This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Poem says:

When Chaos was yet undivided, heaven and earth lay in disarray, vast and dim, unseen by any living eye. Since Pangu first rent the primal mists, from that time purity and turbidness have been made distinct. He upheld and bore all beings; by bringing forth all things he made them upright and good. If one would know the primordial art by which Heaven and Earth are ordered, one must read the Tale of Release from Calamity in the Western Journey.

It is said there are one hundred twenty-nine thousand six hundred years in one great cycle (one 元). One cycle is divided into twelve periods, the zodiac branches Zi, Chou, Yin, Mao, Chen, Si, Wu, Wei, Shen, You, Xu, Hai, and then the cycle turns again. Each period is ten thousand eight hundred years. If one examines a day in the same way: in the Zi hour the yang qi is received, and in Chou the rooster crows; in Yin there is no daylight, and in Mao the sun rises; in Chen it is after a meal, and in Si comes the full heat of the day; in Wu the sun is in mid-heaven, and in Wei it moves westward; in Shen comes the afternoon, at You sunset, at Xu twilight falls, and at Hai people come to rest. For this reckoning, when one reaches the end of the Xu phase, heaven and earth grow dim and all things decline. Then, going back five thousand four hundred years to the beginning of the Hai phase, there is darkness, and no creatures remain between heaven and earth; hence it is called confusion. Going on another five thousand four hundred years, as Hai comes to its end and near the arrival of Zi, the primal source rises and things gradually become clear. Shao Kangjie said: “At the winter solstice, in the middle of Zi, heaven’s heart does not change. When the first yang motion appears, all things are not yet born.” From this point heaven begins to have its root. After another five thousand four hundred years, at the true center of Zi, the clean light rises upward. There is the sun, moon, stars, and constellations. Sun, moon, stars, and constellations are called the Four Forms. Therefore it is said, “Heaven opens at Zi.” After yet another five thousand four hundred years, when Zi draws toward Chou, things gradually become firm and stable. The Yijing says: “Great is the Great Origin of Qian, lofty is the Great Origin of Kun. All things are generated by receiving their support, and all follow Heaven.” By this time the earth begins to congeal. After another five thousand four hundred years, in Chou there is heavy turbidity settling: water, fire, mountains, stones, and earth. These are called the Five Forms. Thus it is said that earth opened in Chou. After another five thousand four hundred years, when Chou ends and Yin begins, all things arise. “Heaven qi descends, earth qi rises; heaven and earth join, and all beings are born,” says the calendar. Thus heaven becomes clear, earth becomes bright, and yin and yang combine. After another five thousand four hundred years, at the proper time of Yin, humans are born, beasts are born, and birds are born; this is the positioning of the three powers of heaven, earth, and humanity. Thus it says humans are born in Yin.

Because Pangu opened the universe, then the Three August Sovereigns ruled and the Five Emperors set the order, the world among the heavens was divided into four great continents: Dongsheng Shenzhou, Xiniuhe Zhou, Nanshenbu Zhou, and Beikulu Zhou. This book opens with Dongsheng Shenzhou. Beyond the sea there is a country named Aolai. The country is near the Great Ocean, and in that sea stands a mountain called Flower-Fruit Mountain. This mountain is the ancestral vein of the Ten Continents, the spiritual origin of the Three Isles, born when pure and turbid were separated and formed after the primal chaos was dispelled. Truly a wondrous mountain! A verse testifies to it:

Its influence commands the vast waters; its might calms and secures the Yao Sea. Its influence restrains the great waters: tides surge as silver hills where fish slip into caves. Its power pacifies the Yao Sea, where snow-like waves rise and phantom-beings break from the abyss. In the corners where water and fire gather are piled heights; at the East Sea it rises into lofty crags. Crimson cliffs of strange rocks, with knife-like faces and strange peaks. On the red cliffs two colored phoenixes cry; before the sheer face a lone qilin lies. At the peak-top one can hear a brocade-cock cry, and from the stone caves one often sees dragons come and go. In the woods are long-lived deer and immortal foxes; on trees are mystic birds and black cranes. Jade grasses and rare blossoms do not wither; green pines and lush cypresses are ever-vivid. Immortal peaches bear fruit constantly, and slender bamboo always gathers in clouds. A ravine with dense vines and tendrils, and around four sides the original banks are newly green. Rightly, this is the pillar that holds up all converging rivers, the root of earth unmoving through countless ages.

On its very summit stood a sacred stone, three zhang six chi five cun in height and two zhang four chi in circumference. Three zhang six chi five cun corresponds to the heavens’ three hundred sixty-five degrees; two zhang four chi corresponds to the twenty-four seasonal qi. It has nine apertures and eight cavities, as do the Nine Palaces and the Eight Trigrams. No trees block its shadows on any of its four sides, and to left and right, luxuriant orchids of fragrant orchid-like sheen stand in harmony. Since the time of creation, it had continually absorbed the heavenly purity and earthly brilliance, the essences of sun and moon. Long impressed by these, it awakened to numinous awareness. Within it grew an immortal embryo. One day it split apart and produced a stone egg, round and large as a cue ball. By the wind it was transformed into a stone monkey, complete in five features and all limbs sound. Then it learned to crawl, then to walk, and paid homage to the four quarters. Its eyes sent forth two rays of golden light straight toward the constellation chamber, startling the Great Celestial Compassionate Lord, the Jade Emperor, Supreme Celestial Venerable, the Mysterious Vault High God of the Highest Heaven. Seated on golden-tiered cloud palaces, in the Lingxiao Precious Vault Hall, he assembled immortals and, seeing golden fire-flame, ordered Qianliyan and Shunfeng’er to open the Southern Gate of Heaven and investigate. The two attendants obeyed at once, sharp of sight and keen of hearing. Soon they returned: "As ordered, we have seen. The light comes from the borderlands of a small realm called Aolai east of Dongsheng Shenzhou within this sea. Upon Flower-Fruit Mountain stands a sacred stone from which issued an egg that became a stone monkey in the wind. He worships the four directions there, and his eyes beam gold toward the starry chambers. He now feeds on herbs and stream-water, and the golden light is beginning to subside." The Jade Emperor, with mercy, declared, "The things below are all born of heaven-and-earth essence; there is no cause for wonder."

That monkey in the mountain could walk and leap, ate grasses and wood, drank from stream springs, gathered mountain flowers, and sought fruit; it kept wolves and crawling creatures as companions, had tigers and leopards as a band, roes and deer as friends, and macaques as kin. At night it slept below the stone cliffs, and at dawn it roamed among peak caves. Truly: “In the mountains there is no reckoning of Jiazi years; one does not know when the winter has ended.”

One day, in hot weather, the band of monkeys sought shade from the heat beneath fir trees and played in wildness together. Look at each and every one of them:

Springing to trees and climbing boughs, plucking flowers, seeking fruit. Throwing seed-balls, chasing at the game. Digging sand nests, building miniature pagodas. Pursuing dragonflies, swatting gossamer pests. Wrestling old trunks, bowing to Bodhisattvas. Tearing creepers, braiding wisped grass. Catching lice, biting and pinching. Grooming their fur, scraping their nails. Pushing and pushing, rubbing and rubbing. Shoving and shoving, pressing and pressing. Tearing and tearing, pulling and pulling. Under green pinewood they ran wild; at the edges of verdant streams they laughed and washed.

After a while this troop went to bathe in a mountain brook. They saw the rushing water leaping like rolling melons bursting into spray. It is said of old: ‘Birds have their own speech, beasts their own tongue.’ All cried, ‘Who knows whence this water comes? Today we are free of other duties. Let us play along the stream and follow it upward to seek the source.’ One cry and they came all together, lads and lasses, brothers and siblings, scrambling toward the headwaters, climbing the mountain along the brook until they found a waterfall and spring. There they beheld:

A white arc rose in a single sweep; for a thousand fathoms snow-mixed waves took flight. Sea-wind blows unbroken; the river moon still lights it still. Cool breath splits the blue ridges; lingering current moistens the green haze. That murmuring fall is called a waterfall, as if curtain upon curtain were hung.

The monkeys clapped their hands in praise: ‘Fine water, fine water! It reaches far beneath this mountain foot straight to the waves of the Great Sea.’ Then one said, ‘Let the strongest monkey dive in and find the source, return alive and unhurt; we will make him our king.’ Three times they called, and then from among the crowd leapt a stone monkey in answer, crying, ‘I will go in, I will go in.’ Good monkey, indeed it was he:

Today fame is made manifest, and an age of fortune has come. Fortune and destiny have placed him here; by heaven’s whim he shall enter the halls of immortals.

See how he closed his eyes, crouched low, and with one bound plunged into the cataract spring. He opened his eyes and looked upward; there, beyond, was no water or surge but a clear, lucid span like a bridge. He steadied himself, fixed his mind, and looked again: it was a plate of iron, a bridge of iron plates. Water beneath streamed through holes in rock and ran upside down out beneath, blocking the bridge gates. He stooped and rose to the bridgehead, stepping out again; looking about, he saw a dwelling fit for humans, truly a fine place indeed:

Moss is heaped in blue green; white clouds drift like floating jade. Light shivers among ribbons of rosy cloud. Empty windows, still chambers, smooth benches on which flowers seem to bloom. In milk-white caves, dragon-jewel clusters hang; strange blossoms swirl across the ground. By cliffside hearths faint traces of old fire remain; wine vessels beside tables hold offerings and remains. Stone seats and stone beds are charms to behold; stone bowls and stone trays can be praised the more. Beyond, two, three slender bamboos and a few plums in bloom appear. Several pines forever with dampened leaves make the whole seem like a true dwelling.

After looking for some time, he leapt to the center of the bridge and looked right and left. There, right in the middle, stood a stone tablet with bold regular-script characters carved upon it: "Flower-Fruit Mountain blessed land, Water-Curtain Cave, celestial grotto-heaven."

The stone ape was overjoyed beyond measure. He leapt out, crouched, and rose from the water, saying twice, “Great craftsmanship of Heaven! Great craftsmanship of Heaven!” The monkeys closed around him, asking, “What is inside? How deep is the water?” He answered, “No water at all! It is an iron plate bridge; beyond it lies a home built by Heaven and Earth itself.” They asked, “How can that be a home?” He laughed: “That stream beneath is only the water from above forcing through the stone bridge and hanging down to hide the gate. Beside the bridge are flowers and trees; there is indeed a stone chamber. Within the cave are stone cubicles, stone hearths, stone bowls, stone basins, stone beds, and stone benches. In the center, a stone tablet is engraved: ‘Flower-Fruit Mountain blessed land, Water-Curtain Cave, celestial grotto-heaven.’ Truly it is our place of dwelling. It is broad enough for a hundred households and all kinds of children and elders. We may all enter and live here, safe from Heaven’s harsh breath. Here:

There are places to shelter from wind. In rain one may hold fast and keep one’s shape. Frost and snow cannot alarm. Thunder is never heard. Mists and halos glow always. Auspicious vapors rise in fragrance. Pines and bamboos are ever lush; strange flowers are born anew each day.

Hearing this, the monkeys all rejoiced and one by one said, ‘You go first and lead us in.’ The stone monkey crouched, jumped inside, and called, ‘All follow me in, all in.’ The bold jumped in at once. The timid peered out, drew in their necks, scratched ears and cheeks, and shouted loudly, yet in the end they too entered. Across the bridgehead each scrambled for basins and bowls, fought over hearths and beds, moved and carried things about. Such is monkey-nature—restless, unruly—and only when strength failed and minds grew weary did they stop. The stone ape sat above and said, “Gentles, there is the saying: ‘A man with no trust is fit for nothing.’ You said earlier that whoever could enter and leave here unhurt should be King. I have entered, and gone out; gone out and come in. I have found this cave-heaven where you may rest and sleep in safety, and each may share domestic blessings. Why then do you not honor me as king?” They heard him and with no dissent lowered themselves in homage, lined up by seniority, and knelt upward in reverence, calling him “Thousand-Year Great King.” Thereafter the Stone Ape rose to kingly seat, hiding the word “Stone” in his name and calling himself “Beautiful Monkey King.” A verse records this:

Where sun and moon together gave rise to all life, the immortal stone womb held their essence of sun and moon. Through an egg transformed, he became a perfect monkey, taking name and rank to join the crimson path. Within he perceived formlessness and cause; without he learned to assume manifest shape. Through the ages all men belong to this line, calling him king, calling him sage, roaming unconstrained.

The Beautiful Monkey King led a crowd of macaques, apes, and monkey-kinds, and appointed ministers and assistants among the sovereign officers. By day he roamed Flower-Fruit Mountain; by night they lodged in Water-Curtain Cave. They kept to shared accord and affection, did not join flocks of birds nor bands of beasts, and ruled by themselves alone, rejoicing beyond compare. Therefore:

In spring they gathered hundreds of flowers for food, In summer they sought fruit to make a living, In autumn they harvested yams and chestnuts as the seasons turned, In winter they sought huangjing to pass the passing of the years.

The Beautiful Monkey King enjoyed pure Heaven-born delight for some three or five hundred years. One day, at the height of a feast among monkeys, sudden sorrow overtook him and he wept. His retinue hurried and knelt, crying, “Great King, why this trouble?” He said, “Though I stand in joy, there is one small yet far-reaching worry.” The others laughed: “Great King, how little is your contentment! Each day we feast in joy, in an immortal mountain blessed land and cavernous divine isle; we bow to no qilin command, no phoenix decree, nor are we bound by human royal law. Free and effortless—this is immeasurable blessing. Why should you brood over worries?” The King replied, “Though today we do not submit to mortal kingdoms nor fear the dignity of beasts, in old age blood will thin and grow weak. In secret, Lord Yama oversees the end. If one dies, is it not wasted to have been born to world, unable even for long to dwell within heaven-and-man as the good do?" The monkeys, hearing this, covered their faces and wept, each lamenting impermanence.

Then from the band leaped out a broad-backed ape, voice clear and sharp: “If Your Majesty bears such concern, that is real awakening of the Way indeed. Of all creatures of the fivefold world, only three kinds of name and form are not subject to Lord Yama’s command.” The king asked, “What are these three?” The ape replied, “They are Buddha, Immortal, and Divine-Saint, three kinds who escape the wheel of rebirth and do not perish, sharing longevity with Heaven, Earth, and mountain-rivers.” The king asked, “Where do these three abide?” The ape said, “Only within this Yanfu world, in the immortal mountains of this great sea-continent.” When he heard this, the king’s heart overflowed with joy: “Tomorrow I will take leave of you all and descend the hill to roam the sea’s edges and distant horizons. I will surely seek these three and learn how to live beyond age, forever avoiding Lord Yama’s peril.” With that sentence, the net of rebirth was pierced, leading to the making of the Great Sage Who Equaled Heaven. The monkeys applauded and praised: “Excellent indeed! Excellent indeed! Tomorrow we will climb over the ridge and gather fruits in abundance, prepare a grand feast, and send our lord forth.”

The next day the monkeys truly went to pick immortal peaches, gather strange fruit, dig mountain yam, and dig up huangjing. Aromatic orchids, precious herbs, and wondrous heavenly grasses appeared in complete batches, all laid out in proper rows on stone stools and stone tables, with immortal wine and immortal dishes arranged. As they looked on:

Gold-round, pearl-like fruits and red-split, yellow-plump produce. Golden-orbed wax cherries, truly sweet and beautiful; plums split red and yellow and ripe, whose flavor was fragrant and pleasantly sour. Fresh dragon eyes, sweet flesh with thin skin; Fiery lychee, small seed in red sacs. Apples with blue-green flesh offered in clusters, loquats with pale buds and leaves held upright. Rabbit-headed pears and chicken-hearted jujubes, which quenched thirst, removed vexation, and dispersed drunkenness. Fragrant peaches and ripe apricots, sweet as jade-wine nectar; Crisp plums and yángméi, softly sour like rich creamy paste. Ripe watermelons with red sacs and black seeds, great persimmons with yellow fourfold rinds. Split-open pomegranates, whose cinnabar-like kernels shone like fire-crystal beads; Yam and chestnuts cut open, with hard flesh clumped like golden agate. Walnuts and ginkgo nuts could be steeped into tea; coconuts and grapes could make wine. Hazelnuts, pine nuts, and related nuts filled the trays, while citrus, sugarcane, mandarin orange, and tangerine filled the table. Cooked mountain yam and fully boiled huangjing. Poria and coix seed were pounded and simmered in a stone pot over low fire into gruel. No matter how fine delicacies are in the human world, how could they compare to the monk joy of mountain monkeys.

The troop honored the Beautiful Monkey King above, and all sat by age and rank below. One by one they came forward with wine, flowers, and fruit, and drank in deep measure for an entire day.

The next morning, the Beautiful Monkey King rose early and said: “You little ones, gather some dead pines and weave a raft, take a bamboo pole for a paddle, and pack the fruit I need. I am going.” Alone he stepped onto the raft, pushing it with all his strength, drifting and floating until he reached the mid-sea swells and, catching the sky wind, crossed toward the southern Yanshan Continent boundary. That departure was thus:

Heaven fashioned this immortal ape’s Dao-path in splendor; leaving the mountain he paddled a raft on celestial wind. He sailed the oceans in search of the Way, setting his heart to achieve a mighty work. Born of fate and shared by affinity, he renounced worldly vows. He would surely meet a knowing friend who could explain the source and flow of all Dharma.

This time, as fate had decreed, after he boarded the wooden raft, persistent southeast winds for many days carried him to the northwest shore, which was the boundary of Nanshenbu. He tested the water with his pole, happened upon shallow water, abandoned the raft, and leapt ashore. At the beach there were people catching fish, hunting geese, digging clams, and skimming salt. He came near and put on a show, masquerading as a tiger so they saw, and those people dropped baskets and nets, then scattered in all directions. Seizing one who could not run, he stripped him and put on his clothes. Swaying and staggering, he passed through prefectures and government streets, and in the market towns learned human courtesy and human speech. He ate by day and slept by night, all the while asking after Buddha, Immortal, and Divine-Saint methods, seeking the way of lifelong life and no aging. He saw that men were all for gain and fame, not for preserving life itself. The scene is aptly said in verse:

When will the contest for fame and profit ever end? Late rising and late resting bring no freedom. Riding donkeys yet hoping for fine horses, they seek official rank as ministers and hopes for princes and lords. They only fear weariness from labor over food and clothing, and what if King Yan grabs them with his hook? Sons-in-law and nephews seek wealth and rank; there is scarcely one who would turn back.

The Great Sage once traveled in search of the path of immortality, but by fate had not yet met one. In the Nanzhanbu Continent, he traversed the Great Wall and roamed through small counties, not noticing eight or nine years pass. Suddenly he came to the Great Western Ocean. Thinking that there had to be immortals overseas, he once again made a raft as before and drifted across the western sea until he came to the land of Xiniuhe Continent. After getting off, he searched for a long time, then suddenly saw a beautiful high mountain. Its wooded slopes were deep and secluded. He was not afraid of wild beasts nor of tigers and leopards, so he climbed to the top to look. It was truly a fine mountain:

A thousand peaks stood in ranks like spears, and ten thousand crags opened like unfurling screens. Sunlight reflected on the cloud-ridge, lightly locking green light; rain-cooled indigo held a cool, deep blue. Slender rattan twined around old trees, and the ancient secluded path was hidden. Strange flowers and auspicious grasses, fine bamboo and towering pines. Fine bamboo and towering pines, evergreen for ten thousand ages, outshone blessed lands; Strange flowers and auspicious grasses never faded in any season, like rivals to Penglai. Hidden birds called nearby, and clear springs sang with rushing notes. Valley after valley and gully after gully, orchids and ferns wound through, cliffs everywhere covered with moss. The ridge crests rose and fell in dragon veins; surely a great hermit hid his name there.

He was still watching when he suddenly heard voices from deep in the forest. He hastened forward, slipped among the trees, and listened closely. It was singing. The song was:

"I watch the board of chess grow tattered, axe-clacking in timber-girding strike; at the cloud-edge, in the mouth of the pass, I walk slowly. I sell firewood and buy wine, laughing wildly, drowning my cares in my own intoxication. In the high autumn void I keep the moon in my sight, and by a pine root I rest until dawn. I know the old woods; I climb the cliffs and cross the ridges, axe in hand I cut dead vines. I carry the load back on my back, singing through the market, trading it for three measures of rice. No one argues there, no crowding for quarrel; prices stay plain and fair. I know no crafty schemes, no clever accounting—without honor or shame I drift in gentle ease. Where we happen upon one another, it is either immortals or the Way: sit in stillness and speak on the Huangting."

When the Great Sage heard those words, he was filled with joy and said, "So immortals really are hiding here!" He leapt in at once and looked carefully. It was only a woodcutter, chopping wood there, but even his attire was very unusual:

On his head he wore a rattan hat made from the first sheathing of fresh bamboo shoots. On his body a plain cloth garment, made from tree-cotton spun into silk. Around his waist a rope belt, twined from thread spun from old silkworm mouths. At his feet, grass sandals made from withered rushes. In his hand he held a hard-steel axe, with a hemp rope for hauling. Splitting pines and hewing dead trees, no woodman could match this one.

The Monkey called out as he drew near: "Old immortal, this disciple offers respectful greeting." The woodcutter flustered, dropped his axe, turned, and returned the salute, saying, "Not worthy, not worthy. I am a poor woodman with only enough food and clothing, how can I dare to be called 'immortal'?" The Monkey asked, "If you are not an immortal, how do you speak immortal words?" The woodcutter said, "What immortal words have I spoken?" The Monkey answered, "I only just came to the forest edge and heard you saying: 'Where one meets someone, it is either immortal or Dao; in quiet one sits and talks about the Huangting.' The Huangting is true doctrine of morality and the Dao. Who but an immortal says that?" The woodcutter laughed, "I will not deceive you: this verse is called 'Mantingfang,' taught by an immortal. That immortal lives next door to my hut. Seeing my home full of hardship and worry, he told me that whenever troubles come, I should chant this verse—first to settle my heart, then to untie hardship. I have a few things I cannot figure out, so I recite it; I never expected you to hear it." The Monkey said, "If your home is next to him, why don't you learn from him and gain a method against old age?"

The Monkey said, "From what you say, you are a filial gentleman; in time you will receive good fortune. But if you would show me the abode of that immortal, I would be happy to pay my respects." The woodcutter answered, "Not far, not far. This mountain is called Mount Lingtai Fangcun. In it is the Slanting Moon Three-Star Cave, and in that cave dwells an immortal named Patriarch Subhūti. Disciples of his come and go in numbers beyond counting; even now there are three or four dozen practicing under him. Take that little path, go south for seven or eight li, and there you will find his dwelling." The Monkey seized the woodcutter’s arm. "Brother, come with me. If there is blessing to be had, I will not forget your guidance." The woodcutter replied, "You understand change poorly. I just explained all this to you and yet you did not understand. If I go with you, will I not ruin my trade? Who would care for old mother? I must cut firewood; you go, and go now."

The Monkey took his leave, got onto the path, and after passing over a hillock of about seven or eight li he truly saw a cave residence. He stood and looked; it was truly a splendid place! But he saw:

Mist and colored cloud-scatter, sun and moon swayed with light. A thousand old cypresses, ten thousand upright bamboo culms. The thousand old cypresses, rain-dark and half-airborne, green and drifting; the ten thousand bamboo culms, with smoky haze, one ravine in deep blue. Outside the gate, wondrous flowers spread like brocade; by the bridge, yaocao sent out fragrance. The stone cliffs stood abrupt, smooth with fresh moss; hanging walls rose with long lengths of green lichen. One heard the cries of immortal cranes, and oft one saw a phoenix take to the air. When the crane cried, its voice shook the nine-rough marshes and far heavens; when the phoenix rose, its five colors shone like rainbow light. Black monkeys and white deer appeared and hid at times; gold lions and jade elephants wandered freely. In this sacred blessed land, it truly surpassed heaven itself.

After a while, he heard a sharp cry and the cave gate opened. A celestial boy came out—truly graceful and dignified, with an extraordinary appearance, quite unlike common folk. Yet he looked:

A chignon bound with two silk strands, A wide robe, both sleeves fluttering in the wind. His appearance and form were distinct, his body and mind both empty and clear. A guest beyond worldly dust, a long-lived boy in the mountain. Not a single speck of dust stained him, through one full jiazi-cycle he could still whirl and turn.

After a short time, he suddenly heard a sharp sound and the cave-door opened. A celestial youth came out. He was truly graceful and mighty, his appearance oddly transcendent, wholly unlike ordinary folk. This is how he appeared:

His hair tied in two twisted strands, a wide robe, both sleeves stirring in the wind. His face and form were strange and distinct, his mind and body already clear and empty. A mountain-dwelling guest from beyond the mundane world, the child of eternal life in the hills. Not one dust-particle clings to him; through ten-year cycles he may turn and whirl unharmed.

When the youth came to the gate and called out, "Who is this who disturbs here?" The Monkey leapt from the tree and, bowing, said, "Immortal child, I am a student who has come to seek the Way and study the immortal path. I dare not disturb here." The youth laughed. "You are one who seeks the Way, then?" "Yes," said the Monkey. The youth replied, "My master has only just risen from his couch and mounted the platform to speak on the Way. He had not yet explained the core when he told me to come open the door and said, 'A cultivator has come from outside; go receive him.' I thought it might be you." The Monkey smiled. "It is me. It is me." The youth said, "Come in with me."

The Monkey straightened his clothing and stood respectfully, then followed the youth deep into the cave realm. Layer after layer he beheld deep hall and jade pavilions, inner court after inner court of pearl palaces and shell towers; he could not exhaust the quiet, secluded dwellings. At last, beneath the jade platform, he saw Patriarch Subhūti seated upright. On either side beneath him stood thirty small immortals. He was indeed:

Great-awakened Golden Immortal, stainless in form, Bodhi of the wondrous form of the Western Way. Neither born nor ending, the three-are-as-Three all abide, whole in breath and spirit, all-compassionate in ten thousand hearts. Empty and still, he follows transformation naturally; true-essence as original nature, he lets things be. Body and life share heaven’s own duration, the Great Dharma Master who clarifies mind across aeons.

At first sight, the Great Monkey fell and knelt in full prostration, bowing again and again without count, crying, "Master, Master, this disciple’s heart is set on your instruction; this disciple offers homage with all his heart." The Patriarch said, "From what region are you? Speak your home and name clearly, then bow again." The Monkey said, "My disciple is from the Flower-Fruit Mountain, Hua Guo cave of the Water-curtain in the Aolai Kingdom, on the continent of Dongsheng." The Patriarch snapped: "Get out! You are clearly one who feigns holiness and stirs up emptiness. What kind of fruit of the Way could you seek here?" The Monkey hastened to bow and pleaded, "My disciple speaks plainly; there is no deceit." The Patriarch said, "If you are truly plain, how do you call this place Dongsheng? Between there and here lie two great seas and the Nanzhanbu Continent. How did you come all this way?" The Monkey prostrated: "My disciple crossed the sea, visited the worlds by crossing borders, and after ten or so years only now found this place."

The Patriarch said, "Since you have come gradually, that is enough. What is your surname?" The Monkey answered, "I have no surname. If people scold me, I am not angry; if they strike me, I do not resent. I only make the courtesy of greeting; I have had no surname for life." The Patriarch said, "That is not this 'nature'. What were your parents' surnames?" The Monkey said, "I have no father or mother." The Patriarch said, "If you have no parents, perhaps you were born from a tree?" The Monkey said, "Though I was not born from a tree, I was born from stone. I only remember that on Flower-Fruit Mountain there was one sacred stone; in the year it split open, I came into being." Hearing this, the Patriarch was pleased inwardly: "This indeed is a heaven-born one. Stand up and I will look at you walk about." The Monkey leapt up, turning and circling twice. The Patriarch smiled, "Though your body is crude, you look like a monkey that cracks pine nuts. I will give you a surname, and the idea is to call it 'Hu'. Take away the beast radical from 'hu'; it becomes 古 and 月. 古 means old; 月 means yin. Old yin cannot nurture and generate, so 'Sun' is better. Take away the beast radical from 'Sun'; it becomes 子 and 系. 子 means a son, and 系 means the helpless tender child, fitting the nature of infancy. Let your surname be 'Sun'." The Monkey, pleased, knelt and said, "Good! good! good! Today I at last know my surname. I beg the Master for mercy: now that I have a surname, please grant my name so I may be called." The Patriarch said, "In my sect there are twelve characters used for naming; you are the tenth generation of junior disciple." The Monkey asked, "What are the twelve?" The Patriarch answered, "They are Guang, Da, Zhi, Hui, Zhen, Ru, Xing, Hai, Ying, Wu, Yuan, and Jue. For you comes the character 'Wu'. Your Dharma name shall be 'Sun Wukong'. Is it good?" The Monkey laughed, "Good! Good! good! From now on I shall be called Sun Wukong." It was said:

Before vast chaos was opened, there was no surname at all; to split the stubborn void, one must become Wukong.

In the end, what sort of Way and fruition he would go on to cultivate was still unknown. Hear on in the next installment.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Once the Handsome Monkey King was given his name, he rejoiced and bowed before Patriarch Bodhi to offer thanks. The Patriarch immediately ordered the assembly to escort Sun Wukong beyond the second gate and taught him the rules for sweeping and cleaning, responding, and advancing or retreating with proper timing. The immortals obeyed and took him out. Sun Wukong, outside the gate, bowed again to the elder brothers and arranged his bedding between the hall colonnades. The next morning he studied with them: speech and etiquette, discussing sutras and doctrine, practicing calligraphy, and burning incense. Every day went on like this. In his spare time he swept the ground, dug the garden, tended flowers and trees, gathered firewood and kindled the fire, fetched water, and hauled gruel. For all household needs, nothing was lacking. In the cave he passed six or seven years without realizing it.

Flowers fell like blossoms from the sky, and golden lotuses surged forth from the earth. He wondrously expounded the three trainings, and the subtle Dharma in full was complete. Gently he swayed the yak-tail whisk, spouting pearls and jade. Its peal rang like thunder, shaking the Ninth Heaven. At times he spoke of the Dao; at times he explained Chan. The three teachings moved together, each true in harmony. He opened the one-syllable path of luminous faith and returning, guiding toward non-born awakened nature, profound and wondrous.

Sun Wukong heard the sermon from nearby and, delighted, pulled his ears and scratched his cheek, brows arched, eyes laughing. He could not help but have his hands dance and his feet move. Suddenly the Patriarch noticed him and called out, “In this assembly, why are you leaping and capering wildly, not listening to my teaching?” Sun Wukong replied, “Disciple listened with a sincere heart. Hearing the Master’s wondrous tones, joy overflowed and I could not restrain myself from this lively movement. Please forgive this offense.” The Patriarch said, “You already recognize the wondrous sound. Then tell me, how long have you been in this cave?” Sun Wukong said, “Disciple was originally obtuse and does not know how long it has been. Only this I remember: there was no fire under the stove, so I often went behind the mountain to gather firewood, found a good peach tree, and ate my fill there seven times.” The Patriarch said, “That mountain is called Rotten Peach Mountain. Since you ate seven times there, you must have been seven years. What is it you wish to learn from me now?” Sun Wukong said, “As for the Master’s instruction, whatever is taught, if it be even a little Dao-qi, disciple will study it.”

The Patriarch said, “Within the gate of the character Dao there are three hundred and sixty side-gates, and each side-gate has its own attainment. Do you know which one you want to learn?” Sun Wukong said, “As the Venerable Master wills, disciple listens with all his heart.” The Patriarch said, “I’ll teach you the way of the gate called Shu. What do you think?” Sun Wukong asked, “What is the doctrine of the Shu gate?” The Patriarch said, “The Shu gate contains arts of summoning immortals, invoking phoenixes, divination, and divining with yarrow stalks, knowing how to seek auspiciousness and avoid misfortune.” Sun Wukong asked, “Can one gain longevity this way?” The Patriarch said, “No, no.” Sun Wukong said, “Then no, I won’t learn it.”

The Patriarch said again, "I will teach you the way of the gate called Liu; how does it sound?" Sun Wukong asked again, "What principle lies in the Liu gate?" The Patriarch said, "In the Liu gate are the teachings of the Confucians, Buddhists, Daoists, Yin-Yang masters, Mohists, and physicians: reading sutras, reciting Buddha, and worshipping descending spirits and ascendant sages." Sun Wukong asked, "Will this attain longevity?" The Patriarch said, "If you seek longevity, this is like setting a pillar inside the wall." Sun Wukong said, "Master, I am plainspoken and do not understand market-tongue. What does it mean, a pillar set inside the wall?" The Patriarch said, "When building a house to make it sturdy, people set a beam between two walls. If one day the great hall topples, that beam will surely rot first." Sun Wukong said, "From this it is not lasting. No, I will not learn it."

The Patriarch said, "I will teach you the way of the gate called Jing; how does it sound?" Sun Wukong asked, "What fruit comes from the gate of Jing?" The Patriarch said, "It is fasting and guarding grain, practicing quietude and non-action, Chan contemplation and seated meditation, mantra recitation and keeping fasts, sometimes sleeping cultivation, sometimes standing cultivation, and also entering stillness, sealing in meditation, and all that sort." Sun Wukong asked, "Can this too lead to longevity?" The Patriarch said, "It is like unfired kiln bricks." Sun Wukong laughed. "Master, you truly possess some subtle art. Disciple cannot play market talk. How is that a 'unfired kiln brick'?" The Patriarch said, "Just as bricks and tiles shaped at a kiln yard have form already, yet have not been tempered by water and fire; when a torrential rain comes, they will all be ruined." Sun Wukong said, "Not enduring. No, I will not learn it."

The Patriarch said, “I will teach you the gate of Dong. How is it?” Sun Wukong asked, “What is the Dong gate?” The Patriarch said, “This is active technique: taking yin and supplementing yang, drawing a bow and using a crossbow, pressing the navel to pass the qi, making formulas and elixirs, firing hemp and forging cauldrons, ingesting red lead, refining autumnal stones, and also taking women’s milk, among others.” Sun Wukong asked, “Could one gain longevity by this?” The Patriarch said, “Seeking longevity this way is like trying to snatch the moon from the water.” Sun Wukong said, “Master, again—what do you mean by ‘snatching the moon from the water’?” The Patriarch said, “The moon is in the high heavens; in the water there is only its reflection. You can see it, but there is no point to grasp.” Sun Wukong said, “Also not. I will not learn it.”

Hearing this, the Patriarch cried out sharply, leapt down from the high dais, and, holding the disciple’s admonitory ruler, pointed at Sun Wukong: "You wild monkey, refusing this one, refusing that one—what do you expect?" He stepped forward and struck the top of Sun Wukong’s head three times. With his hands still behind his back, he walked inside, shut the center gate, and left the assembly behind him. The gathered disciples were startled into fear; all complained against Sun Wukong: "You reckless monkey, utterly shameless. The Patriarch imparts the teachings and you refuse to learn, then argue with him? You offended him so—who can say when he will let you out?" The whole assembly blamed him, looked down on him, and felt contempt. Sun Wukong was not even angry; only a smile of obedience sat on his face. The Monkey King had already broken the hidden riddle of the Patriarch’s words in his heart, and therefore he did not contend with others, choosing only to endure in silence. The three blows from the Patriarch taught him that he should keep intent through the third watch; the hands-behind-back gait into the hall and the shutting of the central gate taught him to come through the back gate and receive the secret transmission.

That day, Sun Wukong and the others were all in delighted mood in front of the Three-Star Cave, waiting for dusk and unable to bear the coming night. At evening they lay down together and, feigning sleep, steadied their breath and preserved their spirit. No watch was beaten in the mountain, and no one rang the bell, so he could not know the hour; he simply regulated the flow of breath in his own nostrils. Around the stroke of midnight he rose softly, put on his robes, slipped out through the front gate, avoided the assembly, and went out into the open. Raising his head, he looked up, and there before him was precisely:

Moonlight clear, the dew cold and bright; the eight directions far, untouched by dust. Deep trees where secret birds keep their roost, and at the source the water threads and slips away. Firefly light scatters shadows; migrating geese trace lines through the clouds. The third watch is exactly upon us; this is the moment to seek the True Dao.

You can see he came by the old path to the back gate and found the door half-open and half-shut. Sun Wukong rejoiced: “The Venerable Master truly intended to transmit the Dao to me, so he has left this gate open.” He stepped forward, sidled in, and went only as far as under the Patriarch’s bed. He saw the Patriarch crouched with knees drawn up, sleeping inward-facing. Sun Wukong did not dare to wake him and knelt by the bed. After a moment the Patriarch woke, stretched his two feet, and began softly chanting:

"Difficult! Difficult! Difficult! The Dao is most profound. Do not treat the Golden Elixir as common. Without meeting a perfect master who can transmit the wondrous secret, empty words only dry out the tongue and throat!"

Sun Wukong answered at once, “Master, disciple has been kneeling and waiting here for a long while.” Hearing it was Sun Wukong’s voice, the Patriarch rose, pulled on his robe, sat cross-legged, and cried, “You monkey, why were you not sleeping in front with the others and then come behind me at this time?” Sun Wukong replied, “Yesterday before everyone on the platform, you had already granted that at the third watch you would transmit the Dao through the back gate to me, so I boldly came straight here to bow at the foot of your bed.” The Patriarch, greatly pleased, thought inwardly, “This fellow is truly born of Heaven and Earth—how else could he have broken through my hidden riddle from within the bowl?” Sun Wukong said, “There is no other person here, only disciple alone. Please be gracious, Master, and pass on the way to long life; I will never forget your kindness.” The Patriarch said, “You now have affinity with this teaching; I am also glad to speak. Since you have understood the hidden bowl-riddle, come nearer and listen carefully; I will now transmit to you the wondrous way of long life.” Sun Wukong knelt in thanks and listened with all his ear and heart, kneeling beneath the bed. The Patriarch spoke:

The true wondrous secret of the perfect and complete esoteric transmission, for the cultivation of life and nature—there is no other doctrine to say. In all things is merely essence, vital breath, and spirit: guard them securely, seal them firmly, do not let them leak. Let there be no leakage; keep it stored in the body. If you receive my transmission of the Dao, it will thrive. Memorize the oral formula; it contains many benefits. Remove perverse desire and you will become cool and clear. When clear and cool, your light is pure and bright, fit to stand at the elixir altar and admire the bright moon. The moon hides the jade rabbit; the sun hides the crow. Therein are the tortoise and serpent coiling together. When they are coiled together, life and nature are made firm; then one can sow golden lotuses in fire. Gather together the five phases and apply them in reversal; when the work is complete, one may become Buddha and immortal together.

At that moment he had disclosed the root source, and Sun Wukong’s spirit was illuminated; he remembered every syllable of the formula exactly. He thanked the Patriarch deeply for boundless grace, then left by the back gate to look out. He saw the eastern sky just barely whitening and golden light blazing clear in the west. He returned by the same path to the front gate and quietly pushed it open. He sat back in his original place, and then shook the bed frame so it rattled, calling out, "Daylight has come, daylight has come—rise!" The assembly was still sleeping and did not know Sun Wukong had obtained the precious teaching. From that morning onward he moved about as before, hiding inwardly what he had gained, and by noon he practiced and regulated his breath.

Three years passed. The Patriarch again mounted the precious seat and taught the assembly. He spoke of precedents and parables, and discoursed on outer forms and skins. Suddenly he asked, "Where is Wukong?" Sun Wukong came forward and knelt: "Disciple is here." The Patriarch said, "What sort of Dao have you been practicing lately?" Sun Wukong answered, "Disciple’s understanding of Dharma has become fairly thorough; the root source is growing firm as well." The Patriarch said, "If you already comprehend the Dharma nature and know the root, and have already placed the spirit in the body, then still guard yourself against three dangers and harms." Sun Wukong reflected and after long thought said, "Your words are mistaken, Master. I have heard that the higher Way and lofty virtue lengthen life to equal Heaven; when water and fire are in harmony, a hundred illnesses do not arise. Then how can there be these three dangers and harms?" The Patriarch said, "This is an extraordinary Way: it seizes Heaven and Earth’s creative qi and intrudes on the secret mechanisms of sun and moon. Once the elixir is perfected, ghosts and spirits cannot endure it. Though it fixes the countenance and adds years, after five hundred years Heaven will bring down thunder and strike you; you must know your nature, awaken your mind, and avoid it in advance. If you evade it, your life will equal Heaven; if you do not, your life ends there. Five hundred years later, Heaven will send fire to burn you. This fire is neither heavenly fire nor common fire; it is called 'yin-fire'. It rises from your own Yongquan source point, burns through to the lower dantian hall, the five viscera become ash, and the limbs rot away, so all your thousand years of hard practice become illusion. Five hundred years again, Heaven will send wind to crush you. This is not wind from the east, south, west, or north; not aromatic gold wind, nor plum, willow, pine, or bamboo wind. It is called 'bì-feng' wind. It enters from the heart gate into the six bowels, passes the dantian, pierces the nine orifices, and the flesh and bones grow loose, the body coming apart. Therefore one must outwit all three calamities."

Sun Wukong heard this and shivered. He knelt and bowed, saying, "Please, Venerable Master, show mercy and pass on the methods for avoiding the three disasters; I dare not forget this kindness." The Patriarch said, "This is not difficult, but you are not like others, so it cannot be handed to everyone." Sun Wukong replied, "My head is round, touching heaven; my feet are square, treading earth. Like others I have nine apertures, four limbs, five viscera, six bowels. In what way am I different from other men?" The Patriarch said, "Though you look like a man, you have one less cheek." Indeed the monkey had a hooked face and hollow cheeks with a pointed muzzle. Sun Wukong reached up, felt his face, and laughed, "Master has not weighed it well. Though I have one less cheek, I have this plain-white pouch more than men, and that should make up the deficit as well." The Patriarch said, "Enough. What do you wish to study? There is the celestial-number arts: thirty-six transformations. There is also the earth-number arts: seventy-two transformations." Sun Wukong said, "Disciple would like to feel and seize the measure and learn one earth-number transformation." The Patriarch said, "Then come forward; I will transmit the oral formula." He bent close to Sun Wukong’s ear and whispered softly, no one knowing what wondrous methods were spoken. The Monkey King, once one aperture opened, had all the hundred opened at once; he promptly practiced the formula, self-cultivated and self-refined, and mastered all seventy-two transformations.

One day, the Patriarch and the assembly in the Three-Star Cave played and lingered into dusk. The Patriarch asked, "Wukong, have you accomplished your task?" Sun Wukong said, "Thanks to the Master’s vast grace, disciple’s results are complete and perfected; I can already mount and rise through rosy cloud-flight." The Patriarch said, "Show me this cloud-raising flight." Sun Wukong displayed his art: he straightened his body, made one linked backward-somersault, leapt five or six zhang into the air, rose on cloud and mist, and returned in less than one return of a meal-time. He landed before the Master and said, "Reverend Father, this is what is called cloud-rising and lifting." The Patriarch laughed, "That does not count as rising through clouds; it is only climbing them. From old times the saying runs: 'A true immortal goes north to the sea at dawn and to Cangwu by dusk.' In half a day, if you cannot go beyond three li and are only climbing the clouds, it is still not enough." Sun Wukong asked, "How does one 'go to Cangwu by dusk after leaving for the north sea at dawn'?" The Patriarch said, "One who truly flies the cloud rises from the North Sea at first light, travels the East, West, and South Seas, then turns to Cangwu. Cangwu is but a term for Lingling in the North Sea. Only one who goes to all four seas within a single day may be said to have ridden cloud and risen." Sun Wukong said, "That is hard. Very hard." The Patriarch replied, "Nothing is hard in this world; only let the heart be determined." Hearing this, Sun Wukong knelt and implored, "Teacher, if a man is to be thorough, then by great mercy reveal this cloud-rising method to me at once. I will never forget this debt." The Patriarch said, "All immortals who rise cloud and ascend do so by stamping and leaping up. You are not of that sort. I have just seen you: you only twisted and somersaulted in order to jump up. Given your present movement, I will teach you only a jindou cloud." Sun Wukong again bowed and begged, and the Patriarch passed on the oral formula: "With this cloud, seize the method, chant the true mantra, clench your fists tight, give your body a shake, and leap. In one jindou cloud you travel ten thousand and eight thousand li." The disciples heard and all burst into laughter: "Wukong’s destiny! If he can truly use this technique, he could serve as courier, messenger, or errand runner for anyone and always find something to eat, wherever he goes." Master and disciples returned to their caves as dusk fell.

That very night Sun Wukong refined his spirit and practiced the art, and he came to master the jindou cloud. Day by day he roamed unrestrained, free and untroubled, at ease in complete freedom—that, too, was the splendor of long life.

One day, spring turning toward summer solstice, the assembly gathered under the pine trees for long discourse. The disciples said, "Wukong, what root-practice of this life have you come to inherit? When, not long ago, our Teacher leaned to your ear and whispered to you the methods for dodging three disasters and transformations, have you mastered them all?" Sun Wukong laughed: "I will not hide from my elder brothers: first, it was the Master’s instruction; second, I applied myself night and day with diligence. I have learned all those skills." The assembly said, "At this good hour, try a demonstration so we may see." Sun Wukong, hearing this, straightened himself and showed off: "Respected brothers, please set a subject. Into what must I transform?" They said, "Transform into a pine tree." Sun Wukong took up the formula, recited the incantation, and shook his body—he became a pine tree. Truly it was:

Lush and smoky with life, through four seasons it bears smoke, rising straight through the clouds, its noble form upright. Not one trace of monkey demon remains, only frost-enduring, snow-beaten branches.

The assembly clapped and laughed aloud, and crying "Good monkey, good monkey!" Their uproar rose until it startled the Patriarch. He quickly came out with his staff and asked, "Who is making such noise here?" Hearing him, the assembly hurriedly composed themselves and adjusted their robes to face forward. Sun Wukong also took back his original form and among the crowd said, "Respectful Master, we were here in mutual discussion; no outsider noise was made." The Patriarch shouted in anger, "You all raise your voices and cry out; you do not look like practitioners at all. For one who cultivates the Way, loose mouth scatters spirit, and moving the tongue gives birth to disputes. How can you shout and laugh so here?" The assembly answered, "We do not dare to conceal it, Master: not long ago Sun Wukong demonstrated a transformation for us. We instructed him to become a pine tree and he indeed became one. All the brothers praised and applauded him, thus we raised our voices and disturbed you by mistake. Please forgive this fault."

The Patriarch said, 'You all, go and leave.' Then he called out, 'Sun Wukong, come here! I ask what divine art you have now shown, and why you changed yourself into a pine-tree. Is this an occasion to display such tricks before people? If you see another possessing this, why do you not ask him? If others see that you have it, they will certainly beg of you. If you fear calamity and still pass it on to him, fine; if you do not, he will surely harm you, and then even your life cannot be kept safe.' Sun Wukong knelt and said, 'Master, only grant me Your pardon.' The Patriarch said, 'I do not blame you; only go on your way.' At these words Sun Wukong burst into tears: 'Master, where are you sending me?' The Patriarch replied, 'Return from where you came, and that is all.' Sun Wukong suddenly awakened and said, 'I am from the Water-curtain Cave of Mount Huaguo in the kingdom of Aolai, on the Divine Continent of Dongsheng.' The Patriarch said, 'Go back at once and preserve your life; while you stay here, it must not be.' Taking this as penalty, Sun Wukong reported to his honored teacher: 'It has been twenty years since I left home. Though I look back and think of my children and grandchildren of old, I dare not return, for I still have not repaid the Master's great grace.' The Patriarch said, 'What great favor is there in that? As long as you do not stir up trouble and do not drag me into it, that is enough.'

Sun Wukong had no way to resist, so he bade farewell and parted from everyone. The Patriarch said, 'By going there you will surely produce evil. How can you provoke chaos and commit violence yet claim to be my disciple? If you utter even half a word, I will know. I will strip your skin, break your bones, cast your soul down to the Ninth Abyss, and make you unable to rise for ten thousand kalpas.' Sun Wukong said, 'I dare not even mention the Master for a single word. I will say only that all this is by my own cultivation.'

After thanking him, Sun Wukong withdrew, twirled the formula in his hand, snapped a cloud-summon, and leapt up on a jinding cloud straight back to the Eastern Victory Continent. In about one watch he already saw the Water-curtain Cave of Flower-Fruit Mountain. The Great Sage to himself murmured:

When I left, my mortal bones and flesh were heavy, yet once I obtained the Way my body became light. In all the world no one was willing to make a firm resolve; when one truly seeks the subtle Way, it becomes clear of itself. At that time crossing the sea, the waves were hard to push through; now in returning it is easy indeed. The separating instructions still ring in my ears—how, in a single instant, do I now behold the Eastern Ocean?

Sun Wukong settled the cloud beneath him and went straight to Mount Huaguo, searching out the road. Suddenly he heard the cry of cranes and the wailing of monkeys: the cranes shouted through the high heavens, and the monkey cries were so grievous and piercing. He called out, 'Children, I have come!' At the stone ledges beneath the cliff, in the flowers and grasses, in the trees, monkeys of every size bounded forth by the tens and tens of thousands and surrounded the beautiful Great Monkey King, then knelt and called, 'Great King, we may now rest easy of mind—why have you been away so long? We have all sat waiting here for you, hungry and thirsty at heart. Lately a demon has bullied us here, forcing himself to seize our Water-curtain Cave. We have fought with him, ready to sacrifice life and forswear breath and life itself. These past days he has stolen our hearth-fire, captured many of our sons and nephews, and made us sleepless day and night while we guard our household. If we had not seen you now, if you had not returned for another year, even the mountain-cave would all have been his.' When Sun Wukong heard this, he grew furious: 'What demon dares such shamelessness? Describe it carefully, and I will seek him out and avenge this.' The monkeys knelt and said, 'Tell His Highness: that brute calls himself the Chaos-Disrupting Demon King and lives in the direction of the true north.' Sun Wukong asked, 'How far is it from here to that place?' The monkeys answered, 'When he comes it is with clouds, when he goes it is with mist, now wind now rain, now lightning, now thunder—we know not how far the road is.' Sun Wukong said, 'Then do not fear; play and keep yourselves busy. I will go and find him.'

The good monkey king sprang once with his body and leapt ahead, coursing along on swift cloud-power until he came to the northern slope and saw a towering mountain, truly most perilous. A fitting mountain:

Peak-prongs rose upright, and crooked ravines sank deep; peak-prongs rose like brushstrokes, piercing the high vault of heaven, and bent ravines led down to the gate of the earth. On both cliffs the flowers and trees strove to outshine one another; here and there pine and bamboo contended in lush green. On the left, dragons—sleek and docile; on the right, tigers—flat and lying in ease. Where one sees the iron-bull plow, one often finds mounds of coin-seed. Hidden birds cry with wary throats, and vermilion phoenixes stand facing the rising sun. Stones glitter, ripples run clear; strange, crooked paths and uncanny bends seem fiercely grim. In this world there are numberless famous peaks, where flowers bloom and fade and bloom again. A sight to contend for, yet enduring forever—eight solar terms and four seasons remain unmoved. Truly this is the Well of Three-Realms source-mountain, nourishing the Water-Organ Cave of the Five Elements.

The Great Monkey King watched the scenery in silence, and then, hearing voices, immediately descended to seek out the source. That sheer cliff before him was in fact the Shui-zang Cave. Outside the cave mouth a few small demons were dancing, and when they saw Sun Wukong they ran. Sun Wukong said, 'Do not run! Speak in your own mouth and carry my words: I am the true master of the Water-curtain Cave of Mount Huaguo in the south. What is this rioting bird-spirit-demon in your place that has repeatedly bullied my sons and grandsons? I have come expressly to meet him and settle this matter.'

The little demon, on hearing this, hurried into the cave to report: 'Your Majesty, calamity has come!' The Demon King said, 'What calamity?' The little demon said, 'Outside the cave there is a monkey chieftain calling himself the lord of the Water-curtain Cave of Mount Huaguo. He says you have repeatedly abused his sons and grandsons, and he has come in person to settle terms with you.' The Demon King laughed and said, 'I have often heard these monkey spirits speak of him as having a Great King, one who went off to become a hermit; perhaps this is that very one coming now. What does he look like, and what weapon does he carry?' The little demon said, 'He carries almost nothing, only a bare head, a red garment, a yellow sash tied at the waist, and a pair of black boots. He is neither monk nor layman, neither Taoist nor immortal. He comes barehanded and unarmed, crying out at the gate.' Hearing this, the Demon King said, 'Bring out my mail and weapon.' The little one instantly brought them out.

The Demon King donned his armor, took up a broad sword, and came out with all the demons at the gate. He called out loudly, 'Who is this master of the Water-curtain Cave?' Sun Wukong quickly stared and saw the Demon King:

On his head he wore a black-gold helm, shining with the sunlight. Across his body hung a black gauze robe, fluttering in the wind. Beneath was black iron mail, cinched with leather straps. On his feet were pleated flower-pattern boots; he was as imposing as a field commander. His waist was broad across ten spans, his height three zhang. In his hand he held a blade, whose keen edge flashed brightly. He was called the Chaos-Disrupting Demon, with a broad and fierce aspect.

The Monkey King cried out, 'You wild demon, with eyes so bloodshot you cannot even see Old-Sun.' The Demon King, seeing him, laughed: 'You are not even four chi tall and no more than three decades old, with no weapon in your hands. How dare you be so wild and seek me face to face?' Sun Wukong shouted back, 'You wild demon, you truly have no eyes. If you think me small, it is no hardship to enlarge me; if you think me unarmed, these two hands grasp the moon on the edge of heaven. Do not fear—I will eat only one punch from this old Sun.' He leapt up and struck straight at the face. The Demon King raised his hand to parry, saying, 'You are so squat and low, I so tall and long. If you use fists, I use my blade; with a blade I would kill you, and men would laugh at me. Put down that blade and test your boxing against mine.' Sun Wukong said, 'It is fair. Good man—come.' Then the Demon King dropped his boasting and attacked at once. Sun Wukong slipped in and the two rushed into collision. They exchanged punches, kicks, thrusts, and rams: the long form seemed empty in the air, yet the short strikes were hard as iron. The Demon King was hit by Sun Wukong at the ribs and groin; in a few knuckle-jumps he was struck so hard he reeled. He sidestepped, picked up the large steel knife, and swung down to cleave Sun Wukong. Sun Wukong drew back at once; the blow sliced empty air. Seeing the demon grow fiercer, he used the external-body art, pulled out a lock of his own hair, chewed it to pieces in his mouth, spat it upward, and cried, 'Change!' At once he became three or two hundred little monkeys, gathering around in a dense cluster.

To become an immortal is to possess a body whose transformations know no bounds. It is not known that ever since this monkey king gained the Way he carries eighty-four thousand hairs, each hair able to transform, each transforming according to circumstance and heart. Those little monkeys, agile and clever in movement, could not be cut by swords nor wounded by spears. See how he bounded forward, leapt backward, dived upward, circled the Demon King, hugging and wrenching, poking at his waist, wrenching his feet, kicking and striking, pressing at his side, pinching eyes, pinching nose, lifting and shuffling him in confusion, making a full knot of battle around him. Only then did Sun Wukong wrest the sword away, part the little monkeys, strike once at the crown, and cut it into two pieces. He led the troop into the cave and slew all the demons, great and small. Then, shaking his hairs, he drew his scattered forms back to his own body; but the one who did not return was the monkey the Demon King had seized from the Water-curtain Cave. Sun Wukong said, 'Why have you all come here?' Of about fifty of them, all with tears, said, 'After Your Majesty ascended to cultivation, in these two years he has quarreled and taken us all by force. Is not that our cave’s hearth-fire? Even the stone basin and stone bowls were taken by this brute.' Sun Wukong said, 'If this is our household fire, carry all of it out.' At once he set the cave alight; he burned that Shui-zang Cave dry and made it all return to single ash. Then he told the group, 'Follow me back.' The monkeys replied, 'Great King, when we came we only heard the wind singing at our ears, drifting here on emptiness and mist, and we did not know the road at all. How can we return home now?' Sun Wukong answered, 'It is a trick of his sorcery. What is difficult? I can now pass through one opening and all openings; I can do the same. All of you close your eyes together and do not fear.'

When the monkeys gathered at the cave mouth, they crowded together and entered in order, then all kneeling they paid homage to the Monkey King. They prepared wine and fruit, welcomed the celebration, and asked him about the demon-subduing rescue of their sons. Sun Wukong explained it all in detail, and the monkeys praised him without end: “Great King, going to that place, how could you have learned such arts?” He went on: "When I left you, I was carried by the waves and drifted across the Eastern Ocean to Xiniuhe, then straight to Śāṅsāmana (South Jambudvipa), where I learned how to appear as a man. In these clothes, in these shoes—tottering and swaying—I roamed the clouds for eight or nine years and had not yet learned the Way. Again I crossed the Western Ocean, came to Xiniuhe, stayed long in inquiry, and by good fortune met an old patriarch who transmitted to me the true and complete art and fruit of long life with Heaven’s span, the Great Dharma of deathless longevity." The monkeys rejoiced: "Such a chance is hard to find in ten thousand ages!" Sun Wukong smiled: "Now, everyone among us has a surname." "Great King, what is your surname?" they asked. "I bear the surname Sun, and my dharma-name is Wukong," he said. Hearing this, they clapped and rejoiced: "The Great King is Old Sun; we are Er-sun, San-sun, Xi-sun, Xiao-sun … one family of Suns, one country of Suns, one nest of Suns!" Then all came to honor Old Sun, offering large vats and small cups of coconut wine and grape wine, celestial flowers and celestial fruit; it was genuine family joy. Aha!

Through one shared surname the body returns to its source, and then one only awaits promotion into the Immortal Register.

Yet how it all ends, and how this realm is to be endured to the end, remains uncertain for now. Listen, and we shall resolve it in the next instalment.
chapters.title: Chapter 2: The true and wondrous principle of Bodhi is fully understood; demons are cut off and restored to the primal spirit.
