This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

When all was said, the Handsome Monkey King returned triumphantly to his native land, having on his own subdued the troublesome demon king and taken a great broadsword. Day after day he drilled in martial arts, teaching the young monkeys to use bamboo poles as targets, to carve wood into mock swords, set up banners, blow whistles, advance and retreat, camp and encamp, and make rough martial play. Suddenly, while sitting quietly, he thought: "If we continue this play, it may become real. It might alarm the human king, and some king of birds or beasts might notice this mock mobilisation and report that we are raising troops to rebel, inviting an army to come and kill us. You all have only bamboo poles and wooden blades—how can we stand against an enemy? We need sharp swords and halberds. What are we to do now?" The monkeys all listened in alarm, each saying, "The King’s insight is far-reaching, but there is nowhere to obtain them." Just then four old monkeys came forward: two were red-bottomed macaques and two were broad-back apes. They said: "Great King, if sharp weapons are needed, it is not difficult at all." Wukong asked, "How can it be easy?" The four said: "To the east of this mountain there is two hundred li of open water; beyond is the border of Aolai. In that border there is a royal seat and many soldiers and citizens, and surely many gold, silver, copper and iron craftsmen. If Your Majesty goes there, you can buy or make weapons and then train us to defend this mountain. That is truly the sure means to safeguard it for long." Hearing this, Wukong was filled with joy and said, "You all stay here and keep playing. I’ll go and return."

When he set out, the Handsome Monkey King immediately mounted his somersaulting cloud, and in a moment crossed the two-hundred-li expanse of water. He indeed saw across the way a walled city with six streets and three markets, ten-thousand households and a thousand gates, with crowds moving about in broad daylight. In his mind he thought: "This place surely has ready weapons. Better I were to use my arts and fetch them instead of merely going down to buy some." He then formed his spell, drew in a breath from the southeast, and blew with a shout. Instantly a raging wind rose, blowing sand and stones and terrifying everyone:

Cannons’ smoke-clouds rose and tossed the heavens and earth, black haze and gloom dimmed the world, waves in river and sea heaved, fish and crabs were terrified, mountains and forests cracked, and tigers and wolves fled, all kinds of commerce had no traveling merchants, all ordinary livelihoods disappeared, the king withdrew to the inner chambers of the palace, and in front of the steps the civil and military officials paced the corridors in confusion, the throne of a thousand autumns was blown down, and the high five-phoenix towers shook from their roots.

The gale swept through the kingdom of Aolai and startled its king; its three markets and six streets were thrown into chaos as doors were shut and no one dared move in the streets. Sun Wukong set his cloud down and cut straight through the palace gate, going straight to the armory and weapons hall. He opened the gates and looked: there were endless kinds of arms—swords, spears, jian, halberds, axes, broad axes, flails, sickles, whips, maces, war clubs, bows, crossbows, prongs, and pikes—every sort fully stocked. Delighted, he said, “How many of these can I carry in my own hands? Better I use the cloning art and bring them all back.” The Great Monkey King plucked out a single hair, chewed it in his mouth, spat it forth, and with a spell cried, “Transform!” It became a hundred and thousand little monkeys that rushed in tumult, each carrying and snatching arms. Some strong ones took five or seven at a time; even the light-handed ones hauled two or three. Soon all were taken away, every piece. He mounted the cloud again and used a gathering spell, summoning a mad wind to lead the monkeys home.

At Flower Fruit Mountain, the young and old monkeys were still at play outside the cave mouth when the roar of wind came. In the sky they saw monkey-forms with outstretched limbs and no end of bounds, and they scattered in fear and confusion. In due time the Great Monkey King descended from the cloud, drew back the vapors, shook himself, pulled in his hairs, and piled the weapons in disorder at the front of the mountain. He called out, “Children, come receive your weapons.” All the monkeys saw Wukong standing alone on the flat ground of Pingyang; they ran up and knelt, asking why. He told them in full how he had raised the storm and fetched the armaments. Once he finished, every monkey, after offering thanks, lunged to seize their swords and daggers, to snatch whips and axes, to haul bows and crossbows, shouting as they competed. All day long they played with them.

The next day, as before, he set up camp again. Wukong gathered the assembly and counted over forty-seven thousand mouths. Soon the mountain’s strange beasts were all alarmed: wolves, worms and insects, tigers, leopards, 麖, 麂, 獐, 𤜱, foxes, polecats, badgers, bear-cats, lions, elephants,狻猊, apes, bears, deer, wild boars, mountain cattle, antelope, blue rhinoceroses, trickster-beasts, and divine mastiffs—seven kinds of demon kings from all over, coming from seventy-two caves, all came to pay homage to the Monkey King as their lord. Each year they paid tribute; in all four seasons there were periodic muster calls. Some came for drill, some came to haul provisions on schedule. In strict ranks they made Flower-Fruit Mountain look like an iron-bucket, gold-plated fortress. From every side, demon kings came with gongs, drums, banners, and armor and helmets, gathering in crowds day after day and practicing as if to field an army.

Just as the Handsome Monkey King was in good spirits, he suddenly spoke to the group: "You are all skilled with bows and crossbows, and expert with weapons, yet this blade I have is truly rough and blunt and does not suit my mind. What am I to do?" The four old monkeys came forward to remonstrate: "Your Majesty is an immortal sage; ordinary weapons are not fit for You. But who knows if You can go into water?" Wukong said: "Since I learned the Way, I have the powers of the seventy-two earth-and-fiend transformations and the immeasurable power of my somersault cloud. I can hide body and spirit, and wield the summoning and seizing spell. In Heaven there are paths; in the earth there are gates. I can pass through days and months with no shadow; I can enter metal and stone without obstruction. Water cannot drown me; fire cannot burn me. How could I not be able to go there?" The four old monkeys answered: "Under our iron-plank bridge, the waters lead to the Dragon Palace of the Eastern Sea. If Your Majesty goes down there and asks the Old Dragon King for weapons, that would suit our needs completely." Wukong, rejoicing, said: "Then let me go and return."

The Monkey King leaped to the bridgehead, cast a water-sealing art, twisted the spell formula, dived with a splash, parted the waters, and went straight to the bottom of the Eastern Ocean. As he moved, a sea yaksha on patrol stopped him and asked, “Who is this one that comes driving the waters? Tell us clearly so we can report and receive you properly.” Sun Wukong replied, “I am the Celestial Saint of Birth, Sun Wukong of Flower-Fruit Mountain, the close neighbor of your Old Dragon King. How is it you do not know me?” The yaksha ran at once to the Crystal Palace and reported: “Your Majesty, outside there is a Celestial Saint of Flower-Fruit Mountain, Sun Wukong, who calls himself your close neighbor and is coming in.” Ao Guang, Dragon King of the Eastern Sea, immediately rose and came out with dragon sons, dragon attendants, and the soldiers to welcome him: “Immortal, please enter, please enter.” They brought him into the hall, offered tea while seated, and then asked, “Since when did you attain the Way, and what divine art have you mastered?” Sun Wukong answered, “Since I was born I left home and practiced, obtaining a body that is neither born nor extinct. Lately I have been teaching my children and grandchildren to guard the mountain cave, but we have no weapons at all. I have long heard that in your heavenly-garlanded, treasure-rich palace there must be many extra divine armaments, so I came to ask for one.” Seeing this, the Dragon King could not bring himself to refuse and had the commander of the crocodile troops bring out a great bar-staff and present it. Sun Wukong said, “Old Monkey cannot wield a blade; please grant me another one.” Ao Guang then had the commander of eel-men bring out a nine-pronged fork. Sun Wukong took it, used it once all the way through, set it down, and said, “Light. Light. Light. Still not fitting.” Ao Guang said with a laugh, “Venerable, have you not seen? This fork weighs 3,600 jin.” Sun Wukong replied, “Not fitting, still not fitting.” Afraid, the Dragon King then had the turtle-bat captain and carp general raise a large rectangular-staff Fangtian halberd. That halberd weighed 7,200 jin. Sun Wukong stepped close, took it, tossed out a few postures and tricks, planted it in the middle, and said, “Still light. Light. Light.” The Dragon King, suddenly alarmed, said, “Venerable, in my palace there is only this halberd and then no more weapons.” Sun Wukong laughed and said, “The ancients said, ‘The Chouhai Dragon King has no treasure.’ Go on and look again. If there is anything you deem fitting, bring it out one by one.” Ao Guang answered, “I swear, none.”

As he spoke, Dragon Mother and Dragon Daughter came from behind and said, “Your Majesty, just look at this holy one—he is no small matter. In the sea treasury there is a piece of divine iron from the bed of the celestial river used to regulate the depths when Yu the Great did flood control. These past days it has burned with rosy brilliance and auspicious vapor. Could this be the time for it to appear and meet this holy one?” The Dragon King said, “That is the divine iron fixed to regulate the depth of the rivers and seas; what purpose could it serve?” Dragon Mother answered, “Whether it has use or not, just give it to him. Let him fashion it as he wishes and be done with it—just send it out through the palace gate.” Following this, the Dragon King explained fully to Sun Wukong. Sun Wukong said, “Bring it out so I may look at it.” Ao Guang waved his hands and said, “I cannot lift it, cannot even raise it. The Immortal must go and see it in person.” Sun Wukong asked, “Where is it? Take me there.”

The Dragon King led him to the center of the sea store, and at once many streams of gold light flashed. He pointed and said, “That glowing one is it.” Sun Wukong drew up his robe, stepped forward, and touched it. It was an iron pillar, about one du in thickness and more than two zhang long. He held it with both hands and gave it a testful toss, saying, “It is too thick, too long—better if it were shorter and finer.” As soon as he spoke, the treasure shortened by a few chi and narrowed a little. He turned it once and said again, “A little shorter and finer would be better.” The treasure then shrank a bit more. Delighted, he took it out of the sea store and saw that it had two golden hoops on both ends with a segment of black iron in the middle. Near the hoops was engraved a line of characters: “如意金箍棒，重一萬三千五百斤.” “Surely,” he thought, “this treasure is exactly to my liking.” As he walked and recited while turning it in his hand, he kept saying, “A little shorter and finer is even better.” Outside it was only about two zhang long and bowl-mouth wide.

Watch him work his divine arts: he cast off tricks, spun maneuvers, and whirled through the Crystal Palace. Old Dragon King was shaken in heart and spirit, the Dragon Son nearly lost his soul, turtles, tortoises, and sea turtles all drew in their necks, while fish, shrimp, ao, and crabs hid their heads. Holding the treasure in hand, Sun Wukong sat on the Crystal Palace hall and smiled at the Dragon King: “Thank you, worthy neighbor, for your kindness.” The Dragon King replied, “Please, no.” Sun Wukong said, “Though this iron is very good to use, there is still one more matter.” The Dragon King asked, “Venerable, what more?” Sun Wukong said, “If there had been no such iron, it would have been fine. Now that I hold it in my hand, there is nothing on my body that will match it. What of it? If you have any harnesses or robes here, simply send one set so I may take my leave in thanks.” The Dragon King said, “This one does not exist.” Sun Wukong said, “One guest does not offend two masters. If there is no one, I will not leave this gate.” The Dragon King said, “Venerable, turn to another sea again; perhaps there is something there.” Sun Wukong said, “Visiting three homes is not as good as staying in one. Please, by all means, send one complete set.” The Dragon King said, “I truly do not have it; if there is, I will present it with ceremony.” Sun Wukong asked, “Truly none? Then let me try this iron with you.” The Dragon King panicked: “Venerable, do not strike, do not strike it. Let me see where my younger brothers are; I will send one set.” Sun Wukong asked, “Where are your brothers?” The Dragon King replied, “The younger brothers are South Sea Dragon King Ao Qin, North Sea Dragon King Ao Shun, and West Sea Dragon King Ao Run.” Sun Wukong said, “Old Monkey will not go, will not go. As the old saying goes, ‘Borrowing at three does not win when facing two.’ Just send one set here, no matter high or low.” The Dragon King said, “No need, Venerable, to go there. Here I have an iron drum and a golden bell: if there is urgency, if one beats the drum and rings the bell, the brothers come at once.” Sun Wukong said, “If so, then have it done quickly.” Indeed, the toad general went to strike the bell, and the turtle captain came beating the drum.

In a short while, when the drums and bells sounded, it truly alarmed the three Sea Dragon Kings, who all came at once and gathered outside. Ao Qin said, “Elder brother, what matter is it that requires the drums and bells?” The elder king replied, “Good younger brother, it cannot be spoken lightly. A self-born holy man from Mount Huaguo came and made himself known as my neighbor. At first he asked for one weapon: he said the steel fork was too small, the painted halberd was too light. He then took out of the very bottom of the Celestial River a divine treasure of iron and toyed with it himself. Now he sits in the hall and asks for even more clothing and gear. I have none, so I rang bells and drums to summon you. If any of you has a set of armor or robes, send him one and dispatch him out. Hearing this, Ao Qin was furious: “Could the four of us raise troops and seize him?” The elder king said, “Don’t say seize him. Don’t say seize him. That piece of iron, if dragged a little, can kill; if struck a little, can slay; if merely brushed, breaks skin and leaves wounds. So he is dangerous.” The King of the West Sea, Ao Run, said, “Second brother, do not fight him. Just give him a set of robes and send him out, then submit a memorial to Heaven and let Heaven punish him.” Ao Shun of the North Sea said, “Well said. I have a pair of lotus-silk cloud-soled boots.” Ao Run said, “I brought a coat of linked-golden chain armor.” Ao Qin said, “I have a phoenix-feathered purple-gold crown.” Greatly pleased, the elder dragon king brought him into the Crystal Palace and offered these. Sun Wukong put on the crown, armor and cloud boots in order, then brandished the Ruyi staff and strode out. “Noisy, noisy,” he said to the four sea kings. The Four Seas Dragon Kings were greatly displeased and discussed submitting memorials to Heaven; this is left unmentioned.

Look at this Monkey King: he parted the waterway, returned directly to the Iron-Plank Bridgehead, and climbed up. He saw four old monkeys leading the others waiting by the bridge. Suddenly he emerged from the waves; not a drop of water clung to his body, and he walked onto the bridge shining bright and gold. Startled, all the monkeys knelt and cried, “Your Majesty, how splendid and striking! how splendid and striking!” Wukong, his face full of joy, climbed the treasure seat and planted the iron staff upright in the middle. Those monkeys, not knowing its true weight, came to seize the treasure, but it was like a dragonfly shaking an iron tree—could not be moved not even a hair. One by one they bit their fingers and stuck out their tongues, saying, “Grandfather, such heaviness—how did you bring it?” Wukong came forward, spread out his hands, and with one stroke lifted it, laughing at the assembly. “All things have their rightful master. This treasure has been in the sea storehouse for thousands of years and this year it suddenly radiated light. The Dragon King only thought it a piece of black iron and called it the heavenly-river-below-great-cosmic-precious iron. That brute could not carry it at all, so he told me to go and fetch it myself. Then it was over two zhang long and about one dǒu in girth. I struck it once and thought it too large; it became much smaller. Again I made it smaller and it became smaller again; again I made it smaller and it became smaller again. Stand back and make room, I will have it change again.” He turned the treasure in his hand and called, “Small! Small! Small!” At once it became like an embroidered pin, small enough to be tucked inside the ear. The monkeys, astonished, cried, “Great King, bring it out and show it again.” The Monkey King truly drew it from his ear and placed it on his palm, saying, “Great! Great! Great!” At once it became thick again, du in girth and two zhang long. Delighted, he jumped up the bridge and came out of the cave, holding the treasure in his hand, and used a heavenly-earth-shifting art; bending at the waist he cried, “Long!” Instantly it rose ten thousand zhang: his head was like Mount Tai, his waist like a steep ridge, his eyes like lightning, his mouth like a blood bowl, and his teeth like halberd blades. In his hand the staff reached from the Thirty-Third Heaven down to the Eighteenth Hell. Tigers, leopards, wolves, worms and insects, all mountain demons, and the demon kings of seventy-two caves all knelt and offered obeisance in terror, trembling as their spirits fled. In an instant he withdrew the spell and once again reduced the treasure to an embroidered pin, tucked it into his ear, and returned to the cave residence. In their panic, the demon kings from all the other caves came to offer congratulations.

Thereupon he set great drums and gongs resounding, rang the brass gongs aloud, spread a lavish feast of rare and varied delicacies, and filled cups with coconut juice and grape liquor, drinking with the whole company for a long while before ordering another entertainment. The Monkey King appointed the four elder monkeys as commanders-in-chief: he named the two red-buttock horse-monkeys Ma Liu and Er, and the two broad-backed ape warriors Bongba as generals. He entrusted the establishment of camps, encampment order, rewards and punishments, and all other matters to those four captains to maintain.

With his mind at ease, day after day he rode the clouds and cut through mist, roaming the four seas and the thousand peaks in bliss. He practiced martial arts and sought out heroes; displayed divine powers and made worthy friends. This time he gathered seven sworn younger brothers: the Bull Demon King, the Jiao Demon King, the Peng Demon King, the Lion-Camel King, the Macaque King, the Rong King, and himself (seven in all). Day after day they discussed literature and warfare, passed cups, sang to strings and danced, leaving in the morning and returning at dusk, with nothing that did not bring delight. They thought a span of ten thousand li was no farther than the road to a courtyard gate; they spoke of a nod taking them three thousand li and a twist of the waist carrying them more than eight hundred li.

...The demons and ghost soldiers rushed up to the 森羅殿 (Senluo Hall), crying out, "Great King, disaster! Disaster! A hairy-faced Lei Gong has come striding in!"

Sun Wukong said, "I am Sun Wukong, a naturally sanctified one born in Water-curtain Cave of Flower-Fruit Mountain. What offices do you hold?" The ten kings bowed and said, "We are the ten Netherworld kings of the netherworld." Sun Wukong said, "Quickly report my name, then no need for further violence." They answered, "We are Qin Guangwang, Chujiangwang, Songdiwang, Wuguanwang, Yama King, Pingdengwang, Taishanwang, Dushiwang, Bianchengwang, and Zhuanlunwang."

Sun Wukong took his staff and strode straight into the Hall of the Net of Worlds, sat facing south at the center. The ten kings ordered the clerk in charge of the casebook to bring out the ledgers. The clerk did not dare delay. He brought out five or six documents and the ten category registers from the Records Hall. He checked one by one: worms of the body, hair-worms, feathered insects, other creeping creatures, scales and shells—all contained no such name. He then saw the section for monkey-kind: this monkey looked like a human yet did not appear in the human register; like a blindworm yet no domestic boundary; like a beast yet not under Qilin jurisdiction; like a bird yet not under Phoenix authority. In another ledger, which Sun Wukong read himself, he searched until the 1350th entry under the character “soul,” and there it was: Sun Wukong, born of a heavenly stone monkey, lifespan three hundred and forty-two years, dies well. Sun Wukong said, “I do not even keep my own years in mind; this name is enough. Bring me a brush.” The clerk hurriedly brought brush and ink, saturated darkly. Sun Wukong took the register and for every named being among monkey-kind he marked and crossed all of them. He slapped the book shut and said, “Account closed. Account closed. This time you have no authority over me.” With one swing of his staff he drove his way out of the Underworld realm. The ten kings dared not come near. They all returned to the Cuilun Palace and with joint bows to Dizang King Bodhisattva discussed submitting a memorial to Heaven, which was later taken up, no more here to narrate.

He suddenly caught on a straw mat, stumbled with a backward fall and jolted awake; it had all been a dream, a Nanke dream. As he stood, he heard the four captains and all the monkeys calling out, "Great King, you drank too much and slept all night; why do you not wake?" Sun Wukong answered, "I only dozed. I dreamed that two soul-catchers came and dragged me, carrying me beyond the gate of the Underworld. When I woke, I knew it was but a dream. I flashed forth my powers, strode straight to the Senluo Hall, argued with the ten kings, and had our life-death register checked. In the entries of our ranks, all the names were struck out by me, so we are not subject to that lord's jurisdiction either."

When Sun Wukong had finished recounting what happened, he sent word through the four captains to the monster kings of each cave; they all came to offer congratulations and joy. Not long after, the six sworn brothers came again to offer congratulations; hearing the reason for his name’s erasure, each of them rejoiced. Their daily gatherings of delight need not be told further.

One day, while the Jade Emperor, Great Sage Yuhuang Tai Shangren (Xuanqiong Gaoshangdi), rode in state at the Golden Ridge Cloud Palace, Lingxiao Baodian, and the civil and martial immortals were assembled for the morning audience, Qiu Hongji Zhenren came forward to report: “Your Majesty, at the Hall of Tongming, outside, the Dragon King of the East Sea, Ao Guang, has submitted a memorial. Please have your decree announced to him.” The Jade Emperor ordered, “Have him summoned.” Ao Guang came down to the Lingxiao Hall, paid homage, and a child attendant presented the memorial. The Jade Emperor read it from beginning to end. The memorial read:

Afterward the Emperor ordered, “Send the Dragon King back to the sea. I shall dispatch commanders to seize him.” The old Dragon King bowed deeply and withdrew in thanks.

Another report was then presented by Elder Ge Xianweng, the Celestial Master, saying: “Your Majesty, the Underworld King Qin Guangwang has received and presented a memorial from Dizangwang Bodhisattva, the Dharma Lord of the Dark Realm, to be presented above.” A heavenly maiden followed by presenting the memorial text; the Jade Emperor also read it through from start to end. The memorial stated:

“The nether region is the underworld of this world. Heaven has spirits and earth has ghosts; Yin and yang revolve in turn. Birds are born and beasts die, and life transforms and cycles; females become males, males become females. This is the natural order and cannot be changed. Now there is a demon monkey, Sun Wukong of Water-Curtain Cave beneath Huaguo Mountain in the Eastern Victory Divine Continent, who commits evil and violence and refuses to submit to summons. He brandishes divine arts and skills, has cut off the Nine-Underworld ghost messengers, and with his power has terrified and wounded the Ten-Dai Ciwangs. He rampages through the nether world and brags of a name and rank. As a result, the monkey tribes are no longer restrained; monkeys and macaques breed with abnormal longevity. The cycles of cessation and rebirth are disrupted, and beings have neither proper life nor death. Your humble monk begs to submit this memorial and has dared to affront Heaven’s majesty. Please dispatch divine troops to bring this demon under control, suppress him, and restore Yin and Yang in order, so that the underworld may be at peace forever. I humbly submit.”

After the Jade Emperor read it, he ordered, “Instruct the King of Darkness to return to the Netherworld; I shall dispatch generals to capture him.” Qin Guangwang likewise bowed and withdrew in gratitude.

The Great Heaven Sovereign then addressed the assembled civil and martial immortals: “This demon monkey was born when, and in what age? In which age did he come forth, and how did he come to attain such Way?” Before he had finished, from among the ranks flashed out Qiānlǐyǎn and Shùnfēng'ěr and said, “This monkey was a heavenly-stone monkey produced three hundred years ago. In those days no one reckoned him as anything, and we know not in which places over these years he cultivated and became an immortal, able to subdue dragons and tigers, and to erase the dead-register.” The Jade Emperor asked, “Which heavenly general shall descend to the mortal realm and subdue him?” Again from the ranks flashed out Taibai Changgengxing, who knelt and offered: “Your Majesty, among beings in the Three Realms, all with nine orifices may cultivate immortality. Yet this monkey was formed by Heaven and Earth and shaped by sun and moon. He now soars heaven and traverses earth, drinks dew and dines on dawn clouds; having already attained the Dao, he has powers to subdue dragons and tigers—what else is he different from us? I advise Your Majesty to remember the Compassionate Favor of life and allow his arrest through beneficence: issue one decree of pacification, summon him up to the Upper Court, give him an office small or great, enter his name in the rosters, and thus restrain this matter. If he accepts Heaven’s Mandate, grant him promotion later; if he defies it, then capture him. Thus you avoid wasting armies and likewise gather one who has truly followed the Dao.” The Jade Emperor rejoiced at this and said, “As you have advised.” He then ordered the Lord of Wénqū Star to draft an edict and sent Taibai Jinxing as envoy to recruit him.

When Gold Star received the command, he passed out through the southern gate of Heaven, descended the auspicious cloud directly to Water-Curtain Cave on Flower-Fruit Mountain, and told the gathered young monkeys: “I am the heavenly envoy. The Sacred Edict commands your Great King to ascend to Heaven. Go quickly and inform him.” The monkeys inside conveyed the news from gate to gate into the deepest reaches of the cave realm: “Your Majesty, there is an elder outside bearing a one-cornered official document; he says he is the celestial envoy sent by Heaven, with a sacred order asking for you.” Sun Wukong heard this with delight, saying, “These last two days I had been thinking to go up to Heaven for a stroll; now an envoy has come to invite me.” He called, “Bring him in at once.” Sun Wukong hastily set his robes in order as the monkeys welcomed him at the gate. Gold Star entered immediately and faced south, saying, “I am Taibai Jinxing of the Western Firmament. I bear the Jade Emperor’s edict of pacification; I am sent below to invite you to ascend and receive an immortal tally.” Sun Wukong smiled: “Much obliged, Elder Star, for descending.” He told his monkeys to prepare a feast and hospitality. Gold Star replied, “The decree is with me; I cannot tarry long. Please come with me at once. After your promotion to honor, we can talk at leisure.” Sun Wukong answered, “Your grace is honored; return for now, return for now.” He summoned the four captains and instructed, “Teach and train the young ones carefully; when I go up and inspect the paths, I will later bring you all up there to live together.” The four captains assented.

The Monkey King ascended with Gold Star, their cloud-heads rising skyward, and soared into the high empty heaven. Then it was so:

As to what official rank he was at last granted, listen to the next chapter for the rest of the tale.
chapters.title: Chapter 3: All under heaven and a thousand peaks submit in submission; in nine abysses and ten realms the evil names are erased.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Taibai Jinxing and the Handsome Monkey King left together from the depths of their cave-heaven and rose on clouds together. Wukong’s cloud was unlike all others, far swifter than most, so he left the Golden Star behind and reached the outer South Heavenly Gate first. As he was about to gather the clouds and move forward, Taizhang Tianwang came leading the soldiers Peng, Liu, Gou, Bi, Deng, Xin, Zhang, and Tao—greatly armed heavenly guards with spears, sabres, and halberds—blocking the gate and refusing passage. The Monkey King said, “This old Golden Star is a deceitful rogue. Since he invited Old-Sun, why did he have these men brandish spears and swords to block the way?” While he was still scolding, Jinxing suddenly arrived. Wukong turned on him in anger: “Old fellow, how are you fooling me? You told me you came with the Jade Emperor’s recruitment edict to summon me, yet you made these people block the gate and not let Old-Sun pass!” Jinxing laughed: “Great King, calm yourself. You have never been to this Heaven before and are unknown here. These heavenly attendants do not know you. How could they let you in at once? Once you have seen the Celestial Lord and been given your divine tally and title, from then on you will move in and out with these attendants and none will dare to block you again.” Wukong said, “If it is like that, all right—I will not go in.” Jinxing grabbed him by the arm and said, “You will come in with me.”

As they approached the Heavenly Gate, Taibai Jinxing cried out: “That’s the gate commanders, great and small, open the way. This is an immortal from the lower world; I bring him under the Jade Emperor’s sacred edict and proclaim his coming.” Then Taizhang Tianwang and all the heavenly guards withdrew their weapons and stepped aside. The Monkey King then believed him and, with Jinxing, walked in more slowly to see. Truly:

First he ascended into the heavens, newly entering Heaven. A myriad golden rays rolled into red rainbows; ten thousand auspicious qi-veils burst up as purple mists. The South Heaven Gate was before him, deep blue and made of crystal; bright and lustrous, built with precious jade. On both sides stood dozens of sky-general captains, each braced by a pillar, holding halberds and carrying banners; around on all sides were ten or so groups of golden-armor gods, each brandishing halberds and lash-crooks, with knives and swords. The outer side was tolerable; within it was astonishing: there were massive pillars in the inner hall, wrapped with red-bearded, sun-glinting, golden-scaled dragons; there were also several long bridges where vermilion-crested peacocks with patterned feathers wheeled through empty air. Bright rosy clouds shimmered reflecting heaven’s light; blue mist, dense and dim, concealed the gate-mouthed sky. In Heaven there were thirty-three palaces: the Dispatched-Cloud Hall, the Bisha Hall, the Wuxing Hall, the Sun Hall, the Flower-Music Hall, and so on—each roof-ridge with a golden-locked stable beast atop it. There were also seventy-two layered treasure halls: the Assembly Hall, the Soaring-Hollow Hall, the Hall of Radiant Splendour, the Heavenly King’s Hall, and the Spirit-Official Hall, and so on—each hall’s columns lined with jade qilin. On the Terrace of Longevity stood famous flowers that do not lose their fragrance for thousands of years; by the alchemical furnace grew embroidered grasses that stay ever green for ten thousand years. He came to the Hall of Holy Audience: crimson gauze robes, stars shining; lotus crowns, and bright golden discs of radiance. Jadespread hairpins, pearl sandals, purple ribbons, and golden seals with plaques. Golden bells crashed; three Censorates of the gods advanced to the cinnabar threshold; when the heavenly drums sounded, ten thousand sacred kings attended before the Jade Emperor. Then to Lingxiao Treasure Hall: doors of jade fixed with gold nails, vermilion doors before which colourful phoenixes danced. There were corridors turning back and forth, everywhere exquisitely translucent; triple-eaved, cluster-like roofs, layer upon layer with dragons and phoenixes soaring. Above was a purple lofty mass—shining, luminous, round and bright—with a great golden gourd on top. Below stood a heavenly maiden with a suspended fan, jade maidens carrying immortal kerchiefs, fierce-faced gate gods, and proud immortals guarding the palanquin-bearing retinue. In the centre, in a glass basin, were heaped many tiered piles of Taiyi pills; in onyx bottles stood a few crooked-curved coral trees. Truly there are all sorts of wonders in Heaven—items like those have no counterpart on earth. Golden-pavilions and silver litters, Purple Courts, together with wondrous stones, divine grasses, and pearl-like blossoms. Passing by the Jade Rabbit altar before the Court King, he saw the golden crows of the participating saints soaring in the lowest sky. Wukong had by fate entered the realm of Heaven, and would not fall back to stain the muddy world below.

Taibai Jinxing led the Beautiful Monkey King to the outside of Lingxiao Hall, and instead of waiting to read out an edict, he went straight to the imperial presence and bowed. Wukong stood upright at his side, and did not kneel at first, only listening closely to Jinxing’s report. Jinxing said, “I have received the sacred command and have announced that the demon-immortal has arrived.” The Jade Emperor lowered the curtain and asked, “Who is that demon-immortal?” Wukong then bent and answered, “Old-Sun, it is I.” The immortals were shocked and pale: “This wild monkey—how can he not bow to pay court and yet say so plainly, ‘Old-Sun, it is I’? He deserves death, indeed death.” The Jade Emperor ordered, “That Sun Wukong is a demon-spirit from the lower world; at first he obtained a human body and does not know court ritual. For now, pardon his fault.” The immortals cried, “Thank you for your grace.” Wukong then made a deep respectful bow. The Jade Emperor reviewed the ranks of martial and immortal officials and asked where he might be given an office; then he said, “Grant him an appointment.” Wuqü Star Lord spoke up from the side: “Across the heavenly palaces and halls and in all quarters, there is no office lacking, except that the Imperial Stable Office lacks one chief attendant in charge.” The Jade Emperor decreed, “Then make him a Bi Ma Wen.” The ministers thanked him, and he only bowed once more. The Jade Emperor again sent Mudé Star Officer to take him to the Imperial Stable Office for audience and induction.

At that time the Monkey King, delighted, went directly with Officer Mude to take up his post. When the work was done, Mude returned to the palace. In the stable office, he gathered the deputy supervisor, deputy manager, registrar, strongmen, and officials of every rank and checked the records. There were only one thousand heavenly horses. They were:

Hu Liao and Qiji; Lu Rui and Xianli; Longmei and Ziyan; Xieyi and Sushuang; Jue Ti and Yao Niao Fei Huang; Tao Tu and Chi Tu; Yuhui and Mijing; Tengwu and Shenghuang; Zhui Feng and Jue Di, Fei𦑭 Benxia; Yipiao and Chidian; Tongjue and Fuyun; Conglong and Huguan; Juechen and Zuling— four extreme superb steeds, eight eminent chargers, and nine extraordinary steeds, a stock beyond compare by a thousand li. Each of these excellent horses had wind-like neighing and lightning-like vigor, with spirits and strength that only grew in cloud and mist.

The Monkey King reviewed the registers and accounted for each horse. In the office, the registrar prepared fodder lists and grain; the wrestlers’ officers handled washing the horses, binding hay, watering, and cooking feed; the deputy and assistant overseers assisted and urged the work. As Bimawen, he neither slept by day nor by night, nourishing the horses. By day he played with them capably; by night he tended to them diligently. When they slept he roused them to eat; when they strayed he caught them and brought them back to their stalls. Those heavenly steeds, upon seeing him, lowered their ears and gathered their hooves together. He fattened them well and filled them with meat and strength. Before he knew it, more than half a month had passed.

One day, in a moment of leisure, all the bureau officials arranged a banquet for him, partly to welcome him and partly to congratulate him. In the midst of their joyous drinking, the Monkey King set down his cup and asked, “What rank of office is this Bimawen I hold?” They answered, “That is its name.” He asked, “And of what grade is this rank?” They replied, “It has no grade.” Sun Wukong said, “No grade—surely that is the highest?” They said, “Not high—not at all. It is simply called lowly, beneath the stream.” The Monkey King asked, “Why call it ‘beneath the stream’?” They explained, “Meanly low and lowest of all. It lets you do little but tend horses. Once you arrive and serve with care, if you fatten the steeds well, you might hear only one word of praise—‘good.’ But if they are even slightly lean, you are blamed; if they are badly damaged, you are fined and put on trial.” Hearing this, his heart flared and he growled through clenched teeth, “Such contempt toward Old Sun! In Flower-Fruit Mountain I am king and ancestor to all—how could they trick me into caring for their horses? To raise horses is an ignoble task for youngsters and inferiors. It is not for one like me. I will not do it.” He shouted, and at once knocked over the public desk; from his ear he drew his precious treasure, made it flash, and struck with one sweep—clearing all at hand—then broke out of the stable office, racing straight for the South Heavenly Gate. The celestial guards, knowing he had received the divine tally and was a Bimawen, dared not restrain him; they let him pass out of Heaven unhindered.

After a short while he descended in cloud, returning to Flower-Fruit Mountain. He saw the four bodyguards and demon kings of the caves in drill with their troops. The Monkey King shouted loudly, “Attend! Old Sun has returned.” A band of monkeys came to kneel and bow, then guided him back into the deep cave-heavens and invited him to take the treasured seat. He ascended the hall and, on one side, had wine made ready to greet him. They said, “Congratulations, Great King. You have been in the upper world for more than ten years and surely returned in glory?” Wukong said, “I have been there for only half a month, how ten years?” They replied, “Great King, in Heaven one day equals one year below. Tell us, what office did you hold?” He waved his hand: “It is hard to say, very hard to say—so shameful it could kill the living. The Jade Emperor does not know how to use talent. Seeing my appearance, he gave me this ‘Bimawen’ title—intending me, in truth, to be a horse-tender, a lowest grade matter. On first arrival I knew nothing and only played foolishly in the horse bureau. Only today, asking the others, did I learn this is such a despised office. Wukong was greatly enraged; he overturned the seats and refused the title, and so returned.” The monkeys cried, “Well done, well done! In this blessed cavern-heaven, as king you enjoy much honour and joy—why would you become a horseman for him?” They ordered everyone to bring wine quickly and cheer the king to lighten his heart.

While they were still in good cheer and wine drinking, someone reported: “Great King, there are two one-horned demon kings at the gate seeking audience.” The Monkey King said, “Let them come in.” The pair entered, dressed in order, and prostrated themselves. Wukong asked, “Why have you come before me?” One said, “We have long heard that Great King gathers worthy men but had no chance to see you. Now that you have received Heaven’s tally and returned in triumph, we have brought a reddish-yellow robe to celebrate you. If Your Greatness would not spurn our low station, I beg you to accept it; then I may render but dog-like service.” Wukong was greatly pleased and put on the robe. All rejoiced and lined up to make obeisance. He next invested the envoy as a forward commander-general of the fore corps. After he had offered thanks, the king asked, “When you have stayed in Heaven so long, what rank was granted you?” Wukong replied, “By the Jade Emperor’s favour I was made some manner of ‘Bimawen.’” The ghost king, hearing this, spoke again: “If the Great King has such divine might, why serve him in horse-keeping? Why not be called the Great Sage Equal to Heaven? Why not indeed?” Wukong rejoiced and could barely contain himself, crying “Good! Good! Good!” three times, then told the four bodyguards: “Immediately set banners and pennants. Write on the standard four great characters: ‘Equal to Heaven, Great Sage.’ Erect poles and hang them high. Henceforth they must call me the Great Sage of Equal-Heaven and never again Great King. Also send this to every cave king so all may know at once.” This need not be described further here.

The next day, the Jade Emperor held court. Then Zhang Tian Shi arrived with the superintendent and deputy of the imperial stables and knelt on the vermilion steps to report: “Long live the Son of Heaven. The newly appointed Bimawen Sun Wukong, displeased by the lowly rank, left the Heaven Court yesterday.” As he spoke, Zengzhang Tianwang was also seen outside the South Gate, leading his heavenly soldiers, and reported, “This Bimawen, for no clear reason, has walked out through the South Gate.” Hearing this, the Jade Emperor issued: “Have the two battalions return to their own duties. I will send heavenly troops to seize this rogue.” From the ranks leapt Tuo-ta Li Tianwang and Nezha, Third Prince. Stepping forward they petitioned, “Your Majesty, this servant is incompetent; please issue the command to subdue this demon.” The Jade Emperor was pleased and appointed Li Tianwang Tuo-ta as Commander-in-Chief for Subduing Demons, and Nezha, Third Prince, as the Great Deity of the Triple-Altar Sea Assembly, and immediately ordered the campaign to begin below.

Li Tianwang and Nezha knelt and gave thanks, then went straight to his hall. He raised the three armies and led all heads of the battalions, appointing Juling Shen as vanguard, Yudu to the rear, and Yacha to urge the troops on. In an instant they came out beyond the South Gate and went straight to Flower-Fruit Mountain, chose a level place and set up camp, then ordered Juling Shen to issue the challenge. Juling Shen obeyed, formed the ranks in order, brandished his floral axe, and came to the outside of Water-Curtain Cave. Outside the small cave gate stood many demons—of wolves, bugs, tigers, leopards and the like—brandishing spears and dancing with swords, leaping and roaring. Juling Shen shouted: “You evil brutes! Go quickly and report to the Bimawen. I am a supreme general from Above, sent by the Jade Emperor’s decree to subdue you. Tell him to come out and surrender early, lest all of you be maimed.” The demons ran back in panic and reported in the cave: “A calamity! A calamity!” The Monkey King asked, “What calamity?” They answered, “Outside stands a heavenly general. He says he holds office of Great Sage and bears the Jade Emperor’s order to subdue you; he told him to come out and submit at once, lest all our lives be ruined.” The Monkey King said, “Fetch my armor.” He put on the purple-gold crown, buckled on the golden mail, put on his cloud-sandals, took the Ruyi Golden Hooped Cudgel, led out his followers, and formed an array. Juling Shen then regarded him and spoke in verse:

Body clad in bright golden armor, shining and splendidly clear. Golden crown on his head, its radiance shining in return. In his hand a single Ruyi Golden Hoop Staff. Cloud-sandals on his feet; all of it fitting perfectly. His two strange eyes like stars; his two ears hung hard past his shoulders. Tall, upright and broad of frame; he knew many transformations. His voice rang out clear, like bronze bells and sounding stones. Sharp nose, sharp fangs: a Bimawen in form, Yet high-spirited, he sought to make himself Great Sage Equal to Heaven.

Juling God barked in a harsh cry, “You wild monkey! Do you know me?” The Great Sage asked sharply, “What sort of hairy spirit are you? Old Sun has never met you. Give your name at once.” Juling God said, “You are a deceitful ape! You do not even recognize me. I am Juling, a vanguard Juling heavenly commander under Li Tianwang of the High Divine Canopy, sent here under the Jade Emperor’s edict to subdue you. Quickly strip your gear and submit to Heaven’s grace, otherwise these beasts on the mountain will all be destroyed; if you speak even a single word against this, I will turn you to powder at once.” Sun Wukong heard this and was furious: “Rabid-haired spirit! Don’t strut so much or wag your long tongue. I had meant to kill you with one stroke at first, but then who would carry the message back? Yet I spare your life—go quickly and tell the Jade Emperor: he is quite unworthy of me. Old Sun has endless powers, so why set me to tending his horse? Look at the inscription on this banner; if he grants me promotion by this title, I will not raise blade or spear and Heaven and Earth will be at peace. If he refuses, I will at once strike at Lingxiao Treasure Hall and make him unable to sit easy on his dragon couch.” Hearing this, Juling God squinted into the wind and looked out. Sure enough, outside the gate stood a tall pole with a banner bearing four bold characters: “Great Sage Equal to Heaven.” Juling God sneered three times: “This wild monkey—so ignorant, so uncouth—dared to claim he is Great Sage Equal to Heaven. Then I’ll make you truly taste my axe.” He lunged forward to hack. The Monkey King, quick to respond and not at all flustered, met him with the Golden-hooped staff in hand. This was a fierce battle:

The staff was named Ruyi, the axe named Xuanhua. They met for the first time, not knowing which was deeper. Staff and axe traded blows left and right. One concealed divine subtlety, the other boasted loudly. Using their arts, they sent up clouded haze; with an outstretched hand they raised dust and flung sand. The heavenly general had divine arts, yet the Monkey King’s transformations were truly without limit. He swung his staff like a dragon frolicking in water; and the axe came down like a phoenix cleaving blossoms. Juling’s renown was famed across the world, yet in truth his skill was not equal to him: The Great Sage lightly moved the iron staff, one strike to the head that numbed him all over.

Jiling God could not endure facing him. The Monkey King struck once at the head with his staff; Jiling, in panic, raised his axe as guard, and with a crack the haft split in two. He withdrew in disorder and fled from the field. Sun Wukong laughed: “Pus-headed one, pus-filled one. I have spared you. Run and report at once—quick, report at once.”

Juling God returned to the camp gate and at once saw Li Tianwang. He knelt in haste and said, “Bimawen is truly all-powerful; this junior general could not withstand him, so I return defeated to atone for this failure.” Li Tianwang grew angry: “That brute has shattered my proud momentum—drag him out and execute him!” From the side, Nezha, the Crown Prince, stepped forward to intercede: “Father King, calm your anger and pardon Juling’s offense for now. Let your son go out once; then you will know the measure of him.” The King heeded the counsel and sent him back to camp to await punishment.”

That was Nezha, the Third Prince, his armor perfectly arranged, leaping from camp and barreling to the mouth of Water Curtain Cave. At that moment Sun Wukong was ordering his troops, and on seeing how boldly Nezha arrived, he spoke: “Good prince.”

The angle of his brows was small and neat, his young body hair scarcely yet covered his shoulders. His wits were keen and his senses quick, and his bones and form were even finer and cleaner; truly a heavenly qilin-born, surely a phoenix of cloud and rosy radiance. A child of dragon stock by nature, never of mundane appearance; in such young years he was not like ordinary dust-bound men. He carried six divine weapons and could fly and transform without limit. Now, by the Jade Emperor’s golden-mouthed decree, he had been appointed and titled as the one of the Three Altars.

Sun Wukong advanced and asked, “Who are you, young lord? You have broken into my gate—what is your business?” Nezha shouted, “Demon ape! Do you not recognize me? I am Nezha, Third Prince of the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King. By the Jade Emperor’s order I have come down to seize you.” Sun Wukong laughed. “Young prince, your milk teeth have not yet fallen and your downy hair is not yet dry; how dare you boast like this? I will let your life be spared and not strike you. Look at what is written on my banner—if that is my official title, then all can stop, and I will submit. If my wish is not met, I will strike up to the Lingxiao Hall.” Nezha looked up and saw the four words: “齊天大聖.” Nezha said, “How can this demon ape have such divine power to dare that title? Do not flinch—take this one stroke of my sword.” Sun Wukong answered, “I will simply stand still. Cut away with as many strikes as you can.” Enraged, Nezha shouted “Transform!” and became three-headed and six-armed, furious, wielding six weapons: the Demon-Slaying Sword, Demon-Splitting Blade, Demon-Binding Net, Demon-Subduing Mace, Embroidered Bolas, Fire Wheels, and a pair of ya-ya forks, then charged in to strike. Sun Wukong saw this and said in alarm, “This little lord does know some tactics. No need for such impudence—watch my divine arts.” “Great Sage,” he shouted, “Transform!” and himself became three-headed and six-armed. He flicked the Golden Hoop Staff and it became three rods. His six hands took those three rods and held them firm. The battle now made the earth shake and the mountains sway; it was indeed grimly slaughterous:

Six-armed Nezha, the crown prince, and the heaven-born handsome stone-king ape met as true opponents, each the source of his line. One came down from Heaven on a divine commission; the other stirred this world in arrogant strife. The Demon-Slaying Treasure Sword flashed with keen edge; the Demon-Splitting Blade was so fierce that ghosts and spirits trembled; The Demon-Binding Net moved like a flying python, the demon-subduing club like a wolf’s head; The Fire Wheels whipped sparks of lightning; the embroidered boluses rolled fiercely in constant loops. The Great Sage’s three As-You-Will rods blocked and defended before and behind with tactical dexterity. In fierce combat there was no clear superior in many rounds; in his heart the prince would not relent. He made his six weapons transform repeatedly, casting billions to strike at his head. The Monkey King did not fear, and laughed aloud as he made his iron staff turn and plan its own stratagem. With one change into a thousand and another into ten thousand, he danced chaotically through the sky like a soaring dragon. It scared every demon king in every cave to lock their doors and all mountain spirits and monsters to hide their heads. The divine soldiers’ wrath gathered darkly like storm-clouds; the golden-hooped iron staff rang with a rushing sound. On this side heavenly lieutenants shouted, and everyone feared; on that side the monkey fiends shook banners and all were sorrowful. Both sides, fierce and enraged, fought with all strength; none could yet tell which was hard and which was soft.

The Third Prince and Sun Wukong each displayed their divine might, and fought for thirty rounds. The prince’s six weapons transformed into ten-thousands and ten-thousands more; Sun Wukong’s Golden-Hoop Staff became ten-thousands and tens of thousands. In midair they were like rain drops and falling meteors, with no winner decided.

Right then, as chaos was at its height, Sun Wukong plucked up one hair from his body and called, “Transform!” He changed into his true form, holding out his staff and taking the figure of Nezha, while his true body in one bound leapt behind Nezha’s head and struck a blow to his left arm. As Nezha was in the middle of casting his arts, he heard the wind-sound at the club’s head and tried to dodge, but could not evade in time; he was struck, hurt, and fled. Gathering up his arts, he drew the six weapons back to himself as before and returned in defeat.

Li Tianwang had already seen the fray and wanted to call in troops to aid the fight when suddenly the prince came before him, trembling, and reported: “Father, Bimawen truly has power; with this level of magic, even my arm cannot prevail against him—I have already been struck and injured.” Li Tianwang turned pale: “With powers like this, how can this rogue be taken?” The prince said, “Outside his cave he raised a staff-flown flag, with four characters: ‘齊天大聖.’ He claimed it himself as a spoken boast and said that if the Jade Emperor had bestowed this title on him, everything was done; if it was not this title, he would strike at the Lingxiao Hall.” Li Tianwang said, “If so, do not continue to spar with him. Go now to court and submit this report, then send more heavenly troops to encircle and seize this fellow; it is not yet too late.” The prince, in pain and unable to continue combat, therefore returned with his father to Heaven to report.

You see that the Monkey King returned triumphant to the mountain. The seventy-two cave demon lords and the six brothers all came to congratulate him, and in their cave-heavens and blessed lands they feasted in unmatched delight. Then he told the six brothers: “Since I have been called Great Sage Equal to Heaven, you too may call yourselves Great Sage.” At once the Bull Demon King suddenly cried out, “My worthy younger brother’s words are just. I will be called Great Sage Pacifying Heaven.” The Snaking-Demon King said, “I will be called Great Sage Who Overcomes the Sea.” The Peng Demon King said, “I will be called Great Sage Who Mixes the Heavens.” The Lion- Ape King said, “I will be called Great Sage Who Moves Mountains.” The Macaque King said, “I will be called Great Sage Who Passes Through the Winds.” The Yaruang King said, “I will be called Great Sage Who Drives Away Gods.” At this point the seven Great Sages self-appointed themselves with self-chosen titles, frolicked in fun for a day, then each dispersed back to his own place.

Li Tianwang and the Third Prince, leading all their generals, went straight to the Lingxiao Palace and reported: “Your Majesty, on Your order we marched on a heavenly mission to suppress the demon-celestial Sun Wukong. Unexpectedly, he has vast powers; we could not defeat him. We still beg Your Majesty to send additional troops to eliminate him.” The Jade Emperor said, “How much can a demon ape have, that even more troops are still needed?” The prince stepped forward again and reported: “Please pardon this servant’s fault, Your Majesty. That demon ape, with one iron rod, first defeated the Great Spirit God and also struck my arm. Outside his cave he set up one pole-flag with four words: ‘齊天大聖.’ It is said that if he is granted this official title he will at once lay down arms; if not, he threatens to assault the Lingxiao Palace.” On hearing this, the Jade Emperor cried in astonishment, “How dare this demon ape speak so wildly? Order all the generals to execute him at once.”

Just then, Taibai Jinxing appeared from the retinue and reported: “That troublesome monkey only knows how to bark and argue; he knows no sense of rank. If we send troops to fight him, we cannot subdue him at once and will only waste the army. It would be better, with Your Majesty’s mercy, to issue a pacifying edict and summon him into service, making him Great Sage Equal to Heaven. Just give him only an empty title—an office without duties and no stipend will suffice.” The Jade Emperor asked, “How can it be called ‘an office without stipend’?” Jinxing said, “His title is Great Sage Equal to Heaven, but do not entrust him with administration, and give him no pay. Keep him living between Heaven and Earth, so his wickedness is contained and arrogance does not take root; then the world and seas will come to peace.” The Jade Emperor agreed: “As you have advised.” He issued the edict at once and again ordered Jinxing to carry it.

Jinxing went again to the Southern Heavenly Gate and then to the entrance of Water Curtain Cave to look around. This time it differed from before: he could feel towering majesty and dense killing intent; every sort of demon and spirit was armed and roaring. One after another they held swords, spears, knives, and rods, howling and leaping about. At the sight of Jinxing, each rushed forward to attack. Jinxing said, “All leaders, return and report this to the Great Sage: I am an envoy from Heaven, come by imperial command. A royal decree awaits him.” They all ran in and said, “Outside is an old man. He says he is Heaven’s envoy with an imperial summons for you.” Sun Wukong said, “He comes well. He comes well. It must be that Taibai Jinxing from before. The time he first summoned me, though the ranks were not worthy, I did go once and learned the way in and out of the Heavenly gates. He returns now, surely with good intent.” He ordered the captains to raise the flags and drums in full array. The Great Sage led all the monkeys out, crowned and armored, with a red-yellow robe over his mail and cloud sandals on his feet. He hurried out of the cave, bowed low and paid respect, then shouted, “Old star, please enter. Forgive my poor reception.”

Jinxing stepped forward and entered directly into the cavern, facing south, and said: “Now, to inform the Great Sage: formerly, when the Great Sage disliked the lowly office and withdrew from the imperial stable watch, he was reported by local officials of this yamen to the Jade Emperor. The Jade Emperor decreed, ‘All offices are conferred from low to high. Why complain of low rank?’ Thus Li Tianwang came down with Nezha to battle. Unaware of the Great Sage’s powers, he was defeated and returned to Heaven to report: ‘The Great Sage raised one banner and demands to be Great Sage Equal to Heaven. The armed officials still tarried and haggled. It was this old rogue who, taking the blame of Great Sage, interceded to forestall war and begged Your Majesty to confer the register.’ The Jade Emperor approved. Therefore I have come.” Sun Wukong laughed. “You labored before; now you are gracious again. My thanks, my thanks. Yet tell me plainly: can Heaven truly grant me the title Great Sage Equal to Heaven?” Jinxing said, “The old fellow dared to bring this title in petition only because I had already secured your approval. I came only on the edict. If it is not fulfilled, then let blame fall on me.”

Greatly delighted, Sun Wukong refused to stay for a banquet and would not accept; so he followed Jinxing, riding auspicious clouds to the south of the Heavenly Gate. The heavenly soldiers and generals there greeted him with clasped hands. He entered Lingxiao Hall straight away. Jinxing knelt and reported, “Your Majesty, in obedience to Your decree, I present Bima Wen, Sun Wukong, who has arrived.” The Jade Emperor said, “Bring in Sun Wukong. Today I hereby confer on you the office of Great Sage Equal to Heaven, your rank is the highest—yet do nothing reckless.” The monkey made one respectful bow and said, “Thank You for Your grace.” The Jade Emperor ordered the palace engineers Zhang and Lu to build a Great Sage Equal to Heaven residence to the right of the Peach Garden of Immortality. Within it he established two bureaus: one named the Anjing Office and one named the Ningshen Office. Each had celestial clerks attending on either side. He also sent the Lord of the Fifth Dipper Star to escort Wukong to his post and granted him two flasks of celestial wine and ten golden flowers, telling him to keep his heart at peace and steady his resolve, and never again act recklessly.

The monkey king accepted these commands and followed the Five-Dipper Star official to the new offices that very day. He opened the wine vessels and drank them all with his retinue. After the star official had returned to his own palace, he found himself content and completely satisfied, rejoicing in heaven with no burden, no obstruction, and all things at ease. It was said:

In the immortal register his holy name is forever preserved; Not to fall again into cyclic re-birth, so shall it be told through ten thousand ages.

What befell afterward remains unsaid for now. Read on in the next installment.
chapters.title: Chapter 4: What worth is an official horse-tamer’s seal? The title “Equal to Heaven” still leaves his mind at restlessness.
