This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Poem:

Great was the Tang king who issued the decree and appointment, appointing Xuanzang as his trusted envoy to inquire into Ch'an. With mind made firm and refined, he searched for the Dragon’s Cave, and with care practiced on Mount Shangjiu. To the frontier he journeyed across many realms, passing through boundless layers of cloud-wrapped mountains. From this day he sets out westward, carrying the Dharma, to realize the Great Emptiness.

It is said that on the third day before the full-moon of the ninth month in the thirteenth year of Zhenguan, Tripitaka was sent out of Chang’an with the Tang king and many officials. In a day or two, without stopping the horse, he arrived early at Famen Temple. The abbot and the upper-hall elder, leading more than five hundred monks, lined them up on both sides to receive him inside, and they met to offer tea. After tea they took the morning meal, and after the meal they did not notice that evening had fallen. It was indeed as follows:

Shadows stirred near the river of stars, and the moonlight shone without a speck of dust. From far Han came the call of wild geese; the drone of querns sounded from the western neighborhood. Returning birds settled on withered trees, and Chan monks chanted Sanskrit tones. On a reed-and-cushion bed they sat until night was near its end.

The monks debated by lamplight about the true meaning of Buddhism and why they should journey to the Western Heaven: some said the water was far and the mountains high, some said there were tigers and leopards along the way; some said the steep ridges and sheer cliffs were impossible to cross, some said venomous demons and evil spirits were hard to subdue. Tripitaka kept silent, only pointing to his own heart with his fingers and nodding several times. The monks could not understand, so with palms together they asked, “Venerable, why did you point to your heart and nod?” Tripitaka answered, “When the mind arises, many demons arise; when the mind ceases, many demons cease. I, your disciple, once stood before the Buddha in Huasheng Monastery and spoke a great, loud vow; therefore I cannot fail in this resolution. On this going I must go to the Western Heaven, meet the Buddha, and ask for sutras so that our Dharma wheel may turn again, and may I pray that the august emperor’s order endure forever.” Hearing this, each monk praised him, everyone praised and spread the word, all crying one voice: “A master of faithful, red-hearted, great Dharma exposition!” They could not stop praising him and invited the Master to retire and sleep.

Again at dawn it was as if bamboo tapping and the waning moon was setting; the rooster called and dawn-mist was born. The monks rose, packed away tea and early fare. Xuanzang donned his robe and entered the main hall, bowed before the Buddha, and declared: “Your disciple, Xuanzang, goes to the Western Heaven to fetch scriptures, but my fleshly eyes are dull and deluded and cannot know the true form of the living Buddha. Now I vow: on the road, should I pass a temple, I will burn incense; if I meet Buddha, I will worship; if I meet a stupa, I will sweep it. May my Buddha be compassionate, manifest soon the six-hundred-sixteen-cubit golden form, and grant true sūtras to pass on in the Eastern lands.” After completing the vow, he returned to the abbot and entered the meal hall for food. After eating, the two attendants tidied saddle and horse and hurried the departure. Tripitaka left the monastery gate and bid farewell to the monks. Unwilling to part, they escorted him for ten li and returned with tears in their eyes. Tripitaka then pressed straight westward. It was already early autumn weather, yet it seemed:

In many villages the trees were stripped and the cattail blossoms lay scattered, A few trees of maple and willow dropped red leaves. Along the road through smoke and rain, old friends were sparse; yellow chrysanthemums were bright, mountain ridges thin, water was cold, lotus leaves split, and people looked worn. White duckweed and red knotweed, frost and sky-snow above; Sunset glow dropped, and a lone wild goose floated down into the wide emptiness. Faint and dim, wild clouds drifted; the dark birds departed, guest geese arrived, and sharp, clear cries split the long night.

After several days of travel, the masters reached Gongzhou city, and officials and soldiers of the city had already come to welcome them and lead them in. They rested one night, and next morning left the city. With little food and little water as they went, traveling by night and by dawn, in two or three days they arrived at Hezhou Guard. This was the frontier of Great Tang’s borderlands. Already the frontier commandant and the local monks and priests had heard that an imperial commissioner, a royal monk, was going westward to see the Buddha, and all offered deep reverence. They brought him inside and provided offerings, then the lead monk told them to rest at Fuyuan Temple. At that temple the monks all came to pay their respects in turn and arranged the evening meal. After the meal, he ordered the two attendants to feed the horses to fullness; once it was lightening day, they set out.

At cockcrow they summoned the attendants again and once more roused the temple monks to arrange tea and offerings for the morning meal. After the meal they crossed beyond the border. This abbey elder was anxious, rising far too early. In truth, at this season of deep autumn, the cocks called early; it was only about the fourth watch. The three of them, with four mounts, followed the crisp dew and walked by moonlight for many tens of li, saw a mountain ridge, and had to push through grass to seek a path. The ground was too rough to describe, and they feared losing the road. Just as they were pondering this, they suddenly lost their footing and all three men and horses slipped down into a pit. Tripitaka was terrified, the attendants’ courage failed. Yet in fresh alarm they then heard roaring and high shouts from inside: “Take him! Take him here!” There came a rolling gale; five or six dozen malevolent spirits rushed out and seized Tripitaka and the attendants. The Master trembled and peered in fear at the one on top—the demon king was ferociously evil indeed. Truly he was:

His mighty presence was cold and imposing, his fierce breath and manner grand. Lightning flashed in his eyes, their glare dazzling; his thunderous voice shook the four quarters. Sawtoothed mouth and parted lips, chiseled fangs showed at the cheeks. Brocade-like ornaments clung to his body, mottled marks wrapped his spine. Steel-colored whiskers, a few strands of flesh showing; hooked claws keen as frost. Even the Yellow Lord of the Eastern Sea feared him; the White-Browed King of the Southern Mountain stood in awe. Tripitaka’s soul seemed to leave his body in fright, and the two attendants felt their bones soften and their sinews turn numb. The demon king ordered them bound. All the spirits tied the three with ropes. Just as they were about to set about eating them, noise came from outside and someone reported, “Bear Mountain Lord and the Special Hermit are coming.” Tripitaka looked up and saw the one ahead was a black man. If you ask what he was like: He was imposing, brave beyond measure, and moved with fierce, light agility. In water-crossing he had ferocious strength; in the woods he ran to display wrathful power. Formerly only an omen-bound omen, now he revealed his heroic form. He could climb and bend green trees and knew how to instruct the cold at the right hour. His spirit showed itself plainly there; therefore he is called Bear Mountain Lord. Behind him came a stout fellow. If you ask what he looked like: He wore a lofty double-horned crown, his broad shoulders and back severe and upright. Clothed in blue, his steps with hooves were slow and deliberate. His clan name was Gu, his mother called him Zi. Because he was skilled at fieldwork, he gained the name Special Hermit.

The two shuffled in, swaying and striding in together, and the alarmed demon king ran out to greet them. Bear Mountain Lord said, “General Yin has always been so impressive—congratulations, congratulations.” Special Hermit said, “General Yin’s handsome form surpasses all, truly pleasing, truly pleasing.” The demon king asked, “How have the two of you fared in recent days?” Bear Mountain Lord replied, “Only keeping guard, no change.” Special Hermit replied, “Only following events as they unfold.” The three then finished speaking and sat to talk and laugh together.

Only then the attendants tied in pain cried out. The black giant said, “Where have these three come from?” The demon king answered, “They came straight to our gate.” Special Hermit laughed, “Could we entertain them as guests?” The demon king said, “Indeed, indeed.” Bear Mountain Lord added, “Do not consume all; eat the two and keep one.” The demon king agreed, then called his lieutenants and had the two attendants’ bellies opened, their hearts cut out, their bodies chopped into pieces. He presented their heads and livers to the two guests, ate the four limbs himself, and shared the remaining flesh and bones among the other demons. There was only the sound of greedy crunching, like a tiger devouring a lamb; in but a moment all was gone. It brought one of the abbots almost to fear-induced death. This was the first severe hardship from leaving Chang’an.

In the midst of that desperate commotion, the east gradually turned pale. The two monsters did not depart until dawn, and they both said, “For today’s disturbance, please allow us to redouble our sincere service.” Then they left together in a mass.

Not long after, a high red sun climbed, and Tripitaka was dully dazed, unable to tell east from south from west or north. At that helpless moment, a gray-haired old man appeared approaching with a staff in hand. As he stepped forward, one touch of his hand with the air severed the ropes. Facing Tripitaka, he blew once, and Tripitaka revived. Falling to his knees he said, “Much thanks, old sir, for rescuing this poor monk’s life.” The old man bowed in return and said, “Rise. Have you lost anything?” Tripitaka replied, “The attendant of this poor monk has already been eaten by demons. I only do not know where my baggage and horses are.” The old man pointed with his staff, “Is there not a horse and two packs over there?” Tripitaka looked back and indeed there were his possessions, not lost, and his heart was slightly eased. He asked, “Old sir, what place is this? Why are you here?” The old man said, “This is Shuangcha Ridge, a haunt of tigers and wolves. Why did you fall here?” Tripitaka said, “At cockcrow I left Hezhou Guard boundary and, rising too early, braved the frost and cut through the dew, only to find myself fallen here. I saw a demon king, fierce beyond measure, who bound me and my two attendants. I also saw a black giant called Bear Mountain Lord, and a stout giant called Special Hermit. They entered and told me that demon king was General Yin. The three of them ate my two attendants before dawn had faded. I do not know by what great fate and great fortune I was granted this great rescue.” The old man said, “The Special Hermit is a wild-bull demon; the Mountain Lord is a bear spirit; General Yin is a tiger spirit. All the other monsters are mountain spirits, tree spirits, and strange-beast blue wolves. Because your essential nature is primordial and bright, they cannot eat you. Come with me; I will guide you on your way.”

Tripitaka, deeply grateful, lashed his sacks to the horse, held the bridle and followed the old man straight out of the pit and up to the main road. He tied the horse to roadside grass, turned back to bow and thank the old sir, and that old sir turned into a drifting clear wind, mounted a vermilion-crowned white crane, and rose into the sky. Only a gust remained, and a short note fell from him, bearing four lines of verse:

I am the Great White Star of the Western Heaven, I came to rescue your life in particular. As you go forward, divine attendants will aid you; do not complain to hardships and misfortunes for the sutra.

Tripitaka looked on and prayed to Heaven: 'Many thanks to the Golden Star for carrying me beyond this danger.' After he had finished bowing, he took the horse by the reins and, utterly alone, desolate and forlorn, pushed forward with effort. On this ridge it was truly:

The rain-forest wind blew in a cold hiss, and in the ravine below the water ran in murmuring streams. Wild blossoms opened with heavy fragrance, dense thickets clumped among heaps of jagged stone. Loud were the cries of deer and monkeys, in bands the roe deer and musk deer came. Birds cried in noisy multitude, but human doings were silent and still. The Venerable elder, in his heart, trembled with fear and unrest; the horse, weak in strength, could scarcely lift its hooves.

Tripitaka threw himself into danger and climbed among the high ridges. After half the day’s travel he still saw no sign of village or homestead. First, his belly was hungry; second, the road was rough and uneven. At the very brink of peril he saw two raging tiger tigers roaring ahead, and behind him several long snakes winding about. Poisonous insects were on the left, strange beasts on the right. Tripitaka, alone and helpless, could only lay his body and mind down and leave all to Heaven. Then the horse itself became frail, its haunches soft and its knees weak, and at once it knelt and collapsed. It could not rise by a single push, and it could not be lifted by pulling. The Dharma Master had no place to set his body securely and was in ten thousand parts sorrowful; he knew he must surely die and could do nothing.

He had calamity in his lot, yet relief would come. Right there, where life itself seemed lost, he suddenly saw poisonous creatures run off, demons and beasts fly away, ferocious tigers disappear, and long snakes hide their traces. Tripitaka looked up and saw a man emerge from the slope before him, indeed a stalwart fellow. He looked so:

On his head sat a leopard-skin cap, speckled like mugwort leaves, on his body a woolen brocade robe in many-hued weave, at his waist a lion-man sash, below his feet a pair of antelope-skin boots. He had round ringed eyes like a watchful graveyard keeper, his whiskers in wild knots like drifting river-light. Across his shoulder hung a pouch of poisoned bow and arrows, in his hand a stout steel three-pronged fork. A peal of thunder broke the heart of mountain vermin, and his bold courage could scatter even the spirits of wild pheasants.

As Tripitaka saw him draw nearer, he knelt by the road, pressed palms together, and cried out, 'Great lord, save my life! Great lord, save my life!' That robust man came forward, set down the fork, and with both hands helped him up: 'Venerable elder, fear nothing. I am no villain. I am a hunter on this mountain, surname Liu, named Boqin, nicknamed Mountain-Terrace Great Guard. I have just come to seek two mountain beasts for food. I did not expect to meet you, and I have brought collision upon you instead.' Tripitaka said, 'I am a monk, humble in appointment from under the Great Tang emperor, going to the Western Heaven to beg the Buddha for the sūtras. Just now upon reaching this place, I met wolves, tigers, and snakes surrounding me on all sides and could not advance. When I saw the Great Guard arrive, all the beasts fled. My life was saved by this meeting. I offer repeated thanks.' Liu Boqin said, 'I live in these places and make my living by striking down wolves and tigers, catching snakes and vermin. So all these beasts fear me and keep away. Since you come from Tang, you and I are from the same place. This is still within Great Tang’s domain, and I too am a Tang subject. We drink the same sovereign’s water and eat the same land’s grain; truly we are people of one state. Do not be afraid. Come with me; rest your horse at my dwelling, and tomorrow I will send you on your way.' Tripitaka heard this and, full of joy, thanked Liu Boqin and followed, leading the horse.

Past the slope they heard the roar of the wind. Liu Boqin said, 'Venerable, do not go forward. Sit here. This wind-breath means a wildcat is coming; wait, I will take it and have it prepared for you.' Tripitaka grew more frightened and dared not move a step. Liu Boqin took up the steel fork and strode out with strong tread. A mottled tiger met him face to face. When it saw Liu Boqin, it turned and fled at once. Liu Boqin thundered, 'You beast, where do you run away to?' Pursued hard, the tiger turned and swung its paw to pounce. Liu Boqin raised the three-pronged fork in front to meet it. So fierce was the scene that Tripitaka nearly collapsed limp upon the grass. From the moment the monk was born, he had never seen such perilous rough play. Taibao and the tiger below the slope clashed against one another, and it was indeed a grand struggle. Then:

Anger everywhere, furious; wild wind rolling on and on. Anger everywhere, Taibao rose to the forehead with giant strength; wild wind rolling on and on, the spotted tiger flaunted itself, spitting up red dust. This one bared teeth and swirled its clawed paws; that one turned and sprang back. The three-pronged fork lifted to heaven, as if to eclipse the sun; the tiger’s thousand-flower tail stirred mist and sent clouds flying. One stabbed wildly at the chest, the other lunged in open-faced seizure. The one who dodged kept his life; the one that struck straight was to behold Lord Yan. You could hear the tiger’s roar; hear too Taibao’s harsh shout. The tiger’s roar split mountain and stream and startled birds and beasts; Taibao’s fierce cry split open the heavenly court and brought stars to view. One with golden eyes burned with wrath; one with stout heart gave birth to anger. Admirable is Liu Boqin, the Mountain-Guard, worthy of praise as lord among the beasts of this ground. When man and tiger fight over life and victory, a fool may lose all three souls.

They fought for about an hour. Then the tiger’s paws slackened, its waist loosened, and Liu Boqin raised the fork and drove it flat through the chest and felled it. The cruel point pierced heart and liver, and in an instant blood spread full on the ground. He pulled it by the ear and brought it back along the path. The fine man did not pant for breath, and his face did not change. He said to Tripitaka: 'Providence, Providence. This mountain tiger is enough for the Venerable to eat for one day.' Tripitaka praised him without end, saying, 'Taibao is truly a mountain deity as if he were born in the heights.' Liu Boqin said, 'What skill have I that deserves such reward? This is the Venerable’s meritorious blessing. Come, hurry and skin it, cook some meat, and prepare fare for him.'

With one hand he held the fork, with the other he dragged the tiger along, guiding the way. Tripitaka led the horse behind him. As they made their way on through the slope’s curves, they suddenly saw a rural settlement. At its front it truly was:

Ancient trees rose to the sky, wild vines covered the road. Ten thousand ravines, and wind-borne dust ran cold; a thousand cliffs made strange and solemn spectacle. Along one path wildflowers breathed their scent against the body; a few poles of secluded bamboo stood close and green. There was a grass gate and thatched hall, hedged yards, stone slabs for a bridge, white-earth walls—truly joyous, truly spare. Autumn air lay austere and desolate, clean wind proud and high. By the roadside yellow leaves fell, on the ridge white clouds drifted. In thin woods mountain birds chirped loudly; outside the gate, tiny dogs barked thinly and keen.

When Liu Boqin reached the gate, he tossed down the dead tiger and called, 'Where are my boys?' Three or four household youths came out, all of odd and fearsome form, and lumberingly carried the tiger inside. Liu Boqin ordered them to skin it quickly and prepare food for the guest. Then he turned, invited Tripitaka in, and they met each other. Tripitaka again bowed and thanked Liu Boqin deeply for the mercy and compassion that saved his life. Liu Boqin said, 'We are people of the same homeland; why offer thanks?' After tea was served and they sat down, an old woman came out leading a daughter-in-law and offered courtesy to Tripitaka. Liu Boqin said, 'This is my mother and my young wife.' Tripitaka said, 'Please let my mother sit. I, a poor monk, bow to her.' The old woman said, 'Elder traveler, each of you cherish yourselves; do not trouble with bows.' Liu Boqin said, 'Mother, he is an envoy of the Tang court, sent to the West to seek the Buddha’s sūtras. He came to this mountain pass and met me by chance; being from the same state, I invited him to my house to rest his horse, and tomorrow I shall send him onward.' Hearing this, the old woman was delighted beyond measure and said, 'Good, good, good. Only to invite him was right, yet such timely good fortune is rare. Tomorrow is Father’s weekly memorial; ask him kindly, Elder, to do a virtue-work, recite a roll of scripture, and send him off the next day.' Though this Liu Boqin was a tiger-slaughtering hand and a mountain protector, he had a filial heart. On hearing his mother, he moved to prepare incense paper and keep Tripitaka at home.

As they spoke, before they knew it the daylight had already been drawing late. The servants spread tables and stools and brought several dishes of well-cooked tiger meat, steaming, and set them out. Liu Boqin invited Tripitaka to serve himself, and to arrange another meal as well. Tripitaka clasped his palms to his chest and said, 'How kind! I will not hide the truth from Taibao: from birth in my mother’s womb I have been a monk and know nothing of eating meat.' Hearing this, Liu Boqin fell silent for a moment and said, 'Venerable, in our family through the generations, we have not known vegetarian cooking. If there is any bamboo shoot, any wood-ear, any dry vegetable, if we make tofu, they are all fried in the oil and fat of roe, deer, tiger, and leopard. There is scarcely any pure vegetarian fare. Even the two iron wok-lids are soaked through with grease. What can be done? It was a fault of mine to invite the Venerable.' Tripitaka said, 'Taibao need not burden himself. Pray, eat what you like. I, this poor monk, can bear three or five days without meals, even hunger. I only dare not violate my fast-day precepts.' Liu Boqin said, 'If you were to die of hunger, what then?' Tripitaka replied, 'Through your grace from heaven I was saved from the circle of tigers and wolves. If I should die of hunger, even that would be better than feeding a tiger.'

Liu Boqin’s mother heard and called out, 'Son, do not chatter idly with the Venerable. I have my own vegetables; I can provide vegetarian fare.' Liu Boqin said, 'Where are they coming from?' The mother said, 'Do not manage me, I have the vegetarian dishes.' She called for the daughter-in-law and had her fetch the small pot. She set it on the fire and burned out the grease, scrubbed and scrubbed again, washed it again and still set it on the stove. She first boiled half a pot of water and set it aside. Then she took some mountain elm leaves and simmered them to make tea. Afterward she cooked some yellow millet into rice, and cooked some dry vegetables to tenderness. She poured two bowls and brought them out, placing them on the table. The old mother said to Tripitaka, 'Venerable, please keep your fast. This is tea and rice, and everything is as clean as can be, prepared by this old mother and the daughter-in-law with our own hands.' Tripitaka thanked her and only then sat down.

Boqin set aside another place and laid out dishes of tiger meat, musk-deer meat, python meat, fox meat, and rabbit, all without salt or sauce, and a little minced dried venison. He filled plate upon plate and bowl upon bowl to accompany Tripitaka at his vegetarian meal. When Tripitaka sat down and was about to lift his chopsticks, he saw the monk join his hands and chant a scripture; frightened, Boqin did not dare to move his chopsticks and hastily rose to stand beside him. After reciting only a few lines, Tripitaka said that the meal could be offered. Boqin asked, “Are you a monk that recites only a short-cut sutra?” Tripitaka replied, “This is not a sutra, but a spell used to open the fasting meal.” Boqin said, “Your ordained folk are so particular—while eating, you keep reciting and reciting.”

After the meal, they cleared away the plates and bowls, and evening gradually came. Boqin led Tripitaka out of the main hall and walked on toward the rear. Passing along the narrow lane-path, they came to a thatched pavilion. He pushed open the gate and entered. There he saw several heavy bows and stout crossbows hanging on the four walls, with several jars of arrows inserted; across the lintel were two blood-stained tiger skins; at the base of the wall were set many spears, sabres, forks, and rods. In the center stood two seats for sitting. Boqin invited Tripitaka to sit. But seeing how fierce and rank with blood the place looked, Tripitaka dared not sit long and so left the pavilion. They went farther back to a broad garden. He saw an endless stretch of clusters of chrysanthemums turning yellow and row upon row of maples and poplars hung with red. Then suddenly he heard a cry; around ten or more plump deer burst out, followed by a crowd of yellow antlered roe, and seeing people they came running with dull, dazed faces, showing no fear. Tripitaka said, “These antelope and deer must have been well kept in your household?” Boqin answered, “As in Chang’an, households with money gather treasure and estates with grain. As hunters, we can only raise a few wild beasts to store against bad weather.” The two talked while they strolled idly, and without noticing had let dusk come. They returned to the front house and rested for the night.

The next morning the whole household, young and old, rose and prepared a pure vegetarian meal, attending to the elder monk and inviting him to begin the recitation. The monk washed his hands, then before the Taibao family shrine held incense and made a bow. Tripitaka rang the wooden fish, first recited the mantra of purifying false speech, then the mantra that purifies body and mind, and then opened the Sutra of Delivering the Dead. Afterward he finished, Boqin asked that a memorial for the dead be written, then asked him to read the Diamond Sutra and the Guan Yin Sutra. One after another he chanted them clearly and loudly. When those were done he ate the midday offering, then recited the Lotus Sutra and the Amitabha Sutra, several more scrolls, and also one scroll of the Peacock Sutra, and spoke on the story of Bichu’s karma-cleansing. Before he knew it, evening had already come. They made all manner of incense and fire offerings, burned votive paper horses for the gods, and burned the memorial text for the dead. The Buddhist rites were complete, and all then retired to rest.

Yet Boqin’s father’s spirit, lifted up and released from sinking misery, arrived early as a ghost at dawn and in a dream told the older and younger members of the household: “In the court of the judges below, my suffering is hard and unending, and I cannot escape transmigration. Now, by good fortune, the holy monk recited scriptures and has removed my sins. The King of Yama has dispatched me to be sent to Zhonghua’s fertile lands, where I will be born into a respectable household. You must make sure to thank this elder well; do not be negligent, do not be negligent. Now I depart.” Thus it was: in the magnificence of all Dharma there is purpose, to send the dead beyond suffering and lift them from the abyss. While still the household was waking from its dream, the sun had already climbed in the east. Boqin’s wife said, “Husband, last night I dreamed our old father came home and said he had suffered deep torment in the spirit court and could not be released for a long time. Now, by this holy monk’s recitation, his sins have been cleared; the King of Yama has sent him to Zhonghua’s rich lands to be reborn in a wealthy household. He told us to thank the elder properly and not to neglect him.” Saying this, she hurried out and paced back and forth. They called for him, but he did not heed. When she awoke it had been only a dream. Boqin said, “I had the same kind of dream—just as you did. Let us go and tell Mother.” As the two were about to do so, the old mother called, “Boqin, come here—I want to speak with you.” The couple came to the front; Mother was sitting on the bed. She said, “My son, I too had a dream in the night. I saw your father return home. He said that by the elder’s compassionate aid he had been delivered, his sins erased; he had gone to Zhonghua’s rich land and to be born in a wealthy household.” At once the couple and all present laughed heartily: “Both my wife and I had this dream; we were just coming to report it, and just then Mother called us—surely it was the same dream.” They called everyone in the family, arranged offerings of gratitude, and had the horses made ready; all of them came forward and bowed, saying, “We thank the elder for lifting my late father out of hardship and into a released rebirth. Our debt cannot be repaid.” Tripitaka said, “What power does this poor monk have to do anything? How can you trouble me with such thanks?”

Boqin explained the dreams of the three people of the household to Tripitaka. Tripitaka also rejoiced. Early the next morning he was served another vegetarian meal, and the family presented one tael of silver as gratitude. Tripitaka would not take a coin. The household pleaded and begged, yet still he accepted not a single coin, saying only, “You were willing to show compassion and send me so far on my journey; that is gratitude enough, my great joy.” Boqin and his mother and wife were helpless and hastily made coarse flour cakes and dried provisions, telling Boqin to see the monk off as far as he could. Tripitaka cheerfully accepted them. Taibao took his mother’s instruction, then called two or three household retainers, each with hunting gear, and they set out together on the high road. They beheld unending mountain wilds and fine scenery on the ridges.

After half a day’s travel they saw ahead a great mountain, high indeed to touch the blue sky, towering and perilous. Tripitaka had not long reached its edge when Taibao climbed it as easily as if it were level ground. As they reached the middle of the slope, Boqin turned around and stood at the foot of the path saying, “Elder, please go ahead and proceed; I must return.” Tripitaka, hearing this, dismounted with a leap and stepped down. “Please do not, for kindness’ sake, trouble yourself to escort me any farther.” Boqin said, “The elder does not know. This mountain is called the Double-Borders Mountain. The eastern half is under our Great Tang, and the western half lies in the land of the Tatar. The wolves and tigers on that side do not submit to me, and I myself cannot cross the border. You must go on yourself.” Tripitaka grew alarmed, lifted his sleeves, grabbed his robe, and could not keep his tears from falling. At just the moment of this parting warning, they had scarcely finished bowing and bidding farewell when, from the foot of the mountain, came a thunderous shout: “My master has come! My master has come!” At that Boqin was startled in fright.

It was still unclear who had shouted. The resolution lies in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 13: Into Tiger-Nest Grotto, Venus rescues him from calamity; at Shuangcha Ridge, Master Beqin holds the monk.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Buddha is the mind, and the mind is Buddha; from the beginning, Buddha and mind both are tied to form. If one truly knows there is neither object nor mind, then that is the True-Mind Dharmakāya Buddha. The Dharmakāya Buddha has no image at all, a single round radiance containing ten thousand forms. The body of no-body is the true body; the appearance of no-appearance is the true reality. It is neither color nor emptiness nor non-emptiness, neither coming nor moving toward nor turning back. No difference, no sameness, no being and no non-being—hard to abandon, hard to seize, hard to listen and behold. Within and without, spiritual light is equal everywhere; one Buddha realm is held in a single grain of sand. One grain of sand contains the Great Thousand World-Systems; one body-mind and all dharmas are one. One must understand the art of not-mind to know this; unsullied and unstuck, it becomes pure karma. With good and evil branching by the thousand, if no action is taken, this is Namo Shijie.

Liu Baqin and Tripitaka were frightened and flustered, and again they heard a cry: “Master, here it is.” Some of the household attendants said, “That shout must be the old ape in the stone casket at the mountain foot.” Taibao said, “It is him, it is him.” Tripitaka asked, “What kind of old ape is that?” Taibao answered, “This mountain was once called Wuxing Mountain; when my Great Tang emperor marched west to pacify the lands, he renamed it Liangjie Mountain. In earlier years I have heard the elders say this: when Wang Mang usurped the Han, heaven dropped this mountain and pressed down a divine monkey. It did not fear cold or heat, nor did it eat food or drink. An earth god kept watch over it and ordered it to eat iron pellets when hungry and drink liquid copper when thirsty. From then until now, it has not died from freezing or hunger. This must be that one. Venerable Master, do not be afraid. Let us go down the mountain and see for ourselves.” Tripitaka had no choice but to follow and led the horse down. After only a short distance, he saw that among the stone caskets there truly was a monkey, thrusting out its head and stretching out a hand in frantic waves. “Master, why did you come only now? You have come at the right time. Save me, and I will take you to the Western Heaven.” The elder moved closer and looked carefully. You may ask what he looked like:

Narrow beak and shrunken cheeks, golden eyes and fiery stare. Moss and lichen piled on the head, vines growing from the ears. Scant hair at the temples, more green grass than hair; beneath the chin no beard, green rushes instead. Mud between the brows, a hollow nose packed with earth, utterly disheveled; thick fingers and broad palms, coated with dust and grime. Yet his eyes kept turning, and his tongue and throat still spoke clearly. His words were quick and clear, though his body was wild and ragged. It was indeed the Great Sage Sun from five hundred years before, still trapped this morning by heaven's net.

Liu Taibao, truly bold-hearted, stepped forward, pulled away the grass at the monkey’s temples and the sedge under his chin, and asked, “What is it you want to say?” The monkey answered, “I have nothing to say. Tell that monk to come up; I have only one question for him.” Tripitaka asked, “What do you ask me?” The monkey said, “Are you the monk sent by the king of the Eastern Lands to fetch the scriptures from the Western Heaven?” Tripitaka answered, “I am. Why do you ask?” The monkey said, “I am Sun Great Sage, the one who threw havoc in Heaven Five Hundred Years Ago. For the crime of deceiving my superiors, I was pressed down here by the Buddha. Formerly there was Guanyin, who came under Buddha’s command to the Eastern Lands to summon a pilgrim for the scriptures. He told me to save myself no more by violence, to return and take refuge in the Buddha’s Way. He urged me to guard the scripture-seeker to the utmost, so that he might go west to worship Buddha; afterward there would be great blessing. So I have kept myself watchful day and night, my heart tied tight from dawn till dusk, waiting only for the Master to come and release me. I will protect your journey for scripture and be your disciple.” Hearing this, Tripitaka’s heart rejoiced: “Though you have such kindness, and though Bodhisattva has taught you well, you now wish to enter the monastic path—but I have no axe or adze. How can I rescue you?” The monkey replied, “No axe or adze is needed. If you only care to save me, I can come out myself.” Tripitaka said, “If I save you, how can you come out?” The monkey said, “On the top of this mountain is a gold-inscribed pressure seal of Buddha Tathagata. Go up, lift that seal, and I will come out.” Tripitaka said so, then turned and begged Liu Baqin, “Taibao, come with me up the mountain once more.” Baqin asked, “How can we know whether he is real?” From below the monkey shouted, “It is true—I will not lie.”

Liu Baqin could only call the household men and take the horses. He then supported Tripitaka and brought him back up the high mountain. They climbed by vines and kudzu and reached the very summit. There indeed was a brilliance of golden light in all directions, auspicious vapors flowing in hundreds of streams, and a great square stone. On that stone a sheet of paper had been pasted, bearing six gold characters: “唵嘛呢叭𠺗吽.” Tripitaka went forward, knelt, faced the characters, made several prostrations, and prayed toward the west: “My disciple Chen Xuanzang, by imperial order, seeks the Dharma. If indeed I am entitled to have a disciple, may I lift these gold words, rescue the divine monkey, and together realize the Spirit-Mountain; if I am not meant to have a disciple, this is but a ferocious and unruly brute seeking to fool a disciple. I do not seek auspiciousness from such deceit, and let me not be able to lift it.” He finished praying and bowed again. Afterward he stepped forward and gently pulled down the six gold characters. At once he heard a fragrant wind, and a hand struck and scraped the seal through the air; a voice rang out, “I am the officer who kept the Great Sage in confinement. Today his term has ended. We go before the Buddha to deliver this seal.” So frightened were Tripitaka and Liu Baqin’s whole party that they all looked up and bowed to the sky. Then they descended by the straight mountain path to the stone casket again. The monkey addressed Tripitaka: “The seal is lifted. Come out now.” The monkey joyfully called, “Master, please move aside a little. I am going out so you are not startled.”

Hearing this, Baqin led Tripitaka and their party eastward. After traveling five to seven li they heard the monkey cry out again: “Go on, go on!” Tripitaka walked yet farther downhill. Then there came a crashing roar—truly the mountain split and crumbled apart. All were terrified. The monkey had already reached the front of Tripitaka’s horse. He knelt there, wet-red and bright, and called, “Master, I have come out.” He made four prostrations to Tripitaka, then rose at once. Bowing deeply, he thanked both Tripitaka and Baqin: “You have gone far and labored to escort my Master; and Brother has also spared me the pain of weeds on my face. I am obliged.” Then he set about gathering the baggage and saddled the horse. When the horse saw him, its waist weakened, its hoofs shortened, and it trembled so that it could scarcely stand. This was because the monkey had once been Bima-wen, guardian of Dragon Horses in Heaven, with certain methods and powers; for that reason, ordinary horses were afraid of him.

Tripitaka, seeing his intention and finding him truly good-hearted, like a true monk, called out, “Disciple, what is your surname?” The Monkey King answered, “I am of the surname Sun.” Tripitaka said, “I shall give you a Dharma name for calling you.” The Monkey King replied, “Please do not take the trouble, Master. I already have a Dharma name: Sun Wukong.” Tripitaka said joyfully, “It suits the order to which we belong. With this appearance you are like a small bhikkhu. I will give you a mixed name and call you Xingzhe. Will that do?” Wukong said, “Good, good, good.” From then on he was also called Sun Xingzhe.

Then Baqin saw Sun Xingzhe gathering himself as if ready to set out in one mind and thought fixed. He turned around, made a deep bow to Tripitaka and said, “Venerable Master, you have in this place obtained an excellent disciple. I am truly glad, truly glad. This man can indeed go with you. I will report back.” Tripitaka bowed in thanks, saying, “I have delayed you with many steps. My gratitude is beyond words. Please send my sincere regards to your mother, the Elder Lady, and to Lady Jing. I have caused much disturbance in your residence; please accept my apology until I return.” Baqin returned the salute, and the two parted.

Now Sun Xingzhe told Tripitaka to mount the horse. He walked ahead carrying the luggage, bare-limbed, limping in quick sways. Before long, having crossed Liangjie Mountain, they suddenly saw a fierce tiger roaring and running at them with its tail lashing. Tripitaka on the horse was alarmed. The Xingzhe, at the roadside and smiling, said, “Do not fear him, Master; he is bringing me some clothes.” He set down the luggage, pulled a needle from his ear, and with a flick of the wind it flashed out as a iron bar as thick as a bowl’s rim. He took the treasure in his hand and laughed, “This good thing has not been used for more than five hundred years. I shall bring it out now and take a bit of clothing to wear.” Then he strode forward and shouted at the tiger, “Beast of karma! Where are you going?” The tiger squatted down in the dust and dared not move. He struck it once on the head, splitting it so the brain burst in ten-thousand scarlet drops, and from its teeth flew a few bead-sized chunks like jade. Tripitaka was so startled he rolled from the saddle, biting his fingers and crying, “Heavens! Heavens! The tiger Liu Taibao fought two days ago is a mottled one; he battled this one for half a day. Today Sun Wukong did not need to contest at all—one staff-blow and he turns it to gore. Truly, when there is strength there is always a stronger one!”

The Xingzhe dragged the tiger and said, “Master, wait a little and sit awhile; let me take off its clothing so I can wear it while we travel.” Tripitaka said, “Where could it have any clothing?” The Xingzhe said, “Do not worry about me; I can make do.” The noble king pulled out one hair, blew a breath of immortal air, and shouted, “Transform!” It became a sharp knife of ox-ear point. He pried open the tiger’s belly skin, then peeled downward and stripped off one entire skin. He chopped off the claw and nails, cut off the head, and cut out a neat square piece of tiger hide. Lifting it, he measured it and said, “It is a bit wide; one piece can make two.” He took up the blade and cut it into two pieces. He kept one piece and wrapped the other around his waist. From the roadside he tore a length of kudzu vine and bound it tight across his lower body to cover himself. “Master, come on, come on. When we reach a house, we can borrow needle and thread and stitch it later.” He twirled the iron bar once; once again it became like a small needle, and he put it back in his ear. He shouldered the luggage and asked Master to mount the horse once more.

The two proceeded. Tripitaka, from horseback, asked, 'Wukong, the iron staff with which you just struck the tiger—where is it now?' Wukong smiled and said, 'Master, you do not know. This staff, which came from the Dragon Palace in the Eastern Sea, is called the Celestial-River-Bottom Holy Iron, and is also called the Golden-Hooped Staff. In the old days when I rose in revolt against Heaven, it was of great use to me. It changes with me: when I wish it to be large, it becomes large; when I wish it small, it becomes small. Just a moment ago I changed it into the shape of a little embroidered needle and tucked it into my ear. It can be taken out only when needed.' Hearing this, Tripitaka rejoiced inwardly, then asked, 'The tiger just now saw you and you could have finished him. Why did you not act? Why did you let him go?' Wukong replied, 'I should not hide it from Master. Do not say he was only a tiger; he was a dragon, and at the sight of me he did not dare to be rude. I, old Sun, am no stranger to subduing dragons and taming tigers; my powers can turn rivers and stir seas. I read appearance and discern disposition, I listen and judge meanings. If I make myself great, I can stretch to the measure of the universe; if small, I can be held in a single hair. My transformations have no bounds, never fixed, ever hidden and revealed beyond measure. To strip this tiger skin, what rarity is there in that? If we come to a true difficulty, then watch me display my art.' Tripitaka heard this and became even more at ease, and he urged his horse forward.

The two disciples went on, talking as they walked, never noticing the sun setting. Then they saw:

Flickering slanting light threw its glow back, and cloud-clusters returned to the edges of heaven and sea. In a thousand hills, birds and small creatures cried densely in chorus, flocking to trees in search of night roosts. Wild beasts came in pairs, pair to pair, tribe to tribe, returning to their home. A hooklike new moon split the dusk. A myriad starlights spread their bright halos.

Wukong said, 'Master, let us quicken our pace. The light is getting late. There, on that side, the trees are dense; surely it is some household courtyard. Let us hurry and ask for the night there.' Tripitaka at once spurred his horse forward, and they rode directly toward the house. At its gate, he dismounted. Wukong dropped the baggage and went ahead, calling out, 'Open the gate! Open the gate!' An old man came out leaning on a cane and pulled the door open with a rough clatter. Seeing Wukong’s fierce appearance, with a tiger skin tied about his waist like a little thunder-god, he went pale, his legs weakened, his body numb, and he stammered, 'A ghost has come! A ghost has come!' Tripitaka came forward and steadied him: 'Good elder, do not fear. He is my humble monk’s disciple, not a demon.' The old man lifted his gaze and, seeing Tripitaka’s peculiar and noble face, only then composed himself, and asked, 'Which temple sent you, monk, to bring such a wicked man to my gate?' Tripitaka said, 'I am a monk from the Tang, going west to seek the Buddha’s scriptures. I happened upon this place at dusk and ask leave to rest one night in your hall, and depart before daylight tomorrow. The old man said, 'Even if you are from the Tang, this one is no man of your land.' Wukong raised his voice in anger: 'You old fellow, you cannot read a face at all! The Tang man is my master, and I am his disciple. I am no ordinary Tangese monk, no trickster either—I am the Great Sage, Equal to Heaven! In this village too, some people know me. I have even seen you before.' The old man asked, 'Where did you see me?' Wukong said, 'When you were a child, did you not carry wood before me? Did you not pick greens before my face?' The old man said, 'This wretch lies. Where did you live, and where did I live? When I came before you, did you have me carrying wood and picking vegetables?' Wukong said, 'My son is only talking nonsense. You do not recognize me. I am the Great Sage from the stone chamber of the Two Realms Mountain; look again and see.' Only then did the old man awaken and say, 'You are somewhat like him. But how did you come out like this?' Wukong then explained in full to the old man the Bodhisattva’s counsel and asked him to wait until Tripitaka showed his credentials and set him free.

The old man immediately bowed and invited Tripitaka inside, calling wife and children to come out, explaining the matter. All rejoiced to hear it, and he ordered tea. After tea, he asked Wukong, 'Great Sage, you also have quite an age on you, do you not?' Wukong asked, 'How old are you this year?' The old man said, 'I have passed one hundred and thirty years.' Wukong said, 'Then I am surely your great-grandson and later-born grandson.' He added, 'I do not remember when I was born, but I have already been under this mountain foot for more than five hundred years.' The old man said, 'Yes, yes. I remember my grandfather saying this mountain had fallen from heaven and pressed down a divine monkey. Only now have you shed that form. When I saw you as a child, there was grass on your head and mud on your face, yet I was not afraid of you. Now there is no mud on your face, no grass on your head, and you seem a little thinner. Add a big tiger skin at your waist, and how different can you be from a ghost or monster?' Everyone in that household, hearing this, all laughed heartily.

This old man proved a decent man, and promptly arranged a vegetarian meal. Afterward, Wukong asked, 'What is your surname, elder?' The old man replied, 'In our house we bear the surname Chen.' When Tripitaka heard this, he came down and respectfully offered his hands: 'Good elder, my humble monk is of the Hua line.' Wukong said, 'Master, if your surname is Tang, how are you of the same surname with him?' Tripitaka said, 'My secular name was also Chen. I am from Juxian Village, Hongnong Commandery, in Haizhou of the Great Tang. My Dharma name is Chen Xuanzang. Because the Great Tang Taizong bestowed upon me the title of a palace brother and made me Tripitaka, he took Tang as my surname, and thus I am also called Tang Monk.' The old man, hearing that they shared a surname, was delighted.

Wukong said, 'Old Chen, we have disturbed your household. I have gone without bathing for more than five hundred years. Please have some hot water boiled and bring tubs, so I and my disciples may wash before we leave and pay our thanks.' The old man at once ordered hot water and basins, and held lamp-welfare. The three travelers bathed and sat before the light. Wukong said, 'Old Chen, I have one more matter that burdens you: lend me a needle and thread.' The old man said, 'Yes, yes, yes,' and told his wife to bring needle and thread, then handed it to Wukong. Wukong then looked with a glance. Seeing Master bathing, he noticed a white cotton short straight robe laid there, not yet worn. He pulled it over and on to himself. He took off the tiger skin, sewed the edges at one spot, folded it into a horse-face shape, wrapped it about his waist, and tightened it with a rattan strap. Coming before Tripitaka he said, 'How does old Sun look today compared with yesterday?' Tripitaka said, 'Good, good, good. This way you look like a proper pilgrim.' Tripitaka said, 'Disciple, if you do not mind this old rag, then wear that short robe.' Wukong did a brief bow and said, 'My gratitude, my gratitude.' He went to find some straw and fed the horse. Then everyone had done what was needed, and Tripitaka, Wukong, and the old man all retired to rest.

At dawn, Wukong rose and asked Master to go on. Tripitaka dressed and told Wukong to gather the bedding and belongings. As he was about to depart, the old man had already prepared soup and a vegetarian meal. After breakfast they set out. Tripitaka mounted his horse, and Wukong led the way. They noticed no hunger, no thirst; they traveled through the night after dawn. It was early winter, and then they saw:

Frost has thinned a thousand woods, red leaves gone thin and dull. On the ridges, a few pines and cypresses still stand bright. Unblown plum buds spread faint fragrance. The short warm daytime, the first hint of spring; chrysanthemums gone, lotuses exhausted, and camellia bushes thick. Old icy bridges and ancient trees vie in branch against branch. A winding ravine murmurs with trickling spring water, while pale clouds float, nearly full of impending snow. A sudden north wind snatches at sleeves—how can one bear the evening cold?

The disciples had been walking some time when a piercing whistle sounded from the side of the path and six men burst out, each carrying a long spear or short sword, sharp blades and taut bows. With one loud cry they shouted, 'That monk, where are you going? Leave the horses and put down the luggage at once, and we will let you live!' Tripitaka was so frightened he nearly lost his soul and dropped off the horse, unable to speak. Wukong steadied him with his hand and said, 'Master, do not worry. It is nothing. They are only here to demand clothes and travel funds from us.' Tripitaka said, 'Wukong, what you say has a flaw. They told us to leave horse and baggage; you ask where their desire is for clothes and money.' Wukong said, 'You guard the clothing, luggage, and horses; let old Sun trade blows with them and see how it goes.' Tripitaka said, 'A single good fighter does not match two fists; two fists are no better than four hands. He has six burly men. How can one so small as you dare grapple with him all at once?'

The courage of the Walking Saint was naturally great, and he did not pause to argue. He strode forward, clasped his hands before his chest, saluted the six men, and said, "Gentlemen, for what reason do you block this poor monk's path?" One said, "We are the king of the six-path cutters, the upright keepers of this mountain. Our great names have long been widely proclaimed; you do not know them. Leave your goods behind quickly and we will let you pass. If you even utter one word of 'no,' we will smash you to pieces and grind your bones to dust." Sun Wukong said, "I too am a hereditary king, a mountain lord by long years, yet I have never heard of your grand fame." One said, "You do not know. Let me tell you: one is called Eye-Watching Joy, one is called Ear-Listening Anger, one is called Nose-Sniffing Love, one is called Tongue-Tasting Thought, one is called Mind-Seeing Desire, and one is called Body-Rooted Worry." Sun Wukong laughed, "So, you are six coarse thieves. You fail to recognize that this monk is your lord, and yet you block the road. Bring out the plunder you have robbed; I will split it evenly into seven parts and spare you." Hearing this, Joy rejoiced, Anger was angry, Love delighted, Thought pondered, Desire desired, and Worry worried. They all rushed forward in disorder, shouting, "This monk has no manners. You have no goods at all, yet you turn to us asking to share!" They brandished spears and swords and came as one, hacking at Sun Wukong in the front with clanging blows—bang and clang—seventy or eighty strikes. Sun Wukong stood in the middle as if unaware. One thief said, "Good monk, your head is truly hard." Sun Wukong laughed, "That is enough to pass as tolerable. Your hands are tired from all this beating. Now let old Sun take out a needle and play with it." One said, "This monk is one of those needle-acupuncture doctors in disguise. We are no patients; why does he speak of needling?"

Sun Wukong reached into his ear and pulled out an embroidered pin. As he flung it into the air, it became an iron rod, as thick as a bowl. He held it up and said, "Do not run. Let old Sun try a staff stroke on you." Those six thieves were terrified and ran in all directions. Snatching out distance in each step, he chased them down one after another and killed them all. He stripped off their clothes, took their travel money, and came back with a smile, saying, "Master, please continue on. Those thieves have all been annihilated by old Sun." Tripitaka said, "You have courted grave trouble. Though they are merely fierce men of the cut-road, even if you brought them before the court it should not be a crime of death. No matter how much skill you have, you only needed to drive them off. Why kill them all? This is taking life without cause. How can you be a monk? A monk, while sweeping the ground, fears to harm even ants, and will cherish moths under the gauze covering a lamp. How can you make no distinctions and slaughter everyone with one brawl? Not the smallest trace of compassion or goodwill of heart. While in the wilds, no one may inspect; if in a city, if someone bumps into you and you swing your staff wildly to injure people, I may become a scapegoat and be held to account—how could I escape?" Sun Wukong said, "Master, if I do not kill them, they will kill you." Tripitaka said, "This monk would rather die than do violence. I may die, but I am only one body. You, however, have slain six. How is this to be explained? If this comes before officials, it cannot be justified even if your father is in office." Sun Wukong said, "Do not dissemble, Master: when I, old Sun, reigned as king over Flower-Fruit Mountain in the age of monsters, I do not know how many people I killed. If we follow your way and carry this to the court, I could at least receive an indictment; then I could not be the Equal-Sky Great Sage." Tripitaka said, "It is precisely because you never curbed yourself, were violent and arrogant among men, deceived heaven and fooled those above, that you suffered the calamity of five hundred years ago. Now that you have entered the monastic life, if you still kill like before, mindlessly harming life, you cannot reach the Western Regions, and you cannot be a monk. Truly evil! Truly evil!"

This monkey in his whole life could not bear people being overbearing. Seeing Tripitaka only keep up a constant stream of nagging talk, he could not hold back the fire in his heart and said, "Since you insist that I cannot be a monk, that I cannot go to the Western Regions, no need to keep this endless babbling and abuse. I will simply return now." Tripitaka did not answer. He gave a bound, and said, "Old Sun, I am leaving!" Tripitaka hurriedly raised his head; he was already gone. He only heard a shout and he turned to the east. Leaving the elder all alone and forlorn, he nodded and sighed in self-reproach, grief and resentment unending: "This brute, so hard to instruct! I only say a few words to him; how is it he disappears without form or sign? Enough, enough, enough. I am not destined by my fate to take a disciple and enter this life. Now I seek him and cannot find him; I call him and he does not answer. Come and go, come and go." It is said: "Give your body and life in devoted risk to go westward; do not depend on another to decide for yourself."

The elder had to gather his belongings and set them on the horse. He neither rode the horse nor moved quickly—one hand on his Golden-Hooped Staff, one hand gripping the reins—he moved westward in a cold, lonely manner. Not long after, on the road ahead he saw an aged mother carrying a padded robe, and on it a flowered hat. As Tripitaka saw her coming near, he hurriedly pulled the reins, stepped to the right side, and gave way. The old mother asked, "Which region are you from, venerable elder, wandering here with such loneliness?" Tripitaka said, "I am a disciple from Great Tang in the Eastern Land, sent on official mission to the Western Buddha to beg the true scriptures." She said, "In the Western land of Buddha, at the Great-Resounding-Drum Temple, in the bounds of Tianzhu, the road is ten thousand and eight thousand li. You are one person alone, one horse, with no companion and no disciple. How can you possibly go?" Tripitaka said, "Today I have just received one disciple. He is violent and unruly by nature. I spoke to him a few words, but he would not accept instruction and so he left at once. She said, "I have this padded robe and a flower-embedded hat. They were my son's things. He became a monk for only three days before his life was cut short. I went to his temple and wept once, bade farewell to his master, and brought home these two garments as remembrance. Venerable elder, since you have a disciple, I give you this robe and hat." Tripitaka said, "I accept your high grace, but this disciple of mine has already gone; I do not dare to receive them." She said, "Which way did he go?" Tripitaka said, "I heard one shout and he turned eastward." She said, "Not far east is my home; surely he has gone there. I also have a spell, called the Heart-Settling Incantation, also known as the Tightening Headband Spell. Learn it in secret, hold it firm in your heart, and do not let anyone else know of it. I will catch up to him and call him back to you; then you can have him put on this robe and hat. If he refuses to obey you, recite this spell silently. He will dare not riot again, and he will dare not go away either." Tripitaka bowed his head in thanks. The old mother turned into a shaft of gold light and went east. Tripitaka knew this was a truth-word bestowed by Guanyin. He quickly pinched up earth, burned incense, and bowed toward the east with earnest prayers. Afterward he took the robe and hat, put them in his pack, sat by the roadside, and practiced that Heart-Settling Incantation, reciting it back and forth several times until he had memorized it perfectly and fixed it well in his heart.

It is said that Sun Wukong, leaving his master, rose on his cloud and turned straight toward the Eastern Sea. He pressed down the cloud-head and split the waterways, reaching the front of the Crystal Palace. The Dragon King was startled and came out to welcome him, then brought him inside to sit. After the courtesies, the Dragon King said, "I have lately heard you, Great Sage, have had much trouble. Congratulations! I suppose you have rebuilt the immortal mountain and returned to your old cave." Sun Wukong said, "I have such intentions too, but I have again become a monk." The Dragon King said, "A monk of what kind?" Sun Wukong said, "It was due to the Bodhisattva of the South Sea persuading me to do good, who taught me the path of true attainment. I follow the Tang monk of the Eastern Lands to the west to worship Buddha, have taken refuge as a monk, and am called Xingzhe." The Dragon King said, "This is truly something to rejoice in, to rejoice in. That is reforming evil and returning to the right, restoring good in the mind. If so, why do you not go west, and why return east again?" Sun Wukong laughed, "It is because Tripitaka does not understand human nature. There were several hairy thieves on the cut-road; I slew them. Tripitaka just kept on chattering and criticized me for many things. Do you think old Sun can stand this bottled-up anger? I left him and was going back to my original mountain; so I first came here for your summons—to beg a cup of tea." The Dragon King said, "Excellent, excellent." Then at once his dragon sons and dragon grandsons presented aromatic tea in offering.

After tea, the Monkey King looked behind him and saw a painting hanging on the back wall titled ‘Yi Bridge, Three Requests for Footwear.’ Sun Wukong asked, ‘What is this scene?’ The Dragon King said, ‘You, Great Sage, came later, so you do not recognize it. It is called The Three Requests for Footwear at Yi Bridge.’ Sun Wukong asked, ‘What does “three requests for footwear” mean?’ The Dragon King said, ‘That immortal is Huang Shigong, and this youth is Zhang Liang of the Han. Huang Shigong was seated on the Yi Bridge when he suddenly lost one shoe below the bridge, and he called Zhang Liang to retrieve it. The boy at once fetched it and knelt to present it. This happened three times; not one trace of arrogance or laziness appeared in Zhang Liang, so Huang Shigong came to love his diligence and, by night, bestowed Heavenly writings on him, charging him to support Han. In time he truly planned in the war chamber and won victory from a thousand li away. After peace was secured, he abandoned office, returned to the mountains, roamed with Chi Songzi, and awakened to Immortal Way. Great Sage, if you do not guard Tripitaka, do not labor wholeheartedly, and do not accept instruction, then in the end you are only a demon-immortal and cannot hope to attain the true fruit.’ Sun Wukong listened and was silent for half a while. The Dragon King said, ‘You, Great Sage, should decide this for yourself; seek no ease and do not ruin your future.’ Sun Wukong said, ‘Enough talking. Old Sun will go and protect him now.’ The Dragon King, rejoicing, said, ‘Since this is so, I dare not detain you. Go promptly in compassion, and do not stay away from your master too long.’

Seeing him urge him to go, the Monkey King quickly sprang up, left the Sea Storage, rode a cloud, and took leave of the Dragon King. As he went, he met the Bodhisattva of the South Sea. The Bodhisattva said, ‘Sun Wukong, why did you fail to accept instruction and not protect Tripitaka? What have you come here for?’ In panic, Sun Wukong, in the midst of the clouds, performed obeisance and said, ‘By the Bodhisattva’s kind words, there indeed came a monk of the Tang. He removed the pressure-seal and saved my life, and I became his disciple. Yet he blamed me as fierce and unruly, so I only slipped away; now I am going to protect him as well.’ The Bodhisattva said, ‘Go at once and do not miss your intent.’ Then they parted ways.

The Monkey King soon saw Tripitaka sitting by the roadside in silence. He came forward and said, ‘Master, why are you not walking? What are you doing here?’ Tripitaka lifted his head and said, ‘Where did you go? You tell me to go, and yet I do not dare to go; I dare not move even then, and here I only sit waiting for you.’ Sun Wukong said, ‘I went to the old Dragon King of the Eastern Sea to fetch tea.’ Tripitaka said, ‘Disciple, one who has left the world should not lie. Not even one moment after you left me, you already claim you went to the Dragon King’s house for tea?’ Sun Wukong laughed, ‘I will not hide it from the Master: I can ride a jindou cloud, and one jindou cloud goes ten thousand eight hundred li, so I can go and return at once.’ Tripitaka said, ‘I spoke too sharply just now; you resented it and gave me this trouble, then left me to starve and wait. You have the power to get tea; I, who cannot go there, can only stand and endure hunger here. You should feel troubled too, should you not?’ Sun Wukong said, ‘Master, if you are hungry, I can make some vegetarian alms for you by transformation.’ Tripitaka said, ‘No need to make alms. In my bundle there are still some dry rations, sent by Liu Taibao’s mother. Go and fetch a bowl and some water, and I will eat a little then continue walking.’

Sun Wukong unfastened the bundle and, in its middle, saw several coarse flour buns. He took them out and passed them to his master. He also saw a bright, glowing cotton robe and a gold-inlaid flower hat. Sun Wukong said, ‘Were these garments brought from the Eastern lands, Master?’ Tripitaka replied offhand, ‘Yes, they were what I wore when I was young. If I wear this hat, I can recite the sutras without study; if I wear this robe, I can perform ceremony without rehearsal.’ Sun Wukong said, ‘Good, Master, then let me put them on.’ Tripitaka said, ‘I only fear the size may not match; if it does, then wear it.’ So the Monkey King took off his old white robe, put on the cotton robe, which fit him exactly, and set the hat on his head. Seeing him so dressed, Tripitaka ceased eating the dry food and silently recited the Tightening Headband Spell once. Sun Wukong cried, ‘Head pain, head pain.’ The master chanted it two or three more times, and the Monkey King writhed until he tore the gold-inlaid flower hat. Tripitaka, fearing he might tear away the golden band, stopped. Without the chanting, the pain ceased. He touched his head and felt a golden wire-like line tightly clamping it—impossible to remove, impossible to pull free, already rooted in place. He then took a needle from his ear, threaded it into the band, and pulled it outward in random tugs. Tripitaka, fearing the band would snap, began chanting again. Sun Wukong still in pain, he stiffened like a dragonfly, rolled in the jindou cloud, ears reddened, face flaming, eyes bulging, body numb. Tripitaka, seeing this, held his breath and stopped chanting again. The pain left the Monkey King’s head. Sun Wukong asked, ‘My head pain—was it the Master who cursed me?’ Tripitaka said, ‘I am reciting the Tightening Headband Spell. When have I ever cursed you?’ Sun Wukong said, ‘Recite once more.’ Tripitaka did so. Sun Wukong immediately suffered again and cried, ‘No more, no more. Whenever you chant it, I hurt. How can this be?’ Tripitaka said, ‘Have you heard my instruction now?’ Sun Wukong said, ‘I have heard it.’ Tripitaka said, ‘Could you still be rude again?’ Sun Wukong said, ‘I do not dare.’

Though he agreed aloud, his heart still held ill will. He swept the needle back and forth, testing its width, and aimed at Tripitaka to strike. Frightened, the old monk chanted the spell two or three times more. The monkey fell to the ground, dropped the iron cudgel, could not raise his hands, and begged, ‘Master, I understand. No more chanting, no more chanting.’ Tripitaka said, ‘Why did you harbor treachery and dare strike me?’ Sun Wukong said, ‘I did not dare strike. Master, who taught you this method?’ Tripitaka said, ‘An old mother taught it to me just now.’ Sun Wukong grew angry, ‘No need for words. That old mother is surely Guanyin. How could that one harm me so? I will go to the South Sea and beat her.’ Tripitaka said, ‘Since this method was bestowed by that one on me, he surely knows it already. If you seek him out, when he chants, would you not die?’ Seeing the point, Sun Wukong truly did not dare to move. He turned back, knelt down, and pleaded with tears, ‘Master, this is the way he used to subdue me, commanding that I go west with you. I will not go to provoke him. You too must not speak as if in everyday scolding; just keep reciting. I vow to protect you and will never regret it again.’ Tripitaka said, ‘Then attend me and mount, and go west with me.’ Only then did that Monkey finally return fully to his senses; he steadied his spirit, tightened his cotton robe, prepared the horse’s harness, packed up the luggage, and raced on westward.

After this departure, there is more to be told. Listen to the next chapter for the full unfolding.
chapters.title: Chapter 14: The Mind-Monkey returns to rectitude; the six thieves leave no trace.
