This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Say that Sun Wukong, serving Tripitaka, went westward. After traveling for several days, it was the cold winter of the twelfth month, the north wind piercing, the world slick with ice and bitterly cold. They were on steep roads of crags and precipices, along rugged ridges and dangerous high mountains. Tripitaka was on horseback, and from a distance he heard a hissing water roar filling the ear. He turned and called, "Sun Wukong, where is that sound of water?" Wukong said, "I remember this place is called Snake-Coiled Mountain Eagle-Grief Ravine, and it must be the water in the ravine." He had scarcely finished when the horse reached the ravine bank. Tripitaka pulled tight on the reins to look. Then they saw:

A narrow cold thread of water passed through the clouds, and clear, limpid waves shone red in the sun. The sound trembles; like night rain it is heard in the dark gorge, and the dawn colors flash, dazzling the sky. Waves rise a thousand zhang and fly, spraying jade-shattering spray; a deep pool roars, and the clean wind echoes. The flow returns toward ten thousand fields of misty waves; gulls and herons forget each other, and no fishhooks are to be seen.

The two disciples and master had just been looking when, in the ravine, a great cry sounded. A dragon shot out, driving forward waves and heaving the water, charging from the cliff and lunging to seize the elder. So startled was Sun Wukong that he dropped the baggage, lifted his master from the horse, and ran back. The dragon could not keep pace: it swallowed Tripitaka’s white horse, with saddle and bridle, in one bite, then lay submerged again in the water to hide its tracks. Wukong placed Tripitaka on a high knoll to sit, then ran back for the horse and load; only one pack-sling remained, and there was no horse in sight. He carried the pack to Tripitaka and said, "Master, that evil dragon has vanished without a trace; it only frightened away my horse." Tripitaka said, "Disciple, then how are we to find the horse now?" Wukong replied, "Do not worry, do not worry. I will go and see."

He gave a whistle, leapt into the air, and with his Fire-Eyed Golden Pupils scanned all around, shading his eyes with his hand. He still could not see even a trace of the horse. Alighting back from the cloud-rim, he reported, "Master, our horse is most likely swallowed by that dragon; I can see no sign of it anywhere." Tripitaka said, "Disciple, how big a mouth can that brute have, to swallow that great horse along with saddle and bridle? Likely it panicked and ran, slipping into one of the mountain hollows. Look again carefully." Wukong said, "You do not know my powers. In broad daylight these eyes of mine often see fortune and disaster along a thousand li. Within a thousand li, even a dragonfly opening its wings I can see; how is it that I do not see that horse?" Tripitaka said, "If it ate it, how shall we go on? Alas, these a thousand mountains and waters—how can we pass them?" As he spoke, tears fell like rain. Seeing him about to cry, Wukong could not bear the sudden vexation and shouted, "Master, do not look so swollen with panic—sit, sit still. Wait while Old Wukong goes and finds that brute, and make him return my horse." Tripitaka caught him and said, "Disciple, where will you go to look? Might he not rise secretly and hurt me as well? At that point we would lose both man and horse—what then?" Hearing this, Wukong’s anger grew even more. He shouted like thunder, "You are so useless, so useless! You want the horse, yet will not let me go. If you mean to stand guard over the baggage like this, then sit until you are old."

He was still bellowing and could barely still his rage when voices rang from the air: "Great Sage Sun, do not be angry; Tripitaka, do not weep. We are deities dispatched by Bodhisattva Guanyin, sent to protect the Journey One covertly." Hearing this, the elder hastily offered a bow. Wukong said, "Who are you all? Declare your names so I may keep account." The gods answered, "We are the Six Ding and Six Jia, the Five-Directions Jie-Di, the Four-Shift Gongcao, and eighteen Gālán that guard the Teaching, each taking turns on watch." Wukong said, "Who begins the watch today?" One of the Jie-Di answered, "The rotation goes: Ding-Jia, Gongcao, Gālán. Of the five-direction Jie-Di, only Golden-Head Jie-Di does not leave either side by day or by night." Wukong said, "Then the non-duty ones should step away. Leave the six Ding generals, the day-watch Gongcao, and all the Jie-Di to guard my master. I will go find the dragon in the ravine and make him return my horse." The gods obeyed. Tripitaka only then relaxed and sat on the cliff, then instructed Wukong to look carefully. Wukong said, "Just take comfort." The good monkey king tied up his cotton robes, lifted his tiger-skin skirt, gripped the Golden-Hooped Staff, steadied himself, came straight to the ravine, and, half in cloud, half in mist, stood above the water and shouted, "Mudskipper, return my horse! Return my horse!"

That dragon which had eaten Tripitaka’s white horse had lain at the middle of the ravine, hidden below, nursing its spirit and strength in secrecy. As soon as it heard someone shouting and abusing for the horse, it could not hold back the fire in its heart. In sudden agitation it sprang up, leaping across the waves, rose and cried, "Who is the one that dares wound me in this watercourse?" When Wukong saw it, he shouted with a roar, "Do not run. Return my horse!" He lifted the staff and struck him at once. The dragon spread fang and claw to seize him. The two fought for a brave and fierce bout by the ravine edge. They saw:

The dragon spread out keen claws; the monkey raised the Golden-Hooped Staff. He has hanging whiskers like white-jade strings; this one has eyes like red-gold lanterns. Under those whiskers pearl-bright mists spray in colored mist; in this one’s hand the iron staff whirls up wild wind. That one is the karmic child of the bewitched mother; this one is the fiendly spirit that dared affront Heaven. Both have met hardship, and now each, seeking success, must show his power.

They went back and forth, fought for quite some time, circled long; then the dragon grew weak in strength and numbed in sinew, unable to withstand. It made one turn and rushed back into the water, diving deep to the ravine bottom and not raising its head again. Sun Wukong cursed it without ceasing; the dragon only pushed as if its ears were stopped.

Wukong, unable to do anything else, could only return and tell Tripitaka, "Master, this monster has been brought out by Wukong’s cursing. He fought with me for a long time and, fearing battle, ran away; now he has hidden himself in the middle of the water and will not come up." Tripitaka said, "How can we be certain that it was he who ate my horse?" Wukong said, "By your own words—if it were not him, would he not have come out to challenge and fight me?" Tripitaka said, "When you fought the tiger earlier, you said you had methods to suppress dragon and tiger. Why today are you not able to suppress this one?" The monkey had no heart to endure being cornered, and when he heard Tripitaka put it in that way, he displayed his divine might and said, "Do not keep saying it; do not keep saying it. Let me meet him once more and finish this."

The Monkey King stepped forward and jumped to the ravine edge, then unleashed the power that can stir seas and turn rivers, and stirred the clear water of the ravine like the swollen, winding waters of the Yellow River at nine bends. The evil dragon, resting in the deep ravine, felt restless and uneasy. Inwardly it thought, "This is indeed twice-a-bad luck, a calamity that does not come alone. I only escaped the Heaven-ordered death danger less than a year ago. In this life of patient drift, I have now run into such a reckless demon; he comes to harm me." The more it thought, the more angry it grew. Unable to bear the humiliation, it bit its teeth and leapt out, shouting, "What sort of splashing demon are you to dare ridicule me so?" Wukong said, "Do not ask where I come from. If you return the horse, I will spare your life." The dragon replied, "The horse is in my belly—I swallowed it. How can I bring it out? If I do not return it, then what can I do?" Wukong said, "If you do not return the horse, watch my staff: I will beat you to death and end it, and that is enough to settle the horse's life." The two again fought hard under the cliff. After only a few rounds, the young dragon truly found it hard to withstand; with one sudden motion it changed into a water-snake and slipped into the grasses.

The Monkey King took up his staff, ran forward, and pushed through the grass to hunt the snake, but found no trace at all. In his anger the three-corpse gods of his being flustered and smoke rose from his seven orifices; he spoke a single cry of the "Om" spell and summoned the local At-fang Earth God and the Mountain God of that place, who came and knelt together, saying, "Mountain God and Earth God come to receive your summons." The traveler said, "Set out your staffs, come forth, and meet with me for five bouts of staff play so Old Sun may vent his temper." The two gods knelt and begged, "Great Sage, if it be your convenience, please allow these little gods to explain." The traveler said, "What is it you would say?" They said, "Great Sage, for so long you have been trapped, and these small gods do not know when you would return, so we never were able to meet you. We beg you, please forgive our fault." The traveler said, "If so, I will not strike you. I ask you: from what quarter did the strange dragon in Eagle-Downpour Ravine come? How did it seize and eat my master's white horse?" The gods replied, "Great Sage, you never had a master from the beginning. You are a Pure and Original One beyond both Heaven and Earth, who bows to neither. How could there be a master's horse for you?" The traveler said, "You do not understand it either. I have endured these five hundred years of suffering because of my former deceit. Now, through the compassion of Guanyin, I have been rescued by a true monk under the Tang court and told to follow him as disciple, going west to bow before Buddha and seek the scriptures. Passing through this place, I lost my master's white horse." The gods said, "So that is it. This ravine has always had no evil in it. It is only steep, deep, broad, and utterly clear; the water shines so pure that even crows and magpies dare not fly over. Because one sees the reflection of oneself, one thinks it is another bird of the same flock and often jumps headlong into the water; therefore it is named 'Eagle-Grieving Precipitous Ravine.' Only in recent times, when Guanyin went out to seek pilgrims, she rescued a jade dragon and sent him here, instructing him to wait for the scripture-seeking pilgrim and not to do evil. When he was hungry, he would come ashore and seize birds or magpies to eat, or catch a marten or deer for food. We do not know by what heedless folly he this day collided with the Great Sage." The traveler said, "The first time he brawled with Old Sun hand to hand, and we wheeled around for several rounds. The second time, when Old Sun cursed him, he did not come out again. So he used a spell that stirs rivers and upheaves seas, churning this ravine until it was muddied. Then he surged up and came on, still seeking to contend. He did not know the weight of my staff; unable to withstand it, he changed into a water snake and slipped into the grass. I came in pursuit, but no trace remained." The Earth God said, "Great Sage does not know. This ravine is connected by myriads of channels and pores, and thus its waves run deep and far. Surely somewhere here there is another hole into which he slipped. There is no need for you, Great Sage, to rage and search here. To seize this thing, simply ask Guanshiyin to come, and it will naturally submit."

The traveler saw this and called the Mountain God and Earth God to come together before Tripitaka, and told him all that had happened. Tripitaka said, "If you must go and invite the bodhisattva, when will you return? How can I, a poor monk, endure hunger and cold?" Before he finished speaking, a voice sounded from the dark sky from Jintou Jie Di: "Great Sage, you need not set out. A small god will go and invite the bodhisattva." The traveler rejoiced and called out, "You have my thanks, you have my thanks. Go quickly, go quickly." Jie Di leapt up on the clouds at once and shot straight toward the Southern Sea. The traveler instructed the Mountain God and Earth God to guard the master, telling the Gongcao in turn to go and seek alms food. After that he went to patrol the ravine banks; no need to set down that here.

Not long thereafter Jintou Jie Di flew in one sweep of cloud and arrived early at the Southern Sea. He followed auspicious radiance straight to Luojia Mountain, into the Purple Bamboo Grove, and through the golden-armed heavenly attendants, with the Wood Guardian and Huian, he conveyed the matter and gained audience with the bodhisattva. She asked, "What brings you here?" Jie Di said, "Tripitaka at Snake-Coiled Mountain, Eagle-Downpour Ravine, has lost his horse, and Sun Wukong is in a bind, unable to advance or retreat. When we asked the local Earth God, he said it was the demon-dragon sent by the bodhisattva here who swallowed the horse. The Great Sage has sent me to beg your arrival and to summon this demon-dragon to return his horse." Upon hearing this, the bodhisattva said, "This brute is in truth the son of Ao Run, lord of the West Sea. He burned the brilliant pearl in the heavenly hall; his father charged him with rebellion, and at court he committed a death offense. I saw him myself before the Jade Emperor and had him brought down, instructing him to serve as foot-strength for Tripitaka. How could he now eat Tripitaka's horse? In any case, let us go." The bodhisattva descended from the lotus throne, left the immortal cave, and with Jie Di rode on auspicious light across the Southern Sea. There is a poem as proof:

The Buddha taught the Mi Tuo Tripiṭaka, and the bodhisattva raised beneficence as a long rampart. Great marvelous speech of Mahā passes through heaven and earth, and Prajñā's true mantra saves spirits and ghosts. So the golden cicada can shed its shell once more, and therefore Tripitaka returns to practice again. Only because the road was blocked by Eagle-Downpour Ravine, the dragon son returned to truth and took horse form.

The bodhisattva and Jie Di arrived at Snake-Coiled Mountain not long afterward and hovered in midair, halting the auspicious clouds, and looked down. Sun Wukong was below on the ravine bank, still shouting and cursing. The bodhisattva told Jie Di to call him. Jie Di drove the cloud steed down without passing Tripitaka and came directly to the ravine edge, telling the traveler, "The bodhisattva has come." Hearing this, the traveler leapt skyward on cloud in haste and shouted, "You, so-called teacher of seven Buddhas, lord of compassion—why did you devise this means to hurt me?" The bodhisattva said, "I, for your brazen sake, this headbanded monkey, crude fool with the red rump—how many times did I spare your life? I drew forth a seeker of scriptures and taught him to rescue your life, and enjoined him to protect you. Why do you not thank me for saving you, yet come and raise such a commotion?" The traveler said, "You have made my lot pitiable. Once you set me free, I should have been allowed to roam and play unhindered. The other day at sea, when you met me, you struck me with a few hard words and ordered me to give my all and serve Tripitaka. Why then did you send him a flowered crown to make me put it on my head and suffer? You fixed this headband upon Old Sun, and taught the old monk to recite this spell of the Tightening Headband Spell, have him chant it over and over, so my head hurt again and yet again. Is this not your doing?" The bodhisattva laughed and said, "You monkey, you do not obey orders, you will not receive proper fruit. If I did not restrain you in this way, you would still deceitfully harass Heaven with no sense of what is right. If once more calamity erupts as before, who will then control it? Only if this demon-head is taken in hand could you enter my path of yoga." The traveler said, "As for this matter, let it be called my demonic role. Yet how could you send that guilty demon-dragon here to take spirit-form and make it eat my master's horse? This is again releasing evil to do evil, utterly unkind." The bodhisattva said, "That dragon—I myself petitioned the Jade Emperor to keep him here, solely to serve as strength for the scripture-seeker. How can an ordinary horse from the Eastern Land endure ten thousand waters and mountains, and how can it reach the Buddha-lands of Ling Mountain? It must have this dragon-horse for the journey." The traveler said, "For one so fearful of Old Sun that he hides and cannot break out, what can be done?" The bodhisattva said to Jie Di, "Go to the ravine edge and call out twice: 'Ao Run Dragon King, third prince of the Jade Dragon, come forth; the South Sea bodhisattva is here.' He will come."

Jie Di did exactly that, calling by the ravine twice. The little dragon leapt up with breakers and waves and rose from the water, transformed into a human figure, stepped upon a cloud-head, and in the air bowed to the bodhisattva saying, "Formerly the bodhisattva granted me the grace that saved my life; I have waited here long and heard no word of the scripture-seeker." The bodhisattva indicated the traveler and said, "Is this not the Great Disciple of the pilgrim?" The little dragon said, "Bodhisattva, this is my foe. Yesterday I was truly starving and did eat his horse. He had some strength, fought me to the point that mine was worn and I withdrew, and then he cursed me so badly I dare not come out again. He had not even mentioned the words 'seeking the scriptures.'" The traveler said, "You never even asked my surname and name, how could I have answered anything?" The little dragon said, "I did not ask where you came from, wild demon. You shouted, 'Who cares where or what place—return my horse at once.' Not once did you speak even half a word of 'Tang.'" The bodhisattva said, "That monkey-chief relies only on his own strength and is never one to praise another. This time, when he goes again, he has come to submit. If he were to ask, if he first utters the word 'Journey to the West'/'seeking the scriptures,' there would be no need to trouble the mind; he would bow of his own accord."

Sun Wukong rejoiced to receive the teaching. Guanyin came forward, took off the bright pearl from the little dragon’s neck, dipped a willow twig in sweet dew, brushed it lightly over him, blew out immortal breath, and called out, “Change!” The dragon at once changed back into the horsehair of his original steed. Then she instructed, “You must clear your karma-obstruction with your heart; once your work is complete, pass beyond ordinary dragons and I will return you to a golden-body true fruition.” The little dragon held a crossbone in its mouth and nodded assent in its heart. Guanyin told Sun Wukong to lead him to Tripitaka. “I am going back to the sea,” Sun Wukong said. He grabbed the Bodhisattva’s sleeve and would not let go. “I am not going, I am not going. The road to the West is that rugged and steep; how can I protect this mortal monk and reach the goal? With so much hardship and trouble, even old Sun’s life may not remain whole, so how could any attainment be completed? I am not going, I am not going.” Guanyin said, “You were not yet fully accomplished before, yet you were willing to apply yourself and awaken; today you escaped heavenly disaster, how can you suddenly fall into laziness? In our way, we realize the true with nirvana, and one must hold faithful hope in right fruit. If you should come to a place of wound and bitter discipline, I permit you to call on heaven to respond and on earth to awaken; once more, if you come to a time hard to survive, I will come in person to save you. Come this way back, and I will grant you another skill of this sort.” Guanyin plucked three willow leaves, put them behind Sun Wukong’s head, and cried, “Change!” They became three strands of life-saving fine hair. She told him, “If the time comes when there is no aid and no master, use them as circumstances require and they will save you from sudden calamity.” Hearing all these good words, Sun Wukong at last thanked the great compassionate Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva then moved with fragrant wind curling around and colorful mist drifting, and went directly back toward Putuo Mountain.

Sun Wukong at once returned from the cloud and pulled the mane from the top of that dragon-horse to go meet Tripitaka: “Master, we have a horse now.” Tripitaka saw him and was greatly glad: “Disciple, how is this horse more fat and sturdy than before? Where did you find it?” Sun Wukong said, “Master, you are still dreaming. The Bodhisattva was invited just now by Golden-Head Jie Di. She came to the stream and transformed the dragon there into our white horse, the same in body and hair as before, only without saddle and reins. Old Sun pulled it here.” Tripitaka was greatly startled and said, “Where is the Bodhisattva? Let me go and thank him.” Sun Wukong said, “The Bodhisattva has already gone to the South Sea; do not delay.” Tripitaka then took up clods, burned incense, faced south, and bowed. After the bowing he rose, and with Sun Wukong prepared to depart. Sun Wukong drove away the mountain spirit and Earth Lord, instructed Jie Di and Gong Cao, and invited Master to mount. Tripitaka said, “How can one ride such a horse with no saddle or reins? Let us first find a boat to cross the gully, then make arrangements.” Sun Wukong said, “Master, you do not understand the times. In these wild lands where does a boat come from? This horse has long stayed here and must know the current. Just ride him across as if he were a boat.”

Tripitaka had no choice and so mounted the bridleless horse as instructed. Sun Wukong carried the packs. When they came to the streambank, they saw upstream an old fisherman drifting down, steering a raft made of dry wood poles with a pole. Sun Wukong saw him and beckoned with his hand: “Old fisherman, over here! I am going to the West to fetch the sutras. My master is in hardship at this place; come and ferry him once.” At once the old fisherman rowed close. Sun Wukong had Master dismount from the horse, while he supported him on each side. Tripitaka boarded the raft, led the horse by the reins, and set down the baggage. The old fisherman pushed off so fast it was like an arrow, and soon they had crossed Eagle-Sorrow Gorge and reached the west bank. Tripitaka told Sun Wukong to untie the pack, took out several paper coins of the Great Tang, and offered them to the old fisherman. The old man pushed hard with one stroke and said, “No money, no money.” Then he drifted away into the wide misty middle waters. Tripitaka felt vexed but only joined his palms and thanked him. Sun Wukong said, “Master, do not make polite greetings. Do you not recognize him? He is the water spirit of this stream. He did not come once to fetch old Sun; old Sun would have beaten him. Now that he spared us, enough! How could he dare ask for money?” Tripitaka seemed half willing, half unwilling to believe, and so again mounted the bridleless horse. Following Sun Wukong he went straight out on the highway and rushed westward. This is exactly so: “With Great Suchness one reaches the far shore; with sincere heart and awakened nature, one ascends to Ling Mountain.”

Then the master and disciples pressed on, and before they knew it the red sun had dropped in the west and evening light was deepening. But behold:

Pale clouds tossed and ruffled, the mountain moon dim and hazy. Frost color filled the sky with cold, and wind from all four sides pierced the body. When the lone bird flew off, the blue islets widened; at the bright glow of evening color, distant hills sank low. Sparse woods and a thousand trees gave out cries; on empty ridges, lone apes called. For the long road there was no trace of travelers; at night, homeward boats entered from ten thousand li away.

As they walked on, Tripitaka and Sun Wukong said nothing for some time before Tripitaka saw ahead a manor-like estate. Tripitaka said, “Wukong, there is a household in front. We can stay the night and travel again at dawn.” Sun Wukong raised his head and said, “Master, this is not a household estate.” Tripitaka asked, “How is it not?” Sun Wukong said, “A household has the ridgeline figures of fish and beasts; this is by all means a temple hall and nunnery.”

The traveling party spoke as they went and soon arrived at the gate. Tripitaka dismounted from the horse and saw three large characters above the gate: “Lishe Shrine,” and entered inside. Inside there was an old man, a string of prayer beads around his neck, who came with palms joined to welcome him and called, “Please sit, Master.” Tripitaka hastily returned the courtesy and went up to the hall to bow before the holy image. The old man called a youth to offer tea. After the tea, Tripitaka asked the old man, “Why is this temple called ‘Lishe’?” The old man said, “This place lies on the border of Habi country of the western lands. Behind this shrine is a household from a village; they came together with devout hearts and established this temple. ‘Li’ means a village territory, and ‘She’ is a local earth deity. On days of spring ploughing, summer weeding, autumn harvest, and winter storing, they make offerings of three sacrificial animals and fruits here, to honor the Earth God so that the four seasons remain auspicious, the five grains be abundant, and the livestock prosper. Hence the name.” Tripitaka nodded and praised, “Exactly as the saying goes, ‘Even three li from home is another village wind and custom.’ In my home village there is not such a practice.” The old man asked, “Where is your holy land, Master?” Tripitaka said, “I am a poor monk of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, commissioned by edict to go west to the Buddha for sutras. As we passed Baofang, dusk was near, so we have taken refuge in this shrine for one night and will travel when morning light comes.” The old man was very pleased, uttered three words of greeting, and again called for the youth to prepare a meal. Tripitaka ate and then thanked him.

Sun Wukong, quick to notice, saw a rope for hanging clothes under the eaves, went over and tore it apart, and tied the horse’s feet with it. The old man laughed and asked, “Where did this horse come from?” Sun Wukong growled, “Old man, you do not know proper rank and ranklessness in your speech. We are pious monks going to the Buddha; would we steal a horse?” The old man laughed: “If it were not stolen, why would a horse come without saddle or reins and then tear apart my line for drying clothes?” Tripitaka placated him: “This impish one is only hot-tempered. If you wish to tie the horse, ask the old gentleman for a rope instead of tearing the clothesline. Old sir, do not be angry, do not be angry. This horse of mine, to be plain with you, is not stolen. Yesterday, coming from the east, at Eagle-Sorrow Gorge there was already a white horse with saddle and reins ready for riding. By chance a wicked dragon in that gorge had formed a spirit and swallowed my horse together with its saddle and reins in one mouth. Fortunately my disciple has some ability, and by luck Guanyin came to the bank, captured that dragon, and taught him to become our original white horse. Its hair was all the same, and so he carries me to the West to worship the Buddha. Today, after crossing the stream, we have not spent even a day and have already reached this holy shrine, and yet we still have no saddle and reins.” The old man said, “Master, do not take offense. I was only joking, but I never imagined your senior disciple would speak seriously. In my youth I had a little coin and could afford a good swift horse. Through years of repeated misfortune and the ruin of fire, I came here with no foundation left, so I became the shrine’s caretaker and serve the incense. Thankfully the benefactors of the manor behind this house feed me through the day. I still have a pair of saddle and reins here, the things I cherished in daily life, and though I am this poor I would not part with them. Only this morning I heard your words and even though even Guanyin would rescue a dragon and make it transform into your mount, this old man cannot withhold even a little help. Tomorrow I will bring those reins and send them to you, Master, with them fastened for your back, and beg you to accept them as a favor.” Tripitaka heard this and thanked him without end. Soon a youth brought out supper. Afterward the meal was done, lamps were lit on the palms, beds were laid, and everyone lay down to rest.

At dawn the next morning, Sun Wukong rose and said, “Master, that shrine-keeper promised us the saddle and reins last night; ask for them and do not let him bear it.” Before he finished speaking, the old man indeed brought out a full set on the veranda: saddle, saddle blanket, harnessing tools, and lead ropes—everything needed for a horse—arranged complete. “Master, here are the saddle and reins,” he said. Tripitaka rejoiced to receive them. He told Sun Wukong to take them up to inspect them on the horse and see whether they would fit. Sun Wukong went forward and examined each item one by one. They truly were excellent pieces. A poem could stand as proof:

The carved saddle shimmered with color, silver stars mirrored in its glow. The padded saddle-tree was layered in plush; the reins were bound with three strands of purple silk. The bit and chin strap at the bridle-end opened like clustered blossoms; gold-painted cloud fan-work showed beasts that seemed to dance. Iron rings and links were well-smoothed from use, and two hanging tufts knotted like wet tassels of hair.

Sun Wukong secretly rejoiced in his heart, buckled the saddle and bridle onto the horse as if they had been measured and prepared exactly for this moment. Tripitaka offered thanks to the old man, who rushed forward and said, “My fear and my fear. Why need you give thanks?” The old fellow did not stay a moment longer. “Venerable Tripitaka, please mount,” he urged, and the monk came out and into the gateway and climbed onto the horse. Sun Wukong took up the baggage. The old man then drew another whip from his sleeve—a short piece with a fragrant canestring handle, its tassel knotted with tiger-sinew cord—and offered it with a respectful bow by the roadside: “Venerable monk, I still have a rein-lash to give you, this is sent with my farewell.” Tripitaka took it while still on the saddle: “I receive your alms; I receive your alms.”

They had scarcely begun to exchange courtesies when the old fellow had already vanished. When he looked back, the roadside shrine was merely an open patch of ground. Then from midair came a voice: “Venerable Tripitaka, forgive my tardiness. I am the mountain spirit and earth god of Mount Loka. At the Bodhisattva’s behest I have sent the saddle and bridle for you all. You must press onward to the West, and never grow sluggish even for a moment.” Flustered, Tripitaka dismounted in a rush and, looking to heaven, prostrated himself again and again: “My disciple is but a flesh-eyed mortal in a mundane body. I do not know your exalted countenance. I beg your pardon for my offense. Please convey my obeisance to the Bodhisattva, whose boundless grace has sheltered me.” He went on bowing to heaven and counting no measure of it. By the roadside, Sun Wukong, the Great Sage, could not help but laugh, for he was delighted with the Monkey King’s joy, and in he came to tug at Tripitaka’s sleeve: “Master, rise up. He has gone far already; he can neither hear your prayers nor see your prostrations. Why do you go on kneeling?” The elder replied, “Disciple, while I bow like this, you do not even bow to him once; you just stand aside and laugh. What sense does that make?” Sun Wukong said, “How can you know? A fellow like him, half-hidden and half-shown, ought to be beaten a good beating. Only for the sake of the Bodhisattva’s face I let him off; enough of that. How dare he receive my obeisance? Old Sun, from childhood, has been a true rough fellow and does not know how to bow to people. Even seeing the Jade Emperor and Laozi, I would only give a token nod.” Tripitaka said, “You are no true son of a house; do not talk such empty words. Rise now; do not lose time on the road.” Only then did the master rise, pack up, and go westward onward.

From then on, for two months the road was tranquil, and what they met were Luo Luo, Hui Hui, wolf-beasts, monstrous vermin, tigers and leopards. Time passed swiftly; it was already early spring. The hills and woods showed brocade-green hues, grass and trees sent up young shoots of green. Plum blossoms had all fallen, and willow eyes were just beginning to open. The trio traveled while roaming in the spring scenery, and then saw the sun falling in the west. Tripitaka pulled in the horse and gazed afar; within a fold of hills were dim tower silhouettes, heavy palatial roofs and halls. He asked, “Wukong, what place is that?” Wukong looked up and said, “Not a palace—it must be a monastery. Let us hurry. We can stay there for the night.” Tripitaka, pleased, agreed and, releasing the Longma, rushed straight forward.

In the end, it was still unknown what place they were heading toward. Listen in the next chapter for the full account of how it turned out.
chapters.title: Chapter 15: At Snake-Coiled Mountain the gods give secret aid; at Eagle’s-Mourning Ravine the unbridled horse of intention is reined.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

At this point, the master and disciple rode in on horseback and came right up to the mountain gate; as he had been told, it truly was a monastery. What they saw was:

Tier upon tier of halls, corridor upon corridor. Outside the gate of the Three Peaks, lofty heights were hidden by ten thousand folds of colored cloud; before the Hall of the Five Blessings, thousands of crimson veils of mist wound in vivid beauty. On both sides stood ranks of pines and bamboos. The twin ranks of pines and bamboos, timeless and beyond count, were naturally quiet and secluded; the stand of cypress and fir had color and complexion, and was proudly handsome. They also saw a tall bell-and-drum tower and a steep pagoda. The monks in meditation were fixed in calm, while birds in the singing trees made sparse sound. Truly desolate and dustless, pure emptiness itself is pure emptiness; in clear spaciousness the fruit of the Way is clarity and emptiness. Poem: On the upper shrine, Jetavana hides within emerald recesses; this vihara’s scene surpasses all Saha. Truly, pure lands in the human world are few; among the world-famous sacred peaks, monks are in the majority.

The Senior Monk dismounted, and the Master set down his load. He was about to enter when a group of monks came out from the gate. See how they looked:

A left-side clerical cap sat on the head. Paired bronze rings hung from the ears. A silk belt wrapped the waist. He walked steadily in straw sandals, with a wooden fish held inside his hand. In his mouth he constantly chanted, "Prajna is my total refuge."

Tripitaka saw them and stood by the gate to offer his greeting. The monk quickly returned the courtesy and, smiling, said, "Forgive me." Then he asked, "Where are you from? Please come in and receive tea in the abbot’s hall." Tripitaka said, "My disciple is an envoy from the Eastland, from Great Tang, come to Leiyin Temple to bow before Buddha and seek the scriptures. We have now reached this place and dusk is near, so I wish to borrow lodging here for one night." The monk said, "Please enter and be seated, please enter and be seated." Tripitaka then called the Master to lead in the horse. When the monk suddenly noticed the Master’s appearance, he was a bit fearful and asked, "What sort of thing is that leading the horse?" Tripitaka whispered, "Keep quiet. Keep quiet. He is quick-tempered; if he hears you call him something, he will be angry. He is my disciple." The monk gave a cold shiver and bit his finger, saying, "With such an ugly face and odd-headed nature, how could he be taken as a disciple?" Tripitaka said, "You cannot tell by looking. He is ugly indeed, but also highly useful."

That monk then went with Tripitaka and Sun Wukong through the gate. Inside the gate, above the main hall were four large characters: "Guanyin Zen Abbey". Tripitaka rejoiced greatly and said, "As a disciple, I have often felt the Bodhisattva’s holy kindness yet had not yet come to thank you. To come to this Zen abbey now is like seeing the Bodhisattva herself; it is most fitting, and I am glad to pay respect." Hearing this, the monk ordered a chan monk to open the hall doors and invited Tripitaka to bow. Sun Wukong untied the horse, dropped the baggage, and went up with Tripitaka. Tripitaka stretched his back and body, lowered himself to the ground, and before the golden image knelt and touched his forehead. The monk went to beat the drum. The Master went to strike the bell. Tripitaka prostrated before the altar and made his prayers. When the worship was over, the monk stopped the drum, yet the Master kept striking the bell without pause, fast and slow, for a long while. The chan monk said, "The worship is finished—why keep striking the bell?" The Master then dropped the bell-mace and laughed, "You cannot know this. I am keeping the rule, 'A monk for one day, a day of bell-striking.'" At that moment this alarmed monks and elders throughout the monastery. Hearing the wild clamor of bell and drum, all came out together and cried, "Which rabble is beating the bell and drum here?" Sun Wukong leapt out and shouted, "It is your old grand-uncle Sun making mischief with the clappers." When those monks saw him, they trembled and rolled on the ground, crying, "Leigong, Grandfather!" The Master said, "Leigong is my own prized grandson. Get up, get up, do not fear. We are lords from the Great Tang in the Eastern Lands." Then they only offered proper reverence. A resident abbot of the monastery said, "Noble ones, please come to the rear hall for tea." So they untied the reins, led in the horse, lifted the baggage, went around the main hall, and went straight into the rear room, where the seating order was set.

The abbey host offered tea, and then arranged the meal. It was still early in the day; Tripitaka had not yet finished his thanks when he saw two novice boys in the rear bringing out an old monk. See how he was dressed:

On his head was a Pílu square hat, with the brilliance of a cat-eye jewel on the crown. On his body he wore a close silk-velvet kasaya with gold-edged borders that shimmered with emerald-like sheen. A pair of monk shoes held together the Eight Treasures; his staff was inlaid with stars among the clouds. Wrinkles covered his whole face, like the old mother of Lishan; his two eyes were dim, yet they resembled the Dragon King of the East Sea. His mouth, with teeth fallen out, could not close against the wind; his back was bent and stooped, and his muscles knotted like twisted cords.

The monks said, "The patriarch has come." Tripitaka bowed and offered proper respect, saying, "Venerable abbey host, my disciple offers greetings." The old monk returned the courtesy and all sat in order. He said, "Only just now my boys informed me that the lord from Tang in the Eastern Land had arrived, so I have come out to pay my respects." Tripitaka said, "I have blundered into your treasure-shrine without understanding its worth; pardon me, pardon me." The old monk said, "No, no." Then he asked, "Sire, how far is it from the Eastern Lands to here?" Tripitaka said, "From the outskirts of Chang’an it is over five thousand li. We passed the Two Realms Mountains, took a number of junior disciples, and along the way passed through Western Barbarians, Xīfān and Habi, and after two months traveled another five or six thousand li to reach this honorable place." The old monk said, "That is ten thousand li away indeed. I, this servant, have wasted my life, never even left the monastery gate, truly what is called 'watching the sky from a well'—a sort of rotting-wood sort of man." Tripitaka asked, "What is the venerable abbey head’s age?" The old monk said, "I am two hundred and seventy, and this is still a little while." Sun Wukong heard this and said, "This is still my great-grandson across ten thousand generations." Tripitaka shot him a look and said, "Speak carefully. Do not forget place and rank, and do not crowd or collide with others." The monk then asked, "Lord, how many years have you lived?" The Master replied, "I dare not say."

The old monk made no more of that mad remark, gave no offense, and did not ask again; he only ordered tea. One boy brought out a lamb-skin jade tray and three blue-lacquered gilt tea cups. Another boy brought a white-bronze kettle and poured three cups of fragrant tea. In truth its color outshone blooming pomegranate flowers, and its flavor surpassed osmanthus blossom. Tripitaka saw it and praised it without limit: "What fine things, what fine things indeed—truly rare food and rare vessels." The old monk said, "Narrow eyes, narrow eyes. You are from the high realm in the Central Kingdom and have broad sight of wonders; for such vessels, praise is unnecessary. Since you come from a foreign land, do you have any treasures you could lend my disciples for a look?" Tripitaka said, "Pitifully, I have no precious things in my eastern land; even if there are, the road is long and such things cannot be carried." Sun Wukong said quietly, "Master, I once saw among the baggage that robe—you know, this kasaya. Why not show it to them to see?" On hearing "kasaya," all the monks each gave a cold laugh. Sun Wukong said, "Why do you laugh?" The abbey host said, "You said a kasaya is a treasure, but your words are really laughable. If you speak of kasaya, for fellows of our kind we have no mere two or three hundred pieces. If we speak of my preceptor, who has been a monk here for two hundred fifty to sixty years, there are at least seven or eight hundred." He said, "Bring it out and let us see." The old monk was showing off in one breath and so ordered the chan monk to open the storeroom. The novice monk lifted the cabinet and brought out twelve chests, set them in the courtyard, and unlocked them. Racks were set on both sides and ropes around all four sides; each kasaya was shaken open and hung up for Tripitaka to view. In truth the whole hall was bright with silk and brocade, and the walls with brocades.

The Master inspected them one by one; they were all robes of flower-inlaid, velvet-worked, and gold-embossed embroidery. He said, "Good, good, good. Put them away, put them away. Bring out ours as well." Tripitaka pulled him aside and whispered, "Disciple, do not compete in wealth with others. We travel alone in the world; this could cause mistakes." The Master said, "Why is it wrong to look at a kasaya?" Tripitaka said, "You have not understood. The ancients said, 'Fine and strange beautiful objects should not be shown to those whose eyes are greedy and deceitful.' If such a thing enters the eyes, it will stir the heart; once the heart is stirred, schemes will arise. You are the one to fear misfortune. If he asks for it, you must give in; if you do not, life may end in ruin. This is no small matter." The Master said, "Do not worry, do not worry; all is with your disciple." Seeing this, he went at once without waiting to be told, opened the bundle, and unwrapped two layers of oiled paper already fastened. When he removed the paper and took out the kasaya, when he shook it open the room filled with red light and the court with colored radiance. Every monk who saw it had no one among them who did not rejoice in heart and praise it aloud: it was indeed a fine kasaya. It bore these lines:

A thousand kinds of craftsmanship, pearl tassels with dazzling luster; ten thousand rare wonders, holy Buddhist treasures gathered together. Above and below, dragon-whiskered brocades laid in colored silks; all four sides trimmed with ribbon-silk borders. Hung on the body, the monsters and specters are eliminated from this day; when worn on the body, the fiends and ogres go down to the Yellow Springs. Made by the hand of the transformed Celestial Immortal; if one is not a true monk, one dares not wear it.

That old monk, when he saw such a treasure, did indeed let a wicked thought take hold of him. He stepped forward, knelt before Tripitaka, and with tears in his eyes said, "My disciple is truly without merit." Tripitaka helped him up and said, "What is it, Venerable monk?" He said, "Your Excellency’s treasure has just now been opened, and dusk had come. My eyes are dim, blurred with age; I cannot see clearly. Is it not because of no destined affinity?" Tripitaka ordered, "Bring the lamp on your palm and let you look again." The old monk replied, "My lord’s treasure is already bright; if I light a lamp, it will flash right in my eyes, and I cannot look closely." Sun Wukong said, "How should I look at it, then?" The old monk said, "If your lordly grace is kind, send the disciple to the rear room and let him inspect it slowly all night. In the morning return it to me before you go west. I do not know your honored intention." Hearing this, Tripitaka was startled and scolded the Great Sage: "It is all your doing, all your doing." The Great Sage laughed: "Why should we fear him? Let me pack it and let him take it to look. Yet if there is any mishap, it will all be through me." Tripitaka could not stop him. He handed the robe to the old monk, saying, "Just look at it. But in the morning, return it to me as before, and do not damage or soil the robe." The old monk rejoiced and commanded the fortunate novice to take the robe inside. He also told the monks to clean the front meditation hall, set out two rattan beds with quilts, and invite the two elders to rest there; in a separate room he had them prepare an early departure meal for the morning. Then everyone dispersed. Master Tripitaka and the disciples closed the meditation hall and slept; there is nothing further to add."

Yet the monk had tricked the robe into his hands. He brought it to the rear room, stood by the lamp, and howled and wept over the robe. The monks of that temple, frightened by what was happening, dared not fall asleep. The happy lucky novice, without knowing why, went and told the other monks: "The Reverend has been crying since the second watch and still has not quieted." Two disciple-monks, whom he loved dearly, stepped forward and asked, "Master, why do you cry?" The old monk said, "I cry out of no fate; I cannot bear to look at Tripitaka’s treasure." A junior monk said, "You are old and have lived long, Master, and are beyond your prime. His robe is right in front of you; simply untie it and look. Why must you cry so?" The old monk said, "To see it for long is impossible. I am two hundred and seventy years old this year. I have turned only hundreds of robes over the years. How could there be such a one? How could this be mine to wear as a Tang monk?" The young monk replied, "Master, you are mistaken. Tripitaka is a wandering monk from afar, who has left home and hearth. You, at this ripe age, have already enjoyed enough of your monastic life; why should you now want to be a traveling monk like him?" The old monk said, "Though I am a monk who lives at ease and finds joy in my old age, I have not yet worn this one. If he let me wear it for one day, even if I die I can close my eyes in peace. That would make my life of being a monk in this world worthwhile." The monks said, "This is no proper way. If you want to wear his robe, what is difficult? Tomorrow we can hold him here one day and then you wear it one day; hold him ten days, you wear it ten days. Enough, why cry like this?" The old monk said, "Even if he stays a whole year, I could only wear it for a year at most. In the end he will have to go anyway. When he departs, he departs with him. How can I keep him for long?"

At that moment, while he was speaking, a young monk named Guangzhi raised his head and said, "If the old monk wants him to stay long, it is simple." At these words the old monk became very joyful and said, "My son, what keen idea do you have?" Guangzhi said, "Tripitaka and the other one are on foot; the hardship of travel has been great. They are asleep now. We should gather a few strong men, take spears and swords, break into the meditation hall, kill them, bury the corpses in the back garden so only we householders know, then at the same time seize his white horse and baggage, but keep this robe as our family heirloom. Is this not a plan for our descendants to hold fast to for many generations?" The old monk heard this, his mind completely delighted, and just wiped away his tears, saying, "Good, good, good; this plan is excellent." At once he made ready the spears and swords."

There was then another young monk named Guangmou, Guangzhi’s fellow disciple. He came forward and said, "This plan is not sound. If we are to kill him, we should first watch for signs. The white-faced one seems easy; the hairy-faced one seems hard. If we fail to kill him, will it not invite ruin on ourselves? I have a way that does not require moving blade or spear. I wonder whether Your Honor approves." The old monk said, "My son, what method do you have?" Guangmou said, "According to Small Sun’s thought, now summon everyone of the East Mountain monk cells, each one to bring a bundle of dry wood. Leave the three meditation halls to one side, arrange the wood all around, and set them alight, leaving him no path to flee, and burn even the horse. The villagers in front of and behind the mountain, upon seeing it, will only say he was careless and set a fire that burned down our hall. Would those two monks not both be burned? Yet it will also shield suspicion. Would not that robe then be our family treasure?" The monks who heard this were all overjoyed and all said, "Strong, strong, strong. This plan is even better, even better." Then he ordered each room to bring in wood. Alas! This was just the plan that made the long-lived old monk’s life run to its end, and turned Guanyin’s Chan hall to dust. In fact, in that temple there were some seventy or eighty monk-houses, with more than two hundred disciples total. That night they all rushed together carrying firewood, surrounded the meditation hall before and behind and on all four sides so it was blocked, and arranged the fire—no further details need be recorded."

Now Tripitaka and the disciples had already settled to rest. The Great Sage, being a spirit-monkey, though he lay down he still gathered spirit and regulated breath, half awake in a blurred state. Suddenly he heard footsteps from outside, and a crackling, gusting sound of wood. He wondered, "At this silent hour, how can someone be walking with such a sound? Could it be robbers, plotting to harm us?" He rose in a single spring and wanted to open the door to look out, but feared waking Master. Watch him summon his energies, shift his body in an instant, and become a bumblebee. He was truly:

Sweetness in his mouth, poison in his tail; a slender waist and a light body. Flying through blossoms and crossing willows like an arrow, he clings for fragrance like falling stars. This small, tiny frame can bear heavy loads; with hasty wings that hum he rides the wind. Then beneath the rafters he bored through and saw clearly."

Only later did they see all the monks moving firewood and carrying brush, already surrounding the meditation hall and setting it alight. The Great Sage inwardly laughed: "As I said to my Master, he intends to take our lives and scheme for my robe, and thus raised this cruel scheme. I was going to take my staff and beat him, but sadly I could not—one strike of the staff would kill him, and then the Master would fault me for the assault. Enough, enough, enough. Let him have a chance at easy thievery; follow his plan as bait, and make him unable to stay."

Good monkey, with one great bound, leaped up into the Heavenly South Gate. A frightened crowd of Pang, Liu, Gou, and Bi bent low, and Ma, Zhao, Wen, and Guan folded their backs; all cried, "Disaster, disaster! The master who disturbed Heaven’s court has come again." Sun Wukong waved his hand and said, "No need for salutations. Do not be alarmed. I have come to seek Guangmu Heavenly King." He had barely said it when the king arrived at once and, greeting the Great Sage, said, "Long time no see, long time no see. I heard before that Guanyin Bodhisattva came to meet the Jade Emperor and borrowed the Four-Duty Magistrates, the Six Ding and Six Jia, along with Jie Di, to protect Tripitaka on his westward journey for the scriptures. They said you became his disciple. How are you free to be here today?" Sun Wukong said, "No need for long greetings. Tripitaka has met villains on the road; they have set fire to him. The matter is urgently urgent. I have come to ask you to lend a fire-proof ward to save him. Bring it quickly so I may use it and return at once." The king said, "You are mistaken. If it is villains setting fire, you should borrow water to save him; why a fire-proof covering?" Sun Wukong said, "You do not understand. If we only borrow water, the fire cannot be put out properly and it will only feed it. With this shield, Tripitaka will be protected from harm, while the rest of it burns as it will. Hurry, hurry, do not waste time with words; a major matter is at hand." The king laughed, "This monkey still has the same narrow heart: only concern for himself, not others." Sun Wukong said, "Quickly, quickly, do not quibble and spoil the task." The king had no choice but not to refuse, and so handed over the ward to Sun Wukong.

Sun Wukong took it, pressed on his cloud-head, and walked straight to the ridge of the meditation hall, covering Tripitaka, the white horse, and the baggage beneath it. Then he went up behind, to the abbot’s chamber where the old monk lived, and sat there to guard the robe. When he saw those people setting the fire, he twisted his seals and chanted an incantation; from the ground to the southeast he drew a breath and blew, and a wind rose, whipping the flames into wild, surging chaos. "Great fire, great fire!" Yet behold:

Black smoke spread dimly, red flames leapt high. Black smoke spread dimly, and in the open sky not a single star was visible; red flames rose high, and the earth was lit red for a thousand li. At first it blazed like a bright gold snake; later it surged like a fierce blood-red horse. From the southern three qi the heroism was spent, and the Great God returning Fortune showed its divine power. Dry tinder made fire ferocious by its nature—what need there is to speak of Sui-ren drilling wood to start flame; in front of hot oil, streaks of colored fire floated, outshining the old patriarch’s furnace. This was merciless firelet rising: how could one prevent this willful slaughter? It did not put out the disaster, but came to increase the cruelty. Following the wind, tongues of flame rose a thousand zhang higher; fire, vaunting its wind-power, sent embers spattering beyond the ninth heavens and the clouds above. "Ping-ping, pang-pang," it sounded like old cracked firecrackers; "plop-plop, rah-rah," it sounded like cannon fire in an army camp. The Buddha statues in that place could not flee; in the east court’s cloisters there was no refuge for the halls. It was like a night of ceaseless battle at Red Cliffs, outdoing the fires within Epang Palace. This was only sparks from a spark, yet they can burn ten thousand mu. In a moment, with wind howling and flame surging, the whole Guanyin monastery was red everywhere. Look: the monks hauled chests, lifted baskets, snatched tables and set down cooking pots, and all the courtyard echoed with cries of grief and pain. Sun Wukong guarded the rear abbot chamber and wrapped the front meditation hall with the fire-warding cover; the rest burned fiercely before and behind, truly red flames blazing in the sky and golden light shining through the walls.

No sooner had the fire begun than it startled a beast-demon of the mountain. Exactly twenty li south of this Guanyin monastery stood Black Wind Mountain, and in its slopes was Black Wind Cave, where a demon spirit was sleeping and turning over. He saw the light through the window cracks and thought it was dawn. When he looked again, however, he saw that the glow flickering from the true north was fire. The demon cried in alarm: "Ah! This must be the fire that has broken out in the Guanyin monastery. These monks are terribly careless. I should go and save them." He rose, lifting his cloud-head at once, and came down beneath the smoke and flames. Indeed, the fire rose to heaven; the front halls were already emptied, and the two corridors burned in a two-sided blaze. He strode in with force and crashed inside, calling out to fetch water, but saw no fire in the back rooms, while on the roof ridge of the hall a man stood fanning wind. At once he understood. He hurried in; at the center of the abbot’s chamber there was a strange rosy light, and upon the altar lay a blue felt bundle. He untied it and found a brocaded saffron robe, truly a precious treasure of the Buddha realm. Wealth moves the heart, does it not? He did not put out the fire, he did not call for water. Taking the robe, he looted in the confusion, hauled it away as he stepped into the clouds, and headed directly for the eastern mountain.

The fire burned until daylight at the fifth watch, and only then subsided. You could see the monks, face and body red and raw, sobbing and crying, all of them going into the ash to search for copper and iron, raking away charred coal, pawing for gold and silver. Some took shelter in wall baskets, patching together makeshift sheds; some kindled fires at the ends of broken hearthstones and set pots to cook. They shouted complaints and grievances, crying and yelling in wild disorder, too much to recount.

Afterward Wukong took the fire-blocking shield, carried it with all his strength up to the Southern Heavenly Gate, and handed it to the Guangmu Heavenly King, saying, "Thanks for lending, thanks for lending." The king took it and said, "Great Sage, such sincerity! I had worried that you would not return my treasure and that I could not trace it; I am glad you have brought it at last." Wukong said, "Am I, old Sun, one who deceives face to face? It is said, 'Borrow well and return well; borrowing again is no hardship.'" The king said, "You have long been out of sight. Please come sit in the palace for a while, what do you think?" Wukong said, "I am not as I was before; no more can I spend time on high talk and easy talk on fine benches. I am now guarding Tripitaka and have no leisure. Let us make an excuse and part." He quickly left at once from the cloud and saw the sun-star again. Then he came to the front of the meditation hall, changed form in an instant, becoming a bee, flew in, and when he showed his true form he saw that the Master was still in deep sleep.

Wukong called out, "Master, dawn has come—get up." Tripitaka had just awakened and said as he rolled over, "Right away." He put on his clothes, opened the door, and came out, then looked up to see only walls of red and black, with the halls and towers all gone. He cried in shock, "Ah! Why have all these halls vanished and only red walls remain?" Wukong said, "You are still dreaming. A fire passed through in the night." Tripitaka said, "How is that I did not know?" Wukong said, "I guarded the meditation hall and saw you in deep sleep, so I did not disturb you." Tripitaka said, "You had the strength to guard the hall—how could you not help with the fire in the other rooms?" Wukong laughed and said, "Excellent Teacher, you had it right from yesterday: they fixed on our robes and plotted to burn and kill us. If old Sun had not been aware, by now we would all be ash and bone." Hearing this, Tripitaka, frightened, said, "Was it their doing that this fire was set?" Wukong said, "Who else would it be?" Tripitaka said, "Could it be that I neglected you and thus you did this in your play?" Wukong said, "Old Sun, a man so lazy as me, would I do such foul work? Truly it was their doing. Seeing their poisoned intent, I did not at all help extinguish the fire; I only, to a small degree, stirred the wind." Tripitaka said, "Heavens! If fire breaks out, one should only summon water. Why instead summon wind?" Wukong said, "You know what the ancients said: 'A tiger has no intent to harm without a tiger's mind, and a man no intent to hurt without human intent.' If he did not set the fire, how could I dare to stir wind?" Tripitaka asked, "Where is the robe now? Could it have been burned?" Wukong said, "No matter; no matter. It is not burned, because the abbot room where the robe was laid had no fire." Tripitaka, angered, said, "I do not care about you, but if there is any damage at all, I will chant and chant mantras upon you, and you will die." Wukong, panicked, said, "Master, do not recite, do not recite. I only need to retrieve your robe and we can set off. Let me fetch it." Tripitaka then led the horse by the rein; Wukong took up the pole and burden and came out of the hall, heading straight for the back abbot chamber.

The monks, who were still wailing in sorrow, suddenly saw their master and disciples coming with the horse and carrying pole. Frightened, each one felt ghostly dread and cried, "A vindictive ghost has come to claim lives." Wukong shouted, "What ghost comes for life? Return my robe at once and leave!" All the monks knelt together and knocked their heads on the ground: "My lord, there is a grudge for a grudge and a debtor for a creditor. If he comes for life, it is no affair of ours. It was all Broad Plan and the old abbot who plotted to ruin you. Do not ask us for your life." Wukong snapped, "You accursed beasts! What life is it you are asking for? Just bring out the robe and go." In the midst of this, two of the braver monks said, "My lord, you were burned to death in the meditation hall; to come back now demanding a robe—are you truly human, or is it a ghost?" Wukong laughed, "These scoundrels, where is your fire now? Go look at the hall in front and then speak." The monks rose and went to see, and the doors and shutters of the hall outside had in no way been scorched. Trembling, they at last recognized that Tripitaka was a true sacred monk and that Wukong was a true guardian of law. All together they came forward and knelt, saying, "We had eyes without wisdom and did not know a true man had descended in mortal form. Your robe lies in the back abbot chamber, near Old Teacher's place." Tripitaka passed through three or five tiers of broken walls, groaning in grief all the while. He saw that the abbot chamber truly had no fire. The monks rushed inside and called out, "Lord, Tripitaka is a divine monk and was not burned; he has only harmed his own household goods. At once take out the robe and return it to him now."

It turned out this old monk had not found his cassock, and had burned the monastery buildings as well. At this moment of utmost distress, when he heard this, how could he dare to give any answer? Having no way of thought, no way to go forward or back, he pulled himself up, bent his back, and smashed himself against the wall. Alas, he only smashed his head so badly that blood flowed, his spirit scattered, his throat choked with breath and broke, and the sand was dyed red. A poem is given as evidence. 詩曰:

How mournful this poor old monk, so dull and deluded, one full life spent in the world. I sought to pass this cassock to distant ages, yet I did not know a Buddha treasure is never ordinary. I hoped to keep things easy and lasting, and in the end I made my ruin through neglect. What use are broad wisdom and deep planning? A scene of harming others and enriching oneself is but an empty victory. The whole host of monks cried out, “Master has broken his skull against the wall and is dead, and yet no one can find the cassock. What is to be done?” The Great Sage said, “I think you have hidden it away. Come out, all of you, and bring your name lists in hand, and I, Old-Sun, will check you one by one.” The warden of the upper and lower quarters made the temple monks, anchorites, young attendants, and Taoist menfolk produce two hand-written name rolls each. In all there were two hundred and thirty persons. The Great Sage made Master sit up high. Then he sang out their names from top to bottom and inspected one by one. Each had to loosen his clothing; he clearly checked them all and found no cassock at all. He also pulled out and examined carefully all the boxes and chests carried from each room, searching through every bit from beginning to end. Not a trace was found. Tripitaka, in vexation, blamed Sun Wukong for not having finished fully, and sat and murmured the spell. The Great Sage suddenly tumbled to the ground, clutching his head, hard-pressed and unable to hold himself back, crying, “Do not chant, do not chant. First, find and bring back the cassock.” The monks saw this and, trembling all over, moved forward, knelt, and pleaded. Only then did Tripitaka close his lips and stop reciting. The Great Sage sprang up like a broken skeleton, and a staff flashed out from his ear; he was about to strike those monks. Tripitaka shouted him down: “Monkey-Head, is your headache not frightening enough for you to be this rude? Do not use force. Do not hurt anyone. Let me question them a little more.” The monks knelt and worshipped, begging Tripitaka: “Master, spare us. We truly did not see it at all. All of this is the doing of that old, dead fool. Last night he watched your cassock till deep in the night and was weeping; he dared not even look long at it, but thinking to make it a long-lasting family treasure, he devised a plan—to burn and kill Master. At the start of the fire, a wild wind rose; everyone only hurried to save the blaze, carrying and seizing whatever they could, and no one knew where the cassock had gone.”

Great Sage grew angry and strode into the abbot’s chamber. He lifted up the corpse of that dead, slain ghost, disrobed it, and examined it closely; there was no treasure on the whole body. He even dug three feet into the floor of that abbot’s room and found no trace. After pondering for a while, he asked, “Are there any demons here who have taken on spirit form?” The warden answered, “Do not ask, Master, nothing may be known. To the southeast, not far off, rises Black Wind Mountain; in Black Wind Cave there is a Black Great King. I, this old monk, have often talked Dao with him—he is a demon. There is nothing else.” The Great Sage said, “How far is that mountain from here?” The warden said, “Just twenty li; you can see the mountain top from here.” The Great Sage laughed. “Master, do not worry. Do not speak more. He surely stole it without a doubt.” Tripitaka said, “He is twenty li away from here; how can you be certain it was him?” Sun Wukong said, “Have you not seen last night’s fire, whose light rose and stretched ten thousand li, bright through three skies? Not just twenty li—even at two hundred li it would have been visible. He must have seen that radiance, and at the right moment crept here in secret. Seeing that our cassock is a treasure, he surely used the confusion and carried it away. Let Old-Sun go and look for him.” Tripitaka asked, “Once you go, what shall I rely on?” Sun Wukong said, “In darkness there are protectors among spirits and gods. By daylight, wait till I summon those monks to wait on me.” He called the monks in and said, “Some of you go bury that old ghost. Some of you attend my Master. Some guard my white horse.” The monks promised to obey. The Great Sage added, “Do not just answer quickly by the mouth for no matter. If I am gone, do not return to flatter me. In caring for my Master, keep your faces pleasant and contented. In caring for my white horse, keep water and fodder in proper balance. If there is even a hair’s deviation, I will match you with the measure of this staff.” He yanked out the staff and struck the fire-scorched brick wall. With one crash it was turned to dust, and seven or eight layers of wall were toppled. The monks saw it and each felt bones gone soft and limbs numb. They knelt, knelt, and wept, crying, “Master, do not worry and go on. We will attend with all devotion, serve you with full devotion, and dare not for a single moment be negligent.”

Good pilgrim, he leapt at once upon the cloud of tight mass, and went straight to Black Wind Mountain to seek this cassock. As it is written:

Golden Wukong seeking the true Way departed beyond the capital bounds, Staff in hand, he rode west across green and blue heights. Tigers, leopards, wolves, and crawling things have their haunts there; men of trade and rank and guest-scholars are rarely seen. On roads through strange lands, ignorant monks are jealous; all depend on the might of the Great Sage Equal to Heaven. Fire blazed and wind rose, the temple went to ruin, and a black bear stole the brocade robe in the night.

After all, whether the cassock is found at all, and whether it brings fortune or disaster, we shall hear it out in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 16: The abbots at Guanyin Monastery scheme for precious jewels; in Black Wind Mountain a fiend steals the monk’s robe.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Great Sage Sun Wukong had just bent his waist to spring off when he startled everyone at the Guanyin Abbey: all the abbots there, from the oldest to the youngest, along with the head monks, lucky boys, and wandering priests, one after another stood up facing Heaven, bowing and saying, "Elder, it is truly a holy one who rides the clouds and fog and descends to this world; how is it that fire could not injure him? Shame on that old skin-flayer who could not know people—today he himself has harmed himself." Tripitaka said, "Please stand up, everyone; do not resent this. If the kasaya robe is recovered, all will be settled. But if we cannot find it, my disciple has an ill-tempered nature; I do not know how your lives will turn out—perhaps not one of you will be spared." Hearing this, the monks, each with heart and gall growing cold, prayed and made vows to Heaven: if they found the robe, each life would be preserved; nothing more was said.

The story turns to the Great Sage. He rose into the air, twisted his waist once, and soon came to Black Wind Mountain. He settled among the clouds and looked closely: it truly was a fine mountain, and it was springtime as well. It appeared as follows:

Ten thousand ravines rushed in rivalry, a thousand cliffs contended in beauty. Birds cry, but no men are seen; fallen blossoms still perfume the trees. After rain, the sky stretches to the emerald cliffs, wet and gleaming; when the wind comes, pines roll and green screen-barricades spread. Mountain grass sprouts, wildflowers bloom, cliffs and crags stand steep and sheer. Ivy grows, fine trees glow, high ridges and broad slopes stretch in balance. No hidden recluse appears—where then to find a woodcutter? By the ravine’s edge two cranes drink; on the rocks, wild monkeys run wild. Towering heaps of dark-green ridges rise in coiled ranks; grand blue-green heights hold and play with the light of mist.

As the Sage was still admiring the landscape, he suddenly heard voices ahead on the fragrant-grass slope. He moved with light steps in stealth, slipped beneath a rock face, and peered in from below. It was three demons seated on the ground: foremost, a black-skinned brute; to the left, a Taoist priest; to the right, a white-robed elegant scholar. They were talking grandly together, speaking of setting cauldrons, fixing furnaces, kneading sand and refining cinnabar, of White-Snow and Yellow-Sprout teachings of the heterodox outer Way. Midway through, the black brute laughed and said, "Tomorrow is my mother’s day of mourning; the two gentlemen should both honor me with a visit." The white-robed scholar said, "Every year on the Great King’s birthday you and I have honored him together; how could there be no way this year?" The black brute said, "Last night I obtained a treasure called the Brocade-Bordered Buddha Robe. It is truly a fine item. Tomorrow I will use it for my birthday banquet, host a great feast, and invite mountain officials from all over to celebrate the robe—shall we call it a Buddha-Robe Festival?" The Taoist priest laughed, "Wonderful, wonderful, wonderful. Tomorrow I’ll come first to pay my respects on the birthday, and the next day I’ll attend the feast."

When the Sage heard him speak of a Buddha robe, he took it at once to be his own. Unable to restrain himself, he leapt from the cliff, lifted his Golden-Hooped Staff in both hands, and shouted, "You rogues and devils! You stole my kasaya and now talk of a Buddha-Robe festival? Return it at once to me!" He cried, "Do not run!" and swung the staff, striking one blow to the head. Startled, the black brute turned into wind and fled; the Taoist took to the clouds and ran. The white-robed youth was struck dead by one blow. Dragging it forward, the Sage found it was only a white-flower snake demon. He took it up and snapped it into five or seven pieces, then went straight into the deep mountain to look for that black brute. Passing sharp peaks and skimming steep ridges, he came again to a sheer cliff where a cave-hall rose up. It looked like this:

Mist and rosy cloud drifted faintly, all else dim and far; pines and cypresses stood thick and dense. The mists floated, filling the gate; pines and cypresses embraced the blue-green doors. A bridge crossed on withered cypress logs, and at the peak ivy wrapped about. Birds came from the cloud-gorge with red petals in their beaks; deer padded through fragrant thickets to a stone terrace. Green willows by the bank gave way to orioles, and beside the bank peach blossoms fluttered with powdery butterflies. Though the wild land has nothing to boast of, it outshines what lies beneath Mount Penglai.

When the Sage reached the doorway, he found both stone doors shut tight. Above stood a long stone slab carved plainly with six bold characters: "Black Wind Mountain, Black Wind Cave." He immediately raised the staff and cried, "Open the gate!" A small demon who tended the door came out and asked, "Who are you, that you dare strike my Immortal Cave?" The Sage abused him: "You miserable beast bringing ruin on yourself! What place is this that you call an Immortal Cave? Who told you to call it an immortal spot? Go right in and report to your black brute. Tell him to bring out my master's kasaya at once, and I may spare your whole nest of lives." The little demon hurried inside and reported: "Great King, the Buddha-Robe feast cannot be held. At the gate is a monkey monk with a thunderlike muzzle and matted hair come to claim the kasaya." The black brute who had been chased from the hillside had locked the gate and was not yet steady when seated; hearing this, he inwardly thought, "This fellow, I do not know where he has come from. Such impudence—how dare he storm my gate?" He ordered his armor put on, quickly strapping up, then taking down a spear with black tassel and stepping out. The Sage stood outside waiting. Wukong held the iron staff and watched closely. He saw the monster was truly menacing:

A blackened bowl-shaped iron helmet blazed with red lacquer, and black-gold armor shone in splendour. A black gauze cloak swaddled him to the wind-fluttered sleeves, with long black-green silk ribbons and tassels. In his hand he bore one black-tasselled spear; on his feet a pair of black-hide boots. His eyes flashed like lightning, and this was indeed the Black Wind King of the mountain.

The Sage laughed softly: "This fellow is just like someone at a burning kiln, a true charcoal-burner by trade, no different from a coal-maker by life—how did he come to be so black all over?" The monster barked, "What kind of monk are you, to dare to be so brazen here in my place?" The Sage took up the iron staff and came up before him, crying in one great roar, "No idle talk. Give back your old grandfather’s kasaya quickly." The monster said, "From which temple are you? Where did your kasaya fall that you come here to claim it?" The Sage said, "My kasaya had been left in the back Dharma Hall of the southern Monastery of Guanyin. In that place fire broke out, and when you caused the commotion you looted and stole it, preparing this Buddha-Robe celebration in your life to welcome your own birthday. How can you deny it? Return it quickly and you may keep your life. If you even utter a single, single word of refusal, I will overturn Black Wind Mountain, level Black Wind Cave flat, and grind every demon in this cave of yours into powdered grain."

The monster, hearing this, let out a cold laugh: "You insolent monkey! So that fire last night was yours after all, was it? You were the one wreaking havoc on the abbot’s roof, and I took a kasaya—you now ask for it as if to seize it. Where do you come from? What is your name? How great are your powers, that you speak so boastfully by the mouth?" The Sage replied, "You cannot even recognize your own great-grandfather. Your so-called old grandfather is Sun, surname Sun, disciple of the Monk Tripitaka from Great Tang; Master of Perfected Path, my name is Sun Wukong, the Great Traveler. If you ask about my powers, I will speak and your soul will scatter and die before your eyes." The monster said, "I do not know your arts. Speak them, and I will hear." The Sage laughed. "Stand firm, little son, and listen. I am as follows:

Since I was young, my spiritual skills were lofty; with the wind I changed forms and displayed prowess. I cultivated my nature and practiced true cultivation through sun and moon, leaping out of the cycle of rebirth to save my life. With one thread of sincere heart I once sought the Way; on Mount Lingtai I gathered healing herbs. On that mountain there was an old immortal elder, whose years were eighty-one thousand. Old Wukong took him as my master, and he showed me one road to long life. He told me that within the body lies the elixir; seeking it only outside is wasted labor. He transmitted the supreme heavenly immortal formula; without its root, one can scarcely endure. Turning back inner light to illumine the mind, I sat at peace; inside my body sun and moon turned to Kan and Li. In all things I thought of nothing, and all craving was set aside; the six senses became clear and the body was made firm.
