To grow old and then become young again can be done, and the path to transcend and become holy is not far. In three years, faultless, I formed a true immortal body, unlike ordinary folk who must suffer and burn away. Over the Ten Continents and the Three Islands I roamed, and circled sea corners and sky horizons once. I deserved to be over three hundred and more years old, and yet could not by that alone rise and fly to the highest ninth heavens. As treasure that subdued the Dragons when I went down to the sea, I gained the Golden-Hooped Staff. At Mount Flower-Fruit I commanded as lord; in Water-curtain Cave I assembled the demon host. The Jade Emperor issued decrees and proclaimed me equal to Heaven’s heights, the very summit in rank. Several times I stormed the Lingxiao Hall; more than once I stole peaches from Queen Mother of Heaven. Ten thousand heavenly soldiers came to subdue me, ranks and files tightly set with spears and blades. I drove them back, and the Heavenly King returned to the upper world; Nezha, in pain, fled leading his forces. The True Manifested Lord could transform, yet old Wukong still risked it all and made them fall. The Dao Ancestor, Guanyin, and the Jade Emperor watched from South Heaven Gate while I slew the demon host. Yet with Old Jun’s help I was taken; Erlang seized me and carried me to the Heavenly Courts. My body was bound to the demon-subduing pillar, and I was ordered for heavenly soldiers to decapitate me. Cut by swords and struck by hammers I could not be broken; then they even called lightning and fire to burn. Old Wukong truly had such arts; not one-half of a grain did I fear. He sent me to Old Jun’s crucible to be forged, where six divine Ding fires cooked me slow and hard. When the sun was full and the furnace opened, I leapt out and ran around the skies with my staff in hand. Wherever I moved, there was no barrier; I threw down havoc through all Thirty-three Heavens. The Buddha Tathagata brought down His law-power, and the Mountain of the Five Elements pinned my waist. It held me tight for a full five hundred years, until I luckily met Tripitaka from the Tang dynasty. Now I return in righteousness to the West, ascending to Leiyin to see the Jade-hued Buddha. Go and ask the four seas of heaven and earth, and ask of all ages—I am renowned as the foremost demon among the ages."

The demon heard and laughed: "So you are that Bimawen who made trouble in Heaven, are you?" The Great Sage hated being called Bimawen more than anything. Hearing those words, he grew furious and shouted, "You thieving fiend! You stole the robe and did not return it, and only wounded old Master. Do not run—fight me with the staff." The black man moved aside, drew a long spear, and came straight on. Their duel was fierce.

The Golden-Hooped Staff, black-sheer spear; the two at the cave-mouth displayed brute strength. With one split-face lunge and one strike that hit arm and crown. This one tossed the dark club broadside, that one thrust three spears in rapid succession. A white tiger scrambled up the slope to test its claws; a yellow dragon coiled in the road and turned in haste. They spat bright mist and flung rays of light; these two demon-sages could not be measured. One was the Great Sage who had corrected Heaven, the other a Great King-turned-demon, black as pitch. This mountain quarrel began only for one matter alone—the coveted robe.

The monster and Wukong fought more than ten rounds and neither gained the upper hand; slowly the sun climbed to noon. The black man held up his spear before the iron staff and said, "Sun Wukong, let’s both hold back. Let me eat first, then I’ll gamble with you in battle again." Wukong replied, "You villain, how dare you call yourself a man? A true fighter asks for food after half a day? I, Old Monk, have held down five hundred years under the mountain root and have not once had tea or water—why should I feel hungry now? No excuses. Do not run. Return my robe first, then go eat." The black man feinted with the spear and withdrew into the cave, barred the stone gate, gathered his lesser demons, and set up a banquet, wrote invitation slips, and invited demon kings from other peaks to celebrate together—no need to describe it further.

Wukong tried to force the gate but could not open it, so he had to return to Guanyin’s temple. The temple’s monks had already buried the old monk, and all were in the abbot’s hall attending Tripitaka. Morning liturgy had ended and the noon meal was already laid out. As they were adding broth and changing water, Wukong descended from the air. The monks saluted and welcomed him into the abbot hall to see Tripitaka. Tripitaka said, "Wukong, you have come—what of the robe?" Wukong said, "There is a reason. I had no ground to wrong these monks; it was that black demon of Black Wind Mountain who stole it. Old Sun sought him in secret and found him with a white-robed handsome scholar and an old daoist, talking before a grassy slope. It was a monster that declared itself outright. Suddenly he spoke: tomorrow is his mother’s mourning day; he was inviting evil spirits to hold his birthday, and by night he had obtained a brocade Buddha robe, planning a grand feast to celebrate the robe and calling it a robe-appreciation gathering. Old Sun rushed forward, struck once, and that black man dissolved into wind and fled; the daoist vanished too, while only the white-robed scholar was killed—he was a white-flower snake spirit turned to power. I hurried to his cave-mouth and called him out to settle it with me. He admitted that he had recovered it. We fought for half a day and still no winner. He went back into the cave and wanted to eat, then shut the stone gate and stayed in, unable to face another fight. I have brought this report to you now. Since we have the robe’s whereabouts, I am not afraid he will not return it."

All the monks heard this; those with palms joined joined them, those who knelt knelt, and everyone called out, "Namo Amitabha Buddha! Today we have found the location, and now only have we found life again." Wukong said, "Do not be too happy yet. I have not recovered it yet, and our Master has not left the monastery. Only when the robe is returned and I can send Master out in safety will you all find peace. If there is even the slightest oversight, old Sun is a rough master to provoke! Have you served my Master good tea and good meal? Have you fed the horse good fodder?" The monks answered with one voice, "Yes, yes, yes. Not even a grain of neglect has touched our treatment of Master." Tripitaka said, "Since you left for this half-day, I have had three rounds of tea and two alms meals; no one dared delay me. But you must still use your strength and bring back the robe." Wukong said, "No need to panic. Since we know where it is, we will surely seize this fellow and return the robe to its rightful owner. Rest easy, rest easy."

At that moment, the head monk of the upper compound prepared another vegetarian offering and invited Wukong to take his meal. He ate a bit, mounted his auspicious cloud, and went searching again. As he walked, a small demon came along the main road, pressing a rosewood box beneath his left arm. Wukong sensed the box must contain some written summons; he lifted his staff and in one sweep struck him. The blow was mercifully irresistible and made him tumble like a meat cake. He dragged the body to the roadside, opened the box, and indeed found an invitation. It read:

In service and reverence, Xiongpi kneels and offers deepest bows, submitting to Great Elder Danfang of the Golden Pool, Hall of the Elixir. Time and again you have bestowed grace; my gratitude is deep. To recover lost blessings in the dark is hard; once rescue failed and I suffered, yet surely the immortal craft has no other harm. By chance I have obtained one Buddha robe, and I wish to host a refined banquet with floral drinks and offerings, to be admired in clear esteem. When the time comes, by a thousand requests I beg you to come with your immortal conveyance and attend briefly. Respectfully submitted. Prepared in advance two days.

When Wukong saw it, he laughed aloud: "That old flayer will not be spared a single hair's worth of loss; he has surely allied himself with a demon spirit. No wonder he has lived two hundred and seventy years—surely that demon taught him some breathing formula and granted him this long life. Old Sun still remembers his face. I will turn into that monk and go into his cave to see where the robe is kept. If I can get it, I will take it back at once and save effort."

The Great Sage intoned the spell, turned with the wind in an instant, and truly became just like that old monk. He hid the staff, adjusted his stride, and came straight to the cave entrance calling, "Open the gate!" The small demon opened it; seeing this form, he hurriedly reported inside: "Great King, Elder Jinchi has arrived." The monster was greatly startled: "I had just sent a junior earlier to send him the summons; it is not yet time there, how could he come so quickly? It must be the little one failed to meet him; surely it is Wukong come to recover the robe. Manager! Hide the Buddha robe; do not let him see it."

Wukong entered the front gate and saw in the courtyard pines and bamboos interwoven with green, peach and plum competing in bloom, clusters of flowers opened and orchids scenting the air. It was, indeed, an abode of heavenly delight. He also saw a couplet above the two doors reading: "In stillness, hide deep in mountains without worldly care; in seclusion, a fairy cave delights in the truth of heaven." Wukong thought privately, "This fellow too is a spirit washed clean of dust and worldly dust, one who accepts his fate." He passed through the gates, entered the outer hall and then another until the third gate; all was carved beam and painted eaves, bright windows and colored doors. There stood the black giant dressed in a black-green felt tunic, with a dark-blue cloud-pattern silk mantle, a black-brimmed soft horn cap, and deer-skin soft-soled boots. Seeing Wukong enter, he adjusted his cloak and turban, descended the steps and greeted him: "Old friend of Jinchi, we have lacked a visit for many days. Please sit, please sit." Wukong offered greeting and courtesy. They sat, and then tea was served. After tea, the demon bowed and said, "I earlier sent a short summons: tomorrow we meet for a gathering. Why have you come today as though to see us now?" Wukong said, "I came in to pay respects and happened upon that matter on the road. Seeing there is a Buddha-robe banquet, I came at once and ask to have audience." The monster laughed. "Old friend, you are mistaken. This robe is Tripitaka’s. He stayed where you were and wore it here—did you not see? And yet you come to inspect it?" Wukong said, "I, a poor monk, only borrowed it; at night I had not yet unwrapped it, then Great King took it. Later we were in the ruined wild hills and lost our household goods in the fire. Tripitaka’s disciple is bold and fierce, so in the turmoil he searched every side and could not find it. Surely it came under your great fortune; therefore I have come to see for myself."

At that moment a patrol demon came running to report: "Great King, disaster! The junior who carried the invitation invite was struck dead by Wukong by the roadside. He held a folded script and changed form to become Elder Jinchi to trick the robe from you." The monster thought, "I already wondered how this elder could arrive so soon and so swiftly today; it must indeed be him." He leapt up, seized his spear, and charged at Wukong. Wukong tore free his club, revealed his true form, caught the spear-tip, and leapt out from the main hall. The fight surged from the courtyard to outside the front gate. The demons in the cave were terrified, all the old and young alike lost their soul of courage. This clash on the mountain was more terrible than before.

The monkey king, bold as a fake monk, this black man hid the Buddha robe in secret in his heart. In words and replies he was subtle and clever, changing with each moment and never missing the occasion. The robe was sought to be seen but could not be seen; this subtle treasure is wondrously profound. A small patrol demon announced the calamity; the old demon blazed with anger and showed divine might. Flipping back from the Black Wind Cave, spear and staff contended to distinguish right from wrong. Staff blocks long-spear; the clash rang clear, the spear met iron staff with bursting light. Wukong’s transformations are rare among humans; a demon with such sorcery is uncommon in the world. This one wants to celebrate to bring home the robe; that one will not willingly let the robe return. This bitter battle cannot be settled and cannot be separated; even a living Buddha descending in mortal form could not unwind this circle.

The two moved from the cave mouth up onto the ridgeline, and from the ridgeline above the clouds, spitting mist and exhaling wind, flying sand and rolling stones. They fought until the red sun sank to the west, no victor in sight. The monster said, "Sun, stay your hand. Evening is near and this cannot be held out now. Go on, go on—come at dawn tomorrow, and then we will decide who lives or dies." Wukong shouted back, "Boy, do not flee. If you wish to fight, fight like one who fights. You cannot set it off with the evening as excuse." Seeing him with neither head nor face, he kept striking with the staff. The black giant transformed into a wind-form, returned to his own cave, slammed the stone gate shut, and would not come out.

Sun Wukong had no good scheme to handle the matter, so he returned to Guanyin’s temple and dismounted from the cloud, calling, "Master." Tripitaka’s eyes were fixed on him with anxious hope; when he finally saw him before him, he was overjoyed. Yet when he noticed Wukong had no cassock in hand, he was again worried. "Why has the cassock still not come back this time?" he asked. Wukong took a small note from his sleeve and handed it to Tripitaka: "Master, that monster and this dead old peeled-skinned fellow were once friends. He sent this note through a small demon, inviting him to the Robe-Offering Gathering. So Wukong killed that small demon, took the form of that old monk, entered his cave, and fooled him into sharing a full measure of tea. When I asked him to show the cassock and hand it over, he would not take it out. While we were still seated, a mountain patrolman suddenly came running a wind-borne message, and he and I fought. We fought until dusk, with neither side above the other. Seeing the sky darken, he slipped away into the cave and fastened the stone gate shut. Wukong had no choice, so he returned for the moment." Tripitaka said, "How do your skills compare with his?" Wukong replied, "I am not much stronger either; it was only a fight to a standstill."

After Tripitaka read the note, he gave it to the abbott and said, "Can your master, perhaps, also be a demon spirit?" The abbott hurriedly knelt and said, "My lord, my master is a human. That Black Great King has cultivated the human path; he comes often to the temple to expound the sutras, and he taught my master some methods for nourishing spirit and regulating the breath, so they call each other friends." Wukong said, "This group of monks has no demon air at all. They all have round, broad heads and square feet, only plumper and taller than old Wukong. They are no demons. Look at the note: it says 'Shisheng Xiongbi'; this must be a black-bear spirit." Tripitaka said, "I have heard the ancients say: 'The bear and the ape are alike.' They are both beasts. How could this one become a demon?" Wukong laughed. "Wukong is also beast-kind; after becoming the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, what is the difference? In this world, anything with nine orifices can cultivate and become immortal." Tripitaka asked again, "You just said his skill was even with yours; how did you manage to prevail and recover my cassock?" Wukong said, "Do not mind, do not mind. I have a way to deal with him."

When the discussion ended, the monks served the evening meal and invited the master and disciples to eat. Tripitaka ordered the lamps to be lit and went to the front meditation hall to rest. All the monks slept leaning against wall and pillar, making rough shelters with blankets, each one settling down; only the rear hall was left for the abbots of the upper and lower courts. At that hour the night was still, and this was seen:

The Milky Way shows its reflection, and the jade firmament is without dust. The whole sky blazes with stars; a lone water-ripple’s trace draws inward. All sounds are stilled, a thousand hills hold no birdsong. At the brook the fisher-fires die away, on the pagoda the Buddha lamps grow dim. Last night the Dharma bells and drums rang, This evening only a single cry of weeping is heard.

That night they slept in the meditation hall. Tripitaka lay thinking of the cassock and could not rest. Suddenly he turned over and saw a pale light through the window; he rose in haste: "Wukong, dawn has come. Go quickly and find the cassock." Wukong leapt up in one bound. Seeing all the monks standing nearby, offering tea and hot water, Wukong said, "You all attend carefully to my master. Wukong is leaving now." Tripitaka got out of bed and held him: "Where are you going?" Wukong answered, "I think this whole affair is due to Guanyin Bodhisattva’s neglect. She has this monastery here, has accepted the household incense from these people, and yet allowed that black demon to live nearby. I will go to the Southern Sea and seek her, tell her to come herself, and have her demand the cassock back from the demon." Tripitaka asked, "If you go, when will you return?" Wukong said, "Soonest by the time of the morning meal, latest by noon. See that those monks attend on him properly. Wukong is off now."

In an instant he reached the Southern Sea, settled on a cloud, and looked about, and saw:

The vast sea spreads wide, its waters rising to the sky. Auspicious radiance wraps heaven and earth; blessed vapors illumine hill and river. A thousand folds of snowy waves roar toward the blue zenith; ten thousand layers of misty surge roll across bright daylight. Water flies in every direction, and waves thunder all around. Water flies in every direction, rolling with thunderous peals. Do not talk of the water’s force; look instead to the center. A hazy five-hued mountain of treasures rises, crimson, yellow, purple, black, green, and blue. There appears the true blessed realm of Guanyin: behold, the Southern Sea Mount Lopakha. A fine place—the peaks rise high, their summits piercing emptiness. In the middle are ten thousand kinds of strange flowers and a hundred kinds of auspicious grasses. The wind shakes jeweled trees; the sun lights the golden lotuses. Guanyin Hall has tile roofs of glazed porcelain; Tide-Voice Cave has doorways inlaid with tortoiseshell. In the shade of green willows parrots chatter; in the purple bamboo grove peacocks call. On veined stone stand the stern Dharma Guardians; before the agate bank stands a powerful wood-carrying guardian.

Wukong gazed at that wondrous scene only briefly, then went straight to the foot of the bamboo grove. Heaven’s attendants were already waiting and said, "Bodhisattva recently declared before everyone that the Great Sage had returned to virtue, and this has been much praised. You are now protecting Tripitaka—how could you have come here with time to spare?" Wukong said, "Because of guarding Tripitaka, we met trouble on the road, so I have come to report this to Bodhisattva directly." The attendants went to the cave entrance and reported; Guanyin summoned him in. Wukong followed the ritual and went down to the Precious Lotus Terrace and bowed. Guanyin asked, "Why have you come?" Wukong said, "Master, on Tripitaka’s road he encountered Your nuns' temple. You have accepted worldly incense there and let a black-bear spirit live near it. It made him steal my master’s cassock, and though he repeatedly asked I have not let me have it. I have come now to ask that it be returned." Guanyin said, "Monkey, your words are disorderly. Since the bear spirit stole your cassock, why do you come to me to reclaim it? It is you, this ill-fated monkey, who flaunted a treasure, let petty folk behold it, then turned violent, called wind and fire, burned my Liuyun Lower Courtyard, and then came to me to make mischief." Wukong, seeing that Bodhisattva spoke as one who knew past and future, hurriedly bowed: "Bodhisattva, forgive this disciple’s fault; certainly it is as you say. Yet since that demon refused to give up the cassock, and my master must recite the spell as well, Wukong cannot bear the ache in his head and so came to beseech you. By your compassion, help me take that demon and bring back the robe to continue westward." Guanyin replied, "That demon has many powers, though not less than yours. Very well, I will go with you and see for myself, for the sake of Tripitaka’s face." Wukong thanked her and bowed again. Then he invited the Bodhisattva out, and together they rode the auspicious cloud, quickly arriving at Black-Wind Mountain, descending from the cloud and searching the way for the cave.

As they walked, there appeared ahead on the slope a Daoist carrying a glass tray, within which sat two pills of immortality, walking straight forward. Wukong collided with him full in the chest, drew out his staff, and struck him once on the head, so blood and brain burst from his skull and mouth. Guanyin was greatly startled: "Monkey, you are as unruly as ever. He did not steal your cassock, he did not know you, and he had no grudge with you. How could you kill him?" Wukong said, "Bodhisattva, you cannot identify him. He is a friend of that black-bear spirit. Yesterday he sat talking with a white-robed scholar on Fragrant-Grass Slope. The day after tomorrow is the demon's birthday, when he has invited them all to celebrate the Robe Ceremony. Today he came first to pay birthday tribute; tomorrow he will attend the robe rite. So I know this is the one who came today on the demon’s behalf." Guanyin said, "If this is all, then it is enough." Wukong then lifted up that Daoist to inspect him and found it was a grey wolf. Beneath the tray were carved four characters: "Made by Lingxuzi."

Wukong laughed: "Fortune indeed; fortune indeed. This helps old Sun and spares the Bodhisattva toil. This fiend essentially confesses on its own and gives us an opening." Guanyin said, "Wukong, how is this to be explained?" Wukong said, "I have a saying, Bodhisattva: 'When you have a plan, use the enemy’s plan against him.' I wonder if Bodhisattva will follow my device?" Guanyin said, "Speak." Wukong replied, "Bodhisattva, these two elixirs in the tray are our tokens to the demon; and the four words carved on its back, 'Made by Lingxuzi,' are the tag that links us to him. If Bodhisattva agrees to follow me, I can make this whole affair a scheme and no weapons need be raised, no campaign fought—the demon is ripe for this now, and the cassock will appear before us. If Bodhisattva does not agree, then Bodhisattva goes west, Wukong goes east; Tripitaka will only be left empty-handed." Guanyin smiled, "This monkey is a sly-tongued one." Wukong said, "No audacity; it is merely a plan." Guanyin asked, "How is your plan arranged?" Wukong said, "The words 'Made by Lingxuzi' on the tray mean the Daoist is called Lingxuzi. If Bodhisattva follows me, she should become that Daoist. I will eat one of these pills and transform, taking one size larger. Then Bodhisattva should hold this tray with both pills and go to the demon to offer birthday homage, giving the larger pill to the demon. When the demon swallows it at once, old Sun will then move in and handle it from inside. If he refuses to hand over the cassock, Wukong will tear out an inner robe from his own gut at once." Bodhisattva had no way around it and could only nod assent. Wukong smiled, "How does that sound?"

At that moment the Bodhisattva, through vast compassion, immeasurable Dharma power, and a myriad forms, with mind joining intention and intention joining body, in a moment of seeming apparition, became the Immortal Lingxu:

The saintly wind of a crane-lined robe sighs, and she drifts as though stepping into the void. Old as pine and cypress is her face; her beauty is beyond the ages. She goes and goes and yet never stays; the suchness of thusness is ever apart in itself. All in the end returns to one Dharma; only the impure body stands apart in opposition. Wukong looked and said, “Wondrous! Wondrous! Still a demon-god, or still a bodhisattva in demon form?” The Bodhisattva laughed: “Wukong, bodhisattva and demon are one thought; in their original nature they are both without any fixed being.” Wukong understood at once. He turned and changed into a tiny immortal pill: Motionless on the rotating plate, round and bright, with no edge to hold. Three-three and hooked-leakages join; six-six, the old master does not yet count it. The golden flame turns pale-yellow as it burns; the Buddha’s white daylight-glow appears. Outside are lead and mercury, not to be measured by easy reckoning.

Wukong changed into that pill, but it remained a little larger than before. The Bodhisattva, certain in his mind, took the glass tray and went straight to the demon-cave gate, and what he saw truly was:

The cliffs are deep, the caves perilous, clouds rising upon the ridges; pines and cypress dark-green, with wind hissing through the woods. Deep ravines and dangerous caves: truly a place where evil spirits lurk, where mortal folk are few. Dark pines and bright cypress also suit true immortals who live apart in withdrawn ways. There are ravines in the mountain and springs in the ravine; rippling water sings softly like a muted zither, enough to cleanse the ear. There are deer upon the cliff and cranes in the woods; in the lone recesses subtle celestial tones stir, also fit to delight the heart. Here a demon-immortal has a destined share of descending to Bodhi, and a vast, immeasurable vow of compassion hangs down in pity.

The Bodhisattva looked and inwardly rejoiced, saying, “Though this wayward beast has occupied this mountain cave, it still bears some trace of the Way.” Already in his heart he had grown compassionate.

When they reached the cave entrance, all the small demons guarding it seemed to recognize him, crying, “Lingxu Immortal has at last arrived,” and summoning him inward as he was led in. One demon had already come out to the gate and said, “Lingxu, what grace that your immortal chariot has come to honor us; this poor dwelling is lit with splendor.” The Bodhisattva said, “This humble Taoist presents one immortal pill; may Your Majesty receive long life of a thousand years.” After the two had knelt and bowed, they sat, then spoke of what had happened the previous day. The Bodhisattva did not respond in turn, but quickly lifted the pill tray and said, “Great King, first see my poor wish.” He set aside one large pill and handed it to the demon: “May the Great King live for a thousand years.” The demon also pushed a pill toward him and gave it to the Bodhisattva, saying, “May it be shared together with Lingxu’s Master.” After the exchange, when the demon tried to swallow, the medicine rolled down by itself smoothly. His true form appeared; he lurched and rolled to the ground. The Bodhisattva returned to his true form and asked the demon to bring a Buddha robe. Wukong had already left by the Bodhisattva’s nostril. The Bodhisattva, fearing the demon might be disrespectful, hurled a hoop onto his head. He rose and picked up his spear to stab. But Wukong and the Bodhisattva had already taken to the air and were chanting the true mantra. The monster still had an unbearable headache in his skull; he threw down the spear and rolled wildly on the ground. In midair the handsome Monkey King laughed, while on the ground he had rolled the black-bear demon about in ruin.

The Bodhisattva said, “Wicked beast, can you take refuge now?” The monster replied with his mouth full, “I have a heart to take refuge; I only beg that you spare my life.” Wukong, fearing delay, wanted to strike at once. The Bodhisattva quickly stopped him: “Do not injure his life; I have use for him elsewhere.” Wukong said, “A monster like this—if we do not kill him, where could he be of any use?” The Bodhisattva said, “Behind my Luojia Mountain there is no one to watch. I will take him to be a Great Guardian of the Mountain.” Wukong laughed: “Surely you are a compassion-bright savior who never harms a single spirit. If this old Sun had such a spell, I could recite it a thousand times by his mother’s name, and all these black bears would be taught a lesson.” The monster had lain insensible for so long and could not endure the righteous pain; he could only kneel in the dust and plead, “Spare my life, and I will return to the right fruit.” The Bodhisattva at once descended with auspicious light and, touching his head in turn, bestowed the precepts, then told him to take up the long spear and follow at one side. The black bear’s one wildness for this day was set, and his endless perversity was then brought to stillness.

The Bodhisattva instructed, “Wukong, go home now. Serve Master Tang well, and hereafter do not be lazy and bring trouble.” Wukong said, “Deeply moved by the Bodhisattva’s far journey here, your disciple should send you off with homage.” The Bodhisattva said, “No need.” Wukong then lifted the kasaya robe, knelt and gave his farewell. The Bodhisattva also took the bear-beast with him and turned back toward the Great Sea. This is proved by a verse:

The holy radiance hangs in hazy gold, a thousand lights in variegated brilliance, truly worthy of praise. He saves all people of the world, bending down in pity, and throughout the Dharma realm he manifests the golden lotus. Coming now, he comes mostly to carry the mission of transmitting the Sutra; leaving, there remains no flaw or blemish in his course. The subdued demon made true and returned to the Great Sea, and the empty gate regained its brocade kasaya once more.

At this point it is not yet known what happens next; listen, then, for the unfolding of the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 17: Sun Wukong storms Black Wind Mountain; Guanyin then subdues the bear-and-lion demon.

chapters.html:
This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

The Great Sage, Sun Wukong, took leave of the bodhisattva, stepped down from the cloud, hung the robe on a fragrant camphor tree, pulled out his staff, and drove it into the Black Wind Cave, where indeed a lesser demon had been inside. It was because, when the demon saw the bodhisattva appear, he had made that old fiend roll on the ground and then everyone had scattered in haste. Sun Wukong then grew suddenly ferocious: he heaped dry firewood on the several gates of the lair, and at once, in front and behind together, set them ablaze, turning Black Wind Cave into Red Wind Cave. He then took up the robe, mounted a beam of blessed light, and turned back, heading straight north.

When Tripitaka looked and saw Sun Wukong not returning in haste, he was deeply troubled. He did not know whether the bodhisattva had failed to come, or whether Sun Wukong had made excuses and run away. While he was in the midst of such frantic guessing, radiant clouds suddenly blazed in the sky, and Sun Wukong suddenly tumbled down to kneel before the steps: 'Master, the robe has come.' Tripitaka rejoiced greatly. The other monks, all of them, could not but be delighted and said, 'Good, good! Only today have our lives remained safe in full.' Tripitaka took the robe and said, 'Wukong, when you left in the morning you said you would be back by midday after the meal. How is it that now the day has reached toward evening?'' Sun Wukong gave a full account of how he had invited the bodhisattva to transform and subdue the demon. Hearing this, Tripitaka set up the incense stand, offered a southward bow, and said, 'Disciple, now that we have the Buddha robe, you may quickly gather the packs and go.' Sun Wukong said, 'No hurry, no hurry. It is late today; this is no time to be on the road. Let us wait and set out early tomorrow.' The monks together knelt and said, 'What Master Sun says is right. First, it is late. Second, among us there are vows to be fulfilled. Now that we are safe and have obtained the treasure, let me return my vows and ask the elder to scatter blessings; tomorrow at first light we can go west again.' Sun Wukong said, 'Exactly, exactly.' See, those monks emptied their satchels and all their stores, each giving whatever remained of what had been pulled from the fire, prepared some vegetarian offering, burned some papers for peace and safety, and chanted several scriptures to avert calamity and evil. That night’s business was finished.

On the next morning, they brushed and prepared the horse, packed the bundles, and set out. The monks sent them on their way from afar and only then turned back. Sun Wukong led the way; it was that season when spring was blending together, and they saw this:

Grass cushions the soft hoofprint of the jade-bay horse, and the new dew on the willows shakes like threads of gold. Peach and apricot trees fill the woods, each contesting beauty; gourd vine coils along the path and gives the place its spirit. On the warm sandbank the mandarin ducks sleep, and in the mountain ravines the flower-scent brings butterflies tame at hand. Autumn has passed, winter has worn away, and half of spring is gone; who can tell in what year this true text will be fulfilled.

The pilgrims traveled five or seven days through wild roads, and one day as evening approached they saw a village home from afar. Tripitaka said, 'Wukong, look there: that manor by the slope is near. Shall we stay one night there and resume tomorrow?' Sun Wukong said, 'Wait. Let old Sun first look into what good and evil this place may bring, then we can decide.' The elder drew in the silk reins, and when he looked with narrowed eyes, it truly was:

竹籬密密，茅屋重重。參天野樹迎門，曲水溪橋映戶。道旁楊柳綠依依，園內花開香馥馥。此時那夕照沉西，處處山林喧鳥雀；晚煙出爨，條條道徑轉牛羊。又見那食飽雞豚眠屋角，醉酣鄰叟唱歌來。

Sun Wukong said, 'Master, please go. It is certainly a good household, fit to spend a night.' The elder urged the white horse on and quickly arrived at the mouth of the street. He then saw a youth, head wrapped in cotton cloth, wearing a blue jacket, carrying an umbrella and bundle, with his drawstring trousers tucked up, and sturdy three-eared straw shoes on his feet, broad-shouldered and striding hard through the street. Sun Wukong casually grabbed him with one hand and said, 'Where are you going? Let me ask you one matter: what is this place called?' The youth kept struggling, and cried out, 'There is no one in our house, just asking me what business?' Sun Wukong grinned and said, 'Layperson, do not be angry. The saying goes, Letting people be at ease is also to let oneself be at ease. Just tell me the name of the place, and I may help untie your worry.' The youth struggled harder; in frustration he jerked and shouted, 'Clumsy, clumsy. The resentment from my household cannot be borne, and I am colliding with this bald head, taking in his sharp breath.' Sun Wukong said, 'If you have the strength, split open my hand and then leave.' The youth twisted left and right, but could not. It was as if an iron clamp held him fast. Enraged, he threw down his bundle, dropped the umbrella, and with both hands, like raindrops, came to seize Sun Wukong. Sun Wukong held the boy’s baggage with one hand and restrained him with the other; however he pleaded and tangled, he still could not grab hold. The more Sun Wukong held, the more he held fast, and he grew so angry he was hot as thunder. Tripitaka said, 'Wukong, where are all these people coming from? You keep asking the same youth and holding him? Just release him.' Sun Wukong laughed: 'Master, since asking others is no fun, we must ask him, otherwise there will be no bargain.' The youth, who had been seized and could not be let go, said at last, 'This is Gaozhuang, on the border of Wusang Country. Most houses there bear the surname Gao; therefore it is called Gaozhuang. Please let me go.' Sun Wukong said again, 'With your appearance you are not one for a near road. Tell me where you are headed and what you truly do, then I will release you.'

The man had no choice but told the matter plainly: 'I am a family retainer of Gao Taigong. My name is Gao Cai. My master has an elder daughter, now twenty years old, and she has never even been matched. Three years ago a demon took her; for these three years that demon has played the role of son-in-law. Master disliked it and said, The daughter who has taken a demon for husband brings no proper law: first, it ruins the household; second, there is no proper in-law ties for kin to come and go. So he has always wanted to drive this demon out. But where a demon would yield? The demon locked the girl in his rear house compound for more than half a year and no longer lets her out to meet the family. Master gave me several taels of silver and told me to seek a teacher who can exorcise that demon. During these times I have had no rest. I have requested three or four people in all; all were useless monks, and puffy-faced Taoist priests who could not subdue the demon. That one just scolded me and said I did not know how to do things. He gave me another five qian to make travel expenses and told me to go back and invite a good teacher again. Unexpectedly I collided with you, and you grabbed me and delayed my road; so inside and out I have been scolded and blamed. I had no way but to shout at you. I did not expect you to have ways to hold a person, so I could not break free, and therefore I tell the plain truth now. Let me go.' Sun Wukong said, 'Your karma and mine are matched in business; this is exactly the proper union of odds and ends. You need not travel far, and you need not waste your silver. We are not those useless monks and puffy-faced Taoist priests; we truly have some arts and are used to catching demons. This is just the saying: First, one may care for the physician in charge; second, one may yet cure one’s eyes. Go back and tell your householder this: we are eminent monks from the Eastern Land, sent forth under imperial authority, going west to the Buddha for sutras, and we are skilled at subduing demons and binding fiends.' Gao Cai said, 'Do not endanger me. I am a man full of grievance; you tricked me, and because you have no real art, if you cannot hold that demon, will you not burden me and bring me scorn again?' Sun Wukong said, 'I will not fail you. Lead me to your doorway.' The youth still had no remedy, truly took up the bundle, took the umbrella, and stepped back, bringing him and the disciples to the gate and saying, 'Two elders, please sit a while on the horse platform and wait; I will go in and report to the master.' Sun Wukong let go of him, dropped the load, and held the horse. The monks and Sun Wukong sat and stood by the gate in wait.

Gao Cai entered through the great gate and walked straight to the main hall, and he happened to run into Gao Taigong. The elder shouted, 'You wild-mouthed brute! Why have you not gone to seek men, and yet you return to do this?' Gao Cai put down the bundle and umbrella and said, 'I report, Master. I had only just stepped out of the street when I suddenly met two monks: one riding a horse and one bearing a shoulder pole. This one (Wukong) grabbed me and would not let go, asking where I was going. I repeatedly did not tell him, and since he held me so tightly I had no way out. So I conveyed all the matters of the householder to him. He was very pleased and said he would capture that demon with us.' 'Where are they from?' asked Gao Taigong. 'He said they are eminent monks sent from the Eastern Land under imperial authority, holy monks going west to the Buddha to seek the scriptures.' said Gao Cai. 'If they have traveled so far, they are surely not without some power,' said Gao Taigong. 'Where are they now?' Gao Cai answered, 'They are waiting outside the gate now.'

Taigong hurriedly changed his clothing and came out with Gao-cai to welcome us, calling, “Elder.” Tripitaka heard it, spun around, and was already at Taigong’s side. The old man wore a black silk kerchief, a pale white Shu brocade robe, a pair of rough calfskin moccasin-like shoes, and a dark green cord; he came out smiling and greeting us. He said, “You two are elders—offer your bows.” Tripitaka returned the courtesy. The Wanderer stayed standing in place. The old man, seeing his fierce, ugly face, did not dare bow to him. The Wanderer said, “Why do you not bow to old Sun?” The elder, somewhat fearful, told Gao-cai, “Can this little rascal not kill me too? I already have an ugly, ferocious, odd-minded son-in-law in my household that I cannot send away, and now you bring this Thunder-lord to torment me as well?” The Wanderer said, “Old Gao, you are already old in years but still so reckless. If you judge a man only by appearance, you are plainly mistaken. Old Sun is ugly by nature, yet he has genuine skill. For your house he catches monsters, seizes ghosts and goblins, and can take your son-in-law and return your daughter to you—that is a good deed. Why go on and on about appearances?” Taigong, on hearing this, trembled and, forcing himself up to strength, said, “Please come in.” Only then did the Wanderer enter, pulling the white horse, telling Gao-cai to carry the baggage, and bringing Tripitaka with him. He ignored all formalities, tied the horse to a post in the hall, hauled a lustrous lacquer chair, and asked Master Tripitaka to sit. He pulled another chair and sat beside him. Gao-lao said, “This young elder is also quite good at living in a household.” The Wanderer said, “If you are willing to keep me for six months, it is still acceptable.”

When seated, Gao-lao asked, “Did your young servant just say that the two elders are from the Eastern Land?” Tripitaka said, “That is so. This poor monk goes by command of the court to the Western Heaven to seek sutras from the Buddha; passing through Baozhuang, we merely borrowed one night’s lodging and will depart at first light.” Gao-lao said, “Since the two of you are only lodging for a night, why speak of taking monsters?” The Wanderer said, “Because we are lodging, we may as well take a few demons and spirits in passing for sport. Now tell me how many monsters there are in your estate.” Gao-lao said, “Heavens! how many could there be? It is only this one demonic son-in-law that has worn us out.” The Wanderer said, “Tell me from the beginning how this demon came to be, and how much power he has.” Gao-lao said, “In this estate, from ancient times to now, we never knew any ghosts, monsters, or wicked spirits. It is just that poor old me is unfortunate and has never had a son, only three daughters: the eldest is Xianglan, the second Yulan, the third Cuilan. The two older ones were matched in this village from childhood. Only the younger remains; I wished to marry in a son-in-law, hoping he would live in my home and old age together, prop up the door and shoulder the household tasks. Unexpectedly, three years ago came a man, seemingly handsome enough. He said he was from Fulin Mountain, surname Zhu, with no parents above and no brothers below, and that he wished to be my son-in-law. Seeing a man so rootless and unbound, I took him in. When he first entered, he was also diligent: he plowed and harrowed fields without oxen, harvested grain without sickle or staff; from dusk to dawn he still seemed fine. Only one thing: he had a way of changing his face. The Wanderer said, “In what way?” Gao-lao said, “At first he arrived as a stout black man, then changed into a long-mouthed, big-eared idiot with a strip of mane at the back of his head, a rough body that frightened people, and a face like a pig. As for appetite, it was immense: one meal required three to five dou of rice, and for breakfast one needed a hundred or more baked cakes to satisfy him. He even liked to abstain from meat and wine, but if he ate meat and drank, then my fields and house assets and the rest would be emptied in less than half a year.” Tripitaka said, “It is because he does that, so he can eat so much.” Gao-lao said, “Eating is only a small matter. Now he can also stir wind: clouds come and go, mists gather and scatter, stones run and sand flies, and he has frightened my whole family and neighbors alike so no one can rest in peace. He has also shut my youngest daughter Cuilan in the rear compound and has not shown himself for half a year in a single visit; no one knows whether she lives or dies. So I know he is a demon, and I invited a master to drive him away.”

The Wanderer said, “What is difficult? Old man, you have no cause to worry. Tonight I will settle this for you and catch him; he will write a return-alliance document and return your daughter, won’t I?” Gao-lao rejoiced greatly and said, “It is enough that I took him in; it did not matter. Yet I have ruined much of my good reputation and offended many kin. As long as he is caught, what documents are needed? Just tell him to leave at once.” The Wanderer said, “Easy, easy. By nightfall you will see it done.”

The old man, very pleased, told them to wipe the tables and chairs and lay out the alms offering. After the meal at evening, Gao-lao asked, “What weapon do you need? How many men will go with you? Prepare early.” The Wanderer said, “I have my own weapons.” Gao-lao said, “You two have only that staff. How can that tin staff strike that demon?” The Wanderer pulled an embroidered pin from behind his ear, held it between his fingers, flicked it into the air, and it became a Golden-Hooped Staff as thick as the rim of a bowl, turning to him and speaking in intent. He pointed to Gao-lao: “Look at this staff. Compared with your household arms, can it beat that demon or not?” Gao-lao said, “If you already have such a weapon, do you need people to accompany you?” The Wanderer said, “I need no man. I only need a few elders of high age and virtue to sit with my master and chat, and I can go alone. When I bring that demon before all of you, I will make him deliver and then remove him for you.” The old man then called for household retainers and invited a few close friends and relations. In a moment all arrived, greetings were exchanged and done. The Wanderer said to Tripitaka, “You sit calmly and steadily; old Sun will go now.”

Look how he swung the iron staff and hauled Gao-lao along: “Take me to the back estate where the demon dwells.” Gao-lao led him to the rear gate. The Wanderer said, “Go and get the key.” Gao-lao said, “You look first. If a key is needed, I will not invite you in.” The Wanderer laughed, “This old man may be advanced in age, but he does not know trickery. I only play at this to deceive you for a moment; take it as truth.” He stepped forward and touched the lock. It was a copper-filled iron lock. Then he smashed it open with one blow of the Golden-Hooped Staff. Inside was black and hollow. The Wanderer said, “Old Gao, call your daughter. See whether she is in there.” The old man, summoning courage, called, “Third Sister!” The daughter recognized her father’s voice and, faintly with weak breath, answered, “Father, I am here.” The Wanderer cast out his divine fiery eyes and looked carefully into the shadows. What kind of figure did she have? She looked like this:

Her cloud-like hair was piled in wild disorder, never combed. Her jade-like face had not yet been washed of dust. A trace of orchid-heart grace remained, all her beauty now drooping in fragile charm. Cherry lips all without blood of life, Her waist and figure bent inward, clinging and frail. Sorrowful, her brows curved dimly; Thin and timid, her voice was low.

She came out, saw Old Gao, and grabbed him by the arm, crying with her head in both hands. The Wanderer said, “Do not cry, do not cry. I ask you, where has the demon gone?” The girl said, “I do not know where he has gone. At daybreak he leaves and at night he comes back. He goes in layers of cloud and mist, and when he returns he does not know to what direction. Since he knows my father intends to drive him out, he is always on guard, and so he comes and goes from dawn to dawn.” The Wanderer said, “That is enough to tell. Old Gao, take her to the front house and speak with her slowly; leave Wukong here to wait for him. If he does not come, do not blame anyone; if he comes, I will certainly cut him off at the roots.” Gao-lao joyfully took his daughter and carried her forward.

The Wanderer then used his powers and changed shape, becoming just like that girl, and sat alone in the room waiting for the demon. Not long passed when a wind arose; truly stones ran and sand flew. A fierce wind:

At first it swayed faintly, lightly and softly; then it spread out and faded into an immeasurable expanse. Softly and faintly it moved; heaven and earth shuddered wide, drifting and vast without any obstruction. Flowers withered, willow branches snapped as if hemp cords were being torn. Trees were overturned, groves crushed as though vegetables were uprooted. Rivers were churned, seas upturned; ghosts and gods were troubled. Stones split, mountains crumbled; heaven and earth turned strange. Flower-eating deer lost their traces, and fruit-picking macaques were bewildered beyond the outer bounds. Seven-storied iron pagodas struck the Buddha’s head, and eight-sided banner poles tore holy jeweled canopies. Golden beams and jade columns rose from their bases, trembling; roof tiles from the houses flew like pieces of swallows. At the tips of the oars people raised vows and prayers, then hurriedly cast off boats crowded with pigs and sheep. In each ward the earth gods abandoned their temple halls; the Dragon Kings of the Four Seas rose and paid homage. By the shore, yaksha boats were battered, and half a wall of the Great Wall was torn down by the gale.

After that furious wind had passed, one could see a demon spirit come through the middle of the air; truly, he was hideously formed: black face and short fur, a long beak and great ears. He wore a straight homespun robe, blue not blue and green not green in hue, and had a flowered cloth strip tied as a headcloth. Sun Wukong quietly laughed: "So this is the sort of business." Good Sun Wukong did not greet him, did not ask after him, but lay in the bed feigning illness, humming and muttering without end. The demon, unable to distinguish true from false, stepped into the room, hugged him in both arms, and tried to kiss him. Sun Wukong smiled inwardly: "So he truly means to fool with Old Sun." He used a seizing trick, cupping the demon’s long snout and giving a little trip. He twitched his head once and with a thud sprang from the bed. The demon got up, gripping the bed edge, and said, "Sister, why are you so strange with me today? Must it be that I came too late?" Sun Wukong said, "No offense, no offense." The demon said, "If you are not offended, why did you make me this fall?" Sun Wukong replied, "How can a little house-born fellow like you hug me and try to kiss me? Because I am a bit unwell today. If I had been well, I would have risen and opened the door for you. You may as well remove your clothes and go to sleep." The demon did not understand, and in fact went to undress. Sun Wukong jumped up and sat upon the cleansing bucket. The demon came back to the bed and, feeling around, could not find him, and cried, "Sister, where have you gone? Take off your clothes and sleep now." Sun Wukong said, "You sleep first; let me go through my courtesy first." The demon in fact undressed and got into bed first.

Sun Wukong suddenly sighed: "My fate is low indeed." The demon said, "Why are you angry? How can fate be low? Since I came to your household, though I ate some tea and grain, I did not eat yours for free. I have also swept your yards and ditches, carried bricks and tiles, hauled and laid earth, built walls, plowed fields and raked the ground, sowed wheat and set in rice; I even helped found your home. Now you wear brocade, wear gold, have fruits and flowers through the year, and at all eight seasonal times there are vegetables cooked for you. Why then these long sighs and short breaths, saying your destiny is low?" Sun Wukong said, "Not that. Today my parents, over the wall that separates us, were hurling brick and tile, beating and scolding me hard." The demon said, "Why did your parents beat and scold you?" Sun Wukong said, "He says I have married you; you are a son-in-law from one of his disciples. He saw not even one proper courtesy. A man with such an ugly beaked face cannot be an uncle-by-affinity, cannot stand seeing his kin; he does not know from where you come and where you go, who your people are, your surname and your name. You ruin his pure character and defile his family honor; therefore he beat and scolded me so, and that is why I am troubled." The demon said, "Though I am somewhat ugly, to be handsome it is not hard. When I first came I had told him, and he willingly invited me. Why raise this again now? I live at Cloud-Deck Cave on Mount Fuling. I take my appearance as my surname, so my surname is Zhu; my official name is Zhu Ganglie. If he comes again and asks about you, tell him this."

Sun Wukong secretly rejoiced: "That demon is honest indeed; without torture he has yielded such a clear statement. Now that we have his place and name, no matter what, we can catch him." Sun Wukong said, "He will ask a Dharma Master to come and seize you." The demon laughed: "Sleep, sleep, ignore him. I have Heavenly-stem transformations, and the nine-toothed spike-clubs; why should I fear monks, priests, or Taoist masters? Even if your old father is devout and summons down from the Nine Heavens the Master of Subduing Demons, I have already known him; he would not dare to act against me." Sun Wukong said, "He says he will summon the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, surname Sun, who made a great tumult in Heaven five hundred years ago, to come and take you." On hearing that name, the demon became somewhat frightened and said, "If it is to be so, then I shall leave; the two of us cannot be husband and wife." Sun Wukong said, "Why are you leaving already?" The demon said, "You do not know: that Bimawen who once made a great tumult in Heaven has some skill. I only fear I may not outdo him and lose face, unbefitting such a show."

After saying this, he put on his clothes, opened the door, and walked out. Sun Wukong caught hold of him, smeared his face and showed his true form, and shouted, "Wicked demon, where do you go? Raise your head and see who I am!" The demon turned his eyes and saw Sun Wukong with fanged, hanging jaw, fire-gold eyes, bristly and battered face, just like a living Lord of Thunder. So frightened, his hands grew numb and his legs went weak; with a hiss he tore through his clothes, transformed into a raging wind, and escaped. Sun Wukong rushed forward, drew the Iron Staff, and struck once in the direction of the wind. The demon turned into ten-thousandfold flame paths and returned straight to his native mountain. Sun Wukong mounted the clouds and followed in pursuit, crying, "Where do you go! If you go up to Heaven, I will chase you to the Douniu Palace; if you go down into the earth, I will pursue you to the Court of Wrongful Death."

Alas! In the end it is still unknown where this pursuit leads or who prevails. Wait and listen for the next chapter to resolve it.
chapters.title: Chapter 18: At Guanyin’s monastery Tang Monk is delivered from danger; Elder Gao of the Gao Manor exorcises the demon.

chapters.html:
This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Then the monster moved forward in flames, while the Great Sage’s colored halo followed behind him. As they walked, they suddenly came upon a high mountain. The monster drew his red light together, revealed his true form, crashed into a cave, and took out a nine-toothed spiked mace to fight. Wukong shouted, 'Stop, demon! From where do you come? What sort of evil spirit are you? How do you know my name, old Sun? Bring out your real skills and show them fully, and I may spare your life.' The monster said, 'You don’t even know my ways; come forward, stand firm, and listen while I tell you. This is what I say:'

Since I was born, my nature was stupidly dull, and I loved idleness and sloth with no end of rest. I never cultivated my nature or practiced true cultivation; my mind, in chaos, wasted away day and night. Suddenly in idleness I met a true immortal, who made me sit down and explain the way. He told me to turn my heart back, not to sink into the world of men, where harming life for one’s own gain creates endless sin. In the end, when my allotted life-span is spent, I will regret it in the eight hardships and the three paths and have no words left to speak. Listening to his words, I turned toward practice and sought the marvelous secret. By merit there, I kneelingly took him as my master, and he showed me the heavenly gates and earthly halls. He transmitted the Great Restoring Elixir of Nine Transformations, and I did not slacken my effort by day or night. From top to bottom, from the Mud-egg Palace at the crown to the Yungquan point at the sole, I coursed the kidney water through the Flower Pool; my dantian filled with steady warm heat. Infant and maiden were matched as yin and yang; lead and mercury mixed together, dividing day and night. I used the Dragon-Gates and Tiger-Void to bring harmony; the spirit turtle drank up the blood of the golden crow. Three flowers gathered atop and returned to root, and the Five Breaths passed through Chaoyuan in perfect transparency. With practice complete and movement fulfilled, I flew upward in ascent; heavenly immortals came in pairs to receive me. Brilliantly, colored clouds rose beneath my feet, and body light and limbs strong, I went forth toward the Golden Threshold. The Jade Emperor held a banquet and convened the host of immortals, assigning each according to rank. He decreed I be titled Marshal, set to govern the Heavenly River, commanding the water soldiery and the rules of order. It happened because the Queen Mother held a banquet for the peaches, opening a feast at the Jade Pool and inviting all guests. Then I was drunk, my thoughts dazed, staggering this way and that, wild and disorderly. I swaggered in and charged into the Palace of the Moon, where graceful immortals came to receive me. Looking at my appearance they stole people’s hearts; the old mundane lust within me could not be extinguished. There was no respect for above and below or for rank, and I dragged Chang'e out, wanting to lie with her. Again and again she refused; she dodged east and west, and I was still unsatisfied in heart. My lust was as broad as heaven, roaring like thunder, and I nearly shook down the gates of heaven. The inspectors and spirit officers reported the matter to the Jade Emperor; that day my fate turned ill. Surrounded in Broad-Cold and cut off from air, I could not enter nor leave and could scarcely escape. Yet the gods seized me; though wine burned in my heart, I still did not tremble. I was taken to Lingxiao to face the Jade Emperor; by the law they asked how to execute me. By good fortune, Tai Bai Li Jinxing, leaving his station, bent low in respectful deference and spoke for me in person. The sentence was reduced yet made severe: two thousand iron blows; flesh split, skin opened, bones nearly broke. I was spared from execution and exiled out of the heavenly gate, demoted beneath heaven, to Fengling Mountain to build my family. Because of my guilt I was cast into this mistaken rebirth. In the mortal world my common name is Zhu Gangye.

When Wukong heard this, he said, 'So you are the Tianpeng Water God fallen to earth, and this is how you know my name, old Sun.' The monster scoffed, 'Hah! You deceiving Bimaun, when you caused that calamity, I know not how many of us you dragged into it. Now you come again to bully people. Don’t be insolent. Taste my mace.' Wukong was not willing to yield and, raising his staff, struck him square on the head. The two of them fought in the middle of the mountain; it was a dark-night brawl. Terrible it was:

The Great Sage’s golden eyes flashed like lightning; the demon’s ringed eyes shone like silver blossoms. This one breathed colored mist; that one breathed out red vapor. Where one exhaled red clouds the dark was lit; where the other breathed color, the dusk gleamed. Golden-Hooped Staff, Nine-toothed Mace—two heroes each worthy of praise: One is the Great Sage in the human world below; one is a marshal fallen from the sky to the edge of Earth. That one lost propriety and became a monster; this one escaped suffering and became a monk. The mace-strike was like a dragon extending its claws, while the staff met it like a phoenix threading flowers. One cried, 'You broke into another’s chamber as if killing one’s father!' The other cried, 'You abused a young maiden; that warrants punishment!' Their words were wild, shouting and clamor, and again and again staff and mace crossed and clashed. See how they fought until daybreak; the demon’s two arms were numb and aching.

The two began at the middle of the second watch and fought straight through until daybreak in the east. The demon could not withstand him and fled the field, turning again into a raging wind and running back to the cave, then shutting the door tightly and no longer showing his head. Wukong stood outside that cave and saw a stone tablet inscribed with the characters Yunzhan Dong ("Cloud-Shelf Cave"). Seeing the demon did not emerge, and with the sky now clearly bright, he thought, 'I am afraid Master is waiting. I should go back and see him first, and come back for this demon without delay.' He pressed the cloud with a footstep, and in a moment arrived at Gao’s estate.

Then Tripitaka and the elders were discussing past and present all through the night and had no sleep. Just when they were thinking that Wukong had not returned, Wukong suddenly stood in the courtyard. He tucked his iron staff away and entered the hall in proper robes. Calling out, 'Master, I have come.' At once all the elders hurried down and bowed, saying, 'Your efforts are much; much indeed.' Tripitaka asked, 'Wukong, you went out last night. Where is the demon you brought?' Wukong said, 'Master, that demon is neither a common-world evil spirit nor a mountain beast. In truth he is the Tianpeng Commander who has come to the mortal plane; because of a mistaken birth, he took a wild pig face, though his spiritual nature still remains. He said his surname is Xiang and his name is Zhu Gangye. I followed him from the rear hall, drew my staff and struck him; he turned into a blast of wind and fled. After being hit once by Wukong with the winded staff, he changed into firelight, ran back to his original mountain cave, took out a nine-toothed pinned mace, and fought Wukong all night. Just before dawn, fearing defeat, he withdrew and shut the cave door tightly, refusing to come out. Wukong wanted to force that door open and finish him, but fearing Master might worry here in doubt and anticipation, I came back first to report.'

After he spoke, that old Gao stepped forward and knelt, saying, 'Long-virtue, you drove him away as far as you could, but after you leave they will return again. What should we do then? Better to let this matter rest with you; arrest him for me. If we root him out, there will be no trouble after this. I dare not delay and am willing to repay in kind: with this family’s estates and fields, I will write deeds with many of my relatives and split them with the elders. Only root him out completely, and do not let my Gao household lose its clean name.' Wukong laughed and said, 'Elder, you do not know limits. That monster told me himself: though his stomach was vast from greed, after eating at your table he did you many good works and in these years brought in many household riches, all through his strength. He did not simply take your goods for free, so why do you insist on expelling him? By his account he came down from the skies as a heavenly god to do errands for your family and never harmed your daughter. For a son-in-law like this—proper match or no—he does not disgrace the family name nor your standing in a great way; it is not beyond forbearance to truly keep him here.' Old Gao said, 'Long-virtue, though he is not openly scandalous, his fame is not very clean: people keep saying, 'The Gao family has taken a demon as son-in-law!' How can I stand that?' Tripitaka said, 'Wukong, since you have already fought him once, settle it in one blow and bring the matter to an end, and only then will all be clear.' Wukong replied, 'I was only testing him with a bit of sparring. I will certainly bring him back for you all to see; do not worry.' He then said, 'Old Gao, see to my Master carefully and decently; I am leaving now.'

With a single cry he disappeared without form or shadow, leapt onto the mountain, came to the cave mouth, and with one thrust of his iron staff shattered both doors to pieces. He shouted, “You pig-brained fool, come out and fight old Sun!”

The monster had been breathing hard in sleep inside the cave. Hearing the crash of the gates and then being called a coarse-livered blockhead, he could barely contain his anger. Dragging out his spade, he roused himself and came running out, voice raised in rage: “You, Bimawen, are truly indolent and lazy. What business have you here? Why did you break open my front gate? Look first at the law: to break into another’s house is a major mortal crime.”

Sun Wukong laughed, “You fool! I only broke the gate, and yet there is still room to judge. If you seize someone else’s woman without witnesses, with no dowry, no tea or wine offered, that should be charged as a true grievous offense.”

The monster said, “Enough talk—show me your spade, old pig.”

Sun Wukong propped his staff and said, “This spade of yours—did you really serve as a hired hand for Old Gao, digging earth and planting crops? What have you to fear if so?”

The monster said, “You mistook me. Is this spade any ordinary thing of the mortal world? Listen carefully:

This is divine ice-iron, forged and polished till it gleams like moonlight. Laozi himself moved the smith’s hammer, the holy spark-master fed it with his own flame. The Five Directions and Five Emperors employed their stratagems; the six Ding and six Jia wore themselves out in contrivance. It formed nine ridged jade-white blades, cast as twin golden leaves that hang in rings. Its body matches the six luminaries and the Five Planets; its form follows the Four Seasons and the Eight Seasonal Nodes. Short and long, above and below, it steadies heaven and earth; left and right, yin and yang part sun and moon. Six-heavenly generals obey the ordinances of heaven; the Eight Trigrams and the stars stand arranged by the Dipper. It is called the Supreme Treasure of Glistening Gold, sent to aid the Jade Emperor in guarding the Cinnabar Bastion. Because I perfected this, I became a Daoist Immortal, raising myself to be a guest of longevity. An edict made me a marshalling captain, named Tianpeng; the Jade Emperor himself conferred this nailed spade as my command token. Lifted, it kindles fierce flames and brilliant rays; lowered, fierce wind whips down auspicious snow. Heaven’s ministers were all astonished, and Yama in the underworld trembled at heart. What is there in the human world like this weapon? In the whole world there is no such iron. At hand it may transform at my will, whirling and surging as heart’s desire commands. Through many ages we have traveled together without parting, and for years it has never left me. I eat three meals by day and never miss them; at night I sleep a whole night without missing one breath. I have carried it for the peach feast and taken it on missions to the imperial court. All this came from drunken violence, only because I relied on strength and raged wildly. Cast down from Heaven to the mortal dust, I now do whatever crimes I can in this world. In a wicked cave of heart I have eaten men; at Gao’s manor I have loved marriage and wedding joy. With this spade I overturned the sea pits of dragon-tortoises and crushed the lairs of tigers and wolves on the mountain. Of all weapons, set them aside—of all, mine is the keenest. Victory in combat is no hardship; there is no need to speak of duels for fame. How can you fear, even with copper head and iron skull and body of steel? If struck by this spade, soul and spirit will be drained away.”

When Sun Wukong heard this, he put away the iron staff and said, “Fool, stop chattering. Old Sun has set this place for your head; give him a swing and see whether your soul disappears and your vigor is emptied.”

The monster truly raised the spade and, with all his strength, struck at it. With a great crash it burst into streaks of flame, and not even a little patch of hair on Sun Wukong’s head was moved. Frightened, his hands went numb and his legs weakened; he cried out, “Good strike! good strike!”

Sun Wukong said, “You do not even know. When old Sun threw a disturbance in Heaven, I stole an immortal pill, stole the peaches of immortality, stole the imperial wine. Erlang the Great Holy Lord captured me and brought me before the Douniu Hall. The Heaven officials hewed me with axes, struck me with hammers, slashed me with swords, stabbed me with spears, burned and thunder-struck me; not one hair was harmed. Again, Lord Laozi took me and put me into the Eight Trigram Furnace, tempered me in divine fire, and made me the Fire-Eyed Golden-Eyed, copper-headed and iron-armed. If you do not believe, strike a few more times and see whether it truly hurts or not.”

The monster said, “You ape, I remember when you caused trouble in Heaven. You once lived in Flower-Fruit Mountain beneath the Water-Curtain Cave in the Ao Lai Country of the Eastern Victor Land, and none has heard your name since. How have you come here to swagger in and strike at me at my gate? Are you certain your father-in-law did not come for you?”

Sun Wukong said, “Your father-in-law did not summon me. Because old Sun turned from evil and returned to the Way, setting aside his former way to serve a monk, he now protects a pilgrim from Great Tang in the Eastern Land, Tripitaka, who travels westward to the Buddha to fetch the scriptures. Passing through Gao’s manor, he lodged there. Old Gao mentioned the matter, and so asked me to save his daughter, seize this pig-brained oaf of yours.”

When the monster heard these words, he dropped the nailed spade, made a deep bow, and said, “Where is the scripture-taking monk? Pray, introduce me.”

Sun Wukong said, “Why do you want to meet him?”

The monster said, “I was a disciple of Guanyin, persuaded toward good and given her precept; here I keep the fast and vegetarian rule. She instructed me to follow the pilgrim to the West to worship Buddha and seek the scriptures, so I might atone for my offenses and attain right fruit. She told me to wait these years, and no news came. Now that you are already his disciple, why did you not tell me of this sooner, and instead rely on violence and force to break in on me?”

Sun Wukong said, “Do not deceive me with soft words and treacherous mind, seeking a way to escape. If it is truly to protect Tripitaka, there is no falsity. Swear to Heaven, and then I will take you to my master.”

The monster fell to his knees and pounded his head as if pounding grain, reciting, “Amitabha Buddha, Namo Buddha. If what I say is not sincere, may I break Heaven’s law and be split to a thousand pieces.”

When Sun Wukong saw his oath and vow, he said, “In that case, light a fire and burn your dwelling, then I will take you.”

The monster truly gathered reeds and thorns, lit a torch, and burned the cloud-stilts cave until it looked like a ruined kiln.

Then he said to Sun Wukong, “Now I have no more entanglements. Lead me to him.”

Sun Wukong said, “Hand me that spade.”

The monster handed over the spade.

Sun Wukong pulled out a strand of hair, breathed out immortal air, and cried, “Transform!” It became a three-braided hemp rope and came forward, binding the monster’s wrists behind him.

The monster truly had his hands bound behind his back, yet however he struggled he could not free himself. Sun Wukong then grabbed his ear and hauled him along, saying, “Move quickly, move quickly.”

The monster said, “Take it gently. Your hands are heavy and my earlobes hurt.”

Sun Wukong said, “I cannot be gentle—I cannot risk it. As the saying goes, ‘A good pig needs a firm grip.’ Only after you see my master and prove true-heartedness will I let you go.”

The two of them, half cloud and half mist, made directly for Gao Manor.

There is a verse as testimony:

Gold is firm and hard, able to master wood; the Mind-Monkey once brought the wooden dragon to submission. Gold and wood, once in accord, become one; the love of wood for gold yields all expression. Master and guest have no separation there; in three-fold pairing and union lies subtle mystery. Temperament and nature both rejoice in faithful congregation, jointly affirming the Western Way without deviation.

In the blink of an eye they arrived before the manor. Sun Wukong held his spade, gripping the monster by the ear, and said, “Look there. Who sits enthroned in the hall? That is my master.”

The Gao household and kin, and Elder Gao as well, seeing Sun Wukong arrive with the monster, back bound and ear-gripped, all came joyfully into the courtyard and cried out, “Venerable elder, venerable elder! He is indeed the son-in-law of our family.”

The monster stepped forward, knelt on both knees with hands bound behind him, kowtowed to Tripitaka, and shouted aloud, “Master, your disciple has failed in proper welcome. Had I known my master lived in my father-in-law’s house, I would have come to pay respect at once—why did so many obstacles arise?”

Tripitaka said, “Wukong, how did you bring him down to take my vows?”

Sun Wukong only then released him, still striking the spade’s handle, and shouted, “Idiot, speak!”

The monster gave a full account of the matter about Guanyin’s instruction to pursue virtue.

Tripitaka was greatly pleased and said, “Elder Gao, bring a fragrance altar.”

Elder Gao quickly lifted a ceremonial altar.

Tripitaka washed his hands and burned incense, then faced south and bowed, saying, “I have greatly received the Bodhisattva’s holy grace.” The older men also added incense and bowed together.

After they had bowed, Tripitaka went to the hall and sat in the high seat and told Sun Wukong to unfasten him. Sun Wukong shook himself once, drew in his body, and the bonds came undone by themselves.

The monster again bowed to Tripitaka, expressing his wish to follow westward. He then bowed to Sun Wukong as well. Since the one who arrived first is elder, he called Sun Wukong “master-brother.”

Tripitaka said, “Since you have truly done good and wish to become a disciple, I shall give you a Dharma name so you may be called easily morning and evening.”

He said, “Master, the Bodhisattva has already given me the precept and bestowed a Dharma name: Zhǔ Wùnéng.”

Tripitaka laughed, “Good, good. Let your master-brother be called Wukong; you shall be Wuneng. In my Dharma lineage, those belong together.”

Wuneng said, “Master, I have received the Bodhisattva precepts and set aside the five pungent and three aversions. At my father-in-law’s house I keep fasting and vegetarian rules and have not touched meat at all. Having met my master today, I have broken my fast.”

Tripitaka said, “No, no. Since you do not eat the five pungents and three aversions, I will give you a separate name as well: call yourself Bājie.”

The fool answered with joy, “Humbly obeying your order.” Thus he was known as Zhu Bajie, or Pig Bǎjiè.

When Old Gao saw that they had turned from wrongness to rightness, he rejoiced even more, and so ordered his household servants to arrange a banquet in thanks to Tripitaka. Zhu Bajie stepped forward and tugged at Old Gao, saying, "Father, please ask my humble sobriquet Juejing to come out so I can pay my respects to the uncles and the elders." Sun Wukong laughed, "Respected brother, since you have entered the order and become a monk, never again speak of that word ‘Juejing.’ In this world there is only a Fire-House Daoist; where is a Fire-House monk to be found? Let us set our seats, eat a vegetarian meal, and set off westward as quickly as we can." Old Gao laid out the table, inviting Tripitaka to sit in the main place; Sun Wukong and Zhu Bajie sat on either side; the relatives sat lower down. He opened a jar of plain wine, filled a cup to the brim, offered it to Heaven and Earth, and then offered it to Tripitaka. Tripitaka said, "I will not hide the truth, good sir: poor monk, I have been vegetarian since before birth and from childhood have never eaten meat." Old Gao replied, "Knowing your purity, I dared not touch meat. This wine is also plain; one cup will do no harm." Tripitaka said, "I do not dare to take wine; wine is the foremost precept of our monastic order." Sha Wujing said anxiously, "Master, I keep vegetarian fasting, yet I have not sworn off wine." Sun Wukong said, "Though old Sun has little stomach and cannot drain a whole jar, I too have not given up drink." Tripitaka said, "In that case, both of you may take some vegetarian wine, only do not drink to the point of intoxication and err." So the two took the first cup. Everyone sat down again as before, and a vegetarian feast was laid out. The abundance of bowls and dishes and the richness of the foods cannot be fully described.

After the banquet, Old Gao brought out a red-lacquered tray and produced two hundred taels of loose bits of gold and silver, presenting them to the three elders as expenses for the road; he also offered three lengths of cotton cloth for robes to wear as upper garments. Tripitaka said, "We are traveling monks; we beg for food wherever we meet it and accept whatever alms are offered. How can we accept gold and silver wealth?" Sun Wukong stepped forward, grabbed a handful in his hand, and said, "Gao Cai, yesterday you brought my Master here, and today you have taken a disciple. I have no valuables to offer thanks; take these bits of gold and silver as travel money and buy straw sandals with them. If afterwards you meet demons, make a few of those into members of my band as well—that will be your repayment." Gao Cai accepted them and knelt, thanking him. Old Gao said again, "Since the masters will not accept gold and silver, please accept this coarse clothing to smile at and take, as a sign of my heart." Tripitaka added, "A monk who accepts even a thread of bribe will need a thousand kalpas to make amends. Only take some of the cakes and fruit left over from the feast as dry rations."

Zhu Bajie said from the side, "Master, Master-brother, do not let this pass. I have been this household’s son-in-law for several years, so as for the travel allowance, three shi would at least be fitting.
