Father-in-law, my straight robe was torn by my elder brother last night; give me a blue-brocade kesa. My shoes have split; give me one good new pair." On hearing this, Old Gao could not refuse. He at once bought a new pair of shoes and, with one length of cotton robe, exchanged it for my old clothing. Shuffling and bowing, Zhu Bajie then addressed the relatives: "Tell my mother-in-law, elder aunt, second aunt, uncle, and all your kin: I am leaving today to become a monk and cannot bid farewell face to face; please do not resent it. Father-in-law, please treat my family gently. I fear if we fail to obtain the Sūtra in time, we may have to return to ordinary life and live as your son-in-law again." Sun Wukong shouted, "Blockhead, do not speak nonsense." Zhu Bajie said, "Not nonsense. I only fear that in one short while there may be some mishap—neither will the monkhood be completed, nor the marriage be avoided; both ways are delayed together."

Tripitaka said, "No more idle talk. Let us set out at once." So he packed a shoulder-borne bundle of luggage, which Zhu Bajie carried. Tripitaka mounted the white horse; Sun Wukong bore the Golden-Hooped Staff on his shoulder and led in front. The three disciples took leave of Old Gao and all the assembled kin and friends, and set out toward the west. A poem is left as testimony:

The ground is full of glowing mist and high tree-color, and this is the hard-to-escape toil of the Tang dynasty Buddha-child. Hungry, he ate from one bowl of alms gathered from a thousand homes; in the cold, he wore a patched kesa held together by a thousand stitches. Let the wayward heart-horse not run wild in your breast, do not let the mischievous mind-monkey cry out. If feeling is harmonious and nature is still, all conditions join as one; when the moon fills Golden Blossom, it is time to shave the hair.

The three proceeded westward; a full month passed. They crossed the Wusang domain and, when they raised their heads, saw a lofty mountain. Tripitaka reined in the horse and said, "Sun Wukong, Sha Wujing, the mountain ahead is high; we must be careful, be very careful." Zhu Bajie said, "No trouble. This mountain is called Futu Mountain. Inside it lives a Wuchao Chan Master, and he is cultivating there. Old Pig has met him before as well." Tripitaka asked, "What does he do?" Zhu Bajie said, "He has some attainment too. He once urged me to cultivate with him, but I did not go." As the masters talked on, after a while they reached the mountain. It was a fine mountain indeed. Look there:

To the south are green pines and blue cypresses; to the north are green willows and red peaches. The place is noisy and lively as mountain birds converse; in graceful motion the immortal cranes fly in rows. Perfume is abundant, flowers in a thousand colors; the green growth is fresh, and strange wild grasses of myriad kinds appear. Beneath the ravines thunders a rush of green water, and before the cliffs gather clusters of auspicious clouds. Truly it was a place of rare and tranquil beauty, and no one could be seen passing by.

Tripitaka, watching from the horse, saw ahead a brush-and-thatch hut before the fragrant cypress. On the left was a deer carrying flowers in its mouth, and on the right a mountain monkey offering fruit. On the tree tops, blue phoenixes and painted phoenixes called together, while dark cranes and brocade roosters all assembled. Zhu Bajie pointed and said, "Is that not Wuchao Chan Master?" Tripitaka spurred the horse and pushed it onward, straight to the foot of the tree.

When the Chan Master saw the three approach, he immediately left his nest and jumped down from the tree. Tripitaka dismounted and bowed. The master put out his hand and raised him, saying, "Holy monk, please rise. My respect and welcome were insufficient." Zhu Bajie said, "Old Chan Master, he has offered courtesy." The master asked in surprise, "You are the rugged boar of Fuling Mountain with bristled hide; how did you come by such great merit to travel with a holy monk?" Zhu Bajie answered, "Last year, after Guanyin persuaded me, I promised to follow him as a disciple." The master rejoiced and said, "Good, good, good!" He then indicated Sun Wukong and asked, "Who is this one?" Sun Wukong laughed, "How can this venerable Chan elder recognize him and not recognize me?" The master said, "I have not known him before." Tripitaka said, "He is my senior disciple Sun Wukong." The master, smiling, said, "I owe him courtesy. I owe him courtesy."

Tripitaka bowed again: "Please tell me, where is the Great Thunder Temple of the Western Heaven?" The master replied, "Far, far away. Yet there are many roads with tigers and leopards, difficult to pass." Tripitaka made respectful entreaties and asked once more, "How far is the road, truly?" The master said, "Though the road is far, there will surely come a day when it is reached, but the demon miasma is hard to dissipate. I have one Heart Sūtra of Great Prajñāpāramitā, in total fifty-four lines, two hundred seventy characters. If you pass a place of demon mists, simply recite this scripture and there will be no harm." Tripitaka knelt to the ground in request, and the master then chanted it for transmission:

The Great Perfection of Wisdom Heart Sūtra: Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, practicing deeply Prajñāpāramitā, saw that the five aggregates are all empty and thus passed beyond all suffering and peril. Shariputra, form is no different from emptiness; emptiness is no different from form. Form is emptiness, emptiness is form. Feeling, perception, intention, and consciousness are likewise. Shariputra, this is the nature of all dharmas: they neither arise nor cease, they are not stained or purified, they do not increase or diminish. Therefore in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no intention, no consciousness. There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no color, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas. There is no realm of the eye, up to and including the realm of consciousness. There is no delusion, and no extinction of delusion. To the end, no old age and no death, and no end of old age and death. No suffering, no extinguishing of suffering, no path, no wisdom, and no gain. Because nothing is gained, the bodhisattva of awakening has no obstruction in mind. With no obstruction, there is no fear. Being distant from distorted dreams and illusions, one reaches nirvana at last. In the Three Times, Buddhas rely on Prajñāpāramitā and attain the unsurpassed and complete Buddhahood. Therefore know that Prajñāpāramitā is the great spell, the bright spell, the highest spell, and the unequalled spell. It can dispel all suffering, true and never false. Therefore it is said that the spell of Prajñāpāramitā is: "Gate gate, pāragate, pāragate, pārasaṃgate, bodhi svāhā!"

At this time, Tripitaka of Tang, though he had a natural root for cultivation, could remember the Heart Sūtra after hearing it only once. From then to this day it has been handed down. This is the complete scripture of real cultivation, the gate to Buddhahood.

After transmitting the text, the Chan Master stepped into the cloud-light to go back up to Wuchao, but Tripitaka held him again and told him he must hear clearly the exact way to the west. The master then laughed and said:

The road is not hard to travel; listen first to what I instruct. A thousand mountains and a thousand waters are deep; where miasma and demons are many. If you meet cliffs that reach the sky, keep your heart steady and do not be frightened. As you come to Mo'er's Cliff, put your footfall to the side. Be cautious in Black-Pine Forest, for fox spirits there block the road often. Spirits fill whole kingdoms, and demon lords dwell across the mountains. An old tiger sits in the zither hall, a dark wolf serves as chief clerk. Lions and elephants all call themselves kings; tigers and leopards all act as attendants. Wild boars carry shoulder poles; water monsters are met in front. A stone monkey who has lived many years—where could he hold anger? Ask those known to you; they will know the road to the west.

When Sun Wukong heard him, he gave a cold laugh and said, 'Let us go. Do not ask him; ask me.' Tripitaka still did not understand. The Chan master took the form of golden light and hurried straight up to the Crow Nest. The elder went up to bow and offer thanks, and Sun Wukong, burning with anger, raised his iron staff and pounded upward in confusion; there appeared ten thousand lotus blooms, and auspicious mist enwrapped a thousand layers. Even with power enough to churn seas and overturn rivers, he could not imagine tugging at the Crow Nest and drawing out even one vine strand. Tripitaka saw this and grabbed Sun Wukong, saying, 'Wukong, with a bodhisattva like this, how can you smash up his nest?' Sun Wukong said, 'He has insulted both my brothers in one go.' Tripitaka said, 'He was speaking of the road to the Western Regions—when has he ever insulted you?' Sun Wukong said, 'How do you understand? When he said, “a wild boar carrying a load-bar,” that was an insult to Bajie; "old monkey of many years" was an insult to Old-Sun. How can you read this?' Zhu Bajie said, 'Brother, hold your anger. This Chan master also knows what happened and what is to come, but look at what he said: "A water demon will be met ahead." Who can say whether that will be fulfilled? Let him go.' Seeing the lotus and auspicious mist near the nest, Sun Wukong had no choice but to ask his master to mount, and they rode down the mountain, going west. That departure:

May the gifts of peace be few among humankind, and thus the Mountain of Calamities fill with demons.

At bottom, no one yet knows how the road ahead will end; listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 19: In Yunchan Cave Wukong takes Pigsy in; on Buddha-Pagoda Mountain Xuanzang receives the Heart Sutra.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

The Dharma-mastery is born from the heart, and it ends when the heart is extinguished. Birth and death are decided by whom? You must tell it apart for yourself. Since all is already one’s own heart, why heed another’s words? Only with hard effort can one wrench blood from iron. A woolen rope through the nostrils, pulling the knot tight in empty space. Tie it to the Tree of Non-Action, and do not let it lurch and worsen. Do not take the thief to be a son; let the heart teachings be utterly forgotten. Do not let him deceive me; I will strike once first with a single fist. The present mind is no-mind as well; then this manifest Dharma ceases too. When one sees neither man nor ox, the azure sky shines pure and bright. As round as the autumn moon, the two are hard to distinguish.

This verse reveals that Tripitaka had fully understood the Multitude-of-Minds Sūtra, and the gate had opened. The elder kept it constantly in recitation and remembrance, and a single gleam of sacred light shone through.

It was then that the three companions on the road ate the wind and slept by the waters, under moon and stars, and by then had reached the scorching days of early summer. Behold:

Flowers have faded; the butterflies move without feeling or care. The tall trees ring with the loud noise of cicadas. Wild silkworms have formed their cocoons and the pomegranate blazes bright; New lotus appears in the marsh.

That day, while they were on the way, dusk came suddenly, and beside the mountain path there appeared a village house. Tripitaka said, “Sun Wukong, look: the setting sun hides like a fire-mirror on the western hill, while the moon rises in the east as an ice wheel. It is lucky that there is a household by the road. Let us borrow lodging for one night and set out again in the morning.” Zhu Bajie said, “You are right. I, this old pig, am a little hungry too, so let us go to a house and beg some vegetarian fare; with that, we shall have strength to carry the packs.” Wukong said, “You sentimental home-lover—you have been away from home only a few days and already begin to complain.” Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, I am not like you, drinking the wind and smoking the incense. Since I’ve followed you all these days, I’ve swallowed almost half a belly of hunger. Can you understand that?” Tripitaka said, “Zhu Bajie, if your heart is still set on home, you are not one who has become a renunciant; go home.” The idiot, alarmed, knelt down: “Master, do not listen to my senior brother’s words. He may have some grievance buried in him. I have not complained at all, but he says I did. I am a fool of straightforwardness. I only said my belly was hungry and wished to seek a household for alms; he called me a homesick ghost. Master, I have taken the Bodhisattva vows and, through your compassion, have been allowed to attend on you to go west. I have no repentance in my vow. This is what is called enduring hard discipline through resentment. How can you say I am not one who has left home?” Tripitaka said, “If this is so, rise up.”

Then that fool sprang to his feet. He muttered continuously and, lifting the pack-frame on his shoulder, obeyed with all his heart and followed on. They came quickly to the front of the house by the roadside. Tripitaka dismounted; Wukong took the reins, and Zhu Bajie set down the load, and all three stood under the green shade. Tripitaka, leaning on his nine-ringed staff, adjusted the rattan-and-lichen raincape with a press of his hand, and hurried first to the gate. He saw an old man leaning askew against a bamboo bed, softly muttering Buddha’s name. Tripitaka, not daring to speak loudly, called gently, “Homeland benefactor, my respects.” The old man sprang up with a start, hurriedly straightened his robe hem and came out with courtesy: “Elder, my welcome was poor. From where do you come? Why come to my poor house?” Tripitaka said, “I am a poor monk from the Great Tang of the Eastern Land. I bear the holy edict and come from Leiyin to worship Buddha and seek the Sūtra. I arrived late in this precious hour and wished to borrow one night at your homestead. I beg you to permit it with convenience.” The old man waved his hand and shook his head: “You cannot go; to the West is no easy way to obtain a Scripture. If you seek scripture, go east instead.” Tripitaka was silent and fell into deep thought: “The Bodhisattva pointed westward, how can this old man bid me go east? Where in the east could there be a sūtra?” He stood, shy and tongue-tied, unable to answer for a while.

Yet Wukong’s disposition was naturally fierce and unruly. He could not bear it and stepped forward to shout: “Old man, for one so advanced in years you understand nothing at all. We are renunciants who came from afar seeking lodging; do not answer such dull words so fierce against me. Your house is indeed narrow and there is no room to sleep; we can sit under a tree and spend the night, not troubling you.” The old man caught at Tripitaka: “Master, you do not speak. But your disciple—his head twisted and jaw jutting, his mouth like Lei Gong’s, red eyes—he looks a leper-like demon. Why does he dare to rush and collide with this old man?” Wukong laughed: “You, old man, truly have no eye for men. As with a handsome fellow of no real substance, handsome to look at and not fit to eat. Though I, old Sun, am small, I am quite sturdy, skin wrapped round with cords of tendon.” The old man said, “You must have some arts.” Wukong said, “I do not dare to boast, but it passes my reckoning.” The old man asked, “Where is your home? Why did you shave your head and become a monk?” Wukong said, “Great-Sun’s ancestral home is the Water-curtain Cave on Flower-Fruit Mountain, in the Kingdom of Aolai to the east of the sea, in Dongsheng-continent. From childhood I learned to be a spirit-beast and was named Wukong. By skill I became the Great Sage Equal to Heaven. Because I would not obey Heaven’s decrees, I rose in rebellion against Heaven’s court and caused a calamity. Now the disaster is passed through, and I have turned to the robe of a monk, going west to seek true merit. To protect our Tang emperor’s disciple here on the road to worship Buddha in the West, why should mountain peaks and risky roads, wide waters and wild waves frighten me? I can catch monsters and subdue demons, pin tigers and seize dragons, kick Heaven and stir wells; I know a little of that sort. If in your house there is anything like hurling bricks, breaking tiles, pots and pans at the door, old Sun can still bring it to order.”

Hearing these words, the old man burst into laughter: “So you are a seasoned beggar-monk with a ready-tongued mouth.” Wukong said, “Your son is indeed a ready-tongued one. These days, because I have gone this far with my master, I have been too lazy to speak.” The old man said, “If you were not tired and not lazy to speak, you’d chatter and deafen me. Since you do have such powers, you may still go west. You may. How many of you are traveling with you? Come inside this thatched hut for the night.” Tripitaka said, “I am greatly indebted to the old benefactor for not driving us off. We are three companions.” The old man said, “Where is that group?” Wukong pointed: “This old man’s sight is weak; is that not the one standing under the shade?” The old man truly squinted, lifted his head to look closely, and when he saw Zhu Bajie’s face at close range he grew frightened, stumbling backward step by step before running inside in panic, crying out, “Close the gate! Close it! A demon has come!” Wukong caught up and restrained him: “Old man, do not be afraid. He is not a demon; he is my junior brother in Dharma.” Trembling, the old man said, “Very well, very well—each monk as ugly as the next.” Zhu Bajie came forward: “Old gentleman, if you judge by looks you miss the mark. We are ugly through and through, yes, but we are useful.”

The old man was still at the gate talking with the three monks when, to the south of the estate, two young men came with an old mother and three or four little boys and girls, clothing bundled up, bare-footed, returning from transplanting seedlings. Seeing a white horse and a carrying pole with luggage at his gate in uproar, they did not know what had happened and all pressed forward to ask: “What are you doing?” Zhu Bajie turned his head, slapped his ears a few times, and stretched his long muzzle. The people were so frightened they swayed and staggered, toppling and falling in all directions. Alarmed, Tripitaka called out repeatedly, “Do not fear, do not fear. We are not villains—we are monks on a journey for the scriptures.” Only then did the old man come out, supporting the old mother: “Old auntie, rise; do not be frightened. This master comes from the Tang dynasty. His disciple’s face is ugly, but he is fierce of look and gentle at heart. Bring the men and women and children in.” Then the mother was led along with the two youths and the children into the house.

Tripitaka nevertheless sat on the bamboo bed in the gatehouse and complained: “Disciple, both of you are ugly in face and rough in speech, and you frightened this household terribly. They are seven losses and eight harms, and you have made sins on my behalf.” Zhu Bajie said, “Not hiding anything from my master, old Pig has improved a good deal since following you. In former days at Gao’s Old Estate, if I sent my face forward one scoop and shook my ears from side to side, I would often frighten twenty to thirty people dead on the spot.” Wukong laughed: “You don’t blurt nonsense, and make your ugliness neat.” Tripitaka said, “You hear what Wukong says? A person’s appearance is innate; how do you ask him to tidy it?” Wukong said, “Put that spade-mouth in your bosom and do not bring it out. Put those fan-eared ears against your back and do not shake them. That is how he is made neat.” And Zhu Bajie truly put his mouth away and tucked his ears back, bowing his head, standing to either side. Wukong brought the luggage inside the gate and tied the white horse to a post.

Only then the old man brought a youth and a wooden tray, holding three cups of clear tea to offer. After tea, he had them begin the meal. The youth then brought an old table with holes and without varnish, placed two broken stools with split legs in the courtyard, and asked the three to sit in the cool place. Tripitaka asked, "Venerable, what is your surname?" The old man answered, "My surname is Wang." "How many children do you have?" he asked. "Two sons and three grandsons." Tripitaka said, "Congratulations, congratulations." Again he asked, "How many years has nature granted you?" "I am sixty-one," came the reply. Sun Wukong said, "Good, good, good. He has met the age of sixty again." Tripitaka asked once more, "Venerable, why did you say at first that the scriptures from the Western Heaven were difficult to obtain?" The old man answered, "The scriptures are not difficult to obtain; it is only that the road is perilous and hard to travel. From here westward is only about thirty li, a mountain called the Eight-Hundred-Li Yellow Wind Ridge, and there are many demons in that mountain. That is why I called it difficult. As for this young monastic of yours, they say he has many arts, yet he still can get through." Sun Wukong said, "No problem, no problem. With old Sun and me, your junior monk companion, no demon, whatever its kind, will dare to provoke me."

As they were speaking, the son came carrying the meal and set it upon the table, saying, "Please take your alms." Tripitaka, palms joined, began chanting the food-ritual verses. Zhu Bajie had already swallowed one bowl. Before Tripitaka had finished a few lines, that boor had eaten three bowls. Sun Wukong said, "That simpleton of a glutton must have run into a hungry ghost." Old Wang, sensing the matter well, saw him eat so fast and said, "This senior monk must be truly famished; quickly add more rice." Zhu Bajie truly had a huge appetite. He did not even raise his head and in one stretch ate nearly ten bowls. Tripitaka and Sun Wukong each ate less than two bowls. Zhu Bajie did not stop, and kept eating. Old Wang said, "In such haste there are no side dishes, I dare not press you on a heavy request. Please bring one more ladle." Tripitaka and Sun Wukong both said, "Enough." Zhu Bajie said, "Old man, why all this dithering? Who are you arguing with and talking about five yáo and six yáo? If there is rice, just keep bringing it." In one sitting he ate all the food prepared by the whole household, and he still claimed he was only half full. Only then did they put out the hearth, and under the gate pavilion they arranged a bamboo bed and boards for sleeping.

At daybreak the next morning, Sun Wukong shouldered up the horse and Zhu Bajie adjusted the shoulder-pole. Old Wang again told his mother to pack some pastries and soup and water for the road, and only then did the three offer thanks before leaving. The old man said, "If some unforeseen matter occurs on the road, you must return here to our thatched hut." Sun Wukong said, "Old man, no idle talk. We are ordained folk; we do not take to going back by another route." So he mounted the horse, lifted the load, and rode westward.

Alas! From this departure, indeed there was no good road toward the Western Lands, and surely evil spirits and demons would soon bring great calamity. The three had gone less than half a day when they met a high mountain, and it seemed exceedingly perilous. Tripitaka brought his horse to the cliff edge and peered obliquely; truly there was this:

Tall was the mountain; steep was the ridge. What rose was cliff, and the ravine was immeasurably deep. The spring resounded, and the flowers shone with color. That mountain: high though it was, its peak met the blue sky. This ravine: though deep, in its bottom one could glimpse the underworld. Before the mountain stood white-cloud masses like bones, and towering odd rocks held them fast; beyond count were cliffs that carried away souls by the thousand-zhang, ten-thousand-zhang drops. Behind the bluff lay a winding, coiling Cave of the Hiding Dragon, and within it rocks dripped with a ding-ding-dang sound. Elsewhere one saw antlered deer with odd, awkward gait, foolish-looking muntjac staring at people, red-scaled snakes winding in loops, and white-faced monkeys making rough sport. At dusk were mountain-tiger lairs and water-drakes that rose in morning surf like waves breaking from streams; when approaching their cave mouths came a loud lu-la-rattle. In the grass, birds burst up with drumming wings; in the woods, beasts scurried with snuffling strides. Suddenly a rush of wolf-snails passed, and people’s hearts thumped and trembled in fright. It was truly that: the cave-mouth ringing, the cave-mouth slanting; the cliff crashing, the mountain collapsing in echoes. The blue-green embankment was dyed like ten-thousand-zhang jade, green gauze covering heaps upon heaps of mist.

The master drew his silver dun to a slower pace, Sun Wukong, the Great Sage, let his clouds stand and walked, and Zhu Bajie, Wuneng, moved the load slowly. While they were still looking at that mountain, a sudden roaring whirl of wind broke out. Tripitaka, on the horse, was startled in heart and said, "Wukong, the wind has risen." Sun Wukong said, "What fear is there of this? This is only the four-season qi of Heaven and Earth." Tripitaka said, "This wind is very sinister; it is unlike the sky wind." Sun Wukong said, "How can you know it is unlike the sky wind?" Tripitaka said, "Look at this wind:

Vast and towering, surging and whirling, it rises in a wild sweep, Its emptiness stretches beyond measure, lifting into blue ether. Crossing the ridges one hears a thousand trees roar; entering the woods one sees ten thousand culms shake. On the banks, willows by the bank shake from root to top, and in the courtyards blossoms are blown, leaves driven in flight. Fishing boats with nets are tightly moored, and guest skiffs with their sails down have all cast anchors. Halfway along the road, messenger-men lose the path; in mountain groves, woodcutters cannot bear to carry their loads. In the groves of heavenly fruit, monkeys scatter; in thickets of strange blossoms, deer run in panic. Before the cliffs, fir and cypress tumble headlong; beneath the ravines, bamboo and rush leaves wither one by one. Dust from the disturbed earth spurts in grains, and river and sea are churned alike in huge, roaring waves. "

Zhu Bajie stepped forward and grabbed Sun Wukong. "Senior brother, the wind is truly fierce. Let us slip aside somewhere first." Sun Wukong laughed. "Brother, that will not do. If one hides whenever the wind is strong, and then happens to meet a demon face to face, what then?" Zhu Bajie said, "Brother, have you not heard, 'Avoid lust as you avoid enmity; avoid wind as you avoid arrows'? If we dodge a while, it is no loss to anyone." Sun Wukong said, "Do not speak yet; wait until I catch a fistful of this wind and smell it." Zhu Bajie laughed. "Brother, again you are making up empty claims and pulling my leg. Wind can be caught and smelled like that? Even if you could catch it, it would fly off through the holes anyway." Sun Wukong said, "Brother, you do not know that old Sun has a method to seize wind." The Great Sage let the gust pass over him, seized the tail of the wind and sniffed it. There was a fishy taint in it. He said, "Indeed it is not a good wind. The flavor of this wind is not that of a tiger wind. It must be a demon wind, and surely there is something strange in it."

Before he could finish, below the mountainside appeared a tiger with a mottled coat and tail tucked tight, hooves flying as it leaped out. Tripitaka was so startled that he lost balance in the saddle, fell from the white horse, and leaned by the roadside, truly like a soul about to fly away. Zhu Bajie dropped the baggage, drew his cleaver-and-spike cudgel, and would not allow Sun Wukong to advance first. He shouted, "Spawn of a demon, where do you think you’re going?" and rushed forward, striking at its head. The tiger rose straight up, lifted its left forepaw, clawed at its own chest, and with one slick scratch pulled off its skin so it stood upright by the roadside. You should see how terrifying it looked. Its form:

Its blood-warm, red-sheared body was naked beneath; its crimson-lustrous, bent limbs and limbs were knotted and fierce. Its two temple-blazes flared up in loose tufts, its hard, straight brows stood like two knives. Four white-steely fangs shone, and its two golden eyes flashed like fire. With proud, rising energy it roared, voice hard and mighty. Its deep-throated, vehement cry split the air. It shouted, "Wait, wait. I am not some other. I am the advanced vanguard on patrol for the Great King of the Yellow Wind. Under my king’s strict command, I patrol this mountain to seize a few ordinary men and make them for sacrificial wine. You who are monks, from where do you come that you dare use weapons against me?" Zhu Bajie shouted back, "You wretch! You do not recognize me. We are not mere passersby of the world. We are disciples of Tripitaka, the elder brother of Great Tang in the East, on imperial command to go west and pay Buddha for the sutras. Clear off to another side at once and give way so as not to frighten my master, and I will spare your life. If you rage on like this, one strike of my spade and you will be left without mercy!" The demon gave him no chance to continue. It rushed close, cast one blocker to catch him at the face. Zhu Bajie dodged, then swung his cleaver at it. The monster, with no weapon of its own, turned and ran; Zhu Bajie followed. At the base of the slope amid tangled rocks, it drew out two red-bronze sabers, raised them quickly, spun and faced him. The two fought back and forth at the front of the slope, charging and colliding as if in a gambling match.

Sun Wukong helped Tripitaka to his feet and said, "Master, do not be afraid. Sit still for now. Let old Sun assist Zhu Bajie and beat down that monster so we may go on." Tripitaka only then sat up, trembling, and in his mouth recited the "Heart Sutra of Great Mind"; no further details are needed.

Sun Wukong snatched up his iron rod and shouted, "Take him!" At this, Zhu Bajie recovered his spirit, and the monster fell back from the contest. Sun Wukong said, "Do not spare him; make sure you catch up." The two raised their spiked hammers and their iron staff and chased downhill together. The demon panicked and, using the Golden Cicada-shedding trick, rolled around, showing its true form and remaining a fierce tiger still. Sun Wukong and Zhu Bajie were not ones to let him go and chased the tiger, determined to cut its root and end it. When the beast saw them come very near, it once again clawed its own chest, tore off its skin, and draped it over a tiger-couching rock, then shed its true body and turned into a violent gust of wind, rushing back toward the path. Suddenly it saw Tripitaka still reciting the "Heart Sutra of Great Mind," grabbed him in that long wind, and snatched him away. Alas for Tripitaka: his destiny in the river of life is fated for many grindings and tribulations; in the gate of Nirvana, progress is hard.

That demon hauled Tripitaka to the cave entrance, held back the wild wind, and told the gatekeeper: "Go report to the king. The tiger vanguard has caught a monk and is waiting outside for your command." The cave chief transmitted the order and told them to bring him in. The tiger vanguard, with two red-copper daggers tucked into his waist, held Tripitaka in both hands and knelt before the king. "Great King, your humble little officer, by Lord Jun’s order, was patrolling the mountain when I happened upon a monk. He is Master Tripitaka of the Great Tang, going west to revere Buddha and seek the scriptures. I have captured him and brought him to you as a token to offer at your table," he said.

When the cave chief heard this, he was startled. "I have heard before from others that Master Tripitaka is the holy monk commissioned by the Great Tang court to fetch the scriptures; he has a disciple named Sun Wukong, with boundless powers and a mind of extraordinary wisdom. How could you have taken him?" the vanguard replied, "He has two disciples. The first wields a nine-pointed spiked mace, long-mouthed and big-eared; the other carries a Golden-Hooped Staff, and he has fire-eyes with golden pupils. While I was pursuing them, they were grappling with me. The younger one used the Golden Cicada-Reliquary trick, slipped away, and took this monk and brought him to offer you, a small gesture to mark our respect." The cave chief said, "Do not eat him yet." The vanguard said, "Whether to eat or not to eat, why call it a matter of small merit?" The cave chief said, "You do not understand. It would not matter if we eat him, but I only fear his two disciples may come and make trouble. Better tie him to the wind-binding stakes in the rear yard. After three or five days, if those two do not come to disturb us, then first we keep his body unblemished, and second we need not endure his cries. We can then, in no hurry, cook him by boiling, steaming, braising, or frying and enjoy him at our leisure." The vanguard was very pleased. "Your Majesty is far-sighted and far-reaching; your reasoning is sound," he said, and ordered, "You men, take him away."

Around him, seven or eight of the binding men came and took Tripitaka away, handling him like a hawk taking a sparrow, winding him in ropes. The monk was the wretched Tripitaka, in this misfortune thinking of his disciple Wuneng. He cried out, "My disciples! I do not know where you chased the demon on the mountain or where you subdued the spirits, and I have been taken by this evil head and suffered this poison. When will we meet again? How bitter this is! If only you had come sooner, my life might still have been saved; if you come too late, there will be no hope at all." While sighing and lamenting, he wept tears as if rain.

At that moment the Great Sage and Pigsy hurried the tiger down the mountain slope. They saw the tiger run and topple, falling in a collapse before the cliff. The Great Sage struck him hard with his staff, and the impact shook his own hand with pain. Pigsy then thrust a spiked cudgel, causing the iron teeth to fly up. It was merely tiger skin stretched over a lying tiger stone. The Great Sage cried out in alarm: "Something has gone wrong—something has gone badly! We have fallen for his trick too!" Pigsy said, "How has he tricked us?" The Great Sage said, "That is the Golden Cicada-Shedding trick: he covered the stone with tiger skin and escaped. We should return and check on our Master, or we may lose him by evil hands." They turned back quickly, only to find Tripitaka no longer there. The Great Sage shouted like thunder, "What now? Our Master has been taken!" Pigsy held the horse and said through tears, "Alas, alas! Where shall we search?" The Great Sage raised his head: "Do not weep, do not weep. One tear and your fighting edge is dulled. This mountain is all we have; let us search it through and through."

The two of them ran straight into the mountain, crossed ridges and scaled passes, and went on a long way until they saw below the cliffs a cave-lair rising from the rock. They studied it carefully and found it truly perilous, yet beautiful. The scene was:

Layered battlements of peaks in tiers; winding ancient ridges like old paths. Green pines and emerald bamboos leaned close together; willow and parasol trees drifted in soft green light. Strange boulders stood in pairs before the cliff; secret birds called in paired whispers within the woods. A distant ravine streamed and struck the cliff wall; tiny spring droplets spread over the sandy embankment. Wild clouds drifted in patches; heavenly grasses spread in delicate threads. Cunning foxes and sly rabbits darted in tangled flurries. Antlered deer and fragrant muntjacs stood in proud rivalry. Old vines hung slanting from split cliffs; thousand-year cypresses hung half over deep ravines. Lofty and grand, they seemed to outshine Huashan; falling blossoms and crying birds rivaled the terraces of heaven.

The Great Sage said, "Elder brother, you can leave the baggage in the hollow of Cangfeng Mountain, loosen the horses, and keep out of sight. I will go to that gate myself and take it as a wager fight with him. I must catch the demon first before we can rescue the Master." Pigsy said, "No need to instruct me. Please go at once."

The Great Sage adjusted his tight robe and tied his tiger-skin waist-wrap, drew his staff, and rushed to the gate. On the door were six large characters reading, "Huang-Feng Ridge, Huang-Feng Cave." He set himself in a T-stance, lifted his staff, and shouted in a loud voice, "Demon, send out my Master at once, else I shall overturn your nest and level your dwelling." The little demons, frightened, trembled and ran inside to report in unison, "Great King, disaster has struck." The Yellow-Wind demon, who was presiding there, asked, "What has happened?" One of them replied, "Outside the cave gate there is a monk with a face like a thunder-god’s bristled mouth, holding an iron staff as thick as a great tree trunk, demanding to be recognized as your monk." The cave lord, in alarm, immediately called for the tiger vanguard: "I told you to patrol and only bring back mountain cattle, wild boars, fat deer, and wild goats. Why did you bring a monk of Tang here and then invite his disciples to come and make this noise? How are we to handle this?" The vanguard replied, "Great King, do not worry. Rest easy and do not be anxious. Though I am but a small and unworthy officer, I can lead fifty young captains out there and bring that one called Sun Wukong in for you to taste." The cave lord said, "Besides the senior and junior captains, I have five to seven hundred junior officers. Choose as many as you like. As long as you seize that Wukong, we can then safely dine on the monk and I will even make you my brother. But if you fail to take him and instead injure yourself, do not come crying that I blamed you." The tiger demon said, "No fear, no fear. I will go."

Sure enough, he gathered fifty robust young demons, set the war drums and banners rocking, and came out through the gate with two red-copper blades in hand, shouting, "Who is this monkey monk from where, to make such loud noises here?" The Great Sage snapped back, "You stripskin beast! What sort of shell-shedding trick is this, in which you seized my Master and then ask who I am? Send my Master out at once, and your life may be spared." The tiger demon said, "Your Master is mine, to be a whole-course banquet for our king. Turn back, and if not, we will seize you and feed you too—why not buy one and spare two?" The Great Sage grew furious within, grinding his teeth together with a clacking cry. Fire-red eyes widened and burned. He drew forth his iron staff and roared, "What great arts have you? Dare you speak such words? Do not run. Face this cudgel." The vanguard swiftly raised his blade to meet it. This clash was no gentle matter. Both unleashed their strengths, and they fought to kill:

That monster was a true goose egg; Wukong was a goose-egg stone. The red-copper blade met the Beautiful Monkey King, like stacked eggs striking stone. How can a magpie contend with a phoenix? How would a turtle-dove dare challenge hawk or kite? The demon blew out wind-dust, filling the whole mountain; Wukong exhaled a fog of cloud to dim the sun. Back and forth they clashed three or five times without pause, and the vanguard’s waist grew weak and lost its strength. He turned, defeated, seeking to flee, but Wukong drove him hard to the point of death.

The tiger demon could no longer stand it and turned to run. Because he had spoken boldly before the cave lord, he did not dare to return indoors but fled up the mountain slope. The Great Sage was not one to release him; gripping the staff, he pursued with all his force, roaring and bellowing without cease until he reached the hollow of Cangfeng Mountain. There he looked up and saw Pigsy there with the horse. At the sound of the roar, Pigsy turned around and saw the tiger demon being driven hard; he dropped the horse, raised his spiked cudgel, and drove it diagonally into the back of the tiger. The poor vanguard tried to slip out by a yellow-silk net and tried to jump away, but he was met again by a fish-caging spirit. Pigsy’s one cudgel blow made nine fresh wounds, and blood poured out; his brain was drained dry. There is a poem to prove it:

For three or five years I returned to the true way, kept precepts in pure fasts, and awakened to true emptiness. With a sincere heart I sought to guard Master Tripitaka; this was the first merit of one who first shouldered the monk’s vows.

The pig stepped and pressed his foot on the demon’s back, then lifted both hands and struck again with his spiked cudgel. The Great Sage, seeing this, said with joy, "Brother, this is exactly it. He gathered a few dozen lesser demons to gamble with old Wukong and I beat him. He could not run back to the cave, so he came here to die. If you had not joined, he would have fled again." Pigsy asked, "Was it he who snatched the Master away with the wind spell?" The Great Sage said, "Yes, it was. This demon has the Master in the cave to serve as a dish for that monstrous king. Old Sun was angry and took this fight out here, and you saved my life by ending him. Brother, this merit is yours. Go back and keep watch of the horse and the luggage. Let me drag this dead tiger away, then I will return to that cave entrance to continue the battle. Only if we take that old demon can we truly rescue Master." Pigsy said, "You are right. You go, you go. If you defeat this old demon, come back here, and I will block him with my body and finish him."

Then the Great Sage, one hand gripping the iron staff and the other dragging the dead tiger by the body, went straight to the cave mouth. It is said:

A master in peril faces a demon; calm nature in harmony brings the chaos-demon to its knees.

After this we still do not yet know whether he will bring the demon under control and save Tripitaka. We shall hear the full resolution in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 20: Tang Monk meets peril at Yellow-Wind Ridge; at Half-Mountain Pigsy jostles ahead to the fore.

chapters.html:
This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Now it is told that the fifty wretched, broken little demons, carrying broken banners and broken drums, barreled into the cave and announced: “Great King, Tiger Vanguard could not stand up against that hairy-faced monk; he chased him back down the Eastern Slope.” Hearing it, the old demon grew exceedingly troubled. He sat with his head bowed, silent and thinking of a plan; then a little demon from the front gate called out, “Great King, Tiger Vanguard was struck down by that hairy-faced monk and dragged to the gate while cursing him.” When the old demon heard this, he grew even more distressed: “This wretch too is ignorant. I did not even eat his teacher. He turned and slew my house’s vanguard—detestable! detestable!” he said. “Bring out my armor. I have only heard stories about this Sun Wukong. Let me go out and see what kind of nine-head, eight-tail monk this is; bring him in, and let him meet my Tiger Vanguard in a life-death match.” The young demons quickly brought out the armor. The old demon finished his gear, lifted a three-pronged steel fork, and, leading his band of demons, leapt out of the cave.

The Great Sage stood outside the gate and saw the demon coming out. He looked truly fierce and valiant. See how he was arrayed:

A golden helm flashed in the sun, and a gold cuirass held the light. On the helm, a fluttering ribbon and a mountain-pheasant tail-trail swayed; a gauze robe covered the armor in a pale goose-yellow. The laced cuirass, coiled like a dragon, glittered with color; a heart-guarding mirror circled his eyes in radiant brilliance. His boots were of deer hide, dyed with flower-bark dye; his brocade skirt and willow-leaf velvet were finely set. In his hand he held a three-pronged steel trident, sharp as a fang. He was no less than the eminent holy heroes of old.

When the old demon came out, he roared, “Who is Sun Wukong?” The Wukong there, wearing a tiger-skin foot-gear and gripping his iron staff as a wish-granting wand, answered: “Your Grandsire Sun Wukong is here. Send out my Master.” The demon examined him closely, saw the Sage’s body was plain, his face gaunt and lean, less than four chi tall. He laughed: “Alas, alas. I had supposed you were some untoppled heroic brute, and yet you are such a skeleton-like sickly ghost.” The Sage laughed: “You whelp, you have no eye for men. Though my Grandsire is but small, if you dare to strike the trident-head at my crown, I’ll grow three chi higher.” The demon said: “You go on with a hard head—take one strike of mine.” The Great Sage showed no fear. The demon indeed struck once. He bent his waist and in an instant his stature lengthened three chi, off by about a full zhang. Startled, the demon lowered his fork and cried, “Sun Wukong, why do you use that body-guarding transformation in front of my gate? Don’t fuss with trickery—come up here, and I’ll see your methods face to face.” The Sage replied: “Whelp, there is an old saying: ‘If one keeps pity, do not raise one’s hand; once one raises it, do not spare.’ My grandfather’s staff hand is heavy and hard—I doubt you can stand this one blow.” The demon gave no room to speak, spun his trident and aimed straight at the Sage’s chest; but the Great Sage was quick both in knowing and speed, not clumsy though the master’s work is difficult, and easy in the work of family. He cleared with the iron staff, used the “Wulong Soaring Through Earth” stance, warded off the trident, and then struck at the crown. At the mouth of the Hwangfeng Cave, this was a fine slaughter:

The demon king flared with rage; the Great Sage displayed majesty. The demon king raged to seize the Sage against the vanguard; the Great Sage wrought power to seize the spirit and save the Elder. A fork met staff and staff answered fork. One was the all-commanding marshal of the mountain-gates, one the protector monkey king. At first all was dust-thick battle, then each moved to the center. He pointed the steel fork, sharp and keen; the 如意棒, black-crowned and golden-yellow. One thrust and a spirit went to the Court of the Dead; one strike and he would have met Yama. All depended on hand-speed and keen eyes, for strength of arm and body was required. The two sides fought as if forgetting life itself, and none could tell who was safe and who was wounded.

The old demon and the Great Sage fought for thirty exchanges and neither gained victory. The Sage then sought achievement and used the art of “body outside the body”: he plucked a clump of his hairs, chewed them to powder in his mouth, spat it upward, and cried, “Transform!” and transformed into a hundred and ten Sun Wukongs, all dressed alike, each holding an iron staff, surrounding the monster in midair. The demon grew afraid, and used an equal art: he sprang back, faced the ground, set his mouth wide open three times, and let out one breath. Instantly, a blast of yellow wind rose from nowhere in the sky. The gale was truly dreadful:

Cold, cold and wheeling, the whole world went strange; form and shadow fled in whirling yellow sand. It cut through groves and bent ridges, knocking pine and plum aside; it heaped dirt and hurled dust that split crags and embankments. Yellow River swells were dashed to the core, mingling into wild torrents like a whole shore in upheaval. The emerald heavens shook; the constellations of Dipper and Ox reeled; palaces of cosmic regiments swayed as if to fall. Five hundred Arhats clamored in the sky; Eight Great Vajras roared in disorder. Manjushri lost his blue-maned lion; Samantabhadra’s white elephant was hard to find. Zhenwu’s tortoise and serpent-spirits lost their ranks; the zitong mule’s saddle-straps flew off. Travellers’ cries shook heaven as they called out vows; officials in the market-hills sought every promised boon. Smoke and wave made life itself a flood; fame and profit-souls, ruined, drifted away in the waters. Celestial peaks and mountain caves went black and dim; islands of seas and immortal isles were dark as dusk. Laojun could not tend his alchemical furnace; the Star of Longevity folded up his dragon-whisk fan. The Queen Mother set out for the Peaches of Immortality, but one wind untied her skirt and loosened her waist-belt. Erlang lost his way of a whole Ganzu city; Nezha could not retrieve the sword from its casket. The Heavenly King could not see the palm-tower; Lu Ban had his golden drill suspended. Leiyin Pagoda collapsed in three tiers; the stone bridge of Zhaozhou split in two. A red sun turned without radiance; the host of stars across the sky grew dim and disordered. Birds of the South Mountain flew to the North Mountain; water of East Lake overflowed into West Lake. Male and female parted, no longer calling one another; mother and child, separated, could not cry out. Dragon-kings searched every sea for yakṣa; Thunder Lord ran here and there hunting lightning-flash. The tenth Yama sought his adjudicators; beneath the earth, Ox-Head pursued Horse-Face. This wind blew down Putuo Mountain, and even sent Guanyin’s Sutra rolling up from the shore. A white lotus rose and flew from the sea’s edge, and twelve halls of bodhisattvas were toppled by its gust. Pangū, to this day, has seen wind before, but none as inauspicious as this. Whu-la-la! Heaven and earth seemed in peril, as if cracking and caving apart; ten thousand leagues of river and land all shook.

The demon’s furious cyclone swept through, making the Little Master’s miniature Sun Wukongs of hair spin in midair like a spinning-wheel of thread. They could not seize a staff and had no way to gather their bodies together. In alarm, the Sage twitched his hairs and drew his form back in. Alone, he raised his staff and advanced to strike. Yet the demon split open his face and blasted another mouthful of yellow wind, rubbing both fire-eyes of his golden pupils shut so tightly he could not open them. Thus he could not use the staff and withdrew from the field in defeat. The demon gathered the wind and returned to the cave; this was not worth further recording.

Pigsy, meanwhile, saw the wild yellow wind rise and the heavens darken. He held the horse, guarded the shoulder pole, and lay in a hollow of the mountain, neither daring to open his eyes nor to lift his head, endlessly chanting Buddha’s name and making vows. He did not know how the Sage’s bout had gone, nor whether the Master still lived. As he stood in this anxious wondering, the wind suddenly settled and the sky cleared. He looked up toward the cave-mouth and saw no soldiers, no drums, no gongs. The pig-idiot dared not ascend the gate, and no one was there to watch horse and baggage; truly he was trapped both ways, sorrowful and alarmed. In that worry he heard Sun Wukong shout from the west, and only then did he incline his body and greet him: “Brother, what a gale! From where did you come?”

The Sage waved his hand: “Terrible! Terrible! I, old Sun, as I know humans, have never seen wind like this. That old demon wielded a three-pronged steel fork and fought me. We had fought over thirty rounds; the Sage used a trick of ‘body outside body’ and surrounded him. He grew frantic and so brought out this wind. It was truly savage, nearly tore me from my stance; I recalled my arts, then fled through it. Ha! What a wind! What a wind! Even I can summon wind and call rain, but I’ve never seen wind this evil.”

Pigsy said, “Senior Brother, how fine is that demon’s martial skill?”

The Sage said, “He is capable enough to be seen through. His fork-form is neat indeed, and we exchanged blows evenly. But it was the wind that was so ferocious; it is hard to defeat him.”

Pigsy asked, “So how can we save the Master?”

The Sage answered, “As for saving the Master, wait and see after we find a moment. I wonder if there is any eye-doctor around here—have him cure mine.”

Pigsy said, “How are your eyes?”

The Sage said, “That demon breathed one blast of wind at me and left my eyes sore and acidic; cold tears run from them this moment.”

Pigsy said, “Brother, it is already late on the lower mountain, and it is nightfall again. Don’t speak of eye doctors—there’s not even a night shelter.”

The Sage replied, “For shelter there is no difficulty. I judge this demon does not yet dare to harm our Master. Let us go to the main road and find a household for the night; after this one night, when dawn comes, we shall return and subdue the demon.”

Pigsy nodded: “Exactly, exactly.”

He led out the horse and shouldered the pole, came up from the mountain hollow, and went to the road’s edge. By then dusk deepened. From below, on the south slope, dogs began to bark. The two stopped to look, and there was a manor house, dim with scattered lights. The two did not concern themselves with whether there was a road or not; they brushed through the grasses and came straight to the gate. There they beheld:

Purple lichens spread thickly; white stones lay sallow and grey. Purple lichens thick upon the grass; white stones grey-green with half-green moss. A few tiny lantern-fire fireflies flashed, while a grove of wild trees stood rank and close. Fragrant orchids filled the air, and young bamboos had just been planted. Clear springs ran through winding gullies; ancient cypresses leaned against deep cliffs. The place was secluded and no visitors came. At the gate, only wildflowers bloomed in the dark.

They did not dare to enter uninvited, so they could only shout once: “Open the gate, open the gate!” There was an old man there, followed by several young farmers with hoes and brooms, all arriving together, and he asked, “Who’s there? Who’s there?” Sun Wukong bowed and said, “We are disciples of Tripitaka, the holy monk of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land. We are going west to bow to Buddha and seek the scriptures. We passed this mountain, and the Yellow Wind King carried off our master; we have not yet rescued him. Night has fallen, so we have come to your dwelling to borrow one night’s lodging and beg you to make it convenient.” The old man replied, “Do forgive us, do forgive us. This is a place with few people and many who are unknown. We have just heard a cry at the gate, so we feared fox spirits, tigers, and mountain brigands of that sort; these rustic lads are simple and unruly and may have rushed at strangers. We did not know you were both elders. Come in, come in.”

His companions brought in the horses and burdens and went straight inside, then tied the horses and set down the poles, and paid their respects to Old Zhuang and sat to exchange courtesies. A dark-headed servant then brought tea. After tea, several bowls of sesame rice porridge were set before them. When the meal was finished, he ordered bedding prepared for the night. Sun Wukong said, “I can stay awake if needed. May I ask, good sir, is there any eye medicine for sale here?” The old man asked, “Which of you elders has an eye ailment?” Wukong said, “To speak plainly, old man, we ordained folk have never been sick from childhood and have never known what it means to have an eye illness.” The old man said, “If you do not suffer eye pain, why ask for medicine?” Wukong said, “Today at the mouth of Yellow Wind Cave, while rescuing our master, that monster suddenly blew one gust of wind at us. The wind made my eyes burn and ache; now I am all watery-eyed, so I seek eye medicine.” The old man said, “Excellent, excellent! You, this elder, so young in years, how can you lie? That Yellow Wind King’s wind is most harmful. His wind is not to be compared with any spring-and-autumn wind, pine-and-bamboo wind, or any east, west, south, and north wind…” Bajie said, “Perhaps it is clasping-head wind, sheep-ear wind, hemp-wind, or crooked-tail wind?” The elder said, “No, no. It is called the Samadhi Divine Wind.” Wukong said, “How do you know that?” The old man said, “That wind can darken heaven and earth, makes ghosts and spirits grieve, splits rocks and makes cliffs fall. When it blows on a person, life departs at once. If you meet such a gust, do you think you can still live? Only immortals can pass through unharmed.” Wukong said, “Indeed, indeed. Though we are not immortals, even immortals are my juniors. This life is not easy to give up, yet it has made only my eyes ache.” The old man said, “Then by this account you are someone with a past. In this poor place I have no eye medicine to sell. But this old man, too, once suffered wind-cold tears in my eyes; long ago I met a strange man and learned one prescription, called Three-Flower Nine-Child Ointment, which can treat all wind-eye disorders.” Wukong, hearing this, nodded his head and said, “I would take some to try.” The old man agreed. He went inside and brought out a small agate jar, untied its seal, and with a jade hairpin drew out a little medicine, applying some to Wukong. He told him not to open his eyes and to lie calmly and sleep; by morning it would be fine. When done, he took back the stone jar and led the young lads back inside.

Bajie unpacked their bundles, spread the bedding, and made arrangements for Wukong to lie down. Wukong sat with his eyes closed, fumbling about. Bajie laughed and said, “Master, where is your bright staff?” Wukong said, “You dolt of a slow fool, why do you treat me as a blind man?” The fool chuckled softly and went to sleep. Wukong sat on the bedding, moved his inner energy through the circulatory arts, and only after the third watch did he finally sleep.

Without noticing, it was already near dawn of the fifth watch. Wukong wiped his face, opened his eyes, and said, “Truly good medicine—far clearer than usual.” Then he looked back over his shoulder. Ah! There was no house, no doorway, no windows there; only old locusts and tall willows, while the brothers were all sleeping on the green grassy mat. Bajie woke and said, “Brother, what is it that you’re crying out for?” Wukong said, “Open your eyes and look.” The fool raised his head at once. Seeing that the place was empty, he panicked and scrambled up saying, “Where is my horse?” Wukong said, “Is it not tied to the tree?” “Where are the luggage?” Wukong said, “Isn’t it by your head?” Bajie said, “The people here are so lazy that they moved it away; how could they do it without calling out to us? If the village head had known, he might have brought us some tea and fruit. It seems they feared we were looking for a proper household, so he must have moved everything away in the night. Alas! We have slept like dead men. How could they tear down his house and not hear even the smallest sound?” Wukong took a small breath and smiled. “Baji, do not make a fuss. Look there on the tree, what is that paper slip?” Bajie moved forward and peeled it off. It said four lines:

This is no mere house of mundane men; a Dharma-protecting shrine, a hermitage of conversion. This wondrous remedy cures your aching eyes; with all your heart, subdue the demon and hesitate no longer.

Wukong said, “That band of fierce spirits, after changing themselves into a Dragon-Horse form, had never summoned him. Yet now he comes back playing false and pretending innocence.” Bajie said, “Brother, do not put on airs. How did he mark your tally?” Wukong said, “Brother, you still do not understand. The Protective Dharma Hall, the Six Ding and Six Jia, the Five-direction Jiedi, and the Four Duty Magistrates, by command of the Bodhisattva, secretly protect my master. Since the day I made my declaration, it has only been since you appeared that I have used them, so I never had occasion to brand a summons.” Bajie said, “Brother, since he is guarding our master under the law and keeping it hidden, he cannot show himself plainly. That is why he transformed this shrine. Do not blame him. Yesterday he not only gave you eye medicine, and he also hosted us for a vegetarian meal, which could indeed be called a full display of care. Do not blame him. Let us go rescue the master now.” Wukong said, “What you say is right. From here to the mouth of Yellow Wind Cave is not far. You should not set out yet; stay in the grove and watch the horses and the baggage. I will go into the cave and inquire about our master’s condition, then contend with him.” Bajie said, “Exactly so. We need to secure firm certainty of life or death. If the master has died, each of us can then know how to proceed with his fate; if he has not died, we will all exert ourselves and apply our hearts.” Wukong said, “Do not speak wildly; I am going.”

He sprang up in one bound and went straight to his gate, but the door was still shut and closed for sleep. Wukong did not call out at the gate, and he did not wish to rouse the demons. Twirling the secret formula, he chanted a spell and transformed himself. His form became that of a small, elegant mosquito with mottled legs. As a proof there is this poem:

Small and restless in shape, with a sharp beak, A soft, shrill buzz, faint as thunder; curtains and gauze screens in a chamber yield easily, And it loves the warm air of a hot day. It fears only pungent incense smoke and flapping fans, Yet in pity for the glow of the lamp it returns, Light and tiny, it burrows swiftly, darting into the demon cave.

At once the little demon by the gate was snoring. Wukong stung him once on the face. The little demon rolled over, woke, and said, “My lord! What a big mosquito! One bite and I’ve got a huge knot.” He blinked open his eyes and said, “It is dawn.” He then heard a sharp sound, and the second gate opened. Wukong hummed in his little tone and flew inside. He saw the old demon ordering everyone to be alert at the gates and to gather weapons on one side of a hall. “If yesterday’s wind did not already blow Sun Wukong to death,” he said, “he will surely come back today, and when he comes, he will certainly lose his life.”

Wukong, hearing this, flew past the hall and came to the rear, only to see a gate there closed so tightly. He slipped through the gap in the door. It was a great open yard, bare and empty. In a corner, at a fixed wind-post bound with ropes and cords, Tripitaka was tied. The master’s tears were already flowing, his thoughts fixed only on Wukong and Sha Wujing, not knowing where they were. Wukong hovered, settled on the top of his head, and called, “Master.” The elder recognized his voice. “Wukong, are you trying to kill me? Where are you calling me from?” Wukong said, “Master, I am on your head. Do not let your heart be hurried; do not worry. We must first catch the demon, and only then can we truly save your life.” Tripitaka said, “Son disciple, when do you expect to seize the demon?” Wukong said, “The tiger demon that seized you has already been killed by Bajie. It is only the old demon’s wind that is ferocious, and we expect to take him this very day. Do not weep. I am going.”

Saying he would go, he hummed and flew to the front. He saw the old demon sitting on the upper side, assigning tally orders to the leaders from all sides. Then he saw a little demon at the cave entrance who had polished the command-banner and came rushing into the hall to report: “Great King, on mountain patrol just now, I had just come out the gate. Had I not run quickly, that long-faced, big-eared monk sitting in the woods would have caught me. I barely escaped. I did not see yesterday’s hairy-faced monk, either.” The old demon said, “Sun Wukong is not here; he was probably killed by the wind. No need to go there to ask for troops.” The demons said, “Great King, if that wind truly blew him to death, that is our good fortune. But we fear he was not blown dead; if he goes and summons divine troops, what are we to do?” The old demon said, “Fear what divine troops? As long as I still hold my wind power, only the coming of Lingji Bodhisattva would matter; nothing else is worth fearing.”

The Great Sage, perched on the roof beam, heard only that one sentence and could not contain his joy. He immediately sprang off, took on his true form, and came out into the woods, calling, “Brother.” Zhu Bajie said, “Elder brother, where have you gone? A moment ago I drove off a demon carrying a command flag.” Sun Wukong laughed: “You did well, you truly did well. Sun Wukong changed into an insect and entered his cave to check on Master, and it turned out Master had been tied to the Dingfeng stake and was crying. Sun Wukong told him not to cry. Then I flew back to the roof beam and listened again. I saw that flag-bearing demon enter, panting, to make his report, saying that only your chasing drove him away and that he had not seen me. The old demon, confused, was guessing wildly, saying I had been killed by the wind, and saying that divine soldiers had been called for me. He even implicated one person himself—how strange, how strange.” Zhu Bajie said, “Who did he expose?” Sun Wukong said, “He said he feared whatever divine troops could still his wind. Only Lingji Bodhisattva would be able to do that. But none of us knows where Lingji is dwelling.”

At that moment of discussion, a man appeared walking along the roadside. Look at what sort of old gentleman he was:

His body was sound, no cane or crutch in his hand; ice-beard and snowy hair were tossed in loose locks. Golden brilliance flashed from his face, yet his expression was half-dazed; His bones were thin, his sinews withered, yet his strength was hard. Bent-backed, head lowered, he walked in slow steps; a broad brow and ruddy face, yet almost childlike. Though he looked like a man by common reckoning, he seemed like a Star of Longevity stepping out of a cave.

Zhu Bajie, seeing him, was greatly pleased and said, “Senior Brother, they say: ‘To know the road below the mountain, one must ask those who go and return.’ Why not go ask this old man?” So indeed the Great Sage tucked away his iron cudgel, loosened his collar, came forward and called, “Old gentleman, my greetings.” The old man gave him a half-answer and a bow: “Where are you a monk from, and what business have you in this wild land?” Sun Wukong replied, “We are holy monks traveling west to fetch the sutras. Yesterday, we lost our Master here, so we have come to ask, if you know, where Lingji Bodhisattva lives.” The old man said, “Lingji is to the south, three thousand li from here. There is a mountain called Little Sumeru; in that mountain is a Dharma Hall, the place where the Bodhisattva expounds scripture. Did you come to take his teachings?” Sun Wukong said, “Not to take his teachings. I have a matter to trouble him with and do not know which road to take.” The old man pointed southward with his hand: “This goat-path is the way.” This made the Great Sage look back at the road, but as he did the old gentleman turned into a gentle wind and disappeared. Only a brief note remained by the roadside, with four lines:

In reply to the Great Sage Equal to Heaven: listen, this old man is called Li Changgeng. At Little Sumeru there is the Flying-Dragon Staff; It was through Lingji, in former days, that Buddha’s soldiers were received.

Sun Wukong took the note, turned and headed south on the road. Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, we’ve been unlucky these past days and have seen ghosts in broad daylight these last two days. Who was the old man who turned into the wind and left?” Sun Wukong handed the note to Zhu Bajie and read it aloud: “Who is this Li Changgeng?” Sun Wukong said, “That is an epithet of Tai Bai Jinxing.” Zhu Bajie, terrified, knelt and bowed to the sky, saying, “Benefactor, benefactor. If this old pig had not secured Tai Bai’s warrant before the Jade Emperor, who knows what my life would have become.” Sun Wukong said, “Brother, you too know gratitude. But do not show yourself. Stay hidden deep in this grove and watch carefully over the baggage and the horses. Wait for me while I go to find Mount Sumeru and summon the Bodhisattva.” Zhu Bajie said, “Understood. I understand. You go quickly. When the old pig learned a turtle trick, he only withdraws his head when the time to hide comes.”

The Great Sage leapt into the air, loosed the cloud of a jindou and flew straight south. His speed was true indeed: in the blink of an instant he passed three thousand li, and with a twist of the waist some eight hundred more. In a moment he saw a high mountain; in its middle rose auspicious clouds, and lucky omens fluttered thickly. In a hollow of the mountain there was indeed a monastery. He heard the temple bells and chime stones echoing, and saw a faint, misty incense smoke. The Great Sage came straight to the gate and saw a Taoist in a scarf of beads, silently chanting Buddha’s name. Sun Wukong said, “A Taoist, I bow.” The man bowed in return and asked, “From where does this lord come?” Sun Wukong asked, “Is this the Dharma hall where Lingji Bodhisattva lectures?” The Taoist answered, “This is the place. What is your message?” Sun Wukong said, “I beg your kind assistance in hearing me out: I am Sun Wukong, Great Sage Equal to Heaven, disciple of Master Tripitaka, monk Xuan Zang of Great Tang. I have a matter to attend to and must see the Bodhisattva.” The Taoist smiled, “Your lord speaks at great length; I cannot hold all that in memory.” Sun Wukong said, “Then just report this: Tripitaka’s disciple Sun Wukong of the Tang monk has arrived.”

The Taoist, as told, went to the hall and relayed the message. The Bodhisattva then donned his robe, added incense, and came out to receive them. As soon as the Great Sage stepped inside, he looked around and saw:

The hall was all brocade and brocade-like splendor, a room of commanding dignity. The disciples together chanted the Lotus Sutra while the senior monk softly struck a gold-cast hand bell. Before the Buddha were arranged heavenly fruits and heavenly flowers; on the tablet stood only plain vegetables and plain fare. Bright treasure candles flamed, long streams of golden fire shooting like rainbows; rich incense drifted in, and jade-colored smoke rose up in flowing colors. Just then, when the lecture had ended and the mind had become still, they entered meditative stillness; white clouds drifted in strips around the pine tips. In silence he gathered the wisdom sword that cuts off demon heads; Prajnaparamita, perfectly understood, rose exalted.

The Bodhisattva arrayed himself and came out to receive him. The Great Sage entered the hall and took a guest seat, then, as ordered, was served tea. Sun Wukong said, “No need to trouble to offer tea. My Master is in danger on Yellow-Wind Mountain; I have come specifically to ask you to exert your great power, subdue the monster, and save him.” The Bodhisattva said, “I received a command from the Buddha and am stationed here to detain the Yellow-Wind demon. The Buddha granted me a Dingfeng pill and a Precious Flying-Dragon staff. When I once caught him, I spared his life and let him return to hide in the mountain, warning him not to harm living beings. I did not know that today he sought to injure our Master, defying the Dharma command. That is my fault.” The Bodhisattva wished to keep the Great Sage for a retreat and conversation, but Sun Wukong politely declined. He then took the Flying-Dragon staff, and together with the Great Sage they rode the cloud onward.

Before long they arrived atop Yellow-Wind Mountain. The Bodhisattva said, “Great Sage, this demon fears me somewhat. I will stay and settle in the cloud heights. You go down and wrestle him, lure him out, and then I can apply my arts.” Sun Wukong obeyed, touched down on the cave, and without a word shattered the cave gate with his iron staff. He shouted, “Monster, return Master to me!” alarmed, the gate-demon hurriedly sent word. The demon replied, “This wild monkey is truly impudent. It refuses to bow and yet dares to break my gate. Once out, I will raise my divine wind array and surely blow him dead.” He then donned his gear, took up the steel fork, and came out through the gate. Seeing the Great Sage, he spoke no more and thrust the fork at his chest; Sun Wukong sidestepped it. Swinging staff to face him, they fought for several exchanges. The monster turned and faced the northeast, then reached for his mouth to summon wind, but from the empty sky above Lingji Bodhisattva flung down the Flying-Dragon staff. He muttered some incantation, and immediately it became an eight-clawed golden dragon, lifting both claws wide and seizing the demon, then lifting him by the head and tossing him two or three times against the mountain cliff edge, where he showed his true form: a yellow-furred marten.

Sun Wukong came up and raised his staff to strike, but the Bodhisattva blocked him and said, “Great Sage, do not harm his life. I still need him to be brought before the Buddha.” Then he said to Sun Wukong: “He was an old mouse of spirit who had attained the Way at the foot of Ling Mountain. He stole the clear oil from a glazed-glass lamp, the lamp-blackened, and fearing that Vajra would seize him, he fled. He then came here and formed a spirit, creating mischief. When the Buddha saw him, death was not his sentence, so I was ordered to detain him; but he still harms living beings and commits evil, so I took him up to Ling Mountain. Now he has again assaulted the Great Sage and betrayed Tripitaka. I am taking him to see the Buddha to make his crimes clear; that is the merit of this task.” At Sun Wukong’s words, he thanked the Bodhisattva, then the Bodhisattva departed westward without further remark.

Then again, Zhu Bajie, in that grove, was still thinking about the Great Sage when he heard a voice from below the slope: “Wuneng, brother, bring horse and carrying poles!” The pig monk recognized it as the Great Sage’s voice, hastily gathered himself, and ran out of the woods. “Brother, what matter is this?” he asked. Sun Wukong said, “I invited Lingji Bodhisattva. He cast forth a Flying-Dragon staff, seized the demon, and it turned out to be a yellow-furred marten spirit. I have taken it to Ling Mountain to present before the Buddha. You and I must go into the cave and rescue Master.” Hearing this, Zhu Bajie was delighted all at once.

The two of them burst inside. They used spiked maces and iron staff to beat to death a whole lot of crafty hares, fox demons, musk deer, and horned deer. Then they went to the back garden and rescued Master. Master came out of the gate and asked, “How did you two seize this demon, and how did you rescue me?” Sun Wukong set out all that he had done in summoning Lingji Bodhisattva to subdue the demon. Master could not sufficiently thank them. The brothers arranged some tea and a meal from the plain provisions in the cave, and only then did they leave the cave and take the broad road westward.

What happens next is still unknown; hear the resolution in the next installment.
chapters.title: Chapter 21: The Dharma-Protector sets a camp to hold the Great Sage; Lingji of Mount Sumeru restrains the wind demon.
