This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

When Tripitaka and the three of his disciples came on, having come out of danger, they crossed Yellow-Wind Ridge in less than a day and stepped westward into a broad band of level, flat country. Time sped by quickly; after summer came autumn, and they passed by cold-calling cicadas and withered willows, while a great heat streamed west. Just then, they saw before them a roaring sheet of water, the waves surging and tumbling in tumult. Tripitaka called out from the saddle in haste: ‘Disciple, look at the water ahead. It is so wide, and I see no boats moving. How are we to cross?’ Zhu Bajie answered, ‘It is exactly a wild flood; there is no boat to pass over.’ The Great Sage leaped into the air, braced himself against the awning and looked, and he too was shaken: ‘Master, it is truly difficult, truly difficult. For this river, if I, Sun Wukong, go, I need only twist my waist once and cross it; but for Master, it is a thousand-fold hard to cross and ten thousand ages hard to travel.’ Tripitaka said, ‘From where I stand it looks endless. How broad is it in fact?’ Wukong said, ‘The width is about eight hundred li.’ Zhu Bajie asked, ‘How can you know such a measure, brother?’ Wukong replied, ‘I will not hide it from worthy younger brother. In broad daylight these eyes of mine often see omens and dangers from a thousand li away. Just now, looking from the sky, I cannot tell how far the river runs above and below, but I can see this passage must be fully eight hundred li across.’ The Elder, worried and distressed, turned the horse, and suddenly they saw a stone stele on the bank. The three came together and saw three seal-script words upon it: “Flowing-Sand River”; below were four short lines in true script:

Across the bounds of eight hundred of the Flowing Sand, the weak waters run three thousand deep. Downy goose feathers cannot stay afloat; reeds and cattail flowers sink to the bottom.

As the three watched the stele, they heard it: the waves surged like mountains and rolled over each other like ridges. From the middle of the river, a demon-skull slid and rose forth, fierce and grotesque:

A head of loose red-flame hair, two round eyes bright as lanterns. His face was neither black nor blue indigo, and his old-dragon voice boomed like thunder. He wore a robe of yellow-goose down and a belt of white vine at his waist. Beneath his throat hung nine skulls, and in his hand he held a jewelled staff, mighty and upright.

The monster came in a whirl, sprinted for the bank, and rushed straight at Tripitaka. Startled, Sun Wukong snatched up the Master and carried him, then quickly climbed to the high bank and withdrew. Zhu Bajie dropped his load, drew his nine-toothed pa, and stepped toward the demon. The demon braced his talismanic staff to block him. The two stood on the bank of the Flowing-Sand River, each matching hero with hero, and there began a fierce contest:

The nine-toothed pa and the demon-subduing staff, the two opposed on the riverbank. This one is the Great Commander Tianpeng, that one the demoted Curtain-Raising General. Once they met in Lingxiao Heaven; today they contend and gamble over strength. This one wields his pa to seek a dragon-claw thrust, that one sets his staff against it like an elephant-bearer’s tusks. They open wide, step square, and stab straight into the oncoming wind. This one grabs as though faceless and headless, that one lets no opening of emptiness be empty. One is the old man-eating spirit that has long held the Flowing-Sand realm, the other the law-bearing, sword-carrying training general. They came and went, fighting through twenty rounds, neither gaining advantage.

Sun Wukong guarded Tripitaka, holding the horse and securing the baggage. Seeing Zhu Bajie and the demon still battling, he growled through clenched teeth, rubbed his palms together, and could not restrain himself from striking. He drew his staff and said, ‘Master, stay seated and do not be afraid. Let old Wukong play with him awhile.’ The Master could not hold him back. He whistled once and leapt to the front. There they found the demon and Zhu Bajie locked in a hard contest, tight and unresolved. Sun Wukong swung his iron cudgel at the demon’s head. The creature spun about, hurriedly dodged, and plunged straight back into the Flowing-Sand River. Furious, Zhu Bajie jumped wildly: ‘Brother, who sent you here? He has been growing slower and slower against my pa; with three or five more rounds I would have captured him. He saw your fierce arrival and fled in defeat—what shall we do?’ Sun Wukong laughed: ‘Brother, I will speak plainly. Since I subdued the Yellow-Wind fiend and came down from the mountain, I have not used my rod for a whole month. I saw how well you were fighting him, and my feet itched, so I came to spar him a little. Who knew that creature does not know how to spar; he just ran away.’

The two returned, still with hands on each other, chatting and laughing, and went back to Tripitaka. Tripitaka asked, ‘Did you manage to catch the demon?’ Sun Wukong answered, ‘The demon could not endure the battle and turned to retreat into the water.’ Tripitaka said, ‘Disciple, this demon has dwelt here long; he knows every depth and shoal. In such boundless weak waters, with no boat or oar at hand, we must get someone to guide us who knows the water’s nature.’ Sun Wukong said, ‘That is exactly what you say. As the saying goes: “Those near cinnabar become red; those near ink become black.” This monster lives here and certainly knows the nature of the water. We should seize him now but not kill him; only make him take the Master across, and then we can deal with him.’ Zhu Bajie said, ‘Brother, do not hesitate. Let you go catch him first, and I will watch over Master.’ Sun Wukong smiled: ‘Younger brother, I will not boast. I do not know water-work very well. If I crossed on foot alone, I would need to form the hand-seal, recite the avoid-water spell again and again, and only then move on; otherwise I must transform into fish, shrimp, crab, turtle and other forms to go. As for fighting arts, what strange odd feats you can do among high mountains and clouds, old Wukong can do all. But in water, the trade is different; there is a special craft to it.’ Zhu Bajie said, ‘In my former days I was Inspector-General of the Heavenly River, commanding eighty thousand water soldiers. I have learned a bit of water’s nature. Still, if there is any old or young in this water’s clan, generations upon generations, all rushing in, I may not withstand them and might be hauled up by them!’ Sun Wukong replied: ‘If you fight him in his waters, do not linger in the contest, and do not seek to win. Draw him out to the surface; then I will come in and strike.’ Zhu Bajie said, ‘You are right. I will go.’ Saying so, he stripped off his blue-brocade robe and shoes, whirled his pa with both hands, split the waterway apart with his old methods, leapt over the waves and broke through the surf, then drove straight down to the river bottom and advanced forward.

The monster, after retreating from that round and just catching his breath, heard the sound of someone driving through the water. He looked up and saw it was Zhu Bajie, his pa churning the current. He raised his staff and called out before Zhu Bajie: ‘You monk, where do you think you’re going? Watch closely and strike true!’ Zhu Bajie held out the pa and asked, ‘What kind of demon are you, that you dare to block the road here?’ The demon said, ‘You do not even know who I am. I am neither a mere demon-spirit nor an unknown wandering outlaw.’ Zhu Bajie replied, ‘If you are no demon-spirit and no nameless one, why do you harm life here? Tell me your true name in honesty, and I will spare your life.’ The monster answered:

Since childhood I have been strong and majestic in spirit, roaming over ten thousand li of Heaven and earth. As a hero under heaven I made my fame known; in brave households I stood in the guise of a champion. Through ten thousand realms and nine provinces I roam at will, and across five lakes and four seas I arrive where I choose. All for this: I studied the Way and roamed the far sky to seek a teacher in boundless lands. My robe and alms-bowl were worn daily and close to my person; my heart and mind could never be scattered. Following the clouds along the ground, I have wandered for dozens of times, roving everywhere in a hundred and more courses. Thus I came to meet a true one, and the Great Radiance of the Way opened before me. First I gathered infants and demoness girls, then I released the Wooden Mother and the Golden Lord. In my bright chamber, kidney waters entered the Flower-Pond, and heavy lofty-liver fire was sent into the heart. After three thousand merits were complete, I worshiped the Countenance of Heaven, my intent fixed on bowing to Bright Splendour. The Jade Emperor then raised my rank and, with his own mouth, sealed me as a Curtain-Raising General. In the South-Heaven Gate I was foremost in esteem; before Lingxiao Hall I was called the one above. At my waist hung a tiger-head tablet; in my hand I held the fixed demon-subduing staff. A golden helmet on my head glittered in sunlight; armour on my body flashed with dawn-cloud light. In coming and going I took the lead of escort, and entered and left wherever I accompanied the court. But when the Queen Mother of the West brought out peaches of immortality and held a feast in the Jade Pool, summoning all the generals, I slipped and broke the jades and glass; all the heavenly gods were stricken and lost their strength. Though the Jade Emperor became wrathful, he ordered him on his left to supervise my punishment: I was stripped of crown and armor, my rank badges removed, and my body was thrown onto the killing field. By the mercy of the Barefooted Celestial Immortal, who petitioned on my behalf, I was spared and released. Spared life and revived with no formal judgment, I was sent down to the east bank of the Flowing-Sand. When full, I sleep and become drowsy on this mountain; when hungry I go through breaking waves to find what I can eat. Woodcutters who met me did not survive; fishermen who saw my form all met their ruin. Many people have I come and gone to, eating and moving on, again and again wounding life and spreading evil qi. You dare to raise violence at my gate; today my belly has some expectation. Do not call me rough and unworthy to chew; seize him, keep still, and I will chop him into pickle and sauce.

When Zhu Bajie heard those words he flared in rage and cursed, ‘You splash-brained brute! You have not an ounce of tact left in you. I, old pig, can still froth up water from my mouth—how dare you say I am coarse and call for me to be chopped up for fish paste? By the way you look, you take me for some old country bumpkin. No such impudence. I’ll bite a lump of your ancestors’ bones with this spade.’

At that the demon, seeing the spade coming, made a “Phoenix Nod” and dodged. The two burst through the water and rose to the surface, each dancing on the waves, each climbing from one breaker to another. This time the duel was no like the previous one. Listen:

Draw back the curtain, Captain of the Heavenly Canopy; both display divine arts so wondrously lovely. There, the demon-subduing treasure staff whirled with a head-crown; here, the nine-pronged spiked spade moved with quickness of hand. They leapt through the waves, shaking mountain and stream, driving back waters and dimming the world. Fierce as Tai Sui striking a battle-banner, vicious as a death-gate heaving up the treasure-lid. This one, his red heart unwavering, defended Tripitaka; that one, crime-lashed, raged on as a water demon. One stroke of the spade made nine gashes; one staff-strike from the other shook spirit and life. Valiant each, they pushed and met in fierce delight, heart set to wrest the bout to a close. If one reckons all this, it was only for the sake of fetching the scriptures, and their fury mounted to the heavens, unbearable. They stirred the gurnard, bream, carp, and snakeheads into retreat, stripping fresh scales from turtles, tortoises, and mud-turtles alike. Scarlet shrimp and purple crabs all met their doom; the gods of the Water Palace went and bowed upward in respect. Only the sound of waves heaving and breakers rolling like thunder was heard; sun and moon lost their light, and heaven and earth seemed struck with wonder.

The two fought on for two full hours, with no clear winner. It was exactly as if a bronze basin met an iron broom, a jade stone-latch met a golden bell.

The two had fought for two whole hours, with neither side winning nor yielding. It was truly like bronze versus iron, chime against bell.

Yet the Great Sage stood by Tripitaka, one on each side, watching them wrestle on the water, yet he did not dare to move. Only then did he see that Zhu Bajie gave a half-deceptive, feigned strike and pretended to be losing, then turned and walked back toward the eastern bank. The demon came after and drew near the bank. The Sage could no longer endure it, so he set Master aside, drew his iron rod, and leapt to the riverside to strike the demon from above. The creature, fearing to engage, whooshed and slipped back into the water. Bajie shouted, ‘You, Bimawen, are all haste and no thought! Go a little slower, and let me lure him to the high ground; then you stop him at the bank so he cannot turn back. If not catch him now, when will he come out again?’ Wukong laughed, ‘Fool, do not shout, do not shout. Let us first go back and report to Master.’

Then Bajie went with the Sage up to the high bank and saw Tripitaka. Tripitaka bowed and said, ‘My disciple, you must be so tired.’ Bajie replied, ‘Not that so much as the matter itself; only if we subdue this fiend and carry you across is all truly secure.’ Tripitaka asked, ‘How did your fight with the demon go?’ Bajie said, ‘The demon’s skill and mine are well matched. As I fought, I feigned defeat, and then only did he dare come all the way to the bank. When he saw my elder brother brandishing a rod, he ran.’ Tripitaka asked, ‘How can this be handled, then?’ Wukong said, ‘Master, do not worry. Do not be anxious. Since the light is already fading, sit here on this cliff-edge for now. Let old Sun go fetch some offerings food. Eat and rest, and tomorrow we will deal with this.’ Bajie said, ‘That is right. Go quickly and come quickly.’

Wukong sprang onto cloud and left at once. He went straight north to a household, transformed a bowl of plain vegetarian fare there, and returned with it, presenting it to Master. When Tripitaka saw how fast he returned, he said, ‘Wukong, let us ask that family a way to cross the river. Is it not wiser than grappling with this demon?’ Wukong laughed, ‘That home is far away—well over five or seven thousand li. How would they know anything of waters and currents? What good is asking them?’ Bajie said, ‘Brother, you are lying again. At five or seven thousand li, how did you come back so quickly?’ Wukong said, ‘You would not know. From my dandelion cloud, one leap spans ten thousand and eight thousand li. For five or seven thousand, I need only nod my head twice, bend my waist once, and return. What is there hard in that?’ Bajie said, ‘Brother, if it is so easy, you could carry Master with a nod and a stoop and simply jump across. Why must we keep beating against this demon so bitterly?’ Wukong said, ‘Can you ride a cloud? Could you carry Master for me? Master’s mortal flesh and bone are as heavy as Mount Tai. I do not mean this for you; only my own cloud can bear him. My cloud is called one that truly bears one through the air; it does travel far or near as needed. If you cannot carry him, how could I bear him? As an old saying goes: “They say Mount Tai can be made as light as a mustard seed, but carrying a mortal out of the red dust is never so easy.” As for this spiteful demon, he can cast spells, stir winds, grab and drag with little tricks, and move only by ground-level trickery, not through the air. Such arts of his I can use too. And there are also concealment arts and the earth-shrinking method; old Sun knows them all. But Master must journey through foreign lands and endure hardships; he cannot yet break free of this sea of suffering. So our task is only guardianship, keeping him alive and intact. Taking on such troubles for him is not possible, nor can we bring the Scriptures that way. Even if one reached Buddha first, Buddha would not hand the scripture to you or me. That is exactly the meaning of: ‘When something is easy, men call it something to take lightly.’ That fool listened and nodded repeatedly. Then he ate a little dry vegetable-free offering food, and the three set down to rest beneath the east bank of the Flowing-Sand River.

At daybreak, Tripitaka asked, ‘Wukong, what is to be done today?’ Wukong replied, ‘There is nothing yet decided. Zhu Bajie must go down into the water again.’ Bajie said, ‘Brother, if you want it clean and clear, leave it to me to go down.’ Wukong said, ‘Good brother, this time I will not be so hasty. Let him lure the demon up; I will hold it off at the bank and let it not return. We must capture it.’

Zhu Bajie, wipe his face, rouse himself, and with both hands took up the spiked spade. He went to the river edge, split the waterway, and again sank down toward the lair. The demon had only just awakened. Suddenly he heard the roar of churning water, turned back at once and opened his eyes to look; seeing Bajie arrive with the spade, he sprang out, blocked him from in front, and shouted, ‘Go slow, go slow—show me the staff.’ Bajie held up his spade in defense and said, ‘What kind of mourning-staff are you calling this? I’ll make your ancestors see the staff indeed!’ The demon said, ‘You brute, you do not understand what this is. Mine is:

The treasure staff, famed before name was set, was first hewn from moonlit Sora-craft. Wu Gang felled a branch of it, and Lu Ban fashioned it with his renowned art. Within it runs a golden sinew-thread, without a thousand bead-strings woven about its skin. It is called the Treasure Staff, excellent at conquering demons, to pacify spirits and subdue monsters for all time. Because I was once appointed Great General, the Jade Emperor granted that I should carry it always. Long or short, as my mood directs; slender or stout, by my will it shifts. It once guarded the Peach Banquet processions, and once accompanied court sessions in the highest heavens. It stood in court before the gathered saints, and with drawn curtains it has seen all immortals bow. By my tending this living divinity, it became a heavenly weapon—not a mere human contrivance. Since I was exiled below Heaven’s gate, I wander the seas at will. I do not boast without cause: in all the world there is no spear or saber equal to mine. As for your rusted spiked spade, it is fit only for tilling fields and building vegetable beds.’

Bajie laughed, ‘I said that you’re the same old slob. Never mind your “building beds”; one hard swing and you’ll have nowhere to put on salve—nine eyes bleeding at once. Even if you do not die, you’ll be left with a lifelong festering of broken wounds.’ The monster flung aside his posture and, from beneath the water, rose again with Bajie. Their combat this time differed still more from before. Look at it:

The staff whirls, the spade-digger plants; their words fail between them, no kinship of tongue. Since the Mother-Wood dagger and the ruler’s hoe-lock meet, each clash drives the other into contact. No clear win, no clear loss, no reverse, no retreat; surf and wave heave and swirl without peace. This one’s rage admits no room, that one’s sorrow can bear no insult. Spade swings, staff blocks, each proclaims itself heroic; water boils and drifting sands turn venomous. Their pride is high, their labor great, for Tripitaka’s westward course cannot be stayed. The spiked spade is terribly fierce; the treasure staff is fully tested and true. One grips to drag him toward the bank; one catches him and drags him back into water. Their sound breaks like thunder that stirs fish and dragons; clouds darken, heaven dims, spirits and ghosts bow down.

This bout went back and forth, through thirty exchanges, with no sign of one side overpowering the other. Bajie again pretended defeat and withdrew with the spade in hand. The demon again rushed after him, heaving surging waves, and came to the cliff edge. Bajie shouted, ‘You foul demon! Come up—this high place has solid ground, good for a real fight.’ The monster jeered, ‘You imbecile, you lured me up and brought your companions. You come down and fight in the water where you can.’ It was then the demon had grown clever; he refused to climb ashore again, and only bickered with Bajie along the water’s edge.

Then Wukong saw he still would not step onto land and was distraught, longing to seize him at once. He said, ‘Master, stay seated and wait. I will do him with the move called the Hungry Eagle Seizes and Eats.’ He set off with cloud stride and jumped into midair; with a sharp dash he dropped down to snatch the demon. The monster, while bickering with Bajie, suddenly heard wind and turned. Seeing Wukong descending from the clouds, it at once withdrew the staff, dived down into the river, and vanished beyond sight. Wukong stood on the bank and told Bajie, ‘Brother, this demon is slippery indeed; if he still refuses to step ashore, what are we to do?’ Bajie said, ‘Hard, hard, hard. I cannot defeat him. I have spent even the strength I had as milk-fed flesh, and can only hold my arms out straight.’ Wukong said, ‘Then go and attend to Master.’

The two had come back to the high bank again, and after seeing Tripitaka they fully reported that the demon was hard to seize. The abbot’s eyes brimmed with tears as he said, 「With hardship such as this, how are we to cross?» Sun Wukong replied, 「Master, do not worry. This monster lies hidden deep in the water and is truly difficult to face. —Zhou Bajie, stay here and guard Master, and fight with him no more. I, old Sun, will go to the Southern Sea and return. Zhu Bajie said, 「Elder brother, what are you doing in the Southern Sea?» Sun Wukong said, 「This whole pilgrimage business was ordained by Guanyin Bodhisattva, and it was Guanyin who also released our shackles. Today the road is blocked by the River of Flowing Sand, and we cannot advance. Without him we cannot deal with this. I had better go and invite him than keep fighting this demon.」 Zhu Bajie said, 「You are right, you are right. Brother, when you go, please send me a report when you return: I have received your instruction many times today as well.」 Tripitaka said, 「Wukong, if you are going to invite the Bodhisattva, do not hesitate at all. Go quickly and come quickly.»

Sun Wukong at once mounted the Cloud-Kicking Machine and flew straight toward the Southern Sea. "Ah!" Before half a watch passed he already caught sight of the lands of Mount Putuo. In a short while he dropped from the cloud outside the Purple Bamboo Grove, where the gods of the twenty-four heavens came forward to meet him and said, 「Great Sage, what brings you here?» "I have come to see the Bodhisattva," Wukong said, "for my Master has met great trouble." Those gods replied, 「Please sit while we report this." The heavenly attendants of the Wheel-Rising court quickly came to the gate of the Cavern of Reverberating Sound and announced, 「Sun Wukong has arrived with an urgent matter to pay homage." At that moment Guanyin was by the balustrade of the Precious Lotus Pond, with the pearl-bearing Dragon Maiden, both hands on the railing, watching the blossoms. Hearing the report, she turned on a cloud, opened the gate, and called him in. The Great Sage entered respectfully, with proper reverence, and made a full prostration.

Guanyin asked, 「Why did you not protect Tripitaka, and why come again to see me?» Sun Wukong knelt and explained, 「Bodhisattva, earlier at Gaozhong Manor my Master once took on another disciple, called Zhu Bajie; by your grace he was even given the Dharma name Wuneng. We have only just passed Yellowwind Ridge, and now we have reached the River of Flowing Sand, three thousand li of weak waters. Master has found it hard to cross. In that river there is a demon whose martial arts are formidable. Wuneng and he have fought on the surface three times, and yet could not win. He blocked us and prevented us from crossing. Therefore I have specially come to inform you and beg your compassion, to save him and let Master cross.」 Guanyin said, 「You monkey is only strutting your pride; why can’t you speak of protecting Tripitaka?" Sun Wukong said, 「We only needed to seize him and order him to ferry my Master across. In water I am not quick in subtle handling. Wuneng spoke with him at his lair three times, but he never heard of the pilgrimage charge or our names.」 Guanyin said, 「The demon of the River of Flowing Sand is Junxian the Great Captain of the celestial realm come down in this life. He is also one of my good believers that I have sought to convert. I told him to protect travelers on this pilgrimage. If you were to tell him plainly that you are pilgrims seeking the Dharma from the Eastern Land, he would not contend with you at all and would yield at once.」 Sun Wukong said, 「But that monster now shuns battle, will not climb the bank, and only haunts the water below. How then can I bring him to submit? How can my Master cross the Weak River?» Guanyin immediately called Hui-an, took out a red gourd from her sleeve, and instructed, 「Take this gourd with Sun Wukong to the surface of the River of Flowing Sand. Call, ‘Wujing,’ and he will come out. First, make him take refuge in Tripitaka. Then gather his nine skulls together, arrange them in a nine-palace pattern, and set this gourd in the center. It will become a Dharma boat and can carry Tripitaka across the boundary of the River of Flowing Sand.»

Hui-an obeyed the instruction and, with the Great Sage, took the gourd and came out of the Reverberating-Sound Cave, taking leave of Purple Bamboo Grove in accordance with the Dharma command. There is a verse as witness.

The five elements, once matched, accord with Heaven’s true nature, and he recognizes his former master. Once refined and set upright, he serves as marvellous use; clear discernment reveals why right is right and evil is evil. Metal returns to its own kind; wood, in seeking pity, goes again to its own sinking place. In both realms the full task ripens in serene silence, and when water and fire are reconciled, not a grain of dust remains.

The two of them soon set down their cloud and came at once to the bank of the River of Flowing Sand. Zhu Bajie recognized the Mu-cha and brought Tripitaka forward in welcome. The Mu-cha and Tripitaka exchanged respectful bows, and then the Mu-cha greeted Zhu Bajie. Zhu Bajie said, 「By the Venerable Master’s instruction, I have now seen the Bodhisattva and, as old Pig, have in truth observed the Dharma teaching; I am glad now to bow to the monk’s way. All along I have been running about in haste on the road and have not yet offered thanks. Please forgive, please forgive.」 Sun Wukong said, 「No need for a long recital. Let us just call that brute over.」 Tripitaka asked, 「Call who?" Sun Wukong said, 「After I went to the Bodhisattva I fully reported our former trouble. The Bodhisattva said the monster of the Flowing Sand was Junxian the Great Captain in human form, fallen here from Heaven because of sins, and having forgotten himself, making trouble. He had once been urged by the Bodhisattva and was willing to go west with Master, but we never told him that this was the pilgrimage. So this bitter fighting kept on. The Bodhisattva now sends this Mu-cha with the gourd and says to make a Dharma boat with him so that he can ferry you across.」 Hearing this, Tripitaka kept bowing without end and said to the Mu-cha, 「Venerable one, I beg you—hasten this at once.」 The Mu-cha lifted the gourd, half cloud and half mist, and went straight to the river surface, calling out in a loud voice, 「Wujing, Wujing. The pilgrim for the scriptures has waited here so long. Why do you still not submit?」

That demon, fearing the Monkey King, had retreated to the bottom and was resting in his lair when he heard his Dharma name called. Knowing it was Guanyin’s command, and hearing also the words “the pilgrim for the scriptures is here,” he was no longer afraid of axe or halberd. He broke the waves and raised his head, and at once recognized the Mu-cha. He came forward with a radiant grin and bowed, saying, 「Venerable one, I failed in courtesy. Where is the Bodhisattva now?" The Mu-cha said, 「The Master has not yet arrived. She sent me first to instruct you: go at once and become a disciple of Tripitaka. Hang the skulls you wear around your neck beside this gourd, arrange them in the nine-palace array to form one Dharma vessel, and ferry him across this Weak River.」 Wujing asked, 「Where is the pilgrim in this case?" The Mu-cha pointed and said, 「That one seated on the eastern bank, is he not?" At seeing Zhu Bajie, Wujing said, 「That one, I do not even know from where he came, and he fought me for two days, never once speaking the words ‘pilgrimage of scriptures.’ Now I see this fellow too, this is the one helping him, and he is fierce indeed; I am not going.」 The Mu-cha said, 「That is Zhu Bajie, and that is Sun Wukong. Both are disciples of Tripitaka and both are beings Guanyin has persuaded and converted. Why should you fear? I will now take you to meet Tripitaka.」

Then Wujing put away his treasure staff, straightened his yellow brocade robe, leapt ashore, and knelt on both knees before Tripitaka: 「Venerable Master, this disciple is blind in heart, unable to recognize your sacred form. I have been at fault and pushed and jostled much; please forgive my offenses.」 Zhu Bajie scolded, 「You pusball! Why did you not take refuge earlier and only keep trying to fight me? What kind of words are these?" Sun Wukong laughed and said, 「Brother, do not blame him. It is simply that we never told them the truth of our pilgrim mission or our names.」 The abbot asked, 「Do you then truly and sincerely wish to take refuge in my teaching?" Wujing said, 「Disciple, by the Bodhisattva’s conversion, was told to take the surname Sha and was given the Dharma name Wujing—how could I fail to follow Master?" Tripitaka said, 「If so,」 and called, 「Wukong, fetch the precept sword and give him the tonsure.」 The Great Sage obeyed, handed the knife, and shaved off his hair. Wujing came and bowed to Tripitaka, and bowed to Sun Wukong and Zhu Bajie, taking the order of seniority. Seeing the manner of his prostration was truly like a monk’s household custom, Tripitaka again called him Sha Monk. The Mu-cha said, 「Since he has already accepted the kasaya precepts, there is no need for needless words. Go make the Dharma boat now."

Wujing, taking no delay, removed the skulls hanging from his neck, tied them together with rope in a ninefold layout, and placed the Bodhisattva’s gourd at the center. He called for the Master to come down the bank. The abbot then boarded the Dharma boat and sat upon it; indeed it was steady as a light skiff. On his left, Zhu Bajie supported him; on his right, Wujing bore him. Behind, Sun Wukong hauled the dragon horse, following in half-cloud and half-mist, and above them the Mu-cha gave protection. The Master passed over the limits of the River of Flowing Sand in ease and steadiness, and the waters were calm and the wind smooth through the weak river. Truly it was as swift as an arrow in flight. Not long after, he set foot on the opposite shore and escaped the raging flood, not dragging mud and water; by good fortune his feet were dry and his hands dry, clean and unentangled. The disciples now had firm ground beneath them. The Mu-cha folded the auspicious cloud and took back the gourd. Then the skulls at once transformed into nine streams of dark wind and vanished into stillness. Tripitaka thanked the Mu-cha and made full prostrations to Guanyin. It was exactly thus:

The Mu-cha returned at once to the Eastern Ocean Sea, while Tripitaka mounted again and rode westward.

In the end, it is not yet known when they will truly obtain the final fruit of seeking the scripture. Hear, in the next installment, how this is resolved.
chapters.title: Chapter 22: Pigsy wages battle at Flowing-Sand River; a wood-guardian monk receives Wujing under the Dharma.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

By the law, setting out westward, I came late on the road; the autumn wind whispers, and frost-flowers fall. The wayward monkey is bound with cord—do not unfasten it; the poor horse, though straining, need not be goaded with more lashings. Mother Wood and Lord Gold are one by original union; the Yellow Crone and the Red Child are not truly different. Gnaw open the iron pellet to learn the true report; Prajnaparamita will come to that house.

This account says that the way of going west to fetch the Sutras is none other than the task of returning to one’s own nature. It says that Tripitaka and his three disciples, having awakened to true suchness, at once broke the shackles of dust, leapt out of the quicksand sea of nature itself, utterly without obstruction, and straightaway came marching west on the main road. They passed through green hills and blue waters, and saw wild grasses and idle flowers without end. Time itself went swiftly, and nine autumns had passed; they had only seen such scenes:

Maple leaves red over all the hills, yellow flowers enduring the late wind. The old cicadas’ singing grew ever more languid; the crickets of sorrowed longing had endless thought. The lotus rends the green silk fans; clusters of orange-scented golden blossoms. Pity, the few lines of geese, tiny specks spread across the distant sky.

Just then, while walking, they did not notice it was late. Tripitaka said: "Disciple, it is getting dark again. Where should we rest tonight?" Sun Wukong said: "Master, those words are mistaken. A monk eats wind and drinks water, sleeps by moonlight and on frost; every place is home. To ask where to rest—why so?" Zhu Bajie said: "Brother, you can walk so lightly; what care if others are worn out? Ever since we crossed the River of Flowing Sand, we have been climbing hills and crossing ridges all this way, with this heavy load on our shoulders. It is hard for an old pig to bear. We need a household: first to brew tea and make a meal, second to restore our spirits. That is only sensible." Sun Wukong said: "Bodhisattva-badger, your words sound as if resentment lurks in them. It is like the ease of idling in some high-lier’s manor, never seeking blessings. Since you are a true monk, you must endure hardship and hardship; only then do you deserve to be a disciple." Zhu Bajie said: "Brother, do you know how much this load weighs?" Sun Wukong said: "Brother, ever since I got you and Sha Wujing, I have not once shouldered it. How would I know how heavy?" Zhu Bajie said: "Brother, count it with me:

Four squares of yellow vine and hemp, eight ropes, long and short. Then to guard against drizzle, three or four layers of felt padding. Even the carrying pole worries us about slipping, nails are set into both ends. A copper-inlaid iron nine-ringed staff, and a great cloak-wrapped bundle bound with rattan vine."

With so much baggage, it is hard for old Zhu Bajie to carry every day; yet you, becoming a disciple of Tripitaka, use me as your day laborer. Sun Wukong laughed: "Blockhead, to whom did you speak this?" Zhu Bajie said: "Brother, I was speaking to you." Sun Wukong said: "Then say it to me instead? No—just to Sun Wukong I only mind the Master’s welfare. You and Sha Wujing should take charge of the baggage and the horse. If you are even a little negligent, I will put down the first hard cudgel on your backside." Zhu Bajie said: "Brother, do not speak of beating; beating means using force to bully someone. I know your lofty pride, you will not agree to carry. But Tripitaka’s horse is so tall and broad, and it bears only the old monk. Ask him to carry a few things too—this is how brothers show feeling."

Sun Wukong said: "You call him a horse, but he is no ordinary horse. He is in truth Dragon Horse, the Third Prince, son of Ao-run, the Dragon King of the Western Sea. Once he set fire to the bright pearl in the hall and was accused by his father as disobedient. He transgressed the Heavenly Law, and only Guanyin saved his life. He long waited for Tripitaka at Eagle-Grief Cliff. Later, by chance the Bodhisattva came in person, took away his scales and horns, removed the pearl from his throat, and made him into this horse so he might bear Tripitaka on the journey to the Western Heaven to worship Buddha. This is all each person’s karmic retribution; do not look down on him." Sha Wujing said: "Brother, is he truly a dragon?" Sun Wukong said: "Yes." Zhu Bajie said: "Brother, I have heard the ancients say: a dragon can breathe out cloud-mist and fog, and spread dust and sand; it has powers to hew mountain ridges and to turn and churn rivers and seas. How is it then that he walks so slowly today?" Sun Wukong said: "If you want him to run quickly, have me do it and you will see."

Sun Wukong made the Golden-Hooped Staff click once in his hands, and ten thousand streams of colored clouds sprang up. The horse, seeing him raise the staff and fearing a blow, panicked: its four hooves flashed like lightning as it tore away at once. Tripitaka’s hands weakened and could not hold the reins; yielding to its poor nature it dashed up the cliff-slope, and only after that did the Master manage to stumble along after it. When his breath finally steadied, Tripitaka raised his head and at a distance saw a grove of pines in shade. Within it there were a few buildings, stately indeed; he saw:

The gate hangs with emerald cypresses, the manor near the blue hills. A few pines rise, one after another; several stalks of bamboo are mottled and brown. By the hedge, wild chrysanthemums with frost-red bloom; by the bridge, hidden orchids mirror crimson on the water. Walls of powdery clay, brickwork forming an enclosed ring. The great hall is splendid in many ways; the mansion is very serene. No cattle or sheep in sight and no dogs or chickens, so perhaps autumn harvest work is done.

While Tripitaka was softly watching while holding the reins, he saw Sun Wukong and the others just arriving. Sha Wujing said: "Master, did you not already dismount?" Tripitaka scolded: "Sun Wukong, this wild monkey, he frightened the horse; if so, I could still have stayed in the saddle." Sun Wukong, with a half-smile, said: "Please do not blame me, Master. It was Zhu Bajie who said the horse was walking too slowly, so I told him to make it go faster." Since Zhu Bajie had hurried the horse, he was breathless and panting, making a sputtering fuss:

Enough, enough—mind your own belly, do not loosen your belt. The load is so heavy I cannot shoulder it up, and he has made me run back and forth driving the horse. Tripitaka said: "Disciple, look over there by that wall—there is an estate. We may take lodging there." Hearing this, Sun Wukong raised his head quickly and looked up. Truly in midair he saw auspicious cloud layers and radiant halos of good omens; he knew it was surely a place touched by Buddha and immortals. He did not dare to reveal divine signs, and merely replied, "Very well, very well. We shall sleep there."

Tripitaka hastily dismounted. They saw a gate tower, with drooping-lotus elephant-trunk forms, painted beams and carved rafters. Sha Wujing set down the pannier; Zhu Bajie led the horse and said: "This household is more than prosperous. It is truly a wealthy and substantial house." Sun Wukong moved to enter, but Tripitaka said: "No. We are monks and must avoid suspicion; do not wander in on our own. Let us wait until someone comes out, and then ask for lodging with courtesy." Zhu Bajie tied the horse and leaned it obliquely under the wall root. Tripitaka sat on a stone drum. Sun Wukong and Sha Wujing sat at the edge of the platform foundation. None came out for a long time; Sun Wukong, impatient, leapt up and entered to look. Inside was a three-room hall facing south with tall-lifting curtains. On the screen door hung a horizontal painting of "Longevity Mountain and Sea of Blessings". On the two gilt columns were pasted two great red-paper couplets reading: "Silken threads drift in the weak willow at dusk beneath the level bridge; snow-dusted fragrant plums make spring in the small courtyard." In the center stood a dull-gloss black-lacquer incense stand, with an ancient bronze beast-urn upon it. Above were six cane-back chairs and hanging screens at both ends, one for each of the four seasons.

As Sun Wukong was still peering about, there came the sound of footsteps from the back gate. A woman of neither old nor young age came out and, in a coquettish voice, asked: "Who are you to enter uninvited through a widow’s gate?" Startled, Sun Wukong kept bowing and answering: "I am a novice monk from the Great Tang of the Eastern Land, ordered to go west to worship Buddha and seek the Sutras. Our party of four disciples is passing Baofang, and night has already fallen, so we hasten to Old Bodhisattva Tan’s residence to beg for one night’s lodging." The woman smiled and invited them in: "Venerable, where are the other three? Please come." Sun Wukong called out loudly: "Master, come in." Tripitaka entered with Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, leading horse and baggage, and the woman came out of the hall to receive them. Zhu Bajie stared sidelong in secret and asked yourself how she was dressed:

She wore a fine robe of woven brocade in official green wool-silk, over it a light red padded coat; she bound a bright-yellow woven silk skirt with knotted bands, beneath it, shoes with tall, decorated soles. Her head was dressed in oiled gauze, floating in place, setting off two-tone dragon-coiled hair. A palace-style ivory comb flashed with vermilion and green, and at an angle she wore two twined gold hairpins. Cloudlike side locks were half-gray, like wings of a flying phoenix; her ears carried double dangling rows of pearl pendants. She wore no powder or rouge and was still beautiful; her beauty and charm were still like those of a young girl in her prime.

Seeing the three of Tripitaka’s party, the woman grew even more pleased and invited them with proper courtesy into the hall and rooms. After each made his greetings and all courtesy was exchanged, she told them all to sit and drink tea. Behind the screen curtain, a maid with hanging braids came forth, carrying a tray of gold and a white-jade cup. Fragrant tea steamed warmly, and strange fruit spread a subtle perfume. The maid had lively sleeves, legs slender as spring shoots; holding up the jade cup, she served tea to each in turn. She offered her salutations to all of them. After tea, she also ordered that a vegetarian meal be prepared. Tripitaka then spoke: "Venerable, what is your surname, and what is the name of this place?" The woman said: "This is the land of Xiniu Hezhou. This poor widow was born a Jia; her husband’s family name was Mo. In childhood she was unfortunate—her father and mother-in-law died early—and with her husband she kept the ancestral estate. There was family wealth of ten thousand strings and fields of a thousand qing. In her husband’s destiny there were no sons, only three daughters. Last year, great misfortune struck again and she lost her husband. As a widow this year she has now completed her mourning period. She has only this land and household remaining, with no clan kin left, only her daughters to carry it on. To marry one of them off to another household is hard if one must give up the estate. Now that the venerable Tripitaka has arrived, I thought perhaps this is the ordained hour: with your four-person pilgrimage and my four maidens, perhaps they may all find husbands among one another; the four of you seem exactly right. I know not whether your honored intention is willing." Tripitaka, hearing this, feigned deaf and dumb, closed his eyes and steadied his heart, and remained silent.

That woman said, "In this homestead there are over three hundred mu of irrigated fields, over three hundred mu of dry fields, and over three hundred mu of orchards and mountain plots. There are more than a thousand yellow water buffaloes, herds of mules and horses, and untold pigs and sheep. To the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast, we have sixty to seventy pasture enclosures in fenced farms. At home there is grain enough to last eight or nine years, ten or more years’ worth of silk and brocade robes we need never wear, and gold and silver enough for a lifetime. It is far richer than those hidden-spring brocade canopies, so what is all this talk of two rows of golden hairpins? If you and your disciples would only change your minds, accept me into your family as groomsmen, then stay in my house at your ease and enjoy wealth and honor instead of laboring for the west.” Tripitaka simply sat there as if stupefied, with no words at all.

That woman said, "I was born at the hour of the Rooster on the third day of the third month in the Dinghai year, so my late husband was three years older than I; I am now forty-five. My eldest daughter is named Zhenzhen and is twenty this year. My second daughter is named Aiai and is eighteen. My youngest daughter is named Lianlian and is sixteen. None of them has ever been betrothed. Though I am a poor, homely woman, by luck the youngest daughters all have some beauty, and each is skilled with needle and thread at everything. Because my former husband had no sons, I raised them as sons. When they were small I even had them learn some Confucian texts, and they all know a little of composing poems and antithetical verse. Though we live in a manor, we are not of the most vulgar sort; one can well imagine they would suit elders of your rank. If you are willing to open your hearts, keep your hair on your head and stay, and make a household with my home, then you could wear brocade and silk and be far better off than a ragged man in a black robe with hemp sandals and a reed hat." Tripitaka sat there like a child startled by thunder and a rain-soaked toad: only dumbfounded, he squirmed, rolled his eyes upward, and sighed.

When Zhu Bajie heard of such riches and such beauty, his heart itched and he could not bear it. Sitting on that stool, he looked as if pricked on the bottom by a needle, twisting left and right, unable to endure it. He came forward, pulled at the Master’s sleeve and said, "Master, this lady has told you so many things. Why do you pretend to ignore them? You should at least take some notice." The Master lifted his head at once, snapped, and sent him away: "You wayward beast! We are ordained people. How could wealth move the mind, or beauty hold our attention, and still be called the Way?"

The woman laughed and said, "Alas, alas. What advantage do monks have?" Tripitaka said, "Lady Bodhisattva, you are a householder. What good has this life given you?" The woman said, "Great Elder, please sit; let me tell you the benefits of household life. Look, there is a verse to prove it."

In spring, fashioning new silks is finest for the season; In summer, changing to light gauze, one delights in green lotus; In autumn there is fresh, sweet glutinous wine with fragrant grain; In winter one comes to warm halls and turns cheeks red with wine. Through all four seasons every comfort is available, and at all eight seasonal festivals there are precious dishes in abundance. Brocade curtains and silk spreads with candlelit nights surpass the merit of roaming in pilgrimage to greet Amitabha.

Tripitaka said, "Lady Bodhisattva, as one in family life you enjoy splendor and wealth, fine things to wear, fine things to eat, sons and daughters together in harmony—indeed that is good. But you do not know that those of us who have left home also have a good side. Look if this is true: there is a verse to prove it."

Taking ordination and setting one’s vow is no ordinary affair; It overturns beforehand the hall of bonds and love. When external things do not provoke idle talk, one’s body contains balanced yin and yang. If merit is fulfilled and conduct completed, one goes on toward the golden gate of morning; seeing one’s nature, enlightening the mind, one returns to one’s original home. Better than a layman in want of blood and flesh, rotting in an old foul-skin body.

When the woman heard this, she grew furious: "This unrestrained monk is impolite! If I had not looked on you with true kindness, men from the far Eastern Lands, I should have driven you out. I came with genuine heart and intention to recruit you disciples into household ties, and you have answered with words that wound me. You have taken vows and made intentions never to return to lay life, and yet you, who are in your charge, insist on such strictness and force this upon me." Tripitaka, seeing her anger, could only mutter repeatedly in deference and call out, "Sun Wukong, stay here." Sun Wukong said, "I never in childhood knew how to handle such matters; ask Zhu Bajie to stay here." Zhu Bajie said, "Brother, let us not make a scandal of others; we should consider this longer term." Tripitaka said, "Since you two will not, then tell Sha Wujing to stay here." Sha Wujing said, "Listen to what Master says. This disciple was encouraged by the bodhisattva and took the precepts and vows. Since Master received me and taught me, and though I have followed him for not even two months, I have not gained even a trace of merit. How could I dare to seek this wealth? I would rather die than do this deceitful-minded deed. I must go westward to the Buddha."

Seeing that they all refused, the woman suddenly rose and retreated behind the screen, and with a thud shut the side gate. The Master and disciples were left outside; there was no tea and no meal at all, and nobody came out. Zhu Bajie, anxious inside, complained to Tripitaka: "Master, you are terribly inept at getting things done; you should have pressed your point and settled it with words and made him offer us some proper food tonight so we could spend a pleasant night. Tomorrow, whether he says yes or no, it will be up to us. Now that the door is shut and no one comes out, how are we to pass one night, with the hearth cold and the stove full of ashes?"

Sha Wujing said, "Second Brother, why don’t you become a son-in-law in that house?" Zhu Bajie said, "Brother, don’t set a snare for people; let us consider this in due time." Sun Wukong said, "What is so hard to consider? If you are willing, then make the Master related to this lady’s family, and become a son-in-law entering at her gate. Her house has such wealth and treasure; she will certainly bring out the bridal treasures, set a feast for a relation visit, and all of us will taste good things. If you renounce it here and return to lay life, is that not beneficial on both sides?" Zhu Bajie said, "It sounds as if that is so, but it would mean I leave the order and then take a wife after wife." Sha Wujing said, "Brother, did he really have a sister-in-law before?" Sun Wukong said, "You still do not understand him. He once was the son-in-law of the old Mr. Gao of Wusang. Because old Sun subdued him, he had at one time received the bodhisattva precepts, yet could not bear it. I captured him and made him a monk, so he abandoned his previous wife and followed Master west to worship the Buddha. He has been separated for so long and then remembered that matter; now, on hearing of this other matter, that old longing has resurfaced at once. Zhu Bajie, then, become a son-in-law in this household. Just bow to old Sun a few more times and, if I do not report you, that is all." Zhu Bajie said, "Nonsense, nonsense. Everyone here has this very thought, and only old pig makes himself the one to be mocked. There is a saying: ‘Monks are lust-hungry ghosts.’ Why must this be so? All the twisting and wriggling, playing at deference, has made everything go to ruin, so now even tea and water cannot even be seen together, and no one attends to the lamps. If we get through this one night, then tomorrow we must carry people on the horse and then walk on. If we are hungry again this night, we may as well be skinned. You both stay. I will go and tend to the horse."

Zhu Bajie hastily untied the reins and pulled the horse out. Sun Wukong said, "Sha Wujing, stay here and keep company with the Master; let me follow him and see where he leads the horse." Tripitaka said, "Sun Wukong, you may go and see, but do not only mock him." Sun Wukong said, "I understand." The Great Sage stepped out of the hall, instantly changed form, became a red dragonfly, flew out through the front gate, and caught up with Zhu Bajie.

Zhu Bajie, pulling the horse, did not allow it to eat grass where there was grass, and with a quick tap-tap he drove it to the back gate. He saw the woman with three daughters waiting outside the back gate, idly standing there playing with chrysanthemums. The women saw Zhu Bajie coming and the three daughters slipped inside in an instant. The woman stood at the gate and asked, "Little Elder, where are you going?" Zhu Bajie dropped the reins and stepped forward, bowing: "Mother, I came to let out the horse." The woman said, "Your Master is too refined and difficult. He has taken a son-in-law into my house yet does not value it, preferring to be a hanging monk and go on the road west?" Zhu Bajie laughed, "They are all following Tang King’s decree and do not dare disobey the kingly order, so they refuse this matter. Just now, in the front hall, they pushed me in front of everyone. Then I had some complaints of my own, only fearing Mother might dislike my long mouth and large ears." The woman said, "I do not mind that. It is only that there is no head of house there; one son-in-law would be enough for me, only I fear the younger girls may be some to dislike ugliness." Zhu Bajie said, "Mother, do not be so picky with this matter. Think of that Tang Monk. Though he is gifted in appearance, he is really of no use. I am ugly, yes, but I have a few lines of boastful strength." The woman said, "What is it that you say?" Zhu Bajie said,

Though ugly in appearance, I am diligent and not without skill. If one says a thousand mu of fields, they need not be ploughed by oxen. With one meal and one spade, sowing can take place in good time. If there is no rain, I can petition for rain; if there is no wind, I can summon wind. If a dwelling seems too low, I can raise it two or three stories. If the ground is not swept, I can sweep it; if the drain in shade is blocked, I can clear it through. All household and neighborhood matters of a household—kicking heaven, handling wells—I can do them all." The woman said, "If you can manage household affairs like this, then go and consult your Master once more; if there is no awkwardness, I shall accept you." Zhu Bajie said, "No need to consult. He is not my natural father and mother; to do or not to do is in my own hand." The woman said, "All right, all right. I will speak with the younger girls." She glancing at it, then swiftly shut the back gate behind her.

Zhu Bajie did not even release the horse; he pulled it forward. Who could know Sun Wukong did not know everything already? He spread his wings and came flying, showing himself in his true form, and first greeted Tripitaka: 「Master, Wuneng has led the horse in.」 Tripitaka said, 「If the horse is not led, it may run off in sheer joy.」 Sun Wukong stood up laughing, and from beginning to end repeated the whole intrigue the woman and Bajie had been talking about; Tripitaka seemed half believing, half not believing it.

After a short while, they saw the clumsy fellow drag the horse up and tie it down. Tripitaka said, 「Is the horse untethered?」 Bajie said, 「There is no good grass, nowhere to let the horse graze.」 Sun Wukong said, 「If there is nowhere to turn it out, is there nowhere to lead it then?」 On hearing this, Bajie knew the message had gotten through; he hung his head, twisted his neck, pursed his lips, frowned, and stood silent for some time. Then came a sudden "yaa!" from within, a gate opened at the waist-level, two pairs of red lanterns, a portable brazier, sandalwood clouds, and tinkling belts and ornaments emerged. The woman came out with her three daughters and called, 「Zhenzhen, Aiai, Lianlian,}」 to bow before the pilgrim company. The three women stood in line in the hall and bent in homage toward the Master. Indeed they were beautiful, and as to them:

One by one their brows arched like moth wings, and their faces bloomed with spring. Their bewitching beauty could stir the heart and shake kingdoms; their supple forms were heartbreakingly alluring. Painted powder and blossoming rouge made every mood an elegant art; embroidered ribbons fluttered, far above the dust of this world. A half-hidden smile opened like budding cherries; with each paced step they exhaled the scent of orchids and musk. Their heads were crowned with pearls and green stones, and countless jewel-pins trembled in their hair; all over their limbs lay a faint fragrance, each strand delicate with gold-threaded floral embroidery. To what words can one say they rival the beauties Chu Wa and the charm of Xi Zi? They were truly nine-heaven maidens descending from above, like Chang’e of the moon stepping forth from the Radiant Hall.

Tripitaka joined his palms and lowered his head. Sun Wukong feigned as if he did not notice, while Sha Wujing turned and faced away. See how Zhu Bajie could not take his eyes off them; his lustful mind was in disarray, his desire shameless and bold. He squirmed forward and murmured softly, 「Thank you, heavenly nun, for descending. Mother, send the elder sisters away.」 The three women went behind a screen, leaving only a pair of gauze lanterns. The woman said, 「Could the four elders take thought to choose one for my young daughter?」 Sha Wujing said, 「We have already discussed it; we will take the man with the pig surname as a son-in-law.」 Bajie said, 「Brother, don't put this on me—don't haggle over it among the elders.」 Sun Wukong said, 「What further haggling? you already agreed at the rear gate, clearly and solemnly; mother has already called. What remains? Tripitaka may stand as the male in-law, the bride’s family become the bride’s side, and let me be the guarantor and Sha Wujing the matchmaker. No need to examine marriage books. Today is an exalted day of heaven’s blessing: you just bow before the Master now and enter as a true son-in-law.」 Bajie said, 「It won’t work, it won’t work—how could we do such a thing?」 Sun Wukong said, 「Bajie, do not bellow on it. From that mouth of yours, mother has been called so many times; what is impossible now? Quickly consent, take us inside and let us share wedding wine. That is best.」 With one hand he hauled Bajie, with the other he drew the woman aside: 「Mother-in-law, bring your son-in-law inside.」 Bajie’s feet shuffled and wobbled as he tried to go. The woman called to the servants: 「Set out chairs and tables, prepare the evening meal, and treat these three in-laws. I will lead the son-in-law to the chamber.」 In another hall she also ordered the cook to lay out the banquet and set tomorrow’s marriage feast. The servants accepted her command and obeyed. After they had eaten their light fare, they quickly spread bedding and all of the three party lay down to rest in the guest seats; no further details need be recorded.

Now it is said that Zhu Bajie followed the mother-in-law inside. Through layer upon layer of rooms—he could not tell how many—he bumped and knocked, tripping over thresholds at every turn. Bajie said, 「Mother, walk a little slower. My footing is poor; you lead me.」 The woman said, 「These are all storehouses, granaries, mills, and room after room of goods—we have not even reached the edge of the kitchen.」 Bajie said, 「A grand house indeed.」 Bumping and clattering, turning and winding, after another interval they finally reached the inner hall rooms. The woman said, 「Son-in-law, your elder brother said today was an especially lucky heavenly day and has invited you to come in. Only in this rush we did not invite an almanac master to arrange the ceremonial tablets or hang the marriage canopies. You may simply kneel and offer your eight bows.」 Bajie said, 「Mother, that is right. Seat yourself; let me bow a few times and that will be counted as the bride’s ceremony and a proper thanks to the in-laws—saving everyone trouble.」 The mother-in-law laughed, 「All right, all right. Truly you are a practical, efficient household son-in-law. I sit; now you bow。」

Ah! The whole hall shone with silver-candle brilliance, and the fool knelt and offered his respect upward. After finishing he said, 「Mother, which sister will you pair with me?」 She said, 「That is exactly the uncertainty: if I give the eldest daughter to you, I fear the second may object; if I give the second, I fear the third may object; if I give the third, I fear the eldest may object. So I have not finally decided.」 Bajie said, 「Mother, since you fear rivalry, give them all to me; then there will be no noisy quarrels, no disorder in household order.」 She said, 「How can this be? Would one man possess my three daughters?」 Bajie said, 「Looking at your words, Mother—doesn’t there exist three wives and four concubines? If needed, add more and this son-in-law will accept them all with a laugh. In my youth I even learned methods of conquest; surely each one would attend and satisfy you all.」 The woman said, 「No, no, no. Here I have a handkerchief. Put it on your head and cover your face, and perform a "heavenly blind wedding." Have my daughters pass by you one by one; when you reach out your hand and seize one, that is the one you marry.」 Bajie followed her instruction and took the cloth, setting it on his head. There is a poem as witness:

Foolish and dim of sense, he knows not the cause beneath, the sword of desire strikes the body—withdraw in secret. Since time immemorial one has trusted in Duke Zhou’s marriage rites, today the groom enters veiled at the brow.

Bajie, with the head covering in place, said, 「Mother, ask your daughters to come out.」 She called, 「Zhenzhen, Aiai, Lianlian, come for this blind heavenly match and pair with your son-in-law.」 One heard only the bright ringing of ornamental belts, and the scent of orchid and musk, as if fair maidens were passing by and among them. Bajie truly reached out to catch someone. He floundered wildly, missing on both sides. Again and again he lunged—left no contact, right no contact. Women moved in and out again and again; who knows how many came and went, but he could not catch a single one. He grabbed a pillar, then the other moment touched a wall board. Running in circles, he became dizzy and unsteady, could no longer stand. Instead of finding balance, he only staggered and fell. He kicked at a door panel, was blocked by a brick wall behind him, crashed and banged; with face swollen and skin blue-black on the head from the blows, he sat upon the ground. Panting and gasping, he said, 「Mother! Your daughters are so slippery and coy—they cannot be caught. I cannot catch even one. What am I to do, what am I to do?」

The woman pulled the covering from his head and said, 「Son-in-law, it is not that my daughters are too slippery. They all showed deference and courtesy and would not invite you forward.」 Bajie said, 「Mother, if they all do not want to take me, then marry me yourself.」 She said, 「Good son-in-law, quiet fool! Is this proper? You are so immodest that you would even take what your own mother-in-law invites? My three daughters are of the craftiest nature. Let each daughter wear one pearl-bowed brocade undershirt. If you can put on whichever one’s, then I will let that one receive you.」 Bajie said, 「Fine, fine, fine—bring all three and I will try them. If I can wear all three, then let me accept all three.」 The woman went into the inner room and brought out only one garment, and handed it to Bajie. Bajie took off his blue brocade straight robe, took the shirt and put it on. Before he had even fastened his belt, there was a sudden heavy thud and he fell flat. In truth, a few cords had been drawn tight. In sharp pain beyond bearing, those people had already disappeared.

Tripitaka, Sun Wukong, and Sha Wujing woke from one sleep and did not realize the eastern sky had turned pale. As soon as Tripitaka opened his eyes and looked up, there was no grand mansion there, no carved beams and painted rafters; instead each of them found himself sleeping in a stand of pines. Startled, the Master hurriedly called to Wukong. Sha Wujing said, 「Brother, enough, enough—we have encountered ghosts.」 Sun Wukong, understanding in his heart, smiled faintly and said, 「What do you mean?」 Tripitaka asked, 「Look where we are sleeping.」 Sun Wukong said, 「This under the pine forest is no bad place to lie. But I do not know where Bajie is and what suffering he endures.」 Tripitaka asked, 「What suffering?」 Sun Wukong laughed, 「Yesterday the mother and daughters of that household—who knows from which bodhisattvas they came—manifested here, descending in such guise to enchant us. They probably left at midnight; only Zhu Bajie bore the suffering.」 On hearing this, Tripitaka joined his palms and bowed. Then from behind, on an old cypress tree, a scrap of paper fluttered and hung. Sha Wujing rushed to fetch it for the Master, and found this eight-line verse:

Mother Lei Mountain once forgot the mundane world; the Bodhisattva of the South Sea summoned us down from the mountain. Puxian and Wenshu were guests there as well, transformed into maidens roaming the woods. The holy monk has virtue and is not yet stained by common ways; Zhu Bajie has no true Chan, and yet remains all worldly. From this on, calm your heart and amend your ways; if negligence returns, the road ahead will be hard.

At that moment the Elder, Sun Wukong, and Sha Wujing were still chanting this verse together when they heard a loud cry from deep in the forest: “Master, he’s killing me—save me! I won’t dare to do it again.” Tripitaka said, “Sun Wukong, is the one shouting that Zhu Bajie?” Sha Wujing said, “It is indeed.” Sun Wukong replied, “Brother, ignore him. Let’s go.” Tripitaka said, “Though that fool is dull and stubborn in nature, he is still only stubbornly direct, and he does have some strength—he can carry the baggage. Remembering what the Bodhisattva intended that day, let us save him and let him go with us; he will surely not dare again.” So Sha Wujing rolled up his blanket and packed the shoulder pole. Sun Wukong unfastened the reins and led the horse, and they entered the forest with Tripitaka to search. Ah! this was exactly:

From upright cultivation one must be diligent; sweep away lust and desire and return to the True.

In the end, it is still not known whether that fool’s fate will be fortunate or otherwise; listen, and let the next chapter explain it.
chapters.title: Chapter 23: Tripitaka never forgets his origin; the Four Holy Ones test the mind of Chan.
