This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Once again those three entered the forest and came inside. They saw the idiot monkey bound to a tree, crying aloud repeatedly, in pain he could not endure. Sun Wukong stepped forward and laughed,

'You fine son-in-law, at this hour you still cannot stand and go to your mother to give thanks, nor can you return to Master with happy news, yet here you are, still making a fool’s show. Tch! Where is your mother? Where is your wife? What a dangling, strained son-in-law you are.' The idiot, seeing him come near, grew shy in embarrassment, bit his teeth, endured the pain, and dared not cry out. Sha Wujing saw this and could not bear it; he set down the luggage, stepped forward, and untied the rope to save him. The monkey only knelt and kowtowed to all of them, and indeed could hardly bear his shame. There is a verse to the tune “West River Moon” that bears witness:

Beauty is a blade that harms the body; to be greedy for it brings inevitable disaster. A fine young woman, beautiful and well adorned, may be fiercer than a mountain demon. It starts from one original root alone; add no small profit to your bag. Keep your capital carefully and store it in due caution. Hold fast, and do not let yourself run wild.

Zhu Bajie pinched some soil, burned incense, and looked to the sky in prayer. Sun Wukong asked, 'Can you recognize those bodhisattvas?' Zhu Bajie replied, 'I already fainted and became dizzy, my vision blurred and spinning. How could I know who they were?' Sun Wukong handed the summons note to him. When Zhu Bajie saw it was a verse form, he became even more ashamed. Sha Wujing laughed, 'Second Brother, with this kind of fortune, four bodhisattvas have come for your marriage.' Zhu Bajie said, 'Brother, do not bring that up again. I am no longer fit to be called a proper son of a family. From now on I will not dare to act recklessly again. Even if I have to break my bones, it is only to bear burdens shoulder to shoulder while going with Master to the Western Regions.' Tripitaka said, 'If that is what you say, then it is right.'

When they came to the mountain, it was truly a lovely sight:

High mountains rose steep and extreme, their vast forms towering in sharp relief. Its roots clung to the veins of Kunlun, and its peaks rubbed against the streams of the Milky Way. White cranes came and went, perching on cypress and fir; dark apes at times hung among tangled vines. Sunshine lit the clear woods, and layers upon layers of red mist coiled around; wind rose in shadowed ravines, and ten thousand colored clouds drifted on the air. Hidden birds chattered wildly in the green bamboo, and patterned roosters battled together among wildflowers. There appeared Thousand-Year Peak, Wufu Peak, and Lotus Peak, majestic and awe-inspiring, giving forth a faint radiance; Wansui Stone, Huyasha Stone, and Three-Heavens Stone, crackling and gleaming, gave forth auspicious vapors. Before the cliffs the grass was lush, on the ridge tops was plum fragrance. Bramble and thorn were dense beyond measure; orchis and orchids gave off a faint scent. Deep in the forest, eagles and phoenixes gathered a thousand birds; in ancient caves, kirins ruled over myriad beasts. The stream water moved with feeling, winding and winding, with curve after curve and bay after bay. Peaks and ridges came without pause, layer upon layer, circling one around another. Again they saw green pagoda trees, mottled bamboos, and blue-green pines, each lingering through a thousand years and bursting into thick clustered bloom. White plums, red peaches, green willows, all bright and vivid, fought each other in the splendor of three springs. Dragons sang and tigers roared; cranes danced while monkeys cried. Elk came forth from among the blossoms, and azure cranes called in reply to the sun. This was truly a blessed immortal mountain, a land of true merit, as if Penglai and Langyuan themselves. Again the mountain top showed scenes of blossoms opening and fading, clouds coming and going over the ridgeline.

Tripitaka, from the saddle, spoke joyfully, 'Disciple, on my way west I have gone through so many mountains and waters, all of them rugged and perilous; none compare to this mountain. If Mount Leiyin is not far, we can go at once and appear before the World-Honored One with proper decorum and solemnity.' Sun Wukong laughed, 'Too soon, too soon—there is no getting there so quickly.' Sha Wujing said, 'Brother, how far is it from here to Leiyin?' Sun Wukong said, 'One hundred and eight thousand li. Of ten relays, not one has been fully walked yet.' Zhu Bajie asked, 'Brother, how many years will it take to get there?' Sun Wukong said, 'If we two worthy younger disciples walk it, we could reach it in about ten days. If I walk it, I can do fifty such spans in a single day and still see the sun rise. For Master? Do not even imagine it.' Tripitaka said, 'Wukong, when do you think we might arrive?' Sun Wukong said, 'From the age you have walked until you grow old, old then young, though you pass through thousands of turns it remains hard; only if your true nature is awakened and your will sincere, and your thought turns inward at each moment, there is Spirit-Mountain.' Sha Wujing said, 'Elder brother, though this is not Leiyin, by its beauty one can tell some noble person dwells here.' Sun Wukong said, 'That is true. Certainly there are no evil spirits here. It is certainly the dwelling of a holy monk or immortal, so we will roam and proceed slowly.' No further details are needed.

This mountain was called Wanshou Mountain. Within it stood an observatory called Wuzhuang Guan. In it lived an immortal with the dharma name Zhenyuanzi, known among the world simply as Tongjun. It produced a strange treasure: it had taken shape as a spiritual root formed at the time of primordial chaos, before the great blur and before heaven and earth had been separated. Among the four great continents of the world, only Wuzhuang Guan on Xiniuhe Continent produced this one, called Caohuan Dan and also known as Ren Shen Fruit. It blossoms every three thousand years, bears fruit every three thousand years, and only after another three thousand years does it fully ripen; only after ten thousand years can it be eaten. In that span of ten thousand years, it yields only thirty fruits. Each fruit is shaped like a child not yet three years old, with all four limbs complete and all five features present. If a man has the right affinity and merely smells it, he can live three hundred and sixty years. If he eats one, he may live forty-seven thousand years.

That day Zhenyuan Daxian received a memorial from Yuanshi Tianzun summoning him to the Miró Palace in Shangqing Heaven to hear a lecture on the Hunyuan Dao Fruit. Among his followers of roaming immortals there were so many he could not count them; among them he had forty-eight disciples now, all perfected and fully true. That day he led forty-six to ascend to the upper realms to attend the lecture, leaving two very young ones to guard the household: one called Qingfeng, one called Mingyue. Qingfeng was only one thousand three hundred and twenty years old, and Mingyue only one thousand two hundred. Zhenyuan Zi instructed the two boys, 'Do not violate the memorial of the Great Celestial Lord. You must go to Miró Palace to attend the teaching. You two remain at home and mind things carefully. A certain old friend will pass this way, so do not be negligent with him. Give him two of my Ren Shen Fruit to eat, to express our old affection.' The two boys said, 'Master, who is this old friend? Please tell us so we may receive him properly.' The immortal said, 'He is a holy monk from the Great Tang court of the East, Dharma name Tripitaka, now going westward to the Western Heaven to seek sutras from the Buddha.' The two boys laughed, 'Confucius said, “When the Way differs, there is no way to conspire together.” We are from the Taiyi Xuanmen tradition. How can we have any acquaintance with that monk?' Zhenyuan Zi replied, 'How do you know? That monk is Jinchanzi reborn, the second disciple of the Buddha of the Western Supreme Old Man, the Tathagata. Five hundred years ago, I met him at the Lanbo Gathering. He personally served me tea, and the Buddha-child honored me; therefore he is indeed an old friend.'

Hearing this, the two immortal boys obeyed the command. When Zhenyuan left, he again instructed them, 'My fruit is limited; you may give only two to him, no more.' Qingfeng said, 'When I opened the orchard, the assembly all ate two, and there are still twenty-eight left on the tree. I dare not give more.' Zhenyuan said, 'Though Tang Sanzang is an old friend, be careful of the noisy household men under him. Do not let him know.' The two children accepted the order. Zhenyuan then took all his disciples and ascended, and went straight to Heaven.

Then Tripitaka and the three companions wandered about the mountain. Suddenly, looking up, they saw a cluster of pines and bamboos and layered towers and pavilions. Tripitaka said, 'Wukong, what place is that?' Wukong looked and said, 'That place is not a mere village or estate; it must be a monastery. Let us walk around there and then we will know clearly.' Not long afterward they came before the gate and saw:

The pine slopes were cool and sparse, the bamboo path tranquil and secluded. White cranes passed back and forth, carrying drifting clouds; monkeys moved up and down among the trees, offering fruit in turn. Before the gate was a broad pool, with long tree shadows; stones split, and mossy blossoms scattered. The buildings stood in dense rank, reaching toward the purple heights; towers and halls stood mist-soft, as if rosy clouds had fallen from above. It truly was a blessed land and spirit-filled terrain, a Penglai cloud-cave. In this clear emptiness human affairs were few, and in the stillness the Way arose in the heart. Blue birds each carried letters from Queen Mother, and purple phoenixes often conveyed the texts of the Elder Lord. One cannot exhaust the vast wind of upright virtue; indeed it is plainly a faintly mysterious dwelling of immortals.

Tripitaka dismounted and stepped down from the horse. He then saw on the left of the gate a stele with ten large characters: 'Wanshou Mountain, blessed land, Wuzhuang Cave-Heaven.' Tripitaka said, 'Disciple, this truly is a monastic estate.' Sha Wujing said, 'Master, this scene is vivid. Anyone who dwells here must be virtuous. Let us enter and see; even if we are to return eastward, this place itself is a landscape worth seeing.' Wukong said, 'Well said.' So they all entered together. Then they saw on the two gateposts a pair of spring couplets: 'Immortal palace of long life and no aging. A Daoist household sharing heaven-lengthened life.' Wukong laughed, 'This Taoist is boasting to frighten people. When I, old Sun, caused a great upheaval in Heaven Palace five hundred years ago, I did not once see such a boast written at Tai Shang Laojun’s gate.' Zhu Bajie said, 'Do not bother with that. Let us enter. Perhaps this Taoist has some true virtue; we cannot yet know.'

When they reached the second gate, they saw an urgent rush of movement within; two young boys came running out. Their appearance was this:

Their bones were clear, their spirits bright; their faces handsome, with topknots and short, tousled hair. Their Taoist robes naturally wrapped the chest in mistlike folds, and their feather garments had sleeves that drifted in the wind. Silk cords were tightly tied in dragon-head knots; light sandals, softly wrapped, held by soft cocoons. Their grace was most extraordinary, unlike ordinary folk. Truly they were the two immortal youths Qingfeng and Mingyue.

That youth bent low, bowing with folded back and outstretched arm, came out to greet him: 'Honored Master, I failed to receive you in time; please be seated.' Tripitaka was pleased, and then he and the two immortal youths entered the main hall to inspect it. The hall complex faced south with five chambers, all latticed carving, bright above and dim below. One immortal youth pushed open the lattice and invited Tripitaka into the hall; on the wall center hung the two great characters for 'Heaven and Earth' in five-colored form. A vermilion carved-lacquered incense table stood there, and on it was a pair of golden incense vessels, with incense prepared neatly beside the brazier.

Tripitaka came forward, took a pinch of incense in his left hand, poured it into the furnace, and made three bows. After bowing, he turned and said, 'Immortal youth, this Wuzhuang Monastery is truly like the immortal realm of the West. Why do you offer incense only to the two words Heaven and Earth, and not to the Three Purities, the Four Emperors, and the officers of Luotian?' The boy smiled: 'I will not hide it from you, Master. Of these two characters, the upper side can still be taken as proper to receive offerings, but the lower side cannot take our incense; this is all our master’s self-flattery.' Tripitaka asked, 'What is this self-flattery?' The boy replied, 'The Three Purities are my master's friends, the Four Emperors his old companions; the Nine Luminaries are his juniors, and Yuancheng is his subordinate guest.' On hearing this, the Great Sage laughed heartily. Zhu Bajie said, 'Brother, why are you laughing?' Wukong said, 'I thought only Old Sun could stir up trouble, and it turns out this Tao boy can stir the wind as well.' Tripitaka asked, 'Where is your master?' The boy said, 'My master, Primordial-Supreme Lord of Heaven, has gone by imperial summons to Miro Hall in Shangqing Heaven to lecture on the mixed-source Dao fruit, so he is not at home.' On hearing this, Wukong could not help shouting, 'What a vulgar Tao boy—you cannot even recognize who stands before you, yet you raise tricks in his presence and brag about empty airs? Who in that Miro Palace is a Taiyi celestial immortal? Go and tell this oaf how you should speak!'

Seeing his fury rise, Tripitaka feared the boy might answer back and stir trouble, so he said, 'Sun Wukong, do not quarrel. Now that we have entered, we should simply leave and appear dignified. As the saying goes, a heron does not eat heron flesh. His master is absent; why disrupt him? You go to the mountain gate and leave the horse, Sha Wujing guard the luggage, and tell Zhu Bajie to unpack and take out some grain. Borrow their stove and cook us one meal. When we are ready to depart, give him a few strings of firewood money and be done. Each of you do your assigned duty. Let me rest here for a while; once we have eaten, we will go.' The three each did as directed and went to their tasks.

Mingyue and Qingfeng praised in whispers without end: 'What a good monk! Truly a saint beloved of the West has descended among mortals, with original purity still intact. Master ordered us to receive Tripitaka and offer him ginseng fruit to show our old ties, and also told us to be watchful that we do not disturb his attendants. Those three are indeed rough-faced and rough-natured. Luckily we have managed to divert them away. If they had been out front, they would never have seen the ginseng fruit.' Qingfeng said, 'Brother, we do not yet know if that monk is Master’s old friend. Better to ask him directly and avoid error.' The two boys stepped forward again: 'May we ask if the monk is Tripitaka, the one from Great Tang traveling west for the scriptures?' Tripitaka bowed and said, 'I am the poor Tripitaka.' The boy said, 'When my master set out, he ordered us disciples to receive you from afar. Unexpectedly the imperial summons came quickly and I failed to welcome you in time. Please be seated, Master; wait while my brother brings tea to serve you.' Tripitaka said, 'I dare not.' Mingyue hurried back to the room, brought one cup of fragrant tea, and offered it to the elder. After he drank, Qingfeng said, 'Brother, do not disobey Master’s order; you and I will go get some fruit.'

The two boys bade farewell to Tripitaka and together went inside. One took the golden clapper, one took a cinnabar tray, and they also put a green cloth under the tray bottom, then went straight to the ginseng orchard. Qingfeng climbed up the tree and knocked the fruit with the golden clapper; Mingyue stood below receiving them in the tray. After a while, two fruits came down and were caught in the tray; he brought them directly to the front hall and offered them: 'Tang Master, Wuzhuang Monastery is on wild, poor ground with nothing else to present. These are two plain ginseng fruits; take them only to quench your thirst.' Tripitaka saw them and, all trembling, stepped back three feet, saying, 'Excellent, excellent! This year has been rich and full of grain; how can this monastery be so barren as to eat people? This is a child not yet three days old. How can he quench my thirst?' Qingfeng thought to himself, 'This monk, always in the arena of disputation, this sea of right and wrong, has no sense of our immortal rarity, so he takes these for ordinary children.' Mingyue stepped forward: 'Master, this is called ginseng fruit; eating one would do no harm.' Tripitaka replied, 'Nonsense. His mother and father must have suffered unspeakable pain carrying him in the womb before he was born. In less than three days, how could they bring him here and offer him as fruit?' Qingfeng said, 'It truly grew on the tree.' Tripitaka said, 'Nonsense, nonsense. Can a tree bear a child? Do not bring him; he is no fruit but a child.'

The two boys, unable to make him eat after endless urging, had no choice but to take the tray back to their room. The fruit itself was strange: it must not be left for long, and if kept too long it would stiffen and become unfit to eat. The two of them entered the room, one each, sat by the bedstead, and simply began to eat.

Ah—so this is how it is. Their Tao chamber shared a close partition wall with the kitchen, and whispers on this side were heard clearly on that side. Zhu Bajie, while cooking in the kitchen, had already heard them mention taking the golden clapper and the cinnabar tray, and it stayed in his mind; he also heard that Tripitaka did not recognize it as ginseng fruit and had taken it in the room to eat. He could not keep saliva in his mouth and muttered, 'How can I get even a bite of something new?' His body was wild and hard to bear, and he could not move freely, so he waited for Wukong to come and argue with him. At the stove-front his mind was on nothing but fire, and he kept poking his head out every now and then to look around. Soon, he saw Wukong bringing in the horse, tying it to a locust tree, and then going back. The brute waved his arms wildly: 'This way, this way.' Wukong turned at the kitchen door and said, 'Bajie, why all this shouting? If we lack rice, let the old monk eat first; after he is full we can go to a rich house ahead and eat again.' Zhu Bajie said, 'You came in, and it is not because there was no rice. There is a treasure in this monastery; do you know it?' Wukong said, 'What treasure?' Zhu Bajie laughed, 'If I tell you, you have never seen it; if I give it to you, you do not recognize it.' Wukong said, 'You stupid one, mocker of old Sun. I have, in five hundred years of seeking the Dao, wandered through sea and sky among immortals; has a thing like this ever not appeared?' Zhu Bajie said, 'Brother, have you ever seen ginseng fruit?' Wukong exclaimed, 'Truly, never. I have only heard people say that ginseng fruit is a life-restoring herb-and-elixir. Whoever eats it gains greatly lengthened life. Where would one get such a thing now?' Zhu Bajie said, 'It exists here. Those youths gave two to Master, but he did not recognize them and said they were infants not yet three days old and he dared not eat. The boy was so indolent that since Master did not eat, he thought it should be for us. He hid it from us and sat in the adjoining room, one each, munching and munching; then came out to leave. That has left my mouth watering. How can I taste something fresh? I thought you were nimble and could slip into their orchard and steal a few to try.' Wukong said, 'Easy enough. Old Sun will have it handled in one reach.' He moved to leave at once. Zhu Bajie grabbed him: 'Brother, I heard him in this room say he was going to take some golden clapper and strike. It must be done cleanly and without spreading wind.' Wukong said, 'I know. I know.'

The Great Sage used a hiding-and-disappearing technique and slipped into the Tao room to look. The two youths had already eaten the fruit and gone to the front hall to speak with Tripitaka; they were no longer inside. Wukong looked all around for the golden clapper, and only saw on the lattice a strip of red-gold hanging there, about two chi long and a finger thick. At its lower end was a garlic-knob-like head, at its upper end a hole, with a green velvet cord tied there. He said, 'This must surely be what they call the golden clapper.' He took it down, left the Tao room, and went straight to the back, pushing open two doors. Lifting his head, he looked and exclaimed, 'This is a garden!':

Vermilion rails and jewel-like balustrades, ridged terraces curving like small hills. Wondrous flowers competed with the radiant sun for beauty; jade bamboos contended with the blue sky for color. Outside the Pavilion of Pouring Cups, a bay of green willows drifted like smoke. Before the Moon-Viewing Terrace, several clusters of lofty pines spread like indigo paint. Scarlet fluttering, brocade-nested pomegranates; green and tender, embroidered-cushion grasses; blue and soft, blue-sand orchids; vast and graceful, set by the stream. Amber osmanthus shone near the golden-well parasol trees, and brocaded locusts lined vermilion rails and jade paving. Some peaches with a thousand leaves were red or white, and chrysanthemums were fragrant or yellow in the ninth autumn. Vining frames threw light onto the peony pavilion; hibiscus terraces linked to peony beds. One could not get to the end of frost-defying gentlemanly bamboos and snow-defying lofty pines. There were also Crane Hall and Deer Hall, square wetlands and round pools; spring water ran like broken jade, the ground mounded in goldlike heaps. The north wind touched and made the white plum blossoms open, while spring came and broke into the pink of flowering begonia. Indeed this is truly the first fairy-scene among all human lands, the foremost floral assemblage of the Western Regions.

Crops for all four seasons were planted: spinach-like greens, chard chives, and young ginger shoots. Bamboo shoots, sweet yams, melons, calabash gourds, white jiaobai, scallions, garlic, coriander, chives, and shallots. Woqu, tonghao, bitter herbs, and eggplant-plants with bottle gourds set out in rows. Mangjing and radishes, sheep-head turnips tucked in, with red amaranth, green bok choy, and purple mustard.

The Great Sage laughed and said, 'He too is a Taoist who grows his own and eats by himself.'

After walking past the vegetable plot, Sun Wukong saw another gate. He pushed it open and peered in, and there in the very center stood a great tree: truly lush green branches, dark and shadowy leaves, the leaves shaped like plantain. It rose straight up more than a thousand chi, and at its root it was seven or eight zhang across, round and broad. The Great Sage leaned against the tree and looked up. On a southern branch he saw a ginseng fruit that truly looked like a child. As it were, it had a stalk at the end, and from its perch on the bough its hands and feet seemed to wriggle, its head bobbing as if nodding, and when the wind passed it seemed to make a sound. Sun Wukong could not contain his joy and praised himself: "Excellent! truly rare, truly rare!" Leaning on the tree, with a breath he climbed up at once. He was the first monkey to know how to climb a tree and steal fruit. He struck it with his golden clapper, and the fruit came down with a thud. He leapt down to follow, but it vanished at once. He searched in the grass on all sides, and there was no trace at all.

Sun Wukong said, "What an odd trick, what an odd trick. I suppose if it can walk it can run, and even if it ran it still could not jump over the wall. I know now: the land spirit of this garden does not allow Old Sun to steal his fruit, so he must have carried it off once I took it." He then chanted a formula, pinched the spell, and intoned a single Om, summoning the Garden Landlord. The spirit came and bowed to him: "The Great Sage summons the little god. What is the command?" Sun Wukong said, "You do not know that Old Sun is a thief famed across Heaven and Earth. In my day I stole peaches of immortality, plundered court wine, and pilfered elixirs of life, yet no one dared share with me. How is it then that today, when I took one ginseng fruit, you snatched it from my head? The fruit hangs on a tree; even birds in the sky should have their share. Old Sun taking one is no great harm. Why, just when it fell, you grabbed it?" The land spirit replied, "Great Sage, you have mistaken the little god. This treasure belongs to an earth-immortal. I am but a ghost-immortal; how dare I touch it? I could not even be worthy of smelling it."

Sun Wukong asked, "If you did not take it, how is it that it disappeared after it fell?" The land spirit answered, "Great Sage, you only know that this treasure prolongs life; you do not know its origin." Sun Wukong asked, "What origin?" The land spirit said, "This treasure blooms every three thousand years, bears fruit every three thousand years, and needs another three thousand to fully ripen. In a brief span of ten thousand years it yields only thirty. One who is fated may sniff it and live three hundred sixty years; one who eats one may live forty-seven thousand years. It obeys only the cycle of the Five Phases." "What does it mean to obey the Five Phases?" Sun Wukong asked. The land spirit explained, "When it meets metal it falls; when it meets wood it withers; when it meets water it dissolves; when it meets fire it scorches and is useless; when it meets earth it sinks into the ground. It should be struck down only with a metal implement. Once knocked down, it must be caught on a tray padded with silk cloth. If placed on wood it will wither, and then it cannot be eaten for longevity. It must be used in porcelain, dissolved in clear water, and eaten. If near fire it becomes charred and useless. If near earth it goes down into it. The earth here is four-thousand and seventy years old—no, forty-seven thousand; even a steel auger cannot bore through a grain of it, it is three or four points harder than raw cast iron. It is because one who eats it thereby gains long life. If the Great Sage does not believe, test the ground here." Sun Wukong flicked out his Golden-Hooped Staff and struck once. A sharp sound burst out as the staff sprang up, yet the ground bore no mark. "Indeed, indeed," said Sun Wukong. "This staff breaks stone like powder and leaves scars on forged iron. How is it that this strike did not damage it at all? Then I have wrongly accused you. Go back." The land spirit returned to his own shrine.

Sun Wukong, however, had a plan. One hand striking with his clapper, with the other he pulled up the hem of his robe of brocade lining and made a pouch. Then he worked his way along the branches and leaves, struck three fruits, and caught them in the fold of his robe. He leapt down and went straight to the kitchen. Zhu Bajie asked, "Brother, is there any?" Sun Wukong said, "Why, this is no ordinary thing. Old Sun has it in hand. As for this fruit, we need not burden Sha Wujing to carry it; call him." "Wujing," Zhu Bajie called. Sha Wujing took down the baggage and ran into the kitchen. "Brother, why did you call me?" he asked. Sun Wukong untucked the robe pouch and said, "Brother, see what this thing is." Sha Wujing saw it and said, "It is ginseng fruit." Sun Wukong said, "Good! You recognize it—you had eaten this before, had you not?" Sha Wujing replied, "Though my junior brother has not eaten it, I once served as a curtain-guard marshal and attended the Phoenix-carriage in the Peach-Peaching banquet, where I saw this fruit offered for the Queen Mother to celebrate her longevity. I saw it then, but did not eat it. Brother, could you let me taste a little?" Sun Wukong said, "No need to talk. Each brother gets one."

The three of them each took one of the three fruits and ate it. Zhu Bajie had a large appetite and an even larger mouth; having heard a young attendant eat, his gluttonous cravings had already stirred. When he saw the fruit he snatched it up, opened his mouth, and gulped it down whole with a gurgling swallow. He then stared with wide, white-rimmed eyes and bawled to Sun Wukong and Sha Wujing, "What are you two eating?" Sha Wujing said, "It is ginseng fruit." Zhu Bajie asked, "What does it taste like?" Sun Wukong said, "Wujing, do not mind him. You ate first and only now ask whose?" Zhu Bajie said, "Brother, I ate in haste and not the way you two do, carefully chewing and tasting it. I do not even know whether there was a pit, so I swallowed it all at once. Brother, I suppose it is wonderful. It has stirred my ravenous craving all over again; let's get another so I can eat slowly, old pig as befits a gentleman." Sun Wukong said, "Brother, you do not know when to stop. This fruit is not like rice gruel or noodles, where eating fills the stomach. A thing that in ten-thousand years yields only thirty fruits—if we now have eaten one, that is by great destiny, not to be wasted. Enough, enough, enough!" He got up, grabbed a golden clapper, slipped it through the window slat, and tossed it into his chamber, completely ignoring him.

The stubborn one went on chattering and muttering nonstop. Unexpectedly those two Dao boys entered the room again to take tea out for offering, and they could hear Zhu Bajie still crying, "The ginseng fruit did not taste quite right; if I could get another one, I should eat it." Qingfeng heard it and wondered, "Mingyue, did you hear the long-mouthed monk? 'I need another ginseng fruit to eat.' Master had warned us before departing: guard what is under our charge, lest he think his men stole our treasure." Mingyue turned around and said, "Brother, it is bad, it is bad! how did the golden clapper end up on the ground? Let us go to the garden and see."

The two of them hurried off at once. They found the garden gate open. Qingfeng said, "I was the one who closed this gate. How was it opened?" Then they rushed around and found the vegetable-garden gate also open. They hurried into the ginseng grove, leaned on the tree, and counted by looking up and down. They could count only twenty-two. Mingyue said, "Can you do arithmetic?" Qingfeng said, "I can. You tell me what we had." Mingyue said, "There should have been thirty. Master opened the garden, and we ate two, so twenty-eight remained. Just now we gave two to Tangjika and he ate them, so there should have been twenty-six. Now only twenty-two remain. That is not one short but four. No need to discuss. It must be those villains, and we should only accuse Master."

The two went out through the gate and came straight to the hall, pointed at Tripitaka, and with both front and back tongues of abuse, filth and obscenity poured from them without pause—loud, foul, and uncontrolled. Tripitaka, unable to bear it, said, "Immortal boys, what is all this noise? Settle down. Say what you have to say in order, do not spread lies." Qingfeng said, "Are your ears deaf? I speak plainly, you do not understand? You have eaten the ginseng fruit, and you do not let me speak." Tripitaka asked, "What does a ginseng fruit look like?" Mingyue said, "You were just given one to eat—did you not say it looked like a child?" Tripitaka said, "Amitabha Buddha! The moment I saw that thing, I was frightened. How could I dare to steal and eat it? Even if this ravenous brute did it, I would never do such wickedness. Do not wrong a man." Qingfeng said, "Even if you did not eat it, your men wish to steal and eat it." Tripitaka said, "That can be true. But do not shout. Let me question them. If they stole it, I will have them compensate you." Mingyue said, "Compensate! With what money can they buy the like of this?" Tripitaka said, "Even if there is money, where can they buy it? As the saying goes, righteousness and loyalty are worth a thousand pieces of gold. Have them pay with a proper apology and that is enough. And we still do not even know whether it was they or not." Mingyue said, "How could it be someone else? They themselves did not divide equally, and they are still shouting there." Tripitaka called out, "Disciples, all of you come." Sha Wujing heard and said, "This is bad. Teacher Father has called us. If the two Dao boys are cursing us, this is not just the old tale of rumor, but something else indeed." Sun Wukong said, "To expose it would be a deadly shame. This is only a matter of food and drink; if we speak of it, we are admitting we stole from them. Simply deny it." Zhu Bajie agreed, "Exactly, exactly. Let us just pretend not to understand." The three then came out of the kitchen and went up to the hall.

In the end, they still did not know how to wriggle out of his accusation. Read on to the next chapter for the resolution.
chapters.title: Chapter 24: Immortal Zhenyuan of Wanshou Mountain detains an old companion; at Wuzhuang Monastery the Wanderer steals people’s ginseng.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Then his two brothers and he came into the hall and said to Tripitaka, “The meal is nearly ready—what are we to do?” Tripitaka replied, “My disciples, this is not about food. In this monastery there are some ginseng fruits, small as a child’s body. Which one of you stole and ate his fruit?” Zhu Bajie said, “I am honest; I do not know. I did not see it.” Qingfeng said, “The one who was smiling was him, the one who was smiling was him.” Wukong shouted, “Old Sun was born with this smile. Has my laughing face become forbidden just because you lost some fruit?” Tripitaka said, “My disciple, restrain your anger. We are ordained men; do not be deceitful or eat food taken in secret. If you truly ate it, then make proper amends. Why deny it so stubbornly?” Seeing that his master spoke reasonably, Wukong spoke frankly: “Master, it was none of my doing. It was that Zhu Bajie heard those two Dao boys eating some ginseng fruit. He wanted to taste one new fruit himself and sent me to fetch three. Each of us brothers ate one. We have already eaten them all. What now should we do?” Mingyue said, “He stole all four of mine, and the monk still says he is no thief.” Zhu Bajie said, “Amitabha Buddha! If four were stolen, why were only three brought out to divide, with one already set aside first?” That fool then blurted out nonsense in return.

The two Dao boys had asked truly, and their insults only increased. The Great Sage ground his iron teeth together, his fire-bright eyes wide, and he shook the Golden-Hooped Staff again and again; enduring and enduring, he said, “If that boy wished me to be beaten in person, let him at least vent some anger on me. I’ll give him a final stratagem—let him and all of them not get to eat a mouthful.” Sun Wukong then plucked one hair from the top of his head, breathed out divine breath, and cried, “Transform!” He became a false Wukong and stood beside Tripitaka with Wuneng and Wujing, enduring the Dao boys’ abuse. From his real body he sent out one spirit, shot upward like a cloud and leapt away, going straight to the ginseng grove. He tugged the Golden-Hooped Staff, struck the tree with a hard clack, and by the force used to move mountains and shift ridges, he pushed it down. Alas, the tree split, leaves flew, and its roots emerged from the ground; the Daoist’s ginseng-root stock was broken off. The Great Sage searched among the branches for fruit, but not even half a fruit could he find. The treasure answered to metal: his staff’s two ends were gilded, and the iron was of fivefold metal, so once it struck, the fruit came raining down; and when they came down, the earth swallowed them. Thus there was none left above. He said, “Good, good, good! Let everyone allay the uproar.” He took up the staff, headed straight forward again, shook the hair, and withdrew his body back in. Mortal naked eyes could not see clearly what had happened.

The two Dao boys had insulted enough. Qingfeng said, “Mingyue, these monks have borne enough cursing. We have been scolding them like a pair of chicks, scolding for half this interval, and there is no sign from them. He must not have stolen. If the tree is tall and the leaves dense, we may not have counted rightly. Do not have wrongfully blamed him; you and I will check again.” Mingyue agreed. The two returned to the orchard. They saw the tree fallen and split wide, with no fruit and no leaves on the ground. Qingfeng was so frightened his legs gave way and he fell backward to the roots; Mingyue’s waist went cold and his limbs failed him. Both were shaken to the core. There is a poem proving this:

Tripitaka came westward to Wanshou Mountain, Wukong cut down the elixir roots. The tree split open, leaves scattered, immortal roots laid bare; Mingyue and Qingfeng felt their hearts turn cold.

The two collapsed in the dust, their speech confused, crying only, “How is this? how is this? We have ruined the elixir foundation of Wuzhuang Monastery, cut off our immortal seed-line. When master comes home, how shall we answer him?” Mingyue said, “Brother, do not bellow. Let us first set our garments straight; do not frighten these monks. There is no other one here. It must be that loud-mouthed fellow with the shaggy face and thunder-mouth who came, made tricks with spirit and magic, and ruined our treasure. If we explain it to him, he will finally deny it and demand a quarrel. If we quarrel, we must come to blows. Think how we two can stand against his four? Better we deceive him first: say the fruits were many, we miscounted, and then make an apology to him. Their meal is already cooked; when he comes to eat, we can give him a little side dish.” One of the boys held a bowl, I stood on the right of the gate and he on the left. I would slam the gate shut, fix the lock, and lock all the gate layers together, not letting him out. When Tripitaka returns home, he can decide what to do. He is master’s old acquaintance, and sparing him would also be master’s kindness. If we do not spare him, we can hold a thief in custody and perhaps avoid our own blame.” Hearing this, Qingfeng said, “You are right, you are right.”

They forced up their spirits and feigned cheer, then came from the rear garden straight to the hall and knelt with bowed backs before Tripitaka: “Master, earlier our words were crude and we spoke out of line in many ways. Do not blame us.” Tripitaka asked, “What is the matter?” Qingfeng said, “There were plenty of fruits. The leaves were high and thick, so we could not see clearly. We went and checked again, and the count is unchanged.” Zhu Bajie broke in, “You child! Being young you do not know things and have come to rant and curse, babbling with your mouth, falsely blaming us too, not fitting for a disciple.” Wukong understood clearly in his heart but said nothing, thinking inwardly, “It is a lie. It is a lie. The fruit is finished and fully settled. How can they speak this way? There must be some way to raise the dead and revive the living.” Tripitaka said, “If so, bring the meal; let us eat and then go.”

Then Zhu Bajie served the rice and Sha Wujing set the stools. The two boys hurriedly brought out the small side dishes, in all seven or eight plates: soy-sauced melon, soy eggplant, fermented radish, vinegar beans, pickled vegetables, and mustard greens. They also brought a good tea jar and two tea cups and stood ready on either side. The four disciples had only just lifted their bowls when the two boys, one on each side, slammed the doors shut and fixed two heavy bronze locks. Zhu Bajie laughed, “This child has gone too far. In this place your customs are poor indeed—why have you closed the doors while we are to eat?” Mingyue said, “Exactly so. At least eat your meal first, then open the gate.” Qingfeng shouted, “You greedy, nosing, bald thief! You stole my immortal fruit and are already guilty of one sin: feeding on a cultivator’s orchard fruit. And you also knocked over my immortal tree, breaking the roots of Wuzhuang Monastery’s sacred stock, and you still dare to speak back. If you can even reach the Western Buddha’s court, only by rolling backward in a cart and taking rebirth again might you survive.” Hearing this, Tripitaka dropped his meal bowl, setting the words in his heart as one would set a stone. The boys locked the front gate and both of the side gates. They returned once more to the central hall gate and hurled curses before and behind, abusing him until dusk darkened, then they ate. After the meal, they went back to their chambers.

Tripitaka rebuked Wukong: “You monkey-headed one, you keep running into disasters. You stole his fruit and only suffered a little of his anger; letting him curse us a few words would have been enough. Why did you topple his tree as well? If this came before an accusation, even if your own father were an official, he would not be able to defend it.” Wukong said, “Master, do not make a fuss. The Dao boys have gone to sleep. When they are truly asleep, we can leave in the middle of the night.” Sha Wujing said, “Elder Brother, many gates are locked. How can we possibly get out?” Wukong laughed, “No matter, no matter. Old Sun has his own way.” Zhu Bajie said, “It’s all your fault for having no methods. You can change form once and a leech-like creature can slip through a lattice slit and fly out. We suffer because we cannot change at all, and must stand here wearing this punishment.” Tripitaka said, “If he makes this kind of racket again, he will not let you and I go out. If I begin to chant the old-folk scripture, how will he bear it?” Hearing this, Zhu Bajie said with a worried laugh, “Master, what kind of words are you saying? In Buddhist scripture I have heard only the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Lotus Sūtra, Peacock Sūtra, Guanyin Sūtra, and Diamond Sūtra. I have never heard anything called an ‘Old-folk Sūtra.’” Wukong said, “Brother, you do not know. The band on my head is what Guanyin bestowed on my master. Master deceived me into wearing it; it grew into my flesh like roots, and there is no way to remove it. It is called the Tightening Headband Spell, also called the Tightening Headband Canon. That ‘old-folk scripture’ is this. But if it is chanted, my head will ache; this is the method by which I am held in check. Master, do not chant it. I will not fail you; by our powers we will all leave together.”

By the time they had finished speaking, dusk had already fallen; they had not even noticed the moon rise in the east. Sun Wukong said, ‘At this hour all sounds are still, the moon is clear and bright; now is the moment to go.’ Zhu Bajie said, ‘Brother, no mischief now—every gate is bolted shut. Where could we go?’ Sun Wukong said, ‘Watch my way.’ Twirling the Golden-Hooped Staff in his hand, he performed an Unlocking Spell and pointed at the gate. There was a sharp clatter, and several layers of doors and their crossbars dropped together; the leaves of the gate flew open with a rasping sound. Zhu Bajie laughed, ‘Fine skill indeed. Even if a little forge-boy used a pry-tool, it would never be so quick and clean.’ Sun Wukong said, ‘This gate is no ordinary one. It is the Nántiān Gate, and I opened it with one finger.’ He invited the Master out, mounted him on the horse, had Zhu Bajie shoulder the pannier, and told Sha Wujing to gather up the horse. Then they rode straight toward the western road. Sun Wukong said, ‘Move slowly. Let me stay and care for those two boys until they sleep it off for a month.’ Tripitaka said, ‘Disciple, do not harm their lives. Otherwise it will be another crime of killing and injuring others for gain.’ Sun Wukong replied, ‘I know.’ He then returned once more and came to the door outside where the boys were sleeping. At his waist he had with him the drowsy insects he had won in a game of knucklebones against Zengzhang, the Heaven King, at the Dongtian Gate. He took out two of them, slid them through a slit of the window, and sent them straight to the boys’ faces. They snored heavily and no one could think to wake. He then set off, extending his Cloud-Walk, caught up with Tripitaka, and, once back on the main road, ran straight west.

That whole night they rode without rest, and came out as dawn broke. Tripitaka said, ‘That monkey of mine has nearly killed me. Because of your mouth, you kept me awake all night.’ Sun Wukong said, ‘Do not complain only. The sky is light; do as I say—find a bit of shelter by the trees along the road, catch a little rest to recover your spirit, and then continue.’ The elder could only dismount, leaning against the root of a pine to fashion a makeshift meditation bed. Sha Wujing set down the shoulder-pole and dozed. Zhu Bajie slept with a stone for a pillow. The Great Sage had a prankster’s bent; you could see him springing among the trees and playing with the branches. As for the four resting, there is nothing more to add.

Later, that Immortal dispersed the assembly in Yuanshi Palace, led his young immortals out of Doushuai, descended to Yao Heaven on auspicious clouds, and came early to the gate of Wanshou Mountain’s Wuzhuang Observatory. He saw that the hall gate stood open and the ground was clean. The Immortal said, ‘Qingfeng and Mingyue, still useful still. In ordinary times, even at this hour one cannot even stretch one’s waist for three zhang; since we are away today, he has gone so early to open the gate and sweep it.’ The young immortals all approved. They entered the hall: all incense and worship were gone, no one was to be seen, and no one else remained where Mingyue and Qingfeng had been. The immortals said, ‘Those two must have taken something away while we were out.’ The Immortal said, ‘Impossible! Can those who cultivate immortality have such wickedness? It is more likely that last night they forgot to close the gate, went to sleep, and have not yet woken this morning.’ The immortals came to the boys’ room door and saw it truly shut; they lay snoring so deep that no clamor at the door could wake them. The immortals pried open the panels and pulled out the bed, yet the boys still would not wake. The Immortal laughed, ‘Good young immortals. A true immortal, with spirit full and whole, should not be this drowsy. Could someone have tampered with them?’ He said, ‘Quick, fetch water.’ One boy hastily took half a cup and handed it to the Immortal. The Immortal spoke his incantation, spat a mouthful, sprayed it on their faces, and at once the sleep-miasma was lifted.

The two only just woke, then suddenly opened their eyes, rubbed their faces, raised their heads, and recognized their Immortal Master, Shitongjun and their brother-immortals. In panic, Qingfeng knelt flat and Mingyue bowed fully, saying, ‘Master, your old acquaintances were monks from the East, a band of brigands, all quite fierce.’ The Immortal laughed and said, ‘Do not fear. Tell it in order.’ Qingfeng said, ‘Master, shortly after we parted, a monk from Eastern-land Tang came. He had four monks in his party and a horse, five mouths in all. As disciples we dared not disobey your order, so we asked after their business and offered two Ren Shen fruits. That monk’s worldly eyes were ignorant and he did not understand our immortal treasure. He said the fruit was not yet fit for children of not even three dawns and refused to eat, again and again. So each disciple ate one. Then among his followers there were three disciples, one surnamed Sun, named Wukong the Walker. He first stole and ate four fruits. The disciples spoke plainly to him a few times. He would not allow it and, within himself, used a spirit-lulled technique. Alas…’ As the two boys spoke, tears kept falling from their cheeks. The immortals said, ‘Did that monk beat you?’ Mingyue said, ‘He did not beat us. He only knocked over our Ren Shen tree.’ Hearing this, the Immortal became no angrier, saying, ‘Do not weep. Do not weep. You do not know that the one surnamed Sun is also a Great Immortal of Taiyi, who once made great trouble in Heaven and whose powers are vast. Since he toppled the treasured tree, do you recognize those monks?’ Qingfeng said, ‘We recognize them all.’ The Immortal said, ‘Since you recognize them, follow me. All disciples, ready the punishments and restraints; wait until I return and strike him.’ The immortals obeyed.

The Immortal lifted up auspicious light with Mingyue and Qingfeng and flew to pursue Tripitaka. In a single instant they were a thousand li away. The Immortal looked westward among the clouds but could not see Tripitaka. When he turned and looked east, he had already overtaken him by more than nine hundred li. In truth, the elder had ridden all night without stopping and traveled only one hundred twenty li; the Immortal’s cloud-step, in one leaping bound, had passed over more than nine hundred li. One heavenly child said, ‘Master, that is Tang Sanzang, seated beneath the tree by the roadside.’ The Immortal said, ‘I see him. You two return and prepare the ropes. I will bring him back myself.’ Qingfeng and Mingyue returned first.

The Immortal landed from the cloud, then shifted his form into a wandering Quanzhen preacher. He looked just so:

Wearing a hundred-patched robe, with a Lu-gong cord tied at the waist. The whisk of peacock tail swung in his hand, and a fisher’s drum tapped softly. Three-eared straw shoes on his feet, a Jiuyang kerchief wrapped about his head. His sleeves were full of drifting wind; he sang in a high, ringing voice. He came straight to the tree and called up toward Tripitaka: ‘Elder, this poor Daoist has arrived.’ Tripitaka hurriedly returned the salutation: ‘My apologies, my apologies.’ The Immortal asked, ‘Elder, where do you come from, and why are you meditating in the middle of the road?’ Tripitaka said, ‘This humble monk is Tripitaka of Great Tang in the Eastern lands, dispatched to go to the Western Heaven for the Sutras. He pauses here only for a brief rest.’ The Immortal feigned surprise, ‘From the East, say you? Did you pass through strange barren mountains?’ Tripitaka said, ‘I do not know, honored immortal, what this precious mountain may be.’ The Immortal said, ‘Wanshou Mountain’s Wuzhuang Monastery is my place of dwelling.’

Hearing this, Sun Wukong, who knew his own mind, hastily answered, ‘No, no, no—we are just on our way onward.’ The Immortal snapped with a half-smile, ‘You rogue monkey! Whom are you trying to fool? You came into my observatory and felled my Ren Shen tree, then in the night you slipped away and passed through this place without owning it. Why hide it so? Do not run. Return and bring back my tree at once.’ Hearing this, Sun Wukong grew angry in his heart. He drew his iron staff and, without yielding room for words, advanced to strike at the Immortal. The Immortal sidestepped, stepped on the auspicious light, and rose into the air. Sun Wukong leapt with cloud-movement and hurried after him. In midair the Immortal showed his true form. Here is his appearance:

On his head a purple-gold crown; a worryless crane cloak draped about him. Shoes on his feet, silk sash fastened at his waist. His body was like that of a youth; his face, handsome as a beauty’s. Three whiskers floated under his chin, and black-neck plumes layered along his temples. He met Sun Wukong with no weapons, only twisting a jade fly-whisk in his hand.

Sun Wukong struck wildly, high and low, hacking with the staff. The Immortal used his sleeve to block left and right, and survived him for two or three exchanges. Then he employed a technique called Universe-in-the-Sleeve: up in the clouds he lightly flung open his robe sleeve into the wind, and with a swish it came forward, enclosing the four monks and the horse all in one sweep. Zhu Bajie said, ‘It is bad. We are caught inside his giant net-bag.’ Sun Wukong said, ‘Idiot, not a net-bag—we are caught inside a robe sleeve.’ Zhu Bajie said, ‘This is no matter; let me strike him with the spike-pedestal and dig him a hole to get us out. Say later he was careless, the net was not secure, and we managed to slip loose.’ The pig then drove his spade wildly at it, but no hole could be made. The hand-swept cloth, though soft, rose up as hard as iron.

The Immortal turned the auspicious cloud and descended to Wuzhuang Monastery, sat down, and ordered his disciples to bring ropes. The young immortals one by one attended. Watch how he drew them from his sleeve as if they were puppets, brought out Tripitaka, and bound him to a pillar under the eaves of the main hall. He brought out the other three as well, binding one to each pillar. He also took out the horse, tied it in the courtyard, and gave it some grass. Their baggage was tossed to the corridor. Then he said, ‘Disciples, this monk is a renunciant; no blades, no polearms, no battle-axes are to be used against him. So bring out the whip; give him a beating and let me vent my anger for my Ren Shen fruit.’ The immortals at once hurried and fetched a whip—not made of cowhide, sheephide, deerhide, or veal-hide, but a dragon-hide seven-star whip, lying soaked in water. He ordered one strong little immortal to hold it fast: ‘Master, whom should I strike first?’ The Immortal said, ‘Tripitaka is the foremost among these monks. Strike him first.’

The Great Sage heard this and thought to himself, “If my old monk does not refrain from striking, and one round of whipping breaks me apart, would that not be my own guilt?” He could not hold back and spoke: “Master, you have it wrong. I stole the fruit, I ate the fruit, and I knocked down the trees too. Why should you not beat me first instead of beating him?” The Immortal laughed. “This unruly monkey speaks in rough tones. Beat him first.” The young immortal asked, “How many lashes?” The Immortal said, “By the number of fruits—thirty.” The young immortal raised his whip and struck. Wukong, fearing the powers of the immortals, stared with wide eyes to see where he was aiming. He turned into two hard iron legs with a cry of “Transform!” and watched how he could strike them. The youth struck him, one stroke after another, all thirty. It was already near noon. The Immortal then said, “Also scold Tripitaka. His instruction has not been strict enough, and he lets wayward monks run wild.” The youth lifted his whip again. Wukong said, “Master, you are mistaken again. When the fruit was stolen, my Master did not know; he was upstairs in the hall speaking with your two boys. Even if there is guilt in insufficient discipline, as his disciple I should have the beating. Strike me again.” The Immortal said, “This bad monkey, though sly and obstinate, still shows some filial feeling. In that case, beat him too.” The young immortal struck thirty more. Wukong bowed his head and looked—both legs shone like polished mirrors from all the blows, and he felt not the slightest pain or itch. By then dusk was coming. The Immortal said, “Soak the whip in water and we will flog him again tomorrow.” The young immortal set aside the whip and went to soak it; each returned to his quarters. Evening food was finished, and all slept soundly; there is no need to add more.

The Patriarch let his eyes fill with tears and reproached the three disciples: “You three brought this disaster and brought me here to suffer. How has this come about?” Wukong said, “Do not complain so. If there must be beating, beat me first—so far you did not receive any blows, and yet you wail?” Tripitaka said, “Though I was not beaten, being tied still makes my body hurt.” Sha Wujing said, "Master, there is still one binding left here." Wukong said, “Do not shout. Wait a little, then we can walk.” Zhu Bajie said, “Elder brother is making grand claims again. This hemp rope here has been drenched and is tied tight; it is worse than being confined in the hall. Yet you used the unlocking spell and walked out through the door.” Wukong said, “I am not bragging. Even if the three-strand hemp rope is drenched, even if the rope is as thick as a bowl, it is still as good as an autumn wind.”

Just then, all sound had ceased, and it was the quiet hour of Heaven’s streets. The Good One now made himself a little smaller, untied the bonds, and said, “Master, go ahead.” Sha Wujing was alarmed: “Brother, save us too.” Wukong said, “Softly, quietly.” He untied Tripitaka, then released Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, tightened his short shirt, fixed the horse’s harness on his back, took the travel bags from the corridor, and all three left the observatory gate. Then he told Zhu Bajie, “Go cut down four willow trees by the cliff.” Zhu Bajie said, “What will they be for?” Wukong said, “They will be useful. Bring them quickly.” That brutish one, with brute strength, took a bite-thing and quickly made off; he bit out four pieces, one at a time, and returned with them all in an armful. Wukong broke off the tips and ordered the two brothers to go back in and tie the original ropes to the pillar again as before. Then the Great Sage recited his spell, bit his tongue tip, spat blood onto the trees, and cried, “Transform!” One tree became Tripitaka, one became himself, and the two others became Sha Wujing and Zhu Bajie; all had the same appearance, with matching faces, and when asked their names they answered correctly. Only then did the two begin to walk and catch up with the Master. That night, as before, horse and riders did not pause and swiftly slipped away from Five-Altars Retreat.

Only when daybreak came, Tripitaka was swaying and dozing on horseback. Seeing this, Wukong said, “Master, you are no easy one; how can a monk work so hard? I, old Wukong, can keep awake for a thousand nights and still not know weariness. Get off the horse. Do not let people walking by see you and laugh at you. Let us rest for a moment in the place below the slope where wind and breath gather, then go on.”

There is no need to say that the disciples and their master stayed on the road for the night. Now in the morning the Immortal rose, ate his early meal, went out to the hall, and ordered, “Bring out the whip. Today we should flog Tripitaka.” The young immortal lifted his whip and said to Tripitaka, “I’ll beat you.” The willow trees answered, “Beat me.” With clashing sounds he struck thirty. He swept the whip toward Zhu Bajie and said, “I’ll beat you.” The willow tree answered, “Beat me.” When he struck Sha Wujing, it too answered to be beaten. When he came to Wukong, the monkey, now on the road, trembled once and cried out, “This is bad!” Tripitaka asked, “What do you mean?” Wukong said, “Yesterday I transformed four willows into our party of four. I only told him he had whipped me twice yesterday, and today he wanted not to whip again, but he has beaten my transformed forms. So my true body shivered. I need to gather in the spell.” The Great Sage hurriedly chanted and withdrew the magic.

See those Dao boys, frightened, throwing down the leather whip, reported: “Master, the one you beat first was the Tang monk. This time the ones being beaten are all merely willow roots.” The Immortal gave a cold laugh and praised without measure: “Sun Wukong is indeed a fine Monkey King. I have heard he once rampaged through Heaven, laid heavenly-net and earth-net, and no one could capture him—there is truth in this. You may go if you wish, but why did you tie these willow trees here as stand-ins in one’s place? Do not spare him. Go and catch him.”

The Immortal cried, “Go!” and rose through the clouds. Looking westward, he saw the monk with his bundle urging a horse along. He dropped from the clouds and shouted, “Wukong, where are you going? Bring back my ginseng tree.” Zhu Bajie heard and said, “Enough—his opponent is here again.” Wukong said, “Master, wrap up the ‘goodness’ talisman and let us release our ferocity; we can finish him in one strike and slip away.” Tripitaka heard this and trembled from fear, but gave no answer. Sha Wujing drew the Precious Staff, Zhu Bajie raised the nail-pick, and the Great Sage wielded the Golden-Hooped Staff. All moved forward together, surrounding the Immortal in the air and striking in a wild flurry. This fierce clash has verse as witness:

Sun Wukong did not know the Zhenyuan Immortal; his wonders were subtler than the age itself. Three divine weapons flared in savage force, while a whisk-like tail drifted of itself. Left blocks right, right blocks left, coming and going in tangled motion; rear blocks before, front meets, every turn and whirl permitted. From night to dawn he cannot yet break loose from this frame—how long can he linger before reaching the Western Heaven?

The three brothers all raised their divine weapons and attacked together. That Immortal only swung a fly-whisk as if setting a stage. In less than half an hour, with one sweep of his robe sleeves he gathered the four disciples, horse, and baggage all at once and brought them off. He returned to the clouds and came back to the observatory, where the assembled immortals came forward. The Immortal sat in the hall and then, from his sleeves, drew each one out in turn: he bound Tripitaka to a low locust tree below the steps; Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing were tied to trees on both sides; Wukong was bound and pinned. Wukong said, “This must be an inquest.” Before long the bindings were secure. He ordered, “Bring out ten bolts of head-cloth.” Wukong laughed, “Bajie, this elder has quite the nerve—bringing out cloth to make us a middle-wrap. Save a little; a single wrap is enough.” The young immortal brought out their household cloth. The Immortal said, “Wrap Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing.” All the immortals moved in and wrapped them all. Wukong laughed, “Good, good, good. A burial wrap is now almost complete.” Soon the wrapping was finished. He then ordered them to bring out the lacquer. The immortals quickly fetched a little raw and cooked lacquer they had self-dried and dried by themselves, and coated all three body-wide, leaving head and face exposed. Zhu Bajie said, “Master, the top is not dangerous, but below there are still holes. We can still step out and make our obeisance.” The Immortal then ordered a great iron pot raised. Wukong laughed, “Bajie, lift out the pot. It must be for cooking our meal.” Zhu Bajie said, “Very well, let us eat some rice; it would look fine for us to become ghosts stuffed full.” The immortals indeed brought forth a large pot and set it beneath the steps. The Immortal ordered kindling piled and fierce fire lit, saying: “Pour clear oil into the pot and set it boiling. When it rolls, plunge Sun Wukong into the cauldron and deep-fry him once, as revenge for my ginseng tree.”

Hearing this, Wukong rejoiced inwardly: “This suits old Wukong’s mind exactly. I have not bathed for some time; my skin is dry and itchy. At least this will cure it, and I will be grateful for the heat.” In but a moment the oil in that pot was boiling. The Great Sage grew more alert, fearing that the Immortal’s spells were hard to match and that in the cauldron he might not have any chance to make handcraft. He turned back and looked around. Below was the east side of the platform, a sundial platform; west was a stone lion. Wukong leapt in one bound, rolled toward the west, bit his tongue tip, and spat on the lion, crying, “Transform!” It changed into his own form as a bound, knotted mass. He then let his original spirit emerge, rose into the clouds, and looked down upon the Taoist below.

One of the little immortals reported, “Master, the oil cauldron has come to a full boil.” The Great Immortal commanded, “Cast Sun Wukong into it.” Four little immortals could not lift him up; eight could not either; adding four more still could not lift him. The immortals said, “This monkey clings to the ground and is hard to move; though small, he is sturdy all the same.” So he ordered twenty young immortals to shoulder him and heave him into the pot. With a crash of cooking, they tossed him in at once. There was a loud frying sound, and a few droplets of boiling oil sprang up, scalding great blisters on the faces of those young Daoist lads. Then came the cry from the fire boy, “The pot is leaking, the pot is leaking.” There was no time to finish the cry: the oil had already leaked out completely, and the pot bottom had torn apart; all along, a stone lion had been placed inside it.

The Great Immortal grew furious: “That unruly monkey—no sign of propriety! You taught him tricks before my face. If he had already left, all right; how is he now smashing up my stove again? This impudent monkey cannot be held even when one tries to seize him; and if one does catch him, it is like shaping sand and trying to handle mercury, grabbing shadows and chasing the wind. Enough, enough, enough. Let him go. Untie Tang Sanzang, fetch another new cauldron, tie him up a bit, and settle the score with that ginseng-tree.” The young immortal then truly set to work and began untying the lacquered bindings.

Sun Wukong heard everything clearly in the open air and thought, “Master is in danger: if he is put into the oil cauldron, one boil and he dies, two boils and he is scorched, and after three or five boils he will be melted into a formless, pasty monk. I should go and save him.” The Great Sage stepped down from his cloud head and came forward, joining his hands as he spoke: “Do not tear apart the lacquered bindings and do not tie up my Master—let me go down into the oil cauldron instead.” The Great Immortal shouted in anger, “I will break you, you monkey! How dare you use tricks and make such a disturbance to my stove?” Sun Wukong laughed and said, “Since you met me, you should have overturned your stove already; what concern of yours is this? I too came to take some share of your hot-oil essence, but I had only been urgent for nature’s call. If I were to break wind in the pot, I might have soiled your prepared oil and you would not be able to season vegetables with it. Now that the matter is fully settled, it is fit for me to enter the pot. Do not tie my Master. Tie me instead.” Hearing this, the Great Immortal gave a cold, chuckling laugh, came out of the hall, and grabbed him by the arm.

In the end, it is still unknown what more was said, nor is it yet clear exactly how he got free. Listen to the next chapter for the resolution.
chapters.title: Chapter 25: Zhenyuan captures the scripture-seeker in a pursuit; Sun Wukong later wreaks havoc in Wuzhuang Monastery.
