This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

A poem says:

In the world, keep your heart upon a blade’s edge; in self-cultivation, remember even the smallest measure. They say the word ‘blade’ stands for life, but think three times before anger and mockery. The noble have never contended through the ages; the saintly hold virtue and carry the era onward. There are always fiercer ones than the fierce, and in the end all becomes emptiness and nothing.

Great Immortal Zhenyuan held Sun Wukong by the arm and said, “I know your talents, and I have heard of your fame; but this time you have grown crafty and too clever with your heart. Even if you can rise and fly, you cannot slip from my hand. I will take you to the Western Lands, see your Buddha, and still I will have my ginseng-berry tree back. Do not use sorcery.” Sun Wukong laughed and said, “You, sir, look like a little household gentleman. If the tree is to live again, what is so hard about it? If you had said this earlier, we might have spared ourselves this quarrel.” Great Immortal Zhenyuan said, “No quarrel. I will generously forgive you.” Sun Wukong said, “If you release my master, I’ll return you a living tree.” Great Immortal Zhenyuan said, “If with your magic you can heal the tree back to life, I will greet you eight times, become your equal, and make us brothers.” Sun Wukong said, “Then free them. Old Wukong will make sure to return you a living tree.”

Great Immortal Zhenyuan guessed that he could not escape, and so he ordered that Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing be released. Sha Wujing said, “Master, I don’t know what ghost your elder brother has stirred up.” Zhu Bajie said, “What ghost? It is what we might call the ghost of present politeness. The tree is dead; can he really heal it alive? He made a flashy medicinal powder to look proper, and while asking for a healer for the tree he tried to flee, yet he even thinks about you and me.” Tripitaka said, “He certainly will not dare to abandon us. Ask him where to ask for medicine.” Then he called out, “Wukong, how did you trick the immortal into releasing us?” Sun Wukong said, “Old Wukong never lies. How could I have tricked him?” Tripitaka said, “Where will you go to seek a remedy?” Sun Wukong said, “The ancients said, ‘A remedy comes from the sea.’ I go now to the Eastern Ocean, to roam the three islands and ten continents, asking elder immortals for a method to raise the dead and restore life. I will surely cure his tree.” Tripitaka said, “When will you be back?” Sun Wukong said, “Only three days.” Tripitaka said, “Then as you say, I set you a limit of three days. Return within three days and all is well. If you do not come back after three days, I will recite the Tightening Headband Spell.” Sun Wukong said, “Understood. Understood.”

See him quickly adjust his tiger-skin skirt, then he went out and said to the Great Immortal, “Master, do not worry. I will go and return quickly. You, however, must serve my master well—three cups of tea and six meals each day, without fail. If even one thing is lacking, when Old Wukong returns he will settle accounts with you and first smash the bottom of your pot. Change his clothes and wash him, wash him and wash him again. If his face turns yellow, I don’t want him; if he loses weight, do not let him go out.” The Great Immortal said, “Go on. Go on. I will not let him remain hungry.”

At once, Sun Wukong leaped onto the clump-cloud and left Five-House Observatory, turning straight toward the Eastern Ocean. In the sky he was as fast as lightning, as swift as a meteor, and soon arrived at the fairyland of Penglai. He settled on the cloud and looked down carefully. It was truly a beautiful place. A poem bears witness:

The earth below is an immortal land where saints are lined in court. In Penglai, tide waves are calmed, parted and gathered by command. The reflection of the Jade Terrace cools the heart of Heaven; bright lights of great towers rise over the sea. Five-hued rosy clouds hold jade-like music; stars and moon in nine heavens cast rays on golden-tusked turtles. At the Western Pond, the Queen Mother often comes there, presenting peaches in blessing to the Three Immortals.

Sun Wukong could not exhaust the fair scenery. He entered Penglai directly. As he walked, he came upon White Cloud Cave. Beneath a pine shade sat three old men around a board game. The one watching the board was Shouxing; the two players were Fuxing and Luxing. Sun Wukong walked up and called, “Elders, my greetings and bows.” The Three Stars saw him, pushed aside the game board, and returned the greeting: “What brings the Great Sage?” Sun Wukong said, “I have come to test my wit with you.” Shouxing said, “I have heard the Great Sage cast off the Way and entered Buddhism, abandoning life itself, and that he protects Tripitaka on the journey west for the sutra, hurrying daily over mountain roads. With such burdens, how can you come here to play?” Sun Wukong said, “I shall not hide anything from you all. On the way westward I met some obstacles in mid-journey. I have come to ask a small matter. Do you grant it?” Fuxing said, “Where? Why were you obstructed? Make it clear so that we may decide.” Sun Wukong said, “On the way we passed Wanshou Mountain, Five-House Observatory, and there was trouble.” The three elders were astonished and said, “Five-House Observatory is the immortal palace of Great Immortal Zhenyuan. Did you perhaps steal his ginseng fruit?” Sun Wukong laughed, “What is there to steal that is so precious?” The three elders said, “Monkey, you do not understand its worth. Smell that fruit and one gains three hundred and sixty years. Eat one and one may live forty-seven thousand years. It is called Wanshou herbal-cinnamon pill. Our practice does not compare with his. He obtains it with ease and can live long as Heaven itself. We still must nourish essence, refine qi, preserve spirit, and harmonize dragon and tiger, seize Kan and fill Li, and do not know how many hours of labor this costs. How can you say what he has has such little value? This is the only such numinous root in all under Heaven.” Sun Wukong said, “A numinous root, a numinous root—I have already made its root snap.” The three elders cried in surprise, “You snapped it how?”

Sun Wukong said, “The other day in his hall Great Immortal Zhenyuan was not at home, and only two young attendants received my master. They offered him three ginseng fruits, but my master did not recognize them and said he was a child not yet three days old, so he refused to eat them again and again. Those boys took them and ate them themselves, never letting us have any. So old Wukong stole three fruits and we three brothers ate them. The attendants, not knowing our measure, cursed and shouted at every turn. Old Wukong got angry, struck the tree with a cudgel and knocked it down. All the fruit was gone; the leaves opened out and dropped, the roots were exposed and the branches broken. It was already dead. Then the boys locked us up, and Wukong twisted the shackles and escaped. The next morning at first light, that immortal came home and entered in haste. In questioning and answering, words clashed; soon we fought. He dodged, spread his robe sleeves open and with one sweep scooped up both Master and disciples with a sleeve. Ropes and bindings were wound about us; with questions and whips he beat us for a full day. That night we escaped again, and he caught up and again netted us. He had no iron weapon at all, only a yak-tail whisk as shield, and with such three kinds of weapons as we had among us, do not imagine he could strike us. On this run he still contrived it: wrapping us in cloth, he lacquers Tripitaka and the two junior disciples, and would have put us under a hot-oil pot. Old Wukong then used an escape technique and walked out, breaking the pot he had. He could not catch me, though he had some resentment.” Again I spoke with him and told him to release my master and two brothers, and I would return and cure his tree. At last both houses found peace. Thinking of, ‘The remedy comes from the sea,’ I came to this fairyland to ask these three elders for a way to save the holy Tripitaka from suffering.”

Hearing this, the Three Stars also felt vexed and said, “You monkey knows nothing of people. Great Immortal Zhenyuan is the ancestor of earthly immortals; we are the lineage of heavenborn immortals. Though you have obtained heavenly immortality, you are still among the scattered teachings of Taiyi, not yet in true current. How can you escape from his hand? If Great Sage can kill and revive beasts that walk, fly, crawl, and are scaled and shelled, my millet-and-rice elixir can restore them. But the ginseng fruit is the root of a heavenly tree—how can it be treated? No formula, no formula at all.” When Sun Wukong heard there was no remedy there, his brows knotted twice and his forehead drew into a thousand lines. Fuxing said, “Great Sage, there is no formula here, but perhaps elsewhere. Why worry?” Sun Wukong said, “I am not blocked by wishing for no formula, if it were easy. I could roam sea’s corners and heaven’s horizons, pass through all thirty-six heavens, and still call it a small matter. But my Tripitaka keeps strict rules and narrow measure. He gives me only a three-day limit. If I fail to return within three days, he will recite the Tightening Headband Spell.” The Three Stars laughed: “Fine, fine, fine. If not for that spell tying you, you would already have pierced the skies again.” Shouxing said, “Great Sage, do not worry. Though that Great Immortal styles himself a senior, he knows us too. First, we have not greeted each other for a long time; second, there is your matter of human kindness. Now the three of us will go and visit him together. Then we will convey this situation and ask that Tripitaka not recite the Tightening Headband Spell. Let him wait three or five days, only until you return with a formula, and then we part.” Sun Wukong said, “I am grateful, I am grateful. Please, please, three elders, go ahead now. I will depart as well.” The Great Sage bade farewell to the Three Stars and left aside further account.

Then the Three Stars set out in auspicious radiance and came to Five-House Observatory. Within that gathering all at once heard cranes cry through the vast sky; those were indeed the three elders arriving with heavenly radiance. They saw:

The sky was full of gentle auspicious light. In the vault of heaven, fragrant mist swirled in abundance. A thousand streaks of colored vapor guarded their feathered robes, and one light cloud lifted a single immortal foot. A blue pheasant flew, a vermilion phoenix wheeled, sleeves drawing fragrant wind that swept the earth. Their staffs tipped with hanging dragons seemed to smile as they came, and snowy beards brushed before chests like carved jade. Childlike faces, joyful, with no trace of worry, vigorous forms and masculine might, richly blessed. They held star-tally rods and sea-like purses, gourds and precious registers hung at the waist. Across ten thousand periods and a thousand springs, blessings of life and age endure by their fate. They often come to the mortal world with a thousand good omens, and each time add a hundred blessings among human beings. They encompass Heaven and Earth and magnify Fortune and Longevity, a boundless joy of bliss and long life at last. The three elders rode the auspicious light to visit Great Immortal Zhenyuan; in the Hall of Blessings, harmony overflowed beyond measure.

That immortal youth saw it at once and hurried to report, “Master, the Three Stars have come from the sea.” Zhenyuanzi had been in easy conversation with Tripitaka and his disciple companions when he heard the report, and at once came down a step to welcome them. When Bajie saw Shou Xing, he stepped forward, grabbed him, and laughed, “You old, meat-headed man, we have not seen you for so long, and you still look so loose—didn’t even bring your cap.” He then took one of his monk caps and tossed it onto his head. Grinning, he laughed and said, “Good, good, good—truly, this is adding the crown and gaining rank.” Shou Xing shoved the hat off and cursed, “You clod of a fellow, old fool, you do not know your place.” Bajie said, “I am no clod. You all are truly servants.” Fu Xing said, “You are the clod indeed, yet you dare call people servants?” Bajie laughed again, “If I am not a servant, why call it ‘adding Longevity,’ ‘adding Fortune,’ ‘adding Rank’?” Tripitaka sent Bajie away in a scolding, then quickly straightened his robes and paid obeisance to the Three Stars.

The three stars greeted the Immortal with the manners of juniors, and only then sat down. Once seated, Shou Xing said, “It has been long since we paid our respects to your noble presence. For this fault of discourtesy, we have now come because Great Sage Sun Wukong has disturbed the Immortal Mountain, and we wanted to meet.” The Immortal said, “Has Sun Wukong gone off to Penglai?” Shou Xing said, “Yes. He damaged your alchemical tree and came to my place to ask for a prescription to treat it. We had no such prescription, and he sought treatment elsewhere, but he may have broken the Tripitaka’s three-day limit for saying the Tightening Headband Spell. So we came now: one, to bow and pay respect; two, to beg for more time.” Hearing this, Tripitaka answered repeatedly, “I dare not say it. I dare not say it.”

While this was being spoken, Bajie came running back again, grabbed Fu Xing, and wanted fruit to eat. He fumbled in his sleeves, dug about his waist, and kept lifting his robes to search him. Tripitaka said laughing, “What kind of rule does Bajie have?” Bajie said, “Not no rule at all—this is what is called ‘fortune every turn.’” Tripitaka again ordered him away. The pig monk stepped out the hall, staring at Fu Xing with eyes that never moved and glaring fiercely. Fu Xing said, “Clod, why should I have angered you? How can you bear such hatred toward me?” Bajie said, “Not hatred. This is ‘turning the head to look for fortune.’” When the fool stepped outside, he saw a child carrying four tea spoons; the boy had just gone to fetch the bell, fruit, and tea. Bajie snatched them in one motion, ran up into the hall, took up a little hand-bell, and banged and beat it wildly, playing tricks with both ends. The Immortal said, “This monk has become even less respectful.” Bajie replied laughing, “Not less respectful—this is the ‘four-season felicity.’"

Leaving aside the matter of Bajie’s bickering and mischief, the Great Sage once again mounted his cloud and left Penglai, reaching Fangzhang Immortal Mountain quite quickly. It was truly a place worth going to. A poem says:

Fangzhang towers high and awe-inspiring, set apart as its own heaven. In the Palace of Great Origin, courts of immortals gather. The light of the Purple Terrace shines along the road of the Three Purities, and flowers and trees cast fragrant five-colored smoke. Golden phoenixes fill the many-hued blossom pavilions, while jade ointment would never be forced to water the ginseng fields. Green peaches and purple plums ripen anew, and once again the immortals keep faith for ten thousand years.

The Great Sage stepped down from the cloud and, with no thought of lingering over the scenery, kept walking. As he moved he heard rich incense-like fragrance in the wind and the cry of a supernatural crane; then in the adjacent hall appeared an immortal. He beheld:

Across the empty sky, myriad streams of rosy light appeared; colorful mists drifted and swirled in unbroken brilliance. The cinnabar phoenix clasping flowers looked all the brighter; the azure-luan bird sang at the cave mouth and the black crane danced on mountain peaks. Fortune like the East Sea, longevity like a mountain; he looked like a young child, yet his body was strong. He held in his hidden-cave heaven an elixir against old age; at his waist hung a talisman of long life for coiling with the sun. In this world many times he descends with auspicious signs. How many times has he taken away disasterful destinies? The Martial Emperor once announced an increase in lifespan, and to the Jade Pool he every so often attends the peaches banquets. He teaches many monks to discard worldly entanglements, and points open toward the Great Way, bright as lightning. He has crossed seas before to bless a thousand autumns, and often goes to Lingshan to see Buddha’s face. His sacred title is the Great Emperor Lord Donghua, the foremost immortal amid fragrant clouds.

Wukong smiled as he faced him and called out, “Your Majesty, we have begun.” The lord hurriedly returned the greeting: “Great Sage, my welcome failed you; please come to this humble house for tea.” And with him he brought Wukong inside. Indeed it was the Bei-Que Immortal Palace, a splendor of Jade-Pool towers impossible to count. After they sat waiting for tea, a child came out from behind the emerald screen. He looked thus:

He wore Dao robes, with cloud-glitter drifting around him. A silken tassel at his waist flashed with patterned light. On his head, a linen cap was marked with the stars of the Dipper. On his feet, reed sandals as he walked like one roaming immortal peaks. A true alchemist, he had shed his old shell; when he had fulfilled his art and practice, he rejoiced in ease. Seeing through original streams of essence, qi, and spirit, the master recognized him without error. He now delights in endless longevity, having left off ambition for fame; even whole Jiazi cycles of heaven and earth could not contain him. He passed through corridors and climbed treasure pavilions, and had plucked heavenly peaches there three times. From the pale-blue cloud emerging behind the jade-green screen came the little immortal himself: it was Dongfang Shuo.

Wukong looked and laughed. “Here is the little thief right here. Did he steal peaches where the lord has none to grant?” Dongfang Shuo came forward and, with a formal offering, answered, “Old thief, why have you come here? My master has no immortal pill for you to steal.”

The lord called, “Mǎn Qiàn, stop your wild talk. Bring tea as well.” Mancián, one of Dongfang Shuo’s Taoist names, hurried inside and brought two cups of tea. After drinking, Wukong said, “Great Sage, I have a matter to petition you. I do not know whether it may be granted.” The lord said, “What matter? Of course—please instruct me.” Wukong said, “Recently, while escorting Tripitaka on the journey westward, we passed Wanshou Mountain at Wuzhuang Observatory. His little child there behaved badly, and in one moment of anger I knocked down the person-living ginseng-fruit tree. For that instant it blocked our way and Tripitaka could not slip away. I have come to your honored place to request one prescription of cure, and I beg you most earnestly to grant it.” The lord said, “You monkey meddles in everything, making trouble wherever you go and caring nothing at all. That Wuzhuang is under Zhenyuanzi. His sacred style is Shitongjun, and he is the ancestor among earth-immortals—how could you have collided with him? That ginseng-fruit tree is a cinnabar root; for you to steal and eat it already deserves punishment, and on top of that you pushed down the tree itself. How could he simply let it pass?” Wukong said, “That is exactly true. We escaped, but when he caught up with us he treated us like a sweat cloth and swept us all up in one sleeve, so we were in a rage. Having no way to avoid it, I begged him for medicine; therefore I made this petition.” The lord said, “I have one Nine-Perfected Taiyi Reverted Elixir-Pill; it can heal living things in the mortal world, but it cannot heal trees. A tree is the spirit of earth and wood, nourished by heavenly dews and earth’s moisture. If it were an ordinary fruit tree among common people, treatment might be possible. But Wanshou Mountain is Primordial blessed terrain, Wuzhuang Observatory is the Cave Heaven of Hezhou, and the ginseng-fruit is a spiritual root opened by heaven and cleft from earth itself. How can it be treated? There is no method, no method at all.”

“There is no method, then, and I shall take my leave,” Wukong said. The lord still wished to detain him and serve a cup of jade liquor, but Wukong said, “The urgent cure is tight; I dare not stay.” He then rode the cloud back to Yíngzhōu and its offshore island, another fine place indeed. A poem attests:

Jade trees glitter and sparkle, shining through purple mist, while Yíngzhōu’s palaces and towers join all the heavens. Green mountains, blue waters, and wondrous jeweled flowers are in full bloom; jade liquor in bronze vessels, hard as ironstone. Five-colored teal pheasants cry at the sea-sun, and a thousand-year red phoenix drinks in scarlet smoke. Men of the human world can never truly investigate the scenes within this flask; beyond appearance, a spring-like radiance lasts for a hundred million years.

When Wukong arrived at Yíngzhōu, just beneath the cinnabar cliffs and jewel trees he saw a few elders with white hair and broad beards, and immortals with youthful faces and crane-black side-locks, where they were playing chess, drinking wine, talking, laughing, and singing. It was truly:

Auspicious light filled all the sky and auspicious vapors floated fragrant. Colorful luan called at the cave mouth; dark cranes danced on the mountain peaks. Crystal lotus and water peaches served for cups of wine; paired pears and fire dates promised life through a thousand autumns. Each one was free of worldly clamor, and yet their immortal tablets were in hand. They roamed carelessly on drifting waves, loose and tranquil in pure seclusion. The heavenly cycles of Jiazi could not bind it; heaven and earth were all alike in freedom. To the sages they offered fruit—black-faced apes, in matched pairs, many and wonderfully cherished. White stags with flowers in their mouths knelt together, their deference exquisitely tender.

Those old ones were still in merry play. The Great Sage then called in a loud voice, “Can you not let me enjoy a little of this too?” The immortals saw him and hurried forward to welcome him. A poem attests:

The spirit-root of the ginseng-fruit tree was broken. The Great Sage came to seek immortals and ask for the wondrous prescription. Through red-gold clouds circling the treasure groves, the Nine Elders of Yíngzhōu came forth to receive him.

Wukong recognized them as the Nine Elders and laughed, “You old brothers are quite free indeed.” The Nine Elders said, “When once you kept the proper path, if you had not stirred trouble in Heaven, you would have been even freer than we are. Now it is different: we hear that you have returned to true practice and are going west to bow to Buddha. How did you find time to come here?” Wukong set out fully the matter of seeking medicine for the tree. The Nine Elders were astonished and said, “You do ask for trouble endlessly, cause trouble endlessly. We truly have no remedy.”

“If there is no remedy,” Wukong said, “I shall take my leave.” The Nine Elders again held him back to drink celestial nectar and eat jade lotus. Wukong would not sit. He stood, drank one cup of nectar, ate one piece of lotus root, and hurriedly departed Yíngzhōu, turning toward the Eastern Ocean. Soon he saw Mount La-ga not far off, so he came down from the cloud and reached Mount Putuo, where he saw Guanyin Bodhisattva in the purple bamboo forest expounding the Dharma with various heavenly divinities, Mu Zha, and the Dragon Maiden. A poem attests:

The Sea-Lord’s city rose high, and auspicious qi was thick; still more, one saw endless marvels and wonders. Know this: within a thousand subtle forms lies the hidden in one—everything comes out of one rare and subtle category. Four holy sages, at the proper time, attain true fruition; the six ordinary beings, hearing this, break free from cage and bondage. Shaolin has another true flavor; the fragrance of blossoms and fruit fills the trees, red and abundant.

The Bodhisattva had already seen the Wandering Sage come, and at once ordered the Great Spirit of Shoushan to go meet him. The Great Spirit came out of the forest and called, “Sun Wukong, where are you going?” Wukong raised his head and barked, “Are you the one who called for Wukong, you black bear? Was it not Old Sun who spared you before? You have already become a corpse-ghost of Black Wind Mountain. Today you followed the Bodhisattva, gained good fruit, dwell on this immortal mountain, and hear the Dharma teachings every day—yet you cannot even address me as ‘laoye’?” That black bear had truly attained the right fruit. Under the Bodhisattva’s charge he now guarded Mount Putuo and was called a Great Spirit, all because of the Monk-Warrior. He could only smile and say, “Great Sage, as the ancients say, ‘A gentleman does not keep resentments from the past.’ Why ask what else? It was the Bodhisattva who sent me to welcome you.” The Monk-Warrior then, with full formality and sincere respect, went with the Great Spirit into the Purple Bamboo Grove and paid respects to the Bodhisattva.

The Bodhisattva asked, “Wukong, where has Tripitaka reached?” Wukong replied, “He reached Mount Wanshou on Xiniuho Isles.” The Bodhisattva said, “There is a Wuzhuang Hall on Mount Wanshou. Have you met Zhenyuan Daxian there?” Wukong bowed and said, “Because he was at Wuzhuang Hall, the disciple did not recognize Zhenyuan Daxian, damaged his ginseng-fruit tree, and colliding with him, he obstructed my teacher from moving forward.” The Bodhisattva, knowing his mind, said in wonder, “You insolent monkey knows nothing of consequence. His ginseng-fruit tree is a sacred root opened from heaven and earth. Zhenyuan is the ancestor of the Earth Immortals. I have even shown him tolerance—how could you strike his tree?” Wukong knelt again and said, “My disciple truly did not know. That day he was out, and only two little immortals were on duty. It was Zhu Bajie who saw he had fruit and wanted to taste one new one; the disciple secretly stole three, and the brothers shared them. The children noticed and scolded us without restraint. In anger, the disciple knocked his tree down. The next day he returned and caught us in an instant, binding us with rope, whipping us, and beating us for a day. We escaped by night, but he caught up again and still cage-dragged us. Three times or two, it was truly hard to escape. I promised to heal his tree, yet only then did I seek a cure from the sea, wandering the three islands, and no gods had any power. For this reason the disciple truly resolved to make proper pilgrimage and especially confessed to the Bodhisattva, hoping for mercy and a gift to save Tripitaka and let him go west soon.” The Bodhisattva said, “Why did you not come to me sooner, and instead go to the islands seeking one?”

Hearing this, Wukong rejoiced within: “How providential, how providential. The Bodhisattva surely has a remedy.” He moved forward again in earnest entreaty. The Bodhisattva said, “In the bottom of my pure bottle is ambrosial dew that can heal immortal trees and spiritual seedlings.” Wukong asked, “Have you tested it?” The Bodhisattva answered, “I have.” “What result?” Wukong asked. The Bodhisattva said, “Once, the Supreme Elder Lord Laozi wagered with me and won. He pulled out my willow twig, put it into the refining furnace, scorched it to ash, and sent it back to me. I put it in the bottle, and after a day and night it regained green branches and leaves, the same as before.” Wukong laughed, “Wonderful destiny, truly. If even charred wood can be revived, how could this toppled tree be difficult?” The Bodhisattva then instructed the assembly, “Guard the forest while I come and go.” She carried the pure bottle in her hand. A white parrot trilled cleverly ahead; Sun Wukong followed close behind. There is a poem to bear witness:

Jade-bristle and gold-horned marks are hard for this world to weigh; it is truly the Compassionate One who rescues beings from suffering. In former kalpas I met the Buddha without stain; till now I have gained a formed body. In so many births, the sea of desire has calmed to still waves, and one field of heart holds not a grain of dust. Ambrosial dew, tested by wondrous true Dharma, instructs the precious tree to keep spring forever.

Elsewhere in the pavilion, the Great Immortal and the Three Elders were speaking quietly when suddenly they saw Sun Wukong alight from his cloud and call out, “The Bodhisattva has come. Quickly, quickly receive her.” Startled, the Three Stars, Zhenyuan Daxian, and Tripitaka’s three disciples all went out together from the Treasure Hall. The Bodhisattva then set down her auspicious cloud, first exchanged words with Zhenyuan Daxian, then paid her respects to the Three Elders. After the bows, she sat. At the steps, Wukong brought Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing to bow to her. The immortals of that retreat also came to pay respects. Wukong said, “Great Immortal, do not delay. Prepare the incense table at once and ask the Bodhisattva to cure that tree of yours.” The Great Immortal bowed and thanked her, saying, “How could this unworthy one dare to trouble the Bodhisattva to descend?” The Bodhisattva said, “Tripitaka is my disciple. Sun Wukong struck at the Master; naturally he must pay compensation for the treasure-tree.” The Three Elders said, “If so, do not keep talking modestly. Please ask the Bodhisattva to all go into the garden and see for yourselves.”

The Great Immortal immediately ordered a ceremonial table to be prepared, had the garden swept, and asked the Bodhisattva to go ahead, with the Three Elders following. When Tripitaka’s master and disciples and all the retreat’s immortals came into the garden, that tree lay fallen on the ground, its roots showing, leaves gone, and branches withered. The Bodhisattva called, “Wukong, extend your hand.” Wukong held out his left hand. The Bodhisattva dipped the willow twig from the bottle’s ambrosial dew and drew, in his palm, a revival glyph of life-restoring power, instructing him to place it under the roots. Wukong was to wait for the water to rise. The Monk-Warrior knelt with a fist, tucked it beneath the roots; in a moment, a clear spring swelled into a pool. The Bodhisattva said, “This water must not be used in any Five-Agents vessel. It must be ladled out with jade dippers. Raise the tree upright, pour it from the top; naturally the root bark will join, buds will rise, branches will green, and fruit will form.” Wukong said, “Young Taoists, bring out jade ladles at once.” Zhenyuan said, “This poor one in the wild mountain has no jade ladle, only jade tea cups and jade wine cups. Could those be used?” The Bodhisattva said, “If it is jade and can scoop water, that will do. Bring them and see.” The Great Immortal immediately ordered the young attendants to bring out some two or three dozen tea cups and four or five dozen wine cups, and those were used to ladle the spring from the roots. Wukong, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing lifted and carried the tree, set it straight, and packed soil around the base. Then, cup after cup of the jade vessels of sweet spring water was carried to the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva sprinkled the water with the willow twig in fine strokes while intoning sutra and incantation. Not long after, the sprinkled water disappeared into the root, and the tree truly returned as before, with dark green, dense leaves, and twenty-three ginseng fruits upon it. The two youths, Qingfeng and Mingyue, said, “When we did not see the fruit yesterday, only twenty-two were counted, inverted upside down. Why does one more appear now that it has revived?” Wukong said, “‘Time reveals human nature.’ The other day, Old Sun stole only three. The one that fell to the ground entered the earth, and the soil spirit said this treasure had gone into the earth. It was only because Zhu Bajie kept shouting that I had struck it off-center; so the wind-borne rumor drifted away and lingered, and only now is the truth plain.” The Bodhisattva said, “What I earlier said about not using Five-Agents vessels was because this thing fears the Five Phases.”

The Great Immortal was greatly delighted and urgently ordered a golden mallet brought. He knocked down ten fruits and asked the Bodhisattva and the Three Elders to return to the Treasure Hall: first, to give thanks for their service; second, to hold a ginseng-fruit banquet. The little immortals then set up tables and chairs and laid out the cinnabar trays. They invited the Bodhisattva to sit on the principal seat, with the Three Elders on her left, Tripitaka on her right, and Zhenyuan in the front seat beside her. They each ate one. There is a poem to bear witness:

In the mid-realm of hidden heaven on Mount Wanshou, the ginseng fruit matures over nine thousand years. Its holy root sprouts out again, damaged branches restored; ambrosial dew nourishes them and the fruit and leaves are complete. The three elders meet joyously, all old allies by bond; the four monks are fortunate to meet this as former affinity. From now on, those who partake of ginseng fruit are all immortals of endless life and youth.

At this point, after the Bodhisattva and the Three Elders each had eaten one, Tripitaka at last understood it was an immortal treasure and ate one. Wukong and the three also each ate one, Zhenyuan ate one, and the immortals of that hall shared one. Only then did Wukong thank the Bodhisattva and return to Mount Putuo, sending the Three Elders directly to Penglai Island. Zhenyuan, however, arranged vegetables and wine again and made brothers with Wukong. This was exactly, not striking does not make acquaintance; the two families became one family. The four disciples and master were happy and in joy; evening had come. Then the elder said:

By destined affinity one may taste the root-replenishing elixir; With long life, enduring the hardships that come from battling demons is still difficult.

As for how they part on the morrow, we shall leave that to the next chapter to explain.
chapters.title: Chapter 26: Wukong sails the Three Islands in search of methods; Guanyin of Sweet-Spring revives a dying tree.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Now, as the tale continues, Tripitaka and his disciples packed up at first light and proceeded onward. Zhenyuanzi had become as a brother to the Great Sage, and the two were so in accord that neither would let go of the other; he made continual arrangements to care for him, and so they stayed on for five or six days at a stretch. The Venerable had taken the miraculous restorative pill and seemed to have changed his whole frame; his spirit felt clear, his body strong and healthy. His resolve to obtain the Tripiṭaka was firm, and he would not delay his journey. In the end he set out.

After parting and taking the road, the master and disciples soon saw a high mountain before them. Tripitaka said, "Disciple, the mountain ahead is steep and dangerous. I fear the horse cannot pass. All of you, be very careful." Sun Wukong replied, "Master, do not worry. We will handle it." The great Monkey King took his staff and crossed it before the horse, hewed out a path through the mountain, and climbed to a high cliff, where the view seemed endless:

Peaks of rock and crag pile upon one another; ravines and gullies wind in looping courses. Tigers and wolves move as ranks, roe deer and stags travel in herds. Countless goats and muntjacs cluster close together; foxes and rabbits gather densely across the whole mountain. A thousand-chi python, a ten-thousand-chi serpent. The great python breathes sorrowful mists; the long snake sends out strange wind. Thorns and briars snarl by the path, and on the ridges the pines stand fair and upright. Ivy fills the eye, and fragrant grasses stretch to the sky. Shadows fall toward the northern Cangming, while in the south the clouds open like the handle of the Northern Dipper. Through all ages it retains its primal energy, ancient and primeval; ten thousand peaks stand in stately ranks, and the sun itself grows cold in their light.

The Venerable, mounted on horseback, was startled at once. Great Sage Sun Wukong displayed his arts, waving his iron staff and roaring once. The sound frightened the wolfish beasts into flinging themselves away, and tigers and leopards ran off in panic.

The companions entered this mountain and, as they were at a rugged stretch, Tripitaka said, "Wukong, I am hungry today. Go make some alms food for me somewhere." Wukong, with an ingratiating smile, said, "How clever you are, Master. In the middle of this mountain there is no hamlet ahead, no inn behind. Even if we had money, there is nowhere to buy food. Where can I go to fetch a meal?" Tripitaka felt displeased inwardly and barked, "You monkey! In the Two-Realms Mountain, you were sealed by Buddha in a stone casket. You can speak, but your feet could not move. Yet I saved your life, bestowed the vows upon you, and made you my disciple. Why will you not apply yourself? Why keep a spirit of laziness always?" Wukong said, "My disciple is also quite zealous; how could I be lazy?" Tripitaka said, "If you are so zealous, why do you not transform alms food for me? How can I carry on with my stomach empty? Besides, this mountain is full of poisonous mist. How shall we still reach Leiyin?" Wukong said, "Master, do not be angry, do not speak too sharply. I know your status is lofty and your pride quick to stir; if I had offended you, I would have to utter the Tightening Headband Spell. You sit the horse and stay steady. I will look for a house where I can obtain alms and prepare food."

Sun Wukong leapt up and vaulted into the clouds, hooked his hands into the cool cloud-surface, and opened his eyes to look around. The western road, poor thing, was utterly desolate, with no village or homestead in sight; it was exactly the sort of place where trees and woods appear often and signs of people are rare. After looking a long while, he saw, far to the south, a high mountain. On its sunny side there was a bright red patch. Sun Wukong dropped the cloud edge and said, "Master, there is something to eat." Tripitaka asked what it was. Wukong said, "There is no house here where I can transform cooked rice. On that southern mountain there is a red patch; it must be ripe mountain peaches. I will pick a few and bring them for your hunger." Tripitaka replied joyfully, "For an ordained monk to have peaches to eat would indeed be most meritorious." Wukong took a bowl, rose up with radiance, and in an instant he seemed to billow like a thunder-cloud, with cold wind whistling around him. In a short moment he flew southward and plucked peaches there; what followed is not set down.

There is a saying: where a mountain is high, monsters arise; where a ridge is steep, spirits take form. In truth, this mountain did have a demon. When Great Sage Sun Wukong arrived, he disturbed the creature. Riding the shadowy wind through the clouds, the demon saw the Master sitting below and exclaimed in delighted wonder: "What fate! What fate! For years people have spoken of the Tang monk of the Eastern Land who seeks the Great Vehicle. This is no mere man; he is an incarnation of a Golden Cicada Child, a primordial body from ten lifetimes of cultivation. If anyone could eat even one piece of his flesh, they would gain long life and longevity. So today he has truly come!" The demon stepped forward to seize him, but seeing two great generals guarding the Master at his left and right, it did not dare close in. It asked who these two generals were. It was Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing. Though neither had remarkable skill, Zhu Bajie was the Marshal of the Heavenly Canopy and Sha Wujing the Curtain-Pulling General; the force of their authority had not yet fully ebbed, so the demon dared not approach. The demon said, "Let me toy with him first and see what comes of it."

The holy monk dismounted beside the rock face, and suddenly a maiden in skirt and hairpin came near. Her green sleeves swayed lightly, cradling jade-bud splendor; her Xiang skirt sat slanting, revealing a golden lotus. Dew beaded upon her powdered face like blossoms wet with morning rain; dust swept her brows, smoky as willow-girl haze. He watched closely, fixing his eyes, and saw her come all the way to his side.

When Tripitaka saw her, he said, "Zhu Bajie, Sha Wujing, Wukong just said this region was wild and uninhabited. Do you see how someone has come out here from somewhere?" Zhu Bajie said, "Master, you and Sha Wujing sit still; let old Bajie go and have a look."

Beneath her icy skin lay jade-like bones, and at her collar the cream of her breast shone. Her willow-dark brows were thick with green-black tint, and her apricot eyes flashed with silver stars. Her face was moon-bright and graceful, her nature naturally clear. Her figure seemed to hide a swallow among willows; her voice sounded like an oriole trilling in the woods. With half-turned cheek she cast forth a dawn-bloom blush, while peonies had just opened as spring weather played.

When Zhu Bajie saw how bewitching she was, the simple brute felt ordinary human desire stir in him and could not stop himself from babbling: "Lady Bodhisattva, where are you going? What is it that you carry in your hands?" He clearly faced a demon, but he could not recognize it. The woman answered again and again: "Master, this blue jar holds fragrant rice, and the green bottle holds fried gluten. I have come only for one reason: by vow, I have come to offer alms to monks." When Zhu Bajie heard this, he was overjoyed, spun around in a pig-like dizzy wind, and ran back to Tripitaka: "Master, good men are surely rewarded by Heaven. You were hungry, and I, your senior brother, went to procure alms; that monkey has gone off plucking peaches and making sport. He has eaten too many peaches and has gotten a little noisy and a little light-headed. See, is this not a Bodhisattva who has come to offer us alms?" Tripitaka did not believe him: "You oaf, your chatter is nonsense. We have gone this far and met not one worthy person. From where would a begging Bodhisattva come?" Zhu Bajie said, "Master, are you sure about this?"

When Tripitaka saw her, he leapt up at once, joined his palms before his chest, and said, "Bodhisattva, where do you live? Whose household are you from? What vow has brought you here to offer alms to monks?" It was clearly a demon, yet even the Venerable did not recognize it. On seeing Tripitaka ask her ancestry, the girl at once played a show of gentle feeling and used flowery words to trick him: "Master, this mountain is called White Tiger Ridge, where serpents fear to return. Just beneath, to the west, is my home. My parents live at home; they listen to the sūtras and are known for doing great alms for monks from near and far. Yet because they have no sons, they prayed to the gods for blessing and gave birth to me. They raised me to marry into another household, but fearing they would have no support in old age, they chose a son-in-law and brought him here to care for us." Tripitaka said, "Bodhisattva, your words are off. The sacred canon says: 'While parents live, one should not wander afar; if one does, one wanders into peril.' Your parents still live in your hall, and you have even taken a husband. If you have a vow, send your husband home and all is in order; why then do you roam these mountains? And you have no maid or attendant to follow you. This is not proper for one keeping the way of a wife." The woman, smiling coyly, quickly returned with flirtatious words: "Master, my husband is in a hollow to the north of this mountain, along with several guests, weeding the fields. This meal was cooked by my maid to feed them. Because these are the hot fifth and sixth months, and there is no one to command, and my parents are old, I came myself to bring it. By chance I met three travelers from afar, and remembering my parents' love for the Dharma, I offer this meal to the monks as alms. If you do not reject it, please accept this humble offering." Tripitaka said, "Excellent, excellent! My disciple has gone off to pluck fruit and will return. I dare not eat. If this monk eats your meal and your husband learns of it, he will scold you—would he not make this poor monk bear blame too?" The woman, seeing Tripitaka would not eat, nevertheless blossomed all over with joy and said, "Master, the alms my parents give is not a small matter for me, and my husband is even better. He spends his life repairing bridges and roads, caring for elders and the poor. Yet if he hears this meal was given to you, his feeling for me as wife will be even different, more intimate than usual." Tripitaka still would not eat.

By the side, Zhu Bajie was already irritated to the point of fury. The dim-witted fellow pursed his lips and grumbled, "There are countless monks under heaven, and never have I seen an old monk so soft as me. The rice that is already cooked, I won’t eat unless it’s more than enough—wait till that monkey comes and finishes it, then I’ll eat my share." He refused to argue, tipped the jar over in one go, and was about to eat. Just then the Great Sage came down from the top of the southern mountain, carrying a few peaches, one bowl and a one-jin scoop. He opened his fiery golden eyes, recognized that the woman was a demon, set down the bowl, drew out his iron staff, and struck her at the crown. The startled Elder pulled him back and said, "Wukong, who are you going to hit now?" Wukong said, "Master, do not take this woman before you as a good person. She is a demon, come to cheat you." Tripitaka answered, "You monkey-head, you once had some judgment then, why babble now? This lady-bodhisattva has such kindness, bringing this food to feed us. How dare you call her a demon?" Wukong laughed, "Master, how much do you really know? When Old Sun made mischief in Water Curtain Cave, if he wanted to eat human flesh he took these forms: gold or silver, a noble pavilion, a drunken man, or a lustful woman. If some infatuated fool came for me, I would enchant him into my cave and indulge my whim—steamed or boiled for my use; if I could not finish him that way, I dried him to keep him from dampness. Master, if I had arrived late, you would surely have fallen into her snare and met her poisoned hand." Tang Sanzang would not believe him and insisted she was kindhearted. Wukong said, "Master, I know you. You have seen her face and surely stirred mortal longing. If that is so, tell Zhu Bajie to fell a few trees, ask Sha Wujing for some straw, and I will act as carpenter and make a shelter here; you can consummate your marriage with her, then we can all go our ways. Is that not a worthy task? Why must we still trudge on to fetch this scripture?" The Elder was a naturally soft-hearted monk and could not bear those words; he flushed from scalp to ears.

As Tang Sanzang stood in discomfort and shame, Wukong’s temper flared again. He drew his iron staff and struck the demon’s face. The monster had a trick and used a corpse-resurrection art. When she saw the staff coming toward him, she roused her spirit, moved away first, and sent a fake corpse head to the ground, which Wukong smashed. Terrified, the Elder trembled and muttered, "This monkey has no manners. Though I have warned him again and again, for no cause he hurts people." Wukong said, "Master, do not blame me; come and see what’s in this jar." Sha Wujing held the Elder forward. When he looked closely, there was no fragrant rice at all—only a jar of long-tailed maggots; not flour either, only several green frogs and toads, all hopping about. Then the Elder had some faith. But Zhu Bajie, unable to bear it, muttered from the side, "Master, about this woman: she is just a peasant woman of this area, out bringing food to the fields, and met us on the road. Why call her a demon? Brother’s staff is heavy; he came and tried a strike, and unexpectedly he killed her. He feared, if you chanted the Tightening Headband Spell, that she might deliberately cast an illusion spell, turn things into this kind of form, and blind your eyes so you would not chant."

From that one word by Tripitaka, misfortune seemed to arrive. As expected, he believed Zhu Bajie’s prompting, formed the hand-seal, and chanted the spell. Wukong cried out, "Headaches, headaches. Don’t chant, don’t chant, if you have something to say, say it." Tripitaka replied, "What is it to be said? A monk should always be practical, with benevolent thought always present—when sweeping, one fears to harm ants; one treasures even moths beneath a gauze-lamp shade. Why do you keep rampaging step by step, killing this ordinary person without cause? What use is it to bring back the Buddhist canon? Go back." Wukong asked, "Master, where do you want me to go back to?" Tripitaka said, "I do not want you to be my disciple." Wukong said, "You may not want me as a disciple, but then how will your journey to the Western Heaven be completed?" Tripitaka said, "My life is written in Heaven. If that demon should steam me and eat me, or boil me, that is not beyond reckoning. In any case, can you save the life span that is mine? Go back quickly." Wukong said, "Master, I can return, that is fine, only I have not yet repaid your grace." Tripitaka said, "What grace have I given you?" Hearing this, the Great Sage hurriedly knelt and knuckled his head to the ground: "Old Sun once wrecked the Heavenly Court and incurred a bodily crisis, and I was pinned beneath the Two-Realms Mountain by the Buddha. By Buddha’s grace, Guanyin gave me the precepts and discipline, and Master saved me. If I do not go with you to the Western Heaven, people will say I forgot a kindness and never repaid it, a name of blame through ten thousand ages." But this Tang Sanzang was a compassionate holy monk; seeing Wukong’s plea, he relented and said, "If that is what you mean, then I forgive you this time. Never be insolent again. If you still do evil, I will chant this spell backwards twenty times." Wukong said, "You may have me chant it thirty times if you wish; I just will not strike anyone now." Then he hurriedly attended Tripitaka, mounted with him, and offered the peaches he had gathered. Tripitaka, once mounted, ate a few himself to appease hunger.

The demon rose into the sky, life spirit gone. Wukong’s strike had not killed her; she had simply slipped out of her form. In the clouds she bit her teeth and hissed in rage: "For years I heard tales of his arts; today they are truly no exaggeration. Tang Sanzang did not recognize me and was about to eat. Had he only lowered his head to sniff once, I could have pulled him in a single grasp—then would he not be mine? Yet he happened to come, wrecked my operation, and nearly got him hit by my staff. To spare this monk would truly be labor for nothing. I will go down again and sport a bit with him."

The trickster demon then descended on a dark cloud and from beneath it changed at the forward slope into an old woman, eighty years old in appearance, leaning on a bent bamboo cane and walking with a wheezy cry at each step. Zhu Bajie saw her and cried out in alarm, "Master, this is bad—the old mother has come searching for someone." Tripitaka asked, "Searching for whom?" Zhu Bajie said, "Surely the daughter is what Brother Wukong said he killed. This must be her mother come to find him." Wukong said, "Brother, do not speak nonsense. That woman was eighteen; this old woman is eighty. How can a woman of sixty more still give birth? She must be false. Let the old Sun go and inspect."

" > She assumes the form of an old woman, white as frost the two temple locks.

Her walking is slow and dragging; her steps are timid and wavering. Her frame is weak, thin, and gaunt; her face is like a dried vegetable leaf. Her cheekbones lift upward, her lips turned downward. Old age is not like youth; her whole face is pleated like folded lotus leaves."

Wukong saw through her and recognized her as a demon. He did not bother with argument; he raised his staff and struck at the top of her head. As before, when she saw the staff coming, she snapped back to life, cast off her true spirit and withdrew it, leaving behind another false corpse head. Wukong struck that down as well beside the mountain path.

At once Tang Sanzang, startled, leapt from the horse, laid himself down by the roadside, and without another word chanted the Tightening Headband Spell in reverse for a full twenty times. The spell tightened Wukong’s head like a squeezed gourd, and the pain was almost unbearable. He rolled over and pleaded, "Master, stop chanting—just tell me what there is to be said." Tripitaka said, "What is it? A monk who hears good words will not fall into hell. I have tried to persuade you, yet why do you only commit acts of violence? You killed one ordinary person, and then killed another one. What does this mean?" Wukong said, "She was a demon." Tripitaka answered, "This monkey lies! Are there really that many demons? You are one naturally inclined toward good yet intent on evil. Go." Wukong said, "Master, you send me away again? If I return, I could return—but there is one part that does not fit." Tripitaka asked, "What does not fit?" Zhu Bajie said, "Master, he wants to split your luggage with you. After doing monkhood behind you for these years, he cannot go back empty-handed; give him two of those old worn shirts or torn hats from your bundle."

Upon hearing this, Wukong flew into a rage and barked, ‘You sharp-mouthed good-for-nothing! Wukong has always followed your precepts as a monk and has not a trace of jealousy or greed. How can you even talk of dividing luggage?’ Tripitaka said, ‘If you are not jealous or greedy, then why should you not go back?’ Wukong said, ‘I will not deceive you, Master. Five hundred years ago, when I flourished as a hero in Water Curtain Cave on Flower-Fruit Mountain, I subjugated the evil spirits of seventy-two caves, with forty thousand seven hundred lesser fiends under me. I wore a purple-gold crown, a saffron-yellow robe, a lanyin-belt at my waist, cloud-walking boots, and held the Ruyi Golden-Hooped Staff in my hand. I had truly once been a man. Since I took Nirvana pardon, shaved my head, and became a true monk to serve you, I became your disciple, and when you tightened this band on my head I could scarcely hope to face my old countrymen if I returned. If you truly do not want me, then chant the loosen-spell once, remove this hoop, entrust it to you, and place it on another’s head; then I would be at ease and could still go on with this journey with you. Is it not that these people have no other intent?’ Tripitaka was greatly startled and said, ‘Wukong, I once received only a hidden copy of the Tightening Headband Spell from the Bodhisattva; there is no loosening spell at all.’ Wukong said, ‘If there is no loosen-spell, you still need take me along and we can go on.’ The elder, helpless, said, ‘Get up. I forgive you this once, but do not become violent again.’ Wukohnsaid, ‘I will not dare again. I will not dare again.’ Then he knelt, attended to his master, mounted behind him, and they pushed on along the road.

That fiend had not, after all, been slain by the Great Sage’s second stroke of the staff. In midair, he praised him without end: ‘What a Monkey King! You still have eyes. I changed forms again and again, yet he recognized me. The monks go fast; once they pass this mountain and go forty li westward, they will be beyond my control. If some other demon carries them off, they will laugh until their mouths split and break my own heart. I will go down and mock him a little.’

The villain turned. In a gust of eerie wind from below, he transformed at the foot of the slope into a true old gentleman:

White hair like Pengzu, Beard as dark-blue as the Star of Longevity. A jade clapper rang at his ear, and a golden speck shimmered in his eye. A dragon-head cane in hand, a light robe like a crane’s wing upon him, Prayer beads pinched in hand, and he muttered a Namo sutra.

Tripitaka, seeing him from horseback, was overjoyed and said, ‘Amitabha Buddha! The Western land is truly blessed. Even that old fellow cannot climb the path, yet still he chants as he moves ahead.’ Zhu Bajie said, ‘Master, do not praise him yet. He is the root of disaster.’ Tripitaka asked, ‘How is he the root of disaster?’ Zhu Bajie replied, ‘Brother Wukong killed his daughter and his old wife. This is just his old father come to search for them. If we should clash with him in his arms, Master, you will die for it and bear grave guilt; I, Zhu Bajie, will be judged to hard service; Sha Wujing will be ordered into official punishment. If Great Sage slips away with a flight spell, will it not still drag the three of us through sorrow?’

Hearing this, Wukong said, ‘This blunt fool, with such nonsense, has it not frightened Master? Let old Wukong go and inspect once more.’ He tucked his staff at his side, stepped forward, and faced the monster, calling out, ‘Old man, where are you going? Why walk and yet keep chanting?’ The demon, having mistaken him for an easy one by the star-name Dingpan, took Wukong for no threat and answered, ‘Great Master, I am an old man who has lived here all my life. I have always been pious, feeding monks, reading sutras, and chanting the Buddha’s name. Fate gave me no son. I had only one little daughter and took in a son-in-law. This morning she carried food to the fields, and I think she must have fallen into the tiger’s mouth. My old wife came first to search for her and has not returned. I had no idea where she had gone. I came only to look; indeed the poor creature was grievously hurt and I could do nothing. I gathered his remains and buried them in a proper mound.’ Wukong laughed, ‘I am an old master of tiger-making; how did you hide that ghost in your sleeve to fool me? You deceived everyone, and I see through it. I know you are a fiend.’ The fiend was startled into silence. Wukong drew out his staff and thought, ‘If I do not strike him, he may make a breeze and haul away Master, and then I will spend my strength rescuing him again. If I strike him, and Master recites that spell, the saying goes, “Even a tiger does not eat its cub.” So I can use my wit and fluent tongue to fool him for a while and then be done.’ The Great Sage chanted and called to the local land-god and mountain spirit: ‘This fiend has mocked my Master three times. This time I will kill him. Be my witnesses in midair and let him not flee.’ The gods who heard, who could disobey? all responded from the cloud banks. At the raising of the staff, the Great Sage knocked the fiend down, ending his spirit-fire at once.

Back on horseback, Tripitaka trembled in fear, scarcely able to speak. Zhu Bajie laughed at his side: ‘Good Wukong, you have stirred up a storm. In only half a day’s distance you have already killed three men.’ Tripitaka was about to recite the spell when Wukong hurried before the horse and called, ‘Master, do not recite, do not recite. Come and see his true form.’ There was only a heap of chalk-white skulls there. Tripitaka exclaimed in great alarm, ‘Wukong, this man is dead—how has he become a pile of bones?’ Wukong said, ‘He was a lurking-ling spirit acting as a jiangshi. Here he had led men astray and ruined them; when I struck him down, his true nature appeared. On his spine there are characters reading, “White Bone Wife.” Tripitaka even believed him. Zhu Bajie at the side interjected, ‘Master, his heavy club and cruel strike kill people; perhaps when you recite that phrase he intentionally changes shape into this form to blind your eyes.’ Tripitaka, being soft-eared as always, believed him and resumed the recitation. Wukong could not endure the pain and knelt by the roadside, crying, ‘Do not recite, do not recite—say what you came to say at once.’ Tripitaka said, ‘Monkey-head, what more is there to tell? A monk doing good is like grass in a spring garden: you do not see it rise, yet it grows from day to day. A doer of evil is like a whetstone: you do not see it diminish, yet it wears down day by day. In this wild wilderness you have killed three people in a row with no one to report it and no opponent to accuse you. If we reach a city, a place with crowds of people and smoke of life, and you seize your wailing-bone staff and beat people about not knowing right from wrong, you will bring a great calamity and tell me how I am to escape. Go back.’ Wukong said, ‘Master, you wrong me. This brute is plainly a fiend; he meant to hurt you, and I have just slain him to remove your danger, but you do not know it. Yet you believe that stupid jibe from Zhu Bajie and have again chased me off. There is a saying: nothing should pass through three attempts. If I do not leave now, I am truly a base and shameless one. I am going, I am going. I am going now, only no one under you can restrain me.’ Tripitaka grew angry: ‘This unruly monkey grows more insolent. If it seems only you are human, then are Wuzheng and Wujing not human?’

When that Great Sage heard Tripitaka speak of Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing as men, he could not hold back his grief and pity. He cried, ‘Alas! When you set out from Chang’an, Liu Beiqin sent you onward. At Two-Worlds Mountain, you saved me and I bowed to you as my master. I passed through ancient caves, entered deep forests, captured demons and spirits, gathered Zhu Bajie, won Sha Wujing, and endured ten thousand hardships. Today, with willfully clouded eyes, you treat me like a fool and bid me return home. This is just as they say: “When the birds are gone, hide the bow; when the rabbit dies, cook the dog!” Enough, enough, enough—only there is this Tightening Headband Spell added to it.’ Tripitaka said, ‘I will recite no more.’ Wukong said, ‘That is hard to know. If we reach a place where poisonous demons torment and cannot escape, and if Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing cannot save you, then at that moment, remembering me, you will not help but chant it again. Even if it is ten thousand li, my head too will ache; if I ever again meet you then, I would rather not have that intention.’

Tripitaka, hearing him, grew more annoyed and dismounted from the saddle in a rush. He told Sha Wujing to take out paper and brush from the pack, and at the stream took water, ground ink on a stone, and wrote a letter of dismissal, handing it to Wukong with these words: ‘Monkey-head, keep this as proof. Do not be my disciple any longer. If I meet you again, I will fall into Avici Hell.’ Wukong at once took the letter and said, ‘No need to swear, old Wukong will go.’ He folded the document and tucked it in his sleeve, yet again spoke gently to Master: ‘Master, I too set out with you and was instructed by the Bodhisattva. Halfway now, this venture is lost and no merit gained. Please sit and allow me to take a bow, so that I can leave in peace.’ Tripitaka turned away and ignored him, muttering to himself, ‘I am a good monk and do not receive a rogue’s courtesy.’ Seeing Master refuse him, the Great Sage used an outer trick, plucked three hairs from the back of his head, blew out immortal qi, and cried, ‘Transform!’ He became three more Wukongs, four in all, and surrounded Tripitaka from four sides as they knelt. The elder could not dodge right or left and at last he too received one bow.

Sun Wukong jumped up, shook himself, drew in his hairs, and once more instructed Sha Wujing: “You are a fine young brother, but only keep watch over Zhu Bajie’s words and whispers, and be doubly careful on the road. If at any time a demon seizes the Master, then say that Old Sun is his senior disciple; the Western Hair Monster, having heard of my methods, would not dare to hurt my Master.” Tripitaka said, “I am a good monk; I won’t speak your villain’s name. Go back now.”

The Great Sage saw the Elder beg three or four times, and he would not be moved or return to kindness, so in the end he had no choice but to go. Look at him:

He wept, knelt in head-bowed prostration, and took leave of the Elder, sorrowful, leaving instructions with full intent to Sha Wujing. He brushed the grass before the slope with one hand, then with both feet kicked up and overturned the vines at his feet. He rose to heaven and dropped to earth like a turning wheel, foremost in leaping over seas and flying mountains. In but a moment his figure was gone from sight; in an instant he hurried back along the old way.

See how he held in his anger, parted from Tripitaka, loosed the Jindou Cloud, and headed straight back to Flower-Fruit Mountain’s Water Curtain Cave. All alone, desolate and heartbroken, he suddenly heard a roar of water in his ears. When the Great Sage looked about in the air, it proved to be the booming of the Eastern Ocean’s tide. As soon as he heard it, he thought of Tripitaka again and could not keep back tears from falling down his cheeks; he stilled both cloud and stride and only after a long while went on.

In the end, no one yet knows what will come of this journey back; listen to the next chapter for resolution.
