This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Then it is told that the monster had bound Sha Wujing but did not come to kill him, did not beat him, and did not curse him even once. He raised his steel blade and thought privately: “Tripitaka is a man of high standing, surely he knows propriety and righteousness. Certainly he is not the sort to spare my life and then have his disciple seize me. Ah, all this is because I must have had some letter sent through him to his country, and the whole matter has been stirred up like a gusty storm. Let me go and ask him about it once.” At once the demon suddenly flared into rage and sought to kill the princess.

The princess, unaware of this, had only just finished dressing herself when she stepped forward. She saw the demon with eyes glowering, brows drawn together, teeth clenched. She greeted him with a coaxing smile: “My lord, what matter troubles you so deeply?” The demon snapped out, “You wretched, worthless woman, your heart is base and you have no human decency. When I first brought you here, you did not once speak. In the matter of the brocade you wear and the gold you bear, if anything was missing I went to seek it. Through the four seasons there have been enjoyments; each day our bond has been intimate. How can you think only of your parents and no longer hold even a trace of a wife’s heart toward your husband?”

The princess, hearing this, was terrified. She fell to her knees: “My lord, why today do you speak of words of separation?” “Do not think this is my parting; it is yours,” he said. “I brought Tripitaka here and planned he should serve for our pleasure. Why did you not first tell me and then let him go? It is plainly because you secretly wrote a letter in private and had him carry and deliver it for you. Otherwise how did these two monks come and strike at my gate, escorting you back? Is this not your doing?” “Lord, you wrong me—you have mistaken. When would I have any such letter?” The old demon said, “You still answer me boldly. Now there is a foe here in your hands; is that not proof?” “Who is it?” The old demon said, “It is Tripitaka’s second disciple, Sha Wujing.” But once one has come to the edge of death, who is willing to admit it? So he could only deal with it loosely. The princess said, “My lord, first calm yourself. Let me go with you and ask him. If there truly is a letter, then kill him and I will accept it. If there is no letter, should we not have spared even this slave from needless death?”

The monster heard her words and allowed no more delay. He lifted up one indigo-blue hand as wide as a winnowing basket, seized the princess’s hair—its strands like gold branches and jade leaves—and pulled her forward, dragging her to the ground. Clutching his steel knife, he came to interrogate Sha Wujing, barking: “Sha Wujing! You two dare to come to our gate with such daring—did this woman send a letter to your king’s land, and did the king command you to come?”

Sha Wujing was bound there. Seeing how ferocious and reckless the demon truly was, having seen him fling the princess down and raise the knife to kill, he thought in his heart: “It is clear he had a letter, and by that he saved my master. This is a vast kindness. If I speak plainly, he will kill the princess. Is that not repaying kindness with enmity? Enough—enough! Sha Wujing has gained no merit in service of my master at all. Since I am bound today, let this life be repaid to my master for that debt.” So he cried out, “Demon, do not be impertinent. Whatever letter he might have brought, you cannot so wrongfully accuse him and seek his life. We came only to ask for the princess for a reason.

Because you captured my master in the cave, my master saw the princess’s appearance and her movements. When we reached the Precious Elephant Kingdom and produced the pass, the emperor showed a painted image of the princess and then inquired in all respects. Upon seeing that portrait he asked my master whether he had seen her on the road. My master then spoke of her. The emperor at once knew she was his daughter. He granted us imperial wine and told us to come for you, that the princess might return to the palace. This is the truth. Never was there any letter. If you insist on killing, then kill this old Sha, but do not falsely harm an innocent person. You ruin both Heaven’s order and human righteousness.”

Seeing that Sha Wujing spoke with such force and vigor, the demon threw down the knife, lifted the princess up with both arms and said, “My roughness was of only one sudden moment. I have much jostled and erred. Do not blame me.” Then he gathered up her blue-black hair, set her jeweled knot upright, and with soft words, gentle tone, and pleasant face and color, he cajoled her inside and invited her to be seated in courtesy. The princess was, by nature, soft and yielding, the way of women; seeing his apparent deference, she changed her mind and said, “My lord, if you cherish the affection of husband and wife, then loosen the rope on Sha Wujing a little.”

The old demon, hearing this, immediately ordered his underlings to untie Sha Wujing but keep him bound there. Sha Wujing, freed from the bonds yet still locked in place, stood up and thought in private with quiet joy: “The ancients said, ‘To make it easy for others is to make it easy for oneself.’ If I do not make things easy for him, how would he be willing to release me?”

The old demon then arranged a banquet and held company with the princess to quiet her fear. As they drank to half-intoxication, he suddenly changed into a brighter robe, took a treasure sword and fastened it at his waist. He turned and touched her, saying: “Husband, stay at home and drink; watch the two boys and see that you do not release Sha Wujing. Since Tripitaka is in that kingdom, I should make haste and go to acknowledge my kin.” The princess said, “You cannot go.” The old demon asked, “How can I not go?” She said, “My father is no petty lord’s mountain won by horse and force. It is the ancestral state his forefathers left him. Since childhood he has ascended as crown prince and has not even gone far beyond the city gate. He has never seen a ferocious man like this. Your face and appearance are so ugly; if he sees you, he may be frightened. That would not be proper. Better not to go than to go and be blamed.” The old demon replied, “If this is how it is, then I will simply change into a handsome man.” The princess said, “Try it once, and I shall see.”

That strange monster transformed during the banquet and in a twinkling became a handsome young man. Truly he looked thus:

Elegant in appearance, with a statuesque and lofty frame. His speech had the air of an official, his conduct fitting for fine youthful manners. In talent he was like Zi Jian’s easy verse, in beauty like Pan’an tossing a fruit lightly. On his head sat a magpie-tail crown, dark as a banked storm cloud. On his body he wore a jade-folded robe, its broad sleeves fluttering and welcoming. At his feet were black pleated shoes, and at his waist a radiant phoenix belt. In complexion and spirit he was truly a wondrous man, lofty, rising and proud, handsome and refined.

The princess rejoiced greatly on seeing him. The demon laughed, “My lord, did the transformation come out well?” She said, “It is good, it is good. When you enter the court this way, my father will receive you as kin and have both civil and military officials stand to host you for banqueting. Yet in the midst of any drinking, be careful a thousand times, careful ten thousand times. Do not reveal your original face or expose your true horse-hoofs; if you let slip, it will no longer be literate conduct.” The old demon said, “No need to instruct me. It is already clear in itself.”

You see, he took to cloud-riding at once and quickly reached the Precious Elephant Kingdom. He came down from the cloud mount and walked to the outside of the hall gate, and said to the gate messenger: “The third royal son-in-law requests audience, please submit and have it conveyed.” The yellow-gate official came to the white-jade steps and announced: “Your Majesty, there are three sons-in-law here to seek an audience. They are now outside the gate awaiting proclamation.” The king, who was then conversing with Tripitaka, heard this. He asked the ministers, “I have only two sons-in-law. How is it that there is also a third?” A minister replied, “If there is a third son-in-law, it must surely be that a demon has arrived.” The king asked, “May he be called in?” Tripitaka, the senior monk, said anxiously, “Your Majesty, this is a demon, yes—but a demon without true spirit is powerless. He can know the past and the future, and he can ride cloud and command mist. Whether you summon him in or not, he will still come in. It is better, then, to summon him; at least it saves some face.”

The king acknowledged the report and ordered him announced and brought to the Golden Steps. He performed the same sort of ritual by dancing and crying out while bowing. The many officials, seeing him handsome and refined, did not dare to take him for a demon spirit. They were merely mortals of flesh and blood, and so they treated him as a good man. The king, seeing him tower and stand skyward as if he were a beam and a pillar meant to aid the age, asked, 'Imperial son-in-law, where do you dwell? From what family? When was it arranged that my princess would marry you? Why only come today to acknowledge the alliance?' The old demon knelt and said, 'Your Majesty, your servant is from Wave-Moon Cave of Wanzi Mountain, east of the city.' The king asked, 'How far is that mountain from here?' The old demon said, 'Not far—only three hundred li.' The king said, 'Three hundred li? How could my princess ever reach there to be matched with you?' The demon-spirit, with clever words and flowing flattery, answered as if in sincere sorrow: 'Your Majesty, I have been fond since childhood of bow and horse, and I made my living by hunting. Thirteen years ago, I led dozens of house boys, with hawks and hounds, and suddenly saw a mottled ferocious tiger carrying a young woman down a slope. Your servant drew one arrow and brought down the tiger, carried the woman to my own estate, and fed her warm water and hot broth to wake her, saving her life. When he asked from where she came, she never spoke the word princess. How could I dare to harbor deceit, and, on my own intent, match myself to the Three Princesses of Your Majesty? If she had truly been a royal daughter, I would have entered the golden hall and sought even a minor post, to dignify myself. It was only because she said she was a peasant girl that your servant kept her at the manor. She was beautiful and he a handsome scholar, so with equal willingness they matched and have done so for these years. After matching her, I wished to slaughter that tiger and invite all the kin, yet the Princess ordered not to kill it. As for not killing it, my reason was in a few good words, and I said:

By heaven and by earth they made us a pair; no matchmaker, no proof is required for marriage.
In a former life a red cord had already tied our feet, and today this tiger has become the matchmaker. By this my words, I untied the tiger and spared his life. Wounded by the arrow, he ran off with tail clipped and hoofs shorn. Unknown to anyone, he retained his life, and in those mountains for these years he cultivated and refined himself into a spirit, intent only on bewitching and harming people. Your servant has heard that in former times there were some who traveled for scripture, and they were all pilgrims of Great Tang, called Tripitaka. I think this tiger ruined Tripitaka, took his credentials, and has taken the form of a scripture-seeker; now, in court, he deceives Your Majesty. Your Majesty, the one seated on the embroidered cushion is exactly that fierce tiger who carried off the princess thirteen years ago, and not the true Tripitaka.'

Look at this king of a watery nature, who is deluded by mortal eyes and cannot know a demon spirit, taking a mere hollow word and making it true. He said, 'Wise imperial son-in-law, how do you recognize this monk as the tiger that carried the princess?' The demon replied, 'Your Majesty, in the mountains your servant ate tiger meat, wore tiger hides, and slept and rose with him; how could I not recognize him?' The king said, 'If you can recognize him, have him show his true form so all may see.' The monster said, 'Grant me half a cup of clear water, and your servant will make him show his true form.' The king ordered an official to fetch water and bring it to the imperial son-in-law.

The monster took the water in hand, rose up and stepped forward, and used the Black-Eye Immobilizing Method. Reciting a charm, he spat a mouthful of water toward Tripitaka and shouted, 'Transform!' The elder monk’s true body, hidden up in the hall, truly became a mottled fierce tiger. At that moment, king and ministers, with mere mortal eyes, beheld the tiger:

White forehead and round head, mottled body, lightning eyes.
Four hooves, upright and lofty, rugged and rising; twenty claws, bent hooks, keen and sharp.
Saw-edged teeth around the mouth, ears sharp and joined to the brows.
Frightful and bulky like a great cat-shaped beast, ferocious and strong like a young ox.
Straight bristled whiskers like silver strips, split tongue crimson and hissing, spitting foul breath.
So it was indeed a fierce mottled tiger, and wave after wave of fearsome wind blew through the precious hall. The king looked once and his spirit was shaken and scattered. Frightened, all the ministers all dodged away. A few bold generals, leading generals and company commanders, rushed forward in a crowd and hacked with all kinds of weapons. This time, either Tripitaka ought not have had life to lose, or else all twenty monks would have been cut to mince. As fate would have it, the gods Ding Jia, Jie Di, Gong Cao, and Hūjiào, guarding unseen in midair, protected him, and so none of their weapons could wound him. The ministers cried out until nightfall; then they captured that tiger alive, bound him with iron rope, put him in an iron cage, and confined him in the inner court.

Yet the king ordered a grand banquet to be laid in the Bright-Essence Hall, giving thanks for the merit of the imperial son-in-law in the rescue, else he almost would have been harmed by that monk. That evening, when the ministers dispersed, the demon entered the Hall of Yinan. He selected eighteen palace attendants and colored-skirted maidens, and with flute and lute they sang and danced, urging the demon to drink and feast. The monster sat alone on the top seat, while all around him were women of alluring form and beauty. See how he took pleasure in drink: by the second watch it had risen, and he could not hold himself. He sprang up and laughed once, showed his true form, and suddenly let loose terrible intent. He spread wide his winnowing-basket-like hands and grabbed a maid who was plucking the pipa, then bit down and took a piece of her head. Frightened, those seventeen palace women, half-dead in fear, ran wildly forward and hiding places all around. You can see:

The court maidens were startled with terror, the painted girls quickly alarmed.
Court maidens in fright were like raindrops striking a lotus cage in a night storm;
the painted girls in panic, like peonies tossed to dance in spring wind.
The one clutching the pipa, to save her life, broke it to pieces and stumbled, bruising zither and lute as she fled.
At the gates they ran north and south, fleeing the hall with no care for east or west.
They battered their jade-bright faces and shattered their fair features.
All ran to save their lives, each seeking a fragment of life. When those women came out, they dared not call out. It was deep into the night, and they dared not alarm the household. They all hid beneath the short wall eaves, trembling and fearful.

The monster sat there, drinking for himself. He drank a cup, pulled a man forward, blood-slicked, and gnawed two mouthfuls. Inside he feasted while outside everyone spread the word: 'Tripitaka is a tiger spirit.' The clamoring of rumors spread all the way to the Golden Pavilion Post. At that time the post had no people, only a white horse in the stall eating hay and grain. He was the Small Dragon King of the Western Sea, who for offense against Heaven had had his horn sawed off and his scales shed, and changed into a white horse to carry Tripitaka west to fetch the sutras. Hearing the talk that Tripitaka was a tiger spirit, he secretly thought, 'My master is clearly a good man; surely a demon has turned him into a tiger spirit and harmed him. What should I do? what should I do? Sun Wukong has been away so long, and Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing have no sign.' He stood on such agitation until the second watch, and at last leapt up and said, 'If I do not save Tripitaka now, this merit and fruit are lost, lost!' He could not bear to hold the reins any longer, loosened bridle and saddle, and quickly appeared in true form as a dragon. He rose on black clouds and flew straight into the ninth heaven to look. A verse bears witness:

Tripitaka comes west to bow before the Buddha, yet on the road there is wicked demon fog.
Tonight he took tiger form, but by a loosening of the white horse reins he will save the master.

The Small Dragon King, in midair, saw the hall of Yinan shining with radiant lamp-flames and candles. There were eight red floor carpets in all, each with a candle lit upon it. Lowering his head through the clouds and looking closely, he saw the demon alone up there forcing out wine while eating human flesh. The little dragon laughed, 'This fellow is no one’s equal, his horse-gait is gone and his disguise is exposed; yet he still pretends and weighs things with false measure. Is it truly a way to continue eating humans? He does not know where my master is, and still meets this wild fiend by chance. Let me go and play him once. If I succeed, I shall seize the demon spirit and then there will be no delay in saving my master.'

The good little dragon, with one transformation, also became a palace maiden, truly light of body and graceful of beauty. He quickly stepped and entered. To the demon he said with reverence, 'Imperial son-in-law, do not harm my life. I have come to fill your cup.' The demon said, 'Pour the wine.' The little dragon took the flask and poured wine into his cup; it rose three to five fen above the rim, yet did not overflow. This was the dragon’s use of the Pressing-Water Technique. The demon, not recognizing it, was glad in his heart and said, 'You have such a technique?' The little dragon replied, 'I can fill it a little higher.' The demon said, 'Pour again, pour again.' He lifted the flask and simply poured; the wine kept rising like a thirteen-tiered treasure pagoda, sharp and full to the top, never spilling. The demon stretched his mouth and took one cup, then with dead flesh in hand took a bite. He asked, 'Can you sing?' The little dragon said, 'I know a little.' She sang a short melody in tune and served him another cup. The demon asked, 'Can you dance?' The little dragon said, 'I know a little, but only with bare hands; my dance is not good to see.' The demon pulled up his clothing, took off the precious sword at his waist, drew out its scabbard, and handed it to the little dragon.

Xiaolong caught the sword and focused. In front of the banquet table he stepped three up, four down, five to the left, six to the right, then set aside the Flower-Blade technique. The monster watched in astonishment. Xiaolong cast away the flower-sign flourish and watched for the demon to come down with a stroke. The fiend was so strange: he sidestepped in alarm, and, flustered in his movements, raised a Mantanghong to block the precious blade. The Mantanghong had in fact been forged from seasoned iron, with the handle weighing eighty or ninety jin. The two came out of Yin’an Hall. Xiaolong revealed his true form, mounted his cloud head, and fought the demon in midair. That bout in the dark was fierce to behold. It may be seen thus:

One was a monster born on Wanzi Mountain, and this one a true dragon from beneath the Western Sea. One cast out radiance like sprayed white lightning; one generated keen qi like red clouds bursting. One seemed like an ivory-tusked old elephant striding among men; one like a gold-clawed leopard-cat flying down through the world. One was a jade pillar that props the sky; one a golden beam that spans the sea. The silver dragon whirled, the yellow ghost surged and roiled. On either side the treasured swords did not slacken; to and fro they came without ceasing, the Mantanghong and all.

The two fought among the clouds for eight or nine rounds. Xiaolong’s hands grew soft and numb; the old demon’s body was strong and heavy with strength. Xiaolong could not match him, so he rose and swung his sword to cut at the demon. The demon had a way of receiving a cut: with one hand he took the precious sword, and with the other hand he flung down the Mantanghong and struck. Xiaolong was caught off guard, and the demon struck him on the hind leg. In alarm he crashed back onto his cloud horse. By luck, the River-commanding Water saved his life, and Xiaolong dived headfirst into the water. The fiend came searching for him but could not find him. He took the precious sword, took the Mantanghong, returned to Yin’an Hall, and resumed, as before, drinking and sleeping; no further account is given.

That little dragon lay hidden beneath the water. After half a watch, hearing nothing at all, he only then bit his teeth, endured the pain in his leg, and leapt up. He stepped on black clouds and turned straight toward the relay pavilion, then changed back into his ordinary horse form and lay beneath the manger. All of him was drenched, and his leg had a bruised blue mark. At that moment:

The heart-horse and mind-monkey were both scattered. Golden Lord and Wooden Mother were all withered. The Yellow Crone was wounded through to understanding. If moral right becomes remote, how can the Way ever be made whole?

Let it suffice for now to set aside Tripitaka’s danger and Xiaolong’s defeat. As for Zhu Bajie, after parting from Sha Wujing, he hid himself in the grass and made a muddy wallow. He slept through that doze until deep in the night before waking. Upon waking he did not know in what place he was. He rubbed his eyes, steadied his thoughts, and only then listened. Ah! It was exactly the kind of deep mountain where no dogs barked and wild space had little rooster cry. He saw the stars shifting and the Dipper turning, and judged it was about the time of the third watch. In his heart he thought: 'I must go back and rescue Sha Wujing. Truly, a single thread has no line; a lone palm cannot make sound. Enough! I will go into the city, report to the Master, get permission from the present authority, and then choose some brave men and horses to help old pig come tomorrow and rescue Sha Wujing.'

Zhu Bajie rushed up on cloud and headed straight back to the city. In a moment he arrived at the relay station. It was moonlit and quiet. Under the two corridors he could not find Tripitaka, and only saw the white horse sleeping there, entirely wet through, with a blue mark of the size of a small tray on its hind leg. Bajie started in alarm and said, 'Double misfortune indeed. This fellow has not walked a step, yet how is there sweat on his body and a blue mark on his leg? Perhaps villainous men have waylaid the Master and maimed the horse.' The white horse recognized Bajie and suddenly spoke in human words: 'Brother.' Bajie shivered in fright, sprang up and tried to go out. The white horse leaned out and, with one bite, caught hold of his robe and said, 'Brother, do not be afraid of me.' Bajie, trembling, said, 'Brother, why are you speaking today? If you are speaking, there must be great misfortune.' Xiaolong said, 'Do you know if the Master is in danger?' Bajie said, 'I do not know.' Xiaolong said, 'You do not. You and Sha Wujing showed off before the Emperor, planning to take that demon and receive credit and reward. But the demon’s power was great. Your methods were insufficient and you could not suppress him. You sent one back to tell the news, yet no word came at all. That fiend changed into a handsome scholar, crashed into court, and became close to the Emperor. He turned our Master into a mottled fierce tiger; the ministers caught it and locked it in an iron cage in the court room. I heard this sorrow and my heart was cut as by a blade. You have been gone two days and know nothing, fearing that life might be taken at once, I had to change into dragon form and go to rescue. Yet even when I entered the court, I still could not find the Master. When I reached outside Yin’an Hall, I met the demon. I then changed into a palace-maid shape and deceived that monster. The monster told me to show my swordplay as he watched, and so I dropped my guard and cut at him once. He had it dodged. With both hands he raised the Mantanghong and put me to the rout. I swung my sword and struck again, but he caught the blade, drew down the Mantanghong, and struck my hind leg. For this reason I burrowed into the River-commanding Water and escaped with my life. The blue mark on my leg came from his Mantanghong.

Hearing this, Bajie said, 'Could this really have happened?' Xiaolong said, 'Could it be I am deceiving you?' Bajie said, 'How is it then? How is it then? Can you move at all?' Xiaolong said, 'If I can move, what of it?' Bajie said, 'If you can move, then go and swim out to sea. Have the baggage hauled by old pig up to Gao Laozhuang, and go home to become a son-in-law.' When Xiaolong heard this, he bit Bajie’s straight robe and would not let it go. Unable to hold back tears, he said, 'Brother, please do not grow indolent.' Bajie said, 'If it were not laziness, then what? Brother Sha has already been taken by him. I cannot beat him. If we do not seize this moment to disperse the fire at once, what else are we waiting for?'

Xiaolong pondered in silence for half a while, then with tears said, 'Brother, do not speak of venting anger. If you want to save the Master, you only need to ask someone to come.' Bajie said, 'Tell me whom to ask.' Xiaolong said, 'Go quickly, ride the cloud and return to Flower-Fruit Mountain, and invite Great Elder Brother Sun Wukong. He still has great demonic-subduing powers and will surely rescue the Master and give you and me satisfaction for this defeat.' Bajie said, 'Brother, it is enough to invite another man. That monkey and I have some misunderstanding. Earlier on White Tiger Ridge, I killed the White-Bone Lady. He blamed me for goading the Master to recite the Tightening Headband Spell. I thought it was only fooling around, but the old monk actually took it seriously and drove him away. I do not know why, but he is angered with me and will certainly refuse to come. If I do not answer him exactly right in speech, his staff is very heavy; if he lands a few blows without knowing measure, how could I live?' Xiaolong said, 'He would not strike you. He is a monkey king of kindness and righteousness. When you see him, do not even say the Master is in danger. Just say, "The Master misses you." Bring him here with coaxing. Once he comes and sees this situation, he will surely be stirred and determined to contend with that demon; he will with certainty seize that demon and save my Master.' Bajie said, 'Fine, fine. You have shown such thorough care. If I do not go, it would show I lacked feeling. If I go now and the traveler Sun truly comes, I will come together with him. If he does not come, then do not expect me; I will not come either.' Xiaolong said, 'Go, go—he will certainly come.'

The glutton really gathered up his spiked rake, fastened his straight robe, and sprang up. He stepped on clouds and headed directly east. In this time also, it was Tripitaka’s destiny. The fool met a favorable wind and spread his two ears wide, making a good wind sail; he crossed the Eastern Ocean at once and came down upon cloud. Before he realized it, the sun had risen over the stars, and he yet entered the mountains to seek the way.

As he was making his way, he suddenly heard voices. Zhu Bajie peered closely, and it seemed to be Sun Wukong in a mountain hollow gathering a host of demons. He sat on a rocky cliff, and before him were over twelve hundred monkeys arranged in orderly ranks, calling: 'Long live the Great Sage, Grand Lama!' Bajie thought, 'What a life to enjoy, what a life to enjoy. No wonder he refused to become a monk. If he only came home, there are these comforts: such a huge estate and so many young monkeys serving him. If old pig had this kind of mountain domain, he would not be a monk either. Now that I have come here, what then is to be done? I must see him in person.' The glutton felt somewhat afraid of him and yet did not dare to face him plainly, so he slipped along the grassy cliff edge, weaving in among the one thousand two-to-three-hundred monkeys, and, with them, bowed in mock obeisance.

Not knowing that the Great Sage sat so high and that his eyes were both clever and sharp, Sun Wukong saw clearly and asked, "Among this group, the one bowing in disorder is an outsider, a yi-ren. From where has he come? Bring him up." Before the command was done, those small monkeys, in a swarm, pushed Zhu Bajie forward and threw him down on the ground. Sun Wukong said, "Where are you from, outsider?" Zhu Bajie kept his head low and replied, "Forgive me for asking. I am not an outsider; I am acquainted, quite acquainted." Sun Wukong said, "The monkeys under my command all look much the same. Your face and features are of another sort, somewhat rugged and strange. You must be a demon from elsewhere. If you would join my troop, first hand over your roll and give your name, then I can place you in my own ranks. If I do not keep you, dare you make such reverent fuss here?" Zhu Bajie bent his head and with his lips curled said, "No shame? Then this is the face I have. I have served your brothers for several years and yet I have not judged truly, could not tell that I was being called an outsider." Sun Wukong laughed, "Raise your head so I can see." The boor pulled his mouth upward and said, "Will you not recognize me by my face?" Sun Wukong could not help laughing: "Zhu Bajie." Hearing that name once, he sprang up with a jolt and said, "Yes, yes, I am Zhu Bajie." Sun Wukong thought to himself, "Now that he is recognized, talk will be easy."

Sun Wukong said, "You are not with Tripitaka fetching the scriptures, so why did you come here? I imagine you must have offended Master and been sent back. If there was a decree of banishment, show it for me to see." Zhu Bajie said, "I did not offend him at all. There was no banishing decree, and he did not drive me out." Sun Wukong said, "If there is no banishment and he did not drive you out, then why did you come here?" Zhu Bajie said, "Master missed you and sent me to invite you." Sun Wukong said, "He did not miss me, nor did he invite me. That day, before Heaven, he swore and wrote a banishment in his own hand. How could he now miss me and at the same time send you so far to ask me to come? I tell you truly I am not willing to go." Zhu Bajie quickly made a pretext and said, "It is because he misses you, it is because he misses you." Sun Wukong asked, "How is it he misses me then?" Zhu Bajie said, "Master was riding on ahead and calling out 'disciple', but I did not hear it. Sha Wujing also has poor hearing, like one who cannot catch the sound. So Master remembered you and said we are not capable without you, and said that you are still sharp and quick, always answering one with ten. Because he misses you so much, he singled me out to invite you. Please come out and go, if only so his longing is not left unanswered, and so I do not return with my effort wasted in crossing so far." Hearing this, Sun Wukong jumped down from the cliff and caught Zhu Bajie by the arm, saying, "You, worthy brother, have gone far in coming. Come now, let us have a little fun together." Zhu Bajie said, "Elder brother, this place is far from where he waits; I fear Master will be disappointed that I am delayed. I will not play now." Sun Wukong said, "You have come all this way already; at least see how my mountain is." The boor, afraid to argue, dared only to follow him and walk about.

They walked hand in hand, while the small demons followed behind, and climbed to the very summit of Flower-Fruit Mountain. It was a good mountain indeed; since the Great Sage returned home, he had set it in order these past days and made it as it had always been. Now this was seen:

Green as jade newly cut, lofty like cloud-massaging heights. Around are tiger-crouching and dragon-coiling forms, and on all sides monkeys cry while cranes wail. At dawn it rises with clouds at the mountain crest; at dusk the sun hangs among the trees. Running water ripples, sounding like jade pendants; dripping springs in the ravines play like a jade qin. Before it stand cliff-summits and steep crags; behind are flourishing flowers and trees. Above it is linked to the Jade Maiden's hair-washing basin; below it joins the channels of the heavenly river. Heaven and earth gather this beauty, matching Mount Penglai; from pure and turbid streams is grown this true cavern realm. Not easy for the finest painter of Danqing to depict, and heaven-crafted maidens cannot render it with divine art. The strange stones glitter with delicate clarity, the ridge-top peaks tied in bright-hued chains. As sunlight moves, ten thousand streaks of violet glow; as auspicious vapour trembles, ten thousand ribbons of red radiance. This is indeed a blessed, cave-heaven realm in the human world, and all over the mountain are new trees and new flowers.

Zhu Bajie looked at it, never done with looking and full of delight, and said, "Brother, this is a fine place indeed, truly the foremost mountain under heaven." Sun Wukong said, "Brother, can one live out a life here?" Zhu Bajie laughed, "With the words you spoke, saying this treasure place is a blessed cavern-land, how can you speak of merely passing the days there?"

After the two laughed and talked for a while, they came down the mountain. By the roadside were a few small monkeys, kneeling with clusters of violet-dense grapes, fragrant pears and jujubes, yellow loquats, and bright red bayberries, calling, "Great Sage, please come in and take your morning meal." Sun Wukong laughed, "My pig brother has a large stomach, yet I do not take fruit as true food. Very well, very well, do not think this a poor offering; take these as light refreshments." Zhu Bajie said, "Though my appetite is large, I too can adapt to each place. Bring them here, bring them here, I will eat some and sample what is fresh."

After the two ate the fruit, the day had risen high. Zhu Bajie, fearing he had delayed Tripitaka's rescue, kept urging, "Brother, Master is waiting there for me and for you. I hope you go quickly, very quickly." Sun Wukong said, "Brother, go into Water Curtain Cave with me and stay awhile to play." Zhu Bajie earnestly refused, "I am deeply grateful for your kindness, but Master has been waiting long. I will not enter the cave and give you trouble." Sun Wukong said, "Then I cannot remain long. I bid you farewell here." Zhu Bajie said, "Brother, you are not going?" Sun Wukong said, "Where should I go? Here the sky does not seize me and the earth does not govern me; I am free and at ease. If I do not play, what use am I as a monk? I will not go; you go by yourself. But tell Tripitaka this: since he has already driven me off, let him not expect me again." Hearing this, the boor was afraid to press him, yet fearing to inflame his temper, he gave him two quick strokes. In helplessness he could only nod repeatedly in farewell and go his way.

When Sun Wukong saw him leave, he sent two quick little monkeys to follow and listen to what he might say. Truly, the oaf went down the mountain; after no more than three or four li he turned around, pointed at Sun Wukong and cursed in his mouth, "That monkey does not become a monk at all but acts like a demon. That ape-gentleman, I came in kindness to invite him, yet he will not go. If you do not go, then fine." He went a few steps and hurled out a few more curses. The two monkeys ran back in haste to report, "Great Sage, that Zhu Bajie is not quite honest. He goes a little way, then curses a few times." Sun Wukong grew furious and cried, "Bring him here!" The troop of monkeys came flying from all around and caught him up, flipping Zhu Bajie over, grabbing his mane, tugging his ears, pulling his tail, seizing his hair, and dragging him back.

It is still unknown how he will be handled, whether life or death will be his end. Let this be resolved in the next installment.
chapters.title: Chapter 30: An evil demon invades the true Dharma; the wayward horse of intention remembers the Mind-Monkey.

chapters.html:
This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Righteous bonds are formed in the heart, and the Dharma returns to its own nature. Gold humors wood and wood, once tamed, bears perfect fruit; the heart-monkey and Wooden Mother are joined in cinnabar truth. Together we ascend to the Pure Land, coming together through the Gate of Non-Dual Dharma. The Scripture is the complete route of cultivation, and Buddha matches one’s own primordial spirit. Brother and younger brother will form three vows; demon-kind and demon-colors correspond to the five elements. Cut away the six doors of desire, and one at once comes to the Great Sound of Thunder.

The fool had been caught by a troop of monkeys, who hauled him with shouts and pulls, and in the tugging one of his straight robes was torn. Muttering anxiously to himself, he kept saying, “Enough, enough—once I go, there will be a bout of bludgeoning and death.” Not long after, he reached the cave entrance. The Great Sage was seated on a rock cliff and shouted, “You sack-borne dunce! You had gone off already; why do you curse me now?” Zhu Bajie knelt on the ground and said, “Elder brother, I never cursed you. If I had cursed you, I would have chewed out my own tongue. I only said that I would go and report to Tripitaka. How could I dare to curse you?” Sun Wukong said, “How can you hide this from me? Pull up my left ear, and I can hear those in the Thirty-Three Heavens speaking; pull my right ear down, and I can know the accounts of ten generations of King Yama and his judges. You cursed me as you passed. How could I not have heard?” Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, I know your thief-like mind and rat-like cunning; you must have changed into something else again, so you have followed me and listened.” Sun Wukong called, “Little ones, bring a big staff. Give him twenty front-facing stinging blows, then twenty on the back; then let me take my staff and see him off.” Zhu Bajie, in panic, bowed and said, “Brother, for Master’s sake, at least spare me.” Sun Wukong said, “I think that old Master is full of compassion and righteousness.” Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, not for Master’s sake—please look upon the face of the Bodhisattva of the sea and spare me.”

Sun Wukong heard him mention the Bodhisattva and softened by a third and changed course: “Brother, since you say so, I will not strike you. Speak plainly. Do not hide from me. Where does Tripitaka face danger there? Why did you come here and fool me?” Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, there was no real danger. Truly, I missed you.” Sun Wukong scolded, “You good target for beating, bad-natured rogue—you still provoke me? Since I returned to Water Curtain Cave, Sun Wukong’s heart has pursued Tripitaka. At every step the monk is in danger; at every place, calamity looms. If only you had told me in time, there would have been no need for this strike.” Hearing this, Zhu Bajie knelt and told him, “Brother, I was plain about this and told you to come; I did not expect your spirit to be so sharp. Spare me from further blows and let me rise and tell you all.” Sun Wukong said, “All right, rise and speak.” The troop of monkeys loosened their hold. The fool sprang up and looked about wildly to both sides. Sun Wukong said, “What are you peering at?” Zhu Bajie said, “I was checking whether the road was clear, so I could run.” Sun Wukong said, “Run where? I will let you go for three days. Sun Wukong has his own ways to drive you back. Say it quickly. This anger I have now is unbearable; I will not show mercy.”

Zhu Bajie said, “I will not hide it from brother. After you returned, Sha Wujing and I were moving ahead of Tripitaka. We came to a black pine forest. Tripitaka dismounted, then told me to perform his alms rite. I looked out and far around; there was no household, and from the hardship I lay down for a little sleep in the grass. Unexpectedly, Sha Wujing left Tripitaka and came looking for me. You know the monk has no fixed sitting habit; alone he roamed in the woods, seeing the scenery. When we came out of the grove, we saw a golden treasure pagoda shining. He took it for a temple. Unluckily beneath the pagoda there was a demon named Yellow-Robed, who seized him. Later when Sha Wujing and I returned, we found only the White Dragon Horse and the baggage, but no Tripitaka. Following to the cave mouth, we fought with the demon. Master was in the cave; thankfully, a rescuer appeared. It was the third princess of the Kingdom of Baoxiang, who had been taken by that monster. She had written a family letter and asked Tripitaka to carry it home, and so by a convenient arrangement Master was released. When we reached the kingdom and delivered the letter, the king invited Tripitaka to exorcise the demon and recover the princess. Brother, do you know whether that old monk can subdue a fiend? Sha Wujing and I went again to fight. We did not know the demon had far-reaching powers; he captured Sha Wujing again. I was routed and lay prone in the grass. That demon changed into a handsome scholar and entered court, claiming kinship with the king, and made Tripitaka into a tiger. It was again the White Dragon Horse who at night revealed his dragon form and went to seek Master; Tripitaka himself did not spot him. He met the demon instead in the Hall of Silver Peace, where the fiend was drinking. The monster became a palace maid, carried wine and swords for dancing, and meant to take a chance to cut him down, but instead was struck by a red, all-hall blow and the horse’s leg was hurt. It was he who told me to ask elder brother, saying, ‘Brother is humane and upright; a gentleman does not dwell on old wrongdoing, and will surely come for a single peril to save Master.’ I beg, brother, in minding the saying, “one day your teacher, lifelong your father,” please, please save him.”

Sun Wukong said, “You, this fool. When I was leaving, I had warned and warned once again: ‘If demons seize Tripitaka, you must say that Sun Wukong is his senior disciple.’ Why did you not say it then?” Zhu Bajie reflected and said, “Please, this is no match for his pride; let me goad him a bit.” He said, “Brother, if I did not mention you, it would be enough. It is because I speak of you that he is already losing composure.” Sun Wukong said, “How should I speak?” Zhu Bajie said, “I said: ‘Demon, do not be rude, and do not harm my Master. I still have a great elder brother named Sun Wukong. He has vast powers and is skilled at subduing demons. When he comes, he will make you have nowhere in which to bury your bones.’” Hearing this, the demon became even more enraged and shouted, “What Sun Wukong is that? Is he someone to fear me? If he comes, I will skin him, strip him, chew his bones, and eat his heart. Even if he is a thin monkey, I’ll still cut him into pieces and cook him in oil.” When Sun Wukong heard those words, he grabbed his ear and scratched his cheeks, then jumped and raged, “Who is the one bold enough to speak of me so?” Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, cool your temper. It was the Yellow-Robed demon who said that; I taught it to you so you would hear.” Sun Wukong said, “Worthy younger brother, stand up. It is not that I cannot go. Since a demon dared to revile me, I cannot but subdue him. You and I are going together. Five hundred years ago I made havoc in Heaven; whenever I appeared, every heavenly commander beneath the sky saw me, each bowed with back bent and called me Great Sage. This demon shows no courtesy; he dares to curse me before my face and behind it as if it were nothing. I will seize him and break his body into ten thousand pieces to repay this insult against me. When I have done so, I will come back.” Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, exactly so. You take that demon and avenge your insult. Whether you return now or later, leave it to your own decision.”

The Great Sage only then leapt from the cliff, crashed into the cave, and shed the demon’s garment. He straightened his brocade robe, bound up a tiger-skin skirt, took up the Golden-Hooped Staff, and came straight out the gate. The startled monkeys blocked his way and said, “Your Majesty, Great Sage, where are you going? Just take us out and let us play for a few years too.” Sun Wukong said, “You little ones, what words are these? In this whole world above and below, everyone knows Sun Wukong is Tripitaka’s disciple. He did not send me back; he only sent me home to see things and return, as a gift so I might roam and play at ease in my own place. Now there is this matter. You all must watch the household carefully. Plant willows and pines in season. Let nothing decline. As for me, I will go back to guard Tripitaka and bring him through the Journey to the West. After my merits are complete, I will return and share carefree heaven with you all.” The monkeys each took the command and withdrew.

The Great Sage and Zhu Bajie then rode the clouds together, left the cave, crossed the Eastern Ocean and reached the western bank, where they rested in the cloudlight. He called, “Brother, move slowly here and wait. Let me go into the sea and cleanse myself.” Zhu Bajie said, “In all this rushing we rush forward anyway—what is the use of cleansing the body now?” Sun Wukong said, “You wouldn’t know. Since I came back, for these few days I have gathered some demon-qi on my body. Tripitaka is a man who loves cleanliness; he may take offense at it.” From that moment Zhu Bajie came to understand that Sun Wukong was sincere in heart, with nothing else intended.

After a little while they finished washing and again rode the clouds westward. They saw the golden tower shining. Zhu Bajie pointed and said, “Is that not the Yellow-Robed demon’s home? Sha Wujing is still in his place.” Sun Wukong said, “You stay in the sky. I will go down and look at the gatefront and meet the demon in array.” Zhu Bajie said, “Do not go. The demon is not at home.” Sun Wukong said, “I know.” “Good, Monkey King,” he called, “settle in the auspicious light and go straight to the cave entrance and look.” As soon as he arrived, he saw two children at the threshold using curved-head sticks, playing with wool balls and grabbing at a nest in rough play. One was about ten, the other eight or nine. In the middle of their play, Sun Wukong arrived in front of them and, not caring whose family they were of, grabbed them by their topknots and lifted them up. The children shrieked, cursing and crying in a confused din. It startled the small demons of the Moon-Wave Cave, and they hastened to report to the princess: “Lady, we know not who has snatched away the two young princes.” These two children, it turned out, were born of the princess and the demon.

The princess, hearing her words, hurried out through the cave gate. There she saw the Wanderer holding the two children in his arms, standing on the high cliff as if he intended to throw them down. Alarmed, she cried out sharply: "You man, I have nothing to do with you. Why did you take my son away? His father is formidable; if even a small mistake is made, you will not get away with it." Sun Wukong replied, "Do you not recognize me? I am Sun Wukong, Tripitaka’s senior disciple. My junior disciple Sha Wujing is in your cave. Release him, and I will return these two children to you. Two for one—still a bargain for you." Hearing this, the princess rushed inside, drove away the little gate demons, and with her own hands untied Sha Wujing. Sha Wujing said, "Princess, do not release me. I fear your monster may come home, ask for you, and cause you to be blamed." The princess said, "Venerable elder, you are my benefactor. You interpreted the letter for me and saved my life. I was willing to release you as well. Yet just as I went near the gate, you had your great elder brother Sun Wukong arrive, and he ordered me to free you."

Alas! When Sha Wujing heard the three characters "Sun Wukong," it was like ambrosia poured over him, like nectar moistening the heart. Instantly he rejoiced; his whole being was filled with spring. It was no mere report that someone had come—he felt as though he had picked up a lump of gold and jade. Watch him pull his sleeves straight and step out the gate, bowing before the Wanderer: "Elder brother, you truly seem to have descended from the heavens. Please rescue me!" Sun Wukong laughed: "You rascal, can’t you recite the Tightening Headband Spell once to aid me? You speak many spells from your mouth. If we are to protect Tripitaka, how can we fail to go west on the Western journey and instead sit here crouching?" Sha Wujing said, "Elder brother, no need to say more. A worthy man does not reopen an old fault. We are like generals of a lost army; we should not boast. Save me and the children." Sun Wukong said, "Come up." Sha Wujing then leapt and sprang onto the cliff.

At that moment Zhu Bajie hung in the air and, seeing Sha Wujing emerge from the cave, pressed down the cloud and called, "Brother Sha, endure—endure." Sha Wujing said, "Second brother, where have you come from?" Zhu Bajie said, "I was routed yesterday. At night I entered the city and met the White Horse. Learning that Master was in danger, I used the yellow-robe spell and turned into a tiger. The White Horse and I discussed it and asked you, elder brother, to come." Sun Wukong said, "Pigsy, no more chit-chat. Each of you take one child, and go first into Baoxiang City to incite that demon. I will stay here and fight him." Sha Wujing asked, "Brother, how should we provoke him?" Sun Wukong said, "The two of you rise into the air and stand on the Hall of the Golden Wheels. Do not worry about who is right or wrong. Throw the children once before the White-Jade Steps. If anyone asks who you are, say you are the sons of the Yellow-Robed demon, brought here by me and one of my brothers. When the demon hears this, he will certainly return, and I need not enter the city to fight him. If we fought above the city, it would summon cloud and mist and raise dust, disturbing court and officials and all the people, and none would be at peace." Zhu Bajie laughed: "Brother, just do what must be done and leave the rest to us." Sun Wukong said, "How am I to help you?" Zhu Bajie said, "You have taken these two children; you have already broken their courage. Their throats are already hoarse from crying and they’ll surely die soon. If we drop them down at once, they may become mere lumps of flesh. When the demon catches them, he will demand our two lives in return. If not for clean proof there will be no witness at all. Can’t you stand with us?" Sun Wukong said, "If he seizes either of you, you two come here and fight. This place is a wide battlefield; I will wait here to fight him." Sha Wujing said, "Exactly, exactly. What elder brother says is reason. Let us go." Then the two set off with a show of fearsome confidence, carrying the children with them.

Sun Wukong at once leapt down from the cliff to the gate below her tower. The princess said, "You monk, you have no faith at all. You said you would return my children if I released your disciple, but you freed your disciple and kept my children, then came back to stand at my gate. What is this for?" Sun Wukong smiled and said, "Princess, do not take offense. You have been here a long time. I brought your son to let him recognize his grandfather." The princess said, "Monk, do not be impolite. My Yellow-Robed Lord is not like others; if you frighten my child, he will be deeply alarmed." Sun Wukong laughed: "Princess, one born between Heaven and Earth—how can this alone be an offence?" The princess said, "I know." Sun Wukong said, "You are a woman of the household; what do you know of such things?" The princess said, "I was raised in the palace and taught by my parents since childhood. I remember an old text: ‘Among the Three Thousand Punishments, none is greater than filial impiety.’" Sun Wukong said, "Then you are truly one lacking filial piety. For the Classics say, ‘Father bore me, Mother raised me. Alas, mother and father, your efforts and hardship gave me life.’ Thus filiality is the root of all conduct, the source of all virtue. How, then, can you keep company with a demon spirit and not even remember your parents? How else can this not be the crime of unfilial conduct?" At these words the princess grew red in face and ears, ashamed and ashamed. After a while she spoke out: "Venerable elder, your words are best. How could I not remember my parents? This demon spirit tricked and carried me off here. His commands are strict; my movements are constrained, the roads are far, and there is no one through whom I can send word. If I try to die, my parents would suspect I fled, and things would never be made clear. So I had no choice but to prolong my life. Truly I am one great sinner before Heaven." When she had finished, tears streamed from her like a spring.

Sun Wukong said, "Princess, do not grieve. Zhu Bajie told me that you had a letter, and that letter saved my Master’s life. In it there was also your longing for your parents. Let me then take down the demon, bring you back to court, and present you before the Son of Heaven. Then choose a worthy husband and serve your parents till old age. What do you say?" The princess said, "Monk, do not try to end me. Yesterday both your junior brothers, how valiant they are, could not defeat my Yellow-Robed Lord. You, one so meager of flesh and bone, looking like a crab, with bones all outside the skin—what power have you? Dare you talk of capturing demons?" Sun Wukong laughed: "You truly cannot see clearly—you cannot recognize people. A saying goes, ‘Though a bladder be large, it has no weight; though a small scale be tiny, it can still press a thousand pounds.’ As for appearance, theirs is all largeness with no use: they stride against the wind, spend cloth in their robes, their hearts are hollow fire, their crown and waist are weak, and their eating brings no merit. As for old Sun Wukong, though small in body from the start, I am not to be measured by shape." The princess said, "Do you really have such methods?" Sun Wukong said, "You have not yet seen mine. I can certainly subdue demons and am most able to pin down monsters." The princess said, "Do not mislead me." Sun Wukong said, "I will not mislead you." The princess said, "If you can subdue and pin down demons, how will you catch him now?" Sun Wukong said, "Then step aside for now and move away; do not stand before me. If he comes and you interfere, you may become soft toward him through long affection and not be able to let him be struck." The princess said, "How can I fail to be attached? What keeps me here is my compulsion, nothing else." Sun Wukong said, "You were his wife for thirteen years. Are there no feelings? If I see him, he will meet no mockery from me—one staff is one staff, one punch is one punch. Only when he is knocked down will you be free to return to court and face the Son of Heaven."

The princess truly did as Sun Wukong told her, withdrawing to a secluded place to hide. It was her marital fate to end here; thus she came upon the Great Sage’s arrival.

The Monkey King hid the princess away. Then he instantly changed form, becoming exactly like the princess, and returned to the cave, waiting for the monster there.

Then Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing took the two children into Baoxiang and flung them down before the White-Jade Steps. Wretchedly, both became like meat cakes; fresh blood spurted, and their bones were shattered. Alarmed, the officials of the whole court announced, "Disaster! Disaster! Two children have fallen from heaven!" Zhu Bajie shouted in a loud voice: "Those children are the sons of the Yellow-Robed demon, taken here by old Zhu Bajie and Brother Sha!"

The monster was still in Yin'an Hall, still heavy with the wine he had drunk. While he was in sleep he heard someone crying his name. He turned over, raised his head, and looked out. There on the cloud he saw Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing shouting. The demon inwardly thought: "Pigsy is tolerable enough. But Sha Wujing was bound in my house—how could he possibly come out? How could my household release him? And how did my child reach his hands? This is surely a stratagem by Pigsy because he could not come out and fight me directly, so he contrived this device. If I acknowledge these two and fight them, if they throw a block-spade formation at me, this whole swagger may be broken and that key flaw discovered. Yet I am still half-dazed from wine. Let me first go back home and see whether these are truly my children; I can speak with him afterward." Such a demon he was. He did not pause for courtesy and did not make a proper report to the king; he turned through hills and woods and went straight back into the cave to check the matter.

By then the court had already learned he was a demon. At night he had eaten one palace maid and there were also seventeen who had come near death. At dawn he went to the king and reported the whole matter in detail. Because he had already left without presenting himself again, the king grew all the more certain he was a monster. The king then had many officials set guards over the fake tiger; there is no need to elaborate further.

But the monster turned and went straight back to the cave mouth. When the Great Sage saw him coming, he made a show of it: he squeezed his eyes shut, let tears fall in a soft, pattering rain, then stamped his feet and beat his chest, crying and wailing as though his whole body had lost its reason. In the cave, he howled in grief. The monster, not recognizing him at first, came forward and held him, saying, "Hunca, what is it? Why are you so distressed?" The Great Sage spun out his false words, shaping a counterfeit tale, and with tears in his eyes pleaded, "My lord, there is a saying: 'A man with no wife is without master of his fortune; a woman without a husband is left with an empty life.' Yesterday you went to court to acknowledge your kin, and why did you not return? This morning Zhu Bajie abducted Sha Wujing and carried off my two sons. It was he who did it, and he will not grant mercy. He said he would take [them] to court to have them recognized by my grandfather; all this half-day, the children have been unseen, and who knows if they live or die. You have not come home either. How am I to bear this severing? So I cannot stop my tears." The demon, hearing this, grew furious in his heart and asked, "So these are truly my children?" The Great Sage replied, "Yes. Zhu Bajie took them away."

The demon, angry and leaping wildly, said, "Enough, enough. My son was smashed by him and is beyond being alive. The only thing is to take that monk and make him atone for my son's life in revenge. Hunca, do not cry now. How are you feeling in your heart now? Let me treat it." The Great Sage said, "I am not really hurt; I simply cannot bear my sons, and crying has made my heart ache." The demon said, "Never mind. Please rise. I have a treasure here; let me press it on the spot where it pains, and it will not hurt anymore. But be careful. Do not let my thumb touch it. If the thumb touches, you will see my true form." The Great Sage laughed inwardly: "This rough demon, though unruly, is strangely honest. He surrenders without torture; I’ll let him bring out the treasure, then I’ll flick him once and see what kind of fiend he is." The monster led him deeper and farther into a secluded, sealed part of the cave. From his mouth he spat out a treasure the size of a chicken egg, a dazzling reliquary-like inner pill. The Great Sage secretly rejoiced: "Fine stuff indeed. Who knows how many works were needed, how many years of trials, how many turns of yin and yang were spent to refine this inner-relic core. By fate, I have met it today, Old Sun." The monkey took it; there was no place that truly hurt, so he pretended to touch lightly, then snapped one finger at it. The demon panicked and lunged to snatch it. Just then, the monkey swerved and in one movement swallowed it whole. The demon came with clenched fist to strike. The Great Sage blocked the blow with one hand, wiped his face, revealed his true form, and said, "Monster, do not be impertinent. Look closely—do you recognize who I am?"

The demon, on seeing him, was greatly startled and said, "Ah! Hunca, why do you show this sort of face?" The Great Sage barked, "You rotten fiend! Who is this Hunca of yours? You do not even recognize your ancestors." The demon suddenly seemed to realize and said, "I seem to recognize you a little." The Great Sage said, "I will not strike you yet; look again." The monster said, "Though your face seems familiar, I cannot recall your name. Who are you? From where did you come? Where did you lay my Hunca low, then come into my home to trick away my treasure? Truly rude and detestable!" The Great Sage said, "You still do not recognize me. I am Sun Wukong the Pilgrim-walker, Tripitaka’s senior disciple. I am your predecessor from five hundred years ago." The monster said, "No such words. No such words. When I seized Tripitaka, I knew only that he had two disciples, Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing. Who has ever mentioned a man surnamed Sun? You are some odd monster from elsewhere, come here to deceive me." The Great Sage said, "I did not come with those two. My master, because Sun Wukong is in the habit of beating monsters and has killed many, is a compassionate and good-natured man and sent me back, so I did not travel with him. You do not know the names of your own ancestors." The demon said, "How very masculine you are. Once your master drove you away, how can you still have the face to come before others?" The Great Sage said, "You brute, do you not know 'a teacher for one day is a father for life'? 'Between father and son there is no enmity from a single night apart'? You harmed my master; how could I fail to save him? You may have harmed him, but afterward you still curse me behind my back—what kind of words are those?" The demon said, "I never cursed you." The Great Sage said, "It was Zhu Bajie who said it." The demon said, "Do not believe him. Zhu Bajie has a sharp mouth and a tongue like a wife’s gossiping tongue—how can you believe him?" The Great Sage said, "No need to talk of such side matters. Sun Wukong has come to your home today and you have made your guest wait. Though you offer no wine or dishes, you still still have a head to spare. Quickly extend your head; let Sun Wukong strike one staff-blow as your tea." Hearing him speak of beating, the demon laughed hoarsely, "Sun Wukong, you have misjudged. If you had said you would beat him, you should not have entered here. I have hundreds of demons, great and small. Even if you have hands all over your body, you cannot break out of my gate." The Great Sage said, "Do not speak nonsense. Forget to say hundreds. There may be thousands, ten-thousands. As soon as I sort out each one, it is easy to beat them; staff by staff, blow by blow, I will cut off their roots and lines entirely."

The demon, hearing this, hurriedly sent word. The demons on the mountain front and back, in and out of the cave, gathered all at once, each gripping weapons and blocking the three or four gate layers densely so none could pass. The Great Sage saw this and was overjoyed. With both hands arranging his staff, he cried out, "Transform!" and became three heads and six arms. He swung the Golden-Hooped Staff, and it changed into three Golden-Hooped Staffs. Watch those six hands wielding three staves as he went straight on, like a tiger entering a flock of sheep, like an eagle plunging through a chicken pen. That is no pity to the lesser fiends: one blow crushed skulls, another swept blood like running water. He moved and dodged across the field like entering an empty wilderness. Only one old demon remained, who rushed out of the gate and shouted, "You wild monkey—you are truly idle and lazy! How do you come into this doorway and bully folk?" The Great Sage wheeled round at once and beckoned, "Come then, come on. To strike you down is my merit." The demon raised a treasured saber and hacked in from separate angles; the Great Sage drew the iron staff and met him face to face. On the mountain ridge, in half-cloud and half-mist, the killing began there:

The Great Sage’s marvels are mighty, the fiend’s skill is deep. Here one sweeps the iron staff straight, there one lifts a steel sword askew. The blade arcs in a slow glow like dawn-bright cloudlight. The light swing of the staff traces drifting colored cloud. They come and go and guard the peak, again and again, turning all over in circling passes. One changes his face as the wind shifts; one stays on the ground, swaying his whole body. That one glares like fire and stretches ape-arms. That one flashes golden eyes and bends the tiger's waist. You come, I go, and trade in battle; blade meets staff and yields no mercy. The Monkey King’s iron cudgel follows the Three Strategies, the monster’s steel sword keeps the Six Manuals. One relies on habitual methods as demon-lord; one casts out power to guard Tripitaka. The fiercer the Monkey King grows, the fiercer the demon lord becomes. Forgetting life and death, they strike through the air, all in honor of Tripitaka’s distant obeisance to Buddha.

The two fought for five or six dozen rounds and no winner could be seen. The Great Sage thought to himself, "This wild fiend’s sword can indeed withstand old Sun’s staff. If I let old Sun leave him a gap, I’ll see whether he can recognize me." The good monkey king raised both hands with his staff and took a "High-Searching Horse" stance. The demon, not knowing it was a tactic, saw an opening, flourished his treasured sword, and dashed down three directions to hack. The Great Sage swiftly turned into a "Great Central Calm" and deflected his sword, then used a "Steal-Peach Beneath the Leaves" move; he brought the staff to the demon’s crown, and the demon vanished from sight. Gathering in the staff at once, he looked around, but the fiend was nowhere. The Great Sage cried out in shock, "My son, if I strike once I should see him, but he is gone. If he had truly been killed, there should be some pus and blood. How is there not even a trace? Then he must have run." He leaped onto the clouds to look around, and in all four directions there was no movement. "My two eyes see everything, wherever I glance. Yet how could he run off so swiftly? I have understood: the demon who says he recognized me is not an ordinary earthly monster. He is likely an exquisite spirit from heaven."

At last the Great Sage could no longer restrain his anger. He brandished the Iron Staff, struck a thunderous blow, and bounded straight to the Southern Heavenly Gate. Pang, Liu, Gou, Bi, Zhang, Tao, Deng, Xin, and the rest were so flustered that they bowed low on both sides, bending and covering their backs, not daring to block him, and let him charge into the gate all the way to the Hall of Bright Clarity. The four Great Celestial Masters, Zhang, Ge, Xu, and Qiu, were already there and asked, "Great Sage, how did you come?" Wukong said, "It was because I protected Tripitaka to the Precious-Elephant Kingdom. A demon deceived the royal maiden and hurt my Master. Old Sun fought with him. In the midst of the bout the fiend disappeared. I thought that fiend is not a mere mortal demon but a heavenly essence, so I came up here to investigate what demon-spirits passed this way." On hearing this, the Master went at once to the Lingxiao Hall and made his report. By order he inspected the Nine Luminaries, the Twelve Primary Constellations, the Five Dippers of the four directions and centre, the stars of the River of Heaven, the Five Mountains and Four Rivers, and all the deities under Heaven. None had dared leave their posts. He then inspected the outer constellations of the Twenty-Eight Mansions under the Dipper; they should have been twenty-eight, but there were only twenty-seven, with only the Kui-star missing. The Master reported back: "The Kui-mu Wolf has come down from Heaven." The Jade Emperor asked, "How long has it been since he was not in Heaven?" The Master answered, "At every fourth-Mao he is absent; every three days the count is updated, and now it is already thirteen days." The Jade Emperor said, "Thirteen days in Heaven means thirteen years below." He then ordered the local star department to bring him back to the Court.

The twenty-seven mansion-officers took the order and left through the Heavenly Gate, each chanting mantras that stirred the Kui-star. You ask where he had hidden himself. He was a divine general once frightened when Sun Great Sage threw Heaven into uproar; he had slipped into a ravine and concealed himself beneath water vapour, and so no one had seen him. Hearing the officers of his own retinue recite the spells, he dared to appear and followed the host up to Heaven. Wukong blocked the gate and was about to strike him; only the pleading of the other stars prevented that, and he was brought before the Jade Emperor. At his waist the fiend drew out a gold tally and, kneeling at the hall, offered a guilty submission. The Jade Emperor said, "Kui-mu Wolf, in Heaven there are delights without edge or end; if you cannot relish them, why did you wander off by yourself?" The Kui-star knelt and spoke: "Ten thousand years and ages, pardon my mortal offence. The princess of the Precious-Elephant Kingdom is no ordinary human. She was once a jade maiden who served incense in the Hall of Fragrant Offerings. Because she wished to join with me in the mortal world, she first came down and was reborn in the inner court of the imperial palace. I did not break my prior accord. I changed form and became this demon, occupied a famed peak, drew her to a cave residence, and we have been joined as husband and wife for thirteen years. 'A single sip and a single bite are no accident but fate.' Now Sun Great Sage has come and brought this to success here." Hearing him, the Jade Emperor took back the gold tally and demoted him to the Doushui Palace to tend the fire for the Supreme Lord Laozi. With merit, he may return to rank; without merit, his fault will be made even heavier.

When Wukong saw that the Jade Emperor had issued such a release, he rejoiced inwardly, bowed deeply toward Heaven, and said to the assembled gods, "Gentlemen, let us get started." The Master smiled and said, "That monkey is still so rustic; after he has captured the demon spirit for him, he did not thank the heavenly grace, he simply bows and withdraws." The Jade Emperor said, "As long as no trouble results, heaven keeps its peace and that is our good fortune."

The Great Sage settled his radiant light, and at once turned toward Wanzi Mountain's Wave-Moon Cave, found the princess, and plainly recounted the words about her descending to the mortal world to subdue the demon. Suddenly they heard Pigsy and Sha Wujing shouting from midair: "Elder Brother, there are demon spirits! Let us leave a few and we will beat them." Wukong said, "The demon spirits have all been utterly annihilated." Sha Wujing said, "Once the demons are all slain there is no hindrance. Bring the princess into court at once. Do not open your eyes. Brothers, use the Earth-Shortening art."

The princess only heard wind roaring in her ears; in a moment she was brought back into the city. The three brought her up to the Golden Luan Hall. She respectfully bowed to her father-king and mother-empress, met her sisters, and all officials came to take leave. She then opened her memorial: "By the boundless power of Senior Monk Sun, the Yellow-Robed demon has been subdued and brought me back to the kingdom." The king asked, "What sort of demon is this Yellow Robe one?" Wukong said, "Your Majesty’s new consort is the Kui-star from above; the one you call beloved was once a jade maiden in the incense-hall of the Heavenly Chamber. Out of desire to descend, she came down as human and was reborn within the inner apartments. No one can call this a trivial matter; all these marriages are ties from former ties of lives. The monster was reported by Old Sun in Heaven to the Jade Emperor. The Jade Emperor checked that he had been absent from Heaven for thirteen days there, which is thirteen years below—one day in Heaven is one year in the mortal world. By order, the local star officers seized him and brought him back. He was sent to the Doushui Palace, completed service, and earned his rank again. Old Sun also rescued Your Majesty’s beloved." The king thanked Wukong for his grace and said, "Go now and fetch your Master."

The three of them came down from the Precious Hall and, with all the officials, entered the court room. They hauled out the iron cage and unfastened the chains of the false tiger. The others saw a tiger; only Wukong saw a man. The Master had been overwhelmed by the demon spell and could not walk, though his mind remained clear; only his mouth and eyes could hardly open. Wukong laughed, "Monk, you are such a fine monk—how did you make yourself into such a terrible face? You called me a violent bad one and sent me back, saying you would keep to the Way, yet in one breath you made this countenance?" Pigsy said, "Brother, save him now; do not spend all your time teasing at him." Wukong said, "You are forever egging things on. He is your cherished and proud disciple. If you won’t save him, how will you keep searching for Old Sun? I told you before: once the demon was subdued and I had repaid the grudge of being slandered, we would return." Sha Wujing came forward on his knees: "Brother, as the ancients said, 'Do not look at the monk’s face, look at Buddha’s face.' Since Eldest Brother has come this far, I entreat you to save him. If we could save him ourselves, we would not have dared to come so far and call on you." Wukong lifted him by the hand and said, "How could I have peace and not save him? Bring water at once." Pigsy flew to the post-station, fetched the baggage and mounts, took out the purple-gold bowl and filled it halfway with water, then passed it to Wukong. Wukong took the water in his hand, chanted the true mantra, and with one fierce spray cast it into the tiger’s face, expelling the demon spell and releasing the tiger spirit.

The monk returned to his true form, steadied his mind, and opened his eyes, then recognized Wukong. He caught Wukong’s arm and cried, "Wukong, where have you come from?" Sha Wujing stood respectfully at his side and gave a full report: how Wukong had been summoned, how the demon was subdued, how the princess was saved, how the tiger spell was lifted, and how all matters had been brought back to court. Tripitaka could not thank him enough: "Excellent disciple, you have borne the burden of this all; only you have borne it. From now on, go straight to the West, and at once return to the Eastern lands to present to the Tang king. Your merit is foremost." Wukong laughed, "No more of it, no more of it. Need not speak those words; this is enough to show how deeply I am loved." Hearing this, the king once again thanked all four disciples. He had a plain ceremonial banquet arranged and threw wide the East Pavilion. The monk and his disciples received the imperial kindness, bid the king farewell, and headed west. The king, followed by many officials, escorted them far on their way. It is so:

The lord returns to the treasure hall and settles the realm; the monk goes to Leiyin to honor Buddha.

In truth, who knows what happened after this, and when they at last reached the Western Heaven? Let the next chapter explain.
chapters.title: Chapter 31: Pigsy’s righteous fervor rouses the Monkey King; Wukong with wit subdues the demon.
