This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Now it was told that Tripitaka recovered Sun Wukong again; master and disciples, one in heart and one in body, set out together toward the West. After rescuing the princess of the Kingdom of Bao Xiang, and being escorted out westward from the city by king and ministers, their hungry eating, thirsty drinking, sleeping by night and traveling by dawn along the road are beyond telling. Yet they once again arrived in the season of early spring, at this time:

The light breeze made the willows green like silk, and such fair scenery was fit for inscription. Birds called out to the hour of spring; warm moisture coaxed flowers open, and fragrant blossoms spread everywhere. In the begonia courtyards came the paired swallows; this was just the season for spring-gazing. On red-dust roads and violet lanes, brocade, string and flute, and meadow games of passing cups in turn.

While master and disciples were walking while enjoying the spring, they came upon a mountain that blocked the way. Tripitaka said, "Disciples, be careful. Ahead is a high mountain, and perhaps tigers or wolves will block our path." Sun Wukong said, "Master, monks should not talk like householders. Do you remember what monk Wuchao said in his Heart Sūtra: 'Where the mind has no obstructions, no obstructions, then no fear; far from deluded dreams.' He also said, 'Clear the grime from the heart, wash away the dust at the ear. One who does not suffer the sufferings within suffering is not fit to be foremost among men.' Do not worry. So long as old Sun is with you, if Heaven itself were to collapse we could still be safe—why fear tigers and wolves?" Master pulled back the reins and said, "I

In former days I was ordered from Chang’an and remember only coming west to pay homage to the Buddha’s face. In the Kingdom of Sheli, golden images shone in color; in the stupa tower gleamed flecks of jade. I sought across all under Heaven for nameless waters, crossed the whole mortal world, yet never reached the mountains. Layer upon layer of mist and waves overlap; when will this body ever come to rest?" When Sun Wukong heard this, he laughed cheerfully, "Master wants to be at ease. What is difficult? If one’s works are complete, all bonds cease and all dharmas are empty. Then it is natural that there is ease of body, is it not?" Hearing these words, Master at last only laughed and forgot his worries. He tightened the rein and spurred the silver steed, tugging the traces to drive forward the jade-dragon horse.

Master and disciples climbed up the mountain, it was exceedingly steep and difficult, truly imposing and towering. A fine mountain:

Lofty ridges, stern and towering; sharp, sharply pointed peaks. Cupped and encircling are the deep ravines below, and beside them the lone, steep cliffs stand sheer. In the cupped, deep ravines one can only hear water-dragons lurching in their play as they turn over; Beside the lone, precipitous cliffs one sees the tangled-forest tigers with tails lashing as they bound. Looking upward, the hilltops jut up suddenly through the blue vault. Looking back, the gorge below is deep and shadowed, nearly touching the green void. Going up it feels like climbing steps and stools; going down it is like crossing ditches and pits. It is truly a bizarre and uncanny peak-chain, a series of knife-like sheared cliffs. On the summits, men seeking herbs think twice before stepping; before the sheer walls even woodcutters can barely move a pace. Wild goats and wild horses dart as if weaving in confusion, and crafty hares and mountain cattle are lined like battle arrays. The mountain is so high it blocks out sun and hides stars; at times one meets demons and gray wolves. The grass paths are choked and confusing, and horses cannot pass through. How could they yet behold the Buddha of the Roaring-Music Sound?

Master pulled back his horse and gazed at the mountain. At the difficult place, he saw, on a green-sedge slope, a woodcutter standing there. How he was dressed:

On his head he wore an old blue felt hat, on his body a woolen robe of coarse cotton. The old blue felt hat, covering smoke and shading sun, was truly extraordinary. The woolen robe, by which one can truly forget one’s worries, was scarcely seen. In his hand he held a steel axe, bright and newly sharpened, chopping dry timber and bundling it tight. At the edge of spring, the four seasons blended in a quiet softness; Outside ordinary concerns, his idle heart was always dim and calm as three faint stars. He lived to old age simply by following his lot; what are honor and shame but temporary by the mountain? The woodcutter said: He was cutting rotten wood at the slope front, when suddenly he saw the elder coming from the east. He set down his pole and axe outside the trees, stepping off the bank onto the rocky ridge. He called out in a harsh voice toward Master: "Venerable elder going west, halt a moment. I have a word to tell you: this mountain has a band of fierce malignant demons who specialize in eating people going east and west." Hearing this, Master was distraught, his soul nearly fled and his trembling made him barely steady in the saddle. He turned back in haste and called to his disciples, "Did you hear what the woodcutter reported? 'This mountain has evil, ferocious demons.' Who dares go and ask him?" Sun Wukong said, "Master, do not worry. Leave it to old Sun to ask him directly."

The Great Sage, entirely fearless, pulled in his pace and went straight up the mountain, calling to the woodcutter with "Big brother" and offering salutation. The woodcutter replied, "Venerable, what cause has brought you here?" Sun Wukong said, "I will not hide it, brother. We have come from the eastern lands as a mission to the Western Heaven to fetch the sutras. On that horse sits my master, who has some timidity. Just now by providence we have heard of a fierce demonic braggart, so I have come to ask plainly: what years is that demon, what years is that monster? Is he fully grown in rank, or still a cub? Please speak plainly, so that I may go tell the mountain spirits and the Earth gods to raise him up from there." The woodcutter, hearing this, threw back his head and laughed: "So you really are a wind-monk." Sun Wukong said, "I am not one of the winds—this is truth in plain words." The woodcutter said, "If you are so straightforward, how do you dare to say you can get him to rise?" Sun Wukong said, "With such swagger as yours, and your random road-side warning, how could this not mean you are close to him? If not kin, then at least neighbor; if not neighbor, then surely friend." The woodcutter laughed and said, "Reckless monk, your reasoning is off. I only meant well, to come and warn you and tell you to be careful by day and by night as you walk, yet you blame me for it. Do not say I do not know where these demons come from. I do know, however: how can you send him off?" Sun Wukong said, "If it is a heavenly demon, he can be handed to the Jade Emperor; if an earth demon, to the Earth Office. Those of the west belong to Buddha, the east to the Holy Sage; north to true warrior Zhenwu, south to Fire Virtue. A flood-drake spirit belongs to the Sea Lord; a scheming ghost to King Yama. Each has its own landward authority. Old Sun is known everywhere. I can issue an imperial order and by night send him off in flight."

The woodcutter could not stop a cold laugh: "Reckless monk, you wander up and down in the upper clouds, have learned some scripture-sign and talisman-water arts to drive out evil and bind ghosts, and yet have never met a demon of such cruelty." Sun Wukong said, "How do you know he is cruel?" The woodcutter said, "This mountain is about six hundred li across and called Pingting Mountain. In it is a cave called Lotus-Flower Cave. In that cave are two demon chiefs. They draw shadow forms and figures, seeking to capture monks, checking surnames and names, and wanting to eat Tripitaka. If you had come from elsewhere, that might be better, but because you bear the character 'Tang', do not even think of going out alive." Sun Wukong said, "Then it is we who are indeed from the Tang." The woodcutter said, "Then he is surely coming to eat you all." Sun Wukong said, "By fate, indeed. But I do not know how he will eat." The woodcutter said, "How do you think he will eat?" Sun Wukong said, "If he eats the head first, perhaps we can still make a sport of it. If he eats the feet first, it is hard indeed." The woodcutter said, "How can head-first be hard, or feet-first be hard?" Sun Wukong said, "You have not truly encountered it. If it is head-first, one bite takes it off and I am dead. No matter how he fries or stews me, I may not know pain. If it is feet-first, he gnaws the staff, bites through the legs, and eats to the waistbone; I would not die at once, yet it is not in fragments but in pieces of suffering, and that is hard indeed." The woodcutter said, "Monk, he has not that much time. He will simply seize you, bind you in a cage, and steam you whole." Sun Wukong laughed, "That is even better. I could not bear pain itself, but only a little trapped suffocation would pass." The woodcutter said, "Monk, do not jest. That demon carries five treasures and his powers are huge and wide. He has a jade pillar that can prop Heaven and a golden beam that can brace the sea. If even a Tang monk is to be taken, you still must make him swoon several times." Sun Wukong said, "A few times? how many?" The woodcutter said, "You would have to make him swoon three or four times." Sun Wukong said, "No matter. We issue seven or eight hundred swoons in a year. Three or four of these is easy: with a few stuns he will be done.

The Great Sage, utterly without fear, had only one mind: to protect Tripitaka. He tore free of the woodcutter, pulled his stride and turned, going straight to the front of the horse on the mountain slope: "Master, nothing serious. There is a demon-lad here, only that the folk here are timid and keep him in their minds. With me present, what can he do? Move along. Move along." When Master saw this, he could only open his heart and follow. Just as they continued, that woodcutter was already out of sight. Master said, "How has the woodcutter who warned us disappeared?" Sha Wujing said, "Our fate is poor; we have run into a ghost in broad daylight." Sun Wukong said, "Perhaps he has slipped into the woods for firewood. Wait here and I will look."

The Great Sage opened his Fire-Eye Golden Eyes and looked across mountain and ridge, yet there was no trace. Suddenly he raised his head and looked into the clouds; seeing it was the day-appointed official, he leapt through the clouds and caught up, shouting "hairy ghost" a few times: "Why, when you had news to bring, did you not speak it plainly, yet change forms so? How rude to old Sun?" Startled, the official paid homage and said, "Great Sage, I came to report too late; do not punish, do not punish. That demon is truly highly potent in spirits and miracles, with endless transformations. Just watch how cleverly you move your stratagems and keep watchful protection over your master. If you grow careless even a little, do not think you can go to the Western Paradise anymore."

When Sun Wukong heard this, he rebuked and sent the gong-cao officer away, took the matter deeply to heart, mounted the cloud path, and came straight up the mountain. He saw Tripitaka advancing, with Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing clustered around him. Inside, he thought: "If I told Master exactly what the gong-cao said, my Master would not be able to take it and surely begin to weep. But if I do not tell him everything and simply lead him along, there is the old saying, 'The first time one enters a reed marsh, one does not yet know its depth.' If somehow the demons seize him, will I not then be the one to fret over it?

I will first look after Zhu Bajie. I will set him to step forward and fight that fiend once. If he can beat it, that is one merit for him; if he lacks means and gets taken, it will not be too late for old Sun to rescue him later, and then my skill will be made known." As he was still weighing this, he said to himself in his heart: "I only fear Zhu Bajie will hide behind laziness and refuse to come out, and Master has some soft corner for him. So old Sun must rein him in."

"Great Sage, look: he is putting on a fake face, rubbing his eyes again and again until tears come. He comes walking forward to meet Master." Zhu Bajie saw this and hurriedly called, "Sha Wujing, put down the shoulder pole and bring out the baggage. Let the two of us divide it." Sha Wujing said, "Elder Brother, divide what?" Zhu Bajie replied, "Let’s split it. You go back to the Flowing-Sand River and become a demon again; old Pig will go up to Gao the old manor and check on the whole family. Sell the white horse and buy a coffin, then send Master to die. We all disperse the flames, and still we can continue to the Western Heaven, right?"

Tripitaka heard this from the saddle: "That obstinate fool, we are already on the road—what is all this nonsense now?" Zhu Bajie said, "It is your own brat speaking nonsense. Do you not see how Sun Wukong has come crying here? He is a hero who can tunnel through earth and sky, whose ax fears no fire and whose body fears no cauldron of oil, and now he wears a hat of sorrow with eyes brimming with tears. The mountain must be steep and the demon fierce. How can people as weak as us go there?"

Tripitaka said, "Do not babble. Let me ask him and see what he says." He asked, "Wukong, if there is anything to bargain over, say it to me to my face. Why are you troubled with such private grief? With that crybaby face of yours, could you frighten a tiger?"

Sun Wukong said, "Master, the messenger was the gong-cao on duty. He said the demon was ferocious and this place hard to pass; truly the mountain is high and the road steep. We cannot go on now, so we should return another day." Tripitaka, frightened, grasped Sun Wukong's tiger-skin skirt and said, "Disciple, we have already crossed three relays and half a stage. Why do you now speak of giving up and retreating?"

Wukong said, "I have not failed in care. I only fear there are many demons and we move as a lone party. 'Though it is a lump of iron, how many nails can be hammered from one furnace?'" Tripitaka said, "Disciple, you are right. Indeed, one man alone is hard-pressed. The war manual says, 'A few cannot defeat a host.' I still have Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing; they are my disciples. With your command to deploy them as bodyguard and helper, if you work in concert, clear this mountain path together and lead me over, can we not all still attain the true fruit?"

That whole hesitation drew from Sun Wukong these words. He wiped his eyes and said, "Master, if we are to pass this mountain, Zhu Bajie must obey two instructions from me; only then do we have even three parts of a chance. If he does not follow my word, he cannot think of crossing an inch without me, even by half a point."

Zhu Bajie said, "Senior brother, then let us just scatter the fire and stop talking. Do not drag me by the collar." Tripitaka said, "Disciple, let me ask your older brother what he is asking you to do." The fool said truly to Sun Wukong, "Brother, what are you asking me to do?" Wukong said, "First, watch over Master. Second, patrol the mountain." Zhu Bajie said, "Watching the Master means sitting; patrolling means walking. Could I sit for a bit and then walk, then walk and then sit? How can one person mind both?"

Wukong said, "You need not do both at once. Take one duty, and that is all." Zhu Bajie laughed, "That is a better arrangement. But I still do not know how this looks: what is watching Master, what is patrolling? Tell me the exact way to match each task, then I can do it." Wukong said, "Watch Master thus: if Master comes out for obeisance, attend him; if he walks, support him; if he is to take his vegetarian fare, prepare it. If he is a little hungry, you should beat him; if his face turns yellow, you should beat him; if his frame grows thin, you should beat him."

Zhu Bajie panicked: "This is hard, hard, hard. Attending and supporting him is not too hard, even if I never leave his side and carry him, that is still manageable. But if you send me down to the villages to prepare his vegetarian meal, on this road to the West no one will know he is a monk for pilgrimage. They will think I am only a half-grown, half-wild strong boar from the hills. With a crowd, trident and broom in hand, they will surround and knock down old Pig, take him home to butcher, pickle him, and feast on him through New Year. Would that not end in disaster?" Wukong said, "Go patrol the mountain, then."

Zhu Bajie asked, "What is patrolling then?" Wukong said, "Enter this mountain and ask how many demons there are, what mountain, what cave they dwell in, so we can pass correctly." Zhu Bajie said, "If this is so, let old Pig patrol." He gathered up his robes and strode in, lifting his iron rake upright, broad-shouldered and fierce, heading straight into the deep mountain. His spirit rose high as he rushed up the main path.

From behind, Sun Wukong could not help a sly laugh. Tripitaka scolded, "You reckless monkey! The brothers all lack tenderness and always harbor jealous hearts. You have made such sly and crafty words, told him to patrol, yet you stay and laugh at him here."

Wukong said, "I am not laughing at him. I have a different taste in this laughter. See, when Zhu Bajie goes out like this, he will not patrol and will not dare to face demons; he will hide himself somewhere and then invent a lie to fool us."

Tripitaka said, "How can you know that?" Wukong said, "I can guess this. If you doubt me, let me follow him and test. First, I can help him aid in subduing demons; second, I can see whether he truly has a sincere heart to worship Buddha." Tripitaka said, "Good, good, good. Do not go and trick him."

Wukong assented, ran up the slope, and in a body transformation became a cicada-like insect. He made himself light and nimble. One could see:

Thin wings dance in the wind without effort; the waist is sharp and fine as a needle. He threads through reed and brush beneath flower shade, quicker still than a meteor. His eyes shine clear and bright; his voice is faint and whisper-soft. Among all insects he is small, upright and poised, with a hidden steadiness in him. After many days of idling, he rests in secluded woods, his whole body unseen, and not even a thousand eyes can seek him out.

With one sharp whirr of a wing he flew up, caught up and landed behind Zhu Bajie's ear, under the tuft of hair at the root. The fool just kept walking and did not know someone sat upon him. After going seven or eight li, he dropped the iron rake, turned his head back, and, gesturing and pointing at Tripitaka, cursed: "You soft old monk, the Bian-ma-wun, and the mild-faced Sha Wujing—there they sit at ease, fooling me into this long road. We all set out to obtain the true fruit, yet I alone am told to patrol this mountain. Ha!

I have heard there are demons, so I should slip away a bit to dodge them—at least half done. Yet he sends me to go hunting for them. Such ill luck! Where shall I go to sleep? I will sleep a while and return, and in a dazed reply to him I will just say I have already patrolled the mountain and finish the matter." For a moment the fool thought himself lucky, gathered up his rake, and walked on. He saw a curved red-grass slope in a hollow of the mountain. He dived in headfirst, set the rake down, thudded into a bed, and slept on, stretching his waist, and said, "So free. Even that Bima-wun cannot be at ease like I am."

Sun Wukong had been listening to every word from behind his ear root. Unable to restrain himself, he flew up once more and pinched him once. Again he changed form and became a woodpecker beetle. As one could see:

Red-glossed, iron-sharp beak, bright and sleek. Green plumage and plumage of a vivid hue. A pair of steel claws sharp as needles. The belly may be hungry; it cares nothing for the stillness of the forest. It most loves rotten rotten wood and decayed timber, but despises old, lonely trees. Round eyes, decisive tail, spirit that flings forth; the pecking sound itself is worth hearing. This insect was not very large nor very small, weighing only two or three taels. A red-copper beak, black-iron legs. With a shiver of a wing it dropped down in a sweep. Zhu Bajie had fallen on his back and was asleep, and the bug pinched his lips sharply once with its beak.

That oaf, flustered, scrambled up and began shouting wildly: "There’s a demon, there’s a demon! It stabbed me once and ran off, and my mouth hurts so much." He reached out to touch it and blood came out. He said, "Goodness, I have not just had some matter for joy. How did my mouth come to be covered in red?" He looked at the bloody hand and kept muttering, glancing about both sides, yet seeing no movement. "There is no monster at all; how could something stab me?" He lifted his head and, looking up, found it was a pecking bug flying in the air. Biting his teeth, he cursed: "That corpse-brother is only Bimawen trouble-meddling with me; now you are troubling me, too. I understand now. He surely does not know me as a person; he thinks my mouth is just a black, rotten, decayed piece of wood with worms in it, and he pecks this way when hunting them. He pecked me once, just once. Once I tuck my mouth into my breast I can sleep." He muttered on and immediately slipped back to sleep. Sun Wukong returned once more, and, pecking behind his ear again, the fool, in alarm, sprang up and said, "This corpse-thing is vexing me badly. Certainly this must be his nest, where he lays eggs and fledglings. He fears I have taken it, so he bothers me this way. Enough—enough—no more sleeping." Grasping his spade, he strode straight out of Red-Grass Slope, searching for another road. That put Sun Wukong in good spirits; the handsome Monkey King laughed aloud. Wukong said, "This blockhead has his eyes flung wide open and cannot even recognize his own companions."

Great Sage, he shook his body and changed again, becoming a tiny xiao-liao insect, and clung behind Bajie’s ear, never leaving him. The fool went deeper into the mountain, walked on for four or five li, and saw in a hollow three square blue stones the size of a table top. He set down his spade and made a grand obeisance to the stones. Wukong laughed quietly: "This fool, the stones are not people—they cannot speak and cannot return courtesy; why does he bow to them? He is like a blind fool." In truth, the fool took the three stones for Tripitaka, Sha Wujing, and Wukong and rehearsed in front of them. He said to himself, "Now when I return and if he asks whether there is a demon, I will say there is. If he asks what kind of mountain it is and I say it is clay-molded, earth-built, cast in tin, cast in bronze, steamed from dough, paper-covered, painted in brush strokes, then when he hears that he will call me a fool. I will simply say it is Stone Mountain. If he asks what cave, only say it is Stone Cave. If he asks what gate, say the Iron-leaf Gate with nailed leaves. If he asks how far in, say there are three levels. If he asks again to search and asks how many nails are on the gate, I shall only say, "My old pig-heart is too flustered to remember truly." If this fabrication is settled well, I can deceive that Bimawen." The fool gathered himself, dragged his spade, and headed straight back on the original path.

What Wukong heard from behind his ear was all clear. Seeing him return, Wukong at once sprang up with both wings and hurried back ahead, resuming his true form before Master Tripitaka. "Wukong, you have come—how is Wuneng not coming back?" Tripitaka asked. Wukong laughed: "He is there, making up lies as he goes; he should return soon." Tripitaka said, "His ears cover his eyes; he is dull-witted. What lies can he make? What ghost-talk are you putting into him?" Wukong replied, "Master, you only defend him. These are matched questions indeed." He then explained that the fool had slept in the grass, been awakened by the pecking bug, made obeisance to the stones, and fabricated the Stone Mountain, Stone Cave, Iron-leaf Gate, and demon-business beforehand.

When he had finished, soon the fool came back. Fearing he might forget the lie, he kept his head lowered and practiced his words under his breath. Wukong barked, "Bajie, what are you reciting?" Bajie lifted his ears and peered, saying, "Have I reached the place?" He came forward and knelt. Tripitaka helped him up: "Disciple, you are exhausted." Bajie said, "Indeed. For the one on foot, for the one climbing hills—this is the hardest of hardships." Tripitaka asked, "Were there demons?" Bajie answered, "There are demons, there are demons—a whole heap of demons." "How did he send you?" "He called me Pig Forefather and Pig Maternal-Grandfather. He set out some flour-soup vegetarian dishes, fed me a meal, and said he would array drums and flags to send us over the mountain." Wukong said, "He must have fallen asleep in the grass; he was speaking in his sleep." At that, the fool grew two chi shorter and stammered, "Grandfather! If I am asleep, how should I have known?" Wukong moved forward and hauled him by the ear: "Come, let me ask you." The fool, frightened, said, "Ask all you like, why this tugging?" "What mountain is it?" "It is Stone Mountain." "What cave?" "It is Stone Cave." "What gate?" "It is a nailed Iron-leaf Gate." "How far inside?" "It is three levels deep." Wukong said, "You need not continue. I remember the latter part perfectly. If Master does not believe, I will speak it for you." Bajie said, "Brother, you have not even gone there. How do you know those things? Why should you speak for me?" Wukong laughed, "Is this it? 'If he asks how many nails are on the gate, just say, old pig-heart is too busy and cannot remember clearly.'" The fool hurriedly knelt. Wukong said, "You made obeisance toward those stones, taking them as if they were the three of us and answering each question in turn. Is that so? And did you not also say, 'Once I get my lie in order, I can deceive Bimawen'?" The fool at once merely knelt and knocked his head, saying, "Elder Brother, I go on patroling the mountain. Did you truly come with me just to listen?"

Wukong snapped, "You worthless, sackful-of-straw fool! At such an important place you were ordered to patrol, and you slept. Had it not been for the pecking bug waking you, you would still be sleeping there. And once you woke, you even invented such a huge lie—would you not ruin a major matter? Bring out that cane and I will strike you five times to etch a lesson into your head." Bajie panicked, "That mourning-gong club is so heavy. One more strike and it will scrape my skin, wrench my sinews, and tear them; five strikes would be death." Wukong said, "You fear being hit, yet how could you forge such lies?" Bajie said, "Brother, if I get through this time, I will never do it again." Wukong said, "One time, three blows." Bajie said, "Granda-—even half a blow I cannot bear." With nowhere else to turn, Bajie seized Master Tripitaka and pleaded, "Please, Master, ask one be spoken to me." Tripitaka said, "Wukong says you fabricated lies; I do not yet believe him. If it is truly so, you truly deserve punishment. But we are now crossing a mountain with few people to command us. Wukong, spare him for now; after we pass this mountain, punish him then." Wukong said, "The ancients said, 'To follow one’s parents’ words with affection is called great filial piety.' Since Master says no beating, I will spare you this time. Go patrol with him again. If you lie again and upset matters, I will not spare you then even once."

The fool only rose and went again. You can see him rush up onto the main road, fear and hidden ghosts springing in his breast, and at every step he suspected that Wukong had transformed and was following him, so each object he saw made him think it was Wukong. After seven or eight li he saw a tiger running down a mountain slope. He was not afraid and raised his spade, saying, "Brother, have you come to listen while I make up these lies? This time I won’t make any." He went on. Then the mountain wind came, strong enough with one cry to tear a dead log from its place and roll it before him. He stumbled and struck his chest, saying, "Brother, what is this? I said I would not make lies this time, and now this tree comes and strikes me? Why turn into this tree to hit me?" He went forward again; he saw a white-necked old crow ahead, crying sharply with repeated calls. He said, "Brother, don't be ashamed, don’t be ashamed. I said I would not make up lies, and I will not. Why do you keep becoming a crow and speaking? Are you here to listen?" In truth, on this occasion Wukong had not followed him at all; only the fool, frightened by his own panic, wondered and suspected wildly, and therefore in every direction he suspected Wukong was by his side. The fool’s fear and suspicion are enough for now, and go no farther.

Now this mountain was called Pingtong Mountain, and the cave was called Lotus-Flower Cave. In that cave lived two demons: one called Golden-Horn Great King, and one called Silver-Horn Great King. Golden-Horn was seated, and said to Silver-Horn, “Brother, how long has it been since we have patrolled the mountain?” Silver-Horn said, “Half a month.” Golden-Horn said, “Brother, today you go with me to patrol.” Silver-Horn said, “Why patrol today?” Golden-Horn said, “You do not know. Not long ago I heard that in the Eastern Capital of the Great Tang, a monk from the Tang court named Tripitaka had been sent west to pray to Buddha. He travels with four in his company: Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing, and including the horse makes five in all. When you see him, bring him to me.” Silver-Horn said, “We are to eat men. Could we not just catch a few in any case? Since this monk is going west, let him go.” Golden-Horn said, “You do not understand. When I once left the heavenly court, I once heard men say this: Tripitaka is Elder Jinchan descended to the mortal world, a virtuous man of ten lives of cultivation, with not a grain of his original yang released. Whoever eats his flesh gains life-prolonging longevity. Silver-Horn said, “If eating his flesh brings long life, then why should we practice any more—why sit in meditation, do any deeds, forge dragons and tigers, mate male with female? We should just eat him. Let me fetch him.” Golden-Horn said, “Brother, you are too hasty; do not be so quick. If you step out of the cave, no matter what happens, if the monk is brought here and if it is not Tripitaka, he is still not a true son of man. I remember his appearance. I once had his teacher and disciples drawn, a sketch and figure made. You can take it and, when you meet the monk, compare with it. I also gave the name and identity of each person, one by one.” Silver-Horn took the image and names, knew their names, then left the cave and called out thirty small demons, and they came to patrol the mountain.

Elsewhere, Zhu Bajie was walking, and all of a sudden collided with a crowd of demons, who stepped in front of him and blocked the way, asking, “Who is coming here?” The fool only lifted his head and, with his ears flapping, saw they were demons, and he was frightened. In his heart he thought, If I say I am a monk of the pilgrimage, they will haul me off.” So he only said he was merely passing by. One of the little demons reported back, “Great King, he is just walking along.” Among the thirty of them, some recognized him and some did not. A demon beside them, listening to the instructions and speech, said, “Great King, this monk resembles Zhu Bajie from the portrait.” He called for the spirit-image scroll to be raised. When Zhu Bajie saw it he was greatly startled and said, “Ah! Why have I been so listless all this while? It was he who brought over my spirit-image.” The little demon prodded him with a spear, and Silver-Horn pointed with his finger: “The one riding the white horse is Tripitaka. The hairy-faced one is Sun Wukong.” Hearing this, Zhu Bajie cried out, “City God, it can pass without me; one pig-head, three sacrificial victims, twenty-four clear offerings.” He kept muttering and praying. The demon said again, “This dark-skinned tall one is Sha Wujing, and that long-nosed broad-eared one is Zhu Bajie.” Hearing himself called out, the fool hastily shoved his mouth into his bosom and hid it. The demon barked, “Monk, put your mouth out.” Zhu Bajie said, “I am sick in my belly; I cannot stretch it out.” The demon ordered a young one to hook it out with tongs. Startled, the fool stretched out his mouth and said, “It's not a small household form— is this it? If you want to look, then look. What use is a hook?”

When that demon recognized Zhu Bajie, he drew his precious saber and came forward to chop. The fool raised his spiked rake and held it up: “My son, do not be impolite—look at this spiked rake!” The demon laughed, “This monk took lay vows halfway on the road.” Zhu Bajie said, “Good son, you have some spirit. How did you know the master was a lay novice?” The demon said, “You know how to use this rake. You must have stolen it from someone’s garden while they were digging the earth.” Zhu Bajie said, “My son, how do you know this is the master’s rake? It is not a gardener’s rake. This one is:

Cast in giant-toothed form like the claw of a dragon, gilded through with gold, it looks like a tiger’s shape. If it meets an enemy, cold wind sprays; if it holds its ground, sparks of flame arise. It can clear away obstacles for Tripitaka, seize demons along the Western Road. Twisting smoke and rosy cloud to hide sun and moon, it raises dark clouds and dims the stars. It can topple old Tiger of Mount Tai and startle even the old Dragon of the Great Sea by turning it over. Even if you, demon, have methods to spare, one blow of this spiked rake makes nine bloody holes.” Hearing this, the demon would not yield. He drew the Seven-Star Sword, cast and parried in many ways. The two traded blows back and forth in the mountains for twenty rounds, neither giving victory. When Zhu Bajie took his enmity to the utmost, he met him as one prepared to die. Seeing him yank his ears, saliva spraying, brandishing the spiked rake, and shouting and roaring, the demon had some fear at last. He then turned and summoned the lesser demons, all of them to join in. If they had fought one by one, that was still manageable. But when he saw all these little demons rushing in together, he flustered, could not hold up his guard, broke rank, and turned to run. Indeed, the path was uneven and he had not looked carefully. Suddenly he was tripped by a tangle of wild vines and stumbled. He struggled up and went to run, when another little demon knocked him down. Grabbing at his heels, he went down again in a full fall. A group pounced and held him fast, grabbing his mane, wrenching his ears, hauling at his feet and tail, then shouldering and lifting him to carry him into the cave. Ah! It was exactly: A demon-body is hard indeed to burn away, With ten thousand kinds of disasters, removal is hard to achieve.

In the end, we still do not yet know Zhu Bajie’s fate. Listen to the next chapter for explanation.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Just then that monster took Bajie into the cave and said, “Brother, I have brought someone in.” The old demon was pleased and said, “Bring him and let me see.” The second demon said, “Is this it?” The old demon said, “Brother, we brought the wrong one; this monk is useless.” Then Bajie snorted and said, “Great king, send this useless monk away. He is not even fit to be a man’s son.” The second demon said, “Brother, do not release him. Though he is useless, he is one of Tripitaka’s party and is called Zhu Bajie. Put him in the rear purification pool, soak off his pelt, salt-pickle him, dry him out, and then when the sky turns overcast we will drink him.” Hearing this, Bajie said, “By the gods, I have run into a demon that pickles flesh for a living.” The little demon lifted Bajie up, threw him into the water, and left it at that.”

Just then Tripitaka sat before a slope, his ears hot, eyes flickering, body unsettled, and cried out, “Wukong, why has Wuneng gone this far on the mountain patrol and not returned?” Wukong said, “Master, you still do not know his heart.” Tripitaka asked, “What is on his mind?” Wukong replied, “Master, if there were any monster on this mountain, he could not take one step. He would for sure put on a display and run back to report to me. I think there is no monster; the road has been peaceful, and he has kept going.” Tripitaka said, “If he truly has gone on ahead, where are we to meet him? This is wild and open hillside, not like town streets and market squares between wells.” Wukong said, “Master, do not worry. Mount your horse. That fool is a bit lazy and so he walks slowly. Spur the horse some and we will catch up and go together.” Indeed Tripitaka mounted, Sha Wujing took the pack, and Wukong went ahead to lead the way up the mountain.

Just then the old demon called again to the second demon: “Brother, now that you have taken Zhu Bajie, we are certain to have Tripitaka. Go patrol the mountain again, and do not let him pass.” The second demon said, “At once, at once.” He quickly signaled fifty little demons to patrol up the mountain. As they walked, there appeared light drifting auspicious clouds and circling lucky vapour. The second demon said, “Tripitaka has come.” The demons said, “Where is Tripitaka?” The second demon said, “On a good man, auspicious clouds shine above his head; on an evil man, black vapour rises to heaven. Tripitaka is, in truth, the earthly manifestation of Elder Golden Cicada, a good man cultivated across ten lives, so those pale auspicious clouds are around him.” None of the monsters could see him. The second demon pointed and said, “Is that him?” Tripitaka, on horseback, shivered a chill. He pointed again, and again he shivered; yet again he pointed and shivered three times in a row. His spirit uneasy, he said, “Disciple, why do I keep having chills?” Sha Wujing said, “Such a chill means a stomach disease has flared up.” Wukong said, “Nonsense. Master is only walking through these deep heights and ridges and must be afraid at a shadow. Do not fear, do not fear. Let Wukong strike the road with his staff and crush this fright.”

Well done, Wukong, he set his staff before the horse and threw out several maneuvers: up three, down four, left five, right six, employing all the arts of the Six Stratagems and Three Mysteries, bringing forth divine skill. Tripitaka watched from horseback and saw that such prowess was rare in all the world. He cut open the road and advanced, nearly unseating that monster. When the monster saw him from the mountain top, spirit and soul fled; he suddenly cried out, “For years I have heard of Wukong, Great Sage. Today I know the report was true and not false.” The demons came forward and said, “Great king, why does he borrow another’s spirit and ruin his own majesty? Who is he to boast against who?” The old demon said, “Wukong’s magic is vast and his courage exceeds ten thousand men; Tripitaka cannot be eaten by him.” The demons said, “Great king, you have no trick for this. Let some of us go and report to the Great King, summon every soldier from this cave, set the formation, and together in one mind and one body block him so he cannot escape.” The old demon said, “Have you not seen his iron staff? It has the might that not ten thousand men can withstand. In my cave there are only four or five hundred soldiers—how could they resist one strike of that staff?” The demons said, “In that case, Tripitaka cannot be taken by force. Did we perhaps seize Zhu Bajie by mistake? Better send him back now.” The old demon said, “To take him was no mistake; to return him is not to be done lightly. Tripitaka is to be taken in the end, only now it cannot yet be done.” The demons asked, “With such words, how many more years must pass?” The old demon said, “Not long at all. I see only that Tripitaka can be sought through kindness, not by malice. If we seize him by force, we will not even hear of him. Only by goodwill and winning his heart into accord with mine can we, in kindness, devise a way to take him.” The demons asked, “If you have resolved this, may we all be used?” The old demon said, “You all go back to your home strongholds, but do not tell Great King. If he is alarmed, he will surely flee like a windstorm and our plan will fail. I have my own transformative arts and can take him myself.” The demons dispersed.

Then he alone leapt down from the mountain and by the roadside transformed himself into an old Taoist. How was he dressed? One could see him:

The star-crown gleamed, his hair loose and wild like a crane’s crest. Feathered robes and an embroidered sash, cloud shoes bound with yellow-brown cords. His spirit was clear, eyes bright like an immortal guest; his body sound, his body light as an old man with long life. As for what sort of Taoist he claimed, a Clear-Cattle Exorcist, he was even better than Master Suquan. He made a false image seem true, and pressed a fake sincerity to look like true feeling. He stood by the road in the guise of a lame, broken-legged Taoist, blood streaming from his foot, humming through his mouth, and crying only, “Save people! Save people!”

It is said that Tripitaka, relying on Wukong and Sha Wujing, came happily onward. While they were walking, they heard, “Master, save a person!” Tripitaka heard and said, “Excellent, excellent. In this wild mountain wasteland there is no village in any direction. What man is it that cries out? Surely one frightened by tigers, leopards, or worms has fainted away.” Tripitaka turned the swift horse and called, “Who is the one in peril? come out.” That demon crawled out of the grass and, before Tripitaka’s horse, knelt down again and again with a clattering sound. Tripitaka on the horse saw he was a Taoist, and very old at that, and was not at all displeased. He quickly dismounted and said, “Please rise, please rise.” That demon said, “Pain, pain, pain.” He dropped his hand and looked, and saw blood flowing from his foot. Tripitaka asked in alarm, “Master, from where do you come? Why is your honored foot injured?” The demon answered in subtle words and false feeling, speaking as if sincere, “Tripitaka, west of this mountain there is a peaceful and secluded cloister. I am a Taoist from that hall.” Tripitaka said, “You do not serve incense and chanting in your own observatory, why do you wander idly here?” The demon said, “Some time ago, at a donor’s home south of the mountain, householders invited a Taoist group to dispel star-misfortune and spread blessings; we, my master and I, were traveling together on the path. When we reached a deep crossroad, we suddenly met a mottled fierce tiger that seized my disciple and carried him off. I, poor Taoist, trembled in fear, could not run; from one stumble I tumbled down a slope of broken stones and hurt my hips and feet, and cannot find my way back. By this great heavenly affinity today I have met your holiness. I beg the Buddha of great compassion in your heart to save my life. If I can return to the hall, I will sell my body and repay my life-breath with all my weight; I will surely thank your deep grace forever.” Tripitaka, hearing this, believed it to be true and said, “Master, you and I are of one life. I am a monk and you are Taoist; though our garments differ, the way of cultivation is the same. If I do not save you I am no true renunciant. I will save you, and now you cannot walk the road alone.” The demon said, “I can barely stand at all—how can I walk?”

Tripitaka said, “Very well, very well. I can still travel on; let him ride my horse for this stretch, and when he reaches your hall, give me back my horse.” The demon said, “Great Master, I am deeply grateful, but my hip-joint is broken from the fall, and I cannot ride a horse.” Tripitaka said, “True enough.” He told Sha Wujing, “Put the luggage on my horse. Carry him one way.” Sha Wujing said, “I will carry him.” The demon turned sharply and cast a glance at him, saying, “Master, I was terrified by that tiger, and seeing your unlucky-faced holiness made the fear worse. I dare not ask him to carry me.” Tripitaka called, “Wukong, carry him.” Wukong answered repeatedly, “I will carry, I will carry.” Then the demon fixed on Wukong and made him carry; without further words he kept steady. Sha Wujing laughed and said, “This Taoist with no eyes for good and evil—if I carry him it is wrong, it should be inverted that he carries me. If he had seen no one when they reached the Three-Pointed Rock, he would have broken your shoulder-bones to fragments.”

Wukong heard it and laughed, "You wild demon, how dare you come to trouble me? Ask yourself how old old Sun is. With such phantom-talk you can only try to deceive Tripitaka, and then dare to deceive me too? I know you for the monster of this mountain, and I know you want to eat my Master. My Master is no careless wanderer—how can he be your food? If you are going to eat him, then you must give half of him to Old Sun too." The demon, hearing Wukong chant, said, "Master, I am the grandson of a good household; I became a Taoist priest. Today has gone badly—I have met the calamity of tigers and wolves. I am no demon." Wukong said, "If you fear tigers and wolves, why did you not chant the Scripture of the Northern Dipper?" Tripitaka had just mounted, and hearing this, he cursed: "You unruly monkey! ‘To save one life is equal to building a seven-tier pagoda.’ Carry him as a porter and no more is enough—what is all this of the Northern Dipper Scripture and the Southern Dipper Scripture?" Wukong said, "This fellow of a twisted fate! My Master is a compassionate and benevolent man, good outwardly but strange within. If I do not carry you, he will reproach me. Carrying you is one thing, but we must be clear from the start: if it is only to relieve yourself, tell me first; if you let it fall down my spine, the stench is intolerable and my clothes are soiled, and no one will be there to wash me." The demon said, "At this age, do you not know how to judge your own words?" Wukong lifted him up and put him on his back. Together with Tripitaka and Sha Wujing, he hurried westward on the road. Where the mountain rose and dipped, Wukong watched carefully and slowed his step, letting Tripitaka go ahead.

They could hardly go three or five li when Master and Sha Wujing had gone down into a mountain hollow, and Wukong himself could not be seen. Inwardly he grumbled, "Tripitaka is so old and still does not understand the situation. On such a long road, even empty-handed I still feel the weight on my back; I want to smash him down, yet he has made me carry this demon. Even if he were not a demon but a good man, at his age he should already be dead. Why keep carrying him? Let me kill him and be done." The Great Sage was just working out how to strike him, when the demon, seeing this, had already prepared another move and used a mountain-shifting and sea-overturning spell. He pinched a mantra-seal on Wukong's back and chanted the true words, sending a Mount Sumeru into the sky to come crashing straight down upon Wukong. Startled, Wukong tilted his head slightly to one side and let it land on his left shoulder and arm, then laughed: "My child, what sort of heavy-body art is this, trying to crush Old Sun? That I do not fear. It is only that carrying evenly is bearable; carrying at a slant is hard to endure." The demon said, "One mountain does not hold him." He chanted again, sending Mount Emei through the sky to press down. Wukong again moved his head a little to the other side, taking it on his right shoulder and arm. Watching him carry both mountains while rushing like a flying star to catch Tripitaka, the demon trembled all over, sweat beading and his whole body gone limp, and said, "He can really carry mountains." He steadied himself and again chanted the truth words, sending Mount Tai into the air to strike him down. Wukong's strength went soft and numb, and under that Mount Tai-underpinning technique, he was pressed only enough to make the three corpse-gods writhe and the seven orifices spurt red blood.

This dreadful demon, having subdued Wukong with his arts, then drove off in a long wind, rushed after Tripitaka, and from the clouds stretched his hand down and struck the monk from horseback. Startled, Sha Wujing dropped the luggage, drew his demon-subduing staff, and blocked him head-on. The demon raised a Seven-Star Sword to meet him. It was a fierce fight:

The Seven-Star Sword and the Subduing-Monster Staff flashed like ten-thousand mirrored rays of gold. This one had a round eye, feral as the Black-Killer God; that iron-faced one was truly the curtain-rippling General. The demon before the mountain displayed his powers, wholly intent on seizing Tripitaka. The other strove with all his heart to guard the true monk, determined to die rather than release him. The two expelled cloud and mist, blinding the heavenly court, and raised earth and dust to veil the Big Dipper. Their fighting dimmed the red sun until it seemed colorless, and heaven and earth became dark and reeling. They engaged and withdrew eight or nine times, but unexpectedly Sha Wujing ended by losing the battle.

The demon was ferociously violent. He made his gem-sword-mouth trick flash and send down meteor-strikes that wore Sha Wujing down till he was weak and could not resist, turning to flee. He had already trapped him with the precious staff, swung up his large hand and struck him, pinning Sha Wujing beneath his left armpit; with his right hand he took Tripitaka from the horse, hooked the luggage under his toes, opened his mouth and bit the horse's mane; then, using a seizing spell, he swept them all into a gust and carried them to Lotus-Flower Cave, then shouted in a sharp voice, "Elder brother! These monks have all been taken."

The old demon heard this and rejoiced: "Bring him, so I can inspect him." The second demon said, "Is this not him?" The old demon said, "Good younger brother, you brought the wrong one again." The second said, "You said he was Tripitaka." The old one answered, "It is Tripitaka, yes—but we still have not seized the skillful Sun Wukong. Only if we take him too will it be proper to eat Tripitaka. If he is not taken, do not touch the others. The Monkey King has vast powers and endless transformations. If we eat his Master, will he yield willingly? Once he makes a ruckus at our gate, how can we ever expect peace?" The second demon laughed: "Brother, you do put people up too high. If we follow your praise, none in heaven or on earth can match him; from my own view, he is just this, with no extra trick." The old demon asked, "Did you seize him?" The second answered, "He has been pinned down by three mountains I sent and lies beneath them, unable to move even an inch. That is why I fetched Tripitaka, Sha Wujing, and even horse and luggage as well." Hearing this, the old demon's heart was full of joy: "Fate, fate. Catch this one, and Tripitaka becomes truly the morsel in our mouths." He called a minor demon: "Quick, prepare the wine. Offer you two princes a cup of earned success." The second demon said, "Brother, hold the wine. Tell the little ones to haul Zhu Bajie from the water. Then they hung Zhu Bajie on the east gallery, Sha Wujing on the west, Tripitaka in the middle, tied the white horse to a rack, and gathered the baggage inside.

The old demon laughed: "Younger virtuous brother, your methods are excellent—you caught three monks twice already. Yet even though Sun Wukong is pinned beneath mountains, you still need a spell; how can we bring him out in a way fit for steam." The second said, "Elder brother, please sit. If we want to seize Sun Wukong, we need not set out ourselves. Just order two little demons to take two treasures and bring him in that way." The old demon asked, "What treasures should they take?" The second replied, "Take my purple-golden red gourd and your sheep-fat jade pure bottle." The old demon took out the treasures and asked, "Send those two then?" The second said, "Send jinxi ghost and lingli bug, those two." He instructed, "You two carry these treasures straight to the peak of the highest mountain, hold the bottom upward and the mouth downward, and call out: ‘Sun Wukong.’ If he answers, he is already taken inside. Then immediately paste on the talisman: ‘By the urgent law-command of the Supreme Sovereign, the Jade Patriarch, in accord with the imperial decree.’ At once, in three ke he will turn to pus." The two little demons kowtowed, took the treasures, and went out to fetch Wukong—further details are omitted.

Now it is said: Wukong, oppressed by the demon spell beneath the foot of the mountain, thinking hard of Tripitaka and bracing for trouble, cried out to the holy monk, "Master, do you recall when you came to Two Realms Mountain and tore away the sealing tally, and Old Wukong escaped great danger and was instructed to follow and guard the monk? By the Bodhisattva’s bestowed Dharma order, I was to live and practice with you, sharing one affinity, one countenance, one vision, one knowing. At the thought of reaching this place, I have met a demon barrier and once more been pressed down by a moved mountain. Alas, alas! It is your life that is fated to end; poor Sha Wujing, Zhu Bajie, and that small dragon-horse-form are the ones to suffer this ordeal." "Indeed, this is said: The tall tree draws wind, and the wind shakes the tree; for man, high fame brings high loss of fame." After this sigh, his tears fell like rain.

At once the mountain gods, earth god, and the five-direction Jiedi spirits were alarmed. The Gold-Head Jiedi said, "Whose mountain is this?" The Earth Deity answered, "It is ours." "Who is crushed beneath it?" the Earth Deity replied, "We do not know." The Jiedi said, "So you truly did not know. This is the Great Sage Equal-to-Heaven, Sun Wukong, who five hundred years ago made a great uproar in Heaven. He has since returned to proper realization and become Tripitaka’s disciple. Why did you lend the mountain to a demon to crush him? If you are fools enough to think it will pass, and he one day breaks free, will he spare you? Even if we take it lightly, the Earth Deity would be demoted, the Mountain God reassigned to far exile; we too would be subject to grave blame." Then the mountain and earth deities, now fearing, said, "We truly did not know. We only heard the demon lord begin chanting the mountain-sending spell, and so we moved the mountain here. How could we have known it was Great Sage Sun?" The Jiedi said, "You need not fear. The law says, ‘The ignorant do not bear guilt.’ I will be reasonable with you: release him; do not let him take up a weapon against us." The Earth Deity said, "Even if released, he will strike and hit us." The Jiedi replied, "You do not understand. He has a Ruyi Golden-Hooped Staff, deadly indeed: if it strikes, one dies; if it catches hold and drags, one is merely wounded. One tap breaks bones, one brush leaves flesh caving in."

The Earth God and the Mountain Deity were afraid at heart. After conferring with the Five-Direction Jie Di, they came outside the gate of Three-Mountain Pass and called out:「Great Sage, the Mountain Deity, the Earth God, and the Five-Directions have come to see you.」“Good Wukong, he still kept his tiger-like lean vigor and the natural, high-necked air of one in command, and his voice rang out clearly:「What’s this, to gaze on me?」The Earth God said:「Report to the Great Sage that the mountain has been ordered to open. The Great Sage should come out, and pardon the minor gods for their disrespect.」The Great Sage said:「Open the mountain, and no beating for you.」He shouted:「Up with it!」Then, as though an official were releasing prisoners, the gods chanted true-word mantras, sent the mountain back to its own station, and released him. He leapt up, shook off the dust, fixed his skirt, drew the staff from behind his ear, and told the Mountain Deity and Earth God:「Come over here with your staffs. Each of you give two blows first, and let Old Son vent his vexation a little.」The gods were greatly startled:「The Great Sage just commanded us and pardoned our offense. How can he, once he comes out, change his words and ask to hit us?」The Great Sage said:「Good Earth God, good Mountain God, you are not afraid of Old Son, yet you fear a demon?」The Earth God said:「That demon spirit has vast powers and strong magic. He chanted mantras to bind us in his cave, and each of us takes turns standing guard there by the watch."

The Great Sage heard the words 「on duty」 and was startled. He faced heaven and cried out in a loud voice:「Azure Heaven, Azure Heaven! Since chaos first divided, since heaven opened and earth split, this Flower-Fruit Mountain brought me into being. I have roamed through famed masters and learned the secret of longevity. Think of how I can change with the wind, subdue tiger and dragon, and make trouble in Heaven’s Court under the name of Great Sage, yet I have never treated Mountain Gods and Earth Gods as if they were servants in my heart. How can this formless demon now dare to call the Mountain God and Earth God his slaves, and have them take turns standing watch for him? My God! If heaven and earth once birthed Old Sun, why birth such a breed as this one too?」

While the Great Sage was still lamenting, he saw a reddish light blazing from the hollow in the mountain. The Great Sage said:「Mountain God, Earth God, since you stand watch in this cave, what is this thing that gives off light?」The Earth God said:「That is the demon’s treasure shining. I think some evil spirit has brought up a treasure to subdue you.」The Great Sage said:「This one is really playing tricks. Let me ask you first: who in his cave goes along with him?」The Earth God said:「He delights in burning elixirs and making pills, and he likes a Quanzhen Daoist.」The Great Sage said:「No wonder he turned into an old Daoist and deceived my master. In that case, all of you remember this and go back. Let Old Sun take him himself.」The gods all sprang into the air and dispersed at once.

The Great Sage changed himself in an instant into an old perfected man. How might he be dressed?

Hair knotted in twin top-knots, robe patched in a hundred seams. With his hand he struck a fisherman’s drum, with a small clapper in hand. He leaned askew beneath the great road, openly waiting for petty demons. Should one demon arrive, the Monkey King would set his trick in secret.

After a short while, the two little demons arrived. The Great Sage extended the Golden-Hooped Staff. The demon, unprepared, caught his foot and fell with a crash. When he scrambled up and saw the Great Sage, he shouted:「Bei-lan, Bei-lan! If my Great King did not honor you, this traveling monk, we would not be comparing you with one another.」The Great Sage smiled and said:「Comparing what with what? Monks who meet each other are one family.」The monster said:「Why did you lie down here and trip me with this stumble?」The Great Sage said:「The young Daoist boy saw this old Daoist and offered a stumble as a greeting.」The monster said:「My Great King asks only a few taels of silver for a greeting fee. Why make me pay a mere stumble as my greeting fee? You are not a rustic local; certainly not a Daoist of this place.」The Great Sage said:「I am truly not. I am from Mount Penglai."The monster said:「Mount Penglai is the realm of heavenly immortals.」The Great Sage said:「I am not an immortal—who is then?"The monster changed to contrite delight and came forward:「Old Immortal, old Immortal, we of flesh and blood with mortal eyes cannot know. Forgive the roughness of my words. Forgive it.」 The Great Sage said:「I do not hold it against you. As the saying goes: 『An immortal’s body does not tread the mundane earth.』 How do you know that? I have come to your mountain today to take a worthy person to become immortal in truth. Who is willing to go with me?」The Witty Spirit said:「Master, I will go with you.」The Agile Insect said:「Master, I will go with you."

The Great Sage knowingly asked:「From where did the two of you come?」The monster said:「From Lotus-Flower Cave.」「Where are you going?」The monster said:「By my Great King’s command we are to capture Sun Wukong.」The Great Sage said:「Capture whom?」The monster repeated:「Capture Sun Wukong.」The Great Sage said:「Is it that Sun Wukong who goes with Tang Monk to fetch the Buddhist scriptures?」The monster said:「Exactly, exactly. You know him too?」The Great Sage said:「That monkey is a little rude. I know him, and I am a little annoyed with him. If I go with you to seize him too, let that count as helping your merit."The monster said:「Master, you need not aid our merit. My two Great Kings have certain arts: they sent three mountains to pin him beneath them so he cannot move an inch. They told the two of us to bring treasures and trap him in them."The Great Sage said:「What kind of treasures?"The Witty Spirit said:「Mine is a red calabash. His is a Pure Jade Bottle."The Great Sage said:「How do you trap him in those?"The small demon said:「Turn the bottom of this treasure upward and its mouth downward, call him once; if he answers, put him inside. Paste on a placard that reads 『Taishang Laojun, urgent, in accordance with the law, by imperial order』 and in one time and three-ke he turns into pus."The Great Sage, hearing this, thought in alarm:「Dangerous, dangerous! when the reporting clerk once came in the daytime he spoke of five treasures; these are two. I do not know what the other three are."The Great Sage smiled:「You two, let me see your treasures."The little demon, not knowing any secret at all, drew out the two treasures from his sleeve and handed them to the Great Sage. The Great Sage saw them and thought inwardly with joy:「Excellent things, excellent things. If I plucked my tail and leapt away, it would seem like a gift to Old Sun."Then he thought again:「No, no. If I snatch them openly, it only sullies Old Sun’s reputation. This is daylight robbery."He handed them back and said:「You still have not yet seen my treasure.」The monster said:「Does Master have any treasure? Lend it to me, a mortal, and see whether it can ward away calamity."

The good pilgrim lowered his hand, pulled a single hair from his tail, pinched it, and cried:「Change!」In that instant it became a large purple-gold red calabash, a chi and seven cun long. He pulled it from his waist and said:「Look at my calabash.」The Agile Insect took it in hand and, after looking, said:「Master, this calabash is large and handsome and fine to behold, yet it is useless."The Great Sage said:「How is it useless?」The monster said:「Each of my two treasures can hold a thousand people."The Great Sage said:「Your treasures that hold people—how rare are they then? In my calabash I can hold heaven itself.」The monster said:「Can it hold heaven?"The Great Sage said:「It truly can hold heaven."The monster said:「I fear it is a lie. Let us have it hold heaven first before we believe you. Otherwise we will not believe.」The Great Sage said:「If heaven is angered with me, in a month it would still hold it seven or eight times; if heaven is not angered with me, it will not hold it even once for six months."The Agile Insect said:「Elder, if the one that can hold heaven can be traded, then let us trade it.」The Witty Spirit said:「How could he who holds heaven agree to trade for mine that holds people?"The Agile Insect said:「If he will not trade, then at least let him give that Pure Bottle.」The Great Sage thought inwardly with joy:「A calabash for a calabash, and in addition a Pure Bottle: one for two, that is a fitting exchange."He stepped forward and caught the Agile Insect by the arm:「Can we trade for one that holds heaven?」The monster said:「If it holds heaven, then we may trade. If it does not, I will be your son."The Great Sage said:「Fine, fine. I will hold it and let you see."

The Great Sage lowered his head, pinched the spell phrase, and intoned a charm, calling on the Day-Walking God, Night-Walking God, and the Five-Direction Jie Di gods:「Go at once and report to the Jade Emperor. Say that Old Sun has returned to the Right Fruit, seeking the Way and guarding Tripitaka as he goes west to fetch the scriptures; the road is blocked by high mountains and the master meets grievous hardship. For the demon’s treasure, I intend to induce him to exchange it. With ten thousand bows and prostrations, have Heaven lent to Old Sun to enclose him for half an hour, to help bring success. If even half a word he refuses, then I will go at once to Lingxiao Hall and raise blades and spears."

That day, a roaming spirit hurried into the Hall of Lingxiao at the South Gate of Heaven and reported to the Jade Emperor all the previous events. The Jade Emperor said: "That unruly monkey-head speaks thoughtlessly. Earlier Guanyin came and said he should be released so he could protect Tripitaka. I here have again ordered the five Jiedi of the Five Directions and the four Gongcao magistrates to take turns guarding him. Now he wants to borrow heaven to fake it—can Heaven be faked?" Not yet had he finished speaking of faking when, among that company, there flashed forth Nezha, the Third Prince. He said, "May Your Majesty live for ten thousand years. Heaven can indeed be faked." The Jade Emperor asked, "How do you propose to fake Heaven?" Nezha said, "From the first separation of chaos, the light and clarity were made Heaven, and the heavy and turbid made Earth. Heaven is one mass of clear qi that upholds the Jade Heaven palace; in theory, such a thing is difficult to fake. But now Sun Wukong is escorting Tripitaka west to fetch the scriptures. This is truly a blessing worthy of Mount Tai and a great good fortune as deep as the sea. Today we must help him succeed." The Jade Emperor asked, "How will you help?" Nezha said: "Please issue an order: go to the North Gate of Heaven and ask Zhenwu to lend the black carved flag. Unfurl it at the South Gate of Heaven, hiding the sun, moon, and stars. Then those on the other side will see no one, will not see white as white or black as black. Deceive that demon and say Heaven has been dressed up, thereby helping the Great Sage to succeed." Upon hearing this, the Jade Emperor said, "Do as you have submitted." The prince took the command, came to the North Gate, and reported the matter to Zhenwu, relaying everything. The patriarch there at once handed the flag to the prince.

A spirit had already rushed down earlier and whispered in the Great Sage’s ear, "Prince Nezha is coming to help with your task." Sun Wukong looked up and saw auspicious clouds swirling; indeed there was a true divinity. He turned to the little demon and said, "Proceed to feign Heaven." The little demon said, "If it is to be feigned, then feign it—why bother over such a trifle of cotton-wool filth?" Sun Wukong said, "I have just chanted the incantation to summon the divine intent." Both little demons kept their eyes wide open to watch how he would fake Heaven. The Great Sage tossed up a false calabash. Think of it: it had been fashioned from a single strand of hair. The wind from the mountain top carried it; it drifted and swayed, and only after half an hour did it fall down. Above the South Gate of Heaven, Prince Nezha snapped open the flag with a loud flourish and blocked both sun and moon and stars. Truly it was as if Heaven and Earth had been dyed in ink and the universe turned to indigo. The two little demons cried out in shock: "Not long ago we were speaking and it was noon; how did it become dusk at once?" The Great Sage said, "Now that the sky is faked, times are no longer to be distinguished. Why should it not be dusk?" The demon said, "Then why is it this dark?" The Great Sage said, "The sun, moon, and stars are all enclosed within; outside there is no light, so of course it is dark." The demon said, "Master, where are you speaking from over there?" The Great Sage said, "Am I not right in front of you?" The demon reached out and said, "I can only hear speech and still cannot see your face. Master, what place is this?" The Great Sage teased him again: "Do not move your feet. This is the Bohai coast; if your footing gives way and you fall, it would take seven or eight days to reach the bottom." The demon cried, "Enough, enough—release the sky trick. We now know it is that kind of fakery. If we keep this up for a while and fall into the sea, we won't be able to return home."

The Good Sage, seeing he had accepted the truth, chanted the spell again, startled the prince, and had the flag rolled up; then suddenly it was once more noon sunlight. The little demon laughed: "Wonderful! Wonderful! Such a precious thing. If one did not swap it, truly one would be no true child raised under a family roof." The fine demon handed over the calabash, and the clever imp took out a pure bottle and together passed both to the Great Sage. The Great Sage in turn handed the false calabash to the little demon in exchange. Now that the treasure had been exchanged, he pressed the matter to a complete close: he pulled a single hair from beneath his navel, breathed out a breath of immortal qi, and changed it into a copper coin. He called out, "Little boy, take this coin and buy a piece of paper." The demon said, "What is it for?" The Great Sage said, "I will write a contract for you. You have exchanged two of your treasures for humans for my one treasure that can feign Heaven. Fearing human hearts are never entirely at peace, and in later days after years pass one may waver, we make this as written proof for both sides to keep." The demon said, "There is no brush or ink here—let us settle it by a solemn oath." The Great Sage said, "How should the oath be made?" The demon said, "I trade these two treasures that can disguise as humans for your one treasure that can feign Heaven. If one of us later repents, plague will strike four times in the four seasons." The Great Sage laughed, "I will not repent. And if I ever do, I accept that I too will suffer your four-season plague."

After he saw that the Great Sage truly spoke in earnest, he again chanted the spell, startling the prince, who then rolled up the flag. At once there was again mid-day light. The little demon laughed: "Marvelous! Marvelous! A treasure this good—if one does not exchange it, it is surely no child of worthy upbringing." The meticulous demon handed back the calabash; the clever imp brought out the pure bottle and together they passed them to the Great Sage. The Great Sage then handed the false calabash to the little demon in exchange. When the treasures were exchanged, he further tightened the matter by another act: he pulled up his tail and snapped it once, then leapt to the front of the South Gate of Heaven, thanking Prince Nezha for his assistance in waving the banner. The prince returned to the palace to submit the warrant and sent the flag back to Zhenwu; no further account is needed. The Great Sage stood suspended between Heaven and the upper air, watching the little demon.

How things would yet be handled is still uncertain. Hear how it is resolved in the next chapter.
