Yet those two small demons held the fake gourd in their hands and peered at it for a while; then they lifted their heads and Sun Wukong was nowhere to be seen. Lingli said, "Brother, even an immortal can lie. He said he would swap treasures and make us into immortals—how could he leave without so much as asking?" Jingsi said, "If we had done that, it would have profited us immensely. How could he have done such a thing? Bring the gourd here, and let me summon heaven once, just to test it." He truly threw the gourd up, and with a thud it came straight down. Startled, Lingli said, "Why won’t it work? Why won’t it? Could it be that Sun Wukong only pretended to be an immortal, swapped his false gourd for our real one, and escaped?" Jingsi said, "Do not speak nonsense. Sun Wukong is still pinned under the three mountains; how could he get out? Bring it over. I’ll recite a few of the spells and try it." This demon, too, tossed the gourd up into the air and chanted, "If there is even half a word of resistance, then upon Lingxiao Hall I will call out arms and blades." He had no more than begun when it came down again with a thud. The two demons said, "No conjuring, no conjuring—surely it is a fake."

Just as they were shouting, Sun Wukong, in midair, understood clearly. Seeing how things were going, and fearing they would waste too long at the critical moment, he sent a sudden gust of wind, shook himself, and drew the hairs that had formed the counterfeit gourd back onto his body, leaving the two demons empty-handed. Jingsi said, "Brother, bring the gourd." Lingli said, "You’re the one holding it." "Heaven! How did it vanish?" they both went down and groped wildly, probing in the grass, searching under sleeves, patting their waists—where was it to be found? The two demons, frightened and bewildered, said, "What is to be done? What is to be done? At first the Great King gave us this treasure and ordered us to seize Sun Wukong. Now Sun Wukong has not been taken, and the treasure itself is gone too. How can we dare go back and report? This is certain death, and they will beat us dead. What is to be done? what is to be done?" Lingli said, "Let us leave." Jingsi said, "Where should we go?" Lingli said, "Go anywhere. If we return and say the treasure is missing, it is certain death." Jingsi said, "Do not run. Go back. The two Great Lords have always favored you; I will put in a word for you. If he is willing to pardon, you may keep your lives. If he cannot bear it, he will kill you right there. Do not let it come to neither side. Go on, go on." The demon thought it over and then turned and went back toward the mountain.

At once, when Sun Wukong saw them turning back, he changed form in midair and became a fly, then dropped down and followed the demons. You may ask where that treasure is kept if he has become a fly. If he had tossed it on the road, hidden it in the grass, and some mortal had seen and taken it, would not everything have been wasted? He kept it on him still. He kept it on him. A fly is no larger than a bean—how could it hold what it needed to hold? The truth is that his treasure is the Ruyi-Fo Treasure, like his Golden-Hooped Staff: it can change in size and form at will, and therefore it can be carried on one’s person.

With a chirp, Sun Wukong flew down and followed the demons. Soon he reached the cave. He saw the two demons seated there drinking, and the small demon knelt before them. He fixed himself to the door cabinet and listened with a straining ear. The small demon said, "Great Lord." The old demon at once set down his cup: "Have you come?" The small demon said, "We have." Then he asked, "Have you brought Sun Wukong?" The small demon knelt and did not dare to speak. The old demon asked again; he still did not dare to answer, only knelt. Pressed again and again, the little demon prostrated himself on the ground and said, "Forgive us ten thousand deaths, forgive us ten thousand deaths, forgive us ten thousand deaths. We took hold of the treasure and came halfway up the mountain when suddenly we met an immortal of Mount Penglai. He asked where we were going, and we replied: 'To take Sun Wukong.' When that immortal heard the name Sun Wukong, he was angered and wished to lend us help. It was not we who asked him to help. Yet we told him how the treasure was to trap a man. That immortal also had a gourd, skilled in containing heaven. We were foolish and greedy, thinking to trade—his for containing heaven, mine for containing men. So we agreed to swap gourds. It was a gourd for a gourd, and Lingli even handed him a pure bottle. Who would have imagined that an immortal’s object cannot be touched by mortal hands? Just as he tried it, even the person was gone. Please, spare these poor demons for our death-dealing sins."

When the old demon heard this, he burst out like thunder: "Enough! Enough! This is what it is: Sun Wukong disguised himself as an immortal and fooled and swindled us away. That monkey-headed one has immense powers and is feared everywhere; who knows which stray spirit let him out and was deceived out of the treasure?" The second demon said, "Elder brother, moderate your rage. Though that monkey-headed one has indeed been uncouth, and though he has means, if he has escaped, let him go. How could he also have carried off the treasure by deceit? If I cannot catch him, I shall no longer trouble the Western journey as a monster." The old demon said, "How are we to seize him?" The second demon said, "We once had five treasures; two are gone, but three remain, and we must take him by force." The old demon said, "What are those three?" The second demon said, "We still have the Seven-Star Sword and the Banana-leaf Fan with me, and that one golden-hoop rope is being kept by the old mother in the Crushing Dragon Mountain at Crushing-Dragon Cave. Now send the two little demons to ask mother to come and eat Tang Monk’s flesh, and have her bring the golden-hoop rope to take Sun Wukong." The old demon said, "Who should I send for that?" The second demon said, "Do not send such useless creatures for this." He called out once, "Jingsi! Lingli!" The two responded, "Fate, fate—we have not been beaten and we have not been scolded, yet you have spared us." The second demon said, "Call the regular attendants Ba Shan Hu and Yi Hai Long." The two knelt. The second demon ordered, "You must be careful." Both answered, "Careful." He added, "Be very careful." Both answered, "Very careful." Again he asked, "Do you know the old mother’s place?" They answered, "We know it." "Since you know it, go quickly; bow to her many times and tell her we invite her to eat Tang Monk’s flesh. Tell her to bring the golden-hoop rope too, and we are to seize Sun Wukong."

The two demons, receiving the order, ran at full speed. Yet Sun Wukong standing nearby heard everything clearly. He spread his wings, flew after them, and caught up to Ba Shan Hu, clinging himself to his person. After two or three li he was about to kill the two. Then he thought, "What difficulty is there in killing him? Yet the golden-hoop rope is near his mother, and I do not know where it is kept. I will question him first, then strike." The capable Great Sage let out a chirp, slipped away from the little demon, and let them go ahead a hundred or ten paces. Then he changed again and became a little demon, donning a fox-skin cap and fastening a tiger-skin skirt up over his waist, and came running up: "You on the road, wait a moment." The one who was Yi Hai Long turned back and asked, "Who are you, and where did you come from?" Sun Wukong said, "Good brother, you do not even recognize your own folk?" The little demon said, "There is no such one in my family." Sun Wukong said, "How can I not be you? Look again at me." The little demon said, "You look strange, strange; we have never met before." Sun Wukong said, "Indeed. You did not meet me before; I am from outside your band." The little demon said, "An outsider-officer, certainly we have not met. Where are you going?" Sun Wukong said, "The Great King sent you two to ask mother to come and eat Tang Monk’s flesh, and to have her bring the golden-hoop rope to seize Sun Wukong. Fearing that you two are going too slowly, maybe lingering in greed and laziness and ruining the task, he sent me to hurry you on."

Hearing this, the little demon, seeing the glance from beneath his sea-dark eyes, had no further suspicion and took Sun Wukong for one of their own. In a rush he flew ahead. In one breath they ran eight or nine li. Sun Wukong said, "You are running too fast. How far from home now?" A small demon said, "Fifteen or sixteen li." Sun Wukong said, "How much farther is it?" Yi Hai Long pointed and said, "It is at the Ulin grove." Sun Wukong raised his head and saw a strip of dark forest not far away; he reckoned the old monster was just outside the woodland. He stopped there and let the small demon go ahead. Then he drew out his iron cudgel and stepped forward, and with the back of his foot scraped them sharply. He could no longer bear it; he swept the two little demons into one mass of minced flesh. Dragging his feet, he hid them in the deep grasses by the roadside. Then he pulled out one hair and blew a breath of immortal air, saying, "Transform!" He became Ba Shan Hu and at once changed himself into Yi Hai Long. Thus he disguised himself as the two little demons and set out toward Crushing-Dragon Cave to fetch the old mother. This was the supreme power of the Seventy-two Transformations; by mere hand signs he could transmute things to the highest degree.

With three or five great strides he leapt into the grove. Just as he searched for the entrance, he saw two stone gates, half open and half shut, and dared not enter without permission. He called out loudly, "Open the gate! Open the gate!" At once the female demon who watched the gate was startled, and she opened half a door panel, saying, "Where are you from?" Sun Wukong said, "I have come from Lotus Cave on Level-Top Mountain, sent to invite the old mother." The female demon said, "Enter." At the second gate he looked over his shoulder, peered inside, and saw a matriarch seated in the center. As for how she looked, it was like this:

Hair loose and wild like scattered snow, with a glimmer like stars. Her face was ruddy and red, richly wrinkled, with sparse teeth and a stout, imposing air. She seemed of a color like flowers fading under frost, her form like the face of an old pine after the rain. A white silk strip was wrapped around her head and tied into a knot, and at her ears hung gold settings set with jewels.

Sun Wukong saw it and did not dare to enter. He stayed outside the inner gate with a hard face, and burst out crying. You may ask why he cried—could he have been afraid? If it were fear, he would not have to cry. First he had cajoled the creature’s treasure and even killed its young demon; why should he cry for that? At that time he had been boiled in nine cauldrons of oil for seven or eight days and never shed a tear. He only wept because he remembered Tripitaka’s suffering in the journey for the scriptures, and his grief broke him. In his mind he thought: “Since old Sun has already shown his arts and turned into a little demon to fetch this old monster, there is no reason to stand upright and just speak. I must surely make him kowtow first. I have been a worthy man and have bowed only to three: Buddha of the Western Heaven; Guanyin of the Southern Sea; the master of the Two-Worlds Mountain who saved me, to whom I paid four bows. For him I have worn out the heart of my three hairs and seven orifices, my body and all. How much could one volume of scripture be worth? And yet today I must go and bow to this monster. If I do not kneel and bow, I am certain to lose everything. Alas! In the end, it is only for Master’s peril that I, a man, submit to humiliation before others.”

When he came to this point he had no choice. He charged inside and knelt, saying, “Grandmother, I bow to you.” The monster said, “My child, rise.” The Monkey-Wise One thought inwardly, “Excellent, excellent—he called him out with such authority!” The demon-lord asked, “Where are you from?” The Master said, “From Lotus Flower Cave on Flat-Top Mountain. By the order of the two Great Kings I was sent to invite Grandmother to eat Tripitaka’s flesh, and to bring the Golden-Hooped Staff, saying that Sun Wukong should be taken too.” The old monster rejoiced: “Such a filial son!” and went to summon a sedan chair. Sun Wukong said, “My boy, are demon-maids to carry a sedan too?” Right then, from behind, two female demons brought out a cane-liana sedan, set it outside the gate, and hung blue silk curtains on it. The old monster stepped out of the cave and sat in it. Behind him followed several young demon-maids carrying cosmetics, hand mirrors, handkerchiefs, and fragrance boxes. The monster said, “Why have you come? At my own place there is usually no one to attend when my son returns; why have you come to offer such service? Go back home, close the gate, and guard the place.” All of those little demons returned; only the two sedan bearers remained. The old monster asked, “What are the names of the two sent as envoys?” The Master quickly answered, “One is called Bāshān Tiger, and I am called Yǐhăi Dragon.” The monster said, “You two go first and clear the way for me.” The Great Sage reflected, “What bad fortune—after all, the scriptures are still not won, and I am now made a drudge.” Yet he dared not resist force, so he went ahead and cried out with four mighty shouts.

They went about five or six li. He sat on a stone ledge and waited for the sedan-bearers to catch up. Sun Wukong said, “Let us rest a while. My shoulders hurt from carrying the load.” The small demon, ignorant of any arts or tricks, put the sedan down. Behind it the Master plucked one hair from his chest and turned it into a large steamed cake, which he held and ate. A sedan-bearer asked, “Great sir, what are you eating?” The Great Sage said, “Hard to tell. The road is far; I was sent to ask for Grandmother and no reward was given. I’m hungry, and I had only dry provisions with me—let me eat a little and then we go.” The porter said, “Give us some too.” Sun Wukong laughed, “Come now, we are one household—why measure and withhold?” The little demon, not knowing what good was, crowded around and divided his dry food. The Monkey-Wise One drew out his staff and struck once: one fellow was smashed into nothing; another was only grazed and, though injured, still groaned. When the old monster heard that groan, he reached out from the sedan to look. Sun Wukong had already leaped to the front. With one staff blow to the front he made a hole, and brain and blood spurted out in a rush. Dragged out of the sedan, it turned out to be a nine-tailed fox. The Master laughed, “Wayward beast! You called him Grandmother. If you call this one Grandmother, you should at least call old Sun his Great Ancestor, yes?”

“Good Monkey King,” he said, “bring out that shimmering golden rope and hide it in your sleeve.” He was delighted. “Even if that splashing demon has its own arts, from this moment the three treasures belong to the family of Sun.” He then plucked two hairs and turned them into Bāshān Tiger and Yǐhăi Dragon; he plucked two more and made two sedan-bearers. He then changed himself into the old grandmother, and sat in the sedan. Lifting it, he returned by the same road.

Before long they reached the entrance of Lotus Flower Cave. The little demons made from hairs were ahead, crying, “Open the gate! Open the gate!” The gate demon opened and asked, “Have Bāshān Tiger and Yǐhăi Dragon arrived?” One hair-demon replied, “They have.” “And where is the grandmother you invited?” The hair-demon pointed and said, “Isn’t it in that sedan?” The small demon said, “Wait. Let me enter first and report.” He reported: “Great king, the Grandmother has come.” At once the two demon lords ordered an incense table to be brought out for reception. Hearing this, Sun Wukong rejoiced inwardly: “Heaven has turned things—now it is my turn to be a proper person. Earlier I became a little demon and came to invite the old monster, and I made him take just one bow. This time I become him, as his mother, and I shall receive four bows in proper courtesy. Not elegant though, but at least I gain two heads of it.” The Great Sage dismounted from the sedan, shook his clothes, and drew the four hairs back onto himself. The gate demon carried the empty sedan inside. He then followed slowly and deliberately, with graceful, coquettish turns and little twists, acting exactly as the old demon did, and went straight in. Thereafter all small and great demons came kneeling to receive him. Drums, zithers, flutes and pipes sounded in full chorus; in the furnace hall a pale curl of incense smoke drifted up. He came into the main hall and sat facing south. The two demon-lords knelt on both knees, struck their heads to the floor, and cried, “Mother, your child bows in reverence.” The Great Sage said, “My son, rise.”

At that time Zhu Bajie, hanging from the beam, let out a loud laugh. Sha Wujing said, “Second brother, what a good laugh, even hanging upside down.” Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, there is a reason behind my laughter.” Sha Wujing asked, “What reason?” Zhu Bajie said, “We thought grandmother had come and that we were to steam her for a meal. It turns out it was not grandmother—it was an old joke.” Sha Wujing said, “What old joke?” Zhu Bajie laughed, “Bimawen has come.” Sha Wujing asked, “How did you know it was him?” Zhu Bajie said, “He bent his back and said, ‘My child, rise.’ Right behind him he lifted a monkey’s tail. My hanging is higher than yours, so I can see clearly.” Sha Wujing said, “Then keep quiet and just listen to what he says.” Zhu Bajie said, “Exactly, exactly.”

The Great Sage sat in the middle and asked, “My son, what is it you ask my presence for?” The demon-lord said, “Mother, for many days we have been unable to offer proper reverence and have not been filial enough. This morning my foolish brothers took in Tripitaka of the Central Kingdom, but dare not eat him; they invited Mother to come and taste him, so that you may steam him and prolong your life.” The Great Sage said, “My son, I do not eat Tripitaka. I have heard that one of Zhu Bajie’s ears is very fine. Have it cut off, cleaned and fixed, and I shall take it as a drink.” Zhu Bajie, hearing this, panicked and said, “Cursed wretch, you come to cut off my ear—calling this out would not sound good at all.”

Ah! Just for one candid word from that muddle-headed one, the whole play of the Great Sage’s transformations was blown away. Then several patrol demons, and all the gate demons, dashed in and reported, “Great king, disaster has come! Sun Wukong has slain Grandmother and has come in his own guise.” Hearing this, the old demon did not pause to speak. He drew out the Seven-Star Treasure Sword and swung it down to split the Great Sage from front to back. The Great Sage flicked his body aside once; instantly the whole cave was filled with red radiance, and he had already fled. Such was his method—truly a masterful trickster. As the old saying goes, when gathered he forms shape; when scattered he becomes spirit-vapor.

The old demon was so frightened that soul and spirit seemed to fly apart, while the horde of spirits gnawed at their fingers and shook their heads. The old demon said, “Brother, return Tripitaka, Sha Wujing, Zhu Bajie, the White Horse, and all our provisions to that Sun Wukong, and close the gate of contention.” The second demon said, “Older brother, what are you saying? Do you not know how much labor I expended to devise this plan and bring all those monks here? Now, if you are so daunted by Sun Wukong’s strange arts that you send him all of this back, people would call you one who fears a knife and avoids a sword—is that fitting for a man of strength? Sit and do not fear. I’ve heard that Sun Wukong has vast powers. Though I have met him once, we have not yet matched force. Bring my armor and robes; let me seek him for three bouts of fighting. If he cannot defeat me in three rounds, then Tripitaka still remains our meal. If in three rounds I cannot beat him, then to send Tripitaka back to him is no great delay.” The old demon said, “My worthy younger brother speaks rightly.” He ordered his armor and robes to be brought.

He wore a phoenix crown, flashing like winter’s snow, and over his body a suit of battle mail and bright-steeled plate. At his waist was a coiled python-dragon belt; his pale-leather boots folded like petals of plum-blossom. His face was like that of Guankou Huo Zhenjun; his form had no difference from Great Spirit Jiling. In his hand he bore the Seven-Star Treasure Sword; his fierce rage shot upward, terrible as a storm.

The Second Demon shouted, ‘Sun Wukong, return my treasures and come to my mother at once; I will let you go in peace to fetch the sutras with Tripitaka.’ The Great Sage could not hold back himself and cursed: ‘You wild monster, you have mistaken me for your own old grandfather. At once send back my Master, my younger brother in Dharma, the white horse, and our pack; and send me some travel money before I leave westward. If a single “no” escapes your teeth, I will wind a rope myself and go, so that your old-grandfather need not lay a hand on me.’

Heard this, the demon sprang upward on a cloud and leapt into the air, swinging his treasure sword to stab; Wukong drew out the Iron Staff and met him with a split-front clash. The two met in midair, and it was a great killing match:

When chess meets its match, a worthy general appears. In equal chess, stratagem cannot be hidden; in a worthy general, the arts of war are fully tested. The two divine generals met; it was like the tiger of Mount Nan and the dragon of the North Sea struggling. Where the dragon contended, scaled armor flashed with light; where the tiger fought, claws and fangs flew in chaos. Scaled armor flashed, shedding iron-like flakes. One turned and turned in a thousand evasive tricks; the other came and went with no slack at all. The Golden-Hooped Staff was only three finger-widths from the crown point; the Seven-Star Sword rushed toward his heart in a single leap. One’s imperial air chilled the Dipper and Ox; the other’s fury was as perilous as thunder and lightning. They fought for about thirty exchanges and no winner emerged.

Wukong thought to himself: ‘This wild demon can indeed withstand old Sun’s iron staff. I have already taken his three treasures, yet to brawl with him so hard may ruin my timing. Would it not be better to put him in the calabash or purified bottle and be done?’ He thought again: ‘No, no. There is a saying: possessions follow their owner. If I bid him refuse, would that not still spoil our work? Better use the Golden-hooped rope and bind his head.’ The Great Saint held his staff out with one hand to bar the demon’s treasure weapon; with the other he took up the rope and, with a sharp clack, looped it around the monster’s head.

That demon had both a Tightening Rope spell and a Loosening Rope spell. If he bound another, he chanted the Tightening Rope spell and it could not be loosened; if he bound one of his own, he chanted the Loosening Rope spell and harmed no one. Recognizing the ropes as his own, he instantly recited the loosening charm; the knot gave way and he slipped out, then turned to cast it at Wukong—but had already caught the Great Sage.

Wukong was about to use the Body-Thinning Art to free himself, and tried to slip out, but the demon had invoked the Tightening Rope spell and it clamped down hard. He was tightly bound below the neck by a golden ring. The monster gave the rope a yank, yanked it down, and chopped at his shiny head with seven or eight treasure swords. Not even a pink flush rose on Wukong’s scalp.

The demon said, ‘Monkey, your skull is so hard that I will not cut you. I will take you back and beat you later. Bring back those two treasures of mine first.’

Wukong said, ‘What treasures of yours did I take? You ask me to return?’

The demon searched him down to the last seam and pulled out both the calabash and the purified bottle. He kept the rope, pulled him to the cave, and said, ‘Elder brother, I have brought him.’

The Old Demon asked, ‘Brought who?’

The Second Demon said, ‘Sun Wukong. Come, take a look.’

At first sight, the Old Demon recognized him: ‘It is him, it is him. Bind him with that long rope to the pillar and make a plaything of him.’ He tied Wukong up, and the two demons went into the back hall to drink.

Wukong crawled under the base of the pillar and startled Baijie. The fool was hanging from the beam, laughing wildly: ‘Brother, my ears are done for.’

Wukong said, ‘Bajie, can you hang there all right? I am going out now and will surely save you all.’

Bajie replied, ‘Shameful, shameful. You yourself cannot get free, and yet you wish to rescue others. Enough—if we all die here, we can all ask the way in the Yama halls.’

Wukong said, ‘Do not speak nonsense. Watch: I will go out now.’

Bajie said, ‘See how you can go out.’

While Wukong spoke to Bajie, his eyes were on those two demons. Inside they were drinking; several little demons carried trays and cups, lifted jars of wine, and ran back and forth at both ends, so the watch was slightly loosened. Finding no one before him, he worked a spell: he brought out the staff, exhaled a breath of immortals’ air, and called, ‘Change!’

At once he became a steel rasp. He twisted the ring at his throat and with three or five strokes of the rasp split it in two. He opened the rasp’s mouth and got out.

He pulled out one hair and changed it into a decoy body, tying it there. His true body flickered once, became a little demon, and stood aside.

Bajie, still on the beam, cried out, ‘No good, no good—what is tied up is false, what hangs is the true body.’

The Old Demon set down his cup and asked, ‘What is that Pig Bajie shouting about?’

Wukong, already in the little-demon form, came forward: ‘Pig Bajie says that Sun Wukong instructed him to transform and slip away; he refused, so he is still shouting here.’

The Second Demon said, ‘I used to say Pig Bajie was honest; now it turns out he is this way too. He deserves to be beaten with twenty rods.’

Then the Great Sage moved up to take a cudgel to him. Bajie said, ‘Strike softly. If you strike too hard I will cry out and I will recognize you.’

Wukong said, ‘Old Sun’s transformations are only for the two of you, and yet you are the one who has let your nerve go cold? In this cave none of the demons can recognize him; why is it only you who does?’

Bajie said, ‘You may have changed your face and features, but you did not change your rear; are not there two red marks on that backside? That is how I recognize you.’

Wukong went toward the kitchen, took a handful from the pot bottom, rubbed both buttocks black, and returned to the front.

Bajie saw him and laughed, ‘Where did that monkey go and how long did he wander, that he now comes back with a black backside?’

Wukong still stood before the demon, intent on seizing his treasure. The ruffian had real wit.

He went into the hall, and with one pull at one of the demon’s legs said, ‘Great King, see how Sun Wukong is tied to the pillar, scrambling here and there, chafing away that golden rope. It would be best to bring down a thicker rope for him.’

The Old Demon said, ‘You are right,’ and immediately unfastened the lion-bound belt at his waist and handed it to Wukong.

Wukong took the belt and tied the false Wukong with it. He slipped the old rope into his sleeve.

He then pulled out one hair, breathed out celestial breath, and turned it into a fake Golden-hooped rope, and handed that to the demon with both hands.

That demon, drunk with wine and greedy, did not look closely, and simply took it. This was the Great Saint’s art: one hair changed into a Golden-hooped rope.

With that treasure now in hand he turned and leapt out through the gate, revealing his true form, and shouted, ‘Demon!’

The little demon at the gate asked, ‘Who are you, and why are you bawling here?’

Wukong said, ‘Go in at once and report to your outrageous demon: Wukong is here.’

The little demon did as told; the Old Demon cried out in astonishment, ‘You have taken Sun Wukong—then how has this Wukong come?’

The Second Demon said, ‘Brother, why fear him? I have both treasures in my hands. Let me take out the calabash and fetch him in.’

The Old Demon said, ‘Brother, be careful.’

The Second Demon took the calabash and walked out of the mountain gate. He suddenly saw someone who looked exactly like Wukong, only slightly shorter.

‘Who are you, and where do you come from?’ the demon asked.

Wukong said, ‘I am Sun Wukong’s brother. I heard you had seized my elder brother, and so I have come to seek this score with you.’

The demon said, ‘Yes, I took him and he is locked in the cave. Since you are here, there must be battle. I will not exchange troops with you, but I will call out to you first: do you answer me?’

Wukong replied, ‘Shout your ghost-name a thousand times and I will answer ten thousand.’

The demon seized the treasure, leapt into the air with his feet toward the sky and mouth to the ground, and shouted, ‘Zhe Xing Sun.’

Wukong did not answer. In his heart he thought, ‘If I answer, I will be swallowed at once.’

The demon called again, ‘Zhe Xing Sun.’

Wukong counted with his fingers under his breath and said, ‘My true name is Sun Wukong; the spirit-name I was given is Zhe Xing Sun. A true name can be taken on as guise, but a ghost-name cannot be faked so easily.’

Yet he could not restrain himself and answered once. In a rush he was sucked into the calabash and stuck fast like a postage patch.

The truth was that the treasure-spell cared little whether a name was true or false: it captures whoever answers with the right spirit.

When Wukong was in that calabash, he was utterly black. He tried to push his head upward, but it could not lift at all, and it was so tightly packed.

Suddenly he fretted in his heart: ‘When I was on the mountain I met those two little demons, and they told me: whether in calabash or purified bottle, once a person is put inside, in only a little while they turn to pus. Couldn’t they turn me so, too?’

Then, with single-minded thought, he told himself: ‘No matter—he cannot liquefy me. Five hundred years ago, old Sun ravaged Heaven, and the Sovereign was cast into the Eight Trigrams Furnace for forty-nine days, where he was tempered into a body of gold heart and liver, silver lungs and entrails, copper head and iron back, fire eyes and golden pupils. How could one and three moments dissolve me? I will go inside with him and see what he does.’

The Second Demon brought him inside and said, “Brother, it’s been fetched.” The Elder Demon asked, “Brought whom?” The Second Demon replied, “The wandering Sun who is Sun Wukong was what I put inside the gourd.” The Elder Demon, rejoicing, said, “Good younger brother, please sit. Do not move; only when it shakes and makes a sound should you lift the sealing sheet.”

When Sun Wukong heard this he said to himself, “With a body like mine, how can it shake and sound? Only if I transform into thin gruel-like liquid can it rattle. I will relieve myself first; when he hears it rattle, he will surely lift the seal, and I can escape in the air.” Then he thought again, “No, no. Though urine can make a sound, it will soil this plain robe. When he lifts it, I’ll just gather some saliva, spit and slosh until it sounds thick and noisy, trick him into opening, and old Wukong will leave again.” The Great Sage prepared himself, while the demon, drunken and fond of wine, would not shake.

Then Sun Wukong cast a spell, only intending to tease the demon into shaking; suddenly he cried out, “By Heaven! even my walking cane has all been dissolved.” The demon did not shake. Sun Wukong cried out again, “Oh my!” “Even my waist bones are transformed.” The Elder Demon said, “It is transformed to the waist and already all dissolved. Lift the seal and see for yourself.”

Hearing those words, Sun Wukong pulled out a single strand of hair and cried, “Transform!” becoming a half body at the bottom of the gourd. His true form became a tiny louse-larva and was pinned beside the mouth of the gourd. As soon as the two demons raised the seal-paper to look, the Great Sage had already flown away. He rolled once, then changed into an Yi-hai Dragon. The Yi-hai Dragon was the same little demon who had earlier gone to invite the old granny; now that one had shifted form and stood to one side.

The Elder Demon pried open the gourd mouth and spread the lid over it. Seeing a half body moving within, he still could not tell true from false, and hurriedly called, “Brother, cover it, cover it; it has not yet fully transformed.” The Second Demon likewise pressed it back on again. Sun Wukong, from the side, laughed to himself: “He doesn’t yet know that old Sun is already here.”

The Elder Demon took the flask, filled a full cup with wine, and stepped forward with both hands to give it to the Second Demon: “Dear younger brother, let me pass you a cup.” The Second Demon said, “Elder brother, we have already drunk for half a watch. Why give me another?” The Elder Demon said, “You have already captured Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing, and moreover Sun Wukong as well, disguised and packed in the gourd. For such service, you deserve several more cups from me.”

Seeing his elder’s sincerity, the Second Demon, out of respect, dared not refuse. But with one hand he held the gourd and did not dare to receive with the other; instead he handed the gourd to the Yi-hai Dragon and took the cup with both hands. Neither noticed the Yi-hai Dragon was actually Sun Wukong in disguise. See how he bore the gourd, serving with elaborate deference. The Elder Demon drank, and then too tried to send a cup back. The Elder said, “No need to return it; I’ll share one drink with you here.” The two only exchanged formal modesty and polite courtesy.

Carrying the gourd on his head, Sun Wukong fixed his eyes and watched them pass the cups from side to side. Seeing there was no suspicion at all, he slipped the gourd into his sleeve. He plucked one hair and made a fake gourd, exactly alike, and held it in his hand. The demon served a few more cups and, not distinguishing true from false, took up the precious vessel all at once with a firm hand. They all took their seats, sat at ease, and kept on drinking.

Sun Wukong slipped away quietly, got hold of the treasure, and in his heart rejoiced: “Even if this demon has his tricks, the gourd in the end is still one belonging to Sun.”

Still unknown is how it will be handled afterward—how they will save the Master and destroy the demon. Read on for the resolution in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 34: The Demon King’s subtle stratagems entrap the Mind-Monkey; the Great Sage shifts forms and steals the holy treasure.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

My true nature is wholly bright, and the Way opens by itself. Aching to master transformations is not easily done; forging long life is not for ordinary folk. Clear and turbid turn again and again by the tide of fate; open through measureless kalpas, letting east and west shift as they will. To wander carefree through myriads of ages there is no way to count; one point of divine light forever rests upon the void. This verse aligns with the subtle Dao of the Great Sage Sun Wukong. He had obtained that demon’s true treasure, tucked it into his sleeve, and joyfully said, “P’o Demon, you worked so hard to catch me; it is truly like trying to pull the moon from water. If old Sun wants to catch you, it is like playing with ice on fire.” He concealed the gourd, slipped out through the gate in quick little movements, revealed his true form, and shouted in a harsh voice, “Monster, open the gate!” A little demon called out, “Who are you, to come and shout like this?” The Wanderer said, “Report to your old P’o Demon quickly: it is Sun Wukong.”

A little demon rushed inside to report: “Great King, someone called a Wukong has come outside the gate.” The old demon was startled and said, “Brother, this is bad—we’ve stirred up a whole storm. The golden cord is still tying the Great Sage Sun, and the gourd contains him; how could there be another called Sun Wukong? It must be that several of his brothers have come.” The second demon said, “Elder brother, do not worry. My gourd can hold a thousand people; I only just put in that one called Sun. How could there be another Sun Wukong? Let me step out and see; I’ll swallow him in one go.” The old demon said, “Brother, be cautious.”

That second demon took up a fake gourd, looked again as before, broad and swelling with swagger, and walked out to the gate crying, “Who are you and where are you from that you dare shout here?” The Wanderer answered, “You don’t recognize me: I dwell at Flower-Fruit Mountain, my ancestral root is Water-curtain Cave. I only caused the uproar in Heavenly Court, and long since the contention has ended. Now I have escaped disaster and left the path to serve the monk. I carry the teaching up to Mount Leiyin, seeking the Classics and returning to awakened truth. I met the wild and violent demon, and yet I was forced to use my powers. Return the Tang monk to me; we go westward to the Buddha. Let both camps stop this war and keep to our own peace. Do not provoke old Sun Wukong into rage and wound your own life.” The demon said, “Come here. I will not fight you, but if I call your name once, can you answer?” The Wanderer laughed, “If you call me, I answer; if I call you, can you answer?” The demon replied, “If I call you, I have a precious gourd with which to hold people. If you call me, what do you have?” The Wanderer said, “I have a gourd too.” The demon said, “If so, take it out and let me see.” The Wanderer drew forth a gourd from his sleeve: “P’o Demon, look.” He flashed it once, then tucked it back into his sleeve, lest the demon come to seize it.

When the demon saw this he was greatly startled: “Where did this gourd come from? How can it be exactly like mine? Even if two gourds grow on one vine, their sizes and forms differ, one not the same as the other. How can they match so perfectly?” He then called sternly, “Sun Wukong, where did your gourd come from?” The Great Sage feigned ignorance and asked in turn, “Where is your gourd from?” Not seeing that it was a test, the demon answered straightforwardly: “My gourd came from the earliest age when chaos split in two, heaven opened and earth was cleared. There was a Supreme Ancestor called Taishang, who in the form of Nüwa remade the sky with stone and saved the Jambudvipa world. After filling the gap in heaven, he reached the foot of Kunlun and saw, below, a strand of immortal vine, on which hung this purple-gold-red gourd. It is the one Lord Lao left to this day.” The Great Sage, hearing this, replied lightly, “My gourd came from that same place too.” The demon lord said, “How do you know?” Sun Wukong replied, “From the first separation of purity and impurity, heaven unfilled in the northwest and earth unfilled in the southeast, the Taishang Dao Ancestor who repaired Nüwa’s heavenly breach passed the foot of Kunlun and found one vine bearing two gourds. I obtained a male one; yours is a female one.” The monster said, “No matter whether male or female, if it can hold people, it is a good treasure.” The Great Sage said, “You are right. I’ll let you swallow first.”

The monster was very pleased, sprang up at once and leapt into the air, grasping the gourd and calling, “Sun Wukong.” The Great Sage heard it and did not stop to catch breath, but answered back eight or nine times, yet he still could not be taken in. The demon came crashing down, stamping and punching his chest: “Ah! I used to say that worldly conditions never stay. With such a treasure, one still dares not frighten old master: when the female sees the male, it dares not hold him.” The Wanderer laughed, “Put it away and hold still. It is now old Sun’s turn to call you.” He sprang up in an armored-buckler leap, turned the gourd bottom upward and the mouth downward, fixed on the demon, and cried, “King of the Silver Horns.” The monster dared not keep silent; he answered once. Instantly he was swallowed inside; the Wanderer then attached a charm reading, “Tai Shang Laojun, urgent lawful command, with obedience,” to the mouth of the gourd. Inwardly he rejoiced: “My boy, today you are trying a fresh trick too.”

He then pressed down the cloud-crown and, carrying the gourd, kept thinking only to save the Master, moving again toward the Lotus Cave entrance. The mountain path was full of ruts and uneven ground, and he was walking with his legs folded awkwardly, turning this way and that. The gourd in his grasp rattled “khok-khok, soku-soku” without cease. Why did it sound so, you ask? The Great Sage’s body had been tempered by fire and could not be transformed on command; though the demon could ride cloud and mist, that was only in spell and technique. In essence he still bore ordinary mortal flesh, and inside the treasure he would soon be dissolved. But Wukong did not think him dissolved and laughed, “My child, how do I know whether you are urinating or just rinsing your mouth? This is the sort of business old Sun has done. I won’t even lift the lid to check until seven or eight days later and you turn to thin gruel. Why such haste? If it was easy for me to come out, it is best you stay hidden for a thousand days.” He held the gourd and kept speaking. Before he knew it, he had reached the cave mouth, shook the gourd, and once more it rang. He said, “This rattling is like the tube used for casting lots—good indeed for that. I will cast and see when the Master can leave the cave.” His hand kept shaking the gourd and his mouth kept reciting: “King Wen of the Zhou Yi, Sage Confucius, Master Taohua Nü, Master Guiguzi.”

A young demon inside the cave saw and said, “Great King, bad times: Wukong has put the Second Great King into the gourd and is casting lots with it.” When the old demon heard this, he was so frightened his spirit flew and his will left him; bones softened, marrow went numb. He stumbled and fell to the ground, crying out, “My respected brother! I left the upper realm with you, descended to mortal dust, hoping to share glory together and be lords of this cave forever. How did this monk of mine wound your life and sever our brotherly bond?” All the demons in the cave wept together in pain.

Zhu Bajie, hung from the beam, heard them cry all together and called out, “Monster, do not cry yet. Let old Pig speak first. The first one was Sun Wukong, the second was the other called Master Sun, and the last one, Sun Wukong again—those three repeated names all refer to one only, my senior monk-brother. He has seventy-two transformations. He flew in, stole your treasure, and put your younger brother inside. The younger brother is already dead. No need for such mourning. Quickly clean the hearth and stove, prepare fragrant mushrooms, mushrooms, tea buds, bamboo shoots, tofu, noodles, wood-ear, and vegetables. Send my master and disciples down and have him recite the Shòushēng Scripture to your younger brother.” The old demon heard this and his heart surged in fury: “You are right, I thought old Zhu Bajie was honest, but look how honest he is not! He makes mockery and plays jokes on me.” He ordered, “Small demon, stop grieving. Untie Zhu Bajie, steam him until he is soft, and when I am fed I will go take revenge on the Great Sage.” Sha Wujing reproved Bajie, “Now see—you talk too much. A tongue so loose first gets you steamed.” The idiot felt some fear. A little demon beside him said, “Great King, it is hard to steam Pigsy.” Zhu Bajie said, “Amitabha! Which elder brother has gathered merit enough for this? Truly he is hard to steam.” Another demon said, “Strip his skin off first, then he will steam well.” Bajie panicked and said, “Good to steam, good to steam. The skin and bones are rough and stout, but if the soup boils they will fall apart—hu hu.”

Just then, amid the uproar, a little demon outside the front gate reported, “Sun Wukong has come shouting again.” The old demon was startled once more and cried, “This brute thinks it no one but me.” He called, “You little ones, hang Zhu Bajie up as before and check what treasures remain.” The housekeeper demon said, “There are still three treasures in the cave.” The old demon asked, “Which three?” The housekeeper said, “There are still the Seven-Star Sword, the Banana Leaf Fan, and the Pure Bottle.” The old demon said, “The bottle is no use: it works only by calling people, and if someone answers it can swallow them. He even taught that spell to this Sun Wukong and had his own brother swallowed. No need for it—leave it at home. Bring the sword and fan at once.” The housekeeper immediately presented the two treasures. The old demon tucked the fan into the back neck of his robe, held the Seven-Star Sword in his hand, and signaled the gathered host of more than three hundred of the small and large demons to arm themselves with spears and clubs, gripping blades and swinging hooks. The old demon himself donned helmet and armor, draping over himself a silk robe burning bright red. The demons formed battle array to seize the Great Sage Sun Wukong.

The Great Sage Sun Wukong had already known that the two demons had transformed inside the gourd, yet he had tightly bound it shut and fastened it at his waist, holding the Golden-Hooped Staff and preparing to fight. He saw the old demon leap out through the gate, red banners flying. What a terrifying appearance:

On his head the helmet and plume flashed with blazing light; at his waist he wore a bright sash of rosy-cloud color. His body was clad in dragon-scale armor, covered by a red robe like fierce flames. His round eyes opened and flashed like lightning; steel whiskers rose, drifting like smoke. In one hand he lightly held the Seven-Star Sword; in the other a banana-fiber fan half-covered his shoulder. He moved like cloud-streams slipping from sea-peaks, and his voice was like thunder that shook mountains and rivers. In dreadful, awe-filled majesty he dared to defy Heaven, the demon-chief commanding his host of fiends out before the cave.

The old demon quickly ordered the lesser fiends to take formation and yelled, "Monkey, you are outrageously rude. You harmed my brothers, injured my men; this is truly hateful!" The Great Sage snapped back, "You death-seeking fiend! You cannot spare even one demon life. My Master, my junior kinsman, and even the four living creatures hanging uselessly in that cave—I cannot bear it in my heart. Why should I endure this? Quickly bring them out and return them to me, and add a good ransom, and in my good spirits you may leave old Sun to rise and go while I spare your old demon body." The monster did not allow him a word, raised the treasure sword and hacked straight at him at once. The Great Sage lifted his staff to receive him. The fighting outside the cave gate was brutal. Ah!

Golden-Hooped Staff and Seven-Star Sword clashed, and the rosy light flashed like lightning. Vast cold qi pressed in with terrifying force; dark rolling clouds blocked ridge and dam. One side held back by brotherly feeling for his men, this one delayed; this one, for the sake of the pilgrim Tripitaka, would not allow even the slightest delay. Each side kept old enmity, each heart full of brewing rage. It became such slaughter that sky and earth darkened, gods and spirits were startled; the sun grew faint through dense smoke, and dragon and tiger fought in a fiery gale. One ground his teeth as if biting jade pegs; the other flung angering eyes that sent out streaks of gold flame. Back and forth they displayed heroism, staff and sword ceaselessly circling.

The old demon and the Great Sage fought for twenty rounds, no victor in sight. The demon pointed to the tip of his sword and shouted, "Lesser demons, come at once." More than three hundred spirits surged forward and enclosed the Monk in the middle of the formation. The Great Sage showed no fear, brandished the staff, charging left, battering right, blocking rear and front in turn. The little fiends each had tricks: they pressed harder and closer, like fluff winding around a body, clinging to waists and pulling at legs, refusing to yield. The Great Sage, suddenly at a loss, used the outer-body technique. From under his left side he pulled out a handful of hairs, chewed them to pieces, spat them out, and cried, "Transform!" One by one they became copies of the Great Sage. Behold: some used the long body to wield the staff, some the short form to swing fists; even the smallest had nowhere to find a place to strike. He banged the little demons about until they were scattered like stars through broken cloud, and together they cried, "Great King, this cannot be made right—oh impossible! The ground and the mountains are full of Sun Wukong!" By this outer-body art he drove back the swarming fiends, forcing the old demon into the middle of his own encirclement; the old demon then ran east and west with no road to escape.

The old demon, now in panic, held the treasure sword in his left hand, reached behind his neck with his right, and drew out the banana-fiber fan. Aiming toward the southeast at the Bing-Ding fire, straight at the Li Palace, he whipped the fan once with a rush. At once fire blazed from the ground. It turned out this jewel-like treasure could summon flames out of nothing. The monster, utterly merciless, swept out the fan seven or eight times in succession. Sky seemed to burn, earth blazed, wild fire flew high. This fire:

It is not heavenly fire, not forge fire, not fire on a mountain-top, not hearth fire; it is a spark of living light drawn naturally from the Five Elements. This fan is not a common object of the mortal world, nor a product of human making; it is a true treasure formed since Chaos was first opened. With this fan, stirring this fire, it blazes and flares like a bolt of crimson silk in lightning; it glows and gleams as if red clouds were flying on scarlet satin. Not a single strand of blue smoke appears: all the mountain is filled with red flame. It burns the pines on the ridge into trees of fire, and turns the firs before the cliff into lanterns. Beasts in their dens, clinging desperately to life, crash east and west; birds of the forest, fearing for their feathers, fly high and far. This divine fire drifted through the air and burned on, charring stone and drying streams; red lay over all the earth.

The Great Sage saw this wicked fire and, though usually fearless, he trembled and said, "This is bad. My own body cannot endure; hairs are useless. If I fall into this fire, will I not be no better than hair easy to burn?" He shook his body and drew all his hairs back onto himself. He made one hair into a false form and fled, dodging the blaze. His true body, twisting the Fire-Evasion formula, sprang with a cloud-somersault and leapt away, leaving the fire and running straight for the Lotus Flower Cave, thinking to save his Master. He reached the gate in haste, let the cloud-head sink down, and saw outside the doorway more than a hundred little fiends, heads smashed, legs broken, flesh torn, skin split. All of them were those he had wounded by his body-multiplying technique. They stood crying out in pain. When the Great Sage saw them, he could not restrain his brutal, fierce nature. He raised the iron staff and beat his way in. Alas, all the fruit of hard discipline at taking human form had come to nothing: he remained naught but old skin and fur.

The Great Sage slew the little fiends and burst into the cave to free Master. He saw bright blazing firelight inside and, in alarm, flustered and fretted, "Enough, enough—if this fire is rising from the back gate, old Sun will never be able to save Master!" As he stood in terror and looked closely—ah!—it was not fire but a shaft of gold light. He came to himself, peered inside, and saw that it was the pure jade bottle radiating bright. Joy rose in his heart: "What a rare treasure! That bottle had been carried by that little fiend on the mountain and shone there. I got it, but that monster searched and took it back. Today it is hidden here, and of course it glows." Watch him take the bottle in secret; delighted, he did not even save Master. He hurried and bolted out of the cave. As soon as he came out, he saw the demon coming from the south with sword raised and fan in hand. The Great Sage could not avoid him; the old demon raised his sword and hacked at his head. Sun Wukong immediately leapt on a cloud-somersault and rose up, vanishing without trace; no further account is given.

When the demon reached the gate, he saw the ground covered with corpses—his own lieutenants among them. Panic-struck, he threw back his head and wept aloud, "Alas! Woe!" A verse remains:

Cursed is the ape’s unruliness, the horse-like rogue of base deceit, the holy essence misplaced, now cast down to mortal dust. Because I erred from thinking wrongly and left the heavenly court, I forgot my true form and fell to this mountain. A wild goose cut from its flock cries with longing; the demon troops are undone, the clan gone, tears streaming. When, at last, will the heap of sin be emptied, and the lock of transgression opened, to return to root and rise to the Imperial Gate?

The old demon, still ashamed and trembling, walked in crying at each step. He saw that all the vessels and fires were still there, but it was all silence, no human shape in sight; the grief was sharp and the desolation grew. He sat alone in the cave, collapsed upon the stone table, set the treasure sword resting askew on its edge, stuck the fan behind his shoulder, and dozed, dull and silent. Truly this matches the saying: when a man is met with glad news, his spirits brighten; when his heart is heavy and shut in, sleep overtakes him all the more.

Sun Wukong shifted his cloud-somersault and stood before the mountain, thinking of saving Master, fastening the pure bottle tightly at his waist, and came to scout at the cave entrance. He saw the two doors open and all was still, not a sound of movement. He stepped in very quietly and slipped within. There sat the demon, leaning against the stone table, snoring heavily. His banana-fiber fan had slipped from under his shoulder-cloth, half covering the back of his head; the Seven-Star Sword still leaned crooked at the table edge. Sun Wukong quietly advanced and lifted off the fan, and when he did, the monster started with a startled cry and ran out. It was because the fan handle had scraped his hair and roused him. Looking up, he saw Sun Wukong had stolen it; in haste he grabbed his sword and gave chase. The Great Sage had already jumped outside the gate, tied the fan at his waist, and with both hands swung open the iron staff to meet the demon. This was a fierce bout:

You have roused the violent demon king, anger rising over your brow; he cannot swallow the grievance whole, this rage will not release. The fiend cursed the ape: "You old rogue who toy with people, you hurt many of mine and still come to steal my treasure. This contest will not be allowed; now life and death is the only reckoning." The Great Sage roared at the fiend: "You have no manners. My disciple challenges Old Sun—can piles of eggs break stone?" Sword to the fore, staff to the side, neither side showed any trace of mercy. Once and again they traded strike and counterstrike, testing winning and losing. Three turns, four returns, each displaying their arts. All this was for Tripitaka’s pilgrimage to seek Buddha atop Vulture Peak, and so iron met fire out of step, the Five Phases were disturbed and harmony broken. They flaunted splendor and displayed power, making stones leap and sand whirl. As the contest dragged on, the sun neared dusk, and the demon king’s strength failed, so he withdrew first.

The old demon fought with the Great Sage for three or four dozen exchanges. Evening was coming. Unable to withstand him, he was defeated and broke formation, then fled straight for Ya Long Cave in the southwest; no more is recorded.

The Great Sage, Sun Wukong, had only just landed from cloud-somersaulting height and burst into the Lotus-Flower Cave, pulling Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing out of it. The three were saved from peril and thanked Sun Wukong, yet immediately asked, "Where have the demons gone?" Sun Wukong said, "The two demons are still packed in the gourd; by now, they should already have transformed away. The Great Demon was defeated in one round of battle and has gone southwest to Ya Long Mountain. As for the little demons in this cave, Sun Wukong already killed half of them using his body-division technique; of those who returned wounded, he has finished them off as well. Only now have we come here to free you." Tripitaka could never thank him enough: "My disciple, it is all because of your hard labors." Sun Wukong laughed and said, "It truly was hard work. You three were only dangling along being pained while I, old Sun, had no time to settle anywhere, busier than a courier in a relay post, running in and out again and again without end. Only because I stole his treasures could I drive these demons away." Zhu Bajie said, "Brother, take out the gourd and let us see. It may be that the two demons have already transformed." Sun Wukong first unfastened the Pure-Water Bottle, then took out the Golden Rope and the Banana Fan, and then held the gourd in his hand: "Do not look, do not look. He once entered this old monk's body and, while Sun Wukong pretended to gargle, he was tricked into opening the lid, allowing Sun Wukong to escape. We must not lift the lid again, or he may make enough noise and get away." The Master and disciples were overjoyed, and searched the cave for rice flour and vegetables, kindled the stove, set up a simple vegetarian meal, and ate. After a full meal, they slept in the cave and passed a silent night. At daybreak they rose."

Yet the old demon at once marched to Ya Long Mountain. He gathered the female demons, great and small, and spoke of what had happened: his mother killed, his brotherhood guise broken, his demon ranks annihilated, and his treasures stolen. The female demons all cried together for a long while in grief, then said, "Stop lamenting so. I still have this Seven-Star Sword here. When your troop has joined at Ya Long Mountain, I will enlist outside kin, and we will certainly catch hold of Sun Wukong and avenge ourselves." He had barely finished speaking when a little demon from the gate announced, "Great King, your old uncle from behind the mountain has come with troops." On hearing this, the old demon quickly changed into mourning white linen and kowtowed in welcome. That uncle was in fact his mother’s younger brother, called Fox Aqi, Great King. He had heard the scouts report that his sister had been killed by Sun Wukong, who had transformed into the form of a sister and stolen his nephew’s treasures, and that he had been fighting at Pingding Mountain, so he brought more than two hundred demon soldiers from his own cave to join the battle. Thus he had first come here to inquire after the family. As soon as he entered and saw the old demon wearing mourning robes, both of them wept together. After long weeping, the old demon knelt and related the previous events. Fox Aqi grew furious at once, ordered him to change out of the mourning robes, seized his treasure sword, gathered the demonesses in one place, rose with wind and cloud, and headed straight toward the northeast.

The Great Sage then told Sha Wujing to prepare an early meal and then let them continue walking. They had just heard the sound of wind when they looked out the door and found a troop of demons coming from the southwest. Sun Wukong was greatly startled; he darted to his feet and hurriedly called to Zhu Bajie: "Brother, they have summoned reinforcements again." Tripitaka, hearing this, turned pale and said, "Disciple, how can we face this?" Sun Wukong laughed, "No need to worry, no need to worry. Bring all the treasures and give them to me." He tied the gourd and Pure-Water Bottle at his waist, tucked the Golden Rope into his sleeve, slotted the Banana Fan behind his shoulder, and raised the Golden-Hooped Staff in both hands. He told Sha Wujing to guard Master Tripitaka and remain seated firmly in the cave. He ordered Zhu Bajie to take up his Nine-Tusked Halberd and go out with him to meet the enemy.

The demon set out his battle formation. In the front stood Fox Aqi, Great King. He had a jade-faced long beard, brows like steel, ears like blades; he wore a helmet of refined gold and a coat of scale armor, and held a square-heaven halberd in his hand. He shouted, "You insolent, rash monkey! How dare you deceive people so? You stole my treasures, harmed my family, killed my demon soldiers, and yet dare to occupy this cave for so long. Run forward now and one by one hold out your throats and die, so that my sister’s grievance is avenged." Sun Wukong shouted back, "You pack of self-destructive brutes, you know nothing of Sun Wukong’s ways. Do not run—receive one blow from my staff." The demon sidestepped, dodging, and used his square-heaven halberd to meet him. On the mountain ridge the two went back and forth for three or four exchanges; the old demon’s power weakened, and he was beaten and retreated. Sun Wukong charged after him, but the old demon met him. They fought three more rounds. Then Fox Aqi circled back and attacked again. On this side, Zhu Bajie saw it and quickly drew the nine-toothed halberd to block him. One against one, they fought for a long time with no clear winner. The old demon shouted once, and all the demon soldiers closed in around them.

Tripitaka was still inside the Lotus-Flower Cave. Hearing the cries that shook the ground, he called, "Sha Wujing, go out and see how my elder brother is doing in battle." Sha Wujing immediately brought out the subduing staff, shouted, and charged out, beating back the host of demons. Seeing the tide turning against them, Fox Aqi turned and fled, but Zhu Bajie caught up with him and struck from behind with the halberd; nine bright-red wounds gushed forth. Alas, the fox’s true life-breath rushed out in haste. They dragged the body in quickly and tore off its clothing to inspect it; it turned out to be a fox spirit.

The old demon, seeing his old uncle wounded, dropped Sun Wukong from hold and raised the treasure sword to cleave at Zhu Bajie. Zhu Bajie braced with his halberd. While they were in mid-combat, Sha Wujing came close and lifted his staff to strike. Unable to withstand them, the demon rose with wind and cloud and fled south. Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing chased him hard. Sun Wukong saw this, sprang up into the air on cloud and, unfastening the Pure-Water Bottle, enveloped the old demon. He shouted, "Golden-Corner King." The old demon, thinking it was just one of his own surviving little spirits calling, turned and answered once. He was abruptly pulled inside, and Sun Wukong pasted on the summons tablet reading, "Taishang Laojun, by urgent command as by the law, as proclaimed." At once the Seven-Star Sword dropped into the dust and the treasure returned to Sun Wukong. Zhu Bajie asked, "Brother, you have taken the sword—where is the demon-spirit now?" Sun Wukong laughed, "There—it's sealed in this bottle as well." Sha Wujing was greatly pleased to hear it.

By then, having swept away all lurking evil, they returned to the cave and reported good news to Tripitaka: "The mountain is cleared, the demons are all gone. Please, Master, mount and continue the westward road." Tripitaka was overjoyed. After a morning meal, they packed up their baggage and mounts and hurried west to seek the road.

As they proceeded, a beggar suddenly flashed out from beside the road and came forward, seizing Tripitaka’s horse: "Monk, where are you going? Return my treasures." Zhu Bajie cried out in alarm, "Enough—this is the old demon come for the treasures." Sun Wukong looked carefully and saw that it was none other than Taishang Laojun. Flustered, he rushed forward and offered obeisance: "Your Excellency, where are you going?" The old master rose to his jade-seat throne and stood in the high heaven, calling out, "Sun Wukong, return my treasures." Sun Wukong rose into the air and said, "What treasures?" Laojun answered, "The gourd is mine for storing elixirs; the Pure-Water Bottle mine for holding water; the treasure sword mine for forging away demons; the fan mine for fanning fire; the rope mine from the strap of my robe. As for the two demons, one was the boy in charge of my Golden Crucible and one the boy in charge of my Silver Crucible. They stole my treasures, came down to the mortal world, and hid where none could find them. Yet it was you who have now captured them and earned good merit." Sun Wukong said, "You old official are truly impolite. Even if you shelter evil for your household, you should answer for your own lax oversight." Laojun replied, "It is none of my affair; do not wrongfully blame others. This bodhisattva—Guanyin—borrowed them from me three times and placed them here, entrusting him to use demons in order to test whether you disciples truly have heart to go west." As he spoke, Sun Wukong thought to himself, "This bodhisattva is so terribly remiss. At first she saved me and ordered me to protect Tripitaka on the road to the West; I told her the road is harsh and hard. She promised to come in person in dire danger, and now she has let evil sprites torment us instead. There is no point arguing with words; he deserves to go through a lifetime without a husband. If it were not for the old official’s own presence, I would not have handed them over. But since you say this, take them away."

Laojun took back the five treasures, opened the tops of the gourd and the Pure-Water Bottle, and poured out two streams of immortal vapour. With one finger he pointed, and they transformed back into a Golden Boy and a Silver Boy, one on each side. Then he saw ten thousand red-gold rays of divine light. Ah! > In faint, vast stillness they all returned together to the Dousui Court, and in freedom they rose straight up to Great Luo Heaven.

Still unknown is what happens next: how Great Sage Sun Wukong will continue to protect Tripitaka and when he will reach the West. This will be explained in the next chapter.
