Then Sun Wukong pressed the cloud down and told his master, in full, how the bodhisattva had borrowed the boy and how Lao Jun had taken the precious treasure away. Tripitaka thanked him again and again, with complete-hearted devotion, as if willing to give his life for the Western way. He climbed to the saddle, Zhu Bajie hoisted the baggage, Sha Wujing held the horse by the head, and Sun Wukong took up the iron staff, cut the road through the ridge, and marched straight down through the high mountains. One could never exhaust the hardships of riverbank nights and wind-breath meals: they pressed on through frost and dew.

After the pilgrims had gone on for some time, a mountain rose before them and blocked the way. Tripitaka called out from the saddle: “Disciples, look at that towering mountain mass; we must be very watchful, or another demon obstruction may assail us.” Wukong said, “Master, do not let your thoughts scatter. As long as you steady your intent and keep your spirit clear, nothing untoward will happen.” Tripitaka said, “My disciples, how hard is this road to the Western Heaven? From leaving Chang’an, I remember, after four or five years—spring came and ended, summer came, autumn went by, winter arrived—yet we still have not arrived.” Hearing this, Wukong laughed: “Too soon, too soon. We have not yet gone out the great gate.” Bajie said, “Brother, do not tell lies. Is there such a great gate in the human world?” Wukong said, “Brother, we are still inside the main hall circling around.” Sha Wujing said with a laugh, “Elder Brother, do not brag and frighten me with such words. If there were such a hall, there would still be nowhere to buy beams like these.” Wukong said, “Brother, if we count by my reckoning, this blue sky is the roof tile, the sun and moon are the window lattice, the Four Mountains and Five Peaks are the beams, and Heaven and Earth are like one open hall.” Bajie said, “Enough, enough. Let us just turn around for a while and go back.” Wukong said, “No need to talk wildly. Just keep following Wukong on the road.”

The Great Sage hoisted the iron staff sideways, fixed Tripitaka, broke open the mountain path, and went straight forward. The Master, riding and gazing afar, beheld a grand mountain scene indeed:

At the summit the peaks stood sheer and proud, and the treetops seemed to touch the cloud heights. In clotted green-blue smoke, now and again came the ape-cries from valley mouths; In chaotic emerald shade, one could hear cranes crying between the pines. Wind-whistling mountain fiends stood in the streams, teasing the woodcutters; Cunning foxes perched beside the cliffs, startling the hunters. Great mountain! See those eight-sided cliffs, all severe on all sides. Strange tall pines wound in spirals formed green canopies, and withered ancient trees hung down with tangled vines. Spring torrents leapt and poured, and the cold pierced through hair and flesh; At the peaks stood towering spires, while the clear wind shot through eyes and startled body and dream. At times one heard great-beast roars; at times mountain birds called. Sika deer, in herds, ran through brambles, darting back and forth; musk-deer made their bands to seek wild food, leaping ahead and behind. On the grass slopes one glance showed no passing travelers; entering deeper hollows, all around were jackals and wolves. It could not be a place where a Buddha patriarch practiced—only a realm of flying birds and roaming beasts.

The Master, trembling, rode deeper into this mountain with a sore heart and pulled back the horse, calling: “Wukong!

Since we made the Yizhi Mountain oath, King Wuliuxing sent us out of the city gate. On the road we met Sanlingzi; along the way he jangled the bell that urged the horse. Seeking slopes, turning ravines, we searched for jiegai; step by step over ridges and mountains, we bowed to Fuling. Safeguarded like bamboo rind all over, my body feels strained; when shall the fennel offer to court my worship?” Wukong heard this, then gave a cold laugh: “Master, do not let your thoughts cling. Do not worry, just calm yourself and move on; your attainment will come in time.” The companions wandered on through the mountain scene at ease; before they could notice it, the red wheel had already dropped to the west. Exactly thus: A ten-li long pavilion, no guest passes by; on ninefold heavens the stars appear. Boats on the eight rivers have all come into port; seven thousand prefectures and counties have shut their gates. Six palaces and five offices have returned their state officials; in the Four Seas and Three Rivers, the fishing-line is cast aside. On two tower tops, bells and drums sound; one bright full moon fills all heaven and earth.

At the horse’s height, the Master looked out for far as he rode and saw layered pavilion terraces in a mountain hollow, repeated palace halls one behind another. Tripitaka said, “My disciple, it is already late, and luckily there are pavilions not far away on that side. It must be a temple complex; we should stay there for one night and continue tomorrow.” Wukong said, “What you say is true. Do not hurry. Let me look carefully first.” The Great Sage leapt into the air and, with close inspection, it was indeed a mountain gate. He saw:

The brick walls were red-finished and earthen, with gold nails set on both gate doors. Layer upon layer of terraces and pavilions hid beside the ridge, and rank upon rank of palatial halls lay wrapped in the mountain. The Hall of Ten Thousand Buddhas faced the Tathagata Hall; the Morning-Sun Pavilion should correspond to the Great Hero Gate. A seven-story pagoda stood moored among clouds and mists; three Buddha forms shone with radiant splendor. The Wenshu Terrace stood opposite the monastery chamber; the Maitreya Hall stood near the Great Mercy hall. At the mountain tops one saw green light dancing, and at the Hall of Empty-Step, purple clouds rose. Pine passes and bamboo courts clung close in green; every abbot’s meditation hall was utterly clear. Elegant and hushed, they held music-offerings; every stream and roadway sounded with glad receptions. At the Chan chambers monks expounded; in the music rooms many instruments rang. From the Miagao platform, strange flowers fell; before the Dharma-pulpit, sacred leaves sprang up. Truly this was the land of the Three Jewels under woodland cover, a mountain embracing a Brahma king’s palace. Half the side was all flickering light of lamps and smoke; rows of incense formed a hazy vapor.

The Great Sage came down from his cloud and told Tripitaka, “Master, it truly is a temple. We may borrow it for the night. Let us go in.”

The Master dismounted and came straight to the outer gate. Wukong asked, “Master, what temple is this?” Tripitaka said, “Only now has my horse’s hoof really come to rest; my toes have not even left the stirrup, and you ask what temple this is. How little discernment you have.” Wukong said, “You have been a monk since childhood, and must once have lectured on the classics. You just preached the Dharma not long ago, your grasp of doctrine is complete, and then by Tang King’s favor you came. How can you not recognize those great characters hanging on the gate?” The Master retorted, “You unruly monkey! Your words are ignorant. I was just spurring the horse westward and the sunlight was glaring; though there are letters on the gate, dust and grime had dimmed them, so I could not see.” Wukong, hearing this, bent his waist and rose two chi and more, then with his hand wiped away the dust: “Please see.” On it were five large characters: "Diarchi Bao Lin Temple." Wukong folded away his Dharma body and said, “Master, who in this temple may receive us for lodging?” Tripitaka said, “I will go in. Your faces are ugly, your speech rough, your nature hard and proud; if you should clash with the monks here, they may not allow lodging, and that would not be good.” Wukong said, “In that case, please, Master, go in. Do not speak further.”

The Master dropped his robe, unfastened his cloak, adjusted his clothing, and folded his hands as he walked straight into the mountain gate. Within the red-lacquered railings sat two golden-armored figures, statues arranged with fearsome and ugly presence:

One had an iron face and steel beard, seeming as if truly alive; one had a bristled brow and round eyes, bright as crystal. To the left, the knotted fist stood out like raw iron; to the right, the broad palm rose like red copper. Gold scales of linked armor glinted fiercely, and bright helmets and embroidered belts flashed in the wind. To the west there was truly much worship offered to Buddha, and in the stone cauldron the incense fire burned red.

When Tripitaka saw them, he nodded and sighed deeply: “In my Eastern lands, if there were people who molded such great bodhisattvas from clay and burned incense to worship them, my disciples might not have gone to the Western Heaven at all.” Even as he was sighing, he had reached the second gate. There were images of the Four Heavenly Kings: Chiguo, Duo Wen, Zengchang, and Guangmu, arranged in meanings of wind, direction, rain, and order across the corners. After entering the second gate, he saw four tall cypresses; each was thick with a luxuriant green canopy like an umbrella. Raising his head, he saw the Great Hero Hall. The Master joined his palms in refuge and knelt in prostration. Rising, he stepped around the Buddha altar and came beneath the rear gate. He then saw an image of Guanyin seated upside down, universally saving all in the South Sea. On that wall all the well-voiced craftsmen had sculpted shrimp, fish, crabs, and turtles, with heads and tails protruding, leaping in waves like sea play. The Master nodded a few times and sighed, saying with a thousand pangs: “How pitiful! All scaled-beings bow to Buddha; why are human beings not willing to practice?”

While he was praising, a Daoist stepped out from within the third gate. Seeing Tripitaka’s rare appearance and exceptional countenance, he hurried forward, offered obeisance, and asked, “Master, where do you come from?” Tripitaka said, “My disciple has been sent under the seal of the Great Tang in the Eastern Capital to go west to pay Buddha and seek sutras. We have arrived at Baofang now, and evening is near; we ask to stay one night.” The Daoist said, “Master, do not be offended. I am not the head here. I am but the one who sweeps, rings the bell, and labors in the service. Inside there is still a steward, a master monk. I shall go in and report to him. If he allows you to stay, then I will come out and receive you; if he does not, I dare not delay you here.” Tripitaka said, “You have been put to trouble enough."

The Daoist hurried into the abbey hall and reported, “My lord, there is a man outside.” The monk-officer immediately rose, changed his clothes, pressed his Pilu cap into place, threw on his robe, and hurriedly opened the gate to receive him, asking the Daoist, “Where has he come from?” The Daoist pointed with his hand: “Is there not a man back behind the main hall?” Tripitaka had only his head uncovered, wore a robe of twenty-five dharma folds, and had on his feet a pair of muddy, water-dragging sandals, leaning askew at the back gate. Seeing this, the monk-officer grew furious. “Daoist, make less of your noise! Do you not know I am the monk-officer? I only come out to receive those from the city who arrive with incense. For a monk like this, why did you report him to me as if he were genuine? By the look on his face, he is no honest man, more one of those wandering monks of the roads. This late it is likely that he wants to borrow lodging. In our hall there is no place for such disturbance. Tell him to squat down under the front corridor—why come reporting him to me?” He turned away from the matter.

When the Elder heard, tears filled his eyes as he said, “Alas, alas! This is the disgrace of a man far from his homeland. My disciple left home as a child and took the monk’s robes, and never once did he attend a repentance rite with evil intent toward flesh, nor let anger over scripture-reading ruin his meditative mind; nor did he ever throw tiles or bricks and injure a Buddha hall, scraping the true gold from Arhat faces. Ah, alas! Who knows what offense in a former life has wounded heaven and earth, making me in this life always meet wicked men. “Monk, if you do not wish to lodge us, fine—do not. But why then speak this lazy, shameless thing and tell us to crouch under the front corridor? It would have been better not to tell me at all; if you told the monk Wukong, in he comes and with one iron staff stroke he will break your props and canes apart. The Elder said, “Enough, enough. As people say: ‘Ritual and courtesy take precedence.’ Let me go in and ask him once and see what he means.”

The Master followed his footsteps and entered the Dharma hall with him. The monk-officer had taken off his outer robe and sat there breathing hard. Whether he was chanting sutras or writing rites for a household, he seemed occupied; on the table and desk were a pile of slips and papers. Tripitaka did not dare to go further in and so stood in the courtyard, bowing low, calling out, “Abbot, my disciple gives his respects.” The monk-officer, somewhat impatient at his intent to step inside, half answered and half withheld, then returned a courtesy: “From where do you come?” Tripitaka said, “Your disciple is sent from Great Tang in obedience to the Son of Heaven, to go west to the Buddha World and beg the living Buddha for the scriptures. Passing through Baofang, it is late; please let us borrow one night’s lodging. We will leave before we offend the dawn. I beg the abbot to show favor.” The monk-officer rose slightly and asked, “Are you that Tang Sanzang?” Tripitaka replied, “I dare not claim more, but I am that disciple.” The monk-officer said, “If you have gone west for the scriptures, how is it you still do not know the road?” Tripitaka answered, “My disciple has never walked the route of the worthy.” He said, “If you go straight west, it is only four or five li away. There is a thirty-li inn there, a household selling rice with room for easy lodging. This place is not suitable. I cannot keep you here. Please stay elsewhere.” Tripitaka folded his hands. “Abbot, the ancients said: ‘Monasteries and temples are all inns for us monks; at the sight of a monastery gate, each gives three measures of rice.’ Why do you not keep me then? What reason is this?” The monk-officer shouted in anger, “You drifting monk, you speak with oiled tongue and oiled lips.” Tripitaka asked, “What do you mean by oiled tongue and lips?” The monk-officer said, “The ancients said: ‘A tiger enters the city and every house shuts its doors. Though he may not bite, by now his name is already spoiled.’” Tripitaka asked, “How can he be ‘spoiled by name’ if he has not bitten?” He said, “These past years some wandering monks came and sat down at the mountain gate. I saw how poor they were: torn robes, broken sandals, bald heads, bare feet; I pitied their tattered state and hastened to invite them into the hall, seated them, gave them alms meals, lent each old robe, and let them stay a few days. Who knew they were fond of free ease in food and bedding, so thought no thought of leaving, staying for seven or eight years. Staying might be one thing; yet they did many unjust deeds.” Tripitaka asked, “What unjust deeds?” The monk-officer said, “Listen to what I have to tell you:

In idle hours he hurls tiles along the wall, and when he grows bored he pries nails from the wall. In cold weather he leans fire toward the window lattice; in summer he drags the doors across the path. He tears banner cloth into leg straps and steals incense, swapping it for turnips. He often tips oil from crystal vessels and steals bowls and pots to win at gambling. Tripitaka thought to himself, “Alas! Is my disciple truly such a boneless monk?” He wished to weep, but fearing the old monks of the monastery would laugh at him, he quietly drew his sleeve and wiped his tears, swallowed his anger, and quickly went out to meet the three disciples. The Great Sage saw anger on the Master’s face and asked, “Master, did the monks here beat you?” Tripitaka said, “They did not beat me.” Zhu Bajie said, “They surely did. If not, why this sobbing tone?” Sun Wukong said, “Did they scold you?” Tripitaka said, “Not scolded me either.” Wukong said, “If not beaten and not scolded, why such distress? You are homesick, then?” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, this place is not convenient.” Wukong laughed, “Is this place of Daoists, then?” Tripitaka answered sharply, “There are only Daoists in the shrine; in a temple are only monks.” Wukong said, “You are helpless. Yet monks are, after all, like us. As people say: ‘Where one is in the Buddha assembly, there are all connected by destiny.’ Sit, and let me go in and see.”

The Great Sage, setting his golden hoop more firmly upon his head and tying up his waist cloth, took up the iron staff and went straight to the Great Hero Hall, pointing at the three Buddha images. He spoke: “You are merely clay figures with gilded bodies and hollow gold within; where is your sensitivity inside? I, Sun Wukong, escorting Tripitaka, the Holy Monk of Great Tang, am going west to bow to Buddha and seek the true scriptures. Tonight we have come here to lodge; report our names at once. If you do not keep us, then with one single staff-blow I will smash your gilt bodies and make you return to your native shape of mud.”

The Great Sage was still in front, raging and ranting and swinging his staff recklessly, when he saw a Daoist burning evening incense who had set several sticks in the brazier before Buddha. At Sun Wukong’s cry, the man started, staggered, and fell. He rose, saw his face again, and fell once more. Frightened, trembling and stumbling, he ran inside to the monk-official and reported, “My lord, a monk has come from outside.” The monk-officer said, “You Daoists all, be less noisy! You told him once to squat under the front corridor and now you report this again? Say that once more and I’ll strike twenty!” The Daoist said, “My lord, this monk is different from that one: fierce and unruly, without a backbone.” The monk-officer asked, “What sort of face?” The Daoist said, “Round eyes, slanting ears, face full of hair, and a thunder-mouth. He grips a staff in his hand, bares his teeth and, hard as iron, seems set on finding someone to beat.” The monk-officer said, “I will go out and see him.”

He opened the gate at once and saw Wukong bursting in. Truly he was ugly beyond measure: seven-bent and eight-high, a face twisted and lopsided, two yellow eyes, one swollen brow, and fangs jutting outward. He looked like some crab-like sort, flesh within and bones outside. Frightened, the old monk shut the hall gate. Wukong arrived at once, knocked down and split the gate leaves, and said, “At once clean one thousand pure rooms; old Sun will sleep.” The monk-officer, hiding in the room, said to the Daoist, “Can this be simply his ugly face? It is all that he has bragged into this kind of face, saying these wild words. Here my monastery has at most not even three hundred rooms—the monks’ quarters, Buddha hall, bell and drum tower, both corridors together. Yet he demands one thousand rooms to sleep in. From where did that come?” The Daoist said, “Master, I am frightened myself from fear. How can you answer him?” The monk-officer, in high, ragged voice, called out, “Monk, you are asking lodging. This poor wild hill is not convenient; I cannot dare to host you. Go elsewhere and find the night’s lodging.”

Sun Wukong made his staff thick as a basin and stood it upright in the courtyard against the wall, then said, “Monk, if this place is inconvenient, then carry your things out.” The monk-officer said, “The temple I have lived in since childhood was handed down from my ancestors to my teacher, from my teacher to my generation; it must be passed on to descendants far away. He does not know what affair brings him here. With his reckless and disorderly manner, he is telling us to move out.” The Daoist said, “My lord, it is very awkward, but to move out would still be fine; yet this is a place where even a single club-bearing one barges in through the gate.” The monk-officer said, “Do not make such speech. We have four or five hundred monks, young and old. Where should we move to? If we moved out, there would be nowhere for us to stay.” Hearing this, Wukong said, “No place to move—then call out one to test a staff blow.” The old monk called to the Daoist, “You, go outside and test a staff with me.” The Daoist, alarmed, said, “Sir! How can I go out and swing against one with such a great cudgel?” The monk-officer said, “‘To train an army for a thousand days is to use it in one dawn.’ Why do you not go out?” The Daoist said, “That staff, no need say swinging it to strike: if it falls, it will also crush me into paste.” The monk-officer said, “Do not speak only of crushing. It now stands upright in the courtyard; at nightfall while one walks, one might forget and strike a great pit in one’s head.” The Daoist said, “Master, now that you know how heavy this is, why still ask me to go out and fight what sort of staff?” He began to stir and bawl inside the hall.

The Walker heard and said, 'It cannot be prevented. If I were to strike once and kill a man with my staff, my Master, Tripitaka, would later accuse me of doing violence. Wait here while I find something else to strike you with and let you try it on.' He then lifted his head and saw a stone lion outside the abbot’s hall. He raised the staff, brought it down with a hard ping, and smashed it into a spray of powdery fragments. The monk watching from the window saw this, and from fright his bones turned to wax and cotton; in haste he crawled beneath the bed. The Daoist wriggled through the stove-door and kept crying, 'Grandpa, the staff is heavy, the staff is heavy, I cannot hold it back, spare me, spare me!' The Walker said, 'Monk, I am not going to beat you. Tell me: how many monks are in this temple?' Shivering, the monk-official answered, 'From front to back there are two hundred and eighty-five cells, with five hundred monks holding ordained certificates.' The Walker said, 'You go quickly and call all five hundred monks, in strict neat order, put on your long robes and go out to fetch my Master of Tang, then I will not beat you.' The monk-official said, 'Grandpa, if you do not strike, we will lift you in at once.' The Walker said, 'Go at once.' The monk-official called to the Daoist: 'Do not say you are so frightened that your courage breaks; if your heart is broken with fear, still come and call these men, and bring Lord Tripitaka here.'

That Daoist had no recourse. He gave over his life’s nerve, dared not strike the gate, and crawled out through the rear dog-hole, running straight to the main hall. He beat the drum to the east and struck the bell in the west. When the drum and bell rang together, the monks from both corridors, all big and small, were startled and came to the hall asking, 'It is still not very late; why ring the bell and drum?' The Daoist said, 'Change into proper robes at once. In rank with the teacher, go out past the mountain gate and receive the honored lord from the Tang dynasty.' Then all the monks truly assembled in neat order and stood in files to greet them. Some put on kasayas, some wore crosswise jackets, some were clothed in a plain bell-shaped coat; many were so poor that, lacking long robes, they simply pulled up two waist-sheets and draped them over themselves. The Walker saw this and said, 'Monk, what kind of garment is that?' The monk, seeing him grim and ugly, said, 'Grandpa, do not strike—let me explain. This is cloth made by our city folk; there is no tailor here, it is a rough homemade wrap from our poor lot.'

The Walker, hearing him, smiled inwardly and, with the monks under guard, went out beyond the gate and knelt. The monk-official knelt and called out loudly, 'Great Master Tang, please sit in the abbot’s quarters.' Zhu Bajie saw this and said, 'When you came in, Master, you were in no condition—eyes all watery, and oil hanging from your mouth. How could big brother have such wild wisdom as to bid them kneel and bow as a welcome?' Tripitaka said, 'You fool, you know no courtesy. It is said even ghosts fear wicked men.' Seeing their prostrations and bows, Tripitaka was displeased; he stepped forward and called, 'Please rise, all of you.' The monks knelt and said, 'If the lord were to tell your disciples a word of easing and keep the staff from moving, we would kneel for a full month.' Tripitaka said, 'Wukong, do not strike them.' The Walker replied, 'I have not struck. If I had, my staff would already be broken through the middle by now.' Only then did those monks rise. Those who handled the horses handled them, those who bore the poles bore them, lifted Tripitaka on high, carried Zhu Bajie, pulled Sha Wujing, and all together went into the mountain gate, then to the abbot’s rear chamber, and sat in order.'

The monks again performed the kowtow. Tripitaka said, 'Abbot, please rise; no need for formal ceremony. Though we are poor monks, I and you are both disciples in the Buddha’s way.' The monk-official said, 'Great Lord, you are the imperial envoy from the Central Kingdom; these young monks failed in the welcome. Now here in this wild mountain, common folk’s eyes do not know the proper observances, and by coincidence you met with him. Are you to tell us whether on the road you eat vegetarian food or meat, so we can prepare a meal?' Tripitaka said, 'Vegetarian.' The monk-official said, 'Disciple, this lord likes meat well.' The Walker said, 'We eat vegetarian too; all of us are of pure vegetarian making.' The monk said, 'Grandpa! Even such a fierce man eats vegetarian?' A brave monk stepped forward and asked again, 'Since this lord eats vegetarian, how much rice should be cooked to be enough?' Zhu Bajie said, 'Little temple monk, what kind of question is that? A single stone of rice cooked in one household is enough.' The monks all panicked and hurried to scrub pots and hearths, arranging tea and rice in every hall. They raised bright lamps, moved out tables and benches, and prepared a reception for Tripitaka.'

After the Master and disciples had finished the evening meal, the monks cleared the hearth. Tripitaka thanked them, saying, 'Elder abbot, forgive the disturbance to your treasure mountain.' The monk-official said, 'Please do not. I beg your pardon, pardon me, pardon me.' Tripitaka said, 'Where shall my disciples and I rest here?' The monk-official said, 'Master, do not rush. The young monks can make arrangements.' He called, 'Daoist, how many people in that wing can obey commands?' The Daoist said, 'Master, there are.' The monk-official ordered, 'You two go arrange fodder and bring it to feed Lord Tang’s horse. Send a few to the front to clean the three meditation halls, make them spotless, lay the bed-curtains, and hasten, please ask the lord to rest.'

The Daoists heard the order and made all things orderly and ready, then came to invite Lord Tripitaka to sleep. The disciples then, leading horse and poles, went out from the abbot’s hall directly to the entrance of the meditation hall and looked in. Inside, light burned bright; between the two sides were laid four cane-framed cots. When the Walker saw this, he called the Daoist in charge of straw-bedding and had him bring it in and place it in the hall, tied up the white horse, and sent the Daoists all out. Tripitaka sat in the middle. Beneath the lamp, five hundred monks stood in two lines, waiting and attending, not daring to leave. The monk-official came forward and told the crowd, 'Only after escorting and settling the lord should you return.' Tripitaka said, 'This is enough for settling; all of you may now go back.' Only then did they dare to depart.

Tripitaka stepped out of his door for a short bodily visit to the chamber, and when he stepped outside he saw the bright moon hanging in the sky. He called, “Disciples.” Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing all came out to stand in attendance. Feeling the moon’s pure, clear light and the deep brilliance of the jade heavens, he thought, “it is truly a single lantern high above, bright enough to lay the whole earth bare.” In homesick silence, he turned to the moon and spontaneously recited a long old-style verse. He said:

The white-moon disk hangs in mid-sky, a hanging treasure-mirror bright, mountains and rivers shiver in its shadow-reflection, complete in every part. A jade palaces and moonlit towers fill with clean radiance, an ice-lens, a silver tray, with crisp, circling light. Ten thousand li are all this one pure brilliance tonight; in all the year, this is the clearest and brightest. Whole it seems a frost-cake torn from the Blue Sea, yet it appears an ice-wheel set in the verdant sky. In the lone guest-chamber, at a cold window, the lonely traveler sits stifled, in hillside hamlets and wild roadside inns, old men sleep through the cold. Reaching the Han Court Garden, I startle at autumn-white temples, only at Qin Hall’s tower does evening hasten. Yuliang’s verse is carried in the Jin annals, and Yuan Hong cannot sleep, afloat upon a river boat. The reflected light lies weak upon the cup’s surface, cold and without force; it shines clear in the courtyard and the robust immortals seem awake. Everywhere the window pavilions sing of white snow, in every yard and court men of ice-strings tune their chords. I sit in stillness on this mountain temple to sport with this moon; when shall we all be together again, returning to our old homeland?

Hearing him speak, Sun Wukong stepped closer and replied: “Master, you notice only the moon’s beauty, and your heart clings to the old home, but you do not understand what the Moon itself means. It is the rule of pre-celestial signs and measures. On the thirtieth day of the lunar month, the yang qi of the sun-spirit is all exhausted, while yin qi of the moon-spirit fills the wheel, so it is utterly dark and without light, which is called the New Moon. At this point it joins with the sun; between the two days of dark and dawn, it receives sunlight and becomes pregnant. By the third day, one yang appears; by the eighth day, two yang energies arise; in the spirit of the orb, yang and yin are half each, and this evenness is called the Upper Crescent. By the fifteenth day there are three yang complete, therefore it is full, called the Full Moon. On the sixteenth day one yin arises, and on the twenty-second day two yin arise; then yin and yang in the disk are half and half, therefore level as a string, called the Lower Crescent. On the thirtieth day three yin are complete; again it is the New Moon. This is the sense of primordial refinement. If we can nurse the two and eight and perfect the nine-by-nine work, at that season it will be easy to behold Buddha and easy also to return to the old fields. The verse is:

Before first crescent and after the latter crescent, the medicine-flavor stays even and the atmospheric signs are whole. If it is gathered and carried back to the furnace to be refined, mind set with resolve, the fruit of practice truly reaches the Western Heaven.”

Hearing this, the abbot suddenly understood and saw through to the true teaching with perfect clarity. Joy filled him, and he thanked Sun Wukong with thanks.

Sha Wujing, standing nearby with a laugh, said: “What Brother Sun has said is valid, yet he spoke only that before the arc is yang and after it is yin, that within the shade half of yang remains and obtains the golden water. Yet he did not say:

Water and fire entangle each with each, each has its own affinity, all is by Mother Earth’s pairing and destined accord. Three lineages meet as one with no contention, water stays in the Yangtze; the moon abides in heaven.”

Hearing this, the Master also felt his fog of mind lifted. It was exactly thus:

One clear opening makes a thousand openings clear; to break through and speak of non-birth is already to be an immortal.

Zhu Bajie stepped forward and held the abbot’s sleeves: “Master, do not listen to this confusion and lose your sleep. As for this moon:

It is lacking and before long is whole again, like me, never born complete. If I eat, he says my belly is too big; when I lift a bowl he says it’s only because I have sticky saliva. He all has cleverness to cultivate his own blessings; I, being foolish and dull-witted, have only old debts of fate. I tell you, your scripture-taking still has all three realms’ karma to clear, tail wagging and head bobbing, rushing straight up to heaven.”

Tripitaka said, “Enough. My disciples have had a hard walk. Go lie down first. Let me take this scroll of scripture and recite it a little.”

Sun Wukong said, “You have missed the point. You left home young and became a monk. As a child those scriptures, were they not already not fully mastered? Yet you also accepted the imperial command of Tang the Great and go west to the Buddha for the true Great Vehicle canon. Your task is still unfinished; Buddha has not been seen; the scripture has not yet been obtained. Which very copy are you now reciting?”

Tripitaka replied, “Since leaving Chang’an, I have trudged at dawn and raced each day. The scriptures from childhood are surely gone stale in me. Now that I have a moment of leisure tonight, let me warm up and review them.”

Sun Wukong said, “If that is so, we shall go to sleep first.” The three disciples each lay down on separate rattan beds. The Master shut the Chan hall door, raised and stirred the silver censer, spread out the scripture text, and silently read and recited. Exactly then came:

At the head of the hall the first drum sounds, all households fall silent; on the wild riverbank, a fisherman’s boat extinguishes its fire.

In the end, it was still unknown how the abbot would leave the temple; listen to the next chapter for the full account.
chapters.title: Chapter 36: The Mind-Monkey faces all conditions aright; splitting open the side-gate, he sees the moonlit light.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Tripitaka sat in the dharma hall of Baolin Temple beneath the lamp, reciting for a while the Water-Attaining Repentance of the Liang Emperor and reading for a while the True Scripture of the Peacock. He sat on until the third watch of the night before at last bundling the scriptures in his satchel. Just as he was about to rise and go to sleep, he heard a rasping, clattering sound from beyond the gate and then the wind came in hard with scattered, hissing gusts. The elder feared the lamp might be blown out, and in haste covered it with his robe sleeve. Again the lamp wavered from bright to dim, and a little fear stirred in him. Yet sleep settled over him again, and he bent against the scripture stand and dozed. Though his eyes were closed in a hazy stupor, his mind remained clear. In his ears sounded a continuous ringing, while outside the window the cold wind whistled on. What a wind! Truly it was this:

Rustle-shedding, light and misty; drifting and drifting, wavering and swaying. Rustle-shedding, light and misty, fallen leaves drift down; drifting and swaying, they roll up floating clouds. All the stars in heaven were dimmed, and all over the ground the dust was flung about in disorder. One gust rough and fierce, one gust sudden and clear. In the clear gust the pine and bamboo chimed with pure tones; in the rough gust river and lake rolled into turbid waves. The wind made mountain birds unable to roost, their cries choked and broken; the sea fish leapt and splashed in frantic fitful bursts. Doors and windows of the eastern and western halls and pavilions came loose; the front and rear corridors of the building-house seemed to shudder with angry spirits and ghosts. In the Buddha hall, flower vases were blown down, and blue-glass vessels tumbled so the lights of wisdom flickered. The incense brazier tilted, incense ash burst apart; the candle stand was askew and the candle flames smoked. Canopies of banners and treasure parasols all shook apart; the bell-and-drum tower and platform quivered at the roots.

In that half-dreaming stupor, after the wind had raged past for a moment, he again heard a faint call from outside the dharma hall: “Master!” He lifted his head within the dream and looked out. At the doorway stood a man, all of him soaked through, tears in his eyes, crying only "Master!" The monk said, "Are you some fiend, monster, spirit-being, or evil demon, come at this late hour to mock me? I am not one of those creatures ruled by greed or lust. I am a monk, upright and open in daylight, sent by the Great Tang of the Eastern Capital to go to the Western Heaven to seek the Buddha’s scriptures. I have three disciples under me, all heroes who can subdue dragons and bind tigers, strong men who clear away monsters and demons. If he set eyes on you, he would shatter your limbs and reduce your bones to dust. That is only my great mercy and my expedient kindness. Leave at once and flee far; do not step onto my gate of cultivation." The man, leaning against the hall wall, said, "Master, I am no demon-child or wicked spirit, nor am I a monstrous deity." Tripitaka said, "If you are not of that sort, why do you come here in the dead of night?" The man said, "Master, look at me and see." The elder looked closely and fixed his sight. Ah! he saw:

He wore a crown that rose to pierce the sky, a belt of pale jade about his waist, and a robe of clay-yellow silk worked with leaping dragons and dancing phoenixes. On his feet were a pair of cloud-headed slippers, embroidered-mouthed, of the sorrowless pattern, and in his hand he held a white-jade tablet marked by the star of Leidouluo. His face resembled the Changsheng Emperor of Mount Tai, and his form resembled Lord Wenchang, opened to enlighten.

When Tripitaka saw him, he was greatly startled and changed color; he bent quickly and called out in a stern loud voice, "What ruler are you? Please sit." He hurriedly reached out to assist, but only grasped empty space. Returning, he sat down again, and when he looked once more it was still the same man. The elder asked, "Your Majesty, what kingdom and what emperor are you? Your realm must be unsettled, slanderers and tyrants in the court, and you have fled for your life to this hour. What is it you wish to tell me?" The man, with tears at the corners of his face, spoke of old matters and sorrow knotted his brows. He said, "Master, my home is directly to the west. It is only about forty li away. Beyond lies a city, that is where Xingji (the city of foundation) was first raised." Tripitaka asked, "What is it called?" The man replied, "Since you ask, I shall not hide it: this was the realm I founded in my time, and I renamed it the Kingdom of Wuji." Tripitaka asked, "Why then are you so terrified, and for what reason have you come hither?" He said, "Master, five years ago, from one terrible year onward, drought gripped this place. Even grass did not grow; the people all starved to death. It was grievous beyond telling." At this Tripitaka nodded and said with a slight smile, "Your Majesty, anciently it was said, 'When the ruler is upright, heaven and earth are in accord.' If you did not show compassion to your people and thus suffered the calamity of barrenness, then why did you leave the city walls? Open the granaries. Relieve the common people. Repent of your past failures. Restore righteousness and revive good governance. Release those who have been wronged by unlawful judgment. Then heaven and earth will be at peace, rain and wind will be in harmony." The man said, "In my state, the storehouses are empty, grain and money are exhausted. Civil and military officials have been suspended from stipend and salary, and even my own food is without meat. I imitated Yu the Great, and together with my people endured bitter hardship in shared suffering, bathing and fasting, day and night burning incense and praying. For three years this brought only dry rivers and empty wells. When we were truly at the brink, a True Practitioner arrived from Zhongnan Mountain, one who could call wind and summon rain, who could turn stones to gold. He first appeared before my civil and military ministers in turn, and then before me. I immediately invited him to mount the altar and pray. The response was immediate: at the crackling of his talisman, in an instant the rain came down in torrents. I had only hoped to have enough to wet three chi, but he said three years of drought could not be sufficiently moistened, and he sent down an extra two cun of rain. When I saw that this man of devotion thus did what was right, I bowed and made him my companion in eight courtly prostrations, calling him brother." Tripitaka said, "This is a thousandfold joy for Your Majesty." The man asked, "What joy can there be?" Tripitaka said, "If this True Practitioner truly has such powers, whenever rain is needed he can command rain, and whenever gold is needed he can turn stone into it. What else is lacking that drove you from your capital?" The man replied, "I dined and dwelt in that companionship with him for only two years. Again came a spring day when wild apricots and red plums were in bloom. Across households, gentry and commoners alike went out to view flowers, and everywhere ladies and gentlemen went to frolic in spring. At that time the civil and military officials returned to their offices, and the consorts withdrew to their inner courts. I walked hand in hand with that True Practitioner through the imperial garden. All of a sudden we came to the edge of the octagonal glass-and-glaze well. I do not know what object he tossed there, for in the well there flashed forth ten thousand shafts of gold light. He lured me to the well to see some treasure, then his heart turned violent in an instant. With a sudden thud he shoved me into the well, covered the mouth with a stone slab, heaped soil atop it, and moved a banana plant over the top. Alas! I have been dead for three years now, a wronged ghost who perished by falling into a well."

On hearing him declare himself a ghost, Tripitaka was so frightened that his muscles melted and his hair stood in terror. Helpless, he pressed on with questions: "Your Majesty, what you have said makes no sense at all. If you died three years ago, where are all the civil and military officers, and the three royal chambers, the empresses and court ladies? When the three palaces saw his body and came to worship the throne, why did they not search for you?" The man said, "Master, with all the powers he possesses, his skill is truly rare in this world. From the moment he harmed me, he changed his form in the garden and took my appearance, without the slightest difference. He has now occupied my entire realm and has secretly seized my kingdom. He has taken my civil and military officials, four hundred court ministers, and all my three palace empresses and six inner consorts." Tripitaka said, "Your Majesty, you are exceedingly timid." The man asked, "Timid?" Tripitaka replied, "Your Majesty, that fiend does have some divine arts and has taken your form to occupy your state. The ministers cannot recognize the deceit, and the concubines cannot tell the difference. Only you know clearly you are dead. Why do you not go to Yanwang in the Court of the Netherworld and lodge your complaint, laying forth your grievance?" The man said, "His arts are wide and great. The officials are intimate with him: the City-god of the capital forever drinks wine with him; the Sea Dragon Kings are all in his closeness; Lord Chiyuan of Dongyue is his good friend; the tenth generation King Yama is his foster brother. So in this matter, there is no avenue for my appeal."

Tripitaka said, "Your Majesty, since you have no power in the netherworld to accuse him, why have you come into my mortal world?" The man said, "Master, how could a ghost such as I dare to come to your gate? At this mountain gate stand the Dharma-protecting heavenly hosts, the Six Ding and Six Jia, the Jiedi of the Five Directions, the Four Duty Censors, and eighteen guardians of the teaching and the monasteries, all attending close with steeds and tack. Just now, one Breath-and-Walk-of-the-Night Spirit, by a single divine gust, brought me here. He told me that after three years of water calamity, your coming had ripened my plight, and so I should come to pay my respects to you. He said your foremost disciple is the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, foremost at beheading demons and subduing monsters. I have come here in earnest reverence, begging a thousand times that you send men into my kingdom to seize the demon and set right what is wrong. If I can in return return in full and offer recompense, I shall coil grass in my hair and carry a ring of humility in my arms to repay your grace." Tripitaka said, "Your Majesty, did you come to ask that my disciple go and remove that demon?" The man said, "Yes, exactly." Tripitaka said, "My disciples do not do every task well, but to quell monsters and capture demons is exactly what suits them. Yet, although you ask him to seize this monster, I fear that justice in law will be hard to carry through." The man said, "In what way is it hard?" Tripitaka said, "That monster has great and far-reaching powers; he can transform into your form exactly. Every civil and military minister speaks in accord and consents in their hearts; each concubine of the three palaces has sentiments in harmony and affection in accord. Even if my disciples have methods, they dare not lightly draw weapons. If they are seized by many officials and charged with violating a realm and destroying a kingdom, and if they are imprisoned as conspirators in a charge of treason on a grand scale, would that not be like bringing a tiger to paint and a crane to carve?" The man said, "There are still people in my court."

Tripitaka said, “Ah, ah—indeed. It must have been a crown prince of that generation, sent to garrison somewhere, is it not?” The man said, “Not so. In my own palace I have a crown prince, my own son, my rightful heir by birth.” Tripitaka said, “Then that heir must have been cast down by demons?” The man said, “No. He stays in the Hall of the Golden Luan, in the Five-Phenix Pavilion. At one time he debates books with scholars; at another he takes audience with the true practitioners. For three years he has been forbidden from entering the imperial city and is not allowed to meet the Empress Mother.” Tripitaka said, “Why is that?” The man said, “That is one device of the demons. They fear a mother and son meeting and speaking in idle conversation, whereupon some rumour might slip out. So he may never meet either. Then, they think, the prince will remain safe for all time.” Tripitaka said, “Your misfortune, as Heaven gave me mine, may indeed be akin. My father was once grievously wounded by a bandit on the water. My mother was taken by those water-bandits and after three months bore me. I fled and saved my life in the river, and by grace of the Golden Mountain Temple’s abbot was nurtured and made a man. In my youth I had neither father nor mother; this crown prince too has lost both parents. Truly, he is pitiable.”

Tripitaka asked, “Even if I have a crown prince in audience, how can I see him?” The man said, “How can you not see him?” Tripitaka said, “He is held in the grip of demons; even his birth mother cannot see him. I am only a monk—by what right could I seek him?” The man said, “Tomorrow at dawn he comes out.” Tripitaka asked, “For what purpose does he go out?” The man said, “On the morning audience, he will lead three thousand horse and men with hawks and hounds, leave the city, and hunt. Then you can certainly meet him. When he comes, tell him my words; he will believe.” Tripitaka said, “He is a flesh-and-blood prince, deceived by demons and kept in the hall. How would he ever call out his father-king as ‘Father’ and trust my words?” The man said, “If he still will not believe, I will leave him a token with you.” Tripitaka asked, “What token?” The man put down the golden-cased white jade gei he held and said, “This can be such a token.” Tripitaka said, “What is it?” The man said, “That true-follower who turned into my likeness earlier only lacked this treasure. He told the court at the palace that the reclusive Taoist who begged for rain had stolen this gei. From then on, for three years, this item has been missing. If the crown prince sees it, he will remember the person at once, and this old grudge must be avenged.” Tripitaka said, “Very well. Let me remain; have your disciples arrange things. Shall I wait here?” The man said, “I dare not wait. I will go and beg the Night-Walking God for one blast of divine wind, and have me sent into the inner court of the palace. In a dream I will tell my principal queen to reconcile mother and son, and ask that you and your disciples remain of one mind.” Tripitaka nodded in agreement: “Then go.”

The wronged spirit knelt and thanked him with a farewell, then walked ahead to see him out. Somehow he kicked and stumbled, clattering down with a jindou strike, and Tripitaka woke in alarm: it was all a dream. Startled, he looked at the dim lamp and cried out, “Disciples, disciples!” Zhu Bajie woke and said, “What is this ‘earth-god, earth-god’? When I was a decent man before, I only ate flesh and lived from day to day, enjoying strong fishy-smelling food. Yet you took the robe, set us to guard you, and now we are your servants: in daytime carrying packs and leading horses, at night lifting urine jars and attending your feet! You do not sleep morning or night, and still you call for your disciples—why?” Tripitaka said, “Disciples, I had just dozed against the table and had a strange dream.” Sun Wukong sprang up and said, “Master, dreams rise from one’s own thoughts. You have never yet climbed the mountain and already fear all manner of demons; you worry the road to the Western Capital of the Buddha is too distant to reach; you miss Chang’an and do not know when we may return. So your mind is crowded with longing, and so are your dreams. For this old Wukong, my heart is sincere only one matter: to see Buddha in the West. Not one dream touches me.” Tripitaka said, “Disciples, this dream was no homesick dream. When I had just closed my eyes, I saw a fierce wind pass by. Outside the meditation hall’s door stood a king as if newly crowned, saying he was the King of Wuji. His whole body was soaked with water, and his eyes were full of tears.” To this and so on, he recounted every part of the dream to Sun Wukong. Sun Wukong laughed and said, “No need to repeat it. He comes to entrust you in a dream; it is plainly a fiend in that place seizing the throne and plotting the realm. I shall go and test his truth. Such a demon-imp can set up his power anywhere and soon prosper at it.” Tripitaka said, “Disciples, he says this demon has tremendous powers.” Sun Wukong said, “Why should we fear its extent? Once Wukong arrives, he will have nowhere to run.” Tripitaka said, “I also remember I left behind a treasured token.” Zhu Bajie said, “Master, do not vex yourself; it was only a dream, and then why take it as true?” Sha Wujing said, “‘Do not believe only what seems upright; you must guard against what is not truly benevolent.’ Light the fire, open the gate, and let us see what it is.”

As Sun Wukong had said, he opened the gate, and together they looked. In the moonlit starlight they truly saw on the stair-terrace a golden-cased white jade gei. Zhu Bajie came close, lifted it up and said, “Brother, what is this object?” Sun Wukong said, “This is the treasure held in the king’s own hand, called a white-jade gei. Master, since this has appeared, the matter is real. Tomorrow, seizing the demon is all on Wukong’s body. But you have three fated burdens.” Zhu Bajie said, “Well, well, well. It was just a dream, and yet he told him. Those people there are not the sort to toy with others. He only says you have these three lowly fates, yes?” Tripitaka went back in and asked, “What three?” Sun Wukong said, “Tomorrow you must shoulder the vat, endure abuse, and meet the plague.” Zhu Bajie laughed, “One matter is hard enough—how can three be borne?” Tripitaka, a clever elder, asked, “My disciples, how is each explained?” Sun Wukong said, “No need for words. Let me first give you two things.”

“Good Sage,” he said, then pulled out one fine hair, exhaled a strip of immortal breath, and called, “Transform!” He became a red-gilt lacquer casket, placing the white-jade gei within it, and said, “Master, hold this object in your hands. At daybreak, put on the brocade kasaya and sit in the main hall reciting sutra. While I inspect his city. If it truly is a demon, kill him and win our merit here. If not, then do not court misfortune.” Tripitaka said, “Rightly said.” Sun Wukong said, “If the crown prince stays inside the city, all right. If, as the dream foretold, he comes out, I will surely bring him to meet you.” Tripitaka said, “If I meet him, how should I receive him?” Sun Wukong said, “When he comes, I will report first. Open the casket lid a little and let me become a two-inch monk inside it, and you hold me in your hand. When that prince enters this temple, he will surely bow to Buddha. Let him bow as much as he wishes and do not stir. Seeing you unmoving, he will certainly order you seized. Whether he beats you, binds you, or kills you, let him do so.” Tripitaka said, “Ah! His command is over the army. If he truly kills me, what then?” Sun Wukong said, “Do not fret. I am here. If it comes to that tight pass, I will naturally defend you. If he asks, tell him: I am an ordained monk from the Eastern Lands, sent by imperial decree to go west to worship Buddha and fetch the scriptures. He will ask, ‘What treasures have you?’ Then you say it once to him as you show the brocade kasaya: ‘This is a third-rank treasure; there are also first and second-rank fine things besides it.’ Then tell him this: inside this casket is one treasure that knows five hundred years of the past, five hundred of the present, and five hundred of the future; whatever happens in the past and coming past and future for fifteen hundred years, all is fully known. At that time release Wukong. I will convey the words from the dream to that prince. If he believes, he will take that demon, avenge his father-king, and secure our name and integrity. If he does not, show him the white-jade gei. He is still young and may not yet recognize it.” Tripitaka listened and was overjoyed: “Disciple, this plan is wonderful. I hear one treasure called the brocaded kasaya, another called the white-jade gei. What is the name of the treasure you have transformed into?” Sun Wukong said, “Call it Li Di Ho.” Tripitaka remembered it as told. The master and disciples did not sleep at all that night; they waited for dawn, eager to nod the world awake, to call forth the sun of Fusang, and blow away all the stars in the sky.

Soon the east had turned pale. Sun Wukong again instructed Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing: “Do not disturb the monks or come out roaming about. When I have succeeded, then you two go with me.” After seeing them off, he whistled, gave a jindou shout, and leapt into the air. Through his blazing eyes he looked westward and indeed saw a city. How one can see it from there? He told them this city was only forty li from the temple, and therefore was visible from that height. Sun Wukong came nearer and examined it closely. He saw then a sinister mist, dim clouds of sorrow, and demon winds with angry vapour swirling. Looking in the sky he praised:

If a true king ascends the jeweled throne, auspicious five-coloured clouds arise. Only because a demon has invaded the dragon seat; black vapour roars and seals the Golden Gate.

The Great Sage was still sighing when he suddenly heard cannon shots ring out. At once he saw, at the opening of the eastern gate, a stream of riders pour forth. Truly it was a hunting army, and indeed they had mighty force. One could see:

At dawn they came out east of the Forbidden City, spreading through the shallow grass. Colorful banners unfurled, reflecting the sun; white horses dashed, caught by the wind. Tortoise drums boomed in great pounding, spears flashed and clashed in opposing rushes. Eagle troops charged fiercely, and hounds were led by men of ferocity. Cannon fire shook the sky in one long roll, with burning staves glowing red in the light. Every man shouldered a crossbow, every one carried a carved bow. Nets were spread down the mountain slope, corded narrow paths laid out. One thunderclap of alarm—then a thousand riders charged like giant bears. The trickster rabbit could not save his body; the clever stag-roe’s wit was exhausted. The fox met its destined end, the moose was undone in the midst. A mountain pheasant can scarcely fly away; how could a jungle fowl escape the danger? All of them picked hunting grounds across the hills, seizing wild beasts, ruining trees, and shooting at things that flew.

Those men came out of the city and strolled along the eastern outskirts. After not long, at roughly twenty li on high farmland, they reached the center camp, where they saw a small but unmistakable general: helmeted, armored, belly-bound, eighteen folds, wielding a treasured blue-edged sword, seated on a chestnut horse, with a full bow at his belt. Truly he was:

He faintly bore the air of a king, and his face was like that of an imperial lord. His bearing was no small frame; in his movements he truly showed the nature of a dragon.

The Great Sage, happy in secret, said, “There’s no need to ask further—that is the emperor’s own crown prince. I’ll put him through a little trick.” The Great Sage touched down from the cloud-head and dashed into the troop before the prince’s horse, then shifted in a blink into a white hare and ran in circles ahead of the prince’s horse. The prince saw him and was exactly delighted; he drew an arrow, pulled the bow full, and loosed. The arrow struck the hare.

It was indeed the Great Sage’s intention to make him hit. Yet with a quick eye and swift hand he caught the arrowhead, dropped the feathered vane in front, cast it off, and fled with his feet. Seeing that the arrow had struck the jade rabbit, the prince urged on his horse and alone came racing to catch up first. He did not know how: when the horse ran fast, the Great Sage moved like the wind; when the horse moved slowly, the Great Sage walked gently—as if only a short distance ahead the whole time. Watching for a while, he guided the prince along one stretch, one more li, to the gate beneath the mountain temple. The Great Sage showed his true form there. The hare was gone; only an arrow stood in the threshold. He charged straight in, saw Tang Sanzang and said, “Master, he has come, he has come.” Then he changed again, becoming a monk-child no more than two inches tall, and slipped inside the red casket.

The prince, having rushed to the mountain gate, found no jade rabbit; only an arrow with a carved feather head was thrust into the threshold. The prince was greatly startled and pale, saying, “Wondrous! Wondrous! My arrow surely hit the jade rabbit; how does the rabbit disappear when only the arrow remains here? I suppose in the passing of many years it has become a spirit-beast.” He pulled out the arrow, looked up and saw five large characters above the gate: “Imperially Built Bao Lin Monastery.” The prince said, “I see it now. In past years I remember my father king in Jinluan Hall sending officers bearing gold and silk to this monk to repair the Buddha hall and images; never did I imagine I would come here today. Indeed, as the saying goes: passing through the monastery and meeting a monk brings, in this floating life, even half a day’s ease. I shall go in and stroll about.”

The prince leapt from his horse and was about to enter when the escort official and three thousand men and horses caught up with him, crowding in close. The monks of that monastery, in confusion, all came to bow and receive him, leading him into the central hall to pay obeisance before the Buddha image. As he looked about and then meant to wander the corridors, he suddenly saw a monk seated in the center. The prince grew angry: “This monk is without propriety! Now that I, the crown prince, have come early this morning to the mountain, though there has been no summons, he need not avoid me. With my cavalry at the gate he ought to rise in respect. Why does he still sit still?” He barked, “Take him down!” At the single word “take,” both flank captains moved at once, pulled Tang Sanzang down and quickly tied him with rope. The Great Sage, silent in the casket, muttered a charm: “Guarding heavens and guardian deities, Six Ding and Six Jia—today I set out to subdue a demon. This prince does not know it; if he tries to bind my Master with rope, you all must protect him at once. If you truly bind him, all of you will be guilty.” In secret the Great Sage gave instructions; none dared disobey. He set his protection over the Master, and those men could not even touch his bald head—like a wall between them, they could not seize his body.

The prince asked, “Where are you from, and what kind of hidden-invisibility art is this to deceive me?” Tripitaka stepped forward and bowed: “I, your poor monk, possess no art of vanishing. I am Tripitaka, a monk of Tang, one from the Temple of Great Thunder Sound, journeying to worship Buddha and fetch scriptures.” The prince said, “Though your eastern land is in the Central Plains, its poverty is boundless—what treasures do you speak of?” Tripitaka said, “The cassock I wear is the third of the treasures. There are first-rate and second-rate ones even finer.” The prince said, “Your garment covers half your body and leaves half your arm bare; how much is it worth that you dare call it a treasure?” Tripitaka replied, “Though this cassock is not whole, it carries a few verses:

A Buddha-robe worn askew need not be argued over; within it hides true suchness and sheds worldly dust. A myriad threads and thousand stitches bring true attainment; nine jewels and eight treasures gather the primal spirit. Crafted in reverence by celestial maidens and sacred girls, it is bestowed on Chan monks to keep the body unstained. To fail to meet your horse is still bearable in itself; yet your father’s wrong left unredressed makes life itself futile.

Hearing him, the prince burned with anger: “This ragged monk speaks nonsense! With only your tongue, you boast and brag over this half-robe, calling yourself able to trumpet wonders. Why has my father’s grievance not been repaid? Speak and tell me.” Tripitaka stepped forward and asked with joined palms: “Your Highness, for one born between heaven and earth, how many blessings are there?” The prince: “There are four.” Tripitaka: “What four?” The prince: “The favor of Heaven and Earth that bear me, the favor of the sun and moon that give light, the favor of the king’s water and soil, and the favor of my parents who raised and nurtured me.” Tripitaka laughed: “Your Highness has erred in words. A person has Heaven and Earth for cover, sun and moon for light, and the king’s water and soil. Where then is this favor of parents’ nurture?” The prince snapped back: “You monk are a vagabond living on alms, a shaven fool rebelling against one’s lord! A man cannot live without parents’ nurture—where did he come from?” Tripitaka: “Your Highness, your poor monk does not know. But inside this red casket is one treasure called Lidi Huo. It knows five hundred years above, five hundred in the middle, five hundred below—altogether one thousand five hundred years of past and future affairs. Thus it knows that there was no favor of being parented, and poor monk has waited here all this time.”

Hearing this, the prince said, “Bring it and let me see.” Tripitaka pulled open the casket lid, and the Great Sage sprang out with a sharp cry, scurrying and weaving to both sides. The prince said, “This tiny little man—what can he possibly know?” At this, the Great Sage, though slight in form, used his powers, stretching his waist until it became three chi four or five inches. The guardsmen, startled, said, “If he grows this quickly, in only a few days he will split the sky.” The Great Sage returned to his full height. The prince asked, “Lidi Huo—this old monk says you know prosperity and disaster in past and future. Do you use turtle-shell for divination? yarrow stalks for cleromancy? Can written passages alone decide a man’s fortune and misfortune?” The Great Sage said, “I do not use even a hair of it. It is all by one three-inch tongue; thus all things are known.” The prince said, “This knave again lies. Since ancient times, the Book of Changes is most mysterious and can see through all fortunes beneath heaven, letting people know what to pursue and what to avoid; therefore turtles are used to divine, yarrow for fortune-staff casting. On what principle do you speak thus, spreading lies of fortune and disaster and bewildering people’s hearts?”

The Great Sage said, “Your Highness, do not be hasty; let me tell you and you shall hear. You are the crown prince of the King of Wu-ji. Five years ago there was severe drought; in a season of endless suffering, all the people endured hardship, and your father king and his ministers prayed with one heart. When there was still no rain at all, a Daoist from Zhongnan Mountain came. He excelled at calling wind and summoning rain, and at turning stone into gold. My father king favored him so deeply he made him a brother. Is not this so?” The prince said, “It is so, yes—yes. Tell me more.” The Great Sage continued: “For the following three years the Daoist Quanzhen has not been seen. Who is the one you now say is missing?” The prince answered, “Indeed there was such a Quanzhen. My father king and he became brothers, ate from one table, slept under one roof. Three years ago, while roaming in the imperial garden, with a divine gust of wind he seized my father’s white-jade and gilded-sheathed bi, carried it back to Zhongnan Mountain. To this day my father still yearns for him. Not seeing him, he has no heart for pleasure now, and he has kept the garden tightly closed for three years. Who else but my father is the one to be emperor?”

When Wukong heard the words, he laughed aloud without end. The prince asked again, and still he answered with nothing but that derisive laugh. The prince, angry, said, "You speak at length before and yet say nothing now—why laugh so much like this?" Wukong replied, "There is still much to tell, but with all these guards around, this is no place to speak." Seeing that the monk’s words had their reason, the prince extended his robe sleeve and ordered the officers to withdraw for a while. The commander of the mounted guard hurriedly passed the order on, and had the three thousand soldiers and horsemen step out to camp outside the gate. At this moment the hall was empty. The prince sat upon the throne, Tripitaka stood before him, and Wukong stood at his left. All the monks from the monastery withdrew. Wukong then stepped forward with a grave face and said, "Your Highness, the one who sent the wind was your own birth father. The one on the seat is that Quanzhen figure who prayed for rain." The prince said, "Nonsense, nonsense. Since my father left Quanzhen, wind and rain have been timely and the realm has flourished in peace. By your logic he would not be my king at all. I have tolerated you because I am still young; but if my father hears such treasonous words, he will have you torn to pieces." He shouted him down. Wukong said to Tripitaka, "How was it? I said he would not believe me. He did not. Now give him that treasure and exchange the pass document, and let us be off to the Western Regions." Tripitaka handed the vermilion casket to Wukong. Wukong took it, gave a slight shake, and the casket was gone at once. It had been made from one of his hairs and he had reabsorbed it into himself. Then he lifted the White-Jade Tablet in both hands and presented it to the prince.

The prince looked and said, "Good monk, good monk. Five years ago you were a Quanzhen priest and swindled away my family treasure; now you dress up as a monk and come again to present it." He shouted, "Take him!" The order went out, and Tripitaka, startled, pointed at Wukong and cried, "You, Bimawen, are always running into empty calamities and bringing trouble upon me." Wukong stepped up and blocked the way, saying, "No shouting—do not stir up the wind! I am no Li-di-huo; I still have a true name." The prince, enraged, said, "Come here. I will ask your true name and then have you delivered to legal authority for judgment!" Wukong said, "I am the Great Master’s chief disciple, named Sun Wukong. I followed my teacher to the Western Heaven to fetch scriptures, and came here last night to seek lodging. My Master read scriptures through the deep of night, and near the third watch he dreamed. He saw your father in a dream, saying that that Quanzhen had deceived and harmed him, pushing him into the octagonal glazed-jade well in the imperial flower garden, and that Quanzhen had taken his appearance. None of the ministers of the full court knew of it. You were young and could not understand; you were forbidden to enter the palace and the garden was shut up, all for fear the matter should leak out. Your father came tonight especially to summon me to subdue a demon. I doubted whether he was truly evil, so I watched from the air, and indeed he was a demon. As I was about to seize him, you unexpectedly rode out to hunt. The jade hare in your arrow was Old Sun. Old Sun led you here to the monastery, met my Master, and told him all this in his heart; every word was true. Since you have recognized the White-Jade Tablet, how can you not remember your debt and kindness and avenge your parent’s wrong?"

When the prince heard this, he was moved to pity and hurt within himself and thought in sorrow, "If he does not tell the truth, there is at least some truth in what he says. If he is telling the truth, how can I see my father on the throne before me?" Caught between what to do and what to think, his mind wavered, and he wrestled with himself with both mouth and heart. Seeing his uncertainty, Wukong stepped forward again and said, "Your Highness need not doubt any longer. Return to your capital at once and ask your queen mother; ask how deep the love between husband and wife remains compared with three years ago. From this one question, the truth will be known."

The prince straightened himself and thought, "So it is. Let me at once ask my mother and return." He leapt to his feet and grasped the White-Jade Tablet and set off. Wukong caught his sleeve and said, "Send all these men and horses back; if word leaks out, my task will fail. When you enter the city, go alone with only your horse, and do not show yourself or make a display. Do not enter by Zhengyang Gate; go in by the rear gate of Zai. When you meet your mother in the palace, do not raise your voice at all; speak in low whispers. That monster’s powers are vast. If she hears of this for even a moment, both mother and son will not keep their lives." The prince carefully obeyed all instruction. As he reached the mountain gate he told his commander, "Hold this camp as it is; do not move. I have one errand and will return with her, then we will enter the city together." He looked at him:

Give the command, line up the troops, and mount—ride as if on wings as we turn back toward the city.

With him gone on this errand, what words he might bring from the queen mother cannot yet be known. We shall hear them in the next section.
chapters.title: Chapter 37: At night a ghost-king visits Tripitaka; Wukong’s divination draws forth the hidden child.
