This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

The king saw that Sun Wukong knew the art of calling up dragon-messengers and sacred powers, and he was just about to apply the precious seal to the release pass and hand it to Tripitaka so he could proceed west. The three Daoist priests, flustered, prostrated themselves in the Hall of Golden Luan and submitted a memorial. The king came down from the Dragon Throne and, waving his hand, asked, "Why does the Grand Master perform this great ceremony today?" One said, "Your Majesty, we have come here to uphold the state and preserve the peace of the land; for twenty years we have labored to guard this realm. This monk’s tricks, wielding power, have dragged him away and ruined our reputation. Could Your Majesty forgive us for the charge of killing men because of one bout of rain? Is that not making light of our efforts? Please hold the warrant for now and let my two brothers gamble with him once more to see how it is." The king was truly confused, shifting this way and that, then taking back the warrant, he said, "Grand Master, how will you gamble with him?" Huli Great Immortal replied, "I will gamble with him at seated meditation." The king said, "The Master is wrong. That monk is trained in the Zen teaching and must surely understand the gate of meditation before he dares to request the sutra by imperial decree. How could you gamble against him in that?" The immortal said, "My kind of seated meditation is unlike ordinary methods. It has another name, called Cloud-Ladder Manifesting-Saintly Power." The king asked, "What is Cloud-Ladder Manifesting-Saintly Power?" The immortal said, "Take one hundred table boards: stack fifty as a meditation dais and set them one above another. One may not climb by hand, nor mount a ladder or stool. Each rider sits upon a cloud, mounts the dais, and remains still for the appointed number of hours."

When the king saw the difficulty, he issued the command, "Monk, Grand Master wishes to gamble this 'Cloud-Ladder Manifesting-Saintly' seated-meditation with you. Can you do it?" Sun Wukong listened in silence, thinking. Zhu Bajie said, "Elder brother, why do you remain silent?" Wukong said, "Brother, I’ll tell you plainly. If it is kicking heaven, muddling wells, churning seas and reversing rivers, carrying mountains while chasing the moon, moving the Big Dipper and shifting the stars—those clever feats I can all do. Even beheading and cleaving skulls, opening bellies and gouging out hearts, and all strange bodily hardships, I do not fear. But when it comes to seated meditation, I am losing. Where can I have such stillness of posture? You could chain me to an iron pillar; I’ll keep climbing up and down, and you cannot expect me to sit still." Tripitaka spoke at once, "I can sit." Wukong exclaimed happily, "Excellent—excellent. For how long can you sit?" Tripitaka said, "When young, I followed a Zen monk and was taught Dharma. At the root of life and death one can quiet intention and still the spirit. In the gate between life and death, one may sit for two or three years." Wukong said, "If my master sits two or three years, we should abandon the pilgrimage. In no more than two or three hours, I think he will come down." Tripitaka said, "Disciple, he still cannot go up there." Wukong said, "You go ahead and promise this. I’ll send you up."

The elder monk then joined hands over his chest and said, "Your humble one can sit meditation." The king ordered it proclaimed and immediately had two platforms erected. The nation possessed strength enough to turn mountains; in less than half an hour they raised two platforms on either side of the Golden Luan Hall.

Huli Great Immortal descended from the hall and stood at the center of the steps. With one leap he stepped onto a cloud seat and went straight up to sit on the western platform. Sun Wukong pulled out a single hair and turned it into a decoy image, and with him beside Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing he stood below. Then he made a five-colored auspicious cloud, lifted Tripitaka into the air, and went straight to the eastern platform to sit. He then gathered in his light and became a long-bodied jingling bug, flew to Zhu Bajie’s ear, and whispered, "Brother, watch Master carefully and do not speak to Old Monkey’s substitute." The Pig-Fisted one laughed, "I understand. I understand."

Huli Great Immortal sat for a long while on a decorated cushion and watched, and the two on the high platforms were still evenly matched. Then this Daoist gave his fellow-priest one helping move: he plucked one short hair from the back of his head, twisted it into a ball, and flung it upward, landing on Tripitaka’s head and becoming a large stinking bug that bit him. At first the monk only felt an itch, then pain. As seated meditation permits no movement, and moving means loss, he endured, unable to stand it, lowered his head and with his sleeve hem tried to scratch. Zhu Bajie said, "This is bad—Master’s wind has risen in his head." Sha Wujing said, "No, it is not that. His head wind has risen." Wukong heard this and said, "My Master is an upright, sincere man. Since he said he could sit meditation, he will sit without fail. If he cannot, then he truly cannot. A gentleman’s household does not speak falsehoods. You two keep quiet; let me go up and see."

A sharp "eeng" rang out; the Sage flew above Tripitaka’s head and saw a bean-sized stinking bug biting his Master. He hurriedly pinched it down and rubbed around to relieve him. Tripitaka himself seemed neither in pain nor in an itch, and sat upright as before. Sun Wukong thought, "On a monk’s shaven head even a louse cannot stay, so how can such a stinking bug remain there? It must be this Daoist’s trickery, harming my Master. Ha, since I do not even know how this is decided, I’ll punish him myself!" He flew up, dropped near the gold-beast head of the hall, then instantly changed into a seven-inch centipede and went straight to sting the Daoist in the hollow of the nose. The Daoist could not keep his seat, flipped and came tumbling down—nearly losing his life. Fortunately, many high officials and attendants crowded there pulled him up in time. The king, greatly alarmed, ordered the chief Minister to take him away to the Wenhua Hall to bathe and comb his hair. Sun Wukong once again took up his lucky cloud and carried Tripitaka down to the steps; already the elder monk had won.

The king then gave order to release them. Huli Great Immortal also submitted a memorial: "Your Majesty, my senior brother has a secret wind illness. Reaching such a height, he was struck by the sky wind, and the old ailment burst forth, so it was that the monk won. Do keep him here and let me gamble one more time with him in the game of Guessing by Dividing Panels." The king asked, "What is called 'Guessing by Dividing Panels'?" Huli said, "I have a method of divining things behind a partition. Let us see if the monk can match it. If he guesses rightly against me, let him go free. If he fails, then according to Your Majesty’s judgment choose his offense, and avenge the grievance of my brothers, so the grace of twenty years of preserving this country is not made impure." Truly confused, the king accepted this slander and ordered: bring a vermilion-red lacquered cabinet and have an attendant carry it to the hall. He ordered the empresses to place in it a precious item. After a short while it was brought out and set before the white-jade steps, and he told the monk, "Each of you now wager your power and guess what treasure is in this cabinet."

Tripitaka said, "Disciple, how can I know what is in that cabinet?" Sun Wukong drew in his light, changed once more into the long-bodied bug, and fixed himself to Tripitaka’s head: "Master, do not worry. I will go and look." The Great Sage flew lightly to the cabinet, crawled beneath its foot, and saw a narrow board crack. He crept through and found a red-lacquer cinnabar dish within, containing a set of court robes: the Mountain-and-River State-Emblem Coat and the Heaven-and-Earth Geology Skirt. He took it up and shook it loose. Biting the tip of his tongue until it bled, he sprayed a jet of blood, shouted "Transform!" and instantly became a tattered rag and a broken little bell. Before leaving he also left a splash of foul urine. He then came back through the board crack and flew to Tripitaka’s ear: "Master, guess only a torn rag and a small bell." Tripitaka said, "He said to guess a treasure—what treasure is this torn rag and little bell?" Wukong said, "Do not worry; just guess it correctly."

Tripitaka stepped forward one step and was just about to guess when Huli Great Immortal said, "I will guess first: in that cabinet is the Mountain-and-River State-Emblem Coat and the Heaven-and-Earth Geology Skirt." Tripitaka said, "No, no. In the cabinet is a torn rag and a little bell." The king said, "This monk is rude. He dares to mock that my realm has no treasure and guess a mere rag and bell!" "Take him!" the guards moved to seize him. In panic, Tripitaka raised his hands in prayer and shouted, "Your Majesty, pardon this poor monk for one moment. Let the cabinet be opened first. If it is a treasure, I take the blame; if it is no treasure, then do not still claim this poor monk has lost." The king ordered it opened. The chief minister opened it and lifted out the cinnabar dish; inside was indeed a tattered rag and a little bell. The king thundered in anger, "Who set this here?" From behind the dragon seat came one of the imperial empresses: "My lord, the imperial seamstress Zitong placed the State-Emblem Coat and Geology Skirt herself. I do not know how it turned into this." The king said, "Your consort may withdraw. I know it now. Objects used in the inner palace are only satin, silk, and patterned silk-brocade—how could there be such a rag and bell?" He ordered, "Lift it again. I myself will hide one treasure in it, and we shall test again." Turning toward the inner court, the king plucked a great peach from the immortal peach tree in the imperial garden, as large as a bowl, and put it into the cabinet before setting it down to be guessed.

Tripitaka said, "Disciple, we guess again now." Wukong said, "Do not fear; let me look once more." Again came the sharp cry, and he flew there, entered through the board crack again, and saw a peach—exactly what he needed. He resumed his true form, sat in the cabinet, bit through the peach clean, even emptying both cheek sockets, then placed the pit inside. He changed once more into the long-bodied bug, flew out, and settled on Tripitaka’s ear: "Master, you should guess a peach pit." Tripitaka said, "Disciple, do not make a fool of me. Before, with too quick a tongue, I was almost taken for punishment. This time we should guess a real treasure. What treasure is a peach pit?" Wukong said, "Do not fear—just win against him."

Tripitaka was about to speak when he heard Yangli Great Immortal say, 'I, your humble Taoist, first guessed it was a celestial peach.' Tripitaka said, 'Not a peach—a bare peach pit.' The king shouted, 'It is the immortal peach I placed myself. How can it be only a pit? The Royal Preceptor has guessed it right then.' Tripitaka said, 'Your Majesty, let us open it and see.' The palace officer lifted it again, opened it, and brought out the elixir tray. It was indeed only a pit, without skin or flesh. Seeing this, the king, alarmed, said, 'Master, do not gamble with him anymore; let him go. I hid that celestial peach with my own hands; now it is only a pit. Who could have eaten it? It must be that some ghost or god secretly aided him.' Hearing this, Zhu Bajie, smiling faintly at Sha Wujing, said, 'You still do not know how long he has been eating peaches.'

At that very moment, Huli Great Immortal, after bathing and dressing in Wenhua Hall, came up to the hall and said, 'Your Majesty, this monk has an art that carries things across. Bring the cabinet out again. I will break his arts and challenge him once more.' The king asked, 'What does the Royal Preceptor still wish to guess?' Huli said, 'The spell can counter objects, but not the human body. Hide this Dao-child inside; then he cannot exchange himself.' He did so: the little boy was hidden inside the cabinet, the lid closed, lowered, and the order was given, 'The monk must guess again—what is this treasure in this third round?'

Tripitaka said, 'It has come again!' The Great Sage said, 'Wait, I will go check again.' At once he flew again, crawled inside, and saw a small boy. 'What cleverness in this Great Sage,' he thought; 'indeed he is one of the rare clever boys under heaven.' He changed form at once and became an old Taoist, entered the cabinet, and called, 'Disciple.' The boy asked, 'Master, where did you come from?' The Great Sage said, 'I came by means of a disappearing art.' The boy said, 'What instruction have you brought?' The Great Sage said, 'That monk has seen you come in. If he were to guess a Dao-child, would he not lose again? I have come to settle with you: let me shave your head, and then we will guess monk.' The boy said, 'As long as master governs, if we win him all is well. If we lose, our reputation will fail, and the court will not honor us.' The Great Sage said, 'You are right. Come, if you beat him I will reward you handsomely.' He changed the Golden-Hooped Staff into a razor, hugged the child, and said, 'Good child, bear the pain and do not shout. Let me shave you.' In a moment the hair was cut off and packed into a knot at the bottom tie of the cabinet. After putting away the razor, he touched the boy’s smooth head: 'My child, your head already looks like a monk’s. Only the robes do not fit. Remove them, and I will transform you.' The boy removed a pale-greensilk cloud-crowned robe with brocade trim and crane-patterned edges. Wukong breathed out a breath of immortal qi and cried, 'Transform!' and it changed into an earthen-yellow straight robe, which he made him wear. Then he pulled two hairs and turned them into a wooden fish, putting it in the child’s hand: 'Disciple, listen well. If they call out that you are a Dao-child, never come out. If they call you monk, then push open the cabinet lid, strike the wood-fish, chant a Buddhist scripture, and crawl out. Only then will you succeed.' The boy said, 'I only know how to recite the Sūtra of the Three Officials, the Northern Dipper Sūtra, and the Sūtra for Dispelling Disasters. I cannot recite Buddhist scripture.' The Great Sage asked, 'Can you recite Buddha?' The boy replied, 'Amitabha Buddha—I cannot not recite that.' The Great Sage said, 'All right, all right. Just chant Buddha and spare me teaching you again. Remember this: I am leaving.' He changed again into a cicada-like insect, flew out, and whispered at Tripitaka’s ear, 'Master, you should only guess it is a monk.' Tripitaka said, 'This time he will certainly win.' The Great Sage asked, 'How can you be so certain?' Tripitaka said, 'The scripture says:

As they were speaking, Huli Great Immortal said, 'Your Majesty, for the third time it is a Dao-child.' The boy kept quiet and would not come out. Tripitaka joined his palms and said, 'It is a monk.' Zhu Bajie shouted loudly, 'Inside the cabinet there is a monk.' Suddenly the child pushed up the cabinet lid, struck the wood-fish, chanted Buddha, and crawled out. The two groups of civil and military officials cheered in unison. Caught in fear, the three Daoist priests kept silent, unable to speak.

The king said, 'This monk is helped by ghosts and gods. How can a Daoist enter a cabinet and turn into a monk? Even if one entered behind him by Imperial order, he could only have his head shaved; how could his clothing change to fit and his mouth speak Buddha as well? Master, let him go.' Huli Great Immortal said, 'Your Majesty, this is a match for one another; we have found a worthy opponent. The martial arts I learned as a boy on Zhongnan Mountain are enough for me to gamble with him once more.' The king asked, 'What arts?' Huli answered, 'The three of us each have some powers: we can cut off a head and set it back on again; open the belly, scoop out the heart, and have it regrow; and roll in a cauldron of boiling oil as if taking a bath.' The king was greatly startled: 'These three are roads to death.' Huli said, 'It is only because we have such powers that I dare make bold words; we must gamble with him and settle it.' The king cried, 'Monk of the Eastern Land, my Royal Preceptor will not release you. He still wants to gamble with you for beheading, opening the belly, and bathing in a rolling oil cauldron.'

The Great Sage was still in cicada form, running errands. At these words he gathered his hairs and revealed his true form, then laughed aloud: 'Fate, fate—this bargain has come right to my door.' Zhu Bajie said, 'These three things are all life-taking; how can you call that a bargain?' The Great Sage said, 'You still do not know my arts.' Zhu Bajie said, 'Elder Brother, your transformations alone are enough. What more skill can you have?' The Great Sage replied, 'Listen:

If my head is cut off, it can still speak; if my arms are hewn away, they can still strike. If my legs are severed, I can still walk; with the belly split open, the repair is wondrous and perfect. Like folk wrap food in dough—one pinch, one comes out whole. Bathing in a boiling oil pot is still easier, as if warm water for washing off grime.' Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing laughed.

The Great Sage went forward and said, 'Your Majesty, this young monk can have his head cut off.' The king asked, 'How do you know how to decapitate?' The Great Sage said, 'When I was in monastic training, I once met a monk named Fangshang Zhi. He taught me a beheading method. I do not know whether it is good or not, but now let us try it.' The king laughed, 'He is young and does not know the way of the world. How can one try beheading? The head is the principal of the six yang; if it is cut off, one dies at once.' Huli said, 'Your Majesty, this is just what will draw out our qi against him.' The deluded king believed him and ordered, 'Set up the place of execution.'

At the command, three thousand Yulin soldiers were arranged outside the court gate. The king ordered, 'The monk should go first for beheading.' The Great Sage readily answered, 'I will go first, I will go first.' Folding his hands, he shouted, 'Royal Preceptor, forgive my boldness—I beg the first turn.' Turning back, he walked out. Tripitaka grabbed him and said, 'Disciple, be careful. This is no place for play.' The Great Sage replied, 'Why should I be afraid? Let go. I will go and return.'

The Great Sage went straight to the execution ground. The executioners seized him, bound him into a tight bundle, and pressed him upon a high earthen mound. At once there was a cry, 'Cut!' and with a hiss the head was chopped off. An executioner kicked him and he rolled away, like a rolling melon, for some thirty or forty paces. No blood came from the Great Sage’s body at all. From inside came the call: 'Head, come!' Alarmed, Huli Great Immortal, seeing such skill, recited a charm and invoked the local Earth Lords and spirits: 'Hold his head fast. If I defeat this monk and report to the king, I will build for you a great temple from your little shrine, and have your clay images remade as true gilded forms.' Because he had the Five-Thunder arts, those Earth Lords and deities obeyed him and truly held the Sage’s head in place unseen. The Great Sage called again, 'My head!' and it seemed rooted, unable to move at all. Wukong grew anxious, twisted his fist and struggled, and all the binding ropes snapped. He shouted, 'Grow!' and in a rush another head sprang from within his body. This terrified the executioners, and every Yulin soldier stood in fear. The execution captain hurried into court and reported, 'Your Majesty, the young monk had his head cut off, and yet it has grown one again.' Zhu Bajie smirked, 'Sha Wujing, did you know my brother has such skill?' Sha Wujing said, 'He has seventy-two transformations, so he has seventy-two heads.'

Before they could finish speaking, the Great Sage returned, crying, 'Master.' Tripitaka rejoiced, 'Disciple, was it hard?' The Great Sage said, 'Not hard at all—just a fine bit of play.' Zhu Bajie asked, 'Brother, can we use medicine for sword wounds?' The Great Sage said, 'Feel it yourself and see if there is any scar from the blade.' The fool reached out to touch him, and with stunned eyes laughed dumbly, 'Wondrous, wondrous! It is complete as before, not even a tiniest scar from a cut.'

The brothers were all rejoicing when they heard the king call out that the pardon scroll was to be issued: “You are pardoned of guilt. Go—go at once.” Sun Wukong said, “Though I accept this order, the Great Master must also come to the execution ground to have his head cut off first; only then should he be tested whether he can return.” The king said, “Great Master, that monk does not intend to spare you. If you gamble with him and win, do not make me be the one who trembles.” Huli could not resist and went. A few executioners bound him to the ground, and with one sweep cut off his head, then kicked it away. It rolled over thirty paces. No blood came from his throat, yet he called once, “My head!” Sun Wukong quickly pulled out one hair, blew a breath of immortal air, cried “Transform!” and turned into a yellow dog, ran into the field, bit off the Taoist’s head, and then ran straight to the bank of the royal waterway and tossed it away without further matter.

That Taoist cried out three times, but the head did not come back; Wukong’s trick did not work to bring it forth. Red light burst from his bones. He had only the art of calling rain and summoning wind, but how could that compare to Wukong, the true immortals’ peer? In a moment he collapsed in the dust. When the crowd looked, he had become a headless yellow-furred tiger.

The execution officer came again to report: “Your Majesty, the Great Master’s head has been cut off and does not grow back. He lies dead in the dust, a headless yellow tiger.” The king, hearing this, was pale with shock, staring without blinking at the two Taoists. Luli stood up and said, “My senior brother is already dead in life and fate has ended him; how can he be only a yellow tiger? It is that monk’s shameless trickery, disguising my senior brother and turning him into a beast. I will not spare him now; I will gamble with him—I demand my abdomen be opened and my heart gouged out.”

The king then came back to himself. He said, “Young monk, the Second Great Master still wishes to gamble with you.” Sun Wukong said, “I have not eaten grain and flame-cooked food for a long time. Some days ago, coming from the west, I met Master Zhai’s house and was told to eat, so I ate several stuffed buns. These days my belly pains me; surely worms are there. I wish to borrow Your Majesty’s knife, split open my belly, take out my entrails, and wash my spleen and stomach clean, then I can go west to meet Buddha in good order.” The king said, “Take him to the execution ground.” Many pulled at him to carry him, but Sun Wukong freed himself: “There is no need for people to drag me. I can walk on my own. Only this: do not bind my hands, for I need them to wash my organs.” The king ordered, “Do not bind his hands.”

Sun Wukong swayed and walked directly to the slaughter place, leaned his body against a great post, untied his belt, and exposed his belly. One executioner looped a rope around his shoulders and another around his legs, then flashed a short ox-ear knife and made a cut under the belly, boring a hole. Sun Wukong with both hands parted his belly and drew out his intestines. He took them out one by one, yet when enough time passed they remained coiled inside as before. He pinched the belly, blew a breath of immortal air, called, “Chang!” and it was instantly closed again.

The king was greatly startled, holding the pardon order in his hand, saying, “Holy monk, do not fail your voyage to the West. Take this writ and be off.” Sun Wukong laughed: “This writ is a small matter. Please have the Great Master also split and gouge himself—what do you think?” The king said to Luli, “This is none of my business. It is you who sought to oppose him. Go on, go on.” Luli said, “Do not worry. I am certain I will not lose to him.”

See how like the Great Sage Sun he was, swaying and swaying, entering the execution field straightaway. The executioners roped him and the short ox-ear knife flashed with a hiss, slitting open his belly. He, too, drew out the liver and intestines and handled them with his hands. Then Sun Wukong pulled out one hair, blew a breath of immortal air, and shouted, “Transform!” He became a hungry hawk, spread wings and talons, and in a rush swooped down to snatch all the five viscera and liver and carried them away to feast; no one knew where he flew. That Taoist was left as a hollow, open-bellied, blood-dripping thing, a withered soul without organs. The executioners kicked over the great post and dragged the corpse to look at it. Ah! It was a white-furred horned deer.

The frightened execution officer came again and reported: “The Second Great Master is most unfortunate. While he was having his belly split, a hungry hawk carried away all the internal organs and liver. He died there. His true form is also a white-furred horned deer.” The king asked, “How can that be a horned deer?” Yangli Great Immortal spoke again: “My brother is dead already. How can he now appear in beast form? It is that monk’s trickery harming us. I will repay the injury now.” The king asked, “What power do you have to defeat him?” Yangli said, “Let us gamble on going to bathe in a boiling-oil cauldron.” The king ordered that a large pot be brought, filled with fragrant oil, and both of you be sent to gamble. Sun Wukong said, “Much obliged. The young monk has not bathed in some time. In these two days my skin is dry and itchy. I will at least roll about a bit.”

The supervising official ordered the oil vat set, laid dry wood underneath, and burned up a fierce fire until the oil boiled. He said, “Let the monk enter first.” Sun Wukong put his palms together and asked, “Should I take the civil wash or the martial wash?” The king said, “What is civil wash? What is martial wash?” Sun Wukong said, “Civil wash means no robe off: with your hands crossed like this, go down and roll once, then come up, and do not let the robe become soiled with oil. If any trace of grease appears, that is losing. Martial wash means taking a rack and a towel, removing your robe, leaping in, and then turning as you like—cartwheels and all, standing like a dragonfly, as if it were mere sport.” The king asked Yangli, “Which will you choose—civil wash or martial wash?” Yangli said, “If it is civil wash, his robe may have been alchemically strengthened and will resist oil. Let it be martial wash.”

Sun Wukong stepped forward and said, “Forgive this boldness—I have taken the lead repeatedly.” He stripped off his plain robe, removed his tiger-skin skirt, and leapt high, landing in the pot, where he rose and fell in waves, splashing and tossing the oil like a man playing with water itself. Zhu Bajie saw this and bit his finger as he spoke to Sha Wujing, “We judged this monkey wrong. All the time we mocked him and argued with him, daring to taunt his tricks, not knowing he has such real skill. The two of them kept chirping and praising him without end.”

Sun Wukong looked on, skeptical: “That fool laughs at me. Truly, as the saying goes, ‘The clever have heavy labor, the clumsy have time to spare.’ This old monk is so adroit at his dances, yet the fool sits easy. Let me make him a rope and bind him, and see what fright he has.” Midway through his bathing, he sent up a spray of water, cooled himself at the bottom of the oil cauldron, changed into a jujube-kernel peg, and did not rise again.

The execution officer came close and reported again: “Your Majesty, the young monk has been boiled to death in the rolling oil.” The king rejoiced and ordered them to haul up the bones. The executioners put an iron sieve into the pot. The holes in that ladle were broad, and Sun Wukong had become tiny as a pin. Again and again he slipped through the holes; how could they retrieve him? Again the officer reported, “The monk’s body is slight and delicate, all of it fried into ash.” The king ordered, “Take three monks down.” Captains on both sides saw Zhu Bajie’s menacing face and first grabbed him by the ears, dragging him and binding his back at the pot.

Tripitaka cried out urgently, “Your Majesty, please pardon this poor monk for a single moment. Since I entered the way, my disciple has rendered clear and steady merit. Today he has collided with the Great Master and died in the oil pot, yet the one who dies first is counted as spirit. How can I, poor monk that I am, dare to cling to life? This is just as officers of the realm govern the people of the realm. If Your Majesty commands my death, how could this monk not obey? I only ask for a little mercy: grant me half a cup of cooling gruel and rice water and three paper horses, and let me stand at the oil pot to burn one sheet of paper, so my disciple and I may make one last confession; then I will receive punishment thereafter.” Hearing this, the king said, “Indeed, a person of the Central Kingdom has honor.” He ordered that some gruel-rice and yellow coins be brought to him, and they were given to Tripitaka.

Tripitaka said his blessing at the pot, “Disciple Sun Wukong:

Since I accepted the precepts and entered the Chan family, my love in escorting you to the West has run deep. I had hoped that together we would attain the Great Way, but now I had this, that today you go toward darkness. In life I only sought the meaning of the scriptures; after death I still keep remembrance of Buddha. A heroic spirit over ten thousand miles away must wait, a ghost in the netherworld, until it rises to Leiyin.” Zhu Bajie heard and said, “Master, not like this blessing. Sha Wujing, do you prepare the gruel and water for him, and let me pray.” While bound to the ground and panting, he said, “You careless, drunken monkey; ignorant Bima-wen. The doomed, carefree monkey—Bima-wen boiled in oil. Monkey, your camp is done, Bima-wen has no root left.” Hearing the fool’s chaotic abuse from beneath, Sun Wukong could not bear it and revealed his true form, standing in the oil pot, wet-red and bare beneath, saying, “What an awful brute! Who are you cursing?” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, you will frighten me to death!” Sha Wujing said, “Big Brother is practiced in feigning death cleanly.”

Before they could settle it, two groups of civil and military officers came up together to report: “Your Majesty, the monk is not dead; he has come out of the oil pot.” The execution officer, fearing the court might be deceived, said in alarm, “He is dead indeed; only the date is unlucky, and the young monk is showing his spirit.” Sun Wukong heard this and became furious, leapt out of the pot, wiped off the oil, put on his clothes, drew out his staff, and struck the execution officer on the head, turning him into a lump of flesh. He shouted, “What spirit am I to show now?” Terrified, many officials hurriedly untied Zhu Bajie and knelt, pleading, “Forgive us, forgive us.” The king descended from the dragon throne. Sun Wukong pulled him there and said, “Your Majesty, do not go. Let your Third Great Master go down into the oil pot too.” The emperor, in trembling fear, said, “Great Master, you have saved my life. Quickly go down into the pot, or the monk may strike me.”

Sun Wukong came down from the hall, took off his clothes as the Great Sage would, leapt into the oil cauldron, and bathed there with the same feigned ease as before. After releasing the king, he moved to the edge of the cauldron and told the fire tender to add more fuel. He reached in with his hand, and at once cried out, “Ah! the oil that was to be boiling is ice-cold.” He thought to himself: “It was hot when I bathed, yet now it is cold for him. I know now which Dragon King is protecting him here.” Instantly he sprang into the air, chanted the seed syllable “Om,” and summoned the North Sea Dragon King: “You, horned earthworm, scaled mud-gudgeon! How did you dare to aid the Taoist, holding a cold-drake beneath the pot so he could pretend to be holy and defeat me?” Hearing that, the Dragon King nodded nervously and replied, “Ao Shun dare not be of this aid. Great Sage, you do not know: this demon animal practiced austerities for a while and shed its former shell, yet it has only truly received the Five-Thunder rite; all else it learned were side methods, unable to return to the Immortal Way. This is the ‘Great-Burning Split’ he learned at Little Maoshan. The other two had already had their arts broken by you, Great Sage, and had shown their true forms. This one is a cold dragon he forged himself, able only to fool ordinary people with childish tricks—how could it deceive the Great Sage? The young dragon has now reclaimed that cold dragon; I will have it made to have its bones broken and its skin scorched.” Sun Wukong said, “Take him up at once and spare the blows.” The Dragon King raised a whirlwind, went to the edge of the oil cauldron, seized the cold dragon, and carried it back to the sea; no further account is needed.

Sun Wukong came down and stood in front of the hall with Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing. They saw the Taoist master thrashing in the rolling oil pan, unable to climb out. He slipped in a moment, and in an instant his bones came apart, his skin was scorched, and his flesh turned rotten.

The officer in charge of executions came again to report: “Your Majesty, the Three-Realms Taoist master has also been boiled to death.” The king, tears spilling down his eyes, struck the imperial desk and wailed:

"A human body is hard to obtain, indeed hard; without true transmission one should not brew alchemy. Empty are charms that drive off gods and water-spells, with no Elixir of Longevity or life-preserving pills. In this perfect and mingling chaos, how can there be nirvana? By clever artifice alone one’s life finds no peace. Had I foreseen this cruel collapse so soon, why not have eaten in secret and settled in the mountains?" This is exactly: "What is gained by gilding and refining mercury from cinnabar? Summoning rain and wind is all in vain!"

In the end it was still unknown how Master Tripitaka and his disciples would manage, so let the next chapter resolve the matter.
chapters.title: Chapter 46: Heterodox force blusters against the true Dharma; the Mind-Monkey reveals its sanctity and destroys all evil.

Yet it is said that the king, leaning against the dragon bed, wept with tears streaming like a spring, crying without ceasing until evening. Sun Wukong stepped forward and shouted, “Why are you in such a daze? Look—the corpse of the Taoist: one was a tiger, one a deer, and the other from the sheep was a roe-antelope. If you do not believe it, haul up the bones and see; whose human has such a skull? He was a mountain beast that had become a demon spirit, and he came here in collusion to harm you. Seeing that your vigor was still strong, he did not dare to strike. If two more years pass and your fortune declines, he will kill you and your whole realm will belong to him. Lucky that we came in time; by removing this evil spirit we saved your life. Why do you still cry, why keep crying? Have a Guanwen sent at once and dispatch me out.” Hearing this, the king at last regained his senses. The civil and military officials all reported together: “The dead were indeed a white deer and a yellow tiger; what was in the oil pan was truly sheep bones. The holy monk’s words cannot be ignored.” The king said, “Since this is so, I thank the holy monk. The night is already deep,” and ordered, “Tai-shi, invite the holy monk first to Zhiyuan Temple. At the first morning audience tomorrow, open the East Hall, and tell Guanglu Temple to prepare a pure banquet in thanks.” He was then sent to the temple and put up for the night.

At first watch the next morning, the king held court, gathered many officials, and issued an edict: “Immediately print the monk-invitation edict and post it at the four gates and every road.” In one side hall a grand feast was laid out. He prepared the carriage after court, went to the gate of Zhiyuan Temple, invited Tripitaka and the others, and together they entered the East Hall for the banquet. Not repeated here.

The rescued monks who heard of the monk-invitation edict each rejoiced and entered the city to seek Great Sage Sun Wukong, bringing their hairs as gratitude. After the abbot dismissed the banquet, the king changed the Guanwen and, with the empress, consorts, and both civil and military ministers, sent everyone out the gate. There the monks knelt along the roadside and said, “Great Sage, we are the monks saved from the riverside. We heard you swept away the demon and rescued us, and we know our king has posted a bulletin inviting monks. We have come to offer our hairs in thanks for heavenly grace.” Sun Wukong smiled, “How many of you have come?” They said, “Five hundred, not one less.” Sun Wukong gave his body a shake and collected the hairs. He said to king and ministers, monks and layfolk, “These monks were truly released by me. I drove their vehicles myself, and the cart paths were torn and crushed apart on the ridges. I also killed those two demon-priests. Now that the evil is destroyed, you have learned the Chan way has true power. Hereafter, do not act in heedless credulity. See to it that the Three Teachings are joined: honor monks, honor the Dao, and nurture worthy talent. I shall guard your realm in permanence.” The king, following his words, was in endless gratitude, and so he sent Tripitaka out of the city.

From this departure onward, Tripitaka, with sincerity and earnestness, labored in single-minded cultivation. He walked by dawn and stayed by night, drank when thirsty and ate when hungry; before he knew it, spring had passed and summer had waned, and the weather had turned to autumn. One day evening came, and Tripitaka reined in his horse and asked, “Disciple, where shall we rest tonight?” Sun Wukong said, “Master, a monk ought not to speak in terms of householders.” Tripitaka asked, “How do householders do it? How do we, as monks, do it?” Sun Wukong answered, “Householders at this hour lie on warm beds with warm quilts, a child in the arms, a wife at their feet, and sleep freely. How can we do that? We, as ordained men, follow moonlight and wear starlight, eat wind and sleep by water, walking wherever there is a road and resting only when there is none. Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, you consider only one side and not the other. The road is rugged now. I carry the heavy load; truly it is hard to go on. We must find a place to stop, sleep a while, and recover our strength, else I may collapse.” Sun Wukong said, “By the moonlight we can walk a bit farther and stay at some house when we reach one.” With no remedy, the disciples followed Wukong onward.

Not long after, they heard the sound of surging waves. Zhu Bajie said, “Enough, the road seems at its end.” Sha Wujing said, “It is a body of water blocking us.” Tripitaka asked, “How can we cross?” Zhu Bajie said, “Let me test it. I will see whether it is shallow or deep.” Tripitaka said, “Wuneng, do not speak carelessly. How is it that you can test depth?” Zhu Bajie said, “Find a goose-egg-sized stone and throw it in. If bubbles rise up, it is shallow; if it sinks with a sound, it is deep.” Sun Wukong said, “Go and try.” The fool took a stone, cast it into the water, and hearing the stone sink with fish-like splashing all the way to the bottom, he said, “Deep—deep and deep. It cannot be crossed.” Tripitaka said, “Though you have measured the depth, you do not know how wide it is.” Zhu Bajie said, “This part, I do not know.” Sun Wukong said, “I will look.” Great Sage then opened a jindou cloud and leapt into the air, fixing his gaze. He saw:

Expansive light soaked the moon, and vast reflections floated in the sky. A spirit-channel swallowed Huashan, long flow runs through a hundred rivers. A thousand tiers of fierce waves rolled, ten-thousand-ridged steep crests tumbled. No fishing fires at the bank; on the sandbank a heron slept. All was in a daze, like the sea, and as far as one could look there was no farther shore. He hurriedly gathered the cloud head and came down at the riverbank, saying, “Master, it is wide, so wide—cannot be passed! By my Fire-Eyed Golden Pupils, on a bright day I can often see a thousand li; at night, even three or five hundred li. Even now I cannot see the far bank—how could I determine the measure of its width?”

Tripitaka was greatly shocked; he could not speak, and his voice choked as he said, “Disciple, what now is this?” Sha Wujing said, “Master, do not cry. Look there by the water’s edge— is that not a person?” Sun Wukong said, “It must be a fisherman with seine ropes. Let me go and ask.” He took up the iron staff, ran two or three paces forward to where it appeared, and looked—and it was not a person. It was a stone stele. On the stele were three large seal-script characters, and below, ten small characters in two lines. The three large ones were “Tongtian River,” and the ten smaller ones read, “Across eight hundred li, from ancient times only a few men have crossed.” Sun Wukong called out, “Master, come and see.” Tripitaka, seeing it, wept and said, “Disciple, when I left Chang’an I only said in my mind that the Western Heaven was easy to reach. Who knew demons would block the way and the mountains and rivers stand so far apart?”

Zhu Bajie said, “Master, listen, whose drum-and-clapper is that? It seems to be a household making an offering. Let us go and get some offering meal; we can ask for a ford and a boat, and cross tomorrow.” Tripitaka immediately heard it and indeed there was the sound of drum and clappers: “Not Daoist instruments—that is our monastic music. Let us go there.” Sun Wukong led with the horse, and they followed the sound. There was no true road, high or low, only a stretch across the sandbank. They saw a cluster of dwellings, around four or five hundred households, and all were well kept. They looked:

A path runs by the hills and along the bank by the stream. Shutters of thorn-wood are closed everywhere; every house has bamboo courts shut fast. On the sandbank, resting herons keep their dreamlike calm; beyond the willows, calls sound with cold, strained throats. No short flute is heard; the cold stone-beat of the house-shackle is out of tune. Red amaranth branches shake in the moon; yellow reeds clash with the wind. Village dogs bark at the road, through sparse hedges; at the ferry an old fisher sleeps in his boat. The lamps are few, human breath is still, and in the half sky the bright moon hangs like a mirror. Suddenly came a waft of white-watercress fragrance, carried by the west wind across the opposite bank.

Tripitaka dismounted. He saw by the roadside a house with a banner set upright outside its gate, with bright lamps glowing within and rich incense smoke. Tripitaka said, “Wukong, this place is not like that mountain hollow by the riverbank. In a household under a roof one can avoid the cold dew and sleep at peace. You all stay away; let me first go to that alms-house gate and request a night’s lodging. If he allows me, I will summon you. If he does not, do not show your despair. Your faces are ugly and your mouths disfiguring; only for fear of frightening the people and bringing trouble, you would be left without shelter.” Sun Wukong said, “That is reasonable. Please go first, Master; we will wait here.”

The abbot then took off his travel hat, bared his head, shook out his damp robe, and dragged his staff, and went straight to the gate of the house. Seeing the gate half open, half closed, Tripitaka did not dare enter uninvited. After standing there awhile, he saw a man come out from inside: an old one with beads at his neck, chanting “Amitābha Buddha,” who came himself to close the gate. Startled, the monk pressed his palms together and cried out, “Benevolent elder, this poor monk sends his greetings.” The old man replied with courtesy, “Monk, you have come too late.” Tripitaka asked, “How do you mean?” The old man said, “If you come late, there is nothing left. If you had come earlier, my place would have fed monks to their fill—cooked rice three measures, a piece of white cloth, ten wen in copper coins. Why do you only come now?” Tripitaka bowed and said, “Elder, this poor monk is not a guest hurrying to a feast.” The old man said, “If you are not hurrying to a feast, why come here?” Tripitaka said, “I am Tripitaka, the Great Tang envoy sent westward to obtain the scriptures. I have reached your place tonight, and the day is already ending. I heard drum-and-clapper sounds from your house and came to ask for one night’s lodging; at dawn I will depart.” The old man shook his hand and said, “Monk, ordained men should never lie. From the Great Tang to here is fifty-four-thousand li. How could one as you come all alone?” Tripitaka said, “Elder, your words are most apt. Yet I still have three young disciples. They make a road through mountains, lay bridges over waters, and protect the poor monk, so that I could arrive here.” The old man said, “If you have disciples, why did they not come with you?” and said, “Please, please—I have a place in my house for you to rest.” Tripitaka turned back and called, “Disciple, come this way.”

Sun Wukong was by nature impatient; Zhu Bajie was born rough; and Sha Wujing was likewise blunt and reckless. When the three heard their master Tripitaka call, they grabbed the horse and the shoulder-pole, ignored all good order, and, like a sudden wind, charged straight in. The old man saw them and, terrified, fell to the ground, crying only, "It’s a demon! A demon is coming!" Tripitaka helped him up, saying, "Good sir, do not fear. They are not demons—they are my disciples." The old man, still trembling, said, "Such a handsome and worthy master—how did he come to have such ugly disciples?" Tripitaka said, "Though their looks are not pleasing, they can still suppress dragons and tame tigers, seize monsters and capture demons." The old man, as if not fully believing, guided Tripitaka inside slowly.

The three ferocious, unruly men then burst into the hall, tied up the horse, and dropped their baggage. In the hall were already several monks chanting scripture when Zhu Bajie, thrusting out his huge mouth, called out, "Monks, what scripture are you chanting?" The monks heard him and all suddenly looked up:

Watching the newcomers, long were their mouths, broad their ears. The frame was stout, the shoulders broad; their voices thundered. Sun Wukong and Sha Wuking, their faces were even uglier. In the hall no one among the monks there was not afraid. Though the reciter should have continued, the one in front ordered the chanting to stop. They could not mind the bell and clappers; even the Buddha images were tossed aside. All at once they blew out the lamps, and the light scattered in startled flares. They stumbled and scrambled; who had ever crossed the doorway? Your head strikes mine, like a tumbled gourd rack. The clear Dharma hall has become a grand farce. Those three brothers, seeing those people stumbling and crawling, clapped and laughed aloud. The monks grew all the more frightened, knelt and struck their heads on the ground, each guarding his life, and fled away.

Tripitaka supported the old man and walked up into the hall. There was no light at all; the three were still laughing and snickering. Tripitaka scolded, "You wild brutes, this is too improper. Morning and evening I have taught you, every day I have reminded you. As the ancients said: 'If one is good without instruction, what does that make one—a saint? If one becomes good only after instruction, what does that make one—a sage? If instruction does not make one good, what does that make one but a fool?' In this way you rush in with such abandon, you frightened down the old benefactor, scattered the reciting monks, and ruined the household’s good rites. Are you not making me bear the sin?" No one dared to answer. The old man then believed at last that they were indeed his disciples, and hurriedly turned and bowed, saying, "My lord, it is no great matter. We had just put out the lamps, scattered the flowers; the ritual is about to conclude as well." Zhu Bajie said, "If the arrangements are done, set out all the dishes and fetch wine and food. We’ll eat and then sleep." The host called, "Bring the lamps, bring the lamps." Those in the household, hearing him, were startled and alarmed: "In the hall a scripture was being chanted with many incense candles. How can you again ask for lamps?" Several servant lads came out to see. The place was black and dark. Even when they lit torches and lanterns and came in a crowd, when they looked up and saw Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, panic made them drop the torches, and they quickly pulled back and shut the inner door, crying inside, "A demon! A demon!"

Sun Wukong picked up a torch, lit the candles, pulled over a chair, and asked Tripitaka to sit on it; his brothers sat at his sides while the old host sat in front. Just as they were taking their seats, from within the inner door another old man came out leaning on a cane and asked, "What evil spirit is this, to come in my good-household at night?" The old host seated in front sprang up and hurried behind the screen to meet him: "Brother, do not shout. It is not an evil spirit, but an arhat from Great Tang of the East travelling to fetch the scriptures. Though the disciples’ looks are fierce, truly good men can wear cruel faces." Then that host set down his cane, bowed with the four of them, and after the salutes were done also sat in front. "Bring tea. Lay out the fasting rite," he said. He called several times, but the servants, trembling, dared not approach in a group.

Zhu Bajie could not hold back and asked, "Old sir, why do you serve this formal reception from both sides like this?" The host said, "I told them to bring and present the offering to serve my lord." Zhu Bajie said, "How many people serving?" The host said, "Eight." Zhu Bajie said, "Those eight serving whom?" The host said, "They are to serve the four of you." Zhu Bajie said, "That white-faced master needs only one, the shaggy-faced thunder-mouthed one needs only two, the unlucky-faced one needs eight. For me I would need twenty attendants to be enough." The host said, "To speak that way, it seems your appetite is large." Zhu Bajie said, "It is all right if it can pass." The host said, "There are people, there are people," and by calling, had three or four dozen—about seven big and eight small—come out.

After some question-and-answer between the monks and the host, everyone at last stopped fearing. They then laid out one table at the main place and asked Tripitaka to sit there; three tables were placed on each side for his three companions; one table in front was set for the two elders. They first served simple fruits, prepared produce and vegetables, then noodles, rice, light vegetarian snacks, and starch soup, all arranged neat and in order. Tripitaka the elder raised his chopsticks and first chanted through one fascicle of the Sutra of Opening the Fast. Zhu Bajie, both anxious to gulp and somewhat hungry, did not wait for Tripitaka to finish the text. He took a red lacquered wooden bowl, thrust one bowl of white rice straight into his mouth in one motion, and ate it at once. A small servant nearby said, "My lord, you’re all wrong in your calculations. Without even holding the rice in your hands, how did you get it into your mouth without soiling your clothes?" Zhu Bajie laughed. "I did not hold it before my mouth; I already ate it." The servant insisted, "You did not even lift your mouth. How could you have eaten then?" Zhu Bajie said, "Children lie when they say no. I certainly ate it. If you do not believe me, eat again so you can see." The servants again brought another bowl and gave one bowl to Zhu Bajie. The fellow gave one swift toss and swallowed it. The household staff exclaimed, "Master! Your throat is as if built of ground brick—so smooth, so slippery!" Before Tripitaka had even finished one entire scripture, Zhu Bajie had already swallowed five or six bowls. Only then did they together raise their chopsticks and eat in unison. Zhu Bajie, whether rice, noodles, fruit, or snacks, simply scooped everything at once and ate in a messy rush, still shouting from his mouth, "Pass more. Pass more rice." Little by little, he was gone from sight, as if none came back. Sun Wukong called, "You prudent brother, eat less. Better to bear hunger in a mountain hollow and be only half-full." Zhu Bajie said, "As the saying goes: 'A fasting monk who is not full might as well be buried alive.'" Sun Wukong said, "Wind down the household fire, and do not bother with him." The two elders, bowing, said, "Let us not hide the truth from your lordship. In broad daylight we are not afraid. Even this broad-bellied elder could fast for a hundred or ten more. But it is late. We had just finished the final offerings, steaming only one shi of flour-rice, five dou of grain rice, and a few tables of vegetarian fare. We were to invite a few neighbors and all the monks to distribute merit. Unexpectedly you arrived; frightened, all the monks ran off, and even the neighbors did not dare come near. So we have offered everything to you all. If you are still not full, we can steam more." Zhu Bajie said, "Steam more, steam more."

After that, they cleared the domestic fire and tables. Tripitaka knelt and thanked the host for the offering, then asked, "Good benefactor, what is your surname?" The host said, "Chen." Tripitaka joined his palms and said, "I am this poor Tripitaka, from the Hua ancestral line." The host said, "My lord is also surname Chen?" Tripitaka said, "Yes. At home, in secular life too, I was a Chen. May I ask: what kind of fasting rite was this just now?" Zhu Bajie laughed, "Why ask him, master? Surely it was Qingmiao Zhai, Ping’an Zhai, or some Liaozhang Zhai, wasn’t it?" The host said, "No, no." Tripitaka asked again, "Then what exactly was it?" The host answered, "It was a preparatory dead-ancestor zhai, to be offered beforehand." Zhu Bajie laughed so hard he nearly collapsed and said, "Good sir, your discernment is poor. We are kings at stitching lies into bridges to dupe people. How could you deceive us with this lie? Do monks not know ritual matters? There are only pre-repair Grain Storehouse zhai and pre-repayment zhai. Where is a 'preparatory dead zhai'? No one in your house has died. Why hold a dead rite?"

Wukong, hearing this, inwardly rejoiced and said, “This fool has become a bit sensible. —Old grandfather, you have spoken wrongly. What is called ‘Yuxiu Wangzhai’?” The two elders inclined themselves and said, “You are taking the Journey, so why did you not walk the proper road and end up at my place?” Wukong replied, “We were on the proper road. We saw a surge of water blocking our way and could not cross. Hearing the sound of drums and cymbals, we came to your estate to seek lodging.” The elder asked, “When you came to the riverbank, did you see anything?” Wukong said, “Only one stone stele, with the three characters ‘Tongtian River’ above it, and beneath it, in ten characters, ‘Directly passes eight hundred li; through all ages few have walked this path.’ No other thing.” The elder said, “Go farther up the bank and look; only about a li from that stele there is a temple of King Linggan. Did you not see it?” Wukong said, “I did not. Please tell me, what is Linggan?” The two elders together wept and said, “Sir, that Great King:

By one response a temple is raised in a region, his mighty spirit aids the people for a thousand li. Year after year he sends sweet rain on the manor; year after year festive clouds fall on the village. Wukong said, “Sweet rain and falling festive clouds—those are fine. Yet why are you all so sorrowful and distressed?” The old man stamped his feet, struck his chest, and cried out, “Sir, Though grace is great, there is also grievance; though compassionate and benevolent, he still hurts people. Only because he must eat boys and girls; he is not a plainly manifest upright god.” Wukong said, “He must eat boys and girls?” The elder said, “Exactly so.” Wukong said, “So your turn must have come, then?” The elder said, “This year it has come to our house. A hundred families live here. This place lies in Yuanhui County of the land of Chechi, called Chen Family Hamlet. This Great King holds his sacrifice-fair once a year and must be offered one boy and one girl, together with pigs and sheep and sacrificial wine. He eats once, and he keeps us with timely winds and rain; if we do not hold the rite, he brings misfortune and disaster.” Wukong asked, “How many sons do you have in your household?” The elder beat his chest and said, “Poor me! Poor me! To ask of sons makes me ashamed. This is my younger brother, called Chen Qing. Old Jun is called Chen Cheng. I am sixty-three this year, he is fifty-eight, and all our children are in hardship. From age fifty onward I had no son. My kin advised me to take a concubine; unable to refuse, I took another wife, who bore a daughter, just eight this year, named Yicengjin.” Bajie said, “What an expensive name. Why is she called Yicengjin?” The elder said, “I keep only difficult household accounts: repairing bridges, mending roads, building temples and stupas, giving alms to monks. There are ledgers for all this. One time it is three taels, another time five taels. But when a daughter is born, her cost equals thirty catties of gold. Thirty catties make one scale; therefore she is called Yicengjin.” Wukong asked, “And that one’s son?” The elder said, “My younger brother has a son as well, a troublesome one, seven years old, named Chen Guanbao.” Wukong asked, “Why that name?” The elder said, “At home we make offerings to Lord Guan; under Lord Guan’s seat we obtained this son, so we named him Guanbao. My brother and I together are one hundred and two years old and have only these two descendants. We did not expect the sacrifice turn to come to my house, and therefore we cannot dare not offer. Thus the father-son bond is hard to cut and hard to give up. So first we prepare a merit-field rite for the boy. Therefore this is called ‘Yuxiu Wangzhai.’"

Tripitaka heard this and could not keep the tears from welling down his cheeks: “This is exactly what the ancients said: ‘The yellow plum does not fall while the green plum does; Heaven in its partiality harms men with no sons.’ Wukong laughed, “Let me ask him one more thing. Old grandfathers, how much is your household estate?” The two elders said, “Somewhat much: four or five dozen mu of wet fields, six or seven dozen mu of dry fields, eight or nine dozen pasture lots; two or three hundred water buffalo, twenty or thirty donkeys and horses, and countless pigs, sheep, chickens, and geese. At home there is even spare grain we cannot eat and clothes we cannot wear. Our property and holdings are all, as one might reckon, fully counted.” Wukong said, “With such a family estate, you seem to have been very economical in saving it.” The elder said, “How do you see me as economical?” Wukong said, “Since you have this private property, how can you bring yourself to offer away your own sons and daughters? For fifty taels of silver you could buy one boy-child; for one hundred taels you could buy one girl-child. Even if it did not pass two hundred taels in all, is it not better to keep one’s own children and descendants?” The two elders wept, one with the other, “Sir, you do not know. That Great King is most numinous; he often comes walking among our houses.” Wukong said, “When he comes walking, what does he look like? How great or short is his figure?” The elders said, “We do not see his form at all. We only smell one rush of fragrant wind and know at once that the Great King has arrived. We then quickly fill a full bucket of incense and offer it to the smoke. Young and old alike, hearing the wind, kneel and bow. Whatever is ours, from large bowls to little bowls, he knows. He remembers the exact year and month of each child’s birth. He only takes naturally born sons and daughters. Do not say he cannot be bought with two or three hundred taels; even if one had thousands or millions in taels, one cannot buy children of this exact same month and year, perfectly alike.”

Wukong said, “Very well, then. Bring out your son-child at once and let me see him.” Chen Qing hurried inside and brought Guanbao out into the hall and set him before the lamp. The boy, unaware of life and death, held two fists full of fruit in his sleeves and danced about, eating and playing. Wukong saw him, silently recited a spell, and in a turning of his body transformed into the exact form of Guanbao. The two boys held hands and danced before the lamp. Terrified, the old man hastened and knelt in haste. Tripitaka said, “Sir, this is not a true son, not a true son.” The old man said, “This master suddenly speaks, and yet has changed into the form of my son. He calls out once and both children answer and move alike. He has ruined our years of life. Please show your original form; please show your original form.” Wukong wiped his face with a hand and returned to his true form. The old man knelt before him and said, “Sir, now I see what you truly can do.” Wukong laughed and said, “Do you look like your son?” The old man said, “Like, like, like—exactly the same face, exactly the same voice, exactly the same clothing, exactly the same height.” Wukong said, “You have not looked closely enough. Bring a scale and weigh. Is he the same weight as your son?” The elder said, “Yes, yes, yes—exactly the same weight.” Wukong said, “Can this be accepted for the rite?” The elder said, “Too good, too good. It can be offered as sacrifice.”

Wukong said, “I will now offer my life in place of this child’s and leave your household line and incense to continue. I shall go to make the sacrifice to that Great King.” Chen Qing knelt and prostrated himself, saying, “If your kindness is truly compassion, I will send one thousand taels of silver with Tripitaka for him to carry westward.” Wukong said, “Will you not at least thank old Sun?” The elder said, “You have already replaced the sacrifice; if I lose you, what then?” Wukong said, “How can that be losing you?” The elder said, “The Great King has already eaten him.” Wukong said, “Would he dare eat me?” The elder said, “He will not eat you. He says, as a matter of honesty, you are too fishy-smelling.” Wukong laughed, “Let Heaven’s command take its course. If he eats me, my life is short; if he does not, that is my destiny. I am going with you to the rite.”

Chen Qing kept on kneeling and giving thanks, and again offered to send five hundred taels of silver. But Chen Cheng neither knelt nor gave thanks; he only leaned against the screen gate and wept in pain. Wukong understood and came up, held him, and said, “Elder brother, because you do not bow to me, do not thank me—you are because you cannot bear to part with your daughter, are you not?” Chen Cheng only then knelt and said, “Yes, I cannot bear to. With your great favor, it is enough that you have saved my nephew. But I, old and without sons, have only this one daughter. When I die, her crying will be most intense. How can I let her go?” Wukong said, “Quickly steam rice from five dou of grain and prepare fine vegetarian dishes to feed my long-nosed Master. Have him transform into your daughter; my brothers and I will go together for the sacrifice. Let us carry out a yin-zhi stratagem and save the lives of both your son and your daughter. Why not?”

Hearing these words, Bajie was inwardly startled and said, “Brother, you would work your magic and, whether I live or die, you still drag me into it.” Wukong said, “Eldest brother, it is said, ‘A chicken does not eat food gained without labor.’ You and I have entered this house and received this fine offering; how can you say you are not full, yet refuse to save others in their distress?” Bajie said, “Brother, in things of transformation, I cannot do such things.” Wukong said, “You also have thirty-six kinds of transformation; how is this one beyond you?” Tripitaka said, “Wuneng, your elder brother speaks most truly and suitably. It is said, ‘To save one life is better than building a seven-tiered pagoda.’ First, there is deep gratitude for this kindness; second, it gathers hidden merit in virtue; besides, on this cool night, you have no business, so let you two brothers go and play a little.” Bajie said, “You hear what the Master says. I can only transform into mountains, trees, stones, a leprous elephant, a water buffalo, or a large fat man, and that is all. To transform into a little daughter would be difficult.”

Sun Wukong said, “Eldest Brother, do not trust him. Bring out your cherished child and show her.” Chen Cheng hurried inside, carried out the child so precious he seemed worth a scale of gold, and came to the hall. All the wives and concubines of the household, old and young, from inside and outside alike, came out, knelt, and bowed, pleading only for the child’s life to be spared. The girl wore on her head a flower-green circlet of jade and silk with eight treasures and hanging pearl strands; on her body a red-and-yellow woolen jacket, over it a dark-green satin cloak with a board-like, checkered collar; at her waist a broad red floral silk skirt; on her feet a pair of light-red felt shoes with toad-head fronts; on her legs a pair of gauze-gold knee-breeches. She was also holding fruit and eating it. Sun Wukong said, “Zhu Bajie, this is the girl. Change to match her at once; we are going to the sacrifice.” Zhu Bajie said, “Elder Brother, how could I become one so tiny and handsome?” Sun Wukong said, “Hurry. Do not start an argument.” Zhu Bajie, in a panic, said, “Brother, do not hit me. Let me change and then see.”

Zhu Bajie spoke a spell, shook his head a few times, and cried, “Transform!” When he changed, he did look like the girl’s face, but his belly was still large and he did not look like a proper fellow. Sun Wukong laughed, “Change again.” Zhu Bajie said, “With your spell it still will not transform fully—what can I do?” Sun Wukong said, “Have you somehow made a maid’s head onto a monk’s body? You’ve made him neither male nor female. How is that right? Raise your vital force at once.” He blew one breath of immortal qi at him, and at once the boy changed to exactly match the child. Then he instructed, “The two elders, take your treasured household and your son and daughter inside—make no mistake. Soon my brother and I will slip in and play, so he cannot recognize us at once. Give him the good fruit to eat and do not let him cry out, lest the Great King suddenly perceive and take the wind and flee. Wait until my brother and me finish our little antics.”

Then this Great Sage told Sha Wujing to protect Tripitaka: “I will become Chen Guanbao, and Zhu Bajie will become a one-scale-gold boy.” The two were arranged, but he asked, “How will the offering be done? Will he be taken by tying and bundling? Or tied and brought away? Will he be steamed, or chopped into pieces?” Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, do not do this to me. I have no such skill.” The old man said, “No, no. Just use two red-lacquered cinnabar trays. Ask you two to sit inside the trays, place them on the table, and have two young men carry each table and carry you up to the temple.” Sun Wukong said, “Fine, fine, fine—bring out the trays, and let us try.” The old man immediately brought out the two cinnabar trays, and Sun Wukong and Zhu Bajie sat on them. Four young men lifted the two tables, carried them around into the courtyard, then carried them back and set them in the hall. Sun Wukong said joyfully, “Zhu Bajie, if we keep walking and joking about like this, we are no different from temple-platform monks.” Zhu Bajie said, “If they carry us out and carry us back, and carry us from one end to the other till dawn, I am not afraid. But if they carry us into the temple, then they are going to eat us. This is not play.” Sun Wukong said, “You only watch me. When it is my turn to be eaten, then you can go.” Zhu Bajie said, “Who knows how he eats? If he eats a boy first, I can run; if he eats a girl first, what then?” The old man said, “At the annual sacrifice, I always have a brave fool hiding behind the temple or under the offering table, and he has seen him eat the boy first and then the girl.” Zhu Bajie said, “Fate, fate.”

Just while the brothers were in the middle of this talk, they heard outside the crashing din of gongs and drums, torches flaring with light. The household folk opened the front gate and called, “Bring out the boy and the girl.” The old man began to weep and sob, and the four young men carried the two of them outside.

At this point, no one yet knows how their lives will end. Listen to how it is resolved in the next chapter.
