This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

In Chen Family Village, all the believers came together, bringing the sacrificial pig, sheep, and wine, and with Sun Wukong and Zhu Bajie they made such a loud uproar as they carried everything straight into Linggan Temple and set it out, placing the boy and girl first. Wukong turned and saw upon the offering altar the incense, flowers, and candles, and directly in front a gilt plaque with the words “Great King Linggan,” with no other deity image at all. When the believers had arranged themselves in order, they all knelt and bowed toward the tablet and recited: “Great King, this year, this month, this day, this hour, we of Chen Family Village, with Chen Cheng leading the sacrificial host and all the believers present, leave no name uncounted, and carefully keep to the annual rite, offering one boy named Chen Guanbao and one girl named Chen Yichenjin, and the pig-and-sheep and wine in proper amount, for your honored enjoyment. Protect us that wind and rain be in balance and the five grains prosper abundantly.” When the prayer was done they burned paper horses, and everyone went back to his own house; no further account is needed.

After the people dispersed, Zhu Bajie told Wukong, “Let us go home.” Sun Wukong asked, “Where is your home?” Zhu Bajie said, “We are going to old Chen’s place to sleep.” Wukong said, “You fool, you are babbling nonsense again. Since you gave your consent, you must fulfill this vow with him.” Zhu Bajie replied, “You are no fool yourself, yet you call me one. If only we could trick him and amuse him for a while, why treat this as a true sacrifice?” Wukong said, “One must be true and complete in conduct. We must surely wait until that Great King eats first; only then is it full and proper from beginning to end. Otherwise he may bring down calamity and harm us, which would be an ugly end.”

As they were speaking, there came a roaring sound of wind. Zhu Bajie said, “This is bad; that wind means the voice is arriving.” Wukong only said, “No more words. Let me answer.” In a moment a demon stood at the temple gate. Look at what he was like:

His new golden armor and gold helmet flashed with brilliance. Eyes shone like evening stars, white and clear. His teeth stood in rows like stacked saw edges. Beneath his feet, clouds of mist drifted and swayed. Around him hung warm drifting vapors. As he moved, he sent wave after wave of cold, piercing wind; where he stood, rank after rank of ominous energy was hot to the touch. He seemed like a gate spirit lifting a drawn curtain to steer a cart, like the great guardian at a temple gate. That monster blocked the gate and asked, “Which household is making sacrifice this year?” Wukong answered with a smiling countenance, “In answer to your inquiry, the head households are of Chen Cheng and the Chen Qing line.” Hearing this, the monster in his heart seemed doubtful: “This boy is bold, his tongue is witty. Those who come to offer and be fed often, when asked, do not speak at first; ask again and their souls freeze in fright; if one reaches out to seize them, they are already dead. How is it that today this boy answers so well?” The demon did not dare to seize him, and asked again, “What are the names of the boy and girl?” Wukong smiled, “The boy is Chen Guanbao; the girl is Chen Yichenjin.” The demon said, “This sacrifice has been the old custom for years past. I usually receive the offering here, but this year I will eat you.” Wukong said, “I do not dare to refuse; please take your freedom to use it.” Hearing this, the demon still dared not act. He blocked the gate and shouted, “Do not talk back. I usually eat the boy first; this year I will take the girl first.” Zhu Bajie panicked, “Great King, keep the old custom and do not spoil the precedent.”

The monster would not allow further words. He stretched out his hand and tried to seize Zhu Bajie. The fool leapt down, revealed his true form, drew the nail-mace, and in one motion struck. The monster withdrew his hand and moved forward; a single ringing ‘clang’ sounded. Zhu Bajie said, “His armor has been split.” Wukong also revealed his true form and saw, on close sight, two fish scales as large as ice dishes. He shouted, “Pursue.” The two leapt into the air. The demon, who had come to attend the rite and had brought no weapon, stood in the clouds and asked with empty hands, “You monks, from what place? To come here and trouble people, break my incense offerings, and ruin my reputation?” Wukong said, “That ruffian did not know. We are disciples of Tripitaka, the Sacred Monk of the Great Tang of the East, sent by imperial command to go west in pursuit of the Buddha’s teaching. Last night we lodged at the house in Chen Village and heard of an evil spirit that, under the false title of Linggan, each year demands child and maiden sacrifices. Out of compassion for sentient beings, we have caught this rogue. Now speak truthfully and quickly: each year you eat two children here; how many years have you called yourself Great King? How many boys and girls have you eaten? Return them one by one to me, and I may spare you from death.” The demon heard this and left. Zhu Bajie struck again with the nail-mace but did not land a hit; the demon raised a whirl of violent wind and plunged into the Tongtian River.

Wukong said, “No need to chase him now. This demon is a thing of the waters. Tomorrow we will find a way to seize him and then take my master across the river.” Zhu Bajie followed this and went straight back to the temple, moving the sacrificial pigs and sheep and wine, and the whole offering table, over to Chen’s house. At this time Tripitaka and Sha Wujing, with the Chen brothers, were waiting in the hall for the ritual. Suddenly they saw the two of them throw the pigs, sheep, and sacrificial goods into the courtyard. Tripitaka came and asked, “Wukong, how went the sacrifice offering?” Wukong recounted how he had called out the name and chased the demon, who had dived into the river. Both elders were greatly pleased and immediately ordered the side room swept and the beds arranged, and invited their master and disciples to retire for the night. No further matter is recorded.

The demon returned by command and went back into the water, sitting in his palace in silence. The water-clans asked, “Great King, every year when you enjoy the rite you return in joy. Why are you anxious today?” He said, “After each annual feast I usually return with some remnants for you to share. Today I myself have not even had a bite. Misfortune has struck; I met a rival and nearly lost my life.” The waterfolk asked, “Great King, who was it?” The demon said, “It was a disciple of a sacred monk from Great Tang in the East, one going west to worship the Buddha and seek scriptures, who feigned boy and girl and sat at the temple. When he showed his true form, he nearly injured my life. I have heard people say that Tripitaka is a man of great cultivation across ten lifetimes, and that to eat one piece of him brings prolonged life and long span. Who would have expected such a disciple under him? I have ruined my incense and broken my name. I meant to seize Tripitaka, but I fear I may not be able to do it.”

Among the water clan there flashed forth a mottled-clothed guipo woman, who knelt in a few measured bows and smilingly said, “If Great King wants to seize Tripitaka, what difficulty is there? But if he is caught, can you reward me with some wine and meat?” The demon said, “If you have a plan, let us together use our strength and seize Tripitaka. If you do, I will adopt you as brother and sister and we shall share together.” The guipo bowed and answered, “I have long known that Great King has the power to summon wind and rain and the might to stir sea and river. Yet I wonder, can he bring down snow?” The demon said, “I can.” The guipo asked, “If you can bring snow, can you make it cold and freeze?” The demon said, “Even more, I can.” She clapped and laughed, “Then it is easy, easy indeed.” The demon said, “Now tell me this easy art and I will listen.” She said, “Tonight it is the hour of the third watch. Great King need not delay; do the rite at once, raise a cold wind and send a great snowfall, letting the entire Tongtian River freeze through. Send us shapeshifters to take human forms at the road crossing—backpacks on our shoulders, umbrellas in our hands, pushing handcarts—constantly walking upon the ice. Tripitaka is in a hurry to fetch scriptures; seeing such people, he will surely step onto the ice and cross. Great King, silently sit in midstream. When you hear the sound of their footsteps, split the hard ice and make him and his disciples together plunge into the water; one shout is enough.” The demon heard this and was fully delighted: “Wondrous, wondrous indeed.” He then left his water court, rose into the open sky, raised wind and snow, and formed the cold into ice. No more is recorded.

Later Tripitaka and his three disciples rested at Chen’s house. Near dawn they lay cold, chilled and cramped beneath pillows. Zhu Bajie could not sleep, coughing and singing, and called out, “Senior brother, it is cold.” Wukong said, “You blockhead, you are too soft. As one who has left home, heat and cold do not affect us—why fear the cold?” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, it is truly cold. See, it is this:

The heavy quilt gives no warmth; with one’s arms folded it feels as though cradling ice. At this moment fallen leaves hang with frost at their buds; old pines wear hanging frozen bells. The ground cracks from the deep cold; the pond surface hardens into water-ice. A fisher boat is no longer seen; how can one meet a monk at a mountain temple? The woodcutter worries he has too little firewood; the lordly youth is glad his coals can increase. A soldier’s beard is like iron, a poet’s brush like a piece of ice crystal. A leather jacket still feels too thin; even a sable cloak is still too light. The monk on the cane mat is stiff and old; the paper screen startles like a traveling soul. Quilted bedding, heavy bolsters and cushions piled high—still the whole body shivers in tremors. All the disciples could not sleep, so they rose and put on clothing. They opened the gate and saw, to their amazement, that the outside was white and vast: it had begun snowing. Wukong said, “No wonder you called out the cold; it is snow like this.” All four looked at once and this was the snow they saw: Crimson clouds gathered thickly; dark mist sank and soaked the world. Crimson clouds gathered thickly, while the north wind howled piercingly through the emptiness. Dark mist drenched all, and snow in countless streams covered the ground. Truly, it was: six-petaled blossoms, each petal flying like ice jade. In a thousand old groves, each tree stood with each trunk carrying its own jewel. In a moment powder collected and within an instant it turned to salt. The white parakeet lost its pure hue, like the feathers of a white crane. It added the waters of a thousand rivers from Wu to Chu, pressing down several plum trees in the southeast. It seemed as if three million jade dragons had been driven back from battle; truly broken scales and ruined armor filled the sky. There was not a sign then of Dongguo Li, Yuan’an at rest, or Sun Kang reading by lamp-glow. Nor was one to see Ziyou Zhou, Wang Gongbi, and Su Wu dining on felt rugs. Travellers could hardly buy liquor, and gray-haired old men were in pain seeking plum blossom. Drifting and scattering, soft and clear, as if cut butterfly wings, and fluttering like torn goose feathers. Round and swelling, rolling with the wind, piling in layers and layers until the road was lost. Blasts of cold force pierced the small awnings, and the soughing chill seeped through quiet curtains. A fortunate blessing for a good harvest came down from heaven, a truly joyful omen for human affairs. That snow fell in scattered, flickering showers, truly like bits of cut jade and flying cotton.

The master and his disciples had amused themselves for quite some time, and then they saw old Chen of the household: he ordered two servant boys to clear the way, and two more to bring hot water for washing faces. In a moment more, he sent hot tea and milk-cakes and then heaped in coals. They all came to the side chambers and sat to talk. Tripitaka asked, "Householder, in your climate do you not distinguish the four seasons?" Old Chen laughed: "Though this is a remote place, customs and people here are not like the Central Kingdom. As for grain, seedlings, and livestock, all follow heaven and sun together. How can it be that there are not four seasons?" Tripitaka said, "If there is still such a difference of four seasons, then how is it that there is such great snow and such cold now?" Old Chen said, "Though it is now the month of July, yesterday we had already entered Bailu, already the eighth month. Here, through all these years, frost and snow come in August." Tripitaka said, "It is much different from my Eastern Country; where I come from, such things come only with Winter."

During the conversation another boy came with a word of courtesy to set the table and beg them to take porridge. After the porridge, the snow had deepened more than it had in the morning; in a little while there were nearly two feet of snow on level ground. Tripitaka grew anxious and tears welled. Old Chen said, "Do not worry, my lord—do not let the depth of snow trouble you. Under my roof I keep several thousand shi of grain; it can feed you and yours for half a lifetime." Tripitaka said, "Householder, you know not the hardship of this poor monk. In that former time, by Buddha’s grace I was given an edict and sent out in a grand carriage; the Tang emperor himself came to the frontier to see me off, holding aloft his hand with a cup in farewell and asking, ‘When can you return?’ I did not know the dangers of mountains and streams and, offhand, answered: ‘In only three years, I shall fetch the scriptures and return.’ Since our parting, seven or eight full years have passed, yet still I have not beheld the Buddha. I fear that I have failed the sacred deadline; and I fear too the ferocity of demons and monsters. That is why I am so worried. By fate we came to dwell here in Yutan Prefecture; last night these foolish disciples offered a small kindness in return, hoping to obtain a boat and cross the river. But snow fell from the heavens; the roads are lost in white, and I do not know when I shall accomplish my task and return to my homeland." Old Chen said, "Do not fret, my lord. That was only a few days among the many years we must endure. We shall just wait for the weather to clear and the ice to melt. This poor old man will spend what he has and see to it that a boat is sent to take you across."

A servant came again to bring morning meal. After it was taken in the hall, and not long after the noon meal followed in turn. Tripitaka, seeing the dishes so plentiful, still grew uneasy: "You have graciously detained us; but only treat us as your household fare." Old Chen said, "My lord, for saving our lives by your kindness, though I set a tray each day and spread out refreshments, even so I can never hope to repay your gratitude."

Then one servant again brought the morning offering, and they all ate in the hall. Not long after came the noon offering as well. Tripitaka, seeing the richness of the foods, still said, "Since you have already treated us so hospitably, we may only ask to be received like ordinary members of your house." Old Chen said, "My lord, though I have shown you such favor in these days, I cannot ever thank you enough, though I set out a table every day and offer these humble dishes."

When there was no more to do among them, the company sat for a long while within the ice-cave room and spoke with the neighbors about the pilgrimage for the scriptures, then each drank tea. Old Chen asked, "Gentlemen, do any of you drink wine?" Tripitaka said, "The poor monk does not. My little disciples may take a few cups of dry white wine." Old Chen was greatly pleased and ordered, "Bring fruit fit for the table, warm some rice wine, and serve the gentlemen to warm the cold." The servant boys then brought a table to surround the brazier; each of the two neighboring elders drank a few cups, and the house fire was stirred to life.

The day’s light had not yet faded when they were once again invited to the hall for the evening meal. Then they heard people in the street all saying, "What a cold day this is—the Tongtian River is frozen over." Tripitaka said, "Wukong, if the river is frozen, what are we to do?" Old Chen said, "It grew suddenly cold, and suddenly chilly; likely only the shallow water near the riverside is frozen." One passerby said, "It is as if eight hundred li are frozen to a mirror's surface, and people can walk at the crossing." Hearing this, Tripitaka, who had said there were people walking, wanted to go and see. Old Chen said, "My lord, do not rush. It is already late today; we shall go look in the morning." He then dismissed the neighbors. After supper again they rested in the side chambers.

At dawn the next day, Pigsy rose and said, "Elder Brother, last night was even colder; surely the river is still frozen." Tripitaka faced the sky at the gate and offered prayer: "Great guardian deities, this disciple has come westward in devotion, keeping to Buddha through hardships in the mountains and rivers and not once uttering complaint. Now we have arrived here and by Heaven’s aid the river has set hard with ice. This poor disciple has only an empty-hearted thanks. When the scripture journey is fulfilled, I shall report to the Tang Emperor and repay with all my sincerity." After his prayer he instructed Wujing to saddle the horses and take them across the ice. Old Chen also said, "Do not hurry. Wait a few days for the snow to melt and the ice to break. This poor old man will arrange for a boat to send you over." Sha Wujing said, "To go would not be right, and to stay would not be right. What is heard has little weight; what is seen is better than hearsay. Let me load up the horse, and let the Master go and see for himself." Old Chen said, "That is true." He ordered, "Boys, quickly bring our six horses to bear. Do not bring Master Tripitaka’s own horse."

Then six little lads followed. The party went straight to the riverbank to look, and truly it was thus:

Snow heaped high like mountains and rising, the lifted dawn clouds made a clear morning. The cold congealed, the ridges of Chu lay gaunt with a thousand peaks, and river and lake were locked into one level plain. North wind bristled hard; the ice was slick and freezing, hard-edged. Fish in pools nestled in dense weeds; wild birds clung to dead timber. Soldiers of the frontier on the march all stumbled to a stop, while at the riverbank children beat out strange teeth. Serpent bellies split, birds’ feet broken—indeed, ice cliffs of a thousand feet. All the thousand ravines floated in silver, and the single river was steeped in jade-cold. From the east, even dormant silkworm cocoons came out stiff; in the north there were truly only rat-holes. Wang Xiang lay still, Guangwu crossed; in one night even the creek bridge was firm from bank to bottom. Curving marshes set in layered ice, and deep abysses stacked hard with frozen crust. Through the broad waters of Tongtian there were no waves at all; pure, white ice spread like a road of land.

When Tripitaka and the party came to the riverbank and loosed the horses to look, it was indeed true that people were walking on that way at the river mouth. Tripitaka asked, "Householder, where are those people going on the ice?" Old Chen said, "Across this river is the Nüguo of Xiliang. Those are all merchants. A good a hundred cash’s worth of goods from this side is worth ten thousand there; likewise, a hundred cash from that side is worth ten thousand here. When profit is heavier than life itself, people neglect life and death and go. In normal years each family sends five or seven in one boat, or ten or more in one boat, drifting across the far waters. Now that the river is frozen they dare abandon life and walk." Tripitaka said, "In this world, fame and profit are the heaviest matters of all. They who seek gain can forget life and death. As for my disciples, we bear this imperial order in absolute loyalty; we seek only renown, and how different can that be from them?" He told Wukong, "Quickly return to the house and have the baggage packed and the horses prepared, and while this thick ice holds, ride at once toward the Western Regions." Wukong answered with a playful smile.

Sha Wujing said, "Master, there is a saying: ‘Who spends a thousand days is given a thousand sheng of rice.’ Now that we still have shelter at the Chen household, let us stay a few more days and wait for clear weather, then let the ice melt and cross by boat. In this haste, mistakes are easily made." Tripitaka replied, "Wujing, what folly is this? If it were the proper second month, each day could warm by the next, and the ice might be waited out. This is the eighth month, when each day is colder than the one before; how can we expect a thaw at once? Would it not waste half a year of our journey?"

Pigsy jumped down from his horse. "Enough of idle talk. Let the old pig test how thick the ice is." Wukong said, "Bajie, you do not understand. Last night we tested the water by throwing stones; now the ice is thick and broad—how can it be tested so quickly?" Pigsy replied, "You, Elder Brother, do not understand. Let me take up the digging crowbar and strike. If it breaks through, then the ice is thin and we shall not dare to cross; if it will not break, then the ice is thick and we certainly can." Tripitaka said, "You speak truly." The piglet lifted his coat, tugged his step, went up to the bank, raised both hands with the crowbar, and with all his strength gave one great blow. There was a sharp crash; nine white marks were struck. His hands numbed and hurt from the impact. The piglet laughed, "It goes, it goes; even the river bottom is fast-frozen."

When Tripitaka heard this, he rejoiced greatly and, with everyone, returned to the Chen household, instructing that only provisions for the journey be prepared. The two elders could not hold him back and therefore arranged some dried food and roasted snacks, and made baked cakes and mo-mo to send with them. The whole family knelt and offered a plate of scattered gold and silver, kneeling before him and saying, "Because we owe our lives to Your Lordship, please accept this as the least token of one humble meal for your road." Tripitaka waved his hand and shook his head: he would not accept, saying, "A poor monk like me has no use for money and silk. Even while on the road I dare not draw on worldly means; to pass my days on alms from transformation is my true duty. Dried provisions are enough." The two elders begged again and again. Sun Wukong pinched off a tiny piece with his fingertips, about four or five qian by weight, and gave it to Tripitaka: "Master, take this only as a bit of pocket money, so that the elders do not think their goodwill has gone unrewarded."

After bidding farewell to the Chens they walked straight toward the riverbank by the ice. The horse’s hoof slid on the surface, and Tripitaka almost tumbled off. Sha Wujing said, "Master, this is hard to ride." Pigsy said, "Stop there. Ask old Chen to fetch some straw for me." Sun Wukong said, "What use is straw?" Pigsy said, "How would you know? If the horse feet are wrapped with straw, the ice will not be so slick, and the Master will not slip from the saddle." From the bank Chen heard this and hurriedly ordered someone to bring a bundle of straw from the house, and asked Tripitaka to dismount. Pigsy wrapped the straw around the horse’s hooves, then all of them crossed the ice on foot.

When they left old Chen’s place by the river and had gone three or four li, Pigsy handed the nine-ringed iron staff to Tripitaka: "Master, hold this across your body while you are on the horse." Sun Wukong said, "That pig is a deceiver. The monk’s staff was yours to carry; how can you ask the Master to carry it?" Pigsy replied, "You have not walked far in frozen ice and do not know. Whenever the ice is hard, there are treacherous bright patches. If one steps onto such glare and slips, and there is nothing to crosswise prop and carry with, the bones themselves may fall into the water. It would be as if a great cauldron lid had covered you—how could you climb out? It must be arranged like this." Sun Wukong smiled to himself: "This brute has learned to cross ice for many years." So they did as he said: the elder held the nine-ringed staff across his shoulder, Sun Wukong bore the Iron Staff likewise, Sha Wujing carried the demon-subduing treasure staff, and Pigsy took the baggage on his shoulder, with the adze at his belt; then all three rode with confidence. They kept going until evening and ate some dry rations. They still dared not rest long. Looking up at the radiance of stars and moon, the ice glowed sharp and bright in the white waste, so they hurried forward without stopping, really with no idle moment. None of them could close their eyes, and they kept walking all through the night. At dawn they ate a little more dried food and set off westward again.

While they were still moving, they suddenly heard a loud pulalā sound from beneath the ice, and the White Horse was almost frightened off his feet. Tripitaka exclaimed, "Disciples! what is this crashing sound?" Pigsy answered, "This river has frozen hard, and the ice itself is cracking. It may be that the whole width is frozen through to the bottom." Hearing that, Tripitaka was both alarmed and strangely heartened; he pressed the horse onward and rode at speed.

The demon evil, having returned to the Water Palace, gathered his spirits beneath the ice and waited long. When he heard the sound of horse hooves, he worked a trick from below and made the ice split apart with a sliding rush. Startled, Sun Wukong sprang into the air; already the White Horse had fallen into the water, and all three disciples leapt off.

That demon caught Tripitaka, and with all his gathered spirits returned directly to the Water Palace. He shouted, "Where is Gui-sister?" Old Gui-Ma came to the door and bowing said, "Great King, we dare not." The demon said, "Why does this worthy sister speak so? 'Once a word is spoken, even a chariot of four horses cannot catch up.' I told you to follow my plan and seize Tripitaka, making you my brother and sister. Now the stratagem has truly succeeded: Tripitaka is taken—will you throw aside our word now?" He ordered, "You little ones, lift the tabletop, sharpen the knives, split open this monk’s belly and scoop out his heart, flay his skin and carve his flesh. In one chamber set the instruments ringing. Eat together with my sister so that my life may be lengthened and made immortal." Old Gui-Ma said, "Great King, do not eat him yet. I fear his disciples may come searching and make a disturbance. Better endure two days, let that brute not return, and only then open him. Ask the Great King to take a seat, line the clans around him, sound music, songs, and dance, and serve him before him, then eat at ease. Would that not be better?" The demon followed her words, concealed Tripitaka in the rear of the palace, and covered him with a six-foot stone casket.

At once Pigsy and Sha Wujing fished up the baggage from the water, loaded it on the White Horse, and crossed the waterway, surges and waves rising as they came out. They saw Sun Wukong up in the air and he asked, "Where is the Master?" Pigsy said, "The Master’s surname is Chen and his given name Daodi. We cannot find him anywhere now; let us get ashore and make some arrangements." In truth, Pigsy had once been the Marshal of the Ranks under Heaven, formerly in charge of eighty thousand water soldiers in the river of Heaven; Sha Wujing was from the River of Flowing Sand; and the White Horse was a son of the Western Sea Dragon, and so they all knew their way in water. The Great Sage gave directions from the air; in a moment they turned toward the eastern bank, brushed and dried the horses, and wrung and shook out their clothes. Sun Wukong descended with cloud-head and they arrived together at Chen Jiazhuang. Someone had already reported to the two elders: "Of the four who set out on the pilgrimage, only three have returned." The brothers hurried to meet them at the gate; indeed their garments were still wet. They said, "Lords, we begged and begged and kept you back, but you would not stay. We could only let you go this way. Where is Tripitaka, Master, not here?" Pigsy said, "Do not call him Tripitaka now; call him Chen Daodi instead." The two elders wept and said, "Alas, alas! I told you to wait till the snow melted and send a boat, but we would not be persuaded, and that loss of caution has cost a life." Sun Wukong said, "Old one, do not let old grief overtake you on behalf of the dead. My Master will live long, not perish. Old Sun knows this is surely the trick of that Linggan King in demon-magic. You keep your heart at ease: give us our wet garments to wring and dry, and get fodder for the White Horse. Let my brothers and I find that brute and rescue the Master, then we will cut him out by the root and remove this later calamity from your household, so that your people may have peace forever." Hearing this, old Chen was delighted in his heart and immediately ordered that a vegetarian offering be prepared.

The three brothers ate a full meal, handed over the horses and baggage to the Chen household to guard, and in turn gathered their weapons and went straight to the riverbank to seek the Master and capture the monster. This was indeed the point:

To misstep upon layered ice harms one’s true nature; when the great elixir leaks out, how can it be made whole again?

In the end, it is still unknown how they will save Tripitaka. Listen to the next chapter for the full resolution.
chapters.title: Chapter 48: A demon stirs bitter wind and drives down great snow; the monk, in worship, walks on layered ice to Buddha.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Once more it is said that Sun Wukong, with Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, left Old Chen and came to the riverbank. Sun Wukong said, “Brothers, have you two decided who is to enter the water first?” Zhu Bajie said, “Elder brother, since we can’t tell by our own means which method to use, you should go first.” Sun Wukong said, “To be frank, I tell you plainly, worthy brother: if this is a mountain demon, you two need not spend your strength. For matters under water, I cannot handle them. If I go out on the open waters and across the river, I must first intone the Tightening Headband Spell and perhaps transform into the shape of some fish or crab. If I do that, then I cannot swing the Golden-Hooped Staff, cannot use my arts, cannot strike any demon. I know well that both of you are used to water, so I ask you to go in.” Sha Wujing said, “Elder brother, though your junior can enter, I do not know what the river bottom is like. We should all go together. Let you change into whichever form you wish, or let me bear you; we can split the water routes and seek the demon’s lair, and you can go in first to scout. If Master is not injured and still alive somewhere there, then we can press on and subdue it. If this fiend’s trick is not the cause, and he has either sunk Master in the deep or the demon has eaten him, then we need not grind our teeth in sorrow and search all roads forever—why not leave at once for another route?” Sun Wukong said, “You speak with reason. Which one will bear me?” Zhu Bajie laughed inwardly and said, “This monkey has fooled me so many times. This time it seems he truly cannot swim. Let old Pig carry him and let him be fooled again.” The fool laughed with delight and called out, “Elder brother, I will carry you.” Sun Wukong saw through the design and played along: “Fine. You are even stronger than Sha Wujing.” Zhu Bajie hoisted him on his back.

Sha Wujing cut a path through the water, and all the brothers entered the River of Heaven. They went on under the water for a hundred-odd li. Zhu Bajie then sought to tease Sun Wukong. At once Sun Wukong plucked one hair and turned it into a fake body, laying it on Zhu Bajie’s back. His true body changed into a pig louse and clung tight inside the monk’s ear. Zhu Bajie was walking forward; suddenly he lurched and gave Sun Wukong a shove, then with one heave tossed him ahead, and Sun Wukong came down with a thump. The fake body was only a hair-form, and it at once floated up and vanished without trace. Sha Wujing said, “Second brother, what is this? You cannot even walk steadily, to fall into the mud would already be enough, and yet you have cast Elder Brother who knows where he went.” Zhu Bajie said, “That monkey could not help falling; once he fell, he vanished. Brother, whether he lives or dies don’t mind it. Let us first go find Master.” Sha Wujing said, “No. We still need him. He may not know water ways, but he is cleverer than we are. Without him, I will not go with you.” From within Zhu Bajie’s ear Sun Wukong could not refrain from shouting, “Sha Wujing, old Wukong is here too!” Sha Wujing heard and laughed. “Enough. This fool was dead, how dare you mock him so? You’ve made a voice that is heard but no face seen—what a spectacle!” Zhu Bajie, alarmed, knelt in the mud and knuckled his head, “Elder brother, it is my fault. When Master is rescued, I will offer recompense on the bank. Why are you still calling out from there? You frighten me nearly to death. Show yourself now and return in your true form; let me carry you and I will not jostle you again.” Sun Wukong said, “It is still you who are carrying me. I will not toy with you. Go now, go quickly.” The fool kept chattering, muttering apologies, then stood and re-entered with Sha Wujing.

They had gone yet another hundred-odd li when Sun Wukong looked up and saw a pavilion, with four large characters on it: “Water-Urchin Manor.” Sha Wujing said, “This side must be the demon’s dwelling. The two of us do not know its true form. How can we force entry and fight?” Sun Wukong said, “Sha Wujing, is there water outside that gate?” Sha Wujing said, “No water.” Sun Wukong said, “If there is no water, then hide concealed on either side and wait. I’ll go in to inquire.”

Great Sage clambered out of Zhu Bajie’s ear and once again changed form, becoming a long-legged shrimp-witch. With two or three jumps he entered the gate. Looking about, he saw the demon seated there, with many water-creatures lined on both sides; at the side sat a speckled-robed crocodile witch, and they were all in council to eat Tripitaka. Sun Wukong searched this side and that for a matching target and found none. Then he saw a large-bellied shrimp witch coming forward and stepping to stand under the western corridor. Sun Wukong sprang to the front and called, “Mother, the king and the rest are consulting to eat Tripitaka. Where is Tripitaka now?” The shrimp witch replied, “Tripitaka was seized when the King brought down snow and froze him in ice, and yesterday he was taken to the stone casket behind the palace. We wait until tomorrow; if his disciples do not come and make trouble, we will then make music and feast on him.”

Hearing this, Sun Wukong shifted through several changes and went straight to look behind the palace. There was indeed a stone casket, something like the trough in a people’s pigsty and also like a stone coffin of this world, and it measured about six feet long. He lay down above it and listened for a while. He heard Tripitaka inside crying softly, whimpering. Sun Wukong said nothing, and listened again, then the Master ground his teeth, gave a rasping cry, and chanted:

Self-blaming, I was born beneath a river-bound destiny, and from birth this life has been tangled in waters. From my mother’s womb I have been tossed in endless waves, seeking Buddha in the Western Heaven and yet falling into a dim abyss. Once I met the peril of the Black River; now, amid freezing ice, my life is undone. I do not know if my disciples can come in time—might I recover the true scripture and return to my old home? Sun Wukong could not refrain from crying, “Master, do not resent the water disaster. The scripture says, ‘Earth is the mother of the Five Phases, water is the source of the Five Phases. Without earth there is no life; without water there is no growth.’ Old Wukong has come.” Tripitaka heard and called, “Disciple, save me.” Sun Wukong said, “Have no fear. Once we capture the demon, I will see you out of danger.” Tripitaka said, “Act quickly. One more day, and this closeness will choke me.” Sun Wukong said, “No matter, no matter. I am going.”

He immediately turned around, leapt out, and came to the gate in his true form, calling, “Zhu Bajie.” Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing drew close and asked, “Brother, what is it?” Sun Wukong said, “This creature has indeed deceived Master. Master has not been injured. The demon has covered him under the stone casket. The two of you challenge it quickly and let old Wukong rise first above the water. If you can seize it, seize it. If you cannot seize it, make a show of losing, bait it out of the water, and then I will strike it down.” Sha Wujing said, “Brother, go first and be at peace. Let the two of us inspect its face and measure it.” Sun Wukong, rubbing the Tightening Headband Spell, emerged from the river and stood waiting on the bank; no further matter needs recording here.

See how Zhu Bajie, enraged, rushed through to the gate and shouted loudly, “Wretchly demon! Bring Master out at once!” This startled the little demons within, who hurriedly reported, “Great King, one has come from outside asking for Master.” The demon king said, “Surely this is that reckless monk again.” He ordered, “Quickly take out cloaks and weapons.” The young demons swiftly brought out arms and armor. The fiend himself, now armed, ordered the gate opened and came out. Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing lined up on either side to face him. See what a monstrous disguise it bore:

A golden helm rocked and gleamed above his head, his golden armor flashing like a rainbow arc. A precious girdle was wrapped at his waist, with inlaid bead-strands of green jade; strange smoke-gold boots stood on his feet. His nose was tall and steep like a jutting ridge, the brow broad as if a dragon’s court. His eyes burned, round and sudden-sparking; his teeth, sharp and even, were like polished steel. Short matted hair flamed in loose locks; long whiskers rose sharply like gilded spikes. He held in his mouth a fresh, green algae stalk and in his hand a nine-petaled red-copper hammer. One hoarse cry from the gate rang out, like thunder awakening spring beneath three spring storms. Such a form is rarely seen among men; it alone dares to boast of the might of a true spirit king.

The fiend stepped out, followed by over a hundred small demons, each brandishing spears and swords, and they opened in two ranks. The fiend asked Zhu Bajie, “Which monastery’s monk are you, and why cause such clamor here?” Zhu Bajie said, “You, the rabid creature who cannot die! You answered me with insults last night; why today do you pretend ignorance and ask what you are here for? I am a disciple of the Holy Monk of the Great Tang, going west to seek the Buddha’s scriptures. You conjure ghostly tricks and pass as some Great Spirit king, making your lair at Chen family manor to eat children and maidens. I once weighed out a tael of gold from Chen Qing’s house—how do you not know me?” The demon replied, “You are no monk of reason. You changed yourself into a tael of gold; that alone is the offense of usurping another’s identity. I did not even eat you; instead you wounded my wrist. I already spared your life, yet why do you come again to my gate?” Zhu Bajie replied, “If you already spared me, why then call down cold wind and great snow, harden this river with ice, and cause harm to Master? Send Master out now and all this can cease. Do not utter even half an ‘no’; look at the halberd in your own hand and I will spare you none.” The demon gave a slight cold laugh and said, “This monk’s tongue is too long and his boast too broad. It was I who brought the freezing snow to the river and seized your Master. Now you roar to my gate and seek retribution. This is not like the earlier bout: then, because I was off to an appointment and had brought no weapon, I was struck by you by accident. Now you will not run. We shall exchange combat three times. If you can beat me in three rounds, I will return your Master; if you fail, I will eat you both at once.”

Zhu Bajie said, 'Good clever son, this is exactly what I said. Look carefully at this pin.' The demon said, 'So you are, after all, a monk who took vows halfway along the road.' Zhu Bajie said, 'Son, you truly have some spiritual instinct. How did you know I am a halfway monk?' The demon said, 'You can use a pin, so I thought you had been hired in some garden, to drive up a stake and then bring it back by force.' Zhu Bajie said, 'My son, this is not that sort of stake. Look:

Cast from huge tusks, it is shaped like a dragon claw. Its gilt inlay appears like a coiling python. If it meets an enemy in cold wind, it scatters; when the hands lock, it kindles flame. It can aid the holy monk in clearing monsters and catch fiends on the road to the Western Heaven. Waving it, smoke and clouds can hide sun and moon, yet parting them makes the colors of dawn clear and bright. It can level Mount Tai so a thousand tigers fear, and overturn the great sea so ten thousand dragons are startled. You may boast of your powers—one strike of mine can drill nine holes.'

The demon would not believe him and raised the copper hammer to strike right at his head. Zhu Bajie parried with the pin and said, 'You braggart spirit are also a demon spirit who took monkhood only halfway.' The demon said, 'How do you know I am a halfway spirit?' Zhu Bajie said, 'You can wield a copper hammer, so surely you once worked in a silversmith’s forge and, by your hand, stole this out.' The demon said, 'This is no hammer for striking silver. Look:

Nine petals packed into a flower-bud; one pole, a hollow core, green for ten thousand years. Truly, it is not equal to common things in this world; it springs, in origin, from a famed celestial garden. Green chambers and violet flesh, born of Old Motherless pools in Yaochi, with pure fragrance from blue mire. For my years of cultivation and smelting, it became harder than steel, keen through-and-through, and spiritually acute. Spears and swords, all kinds of blades cannot easily contend; no axe or halberd dares to cross it. Even if your pin is sharp, at one touch of my hammer it will crack and bend into spikes.'

Sha Wujing saw the two sparring and could not restrain himself. He came forward and shouted, 'Monster, do not argue on words. As the ancients say: "Words alone are not proof; deeds reveal themselves." Do not run—take a staff from me now.' The demon raised his hammer handle to block and said, 'You too are a monk ordained halfway on the road.' Sha Wujing said, 'How can you know that?' The demon said, 'Your appearance is like a shaving-master scholar.' Sha Wujing said, 'How did you know I am like that?' The demon said, 'You are not a shaving-master scholar, so how can you wield the staff used to pound dough?' Sha Wujing cursed, 'You cursed obstruction! It is true that no one in this world has seen such weapons, so it is hard to know its holy name:

Rare is this weapon among the human world, so few know it by name. It comes from the Moon Palace where no shadow is seen, polished from immortal sorra wood by the master craftsman. Gem-stones are set on the outside and radiate rosy light; within, drilled gold gathers the auspicious Qi. It once once served at the imperial banquet; this morning it bears uprightly Tripitaka's protection. On the road to the Western Heaven it seems small, yet in the higher palaces it has a great name. It is called the True Relic Staff that Subdues Demons; with one strike it can shatter heavenly spirits.'

The demon allowed no further talking and all three of them shifted faces in combat. Under the water this bout was fierce:

Bronze-hammer, precious staff, and pin: Wukong and Wujing battle the demon. One is Tianpeng's heaven-pavilion envoy, one a descending general on the edge of heaven. The two of them pressed the water fiend in concert, each displaying power. One alone might stand against the Divine Monk and that cannot be belittled. By destiny and affinity comes the Great Way; generation and conquest between them holds constant. Earth overcomes water, and water dries to the bottom; water gives rise to wood, and wood in vigor makes flowers bloom. In meditative training the Chan method joins into one, and alchemical refining stills the three households. Earth is the mother, producing golden sprouts; gold gives birth to divine water, producing infant spirits. Water is root, moistened wood in full bloom; wood holds splendor, and fierce fire gives red cloud. Gathered together, the Five Phases each differ, so the changing faces contend in many ways. See that bronze hammer: nine-petaled brilliance is beautiful; the precious staff is a thousand-thread embroidered elegance. The pin follows yin and yang to divide nine lights, and one who lacks number does not understand, as if tangled in hemp. To lay down body and life because a monk is hard to save, to reject life and forget self for Śākyamuni. So the bronze hammer cannot drop in panic; left it shields the staff, right it shields the pin.

For two full hours they fought beneath the water and neither gained the upper hand. Zhu Bajie guessed he could not beat the monster and gave Sha Wujing a knowing glance. The two made a false defeat, feigned retreat, each dragging his weapon as they turned and ran. The demon barked, 'Little ones, hold this place firm and wait till I catch that fellow, then bring him here and all of you can feast on the Tang monk.' See how he, like wind through fallen leaves and rain on crushed blossoms, drove both of them out of the water.

The Great Sage on the east bank kept his eyes unblinking, staring only at the water’s current. Suddenly the waves rose and roared. Zhu Bajie jumped ashore first and called, 'He is coming, he is coming.' Sha Wujing came to the bank too and said, 'He is coming, he is coming.' The demon then called out, 'Where do you run to?' As soon as he looked out, Wukong shouted, 'Watch your staff.' The demon sidestepped, dodged and quickly swung the bronze hammer back. One stood on the surging riverbank, one on shore displayed power. Before the three rounds of contact were completed, the demon could not hold his guard; he struck a splash of flowers in the water and vanished back beneath it, and immediately wind and waves calmed.

Wukong turned and called from the high cliff, 'Brothers, you have labored.' Sha Wujing said, 'Brother, this demon feels hard to catch on land and is all strength beneath the water. I and Second Brother attacked him together and only held him to a draw. How shall we handle this and rescue Master?' Wukong said, 'No need to hesitate. He might wound our Master.' Zhu Bajie said, 'Brother, this time I will draw him out, and you must not speak. Just wait in the air. Guess when he breaks to the surface, and strike a pounding blow on his crown, a true, solid strike. Even if he is not killed, he will be stunned and shaken sick. Then, when I chase him up with my pin, I will settle matters with him.' Wukong said, 'Exactly, exactly. This is called 'inside welcome, outside coordination.' Then the matter can be solved.' The two went back into the water again.

The tale says that the demon fled in rout and returned to his home ground. When he reached it, the many fiends gathered in the hall. Gui Po came forward and asked, 'Great King, where did you drive those two monks?' The demon said, 'Those monks had another helper. The two of them leapt up onto the bank; the helper raised an iron staff and struck me. I dodged and fought him. I never could gauge how heavy that staff was in weight. My bronze hammer could not even hold him. We had not fought through three turns, yet I was forced to retreat.' Gui Po said, 'Great King, do you remember what the helper looks like?' The demon said, 'It is a monk with a shaggy face, a thunder-mouth, slit ears, broken bridge of the nose, and fire-like golden eyes.' When Gui Po heard this, he shivered and said, 'Great King, you have escaped by fortune. If you had gone on three rounds again, you would certainly not have survived whole. That monk—I know him.' The demon said, 'You know who he is?' Gui Po said, 'Long ago in the seas of the Eastern Ocean, I once heard the old Dragon King speak of his fame. He was the one who five hundred years ago made a huge uproar in the Heavenly Court: the Golden Immortal of Supreme Harmony, the Beautiful Monkey King, Subduer of the Sky, the Great Sage, Equal of Heaven. Now he has taken refuge in Buddhism, protects Tripitaka on the way to the West to retrieve the scriptures, and has taken the name Wukong, called the Great Sage. His powers are vast and transformations endless. Great King, why would you provoke him? Never fight him again.'

Before anything more could be said, a young demon came to report from the gate: 'Great King, those two monks have come again to the gate, demanding battle.' The fiend said, 'Sister Xian has watched him for a long time; if we do not come out now, let him find out what we will do. Send at once: lock the gates tight. It is exactly saying,

Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing called out repeatedly, but nothing came. The fool of a pig, uneasy, used the pin to build up force and strike the gate. The gate was now tightly shut and locked; no one could think of breaking it. He struck it seven or eight times with the pin and tore open the gate leaves, yet all inside were earth and stones, piled in a thousand dense layers. Sha Wujing saw this and said, 'Second Brother, this fiend is so frightened he refuses to open the gate. He stayed behind the door and would not come out. Let's return to the river cliff above and take up the matter with elder Brother.' Zhu Bajie obeyed and turned back across to the east bank.

The Great Sage stood in half-cloud, half-mist, waiting with the iron staff in hand. Seeing the two come up, and not seeing the demon, he stepped down the cloud and came to the shore. He asked, 'Brothers, why did he not come up?' Sha Wujing said, 'That monster has shut his house and will not come out to meet us. When Second Brother broke the gate leaves, inside there was only earth and stone stacked tight. So we could not fight. We came to consult with you and see what further plan to rescue Master.' Wukong said, 'In this way there is no other remedy. You two stay on this bank and patrol. Do not let him slip away elsewhere. I will go.' Zhu Bajie said, 'Brother, if you go there, it is too much wasted work, and time is long delayed.' Wukong said, 'Whether it is costly or delayed, do not think of that. I will go and return soon.'

Great Sage, he leapt quickly on the auspicious light-cloud, slipped away from the river mouth, and headed straight for the South Sea. There he spent about half a watch, and soon saw Luojia Mountain not far away. He lowered the cloud and came straight to Putuo Cliff. There he saw the Twenty-Four Heavens together with the Mountain-Protecting Great Deity, Mucha Xingzhe, Shancai Tongzi, and the Pearl-Cupping Dragon Maiden, all step forward, greet him, and say, “Great Sage, what brings you here?” Sun Wukong replied, “I have matters to attend to, and must meet the Bodhisattva.” The gods said, “Guanyin left her cave early this morning and does not allow anyone to follow. She has gone inside the bamboo grove to view and play. Knowing the Great Sage would certainly come today, she ordered us to wait here and receive you, but not to meet her directly. Please sit for a while in front of Green Rock and wait for her to come out.”

The Great Sage followed their words, and before he had even sat down, Shancai Tongzi stepped forward and bowed, saying, “Great Sage Sun, earlier you once showed me such kindness; Guanyin was fortunate not to cast me away but to take me in. At all times I did not stray from her side, only serving beneath the Lotus Terrace, so deeply have I tasted her benevolence.” Sun Wukong knew he was the Red Boy and laughed: “In that time you were a demon-deluded mind, and now at this dawn of right attainment you only see that old Sun is indeed a good man.”

Sun Wukong waited long but saw nothing. Anxious, he said, “Tell her for me, if I am delayed any longer, my Master may be harmed.” The heavenly attendants said, “We dare not report. The Bodhisattva ordered us to wait until he comes out himself.” But the Great Sage was too impatient to wait and at once sprang forward into the grove. Ah!

This handsome Great Monkey King was impatient and quick to probe. The gods could not hold him; he rushed in through the inner grove. He strode into the deep woods and watched with open eyes, peering. From afar he saw the Savior of the Distressed one, seated in lotus-mudra, set against tattered sedge. Lacking care to groom herself, her face remained naturally graceful. A loose knot of silk at the side, and no hair-knot ribbon bound it. She wore no plain blue robe, no snug inner jacket tied tight. A brocaded skirt was loosely knotted at her waist; both feet were bare and red. No embroidered shoulder-belt; her two arms shone with inner light. In jeweled hands she held a steel knife, sharpening bamboo skin. After seeing this, he could not restrain himself and cried out loudly: “Guanyin, your disciple Sun Wukong kneels and offers homage.” Guanyin said, “Wait outside.” Sun Wukong prostrated himself and said, “Guanyin, my Master is in danger. I came specifically to ask the cause of the demon spirit of Tongtian River.” Guanyin said, “Please go out for now and wait; I will come out.”

Sun Wukong did not dare to force his way in and only came out of the bamboo grove, and said to the gods: “So today the Bodhisattva has once again set herself to household matters. Why is she not seated on the Lotus Terrace, not adorned, not ready for ceremony, and here in the woods cutting bamboo strips?” The gods said, “We do not know. This morning she left the cave before dressing or fastening her robes and went into the grove. She also told us to stand here and wait for the Great Sage, so it must be that he has important business.” Sun Wukong had no alternative; he had to wait.”

Soon after, Guanyin emerged from the grove carrying a purple bamboo basket in her hands and said, “Wukong, let us go save Tripitaka.” Sun Wukong hastily knelt and said, “Disciple dares not urge. Please take your seat after putting on your robes.” Guanyin said, “No need to put on robes; we are leaving now.” She set aside the attending gods, rose on an auspicious cloud, and flew into the sky. Sun Wukong could only follow.

In an instant they arrived at the frontier of Tongtian River. Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing saw this and said, “Elder Brother is so hot-tempered—who knows what noise he made in the South Sea that he forced out a Bodhisattva not even dressed yet.” He had not finished speaking before they reached the bank. The two bowed deeply and said, “Bodhisattva, we have presumed wrongly. We have wronged the temple. Wronged it.” Guanyin then untied a silk strap from the knot of her robe, fixed the basket with it, held the strap, stepped half onto drifting cloud-ranks, and tossed the basket into the river. She pulled it up by the head and chanted: “Dead go away, the living stay. Dead go away, the living stay.” After seven recitations she lifted the basket, and in it she saw a bright golden fish, eye-bright with flickering scales. Guanyin called, “Wukong, quickly enter the water and save your Master.” Sun Wukong said, “We have not yet seized the demon evil; how can I save my Master?” Guanyin said, “Is he not in this basket?” Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing asked, “How can this fish have such technique?” Guanyin answered, “He was a goldfish raised by me in the Lotus Pool, rising daily to hear scriptures and cultivating arts. That nine-petaled bronze mace was once an unopened lotus bud that he refined into a weapon. I do not know what day the sea tide surged and drove him here. This morning, as I stood by the rail admiring the flowers, I did not see this brute leave his post. Tracing the lines with my fingers, I calculated that he had become spirit here and harmed your Master. So I had no time to groom myself; I brought up divine power and wove this bamboo basket to capture him.”

Sun Wukong said, “Since this is so, wait a little while. Let us call the devout people of Chen Family Manor so they can see Guanyin’s golden face: first to show our gratitude, and second to tell of this capture of the monster so ordinary people gain faith and offer support.” Guanyin said, “Very well, go quickly and call them.” Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing flew together to the front of the estate and shouted, “Come see the living Guanyin Bodhisattva, come see the living Guanyin Bodhisattva!” Men and women, old and young, rushed toward the riverbank, not minding the mud or water, all kneeling and kowtowing in worship. Among them were artists who made fine images; one passed down an image-spirit, and then this appeared as Fish-Basket Guanyin’s manifestation. At that moment Guanyin returned to the South Sea.

Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing separated the channels and went straight to the turtle-lair to search for their Master. The water-demon fish spirits there were all dead and decayed. They entered the rear chambers, opened a stone coffer, and carried Tripitaka out, leaving the waves, to meet the others. The brothers Chen Qing and their household knelt and thanked him: “Master, because we did not heed your humble men’s request to stay, we have caused you such suffering.” Sun Wukong said, “Say no more. In your village, next year there will be no more sacrificial race. That Great King has been eradicated by the root, and there will never be harm again. Elder Chen, this is now enough to burden you. Please find one boat quickly and send us across the river.” Chen Qing said, “Yes, yes, yes.” Then he ordered a flat-boat to be assembled. Hearing this, all villagers rejoiced. One said, “I will buy the sail.” Another said, “I will provide the setting-poles and paddles.” Some said, “I will provide rope.” Some said, “I will hire boatmen.”

They were all still noisy on the riverbank when a loud cry came from midstream: “Sun Wukong, do not hire a boat; do not spend villagers’ wealth. I will ferry you and your disciples across.” When they heard, each person was startled; the timid ones went home, while the daring lingered and watched in nervous awe. Soon a monster emerged from the water. Ask what he looked like:

He has a broad, strange divine form unlike any common kind; they call him Water Immortal of the ninefold spirit workings. By dragging his tail he can prolong life for a thousand ages; submerged, he keeps his essence hidden in the abyss of a hundred streams. He rose through waves and leapt in broken surf against the riverbank, then lay by the sea’s edge facing the sun and wind. He cultivated inner breath and held true spirit; for many years a white film covered the turtle’s rough, scabby head. The old turtle called again: “Great Sage, do not hire a boat; I will take you and your disciples across.” Those present heard; Sun Wukong raised his iron staff and said, “I am a demon-culling fiend! If you come near the bank I will kill you with one strike.” The old turtle said, “I owe Great Sage a debt of grace and will gladly ferry your whole party across. Why should you try to strike me?” Sun Wukong said, “How much kindness have you shown me?” The old turtle replied, “Great Sage, you do not know my roots. This turtle estate beneath the waters was my home, passed down through generations. Since awakening to my true nature, I gathered spiritual energy here and cultivated it; I repaired my ancestral house into this turtle manor. That monster was the sea-surge wave nine years ago. He chased the crest of the tide, came here, wielded wild ferocity and brute force, fought me, hurt many of my children, and took many of my clan. I could not defeat him, so he had quietly seized my dwelling. Now, thanks to your coming here to rescue Master, and calling Guanyin to cleanse the demon air and take away that monster, my residence is restored to me. Now I and my clan can all live together again; we need never again endure mud and ruin, and may return to our old dwelling. This kindness is as heavy as Mount Cui and as deep as the sea. Not only we are favored: all the folk of this village are spared; each year they are freed from the annual sacrificial rites, and so many children and daughters are saved. This is truly a kindness bringing two gains in one go. How could I not repay it?” Hearing his words, Sun Wukong secretly rejoiced, sheathed his staff, and asked, “Is what you say truly sincere?” The old turtle said, “Because Great Sage’s grace is immense, how could I dare to lie?” Sun Wukong said, “If it is sincere, swear to heaven.” The old turtle gaped red-mouthed and swore upward: “If I am not sincere and do not ferry Tripitaka across this Tongtian River, let my body become blood and water.” Sun Wukong laughed, “Come up, come up.”

The old turtle only just moved close to the near bank, leapt once, and climbed up the river cliff. The crowd drew close to look: it was a huge white shell, round, four zhang across. Sun Wukong said, “Master, we can cross by stepping onto his back.” Tripitaka said, “My disciple, even this thick ice there is difficult to pass; how much more this turtle’s back might be unstable.” The old turtle said, “Master, rest easy. I am firmer than that ice-thick surface, very solid indeed. If I were to tilt even a little, it would not do. Sun Wukong said, “Master, any ordinary sentient being who can speak words as humans will not lie.” Then he called, “Brothers, bring the horses quickly.”

When they reached the riverbank, all the men, women, old and young of Chen Family Village came to bow farewell together. Sun Wukong told them to tether the horse upon the white tortoise’s backboard, invited Tripitaka to stand at the horse’s left by the neck, Sha Wujing to the right, Zhu Bajie behind, and Sun Wukong in front. Fearing the old tortoise might be impolite, he unfastened a tiger-thong strap, threaded it through the old tortoise’s nostril, and pulled it taut as if it were a bridle. Then he set one foot on the board and one on its head; with one hand he grasped the iron staff and with the other he held the rein, calling out, “Old tortoise, go slowly. Give a little lean and I will strike your head once.” The old tortoise replied, “I dare not, I dare not.” Yet it stretched out its four feet and stepped on the surface of the water as if walking on level ground. All the villagers on the bank burned incense, knelt, and chanted, “Namo Amitabha Buddha.” This was truly the moment: a genuine arhat had descended among mortals, a living bodhisattva had appeared. The people kept bowing and staring until they could no longer see form or shadow before returning; nothing further is recorded.

Later, it is said that Tripitaka, riding the white tortoise, crossed the pass of the Heavenly River of eight hundred li in a single day and reached the bank without so much as wetting hand or foot. He climbed the bank and with joined palms gave thanks: “Old tortoise, I have burdened you, and have nothing here to give. When I return from the west with the scriptures, I will then repay my thanks.” The old tortoise answered, “No need for the Master to trouble yourself with thanks. I have heard that the Buddha of the western heaven is beyond cessation and non-origination and can know what has happened and what is yet to come. I have been practicing here for more than thirteen hundred years; though my life has been extended, my body made light, and I can speak human speech, I still cannot cast off this shell. I earnestly hope, revered teacher, when you go to the west, that you will ask the Buddha once: when may I be released from this shell and be granted a human body?” Tripitaka at once assured him, “I will ask, I will ask.” Then the old tortoise at last went down into the water.

Sun Wukong then assisted Tripitaka back onto the horse; Zhu Bajie carried the baggage, Sha Wujing followed on either side, and the disciples took the main road and rushed straight west. These lines describe it:

The holy monk, by decree, bows to Amituo; waters are far, mountains remote, and calamities are many. With steadfast will and sincere heart, unafraid of death, the white tortoise bore them across the Heavenly River.

How much farther road lay ahead, and what misfortune or fortune remained, is still unknown; let it be explained in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 49: Tripitaka meets disaster and sinks into a water-house; Guanyin appears in a fish-basket to save him.
