This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

The tale says that Sun Wukong, having obtained the Golden-Hooped Staff, struck out through the gate, bounded up a high peak, and rejoiced fully before all the gods. Li Tianwang said, "How does your fight stand?" Wukong replied, "Old Sun went into his cave in transformation. The demon there grew ever more boisterous, singing and dancing while he drank victory wine. I still have not found where his treasure lies. I went behind him, and all at once heard the horse cry and the dragon’s roar, so I knew it was a thing of the Fire Division. On the eastern bank, by my Golden-Hooped Staff, is where I bore it in my hand and broke my way out." The gods said, "You have recovered your own treasure; when will ours be in our hands?" Wukong said, "Not difficult, not difficult. With this iron staff in my hand, one way or another I shall beat him down and recover your treasure for you."

Just as he spoke, from below the slope came drums and gongs in unison, and shouts shook the ground. It was the Si Great King leading hosts of spirits to chase the Great Sage. When Wukong saw him he called, "Excellent, excellent. This is just to my mind. All of you, be seated. Old Sun will go and catch him." The Great Sage raised his iron staff and met him face to face: "Run, demon-thief, where are you going? Watch this staff!" The monster braced its spear and shouted, "Thief monkey! Very impudent indeed. How dare you loot my items in broad daylight?" Wukong said, "You, pitiless spawn of a beast! It was you who set a snare by daylight to rob what is mine. Whose thing is that to claim as yours? Do not flee. Take one stroke from the old master’s staff!" The monster swung its spear in guard. This was a fierce battle:

The Great Sage displayed awesome might, while demon and demon did not submit to gentleness. Both sides fought with equal courage; which of them would concede? This iron staff crackles and lashes like a dragon-tail wind, that long spear resembles a python’s head. This staff comes on in a ringing like wind, that spear gives majestic breadth like water in flood. Mists, colored and hazy, darkened the mountain ridges, auspicious cloudbanks pressed over the sorrowful trees. All birds in the sky held their wings still, and foxes and insects in the fields drew in their heads. Among the little demons there were cries, and along this wall the Sage braced himself. One iron staff there was no matching foe, striking from west to western lands. That long spear truly had a match, stout enough to pin even the Golden-Hooped lord. In this encounter there was no easy end; seeing no height or low ground, they swore not to cease. The demon king and Sun Wukong fought for three hours with no clear victory, and soon dusk deepened. The demon king said while still bracing his long spear, "Wukong, pause. At this hour, with daylight fading, this is no time for gambling at combat. Rest awhile and tomorrow we shall compare strength again." Wukong cursed, "Filthy beast, do not prattle! Old Sun’s spirit has only just risen; what matter that night has fallen? I must settle win and loss with you." The monster shouted once, made a feint with its spear, and fled for its life. It gathered its band, withdrew its weapons, entered the cave, and shut its gate tight.

The Great Sage, staff in hand, had barely returned when the gods by the bank praised him, all saying, "This truly is a capable and mighty one, a boundless, limitless master of true skill." Wukong laughed and said, "Thank you. Thank you for the praise." Li Tianwang stepped forward: "Those are no compliments, truly. You are a good hero. This bout is not inferior to the net that once covered and restrained the world under Heaven." Wukong said, "Do not raise old matters. That demon has received this full bout from Old Sun and will surely be tired. I cannot be said to have labored in vain. You all sit easy. Let me go in again and learn the layout, take whatever I can, catch the monster, and recover the weapon to return it to heaven." The Prince said, "It is already late; let us sleep one night and go at dawn." Wukong laughed. "This young lord does not know the world. What sort of robber strikes in broad daylight? Thieves who work by feel and touch must move by night and by day both; only then, without noticing, is trade truly done." Fire Virtue and Lei Gong said, "Do not speak so, Third Prince. We do not know this affair. The Great Sage is well-practiced in such arts; he should act now—first, that demon-head is fatigued; second, the night is dark and unguarded. So send him, send him at once."

The Great Sage, laughing, concealed the iron staff. He leapt down from the peak, returned to the cave mouth, and in a blink changed into a small ragged loom-boy. Indeed:

Lips hard-set, whiskers long, skin black, eyes bright, claws and split toes. In clear wind and moon-bright night, he called along the wall’s edge; the night was still, almost like human speech. Tearful, pale, and desolate the scene appeared, his voice broken and worthy of wonder. At a guest-latticed window it was fearfully like a traveler’s lonely longing to hear him, yet he lay off by the empty stair beneath the bed. Kicking open with his legs, three or five jumps, he leapt to the doorway and slipped in through the crack, crouching at the base of the wall. Facing the light within, he watched closely. He saw all the big and small demons, each with wolf and tiger hunger, all in the midst of eating. Wukong gave a sharp clattering call. After little time, they put out the home fire, and all of them went to set up their beds and settle themselves.

About a watch had passed before Wukong reached the back room. He heard the old demon giving orders: "The small ones at every gate, keep alert; if Wukong comes to change and sneak in, he may steal under cover of night." Some were already on night watch; they clanged bells in crisp, quick rhythm. This Great Sage handled his business more cleverly. Entering the room, he saw a stone bed. On either side were several mountain spirits and tree ghosts, powdering and rouge-faced, laid out with blankets attending the old demon, some removing shoes, some unbuttoning robes, some unfastening coats. He saw that the demon king loosened his robe; on his left shoulder-arm a white, icy-white loop was fitted, like a linked-bead bracelet. See—he did not remove it, but with two quick rubs he tightened it hard against his shoulder and only then lay down to sleep. Wukong saw this and changed again, this time into a yellow flea-like thing, hopped onto the stone bed, burrowed into the bedding, and climbed atop the monster’s shoulder-arm and bit down hard. The demon twitched and growled, "You worthless little slaves! You did not shake the cover or brush the bed—what is this thing that bit me so?" He wound the ring up twice and put it back in place, then slept again. Wukong climbed up the ring and bit again. The demon could not sleep and rolled over, crying, "Bastard, you have nearly killed me!"

Seeing how secure the demon’s guarding was, and the treasure stayed on him, unwilling to remove it, Wukong judged he could not steal it there. He jumped off the bed and changed back to the weaving boy, went out through the door, and returned to the rear, where again he heard dragon-cry and horse-neigh. The inner gates were tightly locked, with the Fire Dragon and Fire Horse hanging inside. Wukong resumed his true form, came to the door, used a lock-breaking art, chanted the spell, and with one sweeping motion the double chains of the lock fell away. He pushed open the door and burst inside to inspect. Inside, the room was bright as daylight with fire devices and implements. He saw, slanting on both sides, several weapons: among them the Third Prince’s demon-cleaving sabre and others, and also the Fire Deity’s fire bow, fire arrows, and such. In the firelight Wukong looked around once more; behind the door he saw a straw basket on a stone table with a bundle of hair lying there. The Great Sage, filled with joy, took up the hair, drew two breaths as if from its heat, cried, "Transform!" and became thirty to fifty small monkeys. He ordered them to take up swords, sabres, maces, chains, wolf-hide shields, bows, arrows, spears, chariots, gourds, fire-crows, fire-mice, and fire horses—every captured implement—and to go, fire-dragon and all, burning outward. Then there came sounds like honghong and hahah and puping—like chains of cannon-fire. The little and great goblins woke in panic, heads wrapped, half-awake, crying and weeping; each had nowhere to go, and half of them died in the flames. Handsome Monkey-King returned in triumph only near the hour of the third watch.

Then on the high peak, Li Tianwang and the gods all noticed the flickering light and came forward in a rush. They saw Wukong riding a dragon, panting and snorting, sending the little monkeys forward, and leaping straight to the summit. He shouted aloud, "Collect the weapons! Collect the weapons!" Huode and Nezha answered in assent. The Sage shook himself once and the hair came back onto his body. Nezha gathered six of Wukong’s weapons. Huode Star Lord collected from the Fire Division the fire dragon and other gear. All smiled and praised Wukong in good cheer; it need not be told here.

Within the Golden-Hooped Cave, the flames swirled and burst; the Si Great King was so frightened that his spirit left him. He quickly rose and opened the chamber door. With both hands he held the ring: pushing eastward, the eastern fire died; pushing westward, the western fire went out. Smoke rose all through the air, sudden fires sputtered through the room. He held the treasure tight and ran it in a circuit, and all the fire and smoke in all directions were extinguished. He hurried to rescue the gathered demons. Already two hundred and some had been burned; men and women alike lay, more than a hundred and ten or so and not all could be accounted for. He then checked the cache of weapons: all were gone. He looked behind and saw Bai Zhuba? and Sha Wujing and Master still bound and unfastened, the White Dragon Horse still at its stall, and the baggage pole still in the house. The demon then grumbled in resentment: "One of these little spirits must have been careless and, through failure to attend the fire, caused this ruin." A nearby attendant reported, "Your Majesty, this fire is no business of our household. It was most likely a small thief from elsewhere, who looted the camp: he released the Fire Division’s gear and stole divine arms." The old demon suddenly woke to full understanding: "There is no one else; surely it is Wukong, that thief. This is why I could not rest while sleeping. That thief monkey must have transformed in, and bit me twice on my shoulder. Certainly it was to steal my treasure; seeing I had bound the ring tightly, he could not act directly. So he stole the weapons, loosed the Fire Dragon, and raised this cruel heart of fire to burn us alive. Monkeys call you thief? You used devices, yet you do not know my powers. If I take this treasure with me, even entering the Great Sea I am never drowned, and entering the sea of fire I am not burned. If now this thief is taken, I will scrape him raw and satisfy my heart."

As they spoke, still angry from the long argument, they did not notice that dawn had arrived and the roosters were crowing. On the high peak, Nezha, the Crown Prince, had obtained six divine weapons. He said to the Great Sage: “Great Sage, the day is bright now. We must not be careless. Let us take this chance while the demon’s edge has been dulled, with the Fire Division and the others to support you, and go on and fight again. Perhaps this time we can catch him.” The Great Sage laughed. “That’s reasonable. Let’s join our minds and go at him.” One after another they shook off weariness, swaggered with martial spirit, and went directly to the cave entrance. The Great Sage called out, “Come out, demon, and fight old Sun.”

Those two stone gates had been reduced to ashes by the heat, and inside there were several little demons sweeping up dust and ash. As soon as they saw the whole host arriving together, they dropped their brooms in fright, tossed aside their ash rakes, ran inside, and cried out, “Sun Wukong has come with many heavenly generals and he is taunting and fighting outside.” When the Rhinoceros King heard the report, he was startled; his steel teeth clicked as he snapped and his eyes bulged round in circles. Leaning on a long spear and brandishing his treasure, he came out and shouted abuse: “You thieving imp who set fire to our camp! How dare you treat me like this? How many tricks do you think you have?” The Great Sage answered with a smiling insult: “You wretched demon! If you want to know what I can do, come forward and I’ll show you:

From childhood I was born with strength and guile, and my fame has spread through the vast underheaven and earth. In my early awakening I took to the way of immortality and learned the method that wards off old age. I set my resolve, offered my heart to cultivation, and earnestly sought the abode of sages. Having mastered boundless arts of transformation, I run wild through the endless cosmos. Idling before the mountain I brought a tiger low; at will I subdued dragons in the seas. I once ruled on Floral-Fruit Peak; in Water-Curtain Cave I displayed my fierceness. More than once I aimed for Heaven’s realm, and more than once in reckless ignorance I ascended there. The Jade Emperor honored me with the title Great Sage Equal to Heaven and also conferred the name Handsome Monkey King. I only slipped in because I was not properly invited to the banquet of the peaches of immortality. I broke into the Jade Pond at night to steal celestial nectar, and in secret drank nectar in a treasure pavilion. I stole and ate dragon’s liver and phoenix marrow, and sampled all manner of precious foods. I enjoyed peaches meant to last a thousand ages, and swallowed elixirs meant to last ten thousand. I took odd things from the heavenly court and tucked away every marvel from the divine halls. When the Jade Emperor learned of my powers, he sent out heavenly troops and set a battlefield. The Nine Luminaries and evil stars were humbled by me; the ferocious asterisms of the five directions were struck down. No divine general in the whole world could withstand me; ten thousand mighty warriors dared not oppose me. By my pressure the Jade Emperor issued orders, and the young saint of Guan Jiang raised the army. We held each other for seventy-two changes, each displaying all our spirit, each formidable. Guanyin from the Southern Sea came to fight for them, and Pure-Bottle and Yangliu aided as well. Laozi then used the Vajra net to seize me and bring me before the High Heaven. Bound, I was taken before the Great Jade Emperor, where officials examined and judged what crimes should be laid. The emperor ordered Great Force to cut down with a blade, and the strokes flamed across my scalp. Through myriad stratagems they failed to kill me, and I was dragged to the Hall of Laozi. In the divine furnace of six Ding fires they forged me; my whole body came out hard as steel. When the seventy-seven measures had passed and the cauldron was opened, I leaped out fiercer than before. The gods shut their doors and offered no refuge; all the holy ones conferred to plead to the Buddha. Truly the Tathagata has vast power, and his wisdom is immeasurably boundless. In his palm he flicked and overturned like a gambling cup, and set a mountain upon me, yet I could not be overpowered. Only after the Jade Emperor held the Heavenly Pacification assembly was the Western Region then praised as the Pure Bliss realm. I was crushed beneath him for five hundred years and tasted no tea or gruel. Elder Golden Cicada descended among the mortal world; in the Eastern Land he was sent to lead this mission before Buddha’s Buddha-land. To fetch the True Scripture and return to the Great Tang, your previous Great Emperor had already passed away. Guanyin persuaded me to return to the way and keep the good teaching, so I would bear the precept and not be wild. Deliverance from the roots of this sacred mountain was no easy matter, so now I go west for the Scripture mission. Do not toy with me with fox-and-deer deceit, wretch. Return my master and let him bow to the Buddha-kings.” The monster listened and pointed at the Great Sage: “So you are indeed a thief who robbed Heaven. Do not run. Eat this spear of mine.” The Great Sage answered with his staff. They locked in combat. At that moment Nezha the Crown Prince grew angry, while Fire Virtue Star Lord grew ferocious; they threw the six divine weapons and the Fire Division’s armaments at the monster’s body. The Great Sage grew even more imposing. Meanwhile the Lord of Thunder used his hooked hook, and the Heavenly King raised his sword; without regard to rank, all surged in together. The demon, broad and cold with laughter, quietly pulled out his treasure from his sleeves, cast it into the air, shouted “Now!” and with a sharp crack snatched up all six divine weapons, the Fire Division supplies, Thunder-god’s hook, the Heavenly King’s blade, and even the Great Sage’s staff. The gods stood bare-handed, and the Great Sage was left with empty fists. The demon, having gained the upper hand, stepped back and said: “Servants, carry stones, rebuild the wall, dig up and repair the house and corridor. Once all is restored, I’ll invite the Three of Tang Monk and make thanks to the earth. Then all of you may feast and enjoy your blessings.” The little demons obeyed, and the matter need not be described further.

That Li Heavenly King then withdrew his host back up the high peak. Fire Virtue was resentful, saying Nezha was too impatient; Leigong blamed the Heavenly King for mischief; only Water Virtue stood mute at his side. The Great Sage saw that they did not meet his eyes. Disturbed in thought and unable to help it, he swallowed his resentment and forced a smile. He said to them all, “Do not be distressed. As the old saying goes: in war, victory and defeat are the way of soldiers. What happened was only this—I tested him in arms, and nothing more. It is only this ring he has that causes trouble and lets him snatch away our weapons. Hold easy. Let Old Sun go and look into what sort of fellow he is.” The Crown Prince said, “You already petitioned the Jade Emperor and scoured the entire heavens. There was no trace left behind. How are we to track him now?” The Great Sage said, “It comes back to me: the Dharma is without bounds. I will go up to the Western Heaven and ask the Buddha, the Tathagata, to look with wisdom over the four great continents. We will see where this demon was born, where he lives, and what treasure his ring is. Whatever it is, I must seize him, relieve your grievance, and send you all back to Heaven in joy.” The gods replied, “If this is your resolve, do not delay. Go quickly, go quickly.”

The Great Sage said, “Very well,” and, as soon as the words were out, he spread into the air on a cloud of many tens of li and quickly arrived at Mount Lingshan. Auspicious radiance descended and he looked about all around; it was truly a fine place:

The sacred peak rises sparse and lofty, tiers of ridges shining clear and fine. On the summit of the immortal mountain, it seems to brush the lapis-blue heavens. Facing the West, one beholds a mighty stronghold; its presence presses upon China. Primal energy flows through earth and sky across vast distances; its majesty fills the terraces and blossoms. One hears long peals of bells and chimes, and whenever one listens, the Dharma sounds bright and clear. Beneath green pines one sees compassionate elders teaching; among emerald cypresses, arhats walk. White cranes with sentiment come to Jiu Ridge. Blue-headed birds linger in quiet pavilions. Dark monkeys, in pairs, bear sacred fruit. Paired deer of long life offer violet-golden shoots. Soft birdcalls come often as if in speech. Strange blossoms of many colors unfurl in forms unknown. Returning peaks wind in layer upon layer; the ancient roads turn, and the land opens in gentle steadiness. Truly this is a pure, clear, numinous and beautiful place, charged with the solemn atmosphere of Great Awakening’s Buddhist sphere. As the Great Sage was still appreciating the scenery, he suddenly heard someone call: “Sun Wukong, where are you coming from and where are you going?” He turned quickly and saw that it was a venerable bhikshuni. The Great Sage greeted her and said, “I have a matter here and wish to see the Tathagata.” She replied, “You mischievous one. If you want to see the Tathagata, why did you not go up to the jeweled shrine and instead stand here admiring the mountain?” The Great Sage said, “It is my first time in this precious land, so I took this liberty.” The bhikshuni said, “Follow me quickly.” The Great Sage followed closely to the foot of the Leiyin Temple gate, where he saw the Eight Great Vajra Kings, grand and fierce, blocking the way on both sides. The bhikshuni said, “Wukong, wait here a moment while I present your petition.” The Great Sage had to stand outside the gate. The bhikshuni went before Buddha and knelt with joined palms: “Sun Wukong has business and wishes to see the Tathagata.” The Buddha gave instructions to admit him, and the vajra guardians then parted the way and let him through.

After bowing his head and finishing his homage, the Tathagata asked, “Wukong, I heard earlier that Bhikshu Guanyin freed your body and that you had taken refuge in the Sakyamuni teaching to protect Tripitaka on this journey for the scriptures. Why have you come here alone? What has happened?” The Great Sage knelt deeply and said, “I respectfully report, my Buddha. Your disciple has kept the monastic discipline since childhood and has come westward with my master from the Tang court to seek the Way. We arrived at the Gold-Dipper Mountain, Gold-Dipper Cave, and met a dreadful demon king named the Rhinoceros King, whose powers are vast. He seized my master, our teacher Tripitaka, and our brothers and captured them in his cave. I sought him and made requests, but there was no good intention in him. When we both resisted him, he used a white, stark haloed ring to steal my iron staff. Fearing he might be a celestial general descended to the mortal world, I hurried upward to search heaven and nether without finding him. The Jade Emperor dispatched Li Heavenly King and son to assist; even then he stole away the Crown Prince’s six battle weapons. Later Fire Virtue was asked to send down fires to burn him, but the demon stole away the fire gear. Then we asked Water Virtue to flood him, yet not a hair of his was touched by a single drop. After spending much strength and qi, I sneaked out and recovered that iron staff and the others, and went again to challenge him. He once again wrested those things from me and turned me away; I could not bring him down. So I came here to beg your compassion and ask you to let your disciple see what sort of being this is by origin. If I can return, I will take his kinsfolk and neighbors, arrest this demon king, rescue my master, and with full reverent devotion seek the true fulfillment of the Dharma.”

As soon as the Buddha heard, he gazed out with his wisdom eye and already knew. He said to Wukong: 'That monster I know, yet I must not tell you. Your monkey mouth is open and reckless; if I tell him I spoke of him, he will not fight you, but will run to Ling Mountain to raise a clamor, and even cause trouble for me. I will now support you with my powers so that you can seize him.'

Wukong knelt again and said, 'What powers will the Buddha give me?' The Buddha then told the eighteen Arhats to open the treasury, take eighteen grains of gold cinnabar, and give them to Wukong as support.

Wukong asked, 'How is this gold cinnabar used?' The Buddha said, 'Go outside the cave and call out that demon for a bout. Make him come out, and then order the arhats to cast the sand, pinning him down so he cannot move his body, cannot wrench back his feet. By your grip and striking he will be finished.'

Wukong laughed: 'Wondrous, wondrous, wondrous—send me quickly.'

Those arhats did not dare to delay. They took out the gold cinnabar and left at once. Wukong again thanked the Buddha. On the way he saw only sixteen arhats and cried out, 'Where is this place, and who has released him?' The arhats said, 'Who has released him?' Wukong said, 'It was ordered that eighteen come, and now only sixteen remain.' Before he could say more, two arhats, Descending Dragon and Subduing Tiger, came out from within.

They stepped forward: 'Wukong, how did you become so evasive? The two of us were behind, awaiting the Buddha's command.'

Wukong said, 'Too much dodging, too much dodging. You delayed only a little in your answering cry—how could you not come out yet?' The arhats laughed cheerfully and mounted auspicious clouds.

In a short while they arrived at the bounds of Gold-Dome Mountain. Li Tianwang, seeing them, led his attendants forward to welcome them and reported what had happened. The arhats said, 'No need for long words. Go call him out at once.' The Great Sage rolled his fist and came to the cave mouth, barking, 'Ravaging wretch, come out and meet your monkey granduncle here and now.'

That little demon flew off to report. The demon king roared, 'This thieving monkey still does not know whom he has invited here to make a racket.'

The little demon said, 'No other general has come, only him alone.'

The demon king said, 'That staff has already been taken back by me—how did another come yet? Does he dare to come to trade blows again?'

Taking his prized treasure in hand and a broad spear on his shoulder, he called a demon to clear away the stones, then leapt from the cave, crying, 'Monkey thief, you have not had your share of fortune for some time; you should avoid me. Why have you come back to shout?'

Wukong said, 'Savage demon, you do not know right from wrong! If you wish your old grand-uncle not to appear, then submit to the binding, offer your submission, and send out my Master and my fellow pilgrims, and I will spare you.'

The fiend said, 'Your three monks I have already washed clean; I will soon slaughter them. You still do not understand? Then go away.'

When Wukong heard the words 'slaughter', sparks of fire flared from his cheeks. He could not hold in his anger; he dropped his pretense, raised his fist, stepped aside at an angle, and moved to strike the demon with a hanging feint. The monster extended its long spear and met him with a split-second slash. Wukong jumped left and right, teasing the demon. Not seeing it as a stratagem, it chanted and ran southward from the cave mouth.

Wukong then called to the arhats: cast the gold cinnabar at the demon all together.

Fine sand it is, and this was indeed it:

Like fog like smoke at first drifting loose, in drifting murk that thickens the world, it descends across the skyline. White and vast, it confuses the eyes wherever one looks; hazy and dim, even in flight one loses the road. The firewood-boy loses his mate while chopping; the immortal-child gathering herbs finds no home. Fine and light, it drifts like flour, roughly it rolls again, like sesame. The world turns blurry, mountain tops darken; the open sky swallows the sun in a smoky shroud. It is no like choking dust behind a swift steed, rare indeed the soft padding of a perfume-carriage. This sand is but insentient matter at heart, covering earth and sky to seize the fiend. Only because a demon trespasses on the True Way, the Arhats enforcing Dharma made proud display. In his hand a bright pearl appears, and with one gust his eyes become flower-clouded.

The arhats stood empty-handed, clouds held still. Wukong came near and asked, 'All the arhats—why did you stop casting the sand?' An arhat said, 'There was just such a sound just now, and the gold cinnabar is gone.'

Wukong laughed: 'Again, he tricked them and snatched it away.'

The Heavenly King and the others said, 'He is so hard to subdue; how will we catch him? On what day can we return to Heaven, and what face shall we show the Jade Emperor?'

Nearby, the arhats Descending Dragon and Subduing Tiger said to Wukong, 'Wukong, do you know why the two of us were late in going out?'

Wukong said, 'Old Sun had only suspected you were dodging and missed the chance, not knowing another matter was to be done.'

An arhat said, 'The Buddha instructed the two of us: "The demon’s powers and arts are broad. If he loses the gold cinnabar, then send Sun Wukong to seek his traces in the Tushita Palace of Liuhen Heaven, under the Grand Supreme Elder's Lushi Hall of Mount Duoshuai. Perhaps he can be captured at one stroke."'

Wukong, hearing this, said, 'It is vexing, truly vexing. The Buddha too has played a trick on old Sun. He should have told me then and not sent you all on so far a voyage.'

Li Tianwang said, 'Since the Buddha has made this clear declaration, Great Sage, you should have risen early.'

The able Wukong said, 'Good,' then spoke the word and leapt with a jindou cloud straight through the gate of the Southern Heaven. Four great marshals stood there with fists raised and hands clasped. 'How goes the taking of the demon?' they asked.

Wukong answered as he moved, 'Not yet, not yet. I have a place now where I must trace a clue.' The four generals did not dare to hinder him and let him in through the Heaven Gate.

He did not enter Lingxiao Hall or enter Dou-ox Palace. He went straight to the outside of the Thirty-Three Heavens, before the Tushita Palace of Liuhen Heaven. There he saw two immortal boys standing guard. He did not ask their names, simply walked straight through.

Startled, the two boys seized him: 'Who are you? Where are you going?'

Wukong said, 'I am Sun Wukong, Great Sage Equal to Heaven, and I wish to seek Master Laozi.'

The boys said, 'How can you be so rough? Stay where you are and let us report.' Wukong would not allow words and gave one shout, then walked straight ahead.

At once Laozi came out from within, meeting him face to face. Wukong bent low and bowed. 'Great Elder, do not fail to look upon me as before.'

Laozi laughed. 'This monkey does not go to fetch scriptures, so why has he come to me?'

Wukong said, 'Fetching Tripitaka is a task with no rest by day or night. There are some obstacles; I have come to this place on business.'

Laozi said, 'The road to the West is obstructed. How does that concern me?'

Wukong said, 'Speak not of the Western Heaven now. If I find the trace, then we shall entangle him together.'

Laozi said, 'This is the palace of the Supreme Immortal; what trace is there to seek here?'

Wukong entered, eyes never straying. Looking east and west, he passed through several halls and then saw, by the cattle pen, a child dozing; the blue ox was no longer in the pen.

Wukong said, 'Elder, the ox has gone, yes the ox has gone.'

Laozi exclaimed in alarm, 'When did that fiend beast leave?'

As he was shouting, the child only then woke and knelt before him: 'Master, I fell asleep; I do not know when it left.'

Laozi scolded, 'How dare you doze off like this?'

The child knelt lower and said, 'In the elixir room, Master, your disciple picked up a cinnabar pill and ate one at once, and so slept here.'

Laozi said, 'It must be the seven-cycle Fire-Demon pill brewed the other day; this one had hung about; he ate one. One such pill should make one sleep for seven days. Because the boy slept, none was there to watch, and the fiend took the chance and left the realm below. It has been seven days by now.'

Now they checked whether he had stolen any treasure. Wukong said, 'No treasures in particular, only saw him with one of those iron rings, which is quite perilous.'

Laozi quickly searched. All kinds of things were present—only the Vajra chisel was missing.

Laozi said, 'This fiend stole my Vajra chisel!'

Wukong said, 'So this is the treasure. It was this thing that beat old Sun. Now in the mortal realm he runs wild and I do not know how many objects he has snatched from me.'

Laozi asked, 'Where is this fiend now?'

Wukong said, 'He now dwells in the cave of Gold-Dou Mountain, Gold-Dou Cave. He seized my Tripitaka and hauled him in, and he robbed me of the Golden-Hooped Staff. He summoned the heavenly soldiers and stole the prince’s divine weapon. He summoned Fire Virtue Star Lord and stole his implements of fire. The Water Lord could not drown him; even so he did not steal his implements. Finally, when the Buddha asked the arhats to come down with sand, he stole even that. For you, old official, by letting the demon loose to plunder and hurt others, what guilt should be laid at your door?'

Laozi said, 'My Vajra chisel is my instrument for taming barbarians at Guan Huan Pass, a treasure I have refined from childhood. By whatever weapon, water, or fire you bring, it can still not come near him. If he stole my banana leaf fan as well, not even I could control him.'

The Great Sage rejoiced with open delight and followed Laozi. Laozi took up the banana leaf fan, drove the auspicious cloud, and went with him. Out of the immortal palace and beyond the South Gate of Heaven, he lowered the cloud-face and came straight to Gold-Dou Mountain.

There he met the eighteen arhats, the Lord of Thunder, the Water Lord, the God of Fire Virtue, and Li Tianwang with his son. He explained once more all that had happened.

Laozi said, 'Sun Wukong will go out again to lure him out. Then I will capture him.'

Sun Wukong, the Great Sage, leapt down from the peakhead and shouted at the top of his voice, “Vile, filthy monster! Come out at once and die!” The little fiend ran off again to report. The old demon said, “That thief monkey, and he does not even know who he has invited!” He quickly snatched up his spear and came out to meet him at the doorway. The Great Sage shouted, “You wild demon, this time you are certainly doomed! Do not run—take one of my blows.” He sprang in a single bound and smashed a backhand slap straight into the monster’s face, then turned and ran. The demon grabbed his spear and chased. From the high peak came a call: “That bull still has not gone home; how much longer must we wait?” The demon lifted his head, saw it was Laozi, and, frightened through and through, stammered, “This thieving monkey truly is an earth-demon, yet how did he manage to get my master here?”

Laozi muttered a spell and waved his fan once. The monster hurled a loop at him, and Laozi caught it in one hand. Again he swished the fan, and the monster’s strength weakened and its sinews went numb as it revealed its true form: it was a green bull. Laozi blew divine breath through the Golden-Steel zhuo, drove it through the monster’s nostrils, took off the knot-rope from his robe sash, tied it to the zhuo, and held it in his hand. To this day they keep a bull-nose tether called Kuer, also known as Binar, and this is its appointed role. After bidding farewell to the gathered gods, Laozi mounted the green bull, rode on a colored cloud, and returned straight to Doushuayuan; with the fiend bound, he ascended high to Lihen Heaven.

Sun Wukong only together with the Heavenly King and the others had entered the cave and killed all one hundred-odd little demons, each with their weapons, and then thanked the Heavenly King and his father and returned to Heaven. Leigong went to his mansion, Huode returned to his palace, the Water Lord returned to the river, and the Arhats headed west. Only then did he release Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing and take up the iron cudgel. The three of them then thanked the Great Sage, packed up the horse and supplies, and the monastic party left the cave, taking the main road forth.

As they were in the middle of departing, they only heard a shout from the roadside: “Tripitaka, go and eat your vegetarian meal.” The elder monk was startled.

In the end they still did not know who it was that called out; listen, and the resolution will be explained in the next installment.
chapters.title: Chapter 52: Wukong wreaks havoc in Gold-Dome Cave; Buddha Shakyamuni hints at the true hero.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

"> Cultivate virtue to the tune of eight hundred measures,

accrue three thousand hidden merits in advance. Set even and impartial self, people, and even the wrongdoer. Then at last it accords with the Original Vow of the Western Heaven. I do not fear the demon-rhinoceros's steel and spears; no use toiling with water and fire when no fault is found. Laozi subdued him and led him before Heaven, then laughed and tugged the Blue Ox around."

By the roadside, who was crying out? It was the Mountain God and the Earth God of Mount Jindou, holding a purple-gold bowl as they called: "Holy Tripitaka, this bowl of food was brought forth through Great Sage Sun Wukong's transformations. Because you would not heed good counsel and blundered into the demon’s hands, Great Sage had to labor through endless hardships, and only today could he rescue you. Come and eat, then continue your road, and do not fail this disciple’s heart of reverence and filial service." Tripitaka said, "Disciple, my gratitude is boundless and words fail me. Had I known not to step out of your protective circle, how could there be such a threat to my life?" Wukong said, "I will not hide it, Master: it is because you did not trust my circle, yet you allowed yourself to fall into another. So much pain. Alas, alas!" Zhu Bajie asked, "How could there be another circle again?" Wukong replied, "It is your accursed tongue and tongue-quick curses, that mule-headed fool, that brought Master into this great calamity and compelled old Sun to turn heaven and earth. He called forth heavenly soldiers, Water and Fire, and Buddha’s cinnabar; all was finally snared in a pale, ghost-white circle. The Buddha signaled the Arhat and told old Sun the demon’s true origin; only then was Laozi invited to subdue him, and it turned out to be a deed of the Blue Ox." Hearing this, Tripitaka said, "Excellent disciple. After this trial, next time I will surely obey your commands."

Then the four shared the food, and though it had been some time, it was still steaming hot. Wukong said, "The food has sat for so long. How can it still be hot?" The Earth God knelt and said, "The little god knew that Great Sage’s task was complete, so it warmed itself to serve you." In a moment, when the meal was finished, he packed away the bowl, took leave of the Earth God and the Mountain God, and only then did Tripitaka climb onto the saddle and pass over the high mountain. It was exactly this: cleanse cares from the mind, wash the heart and return to right awakening, living on wind for food and water for lodging as one goes west.

There being early spring weather, they heard:

The purple swallows whisper, the orioles peer and sing. The purple swallows whisper, their perfumed beaks tired of song; the orioles flash and trill in nimble cadence. All over the ground, fallen red blossoms spread like brocade; across the whole mountain, fresh green unfolds like a piled carpet. On the ridges the green plums plump into bean-like buds, and ancient cypresses at the cliffs hold the drifting cloud. The wild air is damp with faint smoke-light; the sandy banks glow softly in the dimming sun. In several gardens the blossoms open at last, and the return of sunlight brings new willow shoots to the earth."

After walking some distance, it was now early spring weather still. They came upon a small river, clear as polished jade, its cold waves dark and still. Tripitaka drew up the horse and looked across. On the opposite bank, beneath willow shade and beneath a hint of that azure-green light, he saw a few eaves of a thatch cottage. Wukong pointed ahead and said, "There, on that side, is surely the ferryman’s place." Tripitaka said, "I too see the same there, but I saw no boat and could not yet speak." Zhu Bajie quickly unloaded the baggage and called out in a loud voice, "Ferrywoman, bring the boat this way." He called several times, and from the willow shade there appeared, in a quavering voice, a boat slowly pushing out, and after a short while it came close to this bank. The monks examined it closely and saw indeed:

Short oar cleaves the waves, light paddle parts the surf. The cabin is painted in bright lacquer, the deckboards are broad and even. At the bow sits an iron winch with coiled rings; aft a bright little helm-house. Though it is but a reed-borne craft, it is no poorer for lake or sea. Even without embroidered cables or tiger-toothed rigging, it truly has fir piles and cassia paddles. Not like a thousand-mile divine barge, yet it can well carry one across a single river-gap. Its coming and going stays only between two cliffs, in and out, never leaving the ancient ford."

Soon the boat touched shore. The oarsman-catcher shouted, "Those crossing, this way." As Tripitaka rode close, he looked and saw the ferryman’s form to be:

A fine velvet turban wraps her head, with soap-silk shoes on her feet. She wore a padded jacket of a hundred-stitch kind, and around her waist, a thousand-knotened skirted sash. Her wrists are thick-skinned and sinewy, hard with strength; her eyes flowered, brows furrowed, face already worn by time. Her voice was tiny and pretty like a warbler’s song, and up close she was an old boatwoman in an old maid’s pins. Wukong went near the boat’s side and asked, "Are you the ferryman?" The woman said, "Yes." Wukong said, "Where is the oar-master? How come you, an oarswoman, row the boat?" She only smiled faintly, never answering, and drew the gangplank up by hand. Sha Wujing hefted the baggage and stepped in, and Wukong supported Tripitaka up and across, then followed; Zhu Bajie hauled over the white horse, and pulled in the gangplank. The woman set the boat in motion, paddled, and in a moment they had crossed. On arriving at the west bank, Tripitaka asked Sha Wujing to untie the pack and gave her several strings of coins. She did not bargain at all, tied the rope to a post by the water, laughed cheerfully, and walked straight into the village house.

When Tripitaka saw how clear the water was, he soon felt thirsty and told Zhu Bajie, "Take the bowl and scoop some water for me to drink." The boor said, "I was just about to drink some too." So he took the bowl, scooped one, and handed it to the Master. Tripitaka ate perhaps half, leaving still almost half. Zhu Bajie took it and drank it down in one breath, then knelt and helped Tripitaka mount. The three set off westward. Not even half an hour later, Tripitaka groaned on horseback: "My belly hurts." Zhu Bajie immediately added, "I, too, feel pain in my belly." Sha Wujing said, "It must be from drinking cold water." Before he could finish, the Master called out, "The pain is sharp." and Zhu Bajie said the same, "It is sharp indeed." As the two endured, their bellies began to swell gradually. When they pressed their hands, they felt like clots of blood and chunks of flesh, with bones knocking against one another restlessly. Just as Tripitaka’s seat became unsteady, he suddenly noticed by the roadside a village house, with two bundles of straw hung from a treetop. Wukong said, "Master, that is a house selling wine. Let us go there and have them make some hot broth for you; ask whether there is anyone who sells medicine and beg for a plaster to treat your pain."

Tripitaka, delighted to hear this, dismounted from the white horse. In no time they had come to the gate and come down from the horse. On the porch outside sat an old woman on a little thatch mound, spinning hemp. Wukong stepped forward and offered greeting: "Grandmother, this humble monk comes from the Great Tang of the Eastern Capital. My Master is a prince of the Tang court. He drank from the river after crossing and now feels severe abdominal pain." The old woman laughed, "Oh, what a trick you children are! How charming. You drank from the river there, did you?" Wukong answered, "Yes, from the clear water on this eastern bank." She smiled with delight and said, "Very funny indeed, very funny indeed. Come inside and I will tell you."

Wukong helped Tripitaka and Sha Wujing helped Zhu Bajie; both cried out as they went, belly-groaning, faces yellow, brows knotted, each in pain. They sat in the thatched room. Wukong said only, "Grandmother, please boil some hot broth for my Master; we are all grateful." The old woman neither boiled broth nor moved, but laughed with a wheezy titter and ran to the back, crying, "Come out, everyone, come out and see!" From within came three half-young, half-old women, stomping out with clattering steps, all of them staring at Tripitaka and laughing. Wukong grew furious and roared once, showing his teeth. The entire household shrank, stumbling backward and then hurried out of the way. Wukong moved forward, pulled up the old woman, and said, "Burn the broth at once, and I will spare you." She trembled and said, "Sir, even if I boil broth it will not help, and I cannot treat two men’s belly pain. Let me go and explain." Wukong released her. She said, "This is the Woman’s Kingdom of Western Liang, and all under this kingdom are women; there are no men. So you look so unusual and amusing to them. Your Master’s water was unclean. The river is called the Mother-and-Child River. Outside our king’s city is a relay station called the Yingyang Guesthouse, and just outside its gate is the Zhaotai Spring. For people like me, no one over twenty years old may drink from the river water. Those who drink it will feel abdominal pain because the water carries gestation. After three days, at the edge of the Zhaotai Spring at Yingyang Guesthouse, one must look to see whether two reflections appear. If two shadows are seen, a child will be born. Your Master has swallowed the Mother-and-Child water and so has taken on the burden of pregnancy. It is near time for him to bear a child; how could hot broth cure that?"

Tripitaka, hearing this, turned pale and exclaimed, "Disciple! What are we to do now?" Zhu Bajie, bending his waist and moaning, said, "Good grief! If we must give birth, we are men. How can there be a birth passage? How can one ever come out?" Wukong laughed and said, "The elders said, 'Like ripe melon, it falls by itself.' When the hour comes, a hole will surely tear open at the side, and it will crawl out." Hearing this, Zhu Bajie trembled and, no longer able to bear the pain, cried, "Enough, enough! Then I will die, I will die." Sha Wujing said with a laugh, "Second Brother, do not twist. If you keep twisting, you may only worsen a child-carrying pain and turn it into a prenatal trouble." Zhu Bajie became more flustered; tears filled his eyes. He tugged at Wukong’s robe and pleaded, "Brother, ask this old woman to find the calmest midwives now, a few of them. The pains are gripping and coming in waves, like labor already. Hurry—hurry." Sha Wujing laughed once more: "Now that the second brother knows it is labor pain, do not twist. You fear only that you might rupture the embryo bag."

Tripitaka hummed and said, 'Grandma, do you have any physician here? Send my disciple to buy a dose of medicine to bring down the fetus, have him take it, and make him expel it.' The old woman said, 'There is medicine, but it will not help. Here, along Zhengnan Street, stands Mount Jieyang. In the mountain there is a broken cave, and in that cave is a Fall-Pregnancy Spring. Only by drinking a mouthful of that spring water can the fetal qi be dispelled. Yet the water cannot be taken now. Recently a Daoist came, calling himself Ruyi Zhenxian; he changed that broken cave into Juxian Hermitage and guards the spring water there, refusing to share it freely. If one wants the water, one must bring red paper offerings, sheep wine, and a fruit tray, and with earnest devotion make an offering, only then ask him and gain a bowlful. You itinerant monks, how can you have enough money for all that? You can only endure your fate and wait until the time to give birth.' When Wukong heard this, he was joyfully reassured and said, 'Old mother, how far is this to Mount Jieyang?' The old woman replied, 'Thirty li.' Wukong said, 'Good, good. Master, do not worry; I shall bring back some water for you.'

The Great Sage instructed Sha Wujing, 'Watch Master carefully. If this family shows no courtesy and troubles him, use your old methods and scare them at once. I am going to fetch water.' Sha Wujing obeyed. The old woman then brought out a large earthen bowl and handed it to Wukong: 'Take this bowl and fetch plenty, keeping some for us in reserve for emergencies.' Wukong truly took the bowl, left the grass hut, and rose through the clouds. At that moment the old woman looked up in reverence and said, 'My lord! This monk can ride the clouds.' She then went inside and called out several women, who came to kneel before Tripitaka and bow. All addressed him as Arhat Bodhisattva. In one corner someone cooked broth and prepared the meal in offering to Tripitaka; not recorded further.

The narrative says: Sun Great Sage raised a jindou-cloud and in a short while saw a mountain peak blocking the edge of the clouds. He steadied his cloud and looked around. 'What a fine mountain!' he thought, then beheld:

Fragrant flowers sway like brocade, wild grasses lie in blue expanse. The ravine streams join and fall, and the creek-clouds pass in still leisure. Deep valleys and gullies are wrapped in thick vines and vines, far-off peaks and trees spread thickly. Birds cry, geese pass; deer drink, monkeys climb. Green ridges stand like screen walls, blue cliffs resemble braided coiffures. Rolling dust makes it truly hard to reach, and spring stones keep whispering in little rivulets without tiring the eye. Whenever one sees an immortal child gathering herbs, one often meets a woodcutter returning with a load of fuel. Truly it is not less than the scenes of Heaven’s terrace, even surpassing the western splendor of Three Peaks Mountain.

As the Great Sage was still gazing at the mountain, he saw, in the shadow behind it, an estate and heard barking. He descended and went straight to the manor; it too was a fitting place. He saw:

A small bridge crosses living water, thatched cottage leans on green mountain. Village dogs bark amid hedges and fences; the recluse goes and returns.

Not long after, he arrived at the gate and saw an old Daoist seated in lotus posture upon green turf. The Great Sage set down the bowl and came forward to offer greetings. The old Daoist inclined his body and returned the courtesy: 'From which quarter have you come, and what business brings you to this little hermitage?' Wukong said, 'I am Tripitaka, the Dharma Master sent by the Great Tang in the East, by imperial commission, to fetch the scriptures in the Western Heaven. My Master drank from the Child-Mother River by mistake, and now suffers abdominal swelling too great to bear. Inquiring of the locals, we were told he has formed fetal qi and no remedy exists. We learned that in Mount Jieyang the Broken-Child Cave has a Fall-Pregnancy Spring that can clear such qi, so I have come specifically to make obeisance to Ruyi Zhenxian and beg spring water to save Master. Please be so kind as to point the way.' The Daoist smiled, 'This place is the Broken-Child Cave, now changed to Juxian Hermitage. I am no ordinary man; I am the senior disciple of Master Ruyi Zhenxian himself. What is your name? I must report it.' Wukong said, 'I am the senior disciple of Master Tripitaka of the Great Tang, a humble monk named Sun Wukong.' The Daoist asked, 'Where are your red token, wine and offerings?' Wukong said, 'I am a passing traveling monk; I could not make such preparations.' The Daoist laughed: 'You are very naïve. My master guards the mountain spring and has never given it away for nothing. Go and bring the gifts; then I can report it. If not, go back. Do not dare to hope, do not dare.' Wukong said, 'Compassion among people is like an imperial decree. Go tell him my name is Elder Sun Wukong, and he will surely show kindness, perhaps giving me even the whole well.'

That Daoist, after hearing this, went in only to report. He saw the true Immortal plucking the guqin and waited until the instrument was done, then said, 'Master, there is a monk outside claiming to be Sun Wukong, Great Tang Tripitaka’s senior disciple, seeking water from the Fall-Pregnancy Spring to save his Master.' The true immortal did not dismiss it at once. But when he heard Wukong’s name, anger rose at once to the top of his heart and evil flashed to the edge of his gall. He sprang up from the qin bed, shed his plain robe, put on Daoist robes, took up a Ruyi hook, leapt from the hermitage gate, and called out, 'Where is Sun Wukong?' Wukong turned and saw him thus dressed:

On his head a star-studded crown, colors flying and radiant. On his body a crimson Daoist robe woven with golden filigree. Beneath, cloud shoes heaped with brocade and embroidery. A bejewelled belt of exquisite loops around his waist. A pair of embroidered cloud-wave socks, hem of skirt flashes silk in its folds. In his hand a Ruyi golden hook, its iron shaft long and sinewy as a python. Phoenix eyes bright, brows knit in fierce arcs, steel teeth sharp and mouth reddened. Below the brow, whiskers drift like blazing fire, short red hair at temples in loose frizz. His form is menacing as Marshal Wen Yuan-shi, yet his robes and cap are not the same. Wukong joined his palms and bowed, 'I am truly Sun Wukong.' The master laughed, 'You are truly Sun Wukong, but are you one using a false surname and borrowed name?' Wukong said, 'Look at your own words. There is an old saying: a noble man does not change his given name by travel, does not alter his surname while seated. I am Wukong. How could there be any fraud?' The master said, 'Do you recognize me?' Wukong answered, 'Since I entered the True Way of Buddha and hold to the monastic teachings, I have crossed mountains and waters these days. My childhood friends I have forgotten to visit; I scarcely know your honored face. Just by asking those families west of the Child-Mother River I heard that you are Ruyi Zhenxian, and thus I knew of you.' The master said, 'You go your way, I keep my Way; why come to visit me?' Wukong said, 'Because my Master has drunk Child-Mother River water in error; his belly has swollen with fetal qi and is near death. I came to this Immortal Court to ask for one bowl of the spring to save him.'

The master glowered, 'Is your Master indeed Tang Sanzang?' Wukong said, 'Yes indeed.' The master ground his teeth in hatred: 'Have you met the Holy Infant King?' Wukong said, 'That is the nickname for the demon Red Boy of Kusong Ravine and Huoyun Cave. Why does the true Immortal ask about him?' The master said, 'He is my house-nephew, and I am the brother of the Bull Demon King. Formerly my elder brother sent word saying that Sun Wukong, Tang Sanzang’s senior disciple, was lazy and had harmed him. At this place I had no chance to bring him to account. You come here to seek me, and then ask for water?' Wukong smiled and said, 'You are mistaken. Your honored brother also was once my friend; in our youth we were seven sworn brethren. But I have not had the chance to meet your august face. Now your nephew has gained good merit and now follows Guanyin as Shancai Tongzi. Even we are not as good as that; how then could you take offense at me?'

The master shouted, 'You brash monkey, still tossing clever words! My nephew—was he not better being king in freedom, or being slave to others? Do not be so impolite. Take this one hook of mine!' The Great Sage set his staff across and said, 'Master, do not speak of fighting. Give me some water as well.' The master cursed, 'Brash ape! You do not know life and death. If in three rounds I can contend with you, take the water. If you cannot, I will turn you to meat paste, and so repay my nephew.' Wukong snarled, 'You degenerate demon who knows nothing of your own beginning! If you want to fight, draw up and show your staff.' The master’s Ruyi hook came up and met him. At Juxian Hermitage, they clashed savagely:

The holy monk ate wrong and became with fetal swelling; Wukong came seeking Ruyi Immortal. The true Immortal he had sought was, in fact, a demon, leaning on strength to guard the Fall-Pregnancy Spring. When they met and spoke of old enmity, each refused to yield a straightforward resolution. Their words and replies turned to frantic snarling; evil-minded and fierce in heart, each sought redress for grievance. This one came for water to save his Master and risk his life. That one, for his nephew’s death, would not let spring-water pass. The Ruyi hook was harsh as scorpion venom; the Golden-Hooped Staff cruel as a dragon’s summit. Chaos-thrusts at the chest, powers unleashed with ferocity. Footwork and slanting hooks revealed subtle arcana. Underhand staff blows came with no front or back; through-the-shoulder hooks rose and struck near the head like whips. A waist-locking staff, eagle-gripped sparrow; three hooks over the crown, cicadas caught like prey. Over and over they came and went, fighting for victory and defeat, returning and returning again and again. Hook and staff twisted and struck without sequence; no trace of victory or loss was seen. The master and the Great Sage fought for well over ten rounds. The master could not withstand the Great Sage. The Great Sage became even more violent, and his staff was like a roaring comet, striking wildly at the head. The master lost his strength, dragged the Ruyi hook, and withdrew toward the mountain.

Great Sage did not chase him off; instead he came into the hermitage in search of water. That Taoist had already shut the hut door. Holding his tile bowl, Sun Wukong hurried to the gate and, with all his strength, kicked it open and burst inside. He saw the priest lying against the well curb. Sun Wukong called out, raised his staff to strike, and the priest ran backward. Only then did Sun Wukong find the bucket and about to draw water, when the other rushed in front, used the Ruyi Hook to snag him by the foot, and hooked him into a fall, the blow driving him down face-first. Sun Wukong climbed up and struck with his iron cudgel. The priest kept to the side, holding the hook and saying, "See if you can take my water and get away." Sun Wukong cursed, "Come on, come on up! I’ll beat you dead, you demon-mischief!" The priest did not move forward to oppose him, only stayed his ground and forbade him from drawing water. Seeing him unmoving, Sun Wukong used his left hand to brandish the staff and his right to lower the bucket. He had only just let the rope slip down with a rattling clatter when the priest moved again with the hook. Sun Wukong could not brace one hand; the man hooked his foot once more, tugged him into a lurching stumble and pulled him all the way down into the well with the rope. "This brute is utterly impertinent," Sun Wukong said. He got up, both hands lifting the staff, and battered away at him without restraint. The priest still withdrew and did not dare meet him. Sun Wukong tried again to get water, but now he had no bucket and feared being hooked again. Inwardly he thought, "I’d better go summon some help."

Great Sage turned the cloud and headed straight to the village doorway, called out once, "Sha Wujing." Inside, Tripitaka moaned through pain while Zhu Bajie kept grunting nonstop. Hearing the call, the two exulted, "Sha, it is Wukong." Sha Wujing hurried to the door to receive him: "Elder brother, did you bring water?" Sun Wukong entered and told Tripitaka what had happened. Tripitaka, tears in his eyes, said, "My disciple, what is this to me now?" Sun Wukong said, "I came to fetch Sha Wujing to go with me to that hermitage. Let Old Sun struggle there with that fellow, and then Sha Wujing can slip in and bring water to save you." Tripitaka replied, "Both of you who are well have gone, leaving me and the two of us who are sick. Who will attend us then?" The old woman at the side spoke: "Holy arhat, just be at ease. You need not send your disciples; my household will naturally care for and attend to you. When you came this morning, we truly meant kindness. Only now, seeing this Bodhisattva drift in and out through cloud and mist, have we known that you are indeed an arhat-Bodhisattva. My household will never dare to harm you again."

The Great Sage snapped, "You women, how dare you harm him?" The old woman laughed, "Goodness, master, it is your good fortune to have arrived at my house! Had you gone to another house, you would not have gone away whole." Zhu Bajie grunted, "What do you mean, not going away whole?" The old woman said, "There are four or five in my household, all at ages where they still have strength. They have all long ago laid aside all that wind-and-moon business, so they refuse to harm you. But if you go to another house, there are elders, youths, men and women—who among them would let you pass? They will press you into coupling. If you refuse, they will kill you and cut the flesh off your bodies to make incense sachets." Zhu Bajie said, "If that is the case, I won’t mind being hurt. They are all sweet-smelling and perfumed, good for incense bags. I am a stinking pig; if they cut my flesh, it will stink too, and so I can take no harm from that." Sun Wukong laughed, "Don’t argue. Save your strength and do your proper work." The old woman said, "No need to hesitate. Go quickly and ask for water." Sun Wukong asked, "Do you have a bucket at home? Lend me one to use." The woman at once went to the back, brought out a bucket and wound out a rope, then handed them to Sha Wujing. Sha Wujing said, "Take two ropes, in case the well is very deep and needs it."

Sha Wujing took the bucket rope and followed Sun Wukong out of the village house; together they rode on the clouds. In half a watch they reached the boundary of Mount Jieyang. He checked the cloud stride and headed straight to the hermitage edge. Sun Wukong told Sha Wujing: "Keep the bucket and rope and stay hidden on one side. Wait until Old Sun breaks forth and fights him full-on. When you see our struggle at its height, slip in at the right moment, take the water, and leave." Sha Wujing obeyed him carefully.

Sun Wukong drew out his iron cudgel and, near the gate, shouted, "Open the gate, open!" The guard who saw him ran in to report at once: "Master, Sun Wukong has come again." The priest was furious in his heart. "This insolent monkey has no manners. We had heard he had some skill, and only today we truly know it—his staff is indeed hard to withstand." The Taoist assistant said, "Master, though his skill is high, you are by no means inferior to him; he is truly a match." The priest said, "The first two times, he defeated me." "Though he won twice before, it was only one fit of brute force," said the assistant. "In the later two occasions when you were drawing water, you were hooked by him into two falls, were you not? That was no equal match. Earlier you had no choice but to withdraw, and now he has come again. It must be that Master Tripitaka, with his body made so heavy, is in deep complaint and could not stay away. He surely comes with a grudge at your teacher; my master has no doubt will take the decisive victory."

Hearing this, the true immortal’s face lit with delighted composure, his whole manner proud and smiling. He strode out with his Ruyi Hook raised and called, "Impudent monkey! Why have you come again?" Sun Wukong said, "I only came to draw water." The true immortal said, "This spring is the well of my household. Even an emperor or a prime minister must come with formal libation of wine and request before receiving even a little. As for you, you are my enemy, yet you dare come unbidden, hands free, to draw water?" Sun Wukong said, "Do you truly refuse?" The true immortal said, "I refuse, refuse." Sun Wukong swore, "Reprobate demon-thing! If no water, then look at this staff!" He flung in an opening move, charged in like a packed flood, gave him no room to speak, and struck at once. The true immortal sidestepped and quickly used his hook in return. This bout surpassed the earlier ones and was truly deadly:

Golden-Hooped Staff, Ruyi Hook—both men, in anger, each carrying old grudges. Flying sand and rolling stones dim heaven and earth; kicked-up dust leaves sun and moon in sorrow. Sun Wukong, sent by his Master, comes for water; the demon-immortal, nephew of the clans, will not allow it. Both sides strain together, each stake against the other, wagering whether there will be peace. Teeth gritted, they contend for victory, testing hard and soft in stubborn turns. As each move appears, each grows braver, while clouds and mist boil up and make spirits and gods despair. Staff and hook strike with a hard, pounding rhythm; roaring shouts shake the hills and mounds. Raging winds whip the forest trees, murderous aura flashes across the Dipper and Ox. The more Sun Wukong fights, the more joyful he grows; the more the true immortal hits, the more entangled he becomes. With will and intent they wrestle in hatred; life or death undecided, they do not cease. The two of them fought hand to hand outside the hermitage gate, leaping and circling in a dance of combat, and carried it down to the foot of the mountain slope, in fierce and unbroken conflict, which I will not set down in detail.

Now as for Sha Wujing, he took up the bucket and burst through the gate. At once he saw the priest blocking the well and saying, "Who are you, and how dare you draw water?" Sha Wujing set down the bucket, drew out his Subduing Monster Staff, and without a word struck at once. The priest could not dodge in time; the staff broke his left shoulder/arm, and he fell to the ground struggling for life. Sha Wujing shouted, "I want to beat this demon-beast to death, but since you still have a human form, I still pity you and let you go. Let me draw water." The priest screamed to heaven and earth and fled to the rear. Sha Wujing then drew a full bucket of water into the bucket, walked out of the hermitage gate, mounted up into cloud and mist, and called to Sun Wukong: "Elder brother, I have fetched the water. Spare him, spare him."

When Sun Wukong heard him, he at once braced his iron staff against the hook and said, "I had intended to cut him down and annihilate him, but he has not committed a crime. Second, for the sake of your relationship to your elder brother Niu Mo Wang, I held back. Earlier, you hooked me twice and I failed to get the water. This time I used a stratagem to draw the tiger from its mountain, to lure you out into fighting, then let my junior brother fetch the water. If Old Sun truly displayed his full power, I would kill you—whether you are any kind of Ruyi Immortal or even if there were several of you. But it is best to spare a life and let one live a few more years, so let you be for now. If others come for water later, do not dare to harass them." The demon-immortal, not knowing right from wrong, tried one more display and came to hook his foot. Sun Wukong dodged the hook head, rushed up, and shouted, "Don’t run!" The demon, unprepared, gave a single kick and could not wrestle free. Sun Wukong snatched away the Ruyi Hook, snapped it into two pieces; then he took another piece and snapped that into four parts, hurling them to the ground: "Impudent demon-spawn! DARE you be insolent again?" The demon shook with fear, silent and enduring. Laughing, Sun Wukong mounted the clouds and rose. A poem attests:

Pure lead cannot be refined without true water; true water must temper pure quicksilver into dryness. True quicksilver and true lead hold no maternal qi; spiritual sand and sacred medicine are the Immortal’s elixir. A child is mistakenly formed like an unborn image, while Earth Mother exerts her power without difficulty. Topple the side-door teachings and rightfully set doctrines straight, and the Heart-Lord smiles in satisfaction.

The Great Sage cast out auspicious light, caught up with Sha Wujing, got the true water, rejoiced with joy, and returned to their place. He pressed down his cloud and came straight to the village hut. There was Zhu Bajie, belly protruding and taut, leaning against the door lintel, softly humming. The Great Sage came up quietly and said, “Bajie, when did you start to be laid up?” The fool startled and said, “Older brother, do not mock me. Has the water come yet?” The Great Sage kept teasing him, and Sha Wujing came right behind and laughed, “The water has come, the water has come.” Tripitaka, though in pain, bent over and said, “My disciples, you are exhausted, too.” The old woman too was overjoyed and all the mouths there made their respectful exclamation: “O Bodhisattva, what a rare thing—such a rare thing indeed.” She hurried to fetch a flower-patterned porcelain cup, scooped out half a cup, and handed it to Tripitaka, saying, “Honored Master, drink just a little. One sip is enough to settle the qi of childbirth.” Zhu Bajie said, “I won’t use a cup. Give me the hanging bucket and let me drink it all.” The old woman said, “Good sir, don’t do it—you’d scare him to death. If he drinks this bucket-water, it may melt away his whole intestines and belly.” Frightened, the fool dared not play tricks and took only half a cup.

At one of the mealtimes there, both of them had cramping in their bellies; their bowels rumbled with a grumbling, clattering cadence. After the rumbling, the fool could no longer hold himself: both urine and stool flowed at once. Tripitaka too could not hold back and needed to go to a quiet place to relieve himself. The Great Sage said, “Master, do not go out into the wind. If a sudden wind is taken, one may fall into a postpartum illness.” At once the old woman brought two clean buckets and set out a place for each of them. Soon enough, after each had gone a few times, they felt the pain abate, the swelling gradually dissolve, and the clots of blood and flesh break apart. The old woman then boiled some white-rice porridge to restore their weakness. Zhu Bajie said, “Auntie, my body is already truly emptied, no need to replenish it. Boil me some hot water to bathe, then I’ll be able to eat porridge.” Sha Wujing said, “Second Brother, you cannot bathe. Those in postpartum confinement fall ill from bathing in water.” Zhu Bajie said, “I have not really given birth to a great child, just a small one; why fear it? I just want to wash clean.” The old woman truly did just that, boiled some water, and had them wash hands and feet. Tripitaka ate only two small cups of porridge and broth. Zhu Bajie ate more than a dozen bowls and still asked for more. The Great Sage laughed, “You oaf, eat less. Don’t make yourself into a sandbag belly; it does not look proper.” Zhu Bajie said, “It’s nothing, it’s nothing—I’m no old sow, so what is there to fear?” Back in that house, they truly went on tidying and cooking the meal.

The grandmother said to Tripitaka, “Master, give this water to me.” The Great Sage said, “Bajie, no more water-drinking?” Zhu Bajie replied, “My belly no longer hurts. The postpartum qi must have dispersed; now it is easy and easy, so why should I drink again?” The Great Sage said, “Since both of them are well now, send the water to your own home.” The old woman thanked him, put the remaining water into a clay jar, and buried it in the ground at the back. To all the household young and old she said, “This jar of water is enough even for my coffin fund.” Everyone was happy. They set the vegetarian meal in order and moved the tables and stools apart. Tripitaka and his company ate their vegetarian repast and, after settling gently, slept through the night.

The next morning at first light, the pilgrims thanked the grandmother’s house and left the village. Tripitaka climbed to the saddle and mounted, Sha Wujing carried the knapsack, Sun Wukong led the way in front, and Zhu Bajie held the reins. Here is what follows:

With the foul mouth washed clean and the body made clean, the ordinary flesh-body dissolves away of its own accord.

It is not yet known what further matters await them in the domain ahead; listen further for the resolution in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 53: The Zen master swallows a meal and bears a ghost-born conception; the Yellow Crone brings forth water to undo the evil fetus.
