This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Soon, Sun Wukong and Zhu Bajie were about to use their arts to subdue those women when there was suddenly a rushing noise of wind. Sha Wujing bawled out in alarm, and when they turned their heads in haste, Tripitaka was nowhere to be seen. Sun Wukong said, “Who is it that has come and carried off our Master?” Sha Wuking replied, “It is a woman. She raised a whirling storm array and snatched Master away.” Hearing this, the Great Sage whistled sharply and leapt into the clouds, reaching out with his hand and looking in every direction. He saw a mass of dust, the wind roaring heavily, sweeping toward the northwest. He turned back at once and called, “Brothers, mount up in the clouds and chase after Master with me.” In response, Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing threw their packs onto the horse, and with one cry both of them leapt into midair.

The king, ministers, and women of Western Liang were startled and fell to their knees in the dust. They all said, “It was an Arhat that ascended in broad daylight; our lord need not be in fear. Tripitaka is also a Buddhist monk of the Way. We all lacked clear eyes and mistook him for a man from China. We wasted this divine effort for nothing. Please, let Your Majesty return by carriage to the capital.” The queen felt deeply ashamed. All the officials and attendants returned to their own state together; no further account need be given.

Again, the Great Sage and the two brothers rose through cloud and mist, pursuing toward the whirling wind. At length they arrived at a tall mountain. The dust had settled, the wind had dispersed, and still they did not know where the demon had gone. The brothers stepped down from the clouds and searched for a way, when suddenly one side of a wall showed bright green stone, like a screen. The three led the horses around the stone screen. Behind it were two stone gates. On the gate were six great characters reading, “Toxic-Enemy Mountain Pipa Cave.” Zhu Bajie, ignorant of the danger, strode forward to force the gate with his spade and hook. Sun Wukong quickly stopped him: “Brother, do not be in haste. We chased after that whirlwind all this way, and only after searching now have we come upon this gate, still not knowing whether it is shallow or deep. If this is not the proper gate, would it not only attract suspicion? You two take the horses and stand by the stone screen for a little while. I will go in first and inquire, to test whether anything is solid or hollow. Then we can act properly.” Sha Wujing, hearing this, said with approval, “Very good, very good indeed. Coarse in form, fine in thought—you are right: in a crisis one must first hold steady.” The two led the horses back.

Sun Wukong displayed divine power, twisted his chant, recited a spell, and in an instant transformed into a honeybee, truly nimble and light. See him:

His wings are thin and soft, bending with the wind. A narrow waist, light as sunlit silk. His mouth is sweet and once sought the flower’s stamen, His tail is keen and skillful at descending like a toad. His making of honey is not yet deep in craft, Yet his obeisance is humbly modest. Now he works this clever stratagem, And dances, winging into the eaves of the gate. From a flaw in the gate Sun Wukong pierced through and entered, passing over two layers of doors. There, in the pavilion at the center, sat a female demon. On either side stood several maidens in bright-coloured embroidered robes, with side buns in their hair, all in gaiety and joy, talking happily over something they themselves did not know how to stop. The Wukong flew silently onward and clung to the lattice of that flower pavilion, then listened closely. He saw two little girls with uncombed knotted hair carrying two hot trays up to the pavilion, saying, “Madam, one tray is savory buns stuffed with human flesh, and one tray is vegetarian buns stuffed with Deng-sha.” The demoness laughed, “Girls, bring out Tripitaka.” The maidens in embroidered robes moved into the inner room and supported Tripitaka out. The Master’s face was yellow, his lips pale white, his eyes red and wet with tears. In secret Wukong sighed and said, “The Master has been poisoned.”

The demoness came down from the pavilion, her ten fingers of spring-like tenderness, and seized the monk: “Master, do not fear. Though this is not the palace of the women’s kingdom of Western Liang, nor as rich and splendid, this is still quiet and free, truly fit for Buddha recitation and sutra study. Be my Dharma companion here; then one might truly have a hundred years of harmony.” Tripitaka was silent. The demoness continued, “Make no more worries. When you attended the banquet in the women’s kingdom, you ate nothing. Here I have both meat and vegetarian dumpling cakes; take some and calm your terror.” Tripitaka reflected inwardly: “I will not speak. I will not eat. This monster is not like that queen. The queen, at least, was of human form and acted with propriety. This one is a demon spirit. It is likely to harm me. If my three disciples do not know I am trapped here, and if she strikes me, would it not be for nothing a life given away?” He asked himself and, finding no way out, summoned his spirit and said at last, “Which is meat? Which is vegetarian?” The demoness answered, “The meat is stuffed with human flesh; the vegetarian is stuffed with Deng-sha.” Tripitaka said, “I, poor monk, eat only vegetarian food.” She laughed: “Girl, bring hot tea. Have him, your household elder, eat the vegetarian buns.” One maid at once brought a cup of fragrant tea and placed it before the elder monk. The demoness split open one vegetarian bun and handed it to Tripitaka. Tripitaka passed the meat bun, whole, to the demoness. The demoness laughed: “Tripitaka, why did you not split it open for me?” Tripitaka joined his palms and said, “As a monk, I dare not split open meat.” She said, “You are a monk and dare not split meat? Why, the other day at Zimu River you ate the flood-bread in haste, and yet today you want Deng-sha stuffing?” Tripitaka replied, “The flood made the boat go fast, while sinking sand slows the horse.”

In the cracks of the lattice, Wukong listened to the two arguing back and forth. Fearing that Master would lose his true nature, he revealed his true form and drew his Iron Staff, crying, “Abominable beast, you are impertinent!” When the demoness saw him, she exhaled a streak of smoke and covered the flower pavilion, commanding, “Girls, seize the Master.” Then she took up a triple-pronged steel fork, leapt out from the pavilion door, and shouted, “Lazy, insolent monkey! How dare you sneak into my home and spy on my face? Do not run. Take this trident from your old mother.” The Great Sage met her with his staff, and the two fought while pressing and retreating toward the cave mouth. Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing were waiting before the stone screen. At the sight of their furious contest, Zhu Bajie took up the white horse in alarm and said, “Sha Wujing, you guard the baggage and the horse. Let your old pigling come to help in the fight.” The honest fool raised both his spades and hurried up, calling, “Elder brother, move back; let me beat this shameless one.” When the demoness saw Zhu Bajie arrive, she used another art: she shouted once, breath-fire from her nose, smoke from her mouth, shook her body, and the triple-pronged fork swirled out to meet him. She came rolling forward, her head and face hidden, yet of no count of hands. Thus Wukong and Bajie held her at both flanks and fought. The demoness said, “Sun Wukong, you truly know not how to keep distance. I recognize you; you do not recognize me. Even Buddha of the Thunder-Roaring Temple fears me. With these two hairy men, where could you go? Come on, both of you—let me inspect you one by one and beat you properly.” This bout was a rare and fierce contest:

The demoness was long in majesty, and the Monkey King rose in valor. Marshal Tiānpéng and Wukong contended in deeds of valour, wildly lifting pikes and spades to show strength. The one with many hands set down her steel fork, smoke-light coiling tightly. These two, quick-tempered and manful in war, sent dense mist and vapor up and up. The demoness sought a husband only; how could this monk of a man yield his source of life? When yin and yang do not match, each clings and resists; each displays fierce cleverness, and they rage through bitter contention. Yin should rest still and preserve its abundance; Yang should gather and guard love in purity. So there was no peace in either side, as fork and spade and staff gambled on victory. The staff had strength, and the pike seemed stronger; the demoness’s steel fork clanged against it, point for point. Before Poison-Enemy Mountain there was no concession; outside the Pipa Cave, no compassion. That one rejoices at winning Tripitaka as a phoenix-pairing mate; these two must follow the elder monk to win the true scripture. Terrible against heaven and earth, they came to battle, making sun and moon dim and stars and constellations waver. After a long time they fought, but no victor was decided. The demoness then sprang up and used a reverse-horse poison stake, and without warning struck once at the crown of the Great Sage’s head. Wukong cried out, “Agh! It hurts!” and unable to bear it, withdrew in defeat. Zhu Bajie saw the strife had gone wrong and drew back dragging his spade. The demoness, having gained the advantage, withdrew and put away her steel fork.

Wukong held his head, brows knotted, face in pain, and called out, “Peril! Peril!” Zhu Bajie came near and asked, “Brother, why did you, just when the fight was turning well, retreat crying out as if in pain?” Wukong clutched his head and only cried, “It hurts, it hurts, it hurts.” Sha Wujing said, “It seems your head wind has risen.” Wukong jumped up, “No, no.” Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, I never saw you wounded, yet your head hurts. Why is it?” The Great Sage sniffed and said, “No joke. No joke. As we faced him directly, when he saw me break his trident pattern, he sprang up and, I do not know with what weapon, struck my head once. The pain became so hard to endure that I had to leave the field.” Zhu Bajie laughed, “So with such constant boasting in peaceful moments you said your head had been tempered by training, yet you cannot endure this one jab?” Wukong replied, “It is true. This head of mine, since I perfected true being, stole the peaches and immortal wine, stole Laozi’s Golden Elixir, and during the ruckus in Heaven was sent by the Jade Emperor with the Great-Power Ghost King and the Twenty-Eight Constellations to Douniu Palace, where divine generals cut and severed with ax and hammer, and thunder struck and fire burned. And when Laozi later placed me in the Bagua Furnace and refined me for forty-nine days, none of that harmed me. Yet today I do not know what weapon this woman used to wound my head.” Sha Wujing said, “If you let go of your grip, let me see to it. Do not break it yet.” Wukong said, “No, no, do not break it.” Zhu Bajie said, “I will go to Western Liang and fetch some salve for you to apply.” Wukong said, “If it is not to break, how can I apply any salve?” Zhu Bajie laughed. “Brother, I have never had that before and after my birth, and you have managed to make yourself a boil at the brow.”

Sha Wujing said, “Second Brother, stop teasing. It is already dark, Big Brother has hurt his head, and our Master’s life and death are unknown. What are we to do?” Sun Wukong snorted. “Master is safe. When I entered, I turned into a honeybee and flew inside. I saw the woman seated at a flower pavilion. After a while, two maidservants came carrying two trays of mo cakes: one with meat filling, savory; one with dengshā filling, vegetarian. Then two young girls came out and offered to bring Master out so he could eat a calming bite, as if to keep him company. At first Master neither answered the woman nor ate the mo. Later, because of her sweet words, he somehow spoke, and said he wanted the vegetarian one. She split open the vegetarian one and handed it to him. Master gave her the whole savory one. The woman asked, “Why did you not split it apart?” Master replied, “An ordained monk dare not tear apart meat.” She said, “If you do not tear meat, how is it that the other day you drank water at Zimu River and today you are so fond of dengshā filling?” Master did not understand and answered, “The boat had to depart at once, and sand slowed the horse’s stride.” From behind the lattice I heard this and feared Master would lose his composure, so I revealed my true form and struck with my staff. The monster used magic too, spitting out smoke and shouting, “Seize the monk,” then swinging a steel fork, it made holes in Old-Son’s blows.” Sha Wujing heard this, bit his fingers, and said, “That shameless jade-hearted braggart never mind where she came from, yet she came with us and already knew all the details.”

Zhu Bajie said, “If that is how it is, we might as well not rest. Don’t care whether it is dusk or midnight—let us storm her gate, shout and make a din, keep her from sleeping, and stop her from tricking our Master.” Sun Wuking said, “My head hurts. We cannot go.” Sha Wuking said, “No need to force a fight. First, Big Brother has a headache; second, our Master is a true monk and will not let lustful beauty disorder his discipline. Let us remain on the slope below, sit in a sheltered spot tonight, restore our strength, and at daybreak handle it.” So the three of them tied down the white horse, guarded the baggage, and spent the night on the slope, with no further account.”

The demoness cast off her ferocity and arranged her face into delight again, saying, “Children, shut both the front and back doors tightly.” She also put two guards to watch; if they heard any sound at the gate, they were to report at once. Then she ordered, “Girls, set the bedchamber in order; hold the candles and light the incense. Invite Monk Tang, I will unite with him.” She brought the Great Master out from the rear. The demoness assumed a very delicate and alluring manner and said to Tripitaka, “There is a saying: ‘Gold is not the truly precious thing; comfort is worth more.’ Come, let us make merry like husband and wife.” The Master clenched his teeth and made no sound. He wanted to withdraw, but for fear she might take his life, he followed her tremulously into the perfume chamber. He acted as if half-mad and mute, never raising his head or eyes; he did not look at what bedding or curtains were in the room, nor knew of any chests or beauty cases. Even when she spoke in the tones of rain and cloud, he did not hear. A good monk indeed:

He does not look at base sights, nor listen to erotic songs. He takes embroidered loveliness like filthy earth, and gold-and-pearl beauty like mere dust. He loves only meditation all his life, never stepping away from the Buddha realm. What care has he for jade and scented hair, when all he knows is the cultivation of truth and the guarding of nature? She is vivid and lively, with spring longing without edge; this elder monk is still as death, with Chan insight still present. One is like soft jade and gentle fragrance; this one like dead ash, dried wood. One displays the phoenix-pair bed and throbbing lust; this one gathers his robe and keeps a monk’s mind fixed as if on a wall, bound for the mountain to visit Bodhidharma. She undressed, displaying her fragrant skin and soft flesh; Master drew up his robe and tightly hid his rough body and coarse skin. The demoness said, “The bed and quilt are ready—why don’t you sleep?” Tripitaka replied, “With this pounding head, how can I keep you company?” She said, “I would be your former-chapel Lily Cui.” He said, “I am no Yuezhalī monk.” She said, “I am as fair as Xi Shi, still graceful and soft.” He said, “My king of Yue has long lain buried.” She said, “Young Master, do you remember, ‘Better to die beneath blossoms and still be elegant as a ghost?’” He answered, “My true yang is my ultimate treasure; how could I lightly give it to your powdered skull?” Their words and replies continued like that, fighting each other till deep into the night, and Tripitaka remained inwardly unmoving. The demoness pulled and tugged and would not release him; the Master was steady, refusing through and through. It persisted until near midnight when she, annoyed and angry, called, “Girls, bring rope.” Alas, she bound her beloved plaything with a rope into something like a gibbon-shaped knot. She then ordered him dragged to under the veranda, extinguished the silver lamp, and sent everyone to his own bed. It passed as a night without words.

Before they knew it, the rooster called three times. Sun Wukong at the base of the slope bent down and said, “I had this headache earlier, and now it is neither painful nor numb—just a little itchy.” Zhu Bajie laughed, “If it itches, pinch him again; what do you say?” Wukong spat and snapped, “Enough, enough, enough.” Zhu Bajie laughed again, “Enough, enough, enough—my Master had a riotous night, truly a wild one.” Sha Wuking said, “No quarrelling. Daylight is near; hurry and go catch that demon tonight.” Wukong said, “Brother, you stay here and guard the horse, do not stir. Zhu Bajie, go with me.”

The pig monk shook himself awake, smoothed his black brocade robe, and followed Sun Wukong. Each taking weapons, they leapt onto the mountain cliff and went straight to beneath the stone screen. Wukong said, “You stand here. I fear this demon may have harmed Master in the night, so first let me go in and find out. If she has enticed him and spoiled his vital essence, then truly his virtue is broken and our discipline is lost; then we all scatter in flames. If he has not been thrown into confusion and his Chan mind remains unmoved, then hold hard and fight, kill the spirit-beast, and save Master for the Western journey.” Zhu Bajie said, “You are too foolishly quiet. There is a saying: ‘Can one use a cat for a dried-fish pillow?’ Whether this or that, I’ll still grab you a few times.” Wukong said, “Don’t spread reckless doubts. Let me go see.”

The Great Sage turned aside the stone screen, left Zhu Bajie, and changed back into a bee, flying into the gate. He saw two maidservants inside the gate, each resting with handbells tucked under their heads, sleeping soundly. He went to the flower pavilion to look. The demoness, having made a racket the whole half-night, and all the others, seemed not to know it was already dawn; they still slept. Wukong circled behind. He could barely hear nothing but Tripitaka’s voice calling. Suddenly he looked up and saw Tripitaka tied under the corridor with all four limbs bound together. He lightly tapped the Master’s head and called, “Master.” Recognizing the voice, Tripitaka said, “Has Wukong come? Save me quickly.” Wukong asked, “How did matters go last night?” Tripitaka, teeth clenched, said, “I would rather die than consent to this.” Wukong said, “Yesterday I saw her as if she had pity and affection, and yet how has she today reduced you to this humiliation?” Tripitaka said, “She entangled me half the night. My belt was never undone; my body did not touch the bed. When she saw I would not follow her, she bound me here. You must save me and go to fetch the scriptures.”

As the master and disciples were still talking, the demoness was wakened. Though she had become cruel, she still had a lingering attachment, hard to let go. In one turn she rolled over and just then heard the words, “Save me and go get the scriptures.” She came down from the bed, shouted harshly: “If we are not to be husband and wife, then why should he go for scriptures?”

Wukong, flustered, left Master behind, hurriedly spread his wings and flew out. He returned to his true form and called, “Zhu Bajie.” From behind the stone screen, the boar monk said, “Did that matter get settled?” Wukong laughed, “Not yet. Master was not yielding while she teased him, and in her anger she bound him there. He had only just begun telling me the earlier events when that monster woke; I came out in a panic.” Zhu Bajie asked, “What did Master say?” Wukong said, “He said only that his robe was never loosened and his body never touched the bed.” Zhu Bajie laughed, “Excellent, excellent, he is still a true monk. Let’s go save him.”

Zhu Bajie, rough as always and not allowing further words, swung his iron spike and struck the stone gate with all his force, making a loud, clattering crash and hewing it into chunks. Frightened, several maidservants with bells at their heads who had been sleeping ran to the outside of the second gate, crying, “Open the door—the front gate was smashed yesterday by those two ugly men!” The demoness was just stepping out when she heard five maidservants run inside and report: “Madam, those two ugly men who came yesterday have come again and already shattered the front gate.” On hearing this, the monsteress at once called, “Girls, heat water, wash your faces, and comb your hair.” Then she shouted, “Carry in the rope that bound our young Master and put it away in the back room. Wait till I go beat him.”

Imp, come out and face us, holding a three-pronged fork. He shouted, “Muddy monkey! Wild boar! blind fool. How dare you break into my gate?” Zhu Bajie shouted back, “Lewd, base trickster! You first trapped my Master, then dared to snarl at me. My Master is one you lured here to make a husband; send him out at once and I may spare you. If you utter one more word of ‘no,’ this old boar will strike you with my cangue-spike hard enough to shake even a mountain down.” The demon, without giving room for reply, shook his body, resumed his arts, breathed smoke and fire from nose and mouth, and raised the steel fork to jab at Zhu Bajie. Zhu Bajie sidestepped, met it with his spike, and Sun Wukong helped him by driving in with the Iron Staff. The demon again used sorcery, with no one knowing how many hands he had, and blocked them from both sides. After three or five rounds of exchange, with some unknown weapon he even pierced Zhu Bajie on the lip. The glutton dragged off his cangue-spike, mouth twisted in pain, and staggered away to preserve himself. The Great Sage, who had been singed by him too, tossed out a feigned swing, withdrew and retreated. The monster returned victorious and called his attendants to stack stone blocks up before the front gate; no further account is given.

Sha Wujing was out on the slope holding the horse, when he heard Zhu Bajie grunting from that direction. He lifted his head and saw the fool holding his mouth in pain and groaning as he came. Sha Wujing asked, “What happened?” Zhu Bajie groaned, “Unbearable—unbearable. Painful, painful, painful.” He could say no more. Sun Wukong came up then and laughed, “Good fool, yesterday I called it a boil in the forehead; today you’ve even made yourself into a swollen-boil mouth.” Zhu Bajie groaned, “Can’t bear it, can’t bear it. It hurts sharply; this is serious, serious.”

As the three were still in trouble, an old mother appeared, carrying a green bamboo basket in her left hand and coming along the South Mountain path with vegetables. Sha Wujing said, “Eldest brother, that old woman has come near. Let me ask her—what demon is this, what weapon is that, and how can it wound so?” Sun Wukong said, “Hold on. Let old Sun ask.” Sun Wukong looked sharply and saw auspicious clouds covering her head and fragrant mist enveloping her body. He recognized her and called out, “Brothers, kneel at once—the mother is a bodhisattva.” Zhu Bajie, despite his pain, knelt in pain to salute. Sha Wujing pulled the horse and bent low, while Sun Wukong clasped his hands and knelt, calling out, “Namo Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful, Guanyin, Soul-Stirring Bodhisattva of Guanshiyin, Savior of those in suffering and distress.”

Guanyin saw they had recognized her true radiance and stepped on the auspicious clouds, rising into midair, revealing her true form. At first she had been in the likeness of a fish-basket. Sun Wukong hurried into the air, knelt and explained, “Bodhisattva, forgive me for the offense of not receiving you at once. We have been laboring to rescue Tripitaka; we did not know the bodhisattva had descended. Now we face a demon obstruction that we cannot contain. I pray you, please rescue us.” Guanyin said, “That demon is extremely fierce. The three-pronged fork he carries is made from two pincer claws. The thing that makes people cry out in pain is a hook on his tail, called dao-ma poison. In his true form he is a scorpion spirit. Formerly, at Le Yin Temple he heard the Buddha expound the sutras. When the Buddha saw him, he could not even push him away with his hand; the demon immediately turned the hook and stabbed the Buddha’s left thumb once. The Buddha himself could not bear the pain, and ordered the Vajra to seize him. Yet he is here now. If you wish to save Tripitaka, you must summon another helper; I cannot come near this foe. Sun Wukong bowed again and said, “Please indicate, Bodhisattva—who is the one we should summon? I will go at once to invite him.” Guanyin answered, “Go to the Bright Hall at the Eastern Heavenly Gate and petition the Mao-rì Star Officer. Only then can he be subdued.” Saying so, she turned into a shaft of gold light and returned straight to the South Sea.

Sun Wukong then guided the top of his cloud down and said to Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, “Brothers, fear not—our Master has a rescuer now.” Sha Wujing asked, “Where is this rescuer?” Sun Wukong replied, “Just now the bodhisattva instructed me to petition the Mao-rì Star Officer. I am going now, Elder.” Zhu Bajie groaned through his mouth, “Brother, why not ask the Star Officer for some medicine for this pain as well?” Sun Wukong laughed, “No need for medicine—just as yesterday it passed after one night’s pain.” Sha Wujing said, “No need to delay; go quickly.”

Sun Wukong set off quickly and rode the Cloud of the Jidou, and in no time reached the outside of the Eastern Heavenly Gate. Suddenly he saw the Great King Zengzhang standing before him and bowing: “Great Sage, where are you bound?” Sun Wukong said, “I am escorting Tripitaka westward to fetch the scriptures. On the road we are entangled by demon obstruction; I must go to the Bright Hall to see the Mao-rì Star Officer.” Then Tao, Zhang, Xin, and Deng, the Four Great Marshals, asked too where he was headed. Sun Wukong said, “I go to seek the Mao-rì Star Officer to subdue the demon and save my Master.” The marshals said, “The Star Officer this morning, by decree of the Jade Emperor, went to inspect things from the star terrace.” Sun Wukong said, “Can this be true?” Xin Tianjun said, “Your little captains have been with him in the same Douniu Palace; none of us would dare to lie.” Tao Tianjun said, “It has been quite some time; he may have returned by now. Great Sage, go first to the Bright Hall. If he has not come back, then go to the star observatory as well.”

The Great Sage was overjoyed and left them. At the gate of the Bright Hall, there was indeed no one; he withdrew his form and left, when he saw a line of soldiers arrayed by the wall and the Star Officer coming in their wake. The Star Officer still wore ceremonial robes suitable for audience, with a robe all threaded in gold. He appeared as follows:

His crown and hairpin glowed with the golden light of the Five Great Peaks, and his court tablets held jade-like brilliance like mountain and river. His robe hung heavy with clouds of the Seven Stars, and clouds of radiance billowed like a curtain. Tinging pendants chimed in rhythmic notes; his swift speed sounded like bells in the wind. With a green-feathered fan he unfurled the Mao stars, and heavenly fragrance swept through the whole courtyard. The forward soldier saw Sun Wukong standing outside the Bright Hall and quickly turned to report, “Lord, Sun Wukong is here.” The Star Officer drew in the cloud-mist, tidied his ceremonial robes, bade the attendants part on either side, and came forward, bowing: “Great Sage, what brings you here?” Sun Wukong said, “I came only to beg you to relieve one hardship and save the Master.” The Star Officer asked, “What hardship? In what place?” Sun Wukong said, “In Pipa Cave on Mount Dudi in Western Liang.” The Star Officer asked, “What demon is in that cave that you would summon this minor god?” Sun Wukong said, “Guanyin Bodhisattva just manifested a moment ago and said it is a scorpion demon. She specifically recommended you as the one able to cure him, so I have come to ask.” The Star Officer said, “I had intended to report to the Jade Emperor, but now that the Great Sage has come and with Bodhisattva’s recommendation in hand, I fear any delay would fail the task. I will not even dare to request tea; I will go with you to subdue the demon and then later make my court report.”

As soon as he heard this, the Great Sage left at once with him, went through the Eastern Heavenly Gate, and straight to Western Liang, where Mount Dudi was not far. He pointed ahead: “That is the mountain.” The Star Officer pressed down his cloud, and the party arrived below the slope before the stone screen. Sha Wujing saw this and said, “Second brother, stand up. Elder has brought the Star Officer.” The fool, still nursing his mouth, said, “Forgive me, forgive me. I am ill and cannot perform due rites.” The Star Officer said, “You are one who cultivates; what illness is this?” Zhu Bajie said, “Early this morning I fought that demon and he pierced my lip. It still aches.” The Star Officer said, “Come up, let me treat you.” The fool dropped his grip and groaned, “Please heal me thoroughly; when I am well I shall thank you.” The Star Officer touched the wound on the lip and blew once; the pain disappeared. Zhu Bajie joyfully knelt and said, “Wondrous! Wondrous!” Sun Wukong laughed, “Please touch my head as well.” The Star Officer replied, “You are not afflicted by poison. Why would you ask for this?” Sun Wukong said, “Yesterday I was poisoned too; once a night passed, it ceased. There is still some numbness and itching, and I fear latent venom might rise. Please treat me.” The Star Officer truly touched his head and blew once; the remaining poison was cleared, and there was no more numbness or itching. Zhu Bajie, now hardening his spirit, said, “Brother, go strike that vile one.” The Star Officer said, “Exactly, exactly. Call him out together, and then let me subdue him.”

Sun Wukong and Zhu Bajie leapt up onto the slope and went to the back of the stone screen. The fool, speaking nonsense through his swollen mouth, muttered, “His hook is like a hauling-claw,” and with one driving blow of the spike he tore apart the stones piled outside the cave-mouth. He forced his way through the first gate, then with another spike-stroke smashed the second gate to dust. A young demon inside cried out in alarm, “Grandmother, those two ugly men have broken through the second gate as well!” The fiend there had been teaching Tripitaka to be released and asking for plain tea and plain grain to eat. Hearing the second gate broken, he at once leapt out of the flower pavilion, lifted his fork and lunged at Zhu Bajie. Zhu Bajie met him with a spike-stroke; Sun Wukong, standing to one side, struck with the Iron Staff. The demon ran close to make poisoned attacks, and Sun Wukong and Zhu Bajie, recognizing his method, turned and fled back.

After that demon had run past the Stone Screen, the Monkey Monk shouted, “Where is the Mao Star Officer?” At once that Star Officer stood upon the hill slope and revealed his true form. He was in truth a great double-crested cock, raising his head to the height of six or seven feet, and he crowed once at the demon. The demon instantly showed his true form too: a scorpion spirit the size of a pipa. The Star Officer crowed once more, and that monster’s whole body turned limp and soft and died on the slope. A poem gives testimony:

With its flowered crest and embroidered neck, like a twisted plume, its claws firm and hard, its long eyes blazing with wrath. It leaps in virile strength with all five virtues, a towering, mighty form to shame three-fold crowing. What is it to that common bird that cries from a thatch-roofed hut? It is truly a heavenly star revealing a sacred name. A venomous scorpion, wrongly trying to walk as a human, now, returned to source and seen, appears in its true form. Zhu Bajie stepped forward and with one foot pinned the creature on its chest and back: “Curse-beast! This time I’ll not let you use the back-fall venom.” The monster did not move at all; the fool then drove down a single strike with his spiked mace, smashing it into a mass of rotten mash. The Star Officer gathered up his radiance again, mounted the clouds, and departed. The Monk, with Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, faced heaven and thanked him: “You have earned your merit, you have earned your merit. Another day we shall go to the palace and repay our thanks.”

Only after the three had offered their thanks did they pack up their baggage and horses and all go inside the cave. They saw all the maids, both great and small, kneel on both sides and bow, saying: “Master, we are not demons or monsters. We are women of the Xiliang Kingdom, taken here by this scorpion spirit. Your Teacher sits in the rear fragrance chamber and is weeping.” Hearing this, the Monk observed closely and truly saw no demonic aura. He then entered the rear room and called out, “Master.” When Tripitaka saw everyone gathered, he was greatly pleased and said, “Excellent disciples, I have troubled you. How are those women?” Zhu Bajie replied, “That wretch was a great mother scorpion. By Guanyin’s instructions, Senior Brother went to the Heaven Palace and summoned the Mao Sun Star Official to descend, and subdued that thing. Only then did this old pig dare to make it into clay and venture this far in so he could behold the Master’s face.” Tripitaka thanked him without end. They sought some plain rice and plain flour, laid out food, and ate one meal. They drove the women brought here by the spirit back down the mountain and pointed them toward the road home. They lit a torch, burned the few houses to complete ruin. Then they invited Tripitaka to mount, and set out in search of the main road westward. It ran:

Sever the worldly ties, leave behind form and appearance, and with mind unruffled, awaken to the Dharma as in a great metal sea laid dry.

In the end, it is still unknown after how many years they will yet attain true enlightenment. Listen in the next chapter for the full resolution.
chapters.title: Chapter 55: Lustful illusion seduces Tripitaka; steadfast nature keeps his practice from breaking.

chapters.html:
This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

The poem says:

At Ling Terrace there is no thing to name, and yet it is called pure; still and silent, not a single thought is born. Restrain ape and horse, forbear from wildness; keep your spirit and vigilance, and do not rise in proud frenzy. Cast out the six thieves, awaken to the Three Vehicles, and all conditions will cease, each made clear. When lust and evil are forever extinguished, one passes beyond the realm of true purity and rests in bliss in the Western Heaven’s land of joy.

It is said that Tripitaka, biting nails and chewing iron, risked his life and kept from himself an unbroken body; by the help of Sun Wukong and the others, they slew the scorpion demon and rescued Pipa Cave. They traveled on in silence, and already it was the Zhu Ming hour. They saw this:

Warm wind now carried wild orchid scent; after the rain had washed everything clean, the new bamboo was cool. Mugwort leaves filled the hills, yet no travelers came to pluck them; cattail flowers filled the ravines and contended for sweetness in bloom. Pomegranates bloomed in beauty, and bees rejoiced among them; creek-side willows made thick shade while the yellow warblers played wildly. A long road cannot bear even a pair of horned millet-bags; dragon boats belong to mourning on the Miluo River. The master and his disciples admired the Duanwu sights and idled through the midday holiday. Suddenly they saw a high mountain blocking the way. The elder pulled the reins and called back, “Sun Wukong, there is a mountain ahead. It may be where another demon lies in wait, so we must be careful.” The others said, “Master, do not worry. We have returned and pledged our devotion. What demon can frighten us?” Hearing this, the elder was heartened. He cracked the reins and, with a signal, spurred the good horses onward. In a moment they reached the cliff. Looking up, what they saw was: At the summit, pine and cypress touched the cloud-blue heights; rock walls, thorns and briars, and wild vines hung from them. Ten thousand feet of severe ridges, thousand-fold suspended cliffs cutting sharply down. Mosses of green and blue moss spread over the shadowed stones. Old firs and tall locusts together made one vast forest. Deep in the woods, strange birdsong could be heard, subtle and clear enough to invite verse. In the ravine water rushed as though jade were being poured. Flowers along the way lay fallen like heaps of gold. The mountain was so cruel, not fit for passing, and in every ten steps there was not half a step of level ground. Fox and deer came in pairs; a white stag and black ape faced one another. Suddenly, a tiger roar startled one’s courage, and a crane cry rang all the way through the sky and court. Yellow plums and red apricots were fit for eating; wild grasses and stray blooms, whose names were unknown, grew in the shade. The four entered the mountain and moved slowly for a long while, then passed over the crest. Down the westward slope was a stretch of open plain. Zhu Bajie showed off his vigor and told Sha Wujing to carry the load, while he walked ahead with both hands raising his spade, trying to drive the horse. The horse was no more afraid of him; though that fool kept tapping and scolding, it still moved only slowly. Sun Wukong said, “Brother, why make him hurry? Let him go at a slow pace.” Zhu Bajie said, “Evening is coming. Since morning we have climbed and travelled all day, and our bellies are empty. Let us go on a bit, find a household, and break fast.” Sun Wukong heard and said, “Very well. Then wait while I tell him to run.” He flicked the Golden-Hooped Staff once, gave a shout, and the horse slipped the bridle and went off like an arrow down the even road.

You say the horse is not afraid of Zhu Bajie, so what is it that it fears in Sun Wukong? Five hundred years ago he had been appointed by the Jade Emperor in Great Pure Heaven to oversee horse tending in the Horse Bureau, with the title Bimawen. The charge remained in force to this day, and all horses still fear the monkey.

The elder could not hold the reins; he only tightened the cinch on the saddle and let the bridle go. He allowed him to run full course, and only after about twenty li across open fields did he finally slow into an easy stride.

While they were proceeding, suddenly there was a strike of drum and gong; from both sides of the road thirty-odd men burst out, each armed with spear, knife, staff, or club, and blocked the way, saying, “Monk, where do you go?” Tripitaka, startled, trembled so much that he could not sit steady. He fell from the horse and crouched in the roadside grasses, crying only, “Great King, spare my life, Great King, spare my life.” The two men in front said, “We will not strike you; just leave toll money.” Only then the elder understood that this was a band of hard men. He bowed slightly and raised his head to look. He saw that they were:

One had a green face and fang-like teeth, bold as if to insult the Year Lord. One had raging eyes, round as a funeral gate. Red hair at the temples burned like drifting fire; yellow beard beneath the chin stood like inserted needles. The two wore tiger-skin caps with painted cloth and bound ermine-trimmed war sashes at the waist. One held a wolf-tooth staff in hand, the other carried a split cane lash on his shoulder. Truly they were not inferior to the tigers of Bashan and looked very much like dragons come from water. Seeing how wild and terrifying they were, Tripitaka could only rise and bring his palms together at his chest: “Great King, this poor monk is Tripitaka, sent by the Tang king of the Eastern Capital to travel west for scriptures. Since leaving Chang’an, many years have passed; whatever toll money I once had is spent. As a monk he begs only by request for alms—how could he obtain silver and grain? I beg your mercy; let this poor monk pass.” One of those two bandit chiefs came forward: “We set up a tigerheart bandit post here and stop the road to levy tribute. What is this talk of mercy? If you truly have no money, quickly strip off your robe, leave the white horse, and then we will let you through.” Tripitaka replied, “Amitabha Buddha! This robe of mine is patched with cloth from one house, stitched with needles from another, pieced together bit by bit. If you strip it off, will you not kill me with it? One who is a hero in this life may become a beast in another.” Hearing this, the thieves grew furious and drew their clubs. One raised his club and came forward to beat him. The elder gave no reply. In his heart he thought, “How pathetic. He only says he has his club, but he does not know my disciple’s club.” The thief gave no chance to answer, held up his staff and struck at him wildly. A monk never learned to lie, but in this urgent moment with no way out, he had to speak a falsehood: “Great Kings, do not strike yet. I have a young disciple behind; he has a few taels of silver. I will give him to you.” The thief said, “A monk who gives like this may be trying to trick us. Bind him up.” The roughs rushed together, bound him with one rope, and hung him high on a tree.

Then the three calamity fiends arrived running behind. Zhu Bajie laughed aloud, saying, “Master, you escaped quickly. I wonder where you waited for us.” Seeing the elder hanging in a tree, he added, “Look, while we wait this while, he has a heart like this one—he climbs the tree and pulls vines to swing and play like a child.” Sun Wukong saw this and said, “Idiot, stop your chatter. Is not the Master hanging there? You both come slowly; let me go see what has happened.”

Great Sage hurried up a high bank and looked closely. He recognized them as a gang of rough men and thought inwardly, “How fated, how fated—profit has come to my doorstep.” Then he turned and shifted form, becoming a neat little monk. He wore a black robe and looked only about twenty-eight, with a blue cloth bundle on his shoulder. He pulled forward, coming before them, and called, “Master, what is this? What sort of villains are these?” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, why not save me first and then ask all these questions?” Sun Wukong asked, “What are they making such a racket about?” Tripitaka said, “This crowd who blocked the road held me up for toll. I had nothing at hand, so they hung me up here and told me to wait until you came to settle things. If not, give this horse to them.” Sun Wukong, smiling, said, “The master is not wise enough. There are monks under heaven, yes, but few with skin as loose as yours. Emperor Taizong sent you west to see Buddha—who taught you to give away the Dragon Horse?” Tripitaka answered, “Disciple, being hung up like this for toll, what else can I do?” Sun Wukong said, “What did you tell him?” Tripitaka replied, “He beat me hard and drove me to it, so in panic I gave you away.” Sun Wukong said, “Master, you have no sense at all. How could you give my name like that?” Tripitaka replied, “I only said you had some toll money with you and told him not to strike me; that was the only emergency word.” Sun Wukong said, “Very well, very well. Thanks for your help. Exactly the line I needed. If he were willing to trade like this for seventy or eighty turns in a month, Old Sun would have excellent business.”

When the robbers saw Sun Wukong speaking with his master, they dropped their airs and closed in around him, saying, “Little monk, your master has told us there is money tied at your waist. Bring it out at once if you want your lives spared. If he says even one ‘no’, we will all send your life on its way.” Sun Wukong set down his bundle and said, “Officials, do not raise such noise. There is some money in this bundle; not much. There are only about twenty ingots of horse-hoof gold and twenty or thirty pieces of powder-faced silver, not counting scattered small change, which I have not counted. If needed, take the whole bundle at once, but do not strike my master. In the old books it is written: ‘Virtue is the root; wealth is the husk.’ This is trifling. We monks can always take recourse to alms; if we meet a vegetarian elder monk, there is alms money and there are robes enough. What use is this for us? Just let my master be released and I will give everything together.” Hearing that, the robbers were all delighted and said, “This old monk is stingy, but this little monk is generous.” “Let him down,” they ordered. The master, who had gained his life, leapt onto the horse, did not even glance back at Sun Wukong, cracked his whip, and rode swiftly back by the old road.

The Great Sage cried out in haste: “We have gone the wrong way.” He snatched up his bundle and tried to chase them. The gangsters blocked him and said, “Where are you going? Hand over the travel money so we needn’t torture you.” Sun Wukong smiled. “Let us be clear. The travel money should be divided into three shares.” Their leader said, “This little monk is too sly; he wants to hide some of it from his master. Very well, take it out and show it. If there is a lot, I’ll share some with you so you can secretly buy fruit.” Sun Wukong said, “Brother, not so. Do I really have any travel money? You two are looting other people’s gold and silver—surely you should give me a share.” Hearing this, the thief flew into a rage and barked, “This monk knows nothing of life and death. You won’t give me anything and you ask to question me. Don’t run; I’ll show you how.” He lifted a heavy rattan cane and struck Sun Wukong on the shaven head seven or eight times. Sun Wukong acted as if he did not notice and kept smiling broadly: “Brother, if you strike like this, even if you go on all this way until next spring, it would not be the real thing.” The thief was shocked. “This monk has a hard head!” Sun Wukong smiled. “No offense, no offense—thank you for being kind. I can only endure this for now.” The thief gave him no chance to speak; two or three rushed him in disorder and beat at him together. Sun Wukong said, “Everyone calm down. Let me bring it out.”

The Great Sage touched his ear and drew out an embroidered needle. “Everyone, I am a monk; truly I carried no travel money. Take this needle and be done with it.” One thief said, “Ill omen! You let a prosperous monk go free, yet catch this poor, bald donkey. So you can sew, can you? What use is this needle?” Sun Wukong, hearing this, did not argue. He pinched it in his hand, flicked it once, and turned it into a staff the thickness of a bowl. The thief said fearfully, “Though this monk is small, he can truly do magic.” Sun Wukong planted the staff in the ground and said, “If you can move it, I’ll give it to you.” Two thieves surged forward to seize it; they were like dragonflies shaking a stone pillar, unable to move it by even a hair’s breadth. This staff was the Golden-Hooped Staff, weighing 13,500 jin by heavenly scales—how could that lot of robbers know it? Sun Wukong stepped up, lifted it lightly, and with a coiling staff-flip and a twisting foot-step, pointed at the tough one: “Your fate is poor; you have met Sun Wukong.” That thief came forward again, and he was struck fifty or sixty times more.

Sun Wukong laughed. “Your hands are tired of striking, so let old Sun do one staff blow—do not take it as real.” See how he spread the staff and swung it: thick as the curb of a well, seven or eight zhang long, one sweep. One robber crashed to the ground with dirt on his mouth and made no sound. The one who still had breath cursed, “This bald brute is outrageously rude! No travel money, yet you maimed one of our men!” Sun Wukong smiled. “Sit down and quiet yourselves. I will take them one by one; with one strike I’ll cut your root out.” He swung again and felled the second. Frightened, the rest of the rowdies dropped their spears and clubs and fled in all directions.

Now Tripitaka rode on his horse and ran eastward; Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing blocked him. “Master, where are you going? You have taken the wrong way.” Tripitaka turned the horse and said, “Disciple, go at once and tell your elder brother to show restraint with his staff and not to kill those robbers.” Zhu Bajie said, “Master, stay here; I will go.” The pig-brother ran ahead and shouted at full voice, “Brother, Master told you not to hit people.” Sun Wukong said, “Brother, when did I hit anyone?” “Where did those robbers go?” Zhu Bajie asked. “The others have all dispersed; only two captains are still asleep here,” Sun Wukong answered. Zhu Bajie laughed. “You two cursed ones, you must have stayed up all night in misery. After so much hardship, why sleep here instead of elsewhere?” Zhu Bajie went to them and looked: “It’s right up my sleeve to be like me—lying with their mouths wide open, with sticky saliva running out.” Sun Wukong said, “Old Sun has broken tofu loose with one staff swing.” Zhu Bajie said, “Tofu from a man’s head?” Sun Wukong said, “Their brains have been knocked loose.”

When Zhu Bajie heard that he had knocked out their brains, he hurried back to Tripitaka and said, “The lot is scattered.” Tripitaka said, “Good! Good! Which road did they take?” Zhu Bajie said, “They were beaten until their legs went stiff. Where else can they now go?” Tripitaka said, “How can you call that scattered?” Zhu Bajie said, “They were killed. What else is that but scattering?” Tripitaka asked, “What did the beating look like?” Zhu Bajie said, “Two large hollows in their heads.” Tripitaka ordered, “Open the pouch and take out a few bits of money. Quickly fetch two plasters and apply them to both.” Zhu Bajie laughed. “Master, that is no way at all. Plasters can only be pasted on a living person’s wound; how can they be pasted on a dead man’s hole?” Tripitaka asked, “Were they truly dead?” He became angry, his muttering never stopping, monkey-tongue long and monkey-word short. Turning the horse, he went with Sha Wujing and Zhu Bajie to where the dead lay and saw them blood-soaked and fallen below the slope.

This elder could not bear to watch. He ordered Zhu Bajie, “Quickly use the pick and dig a pit to bury them. I will recite the Dao Tou Jing over them.” Zhu Bajie said, “Master, this is what you told him too. Sun Wukong killed people; he should be the one to burn and bury them. Why make old Pig do earthwork?” Sun Wukong was annoyed at Master’s scolding and shouted, “You slovenly idiot! Go bury them at once. If you delay, I’ll give you a staff.” Zhu Bajie panicked. Down the hillside he dug three feet deep, but beneath were stone legs and roots that caught the pick teeth. He dropped the pick and used his mouth to dig. At soft spots he dug 2.5 feet with one snout, 5 feet with both, and buried the two bandit bodies, forming a grave mound. Tripitaka said, “Sun Wukong, bring incense and candles. Let me offer the rite, then I can recite scripture.” Sun Wukong pinched his lips and said, “You have no sense. In this middle of the mountain there is no village in front, no inn behind. Where can we get incense? Even if we had money there is no place to buy it.” Tripitaka muttered angrily, “Monkey-head, go. I will gather soil and burn incense and offer the prayer.” This is where Tripitaka, dismounting, wept beside the wild grave, and the holy monk prayed for this barren tomb. The prayer ran:

Homage to valiant men; hear the cause of this plea: remember my disciple, a monk of the Eastern Land of Tang. By the command of Emperor Taizong, I came to the Western Regions to fetch the Dharma. Coming to this place, I met you many in number, and I do not know what prefecture, district, or county you belong to, yet all of you have formed gangs in these mountains. I spoke kindly and begged you with earnestness, but you did not listen and turned instead to anger. You were struck in the body under Wukong’s staff. I grieve that the bodies lie exposed, and I will cover them and make a grave. Green bamboo is bent for incense candles—no bright flame, but diligent in heart; hard stones are set as food offerings—no taste, but true in sincerity. You may raise words at the Hall of the Net and search roots by overturning trees. He is surnamed Sun and I am surnamed Chen; we belong to different clans. Every grievance has its head, every debt has its claimant. Do not accuse this pilgrim monk of seeking sutras. Zhu Bajie laughed. “Master has purged it cleanly. When he struck, neither of us two was there.” Tripitaka truly took more soil and prayed, “The complaint to heroic men names only Sun Wukong and does not involve Zhu Bajie or Sha Wujing.”

The Great Sage, hearing this, could not hold back his laughter. “Master, you are very lacking in loyalty. For your pilgrimage, how much sincere and strenuous toil I have endured. Now I have beaten these two rough thieves to death, and you still tell me to accuse old Sun. Though I was the one who struck, it was entirely for you. If you had not gone to the West for the scriptures, I would not have become your disciple. How would I have come here and killed anyone? Let me offer him a blessing once.” Clutching the iron staff, he looked at the grave and pounded it three times with it: “Wicked bandits, listen! It was seven or eight blows at first, then seven or eight more. You hit me and I did not flinch, yet you provoked my temper, and in one fault and another I killed you. Report wherever you choose. Old Sun fears no one. The Jade Emperor knows me; the Heavenly King can follow me. The Twenty-Eight Astral Mansions fear me; the Nine Luminous Stars fear me. Prefectural and county city gods kneel before me; the Eastern Peak ruler Tianqi trembles before me. The ten Yama Lords have once had me as a servant; the five-route wild gods have once had me as a sworn younger brother. Regardless of the Three Realms or Five Offices, the stewards of the Ten Directions are all deeply close to me; you can complain wherever you like.” Tripitaka, hearing such evil words, was frightened and said, “Disciple, this prayer of mine was meant to teach you good life-force and virtue, to make you a worthy man. How can you take it all so seriously?” Sun Wukong said, “Master, this is not a proper jesting performance. Come, let us get ready to find lodging quickly.” The elder, annoyed, mounted his horse.

Sun Wukong was not at ease with the others, and Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing likewise carried resentment; master and disciples wore fair faces while inwardly being at odds. As they continued west along the main road, they suddenly saw a manor on the lower ground to the north. Tripitaka tapped his whip and said, 「Let's go there and borrow a night’s lodging.」 Zhu Bajie answered, 「Right.」 So they walked to the edge of the manor and dismounted. When they arrived, it truly was a pleasant place to stay. They saw:

Wildflowers filled the path, and mixed trees covered the gate. On the distant bank flowed river and mountain; on even terraces wheat and marigold had been planted. Reeds and rushes, moistened by dew, held light gulls at rest; the willows in the gentle wind gave weary birds place to settle. Between green cypresses and pines the pines contended for the deepest verdancy; red dock and smartweed contended in fragrance. Village dogs barked, evening hens called; cattle and sheep were fed, and the herdboy went home. Cooking smoke knotted into mist; the yellow millet was done—true that it was the hour when mountain folk went into evening. The abbot went forward. Just then an old man came out through the manor gate and met them to exchange greetings. He asked, 「From where does this monk come?」 Tripitaka said, 「I am a poor monk from the Great Tang in the Eastern Lands, an imperial envoy sent to seek the sutras in the Western Heaven. Passing through Baofang and with dusk coming, I have come here to beg this humble house for a night’s lodging.」 The old man laughed, 「From your noble place to here is a long road. How did you cross waters and climb hills to come alone?」 Tripitaka replied, 「I have three disciples with me.」 The old man asked, 「Where are these high disciples?」 Tripitaka pointed, 「Those standing by the road there.」 The old man looked up sharply, saw their ugly faces, and hurried back inside. Tripitaka grabbed him and said, 「Respected householder, have compassion. Permit us a night’s lodging!」 The old man trembled, could scarcely speak, and with his head shaking and hands waving said, 「N-no, n-no, n-no, this is not the shape of human beings; yes, yes, yes, it is a few demons.」 Tripitaka smiled and said kindly, 「Please do not fear. They are only rough in appearance; they are not demons.」 The old man said, 「My goodness! One looks like a yaksha, one like a horse-faced ghost, and one like Leigong.」 Hearing this, Sun Wukong shouted in a loud voice, 「Leigong is my grandson, the yaksha my great-grandson, and the horse-faced ghost my great-grandgrandson!」 The old man heard it, turned pale, and his soul seemed to rise and flee; he only hurried inside. Tripitaka stayed with him, and led him together to the thatched hall, smiling as he said, 「Old householder, do not fear him. He is only this rough sort, and cannot speak much.」

While he was trying to calm him, a granny came out from behind carrying a child of five or six and said, 「Elder, why are you so frightened?」 The old man called, 「Mother, bring tea.」 The old woman truly set down the child and went in, carrying out two measures of tea. After the tea was served, Tripitaka dismounted and bowed to the old woman, saying, 「I am the poor monk from the Great Tang in the Eastern Lands, sent to go west for the sutras. I have only just come to your place, so I ask your honored house for one night. My three disciples have ugly faces, and this householder, on seeing them, was startled in vain.」 The old woman replied, 「If ugly faces frighten you so, what would happen if one saw a tiger or a wolf?」 The old man said, 「Mother, I see ugly faces are still tolerable; it is the voice that frightens people. I said he looked like a yaksha, horse-face, and Leigong, and then he shouted: Leigong is his grandson, the yaksha his great-grandson, horse-face his great-grandgrandson. When I heard this, I was terrified in truth.」 Tripitaka said, 「No, no. The one like Leigong is my first disciple Sun Wukong. The one like horse-face is my second disciple Zhu Bajie. The one like yaksha is my third disciple Sha Wujing. Though they are ugly, they bear the vows of monks, have taken refuge in the good fruit of Dharma, and are no evil demonic fiends. Why should one fear them?」

The old couple, having heard their names and that they were true monks, settled their fear at once and said, 「Come, come in.」 The abbot called to them from outside and also warned, 「This old fellow just now was greatly troubled by you. When you go in to meet him now, do not be rough, each of you must show proper respect.」 Zhu Bajie said, 「I am handsome, and scholarly; I am not as rash as my elder brother.」 Sun Wukong laughed and said, 「Even with long faces, big ears, and ugly countenances, one can still be a good man.」 Sha Wujing said, 「Do not argue. This is no place for flirtation and banter. Just go in, just go in.」 So they took their bundles and horses into the thatched hall, made a collective bow, and sat. The old woman, wise and kind, immediately gathered the child and ordered rice cooked, arranging a vegetarian meal. The four ate it together.

Night deepened gradually. Lamps were brought out, and all chatted idly in the hall. Then Tripitaka asked, 「What is your surname, householder?」 The old man said, 「Yang.」 He was asked his age. 「Seventy-four.」 How many sons? 「Only one. The child Mother just carried is a grandson.」 Tripitaka invited the son to come and bow. The old man said, 「That brute does not bow. This poor old fool has hard fortune and cannot keep him; he is not at home now.」 Tripitaka asked, 「How is that, exactly?」 The old man nodded sadly. 「Alas, alas! If there were any way to settle him, it would be my good fortune. He was born with evil thoughts, cares only nothing for his proper station, and delights only in robbery and stopping travelers, in killing and arson. The ones he keeps company with are all foxes and jackal-spirits in human form. He went out five days ago and has not returned yet.」 Tripitaka grew anxious but said nothing aloud, secretly thinking, 「Perhaps it was him whom Sun Wukong killed as well.」 The abbot was clearly unsettled and said in a gentle voice, 「Excellent indeed. Excellent indeed. What worthy father and mother—how came such a rebellious son?」

Sun Wukong came forward and said, 「For a child so unruly, dissolute, and full of lust and robbery, who brings trouble upon his parents, what use is he? Let me go find him and kill him.」 The old man answered, 「I too intended to give him up, but there is no one else in the household line. However poor and worthless he is, I must still keep him to bury with this old man.」 Sha Wujing and Zhu Bajie laughed and said, 「Master Brother, mind your own affair. We are not officials. If this house refuses, what is that to us? Ask him, instead, to give us a bundle of straw and we will make bedding on that side and sleep. In morning we will leave by the road.」 The old man rose, sent Sha Wujing to the back garden to fetch two bundles of straw, and told them to settle in the straw-heap there. Sun Wukong took the horse, Zhu Bajie picked up the luggage, and with Tripitaka they all rested in the hay-pit. No further matter need be told.

It turned out that in that gang was indeed the son of Master Yang. Early that morning, before dawn, Sun Wukong had already beaten two bandit heads to death in front of the mountain, and the rest had fled in four directions. About the fourth watch, they regathered and came to beat upon the gate. Hearing the noise, old Yang said, 「Mother, they have come.」 The old woman answered, 「Now that they have come, you open the door and let them in.」 Old Yang then opened the gate. As soon as they entered, all shouted, 「Hungry, hungry.」 The son rushed in first, called out to his wife, and ordered her to cook rice. There was no firewood in the kitchen, so he went to the back garden for wood and then in the kitchen asked his wife, 「Whose white horse is in the back garden?」 She said, 「It belongs to the monk from the Eastern Lands going to fetch the sutras. Last night he lodged here; grandpa and grandma fed him a night of vegetarian fare and told him to sleep in the straw bundle.」

Hearing this, that brute stepped out from the hall, clapped his hands, and laughed. 「Brothers, fate, fate—an enemy is in my own house too!」 「Which enemy?」the bandits asked. He said, 「It is the monk who beat our chief dead, who came to my house for lodging and now sleeps in the straw bundle.」 「Good then, good then.」one of them said. 「Catch these bald-monk rogues and chop each into meat paste: first we get their bundles and white horse; second, we avenge our chief.」 The same one added, 「No hurry yet. Go sharpen your knives. Let me finish cooking first. Once we have all eaten our fill, then all strike at once.」 They truly ground knives against grindstones and sharpened spears upon spear-stones.

The old man heard all this, then quietly went to the back garden and called all four of Tripitaka: 「That brute has gathered the others and come. He knows you are here and intends to harm you. This poor fool, because I have pity on you who came from afar, dare not harm you. Quickly pack your luggage. I will send you out through the back gate.」 Hearing this, Tripitaka, trembling, bowed and thanked the old man, then called Zhu Bajie to lead the horse, Sha Wujing to shoulder the pack, and Sun Wukong to carry the Golden-Hooped Staff. The old man opened the back gate and sent them out. He then returned and, as before, quietly lay down in front.

The gang had finished sharpening swords and spears, eaten their meal, and by first light they reached the garden to look for them. They were gone. They quickly lit lamps and searched for a long while; there was no trace at all, but only the back gate stood open. All said, 「They left by the back gate, they left." Calling out, they gave chase. Each ran like an arrow and together followed all the way to the east as the sun rose, when they suddenly saw Tripitaka. Just then the abbot heard the shouts and looked back. Behind them were two or three dozen men, with spears and blades pressed thick together. He called, 「Disciple! The bandits are upon us. What shall we do?」 Sun Wukong said, 「Do not worry, do not worry. This old grandson will settle them.」 Tripitaka pulled on the reins and said, 「Wukong, do not strike down others. It is enough to frighten them away.」 Sun Wukong would not obey. He jerked out his staff and turned to meet them, shouting, 「Where are you going, all of you?」 The robbers cursed, 「Rude bald monk! Return the life of our King!」 Those rogues formed a ring formation around Sun Wukong and raised spears and blades to hack and thrust at random. The Great Sage made one sweep with the Golden-Hooped Staff, making it swell and narrow from broad as a bowl. He hit that band of brigands so that they scattered like stars in the clouds: those struck full-on died, those dragged in by the impact perished, those hit off-center had bones broken, those merely grazed were skin-scratched. Only a few fled in time; the dull ones all saw King Yama.

Tripitaka was on horseback, and when he saw the Master having beaten down so many men, he panicked and drove his horse hard to the west. Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing hurried after him in close pursuit. Sun Wukong asked the still-living, wounded bandit, “Which of them is old Yang’s son?” The bandit answered with a grunt, “Sir, it is the one wearing yellow.” Sun Wukong stepped forward, snatched up a knife, cut off the head of the yellow-clad man, held the blood-soaked head in his hand, took up the iron staff, broke into cloud-step, and hurried to the front of Tripitaka’s horse. Holding up the severed head, he said, “Master, this is old Yang’s rebellious son. The Great Sage has taken his head as well.” When Tripitaka saw it, he was shaken and pale, and in panic he fell off the horse, shouting, “That wild monkey has nearly scared me to death! Take it away, take it away.” Zhu Bajie stepped forward, kicked the head off to the roadside, and with his spade he heaped a little earth over it.

Sha Wujing set down his load, supported Tripitaka, and said, “Master, please rise.” As he regained his senses on the ground, Tripitaka began chanting the Tightening Headband Spell. It squeezed Sun Wukong so that his ears reddened, his face turned crimson, his eyes bulged, and his head swam as he rolled on the earth, crying only, “Stop the spell, stop the spell.” Tripitaka chanted it more than ten times and still would not stop. Sun Wukong rolled in somersaults and bucked like a cicada on end; unable to bear the pain, he only cried, “Master, forgive my fault and end this. If you must speak, speak now. Don’t chant, don’t chant.” Tripitaka finally stopped and said, “There is nothing to say. I do not want you to stay with us. Go back.” Sun Wukong, enduring the pain, knelt and begged, “Master, why are you sending me away?” Tripitaka said, “You wild monkey are too savage and ferocious; you are not one fit for the pilgrimage. Yesterday, when we were below the slope, you killed those two bandit chiefs, and I already blamed you for your cruelty. Later, when it grew late we came to that old man’s home; he gave us alms for the meal, offered us lodging, and even opened the back gate so we could escape with our lives. His son may be wayward, but it is none of my concern, and it was not right to immediately chop off his head; besides that, you have already killed many men, destroying many lives and injuring heaven and earth’s harmony. I have repeatedly urged you, and there is not one grain of goodwill in your heart. What else could you be aiming for? Go quickly, go quickly, lest I have to chant the true words again.” Sun Wukong, now afraid, only pleaded, “Stop the spell, stop the spell—I’ll go.” He said he would go and then leapt through the clouds in a somersault; without sound or trace he vanished. Aha—this is exactly:

A heart still filled with wild ferocity, uncured by the elixir, has no abiding place for the spirit, and the Way cannot be achieved.

In the end it was still unknown in which direction the Great Sage had gone. Listen now to the explanation that follows.
chapters.title: Chapter 56: Divine frenzy executes the bandits; way-lost thought lets the Mind-Monkey wander astray.
