This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Now it is said that Sun Wukong was all embittered and vexed, rising in the air. He wanted to return to Water Curtain Cave of Flower-Fruit Mountain, but feared the small demons there would laugh at him, saying he had gone out and come back the wrong way and was no true hero’s matter. He thought to throw himself into the Heavenly Court, yet feared he would not be allowed to stay there long. He thought to cast himself to the sea islands, but was ashamed to face the immortals of the Three Isles. He thought to flee to the Dragon Palace, yet would not dare to petition the Dragon King in person. Truly he had no support to rely on. Bitterness rising in his heart, he said to himself, "Enough, enough, enough. I will go back to meet my Master; that is still the true realization."

Then he pressed down his cloud and went straight to Tripitaka’s horse, kneeling before it and saying, "Master, forgive this disciple this time. Hereafter I dare not act with violence—let me atone by your teaching. Above all, this is to preserve you on the way to the West." When Tripitaka saw him, he did not answer, pulled the reins, and began to chant the Tightening Headband Spell. He rolled and writhed, chanting it more than twenty times. He sent the Great Sage lock-spell crashing down; the band sank into the flesh nearly an inch deep. Only then did he stop and say, "If you will not go back, why do you return to pester me again?" Wukong only begged, "Stop chanting, stop chanting. I can live out my days elsewhere; I only fear that without me you cannot reach the Western Regions." Tripitaka grew angry: "You, monkey, you kill and take life and have entangled me in so much trouble. Henceforth I truly have no use for you. Whether I can go or not has nothing to do with you. Go, go, go—if I am delayed any more, I will chant the true words again, and this time I will not stop, and I will squeeze your brain out of your skull." The Great Sage could not bear the pain; seeing the Master still unmoved, he had no choice but to mount the magic cloud again and rise into the air. At once he realized, "This monk has betrayed me. I will go tell Guanyin at Putuo Cliff what has happened."

Thus Great Sage, turning his cloud, in scarcely an hour reached the South Sea. He descended in radiance and straight went to Mount Loka, plunging into the Purple Bamboo Grove. There he saw a Mucha practitioner come forward and bow: "Great Sage, where are you going?" Wukong said, "I am going to see the Bodhisattva." The Mucha led him on to the mouth of the Tide-Resounding Cave, and there Shancai the Child, bowing, asked, "Great Sage, what brings you here?" Wukong said, "I have business to report to the Bodhisattva." Hearing only the word "report," Shancai laughed: "Fine words, you sly-mouthed monkey, and yet like before when I had taken Tripitaka and you deceived me. My Bodhisattva is one of immense compassion and mercy, vast vow and Great Vehicle, saving from pain and disaster, infinite in compassion and merit. If there is anything lacking in the world, tell me. How can you accuse the Bodhisattva?" Wukong, filled with pent-up vexation, heard this and at once his anger flared. With one cry he drove Shancai backward and said, "You treacherous, ungrateful wretch—truly dense and foolish. When you once played tricks and became a demon, I asked the Bodhisattva to receive you, restore you to the righteous path and rightness. Now you enjoy this Great Bliss and long life, free and easy, living with heaven in immortality, and yet you do not bow to old Sun, but only insult and revile him. I have come with business to petition the Bodhisattva, and you call me a crafty monkey here to accuse a Bodhisattva?" Shancai answered with a smile, "You are still a hasty monkey. I was only making sport with you, why did you so quickly change your face?"

While this was being spoken, a white parrot flew back and forth; sensing the Bodhisattva’s summons, the Mucha and Shancai then guided them onward to the foot of the jeweled lotus platform. When Wukong saw the Bodhisattva, he threw himself down and bowed, and tears like springs poured out of him as he cried out. Guanyin said to the Mucha and Shancai, "Raise him up," and said, "Wukong, whatever hurts, speak plainly. Do not cry, do not cry—I can help you relieve hardship and avert disaster." Wukong, tears still running, knelt and said, "In the days before, when I was still a disciple, what was the cause of this grief? By your grace, Bodhisattva, you released me from heavenly calamity, instructed me to become a monk, and sent me to guard Tripitaka in going west to worship Buddha and seek scripture. I spent my life with reckless courage to save him from demons, as if snatching fresh bone from a tiger’s mouth or tearing living scales from a crocodile’s back. I only hoped to return to true fruit, cleanse sin, and end evil. Yet that elder betrayed his duty and forgot his kindness, blinded in one stretch of good fortune, and would not discern right from wrong at all." Guanyin said, "Now tell me all of why this right and wrong matter is." Wukong then gave a full account of the whole sequence of killing and crushing the bandits. It is said Tripitaka, because he had many slain by him, grew resentful and could not distinguish right from wrong; therefore he chanted the Tightening Headband Spell and drove him off several times. With no road in heaven and no gate in earth, he had therefore come to report to the Bodhisattva. Guanyin said, "Tripitaka was sent by Buddha to go west, and with one heart he wishes to keep the monastic vow and not lightly damage life. You have boundless powers—why have you killed so many bandits? Though bandits are unruly, in the end they are human forms and should not be slain. That is unlike demonic birds, monsters, ghosts, and fox and fox-spirit demons. Slaying those might be your merit. To slay human bodies is still your inhumanity. Yet to drive them away was itself a way of protecting your Master. By my judgment, this is still on your side a fault."

Wukong, with tears in his mouth and forehead, knelt and bowed: "Though your disciple has been unkind, he should still have merit offset sin; you should not thus drive him away. I beg the Bodhisattva to extend vast compassion and chant, even once, the spell to loosen the headband, remove the band from my head, return it to you, and let me go back to Water Curtain Cave to save my life." Guanyin smiled and said, "The Tightening Headband Spell was given to me by Buddha. In former days Buddha sent me to the eastern lands to seek the monks who would fetch the scriptures, and bestowed three precious treasures on me: the brocade-banded kasaya, the Golden-Hooped Staff, and three golden tightening headbands. I was secretly entrusted with three spells, but there is no spell for loosening a headband." Wukong said, "If that is so, then I will take my leave of the Bodhisattva." Guanyin said, "Where do you mean to go if you leave me?" Wukong said, "I will go west to Buddha and ask for a loosening spell." Guanyin said, "Stay a while. Let me inspect your auspicious or inauspicious sign." Wukong said, "There is no need. This ill omen is enough already." Guanyin said, "I will not inspect you. I will inspect Tripitaka’s sign."

Well then, the Bodhisattva sat upright on the lotus platform, centered her mind on the three realms, and with wisdom eyes surveyed far, covering all the universe. In an instant she spoke: "Wukong, in this very moment your Master has impending danger to his body; not long from now he will come seeking you. Stay here; I will speak with Tripitaka and tell him to still go with you to fetch the scriptures and complete true attainment." Wukong could only submit, dare not act rashly, and stood in attendance at the foot of the treasure lotus platform.

Then it is told that Tripitaka, after chasing after the Great Sage, ordered Zhu Bajie to lead the horse and Sha Wujing to carry the packs; with all four horses they hurried west, not yet fifty li from where they had come. Tripitaka pulled the horse and said, "Disciple, since we left the village after dawn, that Bima-warm wind had already stirred me in anger; this half-day we are hungry again and still hungry, thirsty again and still thirsty. Who shall we go to now to take alms for me?" Zhu Bajie said, "Master, please dismount. Let me see whether there is a nearby hamlet to turn into alms food." Tripitaka, hearing this, slid off the horse. The Fool rode up his cloud-head and looked carefully through the sky, but all he could see was ridges and hills; no household in sight. He descended the cloud and told Tripitaka, "There is no place for alms. From this far view there is not a dwelling at all." Tripitaka said, "If there is no place for alms, at least get us some water for thirst." Bajie said, "Let me go below to the stream in the south mountain for water." Sha Wujing at once took the alms-bowl and handed it to Bajie. Bajie held the bowl under his arm and rode off on a cloud in the mist. Tripitaka sat by the roadside. After waiting long enough, with no sign of return, his mouth was parched and tongue dry. A poem is given as proof:

Guarding spirit and nurturing breath is called essence; emotion and nature are naturally one and born in the same form. When the mind is scattered, spirit is confused, and every illness arises; the form declines, essence decays, and the Way’s root tips toward ruin. Chasing after the three flowers is vain labor for no gain; the four greats fall into desolation and the struggle is wasted. Earth and wood give no efficacy, metal and water are cut off; with a lax and lazy Dharma-body, when will it truly be formed? Sha Wujing by the side saw Tripitaka unable to bear hunger and thirst and saw that Bajie still had not returned with water. He set the packsecure, tied the white horse firmly, and said, "Master, sit free and still, I will go hasten the water." The elder answered with tears but no words, only a nod. Sha Wujing quickly rode his cloud-light and went south toward the mountain.

The Master, alone, suffered through it himself, and the hardship was extreme. Just as sorrow and panic overtook him, he suddenly heard a loud sound. Frightened, the elder bent forward and looked around. It was that Sun Wukong was kneeling by the roadside, both hands holding a magnetic cup, saying, "Master, without old Sun, you cannot even get water. Here is a cup of very cool water; please take a sip to quench your thirst, and let me go to fetch alms again." Tripitaka said, "I will not drink your water; if I stay this moment I may die of thirst—that is my choice. I have no need for you. Go." Wukong said, "Without me, you cannot go to the west." Tripitaka said, "Whether I can go or not does not concern you. Wicked monkey, why do you keep coming to trouble me?" Wukong’s face changed; in anger and fury he shouted at the Master, "You hard-hearted shaven monk, you despise me too much." He swung his iron staff, threw down the cup, and struck once at the Master’s back. The Master fainted where he stood, dizzy and unable to speak. Wukong took the two blue felt bundles in his hands, mounted his cloud, and left by the wayside unknown.

Now it is told that Zhu Bajie, carrying the alms bowl, ran only down the southern slope of the mountain, when he suddenly saw, in a hollow of the ridge, a thatched cottage that was a household. At first, because the mountain rose high, he had not seen it; only now that he came to the edge did he know there was a dwelling. The Fool thought to himself, "If I keep this ugly, bad-mouthed face, I will surely frighten them, and all this wasted thought will be for nothing—I will never be able to transform and obtain alms food. I must change my face first. I must change my face first."

The fool, twisting the formula in his fingers, muttered a spell, and shook his body up and down seven or eight times. He transformed into a yellow, sickly, pot-bellied monk, and came near the gate with a hoarse, whining hum in his mouth, calling out: "Alms-man, there is leftover rice in the kitchen, and a hungry person on the road. I am a poor monk from the Eastern Lands, coming from the east toward the Western Heaven to fetch the scriptures. My master is hungry and thirsty on the way, and there is some cold rice and pan-crisp in the house—please turn just a little of it into food to save him." In that house the men were not there; they had all gone to transplant the paddy. Only two women were at home. They had just cooked the noon meal and filled two basins, then packed up and hurried out to the fields. A little rice and some scorched-rice bits still remained in the pot, not yet served. Seeing his sickly look, and hearing him speak of going from the Eastern Lands to the Western Heaven, the women thought he might be delirious and babbling from illness, and they also feared he might fall and die at the gate. So with whispers and rustling they filled a bowl to the brim with the leftover rice and pan-crisp and handed it to him. The fool took it back, resumed his true form, and at once returned by the old path.

As they walked, a voice called, "Bajie." When Zhu Bajie raised his head and looked, it was Sha Wujing, standing on the cliff and shouting, "Come here, come here." He descended the cliff and came before them, saying: "I do not dare to draw water from this ravine; where are you going?" Zhu Bajie laughed: "I came this way and saw a house in a mountain hollow. I transformed and fetched this bowl of dry rice from there." Sha Wujing said: "We do need the rice, but Master is parched and thirsty. How are we to get water?" Zhu Bajie replied: "Water is easy too. You hold up this rice in your sleeves, and I will fetch water in the bowl."

The two returned to the road with cheerful faces, and there they saw Tripitaka prostrate face-down in the dust; his body on the ground, and the white horse, with bridle cast loose, neighing and bucking along the roadside. Their baggage pannier was gone from sight. Alarmed, Zhu Bajie stamped his feet and struck his chest, calling and crying out: "No need to speak of explanations—no need to explain! This is no less than the remnant band of the one Sun Wukong drove off; he has come here to slay the master and snatch the luggage." Sha Wujing said, "First, tie up the horse!" then wailed again and again: "What is this? what is this? This is truly to abandon the road halfway, to stop in midstream." He called once, "Master!" and tears poured from his eyes; he sobbed in grief. Zhu Bajie said, "Brother, stop crying for now. Since things have come to this point, do not speak of the journey for scripture anymore. Watch over Master’s body, and let me saddle the horse and ride to a nearby market town of that prefecture and county, sell a few taels of silver, buy a coffin, and bury Master. Then the two of us will each seek our own roads and part company."

Sha Wujing truly could not bear to let it be, so he turned Tripitaka over and placed him face-up, warming the master’s face with his own, and cried out once: "Wretched master!" At once the old master exhaled warm breath from his nose and mouth; his chest was still warm. He called in one breath: "Bajie, come—Master has not been fatally hurt." Only then did the fool come close and help him up. After waking he groaned for a moment, then snapped: "You rude monkey—try to kill me, too." Sha Wujing and Zhu Bajie asked, "Which monkey was that?" The master answered nothing, only sighing. He took some water and drank a few sips, then said: "Disciples, you had just gone, and Wukong came again and tormented me. I stood my ground and refused to yield, so he beat me with a staff and snatched away my blue- felt bundle with the travel cloth and bowl.」 Zhu Bajie heard this and ground his teeth, anger flaring in his chest. He said, "This wayward monkey can never be tolerated! How dare he be so rude?" Then he ordered, "Sha Wujing, stay at master’s side. I’ll go to his house and demand the bundle." Sha Wujing replied, "Do not flare up yet. We will carry Master to that hollow-house family, boil some hot tea there, heat the rice we already transformed, and restore Master first; after that we can go to seek him."

Bajie followed the instruction: he helped Master mount the horse, carried the bowl, wrapped the cold rice in his robe, and went straight to the house door. There was only an old woman in the house; when she saw them, she hurried away in fright. Sha Wujing folded his palms and said, "Good mother, we are those sent from the Tang capital in the Eastern Lands, traveling to the Western Heaven. Master has taken ill; we beg you to boil hot tea and let him eat." The woman said, "A little while ago, a monk sick and yellow and pot-bellied came here saying he was sent from the Eastern Lands, and he already transformed and took the alms. How can there be yet another from the Eastern Lands? I have no one else at home. Please go elsewhere." When she spoke, Tripitaka heard and, supported by Bajie, dismounted and bent his body, saying: "Grandmother, I have three disciples who travel with me, all of one mind and heart, to carry me in protection to Great Thunder-Resounding in Tianzhu and worship the Buddha for scripture. Yet my eldest disciple, Sun Wukong, by nature fierce and violent and unwilling to follow the Way, was sent back by me. But as I did not expect it, he came stealthily and struck me on my back with a staff, then took my baggage and robe-and-basin. I now need one disciple to go fetch him. The road is empty and there is no place here for us to sit, so I came to this household to rest a while. Once he brings back my luggage, we leave at once and will not stay long." The woman said: "Just now a sick-looking yellow monk with a swollen belly came and said he was from the Eastern Lands going to the Western Heaven, and he transformed for alms. How can there be another one?" Zhu Bajie could not help laughing: "That was me. Because my face is long-mouthed and my ears are big, I feared your household would be frightened and not give alms, so I made myself look this way. If you do not believe it, is not this the pot-crisp rice from your pot from earlier in my brother’s robe?"

The woman recognized that it was indeed the rice he had given, and so she offered no refusal; she made them sit. She brewed a kettle of hot tea and passed it to Sha Wujing to soften the rice. He immediately soaked the cold rice and handed it to Master. After Master ate a few mouthfuls, and his condition had settled for a while, he said: "Which one of you will go get the luggage?" Bajie answered: "Last year, because Master sent him back, I once searched for him and recognized his Water-curtain Cave on Flower-Fruit Mountain. Let me go, let me go." Master said: "You cannot go. The monkey and you were never at odds, and you speak roughly. One phrase or two in between and he will strike you. Let Wujing go." Sha Wujing assented: "I will go, I will go." Master further instructed Sha Wujing: "When you reach him, watch the signs and his mood. If he is willing to return the bundle, politely thank him and take it. If he is not, do not contend with him. Go straight to the Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea, report this matter, and ask the Bodhisattva to inquire of him." Sha Wujing listened to all. Turning to Bajie, he said: "I will go search for him now. You must not worry; devote yourself to serving Master. Do not behave roughly with this household, lest he refuse to feed us again. I will return as soon as I can." Bajie nodded: "I understand. But go and come back quickly, whether you gain the bundle or not; do not make this like a balancing pole with firewood slipping from both ends." Sha Wujing then twirled the formula, mounted the cloud-shine, and sped toward the Eastern Shengtian Continent. Truly, he sang:

I am with no shrine and yet roam the heavens, how can a cauldron forge elixir without flame? I seek the Golden Old One from the old woman’s hall, and beg the Wooden Mother to mend my sick-faced body. No one knows what day I shall return from this course, nor when I shall come back from this journey. In the Five Phases, generation and restraint have no peace; only when the mind-monkey re-enters the Pass will it be set right."

Sha Wujing, in midair, crossed three day-nights. Only then did he reach the Eastern Ocean, and he suddenly heard the roar of waves. Looking down, he truly saw black fog rising to the sky, a heavy gloom, and the vast sea swallowing the dawn’s light, making it cold and dim. He had no mind to admire it. He looked over the Immortal Mountain pass and passed beyond Yingzhou, steering straight eastward toward the realm of Flower-Fruit Mountain. Riding the sea wind, feeling the pull of the water, after more time he saw high peaks like spears in formation, sheer cliffs like hanging screens. Reaching the crest, he followed the clouds to find the path down and searched for the Water-curtain Cave. As he drew near, he heard countless monkey spirits in the mountain shouting in a surging din. Drawing closer and looking more carefully, he saw it was Sun Wukong seated high on a stone platform, both hands holding a sheet of paper, reciting aloud:

By edict of Emperor Li of the Great Tang, this missive is issued to the holy monk Chen Xuanzang, to go west to the Tianzhu kingdom, to the Great Vulture Peak of Sarvastivada Sound-Sounding Mountain, to the Great Sound-Hearing Temple of Great Thunder-Resonance, and offer single devotion to the Buddha of the Therefore-Come-Thus for the scriptures. I have fallen into severe illness; my soul wandered to the netherworld. By grace of long life in my fortune, the Lord of the Dark Court granted me return to the living, and I established meritorious rites and built the altar-way for saving the dead. Through the golden-bodied Guanyin Bodhisattva, who appears to relieve the suffering, I was shown that in the West there are Buddha and scripture that can uplift the tormented dead and bring liberation; therefore, I have dispatched Master Xuanzang to journey through a thousand mountains and seek out the verse-mantra of the Buddha. If you pass through the nations of the western border states, do not sever good ties; act in accord with this document. Edict of the former throne hall, auspicious autumn day of the thirteenth year of Zhen Guan in the Great Tang: since departing the Great Country, he has traversed kingdoms and in midjourney has obtained my eldest disciple Sun Wukong, the traveler; second disciple, Zhu Bajie; and third disciple, Sha Wujing, the monk. He read it from the beginning and read it again.

Hearing that it was the passage-clearance document, Sha Wujing could not help but come forward and call out in a raised voice: "Elder brother, how do you recite Master’s edict in this way?" Hearing him, Sun Wukong instantly raised his head. Not recognizing him as Sha Wujing, he shouted: "Bring it, bring it." The monkeys gathered around, dragging Sha Wujing close, and he shouted: "Who are you, and how dare you come near my immortal cave?" Sha Wujing saw that he had changed in countenance and would not recognize him, so he could only bow and report upward: "I respectfully report to my elder brother: earlier, Master, hasty and ferocious, misunderstood you and wrongly cursed you several times and sent you back home. First, my fellow disciples could not reason with him. Second, he and Master then went hungry and thirsty, and we sought water and cooked alms. Unexpectedly, Brother Wukong came with good intentions again, and yet because Master clung stubbornly to strict discipline, he struck Master, knocking him down and sending him into a faint. He also robbed his baggage and robe-and-bowl. After this we rescued Master and have come now to bow to you. If you do not hate Master and if you still remember the grace of our rescue of you in former days, return with your younger brother, take back the luggage, and let us show it to Master and together go west for final liberation. If your resentment runs too deep and you will not go with us, then at least grant the bundle to your younger brother. You may remain in the deep mountains and enjoy a mellow old age with桑榆; that would also be truly a twofold good."

The Great Sage heard him and let out a cold laugh: 'Younger brother, this proposal is wholly contrary to my wishes. I struck Tripitaka and seized the luggage; neither was it because I refuse to go west, nor because I love staying here. I have read the edict clearly now. I will go west myself, worship Buddha, seek the scriptures, and bring them back to the Eastern Land. I alone will succeed; I will have the people of the Nanzhanbu Continent set me up as an ancestor, and my name will be passed down for ten thousand ages.' Sha Wujing laughed: 'Elder, what you said is off the mark. There has never been a saying that Sun Wukong is to fetch the scriptures. The Buddha as Tathagata composed the True Tripitaka, and Guanyin Bodhisattva was already searching in the Eastern Land for someone to seek and bring the scripture. We were to endure a thousand mountains and all kinds of hardship, inquire through many states, and protect that pilgrim. The Bodhisattva said the scripture-seeker is a disciple of the Tathagata, called Elder Golden Cicada. Because he did not heed the Buddha’s teachings, he was demoted from Ling Mountain, reborn in the Eastern Land, and told that he should turn himself toward the West and once again cultivate the Great Way. On the road he was meant to meet demon obstructions; if we free us three and he gains us as guardians, he can complete his charge. Elder, if you cannot get Tripitaka, who would the Buddha bestow the scripture on you? It would be a vain waste of divine effort.' The Great Sage replied: 'Younger brother, you are truly ignorant—you know one thing but not the second. If you claim that you have Tripitaka and are protecting him with me, do I then have no Tripitaka? I can choose another genuinely enlightened monk here to go; I can support him by my own strength alone. What is not possible? I have already resolved to depart at first light tomorrow. If you do not believe me, wait—I will call for him and let you see.' He called, 'You youngsters, quickly ask the Teacher to come out.' Immediately he ran in, led out a white horse, brought forth one Tang Sanzang; behind him walked Zhu Bajie carrying the baggage, and Sha Wujing with a staff.

Sha Wujing, seeing this, grew furious and said, 'I, old Sha Wujing, do not change my name or alter my surname—how can there be another Sha Monk? Do not be discourteous; you will feel my staff once.' The good Sha Wujing raised the demon-subduing staff with both hands and felled the false Sha Monk with one blow to the face. It was a monkey demon. The Great Sage, incensed, brandished the Golden-Hooped Staff, led out the troop of monkeys, and surrounded Sha Wujing. Sha Wujing charged east and west, bashing through to the exit, then fled through mist and clouds, crying, 'That unruly monkey is so shamelessly careless; I will go report this to Guanyin.' The Great Sage saw Sha Wujing had killed one monkey spirit and driven the real Sha Monk away, and though he was angry he did not pursue him. He returned to the cave and told the juniors to drag the dead demon body to one side, skin it, and cook the flesh; they fried it, and with coconut wine and grape wine all the monkeys ate together. He then selected another demon monkey that could shapeshift and made it turn into a Sha Monk again, taught it afresh, and there is no need to set down its later journey westward.

Sha Wujing took to cloud in a single bound from the East Sea and in one day and night traveled to the South Sea. While en route, he saw Mount Luojia not far ahead. He hurried on, dropped among the mists, and searched around for a worthy place. What a spot! In truth it was:

In the recesses of Bao-gan, in the tract of Kua-kun, where a hundred rivers meet and bathe beneath the surging sun-star, where converging currents return as wind and moonlit ripples. The tides surge upward, heaving and rising, transforming like the great Kun; waves overturn in broad billows, while vast turtle-like creatures roam. The waters reach the Northwest Sea, and the waves align toward the Eastern Ocean. The four seas are linked as one earth-vein, and on every fairy isle stand fairy palaces. Need not speak of every ground being Penglai; come see Mount Putuo Cloud Caves. What a beautiful view! Atop the peaks, rosy cloud-light gathers the primal radiance; beneath the cliffs, auspicious breeze stirs moon-bright crystals. In violet bamboo groves peacocks fly, and on green willow boughs spirit parrots converse. Gem flowers and jade grasses bloom year after year, treasure trees and golden lotuses flower season after season. White cranes climb the summit time and again, and pale swan-mandarin ducks come to the mountain pavilion many times. Even roaming fish understand the way of cultivating true nature, leaping through waves and breaking foam to listen to the Dharma. Sha Wujing walked down slowly toward Luojia Mountain and surveyed the immortal realm. A Mucha attendant of the pilgrimage greeted him and asked, 'Sha Wujing, you do not guard Tripitaka on the way to the scriptures—why are you here?' After saluting, Sha Wujing replied, 'I have come on one matter only to have audience with the Bodhisattva; please lead me for an audience.' The Mucha attendant, knowing he was looking for the Great Sage, made no further ado and first informed the Bodhisattva, 'A junior disciple of Tripitaka, Sha Wujing, waits outside to bow.' Hearing this from below the dais, Sun Wukong laughed: 'This must mean Tripitaka is in trouble and Sha Wujing has come to ask the Bodhisattva.' Guanyin ordered the Mucha attendant to call him inside. Sha Wujing bowed fully and, as he rose to report, suddenly saw Sun Wukong standing by his side; he could not wait to speak, so he jerked the demon-subduing staff and struck toward Sun Wukong’s face. The Great Sage did not swing back, but moved aside to avoid it. Sha Wujing cursed wildly: 'You are a rebellious ape-beast guilty of the ten evil deeds! You come again to trick Guanyin!' Guanyin ordered, 'Wujing, do not strike. Tell me first what happened.'

Sha Wujing put away the precious staff and bowed again in the space below, then spoke to the Bodhisattva in a flushed voice: 'This ape has committed violence all along the road without number. The day before yesterday he beat and killed two powerful brigands on the slope below the hill, and Master became angry with him. Then that same evening he lodged at the bandit chief’s house and then beat to death the whole band of thieves, bringing one of their severed heads, all blood and all, to show Master. Master, frightened, staggered down from his horse, scolded him a little, and drove him back. After they parted, Master was tormented by hunger and thirst. He sent Zhu Bajie to look for water. He waited long with no return, and then sent me in search of him as well. Suddenly Sun Wukong, seeing that Zhu and I were both gone, came back, struck Master with an iron staff, and snatched away two blue felt bundles. We returned and revived Master. We then came here to his Water-curtain Cave to demand the bundles, but to our surprise he had changed his face and would not recognize me; he kept reciting the spell that seals the master over and over. I asked what he was doing with that recitation. He said he did not protect Tripitaka; he intended to go to the Western Heaven and fetch the scriptures himself, bring them to the Eastern Land, accumulate his own merit, become an ancestral master, and be praised for ten thousand ages. I said, 'Without Tripitaka, who would Buddha give the sutra to you?' He said he had selected a genuine monk of the Way. He then brought him out: indeed, there was a white horse, a Tripitaka, with Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing following. I said, 'I myself am Sha Monk—where is this other Sha Monk?' I had run up and struck him once with a precious staff, and he proved to be a monkey spirit. Then he marshaled the troop and took me. I came expressly to petition the Bodhisattva. I did not know he could wield the jindu cloud and arrive here in advance. I also did not know what clever speeches and flowery words he used to deceive Guanyin as well.' Guanyin said, 'Wujing, do not shift blame. Sun Wukong has been here for four days now. I have not yet sent him back. By what right did he think he had chosen another Tripitaka and gone off to fetch scriptures?' Sha Wujing said, 'Now, in the Water-curtain Cave there is a Sun Wukong; how can he dare to deceive and swindle?' Guanyin said, 'Then do not grow impatient. Ask Sun Wukong to go with you to Flower-Fruit Mountain and see there. What seems hard to extinguish may be easy to remove; what seems easy to remove may be hard to see through. You will understand there for yourself.'

The Great Sage heard this and, with Sha Wujing, took leave of the Bodhisattva. From there he went to:

Before Flower-Fruit Mountain one can separate black from white; at the entrance of the Water-curtain Cave one may discern true from false.

It remains unknown how to distinguish these things. Listen in the next chapter for the resolution.
chapters.title: Chapter 57: The True Pilgrim voices complaint on Loka Mountain; the false Monkey King copies out petitions in Water-curtain Cave.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

This Great Sage and Sha Wujing took their leave of the Bodhisattva, sent up two auspicious rays, and left the South Sea. At first Sun Wukong’s jindou cloud was quick, but Sha Wujing’s celestial speed seemed slow, so Sun Wukong prepared to go ahead. Sha Wujing caught him and said, “Elder Brother, do not flaunt and hide yourself so. Go first and secure our footing. Wait till I follow with you.” Sun Wukong was a true-hearted elder, and yet Sha Wujing still had his doubt. The two then rode together. Not long afterward, they truly reached Flower-Fruit Mountain. They lowered their cloud and looked out from the cave mouth and saw a monkey seated on a stone terrace, drinking wine and reveling with the troop. He looked just like Great Sage Sun Wukong: yellow hair with a golden band, gold eyes and fire-bright pupils; he also wore a plain cotton robe, a tiger-skin skirt at the waist; in his hand he held a Golden-Hooped Staff; at his feet a pair of deerhide boots. He also had the same shaggy face, thunder mouth, broad forehead, full cheeks, and fangs protruding outward.

This Great Sage flared with anger. He waved his hand away from Sha Wujing, whipped the staff forward, and barked, “What sort of demon are you, that you dare assume my likeness, seize what is mine, squat in my immortal cave, and act with this authority?” The other monkey saw this and answered not at all, but came forward with his staff as well. The two monkey attendants stood together, and indeed it was no easy matter to tell true from false in so severe a contest. He cried, ">Two staves, two monkey spirits: this match is no trifling one. Each must protect Master Tang’s envoy and win renown through worthy merit. The real ape is the true disciple of the monkly teaching, while the false fiend feigns devotion as Buddha’s child. Owing to divine arts that take a thousand transformations, there is no true and false, only two equal forms. One is the Primordial-Unified-Celestial Sage of One Qi, the other a long-tempered thousand-spirit ground-plunging demon. This one wields the Ruyi Golden-Hooped Staff, that one a heart-obedient iron-club soldier. Neither side can break through the other in block and counter; neither side can say who prevails. Before, they fought outside the cave and for a while grappled up into the half-sky. Both then rode upon rays of cloud and leapt into battle within the Ninth-Heaven clouds." The two then fought, each stepping on streaks of cloud.

Sha Wujing stood by, afraid to strike. Watching them fight in this fashion, it was indeed hard to distinguish true from false. He wished to draw his blade to aid them, but he feared injuring the real one. After enduring for a while, he leapt off the cliff and, with the treasure staff for subduing demons, struck near the outside of Water Curtain Cave, scattering the demons and turning over the stone benches, smashing all the vessels of wine and meat in wild disorder. He then looked for his blue felt pack and found it nowhere around. Water Curtain Cave was in truth a curtain made of a cascade and spring, hanging before the cave mouth. From afar it appeared a white drape; near at hand it was but a gush of water, hence the name Water Curtain Cave. Sha Wujing did not know its inner arrangement and so could not find the way. He then rode through clouds and caught up in the Ninth-Heaven clouds, raising the treasure staff, but still had no chance to intervene. Great Sage said, “Sha Wujing, since you cannot aid effectively, go back to the Master and report what happened as it has been. Let me then fight this fiend at Mount Lojia Mountain before the Bodhisattva to sort true from false.” After he spoke, the other ape spoke the same. Sha Wujing, seeing both their faces and voices with no smallest difference, black and white undistinguishable, could only obey, turn the cloud and return to report to Tripitaka. Nothing more to mention.

You may see those two monkey attendants fighting while advancing, straight to the South Sea and straight to Mount Lojia. Their blows and shouts never ceased. It immediately alarmed the heaven-protecting deities, who reported to the pool-sound cave: “Bodhisattva, indeed two Sun Wukongs are fighting their way here.” The Bodhisattva, with Mucha, Shancai Child, and Dragon Maiden, came down to Descending-Lotus Terrace and called out from the gate, “You rogue fiends, where are you from?” The two grabbed hold of each other and said, “Bodhisattva, this brute truly resembles my disciple. Since he came from Water Curtain Cave we have fought for a while and no winner could be determined. Sha Wujing’s eyes are dull and he cannot distinguish them, yet he cannot help in battle and I have sent him back to tell the Master. My disciple and this one fought all the way to Baoshan; ask your Bodhisattva’s insight and let my brother and me know which is true and which is false.” After speaking, the other monkey repeated the same words. The many gods and the Bodhisattva watched for a long while and could not discern them. The Bodhisattva then said, “Let go both; both stand still.” At once the two released their grip and stood. This side cried, “I am the real one.” That side cried, “He is the false one.”

The Bodhisattva called Mucha and Shancai forward and whispered, “One of you hold this one, one hold that one. I will silently recite the Tightening Headband Spell. Whoever cries out from the pain is the true one; the one not in pain is the false one.” The two each clung to one of them exactly as instructed. The Bodhisattva silently intoned the mantra, and both cried out in pain together, clutching their heads and rolling on the ground, calling, “Do not chant it! Do not chant it!” The Bodhisattva stopped chanting, and then they once again seized each other and resumed their loud fight. The Bodhisattva had no further means and so ordered the gods and Mucha to lend aid. The gods feared harming the real one and so did not dare to strike. The Bodhisattva called out, “Sun Wukong!” and both answered at once. The Bodhisattva said, “Long ago when you served as Bimawen, all the divine officers recognized you when you turned the heavens to chaos. Go now to the upper court and answer those who ask.” The Great Sage gave thanks for the grace; the other ape gave thanks as well.

The two tugged and pulled, constantly roaring and fighting, and came right to the outer gate of the South Celestial Capital. Terrified, Heavenly King of Broad Vision, along with Marshal Ma, Zhao, Wen, and Guan, and the gods of the gate with the full host blocked the way with weapons, crying, “Where do you go? Is this a place for fighting?” The Great Sage said, “I protected Tripitaka on the way to the Western Heaven Journey. On the road I slew evil brigands. Because the Third Master sent me back, I came directly to Putuo Cliff to complain before Guanyin Bodhisattva. Unexpectedly this fiend at some time took my form, struck down Tripitaka, and stole the bundle. Sha Wujing came to Flower-Fruit Mountain to look and seek him. This fiend had already occupied my den. Then we returned to Putuo Cliff and begged before the Bodhisattva, and then saw me standing at her platform; yet Sha Wujing misrepresented it, saying that it was I who rode the jindou cloud and that I had first hidden under the Bodhisattva’s care. But the Bodhisattva is truly clear-sighted: she would not believe Sha Wujing’s words and ordered me and him to go to Flower-Fruit Mountain and verify. This fiend really did resemble old Sun. From Water Curtain Cave to Mount Lojia, we have fought before the Bodhisattva and she too could not tell. Therefore we came thus far and now ask all the heavenly gods to test true from false with their vision.” Having spoken, the other ape repeated the same words. The heavenly gods, having looked long enough, still could not distinguish them. The two of them called out together, “Since you cannot tell, clear the road. We are going to see the Jade Emperor!”

The gods could not withstand this and opened the gate, bringing them straight to the Lingxiao Treasure Hall. Marshal Ma and the four heavenly masters Zhang, Ge, Xu, and Qiu submitted a report: “In the mortal realm there are two Sun Wukongs who have broken into Heaven’s gate and claim audience with the King.” Before they could finish, both strode in shouting. Alarmed, the Jade Emperor himself descended in the treasure hall and asked, “Why do you two dare to create such a disturbance in Heaven and come here seeking death before me?” Great Sage said, “Your Majesty, Your Majesty, this servant has returned to obedience under Tripitaka’s teachings and will not again deceive the higher heaven. Only this fiend, taking my form,…” and so on, he set forth all previous happenings and begged, “Please let me discern true and false.” The other ape gave the same full account. The Jade Emperor then ordered Li Heavenly King of the Pagoda to bring the demon-discerning mirror and instruct: “Set it before that one and determine which is false and which is true, annihilating the false and preserving the true.” Li King brought the mirror and held it for the Jade Emperor and all deities to see. In it were two images of Sun Wukong: halo, crown, and garments, all without the smallest variation of a hair. The Jade Emperor too could not tell the difference and sent them from the hall.

The Great Sage laughed coldly, and the other ape laughed in joyous amusement. They pulled at each other’s heads and dusted their necks, then fought their way out through the gate again and fell back along the Western Road, shouting, “I’ll go with you to meet our Master! I’ll go with you to meet our Master!”

Now the account says Sha Wujing, after bidding off the two from Flower-Fruit Mountain, had traveled three days and nights before returning to their abode. He told Tripitaka the events from before in full. Tripitaka, on reflection, said in regret, “At the time I said only that Sun Wukong had struck me with a staff and robbed my bundle, never knowing it had been the fiend in Wukong’s false form.” Sha Wujing also said, “This demon took yet another form, that of an elder monk, and another of a white horse. Then there was one ape carrying our pack that looked like Pigsy, and yet another took my form. I could not bear my rage and struck one dead with my staff; it was a monkey spirit. Thus all were scattered, and I then returned to complain before the Bodhisattva. She ordered me and my senior monk to return and identify which was real and which was false. That fiend truly matched Brother Sun exactly. Since I could not assist, I came first to report back to the Master.” Upon hearing this, Tripitaka turned pale with alarm. Zhu Bajie laughed heartily: “Excellent, excellent, excellent. This matches what that pious housewife said—she spoke of several times there would be such a Journey; is this not another one?”

Then all the elders and children in that household came asking Sha Wujing, “Where have you gone these past days to seek provisions?” Sha Wujing laughed, “I went eastward to Flower-Fruit Mountain in Great Sage’s home world to retrieve our luggage, then to Mount Putuo at the South Sea to pay respects to Guanyin Bodhisattva, and then again to Flower-Fruit Mountain; only just now did I return.” The elder asked, “How many li did you go and come?” Sha Wujing said, “About two hundred thousand li, perhaps more.” The elder marveled, “Good heavens! In these few days only so much distance is possible by walking, unless it is by riding clouds!” Pigsy said, “Without cloud-riding, how could one cross the sea?” Sha Wujing said, “We do not count this as walking. As for our great elder, he could return in just one or two days.” The household then all said they must be immortals. Pigsy added, “Though we are not immortals, the immortals are still our juniors.”

As this was being discussed, a racket and a jumble of shouts rose from the air. Everyone rushed out in alarm to look, only to see two pilgrims brawling as they came together. Zhu Bajie saw them and, unable to hold back, said, “Let me go and see who they are.” The good simple fool leapt up and shouted into the sky, “Brother, do not raise such a din. Old Pig has come!” The two answered at once, “Brother, we are here to beat the demon, we are here to beat the the demon.” The householder, both frightened and glad, said, “Are these two arhat-like figures, soaring in cloud and fog, resting in my home? I have even housed vow-keeping monks, but never such worthy guests. I’ll stop worrying about tea and gruel and offer them more.” He added, “If these two pilgrims keep fighting badly, heaven will be overturned and the earth turned; who can say where calamity will strike?” Tripitaka saw the old host smiling outwardly yet worrying within, and said, “Good patron, do not be at ease. Do not grieve. Your humble monk has subdued this disciple, turning evil to good; you need not fear.” The old man answered in full, “No, no, I dare not.” Sha Wujing said, “Do not speak that, honored one. Master can sit here. Let me and my second brother go; we will drag one of them to you. Then you recite that verse—whichever one aches is the true one, the one with no pain is the counterfeit.” Tripitaka said, “That is absolutely right.”

Sha Wujing at once rose in midair and said, “Hold your hands, both of you. I will go with you to the Master’s side and sort out which is true.” The Great Sage let go. That pilgrim let go, too. Sha Wujing caught hold of one and called, “Second Brother, you catch one too.” He did so at once. They dropped to earth from the clouds and went straight to the hut’s threshold. Tripitaka, seeing this, began to recite the Tightening Headband Spell. The two cried out together, “After such fierce fighting as this, why do you still cast the spell on us? Stop it, stop it!” The abbot’s heart was naturally compassionate, so he fell silent and stopped reciting, yet he still could not tell true from false. The two freed themselves and took to fighting again. The Great Sage said, “Brothers, protect the Master. Let me fight this one until we reach King Yama and settle it there.” The other pilgrim said the same. They grappled and pulled, and after a moment they vanished again.

Zhu Bajie said, “Sha Wujing, when you came to Water Curtain Cave and saw the fake Zhu Bajie carrying the luggage, why didn’t you bring it back?” Sha Wujing said, “The demon saw me strike his fake Sha Wujing with the Golden-Hooped Staff. He rushed in with many of his underlings to seize me, so I withdrew to keep my life and ran. I then informed Guanyin, and returned with my companion to the cave mouth. The two of them fought in the air. I was the one who overturned his stone bench and scattered his small demons. A whole cataract appeared; I could not see where the cave entrance lay. I searched and could not find the luggage, so I returned to the Master with empty hands. Zhu Bajie said, “So that is why—you truly did not know. When I had invited him last year, I first met him outside the cave. After I teased him, he leapt down and slipped inside to change his clothes. As he came out I saw him dive into the water. That stream of falling water is the cave mouth. Surely the fiend has taken our baggage in there.” Tripitaka said, “Since you know where this entrance is, when he is gone go in first and take out the luggage. We can continue on westward. When he comes, I won’t need him.” Zhu Bajie said, “I’ll go.” Sha Wujing said, “Second Brother, there are a thousand or so little monkeys in front of that cave. You alone may not be able to handle him and it would not be proper.” Zhu Bajie laughed, “No fear, no fear at all.” He rushed out, leapt through cloud and fog, and went straight to Flower-Fruit Mountain to fetch the baggage. No more need be said.

It is said that those two pilgrims again shouted and fought behind Yin Mountain, so all the ghosts on that mountain trembled and hid themselves in fear. One who had run first barged straight into the gate of the Netherworld and reported to the Senluo Treasure Hall: “Great King, behind Yin Mountain there are two Qi-Tian-Da-Sheng fighting their way here!” In panic, First Court Qin Guangwang conveyed this to Second Court Chu Jiangwang, Third Court Song Diwang, Fourth Court Bian Chengwang, Fifth Court Yan Luo King, Sixth Court Pingdengwang, Seventh Court Mount Tai King, Eighth Court Dushiwang, Ninth Court Wuguanwang, and Tenth Court Zhuanlunwang, hall to hall, without delay. In a moment all ten kings assembled, and messengers were also sent to Dizang King. Gathered at the Senluo Hall, they brought together ghost troops to capture the true and the false. Then came the rolling gale and the spreading dreadful fog: the two pilgrims, turning and tumbling, arrived before the Senluo Hall.

The Yin Lord stepped forward to block them and asked, “Great Sage, what is this and why do you make such a disturbance in my netherworld?” The Great Sage said, “I follow Tripitaka to fetch the scriptures in the Western Heaven. Passing through Xiliang Country, we reached a mountain where a strong robber gang blocked us and plundered my Master. Old Sun slew a few of them; Master grew angry and sent me away. I went to Guanyin in the South Sea to report it. I do not know how that demon, with no warrant, assumed my appearance and with false words became my image. In the middle of the road he knocked down Master and stole the luggage. Sha Wujing, my junior brother, went to my home mountain to claim our packs. This demon used Master’s name and claimed the form of my brother in order to journey to the West. Sha Wujing fled and when he reached the South Sea met the Bodhisattva; I was there beside him. He explained everything. The Bodhisattva then ordered me to go with him to Flower-Fruit Mountain to inspect. In the end this rogue had seized my dwelling place. I argued with him before Guanyin; our looks and words were equally alike, and the Bodhisattva could not tell true from false. I even fought this one all the way to Heaven, and the gods there could not tell either. Since my Master saw this and tested me with the Tightening Headband Spell, he suffered the same pain as with the real one. So we have come to this hell court; ask the books of life and death to see this counterfeit pilgrim’s origin, pursue his soul at once, and avert two minds from turning to confusion.” The demon repeated the same statement verbatim. Hearing this, the Yin Lord summoned the registrars and judging officials to check from the beginning. Not a name matching that of a false pilgrim could be found. Then he checked the Maochong register: there were one hundred and thirty monkey entries. It was there that in his early youth, when Great Sage first gained the Way, he caused great havoc in the netherworld, and his name was cancelled with one strike. Since then, all monkeys have had no names. When the inquiry was done, he reported in court. With ceremonial tablets in hand, the ten kings addressed the pilgrims: “Great Sage, since the netherworld has no verifiable name for him, you must return to the sunny world and settle it there.”

At that moment, Dizang King Bodhisattva spoke: “Hold on, hold on. Let me call Diting and have him listen with you and tell us the truth.” Diting was, in fact, the name of a beast lying bound beneath Dizang’s scripture desk. If it lies under the ground, in a single instant it can survey the four continents, mountains, rivers, and state altars, the cave-heavens and blessed lands, and creatures of shell, scale, fur, feather, and bug, as well as heavenly, earthbound, divine, human, and ghostly immortals, illuminating good and evil and discerning the wise from the foolish. Obeying Dizang’s command, the beast lay prone in the Senluo court yard. After a moment it raised its head and told Dizang, “The demon has a name, but I may not reveal it to his face, and I also cannot help in seizing him.” Dizang asked, “What if it is spoken to his face?” Diting replied, “If spoken openly, the demon may lash out in rage, disturb the precious hall, and throw the Netherworld into unrest.” Dizang asked, “Why cannot you help apprehend him?” Diting said, “The demon’s mystical power is one with Sun Wukong. How much power do the netherworld gods truly have? Therefore I cannot seize him.” Dizang asked, “How then can this be resolved?” Diting answered, “The Dharma has no bounds.” Dizang immediately understood and said to the pilgrims, “You two look the same, with no difference in powers. If you would know clearly which is true, you must go to Śākyamuni Buddha at Leiyin Temple in the Western Heaven and settle it there.” The two called out together, “That is it, that is it. We shall go with you before the Buddha in the Western Heaven.” The Ten Kings then sent them out, thanked Dizang, and returned to the Green-Cloud Palace, where they ordered the ghost officials to seal up the Netherworld passes. No more is recorded.

See how the two pilgrims flew through cloud and rushed through fog, fighting their way up to the Western Heaven. There is a poem as witness:

A man with two hearts brings calamity; from horizon to sea he gives rise to suspicion. Desiring the three dignities of Precious Mare, he still recalls the first-rank platform of the Golden Throne. The southern campaigns and northern expeditions never rest; eastward blocking and westward clearing are still unresolved. In the Chan gate one must learn the art of no-mind; quietly nurture the babe and form the sacred embryo. They pulled and tugged, grabbed and wrestled in the sky, marching and fighting, and cried all the way until they came outside Leiyin, the jeweled stupa of Mount Lingjiu in Great Western Heaven. Already there, four Great Bodhisattvas, eight Great Vajra Kings, five hundred arhats, three thousand Jie-di, bhikshunis, bhikshus, upāsakas, and upāsikās, and many other great disciples had gathered beneath the Seven-Jewel Lotus Platform to listen purely to the Buddha’s Dharma. The Buddha was then speaking this verse: Neither is there being within being, and no non-being within non-being. Not in color is color, not in emptiness is emptiness. Not the conditioned is ‘is’; not the unconditioned is ‘is not’. Neither is color for color nor emptiness for emptiness. Emptiness is precisely emptiness; color is precisely color. Color has no fixed color; color is emptiness. Emptiness has no fixed emptiness; emptiness is color. To know emptiness as not-empty and color as not-color is called illumination, and only then is the subtle wondrous sound realized. The assembly all bowed in reverence and recited in resonance. As they read aloud, heavenly flowers rained down in profuse brilliance. The Buddha rose from the throne and said to the great assembly, “You are all one-minded; now look, the two with split hearts have come here while in contest.”

The crowd raised their eyes and saw that indeed there were two pilgrims, shouting to heaven and earth and clashing all the way to the Victorious Realm of Thunder-Resonance. Alarmed, the eight Great Vajra Kings stepped forward to block them and asked, 'Where are you going?' The Great Sage said, 'A demon spirit has taken my form and wants to go beneath the Precious Lotus Terrace. I beg the Buddha to determine which of us is real and which is false.' The Vajra Kings could not block them; they rushed down to the terrace and knelt before the Buddha, reporting: 'My disciple has been protecting Master Tripitaka as he seeks the True Scripture on this road, and we have subdued demons and bound monsters along the way. I do not know how much energy it cost. Midway we happened upon a fierce kidnapper, and on that occasion the disciple twice struck and wounded several people. Master rebuked me for rushing back and would not allow me to bow to the Buddha’s Golden Body with him. So I had no choice but to flee to the South Sea and tell Guanyin my sorrow. By chance this demon copied my voice and appearance, knocked Master down, and snatched the baggage. Wukong came in to find me at Flower-Fruit Mountain, and this demon used clever lies, saying this was all for a true monk seeking the scriptures. Wukong escaped to the South Sea and reported everything in full. When Guanyin heard of it, she sent the disciple together with Wukong back to my mountain. So we compared true and false and fought, at one time to the South Sea, at another to Heaven, even as far as the netherworld, and even when seeing Tripitaka, and still could not identify him. Therefore, I dare make this bold, forward request: open widely the gate of expedient grace, extend broad compassion, and make clear true and false for my disciple, so that he can properly protect Tripitaka, make personal obeisance to the Buddha’s Golden Body, return to the Eastern Land with the scripture, and forever promulgate the Great Teaching.' The assembly heard both mouths speaking in one voice, both saying the same words, and none could distinguish. Only the Buddha understood. He was about to expose the truth when, between the downward-pouring multicolored clouds, Guanyin arrived and paid homage to the Buddha.'

The Buddha, palms joined, said, 'Guanyin, you look at those two pilgrims; who is true and who is counterfeit?' The bodhisattva said, 'The other day, in your disciple’s wild retreat, I still could not distinguish him. He also came to Heaven and the Underworld, and in both places he still could not recognize. I have come especially to bow and beg the Buddha—please let him make the distinction clearly, clearly.' The Buddha smiled: 'Your powers are great; you can generally perceive events in the cosmic vault, but you cannot know all things in it, nor can you broadly comprehend all its kinds. As for the kinds in the ten directions: there are five immortals—heaven, earth, spirits, humans, and ghosts. There are five forms of creatures—shell, scale, hair, feather, and insect-kind. This rogue is neither heaven, nor earth, nor spirit, nor human, nor ghost; neither shell nor scale, nor hair nor feather, nor insect. There are also four world-disrupting monkeys that are not of the ten kinds.' Guanyin asked, 'May I dare ask what those four monkeys are?' The Buddha said, 'First is the Luminous-Mind Stone Monkey, who can transform, read heavenly timing, know earthly advantage, and move the stars and replace the stars. Second is the Red-Kneed Horse Monkey, who knows yin and yang, handles human affairs, is skilled in coming and going, and can avoid death and prolong life. Third is the Long-Armed Ape Monkey, who can seize sun and moon, shrink a thousand mountains, discern blessing and blame, and wrestle with heaven and earth. Fourth is the Six-Eared Macaque, who listens keenly, discerns principle, knows before and after, and sees all things clearly. These four monkeys are not among the ten kinds and are beyond the names of the two divisions. This fake Wukong is the Six-Eared Macaque. If this macaque stands in one place, he can know events a thousand li away; he can also understand what ordinary men say. So it is he who listens well, discerns reason, knows past and future, and sees all things clearly. One who matches true Wukong in appearance and voice is a Six-Eared Macaque.'

That macaque, hearing the Buddha speak of his true form, was seized with terror and alarm, sprang up at once, and tried to leave. When the Buddha saw him flee, he ordered the assembly to move. Already present were four bodhisattvas, eight Vajra Kings, five hundred arhats, three thousand Jiedi, monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, Guanyin, and Muxa, all encircling together. Sun Wukong also moved to step forward; the Buddha said, 'Wukong, do not strike. Wait while I have him captured.' The macaque, with hair and bones chilled, sensing he could not escape, swiftly changed shape, became a bumblebee, and flew upward. The Buddha flicked up his gold alms bowl; just as it landed, it covered the bee. The assembly did not know and thought he had escaped. Buddha laughed: 'No need to speak, everyone. The demon has not gone; he is under this bowl of mine.' The assembly rushed forward and lifted the bowl, and truly saw his original form: a Six-Eared Macaque. Sun Wukong could not restrain himself; he raised the Golden-Hooped Staff and with one blow struck him dead, ending that species to this day. The Buddha, unable to bear it, said, 'Excellent! Excellent!' The Great Sage said, 'The Buddha should not spare pity. He injured my Master and robbed our baggage. By law, one should charge him for unlawful gain and bodily harm; he robbed in broad daylight and ought to be sentenced to death.' The Buddha said, 'Go at once and protect Tripitaka now to come here for the scripture.' The Great Sage knelt and thanked him: 'I report to the Buddha: Master is certain not to want me. If I go there and he does not take me in, will that not waste Your thought and effort once more? I beg the Buddha, through convenience, chant the Tightening Headband Spell once, loosen the headband, remove this golden hoop, return it to the Buddha, and let me return to lay life.' The Buddha said, 'Do not think wildly. Do not be troublesome. I will have Guanyin send you; do not fear he will not receive you. Guard him well. When your merit is complete, you will return to the Pure Land, and you too will sit upon the Lotus Terrace.'

Hearing from nearby, Guanyin then joined her palms in thanks for the Buddha’s grace, took Sun Wukong with her, and at once rode away on clouds. Immediately after, Muxa the bodhisattva and the White Parrot hurried after her. Soon they reached a house by the roadside where Sha Wujing had seen them and hastily invited Master Tripitaka to bow at the gate in welcome. Guanyin said, 'Tripitaka, the one who struck you before was the false pilgrim, the Six-Eared Macaque. Thankfully the Buddha has discerned him and Wukong has already killed him. Now you must keep Wukong with you; on the road the demon-obstacles are not yet exhausted, and only he can protect you so you can reach Ling Mountain and see the Buddha to obtain the scripture. Do not be resentful again.' Tripitaka knelt and said, 'I respectfully follow the instruction.'

Just as they were giving thanks, they heard wild winds rolling in from the due east, and Zhu Bajie arrived riding the wind with two baggage bundles on his back. The Pig saw the bodhisattva, threw himself down in full prostration, and said, 'My brother, when I left Master the other day and came to the Water-Curtain Cave of Flower-Fruit Mountain to fetch the pack, I indeed saw a fake Tripitaka and a fake Zhu Bajie, and by my hand I killed both; it was two monkey bodies. I then went inside and only later found the bundle. I checked every item and not one thing was missing; then I caught the wind and came here. I still do not know what has become of those two pilgrims.' Guanyin recounted in full how the Buddha had discerned the demon. The Pig was filled with joy and his thanks were boundless. The disciples and Master thanked her and the bodhisattva returned to the sea. From then on all returned to their former harmony of mind and heart, washing away grievance and anger. They thanked the household there again, packed their baggage and horses in order, and took the great road heading west. It was then:

In the middle road, separating causes the Five Elements to split in confusion; the demon-subduing assembly gathers, resolving to Original Clarity. When the spirit returns and lays aside clinging, meditation finds its seat; when the six consciousnesses are dispelled, the transformative elixir forms of itself.

As for this, it is still not yet known when Tripitaka will get to face the Buddha and seek the scripture. Now listen to the next chapter for its unfolding.
chapters.title: Chapter 58: Two hearts trouble Heaven and earth; one body finds it hard to realize perfect silent nirvana.
