This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Though many kinds are one in their original nature, all are naturally inclusive, like the sea with no bound. A thousand thoughts and myriad concerns always become delusion; every color and shade blends into harmony. On the day the work is complete and the course fulfilled, the complete clear Dharma-nature rises high and lofty. Do not let discrimination run east or west, bound fast in a tight cage. Gather it in and place it in the alchemical furnace; forge it till it glows red like a golden crow. Bright and resplendent, beauteously splendid, it may come and go riding the dragon at will.

Following the Bodhisattva’s command, Tripitaka gathered up Wukong, and together with Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing cut through all divided intention, chained the monkey and the horse, and with one heart and one effort pressed on toward the Western Heaven. Time is beyond telling: it goes like an arrow, the sun and moon like a shuttle. They had passed the searing summer heat, and yet they were meeting again the frosty scenes of the late third month. What they saw was:

Thin clouds were torn apart, and the west wind blew tight, Cranes cried among far ridges, the frost-touched woods like brocade. The scene was cold in spirit; the mountains grew long, and the rivers still longer. The southbound wild geese came to the northern frontier, the dark birds returned toward the southern ways. On the road of a traveller, loneliness was all one feared; a monk’s patched robe catches cold too easily.

As the four pilgrims moved forward, they gradually felt heat rising like steam from men. Tripitaka pulled up the white horse and said, “At this time it is autumn; how then is it so hot?” Pigsy said, “It seems we did not know. On the Western road there is a Śa-hā-lǐ Kingdom, said to be where the sun sets, commonly called the End of Heaven. If you arrive at the hour of shen-you, the king sends men to the city gate to beat drums and blow horns, a din mixed with the roar of a sea boiling. The sun is true fire itself and falls among the Western Sea; as if quenched in water it roars. Without the drums and horns to thrum the ears, it would instantly slay the children of the city. So this heat must be from that place of sunset.” When Wukong heard this he could not help but laugh. “Bǎi, stop babbling. As for Śa-hā-lǐ, you are quite early. With this way of the master changing from this to that, from youth to old and old to youth over three lifetimes, one still would not arrive.” Pigsy said, “Brother! If what you say is true, why is this so hot if it is not the place where the sun sets?” Sha Wujing said, “Perhaps it is because the time is wrong, and autumn is running by summer’s order.” The three continued to argue when they saw by the roadside an estate of red: red-tiled houses, walls of red brick, red-oiled fan handles, red-lacquered plank beds—everything was red. Tripitaka dismounted and said, “Wukong, go ask this household a question. See for what reason this is so hot.”

Wukong set aside his Golden-Hooped Staff, straightened his robes, and struck a refined air, then strode out to the road and went straight to the gate. From the gate suddenly came an old man. He looked as follows:

He wore a loose hemp robe, yellow-red yet not yellow and red, and a bluish-green hat woven of split reed straw, neither clearly blue nor clearly so. In his hand he leaned on a bamboo staff of hard knotted cane, bent yet straight and straight yet bent. On his feet were old-and-new shoes, neither new nor old. His face was like red bronze, his beard like white silk thread. Two long life-brows shaded green-blue eyes, and one broad-lipped grin showed golden teeth. The old man suddenly raised his head. On seeing Wukong he was startled, leaned on his cane, and barked, “What monster are you from where, and what business do you have at my gate?” Wukong bowed and answered, “Elder, do not fear me. I am no monster. I am a poor monk from Great Tang in the Eastern land, an imperial envoy seeking the sutras of the West. The four of us have just come to this treasure land; seeing the steam of heat, for one reason we do not know why, and for another because we do not know the place’s name, we have come to ask for guidance." The old man only then was at ease. He smiled and said, “Great senior, forgive me. My eyes were fleetingly dim and did not recognize your worthy face.” Wukong said, “I dare not.” The old man asked, “Where is your master’s road?” Wukong said, “Is it not on that great road at the southern entrance?” The old man said, “Please come, please come.” Wukong rejoiced. With one motion of his hand, Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing came up, guiding the white horse and carrying their baggage, and all three made obeisance to the old man.

The old man, seeing Tripitaka’s graceful bearing and appearance, and seeing the unusual features of Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, was surprised and pleased. He could only invite them in, had them sit, told the younger ones to brew tea, and set another hall for food. Hearing him speak, Tripitaka rose in thanks and said, “May I ask, esteemed sir: you call this place what in autumn heat is still scorching. Why is it so hot?” The old man said, “Our land is called Huoyan Mountain. It has no spring and no autumn; all four seasons are hot.” Tripitaka asked, “Where is Huoyan Mountain then? Can it block the road westward?” The old man said, “You cannot go west by that way. The mountain lies sixty li from here, directly on the required western route, but there are eight hundred li of flame all around, and no grass grows on all four sides. If one were to cross it, even one with a copper skull and an iron body would be melted into gruel.” When Tripitaka heard this, he was pale with fright and dared ask no more.

Just outside the gate a young man was standing by, pushing a red cart, crying, “Cakes for sale.” Wukong plucked a hair and changed it into a copper coin, then bought a cake from him. The man took it without judging its quality, lifted the covering from the cart, and hot steam rose up. He brought out a cake and handed it to Wukong. Wukong held it in his hand; it was like a heated ember from fire, like a red nail in a coal furnace. He kept shifting it from left to right and right to left, saying, “Hot, hot, hot—hard to eat, hard to eat!” The young man laughed. “If it is too hot, do not come here. This is truly that kind of heat.” Wukong said, “You man lacks understanding. There is a saying: ‘When there is neither cold nor heat, the five grains do not ripen.’ It is so hot here indeed—where does your cake flour come from?” The young man said, “If you ask about flour and rice for cake, ask for Tie-shan Xian.” Wukong said, “How should I know Tie-shan Xian?” The young man said, “Tie-shan Xian has a banana-leaf fan in her hand. One stroke stills the flames, two stir wind, three make rain. Then we can sow and harvest in our fields in time and keep grain alive. Without it, truly not even a blade of grass could grow.”

After hearing him, Wukong quickly walked inside and handed the cake to Tripitaka: “Master, do not worry and do not be burned through another year. Eat it first, and then I will tell you.” Tripitaka took the cake in hand and said to the old householder, “Elder, please accept the cake.” The old man said, “My tea and food have not yet been offered. How could I dare eat your cake?” Wukong laughed. “Elder, tea and food are not needed. I ask you this: where does Tie-shan Xian reside?” The old man asked, “Why do you ask about him?” Wukong said, “The cake seller said that this immortal carries a banana-leaf fan. With one wave it quenches fire, with two it raises wind, with three it brings rain; thus this place can sow and harvest in season and have grain to live by. I want to seek him, take the fan, cross the flame-mountain fire, and make this land able to sow and gather in season and live in peace.” The old man said, “There is indeed such a tale, but you have no gifts, and that holy figure may refuse to come.” Tripitaka asked, “What gifts does he require?” The old man said, “In our families, once in ten years one is granted an audience. Four pigs and four sheep, red-dyed silk and brocade, strange incense, seasonal fruit, chickens and geese, fine wine; bathe with reverence, worship with sincerity, bow up to that immortal mountain and ask him to leave his cave and come here to bestow this aid.” Wukong said, “Where does that mountain stand, what is it called, and how many li away? I need to ask him for the fan.” The old man said, “That mountain is in the southwest, called Cuiyun Mountain. In it there is a cave called Bajiao Cave. From here the worshippers must worship there and then take a month to return, about one thousand four hundred and sixty li.” Wukong laughed, “No matter; I will go and come.” The old man said, “Wait—at least eat some tea and food, prepare dried rations, and take two companions. That road has no households and has many wolves and tigers; it cannot be reached in one day. Do not make this into a game.” Wukong laughed, “No need, no need. I will go now.” At once he spoke and vanished. The old man, flustered, cried, “My lord! He was truly a divine man riding clouds and driving mist.”

We need not continue with how this family honored Tripitaka all the more. As for Wukong, he at once went straight to Cuiyun Mountain, calmed his radiant light, and was searching for the cave opening when he heard a ding-ding sound; it was a woodcutter sawing and hacking in the woodland. Wukong stepped forward. Again he heard this from him:

Near the cloud-edge, the old woodland is dimly known; at broken cliffs, overgrown weeds, the path is hard to find. On the western hills one can see the rain from the morning windward, and at the south ravine, when one returns, the ford is deep. Wukong came near and paid respect: “Woodcutter brother, greetings.” The woodcutter set down his axe and, in answering, returned the courtesy: “Where is the abbott going?” Wukong said, “If I may ask, is this Cuiyun Mountain?” The woodcutter said, “It is exactly.” Wukong said, “Where is the Bajiao Cave of Tie-shan Xian?” The woodcutter laughed. “Though this Bajiao Cave exists, it has no Tie-shan Xian, only an Iron Fan Princess, also named Luocha Nü.” Wukong said, “People say she has a banana fan and can extinguish Huoyan Mountain. Is that she?” The woodcutter said, “Exactly. This saint indeed has that precious thing and can put out fire, protecting the households of this land, thus is called Tie-shan Xian. Around here no one has use of him; they only know her as Luocha Nü, the wife of the Great-Strength Ox-demon King.”

When the Traveler heard this, he was greatly startled and turned white in the face. Inwardly he thought, “Another round of revenge now. Years ago I overpowered Red Boy, and they said this one had raised him. Previously, at Poxie Cave below Jieyang Mountain, I met his uncle and he still would not even give water, meaning to seek revenge; now I have met his parents as well—how can I borrow this fan here?” Seeing Wukong fall into brooding silence, the woodcutter sighed repeatedly and then laughed, “Elder, you are a monk; why so full of anxiety? This path runs east. In no more than five or six li is Banana-leaf Cave. Don’t let your heart burn.” Wukong said, “I will not hide it from you, Woodcutter Brother. I am Sun Wukong, the Tang monk’s senior disciple, sent from the Tang court of the Eastern Land to journey west for the sutras. Last year at Fire-Cloud Cave I had words with the Rakshasa’s son Hong Hai-er. I fear the rakshasa still bears a grudge and may not lend himself to me, so this worry arose.” The woodcutter said, “A true man reads face and manner and goes by the name of borrowing a fan. Do not mistake old words for truth, and you are bound to get it.” Wukong, hearing this, made a deep ceremonial bow and said, “Thank you for your guidance, Woodcutter Brother. I go.”

Then, leaving the woodcutter, he came straight to the mouth of Banana-leaf Cave. He saw the two cave doors tightly closed and bolted, while the scenery outside was beautiful. It was truly a fine place, and indeed:

The mountain has stone for bone, and stone gives soul to earth. Mist and sunset clouds hold old dampness, and moss helps new green bloom. Jagged and towering, the ridges rise, proud as though challenging Peng Island. In the quiet silence, flower fragrance lies like the sea wind. A few stately pines shelter wild cranes; a few withered willows whisper with mountain orioles. Truly it is a thousand-year relic, an immortal trace of ten-thousand years. Blue phoenixes cry beneath lustrous parasol-boughs, living water hides a green dragon. Curving paths hang with creeping ivy; stone stairs are wrapped in vines and kudzu. Ape cries rise from jade cliffs, happy for moonlight above; birds cry in tall trees, delighted in clear skies. Two bamboo groves cool one like rain, a path of flowers thick as embroidered velvet. Then one sees white clouds from far ridges, without fixed shape, wandering with the wind. Sun Wukong called out, “Brother Niu, open the door, open the door.” With a sharp crack the cave-mouth opened, and a young maiden came out, holding a basket of flowers in one hand and a hoe over her shoulder. She was all blue-brocade unadorned, plain and plainhearted, her face full of vigor and a sense of the Dao. Sun Wukong stepped forward, joined his palms, and said, “Girl, run and report to the princess: I am a monk on the western pilgrimage. I passed through Flaming Mountain and have come to borrow the Banana-leaf Fan for one use.” The hair-girl said, “What temple’s monk are you? What name do you bear? Tell me so I may report you properly.” Wukong said, “I come from the Eastern Land, and my name is monk Sun Wukong.”

The hair-girl turned at once and returned to the cave, then knelt before the Rakshasa and said, “Grandmother, there is a monk named Sun Wukong from the Eastern Land waiting outside the cave. He asks to see you and to borrow the Banana-leaf Fan for crossing Flaming Mountain.” When the Rakshasa heard the words “Sun Wukong,” it was as if salt were cast into fire and oil poured on the flames; her whole face flamed red, fury blazing in her chest. She spit out, “That rude monkey! He has come today!” She called, “Maid, bring my armor. Fetch weapons.” Immediately she took out her surcoat, and two emerald-edged jewel swords were brought. Wukong slipped to the side of the cave-mouth and stole a glance at how she dressed. He saw:

A round flowered handkerchief wraps her head. A rich cloud-hued brocade robe is worn upon her body. A tiger-sinew sash is tied at her waist; an embroidered skirt and light scarf part the robe. Her phoenix-beaked shoes are three inches. Dragon-whisker-tipped knee-tights with golden fasteners. She lifts the jewel swords with raised voice. Fierce in face, she is a monstrous beauty.

The Rakshasa came out and shouted, “Where is Sun Wukong?” Wukong stepped forward and bowed, “Sister-in-law, old Sun is here to make obeisance.” The Rakshasa snapped, “Who is your sister-in-law, and who is it you are to bow to?” Wukong said, “In your noble house is Niu Mo Wang, who once made sworn-brother vows with old Sun and is counted among the seven brotherhood ties. Now that I hear the princess is under Brother Niu’s command, how could I not call you sister-in-law?” The Rakshasa said, “You impudent monkey! If you claim brotherly bonds, how did you trap my son?” Wukong asked, feigning ignorance, “Who is your son?” She replied, “My son is Hong Hai-er, Holy Infant Great King of Fire-Cloud Cave in Wugon Valley of the Dry-Pine Mountain, called the Red Boy. You overthrew him; we have nowhere to pursue revenge but to come for you. Now you come to give up your life at my gate; could I spare you?” Wukong smiled broadly and said, “Sister-in-law did not understand the order of things and wrongly blamed old Sun. Your son captured our Master to steam and boil him; luckily Avalokiteśvara Guanyin took him in and saved my Master. He now serves at Guanyin’s side as Shancai Tongzi, has attained true bodhisattva fruit, neither born nor extinguished, neither pure nor impure, long-lived with heaven and earth and enduring as sun and moon. Yet you do not thank old Sun for saving your life and turn to blame him—what is the meaning of that?” The Rakshasa snarled, “You crafty-tongued monkey! Though my life was not broken, as long as you ever come near me, when will you let me see you once?” Wukong laughed, “What is hard for sister-in-law to see your son? First lend me the fan, and let me winnow the flames so I can send my Master through. Then I will go to the Southern Sea Bodhisattva and ask him to come and see you, and I will return the fan to you. What is impossible in that?” He added, “Then see if he has any wound at all; if even a single hair is harmed, you may be right to blame me. If he is as handsome as before, you should thank me.” The Rakshasa said, “Impudent monkey! Speak less. Put out your head and I will strike you with several sword-strokes. If you endure the pain, you shall have the fan; if you cannot bear it, I’ll send you quickly to King Yama.” Wukong folded his palms and stepped forward, “Sister-in-law, do not speak much. Old Sun can bare his shining head and bear whatever number of slashes you choose, and when he lacks strength, that is enough. I simply must borrow the fan to use.” The Rakshasa would not wait for him to finish. She raised both hands and flashed the sword against Wukong’s head with clanging blows—ten or more times—but he did not take it seriously. Fearful now, she turned to leave. Wukong called, “Where are you going, sister-in-law? Lend it to me and let me use it at once.” She replied, “My treasure is not easily lent.” Wukong said, “If you will not lend it, I’ll give you one staff-beat for your old uncle.”

The good Monkey King, with one hand he grabbed her and with the other drew the staff from behind his ear; with one swing it was as thick as a bowl. The Rakshasa tore loose and lifted her sword to meet him. Wukong again swung the staff to strike. On the front of Green-Cloud Mountain, kinship and propriety were gone; only grievance was spoken. This was a fine and deadly clash:

The skirt and hairpins were forensibly an uncanny cultivation gone wild; For a son’s grudge she hurled wrath at the monkey. Though the Monkey King truly turned fiercer in anger, because the road to the Western Sage must continue, he kept his patience soft. Before, he asked to borrow the Banana-leaf Fan and did not display ferocity. The Rakshasa, ignorant, raised her sword to strike; The Monkey King meant only to explain brotherly ties. How can a woman wrestle a man? In the end, manly force outweighs womanly force. The Golden-Hooped Staff is so ferocious; that frost-edged green blade is close and tight in rank. They chop at face and temple, hurl at the head, and bitter hatred and hurt endure without rest. Left blocks and right parries display martial arts; front meets rear, and strange stratagems are cast forth. They fought only until deep exhaustion overtook them, and they did not notice the western sun sinking. The Rakshasa swiftly wielded her true fan and swished it once; the spirits and ghosts were troubled by the moved air. The Rakshasa woman fought with Wukong until dusk. Seeing Wukong’s staff heavy and his counter-moves so closely formed, she reckoned she could not defeat him. So she brought out the Banana-leaf Fan, and with one sweep of dark wind she buffeted Wukong until he was left without even shadow or shape; no thought could keep him. The Rakshasa withdrew, victorious.

The Great Sage drifted and staggered, unable to settle by falling left or right. He was like a storm-tossed broken leaf, streamwater carrying the remnant of fallen flowers. He rolled all night and only at dawn at last came down, clasping a rock of a peak in both arms. After settling his mind for a long while, he looked carefully and only then recognized it as the Little Xumi Mountain. The Great Sage sighed deeply: “What power this woman has! How could she send old Sun all the way here? I once remembered coming to this place and petitioning Bodhisattva Lingji to call down the Yellow Wind demon to save my Master. From Huangfeng Ridge to here there is directly over three thousand li to the south; now, turning on the western road, I am at a southeast corner. Who knows how many ten-thousands of li away?” "I will go down and ask Bodhisattva Lingji for some news, so that I may return by the old way."

Before he had even fully steadied himself, he heard the bell ringing out brightly again. He hurried down the mountain slope and went straight to the Chan monastery. A daoist at the gate, recognizing Sun Wukong’s appearance, ran inside to report: "The shaggy-faced Great Sage who came last year to invite a Bodhisattva to subdue the Yellow-Wind demon has returned." The Bodhisattva saw it was Wukong and quickly descended from the precious seat to welcome him. Going in, he bowed and said, "Congratulations. Have you come to begin the scripture journey?" Wukong replied, "Not yet—not yet truly."

Lingji said, "You have not yet obtained the Le Yin Dharma. Why return from the wild mountains now?" Wukong replied, "Last year, because of your kindness, I brought down the Yellow-Wind demon. Since then I have passed through unknown hardships along the road. I have now reached the Flaming Mountains and cannot move forward. I asked the locals, and they told me there is an Iron-Fan Immortal; with her banana-fiber fan she can put out the flames. I went specially to find her. That Immortal is the wife of the Bull Demon King, mother of Red Boy. She says I made her son a disciple page of Guanyin Bodhisattva so he cannot see him often, and she bears me enmity, refuses to lend the fan, and argued with me. Seeing that my staff was too heavy to hold against her, she gave the fan one great sweep, and it sent me drifting and whirling until I finally came down here. So I dashed to this monastery to ask the way back. I do not know how many li remain to the Flaming Mountains."

Lingji laughed. "That woman is named Luo Sha, also called Iron-Fan Princess. That banana fan was once a numinous treasure formed on the back of Kunlun from the beginning of creation, when Heaven and Earth first opened; it is a leaf born of Taiyin essence, therefore it can quench fire. If she fans at a person, he may be blown for eighty-four thousand li before the cold wind settles. From this place to the Flaming Mountains is just over fifty thousand li. It is because Great Sage has the power to hold back the clouds that you stopped here; if you were an ordinary man, you would not have been able to stand still at all."

Wukong said, "Terrible, terrible! How then will my master cross that way?" Lingji said, "Do not worry, Great Sage. This, too, is by Tripitaka's ordained affinity; it is fitting that Great Sage now bring this through."

Wukong asked, "How can it be made to work?" Lingji said, "In the past I received Buddha's command and was granted one Dingfeng Pill and one Feilong staff. The Feilong staff has already subdued the Wind Demon. The Dingfeng pill has not yet been used. I give it to Great Sage now. It will keep that brute from sweeping at you and holding you in motion. You should take the fan, set him to rest, and fan the fires down. That will complete this task."

Wukong lowered his head and bowed in endless thanks. The Bodhisattva took a small brocade pouch from his sleeve, gave him the one Dingfeng pill, tucked it at Wukong’s collar, and stitched it fast with needle and thread. As he sent him out, he said, "There is no need to stay. Go northwest, and that is the mountain-ground of Luo Sha."

Wukong took his leave of Lingji, mounted the Jidou Cloud, and returned straight to Green Cloud Mountain, arriving in an instant. He struck the cave gate with the Golden-Hooped Staff and called out, "Open the door, open it! Old Sun has come to borrow the fan and try it."

The young maid inside panicked and ran to report, "Grandmother, the one who asks to borrow the fan has come again." Hearing this, the Iron-Fan Princess felt a chill of fear and thought, "That wild monkey truly has real skill. My treasure, when it fans a person, can blow him all the way to eighty-four thousand li before the wind ceases. How is he back already after one sweep? This time I will fan him two or three times in a row and send him off so he cannot find his way home."

She sprang up at once, squared herself, drew her sword in both hands, and came out: "Sun Wukong, you are not afraid of me and have come to seek death again?"

Wukong laughed. "Sister-in-law, do not be stingy. I must borrow this fan and use it so that Tripitaka may cross the mountain, and then I will return it. I am a gentleman with a heart of sincerity; I am not a petty fellow who borrows and never returns."

The princess cursed, "You wild monkey! How shameless, how ignorant! You have not yet repaid the grudge for my taking your son, and as for your hope of borrowing a fan, how can it be satisfied? Do not move—eat my old mother’s blade!"

The Great Sage showed no fear and met her blows with a clear stroke of his ironrod. They traded strike after strike; the princess’s hand was weak and she could not handle the sword well, while Sun Wukong was strong and skilled in battle. Seeing the odds not in her favor, she took up the fan and gave Wukong one sweep. He stood unmoving. Wukong withdrew the Golden-Hooped Staff and said with a knowing smile, "This time is not like the last. Sweep as much as you wish. If Old Sun so much as stirs an inch, I am no true man."

The Iron-Fan Princess swept twice more. Again he did not move. Alarmed, she hurriedly withdrew her treasure, turned back, went into the cave, and shut the door tight.

When Wukong saw she had closed the door, he devised a trick. He opened his collar, held the Dingfeng Pill in his mouth, and changed shape, becoming a jiaoliao insect, then crawled through a crack in the gate. At that moment the princess cried, "I am thirsty, I am thirsty—bring tea at once." A nearby maid gave her a pot of fragrant tea and filled a cup in a rushing pour, with foam hissing and rising. Wukong rejoiced at the sight; with a quick chirr he flew beneath the foam.

The princess was terribly parched. She took the tea and drank three cups in as many breaths. Wukong had already gone into her belly. He returned to his true form and cried in a strong voice, "Sister-in-law, let me use the fan."

The Iron-Fan Princess started in panic, "Children, have you closed the front door?" They said, "It is closed." She said, "Then how can Sun Wukong be crying inside the house?" The maid replied, "He is crying from inside your body."

The princess exclaimed, "Sun Wukong, what trick are you practicing there?" Wukong answered, "Old Sun never uses tricks and spells; this is all real technique, true power. I am already playing tricks in your respectable sister-in-law’s belly and have seen your heart and liver for myself. I know you are hungry and thirsty. I will first send you a cup to ease the thirst."

So he put his foot down inside her. The princess clutched her lower belly, writhed on the ground in pain, and called out in distress.

Wukong said, "Sister-in-law, do not refuse. I will bring you another bite to satisfy your hunger." Then he pushed his head upward. She could bear it no more; she rolled on the ground, face gone pale and yellow, crying, "Uncle Sun, spare my life."

Wukong then withdrew his limbs and said, "Only now do you recognize an uncle? Out of brotherly feeling toward the Niu family, I still spare your life. Bring out the fan so I may use it."

The princess replied, "Uncle, there is a fan, there is a fan. Come out and take it."

Wukong said, "I have seen the fan by taking it out."

She called for a maid to bring a banana-leaf fan and set it by her side. Wukong, peering toward her throat, said, "Sister-in-law, because I spared your life, I did not have to stab a hole below your waist-ribs and come out by force; I could leave by my mouth. Open your mouth wide—widely." She did so, opening it broad.

Wukong once again took the form of the jiaoliao insect and flew out first, alighting upon the banana fan. The princess did not understand, and called out three times, "Uncle, come out." Wukong resumed his true form, took the fan, and said, "I’m over here. Thank you for lending it. Thank you indeed."

He jerked the fan and stepped forward out of the cave. The maidens quickly opened the gate and let him out.

The Great Sage turned his cloud about and returned by the eastern route. In no time he descended from the cloud and stood beneath the red-brick wall. Upon seeing him, Zhu Bajie cried, "Master, brother has come! He has come!" Tripitaka and Sha Wujing went out with the old man of this dwelling to receive him, then went into the inner room together.

Wukong set the banana-fan beside them and said, "Old fellow, is this the fan?"

The elder answered, "Yes, yes."

Tripitaka rejoiced, "My worthy fellow has performed a great deed. To gain this treasure must have cost you such hardship."

Wukong said, "The hardship was not too much to speak of. Who was that Iron-Fan Immortal, you ask? She was in fact the wife of the Bull Demon King and mother of Red Boy, called Luo Sha, also called Iron-Fan Princess. I went to borrow from her outside the cave. She spoke of old enmity and struck at me with several sword blows. I frightened her with my staff, so she used the fan once on me and I drifted and spun all the way to Mount Small Sumeru before landing. By luck I met Lingji Bodhisattva, who gave me a Dingfeng pill and pointed me home. I returned to Green Cloud Mountain and met the princess again. She again used the fan and fanned at me, but I did not move, and she fled back into the cave. Then I transformed into a jiaoliao insect and flew inside. She was asking for tea; I slipped under the foam and entered her belly, working my tricks there. She could not endure the pain and kept crying, asking me to spare her life and even to lend me the fan. I spared her, took the fan, and crossed over the Flaming Mountains. I will still return it after we are across." Tripitaka heard this and thanked him in silence.

The four disciples all took their leave of the old man and headed west. After about forty li, the heat grew progressively more oppressive, steaming the body. Sha Wujing only said, "My feet feel as if they are burning." Zhu Bajie added, "My paws are scorching too."

The horse was even faster than usual, and because the heat was so hard to bear it grew restless and rushed forward. Wukong said, "Master, please dismount. Brothers, do not press on. Let me fan down the flames. After wind and rain the earth will cool; then we can cross the mountain."

Wukong raised the fan and went straight to the fire. He fanned once with all his strength; the flames leapt upward in surging plumes. He fanned again—tenfold greater. He fanned once more—the fire rose a thousand zhang high and slowly began to burn his body. Wukong hurried back; two tufts of his fur had already been scorched away. He ran straight to Tripitaka and shouted, "Go back, go back quickly. The fire has come. The fire has come."

The Master mounted the horse, and with Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing came east again for more than twenty li before he finally rested, saying, “How is it, Wukong?” The Monkey King set down his fan and said, “Can’t stop, can’t stop; that rascal has tricked me.” Tripitaka heard this and furrowed his brows in sorrow; with sorrow pressing on his heart, he could not hold back the tears and said only, “What is to be done?” Zhu Bajie said, “Elder brother, why did you hurry back and call out so?” The Monkey King said, “I fanned once and the flames flared; a second fanning made the fire fiercer; a third made the fire-tongues rise a thousand zhang high. If he had not run fast enough, he would have burned all the hairs off.” Zhu Bajie laughed, “You always say thunder cannot harm you and fire cannot damage you. Why are you afraid of fire now?” The Monkey King said, “You dolt, you understand nothing. Then I had guarded carefully with my mind, so I was not hurt. Today I only stirred the flame to calm it; I did not once use the art of dodging fire, and I did not invoke my protective techniques, so I burned two locks of hair.” Sha Wujing said, “With fire this fierce there is no way west. What is to be done?” Zhu Bajie said, “Just choose any path with no fire and go on.” Tripitaka asked, “Which direction has no fire?” Zhu Bajie said, “East, south, and north are all without fire.” He asked again, “Where is the scripture?” Zhu Bajie said, “In the west is the scripture.” Tripitaka said, “I only mean to go to where the scripture is.” Sha Wujing said, “Where there is scripture there is fire; where there is no fire there is no scripture. Truly it is a dilemma.”

The four were still chattering noisily when someone called out, “Great Sage, do not be anxious. Come and eat a bit of vegetarian meal first, then we will talk.” The four looked back and saw an old man, wearing a wind-whipped cape, a crescent-moon crown on his head, a dragon-head staff in his hand, and iron-toed boots on his feet. Behind him came a grotesque-beaked, fish-cheeked ghost, a copper basin balanced on the ghost’s head, containing some steamed cakes, cakes and gruel, and yellow-grain rice. At the westward road he bowed low and said, “I am the Earth God of Flaming Mountain. Knowing that the Great Sage protected the holy monk and could not go onward, I offer this vegetarian meal especially.” The Monkey King said, “I can be offered the meal, but when will this fire die out so that my Master can pass?” The Earth Lord said, “To extinguish the fire, you must borrow the banana-leaf fan from the Rākṣasī demoness.” Wukong picked up a fan by the wayside and said, “Is this it? The more I fan, the more the fire grips it. Why?” The Earth Lord looked at it and laughed, “This is no true fan; he has deceived you.” The Monkey King said, “How can I get the true one?” The Earth Lord then bowed from the waist again and, smiling faintly, said:

If you still want to borrow the true banana-palm fan, you must seek Great-Force King.

In the end we do not yet know why the Great-Force King is involved. Then listen to the next chapter for the explanation.
chapters.title: Chapter 59: Tripitaka is blocked on the Fire-Fire Mountain road; Wukong adjusts the Banana-Fiber Fan once.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

The Earth God said, “Great-Force King is the Bull Demon King indeed.” Sun Wukong said, “Was this hill where the Bull Demon King set the fire, and was it only given the name Flame Mountain?” The Earth God replied, “No, no. If the Great Sage will pardon this petty spirit’s offense, then I dare speak plainly.” Sun Wukong said, “What fault did you commit? There is no harm in telling me openly.” The Earth God said, “This fire was first set by the Great Sage.” Sun Wukong snapped, “Where was I? Why do you speak such nonsense? Am I a fire-setter?” The Earth God said, “It is you, and still you do not recognize me. This place was not this mountain before. Five hundred years ago, when the Great Sage rampaged in Heaven, the August Saint captured him and sent him to Old Lord Laozi, placing the Great Sage inside the Eight Diagram Furnace. After smelting, the cauldron was opened; you kicked over the alchemical furnace, and several bricks came crashing down. The remaining embers became this Flame Mountain. I was a Daoist from Doushui Palace in charge of the furnace then, and when Old Lord Laozi blamed me for failing to guard it, I was cast down here and made into the Earth God of Flame Mountain.” Zhu Bajie heard this and snapped in anger, “No wonder you dress like that; you were really an Earth spirit transformed from a Daoist.”

Sun Wukong, half believing, half not, said, “Say quickly: why is Great-Force King being sought?” The Earth God said, “Great-Force King is the husband of a rakshasi. He recently left that rakshasi; now he stays in Moyun Cave on Mount Jilei. There was once a ten-thousand-year fox king. When that fox king died, he left a daughter named the Jade-Faced Princess. She had a million pieces of household property with no one to manage it. Two years ago, she sought out the Bull Demon King for his vast powers, and in return for her estate, she took him as husband. That Bull King abandoned the rakshasi and has not returned for long. If the Great Sage can find him and beseech him to come here, then he can obtain the true fan: one, by fanning it he can calm the flames and protect Tripitaka’s progress; two, he can forever remove the fire hazard and protect the living beings here; three, he can forgive me, let me return to Heaven, and return the decree of Old Lord Laozi.” Sun Wukong asked, “Where is Mount Jilei located, and how far is it from here?” The Earth God said, “To the true south. From here to there, it is more than three thousand li.”

When Sun Wukong heard this, he told Sha Wujing and Zhu Bajie to guard Tripitaka, and told the Earth God to stay with them and not return. At once, with a sudden cry, he vanished. Half a watch had not yet passed when a high mountain already stood before him, looming like it touched the sky. He landed on Cloud-head and stood on the ridge crest to survey. It was indeed a beautiful mountain:

Not very high, yet its summit reaches toward the blue sky; not broad, yet its roots pierce to the Yellow Spring. In front of it is warm by day, behind the ridge the wind is cold. Before the mountain, day is warm and for three winters the plants know no cold; behind it, where the wind sweeps, one sees in deep heat the frost that does not melt. Dragon pools link to streamlets that run on and on; tigers’ dens cling to cliffs, and blossoms open early. Streams split into a thousand threads like flying jade. Flowers bloom together, like brocade. Ridgelines wind around the trees, and the stones press against jutting pines. Truly: high are its hills, steep are its ridges; sheer its cliffs, deep its ravines. Fragrant its flowers, sweet are its fruits; red are its vines, purple its bamboos; green are its pines, bright green its willows. Through eight seasons and four periods its coloring never changes, and for ten thousand ages its hue is like a dragon. Sun Wukong watched long enough, then stepped down from the sharp peak and entered the deep mountain to find a path. Just as he had no luck at all, he suddenly saw a woman under the pine shade, plucking a sprig of fragrant orchids, approaching with soft, swaying grace. Sun Wukong slipped behind a crag and fixed his gaze to see what she looked like: Tender and charming, her beauty could topple a kingdom; she moved slowly, like a lotus drifting. Her look was like Wang Qiang’s, her face like a lady of Chu. She spoke in gestures like a flower that understands words, and fragrant like jade newly awakened. Her high hair bun rose darkly, like a blue-black crow, and her twin eyes held green as autumn water lying across. A Xiang skirt half reveals the little bow-like shoes; jade-green sleeves half-unfurl, and long pale-rose wrists show. She spoke of evening rain and morning clouds. Truly, she had red lips and white teeth. Her brows, smooth and bright as the brocaded river, surpassed Wen Jun and Xue Tao. The woman drew nearer to the rocks. Sun Wukong bent in formal greeting and spoke evenly, “Lady Bodhisattva, where are you going?” She had not yet seen him. When she heard the question and looked up, she saw the ugliness of Sun Wukong’s face. Frightened, she nearly fled but could not, tried to move but could not, trembled so hard she could scarcely answer: “From where are you? How dare you ask someone here?” Sun Wukong thought, “If I tell her this is a quest for the fan to rescue Tripitaka, she may have ties to the Bull King. I will only use a pretended intimacy to ask for word from the demon king, then speak and answer.” Seeing him silent, the woman changed color and shouted angrily, “Who are you to dare ask me?” Sun Wukong bowed and forced a smile, saying, “I come from Green-Cloud Mountain. I have only just arrived and do not know the routes. Tell me, Bodhisattva, is this truly Mount Jilei?” The woman said, “It is.” Sun Wukong said, “Where is Moyun Cave?” She said, “Why are you asking for that cave?” Sun Wukong said, “I am from Copper-Palm Cave in Green-Cloud Mountain, a messenger sent by Princess Iron Fan to ask for the Bull Demon King.”

As soon as that woman heard of Princess Iron Fan asking for the Bull Demon King, anger surged through her; her roots of hearing burned red, and she spat out curses: “You worthless maid, truly ignorant. Since the Bull King came to my home, though not yet two years, I do not even know how much pearls, jade, gold, silver, silk, and satin I have given him; every year he took firewood, every month rice, and enjoyed himself at ease. Without a shred of shame, he still comes back to ask after him—how dare he?” Sun Wukong, realizing she was the Jade-Faced Princess, intentionally drew out the Golden-Hooped Staff and roared, “You spit such contempt! You sold your belongings to buy the Bull King for your own husband—indeed you married for payment—and you feel no shame, yet you dare to curse who?” The woman, seeing that, was so terrified that her spirit scattered and her soul fled; her steps collapsed in confusion. She clutched her bodice, trembling, then fled backward. Sun Wukong barked and shouted and followed. Through the pine shade he passed right to the mouth of Moyun Cave. The woman ran in and slammed the door shut. Sun Wukong put away the Golden-Hooped Staff, and then, when he paused and looked about, saw this lovely place:

Dense the woods, and the ridges steep and craggy. Vine and ivy shadows stir softly in the shade. Wisteria and fragrant orchids and sweet herbs perfume the air. Spring water rinses like jade through bamboo, and clever stones seem to guide the fallen petals. Mists and rosy clouds enclose distant peaks. The sun and moon shine over screens of cloud. Dragon song, tiger scream, crane cry, orioles call. One whole pure and tranquil beauty, truly lovable. Precious flowers and heavenly grasses keep the scene bright. It is not inferior to the Heaven Terrace Immortal Cave, and surpasses Penglai in the sea. Enough said of Sun Wukong pausing to admire the scenery. That woman had run off sweating with a face flushed pink, breathless from fear, her chest heaving, then gone straight into the study room. There, the Bull Demon King was quietly reading alchemical books. In great agitation she threw herself into his arms, scratching her ears and temples, crying aloud. The demon king, smiling kindly all over his face, said, “Beauty, do not distress yourself. Speak what you need to say.” The woman sprang up, pounding and cursing, saying, “You wicked demon, you nearly killed me!” The Bull King laughed, “For what matter do you curse me?” She said, “I have no parents to lean on, so I took you to protect and sustain my life. In the river and lake circles people called you a worthy hero, but you are just a cowardly husband!” The Bull King, hearing this, held her to his chest and said, “Beauty, what wrongs have I done? Tell me slowly; I will make amends with you.” She said, “Just now outside the cave I wandered the flower shade, plucking orchids and gathering sweet herbs. Suddenly a monk with shaggy face and a thunder-god mouth came at once, suddenly bowing. He frightened me into a freeze of shock and shock. When I steadied myself and asked who he was, he said he had been sent by Princess Iron Fan to request the Bull Demon King. I spoke two words to him, and he cursed me instead, chasing me with a staff to beat me. Had I not run quickly, he would almost have beaten me to death. Is this not a disaster invited by you? You nearly had me killed!” The Bull King listened, then offered her gifts and stayed close to her, comforting her for a while. Only after a long while did her breathing settle. The demon king then grew stern and said, “Now that such a beautiful lady is in front of me, I cannot hide anything from her. Though Bajiao Cave is secluded, it is still serene and free. My mountain wife has practiced cultivation since childhood and is a female immortal of attainment; her household is strict, and no child under eighteen has ever been indoors there. How could any shaggy monk with a thunder-god mouth come as if invited? This must be some wandering monster from elsewhere, or someone borrowing a false name to arrive here and seek me. Let me go out and see.”

The Bull Demon King rose with a hard jerk, left the study, went into the great hall, got himself into his outer gear, and was done preparing. He took a mixed-iron cudgel, stepped outside, and called in a loud voice, "Who is making a commotion here in my place?" The Great Sage, standing nearby, saw him and noticed he was very different from five hundred years before. He saw:

On his head he wore a silver-bright, water-polished iron helm. His body was clad in plush, brocade and gold-threaded armor, and at his feet were brown-tipped leather boots curled at the toe. At his waist was tied a three-plaited silk lion-mane sash. His two eyes were bright as polished mirrors, his twin brows vivid like red rainbows. His mouth was like a basin of blood, his teeth set like copper plates. His roar shook the mountain spirits with fear; his manner was so majestic that evil spirits were thrown into panic. In the Four Seas he was known by a name of uproarious disorder, and in the west he was called the Bull Demon King, Great Strength. The Great Sage dressed properly and stepped forward, then bowed deeply in a full courtly bow and said, "Elder brother, do you still recognize your younger brother?" The Bull King returned the salute and said, "Are you Sun Wukong, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven?" The Great Sage answered, "Just so. Just so. It has been long since we last met. I just now came here to ask about a girl, and only then could I find my brother. The sight is far finer than I recall; congratulations!" The Bull King shouted, "Enough of clever tongue! I heard you made trouble in Heaven, where Buddha subdued you beneath the Five Element Mountain, and since then you have escaped that heavenly disaster and now guard Master Tang on the westward journey to seek the Buddha. How did you come to injure my young son Niu Shengying here at Mountain Ridge, Dried Pine Ravine, Hu Yun Cave? I have already been angry at you for this. Why do you come back asking for me again?" The Great Sage bowed and said, "Elder brother, do not wrongfully suspect me. At that time your young lord had seized our Master and wanted to eat his flesh. I could not get near him. Then Guanyin, in mercy, wished to save our Master and urged him to return to the true path. Now he has become Shanci Child of Good Fortune, higher than your eldest brother in rank, with easy passage into the Hall of Pure Bliss and the gift of free, endless life. Why should he be faulted?" The Bull King snapped, "You slippery-mouthed monkey! You talked about affection for an injured son when it suited you; now you deceive me and strike at my cherished concubine. Why did you come up to my gate?" The Great Sage laughed: "I sought the long-suffering elder brother but did not find him, so I paid my respects to that lady and asked after the matter. She scolded me several times, and my younger brother, rash and ignorant, startled her. I beg your leniency, my elder brother, be lenient." The Bull King said, "If that is all you say, I still see the old feelings between us and let you go."

The Great Sage said, "I am deeply grateful for your leniency; my thanks are beyond measure. Still, there is one matter for which I humbly beg your aid. May you please give help in abundance." The Bull King growled, "This monkey, so ignorant, not knowing how to show proper posture, you are spared for now yet still linger to trouble me? What is this 'aid in abundance' you ask?" The Great Sage said, "I will not conceal anything, elder brother. Because I am escorting Tripitaka westward, we are blocked by the Flaming Mountain and cannot move forward. From the locals I learned that your dear wife, Lady Luocha, possesses a banana fan; I wished to borrow it for use. Only yesterday I came to the old residence to pay respects to Sister-in-law. She firmly refused to lend it. So I now come to you, asking that from your broad heart, heaven and earth-like, you and I go together to my sister-in-law and, by urgent need, she will lend us it to wave away the flames so Tripitaka may cross the mountain safely, and all will be made complete." The Bull King heard this and his heart flared. He bared his iron teeth and shouted, "You claim you are not impolite, yet all this stems from a pretext to borrow the fan. You first cheated my mountain wife; she refused from jealousy to lend; therefore you came to seek me, and now you also drive away my concubine. It is said: 'A friend's wife must not be betrayed; a friend's concubine must not be harmed.' You harmed mine and robbed my wife of hers. What boldness is this? Go on up and take one staff to me." The Great Sage replied, "If elder brother wishes to strike, younger brother does not fear it. But for now, this is truly my sincere plea only for the Treasure-Barely-Used-Staff to be borrowed." The Bull King said, "If in three exchanges you can meet my strength, I will order my mountain wife to lend it. If you do not hold up, I will kill you and clear my grievance." The Great Sage said, "What brother says is right. I have become lazy and negligent over time, and have not met with my elder brother; I do not know how our martial arts compare with the old days. My elder-brother comrades, let us test our staves once. Then this is a splendid bout:

The Golden-Hooped Staff and the mixed-iron cudgel changed faces and fought without counting each other as friends. One said, "I truly grieve that this monkey harmed my child." The other said, "Your son has attained the Way; set anger aside." One said, "How dare you, in your ignorance, tread upon my gate?" The other said, "I came on purpose to ask after a matter." One demanded the fan to save Tripitaka, one refused the banana fan out of stingy meanness. As they spoke, old ties of friendship were lost; the whole household, bereft of righteousness, rose in wrath. The Bull King’s cudgel rose like a roaring river-dragon; the Great Sage’s staff answered and made demons and ghosts scatter. At first they fought on the mountain slope; later they rode together upon auspicious clouds. In midair they showed divine arts, wondrously deploying in five-colored radiance. Two staves sounded together and shook the gate of heaven; yet winner and loser were not yet in sight. The Great Sage and the Bull King fought for a hundred and ten exchanges with no decisively unequal result. Exactly when they were still hard to separate, someone called from above on the mountain peak: "Bull King, this servant bows to our lord many times. Grant him a swift departure and a place to sit in peace." Hearing this, the Bull King brought his mixed-iron cudgel down to brace against the Golden-Hooped Staff and said, "Monkey, stay still. I must go attend a friend who summoned me." He then placed the staff under control, sent down the cloud and went straight inside the cave, saying to the Jade-Faced Princess, "Beauty, that thunder-mouthed man is Sun Wukong the Monkey. I drove him off with one beating; he will not dare come again. You need not be troubled. I am off to a friend’s place to drink." He then removed his armor, put on a dark blue sheared-felt jacket, and stepped out. He mounted the Pishui Golden-Eyed Beast, told the attendants to watch the gate, and, through half-cloud and half-mist, went off directly toward the northwest.

The Great Sage watched from the high peak and thought inwardly, "This old bull has made some other friendship before and is now gone to visit there. I will follow after him." The Excellent Walker flicked his body once; it shimmered like a blast of clean wind, and he kept pace with him. Not long after, they came to a mountain where the Bull King had vanished entirely. Gathering back his true form, the Great Sage entered and searched the mountain. In that mountain there was a deep pool of clear water and on its bank a stone stele with six great characters: 乱石山碧波潭. The Great Sage thought to himself, "The old bull has definitely descended into the water. The spirit beneath the water, if it is not a jiaozhi, must be dragon spirit, fish spirit, or turtle, terrapin, or caiman spirit. I should go down into the water and look as well."

The Great Sage fingered the secret grip and spoke an incantation, then changed his shape. He became a crab, medium-sized, weighing about thirty-six catties, and in a bound leapt into the water, sinking straight to the bottom of the pool. He suddenly saw a clear, translucent, jewel-bright screenlike pavilion, under which the Pishui Golden-Eyed Beast was tethered. Once he entered the pavilion he found that there was no water within. He climbed in and looked closely; only sounds of music came from its inner halls. He saw:

The vermilion palace halls and shelllike towers seemed no different from this world. Golden roof-tiles, white-jade door pivots. Tortoise-shell armor screens stood open; corridors were edged with coral and pearl inlay. Auspicious clouds and good omens glowed upon the lotus dais, receiving the three radiances above and spreading into the avenues below. Not heaven’s court, not the Sea Treasury; truly this place rivaled Penghu itself. In the high hall a feast was laid, with lords and officials both great and small, crowned and jeweled. The jade maidens hurried to bear ivory dishes, and fairy maidens were called to tune the airs. Great whales called out, giant crabs danced, tortoises blew bamboo reeds, toads beat drums, and black-beaked jewel lights shone over cups and platters. Inscriptions in bird-seal script lined the green balustrades; shrimp-whisker curtains hung the halls. Music of the eight tones sounded in succession, blending heavenly melodies, and the scales and tones resounded clear through the skyward void. Blue-headed fish girls plucked the jade zithers; red-eyed horse youths handled jade flutes. An old gruel-spirited lady offered scented venison jerky, and a dragon maiden set a golden phoenix-taper at her hair. They ate delicacies of eight treasures from the heavenly kitchens, and drank fermented pearl wine from the Purple Court. There, seated above, was the Bull Demon King. On his left and right were three or four jiaozing spirits. In front sat an old dragon spirit, and at the sides sat dragon sons, dragon grandchildren, dragon mothers, and dragon daughters.

At that moment, when cups and goblets were crossed in bustle, the Great Sage kept walking forward and was seen; the old dragon noticed at once and ordered, "Seize that wild crab." Dragon son and dragon grandson came up together and caught the Great Sage. The Great Sage suddenly spoke in human speech: "Spare my life, spare my life." The old dragon said, "What wild crab are you, and how dare you ride to the great hall, trampling where honored guests sit, and run wild in defiance? Quickly present yourself, or die for your offense." The Great Sage feigned foolishness and told the assembly:

I was born in a lake and live by it, making my lair beside the cliff. After long time had passed my body grew supple, so my official role was to wander as a rough, free-roving petty officer. My feet drag in grass and mud, I sink and drag up ditches; I have never learned proper manners. I did not understand the law and dare not challenge royal authority; please let your kindness grant mercy for my sin. The assembled spirits, hearing this, all knelt and told the old dragon, "This crab-officer is newly entered the jade hall and knows not the court’s etiquette. Please, Exalted One, let him go." The old dragon acknowledged the thanks. All the spirits then said, "Release that fellow, but keep watch outside." The Great Sage answered once and fled outward, going straight to the pavilion’s base. In his heart he thought, "The Bull King is here in revelry and will not soon have this finished. Even if it were finished, he still would not lend the fan. Better then: steal his Golden-Eyed Beast, turn it into the Bull Demon King, deceive that demoness Luocha with tricks, and win her fan to send Master Tripitaka over the mountain."

The Great Sage at once resumed his true form, untied the curb-rope of the Golden-Eyed Beast, pounced once, vaulted onto its carved saddle, and rode straight out from under the water. When he reached the far side of the lake, he shifted into the shape of Niu Mo Wang. Riding the beast and leaping among the clouds, he arrived in no time at the mouth of the Banana Cave on Cuilyun Mountain. He called out, “Open the door.” Two maidens inside heard the voice and opened it. Seeing the face of Niu Mo Wang, they rushed in to report: “Granny, Grandfather has come home.” When Ruo Sha heard them, she quickly set her cloud-like hair, hurried forward with a lotus step, and came out to receive him. Sun Wukong dismounted from the carved saddle, led in the Golden-Eyed Beast, and with bold guile deceived the two maidens. The demoness did not recognize him by appearance, so she took his hand and entered in, while her maidens laid out seats for tea. The whole household, seeing him as their lord, behaved with complete deference.

After a while they talked about warmth and comfort. “My Lady has missed you for long,” said the Bull King. Ruo Sha replied, “Great King, ten thousand blessings.” She added, “You have been so fortunate in your new marriage that you abandoned this slave-girl; what wind has blown you here today?” Sun Wukong laughed: “I did not abandon you. It is only that, after receiving the summons of the Jade-Faced Princess, my household burdens have been heavy and I have had many friends to attend to, so I have been delayed outside. I even managed another household.” He went on, “I lately heard that that fellow Wukong, while protecting Tripitaka, has nearly reached the boundary of Flaming Mountain. He may come asking you for the fan. I still resent the injury to my child that he caused and, if he comes, send word at once. I will catch him and cut him into ten thousand pieces to wash away the hatred between husband and wife.” Hearing him, Ruo Sha wept and said, “Great King, the saying goes: ‘A man without a wife lacks household authority; a woman without a husband has no master of her own body.’ My life was nearly lost to this monkey.” Sun Wukong, playing angry, barked, “When did that raving monkey leave?” “Not yet,” she said. “Yesterday he came here to borrow the fan. Because he had harmed my child, I girded myself, drew the precious sword, and went out to strike that monkey. He bore the pain and called me ‘sister-in-law,’ saying your Majesty had sworn brotherhood with him.” Sun Wukong said, “Five hundred years ago he and I became seven sworn brothers.” Ruo Sha replied, “Even when I scolded him he dared not answer back, and I dared not cut him down. Later I swept this fan at him. I do not know by what wind-settling art he got hold of it, but this morning he was calling outside again. I used it again and he did not move an inch. I rushed out with my sword to strike him, but then he would not let me. Fearing the weight of his cudgel, I ran into the cave and locked the door fast. I know not from where he came, but he somehow got inside my belly and nearly took my life. So I called him ‘uncle’ a few times and gave him the fan.”

Sun Wukong feigned striking his chest in regret: “Alas, alas—Lady, you are wrong. How could you hand this precious thing to that monkey? It maddens me.” Ruo Sha laughed: “Great King, calm your temper. What he has is a fake fan; I have merely deceived him.” Sun Wukong asked, “Where is the real fan kept?” She said, “Do not worry; it is in my keeping.” She told the maidservants to prepare wine and celebrate. Then she lifted a cup and offered it, saying, “Great King, though your marriage is newly begun, do not forget your wedded vow; take a cup of water from this village.” Sun Wukong could not decline. He smiled and said, “Lady, drink first. Because I have gone afar to manage outer affairs and have long been separated from you, you watched over the household day and night; this is my token of gratitude.” Ruo Sha refilled the cup and passed it to him: “As the old saying goes, ‘A wife is harmony.’ You are the very father that nourishes the body—what is there to thank for?” The two exchanged modest words, and only then sat to circulate the wine. Sun Wukong, not daring to eat meat, ate only a few fruits and spoke lightly with her.

The wine had gone several rounds when Ruo Sha, half-intoxicated, felt a slight stirring of desire. She drew near Sun Wukong, touching and pressing, hand in hand and coy speech in soft tones, shoulders against his, whispering close. One cup from him and one from her, then fruit between them. Sun Wukong feigned fondness, smiling and playing along, and she and he at last leaned and nestled together. Truly it was:

Cast a bait-hook of verse and sweep the broom of sorrow; with this wine, no trouble remains undone. A man keeps his resolve and opens his heart; a woman forgets herself and breaks into smiling ease. Her face turns red like a peach in bloom. Her body sways like tender willow. Word upon word she babbles, all chatter and sweetness. Her fingers twist and pinch with practiced coquetry. At times I saw her hair flash like wind-cut clouds, and then her slim hands arcing like needles. Again and again her feet lifted and crossed, repeatedly she shook out her sleeves. Her powdered neck sank low by itself, her wild waist slowly began to twist. She never let go of words of amorous accord, and her tender chest was half exposed, the golden clasps loose. Drunk, she truly swayed like a collapsing jade peak, and with half-lidded eyes and swishing play, made him look a fool. When Sun Wukong saw her so thoroughly drunk, he inwardly stayed alert and taunted her lightly: “Lady, where have you kept the real fan? Early or late, it is wise to be careful, for Sun Wukong is full of transformations and may trick you again.” Ruo Sha grinned, and from her mouth she brought out nothing but something the size of an apricot leaf, handing it to him: “Is this not the treasure?” He took it in his hand, yet still did not trust it, thinking to himself, “How could something so small fan out fire across eight hundred li? It may well be fake.” Ruo Sha saw him staring at it and lost herself, stepping forward and touching his painted face with hers. “Darling, put away your doubts, keep drinking; what are you thinking about so deeply?” She asked. Sun Wukong took advantage and asked, “How can something so tiny extinguish a fire of eight thousand? eight? Wait—eight hundred li?” Ruo Sha, drunk and without reserve, spoke out the method: “Great King, it has been two full years since you left. You have been consumed day and night with joy, and after the Jade-Faced Princess damaged your spirit, you have forgotten the affairs of your own home. Merely pinch the seventh red strand on the handle with your left index finger, chant one breath: ‘𠲛噓啊吸嘻吹呼,’ and it will stretch to one zhang and two chi. This treasure changes without limit; even eighty-thousand li of flames can be dispersed by a single swing.”

When Sun Wukong heard her, he committed each word firmly to memory. He then took the fan into his mouth, dabbed his face, and showed his true appearance. In a loud voice he cried, “Ruo Sha woman, look—am I not your true husband? You wrapped me in so many indecent farces. Is there no shame at all?” When the woman saw it was Sun Wukong, she panicked, overturned table and chairs, and sank into the dust, utterly ashamed, crying only, “It has almost killed me in rage! It has almost killed me in rage!”

Without caring whether she lived or died, Sun Wukong tore free and strode out straight from the Banana Cave. It was true of him: though he had no intent to covet beauty, he turned back with a triumphant smile. He leapt upward, stepped on auspicious clouds, and jumped onto a high mountain, brought the fan out, and demonstrated the method. He pinched the seventh red thread near the top of the handle with his left index finger, spoke one breath—“𠲛噓啊吸嘻吹呼”—and indeed it lengthened to one zhang and two chi. He took it in his hand, looked carefully once more and again, and found it different from the earlier fake one. Golden radiance shimmered and auspicious vapors swirled; above it were thirty-six red strands, woven in and out, linked through and through. In truth, he had obtained only a long-form technique, not the little-word incantation; he could only control its length. With no alternative, he lifted it to his shoulder and returned along the old path.

The tale says that Niu Mo Wang, in Blue-Wave Pond with the assembled spirits, had just broken up the banquet and come out, only to find the Golden-Eyed Beast that could split water gone. The Old Dragon King gathered the spirits and asked, “Who has stolen the Bull King’s Golden-Eyed Beast?” The spirits knelt: “No one dared steal it. We were all present before the banquet, presenting wine, lifting dishes, singing, and making music; no one was there in front.” The Old Dragon said, “Jia Le’er surely would not dare. Could any mortal have entered?” Dragon Son and Dragon Grandson said, “Just as we were taking our seats, a crab spirit came here—that was the one.” Hearing this, the Bull King suddenly realized: “Enough said. In the morning my worthy friend sent for me and said a monk named Sun Wukong was escorting Tripitaka and had trouble at Flaming Mountain, and had asked me to borrow a Banana Fan. I did not lend it. He and I gambled and grappled, and no winner was decided. But I fled him and came directly to the feast. That monkey is clever in a thousand devices, full of a hundred stratagems. It must be he who transformed into the crab spirit and came here to probe for news, stole my beast, and then went to the mountain wife and tricked her out of this one Banana Fan.” The spirits, hearing this, were one by one terrified and asked, “Could this be Sun Wukong, the one who caused havoc in Heaven?” Niu Mo Wang said, “It is exactly him. If among you there is any place on the road to the West where things go wrong, make sure to avoid him.” The Old Dragon said, “Given all this, what of the Great King’s fine mount?” Niu Mo Wang laughed, “No worry, no worry. Each of you disperse; let me catch him.”

Then they parted the waterway, leapt up from the bottom of the pool, rode on yellow clouds, and went straight to the Banana-Leaf Cave on Green-Cloud Mountain. At once they heard the Rakshasa lady trampling in, beating her chest, calling out in loud cries. Pushing open the door, there again stood the Golden-Eyed Beast that tames water, tied up below. The Ox King shouted, "Lady, where has Sun Wukong gone?" The maidens, seeing the Bull Demon, knelt together and said, "Has father come?" The Rakshasa woman seized the Ox King, knelt and banged her head, and shouted in abuse, "Damn old heaven! How could you be so careless, to let that macaque steal the Golden-Eyed Beast, take your form, and come here to deceive me?" The Ox King, gritted teeth, said, "Where has that monkey gone?" The Rakshasa kept beating her breast as she cursed, "That wretched monkey made off with my treasure, then showed his true form and left. I am furious to the death!" The Ox King said, "Lady, take care and do not be anxious. Let me catch up with the monkey, recover the treasure, skin him, pulverize his bones, and set out his heart and liver so you may vent your rage." He said, "Bring out a weapon." One maid said, "Your father's weapons are not here." The Ox King said, "Then bring your grandmother's weapons." The attendant maid brought out two jade swords with green blades. The king took off the raven-blue velvet banquet robe, tied up the close-fitting inner garments, drew a sword in each hand, and walked out of the Banana-Leaf Cave, heading straight through to Flaming Mountain in pursuit. It was exactly then:

The ungrateful rogue deceived the lovesick woman; the fiery-tempered demon comes near the wooden-fork man.

In the end, it is not yet known whether this departure will bring luck or ruin. So let us listen as it is untangled in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 60: Ox Demon King ends his war and goes to the imperial banquet; Wukong adjusts the Banana-Fiber Fan twice.
