This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Now the King of Jisae and his high and low ministers saw Great Sage Sun Wukong and Zhu Bajie rise through clouds and mist, carrying the two little demons and flying away in a flash. One after another they faced heaven and bowed, saying, 'The rumors were no idle talk. Only today have we truly known that such immortals of living Buddha nature exist.' When he saw they had vanished from sight, he bowed and thanked Tripitaka and Sha Wujing: 'I am but a mortal flesh-body; I only knew my accomplished disciple had enough strength to seize demon brigands, never imagining he was one of the sky-riding immortals.' Tripitaka said, 'This poor monk has no power. All along on this road, it has been all due to these three junior disciples.' Sha Wujing said, 'I will not hide it from Your Majesty. My elder senior brother, Sun Wukong, is the Great Sage, Equal to Heaven. He once raised great havoc in Heaven, and with the Golden-Hooped Staff not one of ten thousand heavenly soldiers could face him. He frightened even Taishang Laojun, and the Jade Emperor was aghast. My second senior brother, the Marshal Tianpeng, is straightforward and upright; he once commanded eighty thousand water soldiers in the heavenly river. As for me, I am a disciple without power, formerly the Curtain-Raiser General after taking vows. My ignorant brethren are not able in other arts, though in catching demons and binding monsters, taking thieves, seizing criminals, subduing tigers, calling down dragons, kicking heaven and stirring wells, and even churning sea and turning rivers, we know a little. Matters such as riding clouds and driving mist, calling rain and summoning wind, and shifting stars and moving mountains and chasing the moon are but trivial extras—hardly worth speaking of.' Hearing this, the king’s respect only deepened. He invited Tripitaka to sit and called him repeatedly 'Old Buddha,' while he addressed Sha Wujing and the others as 'Bodhisattva.' The whole court of civil and military officials rejoiced, and the entire populace of the kingdom paid their obeisance; this need not be set down.

Sun Wukong and Zhu Bajie whipped up a furious wind and brought the two little demons to the Bi-Po Pond of Luanshi Mountain, fixing their cloud foothold in place. He breathed one breath of immortal qi into the Golden-Hooped Staff and cried, 'Transform!' and it became a jiedao blade. He cut off one black-fish demon’s ear and the eel-spirit’s lower lip, then cast them into the water, and shouted, 'Go at once to the Dragon King of Wansheng and report this: Great Sage Sun Wukong, Equal to Heaven, is here. He must at once send down the original treasure from the Jinguang Monastery tower of Jisae Kingdom, and he will spare the lives of his entire household. If he even utters one word of denial, I will churn this pond clean and have both young and old of his family put to the sword.'

The two little demons, having been spared, dragged themselves in pain to escape and sank back into the water with their bonds. The startled tortoises, turtles, crabs, shrimps, and fish spirits gathered around and asked, 'Why are you both dragging ropes and shackles?' One covered its ear, wagged its head and tail; one pinched at its mouth, stamped its feet, and pummeled its chest. They all shouted and hurried straight to the Dragon King’s palace: 'Report, Great King—the calamity has come.' The Dragon King of the Myriad Saints was drinking with his Nine-Headed Son-in-Law when, seeing the two, he at once set down his cup and asked what the trouble was. The two said, 'Last night, on patrol, we were caught by Tripitaka and Sun Wukong while they were sweeping the tower; we were bound with iron chains. This morning, after appearing before the King, we were seized again by that same Sun and Zhu Bajie. One cut my ear, the other cut my lip, and we were thrown into the water, and told to report here and demand that treasure from the top of the tower.' They then described the whole affair in full. When the old Dragon heard it was Sun Wukong, Great Sage, Equal to Heaven, he was so terrified that his soul seemed not to cling and his spirit scattered to the Nine Heavens. Trembling, he told his son-in-law, 'Son-in-law, with another person there is room to calculate; but if this is he, he is not to be taken lightly.' The son-in-law laughed: 'Great Lord, be at ease. Your humble son-in-law learned some martial arts from childhood. In all the four seas I have met a few heroes. Why should I fear him? Let me go out and engage him in three rounds; I will surely make that brute bow his head and submit, not daring to look up.'

A fierce demon indeed: he leaped up in haste, donned his accoutrements, and took up a weapon called a Moon-Crescent Spade. He stepped out of the palace, split the waterway, and from the surface called, 'Who is this Great Sage, Equal to Heaven? Come up and give your life.' Wukong and Zhu Bajie stood on the bank, watching how the demon was dressed:

He wore a tarnished silver helmet whose brightness mocked white snow; over it was a headgear-and-armor coat gleaming like autumn frost. On top he wore a brocade campaign robe, truly like rainbow clouds enclosing jade. At his waist was tied a rhinoceros-patterned sash, like a flower python winding with gold. He held the Moon-Crescent Spade, fast as light from rosy flying clouds. Pigskin boots on his feet made the water part into ripples. Seen from afar it was one head and one face, yet when seen closely there were all sides filled with men: eyes in front, eyes behind, all eight directions seen through. On the left a mouth, on the right a mouth, nine mouths speaking all at once. One roar shook the high sky, like a crane cry crossing nine heavens. He saw no answer and called again, 'Who is that Great Sage, Equal to Heaven?' Wukong tapped his golden band once, smoothed the iron staff, and said, 'It is old Sun himself.' The demon said, 'Where is your home? From where do you come? How did you get to Jisae and, while that king stands guard at the tower, dare to seize my superior and dare to act violently, then come to my treasure mountain to seek battle?' Wukong cursed him: 'You wretch, you truly do not know your Master Sun. Come forward and hear me: Old Sun lives on Flower-Fruit Mountain, in Water-Curtain Cave in the Great Sea. Since childhood I cultivated to become a body that cannot be ruined. The Jade Emperor appointed me Great Sage, Equal to Heaven. It was only because I once threw the heavens into turmoil in the Douniu Palace that the gods above could not win over me. Then the Buddha was called to show the sublime height, whose boundless wisdom has immeasurable use. In that contest of wondrous tricks my palm was made into a mountain and pressed heavy upon me. Up to this day, five hundred years have passed; only through Guanyin's persuasion have I escaped to keep my life. Tripitaka of Great Tang goes westward, far to Ling Mountain, to bow and seek the Buddha's sutras. I was rescued to free my own body and protect him, to refine demons and cleanse monsters through cultivation. On the road we met the westward Jisae city and your line has harmed three generations of monks. Out of compassion we asked of the old truth, but the top of your tower had no holy light. My master swept the tower and investigated clearly; it was the third watch, and heaven-silence had fallen. We caught the demon spirit and took the facts. He says you stole the treasure. The charges are assembled and named as theft involving the Dragon King; the Princess too calls you among the myriad gods. Blood rain soaked the light atop the tower as he stole the treasure and made use of it. The indictment before the Hall Gate has no falsehood. By your command I have hastened to this place. So we have come here seeking battle—there is no need to ask again the name of Master Sun. Quickly return the treasure and spare your old and young family all together. If you dare in ignorance to force a contest and boast of strength, I will let the waters run dry and make your mountains collapse and your lands stumble.' After hearing this, the son-in-law smiled slightly and said, 'So you are the monk on a scriptural quest; this is no business of your weaving and administration. I stole his treasure, and you pursue Buddhist scripture. What concern is yours, that you come here to brawl?' Wukong said, 'This robberous demon is most unreasonable. Though I have not received the king's favors, and do not live on his water and grain, and therefore should not labor for him, yet he stole his treasure, defiled his pagoda, and year after year has harassed the Jinguang Monastery monks. He is one of my household of the Dharma; how could I not exert myself to set this injustice right?' The son-in-law replied, 'If you insist, then you are seeking a duel. It is said, "One who is not good at martial art should not fight." Only, I fear that at the first exchange I may not spare you, and in a moment your life might be harmed, bringing your western quest astray.'

Sun Wukong raged and snapped, 「You ragged villain! How dare you show such strength and roar so loud? Come up here and take a proper strike of the elder’s staff!」 The Nine-Headed Groom did not flinch. He blocked with the crescent-moon shovel against the iron staff. There, on the broken-stone heights, the battle was truly murderous:

A demon stole the treasure tower’s light, and Wukong seized the fiend and reported to the king. The little monster fled to the water, while the old dragon and the others hastily planned. The Nine-Headed Groom strode out, brandishing power in full display. Great Sage Equal to Heaven flew into a rage; the Golden-Hooped Staff rose hard as tenfold steel. The monster had nine heads and eighteen eyes, pouring forth radiant glows in every direction; this Great Sage had a pair of iron arms with thousand-catty strength, his radiance and omens fluttering everywhere. The shovel shone like the first moon of spring; the staff flashed like frost racing ten thousand li. He said, 「You have no right to rest while the grievance remains unpaid.」 I said, 「You meant to steal the treasure with no better intent. You reckless rabble, boast less and return the treasure if you want peace and safety.」 The staff and shovel met in contest, each vying for the upper hand, with no winner or loser yet in the practice arena. They closed and parted, over and over. They fought through more than thirty rounds with no clear edge. Pigsy stood before the rocks. When he saw the two near their most exact match, he raised the hooked spade and rushed in from the demon’s rear. It turned out the monster, with nine heads, had eyes revolving everywhere and saw all plainly. As Pigsy came from behind, he even caught the spade with the hooked shovel, the shovel head pressing against the iron bar. After another five or seven rounds, unable to hold him from both front and back at once, the demon suddenly rolled, sprang upward into the air, and leapt high, showing its true form: it was a creature of nine heads and insectlike body. Its shape was so cruelly terrible it was enough to make one think of death. It was like this: Feathers and down were spread like rich brocade; its body was knotted and packed like a wad of fluff. Its round and square form measured roughly two zhang; in length and breadth it resembled a turtle and giant salamander. Two pointed forefeet, sharp as hooks; nine heads clustered together in one frame. It spread its wings and flew with uncommon skill, as if Great Wild Peng’s strength were nothing to it. Its cry, when raised, echoed far to the ends of heaven and earth, soaring higher than the cry of an immortal crane. Its many eyes flashed with searing gold light, its spirit proud and unlike any ordinary bird. Pigsy, seeing it, said in alarm, 「Brother, though I am human, I have never seen such a beast so wicked. Of what cruel blood was this creature born?」 Wukong said, 「It is truly rare, truly rare. I will chase and strike him.」 The Great Sage then whipped himself high on a cloud of auspicious air, leapt into the sky, and with the iron staff struck him down on the head. The demon flashed open his true body, spread its wings and flew on a slant; with a hiss it spun, darted to the front of the mountain, and from its half-thigh another head burst forth, mouth opening like a basin of blood. It bit Pigsy by the mane, dragging and hauling him half by half, and carried him off into the Blue-Wave Pond. When they reached the Dragon Palace exterior, it changed back to the earlier form, threw Pigsy to the ground and called, 「Where are my subordinates?」 Inside were fish spirits of mackerel, flounder, carp, and eel, and strange creatures of tortoise, turtle, and great softshell. They crowded together and shouted in one voice, 「Here.」 The Nine-Headed Groom said, 「Bind this monk there and send it to my roving underlings; let them avenge this wrong." The spirits pushed and shouted as they hauled Pigsy up. The Old Dragon King, delighted, came forth: 「Brave son-in-law, you have done well. How did you catch him」? The Nine-Headed Groom explained from start to end. The old dragon then ordered wine to be served in celebration; no further account is needed.

Sun Wukong saw the demon had taken Pigsy and in his heart was afraid: 「This brute is formidable indeed. I meant to go back and report to the Master; I feared the king would laugh at me. If I open my mouth to curse and fight, I am alone, and besides I am not used to affairs on water. I will transform and go in first, and watch how that demon handles the brute. If there is a chance, I will slip him out as well and make use of it.」 The Great Sage twisted the formula and transformed, becoming a crab. He plunged into the water and made directly for the gate pavilion. This route, in fact, was one he had already learned from an earlier raid on Bull Demon King’s stolen golden-eyed beast. All the way to beneath the palace gate, he crawled across sideways. Once he came to the foot of the palace towers, he saw the Old Dragon King and the Nine-Headed Groom’s household rejoicing and drinking. Wukong did not dare to approach too closely. He crossed beneath the east corridor and saw several shrimp and crab spirits chattering in a clamor. After listening for a while, he imitated their speech and tone and asked, 「How is the long-snouted monk your groom brought in now? Is he dead yet」? The spirits answered, 「Not yet. Is he not tied and groaning beneath the west corridor」?

Wukong heard this and quietly crawled along to the west corridor. Indeed Pigsy was tied to a pillar, still groaning. Wukong came up close and whispered, 「Pigsy, do you recognize me?」 Pigsy heard the voice and knew it was Wukong. He said, 「Brother, what has happened? I have been seized by this brute as well.」 Wukong looked around and saw no one nearby, then snapped the gag and the ropes apart and told him to go. Once freed, Pigsy said, 「Brother, my weapon has been taken by him—what shall I do」? Wukong said, 「Do you know where he took it」? Pigsy said, 「The monster carried it into the palace just now.」 Wukong said, 「You go first and wait beneath the gate pavilion.」 Pigsy slipped away and escaped. Wukong returned and crawled back up through the palace. On the left below was a dense brilliance—this was Pigsy’s hooked spade emitting light. Using an invisibility method, he slipped the spade out and went down to the gate platform: 「Pigsy, take your weapon.」 Once Pigsy had it back, he said, 「Brother, you go first. Let Old Pig charge into the palace. If he wins, he may seize their whole household. If he fails and is beaten back, come out to this shore and rescue him.」 Wukong rejoiced deeply and merely instructed him to be careful.

Pigsy buttoned his rough black robe and wrapped both hands around the spade. With one shout, he rushed in. The whole water clansfolk, great and small, rushed in confusion like floodwater. They ran up to the palace crying, 「Disaster! The long-nosed monk has broken his bonds and returned to fight!」 The Old Dragon and the Nine-Headed Groom and their whole household were taken by surprise, jumping and hiding in every direction. Pigsy did not care whether he lived or died. He stormed into the palace, smashing through doors and folding screens with the spade, toppling tables and chairs, and breaking all the wine vessels and household fittings to pieces. For witness, there is a verse:

The mother of wood was seized by a water monster; the heart-monkey could not let the bitterness go, kept searching. By hidden stratagem the lock was forced open, and divine fury flared in righteous wrath. The Nine-Headed Groom hurried to shelter the princess, while the Dragon King trembled and lost his voice. The vermilion gates and windows of the watery palace were torn, and dragon sons and dragon grandsons all lost their spirits. In that bout Pigsy shattered the tortoiseshell screen into powder and hurled it down; he battered a coral tree so badly it withered.

The Nine-Headed Caterpillar hid the princess inside and hurried for the crescent-moon shovel, running to the front hall, and shouted, 「You slinging boorish swine! How dare you frighten our clan by your deceitful heart?」 Pigsy spat back, 「You scoundrel, how dare you capture me? This fight has nothing to do with your own quarrel. It is you who called me to your house to brawl. Return my treasure and I will go back to the king to settle it. If not, not one of you will be spared.」 But that monster gave no room. It ground its teeth and traded blows with Pigsy. The Old Dragon finally steadied himself and led dragon sons and dragon grandsons, each armed with spear and knife, and they all came together to attack. Seeing that the situation did not suit him, Pigsy feinted with the spade once, withdrew his body and withdrew. The dragon then led his band in pursuit. In a moment they emerged from the water and rose in churning waves at the pond’s surface.

Sun Wukong remained on the lake bank waiting. Suddenly he saw them chasing Pigsy, leaving the water. He stepped half into the drifting cloud mist, drew the iron staff, and shouted, 「Do not run!」 At once he struck and split the old dragon’s head to ruin. To pity it, blood splashed across the pond, turning the water red, and bodies floated on the waves with broken scales drifting. The Dragon Prince with nine heads gathered up his corpse and withdrew back to the palace.

Wukong and Pigsy did not pursue, but returned up to shore and reported what had happened. Pigsy said, 「His edge has been blunted; when I went in with the spade, I beat him till he was like flowers falling into running water, with mind and spirit scattered. I was still grappling with that Nine-Headed Groom when the Old Dragon King drove in behind, and my stroke that killed him was due to you. Those fiends have gone back; they will surely hold mourning and hang out mourning robes. They will not dare come out. And now evening has come. What can be done?」 Wukong said, 「What does evening matter? Seize this chance and go back in and fight. You must bring out the treasure, then we can return to court.」 Pigsy was lazy in spirit and evasive, wavering and finding excuses. Wukong urged him, 「Brother, do not doubt. Come as before and draw them out again, then let me take them.」

The two were still conferring when suddenly fierce wind rolled and dark mist thickened. At once, from the east it swept swiftly southward. Wukong looked closely and saw what it was: Erlang Xiansheng, leading the six brothers of Mei Mountain, each with eagles and hounds, balancing foxes and rabbits, carrying roe deer, every one with a bent bow at his waist and a sharp blade in hand, bounding through wind and mist. Wukong said, 「Pigsy, those are my Seven-Sage brothers. Invite them in and have them assist our battle. If this succeeds, it will be a great opening.」 Pigsy said, 「If they are truly brothers, it is only proper to invite them.」 Wukong said, 「But among them is Big Brother Xiansheng Erlang, who once subdued me; it is not good to meet him directly. Go block the cloud front and call out:『Erlang Zhenjun, hold a little, Great Sage Equal to Heaven has come to make courtly obeisance』. If he hears that it is me, he will at once halt. Once he settles down, then I can meet him."

The fool bounded ahead on cloud-hooves, rushed up the mountain to block the path, and shouted in a hard voice: “True Lord, hold the carriage; the Great Sage Equal to Heaven wishes an audience.” Hearing this, the lord gave orders at once, stopped the six brothers, and after meeting with Pigsy asked, “Where is the Great Sage Equal to Heaven?” Pigsy answered, “He is below the mountain, calling out now.” Erlang said, “Brothers, go bring him at once.” The six were Kang, Zhang, Yao, Li, Guo, and Zhi. Each came out from camp and called, “Brother Sun Wukong, our elder brother summons you.” The Monkey came forward and bowed to the assembly, then climbed up together. Erlang welcomed him, took his hand, and said, “Great Sage, you have escaped the Great Peril, taken the monk vows, nearly completed your merit, and can soon mount the lotus seat. Congratulations, congratulations.” Sun Wukong replied, “I dare not. I have only just received your immeasurable kindness and have not yet repaid it even in this short time. Though I have escaped great danger and gone west to seek the Dharma, I know not how good my conduct yet is. By chance I met Ji-sai Kingdom on the road and responded to its plea to save the monks; I am here to capture demons and recover treasure. Seeing your procession, I have the boldness to ask that one of us stay to help. I do not even know from where you came or whether you would be inclined to show favor.” Erlang laughed. “I had nothing to do and, with my brothers, had returned after hunting. It is good that the Great Sage did not turn away this chance of reunion; it suits our old companionship. If ordered to suppress demons by force, how could I not obey? But I do not yet know what strange bandit is this.” The six said, “Elder brother, have you forgotten? This is Luanshi Mountain, and under it, at Bibo Pond, is the Dragon Palace of Wansheng.” Erlang was astonished. “If old Wansheng Dragon never causes disorder, how could he dare to steal the tower treasure?” Sun Wukong said, “He recently took in a match as bridegroom who was a nine-headed worm in spirit-form. The two of them committed banditry together, brought a blood-rain on Ji-sai Kingdom, and stole the Buddha-relic treasure from the top of Golden-light Temple’s pagoda. That king, not understanding the matter, tortured monks in torment. My master came in compassion and swept in at night; I seized two little fiends at the pagoda who had been sent by him to scout. This morning they were brought to court and confessed truly. Then the king asked my master to take them in submission, and my master ordered us to come here. In the first battle the nine-headed monster extended one head from its waist and swallowed Pigsy. I transformed and went under water to rescue him. Then in the real struggle, it was I who slew old Dragon; his fellows took away the body and went to hang mourning cloths. Zhu and I were just ready to press for another battle when your ceremonial retinue arrived; so this was only a light transgression.” Erlang said, “Now that old Dragon is already hurt, it is fitting to attack so that villain cannot find his way; why not wipe out his whole nest as well?” Pigsy said, “Even so, what of the lateness of day?” Erlang said, “As the strategists say: ‘A campaign need not wait for a season.’ Why fear that night is near?”

Kang, Yao, Guo, and Zhi said, “Elder brother, do not rush. That villain’s household is here; surely they have nowhere to flee. Brother Sun is also a worthy guest, and this pig-skinned one has returned to proper fruit. In our camp we have wine and dishes with us; tell the younger men to fetch firewood and set a spread here. One, we celebrate joyfully with the two of you; two, we should also exchange feelings. Let us keep this festivity this very night and, if it is late by morning, what is the delay in seeking battle?” Erlang was greatly delighted and said, “The worthy younger brother spoke very fittingly.” He then gave orders for arrangements. Sun Wukong said, “Your many kindnesses overwhelm me, I do not dare to refuse. But I am now a monk and everyone keeps vegetarian precepts; I fear mixed flesh and fruit will be inconvenient.” Erlang said, “There are fruits that are pure and the wine is also pure.” Beneath the starry moonlight, the brothers raised awnings, sat upon the ground, and lifted their cups to recall old days.

It was a lonely night that only grows longer, while delight grows shorter. Before anyone noticed, dawn had already begun whitening the east. After several cups, Zhu Bajie, half drunk and swaying, said, “Daybreak is near; let old Pig go down into the water to seek battle.” Erlang said, “Commander, pay close attention. So long as he is lured out, my brothers can seize him.” Pigsy laughed, “I know, I know.” See him now: he tightened his robe, wound his spade, used the art of splitting water, and leapt down, going straight beneath the gate tower. He shouted and burst into the hall. At that moment the dragon-son, wrapped in hempen rags, sat crying over the dragon corpse; the dragon-grandson and the groom were behind him arranging a coffin. Pigsy cursed forward; with one heavy blow from the spade’s head he clamped the dragon-son’s brain with it and with one strike punched nine holes into him. That frightened the dragon-mother and the rest into running about inside, crying, “The long-faced monk has struck down my son again!”

Hearing this, the groom drew a crescent-shovel and, with the dragon-grandson, came out to kill them. Pigsy raised his spade to meet him, fighting and retreating at once, then leapt out of the water. On this bank Sun Wukong and the seven brothers surged forward together, thrusting spears and sabers in confusion, chopping the dragon-grandson into chunks of flesh. The groom saw this and did not stop; he rolled in front of the mountain, then returned to his true form, spread his wings, and whirled up in flight. Erlang at once took a golden bow, fitted silver bolts, drew the bow to full, and shot upward. The fiend hurriedly folded its wings, darted to the edge to bite Erlang. Only halfway in its torso did a head come out, and that little dog leapt at it; with one bark-and-bite it tore the head down, blood-soaked, from its body. Wounded, the monster fled in pain and rushed directly to the North Sea. Pigsy moved to chase it, but the Great Sage restrained him: “Do not chase now. It is truly, ‘Do not pursue a driven-out brigand.’ His head is bitten by the little dog; he is certain to die, or at most survive poorly. Then let me change into his likeness; you split the water routes and drive me in, seeking the princess to trick and seize her treasure as well.” Erlang and the six brothers said, “Not chasing him is enough, but leaving this kind in the world will surely harm later generations.” To this day, the nine-headed worm has left a drop of blood, a lingering spawn.

Pigsy obeyed and divided the water channels. Sun Wukong changed into the monster’s form and went ahead; Pigsy gave loud cries and followed behind. Gradually he pursued up to the Dragon Palace, where Princess Wansheng called out, “Groom, why are you in such panic?” Sun Wukong said, “Piggy is winning; he drove me here. I can sense he cannot match me. Hide the treasures quickly.” The princess, unable at once to judge the truth, hurried and from a rear hall brought out a gilt box and handed it to Sun Wukong: “This is the Buddha treasure.” She brought out also a white-jade box and handed that to him as well: “This is the Nine-Leaf Lingzhi. Take these treasures and hide them. Wait until I have fought with Pig Bajie for two or three exchanges to hold him back. When your treasures are hidden, you come out and join the battle.” Sun Wukong tucked both boxes at his side, swiped his face, and resumed his own form: “Princess, am I the groom?” The princess panicked and tried to seize the boxes. Pigsy then ran up and struck her on the back with his spade, knocking her down.

There was also an old dragon-mother who withdrew to leave at once; Pigsy grabbed her and was about to strike down with the spade when Sun Wukong said, “Wait. Do not kill her. Leave one alive so we can report merit in court.” So they brought the dragon-mother up to the water’s surface.

Sun Wukong afterward carried the two boxes ashore and said to Erlang, “By your force, I obtained the treasures and swept away the demon-thieves.” Erlang answered, “First it is the king’s great good fortune under heaven; second, you have boundless divine arts, worthy one—what merit is there in me?” The brothers all said, “Since Brother Sun has already accomplished the task, we shall part here.” Sun Wukong, full of thanks, wished to stay to present himself before the king as well, but the lords refused and so led their men back to Guankou.

Sun Wukong carried the boxes, and Pigsy dragged the dragon-mother, in half cloud and half mist, and in a moment reached the capital. In truth, the monks released from Golden-light Temple were already waiting outside the city. As they came, still amid the drifting cloud and mist, the two knelt forward in reverence and were brought inside the city. The king and Tripitaka were discussing in the hall. A monk who had arrived first, emboldened by his courage, entered the palace gate and reported, “Long live the king, Sun Wukong and Pigsy have captured the demon and recovered the treasure and have come.” Hearing this, the king came down at once, and with Tripitaka and Sha Wujing he received them, praising their divine merit as immeasurable and ordered a feast of thanks. Tripitaka said, “There is no need to offer drink yet. Command your small disciples to retrieve the tower treasure first, then feast may proceed.” He also asked Sun Wukong, “You left the kingdom yesterday; how is it that you only arrive today?” Sun Wukong gave a full account of fighting the groom, striking down the Dragon King, meeting the True Lord, defeating the demon spirit, and using transformed treasure stratagems. Tripitaka, the king, and the civil and military ministers all rejoiced beyond measure.

The king then asked, “Can this dragon-mother speak human language?” Pigsy said, “She is the Dragon King’s wife, mother of many dragon sons and grandsons; does she not know human speech?” The king said, “Since she knows human speech, tell us quickly of all the thefts from beginning to end.” The dragon-mother said, “As for stealing the Buddha treasure, I knew nothing of it. My husband, the Dragon King, and that groom, the nine-headed worm, are the ones. They knew the light above your pagoda was a Buddha relic-casket. Three years ago, during a blood-rain, they stole it. You ask how the Lingzhi was stolen?” She was asked. “It was only my young daughter, Princess Wansheng; she secretly entered before the Lingshao Hall in Great Dipper Heaven and stole the Queen Mother of Heaven’s Nine-Leaf Lingzhi. That relic had been nourished by the herb’s immortal qi and does not decay for a thousand years while giving light for ten thousand ages. Wherever it is swept under ground or on a field, ten thousand rays of rosy light and a thousand auspicious streams appear. Now you have taken it back, and it has killed my husband, destroyed my sons, and taken my son-in-law and my daughter; spare my life.” Pigsy said, “I was not going to spare you.” Sun Wukong said, “There is no household without fault. I will spare you, but only on condition that you guard this pagoda forever.” The dragon-mother said, “Living a cursed life is worse than dying. Since you spare my life, command me as you will.” Sun Wukong called for an iron chain. The charioteer at once brought a length of chain and passed it through the dragon-mother’s pipa-bone. Then he ordered Sha Wujing, “Ask the king to come and see us as we settle matters at the pagoda.”

The king at once hastened to prepare his carriage, and then left court with Master Tripitaka, followed by many civil and military officials, and went to Jinguang Temple. The Monkey King ascended the pagoda, placed the relic in the center of the treasure vase atop the thirteenth storey, and bound the dragon girl to the central pillar of the tower. He intoned the true mantra, summoning the native Land God, the City God, and the temple guardians, and commanded them to send one meal of food for three days to feed this dragon girl; if there was even the slightest error, heads were to be struck off at once. All the spirits took note of this silently. The Monkey King then swept each of the thirteen levels with mugwort, placing the sweepings in the vase to warm and nurture the relic. In an instant it was mended, whole as in former days: myriad rays of rosy light, a thousand streams of auspicious air, visible in all eight directions, and all four realms looked on together. After he came down through the gate of the tower, the king said in gratitude, “Had it not been for the Buddha and the three Bodhisattvas arriving here, how could this matter have been understood?”

The Monkey King said, “Your Majesty, the phrase ‘Jinguang’ is not suitable, for it is not for long residence. Gold is a thing that flows; radiance is flashing qi. Since this humble monk has labored for you in this affair, I shall change this temple into Fulong Temple so it may endure forever.” The king immediately ordered the characters changed and hung up a new plaque reading, “Imperially Established Huguo Fulong Temple.” In one hall an imperial banquet was arranged; in another, painters were summoned to paint the four living figures in red pigments, and in Wufeng Tower the names were inscribed. The king arranged his carriage and saw Master Tripitaka and the disciples off, rewarding them with gold and jade. The disciples politely and firmly refused, accepting no gifts at all. This truly is:

Evils and monsters cut down bring all realms to stillness; the reliquary stupa returns its light and makes the earth shine.

In the end, no one yet knows what the path ahead holds. Listen now for the explanation in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 63: Two monks and their master trouble the Dragon Palace with a demon hunt; all holy ones exorcise evil and win the treasure.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

The king of Sai Country thanked Tripitaka and his four disciples for the grace of recovering the treasure and subduing the demons and for the blessing they had bestowed; of the gold and jade he offered, he did not accept a single grain. He nevertheless ordered the officer in charge to have, for each of the four, two sets of the robes they usually wore, two pairs of shoes and socks each, two silk girdles each, and to provision roasted dry rations. He also exchanged their travel passes, arrayed a full ceremonial caravan, and with both civil and military officers, the whole city’s householders, and the monks of Fulong Temple, sent the four followers out of the city with music and shouting. After about twenty li they first took leave of the king. The others escorted them another twenty li and then turned back. The Fulong Temple monks escorted them for five to six tens of li and did not return: some wished to go west with them; some wished to cultivate in order to serve as attendants. Seeing that no one agreed to go home, the Monkey King made a device of it, plucked thirty to forty hairs from his body, blew out a breath of immortal qi, and cried, “Transform!” so they all turned into mottled ferocious tigers, blocked the road ahead, roared, and bounded with delight. Only then did the monks grow fearful and dare not go forward. Great Sage then led Master Tripitaka, who had his horse spurred, and in short time got far ahead. The monks gave voice to loud weeping and cried, “Old lord of benevolence and duty! We are not fated for this; we will not be ferried across with you.”

The weeping of the monks need not be described first. Now the four disciples went up onto the main road, and only after they had retracted their hair-forms did they proceed straight west. The seasons had already begun to change; it was late winter into early spring, not warm nor cold, perfect for carefree travel. Suddenly they saw a long ridge, with a road on the top of it. Tripitaka reined in and examined it. On that ridge were thorny branch and fork, and kudzu twining around, and though there were traces of a path below, on both sides were only thorn and prickles. Tripitaka said, “Disciple, how can this road be passed?” Sun Wukong answered, “Why cannot it?” He added, “Disciple, the traces are below while the thorns are above. Unless snakes and worms crawled along the ground, it cannot be crossed; if you all walk, your waists cannot even straighten. How can I ride a horse this way?” Zhu Bajie said, “Do not worry. Let me use the pike-shovel hand. I can split the thorns apart; not only riding, but even lifting you in a sedan chair I can get you across.” Tripitaka replied, “Though you have strength, this is far and long. You do not know how long it runs; how can it spend so much spirit?” Sun Wukong said, “Need not discuss it. Let me look.” He leapt into the air and, watching from there, saw for a long while without limit. Truly it was:

Around earth and sky, the smoke lies still, rain clinging to it. On either side of the track soft moss tangles in confusion, all the distant hills spread green canopies. Thick and knotted the fresh-budding leaves, climbing and tugging as fragrance rises. Looking afar, one cannot see where it ends; near at hand it is like a dim green cloud. Dim and soft, lush and vast. Wind sounds drift far away, and the sun’s image shimmers in brilliance. Among it stand pines and cypresses, also bamboo; here and there pears, willows, and even more mulberry. Vines of kudzu wrap old trees, and climbing gourd and kudzu girdle drooping willows. Entwined in coils like a frame, linked together like a bed. In some places flowers bloom, as if embroidered brocade; at no cause the grasses send forth deep far perfume. Who among men is not met by thorns? Who has seen the thorny wilds stretch so far to the West?” After looking long enough, Sun Wukong pressed down his cloud head and said, “Master, this place is very far.” Tripitaka asked, “How far is it?” Sun Wukong said, “From one look it is boundless, seems more than a thousand li.” Tripitaka was greatly startled: “How is this to be passed?” Sha Wujing laughed, “Do not worry, Master. We know how to burn wilderness; set a fire and burn the thorns right through.” Zhu Bajie said, “Do not speak that. To burn wild growth, one must wait ten months or more, when the grasses wither and trees are dry. At present it is in full green growth. How can it be burned?” Sun Wukong said, “Even if it could be burned, it would still imperil people.” Tripitaka said, “At this rate how can we cross?” Zhu Bajie laughed, “If we are to cross, depend on me.”

"Good simpleton, twist the technique, recite a charm, bend your waist once, and cry, ‘Long!’—then the body will grow to twenty or so zhang in height. Shake the spiked rake once, call, ‘Transform!’, and it changes into a rake-handle thirty zhang long. With a long pull of the feet and both hands wielding the rake, he opened the thorns aside to both sides: ‘Master, come behind me.’ Seeing this, Tripitaka rejoiced at once and set his horse, following close behind. Sha Wujing carried the baggage. Sun Wukong too parted the thorns with his iron rod. That day he never stopped at all; they went one hundred and ten li. At the next twilight they saw an open place. On the road there was a stone stele with three large characters: “Jingji Ridge.” Beneath it were two lines in small script, fourteen characters: “Jingji thickets climb eight hundred li; from old times few men have passed by road.” On seeing it, Zhu Bajie laughed and said, “Let old Bajie add two lines: ‘From this day forth, Bajie can break it wide open, And straight to the Western lands the road will at last be level.’ Tripitaka gladly dismounted and said, “Disciple, you are tired as well. We shall stay here for the night and depart again when light comes.” Zhu Bajie said, “Master, do not stop. In this clear weather seize the moment while we are stirred with vigor and go through the night by opening the way."

The abbot could only comply and follow.

After another day and one night of unceasing progress, and still in the evening, they saw ahead a dense thicket and heard, in the wind, a tapping of bamboo and a rustling of pines. Again there was a stretch of open ground, and in its middle stood an ancient temple. Outside the gate there was pine and cypress, cold and deep green, and peach and plum contending in brilliant bloom. Tripitaka dismounted and looked with the three disciples. What they saw was:

A cold current at the clifffoot, the old temple nestled against it, and smoke of ruin locks the ruined mound. In the white-heron thicket the long years of age are hidden, and below green weeds beneath the altar the cycles of spring and autumn return. Bamboo stirs the jade pendants as though speaking; birds make lingering sounds like sorrowful complaint. No chickens or dogs, no traces of people; lone flowers and wild vines wind over the wall edge. Sun Wukong said, “This place is not auspicious but inauspicious; not fit for lingering.” Sha Wujing said, “Elder Brother, you are too suspicious. In such a place with no sign of folk nor any monstrous beast or demon-bird, what have we to fear?” Before he could finish, an eerie wind rose. From behind the temple gate came an old man with a horned kerchief, pale robe, staff in hand, and straw sandals. Behind him followed a ghost-errand of green face, fang-toothed, red-bearded, naked to the waist, and bearing a flat cake upon his head. They knelt and said, “Great Sage, I am the Spirit-warden of Jingji Ridge. Knowing you have arrived and with no means to receive you properly, I prepared one tray of steamed cakes and offer them to you, Master Tripitaka, and each of you for one meal. From here to the next settlement is eight hundred li; there is no village at all. At least this may fill your hunger. Zhu Bajie was pleased and stepped forward to stretch out his hands and take the cakes. Unbeknownst, Sun Wukong had been observing long and now shouted, “Stay! This one is not a good man. Do not be insolent. What land spirit are you, deceiving old Sun? Show me your staff!” When that old one saw him coming, he turned and became a swirl of dark wind, and with one shout snatched up the Master, lifting him and carrying him away, drifting and tossing, none knowing to where. Startled, Great Sage could not follow at once; Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing looked at one another in dismay, and even the White Horse only neighed in fright. The three disciples and horse, four mouths in all, reeled and stared off into the distance, then to the heights, with no trace of him at all; searching back and forth is not worth recounting.

Now it is said that the old man, with a ghostly messenger, carried Tripitaka to stand before a stone cottage wreathed in smoke-like radiance and set him down gently. He drew him beside him and said, ‘Holy monk, do not fear. We are no evil men; we are the Elders of Thorny Ridge, the Eighteen Elders. On this wind-clear, moon-clear night, we have specially invited you to come, for we wished to meet as friends, talk poetry, and pass the evening in fellowship.’

Only then did Tripitaka steady his nerves and open his eyes to look closely. Truly:

Faint drifting mists and clouds drift away, A clear immortal realm, its dwellings and homes. A fitting place to purify the body and cultivate, Suitable for planting bamboo and flowers. At every turn the jade-green crags receive the cranes, And at times one hears the frogs crying in the blue pond. More wondrous even than Heaven’s Terrace and the cinnabar kiln, We still hope for the bright rosy clouds of Mount Hua. What talk is there of tilling clouds and fishing the moon? This reclusive life is itself proud of praise. If one sits long, the hidden thoughts become sea-like, A faint moon rises over the gauze at the window.

Tripitaka had been studying silently; gradually the stars and moon grew clear. He only heard human voices in low conversation. They all said, ‘The Eighteen Elders have invited this holy monk.’

Tripitaka raised his head and looked. There were three elders: the first with a frost-like appearance, the second with green hair and draping locks, the third with a dark blue face. Their features and garments were all different, and all came to offer Tripitaka respect. Tripitaka returned the bow and said, ‘Disciple, what merit has he that he dares trouble the august immortals?’ The Eighteen Elders laughed, ‘We have long heard that the holy monk follows the Way; we have waited many times. If this meeting comes now, it is good fortune. If your generosity is not tight-fisted with pearl and jade, recline with us and share your heart. Then we shall see the true current of Zen insight.’

Tripitaka bent and said, ‘What are your honored names?’ The Eighteen Elders replied, ‘The one of frost-like form is called Guzhi Gong. The one of green hair is called Lingkongzi. The dark-faced one is called Fuyun Sou. This old fool is called Jingjie.’

Tripitaka said, ‘I thank you, honored sirs. All four elders enjoy great longevity, and Elder Jingjie has already surpassed a thousand years. With such age one may still reach realization; your countenance and talent are clear and strange. Are you not, in truth, the Four Worthies of the Han?’

The four said together, ‘You flatter us. No, we are not the Four Worthies. We are the Four Sects of the Deep Mountains. We ask you, holy monk, how old are you?’ Tripitaka joined his palms and bowed, answering:

Forty years ago I came from my mother’s womb, Though not yet born, my life was already marked by disaster. To save my life I was thrown into the water, rolling with the waves, Yet by good fortune on Mount Golden I escaped this mortal shell. I have nourished my nature and read the scriptures without slackness, And with a sincere heart I have dared to worship Buddha through hardship. Now, by imperial order, I have been sent westward, And on the way I have met the mercy of these immortals.

All four said, ‘The holy monk, from birth itself followed Buddhism from the moment you emerged from your mother’s body. Truly, you are a practitioner from youth, and a truly upright monk on the Way indeed.’

Then one and all, ‘By your fortune we have won the grace of your face; we dare ask the Great Teaching. We hope you will instruct us in Zen for a little while so that the whole life may feel fulfilled.’

Tripitaka, hearing this, was moved and unafraid, and said to the assembly:

Zen means stillness, and Dharma means passage. Passage within stillness cannot be completed without awakening. The awakened one is one who washes the heart and clears vexations, who sheds the world and leaves off dust. The human body is hard to obtain, the Central Kingdom hard to be born in, and meeting the true Dharma hard to find: to obtain all three together is the greatest blessing.

Supreme virtue and wondrous Way are vast, remote, and elusive. Then the six roots and six consciousnesses can be swept away. Bodhi means neither death nor birth, no remainder and no lack, emptiness and form in total embrace, saint and ordinary both set aside.

Seek the true and realize the primordial origin; awaken to the genuine method of Buddha. Reveal the images and illusions, and tread and shatter Nirvana. One must awaken within awakening and awaken by deeper awakening. The single point of spiritual light must guard all. Unloose the fierce flame to illuminate the dancing world of forms, and the Dharma realm, stretched in every direction, stands revealed on its own. Even in the most subtle mystery it is further sealed and held fast—who can ever say, at the dark secret gate, who is carried across? I am by original cultivation a monk of Great Awakening Zen; only one with affinity and will can truly be said to have awakened.’

The four elders listened with ears wide open and were joyfully moved without end. Each one bowed in homage and knelt to receive, then rose and thanked him, saying, ‘The holy monk is truly one born with the marrow of Zen insight.’

Fuyun Sou said, ‘Though Chan is stillness, and Dharma is passage, one must still fix the nature and make the heart sincere. Even if one is a truly awakened immortal, in the end he must still sit in the Way of no-birth. The profundity of us is altogether different.’

Tripitaka said, ‘The Way is indeed extraordinary; form and function are one. How, then, are they different?’

Fuyun Sou laughed and said, ‘We are born strong and substantial, and our form and function differ from yours. We owe Heaven and Earth with whom we are born, and rain and dew have nourished our complexion. We laugh and scoff at wind and frost, grinding away sun and moon. One leaf never withers; in a thousand branches our integrity remains in firm season. Such words as this do not strike against emptiness; yet you cling to Brahman speech. The Way, in essence, lies in the Central Kingdom, yet you came seeking proof in the West, wasting your grass sandals in vain, not knowing what you seek.

A stone lion had its heart and liver carved out; wild-fox saliva has soaked through its marrow. Forgetting your source while contemplating Chan and vainly seeking Buddha’s fruit—this is all like the thorny riddles of Thorny Ridge and the tangled nonsense of gourd vines and creeping gourds. How can one guide gentlemen of this kind? With such a standard, how can one bestow the seal of transmission? One must first inspect what appears before one’s eyes. In stillness itself there is one’s course of life.

Water drawn in a basket without a bottom; flowers blooming on a rootless iron tree. Fix your feet at Lingbao Peak, and when you return come to the elegant gathering on Dragon Flower.’

Tripitaka heard these words and knelt and thanked him. Elder Jingjie put out a hand and helped him up; Guzhi Gong pulled him to his feet; Lingkongzi laughed aloud and said, ‘Fuyun’s words are plainly too revealing. Holy monk, please rise; do not believe him entirely. We have taken this moonlit night for no lectures or cultivation. Let us rather recite, sing, and roam in free ease, letting our hearts wander at liberty.’

Fuyun Sou smiled and pointed to the stone cottage, saying, ‘If you wish to recite verses, come inside the small cell for a cup of tea. What say you?’

The abbott truly bent forward and looked toward the front of the stone cottage. On the gate were three large characters: “Wood Immortal Hermitage.” Then all entered, and the seating order was arranged. At once a bare-bodied ghost attendant appeared, carrying a tray of poria paste, and presented five cups of fragrant tea. The four elders invited Tripitaka to begin, but Tripitaka, startled and uncertain, did not dare to. The four elders all ate together; Tripitaka ate only two pieces. Each drank the fragrant tea and withdrew. Tripitaka watched carefully, and he saw dazzling brilliance there, as if moonlight had settled below:

Water flows out from the edge of rock, scent drifts from within flowers. The whole hall is clear and elegant, utterly free of dust. When that abbott beheld this fairy-like scene, he was pleased and delighted, his joy overflowing, and he could not help but recite: “A meditative mind is like moonlight, utterly free of dust.” Jiejie Elder laughed and at once linked a line: “Poetic mood, new as the blue of heaven.” Guzhi Gong said: “What a fine line, cast loose, richer than brocade and embroidery.” Lingkongzi said: “Good prose need not point out odd jewels to be rare and beautiful.” Fuyun Grandmaster said: “The splendor of six dynasties is all washed clean; once more the elegant hymn is carefully revised and divided.” Tripitaka said, “My disciple spoke only in haste and blundered, uttering a few words. Truly it is what they call ‘wielding a hatchet at Ban Gate.’ Now hearing these words from the Immortals, they are fresh and lofty, and truly poetic in the extreme.” Jiejie said, “Venerable monk, there is no need for idle elaboration. In one who has left home, a proper beginning already implies an ending. Since you already have the opening line, why have no closing line? Please bring it to completion.” Tripitaka said, “My disciple cannot do that. If you please, may Elder Shiba conclude it and make it a full piece.” Jiejie said, “You have such a true heart; how can you refuse to finish what you began? To be reluctant to give up pearls and jade is unreasonable.” Tripitaka therefore had to add the next two lines: “Tea in a half-pillowed pine-wind sleep, songing mood light and free, full of spring.” Elder Shiba said, “Excellent! ‘Songing mood light and free, full of spring.’” Guzhi Gong said, “Jiejie, you know well the flavor of poetry, so you may keep savoring it. Why not begin yet another piece?” Elder Shiba also replied, with no reluctance, “I begin by striking the key line: Spring will not boast of beauty, winter will not decay; clouds come and mists go, as if nothing at all.” Lingkongzi said, “I too can strike the answering key line: In windless space the dancing shadows sway; A guest finds joy, pitying the picture of blessings and long life.” Fuyun Grandmaster struck a key line, too: “Its form resembles the western mountain of firm-jointed Elders, clear as the southern land, cold-hearted to itself.” Guzhi Gong also struck a key line: “If the side leaf is called the梁梁 beam, let the hall become a crossing-bough and make a statute of a crow.” The abbott, hearing all this, praised them without end and said, “It is truly the pure white snow of spring, a mighty spirit rising to heaven. My disciple is lacking in talent and dares not add two lines.” Guzhi Gong said, “The holy monk is truly a man of the Way, a great cultivated man. There is no need to keep trying to pair lines further. Please teach us the full piece, so that we may try to match it as best we can.” Tripitaka had no choice but to smile and recite one regulated poem: “With staff and staff-bowl came from the west to bow before the Dharma King, praying to seek wondrous canons and spread them afar. Golden and green flowers bloom threefold on the judges’ verse throne; lotus fragrance rises from a thousand flowering trees. At the top of a hundred-foot pole one must still make progress; In the ten directions and all the realms, let one establish conduct and dwelling. To fashion the body of a worthy jade image; before the Gate of Bliss this is the altar of the Way.” All four elders listened to an end and praised highly. Elder Shiba said, “I am an old fool with no merit, and I have dared to intrude boldly, but I too will try to match this one.” “Jiejie stands aloof, laughing at Wood-king pride; the spirit-cypress does not spread my name. In mountain emptiness, dragon and snake shadows stretch a hundred zhang; a thousand-year spring draws up amber fragrance. Unbinding and sustaining the vital breath of heaven and earth, joy at once changed by wind and rain into hidden and manifest paths. In withered decline I blush to find no fairy-bone in me; only this poria-paste grounds a hall of longevity.” Guzhi Gong said, “This opening is imposing and forceful, the paired lines powerful, but the closing line is too much in self-abasement. Admirable! admirable! This old fool also matches a verse.” “I have always favored the plumage king among roosting birds; Before the Hall of Four Magnificences your great vessel is raised. Heavy dew, pearl tassels veiled by jade-green canopy; a light wind on stone teeth, cold fragrance shattered. In the long corridor the night is still, song-voices thin; ancient hall and autumn shade hide faint reflections. On New Year’s day, while welcoming spring, I once offered life-blessings; In old age I yet send my proud heart to the mountains.” Lingkongzi laughed and said, “Fine poem, fine poem—truly a moon that presses open heaven and heart. How can this old fool answer it? Yet I must not leave it all unsaid; I, too, must speak a few lines.” “The timber-beam timber of Liangdung is material for emperor and king; beyond the Hall of Supreme Clarity, sound rises. A clear pavilion appears like azure vapour arriving; On dark walls, as one passes often, passes along emerald fragrance. Magnificent integrity stands proud through a thousand ages; deep roots are knotted in the Nine Springs. Lingkong’s posture covers the dancing shadows; he does not belong in the showy field of brilliant flowers.” Fuyun Grandmaster said, “The poetry of these three elders is lofty and pure, exactly the opening of a brocade-satin casket. I am weak in strength and empty in talent; under the instruction of these three elders, the knot at my gate has burst open. I have no way but to make a few rough lines—please do not laugh at them.” He recited: “In Qi’ao Garden the Sacred King rejoices; ten thousand mu of Weichuan may be set to flourish. Green bamboo is unsullied by Xiang-goddess tears; a strip of reed, fit to transmit the fragrance of Han histories. Frosted leaves come and go without changing their hue; from the smoke-tipped tops, where now can color hide? Since Master Ziyou has left this world, true listeners are few; across ages he left his name in the hall of brush and ink.”

Tripitaka said: “The four Immortal elders’ poems are truly breathless—phoenixes giving forth pearl and jade, none among Xia can equal them. Your deep feeling and high excellence have moved me greatly. But the night is already deep, and my three young disciples do not know where they are waiting for me. My disciple cannot stay long; I beg leave to return and search them out. My love for them is without bound. Please, revered Immortals, show me the way home.” The four elders laughed and said, “Holy monk, do not worry. Such a strange meeting is one of a thousand-year chance. And though the sky is clear and bright, though night is late it is moonlit as bright as day. Sit a little longer. At daybreak we shall gladly escort you far beyond the ridge, and your disciples will surely meet you then as well.”

Tripitaka said: “Three young disciples are waiting somewhere outside, but I do not know where. They wait for no one but me?”

Just as this was being spoken, outside the stone hut two blue-robed maidens appeared carrying a pair of crimson-silk lanterns, followed by a fairy lady. The lady, twirling a sprig of apricot blossom, entered smiling. What did she look like? She was as follows:

Her complexion was painted azure, her face rosy-red like rouge. Her starry eyes still shone with color, her moth brows were bright and even. Below she wore a faint red five-colored plum skirt; above, a light jacket like fire glimmering through smoke. Her curved shoes had bent phoenix-beaks; her silk stockings dragged patterned silk in the mud. Lithe and seductive as a maiden of Heavenly Terrace, in no way below the famous beauty Daji of old. The four elders bowed and asked, “Where has Xingxian come from?” The woman offered full salutations to all and said: “I learned there were fine guests here giving poetry in response, so I came to visit. I dare ask to be granted one audience.” Eighteen Master pointed to Tripitaka, saying, “The guests are here; why trouble to seek an audience?” Tripitaka bowed low and could not speak. The lady called out, “Serve tea at once.” Then two yellow-robed maidens arrived carrying a red-lacquered cinnabar tray. Within the tray were six tiny porcelain tea bowls, and in the bowls were a few kinds of strange fruit; one carried a spoon across the shoulder. Another held a white-iron tea kettle inlaid with yellow copper, its fragrance strong. When tea was poured, the lady showed the color of spring scallions, and handed a porcelain bowl to Tripitaka first, then to the four elders, and after that took one bowl herself.

Lingkongzi said, “Why does Xingxian not take a seat?” The lady had just now gone to sit down. After tea, she bowed and asked, “The honored immortal’s feast is resplendent tonight—would you teach me one or two fine lines?” Fuyun replied, “We are but rough and common in speech; only the holy monk’s verse is truly grand, truly worthy of great admiration.” The lady said, “If you would be generous in instruction, I beg to read one.” The four elders then recited aloud Tripitaka’s earlier poem and later poem and expounded its Zen doctrine. With a full smile on her face, she spoke to everyone: “I am unworthy and have no talent with which to offer my poor verses. But after hearing these fine lines, it would be unworthy to stay silent. I will, with great effort, offer a matching regulated poem as a follow-up. Pray excuse it.” She then sang clearly:

“On the lid remains the name of Emperor Wu of Han; in Zhou times Confucius raised the altar and sang it forth. Dong Immortal cherished me into a forest’s accumulation; Sun Chu once pitied the fragrance of the cold-food rite. Rain-softens my red complexion, tender and fine; mist-smooths green color makes it plainly appear and yet still conceal it. Knowing my own overripe sourness, each place I fall, year after year I keep company with the wheat fields.” The four elders listened and all praised, saying: “Pure and elegant, free of dust, and the line contains the entire spring mood. Excellent is ‘Rain-softens my red complexion, tender and fine’! Excellent is ‘Rain-softens my red complexion, tender and fine’!” The lady smiled and answered softly: “I am afraid, I am afraid. At the hearing of the holy monk’s poems, my heart is truly brocade-fitted and embroidered. If you are not stingy with pearls and jewels, grant me instruction of one more song?” Tripitaka would not dare to agree. The lady’s interest grew, and she drew closer and closer, inching along, until near the seat. In a low whisper she said: “Excellent guest, do not withhold your attention. Why only stand and toy about? This beautiful night passes quickly—what can one’s life have in it?” Eighteen Master said, “Xingxian possesses lofty feeling that raises her eyes upward; can this holy monk have no intention worthy of yielding in return? If he does not show favor, then he does not understand true amusement.” Guzhi Gong said, “The holy monk is a man famed for the Way, and he does not act carelessly. With such conduct as this, we would indeed be committing offense. To sully a person’s name and spoil a person’s virtue is no route to true attainment. If Xingxian truly means to pursue this, you may make Fuyun and Shiba the betrothal matchmakers, and Lingkongzi and I stand as guarantors. Is that not a fine union?”

Tripitaka listened, and his expression changed at once. He leapt up and cried aloud: "You are all of one kind of demon, tempting me thus. Earlier you used gentle words, speaking of the mysteries and of the Dao—it was one thing. How can you now use a beauty’s snare to harm poor monk Tripitaka? What kind of reason is this?" The four elders saw Tripitaka in a rage and, one by one, bit their fingers in startled fear, then spoke no more. The naked-bodied demon envoy shouted in sudden thunderous rage: "This monk is terribly ignorant of what befits such matters. Are my elder sister and her companions not suitable? Her talent is handsome and her form delicate as precious jade; need we even mention the needle-fine grace of a maid’s hands—this one piece of poetry is enough to match you. Why do you refuse so? Do not let the chance slip away. The words of Guzhigong are quite proper; if you will not take a match here, I will arrange your marriage again." Tripitaka was greatly alarmed and pale. No matter how wildly they spoke, he would not yield. The demon messenger spoke again: "You, this monk, we spoke to you politely and you did not listen. If we release our rustic temper, we will seize you and make it so you cannot be a monk, cannot take a husband or wife, and thereby not live in vain as a man either." The elder’s heart was like gold and stone, unwavering. Silently he thought: "My disciples do not know where they are, to find me." Saying this, he could not stop tears from falling. The woman, still smiling, came near and with her emerald-green sleeve took out a silk handkerchief and dabbed his tears: "Good guest, do not be troubled. I will keep you to precious jade and sweet fragrance and play together." Tripitaka gave one sharp shout and sprang up to leave. They pulled and tugged him, shouting until dawn.

Then came a cry: "Master, Master, where are you speaking?" It was Sun Wukong, leading Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing with the horse and loads on poles. They had not rested all night, crossing through thorns and brambles, searching east and west. Through half-cloud, half-mist they had gone over eight hundred li and descended to the west of Thorn Ridge when they heard Tripitaka shouting; he called at once in turn. Tripitaka burst out: "Wukong, I am here. Quickly come, save me, quickly come." The four elders, the demon envoy, the woman, and the maid all flashed and vanished in an instant.

After a while, Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing both came up to the side and said, "Master, how did you come to this place?" Tripitaka held on to Wukong and said, "Disciples, I have made you work hard all this while. Last night I met that old man who spoke of the Earth God offering alms. It was you who cried out to beat him, and he lifted me to this place. He took my hand and led me in; then I saw three elders come here to meet me. All called me a 'holy monk.' One by one they spoke in elegant words and were excellent at reciting verse. Matching them in turn, I joined in and sang with them. By midnight I saw a beautiful woman with a lantern who also came here to meet me and recited a poem, calling me a 'good guest.' When she saw my face, she sought to take me as spouse, and I then understood. I refused. Yet those acting as matchmakers, as sponsors, and as wedding masters pressed me; I swore I would not agree. Just as I struggled up to leave and scolded with them, suddenly the two of you arrived. First it was dawn, and second, I was afraid of you; at once they pulled and dragged me, and then suddenly disappeared." Wukong asked, "If you talked with them and traded verse, did you not even ask one of them for a name?" Tripitaka replied, "I did ask his title. The first old man was called Shiba-gong, styled Jiejie; the second was called Guzhigong; the third, Lingkongzi; the fourth, Fuyun-sou. The woman was called Xingxian." Zhu Bajie said, "Where are these beings now, and where did they go?" Tripitaka said, "Where they went, I do not know. But the place where we were discussing poems is not far from here."

The three, together with the master, looked around and saw a cliff face with the three characters 'Wood Immortal Hermitage' carved there. Tripitaka said, "Here it is indeed." Wukong looked closely and saw, however, a great hinoki cypress, an old cypress, an old pine, and an old bamboo, with a scarlet maple behind the bamboo. Looking again along the cliff-side, there was also an old apricot, two plum trees, and two osmanthus trees. Wukong laughed: "Did you see any demons?" Zhu Bajie said, "No." Wukong replied, "You do not yet know that these very trees have become spirits here." Zhu Bajie asked, "Brother, how do you know that a spirit-beast is a tree?" Wukong answered: "Shiba-gong is a pine. Guzhigong is a cypress. Lingkongzi is a hinoki cypress. Fuyun-sou is the bamboo pole. The naked-bodied demon is a maple. Xingxian is the apricot tree. The maid is the osmanthus, and she is the plum as well." Hearing this, whether good or bad, Zhu Bajie gave one heavy downward strike with his spade-mace, and in three or five broad blows swept down the two plums, the osmanthus, the old apricot, and the maple; truly, fresh blood flowed from their roots. Tripitaka moved forward and restrained him: "Wukong, do not hurt them. Though they had become spirits, they have not injured me. We should leave and keep going." Wukong said, "Master, do not spare them. If they are left to grow later, they may become great demons and cause great harm." Zhu Bajie, determined, struck once more and felled pine, cypress, hinoki, and bamboo together. Only then did he summon the master back onto the horse, and all proceeded westward together along the main road.

In the end it is still unknown how to proceed; let the next chapter explain.
chapters.title: Chapter 64: On Thicket Ridge Wuneng strives with all his might; at the Wood-Immortal Hermitage Tripitaka converses on verse.
