This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

In this turn, this doctrine of cause and effect urges people toward goodness and forbids evil. Let no one dare to do evil. When a single thought arises, the heavenly spirits behold it, and each follows whatever that thought makes him do. How can a clumsy, stubborn fool like you learn the Way? In either case it is still a medicine without a true heart. While this life still remains, and the Way is at hand, it should be cultivated—do not wasteful-linger. Recognize the root and shed your shell. If you seek the Long Life, you must seize it. At all times keep things clear to your sight and weigh the essence like the finest cream. Push through the three passes and cross the dark sea, and then teach the worthy to ride phoenix and crane. In between, through compassion born of mercy, one rises to the Supreme Bliss.

After this, Tripitaka’s one-minded devotion was sincere; do not speak of heavenly gods offering protection. Even spirits of these grasses and trees would come to escort him. After a single proper night’s meeting, he slipped out from brambles and thorns, and no more vines clung to him. The four disciples pressed westward, and after many stages the late-winter chill had passed; it was exactly the days of early spring:

Nature and flourishing things harmonized; the Dipper’s handle turned toward Yīn. Green shoots of grass spread everywhere, and on every bank the willow tips were all blue-green. One ridge of peach blossoms was painted red as brocade, and half a stream shone clear, misty and blue. Whatever wind and rain had come before, they gave way to boundless feeling of heart. Sunlight brightened the flower hearts into vividness, and swallows lightly picked at mossy stamens. Mountain colors, like Wang Wei’s paintings, held soft gradations; birds’ voices of the season darted to and fro. Spring beauty spread like rich embroidery, but no one came to behold it; yet butterflies danced and bees sang with feeling. The disciples sought out the blossom paths and followed their horses at an easy pace. As they walked, they suddenly saw a tall mountain; from afar it seemed to join the sky itself, breaking through the blue heavens. Tripitaka raised his whip and pointed: “Sun Wukong, I do not know how high that mountain is, but it seems to be touching the heavens and piercing the blue ether.” Wukong said, “There is an old verse: ‘Only Heaven is above; no mountain is on par with it.’ To say that a mountain is exceedingly tall does not make it comparable with Heaven; how could it truly touch Heaven?” Zhu Bajie said, “If it does not touch Heaven, how is Mount Kunlun called the Pillar of Heaven?” Wukong said, “You do not know. From old times it has been said, ‘Heaven is not full in the northwest.’ Kunlun Mountain lies in the northwestern corner, so it has the sense of blocking the sky and filling emptiness—that is why it is called the Heaven Pillar.” Sha Wujing laughed and said, “Elder brother, do not speak these good words to him; if he hears them, he will go off and confuse others. Let us just keep walking. Once we reach the mountain, we’ll know its height.”

That fool drove on behind Sha Wujing, teasing and sparring with him all the way. Master’s horse ran as fast as an arrow. Soon they reached the edge of the cliff and climbed up step by step. The mountain looked like this:

In the forest the wind whistled, and in the ravine the water murmured. Rooks and sparrows could not fly through; even immortals would find it hard. A thousand cliffs, ten thousand gullies, a hundred bends in every curve. Dust rolled in great drifts where no one came, while strange rocks stood thick and did not weary the eye. In places, clouds spread like water; here trees and birdsong were all in abundance. Deer carried away the sacred lingzhi, and monkeys went back with peaches. Fox and marten came and went, leaping upon the cliffs; goral and deer moved in and out of ridge-heads in playful unrest. Suddenly a tiger’s roar made one’s courage shake, and brindled leopards and gray wolves blocked the path. Tripitaka saw it and was alarmed. Wukong, whose divine powers were vast, looked to his Golden-Hooped Staff and gave one roar. He frightened away the wolves, insects, tigers, and leopards, split open a path, and led Master up the mountain. Passing the ridge and descending to level ground in the west, they suddenly saw soft auspicious light and drifting colored mist. There stood rows of towers, pavilions, and halls; faint temple bells and chimes floated out. Tripitaka said, “Disciples, what place is this?” Wukong lifted the brim of his thought and shaded his eyes with his hand, then looked closely. This place was truly: Jeweled towers and precious seats; the upper monastery is called Fang. Empty valleys, echoing with many wild winds; the still realm scattered heavenly fragrance. Green pines veiled with rain sheltered lofty pavilions; jade-green bamboos held the clouds, guarding the lecture hall. Rosy light dimly revealed the Dragon Palace; colored haze drifted long across the river sands. Vermilion railings, jade doors; painted ridges and carved beams. Talk of sutras filled the hall with scent, and the scriptural tablets shone like the moon in the windows. Birds sang from red trees, and cranes drank beside a stone spring. All around the flowers bloomed, in beautiful gem gardens; three-sided gates opened with the radiance of Śewēi. Towers and terraces jutted abruptly, gates facing the ridges; temple bells and chimes rang out in long, empty, slow resonance. Windows opened to a fine wind, curtains drew back into drifting haze. The monks’ mood was quiet and detached, with no trace of common worldliness. Red dust never reaches this true-immortal realm. In this still soil, a splendid Dharma field was made. After seeing it, Wukong answered, “Master, that place is a monastery, yet among its auspicious light there is some fierceness. Its appearance is like Leiyin, yet the paths are not the same. We should not, upon arriving, enter recklessly; else we may be met with poisoned hands.” Tripitaka said, “If it has the appearance of Leiyin, then it must surely be Ling Mountain. Do not delay my sincerity; do not obstruct my purpose.” Wukong said, “No, no. I have walked the road to Ling Mountain several times before. This is not that path.” Zhu Bajie said, “Even if not, some good man must live there.” Sha Wujing said, “Do not be over-suspicious. This road must pass through this gate; whether it is so can be known at a glance.” Wukong said, “Wujing is right.”

Master urged his horse and lashed him on. When he reached the front of the mountain gate, he saw the three characters “Leiyin Temple” and in panic dismounted in a tumble, falling to the ground, muttering, “Impudent ape! You’ve done for me. It is Leiyin Temple and yet it has deceived me.” Wukong smiled and said, “Master, do not be upset; look again. The gate has four characters—how could you have read only three and blame me?” Master trembled and rose, looking again. It truly was four characters: “Small Leiyin Temple.” Tripitaka said, “If this is Small Leiyin Temple, there must certainly be some Buddha within. The scriptures say there are three thousand Buddhas, not confined to one place—Guanyin in the South Sea, Samantabhadra at Mount Emei, Manjushri at Mount Wutai. Who can say which Buddha’s sanctuary this is? The ancients said, ‘Where there is Buddha and sutra, there is no boundary and no jewel. We may enter.’” Wukong said, “Do not enter. This place has little fortune and much peril. If calamity comes, do not blame me.” Tripitaka said, “Even if there is no Buddha, there will certainly be an image. My disciple’s intention is to meet a Buddha and bow before him. How could I fault you?”

At once he ordered Zhu Bajie to fetch the monastic robes, exchange the monk’s cap, and arrange their dress, then step forward. At the gate they heard someone called from inside: “Tripitaka, you have come from the eastern land to pay homage to my Buddha, how can you be so negligent?” Tripitaka at once went down and prostrated himself; Zhu Bajie also knelt in submission, and Sha Wujing knelt as well. Only Wukong held the horses and gathered the luggage behind. Then, on entering the two-story gate, they saw the Great Hall of the Buddha. Beneath the hall’s gate, on a jewel platform, stood five hundred Arhats, three thousand Jie-di, four Vajra Kings, eight Bodhisattvas, nuns, upāsakas, and countless holy monks and Taoist adepts. In truth there was radiant flower and perfume, and auspicious light in full abundance. In his haste, Master and the two disciples made a bow at every step, kneeling up to the spirit platform itself. Wukong openly did not bow. From above the lotus platform came a harsh cry: “Sun Wukong—how dare you not bow before the Buddha?” Wukong looked more closely and saw that it was a sham. He threw aside horse and pack, drew his staff, and shouted, “You rabble of evil beasts, how bold are you! How can you hide beneath Buddha’s name and corrupt the Buddha’s pure virtue? Do not flee.” He raised both hands with the staff and lunged to strike. Then in midair came a sharp ding-dang, and a pair of golden clappers was cast down, enclosing Wukong head and feet together within them. Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing hurried to bring out their heavy spiked staffs, but a cluster of Arhats, Jie-di, holy monks, and Taoist adepts rushed in at once and surrounded them. The two were caught off guard and all were seized. Tripitaka too was taken. All were bound tight with rope and cord and fastened securely.

The one seated on the lotus throne as Buddha was, in fact, a demon king, and all the Arhats and others were only little fiends. The Buddha image was put away and the demon form reappeared. The three from Tripitaka’s party were carried to the rear and locked away. Wukong, kept enclosed in the golden clappers, was never released, set on the treasure platform, and left for three nights and three days to become pus and blood. After that, they put him in an iron cage and steamed him, using him for their feast. It was truly:

Green-eyed ape-men discerned the false as true, and from a trace of Zen they bowed to a golden form. The blind yellow hag performed reverence without sight; the wooden-mother, deluded in affection, discoursed with him. A demonic nature grows fierce and deceives its own root; the demon lord, harboring evil intent, feigned heaven and men. Truly this little demon lord is no small one—he is a great one, and to enter by a side gate has wasted his body in vain. At that time the band of demons stored Tripitaka and his two disciples in the rear, tied the horse behind, and put his robes and monk’s cap into the load on his shoulder. They stored everything there as well. The other side was strictly guarded, no need to describe it further.

Then he said the Great Sage, Sun Wukong, was wedged inside the golden cymbals, dark and hollow, soaked in sweat from the heat; he arched left and collided right, yet could not get out. In desperation he struck the Iron Staff about wildly, and could not move it by a single hair. His plan vanished from his mind. He stretched outward as if he could break through the golden cymbal. He twisted a secret technique and shot up so tall, a thousand- and hundred-zhang height; the cymbal grew with him, and not a hint of seam or glimmer appeared. He twisted the technique again and shrank himself a little, small as a mustard seed; the cymbal shrank with him too, with even fewer tiny pores left. He then blew immortal breath through the Iron Staff and called, 「Change！」 and it became like a banner pole, bracing the cymbal. He plucked two of the longest hairs from the back of his head and called, 「Change！」 At once they became five-petaled plum-blossom drills. Sliding beneath the staff, he drilled and drilled by the hundreds and thousands, producing only a dull ringing, and could not drill further.

Sun Wukong grew urgent. He twisted another technique, chanted the spell, 「唵㘕靜法界，乾元亨利貞」, and called forth the Five-Direction Jiedi, the Six Ding and Six Jia, and eighteen Dharma-guard Jialans. They stood outside the golden cymbal and said: 「Great Sage, we are all protecting Tripitaka so that no demon may hurt him. Why call us here again?」

Sun Wukong replied, 「My Tripitaka will not heed my counsel; if he is killed, I lose nothing. But why cannot you quickly open this cymbal and let me out so I can go on punishing this matter? In here there is no light, and my whole body burns with heat—won’t I be suffocated?」

The gods really tried to lift the cymbal, but it stayed fixed, as if nailed down, and could not be moved at all.

Jingtou Jiedi said, 「Great Sage, I do not know what kind of treasure this is. Up and down it is fused into one solid piece. My strength is too small to lift it.」

Sun Wukong said, 「Even from inside, I do not know how many divine arts I have used, and still I cannot move it.」

When Jiedi heard this, he ordered the Six Ding gods to protect Tripitaka, the Six Jia gods to watch the golden cymbal, and all the Jialans to inspect it before and behind. He then rose in auspicious radiance and in an instant entered the South Heavenly Gate. Without waiting for a summons, he went straight up beneath the Hall of Lingxiao Treasures. There he knelt before the Jade Emperor and reported: 「Your Majesty, I am Jiedi, an envoy of the Five Directions. Today Sun Wukong, the Great Sage of Equalizing Heaven, is escorting Tripitaka to fetch the scriptures. On the road, we met a mountain called Little Leiyin Temple. Tang Monk mistook it and worshiped there, thinking it the sacred Ling Mountains, but it was an illusion set by a demon. The monster captured him and his companions and enclosed the Great Sage inside a pair of golden cymbals, making his progress impossible and facing him with no way out—surely to die there. I thus come to report on this.」

Then he issued his decree: 「Send the Twenty-Eight Constellations at once, quickly descend to remove this calamity and subdue the demon.」

The constellation spirits did not dare to linger. They followed Jiedi out of the Heavenly Gate and reached inside the mountain gate at the second watch. In those hours the larger and smaller demons, having obtained Tang Monk, had all been rewarded by the old demon and each went to sleep. The star spirits were no longer anxious. They came outside the cymbals and announced, 「Great Sage, we are the Twenty-Eight Constellations sent by the Jade Emperor to rescue you.」

When Sun Wukong heard this, he was overjoyed and told them, 「Raise weapons and strike to break it, and old Sun will come out.」

The stars replied, 「We dare not strike. This object is a fused gold treasure; if struck it will ring, and the roar would wake the demons, making rescue impossible. Let us pry it with weapons. Move only where you can see a trace of light.」

Sun Wukong said, 「You are right.」

See them then: those with spears used spears; those with swords used swords; those with knives used knives; those with axes used axes. Some hauled, some lifted, some pried up, some levered. They worked until the third watch. It stayed utterly unmoving, as if it were cast into one piece. Inside, the Great Sage kept turning this way and that, crawling over and rolling, and could see no gleam of light.

Kang Jinlong said, 「Great Sage, be at ease and do not be so agitated. Observe, this treasure must be a wish-granting object and surely can transform. Since you are inside, place your hand upon the seam and wait for my horn tip to push in. Then you can transform and slip out through the loosened opening.」

Sun Wukong did as told and truly groped about in agitation. The constellation spirit shrank his body; the horn tip became like a needle point and entered along the rim seam, advancing inward. He used all his strength of a thousand jin before he could break through. He then synchronized body and horn with his art and cried, 「Long! Long! Long!」 The horn became as thick as a bowl. The rim of the cymbal did not seem cast in metal either; it seemed like living skin and flesh lengthened, clenching tightly around Kang Jinlong’s horn, and on all sides there was not a trace of a pulling gap.

Feeling along the horn, Sun Wukong called out, 「It is of no use. Above and below there is no slack in the slightest. I have no choice but to ask: endure this little pain and carry me out.」 So he transformed the Golden-Hooped Staff into a steel drill and drilled a hole at the tip of that horn. He shrank himself to the size of a mustard seed, crouched and threaded himself through the drilled eye, crying, 「Pull out the horn, pull out the horn！」

That star spirit, spending who knows how much force, only then managed to pull it free and collapsed to the ground, exhausted.

Sun Wukong crawled out through the drilled eye of his horn and reappeared in his true form. He drew out the iron staff and struck the cymbal with a crash: it rang out and split it apart like a toppled bronze mountain, as if a gold mine had been blasted open. Alas, he had reduced a Buddhist rite implement to a thousand scattered pieces of gold.

This frightened the Twenty-Eight Constellations and made the Five-Direction Jiedi stand with bristling hair; all classes of demons woke as if from dreams. The old demon king, startled in his sleep, sprang up, dressed in haste, beating drums, gathering the demons, each of them taking up weapons. By then dawn was near. A great crowd rushed to the foot of the treasure platform and saw Sun Wukong, with the constellations, standing outside the shattered golden cymbal. They were greatly shocked and pale.

He ordered, 「You little ones, lock down the front gate tightly; do not let anyone out.」

When Sun Wukong heard this, he took the star hosts with him, mounted the cloud, and leapt into the sky of nine heavens. The demon king gathered the broken gold, formed ranks of demon soldiers, and deployed them outside the mountain gate. Nursing resentment, he donned his gear and took up a short, pliable wolf-tooth club. He came out from camp and shouted, 「Sun Wukong, a true man does not run far into the high heavens. Come at once and fight me in three rounds.」

Sun Wukong could not endure it. He brought the star cohort with him, set down the cloud, and inspected that demon’s appearance. He saw him:

His hair was tangled, and he wore a thin, flat golden circlet; his eyes were bare, with two yellow brows raised like a pair. He had a dangling nose, and open nostrils; wide-mouthed and sharp-toothed all around. He wore a linked chain-mail of interlocking armor plates and a strip of raw silk gathered with tassels at the waist. On his feet were a pair of black, odd shoes, and in his hand a wolf-tooth club. His shape was like a beast yet not-beastly, his looks not human yet vaguely human.

Sun Wukong held aloft his staff and barked, 「Monster, you need not brag. If this is a wager, then come and take a staff stroke.」

The demon king grinned and set the wolf-tooth club against him. This was a fierce battle:

Two clubs, not alike, yet if you speak of them they have their own forms. One was a short, soft cudgel of Buddhist making; the other hard as Canghai-cang. Both had arts of change at will, and this time they met to contend for strength. The short pliant wolf-tooth, mixed with brocade adornment; the hard Golden-Hooped Staff, like a coiled dragon bound in a gold hoop. Thick or thin, each could rightly be praised; short or long, each could be made exactly fitting. Monkey and demon fought together, this bout was truly without falsehood. Monkey-mind under discipline made its craft; evil monsters played the heavens with false forms. Angry and resentful, each heart merciless; wicked and ferocious, each had its own guise. This one struck first and never let the strike relax; that one parried and smashed down the face; hard to resist or push aside. Clouds were expelled and dimmed the sun; vapors exhaled and veiled the peaks. Staff met staff, staff came and went, and they met each other again and again, forgetting life and death for Tripitaka.

After the two fought through fifty exchanges, no winner or loser appeared.

At the mountain gate, gongs and drums sounded. The demons shouted and waved banners. On this side, the Twenty-Eight heavenly soldiers and the assembly of Five-Direction Jiedi, each with weapons, shouted once and enclosed the demon lord in their midst. That frightened the outer demons so much that they could hardly strike the drums; trembling, their hands went slack and they did not beat them.

The old demon, unafraid, with one hand blocked the crowd with his wolf-tooth club while with the other untied from his waist an old white cloth carry-bag, tossed it upward; with a smooth ringing sound it flew, and in one sweep swallowed Sun Wukong, the Twenty-Eight Constellations, and the Five-Direction Jiedi. He slung the whole burden over his shoulder and strode off. The little demons each returned, happy with victory.

The demon king ordered his minions to bring thirty or fifty hemp ropes. They untied the carry-bag, took one, then bound one. Each was made with soft bones and wrinkled skin. They bound and lifted them to the rear, and without choosing good or bad, threw everyone to the ground. The demon king then ordered a banquet table laid out; they drank freely from dawn till dusk, then dispersed, each returning to its bedchamber. Nothing further is recorded.

Now it was near midnight, and Great Sage Sun Wukong and the gathered gods had remained bound all through the dark hours, when suddenly there came a sound of bitter weeping. He listened closely and found it was Tripitaka’s voice: "Wukong, ah, I:

I alone regret that I did not heed you then, and so today I have fallen into this disaster. Within that golden yoke you were harmed, and I am lashed with hemp rope—who knew of this? Four of us, meeting fate by karma, have suffered bitterly, our three thousand deeds of merit nearly spent and collapsing. By what means can this tangle of hardship be untied, so that we may go straight to the Western Regions and return? Hearing this, the Wanderer said inwardly in compassion: "Though my master did not heed my words before, and now suffers this harm, he still, in this peril, remembers old Wukong. While the night is still and the demons sleep, with no one keeping watch, we should go now and free all of us and save them away."

Good Great Sage, he used a vanishing-body art, reduced his body to small size, slipped his bonds, and came near Tripitaka. He called out, "Master." The elder recognized the voice and said, "Why have you come here?" The Wanderer quietly told him what had just happened. The elder rejoiced: "Disciple, save me quickly. Thenceforth all matters rest with you; I will not press the issue anymore." Sun Wukong moved at once, first unbound the Master, then released Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing. He also freed the Twenty-eight Mansions, the Five-direction Jie-di gods, each one in turn. Then he led the horse forward and told them to leave quickly. Only when they were already at the gate did he realize he did not know where their baggage was, and came back searching. Kang Jinlong said, "You are light enough to carry the load but too heavy-hearted; rescuing your master is enough—why seek baggage still?" Wukong said, "A living person comes first, but robes and bowl are also most important. In the pack are the passage credentials, the brocade-edged kesa, and the purple-gold alms bowl; all are supreme Buddha treasures. How could I leave them?" Zhu Bajie said, "Elder Brother, you go look for it; we will wait along the road." See: the star-spirits crowding around Tripitaka used a capture method together with their arts. In one gust of wind they tore through the wall-circuit and ran to the road, down the mountain slope, and then arrayed themselves on level ground and waited.

At about the third watch, Great Sage Sun Wukong moved about with slow, light steps and entered within. He found the gates layered one inside another and locked tight. Climbing the upper story and peering out, he saw all the windows closed. When he tried to come down, he feared the lattice would rattle and so did not dare to push it. He twirled a charm and changed his form, becoming a fairy mouse, commonly called a bat. You ask what manner of form it took?

Its head was sharp and still mouse-like, and its eyes were bright like a mouse’s eyes. It gives wings at dusk, but in bright white daylight it stays indoors. It hides in cracks in the roof tiles and seeks insects to pounce. It delights in clear, bright moonlight; that is when it knows best to rise and fly. He followed along the unsealed tile edges beneath the eaves and squeezed inside, passing from gate to house and reaching the center. There, beneath a third-tier window, he saw a sharp glittering line of light—neither lamp-flame nor firefly glow, neither rosy cloud-flash nor lightning. Half-flying, half-leaping, as he came near the window he saw it was the bundle giving off radiance. The demoness had taken off Tripitaka’s robe and, without folding it, shoved it in disorder into the pack. That kesa was a Buddha treasure, embroidered with a wish-granting pearl, a Mani pearl, red agate, purple coral, śarīra, and moon-bright pearl; thus it shone through. Seeing this robe and bowl, she rejoiced in her heart, resumed her true shape, took it, and without even straightening the carrying rope, hoisted it to her shoulder and set off downward. But unexpectedly one end slipped loose and it dropped with a thud onto the upper-floor boards. Alas! just so happened: the great old demoness sleeping below was awakened by the sound, sprang up, and cried wildly, "Someone’s here! Someone’s here!" The large and small demons rose, lit lanterns and fires, and all shouted together, rushing ahead and behind to look. Some reported, "Tang Sanzang has gone." Some reported, "Wukong and the others have all gone." The demon lord rushed and ordered commands: "Be careful at every gate." The Wanderer heard and, fearing he might again be netted, leaving the bundle behind was impossible; with a long leap he vaulted out the window and fled.

The demoness searched front and back for Tripitaka and the others and found none. When she saw dawn approaching, she took up her staff and led her troops to give chase. Sun Wukong and the gods were visible beneath the hillside of the western slope, like clouds and mist billowing. The demon king cried out, "Where are they going? I come!" Jiao Mujiao cried out in haste: "Brothers, a monstrous thing is coming!" Kang Jinlong, Di Tufu, Fang Ritu, Xin Yuehu, Wei Huohu, Ji Shuibao, Dou Muxie, Niu Jinniu, Nu Tuhè, Xu Rishu, Wei Yueyan, Shi Huozhu, Bi Shuihóng, Kui Mulang, Lou Jingou, Wei Tuzhi, Mao Riji, Bi Yuewu, Zui Huohou, Shen Shuiyuan, Jing Muxuan, Gui Jinyang, Liu Tuzhang, Xing Rima, Zhang Yuelu, Yi Huosha, and Zhen Shuiyin came with the Golden-Headed Jie-di, Silver-Headed Jie-di, the Six-Jia and Six-Ding gods, and the Hojiao Galan, together with Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing (not bringing Tripitaka and leaving the White Dragon Horse). Each bore arms and surged upward at once. The demon king saw them, laughed cruelly, and sounded a whistle. Four or five thousand large and small demons advanced, each one mighty and powerful. They clashed headlong on the western hillside in one wild battle. A great and dreadful fight:

The demon-chief flung vile evil and mocked true nature; how can gentle true nature withstand evil? A hundred schemes cannot free it from suffering; a thousand clever arts cannot match. All the heavenly courts came to shelter; all the Saints joined with weapons. Show mercy on Mother Mu, fix your resolve, and awaken Lady Huang. The whole battle shook heaven and stirred the earth; the struggle sought to trap and encircle. On that bank they raised flags and shouted; on this bank they pounded drums and clanged gongs. Spears and sabers flashed, a cold glint of blades in dense ranks. Swords and halberds rose in swarming kill, the demon soldiers were fierce and brave; how could divine arms withstand them? Sorrowful clouds hid the sun and moon; dark mist covered mountain and river. In harsh grappling and wrenching combat they fought; all because Tripitaka worshipped Amitabha. The demon king, made all the more vigorous and daring, led his troop forward to smother and slaughter.

Just when neither side could be declared victor, they heard Sun Wukong cry out, "Old Wukong has come!" Zhu Bajie called, "What of the baggage?" Wukong replied, "I can hardly say my own life will survive—how can I speak of baggage now?" Sha Wujing gripped his precious staff and said, "No more words. Go strike the demon now." The star spirits, the Jie-di, and the Dingjia gods had been trapped in the battle center and were being butchered by the fiends together. The old demon swung his staff and struck all three. The Wanderer, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing dropped their staves and staffs and raised nails and spikes to meet it. In truth, the earth seemed dark and the sky dim; they could not gain the upper hand. They even slew so that the Sun star vanished into the mountain root in the west and the Moon star rose over the seahead in the east. Seeing evening draw near, the demon sounded a whistle, ordering every demon to keep vigilance, and then he brought out the treasure. Sun Wukong clearly saw it: the monster unfastened the bundled sack and held it in his hand. Wukong cried, "This is bad—go!" and without heeding Zhu Bajie, Sha Wujing, or the heavenly gods, he leapt in successive bounds straight up into the ninth sky. The gods, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing could not fathom his intent. He tossed them up and even stuffed them all into that bundle before flying away. Then the demon king withdrew his men back toward the temple, ordered rope brought out again, and bound everyone as before. He hung Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing from beams in high suspension, tethered the White Dragon Horse behind, and bound the gods as well, lifting them all into the cellar and sealing it shut. The rest of the demons obeyed and each returned to his place; it need not be further related.

Now it is told that Sun Wukong, who had leapt into the ninth sky, had preserved his life. Seeing the demon troops returning, with no flags raised, he already knew the others had been captured. He suppressed his aura and fell onto the peak of the eastern mountain. Clenching his teeth, he railed against the demon, tears dripping as he thought of Tripitaka, then looked up toward the sky and suddenly was struck mute with a grieving cry. He called out, "Master, in which former life did you shape this tangle of sorrow, that in this life at every step one meets demon spirits? In such misery as this, with no escape, what is to become of us?" Alone, he sighed for a long while, then calmed himself and thought in the silence of his mind: "What kind of bundling sack does this demon carry that it can hold so many objects? And now he has even put in there heaven’s gods and heavenly generals, so many people besides. I must ask Heaven for aid, yet I fear offending the Jade Emperor. I remember there is a True Warrior of the North, called Zhenwu, the Great Lord who Quells Demons. He is now on Wudang Mountain in the Southern Continent. I should go and ask him to come save the Master from this danger." It is said:

The Way of immortality is not yet accomplished; monkeys and horses have scattered. Mind and spirit have no master; the five elements wither.

Still unknown is how this will end in the journey ahead. Listen, then, for the resolution in the next installment.
chapters.title: Chapter 65: A demon falsehood feigns a Little Leiyin rite; all four companions fall into grave misfortune.

chapters.html:
This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

After the Great Sage had no means left to act, he mounted a single auspicious cloud, rode his cloud-cart through the sky, and traveled straight to the Nanzhan Continent to bow at Wudang and petition the Great Deity Subduing Demons to explain the calamities of Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie, Sha Wujing, and the heavenly troops. He did not stop in midair; before the day was out, at dawn he beheld the Patriarch’s immortal realm. He drifted down gently upon the cloud’s crown and fixed his gaze: this was indeed a worthy place:

In the southeast of the great capital, in the middle heaven, lies the divine mountain-range. Lotus Peak rises lofty and proud; Purple-Cap Ridge stands in awesome grandeur. The waters of the Nine Rivers stretch far toward Jingyang; the hundred Yue ridges link together like paired wings. Above is the Treasure Cave of Great Emptiness, below the Vermilion-Ground Spirit Terrace. Gold and bronze gongs sound from thirty-six palaces, while host after host comes bearing incense. Shun and Yu offer prayers, upon jade tablets and golden books. Blue birds fly among pavilions and towers, banners and streamers with scarlet hems ripple in the wind. The earth is the mighty cosmos set in famed peaks; heaven opens into immortal lands, bright and empty. Several wild trees are in bloom, and across the mountain the fairy-grass spreads in color. Dragons lurk beneath ravines; tigers crouch inside cliffs. Their hush is like whispered words; tame deer wander as if they can walk with men. White cranes, with the clouds their mates, roost beside ancient cedars; blue pheasants and vermilion phoenixes sing toward the sun. Here is Yuxu, where the Master’s image abides, true immortal ground, the Golden Ridge gate of compassion that governs the world. The Patriarch of Shangdi was born to the King of Jingle and Empress Shansheng, who dreamed of swallowing the sunlight. When they awoke she conceived, and after fourteen months of pregnancy, in the first month of the first day of Kaihuang, in the year jiashen of that cycle, at midday he was born in the royal palace. In his lineage they said: As a child he was valiant and fierce; in manhood he was spirit-filled and numinous. He did not seize the throne, but devoted himself only to cultivation. His parents could not restrain him; he left the imperial palace behind. He entered perfect stillness and entered meditation in these mountains. His work fulfilled, he completed his practice, and he rose to heaven in broad daylight. The Jade Emperor decreed his title as Zhenwu. In response to Xuanyu he answered, and the turtle and snake formed one shape. He governed the heavens and the six directions, and all the spirits called him the Ten Thousand Spirits. Nothing hidden escaped his discernment; nothing open was beyond his grasp. At each cycle’s end and beginning he cut off demonic essence. Sun Great Sage, delighted by the immortal scenery, came in turn to the First Heaven Gate, the Second, and the Third. When he reached the outer court of the Great Hall of Supreme Harmony, he suddenly saw between auspicious light and omens a cluster of five hundred spirit officers. One stepped forward and asked, “Who comes there?” The Great Sage replied, “I am Sun Wukong, Great Sage Equal to Heaven, and I have come to meet the Master.” They reported him at once. The Patriarch descended, went out to the Great Hall of Supreme Harmony, and received him. The Wanderer bowed and said, “I come to trouble the old master with one matter.” “[What] matter?” the Patriarch asked. “I am escorting Tripitaka to obtain the sutras in the West, but the road is fraught with peril. In the Western Niuhe Continent stands a mountain called Little Western Heaven, and in that Little Leiyin Temple is a demon. When my Master entered the gate, he saw arhats, jiedi, bhikshus, and holy monks lined up in order and, taking them for true Buddhas, lay down in prostration. At once he was seized and bound. Carelessly, I too was taken; he hurled a golden gong over me and enclosed me in it, no seam of thread to pass through, its mouth clamped like tongs. By good fortune, Golden Dragon of the Capable-Serpent thrust his horn through it, entered the jing and drew me out, and I crushed the golden gong, startling the demon. In the fighting he threw a white cloth bundle and packed me, the twenty-eight stars, and the five-direction jiedi inside; then he tied us all up. That night I escaped and saved the stars and my master. Later, searching for the cloth and alms bowl, I again startled that monster and fought with the heavenly soldiers. He brought out another white bundle; while he fussed with it I recognized his voice and slipped away. All the rest were captured and packed by him again. I escaped with no other means, and so I have come to beg the Master’s help.” The Patriarch replied: “In the past, when I suppressed the north, I held the position of Zhenwu and cut down demons across the world by the Jade Emperor’s command. Later I shaved my hair and went barefoot, stepped across the leaping snake-turtle spirit, and took with me the five thunder generals, giant-serpent lions, fierce beasts and venomous dragons. By the summons of Primordial Heaven-Lord, I subdued the demonic haze of the northeast. Today I live peacefully on Wudang Mountain, at ease in the Hall of Supreme Harmony, with sea and mountains tranquil and heaven and earth clear. But now, in both Nanzhanbu and Beijuluo, demons ravage, and evil ghosts prowl in secret. Since the Great Sage has descended, I cannot remain still. Yet in the upper realms there is no imperial order for action, so I dare not stir war on my own. If I send all the gods, I fear punishment from the Jade Emperor; if I abandon the Great Sage entirely, I betray human feeling. I figure that even if demons haunt the western road, they are not yet a great calamity. I will therefore send with you the turtle and snake generals and five divine dragons to give aid; they will capture the demon-spirit and save your monk.”

After bowing his thanks to the Patriarch, the Great Sage set out at once with the turtle, the snake, and the dragon gods, each bringing their chosen elite troops, and turned toward the western continent’s boundary once more. In less than a day they arrived at Little Leiyin Temple, dropped the cloud in midair, and went straight to the gate, calling for battle.

Now it is said the Yellow-Browed Great King had gathered his host of demons beneath the treasure pavilion and was saying, “For two days now, that Monkey-Farer has not come. Who knows where he has gone to borrow soldiers.” As he had no time to finish his speech, a small demon at the front gate reported, “The Wukong has come with several dragon, snake, and turtle allies and is calling for battle outside the gate.” The demon king said, “How did that monkey get dragon, snake, and turtle allies? From where have such creatures come?” He quickly dressed in armor, came out of the gate, and shouted, “Who are these dragon gods, and from what realm do you come to invade my immortal territory?” The Five Dragons and two Generals had towering, fierce countenances and spirits alert, and cried out: “Impudent fiend! I am one of the five dragon gods and the two turtle-snake commanders who serve the Grand Master of the Hunyuan School, the Great Deity Subduing Demons of the Hall of Supreme Harmony at Wudang Mountain. Today, by summons from Sun Wukong, our Master’s seal has called us, and we have come here to capture you. Demon, release Tripitaka, the heavenly stars, and the others, and avoid death. If not, I will split this mountain’s monsters and reduce several halls to ash.” The demon, hearing this, grew furious and replied, “What power has this beast that dares to speak so arrogantly? No more words—come and eat my staff!” The five dragons raised the clouds and summoned rain; the two generals raised dust and sand with their spears and sabers and halberds. Sun Wukong charged behind with his iron staff. It was a ferocious clash:

The fierce demon unleashed force; the Wanderer sought troops. The fierce demon took the precious hall as if it were a Buddha image; the Wanderer sought troops and borrowed dragon gods from a distant holy land. Turtle and snake stirred water and fire; demons drew forth spear and blade. The five dragons came to the western road by imperial command, while the Wanderer held back for his master behind. Swords and halberds flashed like lightning, spears and swords gleamed like shimmering rainbows. That wolf-canine cudgel, hard and short of the wrist; this Golden-Hooped Staff moves as one wills. The clattering roars sounded like firecrackers, and the metallic ringing was like gold being struck. Water and fire came together against the demon, steel and blades swirled around the spirits. Their cries and shouts frightened tigers and wolves; the uproar shook ghosts and gods. The battle was at first too even to tell winner from loser, and the demon again seized treasures and jewels. The Great Sage, with the five dragons and two generals, fought the demon for half a time unit. Then the monster unfastened the bundle from his hand. Sun Wukong saw this and called out, “Hold still, all of you!” The dragon gods, turtle, and snake did not know what he meant and each halted his arms, pressing forward to block. In a flash the demon threw that white bundle into the air. The Great Sage, forgetting the five dragons and two generals, mounted his cloud-cart and leaped into the ninth sky to escape. The demon had packed the dragon gods, turtle, and snake into another bundle and gone off with them. The demon, satisfied with victory, returned to the temple and also bound them with rope, lifting them into a cellar and covering them over—no need to set forth the rest.

Now see: the Great Sage fell from the cloud and slanted against the mountaintop, exhausted and spiritless, muttering in vexed disgust, “That demon is truly formidable.” Unbeknownst to him, his eyes had begun to close as if with sleep. Suddenly he heard someone shout, “Great Sage, do not pretend to sleep—rise at once and seek aid. Your Master’s life hangs by a moment.” The Wanderer opened his eyes sharply and sprang up. It was the civil assistant of the sun-star. Wukong barked, “You little spirit, you always lurk there chasing blood-food and never come to offer a word at the proper hour. Today, yet, you come to startle me. Stretch out your staff and let old Sun beat two blows to relieve my temper.” The gong-cao hurriedly offered obeisance: “Great Sage, you are the joy-immortal among men; why be in a mood? We were ordered by the Bodhisattva at dawn to secretly guard Tripitaka. Together with the local earth gods we dared not leave his side even for a moment, so we could not come often for visits. Why should we be scolded for this?” The Great Sage said, “If you truly guard him, where now are the star host, the jiedi, Kalpa, and my own Master and my fellows? Where are they held and what sufferings do they endure?” The gong-cao answered, “Your master and his brother disciples hang in the pavilion corridor of the treasure hall. The host of stars has all been taken into the cellar and is punished there. For two days we have not heard from the Great Sage. Only now have we just seen the demon seize the divine dragon, the turtle, and the snake and send them again into the cellar, and so it seems you had brought those troops. The little gods came at once to find you. Great Sage, do not hold back, and do not delay. Go quickly, again, for aid.”

Hearing these words, the Great Sage could not help but shed tears and said to the gong-cao, “I now feel shame before the Celestial Court and humiliation before the heavenly sea-store. To ask why the Bodhisattva acted so; to face the Buddha-image of the Tathagata I am filled with sorrow. The ones taken were precisely the turtle, snake, and five dragons of Zhenwu Master’s host. I have no further way to seek rescue now—what am I to do?” The gong-cao smiled: “Do not be so tight of heart, old monkey. I remember a body of fine soldiers; if summoned at once they can certainly bring this under control. While the Great Sage came to Wudang, he passed through the Nanzhan Continent. Those troops are also on that same continent, at Xuyi Mountain in Pin City, now called Sizhōu. There is a Great National Master Bodhisattva Wang there, with broad divine powers. One disciple under him is called Prince Xiao Zhang, and he has four great generals; in former years they subdued the Mother of Medusas. Go to him yourself now; when he comes, his compassion will help, and surely the demon can be caught and your Master saved.” The Great Sage brightened and replied, “You go and protect my Master, let there be no harm to him. I will go and invite him on my own.”

The Great Sage sprang up on his jindou cloud, dodged away from the demon’s place, and rushed straight for Mount Xuyi, arriving in less than a day. On close inspection, it was truly a fine place:

South lies Jiangjin, the north looks onto the Huai River, the east opens to Haijiao, and the west connects with Fengfu. On the peak stand lofty towers and cloisters; in the mountain hollows, spring waters surge forth. Jagged, uncanny rocks and graceful, towering pines fill the slopes. Every kind of fruit is fresh in season; a thousand branches of flowers open to the sun. People move in crowds like ant ranks, and boats drift back like lines of wild geese. Above are Ru Rock-Lit Cave Hall, Dongyue Palace, Wuxian Shrine, and Guishan Temple, where bell-toned incense rises into the blue sky; also Glass Spring, Five-Pagoda Valley, Eight Immortal Terrace, and Apricot-Blossom Garden, and the light and trees reflect Bingcheng. White clouds do not pass across, and lone birds, wearied, sing as they return. How could one sing its beauty? This fairyland here is like the fabled Penglai. The Great Sage could not exhaust the sight, crossed the Huai, entered Bingcheng, and came to the gate of Great Sage Chan Temple. Again he saw imposing halls, bright long corridors, and a steep pagoda towering high. It was truly: Piercing the clouds, high as a thousand zhang, it leans against the river heavens; looking up, one sees gold urns piercing the blue sky. Light gathers from top to bottom to solidify the cosmos; east and west have no shadows, only screen-like reflections. Wind shakes the treasure bells, and heaven’s music is heard; sunlight on the ice-drake faces the Brahma palace. Soaring spirit-birds sometimes cry out; from afar the Huai stretches endless into the distance. The Great Sage walked on while still gazing, until he came under the two-story gate. Master Wang Bodhisattva had already known, and came out with Prince Xiao Zhang to receive him. Formalities completed, the Great Sage said, “I am escorting Tripitaka on his journey to the West for scriptures. On the road there is a Small Leiyin Temple where a yellow-bearded monster impersonates the Buddha. My Master could not tell true from false and prostrated, and was taken. Then the monster covered me with the gold clapper. Fortunately, by stars fallen from Heaven I was saved. I shattered the gold clapper, wrestled with him, and with a cloth bundle-bag I put Tian-shen, Jiedi, Galan, my Master, and my junior master-disciple all inside. I went to Wudang Mountain and begged Xuantian Emperor for aid; he sent five dragons, turtle, and snakes to seize the monster, but he was captured and put into that same bundle. My disciples have no one to rely on, so I come to implore the Bodhisattva. Show your full might, use your arts of drawing in water spirits and saving living beings, and go with this disciple to rescue my Master for one hardship. If we obtain the scriptures and return, their teaching will spread in China forever, proclaiming Buddha’s wisdom and raising the waves of prajñā.” Master Wang said, “What you have done today is truly an enlargement of my Buddha’s teaching, and I should go myself. But now is early summer, when the Huai waters are rising. I have only just taken in the Great Sage of the Water Ape; when he sees water he immediately stirs up trouble, and if I leave, he will run wild in the air with no spirit able to tame him. For now, take this young disciple, lead the four generals, and go with you to give help. Go capture and subdue the demon.”

The Great Sage thanked him, then with the four generals and Prince Xiao Zhang rode on cloud back to Little Western Heaven, straight to Small Leiyin Temple. Prince Xiao Zhang took up a zhu-bai spear; the four great generals brandished four kunhu swords, and Sun Wukong advanced with the Great Sage to exchange taunts and blows. The little demon sent word again. The demon king then rallied his bandits with drums and shouting, and came out, saying, “Monkey, whom have you dared to bring here this time?” Before he could finish, Prince Xiao Zhang gave the signal; the four generals moved up together and called, “Rabid demon spirit! Your face has no skin—do you not know who we are here?” The demon king said, “Which minor commander is that, so bold as to aid him?” The prince replied, “I am disciple of Master Wang Bodhisattva, the Great Sage of Sizhou, leading four great divine generals. By order, I have come to seize you.” The demon king laughed, “You child—what martial art do you have that dares come here with this bravado?” The prince said, “If you wish to know my arts, then hear me:

My family is from the western land of the Country of Flowing Sand; my father once was king of the Sands. Since childhood my body carried many ailments; the malignant star of Hua-gai plagued my destiny. Seeking my master and longing for the Way of Long Life, I was fated to meet him and leave the prescription-way behind. Half a grain of cinnabar-powder eased disease and drove it back, and I swore to practice and forgo becoming king. Having learned, I gained agelessness and heavenly longevity; my face remains forever like a youth’s. I once hurried to the Dragon-Wonder Assembly, and once leapt to the Buddha hall through flying clouds. I seized mist and held wind to capture water monsters, caught dragons and subdued tigers, and stilled mountain grounds. I built lofty Buddha towers to steady the people; in the quiet sea shines the relic-light deep and bright. The tip of this zhu-bai spear can bind fiends; with sleeves of pale black I can bring demons to heel. Here in tranquil Bingcheng my fame now rises—my name is Xiao Zhang!” The demon king listened and gave a light cold smile: “You, little prince, abandoned a kingdom to follow Master Wang Bodhisattva and learned this art of longevity and immortality. It is good only for catching Water-Monster spirits, yet how could you believe monkey Wukong’s lies, cross thousands of hills and rivers, and come here to offer your life? See if you can truly be immortal and ageless?”

Hearing this, the small prince grew very angry, and at once twined his spear and stabbed forward. The four great generals rushed as one; Sun Wukong stepped in with his iron staff and struck again. The demon, a fine demon-spirit indeed, stood without fear. He raised his short, soft wolf-tooth club, blocking left and right, and charged straight and broad. A fierce fight ensued:

The little prince, zhu-bai spear, and the four kunhu swords were even stronger. Wukong again used the Golden-Hooped Staff, and together they encircled and struck at the demon king. The demon king truly had great divine power and feared not a hair’s breadth of either side; he did not mind the slightest resistance. The wolf-tooth club was a treasure from within the Buddha’s realm; with sword and spear-swing he was not easily harmed. One only heard the furious wind roaring, and at once saw evil qi in a vast fog. One side delighted in displaying skill, while this side was singularly focused on the Buddha-mission for scripture. After many charges, after repeated bouts of arrogance, he sprayed cloud and mist, obscured the three lights, and unleashed all manner of anger and wrath in disorder. For a long while, even the unsurpassed Dharma of the Three Vehicles, and all their highest arts, were brought to a painful, humbled close.

After the many-parted battle had gone on for long, there was no clear victory. The demon then opened the bundle-bag again. The Great Sage called out, “All of you, be careful.” Prince Xiao Zhang and the rest did not know what that warning meant. With a single sliding sound, the monster took the four generals and the prince and put them into the bundle one more time. Only the Great Sage, foreknowing, had already slipped away. Victorious, the demon king returned to the temple, ordered ropes brought, had him bound, and sent him to the cellar, sealed in and locked in strong bonds; nothing further is worth recounting.

The Great Sage rose with his jindou cloud and stood in midair. Seeing the monster return with his men and shut the gates, he lowered the auspicious light and stood upon the western hillside, looking out in sorrow and crying:

Since receiving the Dharma and entering the Chan grove, I have deeply benefited from the Bodhisattvas’ deliverance. I guard your journey west for the Great Way, helping together to reach Leiyin. I was told it was a broad and smooth road like a goat’s path; who could have thought a towering monster would invade? In a hundred schemes and a thousand methods I could not save you, running east and west to implore in vain.

At the time the Great Sage was at his most desolate and sad, he saw at once a rainbow-colored cloud descending on the southwest. The whole mountain-head burst into vivid rain. A voice called out, “Wukong, do you recognize me?” The Great Sage hurried forward and looked; that figure was:

Broad ears and a wide, level jaw, broad-shouldered, full-bellied, and sturdy of frame. A chest full of springlike joy, eyes like autumn waters bright and rippling. His sleeves flew open with abundant blessing-luck, and his straw sandals made him stride with great vigor. In the Pure Land of Supreme Bliss, he is first among the venerable ones: Namo Maitreya, the Laughing Monk. Wukong immediately prostrated and said, “Laughing Buddha Maitreya, where do you come from? My disciple failed to avoid him and blundered badly—sins upon sins.” Maitreya said, “I have come only for this Small Leiyin monster of yours.” Wukong said, “I am greatly indebted for your boundless kindness. Please tell me: from where does that monster come, what kind of deluding spirit is he, and where is he from? I do not know what that bundle-bag is; please show it to me.” Maitreya said, “He is one of the yellow-bearded youths before my hall. On the third day of the third month I traveled to the Primordial Origin Assembly and left him in the palace as watchman. He stole those few treasures of mine, posed as a Buddha, and became a true spirit-form. That bundle-bag is my after-nourishing sack, known in common speech as the ‘human-seed sack.’ That wolf-tooth club is actually a clapper for striking the bell.” When Wukong heard this, he cried out, “Fine laughing monk indeed. You let this child escape, taught him to counterfeit you as Buddha and to set up false accusations against Old Sun. This is surely a lapse in household discipline.” Maitreya said, “One fault is mine: I was careless with a lost person. The other is that your disciples’ demonic obstacles are not yet finished, and so in this age many spirits descend and should undergo hardship. I have now come to take him away with you.”

Wukong asked, “The spirit of this demon has vast powers, and you have no weapons. How can you capture him?” Maitreya smiled and said, “Below this mountain slope I have set up a grass hut and planted a melon field. Go to him and challenge him. In combat, never truly win—only appear to lose—and lure him into my melon patch. All my other melons are unripe; you alone must become a great ripe melon. He will insist on eating him, and I will then eat both of you. Once he is in my belly, do whatever you wish to arrange there to him. Then I shall take his bundle-bag and put him back in it.” Wukong said, “Though this plan is clever, how can you tell the melon has ripened? And how will he agree to follow me here?” Maitreya smiled, “I am one who governs the age, my慧眼 is sharp and high; can I fail to know you? Whatever form you take, I know. I only fear the demon may not follow, so I will teach you one art.” Wukong said, “He undoubtedly wraps us in the bundle-bag. How could he then follow me?” Maitreya smiled, “Stretch out your hand.” Wukong immediately relaxed his left hand and held it out. Maitreya wet the tip of his right index finger with divine water from his mouth and wrote the character “禁” on Wukong’s palm, teaching him to clutch a fist. When the demon-spirit sees this and lets go before him, he will follow.

The Journeyer squared his fists and, with pleasure, accepted the challenge. With one hand he brandished the iron staff, marched out in front of the mountain gate, and cried, 「Demon fiend, your Grandpa Sun comes again. Come out at once and settle this with me." The small demon hurried to report. The demon king asked, 「How many troops has he brought this time to call a fight?" The little demon said, 「No troops at all, only him." The king laughed. 「That monkey has exhausted his tricks and his strength. He can call on no one. Certainly he has come to meet his death." Then he composed himself, took up his treasured weapon, raised the light and pliant rhinoceros-horn staff, and came out, crying, 「Sun Wukong, this time you cannot pull through." The Journeyer shouted back, 「You impudent fiend, do you think I cannot contend?" The king said, 「I see the monkey’s schemes have run out and his strength has spent itself. He has no one to go to for help and has come on his own in defiance. I have him now; with no heavenly troop to save him, that is why I say he cannot struggle out." The Journeyer replied, 「This brute knows no life or death. Stop talking. Take this staff from me." The demon king, seeing him swing the rod with one hand, could not help laughing: 「That monkey—watch him, how does he use a cudgel with only one hand and still look so crafty?" The Journeyer said, 「Boy, you cannot stop me with both hands. Even if I do not use my paired-clinch move and even if three or five came at once, they would still lose to Old Sun’s one hand." Hearing this, the king said, 「All right, all right. I will not use the treasure weapon now. I will meet you in fair combat, just strength against strength." He raised the rhinoceros-horn cudgel and came out to duel. The Journeyer faced him squarely, set his fist, and swung both hands with the staff. The demon, bound by an enforced spell and not thinking to retreat, truly did not try the paired-strike; he only chased with his staff. The Journeyer made a feint and withdrew in seeming defeat. The demon kept charging to the foot of the western slope.

The Journeyer saw a melon patch. He rolled, then slipped in and became a great ripe, sweet melon. The demon stopped and looked in all directions, not knowing where the Journeyer had gone. He then chased to the edge of the hermit hut and called, 「Who planted these melons?" Maitreya transformed into an old melon grower and came from the thatched hut to answer, 「Great King, this poor man planted them." The demon king asked, 「Are there ripe melons?" Maitreya said, 「There are ripe ones." The king ordered, 「Pluck me a ripe one. I am thirsty." Immediately Maitreya presented the melon in which the Journeyer had become, and with both hands offered it to the king. The demon king did not suspect the ruse; he took it, and with his mouth bit in. The Journeyer seized this chance and, as one wheel spun, slipped right beneath his throat. He did not pause for a better moment; he moved his hands and feet within, grasping the intestines, turning and wrenching from the roots, setting a skittering motion inside. The demon cried out in pain, tusks of pain in his jaw, eyes brimming with tears, and he rolled the melon field like a threshing ground. His only cry was, 「Enough—enough! Who will come to my rescue?" Then Maitreya revealed his true form, chuckling, and called, 「Accursed beast, do you recognize me?" The demon looked up and, in panic, knelt on the ground, rubbing his belly with both hands and knocking his head, crying only, 「Lord, spare my life, spare my life. I will not dare again." Maitreya stepped forward, grabbed him, untied his after-heaven bag, and took the clapper mallet from him. He said, 「Sun Wukong, for my sake, spare him."

The Journeyer was deeply enraged, but still he struck with his left fist and right foot, digging and pounding wildly inside. The demon writhed in unbearable pain and sank to the ground. Maitreya said again, 「Wukong, he has had enough. Spare him." The Journeyer then said, 「Open wide your mouth and wait for Old Sun to come out." Although the demon suffered gut-rot pain, he had not yet given up his life. As the proverb says, 「A man does not die until he breaks in spirit; when petals fall and leaves fall, the root is already decayed." When he heard to open his mouth, he bore the pain and opened it as wide as he could. The Journeyer then leapt out and returned to his true form. He drew back the staff as if to strike, but by then the Buddha had already packed the demon into a bag and had him slung diagonally at the waist. Holding the clapper in hand, Buddha scolded, 「Abominable creature! Who stole the golden clapper, and where has it gone?" The demon, inside the after-heaven bag, could only whimper in complaint, 「Sun Wukong smashed the clapper." Buddha said, 「If the clapper is broken, return me my gold." The demon answered, 「The broken gold is piled on the lotus platform in the hall."

The Buddha, carrying the bag and holding the clapper, laughed and called, 「Wukong, come with me to recover the gold." Seeing such divine power, the Journeyer dared not disobey. He led the Buddha up the mountain and back to the monastery, and gathered the broken gold. The mountain gate was tightly shut, but the Buddha, with one tap of the clapper and one pointed finger, opened it. When they entered, they saw the small demons, now knowing the old fiend had been captured, all collecting what was in their sacks and trying to run off in all directions. The Journeyer saw one, struck one; saw two, struck two. He beat the five-to-seven hundred small demons all to death. Each showed its true body: mountain spirits, tree demons, beastly fiends, winged birds of evil. The Buddha gathered the gold in one heap, blew out a trace of immortal breath, chanted a spell, and in an instant restored them to their original forms. He recovered a full pair of golden clappers. After seeing the Journeyer off, he mounted a lucky cloud and turned straight for the Western Pure Lands.

Only then did the Great Sage untie and release Tang Sanzang, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing. The Pigsy had hungered for many days and, panicked with hunger, went not to thank the Great Sage at once; instead, with his waist bent, he ran to the kitchen in search of food. It happened that the demon had set out the noon meal, but because the Journeyer had demanded combat, none had eaten yet. Seeing it, he ate half a pot. Then he brought out two bowlfuls and called the Master and his younger brothers to each take two bowls. Only then did he thank the Great Sage. When told about the origin of the demon trouble, the Journeyer recounted in full how he had first invited the Patriarch, then the Turtle and the Snake, then later borrowed the Prince for the Great Sage, and also how Maitreya subdued and captured him. Hearing this, Tripitaka’s thanks could not be exhausted, and he respectfully knelt and bowed to all the heavens, saying, 「Disciples, where are these sacred beings confined?" The Journeyer answered, 「Yesterday the laboring magistrate told old Wukong that all of them are inside the pit." He said, 「Zhu Bajie, you and I will go free them."

With his strength restored by the meal, the Piggy shook himself and gathered his courage. He found his spiked rake-and-shovel weapon and, together with the Great Sage, went to the back. There he opened the underground cellar and untied all the bindings, bringing everyone out beneath the precious tower. Tripitaka put on his kasaya and, facing upward, bowed in thanks to each in turn. Only then did this Great Sage send the Five Dragons and the Two Generals back to Wudang, send young Prince Zhang and his four generals back to Bin City, and then send the Twenty-Eight Mansions back to the Celestial Court, dispatching Jie-di and Jia-lan each to their own realms.

The three disciples only rested there for half a day. After feeding the white horse and repacking their baggage, they set out the next morning. As they were about to depart, they lit a fire and burned the precious tower, the jeweled seat, the tall pavilions, and the lecture hall to ashes.

No attachments and no entanglements — flee danger and tribulation, remove calamity and obstacle, and walk forth in freedom.

Still it remains unknown when they will at last reach Great Thunder Sound. Let us await the next chapter’s resolution.
