This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

With the report, Sun Wukong accompanied an attendant eunuch into the inner palace and stood outside the gate of the inner sleeping chambers. He had three lengths of golden thread brought in and instructed: "Tell the palace ladies or attending eunuchs to tie them first under His Majesty’s left wrist at the cun, guan, and chi points, and then pass the thread ends through the window lattice to me." The eunuch, obeying, invited the king to sit on the dragon couch, tied one end at each of cun, guan, and chi with golden thread, and drew the other end out through the window. Sun Wukong took the ends; with his right thumb he first supported his index finger and read the cun pulse; then he placed his middle finger over his thumb and read the guan pulse; then he settled his thumb against his ring finger and read the chi pulse. He regulated his own breathing and distinguished the pattern into four qi, five congestion, seven outer signs, eight inner signs, nine stages, floating in, sinking out, sinking in, and floating out, and thus made clear the root of deficiency and excess. He then ordered the left hand untied and, as before, tied it below the right wrist. Sun Wukong then checked, with his left hand, each point one by one all the way through, shook his body once, and drew the gold thread back to himself. He shouted in a clear, loud voice: "Your Majesty, the left cun is strong and tight, the left guan is constricted and slow, and the left chi is hollow and sinking; the right cun is floating and slippery, the right guan is slow and knotted, and the right chi is quick and firm. A left cun that is strong and tight means pain in the heart with internal emptiness. A guan that is constricted and slow means perspiration and muscle numbness. A chi that is hollow and sinking means red urine and stools tainted with blood. A floating, slippery right cun means internal knots closing the channels. A delayed, knotted right guan means leftover food and drink retained. A quick and firm right chi means vexation and fullness contending with empty-cold. This serious royal disease is called ‘the two birds losing their flock.’" The king inside heard this. His whole heart rejoiced, he regained his spirit, and he called out loudly: "Your diagnosis through pulse-taking is clear. Your diagnosis is clear—it is exactly this disease. Ask them to bring the medicine and give it now."

Sun Wukong only slowly walked out of the palace. Already, the eunuchs listening nearby had reported the matter to the others. Soon he came out, and Tripitaka asked, "How does it stand?" Sun Wukong replied, "I have examined the pulse; now I will prepare medicine that matches the condition." The officials came forward and said, "The holy monk elder just spoke of the disease called ‘the two birds losing their flock.’ What is it?" Sun Wukong laughed: "There are male and female birds, originally flying together in one place. Suddenly a violent wind and hailstorm frighten them apart; the hen cannot see the rooster, and the rooster cannot see the hen. The hen longs for the rooster; the rooster longs for the hen. Is this not ‘the two birds losing their flock’?" Hearing this, the officials cried together, "Truly a divine monk! Truly a divine physician!" and praised him unceasingly. Then one court physician asked, "The state of the disease is understood, but we do not know what medicine should be used." Sun Wukong answered, "No fixed prescription is required; when I see the medicine, I administer it." The physician said, "The classic says, ‘There are eight hundred and eight kinds of medicine and four hundred and four kinds of illness.’ A disease does not belong to one person only; how can one medicine be fully applicable to all? How can one claim to prescribe from sight of the medicine alone?" Sun Wukong said, "The ancients said, ‘Medicine should not be tied to a fixed formula, but used to fit the case.’ Therefore I must summon all medicines and add or subtract as needed."

The physician said nothing more, then went out beyond the court gate and sent the on-duty officials of the office through the city to all herb shops, asking for fresh and prepared drugs. For each kind he requested three jin and brought them to Sun Wukong. Sun said, "This is no pharmacy. Take the total list and number of all medicines, and all apparatus for compounding, and send them all to the guest hall, and have my two junior brothers take charge." The physician obeyed, sending all eight hundred and eight medicines, three jin each, plus grinding stones, mills, sieves, medicinal milk, milk bowls, and milk pestles, all of it, to the hall and handing everything over in full.

Sun Wukong went to the hall and invited Tripitaka to come and make the medicine there. Tripitaka had just risen when an order came from the inner palace: "Hold the monk here; let him stay the night in Wenhua Hall. When he takes the medicine at dawn and the disease is cured, give thanks and send him off with the gate-pass documents." Tripitaka was greatly alarmed: "Disciple, this means they intend to keep me here as the king in charge. If he is cured, he will gladly send us away joyfully; if he is not cured, my life is ended. You must attend carefully, with utmost devotion and strictness." Sun laughed: "Master, stay at ease. Here in this place my old monkey has a hand fit to cure a state."

With that, Sun Wukong left Tripitaka, bade farewell to the ministers, and went straight back to the hall. Zhu Bajie greeted him with a laugh: "Brother, I know what you’re up to." Sun asked, "What do you know?" Zhu Bajie said, "I know your mission to fetch the scriptures has not gone right. You want to make a living with no root. Seeing this rich place, you are going to set up a drug shop." Sun barked: "Do not speak nonsense. After curing the king, I will leave as soon as dismissed and continue on the road. What drug shop are you talking about?" Zhu Bajie argued, "Not so. These eight hundred and eight medicines, three jin each, total two thousand four hundred twenty-four jin. We are treating only one man—how much can that use? Who knows how many ages it will all be eaten?" Sun said, "Do we need that much? Those court physicians are all dull-witted, so this amount was ordered to make them have no way to guess, and they cannot tell which of my medicines are truly in use, nor can they identify my marvelous prescription."

While they were speaking, two attendants from the hall came forward and knelt, saying: "Please, Great Monk, come and take the evening meal." Sun asked, "Earlier he had this treatment for me; now you kneel and invite me—why?" One attendant knocked his head and said, "When Your Honour arrived, this servant had eyes but no discernment and failed to recognize your honored face. Now that we hear you have displayed threefold strength and cured our ruler, if His Majesty recovers, Your Honour gains reward in this land and we are all his subjects. It is only proper that we kneel and make welcome." Sun Wukong, hearing this, ascended in good spirits and sat down. Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing sat on either side. The meal was laid, and Sha Wujing asked, "Brother, where is Tripitaka now?" Sun said, "Tripitaka was kept by the king as an honored head of the household. He must wait until he cures the king, and then be thanked and sent on his way." Sha asked again, "Does Master have enough to eat there?" Sun said, "How could the king not have attendants? When I came, he already had three attendants and chamber helpers beside him, and he was escorted into Wenhua Hall." Zhu Bajie said, "Then Master is truly fortunate: he has three attendants and you have only two hall men attending us. Forget that—let me the old pig eat a full meal." So the three brothers ate at ease.

It was already late. Sun Wukong called to the attendants: "Clear the household fire and bring plenty of oil lamps and wax; when night is quiet we can make the medicine." The attendants did exactly that, bringing a supply of oil and wax and sending everyone away.

By midnight, the city streets were quiet and all sounds had ceased. Zhu Bajie said, "Brother, what medicine is this? Hurry and work now—I’m nodding off." Sun said, "Take one liang of rhubarb and grind it to a fine powder." Sha Wujing said, "Rhubarb is bitter, cold, and non-poisonous. Its nature is heavy and not rising; its use is to go forward without lingering. It drives away many stases without blockage, settles disorder, and brings order. It is called ‘General.’ This would be a medicinal herb, but with this long illness and weakness it should not be used." Sun laughed: "Younger brother knows nothing. This medicine helps phlegm and smooths qi, disperses the cold-heat knots in the abdomen. Do not interfere. Go take one liang of croton bean, remove shell and membrane, pound out its oil-poison, and grind it fine." Zhu Bajie said, "Croton is pungent, hot, and toxic. It cuts hard accumulations, disperses the cold in lungs and bowels, opens blockages and unblocks paths for water and grain. It is a gate-breaking force and a door-cleaving weapon; not for light use." Sun said, "Younger brother does not understand. This medicine breaks knots and opens the bowels, and can settle distended heart and swelling from gas. Make it at once; I still have subordinate medicines to add and assist."

The two immediately ground the two medicines to fine powder and said, "Brother, which of those dozens are still needed?" Sun said, "No others." Zhu Bajie said, "Eight hundred and eight medicines, three jin each, and you are only using these two liang—surely this is grabbing at everything." Sun handed over a flowered porcelain cup and said, "Younger brother, take this cup and scrape half a cup of ash from the stove-stern and bring it back." Zhu Bajie asked, "For what use?" Sun said, "It is needed inside the medicine." Sha Wujing said, "I have never seen stove-ash used in formulations." Sun replied, "Stove-ash is called ‘Bai Cao Shuang,’ capable of harmonizing a hundred illnesses. You do not know that?" The fool scraped half a cup indeed and ground it fine.

Sun then gave him the cup again: "Now go bring back half a cup of our horse’s urine." Zhu Bajie asked, "What for?" Sun said, "For making the pills." Sha Wujing said with a laugh, "Brother, this is no child’s game. Horse urine is rank and foul—how can it be added to medicine? I have only seen vinegar paste, old rice paste, melted honey, or plain water used as binders for pills. Has horse urine ever been used? The smell alone makes a person with weak spleen and stomach vomit. Add croton and rhubarb, and one could be made to vomit and purge both up and down. Are you jesting?" Sun said, "You do not know what is inside this: my horse is no ordinary horse. He was once a dragon form from the Western Sea. If he can be made willing to pass urine, he will relieve whatever illness you can name. I only need it quickly." When Zhu Bajie heard this, he truly went out to the forecourt. The horse was lying diagonally on the ground, asleep. The fool stamped and kicked it in the belly and waited; after some time, not a drop appeared. He returned and told Sun, "Brother, don’t go yet to treat the emperor. Go treat this horse first. The poor beast is tightly constricted and will not pass a drop." Sun said, "I will go with you." Sha Wujing said, "I’ll go see too."

All three came to the horse. The horse reared up, spoke in human speech, and shouted in a fierce voice: 「Brother, how can you not know? I was a flying dragon of the Western Sea. For having violated heavenly law, Guanyin saved me, sawed off my horns, peeled off my scales, and turned me into a horse, so that I might bear the Master to the Western Heaven in quest of the scriptures and work off my crimes. If I pass over water and urinate, the fish in it become dragons when they eat it; if I pass over mountains and urinate, the mountain grasses take the flavor and become lingzhi, which the celestial maidens pick for long life. How could I be so casually cast away in this dusty world?" Sun Wukong said, 「Brother, speak carefully. This is the realm of the Western King; it is not mere worldly vulgarity, nor is it a place to cast off lightly. As the saying goes, 'Many hairs make one full-lined robe.' We must treat this king of the land. If we cure him, all will be illumined; if not, we may all fail to leave this place." The horse only cried once, 「Wait." See it: he lunged forward once, squatted back once, and with the crackling clack of all its teeth, managed to bring out only a few drops before standing upright. Pigsy said, 「This horseman, this one called Jin-zhi, let him pass a little more." Sun Wukong saw there was only a little over half a cup and said, 「Enough. Enough. Take him away." Sha Wujing was only then overjoyed.

The three returned to the hall, mixed the earlier medicinal ingredients together, and rolled three large pills. Sun Wukong said, 「Brother, that is too big." Pigsy said, 「It is only as big as a walnut; even by my measure it is not enough for one bite." So they put them in a small box, and the brothers, still in their robes, lay down to sleep. Not a word all night; by dawn, it was already morning.

The king, sunk in illness, held court and, on seeing Tripitaka, then ordered the officials to go at once to the reception hall and pay respects to the holy monk Sun Wukong’s master, to go and fetch medicine.

The officials came along to the hall. Bowing on the ground, they said to Sun Wukong, 「His Majesty has specifically commanded us to receive the marvelous remedy." Sun Wukong told Pigsy to fetch the box, lifted the lid, and handed it to the officials. One said, 「What is this medicine called? We must report it to the king clearly." Sun Wukong said, 「Its name is Wujin Dan." Pigsy and the other one laughed quietly, 「Mixed with pot ash? How could that be Wujin?" The officials asked, 「What vehicle or anupana do you use with it?" Sun Wukong said, 「Both kinds work. There is a simple sort: six things, then decocted and taken with the medicine." They asked, 「What six things?" Sun Wukong said, 「The droppings of a raven that flies midair; carp urine borne by swift-flowing water; face powder used by the Queen Mother when she anoints her face; alchemical ash from Laojun's furnace; three pieces torn from the Jade Emperor’s headcloth; and five strands of constrained dragon-whiskers. Decoction of these six with the pill will, when the king takes it, remove his anxious illness." They said, 「Such things are unknown in the mortal world. May I ask what the easier anupana is?" Sun Wukong said, 「Use rootless water." The officials laughed, 「That one is easy." Sun Wukong said, 「How can you call that easy?" One official said, 「In common saying, for rootless water you take a bowl by the well or by the riverbank, scoop up water, turn briskly away without setting it down or turning back, and carry it home to the sick person." Sun Wukong said, 「Water from wells and rivers is all with roots. By rootless water I mean water fallen from heaven and not touching ground when taken." Another official said, 「Even that is easy. Wait until the sky darkens and rains, then give him the medicine."

After giving thanks to Sun Wukong, they took the medicine back and presented it. The king was greatly pleased and ordered attendants to bring it forward. He looked at it and asked, 「What kind of pills are these?" The official said, 「The holy monk called it Wujin Dan, to be taken with rootless water." The king then ordered court attendants to fetch such water. The officials said, 「The monk said rootless water is not from wells or rivers; it must be that which falls from heaven and has not touched earth." The king then called the weather official and ordered him to pray for rain. The officials carried out the decree; no further account is given.

Sun Wukong, in the hall pavilion, called out to Pigsy, 「He allowed rootless water fallen from above, so this is needed for the medicine. It is urgent now—how can we get rainwater at once? I think this king is in truth a ruler of great worth. Why not help him by bringing him some rainwater for the remedy?" Pigsy asked, 「How can we do that?" Sun Wukong said, 「You stand on my left and serve as the Fuxing constellation. And you stand on my right as the Bishou. I will have Elder Sun summon him some rootless water." Then, the Great Sage stepped into the heavenly formula and chanted a mantra; soon an ink-dark cloud rose in the east and inched toward the crown of the hall. He called out, 「Great Sage, Dragon King Ao Guang of the Eastern Sea, come." Sun Wukong said, 「Forgive the disturbance only as necessary. I ask you to help by supplying rootless water for the king’s medicine." The Dragon King replied, 「When I answered your summons, you did not ask for water. I came alone; I brought no rain vessel, and there is no wind, cloud, or thunder. How can rain be brought down?" Sun Wukong said, 「We need none of that now—no wind, no cloud, no thunder, and no driving rain. Only some water enough to guide the medicine will suffice." The Dragon King said, 「If so, let me have two fits of sniveling and spit out a little phlegm and saliva for him to take." Sun Wukong rejoiced, 「Excellent, excellent. No hesitation—act at once."

The old dragon gradually lowered the dark cloud lower in the sky until it was above the palace. He hid his form in concealment and spat a mouthful of saliva, which became sweet rain. The whole court rose in one voice and praised, 「Our sovereign is blessed beyond measure; Heaven itself has sent sweet rain." The king then issued an order: have vessels ready, and whether within or beyond the palace, whether high officials or low, all must store this heavenly sweet water to rescue the sovereign. Look then: all the civil and military officials, the inner court of three palaces and six apartments, the empresses and consorts, three thousand attendants in silk, and eight hundred beauties came with cup and ladle, bowl and goblet, each ready to catch the sweet rain. The old dragon, in midair, dispersed and transformed the saliva, never straying from before and behind the palace. After about an hour, the Dragon King took leave of the Great Sage and returned to the sea. The ministers gathered the cups and bowls and vessels they had collected—some with one or two ladles, some with three to five, and some with none at all—combined them all together to about three cups and presented them on the imperial tray. Truly, strange fragrance flooded the Golden Hall, and rich flavor drifted through the Son of Heaven’s court.

The king dismissed the monk and took the Wujin Dan and sweet rain back into the inner palace. He swallowed one pill and drank one cup. He swallowed another pill and drank another cup. Three times in all: three pills and three cups were taken. Soon the belly roared, sounding like a wheel and shuttle without end. He took a clean bucket and purged three to five times. After drinking some rice gruel, he leaned down and collapsed onto the dragon bed. Two concubines came to inspect the bucket and said there was no end to the foul phlegm and spittle, and within it a single lump of glutinous-rice porridge. One came before the dragon bed to report: 「The root of the illness has all gone down." Hearing this, the king rejoiced greatly and took another serving of rice.

After a short while, he slowly felt his chest and heart expand and ease, his qi and blood brought into harmony, and his spirit bright and vigorous, his legs strength restored. He got off the dragon bed, donned court robes, and went up to the treasure hall. Seeing Tripitaka, he immediately threw himself down and prostrated. The abbott hurriedly returned the courtesy. After the bowing, with an imperial hand he assisted him and said, 「Prepare an invitation slip quickly. Write on it: 'I bow once more in deep obeisance.' Send officials to invite the three senior disciples of the Dharma master. Open the eastern hall and have Guanglu Temple set a banquet in thanks." The officials took the command; the invitations were prepared, the banquet arranged. Truly it was as if the kingdom had strength to move mountains, and in a moment all was complete.

Pigsy, seeing the summons delivered by the officials, could not hide his joy and said, 「Elder brother, this is truly a marvelous remedy. The thanks now—this success is your merit." Sha Wujing said, 「What are you saying, second brother? As the saying goes, 'If one person has fortune, it carries the whole household.' We all made this medicine together and all are men of merit. Just partake and enjoy, and say no more." Ah, look at the three brothers—happy and joyful—they went straight into court.

The officials guided them in. In the east pavilion they saw that Tripitaka, the king, and the ministers had already arranged the feast. Sun Wukong, Pigsy, and Sha Wujing offered a formal bow to their master before the others arrived. Later the full court came in. Up there were four plain tables, each with a spread enough to satisfy at ten glances. In front there was one rich meat table, also ample enough to satisfy ten times over. On both sides stood four or five hundred single tables, arranged in perfect order:

Ancient words say: "The dishes are a hundredfold of every flavor, blessed feast worth a thousand measures of wine. Pearl-like cream and rich curds, silk-threaded fat and red sheen. Treasure-bright floral displays dazzle with color; fruits offer deep fragrance. Sugared dragons coil in battle lines, lion-immortal forms in pairs; oven-drawn cakes and disks are set out like mate phoenixes." The meat side had every kind of pork, lamb, chicken, goose, fish, and duck. The vegetarian side had vegetables, bamboo shoots, wood-ear mushrooms, and fungi. Several kinds of fragrant soup breads appeared, and sugar-crisp confections were repeatedly passed. Soft yellow millet rice and fresh reed-grain gruel were served. Every sort of powdered broth was fragrant and spicy and yet sweet when replaced again and again. The ruler and ministers raised cups before seating themselves, while rank and station were observed and vessels passed in order.

The king took a cup in his imperial hand and first sat Tripitaka properly. Tripitaka said, 「This poor monk does not drink wine." The king said, 「This is plain wine; what if the monk drinks one cup of it?" Tripitaka said, 「For monks, wine is the first precept of abstinence." The king was not pleased and asked, 「The monk abstains from drinking—what then shall I offer as honor?" Tripitaka said, 「Let the three of the unruly disciples drink in his stead." The king then happily set aside the golden ewer and passed it to Sun Wukong. Sun Wukong took the wine, offered obeisance to all, and drank one cup. Seeing he drank with ease, he offered another cup. Sun Wukong, without objecting, drank again. The king laughed, 「Drink from the Three-Treasure cup." Again Sun Wukong drank. The king called for yet another fill, 「Now drink from the Four-Season cup."

Bajie sat at the side. Since no wine was offered to him, he endured the trickle of saliva he kept gulping in noisy bursts and said nothing. Again he saw the king pressing Sun Wukong earnestly, so he called him up and said, “Your Majesty, even I have been harmed by the medicine you took; that medicine contains horse…” Hearing this, Sun Wukong, fearing the fool might spread the word, handed his cup to Bajie. Bajie then drank it but still did not speak. The king asked, “The holy monk said the medicine had horse in it. What kind of horse is it?” Sun Wukong took the cup and said, “My brother’s mouth is naturally broad. He has a reliable prescription from experience, and he is about to tell others. Your Majesty’s morning dose contained ma-duo-ling.” The king asked the officials, “What flavor is ma-duo-ling, and what conditions does it cure?” A physician from the Imperial Medical Office replied: “Your Majesty:

Ma dou ling has a bitter, cold nature, and is not toxic; it is very good for fixing wheezing and dispelling phlegm. It regulates the qi and best removes blood phlegm. It replenishes weakness, quiets cough, and eases the chest.” The king laughed: “Very apt, very apt. Elder Pig, drink another cup.” The fool still did not speak, but he also drank a three-treasure goblet. The king handed wine to Sha Wujing as well; he drank three cups, and then all three returned to their seats.

After long drinking and feasting, the king lifted a great cup again and respectfully offered it to Sun Wukong. Sun Wukong said, “Your Majesty, please sit. Old Sun, by habit, drinks hard and never dares to refuse.” The king said, “The holy monk’s grace is as heavy as a mountain. I cannot repay it. Drink this enormous cup at least once; I have something to say.” Sun Wukong replied, “If there is something to say, Old Sun can drink.” The king said, “For several years I have suffered a malady of worry and suspicion, but after the Holy Monk struck the magical elixir and opened my channels, I was cured.” Sun Wukong laughed, “Yesterday, Old Sun looked at Your Majesty and knew it was the illness of worry and suspicion, but I did not know what you worried about.” The king said, “The ancients said, ‘Family shame should not be spoken beyond the house.’ Yet the holy monk is my benefactor; only if you do not laugh, may I tell it.” Sun Wukong said, “How could I laugh at such a matter? Please speak freely.” The king said, “Holy monk, as you came from the East, do you remember how many states you passed through?” Sun Wukong said, “Five or six places.” “And their principal queens—what are they called there?” “In this kingdom, Your Majesty, we call the main one the Main Palace, and the others the East and West Palaces.” The king said, “My titles are not like that. I call the main one Gold Holy Palace, the east Jade Holy Palace, and the west Silver Holy Palace. Now there are only the Silver and Jade queens in the palace.” Sun Wukong asked, “Then why is the Gold Holy Palace not in the palace?” The king, with tears, said, “It has not been here for three years.” Sun Wukong asked, “Where has she gone?” The king said, “Three years ago, on the Dragon-Boat festival, Your Majesty and the empresses were under the pomegranate pavilion in the royal garden, untying zongzi, hanging mugwort, drinking calamus and realgar wine, and watching dragon-boat races. Suddenly a wind came, and in midair appeared a demon who called himself Sai Tai-sui. He said he lived in Jinxiong Mountain’s Xie-zhi Cave, and that in the cave he lacked a lady; having seen my Gold Holy Palace, who was exquisitely beautiful, he wished to take her as his wife. He told me to send her quickly; if I did not send her after three calls, he would first eat me, then the ministers and officials, and devour all the people of the city. At that time I was troubled for my state and my people and had no choice; I led the Gold Holy Palace out of the pavilion, and with one shout he swept her away. I was deeply frightened by this, then ate that rice dumpling, and something congealed within me; moreover, I worried day and night without pause. Thus this painful sickness had lasted three years. Since taking the holy elixir from the monk, I have purged it several times; each bout cleared away the stagnant matter built up from three years ago, so now my body is sound, my frame light, and my spirit like before. All of this life is granted by you, Holy Monk. Is it not more than a burden as heavy as Mount Tai?”

When Sun Wukong heard these words, he was secretly delighted. He drank down two gulps from the huge cup and smilingly asked the king, “Your Majesty, I see the depth of your distress. Now that you have met Old Sun, you are fortunate to be cured. But tell me, should we bring back the Gold Holy Palace to the capital?” The king, weeping, said, “I think of her day and night with no rest, and no one can capture this demon. How could I then ask for her return?” Sun Wukong said, “How about I go with you and subdue this monster?” The king knelt and said, “If you can rescue my queen, I will hand over my three palaces and nine concubines, leave the city as common folk, and give the whole state and its mountains and rivers to you, making you emperor.” Zhu Bajie, sitting nearby, could not bear this scene of deference and laughed aloud, “This emperor has lost all propriety! To kneel before a monk for a wife and offer to give away an empire—what is this?” Sun Wukong stepped forward and helped the king rise: “Your Majesty, since the demon took the Gold Holy Palace, has it ever come again?” The king answered, “He seized her last year in May. In October he came asking for two palace ladies, saying they were to serve the Lady, and I gave two. In last year’s third month he came for two more; in the seventh month another two; and in this February another two. I do not know when he will come again.” Sun Wukong said, “If he comes so often, does he not frighten you?” The king said, “When he comes, Your Majesty sees this often. For one thing, we fear him, and for another we fear he may bring harm. Last April I ordered workers to build an anti-demon pavilion. But whenever the wind sounded, we knew he was coming, and then I entered with the two queens and the nine beauties and hid there.” Sun Wukong said, “If it does not disturb Your Majesty, why not bring Old Sun there and inspect that pavilion?” The king immediately took Sun Wukong by the left hand and led him out in attendance. The officials all stood. Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, you don’t even observe courtly manners. You leave this imperial wine untouched and this place rattling, and now you want to go look at something?” The king knew Bajie spoke from his mouth, so he ordered two plain tables set with wine for Sun Wukong and said to have them wait outside the pavilion. The fool made no more fuss and, laughing with Tripitaka and Sha Wujing, said, “Let us flip the cushions and go.”

A full complement of officials and attendants guided them: the king and Sun Wukong together made their way hand in hand through the palace, through the royal garden, to a spot where no tower, pavilion, or hall remained. Sun Wukong asked, “Where is the anti-demon pavilion?” He had no time to finish speaking when he saw two eunuchs carrying two red-lacquered carrying poles, lifting a square stone slab from the empty ground. The king said, “This is the place. Beneath it is a pit over three zhang deep, cut out as nine audience chambers. Inside are four great jars, each filled with clear oil and lit with lamps, burning day and night. Whenever I heard the wind sounding, I would come in and hide; outside, men would cover it with the stone slab.” Sun Wukong laughed: “That demon has not harmed you before. If he wanted to harm you, how could he fail to reach you here?” As he was saying this, from the true south came a wild gust—wind roaring, throwing up dust and soil. The courtiers all cried out in panic at once, “This monk, with his salty-fish mouth, keeps saying there is a demon, and now the demon has arrived!” Frightened, the king dropped Sun Wukong and dashed into the underground chamber; Tripitaka followed; the officials too found a clean place to hide.

Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing also moved to hide, but Sun Wukong held both their wrists with his right and left hands and said, “Brothers, do not be afraid. Let me and you look at him and see what kind of monster this is.” Bajie said, “You’re talking nonsense. If we do not know him, why go? The ministers hid, the master hid, the king hid. Why should we stay? Is this a show of family pedigree?” The fool struggled and strained to pull away, but could not escape Sun Wukong’s grip. After a while, they saw a demon flash out in midair. Look at him:

Nine feet high and utterly fierce, his pair of ringed eyes flashed like golden lanterns. Two round ears like paddles spread; four steel fangs stuck out like inserted nails. Red-red hair curled at his temples, brows raised like flames; nose and snout hung down, broad nostrils and bright openings. A few scarlet whisker lines, cheekbones ridged and harsh, face all bruised blue. His arms were red and indigo, and ten sharp claws gripped a spear. A leopard-skin skirt was knotted at his waist; bare feet and wild hair gave him a ghostly form. Sun Wukong asked Sha Wujing, “Can you recognize him?” Sha Wujing said, “I have never met him. How could I know?” Again: “Bajie, can you recognize him?” Bajie said, “I have never met him drinking tea or wine, nor is he friend or neighbor. How could I know him?” Sun Wukong said, “He looks like the painted-faced Golden-Eye Ghost who serves as a gatekeeper under Elder East Peak.” Bajie said, “No, no.” Sun Wukong asked, “How do you know he is not?” Bajie said, “A ghost is a yin spirit. It appears only from the hours of申 to亥, from dusk until nightfall. Now it is the 巳 hour, how could a ghost dare appear? Even if it can raise wind, it can only make one spinning gust. Can such violence be from that? Perhaps he is indeed Sai Tai-sui.” Sun Wukong laughed, “You are a good fool—you have some sense after all. Then you two stay here to hold position; I will go ask him his name, so I can bring him to court and return the Gold Holy Palace.” Bajie said, “Go then, but do not give away where we are.” Sun Wukong made no further reply, leapt upward at once in auspicious light, and sprang after him. Right then, there was a coda: First make peace in the kingdom and cure the ruler’s sickness. To keep to the Way, one must remove both love and hatred from the heart.

It is still unknown what happens once he reaches the sky—whether they win or lose, how he captures the demon and rescues the Gold Holy Palace. Let the next chapter explain all of that.
chapters.title: Chapter 69: The Heart-Lord compounds medicine by night; at court banquet the sovereign debates demons and evil spirits.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Now it is told that Sun Wukong shook himself awake with divine might, took his iron staff, stepped on auspicious radiance, and rose into the air, crying out as he met the foe: “Who are you evil fiend, and where are you heading in your lawless frenzy?” The demon roared back in a hard voice: “We are no common rabble. I am the vanguard subordinate of King Saitai Sui, Great King of Xiezhi Cave on Qilin Mountain, ordered to come here and take two palace women to serve the Golden-Saint Empress. Who are you, to dare ask me?” Sun Wukong replied, “I am Sun Wukong, the Great Sage, Equal to Heaven. I escort Tripitaka from the Eastern Land to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha. Passing through this country, I learned that your band of demons was deceiving and oppressing the ruler, and I came to show true heroism, to set the kingdom right and sweep away evil. I was not merely hunting for you at random; I came here to send you your death.” On hearing this, the demon did not know what to make of it. He lunged with his long spear at Sun Wukong. Sun Wukong raised his iron rod to meet him full in the face. In midair there was a fierce killing bout:

The staff is the treasure that tames the sea in the Dragon Palace; the spear is iron repeatedly smelted in the mortal world. Which mortal weapon dares to compare with heavenly arms, if it carries only a little air of sanctity? The Great Sage was truly a Taiyi immortal; demons and ghosts were all evil fiends. How can shadowy tricksters come near upright men? when uprightness appears, evil is extinguished. He there makes wind and scatters earth to startle kings; he here treads mist and stirs clouds, blinding sun and moon. To throw off airs and bet on gain or loss, who among the weak dares claim heroism? Yet it is the Great Sage, Equal to Heaven, who can: with one ping-pong strike of staff and spear, the spear was split in two at once. The demon was split by one blow of Sun Wukong’s iron staff into two halves at its base. Frightened for his life, he turned with a rush, spun the wind aside, and fled westward.

Sun Wukong did not pursue him. Pressing down his cloud, he came out beyond the demon-warding cave and called, “Master, please come out with His Majesty; the demon has already run off.” Only then did Tripitaka help the king and come out. Looking up, all the sky was clear and bright, with no demonic breath left in it. When they reached the banquet table, the king himself took up the flask and cups, filled a gold cup to the brim, and offered it to Sun Wukong: “Divine monk, my thanks, my thanks.” Sun Wukong took the cup in his hand and had not yet answered when an official came from the palace gate crying, “A fire has broken out at the West Gate.” Sun Wukong, hearing this, flung the gold cup and the wine together into the air. A sharp ring sounded, and the gold cup struck the ground. The king, flustered, hastened to bow and said, “Holy monk, pardon me, pardon me. I am the poor fool. I should have invited you into the hall to offer thanks. Because this wine happened to be here, I offered it here. You threw away the cup thinking I had some demonic intent?” Sun Wukong laughed: “No, no. Not that.” After a short while another official came running: “A great rain has come. The fire at the West Gate has been put out. The streets are all running with water, and all the water smells of wine.” Sun Wukong laughed again: “Your Majesty, you saw me toss the cup and thought I meant to inspect a demon. Not so. The demon had already fled west; I did not chase him. He was the one who raised this fire. This one cup of wine is what I used to put out the demon-fire and save the people inside and outside the west city. How could it have such intent?”

The king grew still more joyful and respectful, and invited Tripitaka and the four attendants up to the treasure hall, with an evident intent to offer him a higher place. Sun Wukong laughed: “Your Majesty, that demon said he was the vanguard under King Saitai Sui, and came here to take palace women. He has now returned in defeat and, surely, will report this. His master will then come to fight me. I fear he may quickly gather troops and in one stroke frighten the people again and endanger Your Majesty. I should go to meet him now, capture him in midair, and fetch back the Holy Empress. But I do not know where to head first. How far is it from here to his mountain cave?” The king replied, “I once sent scouts by night and day to that place to gather word. It took them more than fifty days each way. It lies to the south, about three thousand li.” Sun Wukong said, “Zhu Bajie, Sha Wujing, hold things here. I will go and return.” The king held him back: “Holy monk, stay one day. Let me arrange some toasted dry provisions and a little silver, choose a swift horse, and then set out.” Sun Wukong laughed: “Your Majesty speaks truly. This is talk for one who crosses ridges on foot through Ba Mountain. I will tell you plainly: for three thousand li, this cup of wine would not yet be cold before I turn back.” The king said, “Holy monk, do not blame me. Your appearance is like a monkey’s, and yet how could you have such power for travel?” Sun Wukong answered:

Though my body is ape-kind from the start, since youth I opened the path through life and death. I sought wise masters and learned the Way; before the mountains I practiced without end of day. Relying on Heaven as the crown and Earth as the furnace, I pounded two elixirs into one black-and-white pellet. I took Yin and Yang, water and fire to mingle; in an instant I grasped the mysterious gate. All rests on the Great Hinges of Heaven; with the handle of the Northern Dipper I shift my steps. First retreating into the furnace and then stoking the flame, I do it by timing; I draw lead and add mercury to make them unite. Gathering fivefold transformations, I let the world-form arise; in ordered times I harmonize the four symbols. The two energies return by the yellow way, and three streams converge on the road of Golden-Hooped Staff? no—the road of the Golden Elixir. I comprehended the Law and made it my own in the limbs; naturally my body moves as if aided by gods. One bound I cross the Taihang Mountains, one strike I pass Lingyun Ford. Why fear a few thousand steep ridges? I do not fear long rivers numbering hundreds. It is only because my transformations have no boundaries: one leap can forge ten thousand and eight thousand roads.” Hearing him, the king was both astonished and delighted, smiling as he held out a cup of imperial wine and offered it: “Great monk, your toil was great; accept this cup in goodwill.” The Great Sage had no heart for drinking, his purpose fixed on subduing demons. He only said, “Set it down; when I return I shall drink.” Saying “I go,” he gave one sharp whistle. In a hush, he vanished. As for the king and ministers of that country, they were all astonished; no more need be said.

Sun Wukong then sprang upward. At once he saw a high mountain blocking the edge of the mists. He pressed down the clouds and stood on the summit, then examined it closely. It was a fine mountain:

Reaching to heaven while gripping the earth, it blocked the sun and raised clouds. Where it pierced heaven, sharp peaks rose high; where it held the ground, distant ridges stretched far. What blocks the sun is dense, lush ridge-top pine; what raises clouds is the glistening stone at the mountain’s lower face. The pines are thick and verdant all year through all seasons; the stones lie gleaming and unmoving for ten thousand years. In the woods one hears ape-calls at night; in the ravines one often hears demonic water-serpents pass. Mountain birds cry in choked tones, mountain beasts bellow in full-throated calls. Mountain antelope and deer move in pairs, flinging themselves in busy streams; mountain crows and magpies gather in dense formations and fly in clustered flocks. Mountain grasses and mountain flowers are endless; mountain peaches and fruits shine new with every time. Though dangerous and hard to cross, this is still where demons and immortals hide in seclusion. The Great Sage looked on without tiring and was about to seek the cave-mouth when from a hollow of the mountain came roaring firelight. In an instant it shot skyward, and from the red blaze rose a rank evil smoke, more toxic than the flames themselves. Good smoke! He could see it clearly: Firelight burst in myriad points like golden lamps; a thousand tongues of flame shot up in red arcs. That smoke was not hearth-smoke, not wood-smoke; yet the smoke had five colors: blue, red, white, black, and yellow. It smoked the outer columns beyond the Southern Sky Gate and burned the beams above Hall Lingxiao. It burned the beasts in the dens so their skins tore, and burned the feathers away from the birds of the forest. But such cruel smoke like this—how could one enter the deep mountain where the demon king is hidden?

Sun Wukong, at that moment still feeling a touch of alarm, saw another force burst from within the mountain: a torrent of sand. Wonderful sand—truly, it could cover the sky and block the day. You could see:

Scattering in countless clots, filling the edges of the sky; thudding and dense, it shrouded the whole land. Fine dust blinded men’s eyes wherever it drifted; rough ash rolled through the valleys by the handfuls. Herb-gathering immortal youths lose their companions; woodcutters can no longer find their way home. Bright pearls seem to rise into one’s hands at once, while the wind suddenly makes the eyes blossom with stars. Sun Wukong only watched the display and did not notice the sand-gray blowing into his nose. It tickled him badly, and he sneezed twice. When he turned, he felt under the rocks for two goose-egg pebbles and stuffed them in his nostrils. Shaking his form, he changed into a heat-chasing hawk and flew into the heart of fire and smoke. He darted a few times, and at once the sand haze vanished and the flames were out. He quickly returned to his true form; once more he looked around and heard the peal of a bronze gong—“ding-ding dong-dong.” He said, “I have taken the wrong road. This is not the demon’s lair. That drumbeat is like a mustering drum for troop dispatch. It must be the main road of the whole kingdom, where messengers go out to issue orders. Let old Sun ask this one and hear it.”

As he moved on, he suddenly saw what seemed a small demon child, carrying a yellow flag, with documents on his back and a drum in hand, running like wind. Sun Wukong laughed: “So it is this one beating a drum. He does not know what message he carries. Let me hear him out.” The Great Sage changed into a fierce insect-child and lightly flew to sit on top of his satchel. He heard the demon beating his drum and, in a muttering rhythm, recite to himself: “I know my lord has a heart of evil. Three years ago he forced his way into Zhuzi Country and violently took the Golden-Saint Empress. There has never been a proper bond there; he has never come near her body, only the palace maidens that arrive to serve have suffered. He had two come and they were killed. Four came later and they too were killed. Last year he demanded; this year he demanded again; now he demands again. Now he has run into a rival. The forward scout who came to take palace women was beaten by that Sun Wukong and brought back no women. For this my king is angry and wants to contend with that country, so he sends me with an order of war. If the king there chooses not to fight, all is well; if he fights, he will surely lose. My king will make smoke, flames, and flying sand. In that kingdom the king, his ministers, and the common folk—not one should hope to survive. Then we seize his city. My king will call himself emperor and we become his ministers. Though there may be high and low offices too, heaven’s moral order cannot tolerate such things.”

Sun Wukong listened and silently rejoiced: “This demon may have a good heart. Even from those final two words, where he spoke of ‘Heavenly principle not enduring this,’ he cannot be entirely evil. But he also said that Jinsheng Empress has never had such fate and has never once touched her; I still do not know what that means. I will ask him about it.” With a sharp “ying,” he flapped one wing and left the demon, turned toward the forward road, and after some ten li he shifted form again into a Daoist youth:

His head hair was twisted into twin side braids, and he wore a robe of a hundred patched seams. He tapped a fish-drum with his hands, and with his mouth sang Daoist verses. Around the rise of the hill, he faced the small demon and greeted him: “Officer, where are you going, and what edict are you carrying?” The demon, as though he recognized him, set down his gong-beater, smiled, and returned the courtesy: “My king has sent me to Zhuzi Kingdom with a formal declaration of battle.” Sun Wukong then asked, “That matter in Zhuzi Kingdom—did it proceed with my king’s consent?” The little demon said, “Since last year, when I captured him, a divinity came and presented a five-coloured celestial robe for Jinsheng Palace to adorn herself. The moment she put on that robe, she was covered with needle-prickling pain. My king did not dare touch him even once. Yet when he merely tugged at the hem, the palm of his hand burned in pain—I do not know why. From beginning to now, he has not yet once touched him. This morning he sent outriders to call for palace maidens; one called Sun Wukong beat us in combat. So the king burned with rage and therefore sent me to deliver this battle summon; tomorrow he will fight with him.” Sun Wukong said, “Why should he be so angry?” The demon replied, “That is exactly the reason. Go sing a Daoist song for him and ease his vexation.”

‘Good traveler,’ he made an elegant salutation and withdrew at once. The demon still beat his gong and moved forward. Then Sun Wukong struck in fierceness, drew out his staff, turned back, and with one backward blow at the back of the little demon’s head, crushed him—blood spurted out with the splashing marrow, skin split, neck broken, life overturned. He sheathed the staff and at once reproached himself: “I was hasty and never asked him what name he had. Enough of that.” He took the summons from the demon and tucked it into his sleeve. He hid the yellow banner and bronze drum in the roadside grass. As he pulled his feet to drag the body down toward the ravine, he heard a sharp dang; a gold-inlaid token plate flashed at his waist. It read: “A trusted inner-captain named Youlaiyouqu. Short and stout, broad-faced, beardless. Long river suspended; without the plate, counterfeit.” Sun Wukong laughed: “This brute’s name is Youlaiyouqu; with this one club-strike, he has been hit away beyond return.” He removed the plate and fastened it at his waist. He meant to drag the corpse away, but he again considered the venom of smoke and fire and dared not seek the demon’s lair. So, lifting his staff, he struck the little demon once in the chest and tossed him into the air, then returned directly to his own country, thinking to report a head-worthy deed. Reflecting on this to himself, he gave one whistle and arrived at the border.

Zhu Bajie, who had been guarding the king and Master before the Hall of Golden Lamps, turned and saw Sun Wukong carrying a demon aloft in midair. He complained, “Ah! Not a bad bargain at all. If I had gone and brought him back, my effort would have counted too.” Before he finished, Sun Wukong set the demon down with a thud at the bottom of the steps. Zhu Bajie rushed up and said in a single burst, “That is old Pig’s merit.” Sun Wukong replied, “What merit of yours?” Zhu Bajie said, “Do not blame me—I have the witness myself. Did you not see? One stroke of my spade made nine gaping eyes in him.” Sun Wukong said, “Go see whether he has a head or no head.” Zhu Bajie laughed, “So it is without a head; I thought to myself why, even with one thrust, he would not move.” Sun Wukong asked, “Where is Master now?” Zhu Bajie said, “He is in the hall, talking with the king.” Sun Wukong said, “Then go and ask him to come out.” Zhu Bajie hurried to the hall and nodded. Tripitaka immediately rose and came down from the hall to meet Sun Wukong. Sun Wukong tucked a war summons into Tripitaka’s sleeve and said, “Master, keep this, and do not let the king see it.”

Before he could finish, the king also came down from the hall and greeted Sun Wukong: “So the holy monk elder has arrived? What is the matter with capturing the demon?” Sun Wukong pointed with his hand: “That is no demon below the steps? He was struck down by old Sun.” The king looked and said, “It is indeed a demon corpse, but not Tai Sui. I have seen Tai Sui with my own eyes twice—he was eight zhàng in height, shoulders broad as five ding; his face shone like gold-light and his voice cracked like thunder. How could one be as short and coarse as this?” Sun Wukong smiled: “Your Majesty recognizes correctly. It is certainly not he. This is only a messenger demon who, meeting old Sun, was slain at once. I carried him back to report my merit.” The king was very pleased: “Excellent, excellent, excellent—this surely counts as a first-rate credit. I have often sent people to investigate, and not once found anything certain. As soon as a holy monk of this sort appears, he catches one and brings him back. Truly divine is his power.” He ordered: “Bring warm wine, and let us congratulate the elder.”

Sun Wukong said, “Drinking to celebrate is a small matter. I ask Your Majesty: when Jinsheng left, did she leave any token behind? Give me whatever you can.” The king heard the word ‘token’ and seemed as if a knife had cut his heart; he could not contain tears and said:

In past years, at the festival honoring the Zhu-Ming day, the vicious Tai Sui shouted out. He seized the imperial consort to hold at the fortress-gate, and I offered her up for the sake of all living folk. No last words of meeting, no words of parting—what then of long pavilions and short pavilions? The marked incense-sachet token has vanished without trace; even now I remain forlorn and broken. Sun Wukong said, “Your Majesty is here, so why this grief? Since that lady has left no token, is there any cherished object in your palace? Send me one of them.” The king said, “What do you want?” Sun Wukong said, “That demon king truly has powers. I saw him release smoke, fire, and sand, and it is truly difficult to contain him. Even if I subdued him, when I bring him back, his wife may not know me by face and may refuse to follow. I must bring back some object dear to him in ordinary life, so he will believe me. That is why I ask to bring one away.” The king said, “In the dressing chamber of Zhaoyang Palace hangs a pair of gold precious strings, which were originally worn by Jinsheng. On the Dragon Boat day, he took them off to tie five-coloured threads and never put them back on. This is his fondly loved thing, now kept in the makeup box. When he saw it, he could not bear this separation; at one glance it seems he sees her jade-face, and his illness grows all the worse.” Sun Wukong said, “Do not speak of these feelings. Bring the gold strings at once. If you can spare it, bring me the pair. If not, bring at least one.” The king ordered Yusheng Palace to fetch it. It was brought out and handed to him. On seeing it, the king called out several times, “To my beloved lady who aches from this grief,” and then gave it to Sun Wukong. Sun Wukong took it and tied it upon his upper arm.

The Great Sage did not drink the victory wine, but rode out on his cloud and, with one whistle, returned to Mount Qilin. With no heart for admiring scenery, he went straight in search of the lair. While he walked, he heard loud human voices, so he stood still and fixed his eyes and watched. There, at the mouth of the Xiezhi cave, stood the major officers assigned to the gate, about five hundred in number:

Dense rows upon dense rows, rank upon rank in close formation. Dense rows of guards held spears and clubs, gleaming bright in the sun; Dense rows of banners unfurled, fluttering and flashing in the wind. Tiger captains and bear commanders knew transformation and, with leopard heads and handsome forms, moved with spirited force. Blue wolves were fierce, and the otter-elephant ranks still more ferocious. Trickster hares and pliant deer-mares brandished halberds and spears; Long snakes and great pythons carried sword-bows at their sides. Orangutans understood human speech, ordering the formation and reading the coming wind. Seeing this, Sun Wukong did not dare to go farther and turned back by the old path. You ask why he withdrew? Not because he feared them. He went instead to where he had killed the little demon and found the yellow banner and bronze gong. Facing the wind, he formed the required gesture, then with a thought to spring, shifted at once into the form of Youlaiyouqu, struck the gong with a ringing ping and a pong, and strode forward in great steps straight to the cave. Just as he wished to take in the cave’s sight, he heard the orangutan speak: “Youlaiyouqu, you have returned?” Sun Wukong could only reply, “I have.” The orangutan said, “Hurry. Great king waits on the Skinning Pavilion for your report.”

Sun Wukong heard the words, took up a long stride, beat the drum, and strode directly through the front gate to look around. It turned out to be a sheer cliff wall, a stone hall, emptiness in the chamber, with wondrous flowers and jade grasses on both sides and old cypress and tall pines everywhere in front and behind. Not noticing, he reached inside the second gate; he looked up and saw a bright pavilion with eight windows, and in its center a gilded armchair, on which sat a demon king in an honestly terrifying shape.

Flashing light from sunset rose above his head; fierce, murderous intent burst out before his chest. From his mouth, fanged teeth flashed like keen blades; at his temples, scorched hair smoked red. His whiskers on the lips stood out like fixed arrows; over his whole body the upright bristles were piled like felt. His eyes protruded like bronze bells, challenging the star of the year; in his hand he held an iron pestle as if to split the sky. When Sun Wukong saw him, the demon king, he acted openly and arrogantly and showed no courtesy. He turned his face away and kept striking the drum. The demon king asked, "You have come?" Sun Wukong did not answer. He asked again: "You come and go—so you have come?" still no answer. The king came forward, grabbed him, and said, "Why, once you have reached this house, are you still clanging the drum, and when I ask, why do you not answer?" Sun Wukong slammed the drum to the ground and said, "What ‘why?’, what ‘why?’? I said I was not going, yet you told me to go. When I came there, I saw endless men and horses forming ranks. When they saw me, they all cried, ‘Capture the demon, capture the demon.’ They pushed me, pulled me, dragged me, and hauled me, and carried me into the city. Seeing the king, the king at once ordered: ‘Cut him down.’ Fortunately two groups of advisers said, ‘Two states are at odds; do not behead the envoy.’ So he spared me. He took the battle summons and escorted me out of the city, then before the army gave me thirty blows to the shins and sent me off to report. It will not be long before he comes here to battle with you." The demon king said, "So, it seems you have suffered a loss; no wonder I asked and you still did not speak." Sun Wukong said, "It is not that. I kept silent only because I guarded myself from pain." The demon king asked, "How many men and horses are there there?" Sun Wukong said, "I was frightened dumb and already scared by his blows; how could I check how many troops he had? I only saw endless weapons neatly arrayed there: Bow, arrow, saber, lance, armor, and uniforms; blade and halberd and tied banners. Curved spears, moon-shovels, helmets and cuirasses, great axes, round bucklers, iron caltrops. Long staff clubs, short mallets, steel tridents, guns and drills, and helms. Boots and head wraps, padded coats, riding whips, divine bullets, and bronze hammers. The king laughed: "No matter, no matter. With weapons like these, a single fire leaves them all empty. Go now and report to Golden-Saint Lady that she should not grieve. This morning, when he heard I was fierce and would go to battle, she wept until her eyes were full. Tell her there are so many brave soldiers and horses there and they will surely beat me; give her a little time to loosen her heart."

Sun Wukong, hearing this, was deeply pleased and said, "Exactly what I intended." See how well he knows the way: he turned by a corner gate and crossed the halls. There, everything consisted of lofty buildings and high mansions, nothing like the place in front. He went on to the inner palace and in the distance saw the splendid painted gate, which was the residence of Golden-Saint Lady.

When he entered and looked inside, there were two groups of demon foxes and demon deer, each made up to resemble a beauty, standing on either side. At the center sat the Lady herself, one hand lifting a fragrant cheek, both eyes filled with tears. She truly was:

Her face was delicate and soft, her beauty enchantingly alluring. Hair loosely combed, disheveled tresses gathered like crows; she had no ornamental pins and no crown jewels. Her face wore no face powder and her rouge was pale and cold; her hair was un-oiled and her cloud-locked hair was tousled. Her cherry lips were tight, biting silver teeth; her brows were knitted, and star-bright tears swam in her eyes. Her whole heart remembered only the King of Zhuzi, and for a moment she longed to break free of heaven-and-earth’s net. Truly: since ancient times beautiful women have many short fates; she stood silent and inarticulate, facing the east wind. Sun Wukong stepped forward and offered greeting: "Respectfully." The lady said, "This rude monster is utterly shapeless and uncivilized. When I was in Zhuzi, enjoying honor and glory with the king, the Grand Instructor and the Chancellor, on seeing me, would prostrate in the dust and dare not look up. How can this wild thing call it ‘respectfully’? From where did such a boor come?" The attendants came forward: "My lady, let out your anger. He is a trusted junior officer of the Great King, called You-come-and-go. He was the one who delivered the battle summons this morning." The lady listened and asked, with restrained annoyance, "When you delivered the summons, did you even reach the border of Zhuzi?" Sun Wukong said, "I took the letter directly into the city and to the Hall of Golden Crowns, where I appeared before the king and brought back an answer." The lady asked, "When you faced him, what did he say?" Sun Wukong said, "I only told the Great King about the matter of battle and the deployment of troops. Only, the king has thoughts of concern for you, and one fitting word of the heart; I came specially to convey it. But alas, the people around him are not a place where such words can be spoken."

The lady, upon hearing this, sent away the two groups of foxes and deer. Sun Wukong shut the palace gate, wiped his face, and revealed his true form. He said to the lady, "Do not fear me. I am the monk sent by Great Tang of the Eastern Land to the Leiyin Monastery in Great-West Tianzhu to seek scripture before Buddha. My master is Tripitaka, imperial prince and younger brother of Emperor Tang, and I am his senior disciple Sun Wukong. I passed through your kingdom to exchange travel passes. When I saw your ministers and king posting notices inviting physicians, it was I who, with my three-fold arm-bending art, cured his lovesickness, and they held a banquet to thank me. While drinking, he spoke of how you had been demon-bound. I can restrain Dragon Kings and cow tigers, so he specially asked me to come and capture the monster, and rescue you back to your country. The first vanguard to lose the battle was me; the killing of the small demons was also me. When I saw him run wild outside your gate, I became You-come-and-go in form, risked my own life, and came here to report to you." The lady, after hearing this, was silent and thoughtful. Sun Wukong took out a jewel string and offered it with both hands: "If you do not believe me, look at this object and ask where it came from." When the lady saw it, she dropped her tears and knelt, bowing in thanks: "Venerable Master, if you truly save me and bring me back to court, I will remember your great kindness until I have no teeth left."

Sun Wukong said, "Let me ask you. That thing that emits fire, smoke, and sand—what kind of treasure is it?" The lady replied, "That is no jewel. It is just three golden bells. When he shakes the first one, three hundred zhang of flames burn a person. When he shakes the second, three hundred zhang of smoke chokes a person. When he shakes the third, three hundred zhang of yellow sand confuses a person. The fire and smoke are not yet the worst; the yellow sand is the most poisonous. If it enters one’s nostrils, life can be harmed." Sun Wukong said, "Dangerous, indeed dangerous. I have suffered it before; it made me sneeze twice. But I do not know where he keeps those bells." The lady said, "How would he ever set them down? He always keeps them at his waist and, while standing, walking, sitting, or lying, he never lets them leave his body." Sun Wukong said, "If you truly still intend marriage ties with Zhuzi Country, then you should still meet the king, calm his anxieties and sorrows, put on a charming, joyful countenance, and speak with him of conjugal feeling. Make him place those bells in your keeping. If he gives them to you, I can take them and steal them away and then suppress this demon. Then, in time, I can take you back, and you two may again harmonize like phoenix and pair, sharing peace together." The lady agreed.

Sun Wukong changed back into the trusted junior officer, opened the palace gate, and called in the attendants at either side. The lady said, "You-come-and-go, go quickly to the Front Pavilion and ask your Great King to come so we may speak with him." Sun Wukong answered once and went to the Bopi Pavilion. To the demon king he said, "Great King, the Saintly Palace Lady summons you." The demon king, pleased, said, "The lady always scolds me. How is it that she summons me today?" Sun Wukong said, "The lady asked about the King of Zhuzi, and I told her: 'He no longer wants you; he has raised another empress in his own kingdom.' Upon hearing this, she lost all clarity of thought and only then ordered me to bring you here in summons." The demon king rejoiced and said, "You have served well. After I annihilate him and his kingdom, I will appoint you as a Taizai of the court."

Sun Wukong, offering thanks on the spot, hurried with the demon king to the threshold of the inner palace. The Lady welcomed him with a radiant smile and stepped forward to touch hands. The demon king stepped back and said, “Not so, not so. I dare not, I dare not. I have your Ladyship’s favor in abundance, yet I fear I shall pain my hands if I lean against you.” The Lady said, “Great King, please sit. I have something to say to you.” The king replied, “If you have words, speak them.” She said, “I, honored by your favor, have now been three years since we became one household and yet have not lain together on a shared bed and quilt. This is fate from former lives—we are made into these spouses. I did not expect the Great King to keep his heart elsewhere and not treat me as a wife. I thought if once, as queen in Zhu Zi, any visiting realm brought tribute jewels and gifts, once Your Majesty had seen them, they were surely set aside for the queen. Yet here you have not a single such treasure. You wear marten cloaks and eat blood-food; have you ever seen brocade silk or gold-and-pearl work? There is only skin on the ground and blankets for covering. If any precious things do exist, because I am ‘other’ to you, you do not allow me to see them nor to receive them on your behalf. And I even hear that you have three bells, surely a treasure indeed. Why do you carry them when you go, and carry them too when you sit? Hand them to me to keep. When you need them, take them out and use them. That is no impropriety; as husband and wife we should have this inward trust of one another. If there is no such trust, does it come from anything but keeping me apart?” The demon king laughed and answered, “Lady, this is indeed suspicious of you, suspicious indeed. The treasures are here; today I will leave them with you to keep.” He at once raised his robes and took out the treasure. Sun Wukong stood by, his eyes fixed, watching the monster pull up two or three layers of clothing and remove from his person three bells. He took them down, filled their mouths with cotton, wrapped them in a leopard-skin bundle, and handed it to the Lady, saying, “Though these things are of small and humble worth, they still must be stored with care. You must not shake or jostle them.” The Lady took it and said, “I understand. I shall place it atop this dressing table where no one will move it.” She called, “You attendants, bring the wine. I will share joy and delight with the Great King and drink a few cups.” At her words the maidservants quickly set out fruits and vegetables, brought out some antlered deer, roe deer, and rabbit meat, and poured coconut wine. The Lady put on a coquettish manner, coaxing and wooing the spirits.

Sun Wukong, waiting at the side, edged close and moved quietly, then approached the dressing table, quietly took the three golden bells, and moved step by step, slipping out of the palace gate and heading straight toward the cave hall. At an unguarded place before the Peeling-Skin Pavilion, he opened the leopard-skin wrapping and saw that the middle one was as large as a tea cup and the two on the ends were each as big as a fist. Unaware of the danger, he pulled at the cotton. He heard a sharp clanging sound; smoke, flame, and yellow sand burst up with a rattling crack, and the fire rose hot through the pavilion beyond control. The guard spirits at the gate were frightened and rushed in a crowd into the rear palace, startling the demon king, who hastily barked, “Put out the fire, put out the fire!” When they came out to inspect it, they found that it was the come-and-go intruder who had taken the golden bells. The demon king stepped forward and shouted, “Wretched thief! How dare you steal my precious bells and fool about here?” He cried, “Bring them out, bring them out.” The tiger general, bear master, leopard-head captain, tiger-charming commander, otter-elephant, dark wolf, clever goral, trickster rabbit, long snake, great python, and ape then came at once with the other demons in tight formation.

Sun Wukong, flustered, flung down the bells, returned to his true form, drew out the Golden-Hooped Staff, cast out his escape techniques, and beat wildly forward. The demon king recovered the treasure and gave the command, “Shut the front gate.” The demons heard him: some shut the gate, and those ready for battle went to fight. By a rare good chance Sun Wukong broke free, put away his staff, and changed shape again into a foolish blue-green fly, nailing himself to the wall of fire-proof stone. The demons could not find him and reported, “Great King, the thief has escaped! the thief has escaped!” The king asked, “Did he go out through the gate?” All the demons answered, “The front gate is tightly locked fast; he has not gone out.” The king said only, “Search carefully.” Some took water and sprinkled the flames, others searched thoroughly, but there was no trace. The king growled, “What sort of thief is this? Such boldness—to come and go in the manner of one who passes freely, appear before me and answer, then follow at my side and seize my treasure. He must not have carried it out. If he carries it onto the ridges and meets the heavenly wind, what then?” The tiger general stepped forward and said, “Great King, your blessings are as broad as Heaven and our span of life is not yet exhausted; therefore we sensed this in time.” The bear master stepped forward and said, “Great King, this thief is none other than that vanquished vanguard, Sun Wukong. He must have encountered a come-and-go apparition on the road and, wounded to the brink of death, taken the yellow banner, bronze gong, and tusk tally; he then took Sun Wukong’s shape and has tricked the Great King here.” The demon king said, “Exactly, exactly; that is persuasive indeed.” He then ordered, “You below, search every corner well and guard against escapes; do not open the gate and let him get out.” This is a lesson in karma:

What is done in clever play becomes clumsy; what is done in sport turns real.

In the end it was still unknown how Sun Wukong escaped through the demon gate; listen for the explanation in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 70: The demon’s treasure sends out smoke and sand fire; Wukong plans the theft of the Purple-Gold Bell.
