This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Since ancient days, form is said to be emptiness, and emptiness says that form is just as it appears. If one could truly penetrate color and emptiness in Chan, why must one forge red cinnabar by laboring in alchemical fire? Cultivate complete virtue and conduct without idleness, and by hard endeavor boil and press the practice. In time, when deeds are fulfilled, one may ascend to Heaven at dawn, forever preserving an unchanging immortal countenance.

Sai Tai-sui had tightly barred both the front and back gates and searched for the Traveller, crying out as far as dusk, but no trace was found. Sitting in the Pavilion of Flayed Hide, he gathered the hordes of fiends and issued orders: every gate to ring its bell and shout for alarm, to strike drums and clappers. One by one, they set bowstrings, drew swords from their sheaths, and kept watch through the night.

Great Sage Sun Wukong had in fact turned into a dazed blue fly and fastened himself near the gate. He saw the front defenses were so tight and so he fluffed his wings, flew into the rear palace gatehouse to look within, and there saw Lady Jinsheng bowed over the imperial table, silently wiping tears, making faint sounds of sorrow. The traveller flew in, alighted lightly on her windscattered jade hair, and listened to what she was crying about. After a moment, the lady suddenly said: "My lord... As for me and you:

In a former life I burned severed-head incense; in this life I meet the wild demon king. We were sundered three years ago, when shall we meet again? As paired mandarin ducks in two places, grief deepens. I had already sent a senior monk with word and notice; he frightened the good marriage, and one life was lost. It is only that I cannot even identify the Golden Bell, and my longing has run wilder than before." At this, the Great Sage moved behind her ear and whispered: "Holy Palace Lady, do not fear. I am still you-country’s appointed divine monk, Elder Sun, and no life has been harmed by me. It was my own rash temper: when you and the demon king were drinking, I stole the Golden Bell from near the dressing stand and slipped out privately from the front pavilion; unable to resist, I opened it and peered in. At once, when I pulled the cotton plug, the bell rang out and burst forth smoke, flame, and yellow sand. I panicked, dropped the Golden Bell, returned to my true form, and with my staff fought hard but could not break through. Fearing a lethal blow, I changed into a fly and pinned myself to the gate-hinge, hiding here till now. That demon king has tightened the watch still and refuses to open. You must again receive him with the courtesy of a husband, entice him inside to rest, and then I may slip away and act; otherwise I cannot help save you."

When the lady heard this, she trembled as if her hair were bristling on end; her will sank, her heart thudded like a pounding pestle. With tearful eyes she asked, "Are you a person now, or a ghost?" Sun Wukong answered, "I am neither person nor ghost; I am now only this fly. Do not fear, and go quickly to invite that demon king as well." The lady, still doubtful, said softly, "Do not haunt my sleep." Sun Wukong replied, "How could I haunt you? If you still do not believe, open your hand and let me jump down so you may see." She truly extended her left hand, and he flew down gently to land between her jade palms, like:

Black beans pinned atop a lotus-bud, a wandering bee alighting on a peony; Pearls of sewn thread in a heart of embroidery, grapes dropped there, and thick black specks along the lily branches. Lady Jinsheng raised her jade palm high and called, "Divine monk." Sun Wukong warbled in response, "I am the divine monk in disguise." Then she believed him. In a whisper she asked, "When you sent for the demon king again, what are you to do?" He said, "The ancients said, 'The only thing that can dispatch a life is wine.' They also said, 'Nothing cancels all matters more than wine.' Of all the uses of wine, drink it above all. Bring one attendant who stays close to you, and show her to me. I shall assume her form and lie at his side in attendance, and then the time will be good for striking."

The lady did as told and called, "Where is Chunjiao?" From behind the screen a jade-faced fox stepped out and knelt: "You summoned Chunjiao, Your Grace; what is your command?" The lady said, "Go summon them and light the gauze lamps, burn brain-musk incense, help me into the forecourt, and invite the Great King to lie down." Chunjiao went to the front, called six or eight monstrous fox-demons. They came carrying two pairs of lanterns and one pair of brazier stands, and ranged themselves left and right. The lady bowed and folded her hands; the Great Sage had already flown away. As she advanced, he unfurled his wings, flew to the fox-lady’s head, plucked out one hair, blew a breath of immortal qi, and cried, "Transform!" He became a sleepy insect and placed it gently on her face. The drowsy beetle reached her human mouth, crawled into her nostril and in, and at once she grew sleepy. Chunjiao truly began to feel drowsy by degrees, could scarcely stand, and swayed in a doze; she hurried to her old resting place, fell back, and slept with steady breath. Sun Wukong leapt down, changed himself once more, taking Chunjiao’s exact form, and went with the others to stand in place, not to be further told.

It was at this point that Lady Jinsheng was moving forward when a small demon saw her and reported to Sai Tai-sui, "Great King, the lady has come." The demon king hurried out of the Flayed Hide Pavilion to greet her. She said, "Great King, the fireworks are already out and the thief has vanished; at this deep hour I specially invited you to retire." The king, delighted deep within, said, "Lady, please take care. It is that rogue who was Sun Wukong. He defeated my vanguard and slew my junior officer, entered by transformation, and deceived us all. We searched everywhere, yet he has no trace, so my heart is still uneasy." The lady answered, "That wretch likely slipped away. Great King, set aside your worries and go to sleep." Seeing the lady standing and waiting respectfully, the fiend dared not object. So he ordered all the demons: be attentive to the lamps and guard against thieves. Then he and the lady went straight to the inner palace. The traveller, still in the guise of Chunjiao, followed with two lines of attendants.

The lady said, "Arrange wine to ease the Great King’s fatigue." The demon king laughed, "Exactly so. Bring the wine quickly; I shall comfort the Lady." In her false form, Chunjiao set out fruit with the attendants, arranged some savory meat, and reordered the table and chairs. The lady lifted a cup; the demon king also presented one. The two exchanged cups. The false Chunjiao stood at the side, holding the wine jar: "King and Lady, have this night changed but passed cups in turn. Drink yours dry, and share a double-happiness cup." She truly poured more for each and had them drink it dry. Again the fake Chunjiao said, "Since the King and Lady are in joy, let the attendants who can sing sing, and those who can dance dance." Before she finished speaking, a chorus rose in one key and rhythm, singing and dancing in turn. The two drank more, and the lady bid the singing and dancing to halt. The attendants parted by rank and stood outside the screen. Only fake Chunjiao remained, flask in hand, serving up and down. The lady and the demon king then spoke only in intimate spousal words. You see the lady with cloud-soft, rain-heavy feeling, teasing the king until his bones grew soft and numbed—only luck failed him; they did not come together. Pity indeed—like a cat biting an empty bladder, joy without fruit.

They chatted a while, laughed a while. The lady asked, "Great King, was your treasure damaged at all?" The king answered, "This treasure was cast in primordial metal, how can it be harmed? It was only that that thief pulled away the cotton stopper and burned the leopard-hide bundle." The lady said, "How then to deal with it?" The king said, "No need to deal. I carry it at my waist still." When fake Chunjiao heard this, she pulled out a cluster of hairs and chewed them to powder, then came close to the king and placed the hairs upon him, blowing three gentle immortal breaths and whispering softly, "Transform!" Those hairs instantly became three kinds of vile creatures—lice, fleas, and bedbugs—and worked into the king’s body, biting along the skin. The king, burning and itching intolerably, thrust his hand into his robe and rubbed himself, pinching out a few lice and bringing them near the lamp to inspect. The lady thought privately, "Great King, perhaps your under-robe is soiled and unwashed for too long; that must have bred these things." The king, abashed, said, "I have never had them before. I am exposed tonight." The lady laughed, "Why be ashamed, Great King? It is often said, even an emperor has three imperial lice. Then remove your clothes, and I will help you catch them." The king truly loosened his sash and took off his clothing.

The false Chunjiao stood by, watching attentively the king’s garments. Layer after layer crawled with fleas, every piece packed with gross-scented bugs; the body-louse swarms were thick and tight as ants from a nest. Unawares she peeled to the third layer and reached the flesh, where, upon the Golden Bell itself, there were countless wriggling things. She said, "Great King, hand me the bells and let me pick the lice for you." The king, first shy and then flustered, yet not knowing she was false, handed over the three bells to her. Fake Chunjiao took them in hand and feigned searching awhile, and seeing the king lowering his head while he shook out his clothes, she secreted the true bells and pulled one hair, transforming it into three bells alike in all respects. She held them up toward the lamplight and examined. Then, with a subtle bodily shake, she gathered the lice, bugs, and fleas back onto herself and returned the false bells to the demon. He took them, bewildered and uncertain in the dim light, unable to tell one from another. With both hands he cupped the bell and handed it to the lady: "This time you have kept them carefully; keep watch this time, do not be so careless as before." The lady took it, gently opened her jewel casket, put the false bells away, and locked them with golden chain. She then had the king drink a few more cups and ordered a maid: "Clean the bedside, unroll the brocade quilt. The king and I will share the couch." The king nodded repeatedly, "No good fortune, no good fortune. I dare not keep you company. I shall take a palace maiden and sleep in the West Palace. Lady, do arrange comfort for yourself." So each returned to where to sleep; no further details need be told.

Jia Chunjiao had gained her target and placed his precious token at her waist. She showed her true form, shook her body once, drove away that drowsy little bug, and strode straight ahead. Then the clappers and bells rang together, hammering through the third watch. The worthy traveller, pinching the formula, intoning the true incantation, cast an invisibility art and came as far as the gate, where he saw it was tightly secured with many shackles. He took out the Golden-Hooped Staff, pointed at the door, and used the unlocking art; the gate opened gently. He hurried out and stood down below, then shouted in a loud voice, “Sai Taisui, return my Lady Jinsheng!” He cried it two or three times, alarming demons by the small and the great; they hurriedly gathered and looked, and the front gate was opened. A maid then took a lamp and ran to check the lock, and once more relocked the door. She sent several little demons inside to report: “Great King, there is someone outside the front gate calling out Your Exalted Title and demanding Lady Jinsheng.” From within, a palace maid slipped out and whispered quietly, “Do not call out; the king has only just fallen asleep.” Wukong called out loudly at the gate again, but that small goblin dared not disturb him. He did so three or four times, and none of them dared to pass a report inside. The Great Sage kept shouting and making a din outside, all the way until dawn. Unable to bear it, he lifted the iron staff, stepped forward, and struck at the gate. The demons within the gate and without it were thrown into panic, and the messengers ran to send word. The demon king, waking from a nap, only heard the uproar and tumult, rose, put on his clothes, and came out beyond the gauze curtain, asking, “What is all this yelling for?” The maidservants knelt and said, “Lord, we do not know which fellow outside has been shouting and abusing through half the night, and now he is even pounding the gate.”

The demon king came out of the palace gate. He saw those two little messenger demons bowing in panic and crying out, “There is someone outside calling and cursing, demanding Lady Jinsheng of the palace. If one were to say a single ‘no’ word, he would pour out endless twisted remarks, all of them impossible to bear. Seeing that dawn has come and Your Majesty does not come out, he has even been forced to beat the gate.” The demon king said, “Do not open yet. Go ask where he comes from, what his surname is, and what his name is; come back quickly with the report.” The little demon hurried out and asked through the gate, “Who is it that is battering the gate?” Wukong said, “I am the invited uncle from Zhuzi Country, come to take Lady Shenggong back to the country.” The little demon, hearing this, reported it back. The demon king then went to the inner palace to check the newcomer’s background. As it happened, the Niangniang had just risen and not yet combed and dressed, when a maid reported, “My lord has come.” The Niangniang hurriedly arranged her clothes, untied her dark cloud binding, and came out of the palace to welcome him. She had just sat down and had not yet even asked, when another maid announced, “That uncle outside has broken the gate.” The lady laughed, “My lady, how many generals and horsemen do you have at court?” The Niangniang replied, “In court there are Forty-eight guards and horsemen and a thousand able captains; on each frontier there are many marshals and commanding generals beyond count.” The demon king asked, “Is there any surname Wai among them?” The Niangniang replied, “In this palace I only assist the sovereign within and teach the consorts morning and evening. As for outside affairs, they stretch without bound; how could I remember names and surnames?” The demon king said, “This fellow outside calls himself ‘grand-uncle.’ In the Hundred Family Surnames, there is not even one surname Wai. Your Highness is intelligent and highborn, raised in the inner palace, surely reading many books. Is there not a surname written in one of them?” The Niangniang said, “Only in the Thousand Character Classic, there is a line ‘wai shou fu xun’; that must be it, surely.”

The demon king rejoiced, “It is certain. It is certain.” He rose, took leave of the Niangniang, went to the Flayed-Skin Pavilion, made himself ready, called out the demon troops, opened the gate, and came out directly. In one hand he held a Flower-Stamped Xuanhua Axe, and in a sharp voice he called out, “Who is this maternal grandfather from Zhuzi Country?” Wukong held the Golden-Hooped Staff in his right hand and with his left pointed, saying, “Noble nephew, what am I to you?” Seeing him, the demon king burned within with anger and barked, “You rogue:

A face like a monkey, and a countenance like a macaque. Seven parts truly a ghost, yet you dare to mock and cheat humans." Wukong laughed, “You drunken trickster king deceiver, you who dare to dupe your lord—no eye indeed. When, five hundred years ago, I roared through Heavenly Palace, not one of the Nine Heavens’ divine generals dared to call me with an ‘old’ honorific. You call me waigong? Is that not on your head?” The demon king shouted, “Tell me quickly your surname and name, what arts you wield that you dare run riot here!” Wukong said, “You may avoid asking my name, but if you force me to speak it, you may have no ground to stand on. Stand steady and hear me speak: Heaven and earth are my parents; the essences of sun and moon formed the sacred embryo. A divine stone held the secret, ageless; my spiritual root grew by most wondrous conception. In that year I emerged from the Three-Yang height; today my true form returns, and all ten thousand assemblies become harmonious. I once gathered all sorts of demons and was their chief; I could subdue all strange beings and revere Dan-Ya Mountain. The Jade Emperor issued my appointment and Taibai Jinxing carried down the decree. He invited me to Heaven to assume office; I was made Bi Ma Guard, though I rejoiced not. In early rebellion I plotted against him in my cave, boldly raising troops and storming the heavenly throne steps. I crossed blades with the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King and the Crown Prince; in one clash he was humbled. Again did Jinxing report to the Lord of the Mysterious Vault, and another amnesty edict was sent down. I was then made the True Great Sage Who Equalled Heaven, and at that time I was praised as the timber of the realm. Again I disrupted the Peach Banquet, drank deeply and stole the elixir, bringing down this disaster. Lord Lao of Highest Esteem drove himself in person; the Western Pond Queen Mother awaited me at Jade Terrace. Knowing I broke Heaven’s law, he at once summoned the heavenly troops and lit the alarm banners. Ten-thousand evil stars and malign luminaries, blades and spears in close array. Heavenly nets and earth snares stretched over whole hillsides; the armies raised swords and pikes to full measure. In that fierce battle there was no question of victory; Guanyin recommended Erlang to come. The two sides met in rivalry, each showing what heroes they were; he had brothers of Mount Mei. Each then displayed transformations in valour; the Three Sacred Ones of Heaven opened the clouds at the gate. Lao Jun cast aside the Vajra Collar; all the gods seized me and dragged me to Golden Stair. No need to read out warrants and indictments; as a criminal I was to suffer torment and be beheaded. Axe-hacks and hammer-blows could not harm my life; sword-flashes and blade-cuts could not touch my vital core. Fire and thunder struck me, but all this was so; no method could damage my long life. I was taken to Taiqing Doushuai Academy, arranged and refined in the furnace to the limit. When the prescribed term was full, the cauldron was opened, and I leaped out from within. Raising this Wishing-bar Staff in my palm, I flipped and struck the Yulong Terrace. Star and constellations all withdrew in hiding; I trampled Heaven’s court at will. Li, the Vigilant Spirit, rushed to summon Buddha, and Shakyamuni tested my talent. I turned cūn-dou within my palm and traversed the whole circuit of Heaven and return. A Buddha-wisp magician tried to trick and deceive, and he pinned me at the cliff of heaven. Now for more than five hundred years, once released from bondage, I have broken out and goaded my frail body again. I in particular protected Tripitaka and went west to the Western Regions; Wukong the Traveller is fully aware. On the road to the west, I subdue demon-fiends; what evil monster among them is beyond fear?” The demon king, hearing him speak of Sun Wukong the Wukong the pilgrim, said, “So you are indeed the one who ravaged Heaven. You escaped and now escort Tripitaka westward. Go on your way then. Why meddle in my affairs, serving as a slave for Zhuzi Country only to come here seeking death?” Wukong shouted, “Wicked imp! You are ignorant in speech. I was invited with courtesy by Zhuzi Country, and he bestowed on me the honour to receive and serve me; this Old Monkey stands a thousand times above that throne. He treats me like father and mother and serves me as godhead—you dare to speak of me as ‘a slave’? I will not let this upstart deceiver-king live. Stand still! You shall taste one staff-blow for your waigong.” The demon king was flustered and in a panic. He sidestepped and avoided, then used the Xuanhua Axe to meet the strike. It was a superbly violent clash: Golden-Hooped Staff and Wishing-bar staff, one snarls teeth and gathers fury, one grinds teeth and shows might. This one is the Great Sage Who Equalled Heaven descending into the mortal world; that one is the demon king who came down from earth to make mischief. Both loosed cloud and fog, blinding the heavenly court with dust of sky and stone. Their returns and counterreturns were many; flashes of gold light burst forth again and again. Each showed full measure of art, each staking every miracle for all it was worth. This one sought to carry the Lady back to the Capital of the Deity, that one only loved the Empress, to dwell in mountain barracks. This bout is for no reason at all: each forgets life and death for his king’s cause. He two of them fought for fifty rounds without a clear winner. Seeing Wukong’s methods were so formidable, the demon king used the axe to brace against his iron staff and said, “Wukong, stay still. I have not yet taken my morning meal. Wait until I have eaten, then we will settle who is superior.” Wukong understood he was to seize the bell. He withdrew the iron staff and said, “A true hero does not chase a frightened hare.” He said, “Go, go, eat, and come back for death.”

The demon king turned and dashed back inside. “Quickly bring out the treasure,” he told the Niangniang. The Niangniang asked, “What good is the treasure for?” He said, “This morning the fighter said our opponent is a disciple of the monk on the Sutra trip, named Sun Wukong the Wukong, who falsely calls himself waigong. I have fought him to this point and we are still evenly matched. Let me take the treasure out and release some firework; let us burn that monkey head.” The Niangniang’s heart quivered in pain: if she did not bring out the bells, he might grow suspicious; if she brought them out, she feared she would endanger Wukong’s life. While she was still hesitating and undecided, the demon king pressed again, “Bring it out at once.” The Niangniang, at her wit’s end, opened the lock, handed the three bells to the demon king, and he left the cave. The Niangniang sat in the palace, tears flowing like rain, wondering whether the Wukong might somehow escape with his life. Both had no idea that the bells were fakes.

The demon stepped out through the gate, took up the windward side, and shouted, “Sun Wukong, do not run. Watch me shake my bell.” Sun Wukong laughed. “You have a bell, so do I not have one? If you can shake it, does that mean I cannot?” The demon king said, “What kind of bell do you have? Bring it out and let me see.” Sun Wukong pinched his iron staff into the shape of an embroidered needle and hid it in his ear. He then untied three true treasures from his belt and said to the demon king, “Is this not my purple-gold bell?” When the king saw it, he was startled: “What a trick, what a trick! How can his bell be no different at all from mine? Even if both were cast from one mold, some are worn smooth in different places, one has more scars, another lacks a tassel, and yet not a hair’s breadth do they differ!” He asked again, “Where did your bell come from?” Sun Wukong replied, “Noble nephew, where did that bell of yours come from?” The demon king came clean and said, “My bell was made this way:

Taiching Immortal Lord’s Dao origin is deep; in the Eight-Trigram furnace it was long refined. Forged into a bell, called a supreme treasure; Laozi has kept it until this day. Sun Wukong laughed. “Old Sun’s bell also came from that time.” The king asked, “From where, then, is its provenance?” Sun Wukong said, “Mine was made this way: The Dao Ancestor burned elixirs in the Tusita Palace; the golden bell was stirred in the furnace. In cycles of two, three and six, a rare jewel turns; mine is the female, yours the male.” The demon king said, “A bell is a treasure of gold-great-elixir, not a bird or beast. How can one tell male and female from it? It is enough if it yields treasure when shaken.” Sun Wukong said, “Words prove nothing. Let the doing show it. Let me have you do it first.”

The demon king truly shook one bell three times, and no fire came out. He shook the second one three times, and no smoke appeared. He shook the third one three times, and no yellow sand appeared. He panicked. “How strange! How strange! The world has changed. This bell is surely afraid to release its force. The male beheld the female, and so nothing came out.” Sun Wukong said, “Noble nephew, stop. Let me shake yours and you shall see.” The clever monkey clutched all three bells at once and began shaking them together. Behold, red fire, blue smoke, and yellow sand rolled forth together, burning trees and setting mountains aflame. The Great Sage then recited another charm and called down onto the ground, “Wind, come!” At once, wind drove the flames, and the fire rode the wind’s might: red blaze upon red, black as dusk, firework light across the sky and yellow sand across the earth. The Sai Tai Sui demon was terrified; his soul scattered, his spirit fled, with no path left, and in that fire there was no way to save his life.

Then, from midair, a fierce voice cried, “Sun Wukong, I have arrived.” Sun Wukong hurriedly turned and looked up. It was Guanyin, left hand holding a pure water flask, right hand a willow branch, sprinkling nectar of sweetness to quench the flames. Startled, Sun Wukong hid the bells at his waist and, with palms joined, knelt and prostrated himself. The Bodhisattva swept a few drops of nectar with the willow branch, and in a moment the smoke and flames vanished and the yellow sand was gone. Sun Wukong knelt and said, “I did not know the Great Compassion had descended to the mortal world. I failed to avoid offense. May I ask where you are going, Bodhisattva?” Guanyin said, “I came especially to hunt down this demon.” Sun Wukong said, “What is this demon’s history? You would honorfully descend your august form to take him?” Guanyin said, “He is a golden-maned hound demon ridden by me. While the herdsman slept and failed in his watch, this wretch bit through the iron chain and came away. Yet he comes to bring peace to the King of Zhuzi.” Hearing this, Sun Wukong immediately bowed and said, “The Bodhisattva says one thing, yet he has deceived the sovereign here, defiled the queen, and ruined law and custom, bringing disaster to this land. How then is this peace-making?” Guanyin said, “You do not know it. In the time when the former king of Zhuzi still sat on the throne, this king was still the Crown Prince of the East and had not yet ascended. As a child he loved hunting. He led men and horses and turned loose hawks and hounds, and came to Luofeng Slope. Beneath the hill’s side sat two peacock chicks, male and female, born of the Peacock Great Bright King Bodhisattva, a child of the Western Buddha Mother. The king shot at them and wounded the male peacock; the female returned west carrying an arrow in her side. After repentance, the Buddha Mother instructed him to undergo austerity for three years, and sickness clung to his body. At that time I rode this hound and heard the matter. It happened that this wicked beast took note of it and came here to deceive the queen and remove this calamity from the king. For three years the wrong and the grievance have now been satisfied. Fortunately you have come to cure the king’s plight. I come now only to seize this demonic evil. Sun Wukong said, “Bodhisattva, even if this story be true, he has stained the queen, ruined courtly order, and endangered the people. He deserves death. Since you have compassionately descended yourself, pardon his capital crime if you will, but not his living offense. Let me strike him twenty blows and then take him with you.” Guanyin said, “Wukong, since you know I have come among mortals, grant me this one thing: spare him now. Then it will count as your deed of subduing a demon. If you raise your staff, he will be dead already.” Sun Wukong dared not disobey, and only knelt to say, “If the Bodhisattva takes him back to the sea, he must never again descend secretly among men, where his harm would again be deep.”

Guanyin barked once, “Demon wretch! Return at once to your former form. Why delay?” At once the monster tumbled and showed its original body, shook out its furry coat, and the Bodhisattva mounted him. Guanyin looked at the hound’s neck and did not see three golden bells there. Guanyin said, “Wukong, return my bell.” Sun Wukong said, “Old Sun does not know it.” Guanyin cried out, “You thieving monkey! If you had not stolen that bell, not one Wukong—not even ten—would dare come this near. Bring it out at once.” Sun Wukong laughed, “I truly have not seen it.” Guanyin said, “If you truly did not see it, then I will recite the Tightening Headband Spell.” The monkey panicked and begged, “Do not recite it, do not recite it. The bell is here.” This was exactly the saying: who can untie the bell on the hound’s neck? The one who asks to untie it is the one who tied it. Guanyin fitted the bell around the demon’s neck and leapt to a high seat. Watch him: from all four feet lotus-flame sparks leapt, and his whole body flashed with golden threads like flying needles. Great Compassion returned to the South Sea, without further account.

Sun Great Sage then neatly fastened up his robes, raised his iron staff, and battered his way into Xiezhi Cave, beating to death all the demons and monsters and clearing them all out. He went on to the palace and invited the palace maiden to return to her kingdom. The empress could not prostrate enough in respect. Sun Wukong explained fully the matter of Guanyin’s exorcism and how the phoenix had been broken apart. He gathered some soft grass and braided it into a grass-dragon. “Daughter-in-law, mount it. Close your eyes and do not fear. I will take you back and let you appear before the ruler.” The empress carefully obeyed. Sun Wukong employed his divine powers, and only the rushing of wind in her ears could be heard.

After half an hour he brought her into the capital, set her down on the cloud-platform, and said, “Your Majesty, open your eyes.” The queen opened her eyes and looked about. She recognized the Phoenix Pavilion Dragon Tower, rejoiced inwardly, stepped off the grass-dragon, and climbed with Sun Wukong into the treasure hall. When the king saw her he hurried down from the dragon couch and reached for the queen’s jade hand as if to express reunion and emotion. Suddenly he fell to the ground and cried, “My hand hurts, my hand hurts.” Zhu Bajie laughed loudly: “What a face—so little merit! The moment he saw her, he was already stung to death.” Sun Wukong said, “Bajie, would you dare to poke her?” Zhu Bajie said, “What of it if I touched her?” Sun Wukong said, “The empress has born venomous barbs on her body, and there is stinging poison in her hand. Since she came to Qilin Mountain, she has spent three years with that Sai Tai Sui demon, yet he never touched her skin. The moment he touched her, her body would ache; if he touched her hands, her hands would pain.” The assembled officials heard this: “What can be done?” At that moment those ministers outside were full of misgivings, and inside the concubines were frightened. Near by, in two palaces of the Jade Sage and the Silver Sage, they helped the king to his feet.

While this panic was still at its height, he suddenly heard someone in midair call, “Great Sage, I have come.” Sun Wukong lifted his head and saw this:

A grave crane-cry cleaves the sky, swift and high it comes before the court. Auspicious radiance winds in circles; red and wondrous vapor drifts in fluttering grace. Brown robes draped on his body, raising cloud and smoke; feet in reed shoes, a rare sight. In his hand a dragon-whisk broom of fly-repelling fibers, silk cords wound at his waist. Through heaven and earth he knits human ties, and roams in carefree ease across the wide earth. This is the Purple Cloud Immortal of Great Luo Heaven, descended now in mortal form to dissolve the nightmare. Sun Wukong stepped forward and greeted him, “Where does Zhang Ziyang go?” Zhang Ziyang Zhenren arrived in the hall and bowed, saying, “Great Sage, this humble one is Zhang Baoduan.” Sun Wukong returned the salute: “From where do you come?” The immortal said, “Three years ago I attended Buddha’s assembly. Passing this way, I saw that the King of Zhuzi faced ruin from the Phoenix Matter and feared this demon would defile the empress, ruin human order, and make it impossible for her to be reunited with the king. So I transformed an old brown robe into a fresh, cloud-bright garment, shimmered with five colors, and presented it to the demon king, telling the empress to wear this as new clothing. When she put it on, she was covered with the poison barbs. Those barbs were in that brown robe itself. Now that I know the Great Sage has succeeded, I have come to dispel the nightmare.” Sun Wukong said, “If so, we are in your debt for coming so far; then do it quickly and remove it.” The immortal stepped forward, pointed at the empress with his hand, and took off that robe. The empress at once was as before. He shook the garment once, put it on himself, and said to Sun Wukong, “Great Sage, do not take offense; this little immortal takes leave.” Sun Wukong said, “Wait, let the king offer thanks first.” The immortal smiled, “No need, no need.” With one deep bow he rose and vanished into the sky. The emperor, empress, and all the courtiers and attendants looked up and each offered a bow.

After the saluting and bowing were finished, the king at once ordered the Great East Hall opened and thanked the four monks. The king then led all his people in kneeling obeisance, and only then were husband and wife made reconciled once more. In the middle of the joyous banquet, Sun Wukong called out, "Master, bring that battle report." The Venerable pulled it from his sleeve and passed it to Sun Wukong. Sun Wukong gave it to the king, saying, "This was sent by the little captain dispatched by that monster. That little captain had already been slain by me, and this was sent back as a report of merit. Later I returned to the mountain, changed into the captain, and went back into the cave to report. In that way I came before Her Majesty, stole out the golden bell, and was nearly caught by him. I changed form again, stole it out once more, and engaged him in battle. Luckily, Guanyin appeared, took him away, and told me the reason for the phoenix being split. ..." He recounted the whole matter from beginning to end in full detail. Then all the king’s ministers and common people, inside and outside the realm, praised and thanked him without exception. Tripitaka said, "First, this is the blessing of a worthy king; second, it is the merit of your little disciple. This splendid banquet is more than enough. Let us now take leave; do not detain this poor monk and make him fail in his journey west." The king could not keep him by entreaty, so he changed the travel orders, arranged a full royal procession, and invited Tripitaka to sit safely in the dragon carriage. The king and queen together seized the hubs and pushed the wheels, escorting him as they bade him farewell. It is written:

By one’s destined ties, the disease of anxious doubt is washed away; sever all thought and longing, and the heart grows still and serene.

After all this, we shall see what good or ill is to come later; listen as it is explained in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 71: Wukong assumes a false name to subdue a monster hound; Guanyin manifests and compels the demon king.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

After Tripitaka bade farewell to the King of Zhuzi Kingdom, he had the saddles set in order and moved west. He and his companions traveled through many mountains and plains and passed through endless waterways; without noticing, autumn had passed, winter had ebbed away, and bright spring arrived. The master and disciples were strolling the road and enjoying the spring scenery when they suddenly saw a hermitage grove. Tripitaka dismounted, sliding down from the saddle, and stood by the side of the main road. Sun Wukong asked, "Master, this path is flat and even; why are we not taking it?" Zhu Bajie said, "Brother, you are very inconsiderate. Master has sat on horseback too long; let him dismount and take a breath of fresh air." Tripitaka said, "Not for the wind. I see there is a household there, and I intend to go beg some vegetarian alms." Sun Wukong laughed. "What is Master saying? If you want alms, I can go and ask for them. As the saying goes, 'He who is master for one day is as a father for life.' How could a disciple sit high while the master goes begging?" Tripitaka said, "Not exactly that. On ordinary days with no village in sight, you all go out and beg this way and that. But today there is a house right nearby, so I can call on it and bring back a meal." Zhu Bajie said, "Master is wrong in this matter. As the old saying goes, 'When three go out, it is the junior who suffers.' You are elder like a father, and we are all disciples. The old books say, 'When the master has work, the disciples bear the strain.' Let this old pig go." Tripitaka said, "Disciples, today the weather is clear, unlike the windy and rainy times. At such times, you all can go far away. At this household, I will go. If there is alms or not, I can return to the road afterward." Sha Wujing laughed nearby, "Elder brother, no need for long arguing. Master is this way by temperament; do not oppose him. If we upset him, we can just bring the alms by transformation, though he may not eat it."

Zhu Bajie acted on the words, took out the bowl and robes, changed his clothing and headgear, and strode directly to the front of the manor to look. It was a place that seemed well set for a halt. He saw:

The stone bridge rose tall, and the old trees stood in dense ranks. The lofty stone bridge and rippling water joined the long stream below; the old trees stood dense, while faint birds called from the quiet woods. Beyond the bridge stood a few thatched cottages, pure and elegant like a hermit's hut. There was also a separate thatched pavilion, bright and white, boldly set as if defying the monastery gate. Before the pavilion, he suddenly saw four beautiful women, all of them stitching at their needles and thread, embroidering phoenix-and-bird motifs. Tripitaka saw that household had no men, only four women, and so he did not dare to enter. He stood still, hidden beneath a tall grove. He watched each of the women in turn: Her inner heart was firm as stone; her orchid-like nature rejoiced like spring. Her tender face was framed in rosy cloud-light; her lips were vermilion, her rouge evenly spread. Her brows arched like the moon, low and curved; her fresh layered hair rose like stacked new clouds. If she stood among flowers, even roaming bees might mistake her for another blossom.

For nearly half a watch, a profound stillness fell. No chickens or dogs made a sound. Tripitaka thought to himself: "If I cannot summon a bowl of alms-food, my disciples will laugh at me. How can it be said the master cannot beg alms, while the disciple still can go and worship Buddha?"

Tripitaka found no way out and with reluctance took a few uncertain steps onto the bridge. After a few more paces, he saw inside those thatched buildings a sandalwood pavilion, and beneath it three women were playing ball-kicking. Those three women seemed different from the first four. He saw:

Their green sleeves flew loose, and their reddish- ochre skirts were pulled and swayed. The green sleeves fluttered and drooped, softly cupping slender arms like jade shoots. The ochre skirts were tugged so the narrow lotus-gold feet flashed through the hem. Their bearing was complete in line and poise; stillness and motion, in every step, were a thousand patterns. Lifting the head with measured height, then bending and sending the next move, they made each kick exact. Turning, they kicked the ball beyond the wall-like flowers; withdrawing a step, their movement turned as if crossing a great sea. They brushed a clod of earth lightly, then with a quick thrust struck to the side. On the shining little shoes with pearl shine they pressed sharply with the tips. On narrow bricks they knew just how to handle it, the feet lying like sleeping fish. The waist stayed true, knees folded and bent; the top lifted and the heels turned up in perfect turns. They could spin a stool with one movement; their shoulders were open and free. Their waists twisted to and fro, and their jewelled necks swayed with each move. The kicks made yellow-river waters seem to run backward, as if bargained for on a golden-fish bank. One turned, mistaking head for foot; another spun and struck with the back-step. They raised the ball on the arm and snapped a keen, pointed pull. They lifted their feet from the straw-soled shoes and returned them backward in a sudden gather. A retreating step sent their sleeves to swing; one hook, one move, and they crossed long as basket-lines. Reaching the gate, they reached in to seize; when beauty rose in the heart, all the maidens cried out in one voice. Sweat ran through the powdered faces, spreading through silk robes, and though weariness showed in their spirit they still called out like roaring surf. Words were not enough, and there was a poem to prove it: Kicked in the spring of the third month, the fair game begins. Heaven wind descends, and pure moon-faces glow. Sweat beads the powdered faces, each flower holding dew. Dust in the midge-brows and willow-swayed smoke. Green sleeves droop, cupping jade-shoot wrists; the reddish skirt drags to reveal the narrow golden-lotus feet. After many kicks, the lovely ones grow faint; disheveled cloud-hair, jeweled buns set askew. Tripitaka watched on for quite some time, then climbed to the bridgehead and called out: "Lady Bodhisattva, this poor monk has come by chance and begs for some alms." Those women heard him. One by one, each set aside her stitching and dropped the ball, and all came laughing softly to welcome him at the gate: "Venerable Master, forgive our poor reception. We did not expect a monk to pass this wild house; we would not block alms-going monks. Please come in and sit." Tripitaka thought privately: "Good, good indeed. In these western Buddha lands, even women attend to alms-seeking monks; how much more should men be devout to Buddha."

After they exchanged greetings, Tripitaka entered with the women and passed into the cottage. When he passed by the sandalwood pavilion, he saw no real halls or side corridors. He saw:

Ridge-tops rose high, and the earth veins stretched far. Ridge-tops rose up to brush cloud and haze; the earth-vein ran deep and far, connecting seas and peaks. Near the bridge were nine winding bends of water, circling back upon themselves. In the courtyards, peaches and plums were planted, a thousand trees each in dense flower. Vines of vines and fig hung from three and five trees; orchid and all kinds of fragrance scattered in ten thousand blossoms. From afar, the caves seemed to mock Penglai Islet; up close, the woods and hills pressed down even Taihua. It was truly a place where demons and immortals hide from sight, and with no neighboring homes, it made a household all its own. One woman stepped forward, pushed open both stone doors, and invited Tripitaka inside. Tripitaka had no choice but to enter. When he looked up, everything had been laid with stone tables and stone stools, all cold and bleak. He grew inwardly alarmed and thought, "This place is not auspicious; it is plainly inauspicious." The women smiled and greeted him. Tripitaka could not avoid sitting. After a short while, one spoke gently: "Venerable, from what mountain do you come? By what vow does this begging arise? Are you repairing roads and bridges, building temple courtyards, erecting monastic halls, or carving images of Buddha? Show your merit ledger for us to see." Tripitaka said, "I am not a monk who begs alms as a profession." The woman said, "If you do not beg alms, why come here?" Tripitaka said, "I am a monk sent from Great Tang in the East to go west to Greater Thunder-Voice Mountain for the scriptures. We passed by not long ago, hungry through the road; I came only to this hall to receive a single meal and then depart." The women replied, "Very well. As people say, 'A monk who comes from afar is here to read the sutra.' Sisters, do not delay him. Prepare the alms quickly."

At that time three women stayed with him, talking over this and that, speaking of causes and conditions. The other four went to the kitchen, raising their robes and tucking their sleeves to work the fire and scrub the pans. What was it they had arranged? It was human fat rendered in oil, human flesh slowly fried and stewed; it was cooked to a black mash like dark flour-dough, and human brains were sliced into tofu-like blocks. Two dishes were carried and set down on the stone tables. "Please partake," they told Tripitaka. "In this haste we have not prepared good alms; do just enough to fill your belly. More can be brought later." Tripitaka smelled it and noticed the rank stink. He dared not speak, but bowed with clasped hands and said, "Lady Bodhisattvas, this poor monk is strictly vegetarian from the womb." The women laughed: "Venerable, this is vegetarian." Tripitaka said, "Amitabha Buddha! If this is what passes for vegetarian food, this monk will never see the World-Honored One or obtain the scriptures." The women said, "Venerable, as an ordained monk you must not choose and pick through what is offered." Tripitaka said, "How could I? I am a monk from the Great Tang, sent westward to bring back the teachings. Along this road, life by life is to be preserved; if one is suffering, I save; if I can touch a grain of grain with my fingers and put it in my mouth, if thread threads catch and entangle the body, I dare not step across what is not fitting. How then could I choose one giver over another?" The women laughed. "Venerable, though you say you do not choose, you have just arrived to a strange gate of guests. Do not despise coarse and plain food; eat at least a little." Tripitaka said, "I truly cannot eat. I fear breaking the precepts. For the sake of all life, release this monk and let me go."

Tripitaka struggled to leave, but the women blocked the doors; none were willing to let him out. "For a household where guests have come, this is no easy business," they all said. "You may pass wind and then hide your hand as if embarrassed—where do you think you're going?" Each woman had some martial skill, and their hands and feet were lively; they pulled him, seized him with easy timing, and with one move threw him flat to the ground. The others held him fast, bound him with rope, and hoisted him high from the beams. This hanging form had a name: "Immortal Pointing-Path." At the front, one hand drew a silken rope and pulled up; one hand bound his waist and lifted; the two legs were taken back by another rope. With three ropes Tripitaka was hung from the beam, his back facing upward and his stomach downward. Tripitaka endured the pain, eyes watering, and cursed inwardly: "My life as a monk is such bad fortune. I only said I was going to a good household for a single alms-meal, yet I have fallen into a fire pit. Disciple! Come quickly to save me, and at least let me be seen again. If you are two more periods late, my life will be gone."

Though the Venerable Elder was deeply troubled, he still kept watching those women. The women then held him at arm’s length and proceeded to disrobe. His heart started to race, and he thought to himself: “Now that they have taken off their robes, this must be to strike at my life-force. Or perhaps they mean to consume my vital essence as well.” In fact, those women had only loosened their silk tops, exposing their bellies, and then each displayed her art: from each waist-joint shot forth silk cords, thick as duck eggs, knotted and springing like living threads, flashing jade and silver as they leapt. For the moment they left the manor gate hidden; I leave it unstated here.

Meanwhile the Great Sage Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing were on the roadside by the Great Way. Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing sat their horses and waited, while the Great Sage, as mischievous as ever, climbed a tree, leapt from branch to branch, and plucked leaves and fruit. Suddenly he turned and saw a burst of radiance, and in panic leapt down the tree, crying, “Bad, bad—Tripitaka’s allotted fortune has declined.” The Great Sage pointed and asked, “Look there at that manor-house. What do you see?” Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing looked together. The place shone, white as snow, silver-bright and bright as polished silver. Zhu Bajie said, “Enough—enough. Master has fallen in with a demoness; we should rush to save him.” The Great Sage said, “Good brother, don’t shout. Since you have seen nothing clearly, let Old-Sun go and deal with it.” Sha Wujing said, “Elder brother, be careful.” The Great Sage replied, “I have a way.”

The Great Sage tightened the knot of his tiger-skin skirt, whipped out the Golden-Hooped Staff, pulled up his feet, and in two or three strides ran forward. He saw the cords had hundreds and thousands of tight twists, crossing as if in warp and woof. He pressed on them with his hand; they felt sticky and soft, clinging to the flesh. The Great Sage still did not know what they were. He then raised the staff and said, “With one strike, whether it be merely a thousand layers or as many as ten thousand, I can break them.” He was about to strike, then stopped and said, “If they were hard, I could break them. But this is soft—best I can do is beat against it like a board. If I frightened it and it wound itself around me and bound Old-Sun, that would be less than fitting. Let me ask it first; only then will I strike.”

Who was he asking? He pinched a formula and spoke a charm, making the old earth god in the shrine spin in wild circles like a mill-wheel. The earth lady said, “Old man, why are you spinning so? It looks like a sheep-flag wind has risen.” The earth god replied, “You don’t know. You don’t know at all. The Great Sage Equal to Heaven has come, and I have not received him; from there he has bound me.” The old lady said, “Go meet him, and then why stand spinning here?” The earth god said, “If I go to him, his staff is heavy indeed, and he’ll beat me depending on how he deems me.” She said, “He sees you’re so old—how could he strike you?” The earth god said, “He likes to beat old men who’ve run out of good wine and have no coin.” The two bickered for a while; with no choice, he finally went out, and, trembling, knelt by the roadside, calling, “Great Sage, the local earth lord bows.” Sun Wukong said, “Get up. No need for needless fuss. I will not strike you. Stay where you are. Tell me first: what place is this?” The earth god asked, “Great Sage, from which quarter do you come?” Sun Wukong said, “I come from the Eastern land, traveling west.” The earth god said, “Great Sage, coming from the East—did you pass this mountain ridge?” Sun Wukong said, “I was just there. Our baggage and horses are still resting on that ridge, are they not?” The earth god said, “It is called Pansi Ridge. Below it is a cave named Pansi Cave. Within the cave dwell seven demons.” Sun Wukong asked, “Are they male spirits or female spirits?” The earth god said, “Female spirits.” Sun Wukong said, “How powerful are they?” The earth god said, “Their little power is modest; I know not the full extent of their arts. Only this is known: a little to the south, about three li away, is a Hot Spring of Purification. It is natural hot water, once the bathing pool of the Seven Celestial Maidens. Since the demons came here and took up residence, they have occupied it, and even the celestial maidens did not contend with them, simply yielding it. If heaven-born spirits refrain from provoking demons, then these must possess great power.” Sun Wukong asked, “What use is it for this demon to hold that spring?” The earth god said, “This one has taken over the pool, and three times a day comes out to bathe. The Hour of Si has already passed; now the Hour of Wu is coming.” Hearing this, Sun Wukong said, “Earth Lord, go back now. I’ll handle him myself.” The earth god knelt and struck his head to the ground once, then, trembling, returned to his shrine.

The Great Sage displayed a wondrous transformation and changed himself into a large hairy fly, landing nailed to a tuft of grass beside the road to wait. Soon he heard a susurrant breath like silkworms eating leaves, yet also like the swelling surge of sea tide. Not quite half a teacup’s time passed before the silken ropes all came to an end and the manor and village reappeared as they had been. Then came a sudden “yaa” as a gate sounded shut, and inside rose laughter and noisy chatter. Seven women came out. In the dark he watched closely as each one walked arm in arm, shoulder to shoulder, speaking and smiling as they crossed the bridge. They were indeed strikingly beautiful. One could see:

Sweeter than perfume of jade, and truer than the speech of blossoms, Brow like distant ridges, willow-soft and arched, Hairpins tipped in green jade, golden-lotus hems flashing in vermilion silk, As if Chang’e descended to the mortal world, a celestial beauty fallen into dust. The Great Sage laughed: “No wonder Tripitaka came here to perform this ritual conversion; it is because of beauties like these. If these seven courtesans kept hold of my Master, he would not be enough for one meal, nor even for two days of use. If they all put hands to him by turns, one rough movement would leave him dead. Let me first listen to what plans he is making and then see what he intends.”

The Great Sage, with a clear chirping sound, flew and clung to the cloud-coiffed head-dress of the woman in front. As soon as the group passed onto the bridge, a woman from the back called forward: “Elder sister, we’ve bathed; let us steam that fat monk and eat him.” Sun Wukong laughed inwardly. “These fiends are clever in a strange way—if they are to boil him they would save fuel, why insist on steaming him?” The women moved southward, plucking flowers and pushing through weeds. Before long they reached the bathing pool. There stood a splendid gate and wall, and all around the ground bloomed wild flowers in rich fragrance, with dense mounds of orchids and sweet flag along both sides. A woman stepped forward from the back and with one whistle-like breath pushed open both doors. There, in the center, was a hot spring basin. The water was called:

Since creation began, there were ten solar stars in the heavens. Later Hou Yi drew his bow and shot down nine crows to earth, leaving only the golden crow, the true fire of the sun. In heaven and earth there are nine hot springs, all formed from the flock of crows. Those nine Yang springs are Xiangleng Spring, Banshan Spring, Warm Spring, Donghe Spring, Huangshan Spring, Xiaoan Spring, Guangfen Spring, Tang Spring, and this one, the Purification-of-Impurity Spring. There is a poem in witness: From a single breath there is no winter or summer; three autumns pour out as spring forever. Hot waves boil like a cauldron in upheaval; the white-crowned waves rise fresh as newborn broth. Its channels water the grain; its still flows sweep away common dust. Fine jetlets tremble like pearl tears, while thick surges rise like pearls at the edge of one’s tongue. The mellowing is no brewing, yet clear calmness stays warmly self-born. Auspicious signs show this land to be noble; creation itself is heaven’s plain truth. Where beauties bathe, their frosted skins grow smooth; purged of world-dust, their jade-like forms seem newly made.

That bathing pool was just over five zhang wide and more than ten zhang long, with depth and shallows of about four chi. Its water was clear through and through. Near the bottom it seemed like tumbling jade beads; white and pale gleams rose up, and in all four directions were six or seven outlets from which streams escaped. The water ran on for two or three li, reaching the fields still warm. Above the pool stood three pavilions. In one of them, near the back wall, stood an eight-legged bench; and on two hillocks by the side were two lacquered racks for garments. The Great Sage, delighted to himself, fluttered one wing and fastened himself on the top of a rack.

The women found the water clear and warm, and decided to bathe. They removed their clothes together and draped them on the rack before all going in together. They saw:

They unbuttoned, and unfastened the knots of their silk sashes. Soft breasts shone white like silver; moon-white bodies gleamed as pure as snow. Elbows and shoulders were like laid ice, fragrant shoulders faintly dusted like fine powder. Bellies soft and padded, backs still bright and clean. Ankles and calves were slimly full, the golden-lotus folds narrow as three inches. At the waist a little cleft opened, revealing a flirtatious hidden hollow. All the women leapt into the water, one after another, bouncing in waves and playing with the water in wild delight. The Great Sage thought, “If I strike them, I need only stir the pool with this staff and it will be like throwing hot water over a rat’s nest—there will be a whole brood dead in a moment. Alas, alas! To strike would indeed kill them, but it would tarnish Old-Sun’s name. There is an old saying: ‘A man should not contend with women.’ For me, a mere man, to slay these girls would not be fitting. I won’t strike them. I’ll give them a final stratagem that leaves them unable to move at all—at least that will do.” The Great Sage then formed a seal, spoke a spell, and changed himself into a hungry old eagle. He appeared thus: Fur like frost and snow, eyes like stars. Wherever a demon-fox turns up, its soul is lost; a wily hare at its moment of need is struck to terror. Steel claws flash with sharp gleams, while a fierce, lordly air rolls in mighty force. He can use cruel strength to feed his belly, never shrinking from his own grasp to rise skyward. Through ten thousand miles of cold sky, up and down, he passes through clouds and snatches what he finds. With one beat of his wing he flew forward, spread his talons and snatched away all seven suits of clothing from the rack, then turned straight toward the ridge. There he returned to his true form and came to report to Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing.

Zhu Bajie looked back with a grin and said, 'So it seems Master was dragged off, all the way like goods from a pawnshop.' Sha Wujing asked, 'How can you tell?' Zhu Bajie said, 'Didn’t you see Elder Brother bring back some of his robes?' Sun Wukong set down the Golden-Hooped Staff and said, 'Those are not Tripitaka’s robes; they are clothes worn by a fiend.' Zhu Bajie said, 'How can there be so many?' Sun Wukong replied, 'Seven sets.' Zhu Bajie asked, 'How could you strip them off so easily, and so neatly?' Sun Wukong said, 'I did not strip them. This place is called Pan-Si Ridge, and the village-cottage is called Pan-Si Cave. In the cave are seven female monsters. They seized my master, hung him in the cave, and all went to bathe in the Hot Spring of Cleansing Silt. That spring was formed by Heaven and Earth, a whole pool of hot water. The plan was to bathe first, then steam him and eat him. I followed them there, and when he took off his clothes and went into the water, I wanted to strike him. But I feared soiling my staff, and I feared losing face; so I did not move the staff. Instead I became a hungry old eagle and grabbed his clothing. He endured it all in silent shame and, too ashamed, did not dare raise his head, staying crouched in the water. Let us quickly go free the Master and leave.' Zhu Bajie laughed and said, 'Brother, in every matter leave a root to hold to. Now that you have seen a fiend, how can you not kill him and yet go to free Master? Even if he hides now in shame, by evening he will surely come out. His place still has old garments; he can put one on and chase us. Even if he does not chase, he has stayed there long. Once we secure the Sutra, we can return by that road. There is a saying: “Better to be short of money by the roadside than short of fists by the roadside.” At this moment, he only stopped the clamour, and he is not an enemy, is he?' Sun Wukong said, 'On what plan do you insist?' Zhu Bajie said, 'In my opinion, first kill the fiend and then free Master. This is cutting the weeds at the root.' Sun Wukong said, 'I will not strike him. If you want to strike, then you strike him.'

Zhu Bajie shook himself together, happy and proud, lifted the pick, and strode straight there in great spirits. Suddenly he pushed the door open and saw the seven women crouching in the water, cursing the eagle wildly: 'This shaggy-mouthed beast, this cat-faced carrion, you snatched all our clothes—how are we to do anything now?' Zhu Bajie could not help laughing: 'Ladies Bodhisattvas, you are bathing here too? Let my monk wash as well, shall we?' The fiend saw him and grew angry: 'You monk are extremely impolite. We are household women, and you are a man of renunciation. The old books say, “Men and women should not sit together for seven years.” How can you bathe with us in the same pool?' Zhu Bajie said, 'The weather is hot; I cannot avoid it. Let me wash once. What has a book to do with this—same seat or not same seat?' He would not allow further words. He threw down the pick, removed his silk robe, and with a splash plunged into the water. The fiend, vexed, rushed forward to strike him. Not knowing how at home Zhu Bajie was in the water, he changed once within it and became a smelt spirit. The fiends all tried to grasp for fish, and they could not catch him: when they reached east, he suddenly slipped to the west; when they reached west, he suddenly slipped to the east. So slippery and slick, they only groped in confusion around their thighs and groins. The water was deep and swirling; he turned on the surface for a while, then went down to the bottom, and turned over again. He was all breath and panting, his spirit tired and waning.

Zhu Bajie at last rose up, restored his true form, put on the robe, gripped the pick, and shouted, 'Who is there? How could you take me for a smelt spirit?' The fiend, seeing him, was frightened and trembling. He said, 'At first you came as a monk and in the water changed into a smelt spirit; when I could not catch you and now you appear in this dress, from where did you come to this place? you must surely leave a name behind.' Zhu Bajie said, 'This lot of ruffians truly did not recognize me. I am Wuneng, the disciple of Tripitaka from the Great Tang, Zhu Bajie of the Tianpeng rank. You have hung my master in the cave and devised to steam him and eat him. Is my master even good for steaming? Hold out your head at once; let each of you take up a pick, so I can cut your roots.' On hearing this, the fiends’ spirits left them; in the water they knelt and spoke: 'Please, Great Lord, have mercy! We were blind with arrogance and wrongly seized your master. Though he hangs there, we did not dare to punish him further. Show pity and spare my life. I am willing to offer a little tribute and send Tripitaka westward.' Zhu Bajie shook his head and said, 'No need for that. A proverb says, “One who once had the sugar-seller trick a gentleman will never trust sweet words again.” So with a pick in hand, each of you, strike and be done.'

Zhu Bajie was rough and brutish and showed all his arts, with no compassion in him at all for pity and restraint. He raised the pick and, without pausing to distinguish right or wrong, rushed in and struck wildly. The fiend, flustered, lost all sense of order. When life itself was at stake, there was no concern for shame. He covered his shameful parts, sprang out of the water, and all stood in the pavilion. Then he wrought a spell: from each of their navel-caves bones sprang out as silk cords, and they spread a great silk canopy that hid the sky, enclosing Zhu Bajie within. Zhu Bajie suddenly raised his head and could not see sky or light; he pulled himself out and tried to go, but he could not lift his step. He had laid trip-wires; silk ropes covered the ground everywhere. He moved a foot and tripped and spun—leftward, one face-first fall; rightward, one倒倒-plant fall; he turned quickly and fell with his mouth in the dust; getting up in haste, he fell again like an upstanding dragonfly. No one could say how many turns he had taken. His head swam, his body tingled, his legs were weak and he could hardly crawl. At last he could only lie on the ground and groan.

The fiend captured him but did not strike or wound him. One after another they leapt out of the gate, covering the sky with the silk canopy, then each returned to its own cave. At the stone bridge they stood, chanted a spell, and in an instant drew back the canopy; then the one beneath ran into the cave, bare as he had been, and, lewdly showing himself, ran past Tripitaka with a grin. In the stone chamber he took off and put on several old garments, went straight to the rear gate, and stood calling, 'Where are my children?' The demon had not borne these children in her own body; every one was a foster-son she had sworn with. Their names were Mi, Ma, Lu, Ban, Meng, La, and Qing: Mi means honeybee, Ma means ant-bee, Lu means lu-bee, Ban means ban-hair, Meng means niu-meng, La means wax-slick, and Qing means dragonfly. Originally this monster had cast a net across heaven and earth and captured these seven kinds of insect-bodies to eat them. As the old saying goes, 'Birds have bird speech; beasts have beast speech.' At that time these insects pleaded for mercy and wished to take her as mother. So in spring they gathered a hundred flowers for her, and in summer sought out many plants for the monster to serve. At a sudden call they all came before her and asked, 'Mother, what is your command?' The children said, 'Child, this morning we offended a monk from the Tang court. His disciple caught him in the pond and brought him such humiliation he nearly lost his life. Go out and drive him off. If you gain the upper hand, come to your uncle’s house and meet me.' Those monsters were then free from death and gone, and what further misfortune from that wicked mouth was born need not be set out. See these leech-like insects—each rubs his hands and comes out to meet the enemy.

Zhu Bajie, dizzy and bewildered, then lifted his head and saw that both the silk canopy and the silk lines were gone. He tested each step carefully and crawled himself up, enduring the pain, then found the way back. When he saw Sun Wukong he grabbed him by the sleeve and said, 'Brother, is my head swollen? Is my face blue?' Sun Wukong said, 'How did this happen?' Zhu Bajie said, 'That scoundrel covered me with silk cords and set a tripping snare. I do not know how many somersaults I made; I fell so much that my back is bent and my waist is twisted—I can scarcely move an inch. Only when the silk canopy and cords had all disappeared did I save my life and return.' Sha Wujing saw him and said, 'Enough, enough—you have brought trouble upon yourself. The fiend has surely gone back into the cave to harm Master. We must quickly go and rescue him.'

When Sun Wukong heard this, he pulled up his pace and ran; Zhu Bajie held the horse. They hurried to the manor gate, and there on the stone bridge they saw seven little demons blocking the way: “Slow down, slow down—we are here.” Sun Wukong looked at them and said, “How funny. All these fellows are small persons. They are only two or three chi tall, not even three; even the heaviest are only eight or nine jin, not over ten jin.” He called out, “Who are you?” The monster said, “I am the son of Seventh Celestial Aunt. You insulted my mother and dare, still ignorant, to rush onto my gate. Do not run. Be careful.” At once the monsters came charging in a wild rush. Zhu Bajie, who is naturally fierce when angered, saw that band of little, squat creatures and, infuriated, raised his pike to strike them. When those fiends saw the ferocity of the bald one, each one showed his true form and leapt up, crying, “Transform!” In a moment, one became ten, ten became a hundred, a hundred became a thousand, and a thousand became ten thousand, each one into an unending number. Then this was seen:

All through the sky flew wax-moths, all over the ground dragonflies danced. Honeybees chased head and brow, hornets pierced the eyes. Fleas and horse-flies bit front and back, cicadas stung from above and below. Black, thick faces spread across everything; with rustling whispers, spirits and ghosts were frightened. Zhu Bajie panicked, “Brother, you kept saying it would be easy to fetch the sutras on the western road, but even bugs can bully people there.” Sun Wukong said, “Brother, do not fear. Go straight on and strike.” Zhu Bajie said, “They pummel me on face and body all over, with tenfold layers of stings—how can I fight them?” Sun Wukong replied, “No matter. No matter. I have my own method.” Sha Wujing said, “Brother, whatever your method, use it at once; in a little while my bare head will all be swollen.”

The Great Sage plucked a handful of downy hairs from himself, chewed them to powder, and spat them out; at once they turned into yellow, hemp, drake, white, eagle, fish, and kite-hawks. Zhu Bajie said, “Eldest brother, why are you saying such rough marketplace words—Yellow, hemp, drake, and so on?” Sun Wukong said, “You do not understand. The yellow is a yellow hawk, the hemp is a hemp hawk, the drake is a drake hawk, the white is a white hawk, the eagle is an eagle hawk, the fish is a fish hawk, and the kite is a kite hawk. The demon’s children are seven kinds of insects, while my hairs are seven kinds of hawks.” Hawks are the best at catching insects; one in the beak at a time, claws striking, wings hammering. In a moment they had all been cleared, with no traces left in the air and the ground scoured clean within the span of a foot.

The three brothers had only just forced their way across the bridge and gone straight into the cave when they saw Master Tripitaka hanging there, wheezing and crying. Zhu Bajie stepped forward: “Master, did you come here to hang yourself for sport? You have no idea how many times I have tumbled and rolled because of this.” Sha Wujing said, “First let us unbind Master and then speak of it.” Sun Wukong snapped at the rope and cut it, lowering Master Tripitaka. He asked, “Where has the fiend gone?” Tripitaka said, “Those seven all went bareback to the rear to call for their sons.” Sun Wukong said, “Brothers, come with me and search.”

The three men, each bearing his weapon, went into the back garden to search, but found no trace. They searched all over the peach and plum trees and still found nothing. Zhu Bajie said, “Gone, gone.” Sha Wujing said, “No need to look for him; let me help Master Tripitaka first.” The brothers came back to the front and had Master Tripitaka mounted on the horse. Zhu Bajie said, “You carry Master on foot; let old Pig give one pike strike and knock over this house of his, so that when he comes back he has no place to settle.” Sun Wukong laughed: “To knock it down is too much trouble. Better to fetch some firewood and give him a root-upding.” The fool looked for some rotten pine, broken bamboo, dry willow, and withered vine, lit them with one flame, and in a roaring blaze burned them all cleanly. Only then did Master and disciples feel at ease and come onward.

Ah! In the end, we still do not know what fortune or disaster awaits that fiend. Listen and see how it is resolved in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 72: In Spindle-Silk Cave seven emotions cloud the root mind; at Woguo Spring Pigsy forgets himself.
