This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Once, Great Sage Sun Wukong supported Tripitaka and, with Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, rushed up onto the Great Road, always traveling westward. Not long afterward, they suddenly saw a place of layered towers and pavilions, with grand palace-like buildings looming high. Tripitaka tugged the reins and said, "Disciple, look there—what place is that?" Wukong raised his head to inspect and suddenly saw:

Hills encircle halls and pavilions; streams wind about terrace platforms. Before the gate, mixed trees stand thick and wild, and beyond the dwelling wildflowers perfume the air richly. White egrets rest among the willows, pure as flawless jade out of the mist; orioles sing inside peach groves, yet seem to glow like gold in flame. Coupled wild deer, carefree, tread upon green mossy sward; pairs of mountain birds call and fly, crying together from red treetops. It is truly like Liu Ruan’s Terrace Cave and does not lag behind the Immortal Langyuan estate. Wukong reported: "Master, that place is neither a prince’s manor nor a rich household, yet it resembles a Taoist hermitage-temple. Only when we reach it shall we know for certain." Hearing this, Tripitaka whipped his horse onward. They came before the gate and looked closely. On the lintel was a stone plaque engraved with three characters: Huanghua Monastery. Tripitaka dismounted. Zhu Bajie said, "Huanghua Monastery is the abode of Daoists. It would be good for us to visit and speak with him; though our robes and his are different, our ways of cultivation are of a kind." Sha Wujing said, "That is true. First, let us look at the scenery inside; second, we should open a chance for alms. If the place is suitable, we can arrange some monastic meal for Master to eat."

As he instructed, the four entered together. On the two gate-posts they saw a pair of spring couplets: "House of immortals in yellow sprouts and white snow; flower-scented herb and jade blossom home of a feathered scholar." Wukong laughed: "This is a Taoist who burns reeds, forges medicines, keeps a furnace going, and carries a cauldron." Tripitaka pinched him and said, "Careful, careful. We do not know him, nor are we related; be courteous for the moment." Before he could say more, they entered the inner gate. There, the main hall was shut tight, and on the east gallery a Taoist sat making pills. Wukong glanced and muttered,

He wore a bright red crown with gold-work flashing, and a black, dense robe of pitch-dark cloth; he wore green patterned cloud-topped shoes, and tied about him a yellow, flowing Liu-Gong-style sash. His face was like cast-iron from a melon, his eyes like clear stars. His posture was tall and broad, almost with the look of a Western stranger; his lips and mouth flung open wide like a man of rough habits. His heart was hidden thunder ready to rumble—a true feathered Daoist who could subdue tigers and bring down dragons. When Tripitaka saw him, he called out in a loud respectful voice, "Old immortal, poor monk offers reverence." Startled, the Taoist looked up; seeing him, he dropped the pill in hand, straightened his garment, and came down the steps to receive them, saying, "Teacher-Father, pardon my failure to receive you properly. Please come inside." Master Tripitaka gladly mounted the hall. The door was pushed open: there were statues of the Three Pure Ones, and on the offering table were a brazier and incense. He took incense and placed it on the brazier, made three rounds of worship, and then exchanged courtesies with the Taoist. They then moved to the guest seats and sat with the disciples. He urgently summoned a Daoist youth for tea. Two youths appeared from the inner rooms, brought tea trays in, rinsed teacups, wiped tea-spoons, laid out tea snacks, and ran about in a flurry. This soon disturbed those few enemies inside.

It turned out that the seven female demons from Pansi Cave had been studying arts in this Taoist’s hall. Since they had put on their old garments and summoned their son, they had come straight to this place. They were then behind, cutting and mending clothing, when they saw the child fetching tea and asked, "Boy, has a guest really arrived, that you are so busy and pressed?" The acolyte replied, "Just now, four monks came in; the Master told me to bring tea for them." One of the women asked, "Was there a white, plump monk?" "Yes." She asked, "Was there one with a long mouth and big ears?" "Yes." The woman said, "Quickly take the tea out. Give your Master a glance and sign with your eyes, then bring him in. I have urgent words for him." As expected, the celestial youth carried out five cups of tea. The Taoist tucked in his robe, took a cup in both hands, and handed one to Tripitaka, then to Zhu Bajie, Sha Wujing, and Wukong. When tea was served and the cups taken away, the boy gave a signal. The Taoist then bowed and said, "Kindly be seated, everyone." He told him, "Child, lay aside the tea tray and attend." Then, "I will go and return shortly." At that moment, Tripitaka, the disciples, and one youth went out of the hall to look around. It is not to be retold here.

As for the Taoist, he went into the inner room. There he saw seven women kneeling together, all crying, "Brother, brother, listen to a word from your little sister." The Taoist raised each by hand and said, "When you came earlier, you had something to tell me. Today’s pills could not be prepared in the presence of yin people, so I did not answer then. Now there are guests outside. If there is anything to say, tell it slowly for now." The women said, "With respect, Brother, this matter exists only because of those visitors; only after they depart can we tell it, else it is useless to say it now." The Taoist laughed: "You can hear how virtuous these girls are—only speak when guests are present? Are you mad? Put aside that I am a quiet Daoist adept and not a mundane householder with wife and children and domestic business to finish even after guests depart. How can you be so unfilial and put up this pretense for me? Let me go out first." The women together caught his sleeve and said, "Brother, lower your anger. I ask you: where are those guests who came from ahead of the hall?" The Taoist spat and did not answer. The women said, "A little while ago, the boy entered to take in tea. I heard him say there were four monks." The Taoist, angry, said, "So what if they are monks?" The women said, "Among the four monks, one was white-faced and fat, and one was long-mouthed with big ears. Did you ask where they came from?" The Taoist said, "Among them there is such a pair. How did you know? Where did you happen to see them?"

The women said, "Brother, you did not know this predicament. Those monks are envoys from the Tang court going west to fetch the sutra. This morning they came to our cave to conclude their vegetarian rites. The girls heard Tripitaka’s name and seized him. We have long heard people say that Tripitaka is the true form of one who has cultivated through ten lifetimes; if someone eats but one piece of his flesh, longevity and life extension may come, so we took him. Then the long-mouthed, big-eared monk blocked us in the Purification Spring. He first snatched away our clothing, then used his arts and tried to force himself to bathe with us, and we could not stop him. He jumped into the water and changed into a loach-shaped fish, wriggling in and out at the seams of our thighs, intending lewd deceit, all the while utterly overbold. He then leapt out, revealed his true form. When we refused him company, he took up a nine-pronged hooked battle-axe and sought to kill us. Had we not some discernment, we would almost surely have fallen to his poisoned hand. He then set your foolish nephew to wrestle him, and we know not if either would survive. So we have come seeking elder brother, hoping, because you once and I were companions in the same hall, that you will this day take charge of our redress of grievance." Hearing this, the Taoist grew angry and changed color and voice: "So this monk is indeed so rude and lewd. Never mind—you all be at ease. I will dispose of him." The women thanked him: "Brother, if you take up the matter, we will all come to help you fight him." The Taoist said, "No need to fight, no need to fight. As the saying goes, ‘One blow and one can go down three points.’ You all come with me."

The women followed him on either side. He entered a room, fetched a ladder, circled behind a bed, climbed onto the beam, and took down a small leather chest. The chest was about eight cun high, one chi long, and four cun wide, and it was fastened shut with a small bronze lock. He then took from his sleeve a duck-yellow silk sweat-cloth, and on the cloth’s tassel he had tied a small key. He opened the lock and took out a packet of medicine. This poison was:

The dung of a hundred birds from mountain woods, gathered and swept into a thousand jin. Cooked in a copper pot; the heat and duration in the reduction are perfectly balanced. A thousand jin simmered into one ladle, and one ladle yields three parts refined. The three parts must be fried, then calcined, then smoked again. When made into this venomous drug, it is as precious as treasure and precious jade. If one tastes its flavor, one sees Lord Yama before one’s mouth. To the seven women the Taoist said, "Sisters, this treasure of mine—if eaten by a mere mortal, only one li is needed and he dies upon entering the belly; if eaten by an immortal, three li are enough to end him. These monks may have some Dao cultivation, so three li must be given. Fetch the scales quickly." One woman immediately took a weighing stone and said, "Weigh one fen and two li, divide into four parts." She took twelve red dates, broke them slightly, added one li to each, and divided the mixture into four tea cups; then she put two black dates together for one tea cup and set it on a tray. To the assembled women she said, "Let me ask him—if he is not from the Tang, stop. If he is from the Tang, have him change the tea; you, send this tea out by the child. When they drink it, all of them will die. Then we shall settle this grievance and release ourselves from worry." The seven thanked her beyond measure.

The Taoist had changed into another robe and, with courteous humility, stepped out, then invited Tripitaka and the others back to their guest seats, saying, "Master, please do not take offense. I just went to the back and told my young disciples to pick out some greens and radishes and prepare a vegetarian offering, so I was absent." Tripitaka said, "I, a poor monk, come with empty hands to bow; how can I trouble you to provide a meal?" The Taoist laughed. "You and I are both renunciates. Since we are near a mountain gate there are already three bushels of stipend-grain in one’s allowance. Why talk of empty hands? If I may ask, Master, from what treasure land do you come, and why have you come here?" Tripitaka replied, "I am Tripitaka, an envoy of the Great Tang court, sent west to the Great Thunderous-Sound Temple to fetch the scriptures. I have only just passed the Immortal Palace and have come in sincere devotion." On hearing this, the Taoist’s face brightened in joy. "You are a Dharma Master of loyal virtue and great merit. This humble Taoist did not know to wait for you—pardon me, pardon me." He called, "Child, quickly change the tea, and prepare the meal at once in one hall." The boy ran in, and the women called him: "There is ready fine tea here; take it out." Sure enough, the boy brought out five tea cups. The Taoist hurriedly took a cup with red dates in both hands and presented it to Tripitaka. Seeing Zhu Bajie with his broad build, he took him as the first disciple; seeing Sha Wujing, he took him as the second. Seeing Sun Wukong small in stature, he took him as the third. So the fourth cup was presented to Sun Wukong.

Sun Wukong saw at once and took the tea cup; he had already noticed that the cup contained two black dates. He said, "Master, let us exchange cups." The Taoist said with a smile, "I will not hide it, Venerable One. As a poor Taoist of the hills and fields I did not have fruit prepared in advance, so I went in person to fetch some. I had only these twelve red dates and made four cups for offering in this way. A poor Taoist should not host without an accompaniment, so I added two darkened dates as a side to each cup. This is my sign of respect." Sun Wukong laughed. "What is this talk? The ancients said, ‘A household man is not truly poor; in the wilderness, poor-ness can kill the poor.’ You are a householder; how can you call yourself poor? For us walking monks, that is true poverty indeed. I will trade. I will trade." Tripitaka heard and said, "Wukong, this immortal elder’s intention is only to honor guests. Just drink it and do not trade." Sun Wukong, with no choice, took it in his left hand, covered it with his right, and watched them.

Zhu Bajie, hungry and thirsty—and of course with a huge belly—saw that the cup had three red dates in it, and he swallowed them all at once. Tripitaka ate, and Sha Wujing ate, too. In one moment Zhu Bajie’s face changed color, Sha Wujing’s eyes filled with tears, and Tripitaka began to foam at the mouth. None of them could sit still; they fainted and dropped to the ground.

The Great Sage instantly knew it was poison. He lifted the tea cup and aimed to strike the Taoist in the face. The Taoist raised his robe sleeves to block and with a sharp sound knocked the cup down in shards. The Taoist snapped, "You monk—an utterly stupid village fellow! How could you break my tea cup?" Sun Wukong shouted, "You beast! Look at my three companions—what have we done to you that you would pour poison tea on our people?" The Taoist said, "You rustic brute bring disaster; how do you not see it?" Sun Wukong said, "We had only just entered your gate, arranged our seats, and spoken of our homeland. We did not even exchange lofty words. How could any disaster have been caused there?" The Taoist asked, "Have you ever held a sacrificial rite in Pan-si Cave? Have you ever bathed at Zhuo Gou Spring?" Sun Wukong replied, "Zhuo Gou Spring is the place of seven female monsters. Since you mentioned it, you must have had dealings with them; you must be a demon spirit too. Do not run—take my staff." The Great Sage pulled out the Golden-Hooped Staff from his ear, made it swirl in a flash, and aimed at the Taoist’s face. The Taoist spun around in alarm and dodged; then he drew a precious sword to meet him.

The two cursed and battered each other, and this at once startled the nearby female demons. All seven came rushing out together, crying, "Elder brother, do not worry your heart; let the younger sisters take him." When Sun saw them, his anger rose even more. He raised the iron staff with both hands, swept away his guards, and charged inside to strike in chaos. The seven women opened their chests, flaring their white bellies, and from their navel holes they produced spells. Threads of silk, like bones springing forth, surged up in tangled strings, and with them they raised a canopy over him. Sun saw the trick did not work out for him. He flipped over, intoned a spell, and with one earth-shattering strike smashed through the canopy and broke out. Calming his temper, he hovered in midair to observe. He saw the demon-silk cords flashing and weaving, crossing and interlacing like warp and weft, and in a moment they had covered the towers and halls of the Yellow-Flower Monastery so completely that no shadow remained. Sun said, "Dangerous, dangerous. So it is better not to have touched him earlier. This fellow has already sent trouble to Pig Bajie once or more; how can this be made right? My Master and my junior monk have both taken the poisoned tea. These demons are acting in one accord and one heart. I do not yet know what sort of beings they are. I will go ask the Earth God again."

The Great Sage pressed down Cloud Head, twisted the formula, and chanted the true-syllable spell "Om," bringing the old Earth God back. The old god, trembling, knelt by the roadside and prostrated himself: "Great Sage, you came to save your Master before—why did you return as well?" Sun Wukong said, "After rescuing my Master, not far ahead we encountered a Yellow-Flower Observatory. My Master and I went in to see it. The master there greeted us. While we were speaking, he served poisoned tea-drug to my Master and the others. I was fortunate not to have drunk it, so I struck him with the staff. After that he spoke of Pan-si Cave’s sacrificial feeding and bathing at Zhuo Gou Spring. Then I knew that fellow was a demon. I raised my hand to oppose him, but just then those seven women ran out and released silk ropes. Great Sage escaped by my own sense and eyes. You are the local deity here; you must know his true origin. Tell me plainly what kind of demon spirit he is, so I need not strike at random." The Earth God knelt and said, "That demon has not been here for ten years. I only saw him clearly three years ago after inspection, and then his true form was revealed—he is seven spider demons. The silk cords he throws are spider silk." When Sun Wukong heard this, he was very pleased. "By what you say, he is small indeed. Since this is so, go back. I will perform the rite and subdue him." The Earth God knelt again and withdrew.

Sun Wukong went back outside the Yellow-Flower Monastery, pulled up seventy hairs from his tail, breathed out immortal breath, and cried, "Transform!" He changed into seventy small Wukongs. Then he breathed immortal breath into the staff and cried, "Transform!" and it changed into seventy-one two-horned forked staves. Each small Wukong took one, while Sun kept one for himself. Standing outside, they all attacked and stirred the silk ropes together, gave the signal, and with one effort snapped every cord; each break had over ten catties of weight. From inside, seven spiders were hauled out, each with bodies as large as a bā-dǒu. One by one they clasped hands and feet and grabbed their heads, crying only, "Spare our life, spare our life." At that moment the seventy little Wukongs held down the seven spiders and refused to let them go. Sun said, "Do not beat them yet; just return my Master and my junior disciple." The demon shouted loudly, "Elder brother, return Tripitaka and you may spare my life." The Taoist ran out from inside, crying, "Little sister, I am going to eat Tripitaka. I cannot save you now." Sun Wukong flared with anger and said, "If you do not return my Master, then see what your sister is like." The Great Sage made the forked staff whirl and then changed it back into a single iron cudgel. With both hands raised, he beat the seven spider demons to pieces completely.

Then he shook his tail twice, drew back the hairs, stood alone with the staff, and rushed inside to strike the Taoist. The Taoist, seeing he had killed his sisters, felt deep reluctance of heart, yet went berserk and raised his sword in revenge. Both held grudges and unleashed all their divine arts. It was a fierce encounter, with this verse:

The demoness brandished a treasure sword; Great Sage raised the Golden-Hooped Staff. For Tang Master Tripitaka, first he taught the seven women to howl in fear. Now Great Sage unfurled his grand stratagems and made his splendor visible. With dazzling power he used subtle arts, flaunting the might of the Golden Captain. Great Sage’s divine light was magnificent; demon and immortal alike grew hard in nerve and spirit. His whole form flashed with arts, like flowered brocade; both hands whirled like a revolving spindle. Clang and crack sounded from sword and staff. Bleak wild clouds drifted across the sky. Their words and maneuvers, their counsels and countermoves, moved back and forth like a painted picture. He fought so fiercely that wind roared, sand flew, wolves and tigers feared it. The heavens dimmed, the earth darkened, and the stars seemed to lose their light.

The Taoist and Great Sage battled for five or six rounds of exchange, then gradually felt their strength fail. In a moment their tendons slackened; he loosened his waist sash, and with a sharp ringing sound he tore off his black robe. Sun Wukong laughed, "You little one, if you cannot beat someone, stripping to the skin won’t make it possible either."

The Daoist stripped off his robes, raised both hands, and then two flanks of his body revealed a thousand eyes, each eye hurling out golden light with terrible force:

Dense yellow haze; brilliant golden light, bright as a blaze. Dense yellow haze—below both flanks it seemed to billow like cloud; bright golden light from a thousand eyes, as though fire had been loosed. To the left and right he looked like a golden cistern, while east and west were like bronze bells. This was the power of a demon-immortal, the Daoist displaying divine feats: a flurry of eyes to bewilder heaven and hide sun and moon, a veil of heat and haze to scorch and haze men into confusion; it enclosed Great Sage Sun Wukong, equal to Heaven, within golden light and yellow fog. Sun Wukong was flustered and turned wildly within that golden glow, unable to step forward and unable to step back, like one spinning inside a barrel. Unable to bear the searing pressure, he growled and leapt upward, only to smash through the golden light and land in a backward somersault. He felt a sharp pain in his head. He thrust up his head and pawed it, as if the skin at the crown had been softened from the blow. He panted to himself in panic: "Ill-fated, ill-fated—my head is no good today. In ordinary times, axe and cleaver cannot harm me, yet this golden light has softened my skin and flesh. If nothing is done, it will surely turn to swelling and pus; even if it mends, it will still be a bad wound that may become tetanus." After a moment, again overwhelmed by heat and agitation, he calculated in dismay: "I cannot go forward, cannot go back, cannot go left, cannot go right, cannot go up without smashing into it again. What is to be done? Then let me go downward."

The Great Sage intoned a spell, shook his body, and transformed into a pangolin, also called a lingli-lin. In truth he was:

Four iron claws, drilling through mountain and shattering stone as if pulverizing flour; Scaled all over, this armadillo splits ridges and pierces rock like cutting scallions. Two eyes bright, shining like two trembling stars; One pointed mouth, harder than a steel auger, sharper than a gold drill. It is among medicinal creatures the pangolin kind, commonly called lingli-lin. He lowered himself and drove his head into the earth, burrowing straight down. He had tunneled for more than twenty li before he could break out. The golden light had covered only a bit over ten li. When he came to the surface in his own form, his strength was drained, his whole body aching, and tears would not stop from his eyes. Suddenly he cried out: "Master!" In those days, by your command we left the mountain to journey west and labored so hard together; In the vast and churning seas there was no fear, yet in the Yang-gou I am met by a storm.

At that moment, when Sun Wukong was in deep sorrow, he suddenly heard crying behind the mountain. He bent forward, wiped his eyes, and looked back. There stood a woman in full mourning dress. In her left hand she held a bowl of cool gruel-and-water rice, and in her right several strips of paper spirit money to burn. She came forward with each step sounding, crying all the while. Sun Wukong nodded and sighed, "It is just so: 'Eyes full of tears meet eyes full of tears; a heartbroken one meets another heartbroken one.' Who is this woman mourning? Let me ask her." The woman came nearer and faced him. Sun Wukong bent and asked, "Bodhisattva, who is it that you mourn?" Through tears she said, "My husband quarreled with the Master of Huanghua Monastery over the buying of bamboo poles. He gave him poisoned medicinal tea and killed him. I burn these paper notes to repaid the bond of husband and wife." Hearing this, Sun Wukong wept. The woman, seeing him, snapped, "How ignorant you are. I grieve and grieve for my husband; how do you dare to stand before me with tearful eyes and a sorrowful face, as if your heart were in sport with me?"

Sun Wukong bowed and said, "Bodhisattva, do not be angry. I am Sun Wukong, Great Sage, the senior disciple of Tripitaka, the imperial envoy-monk of the Great Tang in the Eastern Lands. We journey west and once rested at Huanghua Monastery. The Daoist there—I did not know who or what he was—became siblings with seven spider spirits. They in the Spider-Web Cave sought to harm my Master, and I with my junior brothers Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing rescued him and got away. Those spider spirits came here to the Daoist and spread slander that we meant to deceive him. The Daoist then poured out poisoned medicinal tea to Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie, Sha Wujing, and even the four mounts, and all of us were caught in his monastery. I did not drink his tea. I smashed the teacup, and then he fought me. At that moment the seven spider spirits came out, spitting forth silk cords that bound me. By art I broke through. I questioned the Earth Deity and learned the Daoist’s true form. Then I used my splitting-body art to disturb the cords, dragged the demon out, and with one staff strike killed him. This Daoist then came to settle the feud and drew a precious sword to fight me. After sixty rounds we contended; he was defeated and, stripped of his robe, sent out a thousand eyes from both flanks, with ten thousand shafts of golden light, to seal me in place. That is why I was in a bind, unable to go or return, and only by transforming into a lingli-lin did I bore out through the earth. While I was in grief, I suddenly heard your crying, so I asked. When I see you burn these paper notes for your husband, while my Master has been lost and I have nothing with which to repay, I am ashamed and filled with sorrow; how could I have dared to play at teasing?"

The woman set down the bowl of rice-water and the paper money, and with that offering addressed Sun Wukong: "Do not blame me. I did not know you were one in peril. From what you said, you still do not recognize that Daoist. He is in truth a Hundred-Eyed Demon Lord, also called the Many-Eyed fiend. Since you have such transformations, have broken through the golden light, and fought for so long, you surely have divine powers; yet he is still not within your immediate reach. Go and invite a holy worthie: he can break this golden light and subdue the Daoist." Sun Wukong quickly kowtowed, "Bodhisattva, you know this origin. Please teach me. If that holy one is truly as you say, I shall go and ask him, and if he saves my Master I will also settle the revenge for your husband." The woman said, "I have already told you. Go ask him. If he subdues the Daoist, he can help you for vengeance; yet I fear he cannot save your Master." Sun Wukong said, "How could he not?" The woman replied, "That villain’s poison is the most vicious. Once he feeds a person poison, in three days the marrow rots through. By the time you go and return it may be too late; so he cannot be saved." Sun Wukong said, "As long as I can travel, no matter how far, I can do it in half a day." The woman said, "Since you can run like that, listen: from here it is a thousand li away. There is a mountain there called Purple-Cloud Mountain. In that mountain is Thousand-Flowers Cave. Inside is a holy man named Pilan Po, and he can subdue this monster." Sun Wukong asked, "Where does that mountain stand, and from which side do I go?" She pointed with her hand and said, "Straight due south from here." When Sun Wukong turned around, the woman had already vanished. He hurriedly bowed and said, "Who was that Bodhisattva? My disciple is dazed and could not identify her. Please, leave your name so I may offer thanks." From midair came a voice: "Great Sage, it is me." Sun Wukong lifted his head and saw it was Lishan Laomu. He rushed upward and thanked her there: "Old Mother, where did you come from, and for what reason did you instruct me?" Lishan Laomu said, "I have just returned from the Assembly at Dragon-Flower, and seeing your Master in danger, I took the shape of a mourning wife and, in the name of a widow’s grief, spared him from instant death. Go and invite him quickly. But do not reveal that I told you, for that holy man has peculiar ways with many persons."

The Great Sage thanked him, took his leave, and with a single thrust of cloud-power followed to Purple Cloud Mountain. He landed his cloud, and there before him was the Cave of a Thousand Flowers. Just outside that cave:

Green pines shield a land of beauty, and emerald cypresses encircle the dwellings of immortals. Green willows fill the mountain paths; strange flowers fill the stream channels. Fragrant orchids ring the stone rooms, and sweet grasses reflect against the rock recesses. Clear running water joins the brooks, and clouds veil the ancient trees in emptiness. Wild birds chirr loudly, and a shy deer steps slowly. Fine bamboo grows branch upon branch, each sprig splendid. Red plum leaves are fully opened. Chilly crows roost in old trees, and spring birds cry from the high paulownia. Summer wheat fills the wide fields, autumn grain lies everywhere on the ground. Through all four seasons no leaf falls; at all eight seasonal nodes flowers appear. Each growth gives forth auspicious omen, rising to the sky, and happy clouds stream upward to the empty vault. The Great Sage, delighted, walked forward in joy, scene after scene, never able to exhaust the boundless vistas. He entered straight inside; still there was not a soul. It was utterly still and quiet, not even a chicken-and-dog sound. In his heart he thought, “This immortal must have gone away from home.” After going a few li farther, he saw a female daoist nun seated on a couch. Look at her appearance: A five-coloured silk-brocade cap adorned her head; a robe woven with gold hung from her shoulders. Her cloud-sharp shoes ended in phoenix heads; at her waist were silk cords gathered with twin tassels. Her face was like an autumn visage, old with frost; her voice was as charming as a spring swallow before it mates. In her breast she long had known the Dharma of the Three Vehicles; in her heart she always cultivated the Four Truths. She had awakened to emptiness itself, to the true fruit of emptiness, and through refinement became clear and free. She was indeed the Bodhisattva in the Cave of Thousand Flowers, and her name, Pilan, was renowned. The Great Sage could not restrain himself and came forward calling, “Pilan Bodhisattva, my respectful greetings.” The Bodhisattva at once rose from the couch, joined her palms, and returned the greeting: “Great Sage, I failed to receive you.” “From where do you come?” The Great Sage said, “How did you recognize me as the Great Sage?” Pilan replied, “When you once threw Heaven and Earth into chaos, your likeness spread through the whole world; who does not know it? Who would fail to recognize you?” The Great Sage said, “So it is said, ‘Good news does not go out beyond the gate, bad news travels a thousand li.’ I have now returned to the Buddha’s Dharma—have you not known?” Pilan said, “When did you return to the Buddha? My congratulations, my congratulations.” The Great Sage said, “Not long ago, I escaped death and protected Master Tripitaka on the way to the Western Heaven. At the Yellow Flower Assembly, the Daoist there gave him poison in tea. I fought with that fellow, and he wrapped me in golden light. I broke free only by my powers. I heard that the Bodhisattva could dispel his golden light, so I came to ask your help.” The Bodhisattva said, “Who told you this? I attended the Yulan assembly and for three hundred years have not left home. I hid my name and I am unknown to any; how could you know?” The Great Sage said, “I am a local spirit and can inquire and find things wherever they are.” Pilan said, “Very well, very well. I did not intend to go, but since the Great Sage has descended here, the good of seeking the scriptures must not be cut off. I will go with you.”

The Great Sage thanked him and said, “I have been too ignorant to hasten matters of my own accord. I did not know what weapon you had with you.” The bodhisattva said, “I have an embroidered needle that can break that ruffian.” The Great Sage could not hold back: “Old mother, you misled me. Had I known it was an embroidered needle, there would be no need to trouble you. I could have asked Old Sun and he would have had a full load too.” Pilan said, “The stitched needle you possess is only steel, or iron, or gold—of no use. This treasure of mine is neither steel nor iron nor gold; it was refined by my son in the fire of the Sun-Eye.” The Great Sage said, “Who is your son?” Pilan said, “My son is the Officer of the Mao-ri Star.” The Great Sage was greatly startled. He looked ahead and saw the glowing golden light, then turned to Pilan: “That place of golden light is the Yellow Flower Monastery.” Pilan drew an embroidered needle from inside her collar. It was as thick as an eyebrow and five or six cun long. Holding it in her hand, she threw it into the air. In short time there was a crack; the golden light was broken. The Great Sage rejoiced, “Bodhisattva, marvelous, marvelous! Find it, find the needle.” Pilan held it in her palm and said, “Is this not the one?” But the Great Sage immediately pressed down his cloud and entered the hall. He saw the Daoist there with eyes squeezed shut, unable to move a step. The Great Sage shouted, “You demon of a wretch, acting blind on purpose.” He took a staff from his ear and struck. Pilan pulled him away: “Great Sage, do not strike—just see first after what happened to your master.”

The Great Sage went straight to the rear guest seat and saw that all three of them lay on the ground, spitting saliva and phlegm. The Great Sage wept and cried, “How can this be? How can this be?” Pilan said, “Great Sage, do not grieve. This outing of mine has, after all, brought in hidden merit. I have an antidote elixir here and will give you three pellets.” The Great Sage turned and bowed in request. The bodhisattva took out a torn paper packet and gave him three red pellets to hand over, instructing him to place them in their mouths. The Great Sage forced their jaws open and each one took a pellet. Before long, the medicine entered their bellies and all at once they retched and spewed, bringing out the poison-stench and regaining life. Zhu Bajie rose first and said, “I was nearly smothered to death.” Tripitaka and Sha Wujing were both awake and said, “Such dizziness too.” The Great Sage said, “You were all poisoned by the tea. Thanks to Pilan Bodhisattva, you are saved. Come, all of you, and give thanks.” Tripitaka bent low, straightened his robes, and thanked her.

Zhu Bajie said, “Master’s elder brother, where is that Daoist? Let me ask him why he harmed me so.” The Great Sage related from start to finish the earlier matter of the spider spirit. Zhu Bajie growled fiercely, “That fellow, being sister to the spider spirit, must be a demon.” The Great Sage pointed and said, “He is standing outside the hall pretending to be blind.” Zhu Bajie lifted his spade and rushed at him, but Pilan restrained him, saying, “Heavenly Skipper, calm your rage. The Great Sage knows my cave is empty of others; let me take him and post him at the gate.” The Great Sage said, “I am grateful for your kindness and do not mean to withhold my praise, but please make him show his true form so we can see it.” Pilan said, “Easy,” then stepped forward and pointed with her finger. The Daoist collapsed at once into the dust and revealed his true self: he was a centipede demon, seven chi long. Pilan lifted him with her little finger, mounted a fortunate cloud, and at once returned to the Cave of Thousand Flowers.

Zhu Bajie exclaimed in amazement, “This mother of ours can be this formidable—how could she subdue such a wicked thing?” The Great Sage laughed and said, “I asked what weapon could break his golden light, and she said she had an embroidered needle that her son had refined in the Sun-Eye. When I asked who her son was, she said he was the Officer of the Mao-ri Star. I figured the Mao-ri Star is only a rooster, and this old mother must certainly be a hen. Hens are best at subduing centipedes, and so she could bind this one.”

Tripitaka listened and made repeated full prostrations. He said, “Disciples, gather everything and go.” Sha Wujing then searched inside for some grain and prepared some offerings of vegetarian fare; all ate until full. They yoked the horses and loaded the shoulder-poles, then asked Master Tripitaka to set out. The Great Sage set a fire in the kitchen and in an instant burned the entire monastery to ash, then resumed his long stride away.

Tripitaka’s life was restored by Pilan’s grace, and purified in nature, he drove out the many-eyed demon.

As for what awaited further on the road ahead, listen as it is resolved in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 73: Old grudges give rise to calamity and poison; the Mind-Master is beset by a demon yet escapes in good fortune.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

The roots of passion and desire are all alike: where there is attachment, desire naturally abides. Monks and practitioners may go on and on in restless pursuits, but to cut off desire and forget feeling is true Chan. Mark this well—keep the heart firm, not stained by so much as a single grain of dust, as clear as a moonlit sky. As your practice advances, do not err in your steps; when the work is fully accomplished, one reaches the Great Enlightened Immortal state.

Tripitaka and his disciples cast off the net of desire, leapt from the prison of longing, and set off westward. After not much distance, summer had passed and early autumn had begun, and a fresh coolness seeped through their limbs. Then there was this to behold:

The sudden rain had driven off the lingering summer heat; a tung leaf quivered. Fireflies flew along the grassy path at dusk, and crickets sang in the moonlight. Yellow marsh-mallow opened and glimmered with dew; red knotweed spread across the sandy banks. Pussy willow and willow were already shedding, and cold cicadas chirped in season.

As Tripitaka walked, he suddenly saw a high mountain, its peak thrust into the blue heaven, truly a peak that seemed to block out the sun. The Elder’s heart trembled with fear and he called out to Sun Wukong: “Look at the mountain ahead—so lofty. I do not know whether a path passes through it.” Sun Wukong laughed: “Master Tripitaka has said it right: from olden times we have heard, ‘The higher the mountain, the more surely there is a road for travelers; the deeper the water, the more surely there is a boatman.’ How could there be no way through? Have no fear and ride on.” Hearing this, Tripitaka grinned and laughed, cracked his whip, urged his horse onward, and went straight up the high rocks.

After going only a few li, they saw an old man: his sideburns tangled and loose, white hair blowing in disorder; beard sparse and gray, strands of silver swaying. Around his neck hung a string of beads, and he held a staff topped with a dragon head. From afar on the slope he shouted, “Monks going west, hold your horse for a moment and pull tight the reins on that jade-bound strap. On this mountain there is a band of demons who have devoured all manner of folk from Yanfushi. You must not go on.” When Tripitaka heard this, he turned pale with fright. One, the ground under the horse was uneven; two, the saddle was insecure. He toppled off with a thud and lay in the grass, unable to stir. Sun Wukong rushed forward to support him: “Fear not—fear not, I am here.” Tripitaka said, “Did you hear what that old man on the cliff says? This mountain is home to a band of demons who have eaten everyone in the world below. Who would dare question him and get the truth from his own mouth?” Sun Wukong said, “You sit down and wait. I will ask him.” Tripitaka replied, “Your appearance is ugly and your speech rough; you may provoke him and not get a true answer.” Sun Wukong laughed: “I shall change into a more handsome form and go ask him.” Tripitaka said, “You have changed already, in my eyes.” The Great Sage pinched a charm, whirled, and in an instant became a clean little monk: clear-eyed, a neat brow, round head, round fair face; his movements gave off an air of refinement, his words no longer coarse. Shaking out the brocade robes and robes of a young monk, he stepped with dignity toward him and said to Tripitaka, “Master, how do I look?” Tripitaka rejoiced and said, “You look excellent.” Zhu Bajie said, “How could he not look fine? Only you are all of us beaten by comparison. Even this old pig had run through this for two or three years and still could not turn this handsome.”

The Great Sage slipped away from them and went straight up. Bowing low, he said to the old man, “Venerable sir, humble monk here offers his respects.” The old fellow looked at him and, struck by the monk’s handsome, gentle face and youthful figure, could not decide how to answer. He finally returned the bow, reached up to touch the boy’s head, and with laughing eyes asked, “Little monk, where have you come from?” Sun Wukong said, “We have come from Great Tang in the eastern capital, set on journeying west to the Buddha for the scriptures. We only just arrived and heard you had spoken of demons here. My Master is timid and afraid, so he sent me to ask plainly: What demon is this, and how does he dare be so wild? Please explain it fully so I can bring him down and carry him away.” The old man laughed: “You little monk is young and know not your limits; your words do not fit the moment. That demon has powers vast and broad. How can you think to beat him out with easy words and send him packing?” Sun Wukong laughed: “By what you say, you seem to protect him. You must be related to him—some close ally or near friend. Otherwise how could he so display that breadth of rank and manner and not open his heart and tell his lineage?” The old man nodded and smiled: “This monk can indeed wield the tongue. You have traveled with your Master and learned sorceries all over, can drive out monsters and calm evil spirits in one household to another. You have not yet met one truly terrible enough to frighten you.” Sun Wukong asked, “What sort of terrible one?” The old man replied, “That demon sent one missive to Ling mountain; five hundred Arhats came to receive him. A document sent to Heaven, and the Eleven Great Stars in the sky all gave him regard. The Four-Sea Dragons have been his companions; the Immortals of the Eight Caves often meet with him. The ten Yama kings call one another brothers, and the local spirit magistrates and city gods love him as guests and companions.”

Hearing this, the Great Sage could not resist a hearty laugh and tugged at the old man’s sleeve: “Do not go on. This demon is no brother or companion in youthful camaraderie to my little monk self. Even if he had heard I was a young monk, he would have moved here overnight.” The old man said, “You small monk is speaking nonsense and insolently. Which heavenly spirit is that younger attendant of yours?” Sun Wukong smiled, “I will not hide it from you. My home is in Aolai, Flower-Fruit Mountain, Water-curtain Cave. I am called Sun Wukong by surname. In my former life I too had once been a demon and had done mighty things. Once, with all the demons assembled, I drank too many cups of wine and fell asleep. In a dream I saw two men bind me with hooks and drag me to the courts of Yama. In one burst of rage I struck with the Golden-Hooped Staff, wounding the ghostly yamen clerks, knocking Yama himself down, and nearly overturning the Hall of the Net.” Terrified, that clerkly deputy brought out papers, the ten Yama kings signed and wrote their marks, and they told me to spare him and all my beating. They were willing to make me their younger servant.” The old man said in astonishment, “Amitabha Buddha! This monk’s words run wildly—do not try to be any larger than this.” Sun Wukong said, “Officer, a body this large is enough for me.” The old man asked, “How many years old are you?” Sun Wukong answered, “You guess.” The old man said, “Maybe seven or eight.” Sun Wukong laughed: “I have one million seven-eights.” The old man looked puzzled: “How can a face be seven-times-seven?” Sun Wukong answered, “This little monk has seventy-two faces indeed.”

The old man did not understand a thing and kept on asking him. Then Sun Wukong dabbed at his face and a different one appeared at once—the original form: sharp white teeth and a mouth like a pestle, two flanks bright red, a tiger-skin skirt knotted at his waist, and the Golden-Hooped Staff in his hand. He stood at the foot of the stone cliff like a living Lord of Thunder. The old man, on seeing him, turned the color of death from his face; his legs and feet numbed, he could not keep upright, and he fell with a crash. He got up, then stumbled and slipped backward again. The Great Sage stepped forward: “Venerable official, do not be truly startled. We have ugly faces and good hearts—nothing to fear. Now that you have pointed this out kindly, tell me plainly how many monsters are here. Tell me all at once so I can thank you.” That old fellow trembled and shook so hard he could not speak, as if deaf, and uttered not a word.

When Sun Wukong saw him silent, he turned back down the slope. Tripitaka called, “Sun Wukong, you’re back. What did you learn?” Sun Wukong laughed, “No trouble, no trouble. There is certainly a demon-child here; only these locals are timid and have put him in their minds. Fear not. Fear not. I am here.” Tripitaka asked, “Did you ask his name, this mountain, what cave, how many demons, and whether the road leads to Leiyin?” Zhu Bajie said, “Master Tripitaka, do not be angry. If it is a matter of tricking with transformations, making sharp pinches, and fooling folk, the three of us and the four are no match for the elder brother. But if it is honesty, the line-up of him is no better than mine.” Tripitaka said, “Right, right—you still are the honest one.” Zhu Bajie continued, “He did not know how to wind the matter without missing its tail; he asked two questions and then came straight back all awkwardly. Let Zhu Bajie go and ask him for the true facts.” Tripitaka said, “Wuneng, ask carefully.”

The big fool, you tucked your hooked cudgel at your belt, straightened your ochre robe, and with a silly affectation marched up the slope, calling to the old man, “Grandpa, I bow before you.” When the old fellow saw Sun Wukong had returned, he braced himself on his staff and half rose, trembling hard, intending to leave. At the sight of Zhu Bajie, his fear grew. “Grandfather! What evil dream did I have this night to meet this band of ruffians? The monk before me was ugly, yes, but had some of a human face. This one—how can a mouth be this blocky, ears this fan-shaped, face this iron plate, mane about the neck, no more trace of a proper man left in him?” Zhu Bajie laughed: “Old sir, you are no master of reserve. Your judgment of people has both praise and blame. How do you find me? I may be ugly, true, but wait a bit and I look quite handsome enough.” Now that he heard something of a human answer, the old man found his voice and asked, “Where are you from?” Zhu Bajie said, “I am the second disciple of Tripitaka, named Wuneng, called Zhu Bajie. The one I mentioned before who asked first is the Great Sage Sun Wukong, my senior disciple. Master got angry at him for barging up and not asking straightly; so he sent me in his place to pay proper respects and ask. What mountain is this place, what cave, what demon dwells there, and where is the road to the west? Please point these things out.” The old man said, “Can you be straightforward?” Zhu Bajie replied, “My whole life I do not dare to tell one iota that is false.” The old man said, “Do not be slippery in speech like the monk that came first.” Zhu Bajie said, “I am not like him.

The old man leaned on his staff and said to Zhu Bajie, “This mountain is called the Eight-hundred-Li Lion-camel Ridge. In its middle is Lion-camel Cave. Inside are three demon lords.” Zhu Bajie spat: “You old fellow, why such suspicion? Could three demons really take the trouble to come here and bring a warning?” The old man said, “You are not afraid?” Zhu Bajie replied, “To tell you plainly, of these three demons my elder master-brother can kill one with one strike of the Golden-Hooped Staff; I can kill one with one stroke of my pa; I have another junior master-brother, and with his demon-subduing staff he can kill one too. If all three are beaten dead, then my Master can pass through—what difficulty is there?” The old man laughed: “This monk does not know the depth. These three demon heads are immensely powerful. Their lower demons: five thousand on the south ridge, five thousand on the north ridge; ten thousand at the east pass, ten thousand at the west pass; four or five thousand are on patrol, another ten thousand guard the gate; there are countless fire tenders and countless wood-choppers: altogether, counting, forty-seven or forty-eight thousand. All of them wear name plaques and live here only to eat people.”

The fool heard these words and, trembling with fear, ran back, came near Tripitaka, said nothing, set down his pa, and knelt there in salutation. Sun Wukong saw him and cried out, “You do not answer, yet why are you crouching there?” Zhu Bajie said, “I’m scared to the point of losing my composure. Now there is no need to speak—hurry, each of us should look to save our own lives and leave.” Sun Wukong said, “This muddle-headed one—my report made me not afraid, but when you ask about it, you panic like this.” Tripitaka asked, “How is it truly?” Zhu Bajie said, “That old man said this mountain is called the Eight-hundred-Li Lion-camel Mountain. In the middle there is Lion-camel Cave. In it are three old demons and forty-eight thousand little demons, all of them specialized in eating people. If we step near the slopes, we will be eaten by them. Do not think we can pass.” Hearing this, Tripitaka trembled through and through, with shivering skin and bones, and said, “Wukong, what is to be done?” Sun Wukong laughed, “Master, do not be anxious; no great matter. There may only be a few spirits here, but these people are cowardly and, frightened by it, they talk of many and mighty folk. I am here.” Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, what talk is that? Mine is not different from yours—I asked and it is real, not mere invention. The whole mountain and all the valleys are full of demons; how do we go forward?” Sun Wukong laughed, “Simpleton, stop frightening yourself. Even if the mountain and valleys are full of demons, I only have to beat along the way once; in the middle of the night I can sweep them clear.” Zhu Bajie said, “Shameful words, shameful words. Do not boast. Those demons need seven or eight days even for one watch shift; how can you end them so quickly?” Sun Wukong asked, “Then how do you think to fight?” Zhu Bajie said, “Relying on you to seize and throw them, to bind and to pin with the Stillness Spell—there is no way to do it so quickly.” Sun Wukong laughed, “No need for catching, taking, or binding. I pull the two ends of this staff and shout, ‘Long!’ and it becomes forty zhang in length. With one sweep, I shout, ‘Thick!,’ and it becomes eight zhang in round thickness. Roll once to the south and you kill five thousand; roll once to the north and you kill five thousand; roll from east to west once and fear only that four or five thousand will be reduced to pulped meat.” Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, if this is how you beat it fast, perhaps by the second watch all will be done.” Sha Wujing laughed by his side and said, “Master, with Great Brother’s powers like this, why should we be afraid? Please mount and ride.” Tripitaka, hearing them discuss methods, had no way out but to steady his mind, mount, and depart.

While traveling, that messenger old man had vanished. Sha Wujing said, “He is a demon, coming on purpose to show him up and scare us.” Sun Wukong said, “Do not be hasty; let me go see.” The Great Sage leapt to a high peak, scanned all around and saw no trace, then quickly turned and saw bright rosy clouds glimmering in midair. He leaped on the clouds and went up to inspect: it was Tai Bai Jinxing. He came to his side and grabbed him by the arm, calling his childhood name over and over, “Li Chang-gang, Li Chang-gang, you look so tired and lazy. Whatever the matter, speak it face to face, why come posing as an old man of the hills and woods, you old monkey?” Tai Bai Jinxing hurriedly offered courtesy and said, “Great Sage, the report was late; forgive me, forgive me. This demon lord is indeed of vast powers and means to make a display. Only by relying on your transformations and your clever strategies can one get through. If you are even slightly negligent, it will be truly hard to leave.” Sun Wukong thanked him: “I am grateful, grateful. This place is indeed hard to pass. Please tell the elder star above the heavens to report to the Jade Emperor that we need some heavenly soldiers to help this old Sun.” Tai Bai Jinxing said, “Yes, yes, yes—just carry my verbal message back. Even one hundred thousand heavenly soldiers can be obtained.”

After parting from Tai Bai Jinxing, Sun Wukong alighted from the clouds and told Tripitaka, “That old man was indeed Tai Bai Star, come to give us this report.” Tripitaka joined his palms and said, “Disciple, hurry and overtake him. Ask whether there is some other road; then we can turn and avoid this place.” Sun Wukong said, “We cannot turn. This mountain alone stretches eight hundred li, and with four sides whose side paths no one knows, how could we turn?” Tripitaka heard this and could not hold back tears: “Disciple, in such difficulty, how are we to make offerings to Buddha?” Sun Wukong said, “Do not cry, do not cry. If you cry, disaster will be complete. This messenger must have added a good deal of exaggeration; it is only to make us mindful, truly as the saying goes: ‘One who reports has already passed it.’ For now dismount and sit.” Zhu Bajie said, “Any other plan?” Sun Wukong said, “No other plan. You stay here and keep guarding Master carefully. Sha Wujing, watch the baggage and the horse well. Let old Sun go up the ridge first and reconnoiter, and I will see how many demons there are in front and behind. I will seize one and question him thoroughly, have him write a roster, set down his names, and identify every one, young and old, one by one. Then command him to shut the cave gate and forbid it to block the path, and then ask Master to cross quietly and silently; only then will Sun’s method truly show.” Sha Wujing only said, “Be careful, be careful.” Sun Wukong laughed, “No need for instructions. If I go once, I can open a road through the Eastern Ocean, and I can even strike through the gate of an iron-clad silver mountain.”

The Great Sage Sun Wukong gave one whistle, sprang on his cloud, and leapt to the high peak. He tugged vines and creepers and swept across the mountain, and found it quiet and empty. Suddenly he cried, “I was wrong, I was wrong. I should not have let this Tai Bai elder go. He only meant to frighten me. Where would any demons be here? They should have come out to leap, twirl spears and staves, and perform martial arts shows—how could there be none?” As he was still thinking, from behind the mountain he suddenly heard ringing and clattering, a clink-clink and clack-clack of clappers and bells. He turned quickly and saw it was a little demon carrying a banner with the character 令, bells hanging at his waist, and clappers in his hands, walking from north to south. Looking closely, he was about one zhang and two chi tall. Sun Wukong smiled to himself: “He must be a decoy, likely sent with an official dispatch. I will wait and listen to what he says.”

The Great Sage Sun Wukong twitched the formula, chanted a spell, and in a single turn changed into a fly. He flew lightly onto the demon’s hat and cocked his ear to listen. He saw the little demon climb onto the main road, striking his clapper and shaking his bells, muttering as he went, “We, the mountain patrols, each of us must stay alert and guard against Sun Wukong; he can turn into a fly.” Sun Wukong heard this and secretly grew uneasy: “Did this fellow see me? If he did not see me, how does he know my name and also that I can become a fly?” It turned out the little demon had not seen him at all. The demon lord had somehow instructed him with that line; it was a rumor, making him babble such nonsense. Sun Wukong did not know this and instead suspected he had seen him, and was about to bring out his staff to strike. Then he stopped and thought to himself, “I still remember when that fool asked about Tai Bai, he said the old demons are three, and the lesser ones are forty-seven or eighty thousand. Even if there are many more like this little demon, it is not a problem. Yet who knows how vast the arts of these three old demons are? Let me question him once; then to act is no problem.”

“Great Sage, how do you plan to question him?” He leaped down from his hat and landed on the tree trunk, letting that little demon go ahead a few steps first. Then, turning swiftly, he also changed into a little demon, copying him exactly as he struck a wooden clapper, shook a bell, carried a tiny banner, wore the same kind of clothes—only about three or five inches longer—and chanted the same kind of words. He hurried up and called, “You walking ahead, wait for me a moment.” The little demon turned back and said, “Where are you from?” Sun Wukong laughed, “Good fellow, are we not one household that you do not recognize me?” The little demon replied, “You are not one of ours.” Sun Wukong said, “How is it not so? Take another look.” The little demon said, “A stranger’s face; I do not recognize you, I do not recognize you.” Sun Wukong said, “Can a stranger’s face be known by sight? I am one of the fire-tenders. You ought to know me.” The little demon shook his head, “No, no. In our cave, the fire-tending brothers are just those fellows, and none of them has this pointed mouth.” Sun Wukong thought to himself, “That fellow’s nose has somehow become more pointed.” He then lowered his head, rubbed his own mouth with the back of his hand and said, “My mouth is not pointed.” Truly, it was no longer pointed. The little demon said, “You were a pointed-mouth just now. How is it that with one quick rub it is no longer pointed? You are hard to recognize and quite suspicious—not one of our household. Wait a little, wait a little; suspicious, suspicious. Our King’s laws are strict: the fire-tenders only tend fire, and the mountain patrols only patrol the mountain. How then would he make you tend fire and send you to patrol the mountain as well?” Sun Wukong, quick with words, seized the moment and said, “You do not know. The King liked how well I kept the fire and promoted me to patrol the mountain.”

The little demon said, “Very well. Among our mountain patrol there is one squad of forty, ten squads in all, four hundred in total, each with its own age and appearance, each with its own complexion and coloring. The King, fearing we might mix up our shifts and be unable to keep proper watch, gave our whole squad one designation. Do you have a sign?” Seeing the demon’s outfit and the way he announced himself, Sun Wukong took on the same form. He had not seen that demon’s badge, so none hung on his own person. Yet, as the Great Sage, he did not tell him he lacked one and answered readily, “How could I not have one? I have only just received a new one. Take out yours and let me see it.” The little demon, not seeing the trick, raised his clothes and pulled out a gold-lacquered token worn at his side with a woolen cord and handed it to Sun Wukong. Sun Wukong saw on the back of the badge the golden characters 威鎮諸魔 (“Subduing and Quelling All Demons”), and on the front three true characters: 小鑽風 (“Xiao Zuanfeng”). He thought in himself, “No need to explain this. A mountain patrol token should still have a ‘wind’ character hanging from it.” So he said, “Hold out your clothes and step here; let me take out my token for you to see.” He turned, inserted his hand, plucked a single tiny hair from the tip of his tail, twisted it, called, “Change!” and turned it into a gold-lacquered token, strung with a green woolen cord, inscribed with three true characters, “General Zuanfeng.” He handed it over. The little demon exclaimed, “We are all called Little Zuanfeng; why are you called General Zuanfeng?” Sun Wukong had no fault in his response, and his words were fitting: “You truly do not know. The King saw that I tended the fire well, promoted me to wind patrol, and gave me a new token: ‘Chief Patrol-Wind,’ so that I might command this squad of forty brothers of yours.” The demon, on hearing this, hurriedly bowed and said, “Officer, officer, newly appointed and just arrived here, I am indeed a stranger and my words were sharp; do not be offended.” Sun Wukong, with proper respect in laughter, said, “No offense meant. There is only one matter: the entrance fee for meeting is five taels from each person.” The little demon said, “Officer, do not hurry. Let me first go to the southern ridge and gather this whole squad, and then I can send them off all at once.” Sun Wukong said, “Then in that case I will go with you.” The little demon truly went ahead and the Great Sage followed right after.

After not far—a distance of only a few li—they came upon a so-called Brush-Peak. Why it is called Brush-Peak: on the top of that mountain rose a narrow peak about four or five zhang high, like a writing brush planted upright in a stand, and so it was named. Sun Wukong went to the edge, scooped with his tail, leapt up and sat on the tip of the peak. He called out, “Zuanfeng, come on over.” Those little Zuanfenges below bowed and said, “Officer, at your command.” Sun Wukong said, “Do you know why the King assigned me here?” The little demon said, “No.” Sun Wukong said, “The King wants to eat Tripitaka. He fears that Sun Wukong has deep powers and many transformations, so he suspects Tripitaka’s disciple may take the form of a little Zuanfeng and come along this path to spy out news. Thus he promoted me as Chief Zuanfeng to check whether any in your squad are impostors.” The little demons answered together, “Officer, we are all true ones.” Sun Wukong said, “If you are true, do you know the true measure of the King’s power? Tell me.” “I know.” “Then tell me and let me hear. If your answer accords with my knowledge, you are true; if it differs, you are false, and I will take you before the King to punish you.” The little Zuanfeng looked up at him from the height and, with much bluff and noise, had no way but to speak plainly: “My King’s powers are vast and mighty; with one mouth he once swallowed ten thousand heavenly soldiers.” Sun Wukong, hearing this, drew a breath and said, “You are false.” The little Zuanfeng was startled and said, “Officer, respected lord, I am true. How can you say I am false?” Sun Wukong replied, “If you are true, how can you speak nonsense? How large can the King’s body be that with one mouth he swallowed ten thousand heavenly soldiers?” The little Zuanfeng said, “Officer, you truly do not know. My King can transform. When he needs, he can expand enough to support Heaven; when he needs, he can be as small as a mustard seed. That year the Queen Mother held a Peach-Pavilion assembly and invited all the Immortals, and he was not invited with a summons. Wanting to contest Heaven, the Jade Emperor sent ten thousand heavenly soldiers to subdue him. My King transformed his true body, opened his mouth like a city gate, and swallowed them all at once. He terrified the soldiers so they dared not engage, and thus shut the South Heavenly Gate. That is why one mouth once swallowed ten thousand soldiers.” Sun Wukong thought to himself, with a hidden smile, that in mere matters of hand and mouth Old Sun had done the same thing before. Then he said aloud, “What powers does the Second King have?” The little Zuanfeng said, “The Second King is three zhang tall, has silk-caterpillar brows, cinnabar-golden eyes, a beautiful voice, projecting fangs, and a snout like a flood dragon. If he fights, he only needs to roll in one sweep of his nose; even a body of iron-back and copper-plated limbs will lose soul and spirit.” Sun Wukong said, “A demon can be captured by a curling nose—easy enough.” He asked again, “How many arts and tricks does the Third King have?” The little Zuanfeng said, “My Third King is no ordinary monster of the mortal world. His title is Yun Cheng Wanli Peng. In action, he can whip up storms and move the sea, stirring north and south. He always keeps a treasure called the Yin-Yang Double-Essence Bottle. If he puts a person inside it, in a short while the one inside turns into gruel-water.”

Sun Wukong listened and inwardly grew wary: the demon might not be frightening, but he must take care to guard against that bottle. Then he asked aloud, “You have described the Three Great Kings’ powers without missing much; it is much what I already know. Still, what about the matter of which King wants to eat Tripitaka?” The little Zuanfeng said, “Officer, you do not know?” Sun Wukong called out, “I know slightly less than you do. I feared that you might not know the full details, so the King instructed me to question you thoroughly.” The little Zuanfeng said, “My first and second Kings have long lived in Lion-Back Ridge, in Lion-Back Cave. The Third King is not here; his dwelling is four hundred li to the west. Over there is a city called Lion-Back Kingdom. Five hundred years ago he ate this kingdom’s king and civil and military ministers; every man and woman in the city was eaten clean as well, and thus he took over that land. It is now filled only with monsters. It was not long ago that he learned in the Tang court of the Eastern Land that a monk was dispatched from the capital to journey west for the scriptures. That monk, Tripitaka, is a good man of tenfold cultivation. Whoever eats even a piece of his flesh will prolong life and become long-lived and deathless. But because he fears your disciple Sun Wukong is so formidable, with his own person alone difficult to deal with, he came straight here, made brothers with my two kings here, and by common agreement they set out together to seize that monk.”

The Great Sage, Sun Wukong, heard these words and grew furious: “That raging demon is exceedingly impolite. I am here to bring Tripitaka to true Buddhahood, and he plots to eat my man?” With one cry of anger, he gnawed his steel-hard teeth, whipped out his iron staff, leapt from the high peak, and struck the little demon on the head with it—pitifully, one heavy blow, and it became a mere lump of flesh. Then, seeing him for himself, he could not bear it and said, “Ah! he was actually kind, he even told me ordinary household gossip. How could I have finished him in this one moment? Well, well—what must be done, must be done.” Yet this great saint had only sought to block the way for his master; helplessly, he had done this thing. He removed the demon’s token and tied it around his waist, shouldered the banner marked with the character “ling,” hung a bell from his side, and clanged the clapper in his hand. Facing the wind he fingered a sealing gesture, chanted a spell, and in a flash transformed into the form of the little Whirlwind. He stepped back, turned onto the old path, sought the cave-stronghold, and went to probe the true state of the three old demons. It was then that:

A thousand transformations has the Beautiful Monkey King, and ten thousand postures—how true a feat he has to fly and rise! He broke into the deep hills, following the old road. Just as he walked, he suddenly heard cries and the neighing of horses. Looking up, he saw that at the mouth of the Lion-Treaded Cave stood myriad small demons arranged in ranks with spears, knives, swords, and halberds, and with banners and pennons. The Great Sage secretly rejoiced: “Master Li Changgeng was not speaking falsely at all; truly not.” That deployment had a certain method: two hundred and fifty made one large company. He saw forty mixed-colored long banners whipping wildly in the wind, and knew there were ten thousand horse and men. Yet he gauged it in his mind: “As Little Whirlwind, if I go in there and that old demon asks me about patroling the mountains, I must answer according to the moment. If for a moment my words slip and he comes to recognize me, how could I escape death? If I tried to run out then, this band at the gate would block me—how could I get through the gate? To seize the demon lord within the cave, I must first dispatch the host of monsters before the gate.” You ask how he would remove them? The Great Sage thought: “That old demon has not yet met me, yet he knows my fame. I will rely on that name, on my imposing presence, and speak a few grand boasts to scare him first. Truly, when beings under Heaven have affinity and a destined bond, in bringing back the scripture one bold speech of a hero can scatter all those guards at the gate; if one has no affinity and no bond, and cannot obtain the true scripture, even were I to make lotuses bloom at once, I cannot clear the spirits outside the Western Cave.” His mind queried his mouth and his mouth queried his mind; weighing this scheme, he struck the clapper, shook the bell, and went straight into the Lion-Camel Cave gate. Before he arrived, little demons in the forward camp had already blocked him, crying, “Has the Little Whirlwind come?” Sun Wukong did not answer, kept his head lowered, and walked on.

He came to the second camp line, and again a little demon pulled him back: “Has the Little Whirlwind come?” Sun Wukong said, “He has.” The demons said, “This morning you went patrolling on the wind—did you happen to collide with Sun Wukong?” He said, “I did. He is right there, and he is grinding the lever-bar.” The little demons were frightened and asked, “What does he look like? What bar is he grinding?” Sun Wukong said, “He is squatting by that ravine, looking like an opening-road spirit. If he stands up, he seems some ten or twelve zhang tall. In his hand he holds an iron rod, a great bar as thick as a basin, and he scoops water on the cliff face and rubs it there. He mutters again and again: ‘O bar, I have never yet taken you out to display my powers. This time, when I go out, I will have ten thousand demons all cut down for you, and when I have killed those three demon-lords, I shall offer this back to you as sacrifice. Before I clear things first, I will kill your first ten thousand spirits at your gate.’ Hearing those words, each of the little demons was horrified, their hearts flying loose and their souls unsteadied. Sun Wukong added, “Friends, Tang Monk’s flesh is only a few jin, and none of it will be enough for my share. Why should we hold this jar for him? Better that we each scatter separately.” All the demons said, “He speaks correctly; let us each attend to our own lives.” As it turned out, they were all of wolf, worm, tiger, and leopard sorts, beast and bird alike. With one ‘whee,’ they all rushed away in uproar. This did not resemble a few market-boasting words from Great Sage Sun, yet it scattered them as surely as a Chu-chant scatters eight thousand troops.

Sun Wukong privately rejoiced: “Good! The old demon is dead. After hearing this and leaving, how could he dare a face-to-face meeting? This way in is only now best. If it had been otherwise, just when speaking, perhaps one or two of this band of small demons would have gone in to listen and then would not have run off in a rush with the wind. Look at his resolve as he presses toward the old cave, trusting himself to enter deep and boldly.”

After all, one cannot yet know what good or ill fate that old demon head will meet. Hear now how it is resolved in the next chapter.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Now Great Sage Sun Wukong entered the cave mouth and looked around both sides. He saw:

Ridges like skulls, bones thick as a forest. Human hair was laid down into felt-like sheets. Human skin and flesh, rotted through, turned to dusty clay. Human sinews were twisted on the trees, dry and shiny like silver. Truly it was a mountain of carrion and a sea of blood. In fact, the stench was utterly sickening. On the east, a little demon took living men and flayed their flesh; On the west, a pouring demon steamed and cooked fresh human flesh. If not for Sun Wukong’s such heroic nerve, no second ordinary mortal could enter this gate. Not long later, as he walked into the second gate and looked, he cried out: Ah! Here the scene was unlike outside: singularly eerie and elegant, beautiful and broad and level. On both sides grew jade-grass and immortal flowers, and ahead and behind stood tall pines and emerald bamboos. He went on seven or eight li, and only then reached the third gate. Sidling his body and peering from the corner of his eye, he saw three old demons seated high above, all fierce and grotesque. The one in the middle looked like this: He had chiselled teeth and saw-toothed gums, a round head and broad face. His roar was like thunder, his glance like lightning. His upturned nose faced heaven, his red eyebrows flared with flame. As he moved, all beasts were struck with panic; if he sat down, all demonic soldiers had their guts shake. This was Qingmao, the lion monster, king of beasts. The one below on the left looked like this: His eyes were like a phoenix’s, his pupils golden; yellow tusk-teeth and thick legs. A long silvered trunk, its head seeming to be its tail. Round brow, wrinkled lines, body squat and dense. A soft voice like that of a graceful young woman, a jade face like a cow-headed fiend. This was the old yellow-toothed elephant, who had practiced self-cultivation for years. The one below on the right looked like this: A huge-roc head with golden wings, starry eyes and leopard eyes. He stirred north and set his course for south, fierce and brave. He could transform and soar through the air; with a ducklike cackle he seemed as cruel as a dragon. In a whirl of wind, feathered pinions, a hundred birds hid their heads; with sharp talons, all manner of birds lost their courage. This was Yunchengjiuwan, the Great Roc Vulture. Below those three were lined up over one hundred small and large captains, each fully clothed and armored, ordered and orderly, with imposing majesty, murderous aura in abundance.

When the Great Sage saw this, he rejoiced in his heart and was not at all afraid. He strode boldly through the gate, took off his clapper-bell, and called upward: "Great King." The three old demons laughed and asked, "Xiaozuanfeng, you have come?" The Great Sage answered, "I have." "You went patrolling the mountain to inquire about the whereabouts of Sun Wukong. What did you hear?" asked the old demon. "Great King above," replied the Great Sage, "I dare not speak of it." "Why do you dare not speak?" he demanded. "By Your Majesty’s order I was striking my clapper-bell as I walked. At one point I raised my head and saw one person squatting there, sharpening a staff. He resembled a road-opening spirit; if he were to stand up, he would be a good ten zhang tall. He took up water from the cliffside rock, polished and filed it, and softly muttered to himself, saying that his staff had not yet displayed its divine power here; once he polished it clear, he would come to strike the Great King. So I knew it was Sun Wukong, and I came to report it."

When the old demon heard these words, he was all covered in sweat. Frightened, he said with a quivering voice, "Brother, I told you: do not provoke Tripitaka. His disciple’s powers are vast, and he prepared in advance—honing his staff to strike us. What are we to do?" He ordered, "Kids, call in all the small demons from outside, close the gates, and just let him through." One of the captains who knew this reported, "Great King, all the small demons outside have scattered." The old demon said, "Why have they all scattered? Perhaps they heard bad wind. Quickly, quickly close the gates." The demons clanged and shut both the front and rear gates fast and tight.

The Great Sage thought to himself in alarm, "Now they have closed the gate. If he asks me about things inside and outside my house and I cannot answer, then he will seize me unless I make my escape first. Let me frighten him once more, make him open the gate, and run." He stepped forward again: "Great King, what he said was not true." The old demon said, "What else did he say?" The Great Sage said, "He said, ‘First Great King, I will peel your skin. Second Great King, I will flay your bones. Third Great King, I will draw out your tendons. If you close the gates so he cannot go out, he will transform. In an instant he can become a fly and enter through a door crack; then he will seize all of us. What will become of us?’" The old demon said, "Brothers, be careful. In this cave there is no ordinary fly. Yet if a fly comes in, it is Sun Wukong." The Great Sage smiled inwardly: "Then I’ll just become a fly and frighten him once, then open the gate and run." Instantly he shifted to the side, plucked one strand of hair from the back of his head, blew a breath of immortal air and called, "Transform!" At once he became a golden fly and flew toward the old demon, smashing into his face. The old fiend, alarmed, said, "Brother, do not stand still—the thing has gone in through the gate." So frightened, the entire host of major and minor demons, with brooms and tools, surged forward and flailed about the fly in chaos.

The Great Sage could not help but laugh with chattering snorts. Yet this was no place to laugh; in this moment he let his original face show. The third old demon instantly leapt forward and grabbed him: "Brother, I nearly got fooled by him." The old demon said, "Elder brother, who is fooling whom?" The three fiends said, "That little one who just answered was no Xiaozuanfeng. It was Sun Wukong. He must have run into Xiaozuanfeng somehow; I do not know how he struck him dead, but he transformed and tricked us." The Great Sage, alarmed, said, "He recognized me." Then he rubbed himself and told the old demon, "How can I be Sun Wukong? I am Xiaozuanfeng. Your Great King has mistaken him." The old demon laughed, "Brother, he is Xiaozuanfeng. Three times a day he appears before us to report at the dawn-watch; I know him." He asked, "Do you have your token?" The Great Sage replied, "I do." Grasping his robe, he pulled out the token. The old fiend at once confirmed, "Brother, do not restrain him." The three fiends said, "Eldest brother, did you not see him?
