Just now he slipped to the side and laughed once; I saw a thunder-mouth appear. When I grabbed him, he had changed into this exact form." He shouted, "Kids, bring rope." The captains immediately brought out cords.

The three fiends turned the Great Sage over and tied him, as if tethering four horses together. Lifting up his clothing, they looked, and it was indeed a Bimawen. In truth, in Sun Wukong’s seven-and-twenty transformations, if he changes into flying birds, beasts, flowers, vessels, insects, and the like, his whole body can spin away at once. But when he changes into a person, only face and features change, while the body cannot. As expected, his body was all yellow fur, with two red cords and one tail. The old demon said, "It is Sun Wukong’s body with Xiaozuanfeng’s skin. It is him." He ordered, "Kids, prepare wine and bring a cup of merit-drink to your three Great Kings. Now that Sun Wukong is taken, Tripitaka is surely food in our mouths." The three fiends said, "Do not drink yet. Sun Wukong may slip and flee; he has ways to escape. Bring out the bottle and put Sun Wukong inside it first; only then may we drink."

The old demon laughed: "Exactly right, exactly." He immediately signaled thirty-six little demons to enter inside, open the treasury door, and bring out the bottle. How large was that bottle? Only two chi and four cun high. How could thirty-six men carry it? The bottle was a treasure of yin-yang energies, containing the Seven Treasures, the Eight Trigrams, and the Twenty-Four Qi; it required thirty-six people, matching the heavenly-gang number, to lift it at all. Not long after, they brought out the sacred bottle and set it outside the third gate upon a clean spread, then unsealed its lid. They untied the Great Sage, stripped off his clothes, and in the breath from inside the bottle he was inhaled with a whooshing sound; they set the lid down and sealed it tight. Then they drank and said, "Monkey, now that you have entered my precious bottle, you can no longer dream of the western road. If you can still bow to Buddha to seek the scripture, it can only happen when you are flung about and turned over in the turning cart, then reborn to seize another body." As for the host and lesser demons, each one laughed broadly and went off celebrating. Their success is not worth further recording.

Yet it is said that the Great Sage came to the bottle. By that wonder of the vessel his body had been bound small, so he changed form and crouched within it. After a while, on that side there was cool shade, and he suddenly broke into laughter: “This fiend has a fine reputation without real power. How can he tell people that a man in this bottle, in one watch and three ke, became pus and blood? If it stays this cool, he could remain in it for seven or eight years without harm.” Alas, the Great Sage did not know the purpose of that treasure: if a person is enclosed in it, one year of silence, one year in cool shade; but when he hears human speech, fire comes to burn. He had not yet finished speaking when suddenly the whole bottle became flame. Luckily he had his skill; sitting in the middle he twisted his anti-fire secret and was not afraid at all. After half a time-span, forty snakes came burrowing from all around to bite him. The Pilgrim swung out his hands, grabbed and snatched them all, and with all his strength snapped them into eighty pieces. Soon after, three fire-drakes came out and coiled around him above and below, and it was truly hard to withstand. Feeling flustered and at a loss, he said, “This is bad. These three fire-drakes are hard to meet. If they continue and no way opens in a while, the heat will attack my heart—what then?” He thought: “I should only lengthen my body and then burst out.” The Great Sage pinched the secret, intoned a spell, and called, “Long!” At once he lengthened, rising by some number of zhang. The bottle, being close to his body, also grew long. When he shortened his body a little, the bottle too became small again. His heart startled: “Difficult, difficult, difficult. How is it that when I grow I also grow, and when I shrink I also shrink? What is to be done?” He could not finish speaking when pain stirred near his single staff. He quickly reached out and felt it, but the heat had softened it. In dread he said, “What is this now? My single cudgel is melted—have I become a cripple?” He could not hold back tears. This is exactly the saying:

Encounters with demons bring me sorrow, my thoughts fixed on Tripitaka, when disaster appears in danger, I dread for the holy monk. He said, “Master! In former days I returned to orthodoxy by Guanyin’s mercy, heeding the Bodhisattva and escaping heavenly calamity. I have followed you through many mountains, suppressed many fiends, subdued Zhu Bajie, gained Sha Wujing; through countless hardships, I relied on this to attain the Western Realm together with you and together reach the true fruit. Yet today this venomous demon has come upon us. Old Sun, by mistake, entered here and has thrown himself away, leaving you amid the mid-mountain with no way to advance. Surely it is because of my former fame that I endure this misfortune this morning.”

At that desolate moment he suddenly remembered: “The Bodhisattva had once at Snake Coiling Mountain bestowed upon me three life-saving hairs. I do not know if they remain; let me look.” He felt over his whole body and found three hairs on the back of his head, very stiff and upright. Gladly he said, “All my body hair is soft and supple, but these three are hard and needle-sharp—surely they are to save my life.” He bit his teeth, endured the pain, plucked out the hairs, blew out celestial breath, and shouted, “Transform!” One became a gold-steel drill, one became a strip of bamboo, and one became soft cotton rope. He bent the bamboo sliver like a bow and, with the drill pulled through it, gave one fierce whistling thrust beneath the bottle bottom, boring a little eye-hole until light came through. Rejoicing, he said, “Fortune, fortune—it is good; I can leave at last.” Only after he changed his form and emerged did the bottle become cool again. Why was it now cool? He had bored through it and let out the yin and yang qi; therefore it became cool.

The Great Sage picked up his hairs, shrank himself, and changed into a tiny cicada-grub, very quick, as fine as a whisker, as long as an eyebrow hair. He came through the hole, and instead of leaving, he flew and fastened himself upon the old demon’s head. That old demon was drinking wine. He suddenly put down his cup and said, “Third Brother, has Sun Wukong transformed this time?” The Third Demon laughed, “Even now, is it so late?” The old demon ordered the messenger to bring up the bottle. The thirty-six little fiends at once lifted it; it seemed much lighter. In fear they reported, “Great King, the bottle is light.” The old demon roared, “Nonsense. This treasure is the full force of yin and yang qi; how could it be light?” One struggling little fiend lifted it and said, “Do you not see, it is not light?” The old demon opened the lid and saw bright emptiness within, and could not suppress his cry: “The bottle is empty!” On his head, the Great Sage also could not help speaking: “My child, with a quick hiss, go!” The monsters heard and cried, “He’s gone, he’s gone.” And they gave orders: “Shut the gate, shut the gate.”

Then the Great Sage gave a body-shake, gathered back his discarded clothing, resumed his true form, and leapt out of the cave. Turning around, he shouted, “Fiendish spirit, do not be rude. The bottle has been pierced and can no longer hold a man; use it only to present your courtesy.” Happy and delighted, he shouted and laughed in uproar, set foot on the clouds, and went straight to where Tripitaka was. The elder was there kneading soil for incense and praying heavenward. Wukong halted in the clouds and listened to his prayer. The elder joined his palms and prayed:

I implore the heavenly beings of mists and rains, the Six Ding and Six Jia with the gods of heaven. May they protect the worthy disciple Sun Wukong, whose powers are vast and whose dharma has no bounds. Hearing such words, the Great Sage, with even greater effort, drew in his cloud-glow, came near, and called, “Master, I am here.” The elder supported himself and said, “Wukong, you have labored hard. You went scouting far peaks and have not returned for long, and I am deeply anxious. What good or bad now lies in this mountain?” Wukong said with a laugh, “Master, this journey had three causes: first, a karma and predestined tie among the living of the Eastern Land; second, your merit is boundless and immeasurable; and third, the force of your disciple. As for the earlier matter of the drilling wind, falling into the bottle, and escaping, I have told it all in full. To behold your face now is truly a benefit across two lives.” The elder said in boundless gratitude, “You did not even wager a bout with the demon then?” Wukong said, “No.” The elder said, “Then how can I trust that you can protect me over the mountain?” Wukong, who loved rivalry, called out, “How could I fail to protect you when crossing the mountain?” The elder said, “You did not even fight him to a clear result, only in this vague way—how can I dare to go forward?” The Great Sage laughed, “Master, you also do not understand change. It is said, ‘One thread alone cannot form a line; one palm alone cannot clap.’ Those demons are three, the little fiends many thousands—how can old Sun face them all by himself?” The elder said, “One against many, even you are hard pressed. Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing also have abilities. Send them with you to join together, sweep the mountain path clear, and then protect my crossing.” Wukong reflected and said, “Your words are best. Have Sha Wujing guard you and have Zhu Bajie follow me.” The Fool was flustered: “Brother, you have no signal of grace for me. I am clumsy and heavy, of little skill; on a hard road I can only shoulder wind, what help can I be?” Wukong said, “Brother, though you lack skill, you are still a man. As the saying goes, ‘Even a fart can add to the wind.’ You can still bolster my courage.” Zhu Bajie said, “Fine, fine—just lead me properly. But only at places where we must move fast, do not tease me.” The elder said, “Zhu Bajie, keep watch; Sha Wujing and I remain here.”

The Fool shook himself, unleashed his might, and with Wukong rode out on fierce wind, in cloud and mist they leapt up the high mountain and reached the mouth of the cave. Already they saw the cave door tightly shut, and nowhere did they see anyone. Wukong advanced, gripping the iron staff, and shouted in a strong voice, “Monster, open the gate! Come out at once and battle old Sun.” A little fiend reported from inside the cave. The old demon, heart shaken and frightened, said, “For years they have said the monkey is fierce; today I know the rumor has not been in vain.” The two elder fiends at his side asked, “How did he speak, brother?” The old demon said, “This early, the Wanderer changed into a small drilling wind and mixed in; we could not know him. Luckily the three worthy younger brothers recognized him and sealed him in the bottle, but he used artful power, drilled through it, then snatched away his clothing and left. Now he calls for battle outside; who dares to engage him in even one clash?” Again he asked, but no one answered. Again he asked; still no one answered, for all were pretending to be deaf and dumb. The old demon raged and said, “We have long borne a filthy name along the western road. If today Sun Wukong so despises us and I do not go out and meet him in array, our name is diminished. Let me cast off this old life and fight him for three bouts. If in three rounds I can win, Tripitaka will still be in our mouths to eat; if I cannot, then bolt the gate and let him pass.” He then put on his battle garments and emerged, opening the gate as he stepped out.

Sun Wukong and Zhu Bajie were watching beside the gate, and it was truly a strange monster:

Iron-faced, copper-headed, he wore a precious helmet, and its tassels danced in light. Brightly the flash of his double eyes flashed like lightning; bright as he was, his two side locks streamed like drifting clouds. Curved claws, sharp as silver points, keen as chiseled blades, and all in a neat row. He wore gold armor with no seam in it, a dragon-rope belt at the waist, as if it could sense every opening. In one hand he held a steel saber, glaring bright; heroic, mighty, and formidable, rare in all the world. He cried out once, a shout like thunder, asking, “Who is it that knocks at the gate?” The Great Sage turned back and said, “You are Sun Wukong, Great Sage Equal to Heaven.” The old demon laughed: “Are you Sun Wukong? Brazen, wild monkey, I do not provoke you, and yet why do you call for battle here?” Sun Wukong said, “‘Waves rise only when there is wind; without the tide the waters are still.’ You did not provoke me—how could I find you? Only because you and your rabble of foxes and jackals have gathered together and scheme to eat my Master, so I have come to do my duty here.” The old demon said, “You come to bellow before my gate so loudly and so bravely—are you here to fight?” Sun Wukong said, “I am.” The demon said, “Do not run wild. If I should bring out my demon soldiers, draw up formations, wave flags and beat war drums, and then fight you, it would seem I am a villain bullying you in my own house. I will fight you one-on-one, and no helping hands.” At this Sun Wukong called out, “Zhu Bajie, come over and see how this old monk handles it.” The ox-eyed boor of a pig indeed moved off to one side. The old demon said, “You come here and make a trial with me. Let me strike three full blows on that shaven head; then I will let your Tripitaka pass. If I cannot hold him, quickly send me your Tripitaka and I will dine on him at once.” Sun Wukong laughed: “Monster, if there is paper and brush in your cave, bring them out and draw up a contract with you. From this day until next year, I shall not treat this as serious combat.”

The old demon shook himself into a posture of threat, set his feet in the cross-stepped stance, lifted his two-handed blade, and aimed to chop the Great Sage from above. The Great Sage tilted his head upward and there was only a sharp kchak sound; even the skin of his head did not redden. The old demon was startled: “What a hard head this monkey has!” Sun Wukong laughed: “You do not know. Old Sun is made this way:

Born with a bronze head and an iron skull, no one in heaven, earth, or the whole world can match it. Axe blows and hammer strikes cannot break me; in childhood I entered Laojun’s furnace. The stars of the Four-Dipper officers supervised my making; the Twenty-Eight Constellations labored over me. Soaked by water many times, I am never spoiled; around me run tight bands and ribs like layered steel. Tripitaka still feared me not wholly secure, so he had me first bound with the Violet-Gold Headband Spell.” The old demon said, “Monkey, don’t chatter with your mouth. Watch these two cuts. I will not spare your life.” Sun Wukong said, “That is all you can do with your blades.” The old demon said, “Monkey, you do not know this blade: It was made in a golden furnace, its divine power refined through a hundred firings. Its edge follows the Three Canons, and its hardness accords with the Six Arts. Yet it is like a fly’s tail, and like the waist of a white python. Enter the mountain and the clouds roar; descend to the sea and the waves crash. It has been polished without number, seared in the fire through hundreds of rounds. Set in an ancient mountain cave, it has rendered service in battle. Swing it against you, this monk’s heavenly dome, and one stroke can split you into two bowls.” The Great Sage laughed, “This wretch has no sense. He has taken Old Sun for a mere bowlhead. Very well—since I was mistreated and struck unfairly, make another cut and see how that goes.”

The old demon swung the blade again. The Great Sage met it with a nod of his head, and ping-pang—it split in two. The Great Sage rolled on the ground and became two bodies. The demon was thrown into confusion and lowered his steel blade. From far off Zhu Bajie laughed, “The old demon could cut two strokes, and yet now he has become four?” The old demon pointed at Sun Wukong: “I have heard you can use a doubling technique. How is it that by doing so before me, you can make two bodies out of one?” Sun Wukong asked, “What is splitting the body?” The demon said, “Why was your first cut no more than a bruise, and now one cut has made two of you?” Sun Wukong laughed: “Monster, do not be afraid. If I am cut ten thousand times, I can give you twenty thousand.” The demon said, “You monkey only know how to split yourself; you do not know how to gather back into one. If you truly have the skill, gather into one and strike me once with the cudgel.” Sun Wukong said, “Do not lie. You promised three strokes and have only struck me twice. If I strike back and it lands half a blow, I shall no longer be called Sun.” The demon said, “Exactly. Exactly.”

Well then, the Great Sage pulled himself together, rolled, and once more stood as a single body. He brandished his staff and struck straight at the old demon’s head. The old demon raised his blade to block: “Impudent monkey, what kind of wretch-wielding cudgel is this you dare bring to my gate and beat someone with?” The Great Sage roared, “If you ask about this staff, its name is known in heaven and earth.” The demon asked, “How is it famous?” He said:

This staff is cast from cast-iron nine times, then burned in the furnace by Laojun himself. King Yü won it and named it a divine treasure, proved and appraised by the Four Seas and Eight Rivers. Constellations were laid up darkly within it, and gold leaves wrapped both ends. Its carvings are so thick they unsettle spirits and ghosts, with dragon and phoenix inscriptions atop. Its name is the Spirit-Sun Staff, hard to find, hidden in the sea-caverns beyond men’s sight. When it changes form, it must be able to rise and fly; five-colored clouds drift from it. Its color can grow large as a great cauldron, or be small as a strand of iron wire. As thick as Mount Nan, as fine as a needle, long or short at will by my own intent. A mere light movement makes colored clouds arise; lifted lightly it leaps like lightning. When it exhales, chill force makes men shiver; every stroke sends killing mists into the air. It can subdue dragons and constrain tigers and travels wherever I wish. I have brought this staff and laid havoc in Heaven’s court, scattering the Peach Banquet with might. The King of Heaven has never won in challenge against me; even Nezha found me hard to face. Gods and heavenly generals I have beaten; ten thousand soldiers fled like swallows. Thunder hosts were sent, guardians of Lingxiao; I flew up and struck the Palace of Brilliance. Celestial attendants of the Directorate to Heaven all ran about; even the escorted Immortal ministers were thrown into confusion. With this staff I overturned the Palace of the North Dipper and, glancing back, split open the Court of the Southern Pole. The Celestial Emperor in the Purple City saw how fierce this staff was and specially invited the Buddha to meet me. In battles and sieges, victory and defeat are as in a strategist’s book; hardships and disasters are impossible to judge. Through full five hundred years I endured and fought; I was only spared by the intercession of the Bodhisattva of the South Sea. In Great Tang there was a monk who, at Heaven’s feet, took a vast vow. He redeemed ghostly souls in the City of the Dead and at the assembly on the Sacred Peak sought the scripture rolls. On the Western road this demon way is full of monsters and the path is by no means easy. Knowing this staff to be peerless in the world, he begged me to accompany him on the journey. Evil spirits I sent boiling into the nether dark, and their flesh became dust, their bones fine ash. Everywhere below, demons and goblins die beneath this staff; thousands upon thousands fall beyond counting. In the upper realm it smashed the Constellation Court of Dipper and Ox; below it damaged the Hall of the Net of Judgments. Heavenly generals once chased with nine luminaries; the underworld wounded my life-and-death judges. Cast into midair, it hurled mountains and rivers apart, matching the Xinhua Sword of Tai Sui. On this staff alone I guard Tripitaka and have beaten every demon under heaven. Hearing this, the old demon trembled for his life, yet raised his blade to strike. Sun Wukong laughed and advanced with the Iron-Staff in front. At first they wrestled at the cave mouth, then sprang into the air, fighting in midair. The clash was fierce: At the root of the River of Heaven, the Spirit-Treasure Staff is set, The name of this staff is As-You-Will, highest in the world. One boasts of techniques, vexing demon chiefs; the other, strong-armed, wields a blade and law-arts with pride. A scuffle at the gate may still be drawn near; aerial combat in the sky gives no quarter. One shifts face and form at will; the other stands and stretches his waist along the earth. The sky above them grew thick with clouds, the fields below drifted with wild mist. One repeatedly meant to eat Tripitaka; this one poured out all his power to defend him. Both because Buddha sent out the scriptures, the lines of good and evil are clear, and sorrow and hatred are brought to grief. The two fought for more than twenty exchanges, with no clear winner and no loser declared.

Originally, Zhu Bajie saw the two fighting well here below and could not restrain himself. He drew his dagger-hoe and charged, intending to leap forward and strike the demon across the face. The demon panicked. He did not understand that Zhu Bajie had the temperament of a tiger-headed fool, reckless and shocking to others. He only saw the long face and broad ears, and the hard, violent weapon, and thought he had won the formation; he dropped his sword and turned to run. The Great Sage shouted, “After him, after him!” The pig, trusting in his swagger, lifted his spiked pike and hurried down on the demon. The old demon saw him closing in. At the edge of a slope he planted himself, faced the wind, and with a flash returned to his true form, his mouth opening wide as if to swallow Zhu Bajie. Zhu Bajie, in fright, suddenly yanked himself out and dived into the grass, caring nothing for thorny thistles and briars, nor for a scratched, hurting head. He cowered and listened from the grass to the banging blows. When the Great Sage arrived, the monster once again opened its mouth to swallow, but it fell into his trick. The Great Sage gathered in the iron staff, dashed forward, and was swallowed by the old demon in one bite. From the grass, that Bimawen muttered and complained in loud tones: "This Bimawen knows nothing of advance and retreat. The demon came to eat you, yet you did not run and went to meet him. If that mouth swallows you now, today you are still a monk; tomorrow you will be a Great Gong indeed." The old demon left in triumph, and only then did the pigling wriggle out from the grass and slip back along the old path.

Tripitaka had been waiting down below that slope with Sha Wujing when he saw Zhu Bajie come running, breathing hard and wheezing. Tripitaka cried out in alarm: “Bajie, why are you so disheveled? Where has Sun Wukong vanished to?” Zhu Bajie wept and sobbed, “The Elder Brother has been swallowed whole by a demon.” Hearing this, Tripitaka collapsed in fear. After a while he was on the ground, stumbling, then rose and struck his chest with his fists and said, “My disciple! I was told you were good at subduing demons and that you would lead me to the Western Heaven to see Buddha. How is it that today you should die by this monster’s hand? Alas, alas! The merit of all my disciples and companions has turned to dust.” The Master suffered greatly. Look at that clumsy Bajie: he did not come to console him, but instead called, “Sha Wujing, bring the luggage; the two of us can divide it.” Sha Wujing said, “Second Brother, divide what?” Zhu Bajie said, “We split it and each goes his way: you go to the Flowing-Sand River and go back to eating people; I will go to Gaolao Zhuang and look in on my household. Sell the White Horse and buy Master a death casket.” Hearing this, the Elder, furious and gasping, called on Heaven and then wailed loudly. Enough for now.”

The old demon, having swallowed the monk and thinking he had secured a good trick, went straight back to his own cave. The demons who had come out gathered to ask about the battle’s result. The old demon said, “I’ve brought one back.” The second demon asked with delight, “Elder Brother, who have you taken?” The old demon said, “It is Sun Wukong.” The second demon asked, “Where is he?” The old demon replied, “I swallowed him in one bite.” The third demon was alarmed: “Big Brother, you never told me you could do this—Sun Wukong should not be eaten.” The Great Sage in the belly said, “I’m not food to be swallowed, and hunger is already forbidden in me; I can’t be made hungry again.” The little demon was flustered: “Great King, this is bad—Sun Wukong is speaking from inside your belly.” The old demon said, “If he can speak, can’t you either eat him outright or else make him submit? Go boil some salted broth. I’ll make him vomit after I drink it and pour it in, then slowly stew him and drink.” The small demon truly brought half a basin of salt broth. The old demon drank it at one gulp; then he retched and vomited, while the Great Sage down below had set firm roots and did not stir. He once again cleared his throat and vomited out again, but this made him nauseous and dizzy and split with bile; the Wukong grew stiller still. The monster, breath ragged, called out, “Sun Wukong, why do you not come out?” Sun Wukong said, “Not yet. It suits me not to come out now.” The old demon asked, “Then why won’t you come out?” Wukong replied, “This demon-thing truly understands no transformations. I am a monk by cultivation, very plain and sparse. In this season’s coolness I wear nothing but a single robe. But in this belly it is warm and windless, so let me stay through winter and then I will come out.”

The demons all heard and said, “Great King, Sun Wukong means to pass winter in your belly.” The old demon said, “If he is to spend winter there, I’ll enter meditation and use my transporting arts; if he eats nothing for a whole winter, he will starve that Bimawun.” The Great Sage said, “My son, you know nothing. Old Sun has taken Master Tripitaka from afar to fetch sutras, and he carries a folding pot for cooking scraps to eat. I will use your liver, intestines, belly, and lungs, gently and piece by piece, and that will even be enough provision through Qingming.” The second demon was shocked: “Brother, this monkey can really do such a thing?” The third demon said, “Brother, even if he only wants scraps, where is he to set up a cooking pot?” Wukong said, “It would be easy on the three-way bone.” The third asked, “Then if he sets up the pot and lights a fire, the smoke will rise and blow into our noses and make us sneeze?” Wukong laughed: “No danger. When old Sun pokes the Golden-Hooped Staff through the crown gate and makes a hole, it serves first as a skylight and second as a chimney for smoke.”

The old demon, though he claimed not to be afraid, was inwardly shaken, so he hardened himself and said, “Brothers, fear nothing. Bring me my medicinal wine. Let me drink a few cups down and poison that monkey and kill him.” The Great Sage laughed inwardly: “Five hundred years ago, when I caused havoc in Heaven, I ate Laozi’s pills, the Jade Emperor’s wine, the Queen Mother’s peaches, and phoenix marrow and dragon liver. What medicinal wine dares to poison me?” The little demon did filter and pour two jars, filling a full cup and handing it to the old demon. The old demon took it in his hand. The Great Sage, smelling the wine within the belly, said, “Do not let him drink that.” The Great Sage twisted his head and turned it into a trumpet-mouth, placing it just beneath the demon’s throat. The monster swallowed with a gulp, and the Great Sage immediately drank it from that throat. The second cup went in, and the Great Sage drank that too. He in a row drank seven or eight cups, all of which the Wukong took in. The old demon set down the cup and said, “No more. I usually take only two cups and my belly burns. But after seven or eight, even my face is not red!”

The Great Sage was not drunk by much, yet after taking those seven or eight cups, he raised a gale of drunken motion inside the belly: unceasingly he set up brace-postures, fell into flat-somersault forms, kicked with flying-feet kicks, grabbed hold of the liver-flower and made himself a swing, raised a dragonfly shape, turned the head root over, and danced in wild disorder. The monster, unable to bear the pain, fell to the ground.

In the end it was still unknown whether the issue ended in life or death; listen for the resolution in the next episode.
chapters.title: Chapter 75: The Mind-Monkey penetrates yin and yang forms; the demon lord returns at last to the Great Truth.

chapters.html:
This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Sun Wukong lingered inside the old demon’s belly for a moment. The demon lord had fallen in the dust, silent and breathless; if he did not speak one might think him dead, though he still moved his hands. He recovered and called, "Great Sage, Greatly Compassionate and Merciful, Equal to Heaven, Bodhisattva!" Sun Wukong heard and said, "Son, do not waste time—spare a few words and just call me Grandfather Sun." The demon, fearing for his life, did call, "Grandfather, Grandfather—my fault. By one misstep and one mistaken act I swallowed you, and now you have turned to harm me. I beg Great Sage for mercy. Have pity on a life-clinging ant and spare me. I will even send your Master across the mountain." Though heroic, Sun still paused out of concern for Tripitaka. He saw the demon’s pleading words and its obsequious tone, and his heart softened. He called out, "Monster, I will spare you. How will you escort my Master?" The old demon replied, "I have nothing here—not gold, nor silver, nor pearls and jade, nor agate, coral, crystal, amber, or tortoise-shell rare treasures to offer you. My three brothers and I can carry him in a fragrant-vine sedan-bier and take your Master over this mountain." Sun Wukong laughed and said, "If it is to have you carry a sedan, that is better than offering jewels. Open your mouth and I will come out." The demon truly opened his mouth. The three demons came close and whispered: "Big brother, when he comes out, clamp down and bite downward. Chew the monkey to pieces and swallow him; then you will have no trouble with him."

From inside, Sun Wukong, having heard all that, did not come out at once. Instead he pushed out the Golden-Hooped Staff and tested it. The monster tried to bite down at once. There came a crackling sound, and the staff split every one of his front teeth. Sun Wukong withdrew the staff and said, "Wretched demon, I spared your life in allowing you to live, yet you retaliate by biting me and seeking my life. If I stay in, I can kill you dead without delay. I will not come out, no, I will not come out." The old demon complained to the three: "Brothers, you are injuring your own flesh and blood. First invite him out, and now you tell me to bite him. He did not even bite me, and yet my gums are shattered and sore. How could this happen?"

The three demons, seeing the old demon angry, used a provoking trick and shouted in ringing tones: "Sun Wukong—your name thunders through the ears from afar. We hear you exerting power outside the Southern Heavenly Gate, showing off your strength beneath the Lingxiao Hall, and now, on the road to the West, you subdue demons and bind monsters. Yet truly you are but a raw monkey chief." Sun Wukong asked, "Why call me a raw youth?" The three answered, "\"Fine to behold from a thousand li, famed a thousand for another ten thousand.\" Come out and wager battle with me; then you are a true man. How can such monkeying be done in a belly? How else is one not a youth?" Sun Wukong reflected inwardly: "Yes, yes, yes. If I were to tear this fiend open now and cut through his liver and guts, it would be no trouble at all. But it would ruin my reputation. Enough, enough. Open your mouth; I will come out and match you. Yet your opening is narrow and narrow—hard for me to make full use of my arts. We must go to a wider place." Hearing this, the demons ordered the big and small ones. Front and back, all around, over thirty thousand spirits came out, each bearing sharpened weapons, forming a triune battle array, waiting for Sun Wukong to emerge so they could all take the field. The two demons, supporting the old demon, went straight to the cave mouth and called, "Sun Wukong, worthy hero, come out! This is a battlefield for a fierce contest!"

Inside, Sun Wukong heard the cries of crows, the chatter of magpies, and the cries of cranes on the wind, and knew it was an open place. He thought, "If I do not come out, I have broken faith with him; if I do come out, this demon has a man’s face and a beast’s heart: at first he promised to send my Master and tricked me out only to bite me; now he has mustered troops. Very well, very well—let us make this even: I will go out, and leave a tether-root in his belly." He plucked one hair from his tail, blew a pinch of immortal breath, and cried, "Transform!" Instantly it became a rope as thin as a hair, about forty zhang in length. As it traveled outward, the wind made it swell thicker. He tied one end to the demon lord’s heart and made a living loop with it. The loop was not tight when slack, but when pulled it hurt sharply. Holding one end, he laughed, "Once this one thing comes out, I can be satisfied if he sends my Master. If he does not, and he stirs up blade and spear, I have no time to fight him. I need only pull this rope, and it will be the same as when I was in his belly." He made himself tiny and went out. Crawling as far as the throat, he saw the demon’s mouth wide open, upper and lower steel teeth arranged like blades. He thought, "No, no. If I come out through the mouth and pull this rope, fearing pain he may close his jaws and bite—will he not tear it? I should go out where he has no teeth." Then Sun Wukong, guiding the rope, crawled from beneath the upper palate toward the front and reached his way into the nostril. The old demon’s nose itched; with an "A-kui!" he sneezed violently, and Sun Wukong shot straight out.

Seeing the breeze, Sun Wukong bent at the waist and instantly grew to about three zhang. In one hand he held the rope, in the other his iron staff. The demon lord, not understanding anything, saw him come out and raised a steel knife, chopping at his face. Sun Wukong met it with the staff in one hand. He also saw the two demons with spears and the three demon’s halberd, and the faceless ones surged in. Sun Wukong slackened the rope, withdrew the staff, and in a rush leapt onto a cloud and fled. He had no wish to brawl while they crowded him. He left the encampment and went to an open mountain ridge, descended the cloud, and with both hands pulled the rope with all his strength. Only then did the old demon feel pain in his heart. Hurting, he strained upward, and Sun Wukong pulled downward in return. The small demons, far off, shouted together: "Sire, do not provoke him; let him go. This monkey is not one to follow the proper season—Qingming has not come yet and he already wants to fly kites." Hearing this, Sun Wukong pressed with all his strength and kicked. The old demon dropped through the air with a whirring sound, like a spinning-wheel, and crashed into the dust. At the foot of the slope he struck through hard-packed yellow earth and made a pit two chi deep.

The two demons and the three demons, startled, all descended from the clouds together, moved forward to seize the rope, knelt at the foot of the slope, and pleaded: "Great Sage, we thought you were a transcendent with vast, overflowing compassion; who knew you were one with mouse and snail insides. We truly deceived you out, then fought in formation before you. Never did we expect you to tie a rope to our big brother’s heart." Sun Wukong laughed: "You band of savage demons are terribly rude. The last time you deceived me out to bite me; this time you deceived me out and set a battle array against me. It is unreasonable for a few tens of thousands of you to fight one me. Untie the rope, untie it, and let me see my Master." The demons together knelt and touched their heads: "Great Sage, in compassion spare our lives. We will send Master Tripitaka across the mountain." Sun Wukong laughed, "If you want life, take a blade and simply cut the rope." The old demon replied, "Grandfather! If I cut the outer end, this inner end is knotted at the heart, and there is this nauseous, writhing pain in my throat. What am I to do?" Sun Wukong said, "Then open your mouth, and let me go in again to undo this rope." The old demon panicked, "If I let you back in, you may not come out—hard, hard indeed!" Sun Wukong said, "I can untie the inner end from outside. If I untie it, will you truly send my Master?" The old demon said, "If I untie it, I will send him. I do not dare to lie." Sun Wukong accepted that it was sincere, gave his body a shake, and withdrew his hair. At once the demon’s heart pain vanished. This was the Great Sage’s trick of masking his form: by binding the demon’s heart with a hair-tether, he removed the hurt when he withdrew it. The three demons rose, thanked him: "Great Sage, please return and have Tripitaka gather his things. We will bring the sedan and escort him." The demons lowered their arms and let all their weapons lie down, and all returned to the cave.

Sun Wukong gathered up his rope and headed east across the mountain, and from a distance saw Tripitaka lying on the ground, rolling and crying. Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing had undone their pack-sacks and divided the luggage there. Wukong muttered to himself, “No need to make a fuss. This must be that Zhu Bajie told Master I had been eaten by a demon; Master cannot bear to lose me and weeps, while this fool is splitting things and making a mess. Hmm—was it really his intention? I’ll wait and call him once.” He dropped from the cloud-head and called out, “Master.” Sha Wujing heard and complained to Zhu Bajie, “You are a coffin-maker’s wretch, always harming others. Master-brother was not dead, and you said he was, and you do this work here—where do you expect this to end?” Zhu Bajie said, “I clearly saw him swallowed in one bite by a demon. It must be a bad day’s luck; that monkey came back as a manifest spirit.” Wukong stepped up, grabbed Zhu Bajie by the face, and with one slap made him stagger: “Fool! What kind of spirit did I show?” The pig, twisting his face, said, “Brother, you truly were eaten, you…how are you alive again?” Wukong said, “What a useless pus-sore you are. If he had eaten me, I would have clutched his bowels, squeezed his lungs, threaded this rope through his heart, pulled until he could not bear it, and made him kneel and beg one by one before I spared his life. Now he has carried me to escort Master across the mountains in a sedan chair.” On hearing this, Tripitaka, with effort, rose and bowed to Wukong: “Disciple, this has exhausted you. Had I believed Wuneng’s word, I would have been finished.” Wukong swung his fist and cuffed Zhu Bajie, cursing, “This mangy idiot is terribly lax and not at all fit to be a man. Master, do not be upset; that monster may now come to escort you too.” Sha Wujing, deeply ashamed, hurried to cover it up, gathered the baggage, buckled the packs and mounts, and all they did was wait along the road.

Then the three demon chiefs gathered their hordes and returned to the cave. The second demon said, “Brother, I thought he was a Sun Wukong with nine heads and eight tails, but it turned out to be your little monkey. You should not have swallowed him. If you had only fought him, how could he have defeated you and me? In this cave there are so many demons; even their spit could kill him. But you swallowed him into your belly, and then he brought out his arts and made you suffer. How dare you compare? He only claimed he would escort Tripitaka, but that was deceit; in truth his life was what mattered, so he lured him out and will not send him.” The old demon said, “Younger worthy, why then refuse to send him on?” The second demon said, “You set my three thousand little demons in formation; I alone can catch this monkey-head.” The old demon said, “Say not three thousand. If you can take the field and hold him, then all of us share the merit.”

The two demons at once ordered three thousand little demons, went to stand by the roadside, and had a blue-banner messenger run back and forth: “Sun Wukong, come out at once and do battle with your two great lords.” Zhu Bajie heard and laughed, “Brother, there is a saying: ‘A lie does not deceive the people of one village.’ So first they say they have subdued a demon and come carrying the Master’s sedan chair, and then they summon us to fight. Why is that?” Wukong said, “The old demon has been subdued by me and dare not show himself. But hearing the name ‘Sun’ gives him headaches. This must be the two demons, still angry that he was not captured, and so they call for battle. I tell you, brothers, that demon has three brothers and such loyalty; my brothers too are three, why should we have none? I have already subdued the old demon. If the two come out now, you may fight him.” Zhu Bajie said, “Why fear him? Let me have one bout with him.” Wukong said, “If you must go, then go.” Zhu Bajie laughed, “Brother, if I go, lend me that rope to use.” Wukong said, “For what? You cannot wriggle into a stomach like his, and you cannot fasten it to his heart. What use would that be?” Zhu Bajie said, “I’ll tie it around my waist and use it as a lifeline. You and Sha Wujing hold the rear end and release me. If I defeat him, you loosen it and I’ll seize him; if I lose, pull me back and do not let him drag me off.” Wukong laughed inwardly, thinking, “Just a bit of fooling.” He fastened the rope at Zhu Bajie’s waist and sent him into the fight.

The fool ran up the cliff with his hooked spade in hand, shouting, “Demon, come out—fight the Pig Ancestor!” The blue-banner soldier hastened to report, “Great king, a monk with a long snout and broad ears has come.” The two demons then came out of the camp. Seeing Zhu Bajie, they did not speak and thrust their spears straight at him; this fool raised the spade and stepped forward to meet them. The two grappled hand to hand on the slope and fought back and forth seven or eight exchanges, but Zhu Bajie’s strength failed and he could not hold the demon. In panic he turned and cried, “Senior brother, it is bad! Pull the lifeline, pull the lifeline!” On the other side, Wukong heard and relaxed the rope, then cast it away. Zhu Bajie broke rank and ran. The rope dragged behind him and he did not feel it; when it came back he had loosened it, so his feet tangled. He tripped himself and fell, rose, and fell again. At first it was a long-heeled tangle; later he crashed mouth-first into the earth. The demon caught up and, with one snout-grip like a flood-dragon, wound him in one snoutful and brought him back victorious. The demons shouted victory songs together and returned in a crowd.

Tripitaka, seeing this below the slope, accused Wukong: “No wonder Wuneng cursed you to death. So your brotherly relation truly has no sense of loving closeness, only envy and jealousy. He told you to pull the lifeline and you did not pull; instead you threw the rope away. Now he is being endangered—what is to be done?” Wukong laughed and said, “Master is too indulgent, too partial. Enough. When old Sun was taken, you did not worry much; that was exactly a life-pleasing quality. This fool has now been captured and you blame me for it. Let him bear some hardship so you can see how hard this road has become.” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, you go. Do I not worry for you? I know you can transform and will not be harmed. That fool is born like a wolf-dog and cannot even leap well. This journey will bring more ill-luck than good. Go, and save him again.” Wukong said, “Master, do not blame me; I will go save him.”

He leapt up at once, ran up the mountain, and in secret fumed: “That fool cursed me to death; for now let him have no joy. I will follow and see how that demon is handling him; let him suffer a while, then I’ll save him.” He snapped the knot, recited the true mantra, and in one change became a chao-liao insect. He flew there, clinging by the root of Zhu Bajie’s ear, and entered the cave with that demon. The two demons led three thousand little spirits with loud drums and horns and massed at the cave mouth. Bringing Zhu Bajie inside, the old demon said, “Brother, I have caught one.” “Show him to me,” said the old demon. He loosened his nose, hauled Zhu Bajie out and said, “Is this it?” The old demon said, “This brute is useless.” Zhu Bajie answered, “Great lord, put away the useless one, and fetch one that is useful.” The three demons said, “Though he is useless, he is still a disciple of Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie. Bind him and send him to the pond behind. Soak him till his hair is gone, split his belly, salt him, and dry him in the sun. When the sky turns overcast, we will drink him.” Zhu Bajie cried out in alarm, “Enough, enough—alas, I have fallen into the hands of a pickling demon.” All the demons sprang to work, binding him with all four limbs tied together, lifting him and carrying him to the pond edge. With one push toward the middle, he went in and turned over all the way.

Wukong flew up to look again. Zhu Bajie was afloat with his limbs up, paws gouging, half submerged, his mouth snorting and wheezing. It was, absurdly, almost funny: he looked like a large black lotus pod that had fallen in the eighth or ninth month after a frost. Seeing his face and mouth, Wukong both hated him and pitied him and said, “How is this possible? He too is one of the men of the Dragon Flower Assembly. Still, I only regret that he keeps at times dividing the luggage and spreading trouble, and then goads Master to recite the Tightening Headband Spell against me. I once heard Sha Wujing say that he had hidden a private stockpile. I wonder whether he has any still. Let me give him a fright and see.”

The Great Sage flew close to Zhu Bajie’s ear, mimicking another voice and crying, 'Pig Wuneng, Pig Wuneng.' Zhu Bajie panicked: 'What misery! This name Wuneng was given me by Guanyin Bodhisattva. Since I started following Tripitaka I have also been called Bajie. How is it that someone here knows I am called Wuneng?' The Fool could not help asking, 'Who gave me that Dharma name?' The Great Sage said, 'It was me.' The Fool said, 'Who are you?' The Great Sage said, 'I am the catcher sent by the Yama officials.' The Fool was alarmed: 'Officer, where are you from?' The Great Sage said, 'I am sent by the Five Yama Kings to catch you.' The Fool said, 'Officer, go back and report to the Five Yama Kings. He is on excellent terms with my senior brother Sun Wukong; ask him to let me off for one day, and tomorrow I will come and be taken.' The Great Sage said, 'Nonsense. The Lord of the Third Watch is destined to die at the third watch; who dares to keep a man alive to the fourth? Be quick and come with me so you are not roped and dragged.' The Fool said, 'Officer, where is any convenience? Look at my face—do you think I still expect to live? Death is certain, and only one day is left. This demon spirit has carried off my teachers as well; if we meet, all of us will be settled then anyway.' The Great Sage laughed inwardly. 'Very well. I have three men out of my thirty waiting around here; when I bring them, you will gain another day. Do you have any travel coin? Hand over some.' Zhu Bajie said, 'Wretch, how could a monk have any savings?' The Great Sage said, 'If there is no savings, I will seize them and bring you along.' The Fool cried out in fear: 'Do not seize me, officer. I know your rope is called the Life-Pursuing Rope; once one is roped, he is done for. Yes, yes, I do have some, but not much.' The Great Sage said, 'Where is it? Bring it out at once.' Zhu Bajie said, 'Wretch, from that pityless beginning to now, I became a monk. Some faithful householders invited me to a meal; seeing my belly, they put in a little extra alms. I put aside what little I got, and the scraps came to five qian of silver. Since I could not store it neatly, when we first reached town I asked a silversmith to melt it in one place. He was shameless and stole a few pieces, so only four qian and six fen in one piece remained. Take it.' The Great Sage reflected inwardly, 'This fool can hardly find trousers to wear, yet he has hidden some somewhere. Hey! where is your silver?' The Fool said, 'It is tucked inside my left ear-hole. You can take it yourself; I cannot untie it.'

As he spoke, the Great Sage put his hand in the ear-hole and brought it out. Truly, it was a saddle-shaped lump of silver, weighing about four qian and five or six fen. He held it and could not suppress a loud laugh. The Fool, hearing it was the Great Sage’s voice, cursed at him while splashing in the water: 'Demon-catcher Bimawen, in such bitter misery you still come here to swindle coins.' The Great Sage laughed too: 'I, old Sun, guarded the Master and do not know what hardships he has suffered; and you set aside a secret hoard.' Zhu Bajie said, 'Secret hoard? It is all what came scraped from my teeth. I could not spend it on food and kept some to buy cloth for a robe. You frightened me instead. Share a little with me.' The Great Sage said, 'Not even a half coin will be given to you.' Zhu Bajie cursed back: 'Take the money that buys my life and I’ll let it go—if by mercy you can save me too.' The Great Sage said, 'Do not be rash; let me rescue you first.' He hid the silver away, then revealed his true form, drew the Golden-Hooped Staff, hooked the Fool close, hoisted him up by the legs, and pulled him free. Zhu Bajie jumped up, removed his clothes, wrung off the water, gave himself a hard shake, and put back on the damp cloth, saying, 'Brother, let us go out by the back gate.' The Great Sage said, 'Go by the back gate? Is that a fit way out? Better to go up by the front gate.' Zhu Bajie said, 'My legs are tied numb; I cannot run.' The Great Sage said, 'Come with me quickly.'

The Great Sage threw the staff forward to loosen the bonds and struck as he moved. The Fool, only half conscious from numbness, could only follow him. He looked and saw at the lower side gate that his spiked pike was still there. He stepped ahead, pushed aside small demons, dashed forward in a rush, and with the Great Sage struck out three or four gate-houses, not knowing how many little demons he had killed. The old demon heard and told the second demon: 'You captured him well, captured him well. See, Sun Wukong has kidnapped Zhu Bajie, and he has wounded your little demons at the gate as well.' The second demon leaped up at once, spear in hand, and rushed out through the gate. He shouted, 'Reckless monkey! So impudent, how dare you dare to disdain us?' The Great Sage heard and stepped down at once. The demon gave no place for words and stabbed with his spear; the Great Sage, exact and unhurried, drew the Golden-Hooped Staff and met him face to face. Outside the cave door, this was a fierce match:

Yellow-tusked old elephant takes human form; it swears brotherhood with the Lion King. Because the Great demon arrived and joined hands in counsel, together they planned to eat Tripitaka. Great Sage Equal to Heaven, wide in divine power, supports the righteous and drives out evil to destroy the fiendly force. Zhu Bajie, helpless, falls to cruel hands; Wukong rescues him and brings him out. The demon king closes in with fierce strength; spear and staff flash, each showing prowess. One spear strike is like a python slithering through forest, the staff-thrust like a dragon rising from the sea. When the dragon breaches the sea gate, clouds billow; when the python cuts the woods, the mist coils. All this was for Tripitaka, yet the painful mutual struggle has no mercy.

When Zhu Bajie saw the Great Sage battling the demon, he stood above the ridge with the spiked pike and, instead of helping, stared dully. The demon saw that the Great Sage’s cudgel was heavy and that there was no flaw in all his methods; he planted the spear, yanked open his nose, and tried to coil him in. The Great Sage saw through the demon’s trick, raised the Golden-Hooped Staff with both hands, and held it up. The demon, with a twist of his nose, had coiled around his waist and hips, yet had not coiled the hands. See how with both hands at the demon’s nose he played tricks with the staff like a juggler. Zhu Bajie saw and thumped his chest: 'Ah! That demon is cursed. He coiled this fool of mine and got even my hands bound so I could not move. He coiled that slippery one and yet did not get my hands. With those two hands of his and the staff, if he were to prick once into the nostril, the pain would make him cry; how then could he hold him?'

The Great Sage had no such intention at first; Zhu Bajie had taught him this. He flicked the staff once; it was as small as a chick and then grew for a whole zhang, and truly jabbed into the demon’s nostril. The demon, frightened, made a 'sha' sound and released his nose. Then the Great Sage turned his hand and grabbed, pulling with all his force. The demon, in pain, followed the pull, step by step, with him. Only then did Zhu Bajie dare to come near, and with the spiked pike he struck at random at the demon’s hips. The Great Sage said, 'No, no. The pike teeth are so sharp; if they pierce skin and blood spills, Master will see and say we harmed life. Use only the handle to strike.'

Indeed the Fool raised the pike handle; one step forward, one strike. The Great Sage hauled him by the nose, and the two of them looked like two elephant keepers hauling a beast down the slope. Tripitaka fixed his gaze and, seeing them coming in noisy tumult, called out, 'Sha Wujing, what is Wukong dragging?' Sha Wujing laughed: 'Master, Elder Brother Wukong is dragging the demon by the nose, truly eager for killing.' Tripitaka said, 'Excellent, excellent! What a big demon, what a long nose. Ask him: if he is willing to kindly escort us over the mountain, spare him and do not take his life.' Sha Wujing hurried up and called out: 'Master says: if that monster will ferry us across the mountain, do not harm his life.' Hearing this, the monster knelt at once and, muffled, pleaded. In fact, when the Great Sage had him by the nose, he had cramped it so hard, like a hard winter wind gone wild. He cried, 'Sir Tripitaka, if you spare my life, then I will at once lift and carry the sedan-chair.' The Great Sage said, 'My disciples and I are all men of true victory and compassion. As you said, your life is spared. Bring the sedan-chair at once; if you shift your way again, we will seize you and never spare you again.' The monster slipped out of his grip, knelt to the ground, and left. The Great Sage and Zhu Bajie explained everything to Tripitaka. Zhu Bajie, overwhelmed with shame, stood on the slope and aired his clothes, and there was no need to continue.

The second demon, trembling all over, returned to the cave. Before he arrived, a little demon had already reported to the old demon and the third demon that the second had been dragged away by the Great Sage by the nose. Frightened, the old and third demons, leading the soldiers, came out at once. Seeing the second return alone, they all gathered in and asked why he had been let go. The second demon spoke to the assembly, recounting all the words of mercy and compassion from Tripitaka. One by one they looked at each other and dared say nothing. The second demon said, 'Brother, are we to send Tripitaka on?' The old demon said, 'Brother, what are you saying? Sun Wukong is a monkey head full of broad benevolence and righteousness. He was already inside my belly first; if he had wished to take my life, he could have killed a thousand of us. Yet he only gripped your nose. If he had pulled it and not sent you back, he would only have crushed your nose-head, but still he was terrified. At once make arrangements to send him off.' The third demon laughed, 'Send him, send him, send him.' The old demon said, 'Virtuous younger brother, your words still sound resentful. If you do not send him, the two of us will send him.'

The three demons laughed again: "Senior brothers above, if the monk refuses to go with us and slips away this way by himself, then it is only his own fate; if he lets us escort him, he has unknowingly fallen into my tiger-drawn-from-the-mountain trick." The old demon asked, "What do you mean by ‘drawing the tiger away from the mountain’?" The third demon said, "Now we call all the beasts in the cavern. From ten thousand pick a thousand, from a thousand pick a hundred, from a hundred pick sixteen, and pick thirty as well." The old demon asked, "Why need both sixteen and thirty?" The third demon said, "The thirty are for cooking: give them fine rice, fine flour, bamboo shoots, tea buds, fragrant mushrooms, ordinary mushrooms, tofu, and gluten, and send them twenty or thirty li behind us to pitch shelter, set up places for tea and meals, and take care of Tripitaka." The old demon asked, "What use are the sixteen?" The third demon said, "Eight should carry, eight should clear and call the road. My brothers will escort him, staying on either side, for one stage. Going this way, over four hundred li to the west, is my city, where I already have men and horses ready to receive him. When we reach the edge of the city… exactly in this and that way, master and disciples will not be able to look to one another. To seize Tripitaka, success depends entirely on those sixteen." Hearing this, the old demon was beyond joyful; it was truly like waking from drunkenness, like waking from a dream. He said, "Very well, very well, very well," and at once signaled the demons, first selecting thirty and giving them provisions, then selecting sixteen and having a perfumed vine sedan lifted, and all came out together. He further ordered all the demons: "None of you may wander idly up the mountain. Sun Wukong is a monkey with many suspicions. If he sees you coming and going, he will certainly suspect and see through this plan."

The old demon then marched his band to the road by the hillside and shouted loudly, "Elder Master Tang, there is no red-sand offense today; please cross the mountain early." Tripitaka heard this and said, "Wukong, who is calling for me?" The Great Sage pointed and said, "Over there is the demon you subdued, carrying a sedan to escort you." Tripitaka folded his hands to heaven and said, "Excellent! Excellent! If my worthy disciples were not so capable, how could I reach the end of this road?" He went straight forward and, in a respectful turn, said to the assembled demons, "I am deeply grateful for your kindness. I am returning from the western journey with my scriptures to Chang’an; then I shall publicize the blessed results." All the demons knelt and knocked their heads: "Please mount the sedan, Reverend Master." Tripitaka, with ordinary human eyes, did not know there was any trick. The Great Sage, himself the Tàiyǐ Golden Immortal and upright by nature, thought only that he had achieved the merit of capturing and subduing demons and did not expect that they themselves could plot something else. Yet he never examined closely and fully followed the Master’s wishes. He ordered Zhu Bajie to send the baggage with the horse, and had Sha Wujing follow closely behind. He struck forward with his Golden-Hooped Staff to clear the way, casting glances to read omens. Eight demons lifted the sedan, and another eight called out one after the other with a cry; three demons shouldered and carried it. The Master joyfully sat upright in the sedan. They climbed the high mountains and followed the main road.

From there, who could have known that sorrow would return in the midst of joy? The classics say, "When supreme yang is exhausted, yin comes again." At this juncture, fortune met true Tai Sui and also the mourning gate and death-star. Those demons, acting in shared purpose, stood as guards at the sides with strict attention by day and by night. They passed thirty li and offered a vegetarian fast, fifty li and offered another; if it was not yet late they asked to rest; along the whole road everything was in proper order. Three meals a day, each one to full satisfaction. By night they stayed one sleep, in the best places to settle and rest.

They moved more than four hundred li to the west, and suddenly their city came into view. The Great Sage raised his staff, and when he was only one li away from the sedan, seeing the city, he was so startled that he stumbled and nearly could not stand. You would think, from his former courage, how could such a one be frightened? It was because he saw evil qi in that city. Its look was this:

In dense clusters gathered countless demons and monsters; at all four gates stood only wolf spirits. Color-spotted tigers served as city officers, white-faced fierce leopards as chief commanders. Fork-horned deer bore errands and passed messages; clever foxes handled the way. Serpents a thousand zhang in length circled the walls, and ten-thousand-zhang serpents blocked the roads. Beneath the towers, blue wolves acted as signal messengers, and before the platform flowered leopards spoke with human voices. They waved banners and beat war drums—all were demons; patrols and watch posts were all mountain spirits. Cunning rabbits opened their stalls and played at trade, wild boars carried shoulder poles and made a living. It had once been a land of the Heavenly Court, but now it has become a Tiger-Wolf City. The Great Sage was indeed in full terror when he heard a gust of wind behind his ears. He turned sharply and saw the three demons raising in both hands a painted-hand Fangtian halberd, thrusting it toward the Great Sage’s head. The Great Sage at once rolled over, sprang up, and met it face-on with the Golden-Hooped Staff. The two demons were both inwardly furious, hot-breathing, and said not a word; each clenched his teeth and sought to strike. Again they saw the old demon king give the command: he raised a steel dao and hacked at Zhu Bajie. Startled, Zhu Bajie dropped the horse, raised his pike, and rushed forward in chaotic thrusts. The two remaining demons coiled long spears and tried to stab at Sha Wujing; Sha Wujing used his demon-subduing staff to brace, ward, and block them. The three demon lords and the three monks fought, one-to-one, with life and death in mind on the hillside.

Those sixteen minor demons obeyed the order and each did his assigned task. They snatched the white horse and the packs, crowded around Tripitaka, lifted the sedan, and went straight to the edge of the city, shouting at the top of their voices: "Your Majesty the Great King’s design has succeeded: we have already seized Tripitaka." All the young and old demons on and around the city walls came running down and threw the city gates wide open. The order was sent to each camp: roll the banners and stop the drums; no shouting, no beating of gongs and drums. "The Great King has already ordered this at the outset, and you must not frighten Tripitaka. Tripitaka cannot endure being startled: one fright would dissolve his flesh and he would be swallowed." All the demons, joyful and exultant, welcomed Tripitaka, bending with bowed backs to receive the leading monk. They lifted Tripitaka’s sedan up to the Golden Canopy Hall, asked him to sit in the center, and on one side offered tea and meals while attendants moved around him on both sides. The Elder sat dull and drowsy, half-awake, with his eyes vacant and unseeing.

In the end, it is still unknown what will become of life and death; listen to the next installment for the full resolution.
chapters.title: Chapter 76: The mind-spirit abides in its true dwelling and demons return to nature; Mother Mu descends with the monster to reveal their real form.

chapters.html:
This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

There is no need to speak further of Master Tripitaka's hardships. It is said instead that the three demon chiefs, united in one mind and effort, fought with all their might against Sun Wukong and his two brothers within the lower eastern hills of the city. This bout was like an iron broom scraping a copper cauldron—hard, hard, and ringing with force. Terrible slaughter.

Six kinds of bodies and six kinds of weapons, six kinds of frames and six kinds of temper. Six evils and six roots, six desires and six gates of craving, six paths of fate wagering win and loss. Thirty-six palaces in springtime ease, six-by-six forms and colours, all famed for longing. This one with the Golden-Hooped Staff has a thousand ways to solve and counter; That one with the Fang-Tian halberd, a hundred proud and cragged heights. Zhu Bajie with hooked mace and pike is more fierce still, the two fiends with long spears are deft as well. Little Sha Wujing’s precious staff is no common thing and intends to strike dead; The old demon-lord’s steel saber is swift and keen, and when he lifts his arm there is no mercy. These three are the undefeated captains guarding the true monk; those three are lawless spirits, wild and unruly. At first they seemed tolerable; afterward they grew more vicious. All six used sky-soaring arts, and in the cloud layers each one heaved and tumbled. In a moment they blew forth mist, spraying the clouds until heaven and earth were dark, Only roaring bellow and thunderous growls could be heard. As the two brothers fought long, dusk slowly arrived. Then wind and mist spread everywhere, and in a flash it turned black. The cause was Zhu Bajie’s heavy ears and drooping eyelids, making him more and more stupefied; his hands and feet grew slow and could not hold the line. Dragging his forked weapon, he broke and retreated. The old demon swung his knife to cut him down, and death came close. He narrowly avoided a stroke to the head, only to have the blade nick away a few tufts of his mane. He lunged up, snapped his jaws on the foremost one, and was taken into the city and handed to the young demons, tied in the Golden-Roof Hall. The old demon mounted cloud again and rose into midair to lend his strength. Sha Wujing saw that the affair was turning bad, made an empty show with his staff, turned himself about, and ran away. Two fiends seized him by the nose; with one wrench they bound him, took him into the city, and ordered the lesser demons to bind him beneath the hall. Then he rose through the air again to summon the capture of the Great Sage.

When Sun Wukong saw his two brothers captured, he understood that by himself alone he could not bear it: one hand cannot contend with two, and two hands cannot contend with four. He shouted once, split apart the three demons’ weapons with his staff, and leapt on cloud-saddle. As the three demons watched the Great Sage ride, they shook themselves, showed their true shapes, spread their two wings, and chased him. You ask how they could keep up? In the days he once threw Heaven into confusion, even ten thousand heavenly soldiers could not hold him. With his cloud-steed he could in a single sweep travel ten thousand eight hundred li, so none of the gods could catch him. One flap of a demon’s wing was ninety thousand li; with two flaps he had overtaken them. So when Sun Wukong grabbed one, the hand-wrestling and thrashing could not free him. When he sought to run, he could not escape. Even by transformation and flight-vanishing arts, movement back and forth was impossible: he grew larger, and the grip relaxed; he grew smaller, and it tightened again. Sun then carried him back into the city, released his hold, and in a rush of dust shouted orders to the crowd of demons, commanding that Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing be tied in one place, too. The old demon and the second demon came down to meet him. All three demon heads ascended to the treasure hall together. Alas! This was no binding of the Great Sage at all—it was plainly an escort for him.

At the second watch of the night, all the demons had finished meeting together, and they pulled Master Tripitaka out from the hall. In the lamplight, Master saw that all three disciples were bound on the ground, while the Great Sage lay beside them. He wept, ‘My disciples, whenever trouble comes you go out and wield your divine arts to fetch rescue and subdue demons. This time even you were captured—how is this poor monk of mine to keep his life?’

Hearing their master in such anguish, Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing also cried out together in grief. Sun Wukong smiled slightly and said, ‘Master, do not worry. Brothers, do not cry. No matter what he is, he is certain not to wound you. Let the old demon settle, and then we shall leave.’ Zhu Bajie said, ‘Brother, we are at mischief again. Bound in hemp ropes, even if there is a little slack, it still sprays with steam. You may not notice, but this fat one has a pox-like swelling in his flesh. See my arms—two cun are already sunk in. How can I break free?’ Sun Wukong laughed, ‘Even if one is bound with hemp, even if bound with coir rope a bowl’s thickness across, let it pass as an autumn breeze brushing the ear—nothing so terrible as that.’

As the companions were still speaking, the old demon called out, ‘The worthy third brother has strength and cunning, and he has truly made a fine plan. They have taken Master Tripitaka. You youngsters: five to fetch water, seven to scrub the pot, ten to build the fire, twenty to lift the iron cage. Steam the four monks till done, and my brothers and I will take our fill; each of you share one piece and you too will attain long life.’

Zhu Bajie, listening, said in a shivering voice, ‘Brother, hear me: the demon’s plan is to steam and eat us.’ Sun Wukong said, ‘Do not fear. I will see whether this is a fledgling demon, or a seasoned one.’ Sha Wujing cried, ‘Brother, do not speak in comforts. We are already over by Yama’s side—what sense in speaking of fledgling or seasoned now?’

He could not finish when he heard the second demon say, ‘Pig Bajie is not good for steaming.’ Zhu Bajie brightened, ‘Amitabha Buddha! Who is the one with all that accumulated evil who said I am not good for steaming?’ The three demons answered, ‘Not good for steaming; skin him and then steam him.’ Zhu Bajie panicked and shouted, ‘Do not skin me. Coarse or fine, if you peel me I will split when the soup boils.’ The old demon said, ‘If it is not good for steaming, put him in the bottom rack.’ Sun Wukong laughed, ‘Zhu Bajie, do not fear. He is a fledgling, not a seasoned one.’ Sha Wujing asked, ‘How do you know?’ Sun Wukong replied, ‘In general, to steam things, one starts from the top. If it is hard to steam, place it in the upper rack, add fire in layers, keep the heat complete, and it will be done. If it is in the bottom, once its vital breath is sealed, half a year of burning would still not send heat through it. He said Zhu Bajie was hard to steam and put him at the bottom. Then is he not a fledgling? What is he, then?’ Zhu Bajie said, ‘Brother, by your way of speaking he will cook me alive. He cannot find my breath now; he will lift me upside down and, once the fire is set up, burn me through both sides while the middle stays uncooked.’

Just then a young demon came to report, ‘The broth is boiling.’ The old demon gave the order to lift. All the demons moved at once, carrying Zhu Bajie to the bottom rack and Sha Wujing to the second. As Sun Wukong guessed they were about to lift him, he slipped away and said, ‘Right under this lamplight, a trick can be done.’ He plucked one fine hair, breathed out a fairy breath, and cried, ‘Transform!’ He became another Sun Wukong and allowed himself to be bound with hemp ropes. He sent out his true body by spirit and leapt into the upper air, looking down. The demons, unable to tell the real from false, saw a man and lifted him up, setting that false Sun Wukong in the third rack. Then they hauled Tripitaka, yanked him over, bound him, and raised him to the fourth. The dry firewood was stacked, and blazing flames rose in fury. From the clouds the Great Sage lamented, ‘My Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing can endure two boilings; my master, only one boil will ruin him. If I do not use my method to save him, he will be lost in an instant.’

The adept Great Sage, standing in the air, twirled the secret gesture and intoned once, “On lǎn jìng fǎjiè, qiányuánhéng lìzhēn,” summoning in the court of the North Sea King. At once a black cloud in the sky answered with a loud cry: ‘Ao Shun, the little dragon of the North Sea, kneels and bows.’

Sun Wukong said, ‘Rise, rise. I would not trouble you without cause. Tripitaka and I have come here and been taken by the venomous demon and set upon the iron cage to be steamed. Go, hold and protect us; do not let them ruin the steaming.’

The Dragon King immediately changed his form into a gust of cold wind, blew beneath the pot, and circled as a guard. The heat of the fire no longer scorched the pot, and then the three were not harmed.

When almost three watches had passed, the old demon gave out orders: ‘My subordinates, we have labored with stratagem and took the four with Master Tripitaka; and because we have spent our strength escorting them, we have not slept for four days and four nights. They are now bound in the cage and likely cannot break loose; mind them well. Put ten little demons on turn to keep the fire, so we may retire to the palace and rest a little. By the fifth watch, when dawn is about to appear, they will surely be fully cooked. Then arrange the garlic, salt, and vinegar and wake us then, that we may partake with empty stomachs.’

Each demon obeyed the command. The three demon heads each withdrew to their resting palaces.

Sun Wukong heard clearly these instructions from the clouds, yet he lowered his head and did not hear voices from inside the cage. He thought, ‘The heat rises upward, surely it must be hot. Why do they not seem afraid, and why no cry or grumbling from within? Could they already be dead by steaming? I will go closer and listen again.’

The Great Sage trod on the clouds and changed himself into a black-blue fly, clinging outside the iron cage to listen. Then he heard Zhu Bajie inside saying, ‘Ill luck, ill luck—do not know whether this is smother-steaming or vent-steaming.’ Sha Wujing asked, ‘Second Brother, what are “smother-steaming” and “vent-steaming”?’ Zhu Bajie replied, ‘In smother-steaming the cage top is covered; in vent-steaming, it is not covered.’ Master Tripitaka added from above, ‘Disciple, it is not covered.’ Zhu Bajie said, ‘Oh fate! I shall not die tonight; this is vent-steaming.’ When Sun Wukong heard all three speaking and none harmed, he flew over and lightly set the lid of the iron cage over it. Master Tripitaka panicked, ‘Disciple, it is covered.’ Zhu Bajie said, ‘All right then. This is smother-steaming; tonight we must die.’ Sha Wujing and the master sobbed with choked cries. Zhu Bajie said, ‘Do not cry. The fire-watch has just changed shifts now.’ Sha Wujing asked, ‘How did you know?’ Zhu Bajie said, ‘When they first lifted us up, the heat suited me: I have a lingering damp-cold illness and wanted it to steam. But now a cool breath has come in. Hah! If the fire-keeper adds more wood, what is left but your doom?’

Sun Wukong heard it and could not help but laugh to himself. “This buffoon can be handled while he is cold; if he gets hot he will be in danger of dying. I say it again: one more time and the wind will be gone from him—save him at once. Wait. If I am to save him, I must show my true form. If I did, those ten fire-cooking fiends would see me and all shout together, alarming the old demon, and that would be no better than before. Let me first give him a trick.” Then he remembered, “When I was first Great Sage I once gambled at Beitian Gate with the Protector of the Realm Heavenly King and won his drowsy bugs. I still have a few.” He felt at his sash and sash-pocket and found twelve. “Give him ten, and keep two in reserve.” He tossed the bugs so they scattered onto the faces of the ten little fiends, and they burrowed into their nostrils and gradually drifted off, all falling asleep. Only one holding a fire fork could not doze. He rubbed his head, rubbed his face, pinched his nose left and right, sneezing again and again. Sun Wukong said, “This fellow knows his business. I’ll give him another pair of sleep bugs.” He threw another bug onto his face. “Two bugs—left in, right out; right in, left out—there will surely be one that settles.” The little fiend let out two or three big yawns, stretched his waist, dropped the fire fork, and with a thud also sank into sleep, never to turn over again.

Sun Wukong said, “This method is truly marvelous and potent.” Then he returned to his true form, went near and called out, “Master.” Tripitaka heard, “Wukong, save me.” Sha Wujing said, “Brother, are you calling from outside?” Sun Wukong replied, “I am not outside. Am I here to suffer inside with you all?” Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, the scoundrel slipped away and we’re all the ones bottlenecked here, suffering the fumes.” Sun Wukong laughed. “Don’t make such a din, fool. I’m here to save you.” Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, if you save him, save him completely—don’t put him back in the steamer again.” Sun Wukong then lifted the cage lid and untied Master, shook the borrowed hairs of his illusion from himself and drew himself back into his own body; then, layer by layer, he freed Sha Wujing and then Zhu Bajie. The fool only just escaped and wanted to run at once. Sun Wukong said, “No rushing, no rushing.” He chanted a spell and summoned the Dragon God, then told Zhu Bajie: “On our way to the Western Heaven there will still be high mountains and steep ridges. Master is weary and weak in the legs. Wait until I fetch a horse.”

See how lightly he moved, step by step, to Jinluan Hall, and saw that fiends large and small were all asleep. He unfastened the bridle and did not alarm anyone. The horse was in truth a dragon-horse; if it were a human, two hind kicks and a few neighs would have escaped from it. Sun Wukong had once raised horses and held the post of Bimawan, and he was one of their own kind, so he made it neither jump nor cry. He quietly led it over, tightened the belly strap and checked all the fittings, then invited Master to mount. The Abbot, trembling, mounted and was about to leave. Sun Wukong said, “Not yet—not yet. As we go west there are kings we must pass, and we need proper writs before we can go; otherwise, what credential do we have?
