This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Now the officer in brocade robes dragged the counterfeit Tripitaka out of the relay inn, and with troops of the Yulin Guards enclosed and followed him all the way to the gate outside the court, then told the Yellow Gate official, “We have invited Tripitaka to this place; please convey it in report.” The Yellow Gate official hurried into court and, as instructed, reported to the dim king, who ordered him admitted. All the officials knelt at the foot of the stairs, but the false Tripitaka stood upright on the stairs and shouted at the top of his voice, “Monk-King, why do you summon this poor monk?” The king laughed: “I have a disease that has persisted for many days and refuses to heal. By fortune, the Lord Marquess has obtained a prescription and all the medicinal ingredients are ready, only one ingredient remains as an attractor. I have summoned the elder to ask for that drawing ingredient. If I am cured, I will build a shrine for the elder and offer sacrifice four times a year, keeping the state incense burning through the ages.” The false Tripitaka replied, “I am an ordained monk, and I came here alone. I do not know what Your Majesty asked the marquess for as the required bait.” The dim king said, “I ask especially for your heart and liver.” The false Tripitaka said, “I will not hide it from Your Majesty: a heart is one thing, though I do not know what color you ask for.” The marquess at his side pointed and said, “That monk, I need your black heart.” The false Tripitaka said, “If so, bring a knife quickly; open my chest and abdomen. If there is a black heart, I will faithfully obey your order.” The king was delighted and thanked him, then ordered the charioteer to fetch a short horn-handled knife and hand it to the false monk. The monk took the knife, loosened his robes, threw back his chest, wiped his belly with his left hand and held the blade in his right. With a sharp rasping scrape he cut open his belly, and a heap of hearts rolled out from within. The civil officials turned pale and the martial generals went numb. The marquess, seeing this in the hall, said, “This is a monk with many hearts.” The fake monk, bloody and bare, picked out those hearts one by one to show the crowd. They were hearts of red, white, and yellow, avaricious hearts, hungry-for-fame hearts, jealous hearts, calculating hearts, proud-competition hearts, high-standing hearts, contemptuous hearts, killing hearts, cruel hearts, fearful hearts, cautious hearts, deluded hearts, hidden obscure-mind hearts, and all sorts of wicked hearts. Not one was black. The dim king stood astonished and trembling, unable to speak, and in a shaky voice commanded, “Take them away, take them away.” The fake Tripitaka could no longer hold back. He gathered in the spell-heart and revealed his true form: “Your Majesty has no discernment. My monk’s heart is all pure kindness. Only your marquess is black-hearted, fit to be your medicinal bait. If you do not believe me, wait until I draw his out for you to see.”

When the marquess heard this, he snapped his eyes open wide and watched closely. He saw the monk had changed his face and no longer looked the same. Ah!

Recognize me, do you not—Sun Great Sage, named and famed five hundred years past. He stepped back, leapt up on a cloud, and as the Wanderer somersaulted into the air he cried, “Where do you run? Eat this one staff-blow!” The marquess at once raised his coiled-dragon cane to meet him. The two fought that day in midair in a superb battle: The Golden-Hooped Staff, the coiled-dragon cane: in the void, a whole sheet of clouds thick and swirling. Indeed the marquess was a demon spirit, and that was why he had taken the strange demoness for his pretty concubine. The king’s lust and greed had infected his body, and the fiend sought to butcher children. Meeting the Great Sage, he displayed divine powers, seized the demon and saved the people, whose peril could not then be untied. The iron staff struck like a tiger at the mountain’s head, and the cane came up in return, worthy of applause. The sky darkened with a cloud of mist over the city, and the cityfolk turned ashen. Civil and military officers alike seemed to have their spirits fly; consorts and painted maidens lost their former composure. Terrified, that monk-kingly ruler lurked in confusion, rigid with fear. The staff rose like a tiger descending a peak; the cane spun like a dragon leaving the sea. This uproar in the realm of the monk-king made right and wrong stand starkly apart. That demon spirit and the Wanderer fought fiercely for more than twenty rounds. The coiled-dragon cane could not stand against the Golden-Hooped Staff. With one flash of false swing, it turned its body into a blade of cold light, fell into the inner court of the palace, dragged out the tribute-bearing demon concubine through the gate, became cold radiance again, and vanished from sight.

The Great Sage came down from the cloud-head and reached the courtyard before the palace hall, then said to the officials, “Your good marquess!” The officials knelt together in gratitude to thank the divine monk. The Wanderer said, “Do not bow now. Go and see where your stuporous king is hiding.” A minister said, “When the combat broke out, our lord, in panic, hid himself. We know not in which palace he went.” The Wanderer ordered, “Search quickly; do not be led astray by the beautiful empress.” The officials heard and, not distinguishing inner from outer quarters, ran first to the empress’s palace with him. No trace at all could be found; even the Beautiful Empress was nowhere to be seen. The principal hall, the east hall, the west hall, and six inner compounds—all the ladies and consorts—came out to bow and thank the Great Sage. The Wanderer said, “Do not kneel in thanks here. Go now and search for your lord.” Soon they saw four or five eunuchs supporting the dim king, who was coming from behind the hall in a self-contracted carriage of body. All ministers prostrated themselves and together began: “Your Highness, Your Highness, by receiving the divine monk here, the true and false were made clear. The marquess of this state is a demon spirit, and even the Beautiful Empress is missing.” Hearing this, the king invited the Wanderer out of the palace and into the Hall of Treasures, offered thanks, and said, “Elder, when you came earlier your appearance was so handsome and handsome indeed. Why have you changed your countenance now?” The Wanderer laughed and said, “Do not think Your Majesty so naïve. The one who came earlier was my master, Tripitaka of the Tang dynasty. I am his disciple Sun Wukong. He also has two junior disciples, Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, at the Golden Pavilion relay station. Knowing that Your Majesty believed the demon’s lies and wished to take my master’s heart and liver as bait, I, Old Sun, took my master’s form and came here specifically to subdue the demon.” When the king heard this, he issued orders at once: the Court Grand Steward should quickly go to the relay station and summon the whole trio of disciples to court.

When Tripitaka heard that the Wanderer had shown his form and was subduing a demon in the air, he was near to terror with spirit flying and soul scattered. Thankfully Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing remained beside him, and he still had a clay-smeared face. He sat in unease when he heard a cry: “Dharma Master, we are the grand marshal sent by the king of the Monk-King realm, and we are directed to enter court and offer thanks.” Zhu Bajie laughed: “Master, do not fear, do not fear. This is no new request to hand over your heart. It must be elder brother’s victory, and this is but a summons to reward him.” Tripitaka said, “Though this may be a call of victory and invitation, how can I be seen in this dirty, soiled face?” Zhu Bajie said, “There is no remedy. Let us go meet elder brother first; he will explain.” So the venerable monk, with no way out, followed Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, shouldering the burden pole and leading the horse, and together they went up to the relay-yard. When the grand marshal saw them, he flinched and said, “Oh, good sir! They all look like demon-headed, monstrous-minded creatures.” Sha Wujing said, “Courtiers, do not mock because of their ugliness. We are but naturally formed bodies. If my Master comes and sees elder brother, he will be handsome again again.”

The three of them came to court with the rest and, without waiting for summons, went straight to the hall. Seeing them, the Wanderer turned and descended from the hall, stepped forward, tore off Master’s clay-face, blew one immortal breath, and cried, “Transform!” Tripitaka at once returned to his original form, and his spirit felt all the more clear and free. The king came down from the hall and personally welcomed him, calling, “Dharma Master, Great Buddha.” The three masters and disciples tied their horse and all came up into the hall for audience. The Wanderer said, “Your Majesty, do you know from where that demon came? Let Old Sun capture him with you and eliminate the later calamity at once.” The three inner palaces, six apartments, and all the consorts and ladies-in-waiting were behind the jade screen; when they heard the Wanderer speak of cutting away the root of harm, they did not mind distinctions of inner and outer, male and female, but came out together and bowed, imploring: “We all hope the divine monk, Great Buddha, will fully exert your powers, cut the weed by the root and remove him utterly. This would be a boundless grace, and we shall repay you greatly.” The Wanderer hastily answered the bows and only told the king where he wished to stay. The king, embarrassed, confessed, “Three years ago when he came then, I once asked him. He said it was not far from the city, only seventy li to the south, at Qinghua Manor atop Willow-Slope Grove. The marquess is old with no sons; later his wife bore one daughter, sixteen years old, never yet married, and she wished to enter for me. Since I came to adore that girl, I accepted and favored her in the palace. My sickness came unawares. Though the physicians treated repeatedly, all remedies failed. He said, ‘I have a divine prescription: only a broth with a child’s heart as the drawing ingredient will work.’ I, being unworthy, took that word too lightly, and thus selected children from among the people, choosing this very midday for the cut to take their hearts. By sheer mischance, when the divine monk descended, the caged boys at once vanished. He said the monk had practiced true cultivation for ten lifetimes, that his primal yang had not yet leaked, and that this monk’s heart surpassed children’s hearts by ten thousand times. For a moment I erred, not knowing the divine monk discerned the demon spirit through and through. How dare I ask that your great Dharma power should be fully cast down to cut away this later plague; I shall repay, with my kingdom’s all resources, in gratitude.” The Wanderer smiled: “I will not hide the truth from you. The children in the cage are those spared by my Master’s compassion; he told me to hide them. Do not speak of material recompense. Let me first capture the demon; that will be my own merit.” He called, “Zhu Bajie, come with me.” Zhu Bajie said, “I respectfully obey my brother’s command. Yet my stomach is empty; I cannot put forth strength well.” The king then ordered that Guanglu Temple prepare a ceremonial fast meal at once. In no time the offering was ready. Zhu Bajie ate a full meal and revived his spirit; then he rose with the Wanderer and mounted the clouds. The king, the consorts and all the many civil and military officials watched in awe, each bowing toward the sky, and all said, “He truly is a real Immortal, a true Buddha descending to the mortal world.

The Great Sage went with Zhu Bajie straight to a place seventy li to the south, came to stay at Fengyun, and searched for the demon’s lair. But he saw only a clear brook, with banks on both sides, and on those banks millions of weeping willows; he still could not tell where Qinghua Manor was. It was exactly as follows:

Across ten thousand acres of wild fields no eye can grasp the bounds; a thousand dikes, with smudged willow haze, vanish beyond sight. When Sun Wukong could not find anything, he twisted his talisman-seal, chanted once the true-word of the syllable “Om,” and drew forth the local earth deity. The deity trembled forward, knelt, and called: "Great Sage, the Earth Spirit of Willow-Grove Slope bows." Sun Wukong said, "Do not be afraid. I will not strike you. I ask: there is said to be a Qinghua Manor at Willow-Grove Slope. Where is it?" The earth deity said, "There is a Qinghua Cave here, but no Qinghua Manor. This little spirit knows. Great Sage, you must have come from the Bikshu Kingdom." Sun Wukong said, "Yes, yes. The king of Bikshu was deceived by a demon. Old Sun came that way, recognized it as a fiend, and at the time drove it off with a burst of cold light, then it vanished. When I asked the king, he said that three years ago, while he was going near the Beauty Pavilion, the creature said it lived in Qinghua Manor on Willow-Grove Slope, seventy li south of the city walls. Now I have come only to this place and find only the slope, no manor. So I ask you." The earth spirit knelt and implored, "Great Sage, pardon my offense. The king of Bikshu is also master of this land, and this little spirit should have investigated properly. Yet the demon has a terrifying power. If this little spirit had revealed it, the fiend would come and bully me. So I could not manage it. But now that the Great Sage has arrived, go to the root of that one willow tree with nine forked branches on the south bank. Turn left three times, turn right three times, strike the tree together with both hands, and call out "Open the gate" three times; then the Qinghua Hall will appear."

After hearing this, the Great Sage sent the earth spirit back, then crossed the stream with Zhu Bajie and went to find that willow tree. There were indeed nine-pronged branches, all from one trunk. He told Zhu Bajie: "You stay well back. When I call for the gate to be opened and bring out the demon, be ready to receive him." Zhu Bajie obeyed and stationed himself at about half a li away. The Great Sage, following the land spirit’s instruction, circled the root, turned left three times and right three times, slapped both hands upon the tree, and called, "Open the gate, open the gate." In an instant there came a ringing crack, and with a rasping sound two doors snapped open; the tree itself vanished. Beyond was a bright, rosy brilliance, yet no sign of people. As he followed his power, Wukong dashed in. It was a wonderful scene:

The cloud-sheen shimmered, and the sun and moon stole faint light. White clouds rose from the cave all the time; tangled green moss spread thick in the court. One path of strange flowers competed to be most fair; at every step, precious grasses contended in fragrant splendor. The air was warm, the scene always spring-like, entirely like Langyuan, not inferior to Penglai. Slippery stools clung along long vines; level bridges hung with tangled creepers. Bees with red stamens in their mouths came to the rock caves; butterflies played with hidden orchids beyond the stone screen. He hurried forward and, on getting nearer, saw four large characters on the stone screen: "Qinghua Immortal Mansion." He could not help himself and leapt beyond the screen. There he saw the old fiend embracing a beauty, breathing hard, speaking of Bikshu affairs. In one voice the old monster cried, "My chance has come. Three years of this, and today it is finished, yet that monkey head spoiled it." Wukong rushed near and shouted, "You bunch of shaggy wretches! What do you mean by "good chance"? Take this staff!" The fiend dropped the beauty and raised a coiled-dragon cane to face him. The two fought outside the cave; it was a hard battle, unlike the earlier one: The staff rose and scattered gold light; the cane whirled, evil force exploding. The fiend said: "You fool, how dare you enter my gate?" Sun Wukong said: "I have come to capture this demon." The fiend said: "I am attached to the king, and you have no business. Why dare you come to flaunt yourself?" Sun Wukong said: "A monk who upholds the Dharma is naturally compassionate, and does not take pleasure in slaughtering the living." Their words crossed in hatred; staff met cane, striking toward the heart. He stepped hard, tripping the emerald moss and smashing the ground where it was slick. Only by striking did the rosy glow in the cave and the radiant colors above the cliffs grow dim and beaten down. Clang and crash startled birds from flight; the beauty scattered at the terrifying shouts. Only the old demon and the Monkey King remained, with whirling winds battering the earth. Then they burst from the cave together, and ran against Zhu Bajie, whose blunt temper flared. Outside, Zhu Bajie, hearing their commotion, felt his blood rise. He drew his pida, struck one of the nine-pronged willows flat, and hacked several blows. Blood seemed to well out and hiss, as if it had a voice. He said, "Even this tree has become a spirit!" He raised the pida and struck again, then saw Wukong leading the fiend out. The fool spoke no word, rushed forward, and swung the pida. The old demon, already hard-fought against Wukong, felt himself more panicked by Bajie’s pida, lost formation, and in a single motion turned into a streak of cold light and ran east. The two did not relent and chased it eastward.

At that very moment of battle, a wild-crane cry sounded, and a faint, auspicious light appeared. Looking up, it was the star known as the Old Man of the Southern Pole. The elder had enveloped the cold light, and said, "Great Sage, do not come on. Tianpeng, do not chase him further. The old Daoist offers worship here." Sun Wukong replied with ceremony: "Brother Shouxing, where do you come from?" Zhu Bajie laughed, "That flesh-bodied old fellow has covered the cold light; he must have caught the demon." The Old Man smiled: "Here, here. I beg you, both of you, spare the demon." Sun Wukong said, "The fiend has nothing to do with my younger brother; why do you speak of mercy?" Shouxing smiled: "He is one of my subordinate strengths. Unwittingly he ran off and became this demon." Sun Wukong said, "If this is the matter of my brother, then make him show his true form." Hearing this, Shouxing released the cold light and shouted, "You imp of evil! Show your true form at once, and I will spare your life of blame." The fiend spun once, and turned out to be a white deer. Shouxing took up his staff: "This wretch has even stolen my own cane." The deer dropped to the ground, could not speak, and only knelt and wept. It appeared then as:

A body like mottled white jade, two antlers crooked, seven-pronged and bent. Many a time, hungry, it sought the herb garden; when thirsty, it drank where the cloud-water rippled. Through many years it learned the art of flight and ascent; through long practice its form had changed. Now that it sees its master’s call, it appears, tucks its ears, and bows down in the dust of the world. Shouxing thanked Sun Wukong and mounted the deer to go. Wukong pulled him up and said, "Elder brother, wait. Two matters remain undone." Shouxing said, "What two matters?" Wukong said, "First, the beauty has not yet been taken, and we do not know what demon she is. Second, we still must return to Bikshu City and present this truth before that deluded king." Shouxing said, "If so, then I shall wait. Take Tianpeng down into the cave and seize that beauty. Then we can all go and present ourselves." Sun Wukong said, "Elder brother, wait a little. We’ll return immediately after we go there."

Zhu Bajie shook himself and followed Wukong straight into the Qinghua Immortal Mansion, crying out loudly, "Catch the demon! Catch the demon!" The beauty trembled, already hard pressed for escape. Hearing the cries swell, she darted back behind the stone screen, and no back gate appeared from which to come out. Zhu Bajie shouted, "Where are you running? You stinking fiend that deceives men—show your pida!" The beauty had no weapon in her hand and could not meet him. In one instant she flashed into cold light and tried to flee. Sun Wukong blocked the light and struck once with a resounding staff blow. The monster could not stand, fell to the dust, and revealed its true form: a white-faced fox. Zhu Bajie could not restrain himself; he raised his pida and smashed it on the head. The woman of a thousand charms that could stir a kingdom was transformed into a snarled bundle of fur, in fox form. Wukong called, "Do not smash him to bits. Leave this body intact and take him to be shown before the deluded king."

The fool did not mind filth; he seized the tail and hauled and hauled, following Wukong out the gate. There he saw the Old Man of the Southern Pole holding the deer’s head and cursing: "Good beast of evil, how could you betray your master and run off to become spirit-power here? If I had not arrived, Great Sage Sun Wukong surely would have beaten you to death." Wukong stepped out and said, "What are you saying, brother?" Shouxing said, "I had warned the deer, I had warned the deer." Zhu Bajie flung the dead fox at the deer’s feet and said, "Is this your daughter?" The deer nodded its head, moved it about, and sniffed him a few times, making a low sound of reluctance and attachment. Then Shouxing struck the deer with a palm: "Beast of evil, your life has run its course enough—how could he have done this?" He untied the tie-belt from his robe, bound it around the deer’s neck, pulled it up, and said, "Great Sage, I will go with you to meet at Bikshu." Sun Wukong said, "Wait. Let us first clean this side completely, so that no demon-kin can rise again."

On hearing this, Zhu Bajie raised his pida and hacked up the willow tree in disorder. Wukong once more uttered the seed-sound "Om," and again called forth the earth spirit of this place, saying: "Find some dry brushwood. Light a fierce fire. Remove this demon-affliction from this region so it can never again oppress others." The earth spirit turned, and a bleak wind sighed sharply. He marshaled dark soldiers, and brought back yingshuang-grass, qiuqing-grass, liao-jie grass, mountain-bud grass, louhao twigs, dragon-bone wood, and reed-tassel wood—all completely dry, fully cured and hardened with age. They caught fire as if ghee-fed. Wukong said, "Zhu Bajie, do not keep bashing the tree. It is enough to fill the cave with these and set the fire, and burn this thing clean through." Once the flames rose, the Qinghua demon dwelling was burned into a blazing pit of fire.

At that moment he had only just driven away the Earth God when Longevity Star returned, leading the white deer and dragging the fox. They came together before the hall. He said to the king, “Is this your beautiful queen, and do you make a toy of him?” The king was shaken with fear. Then Sun Wukong appeared, leading Longevity Star and the white deer, and all came before the hall. The king, ministers, and entire royal household immediately knelt in prostration. The Great Sage stepped forward, steadied the king, and laughed: “Stop paying respects to me. This white deer is your Guo-zhang; only bow to it.” So ashamed that the king had no face left, he said, “I thank the holy monk for saving my small kingdom. Truly this is heaven’s favor.” He immediately issued an order: let the Ministry of Court Light arrange a vegetarian banquet, open the East Pavilion, and invite the Old Man of the Southern Pole and Tripitaka’s four companions to sit together and receive our gratitude. Tripitaka paid his respects to Longevity Star, and Sha Wujing also paid proper respect. All asked, “Since this white deer belongs to Old Longevity, how did it come here to cause harm?” Longevity Star laughed: “Formerly, when Lord Donghua passed through my wild mountain, I stayed and played one round of chess. The game was still unfinished when this wretch fled away. Later, when I went to look for it and found nothing, I reckoned by my fingers and knew it had wandered here. I came to search for it, and by chance met the Great Sage displaying his majesty. Had I come any later, this beast would have been gone.”

The account could not be finished before a report arrived: “The feast is ready.” A magnificent vegetarian banquet:

Five colors filled the gate, and strange scents filled every seat. Brocaded cloth hung upon the tables glowed like woven silk in bright splendor; red carpets on the floor shimmered with rosy cloud-light. In the treasure-shaped ducks coiled sandalwood incense rose in thin plumes; before the imperial table, the vegetable dishes released fragrant aroma. The trays held piled, towering fruit like stacked pavilion towers; confections and carved sugar animals coiled like dragons at their arrangement. Swan lozenges, lion-sage sweets, each in proper and playful shape; parrot cups and egret-cormorant ladles, formed to almost living likeness. Before the seats the fruits were all bountifully arranged; on the tables the vegetarian fare was meticulously prepared. Full-round chestnuts, fresh lychees and peaches. Date treats and persimmon cakes were sweet; pine nuts and grapes perfumed the scented wine. Several kinds of honey sweets, a few kinds of steamed pastries. Fried sugar cakes, then flower-like trays arranged in layered color. Golden trays heaped high with great dumpling-like mochi, silver bowls filled with aromatic rice. Long noodles in hot fragrant soup followed one upon another, each course replaced with another and still more delicious. Mushrooms, black fungus, tender bamboo shoots, and huang-jing—one can scarcely recount them all—ten-scented vegetables, and delicacies of a hundred flavors. There was no pause in the busy hands passing back and forth; at both entry and exit all sorts were abundantly set. At that time the seating was assigned: Longevity Star took the principal seat, Tripitaka next, the king in the seat before him, and Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing at the side seats. On each side there were two or three learned masters to attend. Then he ordered the music office to play. The king lifted a rosy-purple cup and offered wine one by one. Only Tripitaka did not drink. Zhu Bajie said to Sun Wukong, “Elder Brother, let the fruit be yours; for soups and grain I ask you to let me enjoy them.” The oaf distinguished not between fine and coarse, surged in all at once, and came only to eat everything to emptiness.

After one seating of the feast was complete, Longevity Star took his leave. The king once again came forward and knelt to beseech him for methods to remove illness and lengthen life. Longevity Star smiled: “I came in search of the deer and brought no cinnabar pills. If I told you methods of cultivation, yet your sinews and spirit are weakened; you cannot yet receive the Elixir. In my sleeve are only three jujubes, brought to offer tea to Lord Donghua. I have not eaten them. Take these.” The king swallowed them and gradually felt his body lighten and his illness withdraw. The ones who later gained longevity all traced back to this source. Seeing this, Zhu Bajie called out, “Old Longevity, there are fire-dates—send me a few to eat.” Longevity Star said, “I did not bring any; come another day and I will send you a few jin.” He then left the East Pavilion, returned thanks, called once to the white deer, leapt across and upon it, and went forth on cloud paths. The king, consort, and the palace and townspeople all burned incense and bowed in reverence, not worth further record.

Tripitaka said, “Disciple, prepare and take leave of the king.” The king again earnestly begged for instruction. Sun Wukong said, “Your Majesty, from now on reduce lustful desire, accumulate more hidden merit, and in all matters let your long be added to your short and your short made long; that alone suffices to banish illness and prolong life—that is the teaching.” He then brought out two trays of scattered gold pieces and broken silver, offering them as travel expense. Tripitaka firmly declined and would not take a single coin. The king could not help himself. He ordered a palace carriage to be laid out and asked Tripitaka to take the seat in a phoenix sedan-dragged dragon carriage. The king and the consort together pushed the turning wheels, and only then did they send the party out of court. In the six streets and three markets, all householders and common folk added cups of clear water, burned true incense, and also sent them out of the city.

Suddenly there sounded a wind through midair, and along both sides of the road came down one thousand one hundred and eleven goose cages, each with a child crying inside. In secret, the city guardians who had originally been posted came out—the City God, Earth God, Village Spirit, True Officials, the Five-Directional Jie-di, the Four Duty Magistrates, the Six Ding and Six Jia, the Dharma-Protecting Pagoda and other hosts. They cried out at once: “Great Sage, we were first instructed to seize the children’s goose cages. Now we know your merit-work is complete and you are setting forth; we have brought them here for you one by one.” Then the king, queen, and all ministers and subjects likewise knelt in bowing. Sun Wukong looked up and said, “You have all labored; please each return to your shrines. I will make offerings among the people to thank you.” A hard wind rose with a hiss and whisper, then withdrew as it had come.

Sun Wukong called on the city households to identify the children. As soon as the word spread, everyone came and recognized the children in the cages. Gladly they carried them out, calling “Brother!” “My little one!” “Child!” jumping and laughing; all cried, “Hold onto Tang Zongye! Come to my house and we will repay the grace of rescuing our children.” No matter age, no matter boy or girl, no one cared for how ugly he looked. They lifted Zhu Bajie on their shoulders, bore Sha Wujing, supported Sun Wukong, clutched Tripitaka, led the horse, and carried the poles together, forming one great crowd returning to the city. Even the king could not forbid it. Some houses held feasts; others set out tables. Those who had not been able to make full preparations made monk hats, monk shoes, padded short robes, cloth socks—inside and outside, every size and kind of clothing—and came to send him off. So this loitering lasted nearly a month before they could leave the city. There were also reports from shadow spirits: tablets were raised, and people offered top-bowing, incense, and worship. This was the close:

Yin-merit piled high, layered heavier than a mountain of grace, and saved tens of thousands upon thousands of lives.

In the end it is still unknown what further events await. For that, listen to the explanation in the next chapter.

Once again it was said that in the kingdom of Biqiu, the king, his ministers, and the common people escorted Tripitaka and the four pilgrims out of the city, and even after twenty li they still would not let them go. Tripitaka reluctantly climbed down from the sedan, mounted his horse, and took his leave to depart; those sending him off watched until his figure vanished from sight, and only then turned back. The four-company had traveled a long while. Winter’s remnant had passed, spring was waning, and though the wild blossoms and mountain trees should have been in bloom, the scenes had not yet become full of fragrance. Ahead they saw another towering mountain with steep ridges. Troubled, Tripitaka asked, “Disciple, is there a road over that mountain or not? We must be careful.” Sun Wukong laughed, “Master, these are not the words of one who has long-traveled on the road; they are like those of a young noble looking at the sky from a well’s rim. As the old saying goes: ‘A mountain does not block the road; the road goes through the mountain.’ Why ask whether there is road or no road?” Tripitaka replied, “Though a mountain indeed does not block it, I still fear that monsters may be born among such sheer heights, and fiends may emerge from the deep thickets.” Zhu Bajie said, “Do not worry, do not worry. From this place it is not far to the Pure Land, and surely we will have peace and no trouble.”

The master and disciples had been speaking when, without noticing, they reached the foot of the mountain. Sun Wukong took out the Golden-Hooped Staff, climbed up the rocky bank, and called, “Master, this is the way that winds around the mountain, and it is very passable. Come on, come on.” The elder could only loosen the reins and let the horse go forward. Sha Wujing said, “Second Brother, carry the shoulder pole load.” So Zhu Bajie took it up on one shoulder. Sha Wujing held the reins, and the Master sat steady in the carved saddle while all followed Sun Wukong up onto the broad path of the cliff-side. Then they saw that mountain:

Mist draped the peak tops, and rippling streams surged through the ravines. Fragrance of a hundred flowers filled the road, and ten thousand trees pressed in dense clumps. The plum was green, the pearwood white, the willow green and the peach red. Where the cuckoo cries, spring is nearly gone; Violet swallows chatter as the social songs end. Jagged stones, pines with emerald canopies. The ridge-road is rugged, suddenly abrupt and exquisitely clear. Sheer walls and hanging cliffs stand steep and stern. Vines and undergrowth thicken among the roots and trees. A thousand peaks compete in beauty like spears in rows; ten thousand valleys clash in currents, their far waters surging. Tripitaka gazed calmly at the mountain scene, and hearing birds lament, homesickness rose in him again. He pulled the horse up and called, “Disciple! I, by heavenly tally, received command beneath a brocade screen. Fifteen lantern-watchings westward from the Eastern Land, then only then were Tang the King and heaven and earth set apart. At length dragon and tiger met in wind and cloud, and once more I and the disciples forced the horse onward. We have walked twelve peaks of Wushan, when shall I meet one worthy in this age?” Sun Wukong said, “Master, you are always clinging to homesickness, and it does you little credit as one who has left household life. Just keep walking and do not worry so much. As the old saying has it, ‘If one desires prosperity and rank, one must labor with one’s life on the line.’” Tripitaka said, “Though what you say is sensible, I do not know where exactly the road to the Western Buddha lands lies.” Zhu Bajie said, “Master, the Buddha will not part with the Tripitaka Sutra. He knows we must fetch it, so surely some matter has moved us here; otherwise how could we keep going as we have?” Sha Wujing said, “Stop this and follow Elder Brother. Persevere in your efforts; surely a day of arrival will come.”

At that moment, while the group was still speaking idly, they suddenly came upon a vast dark pine forest. Tang Monk grew afraid and called, “Wukong, we have only just crossed that rough mountain road, and now we meet this deep black pine wood. We must be wary.” Sun Wukong replied, “Why fear it?” Tripitaka said, “What are you saying? ‘Trust not the one who seems utterly upright; beware even the upright that is not upright.’ We have already passed several pine woods together, none as deep and far-reaching as this. Look:

East and west stand dense and close, while north and south keep their own long lines. East and west are crowded tight, rising to the clouds’ edge; North and south stand in line, encroaching into the blue vault. Dense thorns and thornbush encircle all, and knotweed binds and circles upward. Vines coil around kudzu, and kudzu returns the coil upon the vines. When the vines coil around kudzu, east-to-west travel is hard; when kudzu coils around vines, south-to-north trade cannot enter. Spend half a year in this forest and you will lose track of day and month; in a few li you do not even see the Big Dipper. In the shade are a thousand forms of scenery, in the sunlit places are ten thousand flower clusters. There are thousand-year pagoda trees, ten-thousand-year cypresses, hardy pines, wild peaches, wild peony, and drought lotus. Heap upon heap they rise in dense, confused masses, a disorderly splendor no immortal painter could finish. Again one hears a hundred birds: parrots whistle, cuckoos cry; magpies thread the branches, crows return their call; orioles dance, warblers tune their voices; partridges shout, and purple swallows converse; starlings learn to imitate human speech, and the barbet seems ready to read a sutra. There too a great beast swishes its tail, a tiger gnashes its teeth; a fox-wolf-maid, old as ages, howls with a wolf’s voice to rattle the wood. Even if the Heavenly King who once held a pagoda were to come, even if he came to exorcise fiends, he would lose his spirit too.” Great Sage Sun Wukong showed no fear at all. He used his staff to cleave a road ahead and led Tripitaka straight into the deep forest. Lightly and freely they went on for half a day, still having seen no way out. Tang Monk called, “Disciple, traveling west has brought us through endless perilous forests and ridges. By luck this place is calm and refined, and the way has been peaceful. The odd flowers and strange herbs here are truly beautiful. I shall sit awhile: first, to rest the horse; second, I am now hungry. Go there and make some alms-food and bring it.” Sun Wukong said, “Master, dismount. I will go make a little offering food and return.” The elder truly dismounted; Zhu Bajie tied the horse to a tree. Sha Wujing put down the baggage, took the alms bowl, and handed it to Sun Wukong. Sun Wukong said, “Master, sit steady and do not be afraid. I will be back soon.” Tripitaka sat beneath the pine shade, while Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing wandered off to pick flowers and fruit in idle play.

Now Great Sage leapt with his staff and rose to midair, coming to a halt in the cloud-lit air. He turned and looked back, and saw in the pine forest subtle auspicious mists and luminous vapor. Then he cried out, ‘Good! Good!’ Why did he cry out? He was praising Tripitaka, saying that he was the reincarnation of Elder Golden Cicada, a true and worthy man of ten lifetimes’ cultivation, and that was why this auspicious radiance covered over him. “Were it not for me, old Sun, when five hundred years ago I caused havoc in Heaven, roaming sea and horizon, playing wild across the world; gathering cohorts of spirits and calling myself Equal of Heaven; subduing dragons and tigers, erasing my death record. I wore a three-tiered gold crown, dressed in golden armor, held the Golden-Hooped Staff in my hand, and wore cloud-walking boots on my feet. Beneath me stood forty-seven thousand demons, all calling me Great Sage. Yet now, having slipped out of that heavenly uproar and become a humbler being, I have become your disciple. If I see this halo of auspicious clouds and blessed vapor fixed above your head, then when we go back east of course there will be some blessing for us; old Sun too will surely gain a true and complete fruit.”

Then, amid that self-laudatory reverie, he suddenly saw, below to the south of the forest, a streak of black vapor surging upward like the rising of bare bones. Sun Wukong cried out in alarm, ‘In that black vapor there must surely be a demon. Neither Pigsy nor Sha Wujing would be able to exude such black qi.’ The Great Sage hovered in midair, trying to inspect it carefully but could not yet determine its nature.

Tripitaka was sitting in the forest, calming his mind and opening his nature, reciting the Great Prajñā Pāramitā Heart Sutra. He suddenly heard a piping cry of ‘Save me!’ Tripitaka was greatly startled and said, ‘Excellent indeed! How strange, in such a deep wood who calls out? It might be a wolf-crop, tiger or leopard, terrified and panicked—let me see.’ The elder rose, moved forward, and crossed over the thousand-year cypress, broke past the ten-thousand-year pines, clung to vine and climbed through tangles, and came near to look. He saw a woman bound to a tree: the upper half lashed by roots and vines to the trunk, the lower half buried in the soil. The elder set his feet and asked, “Woman-bodhisattva, what is your matter, bound here?” Alas, it was clearly a demon; yet with his ordinary mortal eyes the elder could not recognize it. When she saw him ask, tears streamed from her like springs. Look at her—peach-cheeked with tears, with a beauty to make fish sink and wild geese fall; starry eyes filled with sorrow, with a face whose beauty shamed moon and flowers. The elder, still unwilling to draw near, spoke again, “Woman-bodhisattva, what exactly is your crime? Tell poor monk, and I may save you.” The fiend answered with clever, pretty words and feigned sorrow, hastily agreeing: “Master, my home is in Binpo Country, over two hundred li from here. My parents remain at home; they are very righteous and kind, affectionate all their lives. At Qingming we invited our kinsfolk and close family, old and young, to sweep the ancestral graves. With sedan and horse escorting us, we all came out to a wasteland beyond the city. At the graves we laid out the rites; just after the paper horses were burned, gongs and drums sounded, and a band of ruffians burst forth with knives and cudgels, shouting and advancing in violence. Terrified, our souls nearly flew out of our bodies. My parents and relatives, mounted on horse or borne in sedan, each fled and saved their lives. I was young and could not run. Unable to move, I nearly fainted; they carried me off into the mountain. The Great King wanted me as his primary wife; the second king wished me as a wife; the third and fourth each coveted my beauty. In all, seven or eight scores of households argued together, all angry and contentious, so they bound me in the woodland and dispersed. Five days and five nights have passed; my life seems near ending, and soon I will die. I do not know what merit from former ancestors now answers me, but today I have met this teacher. Have boundless compassion, save my life. Below the nine springs, I will never forget this grace.” Speaking thus, she wept as rain.

Tripitaka’s compassion truly overcame him; he could not help but drop tears, his voice choked as he called, “Disciple.” Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing were then in the forest seeking flowers and fruit. Hearing their master’s pitiful call, Bajie said, “Sha Wujing, Master has found a relation here.” Sha Wujing laughed, “Second Brother, stop your nonsense. We have walked so long and not met a single good person; where could this relation have come from?” Zhu Bajie said, “It is no relation. Why is Master crying with a stranger? I and you should go and see.” Sha Wujing truly returned to the old spot, led the horse and took up the load, then called at the side, “Master, what happened?” Tripitaka pointed with his hand to that tree and said, “Zhu Bajie, unbind that woman-bodhisattva and save her life.” Zhu Bajie, not distinguishing good from evil, moved immediately to act.

Now it is said that the Great Sage, Sun Wukong, again in midair, saw thick black vapour so dense that it completely smothered the auspicious glow. He cried, “Not good, not good! The black miasma covers the holy light. Could it be that a demon-evil has harmed my Master? Making an offering is a trifling matter. I must first go and see my Master.” He turned back with the cloud and alighted in the woods. There he saw Zhu Bajie loosely untying the ropes. Sun Wukong stepped forward, grabbed him by the ear, and with one hard drag sent him crashing down in a tumble. The fool looked up, got to his feet, and said, “Master told me to rescue a person. Why did you rely on your strength and throw me down like that?” Sun Wukong laughed, “Brother, do not untie him. He is a demon, making a racket to trick us.” Tripitaka barked, “You insolent monkey, you are making nonsense again. How could you, at once on seeing a woman, know she is a demon?” Sun Wukong said, “Master, you do not yet know; this is an old trade of old Sun’s, a method for getting human flesh to eat. How would you know it?” Zhu Bajie, with his mouth shut tight, said, “Master, do not believe this Bima-wun to fool you. This woman belongs to a household here. We came from the Eastern Land, far away, no kin and no acquaintance—how can one call her a demon? She sent us on ahead, we were turned away, and yet she turned a juggled trick, used magic and brought us back for some sly business.” Sun Wukong shouted, “Simpleton, do not babble. Since old Sun came west, where have you ever found room for idle kindness? You, this lustful and callous fellow, so forgetting righteousness and chasing gain, do not know right and wrong; you set him up to attract a daughter-in-law and tied him to a tree.” Tripitaka said, “Enough, enough. Zhu Bajie, your elder brother has never been slow to observe; if he says so, do not meddle. Let us leave.” Sun Wukong rejoiced and said, “Good, Master now has Heaven’s intent. Mount up and ride out of the pines, there will be houses where you can receive alms-food.” The four then strode onward together, leaving the monster behind.

The monster, still tied to the tree, ground his teeth in fury and said, “For years people have spoken of Sun Wukong’s vast powers; seeing him today, truly nothing he said was false. Tripitaka, a novice monk from the East, has not yet let out even a drop of vital essence. He intended to seize him and make him match with them and become a Tàiyĭ Jīnxian, yet this monkey saw through my arts and rescued him. If they had cut the rope, let me down, and I seized him at once, would he not be my man? Now he has been carried away by this fellow’s scattered babble—has it not become labor with no gain? Let me call him two more times and see what happens.” The demon did not move the rope. He spoke a few words of seeming kindness and, with a smooth wind, sent a shrill whisper into Tripitaka’s ear. You ask, “What did he call him?” He called out, “Master! You leave a living life unrescued and do not save it; how can you claim to seek scriptures by insincere worship of the Buddha?”

Hearing such calling again from the saddle, Tripitaka pulled the reins and said, “Wukong, go and rescue that woman and bring her down.” Sun Wukong said, “Master, after we were already walking on, why do you think of him again now?” Tripitaka said, “He is still calling there.” Sun Wukong asked, “Zhu Bajie, did you hear?” Zhu Bajie said, “My ears were covered; I did not hear it.” He asked again, “Sha Wujing, did you hear?” Sha Wujing said, “I am ahead bearing the load, not attending to it, and I did not hear either.” Sun Wukong said, “Old Sun also did not hear. Master, what did he call that I did not hear?” Tripitaka said, “His words have sense. He called, ‘Master, you leave a living life and do not rescue it. With what heart do you worship Buddha to take the scripture?’ and again, ‘To save one life is worth building a seven-storied pagoda.’ Go, save him at once; that is better than the pilgrimage and bowing.” Sun Wukong laughed, “When one embraces compassion so, there is no remedy for it. Since you left the Eastern Land and traveled west, you have crossed so many mountain ranges and met many demons. They often take you into their caves. I used my staff and killed them by the hundreds of thousands to rescue you. Today, for one demon’s life, you cannot bear to let him go?” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, the ancients said: ‘Do not refuse a small good; do not do even a small evil.’ Go save him.” Sun Wukong said, “If Master is determined, this is a load old Sun cannot bear. If I urge you, I dare not, for I would only provoke your anger. Do as you will and save him.” Tripitaka said, “Monkey, stop at once. Sit still. Let me and Zhu Bajie go save him.”

Tripitaka returned into the woods and told Zhu Bajie to loosen the upper half of the rope; using a spade he worked loose the lower half of the body. The monster staggered, fluttering his feet and clamping his skirt, and, happy and eager, followed Tripitaka out of the pine forest. On seeing him, Sun Wukong only kept on with a cold laugh. Tripitaka scolded, “You monkey-head, why do you laugh?” Sun Wukong said, “I laugh at you: you came upon an old friend and, in transit, happened upon a pretty woman.” Tripitaka scolded again, “You wild ape is speaking nonsense again. From the moment I left my mother’s womb, I have been a monk. Now I go west by command, devoutly worshiping Buddha and seeking scripture; I am no man of honor and profit. How is this lustfulness?” Sun Wukong laughed, “Master, though you have been a monk since childhood, you only read sutras and recite Buddha’s name and have never seen the proper laws. This woman is young and graceful. We are both ordained men and travel with her; if wicked men meet us, they may seize us and hand us to magistrates. Whether or not one calls it a matter of pilgrimage or Buddhist devotion, they will make it adultery. Even if none of that occurs, they still ask about carrying off a person. Master, with your travel-passes, you would be given a little death. Zhu Bajie would be questioned for penal exile. Sha Wujing also for standing in the square. Old Sun would not remain clean; even with my eloquence, after argument I would still be called in answer.” Tripitaka shouted, “Do not talk nonsense, not so indeed. I save this life; what trouble can it bring? I take him with us; any consequences are upon me.” Sun Wukong said, “Master, though you say the trouble is yours, you do not know: it is not you saving him but hurting him.” Tripitaka said, “I rescue him from the forest and secure his life. How could that hurt him?” Sun Wukong said, “At the moment he was tied in the grove, three or five days, ten days, even half a month without food, he could die of hunger and his whole body return to darkness. Now that you bring him out, you ride like the wind; we must all keep to your pace. Yet her feet are small and hard to move, how can she keep up with the steps? If in a moment you drop him back and she meets wolves, insects, or tigers and is swallowed up, would that not be harming her life?”

Tripitaka said, “You are right, this I overlooked. How should we handle it?” Sun Wukong laughed, “Carry her up and let her ride with you.” Tripitaka murmured, “How can I ride together with her?”—“How could he go there?” Sun Wukong said. Tripitaka said, “Have Zhu Bajie carry him.” Sun Wukong laughed, “The fool has good fortune indeed.” Zhu Bajie said, “‘A long road is no light burden.’ You ask me to carry one on my back—what kind of fortune is that?” Sun Wukong said, “Your mouth is so long; if you carry him, you can turn that mouth back and carry on private talk. Is that not useful?” Upon hearing this, Zhu Bajie thumped his chest and leapt, “No, no. If Master beats me a few times, I can bear the pain. But to carry him would not leave me with a clean heart. My elder brother can hide every wrong and even bury it. I cannot carry him.” Tripitaka said, “Enough, enough. I can still walk a few steps. Let me dismount, and slowly we shall all walk together. Have Zhu Bajie lead the empty horse.” Sun Wukong laughed, “The fool has a fair arrangement; Master will indeed watch over your handling of the reins.” Tripitaka said, “This monkey makes trouble again. As the ancients say, ‘A horse can go a thousand li; no one cannot go on its own.’ If on the road I walk slowly, will you then cast me off? If I walk slowly, you will too. Let us all go down the mountain together with this Bodhisattva-lady, and by the way to a retreat-temple or monastery, a house where people live, we can leave her there—that is also the rescue I have done.” Sun Wukong said, “Master has spoken well; go on quickly.”

Tripitaka led from the front. Sha Wujing shouldered the pack, Zhu Bajie led the empty horse and guided the woman, and Sun Wukong carried the iron staff. In less than twenty or thirty li, evening came on, and they saw a pavilion and hall complex. Tripitaka said, “Disciple, there must surely be a hermitage or monastery there. Let us lodge for the night and set out early tomorrow.” Sun Wukong said, “Master is right. Let everyone keep moving.” In an instant they reached the gate. He said, “You all stand a little apart. I will go in first to ask for lodging; if there is a place of convenience, have someone call you.” The group stood under the willow shade, while Sun Wukong alone held the iron cudgel and kept control of the woman.

The abbot drew nearer and pulled himself forward, and all he saw was the gate leaning in all directions, broken and scattered. When he pushed it open and looked, he could not restrain the desolation in his heart: the corridor was silent, the ancient monastery sparse and forlorn; moss filled the court, weeds of mugwort lined the path; only the fireflies’ flickering lamps moved through the dusk, and frog cries had taken the place of time-marking bells. At once the abbot burst into tears. It was truly so:

The halls had withered and collapsed, the corridor and wings lay leaning into loneliness. Piles upon piles of broken bricks and cracked tiles, and all was bent beams and split columns. Before and behind, only new grass grew; dust covered the rotten incense hall. The bell tower had fallen apart, the drum had no skin; the glazed perfume lamps were shattered. The Buddha’s golden form had lost all color, the arhats lay sprawled east and west. Even Guanyin was weathered into mud, and the willow-brushed pure vase had crashed to the ground. By day no monk was within; by night the foxes all kept their watch there. Only the wind’s roar sounded, like thunder; these were dens where tigers and leopards hid. Around, the walls were all fallen; there were no doors left at all to close. There is a poem as witness: For years no one has repaired this ancient monastery; it has fallen into ruin, poor and forlorn. A fierce wind has torn the temple facade apart; hard rain drenched the remnants atop Buddha’s image. The Vajra image lay broken and battered from endless soaking; the earth has no shelter to keep watch through the night. Worse yet, two things remain to be mourned: the copper bell lies on the ground, its tower no longer above it. Tripitaka steeled himself and entered through the two-tier gate. There he saw that both the bell- and drum-tower had collapsed, and only one bronze bell remained, driven into the ground, its upper half white as snow, its lower half dark indigo blue. In truth, with age and years, rain had bleached the upper half, and the lower had taken on verdigris from the breath of the soil. Tripitaka touched the bell with his hand and cried out, 「Bell, you once hung from lofty towers and thundered forth your voice; you once rang out and your sound traveled through painted beams afar. You once proclaimed dawn when the cock first sang, and you once sent evening down at dusk. I do not know where the daoist who turned you into bronze has gone, nor where the smith who cast you remains. I think both have returned their destinies to the courts of Yin, and they are gone without trace while you lie silent.」

The abbot spoke in a loud voice of praise, and without intending to, he startled the temple’s occupants. A daoist keeper of the incense nearby heard the human voice, rose up, picked a broken tile, and struck the bell. The bell gave a sharp clang. It made the abbot start with fright and stumble backward; he jumped up to leave, then caught his toe on a root and fell again with a crash. Lying in the dust he raised his head and called, 「Bell, I had only been grieving and sighing over you when suddenly a clear clink rang out. Perhaps, for no one has come this way on the road to the Western Heaven for so many years, you have become an enlightened spirit on your own.」

The monk hurried forward and caught him. 「Sir, please rise. This was not a bell becoming a spirit—the ringing came from my strike.」 Tripitaka lifted his head and looked at him. The man’s face was ugly and dark. Tripitaka said, 「Are you some woodland fiend or demon fiend? I am no common man; I come from Great Tang, and I have disciples beneath me who can bring dragons under control and tigers to kneel. If you meet them, your life may not endure." The monk knelt and said, 「Please do not fear. I am no demon. I am the one who tends the incense in this temple. When I heard your good words and praises, I tried to come out and receive you. But I feared perhaps an evil ghost had knocked, so I picked up a broken brick and struck the bell once, just to frighten and reassure the place before I dared step out. Please, sir, rise.」 Tripitaka then steadied himself and said, 「Abbot, you nearly frightened me to death. Bring me inside.」

The monk guided Tripitaka through and led him in; within, it was wholly different from outside. He beheld this:

Blue-green brick made walls like rainbows of cloud, green tile formed halls gleaming like glass. Golden ornament adorned the holy images, white jade formed the tiered terraces. Atop the Great Hero Hall blue light danced; beneath the Pi Luo Hall sharp vitality seemed to breathe. The Manjushri Hall was festooned with gathered hues of flying cloud, and the Wheel-Treasury Hall bore painted blossoms heaped with green. On the ridge of the triple eaves sat the point of a treasure vase; within the Hall of Five Blessings spread a plain embroidered canopy. A thousand green bamboos swayed near the meditation cots, and myriad emerald pines mirrored the Buddha gate. In the Emerald-Cloud Palace golden light poured out, and amid violet mists auspicious vapor drifted. At dawn one could scent fragrant wind across the four wild fields; at dusk one heard mountain-high drums like painted thunder. Could there not be morning sun to mend torn robes? Could one not sit by moonlight with the remaining sūtra passages? There was also, at the rear court, the light of a half-wall lamp; a thread of incense smoke lit the central court. Tripitaka, seeing it, dared not enter and said, 「You monk: how can the front be so pitiably wrecked, and the back so complete and proper?" The monk smiled: 「Sir, this mountain is full of powerful brigands, demons and evil ghosts. On clear days they range the ridges and plunder; when the sky turns dim they retreat here to hide in the temple. They overturn Buddha images to make seats and move timber to light their fires. The monks of this monastery are weak and cannot reason with them. So I left those broken outer rooms for those tough ones to use and, with the support of devotees, raised this newly formed temple. One part was kept apart, one part set anew; this is how things are done in the Western regions.」 Tripitaka said, 「I see.」

As they moved on, above the mountain gate they saw five large characters: 「鎮海禪林寺」. As he stepped inside, a monk came out. See his form:

On his head, a wool-brocade cap tilted to the left; a pair of copper rings hung by each ear-root. He wore a rough wool-knit robe; his eyes were white and bright, like silver. In one hand he shook a small hand-drum, while in his mouth he chanted foreign scriptures unclearly. Tripitaka did not at first recognize him—this was a lama monk from the western route. The lama monk came through the gate. Seeing Tripitaka with clear brows and handsome eyes, broad smooth forehead, ears hanging to the shoulders, and hands longer than the knees, he looked like a descending arhat, very fine and elegant. He stepped forward, grasped his sleeve, and with a face full of cheerful affection pinched his fingers and toes, rubbed his nose, and tugged his ears to show welcome. He led him into the abbot’s hall; after ritual bows, he asked, 「Venerable, where have you come from?」 Tripitaka said, 「This disciple is an imperial envoy of Great Tang, sent west to Tianzhu’s Great Thundering-Reverberation Temple to pay homage to Buddha and fetch the Dharma. By fortunate timing I reached this site late in the evening and hastened up to this monastery to pass one night; at dawn I depart. I beg a little aid.」 The monk smiled, 「Not an ordinary child, not an ordinary child. We did not take to the path of leaving home by choice. All of us were born of parents, and our fates struck the Huagai mark, so home could not hold us; only then did we break off and become ordained. Now that you are a disciple of the Buddha gate, do not speak of hollow emptiness.」 Tripitaka said, 「I speak the truth.」 The monk said, 「From the Eastern Capital to the Western Heaven, how long is that road? There are mountains, caves within the mountains, and spirits inside those caves. Looking at you, so single and so delicate, how could you be one to fetch the scriptures?」 Tripitaka said, 「Abbot, you see truly. How could a poor monk alone do it? I have three disciples. When I meet mountain I make a way; when I meet water I make a bridge; they guard this disciple, so I have come to this monastery.」 The monk grew alarmed: 「Master, do you not know that this place has tigers, wolves, demons, thieves, ghosts, and monsters that wound men? By daylight we do not dare to go far out, and before evening we have already shut the gates. Why keep your people outside at this hour?" He called, 「Disciples, quickly go and invite them in.」

Two young lama boys ran out. Seeing the Wanderer, they started and stumbled backward; seeing Zhu Bajie, they stumbled again. They jumped up and ran back, crying, 「Sir, this ill-fated hour has come and your disciples are nowhere to be seen; there are only three or four demons at the gatepost.」 Tripitaka asked, 「How do they look?" One young monk said, 「One has the face of the Thunder Lord, another a mortar-flat face, one has a blue visage with bared fangs. Beside them is a woman—she is, in fact, a handsome one with an oiled, powdered face." Tripitaka laughed, 「You do not know them. Those three ugly ones are my disciples. And that woman is the one I rescued, her life in peril, in the pine wood." The lama said, 「Master! Such a handsome master—how have you found such ugly disciples?" Tripitaka replied, 「They are ugly by any standard, and yet each is useful. Invite him in quickly. If you delay further, that Thunder-Mouthed one may soon create trouble. He is no ordinary child reared by living parents—he will force himself in at once.」

The young monk at once ran out, knelt trembling, and said, 「The noble lords, Master Tang has sent in his request.」 Zhu Bajie laughed, 「Brother, he has already invited us, yet why this panic?" The Wanderer said, 「They were frightened to see how ugly we look." Zhu Bajie said, 「Is that nonsense? We are naturally ugly—that is all." The Wanderer said, 「At least make that ugliness bearable.」 Zhu Bajie truly tucked his mouth inside his chest, bowed his head, and pulled the horse; Sha Wujing took up the shoulder pole; Sun Wukong followed behind with his staff, escorting the woman. The group went in together. They passed through the fallen corridor and entered the third gate; they tied the horse and put down the pole. In the abbot’s hall, they met the lama monk and took their seats. The lama brought out seventy or eighty young lamas from inside. After bows and greetings, they set in order the alms and arranged the monastic meal for them. It was just then that this line appeared:

Merit must be accumulated through compassion’s heart; when the Buddha’s law flourishes, monks shall praise one another.

In the end it remains unknown how they will eventually leave the monastery. Listen in the next chapter for how it is resolved.
