After Tripitaka and his disciples arrived at Zhenhai Chanlin Temple, the monks met them and arranged a vegetarian meal. After the fourfold assembly had eaten, the girl also gained enough strength from the food. Dusk slowly came, and lamps were lit in the abbot’s hall. The monks gathered in groups beneath the lights: some asking Tripitaka the story of his journey to fetch scriptures, others openly gazing at the girl. Tripitaka said to the lama monk he had first met, ‘Abbot, tomorrow we leave Baoshan and go west. How is the road ahead?’

The monk knelt on both knees. Startled, the Patriarch pulled him up: ‘Abbot, please rise. I am only asking the route—why do you kneel?’

The monk replied, ‘Master is traveling west tomorrow. The way is level and safe; there is no need to worry. Only there is one awkward matter. I meant to say it as soon as I entered, but I feared it might not be proper. Now that the meal is done, I dare speak plainly: Master comes from afar and the road is long and hard. It is best he rest tonight in the junior monks’ quarters. This lady-bodhisattva, however, is not convenient; I do not know where to place her to sleep well.’

Tripitaka said, ‘Abbot, do not suspect us; do not think my disciples and I carry any evil intent. This morning, passing through the Black Pine Grove, we found this woman bound to a tree. My junior disciple Sun Wukong would not rescue her; it was I who, out of bodhicitta, saved her. We brought her here, and she may go wherever you direct.’

The monk thanked him: ‘Since Master is so broad-hearted, let her sleep in the Hall of the Heavenly King—behind the image of the Heavenly King—with a straw mat arranged for her.’

Tripitaka said, ‘Very good, very good.’ The novice monks then led the girl behind the hall to sleep. Tripitaka stayed in the abbot’s hall and let all the abbots rest as they wished; then everyone dispersed. Tripitaka instructed Sun Wukong, ‘You have labored enough. Sleep early and rise early.’ So all of them slept in one place, daring not to leave, guarding the master at his side.

Night deepened, and now it was that:

The jade rabbit rises, and all ten thousand sounds fall silent; the heavenly streets are still, no footsteps stirring. The Silver River gleams, star-lit and bright; from the watchtower drums call the change of watches.

That night’s further talk is omitted. By dawn, Sun Wukong rose and told Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing to pack bundles and horses and asked that Master travel on foot. At this time the Patriarch still clung to sleep, not yet awake. Sun Wukong came close and called, ‘Master.’ The master lifted his head a little but gave no clear answer. Sun Wukong asked, ‘What does Master say?’

The Patriarch groaned, ‘Why is my head hanging like this and my eyes so swollen? My skin and bones all ache.’

Hearing this, Zhu Bajie reached out and touched him; he seemed to be running hot. The foolish monk said, ‘I know it. Last night there was poor rice and many bowls of it at the meal; it went straight to his head when he slept, and he is now sick from overfeeding.’

Sun Wukong barked, ‘Nonsense! Let me ask Master what is truly the matter.’

Tripitaka said, ‘In the middle of the night I rose to relieve myself and had not put on my hat. I think the wind got in.’

Sun Wukong said, ‘That can be so. Can we travel now?’

Tripitaka said, ‘At this moment I cannot sit up; how can I mount a horse? It is just that we might miss the road.’

Sun Wukong said, ‘What is that saying? There is a saying: “One may call oneself a teacher for a day, yet for life one is a father.” We who are your disciples are, in every way, your sons. It is also said: “To raise a son is not to buy him with gold and silver; one may raise affection simply by seeing the proper scene.” Since your body is unwell, why speak of missing the schedule? To endure a few more days is nothing.’

The brothers served the master faithfully. Without noticing, midday came, then dusk again; one fine night had just passed when morning pressed in again.

Time passed quickly. By the next day, three days were already gone.

That day the master rose and called, ‘Wukong, in these two days my illness has pressed heavily on me; I have not asked you: has anyone sent food to that near-to-death bodhisattva?’

Sun Wukong laughed, ‘What is that to you? Care first for your own illness.’

Tripitaka said, ‘That is true. Help me up, bring out my paper, brush, and ink, and borrow an inkstone from the temple.’

Sun Wukong said, ‘In what way?’

The master replied, ‘I want to draft a letter and seal it. You must carry it to Chang’an and present it before Emperor Taizong.’

Sun Wukong said, ‘Easy enough. I, old Wukong, am poor at other arts, but if it is carrying a letter I am first among men below heaven. Have the letter prepared properly and give it to me. I can carry it to Chang’an in one go, hand it to the Tang king, and in another go return with it; your brush and ink will not even be dry by then. But I have no idea why you must send it. First, read the letter’s meaning to me; once I have heard it, I will write it again, and that will not be too late.’

The Patriarch, with tears, dictated:

Your humble monk bows in reverence, thrice prostrating, saluting the long-lived sovereign, Let both civil and martial offices read this, and let the four hundred ministers all know. In former days I departed the Eastern Land by imperial command, hoping to behold the World Honored One on Mount Ling. Unforeseen difficulties met us on the road; who would have expected disaster to appear midway. The monk is sick with deep malaise and cannot press onward; the Buddha’s gate is profound, joining on to Heaven’s gate. I have the scripture yet no life to bear it, laboring in vain—I humbly report that now I should be sent another envoy.

Sun Wukong could not hold back a loud laugh: ‘Master, you are not up to this; at only the least illness you conceive such thoughts. If your sickness were truly grave, if you were about to die or live, ask me alone. Old Wukong has ways of his own. Ask which Yanwang dares to think of it, which judge dares to pass an order, which ghost messenger dares to come to fetch you. If I am annoyed, I will take out the nature with which I once made havoc in Heaven: I’ll knock him into the netherworld with my staff, seize the ten Yama kings, and pull their tendons one by one—there will be no mercy.’

Tripitaka said, ‘Disciple, my illness is severe. Do not speak such grand talk.’

Zhu Bajie came forward and said, ‘Elder brother, Master is in poor shape. You keep saying he is well, which is very awkward. Let us at once decide: sell the horse, rent the packs, buy a coffin and send off the funeral fire.’

Sun Wukong said, ‘You talk nonsense again, dumb-brother. You do not know. Master is Buddha’s second disciple, called Gold-Cicada Abbot in former times. It is only because he once treated the Dharma lightly that he is to endure this great hardship.’

Zhu Bajie said, ‘Brother, if Master has been careless with the Dharma, then being stripped and sent back to the Eastern Land, entering this world of right and wrong, and in courts of argument taking human form by faith, then vowing to go west to seek Buddha for scripture, getting bound by demons, hanged by demon-kings, and enduring many torments—that alone is enough. How can we then also make him fall ill?’

Sun Wukong said, ‘You do not understand. Master did not hear the Buddha’s teaching; he dozed off once, then on the next descent his left foot stepped on a single grain of rice. That is why this three-day illness has come.’

Zhu Bajie cried out in surprise, ‘Like old pig, when it eats with mess and splash, one can never know how many ages of illness it causes!’

Sun Wukong said, ‘Brother, the Buddha has no compassion for your mortal life, and you do not know. As people say:

In the noonday sun, one hoes the fields and the sweat drips into the earth beneath the grain, Who knows that each bowl of food comes from each grain hard-earned? Master will be no worse than yesterday; he will be well tomorrow.’

Tripitaka said, ‘Today I am not as yesterday—I am very thirsty. Go where there is cool water and fetch some for me to drink.’

Sun Wukong said, ‘Good. If Master asks for water, that means he is already improving. I will go and fetch it.’

He took up the bowl at once and went behind the monastery to the Xiangji kitchen to fetch water. He then saw that those monks, one by one, had swollen-red eyes, crying with choked sobs, yet they dared not wail aloud. Wukong said, 'You monks are so soft-tempered. We have stayed here for only a few days. When we depart, we will still repay you for the firewood by the day, as agreed. Why are you all so foul-bellied and helpless?' The monks knelt in alarm and said, 'No offense, no offense.' Wukong said, 'Why do you so much as hesitate? Do you think the broad-mouthed, big-stomached old monk in my troop has eaten too much and injured your own merit?' The monks replied, 'My lord, this barren mountain has a hundred and more monks, big and small. One person can feed Your Reverence for a day; one person can still sustain one for a hundred days. How could we act in deceit and count over meals?' Wukong said, 'If you do not count, why then cry and weep?' The monks said, 'My lord, we do not know what demon from this mountain has entered this temple. At night we send two novice monks to strike the bell and beat the drum; after hearing the ringing and drumming they do not return. The next day we search and find only a monk-cowl and monastic sandals thrown in the rear garden, with bones left behind—the people were eaten. In three days of your stay, six young monks in this temple have vanished. So my brothers, though unwilling, are frightened and cannot help weeping. Because your honored teacher is ailing, we dared not tell him, and we could only let tears fall in secret.'

When Wukong heard this, he was both alarmed and pleased. 'No need to say more. It must be a demon in this place. Let me capture him and clear him away.'

The monks said, 'My lord, a demon that is no true demon will still not show power. He will certainly ride cloud and vanish in mist, certainly go in and out of the dark and shadowed realms. The ancients said well: “Do not trust even in one whose face is upright; beware of people without humanity.” Do not blame us for saying this: if you can seize him, then you will remove this root of disaster from our wild mountain; that would be a blessing over three lives. If you fail to catch him, there will be serious and untoward consequences.'

Wukong said, 'What untoward consequences?'

Those monks said, 'Let us not hide it from your lordship. Though this mountain has a hundred and some monks, all of them were ordained when children. Their hair is grown long and rough, their robes are thin and patched and torn. At dawn they wash their faces, fold their hands and bow in devotion to the Way. At night they gather themselves, light incense, and with sincere hearts bite their lips as they chant Amitabha. Lifting their heads, they behold the nine grades of the Buddha-lotus, the Three Vehicles, the charitable ark of compassion, and the clouds of Dharma, and pray to see Śākyamuni in the Deer Park so that he lowers his head and sees their minds; they receive the Five Precepts, ferry the great thousand-world expanse, and through lives upon lives in the myriad dharmas pray to awaken to blunt emptiness and form emptiness. Lay followers come and go, the old and the young, the tall and the short, the fat and the lean: one by one they strike the wooden fish and ring the bronze bell, bow and bow; two fascicles of the Lotus Sutra, one tract of the Repentance of King Liang. The lay people, both new and old, raw and ripened, village and city alike, all join their hands, close their eyes, and quietly, silently descend into meditation on the meditation mat; they shut the gate beneath the moon. Let orioles sing and birds quarrel, they do not mount the great Dharma-vehicle of my expedient compassion. Therefore they cannot subdue tigers, nor bring down dragons; they do not know demons, they do not know spirits. If you were to rouse that demon, our hundred-and-ten monks would only be able to feed him one full meal. First, we would fall again into the round of sentient life. Second, these chan-clerical traces would be erased. Third, in the Buddha’s assembly even half a spark of radiance would be lost. Those are several very bad consequences.'

Hearing the monks’ words, Wukong grew angry from the heart; wicked heat surged near his gall, and he shouted, 'You monks are all very slow-witted! You only know that demon, and yet you do not know how your old Sun behaves?' The monks softly replied, 'Truly we do not know.'

Wukong said, 'I will tell you a bit of my conduct today, listen well. I have once in Flower-Fruit Mountain subdued tigers and brought down dragons. I once stormed Heaven and roiled the Heavenly Court. Hungry, I nipped two or three of Old Lord Laojun’s pills; thirsty, I lightly called down six or seven measures of the Jade Emperor’s wine. Opening my two gold eyes, neither white nor black, heaven darkens and the moon turns hazy. Grasping the Golden-Hooped Staff, neither too short nor too long, I arrive without shadow and go without track. What is there to fear of big devils or small monsters? Let them even be weary and pus-filled, I can still burn them down.

When one chases, they run; when one chases, they tremble; when one chases, they hide; when one chases, they panic. When one catches them, then I file, I burn, I grind, I pound. It is just like the Eight Immortals crossing the sea: only I display the divine powers.

Monks, let me show you this demon. Then you will recognize me, your old Sun.'

The monks listened and silently nodded in agreement: 'This bald rogue opens his great mouth and boasts; he must have some background.' They all muttered approval again and again. Only the lama monk said, 'Hold for a moment. Your teacher is gravely ill; do not take this demon too suddenly. The saying goes: “One who rises to a feast and is not drunk is not satisfied; a hero before the melee, if not dead, is already wounded.” While the two of you grapple in combat, if your master should be endangered through your doing, things will not turn out right.'

Wukong said, 'Good point, good point. I will first give Master some cool water and then return.' He took up the bowl, filled it with cool water, and returned from the Xiangji kitchen to the abbey hall, calling out, 'Master, here is cool water.' Tripitaka, at the very moment of troublesome thirst, lifted his head, took up the water, and drank one full draught. Truly, when one is parched, even one drop was like nectar; the medicine had found the right prescription and the illness lifted at once.

When Wukong saw that Master’s spirit was becoming clear and his brows and eyes unfolding, he asked, 'Master, can you eat some rice soup?' Tripitaka said, 'This cool water itself is like a divine elixir; the illness is gone by half. I can eat a little soup and rice.' Wukong called out repeatedly and loudly, 'My Master is better. He wants soup and rice.' He ordered those monks to prepare things in haste: wash the rice and cook it, knead dough and bake cakes, steam momo, and make flour gruel, and set out four or five tables.

Tripitaka ate only half a bowl of rice porridge. Wukong and Sha Wujing used only one place each; the rest was all swallowed by Zhu Bajie in one belly-full.

He removed the kitchen fire and lit the lamps; the monks all dispersed.

Tripitaka said, 'How many days have we been staying here?' Wukong said, 'It has been three full days. Tomorrow by evening, it is already the fourth day.' Tripitaka said, 'Three days have wasted a lot of our road distance.' Wukong said, 'Master, that does not count as losing distance. We will leave tomorrow.' Tripitaka said, 'Yes, yes. With even this much illness, we are helpless.' Wukong said, 'If we leave tomorrow, let me at least catch that demon tonight and bring it to you.' Tripitaka exclaimed, 'Catch what demon now?' Wukong said, 'There is a demon in this temple. Let old Sun catch it.'

Tripitaka said, 'Disciple, my body is still sick; how can this thought arise again in your mind? If that monster has powers, and you fail to take him, then you too might be harmed.' Wukong said, 'You are always intent on frightening men into fear. Old Sun has subdued demons everywhere; where do you think I am weak? I need not strike a blow first, but if I do, I must win.' Tripitaka pulled at his sleeve: 'Disciple, as the saying goes, “When a chance is expedient, be expedient; where one can spare, spare. Who is better: to hold worry in the breast, or to let good intent rest? What is higher—fighting for face, or enduring injury with dignity?”'

Seeing that his master had pleaded again and again and would not let him exterminate the demon, Wukong spoke frankly: 'Master, I do not hide the truth from you. That demon has already eaten people here.' Tripitaka was greatly startled: 'What people have he eaten?' Wukong said, 'In the three days we stayed, he has already eaten six young monks from this temple.' The Elder said, '“When a rabbit dies, the fox grieves, for all creatures grieve for their own kind.” Since he has eaten monks of this temple, I too am a monk. I let you go, only be careful and be very attentive.' Wukong said, 'No need to say more. Once Old Sun has his hand on him, he will be gone.'

Before the lamp-light, Sun Wukong ordered Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing to watch Tripitaka. Then, eager and restless, he leapt out of the abbot's hall, went straight to the Buddha Hall, and when he looked, the sky had stars while the moon was not yet up; the hall was dark as night itself. He blew out true fire, lit the glazed lamps, beat a drum on the east side and struck a bell on the west. When the sound died, he changed shape in an instant into a small young monk of only twelve or thirteen years, wearing a yellow silk rag robe and a white linen outer coat, tapping a wooden fish with his hand while reciting sutra. By the first watch there was no sign of movement. By the second, as the waning moon only just rose, he heard only the roaring of wind. That wind:

Black fog veils the sky; grief clouds darken the earth. In the four quarters it is like ink flung across, one wash of indigo. First it whirls dust and flings up soil; then it topples trees and crushes groves. With dust and earth lifted, starlight appears; toppled trees and wrecked woods make moonlight dim. It blows so hard: Chang'e clutches the suro tree, the Jade Rabbit circles and searches for the medicine basin; the Nine-star officials all close their doors, and the Dragon Kings of the Four Seas lock theirs as well; in the temples, city gods seek small ghosts; heavenly maidens in the air do not know how to ride the clouds; in the underworld, Yama looks for Ma Mian, while the judges run about chasing their headscarves. It shakes the stones atop Kunlun, and whirls the waves of rivers and seas into one disorderly flood.

Only after the wind had passed did a scent of sandal and musk fill the air and the jingle of jeweled ornaments sound. Sun Wukong bent slightly and looked up: it was a beautiful maiden straightway stepping into the Buddha Hall. The Monkey kept chanting, muttering "wuli-wula," and all the while recited only the sutra. The woman came near and hugged him. “Little elder, what sutra are you reciting?” Wukong answered, “One I vowed to recite.” She asked, “Everyone else is sleeping at ease; why are you still reciting?” He said, “I vowed it—how could I not recite?” She embraced him, kissed him, and said, “Come play with me in the back.” Wukong deliberately turned his head aside and said, “You understand very little.”

She asked, “Can you read faces?” Wukong said, “A little.” She asked, “What do you see in mine?” He replied, “I see someone who bore a child in secret and was driven out by her parents-in-law.” She said, “Wrong, wrong! I was not driven out by my parents-in-law, nor did I secretly bear a child. My fate in my former life was thin: I was married to a young man who did not understand the bridal chamber, so I fled my husband. Now the stars are bright and the moon is clear; those destined for each other may meet though a thousand miles apart. Come with me to the back garden, and let us join as phoenix mates.” Wukong thought, “Those foolish monks were lured by lust and so lost their lives. Now she has come to deceive me too.” He answered, “My lady, I am still young and know nothing of lovemaking.” She said, “Come with me, and I will teach you.” Wukong laughed inwardly: “Very well. I will follow and see what she intends.”

The two held shoulders and hands, came out of the Buddha Hall, and went straight to the back garden. The demon made Sun Wukong trip over a foot-lift, sending him to the ground. She cried wildly, "heart of my heart, brother," and with her hand reached to pinch his testicles. Sun said, "You little one, you truly want to eat Old Sun, don't you?" He caught her hand and, using a small dropping technique, he flipped and threw her into a whirling tumble onto the ground. The demon still cried out, "Heart of my heart, you can even make your mother tumble," and so on. Sun thought, "If I do not seize the moment and strike now, when else? As the old saying goes: 'The first strike is strongest; the later strike meets trouble.'" So he spread one arm, bent at the waist, leapt up, showed his true form, lifted the Golden-Hooped Staff, and smashed her at once. The demon was shocked. She thought, 'This little monk is this dangerous?' She opened her eyes and saw that he was Tripitaka's disciple with the surname Sun. Even then she did not fear him. You ask what kind of demon this was:

A gold nose, hair dusted white like snow. Burrows made as gates and rooms; wherever she settles, it is secure. Three hundred years of life-force she has fostered, and she has gone to Lingjiu three times. After one offering of incense flowers and candles, she was sent from the Buddha down to the heavenly offices. She is the beloved daughter of Pagoda-Bearing King; Prince Nezha recognizes her as a sister. She is no bird that fills the sea, no turtle bearing a mountain. She fears not Lei Huan's sword, nor does she fear Lü Qian's knife. She comes and goes as she pleases, letting the Han waters run wide; up and down, no matter how mountains stand up in lofty heights. Look at that moon-like face, flower-like and delicate. Who could tell this is an old rat spirit showing off its bragging craft?

Full of herself and proud of her powers, she raised both blades in her hands, they rang out, clashing and weaving left and right, eastward and westward. Although Sun was the stronger, he still could not yet bring her down. Eerie wind rose; the waning moon gave only dim light. Behold in the rear garden a fierce battle:

Dark wind rose from the earth, and the fading moon tossed a dim gleam. In quiet Brahma-space, through shadowed ghost corridors, the back garden became a field of war. Great Saint Sun, heaven-born holy; Hairy Maiden, queen among women: neither yields in contests of divine arts. One twisted wrath in his heart, the other opened wise eyes in new adornment. With both hands their swords flew; who could call that a female bodhisattva? One staff strike was cruel as a living Vajra-great. At each clash the Golden-Hoop flashed like a bolt of lightning; in a moment the white iron sparked like stars. A jade tower caught green jade; the golden hall shattered, pair of mandarin ducks undone. Monkeys cried under the moon; geese called to a long Chu sky. Eighteen arhats watched and secretly cheered, while thirty-two heavenly kings grew flustered.

Sun Wukong, spirit unshaken, made no error with his staff. The demon spirit, feeling she could not defeat him, knit her brow, formed a plan, and pulled back to run. Sun shouted, "You ragged one, where are you going? Come back and submit!" She paid no mind and kept retreating. When Sun rushed close at once, she took off her flowered sandal from her left foot, blew out a breath of immortal air, chanted a spell, and cried out, "Change!" At once she took her true form, made her two swords whirl forward; her true body flashed once, dissolved into a clear wind. Was she not Tripitaka's very disaster-star? She collided straight into the abbot's chamber, lifted Tripitaka onto the crown of a cloud and fled. It was all dim and remote; in the briefest moment she arrived at Mountain Pit of Emptiness, entered the bottomless cave, and told her attendants to arrange a plain wedding banquet; no need to set that part down further.

Sun Wukong, anxious and restless from fighting, slipped through a gap and with one staff blow knocked the demon down. But it was only a flower sandal. He realized he had fallen for her trick, and quickly turned back to look for Tripitaka—where was the Master? There, Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing were still muttering "wu li wu la." His chest full of rage, he cared nothing for consequences and raised his staff again and began striking in a rage, shouting, "I'll beat you dead, I'll beat you dead!" Zhu Bajie panicked and had nowhere to run. Sha Wujing, however, was a great general of Lingjiu and seeing how many matters there were, spoke gently and came forward, kneeling: "Elder Brother, I understand. You think to beat us two to death, yet not go to save Tripitaka and simply return home." Sun replied, "If I were to beat you both to death, I can then go save him." Sha Wujing said with a smile, "Brother, what is that kind of talk? Without the two of you it is impossible: a single thread does not tie a line, one hand cannot sound a drum. Brother, who will guard the baggage and the horses? Better learn to split gold wisely like Guan and Bao; do not imitate Sun and Pang in outwitting each other. As the old saying goes: 'To hunt a tiger, brothers by blood are needed; on the field of battle there must be father and son as soldiers.' For now, Brother, hold your hand from striking. At dawn, with a single heart we will join forces and go to search for our Master." Though Sun Wukong possessed immense powers, he was not without judgment. Seeing Sha Wujing's earnest plea, he returned to sense and said, "Zhu Bajie, Sha Wujing, you both rise. At daybreak we seek the Master. Use all your strength for it." Hearing he was spared, Zhu Bajie wished heaven would lower half the day, and said, "Brother, all this blame is on old Pig." The brothers thought long; they did not get sleep. They wished they could nod and call out the sun of Fusang and with one breath blow the whole sky of stars away.

The three sat until daybreak, packed to go. A temple monk already blocked the gate and asked, "Your Grace, where are you going?" Sun Wukong replied with a laugh, "It is hard to explain. Yesterday I boasted before the crowd that I would take that demon; not once did I catch it, and instead Tripitaka has vanished. We are going to search for him." The monks, afraid, said, "Your Grace, this boy-like matter has only brought trouble on the Teacher. Where are we to go seek him?" Sun said, "There is a place where he can be found." They hurriedly said, "If you are going, do not rush, first have some morning gruel." and quickly brought two or three bowls of soup and rice. Zhu Bajie ate it all cleanly and said, "Good monk, when we find our Master, we shall come back here and play some more." Sun Wukong said, "You still come back here to eat? Go and see whether that woman is in the Heavenly King's Hall." The monks answered, "Your Grace, she is gone, gone. She stayed the night, and by the second day she was no longer here."

Sun Wukong, in high spirits, took leave of the monks and ordered Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing to lead the horses and shoulder the packs, then headed east. Zhu Bajie said, "Brother, you made a mistake. Why are we going east again?" Sun Wukong said, "Can you not understand? The woman we tied in the black pine woods the other day—the one I, Old Sun, with Fire-Eyed Golden Pupils had seen through and you all took for a virtuous one—she is the same one who fed on monks today and also who carried off Tripitaka. You did well to rescue that Bodhisattva-maiden. Now that he has taken the Master, we must continue searching along the old path as well." The two brothers exclaimed in admiration, "Very good, very good. Truly there is refinement inside a rough shell. Go on, go on."

The three hurried into the forest, and saw this:

Clouds were dense and soft; mist spread everywhere. Layer upon layer of rock, and the road coiled in turns. Fox tracks and rabbit tracks crossed each other. Tigers, leopards, jackals, and wolves kept burrowing and darting back and forth. Within the woods there was no demon’s shadow; no one knew where Tripitaka was now. The Great Sage grew anxious, drew out his staff, and by a shift of his body took the form in which he once wreaked havoc in Heaven: three heads and six arms, six hands, brandishing three staves, he lashed about the grove in loud uproar. Zhu Bajie said, "Sha Wujing, Senior Brother is in a rage; since he cannot find Tripitaka, he is now wind-whirling in anger." In fact the Great Sage, as he kept striking along the way, had brought out two old men: one a Mountain God, one an Earth God, who came forward kneeling and said, "Great Sage, the Mountain God and Earth God come to report." Zhu Bajie said, "Good-natured spirit, by striking one stretch you beat out two mountain and earth gods; strike one more stretch and you might even beat out Tai Sui too." Wukong asked, "Mountain God, Earth God, you two are so impudent, colluding here as thieves. When thieves seize their prey, they offer pigs and sheep in sacrifice to you, then join with demons and in a gang carry away my Master. Where is he hidden now? Speak plainly at once and spare me a beating." The two gods, flustered, said, "Great Sage, you have mistaken us. The demon is not on my little god-mountain and not under my jurisdiction. But only at night, where the wind moans, the small gods know a little." Wukong said, "If you know, then tell me everything in order." The Earth God said, "That demon who took your Master went off straight to the south; it is nearly a thousand li from here. There is a mountain there called Xian Kong Mountain. In that mountain there is a cave called Bottomless Cave. It was the demon of that mountain that used his transformations to carry him off this way." On hearing this, Wukong was inwardly startled. He sent the Mountain God and Earth God away with a shout, withdrew his tantric body, returned to his true form, and said to Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, "Tripitaka has gone far away." Zhu Bajie said, "If he is so far, we should rise on the clouds and rush after him."

Good simpleton, a wild wind rose first. Then Sha Wujing mounted the clouds; the white horse, being of dragon lineage, carried the baggage and even drove through wind and fog. The Great Sage at once sprang up into a great charge and came flying southward. Soon they saw a great mountain blocking the cloud path. The three held the horse fast and steadied the cloud hooves. They saw that mountain:

Its summit touched the blue heavens, and its peaks met the high sky. Around it grew ten thousand trees of many kinds, and flying birds came and went, chattering. Tigers and leopards moved in ranks; serow and deer ran in thickets. On the sunny side, fairy flowers and precious herbage spread fragrance; on the shaded side, old snow ice would not melt. Uneven steep ridges, knife-cut cliffs and hanging cliffs. Straight, lofty peaks, and circling bends around deep ravines. Pines stood dense and thick, stones glimmered; the onlooker in that place was chilled in spirit. No wood-gathering woodcutter could be seen; no immortal-errand boy collecting herbs appeared. Right before one’s eyes, tiger and leopard could raise fog; foxes all over the ground stirred the wind into disorder. Zhu Bajie said, "Elder Brother, this mountain is so steep and harsh; surely there are fiends and demons here." Wukong said, "No need to speak. Where mountains stand high, monsters are natural; where ridges are harsh, could there be no spirits?" Then he said, "Sha Wujing, you and I stay here. Let Zhu Bajie go down first into a mountain hollow and ask around. See whether the path is passable, whether there is truly a lair, then see where a gate is opened. Investigate all these carefully, and then we can all go together to seek Tripitaka and save him." Zhu Bajie said, "You unlucky old pig, take me first before you." Wukong said, "You have had this on your own words through the night; how can you then make such a demand?" Zhu Bajie said, "No shouting. Let me go." The fool set down his axe, shook out his clothing, and jumped off the high mountain, empty-handed, to search for the path.

From this point on, still no one knows how all this ends. Listen for the resolution in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 81: At Zhenhai Monastery the Mind-Monkey foresees a fiend; in Black Pine Forest the three pilgrims seek their master.

Then Zhu Bajie came leaping down the mountain and found a small path. He followed it for about five or six li, when suddenly he saw two female demons drawing water at a well. How did he recognize them as two demon women? Their headgear was a bamboo-silk coiled topknot on the head, one chi and two or three cun high, which looked absurdly old-fashioned. Zhu Bajie walked up to them and called out, “Monster.” Hearing this, the demon became furious. The two spoke to one another: “This monk is a boor; we do not even know him, and in ordinary times we are not used to using such language with him—how does he dare to call us demons?” In her anger she raised the water-drawing bar and struck him full at the head.

The fool was unarmed and could not parry at all; after being scooped at a few times he ran back up the mountain with his head knocked and said, “Brother, let’s go back. That demon is fierce.” Sun Wukong said, “How is it fierce?” Zhu Bajie said, “In a hollow on this hill, two female demon spirits were drawing water from the well. I called them ‘monster’ just once, and one of them struck me three or four times with the water pole.” Sun Wukong asked, “For what did you call him that?” Zhu Bajie said, “I called him a monster.” Sun Wukong laughed and said, “Then the beating was too light.” Zhu Bajie said, “Thanks for looking after me. My head is swollen, and you call it little.” Sun Wukong said, “If you go with gentleness, you can pass beneath the heavens; if you are hard and forceful, not a single step will move.” "They are monsters of this place, and we are monks from afar; though your body is all hands and fists, still be a little gentle. You call them monsters, and they do not strike me, why should they strike me? Among men, ritual and courtesy come first." Zhu Bajie said, “I did not understand that at first.” Sun Wukong said, “You have lived since childhood in the mountains eating men. Do you know there are two kinds of wood?” Zhu Bajie said, “I do not. What kind is it?” Sun Wukong said, “One is poplar, one is sandalwood. Poplar is by nature soft; a clever craftsman can carve sacred icons from it, or sculpt the Buddha, coat it with gold and powder, inlay jade, deck it with flowers; then ten thousand people burn incense and make offerings, earning immeasurable merit. Sandalwood is hard in nature. It is taken to the oil room and worked into a pestle, then an iron hoop is placed around its crown, and an iron hammer comes down on it repeatedly. Because it is hard, it suffers this hardship.” Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, if you had told me such sensible words before, that would have been good; then it would not have beaten me.” Sun Wukong said, “Go ask him again, but do it properly.” Zhu Bajie said, “If I go again, he’ll recognize me.” Sun Wukong said, "Then change your form and go." Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, if I have changed, how can I ask him then?” Sun Wukong said, "When you are changed, go before him and make obeisance. Ask how old he is. If she is about our age, call her ‘Girl.’ If she is older than us, call her 'Grandmother.'" Zhu Bajie laughed, “How awkward—so far from home, how can I tell who counts as what relation?” Sun Wukong said, "Not relation, but draw out his words. If it is she who has taken Master, then we can strike at once; if not, we must not get diverted into another matter.” Zhu Bajie said, “That is sound. I’ll go once more.”

The fool tucked his iron pick at his waist, went down into the hollow, and in a twirl changed into a fat, black monk. Swaying heavily, he went near the demon and made a deep obeisance: 'Grandmother, this poor monk makes his bows.' The two demons said, 'This monk is fine—he can offer a proper bow, and he can also speak a smooth, proper answer.' One asked, 'Elder, where do you come from?' Zhu Bajie said, 'Where do I come from?' The same asked, 'Where are you going?' He answered again, 'Where am I going?' Then asked, 'What is your name?' and he answered again, 'What is my name?' The demon laughed: 'This monk is truly decent, but he has no introduction and can answer in one-tongued fashion.' Zhu Bajie said, 'Grandmother, why do you have to draw water?' The demon replied, 'Monk, do you not know? My old mistress has taken hold of a monk on pilgrimage inside our cave tonight; she must feed and care for him. The water in our cave is not clean, so she sent us two to fetch this good yin-yang water, and to set out a vegetarian spread of fruits and vegetables. He must eat with Tripitaka, and this evening they will be united in marriage.'

Hearing this, Zhu Bajie at once pulled himself away and ran back up the mountain. 'Sha Wujing, quickly bring the luggage. Let us split our tasks.' Sha Wujing said, 'Second Brother, what do you mean by splitting?' Zhu Bajie said, 'We split then: you go back to the Flowing-Sand River and eat people, I will go to Gao Laozhuang to visit family, brother will go to Flower-Fruit Mountain to proclaim his sainthood, and the White Dragon Horse will return to the great sea to become a dragon. Master is already in this demon spirit’s cave to marry. Let each of us attend to our own affairs.' Sun Wukong said, 'That fool is lying nonsense again.' Zhu Bajie said, 'Your words are the nonsense. Those two water-drawing demonesses just said she has arranged a pure vegetarian feast for Tripitaka and now they will marry him.' Sun Wukong said, 'That demoness has taken Master into the cave. Master is looking to us in despair for rescue, and you speak such words here.' Zhu Bajie said, 'How to rescue?' Sun Wukong said, "You two lead the horses and shoulder the load poles; we follow those two female demons, use that as a lure and draw her to the gate, then we all strike together."

So Zhu Bajie had no choice but to follow. Sun Wukong kept the two monsters in sight from afar and they gradually entered deep into the mountains. After another ten or twenty li they vanished all at once. Zhu Bajie cried in alarm, 'It must be a day-ghost has taken Master.' Sun Wukong asked, 'Your eyes are keen—how could you see his true form at once?' Zhu Bajie said, 'Those two demons were carrying water and going along, and suddenly they disappeared. Could it be a day-ghost?' Sun Wukong said, 'Probably they have slipped into a cave. Let me go and look.'

Sun Wukong widened his fire-tiger golden eyes at once, looked all around the mountains, and indeed saw no trace of movement. Before the steep cliff he saw a delicate, translucent, ornamented stone gateway, piled in five hues, three eaves and four clusters. The three approached and examined it. Above were six large characters: ‘Pit of Falling Air, Bottomless Cave.’ Sun Wukong said, "Brothers, this demon set this frame here, and we still do not know which way the gate opens." Sha Wujing said, "Not far, not far, look carefully." As they turned, at the base of the gateway, at the foot of the mountain, there was a great slab of stone, roughly ten or more li across, with a perfectly smooth, jar-mouth-wide opening in the center. Zhu Bajie said, 'Brother, this must be the cave where the demon enters and leaves.' Sun Wukong looked and said, "Strange indeed. I, old Sun, must guard Tripitaka; I cannot hide this from you two. The demoness has taken him by some means, yet no such caverns as this have shown themselves. Zhu Bajie, go down first and test how deep it is, and then I can enter and rescue Master.' Zhu Bajie shook his head: 'This is hard; this is hard. My old pig body is clumsy and bulky—if the ground gives way and I hang over the edge, who knows when in two or three years I’d get back from the bottom?' Sun Wukong said, 'How deep is it, then?' Zhu Bajie said, 'You see.' Sun Wukong knelt by the cave edge and looked carefully down. 'Ah! It is deep indeed—more than three hundred li around.' he said on turning back. Zhu Bajie said, 'Then go home. Master cannot be saved.' Sun Wukong said, "What is that talk? Do not grow lazy. Do not let idleness take hold. First put down the luggage and tie the horses to the gateway columns. You use the crowbar, Sha Wujing the staff, to block the cave mouth while I go in to make inquiries. If Master is truly inside, I will beat the demon out with my Golden-Hooped Staff and bring him to the gate; you two stay outside and hold him off. This is the inside-outside coordination. Only when the spirit is killed can Master be saved." The two obeyed.

Sun Wukong at once leapt straight upward and sprang into the cave. Clouds of colored light rose beneath his feet, and a thousand layers of auspicious vapor guarded him from his side. Not long after, he came to a far, deep place where it was bright and clear as day, with a wind, with flowers, grass, and trees. Sun Wukong said with joy, 'What a fine place! If the Great Sage had been born for this world, Heaven would have bestowed this water-curtain cave upon him. This too is a blessed cavernous land.' As he looked, there appeared another gate pavilion with two eaves, all wrapped in pine and bamboo, and inside many chambers. He thought, "This must be the demoness’s dwelling for sure. I should go in and inquire. Yet if I go as I am, she will recognize me. Better that I change and go." He shifted his form and, with a hand gesture, became a fly, then lightly flew upon the pavilion to listen. There he saw the demoness seated high upon a thatched pavilion; her appearance, compared with the one in the pines and the one taken in the monastery, was even more striking:

Her coiffure rose in a cloud-knot, like gathered crows. Her body was dressed in a green velvet embroidered jacket. A pair of golden lotuses were just half-bent, her ten fingers sprouting like spring bamboo shoots. Her round powdered face was like a silver basin, and her lips, bright as cherries, were smooth and glossy. Upright, graceful, perfectly formed, a true beauty; even the moon’s Chang'e would envy her. Today she has caught hold of the monk of the scriptures, and tonight she means to lie with him in delight. Sun Wukong said nothing and just listened. Soon she cracked open cherries and cried, "Servants, quickly set out the pure vegetarian banquet! After eating with Tripitaka, I will marry him tonight!" Sun Wukong laughed inwardly: 'Indeed this is true! I thought Zhu Bajie had only been making jokes and nonsense.' He then flew inward again to look for him. 'How has his heart turned?' he thought. 'If he has been stirred and enticed, then leaving him here is enough.' Spreading his wings, he flew into the inner hall. Beneath the east corridor there were red-paper lattice screens, bright above and dim below, and inside sat Tripitaka.

The Great Sage smashed through the lattice opening with his head, flew over and struck down on Tripitaka’s shaven scalp, and called out, “Master.” Tripitaka recognized the voice and said, “Disciple, save my life!” Sun Wukong said, “Master cannot rescue himself now. The demoness has arranged a banquet and is forcing you to eat and marry her. If one boy and half a girl were to be born, that would still be a monk’s progeny. Why do you worry so?” Tripitaka, grinding his teeth, said, “Disciple, since I left Chang’an and came to Shuangjie Mountain to fetch you, I have gone steadily westward all this time. What moment turned toward flesh? What day brought this crooked intent? Now this demoness has caught me and asks that I take a husband. If I lose my true yang, I will fall into the cycle of rebirth, be struck behind Mount Yin, and never rise again in life after life.” Sun Wukong laughed and said, “Do not swear. Since your heart is sincere about going west for the sutra, I, old Sun, will take you out.” Tripitaka said, “I have forgotten the way I came in.” Sun Wukong replied, “Say no more about forgetfulness. This cave is not entered and left in the ordinary way. One goes in head-first and down through the throat of the earth. Now that I have rescued you, we must bore upward from below. If your fate is high, you will tunnel out through the mouth of the cave; if your fate is low and it is blocked, then a suffocating day of death will follow.” Tripitaka, eyes full of tears, said, “With trouble so great, what is one to do?” Sun Wukong said, “Nothing to fear. Let the demoness prepare wine and food for you. If she insists, drink just one cup. Have her pour quickly, and ask for a cup mixed with a joy-bud. I will become a cicada-like insect and hide beneath the wine foam. Once she swallows me in one bite, I shall tear through her heart and liver, snap her entrails, and kill the demoness so you may escape.” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, hearing this, you are no true son of man.” Sun Wukong said, “Do what is right and let your life go on. The demoness is the root of harm; why should you pity her?” Tripitaka said, “All right, all right. Just keep to my side.”

That Great Sage, Sun Wukong, guards Tripitaka; this monk on pilgrimage lives by the Beauty of the Monkey King alone.

The two did not finish their plans before the demoness, already making her arrangements, came near the east corridor outside, unlatched the gate, and called, “Elder!” Tripitaka dared not answer. She called again; he still would not. Why could he not answer? He thought, “If I open my mouth, my divine spirit scatters; if my tongue moves, right and wrong are born.” Yet in one heart he thought, “If I remain mute, if this wicked one is cruel, he may kill me at once.” It was exactly a mind asking one thing and the mouth another, three thoughts wrestling with two mouths in silence. While he still hesitated, the demoness called again, “Elder.” Tripitaka could not endure it and answered once: “Lady, yes.” When the Elder spoke those words, it felt like a thousand jin fell from his chest. People call Tripitaka a true monk, sincere in going west to worship Buddha for the sutra, so how could he answer a female demoness? Yet at this moment of life and death, he had no choice. Though he answered outwardly, he held no desire within. The demoness, seeing he had answered, pushed open the gate, pulled Tripitaka up, walked with him hand in hand, and whispered at his ear. Watch her move in a thousand charms and ten thousand gestures—how artfully she played the role of beauty, while Tripitaka’s heart was torn with grief. From hiding, Sun Wukong laughed and said, “My Master is so honeyed by her coaxing that I fear he may falter.”

The true monk and demon met a cruel temptress; this wily demon-girl was fair indeed. Fine green brows parted like willow leaves, a bright red face setting off peach blossoms. Embroidered shoes barely showing two hooked phoenix points; her cloud-like hair coiled high, two raven locks at the temples. Smiling, she took his hand, and at that contact her fragrance spread, musk and spikenard, through his robe.

Drawing Tripitaka along, she led him to the grass pavilion and said, “Elder, I have prepared one cup of wine; drink with me.” Tripitaka said, “Lady, poor monk does not eat meat.” She said, “I know you do not. Since the water in this cave is impure, I ordered clear water from the mountain to gather yin and yang purity, and prepared pure vegetarian fruit and vegetables for our banquet to play at marriage with you.” Tripitaka followed her in to see, and truly saw this:

The gate was full of embroidered bindings and bright ribbons; the entire yard reeked sweetly with scented lion incense. Gilded tables were set, with black-oiled wicker-rib boards for platters. On those tables lay curious delicacies; in the platters sat rare vegetarian things. Apples, olives, lotus flesh, grapes, candlenuts, loquats, hazelnuts, pines, lychees, longans, wild chestnuts, hornwort watercress, jujubes, persimmons, walnuts, ginkgo, kumquats, and fragrant oranges—whatever grew in the hills. More fresh vegetables appeared: tofu, flour cakes, wood ear fungus, fresh bamboo shoots, mushrooms, fragrant mushrooms, Chinese yam, and huangjing. Rock-flower greens and daylily buds, stir-fried in green oil; Lablab beans and river beans, sauced and seasoned. Wax gourd and bottle gourd, white nuts, and turnip greens. Eggplant with peeled skin, quail cooked together; scooped winter melon cut in neat cubes. Stewed taro mashing with sugar, and boiled radish glazed in vinegar. Hot peppers and ginger, each dish savory and sharp, salt and sweet in balanced proportion.

The demoness held up her pointed, jewel-like fingers and lifted a golden cup, filled it with fine wine, and offered it to Tripitaka. Through smiling lips she called, “Dear elder brother, wondrous one, have a cup of joy wine with me.” Tripitaka shyly accepted it, tipped a little toward the sky in offering, and inwardly blessed: “Guarding heavens, lords of the Five Directions, Four Officers of Judgment: disciple Chen Xuanzang, dispatched from the East by Guanyin, begs all hidden gods to guard him. I have left the Eastern Land to come to the Thunderous-Voice Buddha and seek the sutra. Now on the road I am seized by this demoness and forced toward forced marriage. She hands me this cup. If this is indeed vegetarian wine, I can reluctantly drink and yet still attain Buddhahood; if it is meaty wine and I violate my precepts, I will fall forever into the misery of rebirth.” But Sun Wukong, at the back of her ear, turned light and close as if he were merely an ear-echo; only Tripitaka heard him, no one else did. He knew Master liked the grape-based vegetarian wine and told him to drink one cup. The Elder had no choice but to drink. He swiftly poured another full cup and handed it back to the demoness. Truly she poured in a joy-bud. Sun Wukong became that cicada-like insect and glided silently beneath the bud of wine. The demoness reached for it, did not drink, set the cup aside, bowed twice to Tripitaka, and in sweet, shy words shared a few love phrases. Only when she raised the cup had the blossom broken apart and the insect been revealed. Not recognizing Sun Wukong in that form, she thought it was only a grub. With her little finger she pinched it up and flicked it downward.

Seeing things go awry, Sun Wukong judged he could not get into her belly and so turned into a famished old hawk. Truly:

Jade claws, golden eyes, iron feathered wings; Manly posture and fierce breath stirred the clouds. Fox spirit and crafty hare, seeing him move, fled a thousand leagues across land and river. Hungry, he runs with the wind to chase sparrows; Sated, he rides high and touches the gate of heaven. His old iron-hard fist is most hurtful to men; proud with success, he soars beyond the sky’s boundary. He rose, spread his jade claws, and with one roar overturned the table setting. He scattered the vegetarian fruits and vegetables, the plates, pitchers, and goblets, all into splinters, brushed Tripitaka aside, and flew out. The demoness was shocked into horror; Tripitaka’s bones and flesh went limp like jelly. Trembling, she hugged Tripitaka and said, “Elder brother, where did this creature come from?” Tripitaka said, “The poor monk does not know.” The demoness said, “I put so much effort into arranging this vegetarian feast for you to amuse yourself, yet I do not know from where this shaggy beast flew in and shattered my hearth. My little fiends! To have broken my fire is one thing, but to splash this purity of dishes across the ground and make them impure—how can it be used?” Tripitaka clearly understood it was Sun Wukong’s doing, but he had no heart to speak. The demoness said, “Servants, I understand. It must be that as I trapped Tripitaka, Heaven and Earth would not permit this, so I have brought this thing down. Pick up the scattered fire and table things. Prepare another round of wine and dishes at once. We will not refuse meat or vegetables; I will take heaven as witness and earth as witness and renew the betrothal with Tripitaka.” She still sent the Elder to sit in the east corridor.

Then Sun Wukong flew out, resumed his true form, and at the cave mouth shouted, “Open the gate!” Zhu Bajie laughed and called out, “Sha Wujing, brother is here.” They both cast aside their weapons. Sun Wukong leapt out. Sha Wujing moved forward and asked, “Is there a demoness? Is Master inside? Is he bound?” Sun Wukong said, “Yes, yes, yes.” Zhu Bajie said, “Master is suffering in there, is he tied up, is he to be steamed or boiled?” Sun Wukong said, “That is not the point. The demoness has arranged a vegetarian feast and plans to carry out that affair with him.” Zhu Bajie said, “You are doomed, you are doomed. Did you come back after drinking the wedding wine with her?” Sun Wukong said, “Fool, Master’s life itself hangs by a thread. What is there to drink with respect to wedding wine?” Zhu Bajie said, “How did you end up back here?” Sun Wukong recounted all he had seen in Tripitaka’s cave form-changing. He said, “Brothers, think no more nonsense. Master is in this place; once I go, old Sun will certainly bring him out alive.”

Turning over again, he entered inside and once more changed into a fly, perching on the gatehouse and listening. He heard the demoness, breathing hotly, calling from the pavilion: “Servants, whether vegetarian or not, bring paper to burn. Let Heaven and Earth stand as witness; I must marry him.” Sun Wukong heard this and laughed inwardly. “This demon has no scrap of shame at all. In broad daylight she has put a monk in her house and made a puppet of him. Do not rush—let the old monkey slip in again and take a look.” With a quick buzzing sound he flew beneath the east corridor. Inside sat Tripitaka, and tears dripped clearly from his cheeks. Wukong slid in beside him and called, “Master.” The Master recognized the voice and leapt up, grinding out in anger: “Monkey! Another man’s courage is still courage inside him; yours is nothing but courage wrapped around your whole body. You used your changeable powers and burst through the household fire—how much is that worth? After you stirred this demon into lustful excitement, she made no distinction between pure and impure and insists on mating with me. What are we to do now?” Wukong, smiling in secret, said, “Do not blame me, Master—there is a way to save you.” Tripitaka asked, “How can you save me?” Wukong answered, “When I flew up just now I saw a garden behind him. Lure him into it and make him play; then I will rescue you.” Tripitaka asked, “How is it to be saved in the garden?” Wukong said, “Go with him to the garden. When you come to the edge of the peach grove, do not move further. I will fly up to the branches and become a red peach. You must take the red fruit first and pick it down. The red one is me. He will certainly pick one too; be sure to give him the red fruit. If he swallows it in one mouthful, I will be inside him. Then I can smash his hide-bag, tear his entrails apart, and kill him, and you will be free.” Tripitaka said, “If you can do it, why not grapple with him yourself? Why hide inside his belly?” Wukong replied, “Master, you do not understand. If his throat-passage were easy to enter and leave, I could wrestle him head-on. But it is crooked and narrow, hard to pass through. If I fought him directly, all that nest of his—old and young alike—would grip even me. What then? Only by this rough-handed handling can we all be cut cleanly away.” Tripitaka nodded and believed him, saying only, “Stay with me.” Wukong said, “Understood. I am on your head.”

The disciples and the Master settled the plan. Tripitaka only then rose, putting his hands on the lattice and called, “Wife, wife.” Hearing it, the demoness ran forward with a soft laugh and said, “Good monk brother, what is to be said?” Tripitaka said, “Wife, since I left Chang’an and came westward, there has been no day without mountains and no day without waters. Yesterday, at Zhenhai Temple, I lodged for the night and came down with a heavy cold and a grave illness; today I broke into a sweat and am only just a little better. And because you were so generous, you brought me into this immortal hall. Yet sitting here all this day, my mind is still unsettled. Would you take me there just to freshen my spirits and play a little?” The demoness was deeply pleased. “Good monk brother, you do seem to have some interest. I will go with you to the garden and we shall play.” She called, “Servants, fetch the keys and open the gate of the garden, and sweep the paths clean.” All the little demons ran off to open the gate and tidy it.

The demoness opened the lattice and helped Tripitaka out. Look at her many little demons: all with oiled heads and powdered faces, pretty and graceful, clustered close, accompanying Tripitaka as they took the path straight to the garden. A good monk, he made no trouble in this embroidered throng, a dumb and deaf creature among a tangle of brocade. If not for that iron-hearted heart fixed on Buddha, no second lusty layman of wine and desire could ever have obtained the Scripture. The whole party reached the garden’s outer edge. The demoness spoke in flirtatious low tones: “Good monk brother, if we sport here, it will truly ease your spirits.” She and Tripitaka took each other’s hands and entered the garden together, lifting their eyes to look around, truly a delightful place.

Winding paths turn and wind, all about them freckled with dark moss; slender latticed windows, everywhere shrouded in muted embroidered foil. At the first movement of the breeze, light brocades of Shu and silk of Wu flutter and spread; the fine rain only just having passed, delicate drops reveal skin like ice and jade. The sun sets the fresh apricots glowing, red as an immortal drying a rainbow garment in sunlight; the moonlight on plantain leaves is blue like the august beauty waving a feather fan. Pink walls on all sides, ten thousand clusters of willows with oriole song; around the quiet halls, the courtyards are full of mountain-ash and fluttering powder-butterflies. Look at the Pavilion of Fragrant Condensation, the Green Moth Pavilion, the Dispelling Intoxication Pavilion, and the Yearning Pavilion, folded one upon another in layered reflections; on red curtains, hooked tassels hold up curled beard-like fringes. Then there are the Growing-Sour Pavilion, the Plain-Robed Pavilion, the Painted-Eyebrow Pavilion, and the Four-Rain Pavilion—each tall and lofty, carved tablets painted with bird-like seal script. Look at the Bathing-Crane Pool, the Wine-Basin Pool, the Moon-Soothing Pool, and the Hair-Rinsing Pool, where blue duckweed and green algae flash like golden scales; there are also Ink-Flower Hall, Strange-Casket Hall, Adept Delights Hall, and Cloud-Coveting Hall, jade ladles and chrysanthemum cups floating on green ants. Between the pools and pavilions stand the Taihu stones, Ziying stones, Yingluo stones, and Jinchuan stones, with tiger-whisker cattails growing verdant. To east and west of hall and pavilion rise the Wooden Rockery, Emerald-Screen Mountain, Whistling-Wind Mountain, and Jade-Fruity Mountain, where phoenix-tail bamboo crowds every place. The gourd-trellis, the rose-trellis, and near them the swing-frame form one vast brocade canopy. The Pine-and-Cypress Pavilion and the Magnolia Pavilion face the Sweet-Wood Pavilion, looking like an emerald-fort embroidered drape. Peony rails, peony thickets—scarlet and purple flowers wrestle in riotous fullness; the Night-Meeting Terrace and the Sweet-Malva Lattice blossom charmingly year after year. Droplets fall in thin threads, purple and smiling, fit to be painted or drawn; splendid scarlet silk-cotton burns the sky, fit to be titled and versified. In judging beauty, do not boast of Langyuan and Penglai; in comparing blossoms, do not number Yaohuang and Weizi. If one compares springtime grasses here, only the Jade-Qiong blossom is lacking in this garden.

The Master, holding the demoness’s arm, walked through the garden, admiring wondrous and strange flowers and trees without end. After passing many pavilions, he truly entered a finer setting. Suddenly he lifted his head and came to the edge of the peach grove. Sun Wukong pinched Tripitaka once on the head, and the Master understood. Wukong flew to a branch of the peach tree, shifted form, and became a red peach, red and enticing. The Master said to the demoness, “Wife, in this garden there is fragrance in the blossoms and ripe fruit on every branch. Bees and wasps compete for the fragrance, and birds quarrel for the ripe fruit. Why are the peaches here mixed in blue and red? Why not the same?” The demoness laughed, “If there were no yin and yang in heaven, the sun and moon would not shine; if there were no yin and yang in earth, grasses and trees would not grow; if there were no yin and yang in people, men and women would not be distinguished. On this peach tree, the fruits on the sunward side, warmed first by sunlight, ripen first and therefore turn red; those in shade ripen slower and remain green. This is the way of yin and yang.” Tripitaka said, “Thank you for your instruction, Wife. Truly this poor monk did not know it.” Then, stepping forward, he reached out and picked a red peach. The demoness also picked a green one. Bowing slightly, Tripitaka held up the red peach to the demoness: “Wife, you love color; please eat this red peach, and let me take the green one.” The demoness truly nodded, and inwardly rejoiced: “What a good monk! He is indeed a true man: even before a husband and wife are joined for even one day, he already shows such affection.” She then honored Tripitaka with delight, fondly and with joy. Tripitaka took the green peach and ate it at once. The demoness, with delight, bit into the red one. Her vermilion lips parted, silver teeth gleaming; before she could close her bite, Sun Wukong—impatient now—spun in a tight somersault and flipped into her throat, straight into her belly. The demoness, frightened, said to Tripitaka, “Great Master, this fruit is fierce! Why did it not break as it was bitten and just roll downward?” Tripitaka said, “Wife, fruit from this newly opened garden is loved for eating, so it goes down quickly.” The demoness said, “She had not yet spat out the stone and already it had vanished.” Tripitaka said, “Wife, the appetite is beautiful and the feeling kind; you enjoyed it so much you did not have time to spit out the stone before swallowing.”

Sun Wukong was in his belly, resumed his true form, and called out, 'Master, do not argue with him. Old Sun Wukong already has him in his grasp.' Tripitaka said, 'Disciple, be more tactful.' The demoness heard and said, 'Who is it that you are speaking with?' Tripitaka said, 'I am speaking with my disciple Sun Wukong.' The demoness said, 'Where is Sun Wukong?' Tripitaka said, 'In your belly, was it not the red peach you just ate?'

The demoness panicked, saying, 'Enough, enough. This monkey-head burrowed into my belly—I am finished. Sun Wukong, by what tricks did you manage to get in my belly by every means?' Sun Wukong, from inside, muttered in resentment, 'No big deal. I have merely eaten your six-fold liver and lungs, your three hairs and seven-orifice heart; I have washed clean your five viscera and made you into a clapper demon.'

Hearing this, the demoness was so frightened that her soul and spirit shook apart. Trembling, she held Tripitaka close and said, 'Venerable Master, I only thought:

Bound in a red thread by former-life ties, fish and water had two hearts in true accord. Yet now the mandarin ducks are broken apart, and who could have expected the phoenixes to drift apart east and west. At Blue Bridge the waters rise and the matter cannot be done; smoke from the Buddha temple drifts, and the blessed meeting is empty. We meant to meet in one affair, and now once more we part—what year will let us meet again?'

Sun Wukong, hearing this from within, feared that the Master's kindness might be swayed again and that he would be duped, so he raised his fists and jumped about, setting himself up and shifting his stance, almost bursting that skin-bag. The demoness could not bear the pain; she crashed to the dust. For a while she dared not speak. Seeing no words from her, Sun Wukong thought she was dead and loosened his grip a little.

She came to herself and called, 'Where are the little ones?' Those little demons, who had entered through the gate earlier, each kept their place as best they could, each wandered to a different spot to gather flowers and wrestle weeds, each playing as they pleased, leaving that demoness and the monk alone to speak as they wished. As soon as they heard her call, they all came running back.

Again they saw her lying on the ground, her color changed, groaning from her mouth, unable to crawl. They hurriedly supported her and clustered together, saying, 'Lady, what is it? Is it from sudden pain of the heart?' The demoness said, 'No, no. Do not ask. There is already one inside my belly. Send this monk out at once and spare my life.'

The little demons truly came to shoulder her. Sun Wukong called from inside, 'Who dares to carry him? If any of you carries my Master out by yourself, once he is out there, I will spare your life.' The fiend, unable to resist, could only think of saving her own life. In haste she rose, lifted Tripitaka onto her back, pulled up her steps, and walked straight out.

The little demons followed, saying, 'Old lady, where are you going?' The demoness replied, 'As long as there is still the bright moon over the Five Lakes, how can there be no place to cast the golden hook? Send this brute out first, then let me go find another head.'

A mighty demoness bounded once through cloud-light and reached the cave mouth. Again came the clatter and clang of arms, weapons clashing in disorder. Tripitaka said, 'Disciple, there is a clanging of weapons outside.' Sun Wukong said, 'It is Zhu Bajie working his crescent spade. Call him.' Tripitaka called, 'Zhu Bajie.' Zhu Bajie heard and said, 'Sha Monk, Master is coming out.' The two drew out the spade and staff, and the demoness carried Tripitaka out on her back.

Ah! it was exactly then:

The Monkey of the Heart should within subdue the wicked fiend, At the Gate of Earth and Wood the holy monk is received.

After all, we do not yet know how the demoness’s life turns out; wait and hear it explained in the next chapter.
