This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

The Great Way is profound and darkly deep—who can fathom it? If one tells it, ghosts and spirits would be startled in alarm. It clasps and shelters the universe, cuts and judges the mysterious light; in the realm of the world there is no happiness to compare with true bliss. Before Spirit-Emu Peak a sacred pearl was lifted, shining with five-hued radiance. It illuminated all beings above and below Heaven and Earth, and to the awakened it granted a life vast as mountains and seas.

The three monks and the four disciples parted from the woodcutter, came off Hidden-Mist Mountain, and rushed onto the great road. After walking for several days, they suddenly saw a city drawing near. Tripitaka said, “Sun Wukong, look at that city ahead. Is that the Tangut-like realm of Tianzhu?” Wukong swished his hand and said, “No, no. Though it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss where the Buddha dwells, there is no city there; it is a great mountain with pavilions and halls inside, named Great Thunderclap Monastery of Sacred Mountain. Even if this were Tianzhu, it still is not where the Buddha resides. And we do not yet know how far Tianzhu lies from Sacred Mountain. This city is likely an outlying county beyond Tianzhu, and only when we near its border will we know clearly.”

In no time they reached the outskirts. Tripitaka dismounted and entered through the three gates, where they found civic life desolate and the streets and avenues deserted. They went on into the market quarter and saw many blue-robed men standing on either side in rows, with several officials wearing official caps and belts beneath the eaves. The four masters walked steadily along the main street, but those men made no way for them to pass. Zhu Bajie, the village fool, puffed up his long snout and shouted, “Make way! Make way!” Seeing this, they raised their heads in panic; their bodies went soft and their muscles slack, and they stumbled, saying, “A demon! A demon has come!” The officials under the eaves, trembling, bent and asked, “From where do you come?” Fearing trouble for them, Tripitaka stepped forward and said to all, “I am the humble monk, Tripitaka, dispatched from the Great Tang by imperial decree to seek scripture from Buddha at Great Thunderclap Monastery in Tianzhu. We passed Baofang, yet knew not the names of the places, and we have not yet entered any household; when we entered this city we showed little courtesy in yielding the way. Please pardon this fault.” The officials then prostrated and said, “This is an outlying county of Tianzhu, called Fengxian County. Consecutive years of drought have come, and the county magistrate has us issue a public notice, calling for a Dharma master to pray for rain and save the people.” Wukong said, “Where is your notice?” The officials said, “It is here; we only just swept the eaves and have not yet hung it out.” Wukong said, “Bring it, I want to see it.” They opened and hung the notice beneath the eave. Wukong and the three disciples moved forward together to read it. It said:

In Fengxian County, an outer district of Great Tianzhu ruled by Governor Shangguan of the Shangguan lineage, this proclamation is posted to invite a true master in Dharma for a great rain rite: because this county is wide and broad and the people and soldiers are numerous and prosperous, there has been many years of fierce drought and repeated failure of rains. Fields are withered and grain is ruined, rivers are shallow and canals empty. Wells are dry and springs have no water at all. The rich can barely keep themselves alive; the poor are near unable to live another day. A bushel of millet costs a hundred gold, a bundle of firewood costs five taels. A ten-year-old girl is exchanged for three sheng of rice, a five-year-old boy is taken away with whoever will. In the city people fear to disobey the law and barter even clothing to keep body and life; in the countryside they mock officials, robbing and abducting people, and still survive somehow. Therefore this decree was posted, calling for the sages of the four directions to pray for rain and rescue the people. Our merit will be deep in return, and I vow to repay with a thousand taels, never an empty promise. Let those who heed this notice come quickly. Wukong, after reading, said, “What is this Shangguan surname? Is it one of the magistrate’s names?” The officials replied, “Shangguan is the family name; it is the name of this county magistrate’s clan.” Wukong laughed, “That surname is rare indeed.” Zhu Bajie said, “Elder brother has never studied; in the Hundred Family Surnames it says, ‘Shangguan, Ouyang.’” Tripitaka said, “Disciples, stop all idle talk. If one can pray for rain, ask him for a rain of sweetness to relieve the people’s suffering; this is the meritorious act of all good works. If he cannot, then let us move on and do not delay our journey.” Wukong said, “What difficulty is there in invoking rain? I, old Wukong, can turn rivers and stir seas, swap constellations, kick heaven and stir wells, exhale mist and spray clouds, carry mountains and chase the moon, summon rain and call wind—aren’t these child’s games from my youth? Why should it be so rare?”

The officials heard this and sent two men running to the magistrate: “My lord, a thousand blessings have arrived.” The magistrate was then burning incense and offering silent prayers. Hearing that there was glad news, he asked, “What is this glad news?” The messenger said, “We have just hung the proclamation at the city gate; four monks have already arrived, saying they are from Great Tang under the imperial court, going to Great Thunderclap Monastery in Tianzhu to seek scripture from Buddha. On seeing the proclamation, they claimed they can pray for sweet rain. I am the one who came to report at once.”

The magistrate then changed his robes and went on foot, without sedan chair, horses, or a crowd, straight to the city gate and paid formal greeting. Suddenly someone called out, “Magistrate Shangguan has come!” and everyone moved aside. The magistrate saw Tripitaka and, untroubled by his ugly disciples, prostrated himself right in the street, saying, “I am Shangguan, magistrate of Fengxian County. I respectfully beg the venerable teacher to pray for rain and save the people. Grant your boundless compassion, move your divine powers, and bring deliverance, deliverance.” Tripitaka replied with courtesy, “This is not a place for such talk; let the humble monk first come to a temple and do the rite there.” The magistrate said, “Come with the teacher to my yamen; there is a clean place prepared.”

So the master and his disciples hauled their horses and load poles and went directly to the magistrate’s hall, where everyone was received in due order. The magistrate ordered tea and a simple meal. Soon a vegetarian meal was served. Zhu Bajie, at will, swallowed his food like a hungry tiger. The serving attendants, terrified, hurried back and forth, adding soup and rice as if chasing a carousel horse. By the time the meal was done he was full and only then did he stop. After the meal Tripitaka thanked him and asked, “Magistrate, how long has your district suffered drought?” The magistrate recited:

Our land belongs to Great Tianzhu; this is Fengxian, an outer county under my governance. For three years in succession we have known great barrenness; even grasses and seed refuse to grow, and the five grains are gone. Great and small households alike struggle in trade; in nine of ten homes, crying and weeping fills the place. In three periods, two people die of hunger; one remains, like a candle in the wind. This humble official has posted notices far and wide seeking the wise and virtuous, and now at last the true monk has arrived in our land. If you can send but one drop of rain to relieve the common people, I will offer a thousand gold in repayment for this vast merit. Hearing this, Wukong smiled broadly and said, “No need, no need. If they offer a thousand gold, there is not a drop of real rain to pay for it. But by one’s accumulated merit and virtue, Wukong will send your county a great rain.” The magistrate, who was truly upright and beloved by his people, invited Wukong to sit and bowed low, saying, “The teacher has indeed given boundless compassion; this humble official dare not fail in moral conduct.” Wukong said, “Don’t speak further. Please rise. But do take care to watch my master while the old Wukong performs the rite.” Sha Wujing asked, “Elder brother, how will you do it?” Wukong said, “You and Zhu Bajie come over here and stay under this hall like wings at my side while I summon the dragon to bring the rain.” Obediently they followed his instructions, and the three stood below in the hall. The magistrate burned incense and paid homage. Tripitaka sat and chanted scripture.

Wukong recited a true mantra and intoned spell formula. Immediately, in the far East, a black cloud appeared and slowly came down to the front of the hall. It was the Old Dragon King of the Eastern Sea, Ao Guang. Ao Guang gathered the tail of the cloud and changed himself into human form, then walked forward and bowed to Wukong, saying, “Great Sage, you called for a dragon. What need brings you to summon me?” Wukong said, “Please rise. You have made the long journey; there is no great matter. This is Fengxian County. In recent years there has been severe drought and the people suffer. How is it that you did not come here to rain?” The dragon king said, “As Your Holiness knows, I can cause rain only as one sent by Heaven. If Heaven has not dispatched me, how dare I come and rain here on my own?” Wukong said, “I come by chance and see that these people suffer under years of drought. I have sent for you to descend here and bring rain to relieve them. How can you make excuses now?” The dragon said, “I dare not refuse. Yet after your call to the true mantra, how could I fail to come? One, I have no imperial order from Heaven. Two, I have not brought the rain ministers with me; how can I move the rain department? Since the Great Sage has the heart to save them, let this little dragon return to the sea to summon the troops. Please return to Heaven and request an edict authorizing rain; ask the water official to release a dragon, and I will then rain according to the decree’s measure.”

Wukong saw the logic in the dragon king’s words and sent him back to the sea by force of law. He then stepped out of the Protective Battle Ring and told Tripitaka what the dragon king had said. Tripitaka said, “In that case, you go and do it—do not utter deceitful words.” Wukong ordered Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, “Protect the master. I am going to Heaven.” He then, in one cry, was gone as if disappeared from silence. The magistrate, frightened to the core, asked, “Where has Master Wukong gone?” Zhu Bajie laughed, “He rides the clouds to Heaven.” The magistrate showed him deep respect, sent out proclamations throughout city streets and lanes, commanding all officials, civilians, soldiers, and common folk—high and low alike—to set out tablets for the Dragon Kings in every household. They should set up jars of clear water with willow branches stuck in them, keep incense flames burning, and offer worship to Heaven; no need to describe it further.

It is now told that Sun Wukong mounted a cloud and rode straight to the outer gate of the Western Heavens. There he soon saw the Protector of the Nation Heavenly King, who had heavenly soldiers and mighty men come forward to welcome him and ask, 'Great Sage, is the matter of obtaining the scriptures done?' Sun Wukong replied, 'It is not far off. Now that we have reached the border of Tianzhu, there is an outlying county called Fengxian County. For three years this place has had no rain, and the people are in great hardship. I, Old Sun, wished to pray for rain to save them. I called the Dragon King there, but he said he had no warrant and dared not act on his own; so I have come now to come before the Jade Emperor to seek instruction.' The Heavenly King said, 'There, by all means, it should not be time for rain. I have heard that that magistrate behaved carelessly, offended Heaven and Earth. The Highest Emperor saw the crime and set three things in place: a Rice Mountain, a Flour Mountain, and a Great Golden Chain. Only when these three are overturned and broken may it then be fitting for rain to fall.' Sun Wukong did not understand this meaning and wished to see the Jade Emperor. The Heavenly King did not dare to block him and let him in. He went directly to the outer hall of the Hall of Bright Illumination, and again saw the Four Great Heavenly Masters coming forth to welcome him, asking, 'Great Sage, what business brings you here?' Sun Wukong said, 'I am protecting Tripitaka on the road, and have come to the Tianzhu border. In Fengxian County there is no rain. The magistrate there requested prayers for rain. Old Sun summoned the Dragon King; he said there was no edict from the Jade Emperor and he dared not act on his own, so I came specifically to ask for an edict, to save the people's suffering.' The Four Great Heavenly Masters said, 'That place ought not to have rain.' Sun Wukong laughed: 'Whether it should or should not, please present it and press the matter; then you may see what face the Great Sage shows.' Ge Xianweng said, 'As the saying goes, "A fly caught in a net—what an enormous nerve for a face."' Xu Jingyang said, 'No idle talk. Just bring him in.'

Qiu Hongji, Zhang Daoling, Ge Xianweng, and Xu Jingyang, the four True Men, brought him to the hall under Lingxiao and presented this report: 'Your Majesty, Sun Wukong has come to the Tianzhu outer county of Fengxian and asks for rain; he has come to request your edict.' The Jade Emperor said, 'That brute, three years ago on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month, when I traveled to inspect all the heavens and roamed the three realms, upon reaching another region I saw that the official Shangguan Zheng was without compassion. He overturned the simple vegetarian food prepared for the Fast of Heaven and fed it to a dog, then spoke filthy words, thereby committing a serious offense. I then set him with three punishments in the Hall of Perfumed Incense. You all take Sun Wukong there to inspect: if the three things are overturned and broken, then give him your decree; if they are not overturned, then refrain from meddling further.'

The four Heavenly Masters then led Sun Wukong to the Hall of Perfumed Incense. There were three things there: a mountain of rice about ten zhang high, and a mountain of flour about twenty zhang high. Beside the Rice Mountain was a chicken the size of a fist, pecking one beakful, then a little beakful, picking away at the rice to eat it. Beside the Flour Mountain was a gold-muzzled hound, with a golden coat, stretching its tongue now long, now short, lapping the flour to eat it. To the left hung an iron frame, and on the frame a great golden lock, about one chi three or four cun long, the lock bar thick as a finger; beneath it burned a bright lamp, and its flame was licking the lock bar. Sun Wukong did not know the meaning and asked a Tian Master, 'What does this mean?' The master answered, 'That fellow offended Heaven, so the Jade Emperor set these three things. Only when that chicken has eaten all the rice, the dog has licked all the flour, and the lamp flame has burned through the lock bar, then and only then should rain descend there.'

Hearing this, Sun Wukong was greatly startled and pale, and he dared not submit a memorial again. He came out of the hall, his face full of shame. The Four Heavenly Masters laughed: 'Great Sage, do not worry. This matter is rightly resolved by doing good. If but one thought of compassion is stirred, moving Heaven above and above, the Rice Mountain and Flour Mountain will topple at once, and the lock bar will break at once. Go and persuade that one to return to the good path, and blessings will come of themselves.' Sun Wukong did as told. He did not return to Lingxiao to take leave of the Jade Emperor, but went straight back to the mortal world. Shortly afterwards, he came again to the Western Heaven gate and met the Protector of the Nation Heavenly King. The king asked, 'What is the result of the request?' Sun Wukong recounted the matter of the Rice Mountain, Flour Mountain, and Golden Lock in full: 'In keeping with your words, he would not transmit any order. Just now the Tian Master who sent me told me to urge him to return to virtue. Then blessing itself would come.' Thus they parted, and he descended on clouds back into the world below.

That magistrate, together with Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie, Sha Wujing, and the various officials and people, came to welcome him and all crowded together in a dense crowd asking questions. Sun Wukong shouted at the magistrate, 'It is all because you, this wretch, three years ago on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month offended Heaven and Earth, bringing hardship on the common people, and now you refuse to call down rain.' Frightened, the magistrate knelt on the ground and said, 'How did Teacher come to know what happened three years ago?' Sun Wukong said, 'How did you overturn the vegetarian offering for the Fast of Heaven and feed it to a dog? Tell it plainly.' The magistrate did not dare conceal it and said, 'Three years ago, on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month, during a Fast of Heaven in my yamen, because my wife was unworthy and we argued with harsh words, in a moment of rage and ignorance I knocked over the offering table and spilled the vegetarian dishes; it is true I called the dog to eat them. These two years my heart has remembered this, my mind has wandered in confusion, and I have had nowhere to explain. I did not know that Heaven had marked this as guilt and thereby harmed the people. Now that Teacher has descended, I earnestly ask that it be made clear. How does the upper court reckon this matter?' Sun Wukong said, 'That very day was the day the Jade Emperor came to this world below. When he saw you overturn the Fast of Heaven offering and feed it to a dog, and heard your obscene words, he instantly set three punishments for you.' Zhu Bajie asked, 'What are those three?' Sun Wukong said, 'In the Hall of Perfumed Incense is a Mountain of Rice, about ten zhang high; and a Mountain of Flour, about twenty zhang high. Beside the Rice Mountain is a small chicken the size of a fist, pecking there one beakful, another beakful, eating that rice. Beside the Flour Mountain is a gold-muzzled hound that there lengthens its tongue and shortens it, lapping up the flour. On the left is another iron stand on which hangs a golden chain, whose shackle is finger-thick. Under it is a bright lamp, whose flame is lapping at the shackle bar. Only when that chicken has eaten all the rice, the dog all the flour, and the flame has burned through the lock bar, is this place then fit for rain.' Zhu Bajie laughed and said, 'No matter, no matter. Brother, if you take me there and I transform my true body, in one meal I can eat all their rice and flour and snap the lock bar; then rain will surely come.' Sun Wukong said, 'Bajie, do not speak foolishly. This is a stratagem set by Heaven; how could you perceive it?' Tripitaka said, 'If this is the way, what should be done?' Sun Wukong said, 'It is not hard. When I departed, the Four Heavenly Masters told me that only good deeds could release it.' The magistrate prostrated himself and pleaded, 'By Teacher's instruction alone, I will take refuge completely.' Sun Wukong said, 'If you can turn your heart toward the good and pray to Buddha and read the scriptures at once, I will still make arrangements for you. If you persist in your former ways, I will also not be able to intercede; not long from now Heaven will punish you, and your life cannot be saved.'

The magistrate knelt, offered obeisance, and swore his vow to take refuge. At once he invited all the local monks and Daoist adepts, and ordered that a Dharma hall be established. One and all wrote petitions and submitted memorials for three days. The magistrate led the crowd in taking incense and bowing, giving thanks to Heaven and apologizing to Earth, and confessing his guilt. Tripitaka also chanted sutras with him. On one side, a flying bulletin went out saying that all householders both within and beyond the city, women and men alike, should burn incense and chant the Buddha's name. From then on, a full sound of goodness filled the air. Sun Wukong at last rejoiced and told Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, 'You two, guard the Master well; let Old Sun go with him once again.' Zhu Bajie asked, 'Brother, where will he go now?' Sun Wukong said, 'This magistrate has believed Old Sun's words and indeed followed the teaching, respectfully and compassionately, and now he chants Buddha with sincerity. I am going once more to present before the Jade Emperor and ask for some rain.' Sha Wujing said, 'Since Brother intends to go, there need be no hesitation; do not delay us from our journey. We must seek rain once and thereby complete our true fruit.'

Well then, Great Sage mounted the cloud head once more and went straight to the outer side of the Heaven gate, meeting again the Protector of the Nation Heavenly King. The king asked, 'Why have you come again?' Sun Wukong said, 'The magistrate there has now turned to good conduct.' The king was overjoyed as well. Just then, a straight-talisman messenger appeared, carrying a Taoist document and a monk's pass, and came to the outer heaven gate to deliver them. Seeing Sun Wukong, the messenger paid respects and said, 'This is the merit from the Great Sage's urging toward good.' Sun Wukong asked, 'Where will you send this sealed document?' The messenger said, 'I will take it directly to the Hall of Bright Illumination, deliver it through the heavenly masters to the Jade Emperor, Great Heavenly Lord.' Sun Wukong said, 'In that case, you go ahead, and I will follow after.' The talisman messenger entered the Heaven Gate. The Protector of the Nation King said, 'Great Sage, there is no need for you to see the Jade Emperor now. Go to the Nine Heavens Yingyuan Office and borrow a few thunder gods, then strike thunder and flash forth with lightning yourself, and rain will come there.'

The Great Sage did as he had been told: he entered through Heaven’s Gate and did not go up to Lingxiao Hall to request a decree, but strode through the air of clouds straight to the Yinyuan Office of the Ninth Heaven. There he found the envoy of the Thunder Gate, the records-correcting clerk, and the inquiry clerk all coming out to greet him. They offered him formal salute and said, "Great Sage, from where do you come?" The Great Sage answered, "I have business to see the Celestials." The three envoys immediately reported it. The Honored One then descended from beneath the nine-phoenix scarlet-cloud screen, adjusted his garments, and came out to receive him. After formal greetings, the Great Sage said, "I have come with one particular request." The Honored One asked, "What is it?" The Great Sage said, "Because I escorted Tripitaka to Fengxian County, I saw the drought there was severe. I promised him I would ask for rain, and so I have come to borrow your thunder officers." The Honored One said, "I know the county lord there has offended Heaven and has three offences on record. I do not know whether rain should be granted." The Great Sage laughed and said, "Yesterday I already saw the Jade Emperor and asked an audience. The Jade Emperor had the Celestial Master lead me to the Hall of Fragrant Incense and show me the three matters: Mount Rice, Mount Flour, and the Golden Lock. Only if those three are overturned and broken can rain be allowed. I worried I might not be able to break them. The Celestial Master taught me to encourage the county lord and all the people to act virtuously, for when people form good intentions, Heaven must respond. If so, they may yet turn heaven’s heart and relieve this disaster. Now good-minded thoughts have suddenly arisen; sounds of devotion fill the air. Moments ago the envoy of the Direct Edict Office already conveyed a memorandum reporting this turn to virtue before the Jade Emperor. Therefore, by special approach to Your Excellency’s court, I beg to borrow officers from your thunder office to lend aid." The Honored One said, "Since this is the case, dispatch Deng, Xin, Zhang, and Tao, command the Lightning Maidens to lead them, and let them follow Sun Wukong down to Fengxian County and send thunder there."

Those four commanders and the Great Sage did not take long to reach the realm of Fengxian County. At midair they began their incantation. At once there sounded a pounding, rattling thunder, and streaking flashes of lightning were seen. Truly it was thus:

Lightning darted like a purple-gold serpent, thunder roared and the hibernating masses stirred. Brilliant fire flew in a glow, and thunderclaps split mountain caverns. Rifts of cloud-lit sky shone full, and heaven’s shock shook earth in long quivers. A scarlet spark flashed and broke forth, and for ten thousand li the land and mountains trembled. Within Fengxian County, inside and outside the city, all the great and small officials and all soldiers and commoners had gone three years without hearing thunder and seeing lightning. Today, at the roar and flash of thunder and lightning, they all knelt down together. Some held incense burners on their heads; others held willow twigs in their hands, and all chanted, "Namo Amitabha Buddha! Namo Amitabha Buddha!" This single thought of virtue truly startled Heaven. As an old verse puts it: When a single thought rises in the human heart, heaven and earth alike know it. If good and evil carried no reckoning, Heaven and Earth would surely be partial.

The text sets aside, for the moment, Sun Wukong commanding the thunder generals, hurling lightning and sounding thunder over Fengxian County, where everyone turned to good. It then says that the direct-edict envoy of the upper world brought the memorials of monk and Daoist households to the Hall of Clear Illumination, and the Four Celestial Masters reported to Lingxiao Hall. When the Jade Emperor saw them he said, "Though those rascals now have good thoughts, what of the three matters?" Just then the officer stationed in charge of the Hall of Fragrant Incense reported: "The set-up Rice Mountain and Flour Mountain have both collapsed. In but a moment, rice and flour are gone, and the lock-bar is also broken." Before that report was finished, the chariot-carrying Celestial Officer arrived, bringing and presenting the land gods of Fengxian County—Earth Lord, City God, and local spirits—who all bowed and reported together: "In this county, the county lord and all families in the town, high and low, none among the people fail to have returned to good and to take refuge in righteousness, bowing to the Buddha and honoring Heaven. Now, by your mercy, let sweet rain descend abundantly to aid the people." Hearing this, the Jade Emperor rejoiced and issued an order: "Direct the Wind Department, Cloud Department, and Rain Department each according to command. Go to the lower realms and in the bounds of Fengxian County, at this very time, send out sonorous thunder through the clouds and make it rain three chi and forty-two fen." Then the Four Great Celestial Masters, upon receiving the order, transmitted it to each department to descend at once, each displaying divine power.

The Great Sage was in the sky with Deng, Xin, Zhang, and Tao, directing the Lightning Maidens to work their art, when all the gods arrived and convened in one heavenly assembly. In the midst of it, wind and cloud met, and sweet rain poured in torrents. The good rain:

Dim and broad clouds hung low, heavy black mist filling all; thunder wagons roared, lightning flashed and blazed; rushing winds rolled in surges, sudden rains poured in torrents; this is what they say: one thought remakes Heaven, all ten thousand people live in hope. All to the Great Sage’s meritorious power, ten thousand li of hills and rivers lay under a single shade. The good rain tipped rivers and overturned the seas, covering fields and confusing sky. Waterfalls hung before the eaves, and beyond the windows rang clear chiming crashes. In ten thousand households and a thousand gates, people chanted the Buddha’s name. In six streets and three markets, waters rushed in floods. East and west waterways brimmed full, north and south creek-bays all opened. Dried shoots found moisture, withered trees revived. The fields bore hemp and wheat, village granaries swelled with grain. Travelers rejoiced and traded freely; farmers loved this season for ploughing and tilling. From now on, millet and sorghum grow in easy abundance, and harvests will naturally be rich. When wind and rain come in harmony, the people rest in peace; sea and river run clear, and all enjoy great peace. In one day the rain came down to the full measure of three chi and forty-two fen. The gods gradually began to withdraw. Then Sun Wukong shouted in a loud voice, "You four department deities, halt the clouds for the moment. I must go and ask the county lord to thank you. Please clear away the mists and show your true forms, so these mortals can see you with their own eyes and thereby give you true faith and offerings." The gods heard him and therefore held still in the sky.

The Great Sage alighted from his cloud-head and went straight into the county. Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing were already there to welcome him, and the county lord came bowing one step at a time in thanks. The Great Sage said, "No need to thank me yet. I have detained the gods of the four departments; you may now summon many and have them together offer gratitude, and instruct them to come here whenever rain is needed." The county lord immediately spread the summons, and all came forth to give incense and homage. At once the four department gods parted the bright cloud mists and revealed their true forms. The four were the Rain Department, the Thunder Department, the Cloud Department, and the Wind Department. Then it appeared:

The Dragon King revealed his image, and the Thunder General stretched his powerful form; A cloud youth appeared, and the Wind Lord displayed his true self. The Dragon King’s form—silver-bearded and blue-faced—was unmatched in this world; The Thunder General stretched to his full form, his hooked mouth and severe countenance beyond compare; The cloud youth appeared, who could match that jade-faced one with a gold crown? The Wind Duke in true form seemed to have an eye-ringed brow and a dry, fierce gaze. Together they appeared in the azure heavens, each standing in proper rank in sacred array. In the realm of Fengxian County now all men of learning came to bow, incense in hand; evil nature turned. Today they faced Heaven’s generals, cleansed their hearts, and turned wholly to devotion. The gods remained for one full period while the people continued to offer worship without end. Sun Wukong rose again among the clouds, bowed to them, and said, "You have labored much, truly much. Please, each of you, return to your own department. As for Sun Wukong, he also teaches the families in this commandery to uphold high spirits and, at each season, make sacrificial thanks. From now on, every five days wind and every ten days rain—then return and save us again and again." The gods followed his words and returned to their respective departments, and nothing more is noted.

The Great Sage dropped from the cloud and said to Tripitaka, "The affair is complete, the people are secure, and we may make ready to travel on." When the county lord heard this, he hurriedly bowed and said, "Master Sun says he can leave at once? This time is an immeasurable, boundless kindness and grace. This servant will send men at once to prepare a small feast in return for this great favor. I will also buy land for the people and have a monastery built in honor of the Great Sage, with a memorial shrine raised in your honor and a stele engraved with your name, to be maintained with offerings through all four seasons. Though my bones and heart are carved and incised, they could never repay even a thousandth part; how can you now speak of setting out on the road?" Tripitaka replied, "The district lord speaks truly. But we are monks of the Western pilgrimage and dare not stay long; within a day or two we are certain to depart." Yet the county lord would not release him. Through that same night he sent many men to prepare the banquet and to build the shrines.

The next day, a great feast was opened in full. Tripitaka was set at the high seat; Sun Wukong sat with Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing in proper places. The county lord, together with his county officials and all subordinate ministers, presented cups and dishes in turn, while soft flutes and light drums accompanied a day of careful hosting. The occasion was indeed joyous. A poem bears witness:

Long-droughted fields now meet sweet rain, and the river routes that carry trade run free throughout the land. With deep gratitude we feel the divine monk’s coming to our commandery, and the Great Sage’s ascent to Heaven’s palace. The three former evils are undone, and one thought of devotion brings forth the ripe fruit of goodness. From now on, may we be like Yao and Shun’s age: five winds and ten rains, abundance for ten thousand years. One banquet for one day, another banquet for two days; gratitude today, thanks tomorrow. The monks would stay for half a month, waiting only until the monastery and memorial shrines were complete. One day the county lord invited the four to inspect it. Tripitaka exclaimed in surprise, "The task was vast—how could it be completed so swiftly?" The county lord said, "This servant pressed the workers hard, day and night without pause, and hastened the work to completion. Please, honored lords, take a look." The Great Sage laughed, "He is indeed a worthy and capable good governor." At once they all came to the new monastery and saw the tall halls and pavilions, and the lofty mountain gate. All praised it without restraint. Sun Wukong asked the Master to assign a name to the monastery. Tripitaka said, "Yes. Let its name be 'Ganlin Puzhi Temple.'" The county lord praised him: "Excellent, excellent." He then used gilded tablets to summon many monks widely for offerings and incense service. On the left side of the main hall he ordered four memorial shrines for the Four to be erected, for seasonal rites each year; he also ordered temples for the Thunder God, Dragon God, and others to repay divine merit. When all had been seen, he ordered the departure preparations.

The people of the county, knowing they could not stay long, each prepared parting gifts and would not receive any payments. So all county officials and the people together raised great drums and raised banners high, escorting the parting party for nearly thirty li from both near and distant. Even so they could not bear to part, so they covered their tears and sent them off until they could no longer see them. It is exactly as in the verse:

The accomplished divine monk leaves after broad mercy and rescue. The Great Sage who aligns Heaven extends wide benevolence.

It is not yet known how many more days it will be before they see the Buddha from this point. Listen for the explanation in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 87: The county of Fengxian is blamed for Heaven-sent drought; Great Sage Sun urges merit and sends down rain.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

After joyfully bidding farewell to the county marquis, Tripitaka, still in the saddle, called to Sun Wukong: “Worthy disciple, this merit of yours is truly greater than the rescue of children in the Bhikṣu kingdom; it is all your doing.” Sha Wujing said: “In the Bhikṣu kingdom only one thousand one hundred and eleven children were saved. How can that compare with this great downpour, all-soaking and life-giving, by which ten thousand times ten thousand lives were preserved? Your junior disciple also praises in secret Brother Sun’s sky-reaching powers and earth-covering benevolence.” Zhu Bajie laughed: “Brother has done kindness, and indeed done good, but only outwardly shows grace and righteousness while hiding peril within. To travel with old Pig, all one gets is to be trodden upon. Where am I being trampled?” Sun Wuking replied: “Where would I trample you?” Zhu Bajie said: “Enough, enough. You always tend my bindings, tend my hanging, tend my boiling, and tend my steaming. Now here in Fengxian County you have shown kindness to myriad people; you should stay for half a year, carry me to eat a few full, carefree meals, and yet only keep pressing us onward.” Hearing this, the Master thundered: “You fool, why are you thinking only about your mouth? Walk on quickly, and do not argue anymore.” Zhu Bajie dared not speak. He cupped his mouth shut, hoisted his pack, and laughed foolishly as they all ran along the great road. At that time the passage of time felt as swift as a shuttle, and it was already deep autumn, but this was seen:

The water stains have withdrawn and the mountains stand lean. Scarlet leaves whirl in torrents, the yellow flowers are at their time. Frost-cleansed moonlight makes the nights feel long, and pale moonlight pierces through windows. In every home, hearth-smoke and evening sun are plenty; everywhere lake-light slips over cold water. The white cattails scent the air; crimson smartweed grows thick. Greenish orange and yellow tangerine, withered willows, flourishing grain. In abandoned villages the geese come down among broken reed blossoms; at wild inns, chickens call out while the sound gathers among beans and peas. After the four had walked for quite a while, they again saw the shadowy outline of city walls. The Master raised his whip, pointed afar, and called out: “Wukong, look there—another city, yet we know not what place.” Sun Wukong answered: “Neither of us has ever been there; how could we know? Let us go up to the edge and ask people.” Before he had finished, suddenly a man came out from a thicket of trees: a bamboo staff in hand, light robes on his body, a pair of brown shoes on his feet, and a flat belt around his waist. Startled, Tripitaka rolled from the saddle and dismounted, stepping forward to offer proper greetings. The old man braced on his staff and returned the courtesy: “Which land has the Elder come from?” Tripitaka joined his palms: “This poor monk is a pilgrim from the Great Tang of the eastern lands, sent to Leiyin to worship Buddha and seek the scriptures. I have arrived in this Precious Territory and, seeing the city walls from afar, do not know its whereabouts; I beg this elder householder to give instruction.” Hearing that, the old man said: “Venerable Patriarch, this humble place is in the Tianzhu kingdom, a lower prefecture called Yuhua County. The lord of this city is a kinsman of the Tianzhu emperor, enfeoffed as King Yuhua. He is a very worthy king, reverent toward monks and Taoist sages alike, and deeply fond of the common people. If you, Reverend Monk, go to meet him, you will be received with great honor.” Tripitaka thanked him. The old man then slipped straight back through the woods and left.

Tripitaka only then turned and briefed the disciples on what had happened. The three disciples were delighted, and helped Master set him back on the horse. Tripitaka said, “There is not much road ahead, no need to ride.” The four therefore walked to the edge of the city street and looked about. It turned out that the households in that district were engaged in buying and selling, with crowds of people gathering and commerce thriving handsomely. By voice and appearance, they were no different from those of China. Tripitaka instructed: “Disciples, be careful; do not be unrestrained in any way.” Zhu Bajie lowered his head, and Sha Wujing covered his face, while only Sun Wukong supported the Master. People came from both sides and pressed for a look, all calling out at once: “Here we only have high monks who can tame dragon-conquering, tiger-subduing spirits; we have never seen a monk who subdues pigs and tames monkeys.” Zhu Bajie could not help himself; he puckered his mouth and said, “Have you ever seen a monk that subdued the Pig King?” In panic, people across the whole street stumbled and sidestepped in both directions. Sun Wukong laughed: “Idiot, hold your mouth in, do not put on a show, and mind your footing over the bridge.” That fool kept his head down and only smiled. After crossing the hanging bridge and entering through the gate, they saw that on the main street stood taverns and songhouses; it was lively and magnificent—truly a capital city of the Central Plains. A poem attests to this:

Brocade city, iron-walled, firm for ten thousand years, set by water and leaning on the hills, its colours vivid. Goods flow from the lakes, and boats enter the market; a thousand homes draw curtains over taverns of wine. In towers and pavilions, smoke from every home stretches wide; every alley in every dawn is loud with guests and merchants. No less beautiful than the scenery of Chang'an, rooster cries and dog barks sound all the same. Tripitaka quietly rejoiced: “People say that the Western Regions are lands of many tribes, and I have never yet arrived there. Looking carefully at this scene, it is no different from our Great Tang. One might call this truly a Pure Land.” He also heard people say that white rice sold for four qian a shi and sesame oil eight li a jin. Truly this is a land of full grain harvests.

After walking for a while, they at last reached the Yuhua King’s compound. To the left and right of the gate were the Hall of the Chief Clerk, the Tribunal Hall, the Household Kitchen Office, and the Guest Pavilion. Tripitaka said: “Disciples, this is the estate office. I will go in, pay homage to the king, and present my credentials.” Zhu Bajie asked, “If Master goes in, may we stand at the yamen gate?” Tripitaka said: “Do you not see these words ‘Guest Pavilion’ above the gate? You all go there and sit. See if there is grass feed, and buy some for the horses. If I am granted a meal there, I will come and call you to share it.” Sun Wukong said: “Master, go in with your mind at ease; Old Monkey will attend to everything.” Sha Wujing carried the luggage into the pavilion. In the pavilion there were officials and attendants, and seeing their ugly faces, they dared not question them nor tell them to leave; they only let them sit down and make no further move.

The master changed his hat and robes, took the travel credentials, and went straight to the front of the king’s hall. He saw at once a ceremonial usher who came out to receive him and asked: “Elder, whence do you come?” Tripitaka said: “A monk from the Great Tang in the eastern lands has been dispatched to Leiyin to worship Buddha and request scriptures. I have come to this noble land and wish to have my credentials accepted and exchanged; therefore I come to pay court to the Lord of a Thousand Years.” The usher immediately conveyed the report. The Yuhua King was indeed wise and capable; he at once issued an order of summons. Tripitaka offered his bows in the hall, and the king invited him up and granted him a seat. Tripitaka presented the credentials. The king read them, saw seals from many countries and the hand impressions beneath, and gladly impressed the royal seal, added vermilion script, and set the folded paper on the desk. He asked: “Venerable Master from the Great Tang, from your homeland to here, having traveled through many kingdoms, how many distances have you covered in all?” Tripitaka answered: “This poor monk has not kept count of the miles. But many years ago, Guanyin Bodhisattva once revealed himself before my sovereign and left a verse, saying that the Western Regions are ten thousand and eight thousand li away. This poor monk, along with this road, has already endured fourteen cycles of cold and warmth.” The king smiled: “Fourteen cycles of cold and warmth means fourteen years. I suppose there must have been some delays along the way?” Tripitaka said: “It is hard to tell in one phrase. A myriad hidden monsters and ten thousand demons—who can know how much suffering was borne to arrive at this Precious Land?” The king was very pleased and instructed the official in charge of the kitchen to prepare a vegetarian meal. Tripitaka said: “I beg to report, Your Majesty: the poor monk has three young disciples waiting outside, and does not dare to receive alms alone, yet fears delay to the journey.” The king ordered: “Summons the hall officials; go quickly and call the Elder’s three disciples, so that they may enter the residence and share this meal.”

The hall official went out to issue the summons at the gate, and all of them said, “Never seen, never seen.” One of the attendants said, “In the Guest Pavilion there are three grim-looking monks seated; surely they must be those.” When the hall official and company came to the pavilion, he asked the host there: “Which is the senior disciple of the Tripitaka monk from the Great Tang? My lord has ordered that they be invited to the meal.” Zhu Bajie had been dozing while seated. Hearing the word “meal,” he could not help himself and sprang up, answering, “We are, we are.” At first glance, the hall official was shaken to the core, his soul seeming to leave him; he spoke timidly, “It is a pig spirit, a pig spirit.” Sun Wukong heard and pulled Zhu Bajie: “Brother, keep more civil, do not act rough and rustic.” The officials then saw Sun Wukong and exclaimed: “It is a monkey spirit, a monkey spirit.” Sha Wujing clasped his hands and said: “Gentlemen, do not be alarmed. All three of us are disciples of Tripitaka.” The officials repeated: “Zaojun, Zaojun.” Sun Wukong then told Zhu Bajie to lead the horse and Sha Wujing to carry the pole-load, and with everyone together they entered the Yuhua King’s residence. The hall official entered first and conveyed the report.

The king lifted his gaze and saw those ugly faces, yet he too was inwardly fearful. Tripitaka folded his hands and said: “Your Majesty, do not worry. Though unruly disciples are hideous in appearance, they all have upright hearts.” Zhu Bajie bowed up to the side and said, “The poor monk makes his respectful greeting.” The king became even more uneasy. Tripitaka explained: “These unruly disciples were taken in from the wilds and fields; they do not know how to observe proper ceremony. Kindly forgive their offense.” Fearful though he was, the king ordered the steward of provisions to invite all the monks to the Canopy Pavilion for the meal. Tripitaka thanked him and, descending from the hall with the Master, complained on the way: “You foolish lump, not knowing a single point of decorum. If only you would keep silent, that would do; why such rudeness? A single word from you could bring down Mount Tai.” Sun Wukong laughed: “Even better if I do not bow at all—then I would save some strength.” Sha Wujing said: “When he does bow, he does so out of time and already begins with shouting through his mouth.” Zhu Bajie said: “A lively rascal, a lively rascal. The day before, Master taught me that greeting and asking after health is proper when meeting a person; today, even in making greetings, you say it is wrong. Why do you tell me to do such a thing?” Tripitaka said: “I taught you to offer greetings after meeting others; I did not teach you to drag the speech this far before a prince. As it is said, ‘There are many kinds of things, and there are many kinds of people.’ How could you fail to distinguish between high and low?” As he said this, the official in charge of offerings came leading attendants, moved out the tables and stools, and set out the meal. The Master and disciples made no remark; each ate the meal in silence.

Then the prince withdrew from the hall and re-entered the palace. There were three young princes in the inner court; seeing his face had lost its colour, they asked, “Why is Father so alarmed today?” He said, “A while ago there came a monk from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, sent on an errand to beg Buddha for the scriptures. He showed me his crossing pass, yet his mien was extraordinary. I made him stay for a vegetarian meal; he said he had disciples at my gate, so I immediately ordered them to be summoned. They arrived shortly, but when they entered and did not make full obeisance to me or give proper greetings, I was not pleased. Then when I raised my head and saw them, each looked ugly as a demon, and I was startled in my heart—hence my face changed color.” It turned out these three young princes were unlike others; each was strong and mighty, so they curled their sleeves and raised their fists, saying, “Could these not be mountain demons from the wild, pretending to be men? Let us take up weapons and check them.”

The eldest prince took a Qimei staff, the second brandished a nine-toothed halberd, and the third wielded an oiled-black staff. Broad-shouldered and proud, they strode out of the pavilion and shouted, “Where is that monk seeking the scriptures?” Some pantry officials knelt and said, “Your Highness, they are at the Baosha Pavilion taking the offered meal.” The little prince, with no judgment of good or evil, pushed straight inside and roared, “Are you men or monsters? Speak at once—if not, I will spare your lives only in words.” Tripitaka was startled, his face paling; he dropped his bowl and bent low: “I am a monk from Tang on a scripture mission. I am a man, not a demon.” The prince said, “You at least look like a man; those three hideous ones are surely monsters.” Zhu Bajie kept right on eating, paying no attention. Sha Wujing and the Monkey King bowed and said, “All four of us are men. Though we have ugly faces, our hearts are good; though our bodies are rough, our natures are kind. You three, where did you come from that you are so loud-mouthed and reckless?” An attendant explained, “The three are Your Highness’s young princes.” Zhu Bajie dropped his bowl and said, “Your Highness, why does each of you have a weapon in hand? Are you going to fight us?”

The second prince stepped forward, twirled the halberd with both hands, and prepared to strike at Zhu Bajie. Zhu Bajie chuckled and said, “Your halberd is only good to be a grandson to mine in such a match.” He stripped off his coat, drew out his own halberd at his waist, gave it a swift whirl, and gold rays streamed in ten thousand shafts. He spoke an incantation, and a thousand threads of auspicious vapour rose. The prince, struck with fright, had weak hands and numb limbs and dared not move. Seeing the eldest prince using a Qimei staff, the Monkey King sprang lightly and, from his ear, took out the Golden-Hooped Staff. He gave it one whirl; it was thin as a bowl in girth, and two or three zhang in length. One thrust to the ground made a pit of three feet, and it stood upright there. He laughed, “Take this staff and be done with it.” Hearing this, the prince dropped his own staff and reached for that one, but even with all his strength in both hands he could not move it a hair’s breadth. He then grasped the other end and shook it—yet it held fast like a rooted tree. The third prince, all reckless fury, came down with the oiled-black staff to strike. Sha Wujing split it open with one hand, brought out the Subduing-Demon Treasured Staff, twisted its tip, and a lustrous light flashed forth in flickering scarlet radiance. Even the pantry officials and attendants stood stunned, dazed and unable to speak. The three young princes knelt together and said, “Revered Master, we are but mortals and do not understand. We beg you, show us some skill. We wish to pay homage and learn.” The Monkey King stepped close, lifted the staff easily, and said, “This place is too narrow to display a full performance. Let me jump into the air and show one sequence—you all watch.”

‘Great Sage’ gave a whistle, shook the cudgel, and with both feet stepping on five-coloured auspicious clouds rose into midair, about three hundred paces above the ground. He flung the Golden-Hooped Staff into a move called ‘Flowers Strewn Like a Canopy,’ then ‘Yellow Dragon Turns Around,’ up and down, left and right, spinning. At first one could see man and staff together, like embroidery adorning silk; later the man disappeared and only a single staff could be seen, rolling through the sky. From below, Zhu Bajie called out in approval and could not hold back. He roared, “Let old Pig go show one too.” The good fool mounted the wind himself and rose into the air, tossing the halberd in sweeping arcs—up three, down four, left five, right six, front seven, back eight—with every part of his body put on display. Only the whistling of wind could be heard. When he reached the uproar’s height, Sha Wujing said to the Master, “Master, let old Sha perform as well.” The good monk leapt, staff in hand, into the air. His aura shimmered, and pale gold light spread far. With both hands he tossed the Subduing-Demon Staff in one move, ‘Phoenix of Vermilion Faces the Sun,’ then ‘Hungry Tiger Pounces,’ closing in, retreating to block, then wheeling and darting in haste. The three brothers showed full divine prowess together, all of them in that half-sky, jointly proclaiming and displaying their power. This was then:

The true Zen vision is extraordinary, peerless and vast, The Way’s origin fills all the heavens. Gold and wood deploy their might, overwhelming the Dharma realm, Blade and ritual measure rotate together in perfect completion. Divine weapons show their keen ranks at every instant, Cinnabar vessels bloom with wonder wherever praised. Though Heaven of the Western Region be lofty, restraint is still the path, Prince Yuhua at last returns to the center. The three young princes were terrified and knelt in the dust. All the staff of the Baosha Pavilion, the old king’s household, and all the city’s soldiers and civilians, men and women, monks and nuns and lay people—all came and chanted Buddha’s name, kowtowed and burned incense in every home and court. Truly: Beholding that form that returns to truth and ferries all the monks, In the world of men, merits are made and peace made plain. From now on one truly treads the Bodhi Way, All become seekers of Chan and worshippers of Buddha. Each of the three had fully displayed his martial power, brought down the auspicious clouds, and gathered his weapon. They came before Tripitaka, made their respects, thanked him for the masterly grace, and sat down. No further account is needed.

The three young princes hurried back into the palace and reported to the old king: “Father, this is a hundred-thousandfold joy—today we have achieved a mighty feat. Just now, did you see the displays in the sky?” The king said, “I only saw auspicious colours in the sky and then, with your mother and the rest, burned incense and offered worship in the palace court. I do not know which immortal descended from where.” The prince replied, “It was not one of those. It was exactly the three ugly disciples of that scripture monk. One wielded a Golden-Hooped Staff, one a nine-toothed nail-fork, one the Subduing-Demon Treasured Staff. They were equal to our weapons; not one was inferior. When we asked them to show one set, he said, ‘The ground is narrow; it is no place to stretch out. Let me rise in the air and show you then.’ They mounted the cloud-head one after another. The whole sky was filled with faint auspicious clouds; bright fragrance-like vapour hung in the air. When they came down, all sat in the Baosha Pavilion. The boy—very happy—wished to make him a disciple, learn his methods, and guard our land. This is truly a meritorious deed of the greatest size. I do not know how Father will think of it.” Hearing this, the king accepted the plea at once with whole-hearted conviction.

At that moment the four father-and-son party came out without pavilion carriage, without canopy, and walked to the Baosha Pavilion. The four attendants gathered their luggage and intended to return to the residence to thank and depart, when by chance they saw King Yuhua and his sons coming up to the pavilion and they immediately prostrated themselves. The startled Master hastily straightened and, falling to the ground, returned the reverence; the Monkey King and others slipped to the side with faint cold smiles. After all had bowed, they invited the four to sit in the hall. All four entered with delight. The king rose and said, “Venerable Tripitaka, I have one wish. I do not know whether your three senior disciples might allow it.” Tripitaka said, “I can only obey the command of the Thousand-Year Elder; my junior disciples dare not refuse.” The king said, “When I first saw you all, I took you only for travelling monks from Tang. In truth, with mortal eyes and mortal flesh, I repeatedly treated you with disrespect. Only when I later saw Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing dance in the sky did I realize you were immortal and Buddha-like. My three sons have all their lives been fond of martial arts. Now I make a sincere appeal, desiring to accept them as disciples and learn some martial arts. I beseech you, with a heart that opens heaven and earth, to set in motion your boat of compassion and guide these children. I will repay you with the wealth of this city.” The Monkey King, hearing this, could not help but laugh and say, “Your Highness, you are truly a poor manager. We ordained folk would love nothing more than to transmit a few disciples. Since your sons have a mind to follow the good, do not speak at all of any profit; if there is feeling between us, that alone is enough.”

The prince heard this and was deeply pleased. He ordered a grand banquet at once. In the main hall of the residence, all the seats were set. With one command, all was completed instantly. Behold:

Tresses of bright-coloured silk streamed in fluttering arcs, and fragrant incense smoke rose dense and rich. Gold-rimmed tables hung with tightly bound gauze dazzled the eye. The painted lacquer chairs, covered in brocade, made the seating radiant. Fresh fruit was arranged, tea steam was fragrant in the air. Three or five kinds of light, sweet snacks were prepared, and one or two baskets of generous buns. The steamed pastries, crisp as a blessing and honey-fried, were marvellous beyond measure; fried sweets drenched with sugar-syrup were truly beautiful. There were a few bottles of fragrant glutinous wine, and once poured out it surpassed nectar; several rounds of Yangxian Immortal tea were presented, and when carried in hand, its fragrance outshone osmanthus bloom. Every single item was in place, every kind surprising. A side pavilion rang with music for songs and dance, with wind and strings for lively play, and staged performances were presented. The master and his disciples, together with the king and his sons, all delighted through the day.

It was already late, and none noticed that night had fallen before the wine feast was dismissed. Then he ordered, at once, that bedding and curtains be laid in the Baosha Pavilion and invited the Master to rest there. By dawn he would burn incense with all sincerity, then bow again and beg to be taught the martial arts. All obeyed; they prepared scented bathwater and invited the Master to bathe, while the rest withdrew to bed. At this moment:

The wild birds settle in high nests, and all grows still; the poet takes leave of his couch and stops his chanting. Milky Way light shines, and heaven grows clearer and brighter. The pounding stones in the side court ring ding-dong. Across the distant passes, empty hills awaken homesickness. The cold crickets cry aloud, knowing men’s hearts, and their rustling at the bed’s head tears apart the dream-thought. One night’s scene was written in this way. At dawn the old king and his sons came again to visit. Yesterday, on their first meeting, they had offered him kingly civility; today they offered him the rite of receiving a Master. The three young princes knelt before Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing and asked, 'Respected Master, could we bring out your weapons and let the disciples see them?' At once Zhu Bajie, delighted, took out his spiked weapon and tossed it to the ground. Sha Wujing set down his precious staff and leaned it against the wall. The second and third princes sprang forward to seize them; like dragonflies shaking a stone pillar, each strained and strained and was left red-faced and hot, unable to move even a hair’s breadth. Seeing this, the eldest said, 'Brothers, do not waste yourselves. The Master’s weapons are all divine arms—who can know how heavy they are?' Zhu Bajie laughed, 'My spiked weapon is not much heavier. As for the shaft and all, it is five thousand forty-eight jin.' The third prince asked Sha Wujing, 'How heavy is the Master’s staff?' Sha Wujing smiled, 'It is also five thousand forty-eight jin.' The eldest asked to see Sun Wukong’s Golden-Hooped Staff. Sun Wukong took a pin from his ear, let it flutter into the wind, and at once it became bowl-wide and stood straight upright before him. All the father and sons of the king were startled; every official’s heart trembled. The three young princes knelt in reverence, saying, 'Pig Master Zhu and Monk Sha keep their weapons hidden under their robes at all times; we can take them out at once. Why does Master Sun draw his from his ear and, facing the wind, make it grow instantly?' Sun Wukong laughed, 'You do not know this staff; such a thing does not exist casually in the mortal world. This is: At the first fog of Great Vastness, bronze-iron was cast and tempered, and the divine craftsman of Great Yu set it forth. Lakes, seas, and rivers, shallow and deep, were all measured by it in turn. When mountains were moved and waters levelled in the age of peace, it drifted to the eastern seas at Dongyang, guarding the sea pass. Through age upon age, it glows with auspicious light, able to shrink, able to lengthen, ever clear and bright. It is destined that Old Monkey will take it in time, with unlimited transformations, obeying but one formula. It can be vast beyond the universe, and yet small as the joint of a needle. Its name is Ruyi, called the Golden-Hooped Staff, and in heaven and on earth it is praised as peerless. Its weight is reckoned one thousand three hundred and fifty jin, and whether thick or thin it can appear and vanish. It has helped me shake the heavenly palace, and with me it has stormed the earthly gates. It passes everywhere to subdue tigers and conquer dragons, and in purging demons and casting out monsters it is utterly penetrating. Lift your head and point once, and the sun itself seems to dim; heaven and earth, ghosts and gods all grow timid. This is the divine relic of Primordial Chaos down to this day, and is no iron of ordinary people.' Hearing this, each prince knelt in repeated, unending bows. The three stepped forward and bowed heavily, and with single-minded hearts sought instruction. Sun Wukong asked, 'You three are not sure which martial arts to learn, are you?' The princes answered, 'Let the one used to cudgels learn cudgel-play, the one used to the spade-lever learn that, and the one who loves staffs learn staff-play.' Sun Wukong laughed, 'To teach them is easy enough, but you lack the strength to wield our weapons; you may learn imperfectly, like trying to draw a tiger and ending with a dog. As the ancients say: The teacher’s fault is lax teaching, and the student’s fault is poor learning. Since you are sincerely willing, burn incense, bow to Heaven and Earth first, and I shall first transmit some divine power; then I will teach the arts.'

The three princes were overjoyed at these words. They personally raised the incense table, washed their hands, burned incense, and bowed toward Heaven. When that was done, they asked the Master to transmit the Dharma. Sun Wukong knelt down and bowed to Tripitaka, saying, 'Tell the honored Teacher to pardon this disciple’s fault. Since the day on Two Realms Mountain when Great Teacher rescued this disciple and with great grace saved me; I took up the monk’s precepts and have come westward all along. I have not repaid my Teacher in full, yet I have crossed waters and climbed mountains, exhausting myself. Now, in the land of the Buddha, it is my fortune to have met the three worthy sons of King Ren, and they come to bow to us, wishing to learn martial arts. Since they are disciples of mine, they are the Teacher’s disciple-children through me. I respectfully report this to my Teacher, hoping he will allow instruction.' Tripitaka was greatly delighted. Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, seeing Sun Wukong bow, turned at once and knelt before Tripitaka: 'Master, we are simple and dull, with blunt tongues and slow faces; we do not know how to speak well. Please sit high in your Dharma seat and let each of us take one disciple to play and practice, so that our journey to the West may have something to remember.' Tripitaka gladly approved.

Sun Wukong then took the three princes to the Quiet Chamber behind the Baosha Pavilion and drew a Gangdou formation. He ordered all three to lie prone within it, eyes closed and spirit settled. There, in silence, he chanted true words and recited spells, blowing immortal qi into the depths of their hearts and drawing their original spirits back to their true dwelling. He transmitted the oral formula and conferred upon each of them strength in the thousandfold measure; he added firepower in perfect timing, and it was like a transfiguration of body and bone. After he made the cycle of Zi and Wu pass through them, the three princes finally awakened. At once they all got up together, wiped their faces, and stood braced with spirit, each one full-bodied and sinewy. The eldest grasped the Golden-Hooped Staff, the second raised the Nine-Tusked Spiked Weapon, and the third lifted the Demon-Subduing Staff.

The king rejoiced beyond measure. He hosted a plain banquet again and offered thanks to the four in the monastic party. Then, before the feast, he taught each according to ability: those who learned staffs showed staff forms, those who learned the spiked weapon showed that art, and those who learned the staff likewise practiced it. Though they could turn a few times and throw out a few techniques, they were still mere mortals and lacked true force: one stretch and they were already panting, unable to endure long. The reason was that their weapons all could transform; their advance and retreat, their attacks and counterstrikes, could all lengthen or shorten at will and carried a natural subtlety. These men were still ordinary people—how could they in a moment arrive at it? The banquet ended that day.

The next day the three princes returned to give thanks and said, 'By your divine grace we have been granted strength. Even though we can wield the Master’s weapons, changing them in form is still difficult. We wish to order craftsmen to forge copies in the same pattern but lighter in weight, if the Master permits. Is that acceptable?' Zhu Bajie said, 'Well said—well said indeed, it is reasonable. Your weapons, one, you cannot wield as we do; two, we must protect the Dharma and subdue demons, and in truth we should make separate ones.' The princes immediately summoned the blacksmiths, bought ten thousand jin of steel, and in the front court of the king’s residence set up a foundry and raised crucibles for casting. On the first day they refined the steel thoroughly. On the next, they asked the three disciples of Sun Wukong to bring out the Golden-Hooped Staff, the Nine-Tusked Spiked Weapon, and the Demon-Subduing Staff, and placed them among the casting sheds as models. From then on they labored day and night without rest.

Ah! These weapons were treasures they always carried upon their persons and could not be apart from even for an instant, each hidden on the body and wrapped in its own light to guard the form. Now that they lay in the foundry court for several days, ten thousand rays of rosy radiance rose to heaven and auspicious vapor of a thousand kinds spread across the earth. That night a demon spirit dwelling about seventy li from the city—his mountain called Leopard-Head Mountain, his cave called Tiger-Mouthed Cave—while sitting in the dark saw, in a flash, the rosy light and auspicious vapor. He rode on clouds to look, and when he saw where the brilliance arose, it was inside the king’s manor. He lowered his cloud platform and came near to inspect. It was these three kinds of weapons shining with light. The demon, both joyful and lustful, said, 'Fine treasures, fine treasures. For whom are these? How can they be set here now? They are under my destined affinity. Take them, take them!' His desire rose, he set himself in terrifying display, and gathered all three weapons in one sweep, then went straight back to his cave. As the line says:

One must not leave the Way even for an instant; if one does, it is not the Way. The divine weapons have fallen into emptiness; all that toiling cultivation is wasted.

Still unknown is how those weapons were ultimately recovered. Listen, and hear the resolution in the next chapter.
