Later, in the courtyard several of the blacksmiths, worn out from days of labor, had all fallen asleep at night. At daybreak they rose to resume forging, and beneath the canopy the three kinds of weapons were not to be found. One and all they stood there, stupefied and frightened, searching all around. Just then the three princes came out of the palace to inspect, and the smiths knelt together and said, “Young master, the three weapons of the holy Master are gone, and no one knows where they are.”

The young prince heard this and, pale with alarm, said, “I suppose Master must have packed them away last night.” He hurried to the pavilion to check, and seeing White Horse still beneath the corridor, could not help crying out, “Is Master still asleep?” Sha Wujing said, “He has risen.” He opened the chamber door and let the prince in to look; when no weapons appeared, he asked in a fluster, “Have you gathered Master’s weapons?” Sun Wukong leapt up and said, “I have not.” The prince said, “All three weapons are missing tonight.” Zhu Bajie scrambled up at once, asking, “Is my pa there?” The prince explained, “A little while ago we all came out and saw everyone searching front and back in vain. The disciple feared Master had collected them, so we came to ask. Master’s treasures can lengthen and shrink at will; surely he has them hidden on him and is teasing the disciples.” Sun Wukong said, “I did not gather them. All of us, go and search.”

Following him to the tent in the courtyard, there was indeed no sign of them. Zhu Bajie said, “It must be these blacksmiths who stole them. Bring them out. If they delay even a little, I will beat them all to death, to death!” The smiths, frightened, knelt and wept, saying, “My lord, we have toiled without rest day after day. We slept through the night, and then when we rose at daybreak everything was gone. We are only common men—how could we carry these off? Please spare our lives, please spare us.” Sun Wukong was silent and inwardly resentful: “The fault is our own. We had already seen the pattern, so we should have kept them on our person. Why did we leave them here? Those treasures shimmered with rosy radiance; surely they startled some rogue and he stole them in the night.” Zhu Bajie refused to believe it: “What are you saying, brother? This is a peaceful land, not some desolate wild mountain. How could a villain come here? It must be the blacksmiths being deceitful. Seeing the brilliance of our weapons, they recognized three precious treasures, slipped out of the prince’s court in a band at night, and lugged them away. Bring them here and strike them, strike them.” The smiths only knelt and swore innocence.

At that clamour, the elder prince came out, heard the matter through, and though his face gave no sign, he paused in thought and said, “The holy Master’s weapons are not like ordinary things—no matter if one hundred or more men tried, they could not force them. As for me, living in this city for five generations, I am no reckless adventurer; I have a modest reputation outside as well. The soldiers, civilians, and makers in this city all fear my discipline and would never dare be dishonest. Ask the holy Master to think it over once more.” Sun Wukong smiled, “There is no need to think further, nor need we burden the blacksmiths. Your Highness, tell me—are there any mountain or forest demons on the edge of this prefecture?” The prince said, “Your question is very reasonable. North of this city is Leopard-Head Mountain. In that mountain is a cave called Tiger-Mouth Cavern. At times people say an immortal dwells within it, at times they say tiger and wolf, at times a demon. I have not gone to confirm it myself; I do not know what in truth it is.” Sun Wukong laughed, “No need to say more. Certainly it is the rogues there. They saw they were treasures and stole all three in one night.” He then ordered, “Zhu Bajie, Sha Wujing—you both stay here to guard Master and protect the city. Let Sun Wukong go searching.” He also told the blacksmiths, “Do not let your furnaces go cold. Continue forging as you can, one by one.”

Good Monkey King, after bidding Tripitaka farewell he whistled sharply; in a moment he vanished and had already crossed to Leopard-Head Mountain. In truth the city was only thirty li away, and he arrived in an instant. He climbed up to look at the mountain’s peak and saw at once a hint of demon air. Truly it was:

The dragon-veins ran long, and the land spread wide. The pointed peaks thrust upward, high as piercing the sky; steep ravines thudded with swift, deep-flowing water. Before the mountain grew jade grass spread like a rug; behind it wondrous flowers lay like brocade. Lofty pines and aged cypresses, old trees and fine bamboos. Mountain crows and magpies flew about in loud, scattered cries; wild cranes and wild monkeys all shrieked. Beneath the cliffs, elk in pairs; before the abrupt walls, badger-foxes in pairs. Rising and sinking in turns, distant dragon-lines bent and folded in nine curves and nine bays, veiling the earth’s veins. At the ridge, it touched Yuhua Prefecture—a place of flourishing glory through ten thousand ages. As Sun Wukong was still at it, he suddenly heard voices behind the mountain. Turning back, he saw two wolf-headed demons speaking loudly, heading up toward the northwest. Sun Wukong thought, “These must be patrolling monsters. I will follow them and listen to what they say.” He pinched his secret, recited a spell, transformed his body, becoming a butterfly. He spread his wings and fluttered in looping flight, giving chase directly. He had truly taken an excellent form: A pair of pink wings, two streaks of silver whiskers. He flew swiftly borne by the wind, and in sunlight danced with gentle ease. He crossed water and cleared walls with quick cleverness, delighted in playful flirtation with scents and drifting petals. His body, light by nature, loved the fragrance of fresh flowers; graceful mood and elegance rose and fell in free play. He hovered over the heads of the demons and listened while they talked. One demon cried out, “Second brother, our king has had great luck lately. Last month he gained a beauty and kept her in the cave, and they were delighted. Last night he gained three weapons—true, they are priceless treasures. Tomorrow we will hold a banquet to celebrate the Dingba.” The other said, “We too have some luck: with these twenty taels of silver we can buy pigs and sheep. Now that we have reached Qianfang Market, we will first drink a few jars of wine. Put up a flowered tent for the matter, spend two or three taels there, and buy some padded robes for the cold—would that not be good?” The two demons kept speaking and laughing, then hurried away down the main road like flying birds.

When Sun Wukong heard that they planned to hold a Dingba banquet, he rejoiced inwardly. He wished to kill them at once, but they were not within his immediate business, and he had no weapon in hand. So he flew forward, returned to his true form, and stood at the road junction. As that demon came close enough to come within sight, Sun Wukong spat out a spell-spit in one breath and cried, “Ān Hōng Zhā Lī,” then employed an immobilization spell, fixing the two wolf-headed spirits in place. Their eyes were open, yet their mouths could not open; their bodies stood rigid and their feet rooted to the ground. He turned them over, stripped them out, and searched. There were indeed twenty taels of silver in each, tied into a sack fastened on the waist-sash; and each wore a light-pink painted token, one bearing the words “Diao-zuan Guai,” the other “Guai Diao-zuan.”

Great Sage, he took their silver and removed the tokens, then hopped back and returned to the prefectural city. He entered the prince’s hall and met the prince, Tripitaka, and the various officials and smiths, and told all that had happened. Zhu Bajie laughed, “It must be that Master’s treasure shone with rosy radiance, so they bought pigs and sheep and prepared a feast to celebrate. But now, how are we to bring it back?” Sun Wukong said, “All three of my brothers and I will go. This silver is for buying the pigs and sheep. First give this silver to the smiths as a reward, and ask Your Highness to get several pigs and sheep. You, Zhu Bajie, become Diao-zuan Guai; I will become Guai Diao-zuan; Sha Wujing will dress as a guest-trader in pigs and sheep. Enter Tiger-Mouth Cave; once you find a good spot, each of you take up a weapon, strike the evil spirits, and return, settling up the road on the way back.” Sha Wujing laughed, “Wonderful, wonderful, wonderful—do not delay, go quickly.” The prince followed this plan and at once ordered his attendants to buy seven or eight pigs and four or five sheep.

After taking leave of Tripitaka, the three of them displayed their powers outside the city. Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, I have never seen that Diao-zuan Guai, and how can I change into that appearance?” Sun Wukong replied, “That demon is fixed by Sun Wukong’s immobilizing spell and will not wake until this time tomorrow. I remember his appearance. Stand still and let me teach you to change. … Just so, exactly like him.” The simple one chanted the spell in his mouth while Sun Wukong blew out immortal breath, and at once he became no different from that Diao-zuan Guai, with one pink token at his waist. Sun Wukong in turn became Guai Diao-zuan, also with a token at his waist. Sha Wujing dressed as a customer in the trade of pigs and sheep. The three moved together, hurrying the pigs along the main road and heading straight for the mountain.

Not long after, they entered a hollow in the mountain and again met a small demon, and his face was every bit as savage as the stories foretold. He looked like this:

Round, glossy eyes, bright as a trembling lantern; a red, bristling tuft of hair on his head, like fire drifting with light. A coarse nose, a grotesque ape-like jaw, and sharp saber teeth; broad ears, a hacked-looking forehead, a green face swollen and puffy. He wore a light yellow robe and sandals of woven reed-fiber; on both sides his frame was wild, as if an evil spirit, rushing and panting like a malicious ghost. He held a painted invitation casket under his left arm, and he called out to Sun Wukong: “You tricky and obstinate oddity, have the two of you come? How many pigs and sheep have you bought?” Sun Wukong said, “Is that not the one driving them?” The demon said to Sha Wujing, “Who is this?” Sun Wukong replied, “He is just a customer buying pigs and sheep. He still owes him a few taels and came home with him to collect. Where are you going?” The demon said, “I am going to Bamboo-Joint Mountain to summon the Great Lord for the assembly at dawn.” From the way he spoke, Sun Wukong asked, “How many are invited?” The demon said, “The Great Lord will be seated first, and with him and the heads of this mountain, about four dozen in all.” While he was still saying this, Zhu Bajie said, “Go on, go on, the pigs and sheep have all scattered away.” Sun Wukong said, “You go on to invite them. I will first inspect his invitation.” Seeing him as one of his own, the demon opened it, took it out, and handed it to Sun Wukong. Sun Wukong unfolded it and read: Honorable tomorrow, with food and wine respectfully prepared, we celebrate the Qingding-pǎ Assembly of the Great Spiked Mace. Deign to cross the mountain and attend a brief audience. Keep this matter secret. Gratefully yours. To be opened before the Great Elder Ziweng, Ancient-Saint of the Nine Spirits, before the august presence. At the feet of my former master, the Golden Lion Sun of the under-room, one hundred reverent bows. After reading, Sun Wukong handed it back to the demon. The demon put it back in the casket and went off straight toward the southeast, rising uphill.

Sha Wujing asked, “Elder brother, what does the invitation say?” Sun Wukong answered, “It is an invitation to the Qingding-pǎ festivity. It says, ‘At the feet of my former master, the Golden Lion Sun of the under-room, one hundred reverent bows.’ The invitee is the Great Elder Zuweng, Nine-Spirit Primordial Saint.” Sha Wujing smiled: “Golden Lion must surely be a gold-maned lion in fox-form. But what is this Nine-Spirit Primordial Saint?” Hearing this, Zhu Bajie laughed: “A trifle of the old pig, surely.” Sun Wukong said, “How do you know it belongs to the old pig?” Zhu Bajie said, “The ancients said: ‘A mange-mothered pig chases after a gold-maned lion spirit.’ So I know this is the old pig’s business too.” The three, talking and laughing, drove onward. Soon they saw the gate of the Tiger-Mouth Cave. They beheld it from outside:

Around it the mountains wound in green, and one thread of breath seemed to link mountain to city. Steep cliffs strained with blue vines, on high precipices purple acacia hung. Deep-tree groves ringed with birdsong, flower-shadows welcoming the cave-mouth. It did not fall short of Peach Blossom Cave, fit to hide one’s mortal world-burden. As they drew nearer the gate they saw a throng of small and big motley demons at the foot of the flowering trees, frolicking and quarreling. Suddenly Zhu Bajie bellowed, and when he hurried the pigs and sheep over, they all came to meet them. Each caught one of the pigs, each took one of the sheep, and all were bundled down together. This stirred up the demon king within, and he came out with a score of little demons and asked, “Have the two of you arrived? How many pigs and sheep did you buy?” Sun Wukong said, “We bought eight pigs and seven sheep, fifteen animals in all. The pork is sixteen taels, the sheep nine taels. I was paid twenty taels in advance and still owe five. This is the customer, here to collect the money.” Hearing this, the demon king said at once, “You little ones, fetch five taels and send him off.” Sun Wukong said, “This customer has come for one thing to claim payment and one to come to see the meeting.” The demon king grew angry and cursed: “You troublesome trickster! You only buy goods, and yet you speak of gatherings and not gatherings?” Zhu Bajie stepped forward: “The lord has obtained a treasure that is indeed a rare marvel of the world. Why should we not let him look?” That demon snapped, “You oddities are enough to disgust me! This treasure came from Yuhua Prefecture, and if this customer saw it then returned to the prefecture and spread rumor of it, when the prince comes on inspection they will ask and trouble us terribly.” Sun Wukong said, “Your lordship, this customer is from beyond Qianfang, far from this prefecture, not a native of Yuhua. How could he carry it anywhere as rumor? Besides, he is hungry in his belly, and so are we two; we have not eaten yet. There is ready wine and food at home. Give him some and send him away.” Before he could finish, a little demon brought five taels and handed them to Sun Wukong. Sun Wukong passed the money to Sha Wujing and said, “Customer, take the silver and come with you behind. We’ll go in and have something to eat.”

Relying on his courage, Sha Wujing entered Tiger-Mouth Cave with Zhu Bajie and Sun Wukong. Reaching the second hall above, he saw in the center of the main table a nine-toothed dingpa set up high in offering, truly dazzling to the eye. On the east side of it leaned a Golden-Hooped Staff. On the west side leaned a demon-subduing staff. The demon king followed and said, “Customer, that object in the center glows in the center of the hall; look well. But when you leave, do not tell any man of it.” Sha Wujing nodded and thanked him.

Ah! Truly this is the principle: when a thing sees its owner, it must be taken. Zhu Bajie had always been a blundering fool, and when he saw the dingpa he did not stop to weigh any further matter. He rushed over, took it down, swung it in his hand, displayed his true form, and with a shout sent it flying, rushing to strike the demon king straight in the face. Sun Wukong and Sha Wujing likewise ran to either side, each taking up a weapon and revealing their true forms. The three brothers together struck in wild confusion. The demon king, alarmed, leapt back and fled, then turned behind. He took up a Four-Ming shovel, the pole long and keen-edged, and charged into the courtyard, bracing all three of their weapons and barking aloud: “Who are you, daring to blaspheme and trick me over my treasure?” Sun Wukong spat, “You band of thieving fur! You do not recognize me. We are disciples of Tripitaka, the holy monk of the Eastern Land. We came to Yuhua Prefecture to exchange travel permits, and at the king’s order the three princes there took us as masters and learned the arts of war. They copied our treasures and forged weapons to their pattern. Then we set them out in the courtyard, and you, band of thieves, sneaked into the city by night and stole them away, and now you claim I am deceiving you about your treasure. Do not run—let us try these three weapons against you in turn, just a few blows.” The demon king lifted the shovel in challenge. From the courtyard into the front gate this bout rolled onward, and when the three monks and the single demon-clump clashed it was a slaughter:

The Hoo-hoo staff ran like wind; the storm of spikes fell like rain. The demon-subduing staff rose into a sky of rosy light; the Four-Ming shovel stretched out and made colored cloud-motes in the air. It seemed like three immortals refining great cinnabar elixir, fire-glow and brilliance startling god and ghost. Sun Wukong manifested power most wondrous, while the demon thief of treasure was rude in all else. Heavenly Canopy Bajie showed wondrous mastery, and General Sha Wujing appeared even more handsome in valor. Brothers combined in counsel and technique, and a battle rose within Tiger-Mouth Cave. That rascally demon-thief boasted of strength and craft, yet four heroes could be matched with him. As the killing rang until sun touched westward, the demon’s evil strength had softened and could scarcely hold. They fought for a long time in Leopard-Head Mountain. At last the demon, unable to match them, shouted to Sha Wujing, “Watch the shovel.” Sha Wujing yielded a body-form sidestep and avoided it. The demon got a clear path and fled, riding the wind to the southeast. Zhu Bajie wanted to chase, but Sun Wukong said, “Let him go. As the ancients say, ‘Do not pursue the cornered foe.’ We will only block his way home.” Zhu Bajie obeyed.

The three went straight to the cave mouth and slew all the demons there, from the huge to the tiny, one hundred or more in all. They were mostly tigers, wolves, leopards, mountain goats, and wild deer and antelopes. By Sun Wukong’s method, every soft-bodied and flimsy creature in the cave, as well as the mixed-bodied animals from the flock they had driven in, were all slain; he brought all of them out along with the captured pigs and sheep. Sha Wujing then took out dry wood and set a fire, while Zhu Bajie flapped wind with both ears, and in a moment burned the whole den clean. Then he set out with all the gathered things and turned back toward the state city.

At that time the city gate still stood open and no one was yet asleep. The old king and his sons, with Tripitaka, were all waiting in the pavilion of open curtains. They saw them arrive, dropping whole a courtyardful of dead demons, pigs, sheep, and soft-bodied creatures in a wild heap. All together they shouted, “Master, we return in victory.” The prince nodded repeatedly in thanks. Tripitaka was all joy. The three young princes knelt on the ground. Sha Wujing helped them up and said, “Do not give thanks yet; come forward and see these things.” The prince asked, “What are all these objects?” Sun Wukong laughed and said, “Those tigers, wolves, leopards, and mountain-goat beasts were all demons in transformed form. We took their weapons and drove them out the gate. Their old lord was a gold-maned lion. He wielded a Four-Ming shovel and fought us till dusk, then was defeated and fled to the southeast. We did not pursue him; instead we blocked his return, slaughtered these bands of demons, searched and took all these objects, and brought them here.” The old lord heard this with joy and worry both: joy at returning in victory, worry that the demon might seek revenge later. Sun Wukong said, “Your Highness, do not worry. I have already thought through it fully and can deal with it in good time. I will sweep him out completely before we depart, so no harm will follow.” Then he added, “At noon, I met a small blue-faced, red-haired demon carrying an invitation. The invitation said: ‘Tomorrow morning, with feasting of food and wine prepared in reverence, we hold the Qingding-pǎ Assembly. Deign to pass the mountain for a brief council. Keep this hidden. Gratefully yours.’ It was addressed to “Before the venerable Great Elder Zuweng, Nine-Spirit Primordial Saint.” The name was, “At the feet of my former master, the Golden Lion Sun, with one hundred full prostrations.” That demon who was defeated today must surely have gone to his elder-lord and, at dawn, surely come seeking us for vengeance. We will therefore clear him out thoroughly.” The king thanked him again, and they set out the evening meal. After the monks had finished their evening repast, each returned to his bedchamber; nothing further need be said.

The demon spirit did indeed run southeast to Bamboo-Knot Mountain. In that mountain there was a cave retreat called Panhuan Cave of the Nine Bends. In the cave, the Nine-Spirits Primordial Sage was his ancestral lord. He did not stop to rest the whole night, and when the fifth watch arrived he came to the cave mouth, knocked, and went in. The junior demon saw him and said, “Great King, last night a green-faced youth came to deliver an invitation; the master kept him here until this morning and meant to go with him to your Dingba gathering. Why have you come so early yourself to invite us again?” The demon spirit replied, “It is hard to speak, hard to speak—this meeting will surely turn out bad.” As he spoke, he saw the green-faced youth come out from inside and say, “Great King, why did you come? The Great King has risen and is going with me to the assembly.” The demon spirit was flustered, merely waving his hands and saying nothing.

After a little while, the old demon rose and called him in. This demon cast aside his weapons, toppled to his knees and bowed, and could not stop tears from streaming down his cheeks. The old demon said, “Worthy grandson, yesterday you sent the invitation; this morning you were about to come to the assembly yourself. Why are you here again, bringing grief and sorrow?” The little demon knocked his head and said, “Last night, while strolling idly by moonlight, I saw that in Yuhua Prefecture there was radiance filling the sky. When I hurried to look, I found three kinds of weapons displaying their brilliance in the Prince’s court: one was a nine-toothed gold-seeping dingba, one a precious staff, and one the Golden-Hooped Staff. Using my divine art, I took them and at once named it a ‘Dingba felicitation assembly’; I made my subordinates buy pigs, sheep, fruits, and other goods, set a banquet, and held a feast to celebrate, inviting Grandfather to reward it all as a joy. After sending the green-faced one to deliver the invitation, I then saw the Diaozuan lad from the group sent to buy pigs and sheep, along with others, hurrying along with several pigs and sheep; they also brought a trader to seek silver. He was determined to see the gathering, and though my grandson feared he might spread rumors outside, he would not let him watch. He then said he was hungry and asked for food, so he was told to eat at the rear. He went inside and saw the weapons, saying they were his. The three then each grabbed one; their true forms appeared: one was a monk with a furry face and a Thunder God mouth, one a monk with a long snout and large ears, one a monk with a dark, inauspicious-faced complexion. He did not distinguish good from bad, only shouted once and fought wildly. My grandson at once hastened to take up the Siming shovel and drive them out, then held on in resistance, and asked who would dare to make such vain show. That one said he is a disciple of Tripitaka, sent from the Great Tang of the Eastern Capital to go westward. Passing through this prefecture, he changed documents, was kept by the Prince to learn martial arts, and had these three weapons modeled and forged, placing them in the yard; I stole them, and thus I became resentful and battled. I do not know what names those three monks bear, yet all three are skilled. One like my grandson cannot match three opponents, so he fled to his old father’s place. I hoped for help with a drawn sword, to take revenge on those monks, and thereby show my grandfather’s affection for his grandson.”

After hearing this, the old demon fell silent for a moment and then laughed. “So it is he indeed,” he said. “Worthy grandson, you have provoked him inappropriately.” The demon spirit said, “Does Grandfather know who he is?” The old demon said, “That one with the long snout and large ears is Zhu Bajie; the one with the sullen, ominous face is Sha Wujing. Those two are still manageable. The furry-faced, Thunder God-mouthed monk is called Sun Wukong. That man truly has vast powers: five hundred years ago he once laid waste to Heaven’s Court, and even ten thousand heavenly soldiers could not catch him. He is intent on seeking out men; he is a captain of raids who searches mountains and reveals seas, breaks through breaches, storms fortresses, and brings chaos. How did you dare to trouble him? Never mind. Come with me; we shall catch that brute, and with him the prince of Yuhua as well, and bring them to vent your anger for you.” The demon spirit heard and instantly knelt to thank him.

The old demon then called for the ape-lion, Snow Lion, Suannei, Baize, Fuli, Tuanxiang and the rest of his grandson-demons; each took up sharp arms and weapons. Yellow Lion led them, and each sent forth wild wind as they rushed straight to the border of Leopard-Head Mountain. They smelled smoke and powder in the air and heard cries of weeping. Looking more closely, it was indeed Diaozuan and Guo Guai crying there, calling for their master and wailing for him. The demon came forward and shouted, “Are you genuine Diaozuan, or merely a fake Diaozuan?” The two fiends knelt, swallowed their tears, and kowtowed. “How are we fake?” they said. “Last night, just at dusk, after receiving silver to buy pigs and sheep, we were on the big road west of the mountain. We saw a monk with a furry face and a Thunder God mouth; he spat at us. At once our legs weakened and our mouths locked up: we could not speak, we could not move. He toppled us, searched us, and took the silver and the tally slips. We two remained in a dazed stupor until we woke only now. When we returned home, we found fires not yet out; every house was burned. Nor could we find the master, or either senior or junior head. So here we are, grieving and crying. We do not know how this fire came about.”

When the demon heard this, he could not stop tears from bursting forth like springs. Both his legs gave way and he crashed down, and his cry shook the sky and earth, cursing, “Tonsured wretch! You have done terrible evil—how could you commit such a venomous deed? You burned my cave dwelling to ash, burned the beautiful women, and left household and kin, old and young, stripped clean. My blood will kill me, my blood will kill me!” The old demon told Mau-Lion to pull him over and said, “Worthy grandson, matters have come to this; to mope now is useless. First preserve all your sharp spirit and go to the prefectural city to seize that monk.” The demon still refused to stop crying. “Master, that mountain site of mine was not built in a day. Now this bald brute has destroyed it completely. What life is there left for me?” He tried to rise, ran to the cliff, and struck his head and head-bowed in rage. Only after Snow Lion, Mau-Lion, and the others urged him hard did he stop.

Then all left that place and fled for the prefectural city. They heard the wind rolling and the mist churning, coming very close. Alarmed, all the people outside the city gates, men and women alike, in haste left home goods behind, all rushed into the city, entered through the gates, and shut them. Someone reported into the Prince’s residence: “Disaster, disaster.” The Prince, Tripitaka, and the others were at Bao-sha Pavilion taking their morning meal when they heard the warning, and came out to inquire. The others said, “A group of demons is approaching the city with flying sand and stones, spitting mist and raising wind.” The old Prince was greatly startled: “What is this?” Sun Wukong smiled and said, “All be at ease, all be at ease. This is the demon spirit of Tiger-Mouth Cave, defeated in battle yesterday, who went southeast and has come here with that one child of the Nine-Spirits Primordial Sage. Let me go out with my brothers.” Then he ordered: “Have the four gates closed; you all set men to guard the city.” The Prince indeed ordered the four gates shut, and ordered the guards to go up to the walls. The father and son, with Tripitaka, stood on the city towers issuing signals; banners covered the sun and cannon-fire connected to the sky. Sun Wukong and the two brothers went out, half in cloud and half in fog, to meet the enemy. This is exactly the case:

Losing the care of prudent vigilance, he made the demons of evil rise up all together.

After all, this does not yet reveal how the battle will end. Let us hear the resolution in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 89: The Yellow Lion spirit feigns a pin-and-bolt feast; Gold-Wood-Tu stirs uproar at Leopard-Head Mountain.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

After this, Great Sage Sun Wukong, with Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, came out beyond the city gate and was met face to face. They saw that the group of demon-kind were all coarse, shaggy lion spirits: the Yellow Lion Spirit led in front; on the left were the Suan-ni Lion and Tuan-xiang Lion, on the right the Bai Ze Lion and Fuli Lion, behind the Nao Lion and Snow Lion, and in the center a Nine-Headed Lion. At its side stood a blue-faced fiend gripping a brocade-gilt flowered treasure banner, close beside the Nine-Headed Lion. The Cunning-and-Twisted and the Twisted-and-Cunning ones waved two red banners. All were arrayed together on the ground of Kanguan.

Zhu Bajie, rash as ever, strode up and cried out, 'You treasure-stealing monster, why did you gather these shaggy brutes to come here?' The Yellow Lion Spirit ground his teeth and snapped back, 'You rough, bald brute! Yesterday it was three against one and I was beaten and had to retreat; this should have satisfied you. Why are you so ruthless now, burning my den, ruining my mountain ground, and wounding my clan? My grudge against you is deep as the sea. Do not run; I will take you with one shovelful.' "Good," said Bajie, and raised his spade to meet him. The two had only just closed, and still no one could claim the upper hand, when the Nao Lion Spirit swung an iron caltrop and the Snow Lion Spirit brought out a three-ridged cane and rushed straight into the fray. Zhu Bajie shouted, 'Well done!' Then Sha Wujing quickly drew the demon-subduing staff and came forward to help. Then the Suan-ni spirit, Bai Ze spirit, Tuan-xiang Lion, and Fuli Lion all rushed together. There Sun Wukong used the Golden-Hooped Staff to hold back the swarm. Suan-ni used a club, Bai Ze a bronze hammer, Tuan-xiang a steel spear, and Fuli an axe. Those seven lion spirits, and these three ferocious monks—what terrible slayers they were:

Clubs, maces, spears, and axes, and three-ridged canes; Caltrops, bone-knots, Four-Ming shovels, every weapon keen; Seven lions and seven instruments, so keenly gleaming, encircled the three monks who roared together; Great Sage’s Golden-Hooped Staff was fierce; Sha Wujing’s treasure staff is seldom seen among men; Zhu Bajie, wild as storm-ridden winds in bearing, made his riveted spade flash with dreadful light; Front to cover and rear to block, each used his arts—left to brace, right to welcome—brave all through; The prince on the city wall added thunder to their valor, drums and gongs clanging in one swell; Hurling and seizing, they displayed their divine arts, and so much slaughter made earth and sky reel and blur.

That band of demons, together with Sun Wukong and the three monks, fought through half a day and only then noticed evening. Zhu Bajie spat with thick saliva, felt his legs go weak, feigned a shuffle with one swing of the spade, and lost the formation and withdrew. The Snow Lion and Nao Lion demons shouted, 'Where do you run? Face us first.' The fool could not dodge; he was struck once along his spine and fell to the ground, saying only, 'Enough. Enough.' The two demons dragged Zhu Bajie by his mane and tail and hauled him off to the Nine-Headed Lion, reporting, 'Grandfather, we have taken one as well.'

Before he could speak, Sha Wujing and the Great Sage also fell in defeat, and all the demons came charging together. Sun Wukong pulled a handful of hairs from his body, chewed them to pieces and spat them out, crying, 'Transform!' and at once became a hundred and ten little Sun Wukongs, circling around. They enclosed the Bai Ze, Suan-ni, Tuan-xiang, Fuli, and the Golden-Mane Lion Spirit in their midst. Sha Wujing and Sun Wukong again moved in to strike. By evening they had taken the Suan-ni and Bai Ze spirits and drove off Fuli and Tuan-xiang. The Golden-Mane Lion Spirit reported to the old demon. Seeing he had lost two lions, he ordered, 'Bind Zhu Bajie. Do not wound him. First let him return my two lion spirits; then return him with them. If he has been ignorant and ruined my two lions, then kill Zhu Bajie as justice.' That night the demons settled outside the city and no further account is worth giving.

Sun Wukong took the two lion spirits up near the city wall. The old king saw this and at once ordered the gate opened. He sent two or three dozen captains to run out with ropes, tie up the lion spirits, and carry them into the city. Sun Wukong retracted his magic hairs and, with Sha Wujing, went straight to the watchtower to meet Tripitaka. Tripitaka said, 'This matter is very dangerous. Do we know whether Wuneng’s life was spared?' Sun Wukong replied, 'No harm. We have taken these two demons, and there he would not dare to injure them. Bind the two spirits tightly, and at first light we will exchange them for Zhu Bajie.' The three young princes kowtowed to the Great Sage and asked, 'Earlier, when Master fought beforehand, we saw only one body. Later he pretended to lose and withdrew, yet how then were there a hundred and ten of his forms? And once he had captured the demons and came near the city, he was only one body again. By what power is this?' The Great Sage laughed and said, 'On my body are eighty-four thousand hairs. One becomes ten, ten becomes a hundred, a hundred becomes a thousand and a thousand becomes myriad and billion—each of those are forms outside the original self. Then each prince in turn bowed. Food for the precept was set at once, and they ate it there on the city tower. At every embrasure they raised lanterns and flags, clappers and bells and gongs, shifted the watch and passed signal arrows, and fired cannon with shouting.

At first light, the old monster summoned the Yellow Lion Spirit and laid plans: 'Today you all use all your mind and strength to take Sun Wukong and Sha Wujing; then I will secretly fly in the air up to the city, seize his Master, and seize the old king and his sons as well, and first turn to Nine-Curve Coiling Cave. When you return in victory, come back and report.' Following that plan, the Yellow Lion led the Nao Lion, Snow Lion, Tuan-xiang, and Fuli, each bearing weapons, to the city edge, and the battle began in wind and mist. The Great Sage and Sha Wujing jumped from the city top and shouted in fierce voices, 'You wretched demons! Quickly send back my junior monk Zhu Bajie and I will spare your lives. Otherwise I will make your bones to dust.' The demons had no room to speak; they closed in together in one rush. The two brothers used all their stratagems and blocked the five lion spirits. This fight was much different from yesterday:

The earth was scourged by howling wind; dark thick fog concealed the sky; stones rolled and sand flew, and spirits and ghosts trembled, trees were toppled and beasts startled; steel spears were cruel, axes flashed bright, caltrops, canes, and poisoned shovels were all deadly; They wished to swallow the Great Sage whole and drag little Sha Wujing down and seize him alive; Sun Wukong’s one Ruyi rod expanded, contracted, extended, and folded with wondrous skill; Sha Wujing’s demon-subduing staff had a name beyond the Hall of Lingxiao; This time he employed his powers broadly, and in the Western Regions he swept the spirits away. The five coarse-haired lion spirits and Sun Wukong and Sha Wujing were already in the heart of the slaughter when the old monster rode a black cloud and rose straight to the city tower. He shook his head once, and the civil and military officials and guards on the city ramparts all fled down in fright. He then ran into the tower, opened his mouths, and snatched out Tripitaka and the old king and his sons; then he returned to the depths below Kanguan and in the same way took Zhu Bajie as well. In truth he had nine heads, and therefore nine mouths: one held Tripitaka, one held Zhu Bajie, one held the old king, one held the first prince, one held the second prince, and one held the third prince—six mouths for six people, leaving three mouths empty. He shouted, 'I go first.' Those five small lion demons, seeing their lord win, each displayed even greater prowess.

When Sun Wukong heard the shouting and outcry from atop the city, he realized he had fallen into their scheme and at once called urgently for Sha Wujing to be ready. He then pulled off all the hairs from his arm, chewed and spat them out, and turned into a hundred or more little Sun Wukongs. At once he knocked down the Nao Lion, captured the Snow Lion alive, seized the Tuan-xiang Lion, hurled the Fuli Lion over with force, and killed the Yellow Lion; he shouted in a ringing voice down to the lower city. He turned and withdrew, and in doing so the blue-faced one, along with the Cunning-and-Twisted and the Twisted-and-Cunning demons, slipped away. Seeing this, the officials on the city wall opened the gate again, tied up the five lion spirits with ropes, and carried them back into the city. Before there was any resolution, the queen came crying, weeping, and kneeling before the Great Sage said, 'Divine Master, our prince and his father with your Master Tripitaka—let their lives be spared. What will become of this lone city?' Sun Wukong gathered in his hairs and bowed to her: 'Noble lady, do not fret. I have taken his seven lion spirits. That old demon used a grasping spell to seize your lord, your father, your prince, and Tripitaka; they are all likely unharmed. At first light tomorrow, my brother and I will go into that mountain and surely seize the old demon, returning your four princes.' The queen, with a cluster of her ladies, heard these words, and all knelt before Sun Wukong saying, 'May your prince and the king’s father and sons all live, and may the realm stand firm.' When they had finished bowing, each one returned to the palace with tears. Sun Wukong then ordered the officials, 'Skim the hide off the dead Yellow Lion Spirit. Bind the six living lion spirits securely in heavy chains. Bring out some vegetarian food; we will eat and sleep. You all take heart: you will have no trouble.'

By the next day, the Great Sage led Sha Wujing onto an auspicious cloud. Not long after, they reached the crest of Bamboo-Node Mountain. Gazing from the cloud there, it was a grand height indeed:

Peaks rose abrupt and abrupt, ridges steep and jagged. Deep ravines below, with murmuring waters running and rinsing; before sheer cliffs, flowers in brocade-lacquered splendor smelled sweet. Returning ridges overlapped; ancient roads turned through circling bays. Truly, cranes come with pines for company, while clouds departing leave stones with no companion. Dark-green apes sought fruit in clear sunshine; deer sought blossoms on warm days with joy. The cries of blue cranes came in fine drizzling notes, and yellow birds spoke with long tangled song. In spring the peach and plum contended in beauty; at midsummer willow and pagoda-tree flourished alike. When autumn came, yellow flowers spread like brocade; when winter settled, white snow drifted in tufts. Through four seasons and eight festivals the scenery was fine beyond compare, no less than the immortals’ wonderland of Yingzhou. The two were still looking when suddenly the blue-faced fiend with a short club came running out between the ravines. Sun Wukong shouted, 'Where are you going? It is Sun who comes!' Frightened, the small demon ran, rolling and flipping down the ravine. They pursued but lost his trace. After going forward a few more steps, there appeared a cave dwelling with two spotted stone doors tightly shut. Set in the threshold was a stone slab, in regular script with ten large characters reading: 'Wuling Bamboo-Joint Mountain, Nine-Curve Coiling Cave.'

The little demon had, in fact, run into the cave and shut the cave-door behind him. In the meantime he told the old demon, “Grandfather, two more monks have come outside.” The old demon asked, “Did your Great King and the monkey-lion, the snow-lion, the coiling elephant, and the crouching fox come?” The little demon said, “No, no, not at all. It is only that two monks are looking out from a high mountain peak. I saw them and turned back at once; he chased me after, and I came back and closed the door.” The old demon, on hearing this, lowered his head in silence. After a while he suddenly burst into tears and cried, “Alas! My Yellow Lion Grandson is dead, and Niao-lion Grandson and the others have all been caught by monks and taken into the city. How can this vengeance be repaid?” Zhu Bajie lay bound nearby, together with the king and prince and Tripitaka, all crowded together, distressed and in fear. On hearing the old demon say that all those sons had been captured by monks and taken into the city, Tripitaka thought privately, “Master, do not fear. Your Highness, do not sorrow. My elder brother has already won; he seized all the monsters and has come here to rescue us all.” Saying this, he then heard the old demon shout, “You little ones, stand guard here. I will go out and bring in those two monks; then at once we will punish them all.”

You can see he came forward with no armor and no weapon in hand, striding in big steps, and one only heard Sun Wukong crying out. He opened the cave-mouth wide without replying and ran straight at the Great Sage. Sun Wukong met him with his Iron Rod, blocking him head-on. Sha Wujing swung his precious staff and struck. The old demon shook its head once; all eight heads opened their mouths together and, with a light motion, took Sun Wukong and Sha Wujing both and drew them back inside the cave. “Bring rope,” it ordered. The two crafty and devious little demons—the devious and crafty ones, together with the green-faced one—were the pair who had escaped and returned from last night. They took two ropes and bound the two men tightly. The old demon said, “You wild monkey, you have captured my seven sons and grandsons. Today I have caught your four monks and four sons of the royal household; that is enough to pay for my young ones’ lives. Kids, bring willow clubs and take this monkey-head for a beating, so I can settle the grudge for Yellow Lion Grandson.” The three little demons each held a willow staff and targeted only the Great Sage. The Great Sage was a body tempered by alchemical fire; those willow rods merely tickled him. He made no outcry, no matter how hard they struck him, not even a flinch. Zhu Bajie, Tripitaka, and the prince, seeing this, were each horrified to the marrow. After little time the willow clubs were snapped. The beating went on to dusk and was beyond count. Sha Wujing, seeing that it had gone on too long, said, “Let me strike him a hundred and ten times in his place.” The old demon said, “Do not be hasty; tomorrow I will beat you until your turn comes, one by one.” Zhu Bajie blurted, “Then the day after, I, your old pig, will be beaten too.” The beating dragged on as the sky darkened. The old demon said, “Kids, hold for a moment. Light the lamps, eat some food, and let me go to Jin Cloud Nook and sleep a bit. You three have all already been harmed before; keep watch carefully and we will continue at dawn.” The three little demons moved the lights closer and struck Sun Wukong on the top of the head with willow staffs as if knocking a wooden clapper, tik-tak, tok-tok, quick and slow, slow and quick. Night deepened and they all began to doze off.

The Great Sage used a vanish technique, shrank his body to small, and slipped free from the ropes. He shook out the hairs on his head and smoothed his clothes in place. From within his ear he pulled out his staff, gave it a flick; it was as thick as a hanging bucket and two zhang long. Pointing it at the three little demons he said, “You wretched beast, you lashed your lord with so many clubs. The lord is still as before. I’ll press this staff against you and see what happens.” He gave the three little demons each a light shove, and at once turned them into three meat cakes. He brightened the lamp again and released Sha Wujing. Zhu Bajie, still badly bound, could not bear it and cried out loudly, “Eldest brother, my hands and feet are swollen from the binding—could you not free me first?” That fool of a pig cried out once, and it had already startled the old demon. The old demon, half-crouching, scrambled up and said, “Who released him?” Sun Wukong heard it; with one breath he blew out the lamp and, without regard for Sha Wujing and the rest, struck with the Iron Rod, breaking through several gates as he ran away.

The old demon called in the central hall, “Kids, why is the light gone? Did no one run off with anyone?” He called once, and no one answered; he called again, and still no one answered. When he took up the light and looked, he saw only three blood-soaked meat cakes on the ground. The king and his son, Tripitaka, and Zhu Bajie were all there, but Sun Wukong and Sha Wujing were no longer present. He lit the light and hurried to search front and back. He saw that Sha Wujing was still standing with his back pinned against the corridor rail. He seized him at once, dragged him down, and bound him as before. He searched for Sun Wukong; he saw that several layers of gate had all been broken apart, so he knew that the Great Sage had beaten through and fled. He did not give chase. He patched broken gates and sealed breaches, and kept to guarding the household; nothing more to record.

The Great Sage left the Nine-turn Labyrinth Cave, rode a cloud of good omen, and headed straight to Yuhua Prefecture. He saw on the city walls gods of every quarter, local earth deities, and the City God waiting in the sky to bow before him. Sun Wukong asked, “Why do you only meet me at this hour?” The City God replied, “The little spirits knew the Great Sage had descended to Yuhua Prefecture; since Your Majesty had been invited by the royal prince, they did not dare to show themselves before you. Now that we know the king and his family have met a demon, and that the Great Sage has come to subdue it, they have come especially to come forward and welcome.” Just then, while Wukong was still vexed, he saw Gold-Head Jie Di and the Six Jia Six Ding generals of heaven leading a local land spirit in chains. They knelt before him and said, “Great Sage, we have seized this ghost of this land.” Sun Wukong shouted, “You were not stationed on Bamboo-Joint Mountain to guard my master, so why are you making noise here?” The Ding-Jia general said, “Great Sage, when this demon escaped from you, it seized the Curtain-roller General and still bound him. We saw that the demon’s powers were vast, so we brought this Bamboo-Joint Mountain land spirit here in custody. He knows that demon’s origin. Ask him one question for the Great Sage, and he can be judged and punished, to relieve the sufferings of the Holy Monk and of the wise king.” Hearing this, Wukong rejoiced greatly. The land spirit, trembling, knelt and said, “The old demon came down to Bamboo-Joint Mountain last year. The Nine-turn Labyrinth Cave was originally the den of six lions. When this old demon arrived, those six lions all bowed to him as their ancestral lord. The ancestral lord is a nine-headed lion, called Nine-Spirit Primordial Sage. To destroy him, one must go to the Mystic Rock Palace in the Far East and summon his principal owner; only then can he be subdued. No one else can dream of capturing him.” Wukong thought for a while and said, “The Mystic Rock Palace in the Far East—that is the domain of Taiyi Jiuku, is it not? He is itself none other than a nine-headed lion. So it is.” He then ordered, “Jie Di, Gold-Armour, go back with the land spirit and secretly protect my master, my fellow disciple, and the king’s father-son household; let the City God of this place guard the city.” The deities each did as commanded and withdrew.

The Great Sage gathered momentum on a cloud and traveled through the night. Around the hour of the tiger he reached the outside of the East Heaven Gate and happened upon Guangmu Heavenly King with a company of heavenly soldiers and strength-bound attendants. All of them stopped, bowed with joined palms, and said, “Where does the Great Sage go?” After offering proper salutations, Wukong said, “I am going to the Mystic Rock Palace for a visit.” The King said, “You did not go by the Western route; why come to the East Heaven for this?” Wukong replied, “When I came to Yuhua Prefecture, Lord Yuhua’s son invited me, and he sent three sons to bow to my brothers and me as teachers and learn martial arts. Unexpectedly I met a pack of lion demons. Now I have learned that the master of the Mystic Rock Palace, Taiyi Jiuku, is this demon’s host; I have come to invite him to descend and subdue the fiend to save the master.” The Heavenly King said, “That is because you wish to become a teacher of men, so this nest of lions has thus been stirred up.” The Great Sage laughed, “Precisely for that, precisely for that.” The heavenly attendants and strongmen bowed one by one, made way, and withdrew. The Great Sage entered East Heaven Gate; before long he came before the Mystic Rock Palace and saw:

Overlapping layers of colored clouds, purple qi lush and dense. Golden wave-like flames shimmer on tiled roofs; jade-beast-like gates stand in grand procession. The twin gate towers are heavy with blossoms, red clouds circling, while sunlight washes forested groves in green mist. It truly is a ring of ten thousand true beings and a flourishing of a thousand saints. Halls and pavilions rise in layered brocade; every window and veranda is open. Azure dragons coil in guard, divine radiance soft and broad; the yellowway glows with concentrated auspicious light. This is the domain of Green Radiance and Everlasting Joy: the Mystic Rock Palace of the Far East. At the palace gate stood a child-immortal in a rainbow skirt. Seeing Sun Wukong, he immediately entered and reported, “Great one, the Qi Tian Daxia—the Great Sage of Heaven’s Court is here.” Taiyi Jiuku heard this and called guards and celestials to receive him. Guided in, he came to the hall where the Honored One sat high upon a nine-colored lotus throne amid hundreds of billions of radiant omens. He saw the Great Sage, descended from his seat, and came down to meet him. Wukong offered his bow. Taiyi Jiuku returned the salute and said, “Great Sage, we have not seen you these years. Earlier we heard you abandoned Dao and returned to Buddha, protecting Tripitaka’s pilgrimage to the West—likely your merit now complete?” Wukong said, “The merit is not yet complete, but near so. Now, while protecting Tripitaka to Yuhua Prefecture, we were welcomed by the prince; he had three sons bow to the Great Sage and my brothers as teachers to study martial arts. Our three divine weapons were forged in like manner as before, but unexpectedly the thieves stole them in the night. At daybreak we searched and found that it was a golden-maned lion spirit in a Tiger-Mouth Cave of Leopard-Head Mountain north of the city that had stolen them. Sun Wukong used a stratagem and brought it out, and that spirit rounded up several lion spirits and roared in great uproar with me. Inside it was a nine-headed lion of extensive powers. He carried my master, Zhu Bajie, and four of the royal household to the Nine-turn Labyrinth Cave on Bamboo-Joint Mountain. The next day, Sun Wukong and Sha Wujing followed and were likewise carried off. Sun Wukong was bound and beaten beyond count, but by chance escaped by means of art. They are still enduring punishment there. After questioning the local district land spirit, it became known that you are the Honored One’s lord, so I have come in reverence to invite you to bring the demon down and rescue them.

The Celestial Venerable heard the report and at once ordered a celestial general to go to the Lion Quarters and summon the lion slave for questioning. The lion slave had been fast asleep; the assembled generals shook him until he woke, then dragged him into the main hall. The Celestial asked, "Where is the lion beast?" The slave knelt with tears and said only, "Spare my life, spare my life." The Celestial said, "The Great Sage Sun Wukong is here. I will not beat you for now. Tell me quickly why, through carelessness, you let the Nine-Headed Lion escape." The lion slave said, "Sir, the other day in the Hall of Ganjiu of the Great Expanse I saw a bottle of wine. I do not know when I stole it and drank it, I fell into deep stupor and forgot the restraints, so it fled." The Celestial said, "That wine was sent by Laozi and called Reincarnation-Elixir. If you drink it, you should be drunk and not wake for three days. How long has that lion-beast been away now?" The Great Sage said, "By the report of the local mountain Earth God, it descended two years ago and has been gone for two or three years." The Celestial laughed, "Yes, yes. A day in the Heavenly Court is a year in the mortal world." He then said to the lion slave, "Get up. I pardon your death penalty. Go with me and the Great Sage below to fetch him. You and the rest of the immortals should return; you need not follow."

The Celestial then went with Sun Wukong and the lion slave, stepping along cloud paths to Bamboo-Joint Mountain. There the Five-Directional Jiedi, the Six Ding and Six Jia, and the Mountain’s Own Earth God all came and knelt to receive them. The Great Sage asked, "Did you protect and guard properly? Did you hurt my master?" The assembled deities replied, "The demon spirit had been overtaken by maddening sleep and did not move the master at all, nor did it inflict any punishment." The Celestial said, "That Great Saint of mine is truly a true spirit who has long cultivated the Way; with one cry he can rise through the Three Saints above and penetrate Nine Springs below, and without effort he does not harm living beings. Sun Wukong, go to his gate and challenge him, draw him out. Then I will take him in."

The Great Sage obeyed. He drew the Golden-Hooped Staff in one pull and leapt near the cave mouth, shouting, "Villainous demon, return him to me! Villainous demon, return him to me!" He called several times in succession. The old demon merely slept and gave no answer. Impatient, the Great Sage raised the iron staff and struck inward, keeping up his cries all the while. That old demon then startled awake in anger. He rose and shouted, "Fight!" he shook his head and opened his jaws to bite. The Great Sage turned and leapt out. The demon chased out and shouted, "Thief monkey, where are you running?" The Great Sage stood upon a high cliff and laughed, "You still dare such bold disrespect? Do you not know whether this is your life or your death? Is this not where your master and lord is present?" The demon reached the cliff edge, but already the Celestial had chanted a spell and cried out, "Yuansheng-er, I have come." Recognizing the master, it dared no struggle, planted its four feet to the ground, and only knelt and bowing. The lion slave ran over, seized a lock of hair at the neck, and with his fist struck the neck for well over a hundred blows, cursing, "Beast, why did you steal and make me bear fault?" The lion beast said nothing and did not dare to move. The lion slave was fatigued from striking when only then he stopped, and fastened a brocaded collar-halter on it. The Celestial mounted, shouted the order to depart, and then the lion rose at once and rode on the colored cloud, turning straight toward Miao-rock Palace.

The Great Sage looked up and offered thanks, then entered the cave. He first unbound the Yuhua King, then Tripitaka, then Zhu Bajie, Sha Wujing, and the three princes. They searched the cave thoroughly for objects, lingered and moved about as they wished, then led everyone out through the gate. Zhu Bajie took several bundles of dry wood, stacked them before and behind, set them alight, and burned the nine-turn winding cave into charred, broken-paned ruin. The Great Sage also dismissed the gathered gods and ordered the local Earth God to guard there. He then told Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing each to use their arts and carry the king and his sons back to the prefecture. The Great Sage supported Tripitaka. Before long they reached the prefectural city as dusk deepened. Then the consorts, empresses, and officials all came to receive them. A vegetarian feast was laid out and all sat together to partake. The master and disciples still rested at ease in the Baosha Pavilion. The princes entered the palace and each retired to sleep. One night passed without a word.

The next day, the king issued a new edict and held a grand plain-meat banquet. All officials of the household came and thanked their thanks in turn. The Great Sage again called for the slaughterman, who killed the six living lions. He had the skin removed from all of the yellow lions and arranged the meat for use. The prince was greatly delighted and immediately ordered: "Keep one for the household and its outer staff to use; give one to the chief steward of the palace and other officials to share; chop the remaining five into chunks of one or two taels and send captains to distribute them to soldiers and townsfolk inside and outside the prefecture, that each may taste a bit: one to sample the flavor, two to stir fear." Every household, all alike, could not fail to gaze in awe.

Again the blacksmiths who had forged the three kinds of weapons knelt before the Great Sage and said, "Sir, the work is complete." They were asked, "How much does each weigh, in catties and taels?" The smith said, "The Golden-Hooped Staff weighs a thousand catties; the Nine-Toothed Axe and the Demon-Subduing Staff each weigh eight hundred catties." The Great Sage said, "Very well." He ordered the three princes out, and each took up a weapon. The three sons told their father, "Father, the weapons are ready today." The old king said, "For these weapons, our father and sons’ lives were nearly lost." The youngest prince said, "By the holy teacher’s spells we were saved, yet again swept through demons and removed future trouble. Truly this is a world where seas are calm and rivers clear, and peace prevails." At that moment the king and his sons rewarded the craftsmen, then went to the Baosha Pavilion to bow and thank the teacher’s grace.

Tripitaka again told the Great Sage and companions to teach martial arts quickly so as not to miss the journey schedule. The three of them then each took up weapons in the king’s courtyard and taught all motions one by one. In no more than several days all three princes had practiced to full competence. As for the other methods of attack and retreat, of tightening and releasing, each had seventy-two ways of release and none was unknown to them. One reason was the princes’ firm minds; another was that the Great Sage had earlier already bestowed divine strength upon them. Thus they could all lift and carry a thousand-cattie staff and eight-hundred-cattie axe or staff. Compared with the fighting arts they had once learned on their own, this was truly a world apart. A poem attests:

By good fortune, in fortunate meeting with the holy teacher, who could have expected to train against this monstrous lion? Sweeping away bands of demons and securing the state, one true body returns, the frontier pacified. The nine spirits and numerals join in the principle of primal yang; in all four quarters they are skilled in Way and fruit. The bestowed clear mind is transmitted through ten thousand ages; Yuhua abides in eternal joy and peace. The prince then opened a grand banquet again to thank the teaching and took out a large tray of gold and silver as a token of gratitude. The Great Sage laughed, "Carry it in, carry it in quickly. We are people of the monastic path; what need have we for these?" Zhu Bajie said in an aside, "We truly dare not accept gold and silver. But my robe was torn by those lion demons; if they will exchange one set of robes for us, that would be enough as a token of love." The prince accordingly ordered the seamstress workers, and by matching colors and patterns took several lengths of blue brocade, red brocade, and tea-brown brocade and made one robe for each of the three. The three gladly accepted, put on straight-collared brocade jackets, gathered their travel packs, and set out. Then in and beyond the city, whether great or small, there was not one who did not call them Arhats come to the mortal world, Living Buddhas descending from above. Drum and music sounded; banners and colors filled the streets and blocked the roads. Indeed, in every household incense was burned and everywhere before every doorway offered colorful lanterns. When they had gone a long way to the west, only then did the four leave the city westward. This departure shed all the lion host, and their hearts turned in earnest to the true fruition. As it was: With no worry and no anxiety they come toward the Buddha realm, With sincere heart and true intent they rise to Leiyin.

Still it is not yet known how much farther the road to Spirit Mountain remains or when they will arrive there. Listen and settle this in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 90: The Lion Master grants and receives in unity; the thief on the path entangles nine spirits in stillness.
