This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

What use is this effort in Chan, if your discipline is no better than a lame horse and a frenzied ape? Quickly cut them away. Hold fast and bind tight the life of five colours; if it pauses and stays even a little, it falls into the three destinies. If the freely governed divine elixir leaks and you let it go at your leisure, then the jade nature will soon wither. Anger, joy, sorrow, and brooding thought must all be swept clean; to obtain the profound and wondrous is exactly to be as nothing.

At first Tripitaka and the four companions left Yuhua City. The way was smooth, truly what one might call a village of bliss. After five or six days of travel, they saw another city. Tripitaka asked Wukong, "What place is this?" Wukong said, "It is a city. But I do not see banners on the battlements; I do not know where it lies. Let us go closer and ask." They reached the east gate quarter and saw teahouses and taverns clamoring on both sides, and a noisy place of rice markets and oil shops. Along the streets there were a few idle ruffians, idle youths with nothing to do. Seeing Zhu Bajie with his long mouth, Sha Wujing with his black face, and Wukong with his reddened eyes, they crowded around and stared, but did not dare come near enough to speak. Tripitaka clenched his hands with sweat in fear, worrying they might cause trouble. After passing several more alleyways, they had not yet entered the city when they saw a mountain gate with the three characters "Ciyun Temple" on it. Tripitaka said, "Let us come in here a little, rest the horses, and take a meal offering, shall we?" Wukong said, "Good, good." The four entered together. There they saw:

Magnificent are the jewel halls, and the great jeweled seats stand proud and towering. The Buddha pavilion rises above the high drifting clouds. In the still moon, the monks' cells are quiet. Rosy clouds drift in the far mist; the pagoda rises, remote and fine, while dark-green trees stand in secluded depth. Truly this seems a pure land, though it wears a false Dragon Palace; above the Great Hero Hall, violet clouds enshroud the air. Neither the twin corridors nor the unending passages are bereft of idle folk at play; a single tower is always open and guests are ever ascending it. Incense burns in the furnaces from time to time, and lamp-flowers gleam on the platform every night. Then came the sonorous gold bell of the abbot’s hall, answering the Buddhists who clearly and deeply chanted the scriptures. While the four were still looking, a monk came out beneath the corridor and bowed to Tripitaka: "Teacher, where do you come from?" Tripitaka answered, "Your disciple comes from the Tang capital of Zhonghua." The monk threw himself down in full prostration. Startled, Tripitaka helped him up: "Abbot, why do you render this great courtesy?" The monk pressed his palms together and said, "Among the virtuous here, all who recite the Dharma and chant the Buddha-Breathing teachings hope only for rebirth in your land of Zhonghua. Now on seeing your handsome bearing, robes, and cap, I know indeed that in former lives you cultivated this and so may enjoy this result, and therefore I bow at once." Tripitaka smiled: "How terrifying for me! I am only a traveling monk with no merit or luxury. If the abbot here can linger at ease, then truly that is happiness." The monk then led Tripitaka into the main hall; after he paid homage to the Buddha image, Tripitaka then summoned the disciples inside. Wukong and the other two had stood nearby with dark faces, one leading the horse and another bearing the baggage, since when that monk spoke with the master they had felt no place in his thoughts. Only when they heard Tripitaka call "disciples" did the three turn around. Seeing them, the monk cried out, "Goodness, what strange ugly faces your foremost disciples have!" Tripitaka said, "Though they are ugly, they are nevertheless potent in magic. They have protected me all along this road."

While this was being spoken, several monks came out from inside and bowed. The monk who spoke first said to those arriving later, "This teacher is a person of the Great Tang of Zhonghua, and those three are his senior disciples." The gathered monks were both glad and startled: "A teacher from the Great Tang of the central realm, why has he come here?" Tripitaka said, "I carry the holy command of the Tang king, going to Lingshan to worship Buddha and seek the scriptures. I have just passed Baofang and now hasten uphill toward the holy mountain: one aim is to ask about direction, and another is to take alms and a meal before departing." All the monks were overjoyed and invited them into the hall. In that hall were more monks preparing alms-offerings. The one who had entered first called out, "Come all of you and look at this person from Zhonghua. In Zhonghua there are handsome men and ugly men. The handsome are truly beyond description and painting; the ugly ones, though, are singularly strange." So all the monks here and the alms host came to meet them. After seeing them all, everyone sat down. After tea, Tripitaka asked, "What is the name of this place?" They replied, "This is Jinping Prefecture, a district outside Tianzhu." Tripitaka asked, "How far is your prefecture from Lingshan?" The monks said, "From here to the capital it is two thousand li; that is the distance we have traversed. Westward to Lingshan, we have not gone, and we do not dare presume to answer how much farther remains." Tripitaka thanked them.

After a short time, a meal was served. When the meal ended, Tripitaka prepared to leave, but the monks and the alms host together detained him: "Teacher, stay and make your home here one or two days. After Yuanxiao, there will be no harm in setting off." Tripitaka asked anxiously, "On the road one sees only mountains and waters, and fears meeting monsters and demons; I fear the time may all be wasted. I do not even know when the Yuanxiao festival arrives." The monks laughed: "Since you worship Buddha and place your heart on awakening in Chan, you do not need to be concerned. Today is the thirteenth day of the first month; by evening they try out the lamps. The fifteenth is Shangyuan. It is only on the eighteenth and ninth that the lights are finally thanked away and put out. In this place every household keeps good fortune; our magistrate cherishes the people and every quarter here is hung with high lamps, music and flutes sounding all night. There is even a Golden-Lamp Bridge, kept since antiquity and still flourishing. If the abbots of this place ask you to stay several days, this poor mountain monastery can surely shelter you." Tripitaka had no alternative and stayed. That evening he could only hear the temple bells and drums ringing like heaven above the Buddha hall, for the neighborhood devotees had brought lanterns to present to Buddha. Tripitaka and the others came out of the abbot’s hall and watched the lights, and then each retired for the night.

The next day the temple monks offered another meal. After eating, they all went out to pass the time in the garden. It truly was a wonderful place:

It is the first month, the year has reached new spring. The gardens are secluded and graceful; the scenes are lush and beautiful. Through all the seasons flowers and trees compete for wonder, while ridges and peaks in one stretch pile green upon green. Fragrant grasses stir on the steps; old plum branches begin to scent the air. Peach blossoms turn to tender red; willow buds return with fresh green. The Garden of Golden Valley is splendid, but make no boasts; the famed Wanchuan Scroll whispers of its own flowing wind. Across the stream, wild ducks appear and vanish unpredictably. A thousand stands of bamboo rise; poets still pause and deliberate. Peonies, peonies, azaleas, and smiling-flowers wake the hidden scheme of heaven; camellias, red plums, vernal welcoming blooms, and osmanthus uncover their splendid colors first. On shady cliffs, the old snow still holds its frost, while distant trees send out spring haze. Again one may see a deer at the pond, reflecting its image; a crane comes beneath a pine to listen as if to a qin. To the east are guest cabins; to the west, pavilions where travelers may lodge. To the south, assembly halls; to the north, a tower where monks sit in quiet meditation. Among the flower grounds stand one or two Nurturing-Nature pavilions with broad eaves arcing high. Within hills and streams there are three or four demon-refining chambers, with quiet benches and clear windows. Truly this is a place fashioned by nature itself for seclusion; why seek Penglai elsewhere? The disciples spent a whole day in play and contemplation, then after seeing the lamps in the hall, all went to watch the lantern displays. But they saw: A city of agate blossoms, crystal caves of immortals, and micastral palaces of crystal: layer upon layer of brocade-like magnificence, dense upon dense with lucid intricacy. The reflected light of the star-bridge trembles and stirs heaven and earth; a few trees of flame sway red. In six streets, flutes and drums; at a thousand gates, moonlike brightness; in ten-thousand households, a wind perfumed with incense. On many places, lofty tortoise-crag pavilions rise; fish-drakes rise from the sea, and phoenix-and-feng glide in the air. The lamp-light and moon-glow are alike, and the atmosphere is warm and harmonious. In the silk-brocade processions, all are delighted to hear reeds and songs. Carriages and horses thunder on: one can never get one’s fill of beautiful faces and jade-like features; gallant beauty and graceful elegance, a boundless fine scene. Tripitaka and the monks watched the lanterns in the temple, then went through the streets of the east gate quarter to join the festival crowds. They returned home only by the second watch of the night.

The next day Tripitaka said to the monks, "My disciple has a preexisting vow to sweep a pagoda. On this festive day of Shangyuan, please have the abbot open the pagoda gates so that I may fulfill this intention." The monks opened the gates at once. Sha Wujing took a kasaya and followed Tripitaka. Upon reaching the first level, he put on the kasaya, worshipped Buddha and offered prayers, then swept one level with a broom, removed the kasaya, and handed it back to Sha Wujing. ... He then swept the second level. Level after level, he swept straight on to the topmost point. On the tower, tiers and tiers of Buddha-images faced outward, and windows opened everywhere. Each level he swept was a level he also admired, admired, and praised. When all was done and he had come down, dusk had already darkened, and the lamps were all lit.

This night is truly the fifteenth of the Lantern Festival. The monks said, "Master, only last night we watched lanterns on the barren mountains and at the frontier watchposts; tonight is the proper day of the festival—let us go into the city and see how the golden lamps are displayed." Tripitaka gladly agreed, and the three companions and many monks from this temple entered the city to watch the lamps. Just then:

On this happy Three-Five night, the upper-lantern spring season is in tune. Flowery lanterns hang through the noisy city, and all sing together the songs of peace. Again I saw lamps glow on six streets and three markets, and a half-sky silver mirror rise. The moon rose like Fengyi lifting a blazing silver tray, and the lanterns seemed woven by immortals into a brocade spread on the ground. The lamp light, facing the moon, doubled its brilliance; the moonlight on the lamps added tenfold brilliance. One could not exhaust the star bridges of chained iron, nor could one fully behold the fire-trees and blossom-lights. Snow-flower lamps, plum-flower lamps, broke like spring ice. Embroidered-screen lamps, painted-screen lamps, amassed all five colors. Walnut lamps, lotus-lotus lamps, hung high on lofty lamp towers. Green-lion lamps, white-elephant lamps, mounted on high lamp frames. Shrimp lamps, turtle lamps, raised high before the stalls. Goat-lamps, hare-lamps, spirit-tuned beneath the eaves. Hawk-lamps, phoenix-lamps, linked together. Tiger-lamps, horse-lamps, moving side by side. Immortal-crane lamps, white-deer lamps, where the Star of Longevity rides in pride. Goldfish lamps, great-whale lamps, Li Bai ridden aloft. Ao-shan lamps, where immortals convene. Running-horse lamps, where generals clash in rank. Ten thousand household lamp-towers shone, a few tens of li of cloud-like, smoke-filled world. On that side, jade tassels and clasps clinked and flew in; on this side, rumbling carts of perfume passed. On the red-gowned upper rooms, by railings through curtains, with shoulders touching, hands clasped, pairs of beauties reveled in pleasure; by the Green-Water Bridge there was uproar and clamor, brocade clustered thick, wine-drunk laughter, and merry-playing guests in couples. Through the whole city, flute and drum sounded in tumult, and all night long music and song never ceased. There is verse to bear witness: In brocaded courts we sing of painted lotuses, In realms of peace, human crowds cluster. Lamps and moonlight bright on this Lantern night of the full moon, Rain is timely, wind in tune; the harvest will be abundant. Now was it truly an age when the Golden Guards were no longer restraining, all in tumult, and countless multitudes of people and hearth-flames. Dancers danced, tiptoe dancers, ghost-imitators, elephant riders—one crowd to the east, another to the west, impossible to see them all.

It was only as soon as they came to the Golden-Lantern Bridge that Tripitaka and the monks came close enough to see. It was in fact three golden lanterns. Each lantern was as big as a vat and cast light over a delicate, translucent two-story pavilion. All were braided of fine golden wire, with thin sheets of glassware supporting the frame inside. The light flashed like polished brightness, and the oil gave out fragrance. Tripitaka turned to the monks and asked, "What oil is this? How can such unusual fragrance fill the air?" The monks said, "Master, I do not know. In my prefecture there is a county called Mintian County, two hundred and forty li across. Each year in assigned levies there are two hundred and forty major oil households. The regular levies of the prefecture and county are manageable, but this one is especially burdensome: each household is assessed over two hundred taels of silver for the year. This is no ordinary oil—it is suhe-fragrant oil. Each tael of it is worth two taels of silver; each jin is worth thirty-two taels of silver. For each of the three lamps, each vat holds five hundred jin; three vats hold one thousand five hundred jin in all, costing forty-eight thousand taels in all. With incidental levies and charges there is above fifty thousand taels, and yet it burns only for three nights." Sun Wukong asked, "How can so much oil be spent in only three nights?" The monks replied, "In each vat there are forty-nine great lamp-horses. They are lamp-grass bundles wrapped in cotton with silk, thick as a hen's egg. Burned for this very night, if Buddha appears in person, then by tomorrow night the oil is gone and the lamps grow dim." Zhu Bajie laughed nearby and said, "It must be that even Buddha has taken away the oil." The monks said, "That is exactly the saying. In this city, from old times to now, this is how people speak. When the oil is exhausted, everyone says the Buddha took the lamp-offering, and naturally the five grains are plentiful. But if in a year it does not run out, then there is drought in that season and wind and rain are out of balance. So households must make this offering."

Just then, while the talk was still mid-sentence, there came the whoo of wind from midair. It startled those watching the lanterns, and they all scattered. Even the monks could not stand firm and said, "Master, let us return. The wind has come; that is Buddha's auspicious descent, to watch these lanterns here as well." Tripitaka said, "How do you know it is Buddha coming to see the lamps?" The monks answered, "Year after year, before the three watches are done, this wind comes. We know the Buddhas descend in blessing, and so everyone gives way." Tripitaka said, "My disciples are by nature to think on Buddha, bow to Buddha, and worship Buddha. Now that we have met this fair scene, if Buddhas truly descend, then to worship here is surely good." The monks implored him again and again, but could not turn him. After a short while, in the wind there indeed appeared three Buddha bodies, approaching the lanterns. Alarmed, Tripitaka ran to the top of the bridge and threw himself prostrate. Sun Wukong hurriedly pulled him up and said, "Master, these are not good men; surely they are demons." Before he could finish, the lantern light grew dim. With one sudden cry he lifted Tripitaka and rode the wind away. Alas, who knows what mountain or what cave this true demon came from, having for years feigned Buddha to watch the Golden-Lantern rite? Zhu Bajie, frightened, searched on both sides, and Sha Wujing called from both flanks. Sun Wukong said, "Brothers, do not shout here. My Master was filled with joy, and joy has turned to sorrow; he has already been taken by a demon spirit." The few monks, in fear, asked, "Sir, how do you know he was taken by a demon spirit?" Sun Wukong laughed: "You men of this world have been ignorant for years and were deluded, so you kept saying this was the true Buddha descending and accepted this lamp offering. The three who appeared with the wind were three demons. Even my Master could not recognize them. As he ascended the bridge-top to bow, they dimmed the lamps, took up the vessel that held the oil, and seized my Master as well. I was only a little late in moving, so those three turned into wind and fled." Sha Wujing asked, "Elder Brother, what are we to do now?" Sun Wukong said, "Do not hesitate. You two and the rest return to the monastery, guard the horses and luggage. Let Old Monkey use this wind to pursue."

Great Sage leapt at once onto a Jindou cloud, rose into midair, caught the rank wind-scent, and raced northeast. He pursued until near dawn, when the wind suddenly ceased. He saw a very steep mountain, truly severe and rugged, with real grandeur:

Layer upon layer were valleys and ravines, winding springs among them. Vines hung from jagged cliffs, pines and cypresses stood straight on bare crags. In the morning mist cranes called; in the dawn clouds geese cried. Lofty peaks stood rank upon rank, ridges thrust like spear rows, with rough stones stacked in dazzling masses. The summit rose ten thousand fathoms high, and sharp ridges piled into a thousand folds. Wild flowers and good trees knew spring had arrived, and cuckoos and orioles answered in fitting color. It could be majestic and imposing, truly cliff-rugged, ancient, strange, steep, and hard to pass. After lingering for long, no one spoke; only tiger and leopard voices rumbled in thunderous snoring. Fragrant deer and white deer came and went, jade rabbits and blue wolves went out and returned. Deep ravines streamed for ten thousand li, returning rapids striking stones with murmuring chatter. The Great Sage was searching the cliff face for a route when he saw four men driving three sheep down from the western slope, all calling together, "Open Tai." Sun Wukong, flashing his discerning eyes, peered closely and recognized them as the envoy officials of the four marks of year, month, day, and hour, disguised in hidden form. He drew out the Golden-Hooped Staff, snapped it once, broad as a basin in girth and two zhang long, and leapt from the cliff, shouting, "Where have you all gone hiding and shrinking your heads and necks?" The four duty officers, seeing him speak of wind signs, quickly drove off the three sheep and, revealing their true forms, slipped to the roadside and bowed, saying, "Great Sage, forgive us, forgive us." Sun Wukong said, "You have not been put to use by me in this time before. Since you saw Old Monkey in no hurry, each of you grew careless; not one of you came to pay me a visit. What is this? Why did you not secretly protect my Master in secret? Where are you all going?" They answered, "Your Master loosened his Chan composure and grew indulgent at Ciyun Temple of Jinping Prefecture; when fullness reaches its height, sorrow follows, and now he has been captured by demon spirits. He is under protection of Dharma guardians of the temple. We know the Great Sage pursued overnight and feared you might not know this wilderness, so we came to report." Sun Wukong said, "If you have delivered the news, why do you hide your names and run about with three sheep, shouting and crying?" The officers said, "These three sheep were set in order to answer the phrase 'Open Tai.' They are called 'Three Yang, Great Opening.' It is to break your Master's blockage." Sun Wukong, with angry intent, was about to strike them, then seeing this intent ceased, withdrew the staff and, changing anger into delight, asked, "Is this mountain a demon haunt?" The officers said, "It is indeed. This is Qinglong Mountain, with a cave called Xuaning Cave. Inside are three demons. The eldest is called King Bihan, the second King Bishu, and the third King Bichen. These demons have been here for a thousand years. From childhood they loved to eat suhe-fragrant oil, and in time they became spirits. They feigned Buddha images, deceived the officials and people of Jinping Prefecture, and set up this Golden-Lantern rite, using suhe-fragrant oil for the lamp fuel. Year after year, on this first month's fifteenth, they transform into Buddha forms and collect the oil. This year, seeing your Master, they recognized him as a holy monk, took him into the cave, and soon intend to cut and cook his flesh in suhe-fragrant oil. Be quick and use all your powers to rescue him."

The Pilgrim heard and dismissed the four Captains, then turned around the mountain brow in search of the cave dwelling. He had gone only a few li when he saw a stone cliff by the ravine. Beneath it stood a rock house with two stone doors, half open and half shut. By the gate was a stone stele with six characters: “Qinglong Mountain, Xuanying Cave.” The Pilgrim did not dare to enter at once; he set his feet and called out, “Demon! Send out my Master immediately.” A hoarse cry sounded there; the door burst open, and a troop of ox-headed fiends dashed out. One of them, thick-faced and dull, asked, “Who are you, to shout out in this place?” Sun Wukong replied, “I am the senior disciple of Tripitaka, the holy monk from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, who goes west for the scriptures. While we passed through the lantern-gazing at Ci Yun Temple in Jinping Prefecture, your demon lord seized my Master. Send him back quickly and I will spare your lives; otherwise I will turn your whole den upside down and make all your spirits into pus and blood.”

Those small demons heard this and hurried inside to report: “Great King, there is misfortune—misfortune!” The three old fiends were holding Tang Sanzang deep in the cave’s far recesses, where, without wasting time on questions of right and wrong, they had ordered the young ones to strip off his robes, wash him clean in the rushing stream water, and then plan to cut him into fine pieces and fry him in butter and sesame oil. At that moment they heard the cry of calamity. The elder fiend, startled, asked what had happened. A little demon said, “In front of the outer gate, a shaggy-faced, thunder-mouth monk was shouting: ‘A monkey-monk took our lord’s Buddha image and says you have abducted his Master. Send my Master back at once and spare our lives. If not, he will overturn the nest and turn us all into pus and blood.’ Hearing this, the old demons all grew alarmed. “We have only just captured this fellow and have not yet asked his name or origin. You youngsters, put robes on him and bring him out; we shall examine him fully and learn who he is and from where he came.”

A crowd of fiends came up, untied Tang Sanzang, put robes back on him, and pushed him before the seat. Terrified, Tang Sanzang knelt beneath them and trembled, crying only, “Great King, spare my life.” The three demons spoke in one voice: “From where do you come, monk? Why did you not avoid the Buddha image and yet crash into my cloud-road?” Tang Sanzang knelt and said, “I beg your pardon, this poor monk came from the Great Tang by imperial decree of the emperor to NIRUTRA [the Western Region], to Long Sound Temple (Da Le Yin) to worship the Buddha and fetch the scriptures. Passing through Jinping Prefecture, I came to Ci Yun Temple and joined the alms-round. By your lord’s monkly grace, the temple monks let me stay through the Lantern Festival to watch the lanterns. At the Golden-Lamp Bridge I saw the Buddha image manifest before your lord. I am but mortal flesh and blood; seeing Buddha, I bowed, and in that I crashed into your lord’s cloud-road.” One fiend asked, “From the Eastern Land to here is a long way. How many are you in one group? What are your names? Speak plainly and I may spare your life.” Tang Sanzang said, “In the secular world I am called Chen Xuanzang. Since childhood I was a monk of Jinshan Temple. Later, by imperial edict, I was ordained as monk-official at Hongfu Temple in Chang’an. Then, when Chancellor Wei Zheng dreamed he cut the old dragon of the Jing River, the Tang Emperor journeyed to the Netherworld, returned to life, and held a great Water-and-Land assembly to deliver the dead from the dark realms. Therefore the emperor selected this poor monk as altar master and later as interpreter of the great canons. By good fortune Guanyin Bodhisattva appeared, transformed this poor monk’s mind, and said that at Great Sound Temple in the Western Heaven are the true Tripiṭaka scriptures, which can raise departed spirits toward Heaven. Thus I was sent. I was given the name “Tripitaka,” and because I bore the surname Tang, all now call me Tang Sanzang. I have three disciples. The first is surnamed Sun, named Wukong, the Pilgrim, once the Great Sage Who Equaled Heaven, now restored to true alignment. The second is surnamed Zhu, named Wuneng, Bajie, the former Heavenly Trellic Commander in former life. The third is surnamed Sha, named Wujing, a monk, formerly the general Juanlian in descending to the mortal world.” Hearing this name, the fiends were suddenly startled and said, “Is that Great Sage Who Equaled Heaven the one who threw the Heavenly Court into uproar five hundred years ago?” Tang Sanzang answered, “Yes, yes.” “The second is surnamed Zhu, named Wuneng Bajie, the former commander of Heavenly Skies. The third is surnamed Sha, named Wujing, who once served as General Jüanlian in descending here,” the first added, “are known as what you have heard.”

The three demon kings heard this and, each in alarm, said, “We have not yet eaten him. Younglings, tie Tang Sanzang with iron chains at the back. When we get his three disciples, we shall have enough for the meal.” So they summoned a mob of mountain-buffalo spirits, water-buffalo spirits, and yellow-buffalo spirits, each bearing arms, and they came out the gate, taking up drumbeats and banners. The three demon lords dressed themselves in orderly array and stepped outside, crying, “Who is this who dares to shout here?” Sun Wukong waited upon the stone brow and watched closely as they appeared: they were as follows.

Their faces were painted and ringed with bright eyes, two horns hard and jutting. Keen and sharp, four ears, spirit-orifices flashing with light. Their bodies were patterned in variegated design, all as if painted, all over in brocaded plumage like flying petals. The first, with a fox-fur flowered cap atop his head, had one flushed, raised snout steaming with fierce heat. The second wore light gauze, aflame like leaping fire, with four jewel-bright hooves that rang. The third roared with a mighty lion-like sound, thunderous as a drum; his fangs were sharp, like silver needles. All were brave and fierce; each held one of three weapons—one an axe, one a great knife—and the third carried across his shoulder a vine-whip cudgel. Also seen were many small and large ox-headed fiends, some tall, some short, some stout, some thin, all in varied size, all spears and clubs in hand. Three large banners were there, clearly written: “Bi-han Great King,” “Bi-shu Great King,” “Bi-chen Great King.”

Sun Wukong watched a while and could not bear it; he stepped forward and shouted, “You thieves and fiends! Do you recognize Old Sun?” One demon answered, “You are the Sun Wukong who once threw Heaven into chaos? I have heard your name but never seen you; even to behold you is shame for a heavenly god. So this is what kind of monkey-brute you are?” The Pilgrim was furious and cursed, “You oil-stealing, smooth-tongued fiend—stop your empty talk and return my Master at once.” He lunged forward and swung his iron staff. The three demon kings raised all three kinds of weapons to meet him. What followed in the mountain hollow was a grim battle:

Axe, steel sabre, and vine-whip flew up and down, while the Monkey King met them with one single staff. Bi-han, Bi-shu, and Bi-chen fiends, knowing the name of the Great Sage Who Equaled Heaven, made the spirits and ghosts fear when the staff rose; axes and knives flew, chopping in wild arcs. What a true image of Perfect Emptiness and Real Method the one who held it was, standing firm against three fiends in counterfeit Buddha shape. Those three oil-stealing, nose-slick fiends set this year to seize an envoy monk sent from the Emperor’s court. One, because of me he did not fear the long road to the Dharma; another, with that face, long had prepared incense and lamps. Ping-pang, only the clashing of knives and axes was heard; only the staff split the air with its sound. Ramming and crashing, they clashed in threes, parrying and blocking, each showing his skill. Once the fight reached dusk, no one knew which had yielded and which had prevailed. For one hundred and fifty exchanges Sun Wukong fought the three fiends, and as evening came the outcome was still undecided. Then Bi-chen Great King flicked his vine-whip once, leapt past the front, and gave the banner a shake. A horde of ox-headed fiends surged forward and surrounded Sun Wukong in their center, brandishing weapons and striking wildly. Seeing that all was not going well for him, Sun Wukong gave a ringing cry, mounted his cloud-kicking somersault, and withdrew in disorder. The demons did not chase. They called the fiends back, laid out the evening meal, and all ate heartily. They also ordered a bowl sent to Tang Sanzang, saying they would have the two together before setting everything in order. As for the Master, he kept an extended fast and, in sorrow, wept and sobbed; out of fear he did not dare touch even a grain of food.

Then Sun Wukong rode his cloud back into Ci Yun Temple and called, “Brothers-in-faith.” Ba Jie and Sha Monk were waiting and discussing together. Hearing the call, both came out to receive him. “Brother, how did you return so quickly in one day? What is the Master’s whereabouts?” The Pilgrim smiled and said, “Last night, hearing the wind of this affair, I hurried on, reached a mountain by dawn and went a short distance on, and saw nothing. By good fortune I heard from the four Captains that the mountain is Qinglong Mountain, and in it a cave called Xuanying Cave. Within are three fiends named the Bi-han Great King, Bi-shu Great King, and Bi-chen Great King. For years they have stolen oil, feigned Buddha images, and tricked officials and people in Jinping Prefecture. When they met us this time, they did not know what was right or wrong and even seized the Master. Sensing the whole matter, Old Sun ordered the Captains and others to guard the Master from afar in secret. I then moved close to the gate and shouted in reproach. Those three fiends came out together; each was like an ox-headed ghost. The first wielded a battle axe, the second a great sabre, and the third a vine-club. They brought out a whole crowd of ox-headed goblins, raised banners and drums, and fought with Old Sun for a full day until blood-slick and fierce. When the demon king raised his banner, the small fiends all joined. It grew late; fearing I could not force a victory, I rode my cloud-somersault and returned.” Ba Jie said, “Could this be the Ghost King of Fengdu causing a commotion?” Sha Monk asked, “How did you guess it was some uproar made by the Ghost King of Fengdu?” Ba Jie laughed, “Brother said they were ox-headed fiends—so I knew, no doubt.” Sun Wukong said, “No, no. In my judgment, those beasts were made from three rhinoceroses.” Ba Jie said, “If they are rhinoceroses, then seize him, saw off his horn, and you would fetch a good few taels of silver.”

Just then, amid the conversation, the monks said, “Sun Wukong, will you take the evening meal?” The Traveler said, “I can eat a little for convenience; if not, no matter.” The monks replied, “Elder Master, after all this day of fighting, are you not hungry?” Sun Wukong laughed, “How could I be hungry after this day’s going? Old Sun has gone five hundred years without food or drink.” The monks did not know he spoke truly and took it for a jest. Soon the food was brought, and the Traveler ate as well. He said, “Now get ready and prepare to sleep. Tomorrow we all go together to engage him, seize the demon king, and perhaps save the Tripitaka.” Sha Wujing spoke beside him: “Brother, your words do not suffice! As the saying has it, ‘Delay steals one’s wisdom.’ If this demon, this night, should not sleep and harms the Tripitaka, what then? It would be better if we go now and seize him while he is taken by surprise in this moonlight; only then can we save the Master. If we delay even a little, we may lose the moment.” Zhu Bajie, hearing this, stirred his strength and declared, “Brother Sha speaks well. Let us all take this moonlight and descend now to subdue the demon.” Sun Wukong followed their counsel and immediately ordered the temple monks: “Guard the baggage and the horses. Once we bring in the demon, we should present him before the magistrate here in this prefecture, prove him a false Buddha, and spare the poor common folk of Su Gai County from the drain of lamp oil. Would that not be the better way?” The monks obeyed. The three then rose upon auspicious clouds and left the city. It was just then that this verse fell:

Slack and careless, Zen uncouth, and wayward nature scattered; danger and misfortune, in time, veil the path of the mind.

After all, it remains to be seen how victory or defeat in this affair will turn out; wait to hear how it is resolved in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 91: At Jinping Prefecture a New-Year lantern rite is seen; in Xuanying Cave Tripitaka submits his memorial.

Once thereupon, Great Sage Sun Wukong, together with his two younger brothers, rolled in the whirling wind, mounted on the cloud, and in a trice arrived at the mouth of Xuan-Ying Cave at Qinglong Mountain in the northeast direction. The Classics say, “When fortune reaches its extreme, can it not return?” In the best of times, perils are indeed certain. Of the two horns he had brought, leave one in the prefectural hall vault as perpetual evidence that lamp oil taxes are exempt thereafter; take one with us to offer before Buddha on Spirit-Treasured Mountain. The four stars rejoiced in their hearts. At once they bowed farewell to Great Sage, mounted in colorful clouds, and hastened back in report.

The county officials detained the four monks in honor, setting a great vegetarian feast and asking all local officials to attend. In one quarter a proclamation was posted, informing the military and commoners that next year no Golden Lamps were to be set, and the annual levy on the two hundred and forty oil-household contributors was forever remitted. In another quarter the butchers were ordered to slaughter and skin the rhinoceros; the hide was cured and dried with sulfur smoke and made into armor, and its meat was shared among the officials and people. In another quarter they raised funds from fines and grain assessments without obstruction and bought vacant village land, then built a temple to the four stars who had subdued the demon, and also raised memorial shrines for Tripitaka’s party. In each place stelae were carved with inscriptions, to be passed on for a thousand generations, as thanks and recompense.

The party of four accepted all this with broad hearts. Then the two hundred and forty lamp-oil households and one family and another household all made their recompense and invitations in turn, with not a moment unspent. Zhu Bajie, fully satisfied and content, gathered treasures taken from the cave and put a little of each into his sleeves as gifts for each household’s ceremonial banquet. They stayed for a month, yet still could not rise to depart. Tripitaka then ordered, “Wukong, send all the remaining treasures to the monks of Ciyun Temple as presents. Slip away before the daylight from the houses of those great oil households. To linger among them will only feed greed and joy, and we may miss the pilgrimage, inviting blame from Buddha and bringing fresh calamity on us. It is very improper.” Wukong obeyed and handed out the previous items one by one.

At dawn of the next day, at the fifth watch, Tripitaka called for Zhu Bajie to prepare the horses. The fool, having eaten generous wine and rice, woke from a heavy sleep and groggily asked, “Why so early to prepare the horses?” Wukong shouted, “The Master has ordered us to set out.” The fool rubbed his face and said, “Again this abbot is no proper person. Two hundred and forty great households all invited; we have had thirty-odd full vegetarian banquets, and now again you make this old hog fast?” Upon hearing this, the Master scolded, “You stupid boor, stop your nonsense. Rise quickly, and if you continue this bad mouth, I’ll have Wukong strike you and break your teeth with the Golden-Hooped Staff.” Hearing “strike,” the fool panicked and said, “Master has changed this time. At other times he pities me, loves me, and says I am foolish but dear; when he wanted to beat me, he would mediate. Why today this anger and now he orders beating?” Wukong said, “The Master’s displeasure is with your tongue, which has delayed our road. Quickly gather the baggage, saddle the horses, and there will be no blows.” Truly fearing beating, he leapt up and dressed, then called out to Sha Wujing, “Quickly rise, he is coming to strike.” Sha Wujing rose too, and all the packing was finished. The Master gestured: “Quietly and silently; do not wake the temple monks.” They then hurriedly mounted, opened the mountain gate, and sought the road onward. As goes the saying:

Secretly he opened the jade cage and let a painted phoenix fly; privately he unfastened the golden lock and released the scale-dragon.

As for what came of the recompense from those grateful households before dawn, listen and unravel it in the next installment.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Whenever thought rises and clings all at once, love held on will surely bring disaster. Clarity of spirit cannot tell apart the three platforms. When the course is fulfilled, one naturally returns to the Primordial Sea. Whether one becomes an immortal or becomes Buddha, it must be settled from within. Pure and clean, free from all dust. Then truly one’s fruit will rise and ascend to the upper realms.

Now it is said that Temple-Monk Tianming did not find Tripitaka and his three disciples, and all said, “We did not keep them, we did not see them off, we did not even hear them ask to leave; somehow we let a living Bodhisattva go away plainly and unimpeded.” Just then, several householders from the south gate side came to make requests. The monks clapped their hands and said, “Last night we had no guard to stop them; tonight they all took to the clouds and left.” Everyone at once looked up into the air and bowed in thanks. When this was spoken, every official and commoner in the city all came to know it. Those same wealthy houses were all ordered to organize full sacrificial offerings—five kinds of livestock and flowers and fruits—and to make offerings at the Shrine of Rebirth in thanks; the particulars need not be recorded.

Yet Tripitaka and his four companions had eaten wind and drunk water, lodging only by the road, and after more than half a month of travel, all was peaceful. Suddenly one day they came upon a high mountain. Tripitaka said in alarm, “Disciple, the mountain ridge in front is steep and formidable; we must be careful.” Wukong laughed, “This road is near the Buddha lands, so surely there are no fiends or demons here. Master, keep your heart at ease and do not worry.” Tripitaka replied, “Disciple, although the Buddha lands are not far, that temple monk said only recently that from here to Heaven-India is two thousand li; we still do not know how much farther remains.” Wukong said, “Master, have you once again forgotten what Wuchao Chan Master taught as the Heart Sūtra?” Tripitaka said, “The Prajñā Heart Sūtra is stitched into my robe and alms bowl. Since Wuchao Chan Master taught it to me, on what day did I not recite it? At what moment could I have forgotten? Even if recited in reverse I can still recite it; how could I forget?” Wukong said, “Master, you only recite it, but you never asked the master for explanation.” Tripitaka said, “Monkey-head, how can you say I did not understand? Do you understand it?” Wukong said, “I understand. I understand.” From then on, Tripitaka and Wukong were silent. At that moment Zhu Bajie laughed himself into fits, and Sha Wujing was just as delighted, saying, “Mouthful one, you were born, like me, as a demon spirit; you have not heard this Chan and Zi kind hear teachings, nor have you seen any Buddha monk give Dharma talks. You swagger with an empty head, looking for a pose, saying things like ‘I know’ and ‘I understand.’ Why are you now silent? Please explain for us to hear.” Sha Wujing said, “Second Brother, do you even believe him? The Elder Brother is spinning long words to lead Master astray on the path. He only knows how to use the staff—how could he understand a sermon?” Tripitaka said, “Wuneng, Wujing, stop talking nonsense. Sun Wukong’s understanding is not in words and letters; it is genuine understanding.”

Their party kept walking while speaking and had already gone many paces, passed a few hills, and now beside the road saw a large monastery. Tripitaka said, “Wukong, there is a monastery ahead. Look at that temple:

It is neither small nor large, yet it has green-glazed-tile roofs; Half-new and half-old, yet it has red walls in the Eight-Character pattern. Dimly one sees dark pines spreading overhead, and one cannot know how many hundreds or thousands of years it has remained until now; Water runs on, murmuring like music-struck strings, and one cannot tell to which age the cleaving of the mountain belonged. On the gate is written in large characters: ‘Bujin Chan Monastery’; on the hanging plaque is inscribed: ‘Remnant of Antiquity.’” Wukong saw that it was “Bujin Chan Monastery,” and Zhu Bajie also called it “Bujin Chan Monastery.” On horseback, Tripitaka thought to himself, “‘Bujin’…‘Bujin’… Could this not be the border of Śrāvastī?” Zhu Bajie said, “Master, wondrous! After these years with you I have not seen any roads; today I can recognize one?” Tripitaka said, “No. I have often read sutras and histories: it says that in Śrāvastī, in Jīvaka’s Park, Buddha gave teachings under a sacred tree. The park was that of the lay patron Jiguodu, who asked the prince to sell it. The prince replied, ‘I will not sell this park. If he wants to buy it, he must spread gold across the entire grounds.’ Jiguodu did so, laying gold bricks thickly over the land and bought the park, then invited the World-Honored One to teach Dharma. I am thinking this Bujin monastery may be that very story?” Zhu Bajie laughed, “By fate, if this is truly that story, we can even go and feel a brick and give one to him.” Everyone laughed for a while, and then Tripitaka dismounted.

As they entered the mountain gate, under it were porters with shoulder poles, pack-carriers, cart-drivers, and carts fully settled in place; some went to sleep and some went on talking. Suddenly seeing Tripitaka’s party of four—handsome and more handsome, ugly and more ugly—everyone seemed a little afraid, yet they made some room to let them pass. Fearing to cause trouble, Tripitaka kept crying out, “Polite ones, polite ones.” At that moment everyone all at once grew restrained. After passing the Vajra Hall, a Chan monk appeared with extraordinary composure, truly:

His face was as bright as full moonlight, his body like a bodhi tree. With robe sleeves over the shoulder, wind rose in them; his straw sandals met the stony road. Tripitaka asked and offered courtesy. The monk hastened back with a bow and asked, “Where do you come from, Master?” Tripitaka said, “My disciple is Tripitaka, sent by order of the Great Tang Emperor of the Eastern Land to go to the Western Heaven to worship Buddha and seek the scriptures. Passing through Baofang, I respectfully request one night lodging, and will depart tomorrow.” The monk said, “This remote mountain is always home to those dwelling in all ten directions; all may be joyfully welcomed. How much more so, venerable elder from Great Tang—if you can make offerings, it is indeed a great blessing.” Tripitaka thanked him and at once invited all three of them to walk with him. After passing the incense-circling corridor they went directly into the abbot’s hall. Courtesy was exchanged, and host and guest sat in order. Wukong and the two others also sat down with hands respectfully hanging at their sides.

At this time, hearing that a monk from Great Tang had come to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven, every monk in the temple—great or small, whether long-staying resident, bed-matted elder, master, or young attendant—came to pay respects. After tea was finished, the monastic meal was set out. At that moment the elder was still opening the fast reciting verse; Zhu Bajie, of course, being eager, swallowed steamed buns, vegetarian fare, and flour soup all in a rush. There were many in the abbot’s hall: those with learning praised Tripitaka’s dignified bearing, and those fond of mockery just watched Zhu Bajie eat. Sha Wujing, stealing a glance, saw at the crown of his head and pinched Zhu Bajie hard, saying, “Polite ones.” Zhu Bajie, startled, quickly stood and said, “Polite ones, polite ones, my belly is empty.” Sha Wujing laughed and said, “Second Brother, you don’t know. Across all under heaven, when it comes to the belly, it is exactly the same as for you and me.” Only then did Zhu Bajie agree to sit still. Tripitaka finished the meal, the attendants cleared the seats on both sides, and Tripitaka expressed thanks.

The temple monk asked about the reason for Tripitaka coming from the Eastern Land. Tripitaka spoke of ancient sites, and only then asked why the Bujin monastery bore that name. The monk replied, “This temple was originally the Gift-Solitary Patron’s Garden Monastery of Śrāvastī, also called Jetavana. Because the patron Jiguodu invited Buddha to preach and covered the ground with golden bricks, the name later changed. From where one can see this monastery from afar, this was once Śrāvastī. At that time Jiguodu was living in Śrāvastī, and this wild mountain was originally the patron’s Jetavana, so it came to be called Gegu Bujin Monastery. At the back of this temple there is still the site of the Jetavana foundations. In recent years, when a heavy downpour comes, gold and silver beads still seep out. Some fortunate folk often pick them up.” Tripitaka said, “I take these words as no fiction.” He asked again, “We just entered Baoshan and saw along the two side corridors many mule-and-horse carts and laborers with loads. Why are they lodging here?” The monks said, “This mountain is called Baijiao Mountain. In earlier years it was all peace; of late, for reasons no one can quite explain, several centipede spirits have appeared and often wound travelers on the road below. Though they do not actually kill, people still dare not travel. At the foot of the mountain is a pass called Cockcrow Pass, but only when it is cockcrow can one dare to pass. Those travelers arrive late, and fearing inconvenience, they borrow this desolate mountain for one night, then wait and travel after cockcrow.” Tripitaka said, “We too shall wait until cockcrow and then go.” As they were still speaking, food was brought again, and they ate together with Tripitaka.

At this moment the waxing moon was bright. Tripitaka and Sun Wukong walked at ease in its light when a Daoist messenger came with the words, “Our teacher wishes to meet a person from Zhonghua.” Tripitaka turned quickly and saw an old monk holding a bamboo staff. He stepped forward and bowed, saying, “Is this the master who has come from Zhonghua?” Tripitaka answered with folded hands, “I dare not say so.” The old monk praised him endlessly, then asked, “How long have you lived, Master?” Tripitaka replied, “I have already lived forty-five years. May I ask the abbot’s age?” The old monk laughed and said, “I am older than you by six full decades.” Sun Wukong said, “I am now one hundred and five years old. Tell me what my age looks like to you.” The monk said, “Your face is ancient and spirit-clear; and on a moonlit night one’s eyesight can blur. I cannot read it at a glance.” After talking awhile, he looked back toward the rear corridor. Tripitaka asked, “You only just spoke of the Ji-gu Garden site—where is it?” The monk replied, “It is just outside the back gate. Open it quickly.” They saw only an open patch of ground, and a wall base stacked from broken stones. Tripitaka joined his palms and sighed:

“I remember, in past days, Tana-mu-su-da-duo, who once used gold and treasure to relieve the poor and the afflicted. In Jiyuan the name remains through ages unending; O elder, where now is companion Jueluo?” He moved on under the moon, strolling slowly. As he neared the back gate and came to the platform, he sat down for a while, and suddenly heard weeping. Tripitaka listened carefully. It was the sound of children crying out their mother and father’s grief, in language no one in the room could grasp. Moved to the heart, tears fell before he could stop them, and he asked all the monks, “Where is this one who cries so bitterly?” The old monk, seeing the question, ordered the monks first to return and prepare tea. When none were near, he only then bowed before Tripitaka and Sun Wukong. Tripitaka lifted him and said, “Abbot, why offer me such worship?” The monk said, “I am past a hundred years of age and only loosely know worldly matters, yet in moments of meditative stillness I have seen several scenes. As for you and your disciples, holy monk, I understand you in part—you are unlike the rest. As for this matter of sorrow, this disciple thinks Tripitaka alone cannot fully discern it.” Sun Wukong said, “Then speak: what is it?” The monk said, “Last year today, when I was in that hour of bright-moon contemplation, I suddenly heard the wind and a cry of grief. I got up and went to the Jiyuan platform, and saw there was a beautiful, refined young woman. I asked her, ‘Which house do you belong to, and why have you come here?’ She answered, ‘I am a princess of Tianzhu. While watching flowers under the moon, I was blown here by the wind.’ I confined her in an empty broken room and made it like a prison cell, leaving only a small hole in the door through which I passed her a bowl. That day I told the monks, ‘It is a demon spirit; I have bound it.’ But I am a monk, and one of compassion, and would not dare take her life. I have fed her two rough meals each day, simple tea and plain gruel, to keep her alive. The girl understood my intent at once. Fearing she would taint the monks, she feigned wind-spirits, and slept in urine, and lay in filth. By day she muttered foolish words, vacant and muddled; when night fell silent she thought on crying for her parents. I made several trips into the city to investigate the matter of the real princess and found nothing. So I kept the shackles tightened and did not release her. Now that you have come to this country, I hope when you reach the capital you will broadly exert your powers and make the truth clear—first to rescue the innocent and compassionate, and second to manifest divine attainment.” Tripitaka and Sun Wukong listened, and both held the words deeply in their hearts.

They were still speaking when two young monks came to offer tea and make ready, then withdrew. In the abbey hall, Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing muttered in a low rumble, “We are to start at rooster-crow. Why are you not asleep at this late hour?” Sun Wukong said, “What is that muddle-headed fool saying now?” Zhu Bajie said, “Come to sleep. It is so late—what beauty of scene remains to watch?” The old monk dispersed, and Tripitaka lay down to rest. At that time, truly,

The night grows still; moonlit blossoms keep silent dreams. A warm wind slips lightly through wall and gauze. Copper kettles dip and clink for three small pails, The River of Heaven shines bright over Nine-hua. Before long, before he had slept much, he heard the rooster. The merchants ahead all rose in a bustle, lit lamps, and began cooking. The abbess awakened also, calling Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, saddling the horse and gathering things; Sun Wukong called for lamps. The temple monks had already risen, and they set out tea, broth, and light fare, waiting afterward in attendance. Zhu Bajie was delighted and ate a plate of cakes, then had their luggage and horses led out. Tripitaka and Sun Wukong thanked the rest. The old monk once more said to Sun Wukong, “That sorrowful matter I spoke of is in your heart.” Sun Wukong laughed, “I understand; I understand. In town I can hear and test what is true, and by face and mien distinguish colors of intent.” A group of merchants, loud and noisy, followed them onto the highway. At the hour of the tiger, they passed the Rooster-Crow checkpoint. By the hour of the snake, the city wall came into view. It was truly a city of cast-iron walls and gold-locked battlements, a heavenly estate of this divine isles. The city was: Tiger-coiled high, dragon-entwined in lordly posture; Phoenix pavilions, qilin halls, with colored light swaying. The royal moat flows like a circling belt; Blessed land, with banners along hills like brocade spires. At dawn, banners and standards light the avenues; Spring wind drums and flutes ring across every bridge. The king’s rule is orderly, robes and caps in noble rank; Five grains are full, and prosperity shows the worth of its lords. That day they entered the East Market street, and the merchants went to various inns. Tripitaka and his disciples entered the city; while crossing, they came to a guest inn- and yamen hall and entered directly. The clerk inside reported to the station chief: “Outside there are four unusual monks and a white horse.” On hearing of a horse, the station chief knew they must be officials’ escorts and came out to receive them. Tripitaka bowed and said, “I am a poor monk from Great Tang in the Eastern Land, a humble envoy sent by the Son of Heaven to Mount Lingji’s Great Thunder-voice assembly to seek the Tripitaka scroll, with credentials on my person to present at court. Please allow a halt in your exalted office; once my business is finished I will go.” The station chief answered with courtesy, “This office was established to receive messengers and envoys; naturally we should welcome you. Please, please come in.” Tripitaka rejoiced and had his disciples come forth for introductions. The station chief, seeing their ugly faces, was secretly alarmed and could not tell whether they were men or ghosts; trembling, he merely arranged tea and a vegetarian meal. Tripitaka saw his fear and said, “Do not be startled, Great Officer. Though my three disciples look severe, our hearts are all good. As the saying goes, ‘A man may look grim and yet be gentle in spirit.’ Why should you fear?”

The station chief, now somewhat steady, asked, “Master of the Scriptures, where is Tang in this world?” Tripitaka answered, “In the land of Zhonghua on South Shengtu and the four continents.” The chief asked, “When did you leave home?” Tripitaka replied, “In the thirteenth year of Zhenguan, and now fourteen years have passed, and I have borne down through ten thousand waters and a thousand mountains to arrive here.” The station chief said, “Divine monk, divine monk!” Tripitaka asked, “How old is your upper kingdom now?” The station chief answered, “This place is the great Tianzhu kingdom. From Great Ancestor and Great Ancestor’s successor down to now, more than five hundred years have passed. Now the reigning father-emperor, who loves mountains, waters, and flowers, is known as Emperor Yizong, with the reign title Jingyan; twenty-eight years have elapsed.” Tripitaka said, “Today I must go to present my credential paper and seek audience; I do not know whether I will be able to meet the court.” The station chief replied, “Good, good—just right. At present, the princess of this realm has just entered her twentieth spring. At the Crossroads Street she now has a silk-crowned pavilion where she throws embroidered balls and seeks a husband by divine match. It is in the thick of festivity. The king himself has not yet left court; if you want to present your pass, now is the time to go.” Tripitaka gladly prepared to depart, but they brought out the meal first, and he then ate with the station chief and Sun Wukong.

It was past noon. Tripitaka said, “I should go now.” Sun Wukong said, “I will go with Master.” Zhu Bajie said, “I will go.” Sha Wujing said, “Let the second elder go. Why should you, with your face, go before the gates and pretend to be corpulent? Let your elder brother go.” Tripitaka said, “Sha Wujing said well. The bungling one is rough in manner; Sun Wukong has at least a little more subtlety.” The bungler cupped his mouth and said, “Apart from Master, the three of us look no different in face.” Tripitaka put on his kasaya anyway, and Sun Wukong took the lamp-bag and went with him. In every quarter, scholars, farmers, artisans, merchants, literati, clerks and ordinary folk all said in passing, “Go and watch the embroidered-ball game!” Tripitaka stood by the roadside and told Sun Wukong, “The people here, their dress and hats, their palaces and furnishings, their speech and manner, are very much like our Great Tang. I thought that in my former life as a layman too, they played the silk-ball tossing game, and by that old bond of destiny husband and wife were joined. Here the same custom exists.” Sun Wukong said, “Shall we go and look?” Tripitaka said, “No, no. Your robes and complexion are not fitting; they may take suspicion.” Sun Wukong said, “Master, have you forgotten what the monk at Ji-gu Temple said? One: go look at the pavilion. Two: examine true and false. In this rush, if we go there, the emperor will be occupied with the princess’s glad announcement and not with court business. So we should both go and come.” Tripitaka, hearing this, truly followed Sun Wukong and saw all the crowds watching the match. Ah—what they had gone to see would be this:

The old fisherman cast out hook and line; From this day onward he will haul in contention.

Now this is how it came to be in the Tianzhu kingdom: Because the king loved mountains, waters, and blossoms, he had last year taken his queen and princess to the imperial flower garden and in moonlit viewing set loose all manner of distraction. That stirred a demon spirit, which carried off the true princess and made it become a counterfeit princess in her place. Knowing that Tripitaka would arrive this year, this month, this very day and hour, he feigned the abundance of his kingdom, raised the silk-bannered pleasure pavilion, and sought to invite Tripitaka as a companion, to draw out his primal yang essence and thereby become the Supreme Immortal of Taiyi.

At exactly the third quarter of the noon hour, Tripitaka and Sun Wukong mixed into the crowd and came near the base of the tower. Only then the Princess lifted incense, set it burning, and offered her blessing to Heaven and Earth. On either side stood five or seventy coy, rouged embroidery girls, attendants holding embroidered balls. The tower was filigreed with eight bright windows. The Princess turned her gaze and saw Tripitaka nearing; she took the embroidered ball in hand and threw it herself onto Tripitaka’s head. Tripitaka was startled; his Pilu hat was knocked sideways, and with both hands he hurriedly held on to the ball. The ball rattled and rolled, coming to rest inside his robe sleeve. From above in the tower there was a single loud cry: “A monk has been struck, a monk has been struck.” At the cross-shaped street, the merchants and buyers, thick in noisy clusters, rushed in to seize the ball. Sun Wukong shouted once, let out a hard clacking sound with his tooth-implement, bent his waist in a crouch, and his divine might rose as if he were three zhang tall, making a grotesque face. The men, frightened, stumbled and crawled away, unwilling to come near; at once they dispersed. Sun Wukong then resumed his true form.

Those embroidered girls, palace maidens, and high and low eunuchs came down from the tower and knelt before Tripitaka: “Noble one, noble one, please enter the court hall and share our joy.” Tripitaka hastily returned their courtesy, raised them, and then turned to scold Sun Wukong: “You monkey head, why are you teasing me again?” Sun Wukong laughed: “The embroidered ball struck you and rolled into your sleeve; what is that my affair? Why complain?” Tripitaka asked, “What should I do now?” Sun Wukong said, “Master, do not worry. Go in and present yourself before the king. I’ll return to the relay station and tell Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing to wait. If the Princess does not summon you, then leave and we can simply exchange the travel permit. If she must summon you, tell the king: ‘Call my disciples, I have a word for them to hear.’ If I bring these three in then, I can distinguish the truth from falsehood then and there. This is the strategy of taming a monster through a marriage bargain.” Tripitaka could not help but accept his words, and Sun Wukong turned back toward the station.

The elder monk was surrounded and escorted by the palace maidens and eunuchs to the front of the tower. The Princess came down, took his jeweled hands together with her own, and mounted the jewel-litter; the ceremonial order was arranged, and they turned back to the gate. A gate official had already announced, “May Your Majesty live long. The Princess, carrying a monk, believes he was struck by the embroidered-ball toss and now waits beyond the noon gate for an audience.” The king heard and was quite displeased, wanting to send him away, but not knowing the Princess’s intention, he could only graciously allow him in. The Princess and Tripitaka then came to the Hall of Golden Lanterns. It was just then a pair of spouses called out blessings for ten thousand years, with both proper and improper doors bowing in reverence for a thousand autumns. After the rites were complete, they were again summoned to the upper hall. The king asked, “From where does this monk come, and how did he come by your throwing him the embroidered ball?” Tripitaka knelt and said, “This poor monk is sent by the emperor of Great Tang in the Southern Ocean to go west to Great Sound of Thunder Monastery to worship the Buddha and seek the sutras. As there is a long-road permit, I came to beg your Majesty to exchange it. Passing beneath the painted tower at Crossroads Street, I did not expect the Princess to cast the embroidered ball and strike it upon my head. I am a monk, one who has left home, who follows another teaching; how could I dare to be paired with one of jade leaf and golden bough? I beg that my death offense be forgiven, that my travel pass be exchanged, and that I be sent at once toward Ling Mountain to meet the Buddha for the sutras, and return to my land to bring long favor upon Your Majesty.” The king said, “You are a holy monk from the Eastern land, truly one of those fated by a thread from a thousand li. My Princess, now twenty years of age and unmarried, chose today’s date and hour as auspicious, and so held this painted tower ball game to seek an ideal bridegroom. Yet the ball struck you. Though Your Majesty says you are not to my taste, I do not know what the Princess intends.” The Princess knelt and said, “Father king, it is said, ‘Marry the rooster for a rooster, marry the dog for a dog.’ I had a vow in advance. When I tied this ball and proclaimed before Heaven, Earth, and the spirits that I was striking for a sky-wedded marriage, I struck today’s holy monk. This is the fate of a former life and therefore the meeting of this life; how could I change it now? I wish to take him as my prince-consort.” The king rejoiced and immediately ordered the Astronomical Office and Court Bureau to choose an auspicious date. In one hall the bridal ornaments and furnishings were readied, and then an imperial order was issued to announce it throughout the realm.

After hearing this, Tripitaka offered no more thanks and simply called out, “Pardon, pardon, pardon.” The king said, “This monk does not understand. I, with a kingdom’s wealth, invite you to be my son-in-law, and why should you not enjoy yourself here? Your only thought is still obtaining sutras. If you persist in refusing, I will have the brocade-clad guards drag you out and behead you.” Tripitaka was so frightened he seemed not in his body, and at last, trembling, he knelt and appealed, “With Your Majesty’s heavenly grace, I am your debtor. Yet this poor monk has three disciples traveling with me, and they are still outside. When I now receive you as a son-in-law, I have not had one word to give them. Please summon them here, exchange the permit, and send them on at once, so as not to delay the purpose of our western journey.” The king asked, “Where are your disciples?” Tripitaka answered, “They are at the Huitong Relay Station.” An official was immediately sent to summon the holy monk’s disciples, to send them out west, leaving the holy monk here as prince-consort. Tripitaka only then rose and stood attending. There is a poem in evidence:

The Great Elixir must not leak; one must bring it to fulfillment in all three, else painful asceticism cannot conquer a bitter bond. The Way is in the holy transmission, but cultivation must be in oneself; merit is accumulated by man, blessing descends from heaven. Do not let the six sense gates run after greed and desire; instantly open the original single nature. With no attachment and no brooding, keep your purity clear; and surely release will arise to transcendence. At that time officials were dispatched to the Huitong Relay Station to summon Tripitaka’s disciples, and there is no further notice.

After this, Sun Wukong took leave of Tripitaka beneath the painted tower, walked two steps, laughed twice, and returned to the station in good spirits. Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing met him and said, “Elder Brother, why are you smiling so?” “How is Master now?” Sun Wukong said, “Master is pleased.” Zhu Bajie said, “We have not even reached the end of the road and have not seen you returned from Buddha with the sutras; why this joy?” Sun Wukong laughed: “Bajie and I only walked with Master as far as the base of the painted tower at Crossroads Street, where by sheer luck the reigning Princess’s embroidered ball struck Master. She then had palace girls, embroidery girls, and eunuchs escort him to the tower front, and together with the Princess he entered the court and was called as prince-consort. What else could be joyful?” Hearing this, Zhu Bajie stamped his feet and thumped his chest: “If I had known I would have come here sooner. It was all that Sha Wujing was indolent. If you had not stopped me, I would have run straight under the painted tower; if just one embroidered ball struck me, old boar, and the Princess chose me, would that not be splendid and fitting? Handsome and handsome to look at, proper and complete in shape, and fate making a playful match between us—how entertaining!” Sha Wujing stepped forward and smacked his face: “No shame, no shame, what kind of mouth you have. For three silver pieces you bought an old donkey, yet you brag that you can ride it well. If one embroidered ball had struck you, we would have burned the return papers and gone back that very night, and still have called it too late. How could we let such bad luck as you into the gate?” Zhu Bajie retorted, “You dark-skinned brute know no propriety. Hideous you may be, but it has some charm. As it has been said from old times: ‘Rough skin and flesh, sturdy bones; each has its own kind of worth.’” Sun Wukong said, “Don’t ramble with lustful words, fool. Prepare your baggage. I fear Master may panic and call for us; we should get to court and protect him.” Zhu Bajie said, “You are mistaken again. If Master is now a prince-consort, he will be in the palace making love with the king’s daughter. This is not like climbing hills and rugged roads where demons and monsters appear. Why do you need to protect him? At that age of his, he barely knows what is done in the nest; do you expect me to hold up his bedchamber?” Sun Wukong grabbed him by the ear, drew up his fist, and shouted, “You lecherous oaf, what filth is that you are saying?”

While they were still arguing, a station chief arrived with the report: “His Majesty commands. Officials have come to fetch the three holy monks.” Zhu Bajie asked, “For what purpose are we summoned?” The station chief said, “The holy monk was fortunate in being struck by the Princess’s embroidered-ball throw and chosen as prince-consort, so officials have come to invite him.” Sun Wukong said, “Where is that official? Bring him in.” The official, after saluting Sun Wukong, bowed through the ceremony and dared not look up; inside, he muttered in fear, “Is it a ghost? A monster? A Thunder Lord? A yaksha?” Sun Wukong said, “Official, if you have something to say, why this hesitation?” The official, trembling all over, held out the imperial order in both hands and stammered, “The Princess has invited for the marriage rite; my sovereign king has invited for the imperial audience.” Zhu Bajie said, “I have no instruments here to punish you; I will not strike you, so speak slowly and do not fear.” Sun Wukong said, “Are we to think you are afraid of being beaten? You are afraid of what your own face looks like. Quickly pack the pole-bundles and harness the horses; we are going to court to meet Master and discuss matters.” This was just so:

On a narrow road one cannot avoid being trapped; intense love can be forced into enmity.

In the end we still do not yet know what the king said after seeing him. Listen and await its explanation in the next installment.
chapters.title: Chapter 93: In Geiguyuan they question antiquity and speak of causes; in Tianzhu kingly court, the ruler meets his destined mate.
