This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing followed the summoning officer to the outside of Wumen Gate. The Yellow-Gate officer at once announced them for audience. The three stood evenly and did not kneel. The king asked, "Who are these three disciples, the foremost disciples of the holy monk who is to be my son-in-law? What are your surnames and names? Where do you live? For what reason did you leave home and take vows? Which scripture have you come to fetch?" Wukong moved forward as if to mount the hall. A guard beside him shouted, "Do not advance. If you have something to say, speak it here." Wukong laughed: "We are monastics; once we have one step, we take the next." Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing then stepped forward as well. Tripitaka, fearing the king might be startled by him, rose and called, "Disciple, His Majesty asks why you have come; report it at once." Seeing Tripitaka, who was standing beside him as master, Wukong could not restrain himself and cried out, "Your Majesty looks down on me and also on yourself. Since you invited my master to be your future son-in-law, how can you keep him standing on guard? In this world, those called husband to a princess are honored persons; is it proper that an honored person does not sit?" Hearing this, the king turned pale and, startled, wanted to leave the hall for fear of losing face before the crowd. He forced himself to stand firm and ordered an attendant to bring a brocade cushion, then asked Tripitaka to be seated. Only then did Wukong present his report:

I, Old Wukong, was originally from the Flower-Fruit Mountain, the Water-Curtain Cave, in the sovereign land of Dongsheng and the proud kingdom beyond. My mother was earth, my father heaven; I was born when a stone split. I once bowed to a Perfect Person and mastered the Great Way. Returning again to the Immortal lands, I roamed with a cry among blessed heavenly realms. I descended into the sea to tame dragons, climbed mountains and seized beasts. I destroyed my dead-name, rose with a new life, and was appointed Great Sage Equal to Heaven. I delighted in jade towers and loved roaming jeweled pavilions, and I met heavenly immortals, singing in joy each day; in the sacred lands I woke to happiness each morning. Only because I once disrupted the peach banquet and rebelled against the Heavenly Court, Buddha himself seized and subdued me. I was pressed beneath the Five-Element Mountain; hungry, I ate iron pellets, thirsty, I drank molten copper, and for five hundred years I had not tasted even tea and grain. It was fortunate that my master came from the Eastern Land, bowed to the West, and Guanyin commanded him to free me from heavenly disaster and great danger, and to take refuge beneath the Yoga gate. My former name was Wukong; I am now called Wukong the Wanderer. The king, hearing this weight of name and deed, was startled and leapt from the dragon couch, coming forward with a royal hand to hold Tripitaka down and say, "My future son-in-law is indeed my heavenly fate: to have found such an immortal husband for my daughter." Tripitaka, filled with gratitude, bowed his thanks and invited the king to resume his throne.

He asked again: "Who is your second senior disciple?" Zhu Bajie cupped his mouth and barked with showy boldness:

In a former life I was a man, greedy for pleasure and wholly lazy. All my life I was muddled, my nature disorderly and my heart confused. I knew nothing of Heaven's height or Earth's breadth, and could not understand how wide the sea ran or how far the mountains stretched. At a time of seclusion, I suddenly met a true person. In half a sentence he untangled my net of sin; in two or three words he split open the gate of calamity. At that moment I awakened, cast myself down at the master's feet, and diligently practiced the disciplines of the twonines; with reverence I perfected the three-three methods before and after. When my practice was complete I rose into heaven and surpassed the Celestial Treasury. Through the Great Emperor's great favor I was appointed Tianpeng Yuanshuai, entrusted with the river troops, and roamed with ease in the Han Hall. But because I drank at the peach banquet and mocked Chang'e in drunken play, I was stripped of rank and banished to the mortal world; by mistaken rebirth I was cast in a pig form. I dwelt at Mount Fuling and committed endless misdeeds. Then I met Guanyin, who pointed out the Way of good. I took refuge in Buddhism, protected Tang Sanzang, and went straight to the Western Heaven to seek the subtle scripture. My Dharma name is Wuneng; they call me Zhu Bajie." The king listened, blood-cold and fearful in his heart, and dared not even glance at him. The pig then stirred up his spirit still more, shaking his head, cupping his mouth, wrinkling his ears, and laughing loudly. Tripitaka, still fearing he might alarm the ruler, shouted, "Zhu Bajie, be restrained!" Only then did he cross his hands, bow with ceremony, and feign composure.

He asked again: "Who is the third disciple, and why did he take refuge?" Sha Wujing folded his hands:

Old Sha was originally an ordinary man; fearing the cycle of rebirth, I journeyed in search of the Way. I roamed by cloud over the sea's edges and drifted to the sky's far shores. Robe and beggar's bowl were always at my side, and each time I refined my heart and spirit in retreat. Through faithfulness I met an immortal couple. I reared a boy and through karmic accord was matched with a demoness. My skill was complete in three thousand measures; my three-and-four virtues were in harmony. I rose and surpassed the heavenly realm, bowed before Xuanqiong, was granted command of the Curtain-Raising General, and served in the phoenix-laden carriage and dragon carriages; I was enfeoffed as a general. Yet at the peach banquet too I accidentally broke a crystal goblet, was banished to the River of Flowing Sand, changed face and appearance, and committed misdeeds that harmed life. In good fortune, the Bodhisattva journeyed far to the East and urged me to take refuge; I waited for the Buddha-child of the Tang court, and then to go west for the true fruit of scripture.

From that point I renewed myself and again cultivated Great Awakening. I took my surname from the river. My Dharma name is Wujing, and I am called a monk. The king, hearing this, was both terrified and joyful: joyful that his daughter had gained a living Buddha, fearful that all three were indeed demons and spirits. As he was still wavering, the Yin-Yang Office officer from the main platform announced: "The wedding date is fixed for this year, this month, on the twelfth day, the Renzichen lucky day; the hall is auspicious and marriage may proceed." The king asked, "What is today by the calendar?" The officer reported, "Today is the initial eighth day, the Wushen day; a monkey brings fruit, so this is precisely the time to welcome worthy matter and settle marriage." The king rejoiced greatly and ordered the chief steward to sweep and prepare the outer palace gardens, pavilions, towers, and terraces. He also instructed that the would-be son-in-law and the three senior disciples be given lodging there. Afterwards, he would arrange a proper ceremonial banquet and match the princess. All obeyed. The king ended court and withdrew; many officials dispersed, and the matter ends here for now.

Thereafter the three disciples of Tripitaka arrived in the imperial flower garden. Evening deepened, and they spread a simple vegetarian meal. Zhu Bajie said happily, "Today we should also eat at last." The attendants brought in sacks of plain rice, noodle rice, and other foods. Zhuk Bajie ate and then added more, and again and again he ate until his belly was full and hard with fullness, then finally stopped. Soon after, they lit the lamps, laid out bedding, and each retired to sleep.

When Tripitaka saw that there was no one beside him, he reproached Wukong bitterly and cried out angrily, "Wukong, you ape, again and again you ruin me. I said we were only going to switch the credentials document, and not to go before the painted pavilion; why did you insist on dragging me there? Now, what have we seen? What trouble have you brought? What am I to do?" Wukong smiled and replied, "Master once said: 'If one first throws embroidered balls, and there is old affinity, husband and wife may still be made.' I judged this to suit an old custom and so brought you there. I also remembered what the abbot at Jigubojin Temple had said, so I wished to test true and false. When I saw the emperor's face, it looked a little darkened, but I did not yet see how the princess truly was." Tripitaka asked, "So what if you see the princess?" Wukong said, "With my Fire-Eyes Golden-Gleam vision, the moment I see a face I can tell true from false, good from evil, wealth from poverty, and I can clearly discern the upright from the crooked." Sha Wujing and Zhu Bajie laughed and said, "Brother has even learned face-reading again." Wukong answered, "As for face readers, I am as if their grandson." Tripitaka shouted, "Hold your tongue. She is fixed on taking me as her husband; what are we to do now?" Wukong said, "Wait until the twelfth-day congratulatory rites. The princess will then come out to bow to her parents, and I will stand nearby to watch. If she is truly a woman, then become a son-in-law and enjoy the honor within this realm." Hearing this, Tripitaka grew even more angry and cursed, "You rogue ape! You have harmed me again. It was Wuneng who said this, and we are already well past nine and nearly three-quarters through the tenth of ten measures; yet you still wag your hot tongue at me. Close it quickly. If you speak out of turn again, I will recite a spell and make you feel what cannot be borne." Wukong, hearing the threat of a spell, flinched and knelt before him: "Do not recite, do not recite. If she is truly a woman, then at the wedding hall we will all raise such a riot in the palace, and take you away too."

The disciples kept talking and did not realize they had entered the deeper watch of the night. It was exactly:

The palace water-clock dripped on in heavy measure, and dense fragrance of blossoms hung in the air. Pearled bead-curtains drooped from embroidered doors while the quiet courts had no torchlight. The cold swings left only emptiness and shadow in the air, and the qingdi melody of the reed flute faded into stillness across all directions. Flower cages circling the house shone in moonlight; beyond, with no trees in the open sky, stars alone flickered. The cuckoo's call had ended, and the butterfly's dream went on long. The Silver River stretched across the heavens; white clouds returned to their homeland. It is the keenest hour of parting in the heart, when wind-shaken young willows feel even more desolate. Zhu Bajie said, "Master, it is late. Let us discuss matters in the morning. Sleep now." The three disciples truly passed one night in rest.

At dawn, roosters with golden combs sang at daybreak. The king ascended the hall and held morning court. Thereupon:

The palace court opened in radiance, purple qi rose high, and spring wind blew imperial music up into the blue heavens. Cloud banks moved, leopard-tail banners swayed, and sunlight made the jade pendants on dragon-head finials tremble. Fragrant mist slightly deepened the green of palace willows, and dew beads moistened the blossoms of the gardens. A cry of joy rose as ministers and officials danced in line; sea calm and rivers clear, one realm in perfect order. After the civil and military officials had finished court, the king also proclaimed: "The Palace of the Imperial Household shall prepare the joyous twelfth-day wedding banquet. Today, polish and set out the spring vessels and let the would-be son-in-law relax and stroll in the imperial flower garden." He ordered the Ritual Office to lead the three worthy attendants to a side hall so they might sit briefly with others, while the Imperial Household should arrange three vegetarian seats there as accompaniment. Both gardens and courts were set to music by the Music Bureau, with attendants in attendance to enjoy the spring scene and withhold the day. Hearing this, Zhu Bajie answered at once, "Your Majesty, my master and I are constantly together and do not have one moment apart. Since we are to banquet today in the imperial flower garden, take us there for two days of recreation; then teach my master to serve as son-in-law to your family. Otherwise this business cannot be closed." The king, seeing his ugliness and hearing his coarse speech, then saw him also twist his head, pinch and knot his neck, cup his mouth, and shake his ears; it was as though the whole style would ruin the engagement. He therefore yielded and ordered, "In the Eternal-Anchor Huayi Pavilion arrange two seats; I will sit there with the would-be son-in-law. On the Keep-Spring Terrace arrange three seats and ask the three of you not to sit there, lest master and disciples be arranged awkwardly." The fool then looked up, offered a courtly bow, and said, "Many thanks." All withdrew in turn. Another edict was then sent to the inner palace officials to arrange the banquet, summoning consorts from three courts and six chambers, including the princess, to prepare and beautify the gifts in waiting for the twelfth-day marriage.

By the Hour of Si it was time, and the king had his carriage arranged and invited Tripitaka to bring everyone to the Imperial Flower Garden to view it. It was a beautiful place:

The paths are paved with bright-colored stone, and the fences are carved with sculpted railings. The pathways are paved with painted stone; by the sides of the path, beside the rocks, strange blossoms grow long and high. In and beyond the railings bloom unusual flowers. The peach trees sway among emerald hues, and the young willows glitter with yellow orioles. As one walks, faint fragrance fills one’s sleeves; each step brings a clean, clear fragrance up onto the robe. A Phoenix Terrace and Dragon Pools; bamboo pavilions and pine bungalows. On the Phoenix Terrace, the rite of sounding reed flute calls the phoenix down. In the Dragon Pools, fish are reared and then changed into dragons as they leave. The bamboo pavilion holds poems, refined by endless revision, cut and smoothed like white snow. In the pine pavilion are literary anthologies, shaped to pearl-and-jade brilliance and glossed in blue-threaded volumes. Faux mountains of green, rocks like clusters of jade, and winding water with deep blue ripples. Peony pavilions, rose trellises, layered brocade laid like velvet. Jasmine cages and crabapple beds, piles of rosy light and jade-inlaid settings. Peonies with strange scent, and wild hibiscus with extraordinary brilliance. White pears and red apricots compete in their blossom; purple fragrant herb and golden chrysanthemum vie in glowing splendor. Lichun flowers, pencil-flowers, azaleas—glimmering and bright. Smiling flower, balsam, and fritillary—stately and imposing. In every place the red has soaked through like warm rouge; in every clump the rich fragrance is thick as stitched brocade. Still more delightful is the east wind returning with mild sunshine; the whole garden’s charm has found full force.

A whole set of kings and officials admired it for a long time. Already officials from the ceremonial bureau had invited the three disciples into Liuchun Pavilion. The king led Tripitaka to Huayi Pavilion, and each went to feast. The singing, dancing, flute-playing, and instrumental music, together with all the arrangements and displays, were truly this:

Lofty rises the Vermilion Gate as dawn-light is born, while phoenix towers and dragon halls stretch beneath auspicious haze. Spring color is finely spread in embroidered flowers and grasses; far-off sunlight sends a clear brightness across brocade robes. Melody and flute-song twine together like a fair of immortals; cups pass hand to hand with pure jade-like wine. Lord and ministers rejoice together in shared delight at the sights; in Huayi may peace and prosperity be secured for all ages.

At this moment Tripitaka saw how the king honored him, and there was no way to resist; he could only offer reluctant acquiescence. He was outwardly cheerful, inwardly troubled. While seated, he saw that on the wall hung four gilded folding screens painted with scenes of spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Each scene had inscriptions, and all the verses were poems by renowned Hanlin scholars.

"Spring-Scenery Poem" says:

One cosmic breath of Heaven turns in majestic balance; the great earth flourishes, and all ten thousand things are made new. Peach and plum contend in beauty, and blossoms overflow in brilliance; swallows arrive, piling fragrance-dust upon painted rafters.

"Summer-Scenery Poem" says:

The perfumed wind drifts, slow and lingering with longing; in palace courtyards, pomegranate and sunflower glow in the sun. The tone of a jade flute startles the noon dream; lotus-lily fragrance spreads across the hanging curtains.

"Autumn-Scenery Poem" says:

By the Golden Well a tung-leaf turns yellow; pearl curtains need not be drawn when frost came in the night. The swallows know the day to leave the nest, and geese bend through reedbeds and pass beyond their homeland.

"Winter-Scenery Poem" says:

Rain in the sky and flying clouds grow bleak with cold; north winds drive snow, piling on a thousand mountains. In the innermost palace there is always a red brazier’s warmth; news comes that plum blossoms have opened, filling jade-banded rails.

Then the king saw Tripitaka viewing the poems freely and said, "The Prince-Consort delights in savoring the flavour of verse and must surely be skilled at reciting. If you would not refuse, please match each rhyme in turn. How does that sound?" Tripitaka was one who had forgotten himself in scene and feeling, set in sudden seeing and essence. Seeing the king’s respect, he ordered that he would answer in the same rhyme, and without notice he recited one line: "When the sun warms, ice melts, and earth settles into accord." The king rejoiced greatly and called to his attendant guards: "Bring the four treasures of the writing studio. Ask the Prince-Consort to finish the matching lines, and I will have them recorded in good time." Tripitaka, delighted, made no refusal, lifted his brush, and replied in matching verse.

"Composed Spring-Poem" says:

The sun grows warm and the ice dissolves, and the whole earth is made new. The imperial garden’s flowers and plants flourish once more. Gentle wind and rich rain moisten the people with grace; sea and river run clear, far from worldly dust.

"Composed Summer-Poem" says:

The Dipper points south, while daylight in the southern quarter lingers slow; sophora clouds and pomegranate fire wrestle in radiance. Golden orioles and purple swallows cry in the palace willows; dual tones turn cleverly into the red-purple curtains.

"Composed Autumn-Poem" says:

Fragrance drifts through orange-green and orange-yellow leaves; pine and cypress remain green and rejoice when frost descends. Hedge chrysanthemums half-open, heaping brocade-like splendor; the charm of reed pipe and song carries to water and cloud country.

"Composed Winter-Poem" says:

Auspicious snow clears to a cold, crisp air; strange peaks, cunning stones, and jade-massed mountains. The stove burns beast-charcoal and toasts soft curd; with arms on hips, one sings high while leaning on the green balustrade.

The king, delighted at the matching poem, said aloud in praise, "What a line: 'With folded arms I sing, leaning on the green balustrade'!" He then ordered the music office to play the new verses, and they scattered only at day’s end.

The three disciples in Liuchun Pavilion had also fully enjoyed themselves; each had drunk a few cups and all were somewhat tipsy. As they were about to go look for Tripitaka, they saw that he was already in a pavilion with the king. Zhu Bajie’s stupid humor flared and he called out at once: "What good cheer, what ease! We have had enough of this enjoyment today. It’s time to go and sleep while still full." Sha Wujing laughed: "Brother Two is very little restrained. With this food and drink in the body, how can one sleep?" Zhu Bajie said, "How do you know? As the saying goes, 'After a full meal, nobody wants to lie still like a corpse while there is no grease in the belly.'"

After parting from the king, Tripitaka returned to the pavilion and rebuked Zhu Bajie: "This ox, he grows even more rustic. What sort of place is this, all he does is bawling and calling out? If he should offend the king, might he not strike at his life in anger?" Zhu Bajie replied, "No trouble, no trouble. We paid him proper family respects and exchanged greetings; that won’t make him resentful. As the saying goes, 'you cannot beat a relative and you cannot stop scolding a neighbour.' We are all fooling around—why should we fear him?" Tripitaka shouted at him, ordering him brought over to be struck with twenty staff blows. Sun Wukong grabbed him and hauled him over at once; Tripitaka raised the staff and struck. The fool cried out, "Prince-Consort, Mercy! Mercy!" A banquet officer nearby moved to intercede. The fellow scrambled up, muttering: "Fine lord, fine Prince-Consort. Before the betrothal is even settled, you’ve already begun to apply royal law." Sun Wukong sneered at him and said, "No nonsense, no nonsense—go to sleep early."

They stayed in Liuchun Pavilion for one more night. By dawn they held the entertainments again.

They did not realize they had been celebrating for three or four days when it was the twelfth day, an auspicious date. Three offices of the Ministry of Merit and Rewards submitted a joint report: "Since the eighth, in obedience to Your Majesty’s edict, the Prince-Consort’s hall has all been completed, and we have only been waiting to arrange the bridal chamber and furnishings. The wedding banquet has also been completed, with more than five hundred tables set for meat and vegetarian dishes each." The king rejoiced and wished to invite the Prince-Consort to take his seat, but an inner-court official then informed him at court, "Your Majesty, the Empress in the inner chambers requests your presence." The king withdrew into the inner palace. There, in Zhaoyang Palace, the three principal empresses, the six chamber consorts, and the princess were laughing and talking together. It was truly clusters of floral brilliance and embroidered splendor, a scene so rich and alluring it seemed to surpass the moonlit halls of heaven, no less than the jade palace of the immortals. Four new songs for the joyful union were offered as proof:

"Happiness Song" says:

Joy, joy, joy—rejoice, this is delight. A marriage-bond, beauty in affectionate love. So exquisite the palace adornment, what is Chang'e compared to it? Dragon hairpin and phoenix hairpin, dazzling in flying gold threads. Lips like cherries, teeth white as snow, cheeks rosy; her light form is flower-slender. Layer upon layer of brocade in heaps of five-colour bloom; incense-like fragrance drifts, with a retinue worth a thousand pieces of gold.

"Meeting Song" says:

Meeting, meeting, meeting—bewitching and graceful. More alluring than a fox-maiden, outshining every beloved beauty. She can topple states and enthrall cities, flower against jewel. Her makeup and attire become ever more radiant, her pins and bracelets richly brilliant. Her heart is orchid-like, character like refined iris, her powdered face with icy skin rich in noble grace. Brows of ink one fine line, like distant hills in stillness; she gathers fine, coquettish beauty in ranks of brocade.

"Fairness Song" says:

Fair, fair, fair—jade maid, immortal girl. So very lovable, truly worthy of praise. Strange fragrance is dense and perfumes and rouge are woven together. The blessed land of Heaven’s Terrace is far; how could it rival the king’s own house? Laughing and babbling in graceful poses, flute and song whirl in bright uproar. Flower mounds and brocaded terraces, a thousand beauties; what in the mortal world can match her?

"Marriage Song" says:

Marriage, marriage, marriage—fragrant musk and sandal rise. A host of fairy maidens, a throng of beauties. Concubines change silks; the palace mistress puts on fresh adornment. Hair-knots piled cloud-black in her crown, rainbow robes crushing the phoenix skirt. One line of pure celestial melody rings out, two lines of vermilion and purple glitter. In former days there was once a vow of riding the phoenix-chariot; today at last we are glad to witness this good marriage.

But the king arrived, and the empresses and consorts escorted the princess and the court maidens to welcome them. The king was overjoyed as he sat in Zhaoyang Palace. After the salutations, he said: "My worthy daughter, since the eighth you have spent the day with ribbons and tossed balls. To have met a holy monk must mean your wishes are fulfilled. All the court offices have understood my intentions; all arrangements are complete. Today is the proper day. Do not miss the hour—go soon to the joining banquet." The princess came near and knelt deeply, then spoke: "Father, forgive your daughter’s thousand faults. I have one petition: in these past days I have heard the palace officials say that the holy monk Tripitaka has three disciples and is exceedingly ugly. My daughter cannot face him, for fear I will be terrified at the sight. Please allow him to be released beyond the city walls, so he may not frighten my frail body and bring danger upon us all." The king said, "Child, do not speak further; I was almost forgetting. He truly is ugly. I have had him kept all these days at the Liuchun pavilion in the Imperial Garden. Let him come to court today, and then send him away beyond the city gate; only then should the banquet proceed." The princess knelt again and thanked him. The king then left and went to the hall, ordering that the Prince-Consort and his three companions be summoned.

Tripitaka had been counting the days by pinching his fingers, and by dawn he reached the twelfth day. Before first light he asked the three of them, "Today it is already the twelfth day. How shall we handle this matter?" Sun Wukong said, "I have already understood that the king has a touch of inauspicious destiny but has not yet touched us with harm. The only point is that the princess must not see him. If we can get out of this place, old Sun will have one glance and know what is real, and then we will act. You keep your heart at ease. He will certainly come to summon us and send us out of the city. You should accept it without fear. I will slip out unseen and come back, and then stay close to guard you."

"This time, before dawn on the twelfth day, Tripitaka had already been counting the days on his fingers. He had kept the three together and said, 'Today is the twelfth; how should we arrange this?' Sun Wukong replied, 'I have already judged that the king has a trace of inauspiciousness, and though he has not yet touched us, it has not become grave harm. Only this: he must not be faced by the princess. If we can get outside, old Sun will have one glance and see what is true, and then we can act. You just trust me. He will surely come and ask for us and send us out of the city. Do not be afraid—you rest assured; I will slip out first and then come right back, staying close to protect you.'"

The disciples were still talking when they saw an official of the royal horse-and-ceremonial office come to summon them. Sun Wukong laughed, “Come now, come now. This is surely an escort to send us off so we can still meet the Master again.” Zhu Bajie said, “If it is a send-off, there will surely be hundreds and thousands of taels of gold and silver, and we can buy some favors with people to carry back. When I get to my father-in-law’s home, I can also visit my own children.” Sha Wujing said, “Second Brother, hold your tongue and do not speak recklessly. Just follow Elder Brother’s lead.”

At once, all their baggage and horses were sent with the officials down to the vermilion steps. When the king saw them, he called Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing forward and said: “You all bring out your travel passes. I will apply the jade and stamped seal and entrust them to you, and besides I will prepare ample travel expenses so the three of you can set out quickly for Ling Mountain to see Buddha. If you return with the scriptures, there will be a heavier reward. Leave the Crown Prince here; do not worry about him.” Sun Wukong offered his thanks. He then told Sha Wujing to take out the pass document and hand it up. The king read it, then used the seal and stamped the red characters, and also gave ten ingots of gold and twenty ingots of silver as an initial courtesy gift. Zhu Bajie, who was always fond of money, immediately stepped forward to take them. Sun Wukong bowed to the throne and said, “Hurry, hurry,” then turned and was about to leave. Alarmed, Tripitaka scrambled up in a rush and clutched Sun Wukong, biting down in agitation: “You are all leaving me behind?” Sun Wukong held his hand and, with a sidelong glance, said, “You stay here with a calm mind and cheerful company. Once we fetch the scriptures, we will come back and see you.” The Master, as if unsure whether to believe him, did not let go. The officials all took this as if it were truly a final parting before departure. Very soon the king invited the Crown Prince back to the hall and ordered many officers to escort the three out of the city. The Master had no choice but to release his grip and go up the hall.

Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing left the Hall Gate with the others and parted from one another. Zhu Bajie said, “Are we really leaving now?” Sun Wukong said nothing, only walked on to the relay station. The station master greeted them, served tea, and set out food. Sun Wukong told Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, “The two of you stay right here. Do not show yourselves. If the station master asks anything, answer vaguely. Speak with me no more. I will go to guard the Master.”

The Great Sage pulled out a single hair from his whisker, blew a breath of immortal air, and shouted, “Transform!” and at once became his own form, appearing in the station with Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing. His true form, however, suddenly leapt up into the air and turned into a honeybee. See:

Yellow wings, a yellow mouth, and a keen tail sweet as nectar; with the wind it drifts and whirls, wildly and madly. Most skilled at plucking stamens and stealing perfume, it passes through willows and swings among flowers. After many hard stirrings and straining, it flits back and forth in vain. How could a rich sweetness ever be brewed? In the end only a name is left. You could see it flying gently into the court. From afar it saw Tripitaka seated on an embroidered cushion to the king’s left, with brows drawn and a scorched heart. It flew straight to Tripitaka’s bilu hat, quietly crawled to his ear, and called out: “Master, I am here. Do not worry.” Only Tripitaka heard this; those ordinary men could not feel it at all. On hearing it, Tripitaka finally felt relieved. Before long, a palace official came to invite him: “Your Majesty, the joyful banquet has been arranged in the Zique Palace; the empress and the princess are both in attendance, and they wish to invite Your Majesty and the honored lords to join them.” The king, delighted beyond measure, went into the palace with the Crown Prince. It was exactly as said: The evil ruler loves flowers and makes disaster of them; a meditative mind, once a thought stirs, gives birth to sorrow.

As it turns out, we still do not yet know how Tripitaka will be released from the inner palace; await the next chapter for the resolution.
chapters.title: Chapter 94: Four monks feast in the imperial flower garden; one monster clings inwardly to lust and joy.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

Now it is said that Tripitaka, anxious and sorrowful, followed the king into the rear palace. He only heard drums and music roaring to the sky, and then caught a strange fragrance in his nose. He kept his head lowered, not daring to look up. Sun Wukong, concealed, rejoiced inwardly, and from the top of his Bilu hat drew forth divine light, opening his blazing-golden eyes to watch. Then he saw those two ranks of painted maidens, lined up like an otherworldly pavilion of celestial ladies, even lovelier than a brocade canopy stirred by spring wind. Indeed it was:

Delicate and graceful, slender and yielding, jade-like in complexion and icy in skin. Pair after pair of charming ones shamed the women of Chu, and pair after pair could rival the beauty of Xishi. Her cloud-like hair knot rose high, sending out painted phoenixes; tiny butterfly brows faintly showed, like distant hills low on the horizon. The flute and shawm played in refined tones, the xiao and drums blew often. The modes gong, shang, jiao, zhi, yu rose and fell in equal harmony. Clear songs and wondrous dances were always lovable; in brocade inlaid courts, flower-garlands of every color brought joy. Seeing that his master never stirred from distraction, Sun Wukong silently chewed in approval: "Good monk, good monk. He dwells amid brocade and beauty, yet his heart is without desire; though his step falls on jade and jade dust, his mind is not bewitched."

After a little while, the empress and court consorts crowded about and brought the princess out of Ziqe Palace to greet everyone together, all crying, "Long live the king for ten thousand years, ten thousand times over!" The elder monk trembled in panic, not knowing what to do. Sun Wukong had already known it; seeing a faint demon aura just showing atop the princess’s head, though not wholly ferocious, he quickly crept near her ear and called out, "Master, the princess is false." The elder said, "She is false, but how can we let him show his true form?" Sun Wukong said, "Use my Dharma body and seize him at once." The elder said, "No, no, no. It may frighten the sovereign. Let Your Majesties, the king and queen, disperse first, then use your power."

The Great Sage was naturally hasty and could not bear it. He roared once, showed his true form, rushed forward, seized the princess, and shouted: "Wretched beast! You make falsehood look true here, and only indulge in such pleasures—is that not enough? And still you are not satisfied. You would even deceive my master, break his true yang, and satisfy your lust." The king stood stunned and helpless; the empresses and consorts scrambled in confusion, tripped and fell, and the palace attendants and maidens all darted this way and that to save their lives. It was as if:

Spring wind ripples, autumn air sighs thin. Spring wind ripples through the gardens, a thousand flowers sway; autumn air comes into the royal park, ten thousand leaves flutter. It snaps peonies beneath the balustrade, and blows the peony blossoms askew along the beds. Wild lotus by the pond bank shakes in disarray; the terrace base is piled high with chrysanthemum hearts. Begonia bends without strength and falls into dust; roses, fragrant, half doze in wild grounds. Spring wind breaks the split stems of cane and lotus; winter snow has bent the young plum buds. Pomegranate petals scatter in disorder through the inner court, east and west; willow branches by the bank droop askew, from south to north across the palace. All in one night of wind and rain the fine flowers went wild; countless broken reds lay spread upon the ground like brocade. Tripitaka, suddenly flustered, lost his composure, trembling, and clutched the king, only crying, "Your Majesty, do not fear, do not fear. This is my unruly disciple using divine power to distinguish true from false."

The demoness found the matter unfavorable, tore loose, stripped off her clothes, shook out her hair, and dropped her hairpins and ornaments. She ran to the temple of the field-spirit in the imperial garden, took out a short club with a pestle-like mouth, spun sharply, and came back to randomly strike Sun Wukong. Sun Wukong followed at once, and with the iron staff met her blow-to-blow. The two shouted and screamed and began combat in the garden. Then they later displayed great powers, each riding cloud-mist and clashing in the air. This bout:

The Golden-Hooped Staff is renowned; none knows the short cudgel with a mortar-mouth. One has come to this land to fetch the True Scripture; the other came to live by strange flowers, seized by love of their beauty. That demon, long knowing the holy monk of Tang, sought to pair with the primal essence and vital fluid. Last year he took the true princess, took on a human body, and was dearly cherished. Now, meeting the Great Sage and recognizing the demon aura, life was saved by separating false from true. The short cudgel rushes in violence with a top-hurling strike; the iron staff answers with power, smashing straight at the face. Shouting and shouting, the two held on, and cloud and mist filled the sky, covering the white daylight. The two then fought in midair, wagering life for life. The whole city panicked; citizens and officials alike were terrified. The elder held the king and said only, "Do not be afraid. Please ask the empress and everyone else not to fear. Your princess is a false one taking true form. When my disciple catches him, then you will know good from bad." The braver consorts took those garments, hairpins, and ornaments to the empress and said, "These are what the princess wore. She has cast them off and now, with only her spirit form, is fighting the monk in the air with him. She must be a demonic being." At that moment the king, empress, and the rest regained themselves and looked up into the sky and so it need not be told further.

The record says the demon and the Great Sage fought for half a day and could not determine a winner. Sun Wukong threw up his staff and shouted, "Transform!" then used one to become ten, ten to become one hundred, one hundred to become one thousand; in half a day he seemed like snakes and pythons churning, striking wildly at the demon. The demon, flustered, changed into a pure breeze and fled up into the blue sky. Sun Wukong recited a spell, collapsed the iron staff into one rod, and drove on with a straight line of divine light. Nearing the Western Heaven Gate, he saw flashing banners and cried out sharply, "Those at the Heaven Gate, block it and stop the demon—do not let him pass!" Truly on the gate were the Protector-of-the-Nation Heavenly King and four great marshals, Pang, Liu, Gou, and Bi, each displaying weapons to hinder him. The demon could not go forward; hurriedly he turned back, used the cudgel, and again grappled with Sun Wukong.

That Great Sage, lashing out with his iron staff and watching closely, saw that the short cudgel had one end thick and one end slender, like the pounding head of a mortar. He barked once and shouted, "Wicked beast! What kind of weapon do you carry to dare oppose Old Sun? Hurry and submit, or this one blow will break your Heavenly spirit." The demon said through clenched teeth, "You do not know this weapon of mine. Listen:

Its sacred root is a chunk of mutton-fat jade, shaped by carving over uncounted years. When the chaos opened, I had already obtained it; in Hongmeng it was decreed I should come first. It is no ordinary matter of the mortal world; its essence is born of heaven above. A single body of golden light, with four forms, fivefold auspicious qi, and three circles joined. For long I dwelt within the moon palace, dwelling near the osmanthus hall. Loving flowers upon the human world, therefore I came to Tianzhu, feigning a beautiful maid. There was no other intent in rejoicing with you; I came for the destined union with Tripitaka. How can you, with deceitful heart, shatter good fortune, driving me into this battle in savage rage? This weapon has a vast name before your Golden-Hooped Staff. In the Bright and Cold Palace I was a medicine-pounding mace, one strike from it sends life back to the spring source." Sun Wukong heard and gave a cold laugh, "You shambling monster! Since you once lived in the lunar palace, you still do not know Old Sun’s methods, yet you dare to quibble here? Show your true form and submit at once, and I will spare your life." The demon replied, "I recognize you as the Bima Wen who threw heaven and earth into uproar five hundred years ago, so in truth I should let you pass. Yet this is no matter of making love. It is as bitter as a grudge of murdering parents, and my reasoning cannot accept it; I must fight you, Bima Wen who deceives heaven itself." That made the Great Sage furious at the words "Bima Wen." Hitting his mark, he raised the iron staff and struck full in front; the demon swung his mace to meet him. At the gate of the West they fought in fury. This scene: The Golden-Hooped Staff and the medicine-pounding mace are truly worthy of comparison as two celestial weapons. One came down to seal this world in wedding marriage, the other came to protect Tripitaka until here. Truly it is because the king’s heart was not upright and his love of flowers delighted the demon. So now hatred and suffering contend, and both sides have stirred from stubborn intent. Clash after clash, jostling and striking, they traded taunts and matching words. A hero’s medicine-cudgel is rare in the world, yet the divine might of the iron staff is even finer. Golden light flooded bright, shivering before Heaven’s gate, and colored mists gleamed, reaching all the way down to the earth. They fought ten-some times back and forth; the demon grew weak and could not resist. The demon and the Great Sage fought ten or more rounds more. Seeing the density of the Great Sage’s staff movements, he judged he could not win. He feigned dropping one cudgel, flashed his body, and in ten thousand streams of golden light fled straight southward in defeat. The Great Sage pursued right after. Suddenly they came before a great mountain; the demon, by the guidance of the gold light, slipped into a cave and vanished in silence. Fearing that he might slip back to his country and secretly harm Tripitaka, he judged the scale of this mountain, turned around with cloud-head and headed straight back into the kingdom.

Now it was already the hour of Shen. The king was clutching Tripitaka, trembling and frightened, only crying, “Holy Monk, save me.” The empress and the consorts were also in such distress. At that moment the Great Sage came down from a cloud and called, “Master, I have come.” Tripitaka said, “Wukong, stop; do not startle the holy body. I ask you: what is really the matter with the false princess?” The Great Sage, standing outside the Jade-Sparrow Palace, placed his crossed hands to his chest and said, “The false princess is a demonic spirit. At first I fought with her for half a day. She could not defeat me, so she changed into pure wind and ran for Heaven’s Gate. I shouted and the heavenly gods blocked her way. She resumed her form and fought me for ten or so rounds, then changed her body into golden light and fled back to a mountain in the far south. I hurried there and chased her, but could not find her. Fearing she might come here to harm you, I hurried back only to check on you.” The king, still gripping Tripitaka, said, “If the false princess is truly a demon, where is my real princess?” The Great Sage answered, “Once I seize the false princess, your real princess will naturally come back.” Upon hearing this, the empresses and concubines released their fear, and one after another they stepped forward and knelt, pleading, “May the holy monk save back my real princess and make clear truth from falsehood; we will then give our deepest thanks.” The Sage said, “This is not a place for our talk. Please, Your Majesty, and my Master, leave the palace and go up to the hall. Empress and ladies, return each to the inner quarters. Summon my fellow disciples Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing to protect the Master. I will then go to subdue the demon. In this way, the inner and outer courts are separated, and I will not be hung around. I will make the case plain and show my full effort.” The king followed his words and thanked him deeply. Then he and Tripitaka went hand in hand out of the palace and straight to the hall. The concubines all returned to their quarters. On one side officials prepared plain vegetarian fare, and on the other side they summoned Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing. Before long the two arrived. The Great Sage reported the prior events and told them to protect the Master with utmost care. He then jumped onto a cloud and flew into the sky. Many officials before the hall each raised their eyes to the heavens and bowed in reverence; this need not be further recorded.

Sun Wukong went straight to the mountain in the true south to search. The demon, defeated in battle, had come to this mountain, slipped into a burrow, blocked the entrance with stones, and hidden in a timid, furtive way without emerging. Wukong searched for a while and saw no movement; he was very anxious. He twisted the mantra, recited the true incantation, and called forth the mountain land and mountain god for questioning. After a short time the two spirits arrived and knelt, saying, “We do not know, we do not know. We know only from far off. Please forgive our offense.” The Sage said, “I will not strike you now. I ask: what is the name of this mountain? How many demons dwell here? Speak truthfully, and I will spare you your punishment.” The two replied, “Great Sage, this mountain is called Maoying Mountain. In it there are only three rabbit holes; from ancient times to now there have been no real demons. It is a blessed land of Five Rings. If Great Sage seeks the demon, he must be elsewhere on the road to the West.” The Great Sage said, “When I reached the Western Heaven, King of Tianzhu had a princess taken by a demon and cast out into a wild waste. That one took on the form of a princess, mocked the king with play, built a multicolored pavilion, and tossed embroidered balls to lure a marriage prince. I brought Tripitaka to the pavilion below, and the demon set a trap to strike at Tripitaka, intending to take him as a husband and draw out his yuan-yang. I saw through it and manifested in the palace to seize her. She then took off the human garments and ornaments, made herself a short staff and called it a mortar-beating pestle, and fought with me for half a day. She turned into pure wind and fled. I chased her to the Western Gate and fought there for more than ten rounds. Thinking she could not win, she changed into golden radiance and escaped here. How is it that she is no longer found?”

The two spirits, hearing this, immediately led Wukong to search among the three caves. Beginning at the edge of the cave by the foothill they looked there and saw several grass rabbits, which were frightened and ran off. After searching to the cave atop the summit, they saw two great stones blocking the cave mouth. The Earth Deity said, “This place must surely be the demon; force your way in at once.” Wukong used the Golden-Hooped Staff to pry the stones apart. The demon was indeed hiding inside. At one roar it sprang out, raised the pestle and struck; Wukong lifted his staff to meet it. Even the mountain spirit was frightened and stepped back, while the land deity hurried away. The demon muttered and snarled at the mountain spirit and land god, saying, “Who told you to lead him to come here and search?” Leaning hard with shoulder and arm against the Golden-Hooped Staff, he fought and withdrew, then ran into the air.

At that critical moment evening had also come. The Great Sage, fiercer still, tightened his grip, wishing he could kill in one stroke. Suddenly he heard someone call through the cobalt void of the nine heavens: “Great Sage, do not move—do not move. Show mercy beneath your staff.” He looked back and saw it was the Lord of Taiyin Star, followed by Chang’e, descending in rainbow clouds before him. Startled, Wukong put down the Golden-Hooped Staff and bowed deeply, saying, “Great Lady Taiyin, where are you going? I have failed to avoid my offense.” Taiyin said, “The demon you are contending with is the jade rabbit that grinds the Immortal Frost Herb in Guanghan Palace. He secretly broke open the Golden-Locked Jade Gate and left the palace; he has been wandering for a year now. I judge that he now faces a calamity of life and death, so I have come to save him. Please, Great Sage, for my sake, spare him.” Wukong nodded repeatedly, saying, “Forgive me, forgive me. I did not know that he could use the medicine-pestle; indeed he is a jade rabbit. Great Lady Yin did not know he had kidnapped the princess of Tianzhu and then pretended to be the true one in order to violate the Master’s yuan-yang. Such intent and such sin—how can it be pardoned so lightly?” Taiyin replied, “You also do not know that the king’s princess is no ordinary mortal, but Suo'e, the pure maid of the Moon Palace. Eighteen years ago he struck that jade rabbit with his palm, and because of it the rabbit resolved to descend to the mortal world. A beam of spirit went down and took form in the womb of this king’s principal queen, and was born then. This jade rabbit, holding on to that single palm strike as a grudge, secretly left the palace last year and cast Suo’e into the wilderness. But he still had no right to seek Tripitaka as husband; that crime is truly inexcusable. Happily you were alert and uncovered true and false, and you did not harm your Master. I beg you, for my sake, show mercy and let me take him away.” Wukong said with a smile, “Since these are the causes and retributions, Wukong does not dare to oppose you. But if you take the jade rabbit now, I fear the king may not believe. Kindly, at my request, with your attendant immortals, bring this jade rabbit over there and clearly prove it before the king: first, show that Wukong’s method has worked; second, explain the cause of Suo’e’s descent from the Moon. Then the king can recover the body of Princess Suo'e and see that recompense is made manifest.”

Taiyin Lord believed his words and, pointing at the demon, shouted, “That fiend, return to proper form and come here at once.” The jade rabbit rolled over and revealed its true form. Truly it was:

Lips are narrow, teeth are sharp, ears long, whiskers sparse. A compact body, one coat of fur like jade, with feet that, when extended, leap as if over a thousand peaks. A straight nose with drooping, soft tip; the muzzle is creamy and white, filling the face like powdered frost. Two red eyes gleam, as if mocking points of rouge on fresh snow. Lying on the ground, it was a white, fluffy heap of pure cotton. Spreading its waist, a pale bell rang with a framework of silver threads. It has often gone out to breathe the leftover clear dawn dews of the Jade heavens, A wondrous jade mortar-pestle for pounding the elixir of long life. The Great Sage, seeing this, was filled with joy and stepped on cloud-light, leading the way forward. Taiyin Lord, with all the Chang'e fairies, took the jade rabbit and turned directly toward the borders of Tianzhu. At this moment it was dusk, and the moon had just risen. Upon reaching the edge of the city, he heard drums beaten from the Qiao tower. The king and Tripitaka were still in the hall; Zhu Bajie, Sha Wujing, and many officials were at the steps, just concluding court, when suddenly a broad sheet of colored cloud in the true south shone brighter than day. As all looked up, they heard Sun Wukong cry out in a stern voice, “Heavenly King of Tianzhu, command your empress, your consorts, your palace maids, and the colorful maidens to come and witness the sky. Under this treasure banner is the Taiyin Star Lord of the Moon Palace, and on either side are the celestial maidens Chang'e from the moon. This jade rabbit is the false princess of your house, showing his true appearance now.” The king hastily summoned his empress, concubines, palace ladies, and dancing maidens, all to make offerings and offer worship toward heaven; he, with Tripitaka and the officials, also looked upward and bowed in thanks. In every household throughout the city none failed to set out incense tables and kneel in Buddhist remembrance. At just this moment Zhu Bajie became lustful; unable to restrain himself, he leapt into the air and seized the Celestial Lady in rainbow robes, saying, “Sister, we are old acquaintances. Let us go off and play.” Wukong came forward, grabbed Zhu Bajie, and slapped him twice, shouting, “You vulgar, vulgar fool! In what place is this, that you dare let lustful intent rise?” Zhu Bajie said, “I only meant to pass time and banish loneliness by playing.” Taiyin Lord ordered the celestial banner turned about, and with all the Chang'e maidens took back the jade rabbit and went straight to the Moon Palace. The Great Sage pulled Zhu Bajie down to the dust.

The king in the hall had offered thanks to the Great Sage and then asked about the prior cause: “By your great spiritual power, holy monk, you have captured the false princess. But where now is my true princess?” Sun Wukong replied: “That true princess of yours was not of ordinary flesh. She was in fact Suo’e, a fairy of the Moon Palace. Eighteen years ago, he struck the Jade Rabbit child with one slap; moved by resentment, the Rabbit descended to this world and entered your chief queen’s womb to be born. Because the Jade Rabbit harbored an old grudge, in former years it quietly opened the Jade Barrier and the Golden Lock and came down, casting Suo’e into a wild waste, then changing form to deceive you. This chain of cause and effect was told to me by Lord Taiyin himself. Since today the false one has been removed, tomorrow please take Your Majesty’s carriage and go in search of the true one.” Upon hearing this, the king, ashamed and distraught, could not hold back tears: “Son, I came to the throne as a child. I have not even gone beyond the city gate in all my life—how can I possibly be told where to find her?” Sun Wukong laughed: “No need for anxiety. Your princess now feigns a wind-affliction at Jigubujin Temple. For now, let everyone disperse, and at dawn I will return to you a true princess.” The officials knelt and saluted together: “May Your Majesty settle your heart. These divine monks ride cloud and move through fog; surely they know the causes of past and future. Tomorrow, if Your Majesty asks them to go with you, all will become clear.” The king followed their words and invited the court to the Hall of Lingchun to hold a light meal and rest. It was already near the second watch of the night. Just then, it was:

Copper-urn time-dropper, moonlight all clear; gilt bells clink, and the wind carries their sound. The cuckoo cries on: spring is half gone; fallen petals, with no road to return, come to the hour of the third watch. In the deserted imperial garden the swing-shadow is lonely; in the empty blue firmament the Silver River drifts in a line. In three markets and six streets no guest is running; all night the stars and constellations shine with a clear light. That night all went to rest; nothing further to record.

That night, the king’s demonic influence departed, and his spirit revived at once. By the third point of the fifth watch, he once again came out to hold court. Court dismissed, he ordered Tripitaka and the four disciples to discuss finding the princess. The Master came and presented homage. The Great Sage and three others offered greetings together. The king bowed and said: “What you told us yesterday about the daughter, I beg the holy monk to seek her out and save her.” Tripitaka said: “The humble monk came from the east the day before and reached the city at dusk. I came upon a temple called Jigubujin Temple and sought to stay the night; the temple monks received me. After the evening meal, I strolled under the moon and came to the old Jigubujin garden, looked upon the foundations, and suddenly heard weeping. I asked into what cause. In this temple there is an old monk, more than a hundred years old. He sent away his attendants, then explained everything clearly: ‘The crying voice came from the deep spring of former years. That old monk, while observing his life-discipline, suddenly saw a gust of wind. He saw a woman thrown to the ground. He asked her who she was, and she said, “I am the princess of Tianzhu. One moonlit night, I was out playing with flowers and moonlight and was blown here by the wind.” The old monk, versed in propriety, locked the princess in a quiet room. Fearing to pollute this temple with his unruly priests, he only said she was a demon spirit and kept her confined. The princess understood this and by day spoke nonsense, asking for tea and food; at deep night, when no one was near, she would weep for her parents. That old monk had also come to the state to ask several times, saw that the princess was safe in the palace, and so did not dare to report it. Seeing that my disciple had some powers, that old monk repeatedly begged me to come here and investigate. But in fact it was the Moon Rabbit from the lunar palace, using a counterfeit form, taking the princess’s shape. He even had designs to break my Yuanyang. Fortunately, my disciple displayed might and divine law, distinguishing real from false. He has now been taken back by Lord Taiyin. The virtuous princess is presently at Jigubujin Temple, feigning wind affliction.’”

When the king heard this full account, he wept aloud. It startled the three palaces and six inner courts, and all came to ask about the earlier cause, none without tears. After a while the king asked: “How far is Jigubujin Temple from the city?” Tripitaka said: “Only sixty li.” The king at once issued orders: “Have the eastern and western palace households guard the hall and keep the court safe with the Grand Minister and the guards. I myself, with the principal Empress, will go with many officials and the four holy monks to fetch the princess from the temple.” At once the imperial departure was arranged, and the party left the court.

You see, the Great Sage sprang up into the air, twisted his waist once, and arrived at the temple first. The monks hurried and knelt in greeting: “My lord, when you left just now you all came on foot. How is it you come down from the heavens today?” Sun Wukong laughed: “Where is your abbot? Quickly summon him. Set up a fragrant altar to receive the carriage. The King of Tianzhu, the Empress, many officials, and my Master are all here.” The monks did not understand his meaning, so they asked the old monk to come out. Seeing the Great Sage, the old monk prostrated fully and asked: “My lord, what of the princess?” Sun Wukong described again how he had tossed the false princess like an embroidered ball, intended to pair her with Tripitaka, and had chased and captured the trickster, telling also how Lord Taiyin had taken back the Jade Rabbit. The old monk knelt again and thanked him. Sun Wukong helped him up: “No need to bow. No need to bow. Prepare the reception at once.” The monks then understood that the one locked in the back chamber was a woman; one and all, astonished and overjoyed, set out incense tables outside the gate, put on robes, and set the bells and drums ringing while waiting.

Not long after, the imperial carriage arrived early. It truly was:

Rich auspicious mists filled the sky with fragrance; a wild hill was suddenly graced with good omens. For a thousand ages a rainbow-like stream ran through the clear river-sea; lightning coiled through Eternal Spring, like Yu and Tang contending. Plant and tree, touched by grace, gained richer hue; wildflowers, once dried, found surplus fragrance. From ancient times a hermit left relics here—today we rejoice that the Bright Monarch descends upon the Treasure Hall. The king arrived before the mountain gate and saw the monks all lined in orderly rows, kneeling and receiving him; he also saw Sun Wukong standing in the center. The king asked, “How did this holy monk arrive here first?” Sun Wukong laughed: “Old Sun merely twisted his waist a little and came. Why did all of you take this long a way?” Then Tripitaka and the others came. The Master guided the carriage to the side of the back chamber, where the princess was still pretending to be wind-crazed and speaking nonsense. The old monk knelt and pointed: “The lady in this room is the princess blown in by wind in past years.” The king ordered the door opened. At once the iron chain locks were undone and the door opened. The king and empress saw the princess, recognized her face, and set aside all disgust. They rushed forward and embraced her: “My child, my child who has suffered! What torments have you endured, and what suffering have you borne here?” It was a reunion of parents and daughter unlike any other, and the three wept with heads together. After they had wept a while and told and listened to what had passed, the king ordered scented bathwater, had the princess bathe and change clothes, and had her mount the sedan back to the capital.

Sun Wukong then bowed and said to the king: “There is one more matter, Master would humbly submit.” The king returned the courtesy: “If the holy monk has matters to command, I will immediately follow.” Sun Wukong said: “This mountain is called Baijiao Mountain. Lately it is said that a centipede spirit has taken form there, wounding people at night and causing great inconvenience to travelers. I considered that only roosters can subdue a centipede. Select a thousand fine, vigorous roosters and release them into the mountain to clear away that poison vermin. Then rename this mountain, issue an imperial edict and grant it a charter, as compensation for the merit of this monk’s nourishing your princess.” The king rejoiced and promised to do so. He then sent officials into the city for chickens; he also changed the mountain name to Baohua Mountain. He further ordered the Ministry of Public Works to arrange materials for extensive rebuilding, and bestowed the title: “Imperially Established Baohua Mountain Jigubujin Temple.” The old monk was appointed as the “State-Repaying Monastic Officer,” hereditary in perpetuity, and granted a stipend of thirty-six piculs. The monastic community thanked the royal favor and saw the procession back to court.

The princess returned to the palace and paid visits to everyone. A feast was arranged, and all celebrated to ease her sorrow and rejoice. The queen-mothers and son and daughterly ranks were gathered together once more in harmony. King and ministers rejoiced as well; they dined through the night—nothing further to set down.

The next morning, the king ordered an edict: summon artists to portray the happy likenesses of Tripitaka and the four disciples in pigment, and set them on worship in the Hua Yi Tower. He also had the princess remade and made neat, and asked her to come forth and thank Tripitaka and his three disciples for rescuing her from suffering. After thanks were made, Tripitaka took leave of the king and set off westward. The king would not allow him to depart. He arranged grand banquets, continuing for five or six consecutive days, truly entertaining them with generosity and opening up his whole capacity for hospitality.

Seeing their devotion to the Buddha in daily worship and their wish to keep them, the king could not bear to let them go. He took two hundred silver ingots and one tray of jewels and relics as tribute. Not one of the master and disciples accepted them. He ordered the sedan set, invited the Teacher Father to mount it, and sent officials far on the road in escort. The queen-mothers, ministers, and subjects all bowed in thanks without end. When at last they reached the road, they again saw many monks kneeling in farewell, and none could bear to part. Seeing that the send-off party would not return, Sun Wukong, unable to bear it, pinched the mantra-knot, blew out a clouded immortal breath toward the southeast ground, and a sudden dark wind blinded all who were seeing them off. Only then could he get away.

Bathed in purifying grace, he returned to his true nature; leaving the Golden Sea, he awakened to the true emptiness.

As yet it is not known what lies ahead. For now, listen for the resolution in the next chapter.
