After Hua Biao Kou Yüanwai had recovered to life, he once more set in order banners and drums. The monks, Daoists, and close friends still bid him farewell as before—there is no need to record more.

Later Tang Sanzang and the four disciples set out onto the high road. Truly, this Buddha-land of the Western Regions differed from others: they saw mysterious flowers and jade-like grasses, ancient cypresses and deep green pines. In every place they passed, households practiced virtue, and every home kept a vegetarian offering for monks. At every mountain foot, whenever they encountered mountain people in cultivation, travelers in the woods were also seen reciting sūtras.

At night the master and disciples lodged, and at dawn they went forward; after six or seven days, they suddenly beheld a band of lofty buildings, several tiers of exquisite pavilions. It was indeed:

Reaching the sky a hundred feet, it rose in proud majesty, piercing the empty vault above. Bending low, one views the setting sun; one might stretch out a hand and pluck a flying star. Spacious windows and eaves seem to swallow the cosmos, while ridged roofs and towers join the cloud-curtain. The yellow crane’s arrival has withered the autumn trees, and at evening’s clear wind come the painted-phenix letters. This is a spirit palace and treasure hall, a jade pavilion and pearl court. In true halls they converse on the Dao; through heaven and earth the sūtras are transmitted. Spring brings blossoms at their finest, and pines stand a deep green after rain. Purple-golden fairy fruit ripens splendidly year after year; vermilion phoenix standards soar with myriad numinous feelings. Tripitaka raised his whip and pointed from afar: “Wukong, what a fine place this is!” The Great Sage replied: “Master, when this was a false terrain, in front of false Buddha images, you had gone to the ground and bowed. Now that we have reached this true realm, before true Buddha images you still have not dismounted. What do you make of that?” Hearing this, Tripitaka was startled and leapt down from the horse, arriving at the gate of those towers. There stood a Taoist youth leaning at the mountain gate, calling out, “You three from the Eastland are seekers of the sūtras, are you not?” Tripitaka hastily straightened his robes and looked up. Seeing him: Robed in brocade, he wielded a jade whisk in his hand. In robes of brocade, to pearl pavilions and Jade-Pool palaces he goes oft to banquets; with jade whisk in hand he waves, and with each sweep he clears the dust from crimson terraces and purple courts. A divine chart hangs at his elbow, his feet in ceremonial shoes; he floats like a true feathered hermit, handsome and strangely striking. He forged this long life in realms above the peaks, and cultivated it to a blissful immortality, shaking off the dust. To shackle the worldly monk with holy knowledge he was unknown; in former days, the Great Golden-Crowned Immortal of Yuzhen Hall had once come here. The Great Sage recognized him at once and said, “Master, this is Jinzding Xian, the Golden-Crowned Immortal from the foot of Ling Mountain, and he has come to receive us.” Only then did Tripitaka understand, and advanced to offer reverence. The Immortal smiled: “The holy monk has just arrived this year. Guanyin deceived me: she had taken a jade edict from Buddha and gone east to seek you from the Central Land, saying that in two or three years she would bring you here. Year after year I waited, no message at all—only to meet you this year.” With palms joined, Tripitaka said, “Great Immortal, your intentions are appreciated. I am grateful, truly grateful.” Then the four entered together, guiding the horses and shoulder-poles, and went inside to visit the Immortal one by one. He ordered tea to be served and the vegetarian meal prepared. He also told a young attendant to boil fragrant water and bathe the holy monk so he could ascend the Buddha realm. Truly then it was said: For merit completed and practice fulfilled, one must bathe and be made clean; By subduing one’s nature at last, one rejoins heaven’s true root. Ten thousand pains and hardships now at last are stilled; by nine vows and three refuges, one is newly born. When demons are exhausted one truly reaches Buddha-land; when calamity is quelled, one comes to behold the Sha-men. To wash away dust and stain without taint at all, returning to the root, one’s form remains unbroken. After bathing, though evening was near, they settled for the night in Yuzhen Hall.

Next morning, Tang Sanzang changed clothes, donned a brocade-bordered monk’s robe, put on a Pilu hat, and took up his iron staff before ascending to bid the Immortal farewell. The Immortal smiled: “Yesterday you came in rags; today you are resplendent. From this countenance one can tell you are truly a child of Buddha.” Tripitaka took leave and set out. The Immortal said, “Wait. Let me send you on.” The Great Sage spoke: “You need not bother. Old Monkey knows the way.” The Immortal replied, “What you know is the Cloud Road, but the holy monk has not yet mounted the Cloud Road. You must travel by the path that leads here.” The Great Sage said, “That is as you say. Though Old Monkey has walked this way many times, I only pass by cloud routes. In truth I have never set my feet here. Since there is an original road, I ask that you see us to it. My Master’s heart is earnest in worshipping Buddha—do not delay.” The Immortal, smiling contentedly, took Tang Sanzang’s hand and led him in to the guiding Dharma gate. The way needed no leaving the gate: from the inner hall it moved on through the courtyard and came out by the back gate. Then the Immortal pointed: “Master, there in the middle heavens is a five-colored auspicious radiance, auspicious signs in endless layers—that is the peak of Lingjiu, the holy precinct of the Buddha-ancestor.” Tripitaka, seeing it, knelt in reverence. Wukong said, “Master, we have not yet come to the place of prostration. As the saying goes, ‘Only when you reach the mountain can you dismount.’ From this watchpoint there is still much distance. What good is kneeling now? If we bow at the top, how many times would we strike the earth?” The Immortal said, “Holy monk, with Great Sage, Celestial-Swift, and those of rolled-curtain and so forth, you have already reached the blessed land. Since you have seen Ling Mountain, I shall return.” Thus Tripitaka took leave and went on.

The Great Sage led Tang Sanzang and the others, slowly and steadily, and climbed toward Ling Mountain. After not even five or six li, they came upon a living stream whose sound rushed and surged in waves and flying currents, about eight or nine li wide, with no human tracks in sight. Tripitaka said in alarm, “Wukong, this route has gone awry. Could the Immortal have misdirected us? How can we cross this wide and turbulent water with no boat in sight?” The Great Sage laughed: “No mistake. Look there—on the other side is not a riverbank but a bridge. Only when we cross that bridge we will truly fulfill our goal.” When they drew nearer, at the edge of the bridge stood a board on which were written three characters: “Lingyun Ferry.” It was, in truth, a one-log bridge. It was exactly:

From afar it sprawls across the sky like a beam of jade; Close at hand the river is severed by this single dried-log span. A way across the Great River and sea may be made with ease, but how can one step on one lone timber? Ten thousand zhang of rainbow and lustrous veil lie flat in shadow, A thousand-fathom white silk ribbon connects to the horizon. It is fine and slippery, impossible in truth to cross, save for heavenly beings who can stride through painted rosy clouds. Tripitaka, frightened to the quick, said, “Wukong, this bridge is not for people to cross; let us seek another path.” Wukong replied, “It is the road. It is the road.” Baijie, uneasy, said, “A road? Who would go? The water is wide, the waves surge, and a single slim log, both thin and slick, does not allow one to set one’s feet. How can one move?” Wukong said, “Both of you stand down there, and wait till I run across first so you can see.”

The Great Sage pulled out his stride and jumped onto the one-log bridge. He swayed and staggered, and in a moment ran all the way across, then called from the far side, “Come, come.” Tripitaka gestured with his hand uncertainly. Bajie and Shaseng bit their fingers and said together, “Impossible, impossible, impossible.” The Great Sage returned running across and grabbed Bajie, saying, “Dunce, follow me, follow me.” Bajie collapsed on the ground: “Slick, slick, slick—cannot step! Have mercy and let me pass by wind and fog.” Wukong held him fast: “What kind of place is this that I should let you ride the wind and fog? You must cross this bridge; only then can you become Buddha.” Bajie said, “Brother, if I cannot become Buddha, let it be. Truly I cannot walk it.” The two struggled there by the bridge, tugging and pulling in a playful rough-and-tumble. Sha Monk went to soothe them and at last he released them.

Tripitaka turned back and suddenly saw downstream a man coming with a small boat, calling, “Board here, board here.” Tripitaka, greatly relieved, said, “Disciple, do not cause confusion. A boat has come.” The three jumped up and stood still, watching together. As the vessel came near, it proved to be bottomless. The Great Sage’s fiery eyes had long since recognized him as the Buddha-guide, also called Namo Baozhuang Guangwang Buddha. Wukong did not expose that fact, but only cried, “Bring it here, pole it over.” At once it came near shore and called again, “Board now, board now.” Tripitaka saw it and said in alarm again, “How can this bottomless leaky boat carry people?” The Buddha-guide spoke:

At the first judging of all this vastness, a name was made renowned; by my piloting it comes unchanged. With waves and wind I remain at ease, and without beginning or end all rise in peace. Untouched by the six dusts, one can return to unity; through ten thousand kalpas one moves in unbound freedom. A bottomless boat cannot ford the seas—yet today, old and new alike, it ferries living beings. The Great Sage joined palms and praised thanks: “I accept your kindness in receiving my Master. Master, climb aboard. Though this boat is without bottom, it is steady; even wind and wave cannot overturn it.” Tripitaka still felt dazed, and Wukong gave him a shove. The Master could not keep his footing and stumbled, splashing heavily into the water; instantly the boatman seized him and hauled him aboard. The Master was still shaking out his robe and dusting the mud from his cloth, complaining about Wukong. Wukong then brought up Sha Monk and Bajie and led in horse and shoulder-pole as well, and all stood on the boat’s deck. With a light stroke the Buddha-guide set the pole and pulled; only then a corpse rose upstream and downstream. Tripitaka was startled. Wukong said, “Do not fear, Master. That one was you.” Bajie said too, “It was you, it was you.” Shaseng clapped his hands and said, “It was you, it was you.” The boatman, chanting as he rowed, said, “That is you—congratulations, congratulations.” The three answered in one voice. They kept the boat moving and without long delay crossed Lingyun Ferry securely and steadily. Tripitaka then turned and lightly leapt onto the far bank. As proof, there was this verse: Casting off the flesh of mother and father, this body of bones and skin, Inherent spirit remains in loving union. This morning’s complete journey is almost Buddhahood achieved, today the sixfold dust of long years is washed away. This is truly vast wisdom—thus is the boundless Dharma of crossing to the farther shore.

The Four Great Ones crossed to the far bank and looked back; even the bottomless skiff did not know where it had gone. Master Wukong then explained that it had been the Buddha’s divine guide who brought them. Tripitaka only just awakened to understanding, and he turned swiftly around, offering thanks again to the three disciples. Wukong said, “Do not thank one another at all. We have each supported the other. Because of Master, we have been able to escape and, by this way, cultivated until we achieved the true fruit; and Master also owes us, for the protection of our Dharma journey, joyfully cast off the mortal flesh. Master, look at this realm before us—flowers, grasses, pines, and thick bamboo, the flourishing land of luan, phoenix, cranes, and deer. Compared with the place where the demon appeared, which is beautiful and which is ugly, what is good and what is dangerous?” Tripitaka could only continue giving thanks and could not stop himself. One by one they grew light in body and swift of step, and climbed up Ling Mountain. Soon they saw the ancient monastery of Thunder-Sound:

Its crest seems to touch the starry vault, its roots join the Sumeru vein. Peaks lie in clever array, strange rocks jut askew. Beneath a precipice bloom celestial grasses and queer flowers; windings of path by violet-ground myrtle and fragrant orchids. Immortal apes pluck fruit in a peach grove, seeming like gold ablaze; a white crane perches on a pine bough and stands there as though mist cupped jade. Pairs of colored phoenixes, pairs of green luan, all in twos. Two bright phoenixes cry in the same moment, and the omen blesses all under Heaven; paired green luan, turning into the wind and shining in dance, are rare in all the world. Again there were dense clusters of yellow-gold tile, layered like mandarin ducks, and bright shining flower-brick paving of agate. One stretch east, another west—everywhere were flower pavilions and jeweled towers; one belt to the south, another to the north—one could not take in all the jewel halls and precious mansions. From the Hall of the Heavenly Kings spread streaks of sunset glow, and before the Hall of the Protecting Dharma rose purple flames. The Buddha stupa shone forth, and the fragrance of yü-po blossoms drifted. Truly this was a place where earth’s excellences made heaven seem another realm; the clear clouds made the day seem long. Dust of the mundane world did not reach here, and all ties had come to an end; this was the Great Hall of Dharma, unblemished through ten thousand eons. The four moved in free and untroubled grace and reached the summit of Ling Mountain. Once more they saw under the green pines the ranks of upāsakas, and among clusters of emerald cypresses the virtuous assembled. The elder quickly made formal reverence, whereupon the upāsakas, upāsikās, bhikṣus, and bhikṣuṇīs clasped their hands and said, “Venerable monk, hold, do not pay your respects yet. Bow first to the Tathāgata, and then we shall speak.” Wukong laughed, “Enough already—enough already. Go on, let us pay our respects to the superior ones.”

That elder danced, hands and feet moving with joy, and followed Wukong straight to the gate of the Thunder-Sound monastery. There were four Great Vajras stationed there who called out, “Venerable monk, have you arrived?” Tripitaka bowed and replied, “Yes. Disciple Tripitaka has arrived.” As soon as he answered, he was about to enter. The Vajra said, “Venerable monk, wait a little. Let word be given and you shall enter after that.” The Vajra dashed to the first mountain gate and informed the four Great Vajras above that Tang monk had arrived. They passed the word to the next gate, and it was passed again to the third gate. Within the three gates were divine monks serving offerings; on hearing that Tang monk had arrived, they hurried to the Great Hero Hall and reported to Buddha Śākyamuni, “A holy monk of the Tang court has arrived at Treasure Mountain to seek the sūtras.” Buddha was greatly pleased. At once he called together eight bodhisattvas, four Great Vajras, five hundred arhats, three thousand Jiedi, eleven Great Yao, and eighteen Ga-lans, and arranged them in two lines. A divine command then went forth to summon Tripitaka inside. One level, one hall at a time, and all obeyed the Buddha’s command, crying out, “Holy monk, please come in.” Tripitaka proceeded in strict order, and with Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing, leading the horse and carrying his panniers, he strode straight into the gate. It was then sung:

In earlier years, with resolve I obeyed the imperial order, took the decree, and left the royal jade stair. At dawn I climbed the mountain to greet the mist and dew; at dusk I rested my head on stone through drifting cloud haze. Bearing the Zen bundle, I strode across three thousand waters; with robes streaming, I walked ten thousand ridges. Every thought fixed upon the true fruit, and this morning at last I behold the Tathāgata.

The four reached the front of the Great Hero Hall and bowed fully before the Buddha, then, left and right, they bowed again. After three rounds each, they knelt again before the Buddha and offered the pass permit. The Buddha examined them one by one and passed them to Tripitaka. Tripitaka, lowering his head in reverence, spoke: “Disciple Tripitaka, by command of the Great Tang emperor in the Eastern Land, has traveled from afar to this Treasure Mountain to beg for true scripture so that all beings may be delivered. May my Buddha master have compassion and quickly grant safe return to my homeland.” Then Buddha opened his merciful mouth and awakened his heart of vast compassion, and spoke to Tripitaka: “You know your Eastern Land is the Nanshan Continent. Because of heaven high and earth thick, of plentiful creation and crowded people, there is too much greed, too much killing, too much lust, too much deceit, too much cheating. They do not keep the Buddha Dharma, do not incline to wholesome causes, do not honor the Three Lights, do not cherish the Five Grains; they are not loyal, not filial, not just, not humane, they cloak their hearts, deceive themselves, and use large measures against small—taking life and slaughtering creatures. They create boundless sin, fill themselves with evil to overflowing, and so invite the disaster of hell. Hence they sink endlessly into darkness and endure immeasurable grinding, pounding, and crushing, changing into beast forms. So many return with forms covered in hair and crowned with horns, paying back their debts with their own bodies, feeding their flesh to men. Those who forever fall into Avīci and cannot rise beyond it are all for this reason. Though Confucius there has set down teachings of benevolence, righteousness, rites, and wisdom, kings have followed in succession and governance includes punishments like strangling and beheading, yet how can the ignorant and the unrestrained run rampant? As for me, I now possess the Tripiṭaka with which one may pass beyond sorrow and clarify calamity and transgression. In the Tripiṭaka there is one basket of Dharma about Heaven, one basket of treatises about Earth, and one basket of sūtras that guide spirits. Altogether there are thirty-five divisions, totalling fifteen thousand one hundred and forty-four rolls. This is truly the path to true cultivation, the gate of right virtue. Of the four great continents under Heaven, all there is of astronomy, geography, persons, beasts and birds, flowers and trees, tools and uses, and human affairs has been recorded. You have come from afar. I intend to give you all of it to take away. Yet the people in that land are dull, vulgar, and stubborn, slandering true words and failing to comprehend the monk’s secret intent.” Then he called, “Ahuo, Jiaye—both of you—lead the four disciples down to the Pavilion of Treasures and first offer them vegetarian alms-food. When the repast is complete, open the treasure hall and select several rolls from my Tripiṭaka among the thirty-five divisions to give him. Teach him to transmit them into the Eastern Land, and thereby inscribe my boundless grace forever.

The two Venerable Elders at once obeyed Buddha’s command and led the four disciples downstairs. They could not exhaustively behold the strange treasures and marvels, set out without limit. Then they saw the gods who had arranged the offering laying out a banquet: all of it was celestial fare—immortal dishes, immortal tea, immortal fruit—with precious delicacies of countless tastes, all unlike the mundane world. Tripitaka and the disciples bowed in thanks for Buddha’s mercy and ate according to their hearts. In truth, this was:

Jewel-flame and golden light shone to dazzle the eyes, fragrant rarities and wondrous things still more subtle and fine. The thousand-tiered golden pavilions were endless in beauty; a single strain of immortal music entered the ear, clear. Unto ordinary men, plain-tasting immortal flowers are rarely seen; with scented tea and uncanny foods one receives long life. All along we have suffered a thousand hardships; today joy at glory and success has at last arrived. That blessing made a good turn for Pigsy, and made Sha Wujing’s lot favorable as well. In the Buddha’s realm of true, life-bestowing longevity, there was fare of rebirth-from-skin-and-bone, and each could partake at full. After sharing the meal with the four, the two elders went into the treasure hall and opened the doors to inspect it. On one side, rosy light and auspicious vapors cloaked all in layer upon layer; rosy clouds and auspicious mist spread across the sky in all directions. On the scripture caskets and outer jeweled chests were pasted red slips in regular script, bearing the names of the volumes: The Nirvana Sūtra, one text ... 748 volumes. The Bodhisattva Sūtra, one text ... 1,021 volumes. The Śūnyatā-Treasury Sūtra, one text ... 400 volumes. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra, one text ... 110 volumes. The Great Compilation of the Sūtra of Kind Intent, one text ... 50 volumes. The Treatise on Determinative Dharma, one text ... 140 volumes. The Precious-Treasure Sūtra, one text ... 45 volumes. The Avataṁsaka Sūtra, one text ... 500 volumes. The Sūtra Honoring True Suchness, one text ... 90 volumes. The Great Prajñā Sūtra, one text ... 916 volumes. The Radiance Sūtra, one text ... 300 volumes. The Sūtra of Never-Being-Seen, one text ... 1,110 volumes. The Vimalakīrti Sūtra, one text ... 170 volumes. The Separate Sūtra of the Three Treatises, one text ... 270 volumes. The Diamond Sūtra, one text ... 100 volumes. The Treatise on the Correct Dharma, one text ... 120 volumes. The Sūtra of Buddha’s Original Practice, one text ... 800 volumes. The Five-Dragons Sūtra, one text ... 32 volumes. The Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtra, one text ... 116 volumes. The Great Collection Sūtra, one text ... 130 volumes. The Mojie Sūtra, one text ... 350 volumes. The Lotus Sūtra, one text ... 100 volumes. The Yoga Sūtra, one text ... 100 volumes. The Constant-Treasure Sūtra, one text ... 220 volumes. The Western-Heaven Treatise Sūtra, one text ... 130 volumes. The Sengqi Sūtra, one text ... 157 volumes. The Miscellaneous Sūtras of Buddha Realms, one text ... 1,950 volumes. The Treatise on the Arising of Faith, one text ... 1,000 volumes. The Great Vehicle-to-Liberation Sūtra, one text ... 1,080 volumes. The Great-Might Sūtra, one text ... 1,280 volumes. The Benge Sūtra, one text ... 850 volumes. The Correct-Meter Writings Sūtra, one text ... 200 volumes. The Great Peacock Sūtra, one text ... 220 volumes. The Vijñāna (Consciousness) Theory Sūtra, one text ... 100 volumes. The Juxie Treatise Sūtra, one text ... 200 volumes. Ahua and Jiaye brought Tripitaka over the titles one by one and said to him, "A holy monk from the Eastern Land has arrived here. Did someone in your land send us anything? Bring it out quickly, and we shall transmit the scriptures to you and let you go." On hearing this, Tripitaka said, "Your disciple is Xuanzang; my journey has been long, and I have made no preparations." The two elders laughed: "Very well, very well, very well. Passing on scriptures to posterity with empty hands—later men will starve to death." When Monkey King saw him hedging and refusing to pass the scripture, he could not help but shout, "Master, let us report to Śākyamuni and ask him to come himself to give the texts to Old Monkey as well." Ahua said, "Do not shout. What sort of place is this, that you still run wild and misbehave? Come here and receive the scriptures." Pigsy and Sha Wujing restrained themselves and reined in Sun Wukong. Turning back, they gathered the books one by one into a bundle, loaded the load on the horse, and tied two extra shoulder-bundles, which Pigsy and Sha Wujing carried on poles. Then they came to Buddha’s seat and knelt in full prostration to thank him, and left directly out the gate. Wherever they met a Buddha, they bowed two times; wherever they saw a bodhisattva, they bowed two times. At the great gate they bowed to the bhikṣus, the bhikṣuṇīs, and the upāsakas and upāsikās, bidding farewell one by one, then hurried down the mountain road—there is no need to record it further.

Now, on that treasure hall there was an ancient Buddha named Rendan, who sat above and listened silently to the matter of transmitting the scripture. In his heart he understood clearly: Ahua and Jiaye were sending off the scriptural texts with no characters upon them. He smiled to himself: "The disciples of the Eastern Land are ignorant and deluded; they cannot recognize the scriptures without characters. Have they not made the holy monk’s whole pilgrimage useless?" He asked, "Who is it that is here beside your seat?" and Ahua appeared at once. The ancient Buddha instructed him: "Raise your divine might, fly like a star, and overtake the Tang Monk. Snatch away that blank, uninscribed scripture, and make him come again to seek the true written scripture." So the Baixiong Venerable rode forth in a wild wind and rushed beyond the gates of Mount Leiyin, setting up his divine terror. The wind of that moment was truly:

The warrior before Buddha, no equal to even two wind-gods of Xun. The immortal throat thundered in rage, its blast surpassing maidens blowing pipes. In this gust, fish and dragons lost their lairs; the river and sea heaved with reversed waves. A dark ape could scarcely carry fruit forward to offer; the yellow crane turned in the clouds to seek an old nest. The vermilion phoenix’s pure notes came out not as sweet, and the brocade rooster cried in shrill discord. Green pines snapped their branches; yubo flowers were scattered. Jade bamboos bent and fell, golden lotuses swayed in clusters. Bells were heard afar, sending three thousand li; the scripture-music floated high above ten thousand ravines. Beneath the cliffs strange blossoms withered half their beauty; by the roadside jade-grass lay folded and fresh. Rainbow-hued phoenixes could not dance their wings; white deer hid by the mountain face. Vast and roaming fragrances filled the cosmos; pure wind-breath pierced through the clouds. At that moment Tang Monk was walking on, and he suddenly felt a billowing fragrant wind and took it for an auspicious portent from Buddha, with no guard at all. Then another sound came, and from mid-air a hand reached down and lightly snatched the saddle-carried scripture bundle. Sanzang, startled, struck his breast and shouted. Pigsy rolled on the ground and gave chase; Sha Wujing guarded the load of scriptures, while Sun Wukong hurried after it as fast as flight. Seeing Sun Wukong almost upon him, Baixiong Venerable, for fear of missing his chance to strike the monkey’s staff-headed staff and blind-side him, acted rashly without good discernment, struck him, and wounded him. He ripped the scripture bundle apart at once and cast it down into the dust. When Sun Wukong saw the bundle torn and fallen, and then be blown about by scented wind, he steadied his cloud-head to tend the scriptures and did not pursue. Baixiong Venerable then gathered the wind, gathered the mist, and returned to report to the ancient Buddha; nothing more to record.

Pigsy followed after in pursuit and saw the copied scriptures falling down; then he and Sun Wukong gathered them and returned, carrying them on their backs, to the Tang Monk. Tang Monk, with tears filling his eyes, said, "My disciple, even in this Western Paradise there remain ferocious demons who harass and deceive." Sha Wujing caught the scattered scriptures in his arms and, on opening one, found it white as snow, with not a single character. In haste he handed it to Tripitaka: "Master, this volume has no writing." Sun Wukong opened another volume and found none either. Pigsy opened another volume, and there were none as well. The elder sighed deeply and said, "My people of the Eastern Land truly have no blessing. What use is such an empty, blank copy for me to bring back? How could I dare face Emperor Tang? The offense of deceiving the sovereign is truly one that cannot be forgiven." Sun Wukong had already understood and told Tripitaka, "Master, there is no need for further talk. Ahua and Jiaye, those rascals, asked for human gifts and, finding none, gave us these blank sheets of paper. Go quickly back and report before Śākyamuni himself, and question him about the offense of cheating for wealth." Pigsy shouted, "That is so, that is so—go complain." The four attendants hastened back to the mountain with hurried steps, and then in haste turned and rode again toward Mount Leiyin.

Not long afterward they arrived outside the mountain gate. All greeted them with folded hands and smiles: “Holy monk, you are the one sent to exchange the sūtra?” Tripitaka nodded and thanked them. Even the Vajra Kings did not block him, but let him pass all the way to the front of the Great Hero Hall. Wukong shouted, “Buddha Tathagata, my master and disciples have endured myriad torments and endless hardship, traveling from the Eastern Land to this place. Your grace had ordered us to transmit the true scripture. Yet Ahua and Jia‑ye, unable to squeeze gifts from this monk, conspired to cheat us and deliberately told us to take a white copy of blank paper. What use is that to us? Please instruct and correct this matter.” Buddha smiled and said, “Be quiet and stop shouting. I know why those two sought gifts from you. But a scripture should not be passed around carelessly, and it should not be taken in emptiness. Earlier, when that band of monks, among them the holy monk, came down from the mountain, the scripture was recited once at Elder Zhao’s house in Śrāvastī; it safeguarded the living members of his household and sent the departed beyond, yet they gained only three dou three sheng of grain and a little gold in return. I said they sold it far too cheaply, leaving their descendants without means. You have come now to receive it with empty hands, so what was given was only the white copy. This white copy is a wordless true scripture; that too is good. Since the beings of your Eastern Land are ignorant and deluded, this is only what can be passed to them.” Then he called, “Ahua, Jia‑ye, quickly take several written true sutra volumes from each section and bring them here to report the tally.”

The two elders again led the four to the foot of the Precious Hall and Treasure Pavilion and once more asked Tripitaka for gifts. Tripitaka had nothing worthy to offer, so he ordered Sha Wujing to bring out the purple-gold alms bowl, and with both hands presented it saying, “This disciple is poor, with scant means and a long journey, and has not prepared gifts. This bowl was personally bestowed by the Tang king and used by me along the road in giving alms. I now offer it as a token of my small heart. I beg you, honored ones, to take it; upon my return, I can present it at court to King Tang, and he will surely reward this deeply. If you bestow a written true scripture in return, at least this labor of far travel on imperial commission will not be in vain.” Ahua took it, but only smiled faintly. Then those keepers of the pavilion, the stewards of the incense kitchens, and the supervising elders, one smeared his face, one struck his back, one snapped fingers, one twisted his lips, all of them laughing: “No shame, no shame—asking for gifts in order to obtain scripture.” In a moment their faces were all wrinkled in embarrassment, but they still would not let go of the bowl. Jia‑ye only then entered the pavilion and examined the scriptures one by one with Tripitaka. Tripitaka called out, “Disciples, all of you, look closely; do not behave like before.” They took one scroll after another, and each was indeed written on. Five thousand and forty-eight volumes were transmitted, the total of one entire canon. Everything was neatly packed and loaded on horses; what remained was carried in an extra load, with Zhu Bajie shouldering it. Tripitaka’s own baggage was shouldered by Sha Wujing. Wukong led the horse, Tripitaka took up his staff, tapped the Pilu cap once, shook out his brocade robe, and then, full of joy, came before Buddha. And then came:

The Great Scripture tastes sweet beyond measure, and Buddha has made it with perfect severity. Know that Tripitaka’s climb from the West was full of hardship; laughable that Ahua loved money more than truth. In the first transfer there was no clear accounting to the Ancient Buddhas; only later does certainty truly arrive. Even now, with triumph it is carried to the Eastern Land; all hearers are bathed alike in rain and dew.

Ahua and Jia‑ye brought Tripitaka to meet Buddha. Buddha ascended the Lotus Throne and ordered the two great Arhats Long-Subduer and Tiger-Subduer to strike the cloud gongs, then invited three thousand Buddhas, three thousand Jieti, eight Vajra Kings, four bodhisattvas, five hundred Arhats, eight hundred bhikṣus, all laymen and laywomen upāsakas and upāsikās, the bhikṣuṇīs, and all heavenly halls, pure lands, and sacred peaks—great and small elders and monks—to come. Those who should sit were invited to throne seats, those who should stand took places at either side. At once heavenly music could be heard in the distance, celestial song rang clear, auspicious light layered through the sky, and clouds of blessed omen thickened. All Buddhas assembled and came to witness Buddha Tathagata. Buddha asked, “Ahua, Jia‑ye, how many scripture volumes have been passed to him? Report each number.” The two elders then reported:

《涅槃經》 …………………………… 400 volumes 《菩薩經》 ……………………… 360 volumes 《虛空藏經》 ………………………… 20 volumes 《首楞嚴經》 ………………………… 30 volumes 《恩意經大集》 ……………………… 40 volumes 《決定經》 …………………………… 40 volumes 《寶藏經》 …………………………… 20 volumes 《華嚴經》 ………………………… 81 volumes 《禮真如經》 ………………………… 30 volumes 《大般若經》 ………………………… 600 volumes 《大光明經》 ………………………… 50 volumes 《未曾有經》 …………………… 550 volumes 《維摩經》 …………………………… 30 volumes 《三論別經》 ……………………… 42 volumes 《金剛經》 ……………………………… 1 volume 《正法論經》 ………………………… 20 volumes 《佛本行經》 ………………… 116 volumes 《五龍經》 …………………………… 20 volumes 《菩薩戒經》 ………………………… 60 volumes 《大集經》 …………………………… 30 volumes 《摩竭經》 ……………………… 140 volumes 《法華經》 ……………………………… 10 volumes 《瑜伽經》 …………………………… 30 volumes 《寶常經》 ……………………… 170 volumes 《西天論經》 ………………………… 30 volumes 《僧祗經》 ……………………… 110 volumes 《佛國雜經》 …………… 1,638 volumes 《起信論經》 ………………………… 50 volumes 《大智度經》 ………………………… 90 volumes 《寶威經》 ……………………… 140 volumes 《本閣經》 ………………………… 56 volumes 《正律文經》 …………………………… 10 volumes 《大孔雀經》 ………………………… 14 volumes 《維識論經》 …………………………… 10 volumes 《具舍論經》 …………………………… 10 volumes There are thirty-five sections in this whole canon; in each, five thousand and forty-eight volumes were checked out and delivered, and the remainder was left with the holy monk to carry east to Tang. Now all have been set in order, mounted on horse-litters and head-poles, and all are sent away in thanks.

Tripitaka and the four disciples bound the horses and set down their loads. One by one they folded their hands and knelt in deep bows. Buddha addressed Tripitaka: “The merit of this scripture cannot be measured. Though it is a mirror of my gate, it is in truth the source-stream of the Three Teachings. When you reach your Nanzhanbu Continent, reveal it to all beings, and do not treat it lightly. Do not open the volumes except after bathing and keeping a fast-day observance. Treasure it, and hold it dear. Within this lie the subtleties of becoming immortal through the Way, and marvelous methods for revealing the ten thousand transformations. ” Tripitaka knelt and thanked Buddha, accepted and put faith into practice, and once more made three full circuits of reverence before Buddha, then departed respectfully receiving the sutra. When they came to the three mountain gates, they again thanked all the saints; no more need be said.

After dispatching Tripitaka, Buddha then dismissed the scripture-transmission assembly. Later, Guanyin came with folded hands and spoke to Buddha: “When I was once ordered by the Golden Edict to go east to seek sutras, the mission has now been fulfilled. In total it has taken fourteen years, five thousand and forty days—eight days short of the full canon count. I beg my World-Honored One to soon grant the holy monk leave to return eastward, and then bring him back westward; this must be completed within eight days, so that the canon tally be made whole. Please grant me leave to return the Golden Edict.” Buddha rejoiced and said, “What you say is entirely right; you may return the Golden Edict.” He immediately ordered the Eight Great Vajra Kings: “Quickly send forth your divine might, escort the holy monk back east, leave the true canon there, and then bring him westward again. It must all be finished within eight days; do not be late.” The vajra kings at once overtook Tripitaka and called, “One who fetched the sūtra, follow me.” Tripitaka and the others became light and fit in body, drifting gracefully as they followed; with the kings they rose riding on clouds. Then was this saying:

See true nature and brighten the mind and contemplate Buddha. When virtue is complete and the journey fulfilled, one ascends at once.

It remains unknown how to transmit it upon returning to the Eastern Land. Listen as the next chapter unfolds to explain.
chapters.title: Chapter 98: A monkey can ripen only when the horse is fully tamed and the shell left behind; work fulfilled, the Way is complete.

This is a fresh, complete English translation of Wu Cheng’en’s public-domain one-hundred-chapter novel, produced with GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark assistance. It is an AI-assisted first edition, not a reproduction of an existing translation.

As for the part where the Eight Golden Vajra Kings had already sent Tripitaka back to his homeland, it need not be set down further. Beneath the Three-Tier Gate were the Five Directions Jiedi, the Four-Time Functionaries, the Six Ding and Six Jia, and the Defenders of the Dharma Sanctuary. They went before Bodhisattva Guanyin and said, “At your Dharma command, our disciples have protected the Holy Monk in secret. Today the Holy Monk has completed his journey; you have received Buddha’s golden decree. We ask that you grant approval for submitting the decree.” Guanyin rejoiced and said, “Approved. Approved.” She asked again, “How were Tripitaka and the four companions in heart and conduct along the way?” The divine attendants replied, “Their hearts were truly sincere and devout, and no one could hide from Guanyin’s insight. Only the suffering he bore is truly beyond telling. Every calamity and hardship he met on the road, your disciple has carefully remembered. This is the book of his tribulations.” Guanyin read it all the way through. It read:

By order of Mengcha Jiedi, in reverent submission, I have carefully kept a clear count of Tripitaka’s hardships: Gold Cicada demoted — first hardship. Nearly slain at birth — second hardship. Cast into the river on the full-moon day — third hardship. Searching for kin to redress injustice — fourth hardship. Meeting a tiger on leaving the city — fifth hardship. Tumbled into a pit from a divided road — sixth hardship. On Double-Fork Ridge — seventh hardship. At Two-Realms Mountain — eighth hardship. Horse changed at the precipitous ravine — ninth hardship. Burned by night — tenth hardship. Losing the kasaya robe — eleventh hardship. Capturing and subduing Zhu Bajie — twelfth hardship. Obstructed by the Yellow Wind demon — thirteenth hardship. Petitioning Lingji — fourteenth hardship. Struggling through Flowing-Sand waters — fifteenth hardship. Capturing and securing Sha Wujing — sixteenth hardship. Four holy ones manifesting themselves — seventeenth hardship. In Wuzhuang Hall — eighteenth hardship. Keeping the life-ginseng alive — nineteenth hardship. The heart-monkey again cast down — twentieth hardship. Scattered in Black-Pine Forest — twenty-first hardship. Bearer of the letter from Treasure-Elephant Kingdom — twenty-second hardship. Golden-Luan Hall turning into a tiger — twenty-third hardship. Meeting a demon on Mount Pingding — twenty-fourth hardship. Lotus Cave suspended high — twenty-fifth hardship. Rescue in Crow-Chicken Kingdom — twenty-sixth hardship. Possessed and transformed by demon magic — twenty-seventh hardship. Meeting monsters at Mount Hao — twenty-eighth hardship. Wind seizing the Holy Monk — twenty-ninth hardship. The mind-monkey harmed — thirtieth hardship. Inviting the Holy One to subdue demons — thirty-first hardship. Sinking into the Black River — thirty-second hardship. Delayed in transporting the vehicle — thirty-third hardship. Great gambling won and lost — thirty-fourth hardship. Banishing evil to uplift the monkhood — thirty-fifth hardship. Meeting a vast flood on the road — thirty-sixth hardship. Falling into the Celestial River — thirty-seventh hardship. The fish basket appeared — thirty-eighth hardship. Monster encountered on Mount Doushan — thirty-ninth hardship. The gods of heaven all could not be subdued — fortieth hardship. Inquiring into Buddha’s source — forty-first hardship. Poisoned by drank water — forty-second hardship. In West Liang, lingering for a marriage — forty-third hardship. Suffering in Pipa Cave — forty-fourth hardship. Again the heart-monkey was demoted — forty-fifth hardship. Unable to tell the true from the macaque — forty-sixth hardship. Journey blocked at Flame-Mountain — forty-seventh hardship. Seeking the plantain fan — forty-eighth hardship. Binding the demon king — forty-ninth hardship. Sweeping the tower at Saicheng — fiftieth hardship. Recovering treasure to rescue the monk — fifty-first hardship. Recitation among thorny thickets — fifty-second hardship. Small Leiyin met with misfortune — fifty-third hardship. Celestial deities themselves trapped in trouble — fifty-fourth hardship. Obstruction by the foul passage of Xishitong — fifty-fifth hardship. Practicing medicine in Violet-Purple Kingdom — fifty-sixth hardship. Rescuing the sick with urinary blockage — fifty-seventh hardship. Subduing demons and taking back the queen — fifty-eighth hardship. Drowned in the seven emotions — fifty-ninth hardship. Wounded by the many-eyed foe — sixtieth hardship. Lion-camel blocked the road — sixty-first hardship. Monsters divided into three colors — sixty-second hardship. Disaster in the city — sixty-third hardship. Inviting Buddha to take in the demons — sixty-fourth hardship. Monk saved a child — sixty-fifth hardship. Discerning true from false — sixty-sixth hardship. Rescue of a monster in a pine forest — sixty-seventh hardship. The monk’s chamber with fevered sickness — sixty-eighth hardship. Trapped in a bottomless pit — sixty-ninth hardship. Hard to proceed in the kingdom that destroys the Dharma — seventieth hardship. Encountered a demon on Mist-Hiding Mountain — seventy-first hardship. Rain requested in Fengxian Prefecture — seventy-second hardship. Weapon lost — seventy-third hardship. Huoqing and the pinning of the halberd — seventy-fourth hardship. Beset at Bamboo-Node Mountain — seventy-fifth hardship. Suffering in Xuanying Cave — seventy-sixth hardship. Chasing and capturing the rhinoceros — seventy-seventh hardship. Summoned to marriage in Tianzhu — seventy-eighth hardship. Imprisoned in Tongtai Office — seventy-ninth hardship. Crossing Lingyun and shedding the mortal flesh — eightieth hardship. The road covered ten-thousand-eight-thousand li. The master’s record of tribulations was perfectly clear. Guanyin perused the ledger and said quickly, “In the Buddha’s law, nine by nine returns to Truth. Tripitaka has endured eighty hardships, still one short, and the number is not complete.” She then ordered Mengcha Jiedi, “Catch the Golden Vajra one and bring forth another hardship for him.”

Mengcha Jiedi, obeying this command, rode a cloud in a single run to the east, and by dawn and dusk in one day and night caught up with the Eight Great Golden Vajra Kings. Whispering in his ear, he said, “... In this way, in this way: we have carefully observed Bodhisattva Guanyin’s instruction and must not err.” Hearing him, the Great Vajra one snapped and pressed down the wind, and sent the four companions with their horses and the sutra tumbling to the ground. Alas! It was precisely the moment of:

On the path of truth regained through ninety-nine, hardship is the road of practice. Keep steadfast and firm in resolve, and set the mysterious gate. Evil magics must be bitterly tempered and driven off; hold the right Dharma and restore it. Do not treat the scripture chapters as something easy: the Holy Monk has borne far more than you think. From olden times, perfect accord and inward agreement meet as one; even a single hair out of place prevents the forming of the elixir. Tripitaka’s feet touched the mortal earth and he felt sudden dread. Zhu Bajie laughed, "Haha, good, good, good—this is exactly why this would have to be delayed." Sha Wujing said, "Good, good, good. We have traveled too fast this time; we are to rest here for a while." Sun Wukong said, "There is a saying: ‘Sit at one ford for nine days; in one day you may cross nine fords.’" Tripitaka said, "The three of you stop your bickering, set your bearings, and see what place this is." Sha Wujing looked around and said, "It is here, it is here. Master, listen to the sound of the water." Sun Wukong said, "The sound of water seems like it comes from your homeland." Zhu Bajie said, "His homeland is Flowing-Sand River." Sha Wujing said, "No, no, this is Tongtian River." Tripitaka said, "My disciples, look closely at that bank." Sun Wukong sprang up and leaned on the cool awning frame to look carefully, then came down and said, "Master, this is the west bank of the Tongtian River." Tripitaka said, "I remember now. On the east bank there was once a Chen family manor. In that year when we came here, because you had saved his children, he was deeply grateful. He made a boat for us to send us off, and thankfully the White Tortoise offered passage. I remember the west bank was devoid of human settlement. What are we to do now?" Zhu Bajie said, "I only thought ordinary people could cheat; it seems even the Golden Vajra before Buddha can cheat. He obeys Buddha’s order and tells us to carry Tripitaka homeward, yet how has he left us half a way here? Now are we not in a hopeless dilemma? How are we to cross?" Sha Wujing said, "Second Bro, do not complain. Our Master has already obtained the Way; he shed his mortal body at Lingyun Ford before. This time he will not fall into the water. Teacher and I, together with you, will all use the restraint-art and carry the Master across." Sun Wukong laughed quietly to himself, "Cannot carry him, cannot carry him." See how he just says ‘cannot carry him’! If he truly exerted divine power and laid bare the secret of flying ascent, the teacher and disciples would cross a thousand rivers at once. But because in his heart he knew Tripitaka’s ninety-nine trials were not yet complete and one more trial still remained, he was held back here on purpose.

The disciples chattered as they walked, footstep by footstep, until they reached the riverbank. Suddenly someone called out, “Tang Sage, Tang Sage, this way, this way.” All four were startled. They looked up to see no one in sight and no boat or ferry, only a great white tortoise with a bald head raising its head from the bank and crying out: “Master, I have waited for you these many years, and only now have you returned?” Wukong laughed: “Old turtle, I have been counting these years for you; now, this year, we meet at last.” Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing were filled with endless joy. Wukong said, “Old turtle, if you truly mean to receive us, come up ashore.” The turtle at once leapt onto the bank. Wukong ordered them to lead the horse up onto him. Zhu Bajie still crouched behind the horse’s tail, Tripitaka stood to the horse’s left, and Sha Wujing to his right. Wukong put one foot on the turtle’s neck and one on its head and called, “Old turtle, walk steadily and keep your footing.” The old turtle kicked out its four legs and stepped on the water as if on level ground, carrying the four disciples and the horse—five mouths in all—on its back and returning straight to the east bank. As the saying goes:

In the Gate of No-Duality the Dharma is deep and mysterious; all demons are driven back, whether of man or heaven. The original face is now seen; the one essence and cause are made whole. With the proof of the Three Vehicles, entering and leaving in turn, perfected cinnabar turns nine times and moves through all. Even of staff and bundle, and of speeches about flying through battle, none can be spoken of—thankfully, at my return to origin, I met the old turtle. With the turtle bearing them, skipping over waves, they traveled most of the day and as dusk came they came close to the east bank. Suddenly it asked, “Master, in earlier years I petitioned the West before my Buddha, the Tathagata, and asked him about my years of life, whether there was any remaining term. Did he ever ask me that?” Since that Elder had, after coming west to Yujing Hall, bathed there, crossed Lingyun, climbed to Lingshan, and devoted himself wholly to worshipping Buddha and paying homage to Buddha, bodhisattvas, and holy monks; his mind was fixed only on taking the sutras, he had not inquired at all about the turtle’s lifespan, and could not answer. Yet he dared not deceive, and after a long pause he remained silent. The turtle knew at once he had never asked on its behalf. In an instant it shook its body and with a sharp splash plunged into the water, pulling all four disciples and even the horse beneath it. Alas! Fortunately Tripitaka had shed mortal birth and become a sage; had it been in earlier times he would already have gone to the bottom. Fortunate too that the white horse was a dragon and that Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing could swim. Wukong gave a faint smile and showed his divine powers, lifted Tripitaka out of the water, and got them onto the east bank. Only the scripture case, robes, and saddle tackle were wet.

After the party had just reached the bank and set things in order, a furious gale suddenly rose. The sky darkened, lightning flashed, stones and sand flew. What they then saw was this:

A blast of wind, and the cosmos was shaken in all directions; a crack of thunder shook all mountains and rivers. A glare flashed, boring through the clouds in fire; A whole fog of daylight veiled the earth. The wind screamed; thunder roared, fierce and relentless. The glare jerked out red fire, and fog confused both stars and moon. Wind-driven dust struck their faces, and terrorized by thunder, tigers and leopards hid their forms. The glare-wilted birds cried out, and trees vanished beneath drifting fog. That wind roused the River of Heaven so its waves rose in towering swells; that thunder made the fish and dragons of the River of Heaven lose heart. That glare lit the River of Heaven bright as day; that fog covered its banks and cliffs in dim gloom. A fine wind: collapsing hills, shattered stones, pines and bamboos overturned. A fine thunder: frightening, striking, and perilous to men with mighty force. A fine glare: streaking heavenward, lighting wild golden snakes. A fine fog: thickly spread, obscuring the ninth sky. The commotion made Tripitaka clutch the sutra, Sha Wujing hold down the scripture pannier, Zhu Bajie hold the white horse, while Wukong spun his Golden-Hooped Staff with both hands and protected them on both sides. In truth that wind, fog, thunder, and glare were yin demons in disguise, seeking to steal the scriptures. They roared and raged for a whole night, and only at dawn did it cease. Tripitaka, still in wet robes, trembled and asked, “Wukong, how did this come about?” Wukong replied in a breathless tone: “Master, you do not know this. We guard you so that you may obtain these sutras; this is to take up the work of heaven and earth’s cosmic patterning. It can last as long as Heaven and Earth, with the sun and moon shining equally, and grant long springlike life and an undying Dharma body. That is why heaven and earth do not tolerate it, and ghosts and gods resent it—it comes secretly to steal your scriptures. First, this sutra is soaked through with water; second, your upright Dharma body presses it down so thunder cannot strike, lightning cannot reveal, and fog cannot confuse; also, Old Sun circles with the Golden-Hooped Staff, bringing pure yang energy to guard it; and by dawn, yang qi had risen again. So it could not be taken.” Tripitaka, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing only then understood and offered endless thanks.

After a short while the sun rose high. They moved the sutras up to a high cliff and opened the package to dry them. The stone where the texts were dried there still remains to this day. Then they dried their robes and sandals along the cliff. Some stood, some sat, some jumped about. Truly:

In one body of pure yang, one turns joyfully toward the sun. The yin demons dare not assert themselves with brute force. Know that this true Water-conquering scripture does not fear wind, thunder, glare, or fog. From now on peace returns to true awakening; from this day on, peaceful ease reaches the land of immortals. On the scripture-drying stone remains a trace, and no demon has ever come here through the ages. The four checked the scripture copies one by one, laying them out in the sun. Soon several fishermen came to the bank and raised their heads to look. One among them recognized them: “Master, were you not the ones who came this way two years ago, crossed this river, and went west to fetch sutras?” Zhu Bajie said, “Yes, yes indeed. Which place are you from, and how do you recognize us?” The fisherman answered, “We are from above Chenjia Village.” Zhu Bajie asked, “How far is Chenjia from here?” The fisherman replied, “If one crosses Nan-chong and goes south, it is twenty li.” Zhu Bajie said, “Master, why not take our scriptures to Chenjia and dry them there? They have a place to stay, a place to sit, and we can get food there too. If we ask them, they can wash our robes.” Tripitaka said, “No need. Let them dry fully here, then we will gather our things and find our road home.”

The fishermen went on across Nan-chong and happened to meet Chen Cheng, calling out, “Second Master, we are the clerics who came to your house two years ago to serve in the rite for your child.” Chen Cheng asked, “Where did you see them?” They pointed and said, “Up on that stone, they are drying scriptures.” Chen Cheng took a few tenant households with him and walked over the ford to look. As he drew near he knelt down: “Holy Master, you have returned with the scripture complete, your work fulfilled. Why not come to the house, and instead linger here? Please, please come to the manor at once.” Wukong said, “Once the scriptures are dried, we will come with you.” Chen Cheng asked, “How did the scriptures and robes of the Master get wet?” Tripitaka said, “Last year a white turtle ferried us west across the river; this year we were once again carried east by it. When we came near the bank, it asked whether I had ever asked the Buddha in the west the matter of its own years. I had not asked, so it plunged in and drenched us, and this is why we are wet.” He then explained everything that had happened before and after. Chen Cheng’s request was earnest, and Tripitaka could not refuse; he gathered the sutra scrolls. Yet on the drying-stone, several fascicles of the Fo Benxingjing had become wet and the tail end of the text tore. That is why to this day the Fo Benxingjing is not complete, though traces of writing remain on the drying-stone. Tripitaka regretted, “We were negligent and failed to look after it.” Wukong laughed: “Not here, not here. Heaven and Earth are not complete in all things; this scripture was whole as it was. To have been wet and torn now is the hidden principle of its seeming incompleteness. This is no fault of human power.” When all had packed their things, they followed Chen Cheng to the manor.

At that manor all the householders spread the news—one told ten, ten told a hundred, and a hundred became a thousand. Young and old all came to see. Hearing of their arrival, Chen Qing laid out a fragrance altar at the gate to welcome them and ordered drums and music. After a short while they arrived and were brought in. Chen Qing, leading the whole household, came out and bowed to pay thanks for the former grace of saving his sons and daughters. He then ordered tea and set out a vegetarian offering. Tripitaka had accepted holy food and heavenly fare from Buddha and shed mortal flesh to become a Buddha; he no longer thought of ordinary food. The two elders urged him repeatedly and at last accepted his small assent. Wukong, who had never before eaten grain and mortal cookery, said, “Enough.” Sha Wujing, too, ate little. Zhu Bajie too, unlike before, put down his bowl. Wukong said, “Is the Bungler also not eating now?” Zhu Bajie replied, “I do not know why—my spleen and stomach are suddenly weak.” Thus they all ended the meal and at once asked about the matter of obtaining the sutras. Tripitaka then recounted in full how he had first gone to Yujing Hall in the west to bathe, crossed through Lingyun and stepped upward with a lightened body, then reached Liyin Temple to meet the Tathagata, where he was given banquet in the Precious Pavilion and transmitted the scriptural teaching in the Precious Hall. Because two dignitaries failed in their attempt to draw him into a private matter, they later transmitted him a sutra with no script characters. He then again bowed before the Buddha and was granted the number of one full collection, and he recounted as well the whole matter of the white turtle being dipped and the shadowy demons trying to steal the books in secret, all in detail, and was about to take leave.

Those elders and their whole households would not let us go, saying: "Long ago we were saved by you, rescuing our son and daughter from sacrifice; our deep gratitude cannot be repaid. We have already built a monastery and named it Jiusheng Temple, where incense is now tended without cease." They also summoned forth Chen Guanbao and Yichengjin, the children once set aside for sacrifice, and they knelt to offer thanks. They again begged us to come and see the temple. Tripitaka then took the scripture bundle and set it on the hall-front of their house, and recited one volume of the Baochang Sutra for him. When he arrived at the temple, he saw that the Chens had also arranged another banquet there. He had not yet sat down when they invited again; he had not yet lifted his chopsticks when they invited again. Invitations came in unending succession, one crowding on another, impossible to manage. Tripitaka could not dare refuse; he only feigned a little assent. He saw, all at once, that the temple had been built in complete order:

The mountain gate is vermilion and smooth, all thanks to the donor’s virtue. A pavilion now stands, with towers rising high, and from now two gallery-halls prosper as well. Crimson-red partition screens in jeweled filigree gleam sevenfold. Fragrance drifts, filling the Milky Way; pure radiance fills the heavens. A few young cypresses have only just been watered, while several trunks of lofty pines are yet without full clusters. Living waters answer the front, layering to heaven in swelling waves; a high cliff leans behind, and mountain ridges join the earth-dragons in many folds. After reading this, Tripitaka only then ascended the high tower. On the upper level were, as if sculpted, images of the four of them. Zhu Bajie saw this and tugged Sun Wukong’s sleeve: "Elder Brother, your likeness is very much right." Sha Wujing said, "Second brother, yours is also true enough; only Master’s turns out a little too handsome." Tripitaka said, "Excellent, excellent." He then came down. In the front hall and the rear corridor below, further tables for offering meals were still awaiting invitation. Sun Wukong asked, "What has become of the Former-Sun Great King Temple?" The elders replied, "That temple was torn down long ago. Since this temple was built, every year has ripened and every year yielded abundance; all this is owing to Your Grace’s blessing." Sun Wukong laughed: "This is the gift of Heaven; what has it to do with us? Yet from this day onward, after we depart, may your household and descendants in this village increase in number; may all your livestock live in peace; may the winds be timely and the rains right each year, year after year." All of them bowed and thanked him with their foreheads to the ground.

Behind and before, and all along beyond, there were endless households presenting fruit and offering vegetarian meals. Zhu Bajie laughed: "I have been in such a muddle. In those times when we ate, there was not a single household that did not invite me again and again, ten times over. Today I cannot get one meal through, and already another house comes in turn." Though indignantly hot with vexation, he moved his hands a little and ate enough to cover eight or nine vegetarian dishes; though his stomach was already sore, he also ate two or three dozen buns. He was fully sated, and yet another household came inviting again. Tripitaka said, "How can this disciple accept? We are deeply touched by this great kindness. Let us halt for this evening, and accept again tomorrow morning."

It was already deep into the night. Tripitaka kept guard over the True Scripture and dared not leave even briefly, so he sat below in meditation as a watchman. Near the third watch, Tripitaka whispered softly, "Wukong, the people here know our mission is complete. As the old saying goes, ‘A true person does not reveal his aspect; one who reveals himself is no true person.’ I fear that by lingering too long we may lose the great affair." Sun Wukong replied, "What the Master says is sound. We should make use of this deep night, while the households sleep, and go quietly." Zhu Bajie also became aware, and Sha Wujing was entirely clear as well; even the white horse understood. Then they rose, raised themselves, gently set the shoulder-pole load, and by the covered corridor carried it out toward the gate. At the gate they saw it locked. Sun Wukong used a lock-breaking method, opened the two inner doors and the main gate, and found a road and set out eastward. Then from midair came a cry from the Eight Great Vajra Kings: "Those who flee, follow me." The elder heard it with a wind of perfume wavering all about, and rose into the air. It was just here that the line was spoken:

When the cinnabar is made complete, one recognizes one’s original face. The body remains robust and true, bowing to the Master as it is.

In the end, how they eventually came to see the Tang King remains unknown; hear the resolution in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Chapter 99: When ninety-nine reckonings are complete, all demons are cut down; when three-by-three are complete, the Way returns to its root.
